# Patrologia Latina, volume 107 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, vol. 107

## Complete Course of Patrology

Or universal library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, comprising all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the modesty of the price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time brought together in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold in 1,200 volumes; the Greek-Latin in 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# The Complete Works of Blessed Rabanus Maurus

[Col. 0009]

## Preliminary materials to the works of Blessed Rabanus Maurus

[Col. 0009A]

# A Historical Eulogy of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, by Mabillon

## Chapter One

### Rabanus’s names, homeland, parents, and time of birth

1. Rabanus, so called by his native name, received the other name Maurus from his teacher Alcuin, as he himself testifies in the preface prefixed to his Commentaries on the Books of Kings. There he says that in those passages which he explains himself he “marked in the margin the letter M, expressing the name Maurus; for,” he says, “my teacher, Albinus of blessed memory, gave me this name.”

For in that age a custom had become established among learned men living in these regions: besides their family name, which was generally somewhat harsh in sound, they adopted another name from the Latins or Greeks, and more rarely from the Hebrews, in their desire to cultivate the smoothness of a more polished form of speech. Thus Hadrian was given to Saint Frichorius; Benedictus to Bisco, that is, a second name; Clemens to Willibrord; Bonifacius to Winfrid; Aquila to Arno, bishop of Salzburg; Albinus Flaccus to Alcuin; David to Charlemagne; Homer to Angilbert; Damoetas to Riculf; Antonius to Adalhard; Arsenius and Hieremias to Wala; Paschasius to Ratbert; and Placidius to Warin, abbot of Corbie the New. Other names were similarly substituted for others.

[Col. 0009B]

The following words of Hariulf, the chronicler of Centula, concerning Saint Frichorius, in Book I, chapter 6, deserve notice: “Because the other name seemed unsuitable on account of the articulation of the barbarian tongue, it is said to have been changed by those who came before, and is written Hadrianus.”

So zealously, indeed, did people of that time pursue this smoothness that they scarcely dared pronounce such popular names, as though they were barbarous, without first asking the readers’ indulgence. [Col. 0009C]

This is the point of Servatus Lupus in the preface to his book On the Life of Saint Wigbert, abbot:

“May I obtain this also from the goodwill of the learned reader: wherever the smoothness of the Latin language is made harsh by the vernacular forms of the German language in persons or places, may he bear it patiently and remember that I am not writing a poem, in which poetic license sometimes mutilates names and adjusts them to the sonority of Roman speech, or completely changes them, but a history that refuses to be obscured by the obliquities of embellishment.”

[Col. 0010A]

This, then, is the reason why Alcuin gave Rabanus the byname, or second name, Maurus, by which he commonly addresses him in letters and poems written to him. Those who had been given two names used only one or the other separately, rarely both together; and it was customary for others to do the same. Nevertheless, in a letter of Humbert, bishop of Würzburg, to Rabanus, prefixed to the Commentaries on the Books of Judges and Ruth, I read this heading:

“To the illustrious, deservedly distinguished, and most excellent Father H. Rabanus Maurus, Humbert.”

The same conjunction of names is also found at the head of Emperor Lothar’s letter prefixed to the exposition of Ezekiel.

Finally, Rabanus calls this his additional name in the preface to the Gospel of Matthew. Johannes Trithemius frequently calls Rabanus Magnentius, from the family of the Magnentii, from which he believed him to have descended. Among ancient writers, no one, so far as I know, assigns this name to Rabanus before Ademar of Chabannes, a monk who composed his chronicle from the year 600 onward, and Sigebert, his contemporary, in Book 89 of his work On Ecclesiastical Writers, where Rabanus is called “Rabanus, otherwise Maurus or Magnentius.”

[Col. 0010B]

Rabanus—whom others write Rabanus or Rhabanus—likes to write his name with an aspirate prefixed, just as H. Ludovicus and H. Lotharius, according to the custom of that age.

2. Different people assign Rabanus different homelands, each according to his own preference: some England, others Scotland. [Col. 0013C]

It is not worth the trouble to refute such nonsense. It is certain that he was a Frank, that is, born in eastern Francia—not at Fulda, but at Mainz. [Col. 0010C]

Hear Rabanus himself, offering his books On the Cross to the pope in Alcuin’s person, and speaking of himself as follows:

> He is indeed Frank by descent, and an inhabitant of the  
> Bochonian forest, etc.

He was a monk at Fulda, a town situated in the Bochonian forest; yet he was not born there, but in the city of Mainz, as he himself sings in his epitaph:

> In this city I was indeed born, and reborn in the sacred font;  
> At Fulda afterward I learned the sacred teaching.

[Col. 0011A]

Nor should we listen to those who place punctuation after the words “at Fulda.” For Rabanus had designated his burial at Mainz, in the monastery of Saint Alban; therefore the words “In this city I was indeed born” must be understood of Mainz. An ancient anonymous writer interpreted them in precisely this way; we shall report his opinion below, in section 39.

3. Johannes Trithemius attributes to Rabanus the following parents: “Ruthard, descended from the family of the Magnentii, a wealthy and powerful man who had served vigorously for a long time under the Frankish princes; and Aldegund, a woman of most honorable conduct.”

But since Trithemius was mistaken in identifying Rabanus’s birthplace, I fear that he cannot safely be trusted concerning the names and rank of his parents, of whom the ancients make no mention. Nevertheless, it is certain that Rabanus was born of an illustrious family, since he had a brother named Tutin, a man of the highest nobility, as Rabanus testifies in his epitaph; and a nephew, Gundramnus the Levite, superior of the cell of Saint Solus and chaplain of Louis, king of Germany.

Tutin’s epitaph is as follows:

> Here lies buried an illustrious man named Tutin,  
> Completing the common day summoned by fate.  
> Born of the high stock of famous parents,  
> He equaled in every custom his noble grandfathers.  
> In talent, integrity, faith, and dignity of speech,  
> He lived with royal men in honor.  
> Grace of his great Lord caused him,  
> A young man, to fall bravely amid the weapons of war.  
> He was the brother of the bishop, swift in arms,  
> Who brought here the bones of his brother.  
> Bend your knee and raise your hands, good reader, and pray;  
> Say: “I beg you, God, be gracious to both.”

That this must be understood of Rabanus the pontiff, and not of someone else, is shown by the fact that he does not name the pontiff and asks for prayers for both brothers. [Col. 0011B]

If this does not seem sufficiently established to someone, he must at least concede that Gundramnus, a court official, was Rabanus’s nephew.

[Col. 0011C]

We have a reliable authority for this—not only Ermanricus, his contemporary, in his book On the Deeds of Saint Solus, but also Gundramnus himself. In order to induce Ermanricus to write the Life of Solus, Gundramnus says that he conveys “the permission of the lord abbot, my uncle.” Who this abbot was is made clear by Ermanricus in chapter 6 of that Life, namely the abbot of the monastery of Fulda:

“Where, by God’s providence, the most holy lord abbot Rabanus, most skilled in every art, now shines with discernment. Ermanricus presents Gundramnus, his dearest deacon, as sacristan of the cell of Saint Solus and chaplain of the king.”

In chapter 10 Ermanricus introduces him speaking as follows:

> “For I am here, dearest brother, by command of my lord the king, in obedience to my uncle [*patrui*] and my dearest lord, and to his brothers

[Col. 0011D] who live with him in the monastic community, assigned, as you see, to this most narrow and barren place.”

This can be understood of no one other than Rabanus, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, on whom the cell of Saint Solus depended.

Gundramnus continues:

> “Moreover, this also frequently troubles my mind: what good my lord the king could have found in me, that he deemed my service desirable; or why he wished to draw me away from the most peaceful life of the monastery—although until then I was not bound to it—and bring me up in it, and set me upon these most rugged mountain ridges.”

[Col. 0012A]

There was evidently a royal villa or residence near the cell of Saint Solus, as is clear from Gundramnus’s subsequent words. Gundramnus was prefect of this villa, and he laments that he had been forcibly removed from the monastery “and now enrolled among the court officials.”

This Gundramnus seems to me to be a different person from the Gundramnus whose epitaph, as well as that of his wife Otdrudis, Rabanus composed, since the former was a Levite and the latter married.

This is what may be said about Rabanus’s parents; from what has already been stated it is clear that they were illustrious.

4. Trithemius confidently specifies Rabanus’s birthday and year as “the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the year 788.” I do not know where he obtained the day; he came close to the truth concerning the year. I shall show below that Rabanus was promoted to the diaconate in the year 801. If he observed the ancient laws and regulations of the Church in this matter, he was then at least twenty-five years old. [Col. 0012B] For the ancient canons require this age unless a dispensation has been granted. Rabanus was therefore born about the year 776.

Certainly, he undertook to write the two books On the Praises of the Holy Cross before the year 810, by which time he had completed six lustra, that is, thirty years.

# Chapter Two

## Monastic profession and the diaconate; studies under Alcuin; fellow students

5. “He was a monk at Fulda from childhood,” according to the Anonymous writer whom we shall cite below. This is also sufficiently indicated in his own epitaph, where, immediately after receiving baptism, he says that at Fulda he learned the sacred teaching, that is, the rules of Christian and monastic life.

[Col. 0012C]

In the very ancient Annals of Fulda, which end in the fourth year of the reign of Louis the Pious, Rabanus is recorded as having been made a deacon in the thirty-third year of the reign of Charlemagne, that is, in the year 801.

6. When Rabanus was already a young man and had acquired some education, Ratgar, abbot of Fulda from 811 for sixteen years, “sent Rabanus, together with Hatto, to Albinus the teacher at Tours, for the purpose of learning the liberal arts,” as Browerus reports from an ancient Fulda manuscript in his notes on Rabanus’s poem 13.

Rabanus himself seems to credit this to Ratgar in that poem, in which several verses deserve attention here:

> Your goodness has now granted me permission to study books;  
> But poverty chokes the powers of my mind.  
> Whatever my teachers have taught with their lips,  
> Lest my wandering mind lose it, I have committed all to leaves.

[Col. 0012D]

In the poem prefixed to the books On the Holy Cross, he introduces Albinus, or Alcuin, his teacher, asking Saint Martin on his behalf:

> Holy bishop of God, living through your merits forever,  
> Receive with pious mind the cause that we bring.  
> When I was the humble guardian and minister  
> Of this church, reading the sacred teachings,  
> I taught this boy, through the utterance of the divine word,  
> The ethical precepts and the studies of wisdom.  
> He is indeed Frank by descent, and an inhabitant  
> Of the Bochonian forest, sent here to learn the words of God.  
> For his abbot, ruler of the Fulda flock,  
> Sent him here to your dwelling, Father,  
> So that with me he might read the schoolmaster’s art of meter,  
> And eagerly prepare the sacred Scripture in due form.

[Col. 0013A]

These verses misled Trithemius and others into saying that Rabanus studied literature under Alcuin at Rome. They thought that this poem, addressed to Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, should be understood as referring to the Roman pontiff and to the Roman Church, in which Alcuin had taught literature.

7. Rabanus had as fellow students at the academy of Tours Hatto, whom we have mentioned and who later succeeded him in the abbatial office; and Emmo or Haimo, later bishop of Halberstadt. This is gathered from the preface to the work On the Universe, dedicated to Haimo, in these words:

> “I remember your good zeal, holy Father, which you displayed in childhood and youth in the exercise of letters and the meditation of sacred literature, when with me you read not only the divine books and the explanations of the holy Fathers concerning them, [Col. 0013B]

but also the diligent investigations of the wise men of this world concerning the natures of things, which they composed in their account of the liberal arts and in their inquiry into other matters.”

He also had Samuel as a companion, as will become clear from section 10. I do not wish to speculate about his other companions.

# Chapter Three

## Direction and renown of the school of Fulda; other teachers; Rabanus’s pupils and successor in teaching

8. After returning from Tours, Rabanus was placed in charge of the Fulda schools under Abbot Ratgar, who was little disposed toward letters and learned men. Rabanus assumed this responsibility while Alcuin was still alive. In letter 55, addressed to “the blessed child of Saint Benedict, Maurus,” that is, Rabanus, Alcuin wishes him and his pupils happiness.

Thus, if Rabanus was sent from Abbot Ratgar—who is known to have assumed the direction of Fulda in 802—to Alcuin’s school; and if Alcuin died in May 804, Rabanus listened to Alcuin as his teacher at Tours for only a short time.

9. While Rabanus was teaching literature, the academy of Fulda enjoyed great renown. It abounded in books of every discipline and produced distinguished teachers for the Christian world. Rabanus shows us how extensive the holdings of the Fulda library were in poem 16, addressed to the priest Gerhoh, to whom it had been entrusted and whom he therefore calls his “key-wielding brother”:

> What can I say about the great praise of the books  
> Which you keep under your key, beloved brother?  
> Whatever God of heaven sent forth from the citadel into the world,  
> Through the pious words of men, as Holy Scripture—  
> You will find it there; whatever the wisdom of the world  
> Has brought forth into the world at different times.

[Col. 0013D]

10. Rabanus was not the only one teaching in these schools, although he was the principal teacher. He had as assistant and companion Samuel, later bishop of Worms, who had also been his fellow student under Alcuin.

Both facts are established by poem 21:

> Once I rejoiced that you were my companion  
> Among the readers, beloved brother, with me.  
> Now also I rejoice that you retain the authority of a teacher,  
> Growing in virtue and taking the place of your father.

By these verses he indicates that Samuel had once shared with him the office of teacher or reader, which he retained after being made a bishop. After two verses he adds that Albinus had also been their common teacher:

[Col. 0014A]

> What Albinus once taught properly as a teacher,  
> May this breast retain, and may all this work approve.

While Rabanus was in charge of the Fulda schools, Gildas the Irish, at his request, issued a book On Computation in ninety-nine chapters and dedicated it to him. Usserius published the dedicatory letter from the Cotton Library among his Irish writings. In that letter Gildas explains the subject of the work, giving thanks to God,

> “who,” he says, “inspired you with love for it, and makes you adorned with his radiance and beneficial to those near you.”

11. He had very many pupils, among them Walahfrid Strabo, Servatus Lupus, Rudolf, the subsequent author of the Life, and Otfrid. A few things concerning them should be noted here.

[Col. 0014B]

Walahfrid Strabo, later abbot of Reichenau, counts himself among Rabanus’s pupils in a poem written to his teacher Rabanus. Lupus writes in letter 1 that he had been sent by his metropolitan Aldric “to the venerable Rabanus, in order to receive from him an introduction to the divine Scriptures.”

He addresses letter 40 to that most reverend Father and distinguished teacher of his; in turn, after Lupus’s departure from him, Rabanus dedicated to Lupus his Collection on the Epistles of Paul.

Rudolf likewise calls Rabanus his teacher and master in the following Life.

Otfrid, priest and monk of Weissenburg near Speyer in the territory of the Nemetes, wrote to Liutbert, archbishop of Mainz, concerning the translation he had made of the Gospels into the Theodisc language:

> “I have therefore taken care to send this book for the approval of your discerning prudence. And because my small self was educated by Rabanus

[Col. 0014C] of venerable memory, formerly a worthy bishop of your see, I have taken care to commend it to the dignity and wisdom of your episcopate.”

12. After becoming abbot, the holy man entrusted the care of teaching the liberal arts to others, reserving for himself the task of interpreting the sacred Scriptures. For Lupus was sent to him when he was already abbot, in order to learn from him the beginnings of this discipline, as we have seen.

[Col. 0014D]

During his abbacy, the monk Candidus taught the scholars the humane letters. At the beginning of the little book he composed On the Life of Abbot Eigil, he writes:

> “I also make known to your charity that last year, when I complained to the lord Abbot Rabanus that I did not have anyone among my associates with whom I could advance by disputing and reading in the divine lesson, he gave me this answer: ‘Exercise yourself by reading,’ he said, ‘and add some useful contribution by dictating. For when I lived in the same place where you now dwell, I began, by divine grace inspiring me, a book in prose and verse in praise of the holy cross.’”

Rabanus undertook that work while he was teaching the humane disciplines in the monastery school. Consequently, when Candidus was writing the Life of Eigil, he held the office of teacher there.

# Chapter Four

## Priesthood, persecution, and the journey to Jerusalem

13. He received the rank of the priestly order from Haistulf, archbishop of Mainz. He himself testifies to this in a letter to Haistulf, prefixed to the books On the Instruction of Clerics, in these words:

> “For I willingly submit myself to your teaching, from whom I remember having received ecclesiastical dignity,”

that is, priestly ordination.

[Col. 0015A]

Rabanus wrote this letter in 819, as is indicated by the verses addressed to Haistulf at the beginning of those books. In that year the basilica of Fulda was dedicated, and Rabanus attended it already as a priest, according to Candidus in the Life of Saint Eigil.

Haistulf is said by Serarius to have assumed the see of Mainz in 815; consequently Rabanus was ordained by him at about that time. Certainly the word “I remember,” which he used in the aforementioned letter addressed to Haistulf in 819, sufficiently suggests that some time had already elapsed since his ordination.

[Col. 0015B]

After I had made these observations, the second volume of the Lambecian Library came into my hands. It contains the very ancient Annals of Fulda already mentioned, where I read the following concerning Rabanus’s priesthood:

> “In the first year of Louis the Pious, Rabanus was ordained priest on the tenth day before the Kalends of January by Haistulf, archbishop of Mainz.”

Therefore this occurred at the end of 814, by which time Haistulf was already presiding over the church of Mainz.

14. During this period disturbances and conflicts arose in the monastery of Fulda: a terrible plague with which that community was afflicted more than once—first under Abbot Sturm, then, as I conjecture, while Baugulf was governing, who appears to have resigned the government for that reason; then under Ratgar, who was deposed by order of Louis Augustus; and finally under Rabanus, whom a faction of his monks forced to resign the abbacy.

[Col. 0015C]

Sturm, by order of Pepin, was sent into exile “to a great monastery called Unnedica,” as it is written in his Life. Browerus, the first editor of the Life, regarded the word *Unnedica* as suspect. The distinguished Hadrian Valesius thinks that one should read *Gemedico*, Jumièges, which is called *Gemedicum*, *Gemeticum*, and *Gimeticum*, situated in the district of Rouen on the Seine.

The change of the letter G into V is certainly easy among the Germans and Franks, so that *Gimedico* may have been written *Vimedico* in the Acts of Sturm, in place of which Browerus may have read *Unnedico*. I therefore consider it unquestionable that the place of Sturm’s exile was Gemeticum.

[Col. 0015D]

The monks’ agitation against Sturm and Rabanus was unjust; against Ratgar, however, it was just, moderate, and necessary. As soon as Ratgar assumed pastoral responsibility, he almost entirely overturned the state of Fulda’s monastic discipline, censuring the customs of other monasteries, let alone his own, “as though they were not living according to the rule.”

He deprived his monks of necessary things and forced them into continual manual labor, abolishing the customary prayers, frequent celebration of Masses, and not a few feast days. Hence the monks lodged complaints with Charlemagne. I have reported their petition concerning this matter after the Life of Saint Eigil, abbot of Fulda.

[Note: [Col. 0015D] See volume 105 of Patrologia.]

By order of Charlemagne, Ratgar’s severity was restrained; but after Charlemagne’s death it began to rage again. Ratgar drove his men into labor more than

[Col. 0016A]

servile and forbade them books and the use of study.

At first they addressed the matter through petitions to him himself, falling upon their knees and begging that he deal more gently with them. Rabanus himself, whose small collection of books had been taken away, tried to soften the abbot’s harsh and savage spirit with these verses:

> You, kindly Father, excellent man and shepherd of monks,  
> I, your servant, invoke as gracious:  
> May your fatherly goodness now hear me, wretched as I am,  
> Crying out to you, pious ruler everywhere.  
> Your goodness has granted me permission to study books;  
> But poverty chokes the powers of my mind.  
> Whatever my teachers have taught with their lips,  
> Lest my wandering mind lose it, I have committed all to leaves.  
> Hence also there remain glosses and little books,  
> Which I beg you to order returned to the unworthy.  
> Whatever servants possess is held by right of their masters.  
> Thus you rightly possess all that I have written.  
> I do not arrogantly claim these writings as my own,

[Col. 0016B]

> But submit everything to your judgment.  
> Whether you grant these things to me or not, nevertheless may  
> The divinity of the Almighty always grant you every good;  
> And may he complete the good contest in an honorable course,  
> So that you may remain forever with Christ in the citadel of heaven.

Such a just and modest prayer might have moved a heart of iron; but it was spoken to stone.

Hence came immense evil: the monks’ secession and exiles, and solitude within solitude itself. Rabanus describes the mournful condition at Fulda *pathetically* [Greek: *pathetikōs*] in poem 30, addressed to a certain Fulda monk who was rejoicing. It will not be out of place to quote it here, so that pastors may at last understand how great an evil immoderate severity produces.

> A letter running from afar announces at the gate  
> To the beloved Brother the grievous gifts  
> Which the unhappy hour of time had brought.  
> Him whom an evil fate had recently snatched away,

[Col. 0016C]

> Noise, deceit, grief, and immense labor  
> Had compelled to seek distant lands.  
> One part was taken away, another remained;  
> When one man is divided, alas, the same person  
> Is one in desire and soul, but two in body.  
> After you, brother, my one-minded companion, departed,  
> Soon, amid various torments everywhere,  
> I became the victim of misfortune, wounded by black hatreds.  
> But now … I grieve with a sorrowful heart  
> That a common evil, alas, has such great power,  
> Rather than that I might conceal harm to myself alone.  
> Since a harmful sedition arose among us long ago,  
> No one was able to soften it by prayers  
> Or bring it to an end.  
> But as it grew for a very long time,  
> It increased day by day through evil fortune  
> And devastated the Father’s people because of his anger.  
> He hardens his heart and does not know how to yield;  
> The savage drives away the sheep and stains himself with slaughter;  
> He pities no one and rages against all.  
> Moved by these evils, the crowd abandoned  
> The ancient fold and became a wandering people.

[Col. 0016D]  
> For the injured, the only salvation is to go far [L.: *longe*, “far”].  
> The final day came, the bitter time,  
> When the crowd, forced to endure extremes,  
> Was compelled by its sufferings to leave its dwelling.  
> All the brothers gathered from every side,  
> United in mind and equal in will,  
> To strive by prayers to bend the unyielding man.  
> But he, hardened in spirit, who had despised all [for *sprevit*, “despised”]  
> And provoked the people [the monks], drove the monks from the church;  
> He caused them to despair of the Father’s love.  
> Meanwhile, within the walls, grief of different kinds  
> Is mingled; cymbals resound together,  
> And the church’s signal summons everyone.  
> They hasten to the tomb of the blessed martyr;  
> The younger people weep mingled with the elders;  
> They draw groans from the depths of their hearts  
> And extend their hands with poured-out prayer.

Thus the mutilated codex ends, from which we learn enough about the end of this tragedy.

[Col. 0017A] The matter was brought before Louis Augustus, who granted the monks of Fulda permission to choose another abbot.

Ratgar was soon deposed, and in 817 Eigil was elected abbot, as is stated in his Life. Under that abbot the desired serenity returned; the monks were gathered together again, restored regular discipline and the practice of study, and did so especially under Rabanus as teacher.

15. I believe that during Ratgar’s storm it happened that Rabanus was compelled to leave his position and went to the holy places. He himself mentions this previously unknown pilgrimage in manuscript commentaries on chapter 11 of the Book of Joshua, at verse 8, where he discusses Sidon:

[Col. 0017B]

> “When I myself had stayed several times in the regions of Sidon, I never discovered that there were two Sidons, one great and the other small, so far as the earthly location is concerned.”

Nor can this journey be referred to the period when he had temporarily ceased to exercise the abbatial office, since he dedicated these commentaries to Frideric, bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine, who was killed in 834, eight years before Rabanus resigned his office.

# Chapter Five

## The office of abbot, his deeds, and his resignation from office

16. After Abbot Eigil had been established in office as I have said, and had died five years later, Rabanus succeeded him in 822, in August or September, as I gather from two charters published by Pistorius. One of them, issued under Abbot Eigil, is dated the sixth day before the Nones of August, p. 528; the other, under Rabanus, is dated in October, the tenth day before the Kalends of November, p. 533. Both belong to the ninth year of Emperor Louis.

[Col. 0017C]

17. It would be difficult to explain all the distinguished deeds accomplished by so great an abbot. Under him monastic discipline was maintained intact; the reputation and fame of the monastery, as well as the religious observance of the monks, increased beyond measure; temporal prosperity was greatly augmented; the study of literature flourished wonderfully; the goodwill of kings and emperors—whose favor and affection he always enjoyed—was won; and, something I should have mentioned earlier, worship was increased through basilicas, sacred altars, and the relics of the saints.

[Col. 0017D]

Trithemius should be heard at this point:

> “Under his rule, the monastery of Fulda grew daily in possessions and persons, and the fame of the holiness of its monks spread throughout the entire kingdom of the Franks. Above all, however, the reputation of Abbot Rabanus for learning and holiness was celebrated and glorious in everyone’s speech, not only among the Franks of Germany but also among the Gauls and Italians. The fame of this man moved kings and princes, bishops and every kind of teacher, even those living at a greater distance, to venerate him. From the whole Frankish kingdom, which at that time was united, Germans and Gauls hastened together to hear him, men skilled in many abilities, and they considered themselves blessed if they were admitted to his familiarity. Many princes, nobles, and citizens also entrusted their sons to Rabanus’s instruction, honoring the teacher with various and magnificent gifts and rewards. He taught them with such diligence that scarcely could anything greater be imagined.”

[Col. 0018A]

18. Rudolf gives us abundant information about what Rabanus did for the relics of the saints and the sacred places in the Life of Rabanus below. He omits only the fact that Rabanus laid the foundations of the church of Hersfeld, as attested by Lambert, a monk of that place, whose words are:

> “In the year 831, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, a Monday, Abbots Brun and Raban dug the foundation of the church of Saint Wigbert.”

Rabanus completed it after Brun’s death and dedicated it in 850. He left a memorial of this event in verse.

[Col. 0018B]

19. At that time, according to Meginfrid’s testimony preserved by Trithemius, there were one hundred and fifty monks in the monastery of Fulda, whom Rabanus instructed no less in virtues than in literary studies.

The reputation of his learning is demonstrated by the conduct of Lupus, who, already a mature man occupied with important affairs and cultivated in letters, nevertheless submitted himself to be instructed in Rabanus’s discipline shortly before the administration of the monastery of Ferrières was entrusted to him, as is clear from his letter 5. Once he himself had become abbot, he thanked his teacher in letter 40.

What he did in the Fulda academy under Rabanus he explains in the following letter to Immo, bishop of Noyon:

> “I was astonished that you had asked to be informed which books I had written or read in Germany, and I could not adequately grasp the reason, unless perhaps you wished cleverly to test me by proposing two alternatives: one of which, if I had remained silent, might have seemed ostentation; the other, childish imprudence. I therefore disclose to you frankly that I devoted my principal effort there to reading, and prepared a few books both as a remedy against forgetfulness

[Col. 0018C] and for the increase of learning. Nor did I take on, out of love for the German language, as certain people most foolishly boasted, the burden of so great and prolonged a labor.”

20. During the time when the sons of Louis Augustus were conspiring against their father, Rabanus conducted himself so prudently and religiously that he retained the goodwill both of the father and of the sons, and became among them an intermediary for concord and peace. He published a book On the Reverence of Sons toward Fathers and of Subjects toward Kings, at the end of which he urges Emperor Louis to show indulgence toward his son and toward the others.

21. What increase in the Fuldense monastery’s temporal resources accrued through him is shown by the charters of donation published by Pistorius and Browerus. Worthy of note is Einhard’s Letter 16, addressed to the most reverend servant of Christ, the venerable abbot Hrabanus [Col. 0018D], in which he asks that a certain Gundhart, one of Hrabanus’s men, be excused from that year’s military expedition. For the Fuldense monastery belonged to the number of those that owed the king gifts and military service (as they call it). In addition, he is said to have obtained an outstanding diploma from Pope Gregory IV, by which the pontiff grants the Fuldenses six privileges:

1. He confirms the monastery’s patrimony.
2. He assigns to Hrabanus and his successors a residence in Rome, namely the monastery of Saint Andrew, called Exavilum, beside the church of Saint Mary at the Cradle.
3. He forbids prelates of every order to celebrate at the principal altar of the Fuldense basilica.
4. He grants the faculty of preaching, the place of precedence, and the first seat in public assemblies, before all the abbots of Gaul and Germany.
5. The use of the dalmatic, leggings, and sandals.
6. That the prelate of Fulda should be blessed or confirmed only by the Apostolic See.

On the Ides of May, by the hand of Benedict, notary and archivist, in the fourteenth indiction—that is, in the year 836. Gretser published this diploma from the Viennese library, as Browerus testifies in his Re-readings of the Fuldense Antiquities: “If this diploma is genuine,” he says, “it confers great distinctions upon Hrabanus.”

22. Trithemius adds that Hrabanus was generous toward the poor, not without the criticism of his own people, and was accustomed to give alms for the refreshment of the dead. When Adelhardus, a Frankish monk and an excessively greedy administrator of the household’s property, had at some point defrauded him of these alms [Col. 0019B], he was, in the year 837, deservedly chastised from heaven. When I read this, I was reminded of that enclosed Adalhardus whose epitaph is found among Hrabanus’s poems.

As for what Trithemius adds—that by a statute he removed women from entering the Fuldense church—Rudolfus, in his book On the Life of Saint Lioba the Abbess, testifies that this had been provided for there from the beginning, from the time when the place began to be inhabited by monks. Nevertheless, something in Trithemius’s words deserves notice:

> “The blessed abbot Hrabanus also made another very necessary regulation, which, as is reported, is observed in the monastery even to the present day. Knowing how dangerous the frequent sight of women is for monks, especially for those who are younger in age and whose minds are still less practiced in the fear of the Lord, after consultation with twelve elders he perpetually forbade all women access to the monastery. And so that this holy regulation might retain perpetual force, he permanently prohibited and denied the female sex passage through the northern gate of the city, outside which the monastery is situated.”

This perhaps should be understood as a confirmation of an ancient custom. As for Trithemius’s statement that this practice was observed down to his own time—with the exception of the feast of Saint Boniface and certain other feast days, on which, by concession of the Roman pontiff, women were allowed to enter the church—it should nevertheless be noted that the elders maintained that on the first occasion when the church was opened in this way, it was struck by fire from heaven and burned down the following day.

23. What remains to be said is that in the year 838 Abbot Hrabanus sent a colony of monks to Hirsau [Col. 0019D], to inhabit the monastery established by Count Erlafrid, placing over them his disciple Liutbertus as abbot, as Trithemius explains more fully in his History of Hirsau.

24. “In the year 842,” says Lambert of Schafnaburg, “Lotharius was expelled from the kingdom, and Abbot Hrabanus left the monastery after having nobly governed it for twenty years,” following Rudolfus. Trithemius, drawing on Meginfridus, reports that this happened because of a disagreement among the monks:

> “In the fifty-seventh year of his life, as Meginfridus, later a monk at Fulda, records, a serious and harmful disagreement arose between him and his monks, at the instigation of the devil; its cause, however, he did not explain. King Louis of Germany—brother of the emperor and king of Italy Lotharius, and son of Louis I—summoned Abbot Hrabanus to him by messengers sent to Fulda and restrained the monks’ rashness by royal authority. He received Hrabanus with honor and kept him with him at the royal court for nearly two years. Meanwhile the Fuldense monks, moved to repentance, sent envoys to the king, humbly begging him to restore to them the abbot who had been taken away. But, because of a reasonable cause, the abbot refused to do so, and the king absolutely declined to agree. Thus the blessed abbot Hrabanus remained at the royal court for two years, until the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, while the monks continued to lament.”

There is a double error here: both the claim that Hrabanus remained at court for two years after relinquishing his office [Col. 0020B], and the statement that after those two years he was promoted to the see of Mainz. For almost five full years he lived in retirement in a remote cell, namely from 842 to 847, when he succeeded Otgar.

The old Acts of the Fuldense abbots, cited by Browerus in Book IV of the Fuldense Antiquities, distinguish the matter more accurately:

> “After Hrabanus had nobly governed the Fuldense church for twenty years, he left the authority he had held beyond the Rhine and went into Lotharius’s kingdom. After him, certain brothers of the monastery were sent out to see whether they could recall him. When he refused, they appointed Hatto as abbot over themselves. But after a few days Hrabanus came to the monastery and, with the agreement of the abbot and his brothers, became a mountaineer on the eastern side of the monastery.”

That is, he was confined in a cell situated on Mount Saint Peter, approximately twelve stades from the monastery. There, “serving God,” says Rudolfus, “he devoted himself to heavenly wisdom.”

Lotharius Augustus’s letter to Hrabanus, prefixed to the Commentary on Ezekiel, must be understood as referring to this retreat:

> “I approve, I say, of your dwelling, if it is believed to be free from all ostentation. For rustic solitude among the mountains delights the inner man more than the regal splendor of cities, where no envious malice feigns a peaceful heart with a cheerful gaze, nor does the cunning crime of mutual deceit fabricate the shadow of flattering speech.”

This letter was given at the time when the turmoil of the wars that drove Lotharius and his brothers to dispute the kingdom was agitating them, as Lotharius indicates at the beginning of the letter.

Stephanus Baluzius, a man of great learning, correctly established the time when Hrabanus relinquished the government in his notes on Lupus’s Letter 40, both from the year 822, which the Fuldense Annals identify as the year when Hrabanus assumed the abbatial dignity, and from the twenty-year period of his rule, which Rudolfus assigns to him up to his deposition from pastoral responsibility.

Nevertheless, an old handwritten catalogue of the Fuldense abbots, cited by Browerus in his notes on Hrabanus’s Poem 28, seems to conflict with this. In that catalogue, “Hatto, called Bonosus,” Hrabanus’s successor, is said to have “undertaken the governance of the abbacy in the year of the Lord 841.”

I think this should be interpreted as the end of the year 841 according to the old reckoning, but as the beginning of the year 842 according to the new. For, according to the evidence already given, Hrabanus succeeded Eigil toward the end of the year 822, namely in September. He relinquished his dignity “after he had governed the monastery for twenty years,” as Rudolfus testifies; consequently, his abdication occurred at the beginning of the year 842, though some referred it to the end of the preceding year.

This reckoning is strongly confirmed by Lupus’s Letter 41, where he says that, after returning safely from Germany, or from the Fuldense school, he was struck by news of the death of Aldricus, bishop of Sens and his foster-father, who, as I have shown in his Life, died toward the end of the year 840, specifically on the sixth day before the Ides of October [Note: [Col. 0021D] See volume CV of Patrologia.]. Yet at the time when Lupus departed from Hrabanus, Hrabanus had already relinquished the office of abbot, as is understood from Lupus’s Letter 40 to him. In it, Lupus, already returned to Gaul, writes that he had heard that Hrabanus had laid down the burden of administration [Col. 0021B]. Consequently, this occurred only at the beginning of the year 842, at which time Lotharius was disputing the kingdom by arms with his brothers, as stated above.

To this may be added certain charters of donation in Pistorius, pages 484 and 558. One of them is said to have been made to Abbot Hrabanus in the second year of Ludharius, the most glorious king of the Franks, on the fourth day before the Nones of April—that is, in the year 842. Another was made to Abbot Hatto on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the third year of Louis, king of the eastern Franks—that is, in the following year.

What the cause of this abdication was, Lupus asks to have reported to him in the aforesaid Letter 40, in these words:

> “Moreover, I have heard that you have laid down the burden of your administration and are now occupied solely with divine matters, while you have left our Hatto the care that is full of toil. I would like to learn the course of this affair, as well as anything else that may seem appropriate, through a letter from Your Blessedness.”

But what reply Lupus received concerning this matter is unknown.

25. During this period of retirement, the pious man devoted himself entirely to the study of sacred literature. At that time he dedicated his work On the Universe to Hemmo, bishop of Halberstadt, to whom he says in the dedicatory letter:

> “After divine providence released me from responsibility for external affairs and raised you to the office of pastoral care, I was considering what I might prepare in writing that would be pleasing and useful to Your Holiness.”

Moreover, “in the year 844,” as the Fuldense Annals report, “Hrabanus the sophist”—that is, the wise man—“second to none among the poets of his time, sent through Aschricus and Hr(u)odbertus, monks of the Fuldense monastery, to Pope Sergius, to be offered to Saint Peter, a book which he had composed in a difficult and marvelous poem, distinguished by a variety of figures, On the Praise of the Holy Cross of Christ.” We shall speak later of his other works published during this period.

Among these works, he dedicated his commentaries on Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, together with his penitential book, to Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, his predecessor. In this connection the complaining letter of the Mainz clergy, published by Chiffletius in Volume II of the History of the Franks, must be explained. In it the people of Mainz ask Emperor Louis to restore Otgar, or Otger, to his own see, “because of the excessive necessity that daily afflicted that very diocese [Col. 0022A], while its shepherd was absent for a long time and dwelling far away.”

I mention this because Serarius makes no reference to the matter in his History of Mainz. This is the Otgar to whom Hrabanus wrote concerning the ordination of the deacon Werdricus, as is confirmed by Einhard’s Letter 4.

## CHAPTER VI

### The Archiepiscopal Dignity and the Deeds of the Archbishop

26. “In the year 847,” the Fuldense Annals record, “Otgar, bishop of Mainz, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May; in his place Hrabanus was ordained on the fifth day before the Kalends of July.”

This raises a difficulty for Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, an erudite priest of the Society of Jesus. In the Preface to a book Against the Jews, which he published under Hrabanus’s name, he maintains that Hrabanus’s ordination took place in the preceding year. He argues this first because, according to ancient custom, episcopal ordinations were to take place on a Sunday, and in that year the fifth day before the Kalends of July fell on a Sunday; and second because of the period of nine years, one month, and four days of rule assigned to Hrabanus in the aforementioned Annals, where his death is referred to the year 856, on the day before the Nones of February. For, counting from the fifth day before the Kalends of July in 847 to that year, a complete nine-year period cannot be found.

For this reason he thinks that the year 847 in these Annals is reckoned according to the old calculation, so that it would be the preceding year according to the new. Both of Chiffletius’s arguments are sound, but the solution to both difficulties must be sought elsewhere.

The month of June, on whose fifth day before the Kalends of July Hrabanus’s ordination is said to have taken place, cannot be assigned to different years according to different reckonings. Only the first three months of our common era can be so shifted; and the old system of computation does not precede the Dionysian and our own modern system.

Thus January, February, and March, up to Easter, belong to the end of the year 847 according to the old reckoning, but to the beginning of the following year according to the Dionysian system, which begins the years with Christ’s nativity, and according to our modern system, which begins them in January.

I know that this practice varied in some places, so that nine months—from the Annunciation, or from the month of March, to Christmas—were occasionally assigned to the year preceding the reckoning that counted years from the Nativity rather than from the Incarnation. According to Covarruvias, this custom prevailed among the people of Pisa. But this method of computation was extremely rare. Therefore, as I have said, the solution to the difficulty proposed by Chiffletius must be sought elsewhere.

It certainly cannot be denied that, according to the ancient custom, episcopal ordinations were ordinarily performed on a Sunday, but not always. For Saints Willibrord and Boniface were ordained at Rome: Boniface on the day before the Kalends of December in the year 823, which then fell on a Tuesday; Willibrord in the year 696, on the feast day of Saint Cecilia, which fell on a Wednesday.

Nevertheless, I think that Hrabanus’s ordination did take place on a Sunday. But since the Fuldense Annals, the Franco-Saxon Annals, and the monk Hermannus testify that it occurred in the year 847, we must acknowledge that an error has entered the date in the Fuldense Annals, and that the sixth day before the Kalends of July should be restored in place of the fifth, as Trithemius reads [Col. 0023A].

Although the Franco-Saxon manuscript Annals, of excellent quality, which otherwise agree here with the Fuldense Annals, place Hrabanus’s ordination on the eighth day before the Kalends of July—that is, on the birthday of Saint John the Baptist—his ordination could readily have taken place on that day because of the solemnity of the feast, even though it was not a Sunday.

Chiffletius’s other argument must be refuted below, when we examine the years of Hrabanus’s pontificate. For now I point out that the book, or letter, Against the Jews, published under Hrabanus’s name, from which Chiffletius drew the principal foundation of his opinion concerning the year of Hrabanus’s ordination, should not be attributed to this pontiff but to Amolo, as I shall later demonstrate.

The deeds of Archbishop Hrabanus must now be briefly explained.

27. In the same year as his ordination, according to the aforementioned Annals, “at the command of King Louis, he held a synod at Mainz around the Kalends of October,” namely in the monastery of Saint Alban. The occasion of this synod was the same as that of the council of Meaux, as Baronius observed.

Since laymen were invading the property, rights, and persons of the churches, and frequent complaints concerning these matters were being brought before the king, he took sufficient action to have a provincial council assembled to remedy these evils. “Archbishop Hrabanus, a man highly distinguished for learning, whom he knew to be second to none in integrity and knowledge, was to preside over it,” says Baronius.

How many bishops attended, and what they decreed, is shown by Hrabanus’s synodal letter sent to King Louis together with the chapters established there; these survive in the collection of Councils. The following words in that letter deserve consideration:

> “We decreed that in each parish, prayers should be offered for you, for your wife, and likewise for your most noble offspring by the bishops and clergy, by the abbots and monks. The total of these prayers is three thousand five hundred Masses and one thousand seven hundred psalters.”

And below:

> “Then, sitting together in the cloister of Saint Alban the Martyr, following the custom by which, in ancient times under Emperor Charles, Hildeboldus and Ricolfus, together with the other bishops and abbots who had assembled there, acted in this way, we began, in the name of God and by common agreement and consent, to discuss together the state of true religion and the welfare and progress of the Christian people. We agreed among ourselves to divide our common college of clergy and monks into two groups, as we indeed did, so that in one group the bishops would sit with the notaries . . . while in the other group the abbots and approved monks sat, carefully reading and discussing the Rule of Saint Benedict, considering how they might, by God’s grace, bring the life of monks to a better condition and greater flourishing; and wherever the regular order had lapsed through the negligence and sloth of its superiors, it was to be restored again according to the norm of Saint Benedict.”

At that synod the case of a certain “false prophetess from the regions of Alamannia, named Thiota,” was also debated. She had greatly disturbed the diocese of Bishop Solomon of Constance with her prophecies, asserting that a certain day for the end of the world had been divinely revealed to her, along with many other matters. “Brought before the bishops at Saint Alban, she was beaten publicly with whips and, to her disgrace, lost the ministry of preaching which she had irrationally assumed,” as is more fully related in the aforementioned Annals, from which we have also extracted what follows.

28. “In the year 848,” King Louis of Germany “reconciled at Mainz with his lord the men of Bishop Hrabanus who had conspired against him, after they had been publicly convicted.

“A certain priest named Gotescalcus”—a monk of the monastery of Orbais, under the parish and jurisdiction of the archbishop of Reims but in the diocese of Soissons—“holding an erroneous opinion concerning God’s predestination, and affirming that the good were predestined by God inevitably to life and the wicked to everlasting death, was reasonably convicted, as it seemed to many, in the assembly of bishops and was sent to his own bishop, Igumarus of Reims, after first confirming by oath that he would not return to King Louis’s realm.”

Hincmar mentions this synod in various places, especially in chapter 11 of his later work Against Gottschalk, where he produces a synodal letter sent to him by Hrabanus concerning Gottschalk. It is extant in Volume III of the Councils of Gaul.

Hrabanus also wrote three letters on this matter: to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims; to Notingus, bishop of Verona; and to Count Heberardus in Italy. Jacobus Sirmondus published them in print in the year 1647.

Trithemius combined the two preceding synods into one in his Hirsaugiensis Chronicle, where, in discussing this synod, he makes many errors. First, he says that the synod was convened at the command of Lotharius, although it was held through the initiative of King Louis. Then, when listing the synod’s fathers, he mentions Altfridus, bishop of Hildesheim, who did not assume that see until the year 851; Hetti, archbishop of Trier; Hildeboldus of Cologne; Ludericus, bishop of Bremen; and Einhardus, abbot of Segenstelten, all of whom had already died. He also mentions Radulphus, abbot of Saint Medard of Soissons and later archbishop of Bourges, although he had obtained the latter dignity long before, namely from the year 840. See Henschenius’s Commentary, no. 51.

29. “In the year 850,” according to the same Fuldense Annals [Col. 0024D], “an exceedingly severe famine afflicted the peoples of Germany, especially those living around the Rhine. For one modius of grain was sold at Mainz for ten shekels of silver.

“At that time Archbishop Hrabanus was staying in a certain village of his diocese called Winzella. Receiving poor people who came from different places, he supported more than three hundred of them with food every day, apart from those who were continually fed in his presence.”

It has already been noted above, from Trithemius, how great Hrabanus’s charity toward the poor was. Winzella will be mentioned again in section 38.

In the same year 850, specifically on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, “the church of Saint Wigbert” in the monastery of Fritzlar “was dedicated by Hrabanus, archbishop of the Mainz church,” according to the Hildesheim Chronicle.

30. “In the year 852 a synod was held, by the will and command of Louis, the most serene prince, in the city of Mainz, the metropolis of Germany. The venerable Hrabanus, archbishop of that city, presided, together with all the bishops and abbots of eastern Francia, Bavaria, and Saxony. They dealt ecclesiastically with the resolution of disputed questions. The king, however, occupied himself with the princes and governors of the provinces in settling public affairs and lawsuits. After approving their synodal decrees by his judgment, he returned to Bavaria.”

Henschenius discusses the bishops who attended this council in his Commentary, no. 51, where he corrects certain errors of Trithemius. In no. 49 he also assigns each bishop his own see among those who were present at Hrabanus’s first council.

In the year 853 a synod was held “in the royal palace of Frankfurt,” in the presence of Louis, king of Germany. There it was determined what rights Gozbertus, bishop of Osnabrück, ought to possess over the churches of the convent of Herford, in the presence of King Louis “and Archbishop Hrabanus, together with the others conducting the synod with him.” The same king granted a diploma concerning this matter, published above in the preliminary observations to the history of the translation of Saint Vitus [Note: [Col. 0025D] See volume CIV of Patrologia, among the Diplomas of Louis the Pious.].

31. Thus occupied with the duties of his office, the most devout prelate scarcely had time to breathe. For this reason, when urged by Freculfus, bishop of Lisieux, to write commentaries on Genesis, he replied:

> “You have instructed me to arrange the Pentateuch . . . But you know better than I how far this exceeds my abilities, since, being engaged in a very difficult position on account of the care of the Lord’s flock, lest it lack what is necessary, I am so occupied that I have neither the opportunity to read through the writings of others nor to devise works of my own.”

## CHAPTER VII

### His Zeal for Writing and His Reverence for the Fathers

32. His love of literature was so great that neither the labor of teaching, nor the duties of the regular life, nor various occupations, nor even illnesses could recall him from his devotion to writing. He was readily obedient to the wishes of his friends and cared only that he might be of benefit to the Church of Christ and to the salvation of others.

This is demonstrated by his preface to the Book of Judges, addressed to Humbertus, bishop of Würzburg, whose words are as follows:

> “Therefore, since Your Paternity has deigned to seek from our littleness some slight assistance for this purpose, for the love of God and also because of your humble affection for him, I humbly profess that in this work I wish to be your servant, and, insofar as divine grace permits, a willing helper in your good undertaking.”

And in his letter to King Louis, at the beginning of his Commentaries on the Books of Maccabees:

> “As long as I live in this little body,” he says, “I strive to labor in the service of Christ insofar as it is possible.”

Although he was placed in charge of the Fuldense school and was occupied with the regular exercises and the instruction of the young [Col. 0026A], he nevertheless did not cease composing commentaries from the opinions of the Fathers, as his letter to Haistulfus, bishop of Mainz, concerning his exposition of Matthew testifies:

> “Intent upon reading these authors, insofar as I was permitted by the countless restraints of monastic service, and for the nourishment of the little ones—which causes us no small trouble and interferes with reading—I, acting as both my own dictator and notary, took care to commit to a sheet what they had explained, either in their very words or, for the sake of brevity, in expressions of my own.”

He imitated the Venerable Bede, whose words are almost identical in his Eulogy, reported in the preceding century [Note: [Col. 0026D] See volume XC of Patrologia, volume I of the Works of the Venerable Bede.].

After becoming abbot, he cultivated the same study, although, “living in desert places, he was kept occupied by the greatest number of duties, by which he was compelled daily to serve and provide what was necessary for the servants of Christ living under the Rule of Saint Benedict, and had no leisure to examine fully the writings of the Fathers,” as he writes in his letter to Freculfus, bishop of Lisieux in Gaul, to whom he sent his exposition of Leviticus. He had said the same in a letter to that same man when he sent him his explanation of Genesis. What the bishop wrote will be seen later.

But—and this is even more remarkable—illnesses did not delay him from this work, as is shown by his letter to Lotharius Augustus concerning the Commentaries on Ezekiel:

> “As for what you requested in third place concerning Ezekiel,” he says, “you have here in the present little work what has been completed, insofar as bodily weakness and the smallness of my intellect allow.”

And in the preface of his little book On the Sacred Orders, addressed to Theotmarus, he speaks as follows:

> “Since I have chosen you as my co-worker in the sacred ministry, I urge you to make known to those who have been ordained to the priesthood and are to exercise the priestly ministry, and to persuade—or rather command—them to learn diligently what has been written in this little work, what I cannot set forth before many people because of bodily weakness. You are younger in age and stronger in body.”

Finally, in the preface to his work on Jeremiah:

> “Pressed by a serious illness, I now lie more often on my little bed than I sit in my study for writing or reading.”

33. The extent of his respect for the holy Fathers is shown by all his works, which he composed from their opinions, adding their names in the margins “so that I might not be accused of stealing the sayings of my elders and presenting them as if they were my own,” as he says in the preface to the Gospel of Matthew.

He did this, as he says there, for the benefit of others:

> “So that the poor reader who does not possess an abundance of books, or who is not permitted to investigate the Fathers’ profound meanings in many volumes, might at least find in this work sufficient material for his need.”

No one who considers the scarcity of books in that period can deny that this was done with excellent judgment. For outside the monasteries there were scarcely any libraries, not even in most cathedral churches, as Freculfus testifies concerning his own church of Lisieux [Col. 0027A] in his letter to Hrabanus. He had asked Hrabanus for commentaries on the Pentateuch composed from the sayings of the Fathers:

> “Therefore, if you attempt to put forward some excuses to avoid undertaking a work of such magnitude and such great labor, and if you try to answer by asking why I do not examine through my own labor of reading the books from which I order these things to be made, gathering whatever I like by selecting it, then let the vigilance of your charity attend to this: we have no abundance of books to enable us to do these things, even if the smallness of our dull intellect were vigorous. For in the episcopal residence entrusted to our littleness I cannot find even the canonical books of the New and Old Testament, much less their expositions.”

And although Hrabanus’s modesty in preferring the opinions of the Fathers to his own deserves praise, there were nevertheless those who criticized him for this. He complains of them in his preface on Ezekiel, addressed to Emperor Lotharius:

> “Nor do I think that this should be left unmentioned: I have learned, from the reports of certain people, that some ignorant men criticized me for marking the names of the holy Fathers when making an excerpt from their writings, or because I used the opinions of others more than I composed works of my own. I can readily answer them on this point. For what fault did I commit in judging the teachers of the Church worthy of veneration and inserting their opinions in my little works, in the places where they were appropriate, just as they had expressed them, together with an indication of their names? It seemed to me more salutary to preserve humility and rely upon the teachings of the holy Fathers than, through arrogance and the pursuit of personal praise, to put forward my own words improperly . . .

> “Let those who seek to be praised and desire to be seen by men dictate or write whatever they wish, and let them acquire for themselves, from wherever they can, praisers and flatterers. But for me, to cling to God all the days of my life is good, and to place my hope in the Lord God, so that I may proclaim all his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion—in those gates, namely, of which it is written: ‘Blessed are those who walk in the paths of life and enter the city through the gates.’”

Would that those who compose new books might walk along these same paths—as indeed many now do—and not through the tangled roads of human inventions and novelties, than which nothing is more harmful in religion!

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0027D]

### Zeal for the Faith and for Integrity of Morals, Authority, and Humility

34. Hrabanus’s zeal for the Christian religion would be demonstrated above all by the letter Against the Jews published under his name by Chiffletius. But since it is more probable that it was the work of Amolo, as we shall later show, it is preferable to offer, as evidence of this zeal, the Martyrology he himself published concerning the saints who glorified the Church by their deeds as well as by their suffering.

All his writings likewise demonstrate this: they breathe the genuine teaching of the Fathers and authentic piety. Most especially this is shown by the decrees he enacted in the various synods he convened for ecclesiastical affairs.

35. Against moral laxity he wrote several homilies, which he dedicated to Haistulfus, archbishop of Mainz, for recitation to the people. Among them is a homily Against Those Who Wearied Themselves with Shouting during an Eclipse of the Moon; another Against Pagan Errors, which certain uneducated Christians followed; and another On the Conduct of Good and Bad Christians.

Nor did he give salutary admonitions for the correction of morals only to common people; he gave them also to kings and bishops. He admonished kings both in the book On the Reverence of Sons toward Their Fathers, concerning the deposition of Louis Augustus, and in the provincial synod of Mainz, which he celebrated in the first year after his ordination.

Finally, he admonished bishops not to devote more time to secular lawsuits than to sacred preaching, in a letter written to Bishop Hemmo at the beginning of the books On the Universe:

> “For it is much better for a bishop to labor in the teaching of the word of God for the salvation of the souls entrusted to him than to devote himself to arranging and deciding civil questions and the various disputes of men, who, because of earthly greed, constantly stir up lawsuits and quarrels, and each strives to surpass the other in these matters. For nowhere in the sacred Scriptures do we read that the Savior himself or his disciples did or taught such things . . . In writing this, my lord, I do not want you to think that I am establishing for you a new rule of life, but only briefly recalling, for remembrance, what was formerly proclaimed by holy men.”

And in his letter concerning chorepiscopi to Dragon, bishop of Metz, he censures the Western, or Gallican, bishops [Col. 0028C] who wished to exclude chorepiscopi from the power of ordaining priests and deacons:

> “It is a great honor to be a minister of Christ, and therefore a great reward follows one who ministers well, so that he may rejoice without end in heavenly blessedness with Christ and his holy angels. For this reason it is not fitting for Christ’s servants to contend over the elevation of honor, but rather to strive over the usefulness of sound preaching and the constancy of good works, so that the people of Christ may hear from their mouths the word of right faith and see in their actions a good example through the mark of humility . . . For it is not right that the conferral of sacred orders should become for Christ’s servants a cause of pride and earthly pleasure, since they find nothing of this kind either in the words or in the examples of the Master himself or of his disciples.”

And so forth.

Hrabanus’s opinion agrees with Letter 39 of Pope Nicholas I, addressed to Rodulfus, bishop of Bourges.

36. Such freedom in speaking did not, as usually happens, provoke the indignation of those to whom he wrote. Rather, it won him authority among all who eagerly desired to be instructed and corrected by his writings and admonitions.

An example is Lotharius Augustus, who, after receiving from him an exposition of the Book of Joshua, thanked him for what he had received. He then asked for additional works, expressing his ardent desire to see and speak with him frequently, as is clear from Lotharius’s letter at the beginning of the Commentary on Ezekiel. This was written to Hrabanus after he had relinquished the abbatial government and displays signs of an exceptional familiarity with him.

Louis Augustus and Louis, his son and king of Germany, were no less favorably disposed toward him. The former visited the Fuldense monastery on Hrabanus’s account, as Hrabanus testifies in his letter to King Louis prefixed to his exposition of the Paralipomenon [Chronicles], where he says that he had recently delivered the Commentaries on Kings in person to Louis’s most sacred father at his own monastery.

The latter summoned Hrabanus to the monastery cell called Ratestorf, where he discussed the sacred Scriptures with him and persuaded him to explain the canticles sung throughout the week at the morning praises, as is related in the letter prefixed to that exposition.

It is remarkable that kings so great, entangled in so many wars and secular affairs, possessed such a thirst for the word of God—a thirst undoubtedly kindled by the man who quenched it, namely Hrabanus.

37. What the holy man thought of himself amid all this he reveals in his own preface to the Commentaries on Ezekiel. Lotharius Augustus had asked him, among other things, to continue the explanation of the book from the point where Gregory the Great had stopped.

> “As for what you requested in third place concerning Ezekiel,” he says, “you have here in the present little work what has been completed, insofar as bodily weakness and the smallness of my intellect allow. For I have not done this as the successor of Pope Gregory and preacher of God’s people, filling out what he began when teaching the people through the form of homilies, but did not bring through to the end of the Prophet. Rather, I have done it as an imitator and disciple, following the footsteps not only of that aforementioned pope but also of the other holy teachers.”

Let these remarks suffice as an example of Hrabanus’s virtues.

## CHAPTER IX

### Death and Age, Burial and Epitaph, Translation, Eulogies, and Commemoration
38. “In the year 856,” as we read in the *Annals of Fulda*, “in the month of February, on the fourth day of the month, Rabanus, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, died, having held the episcopate for nine years, one month, and four days. Karl succeeded him, more by the will of the king and his advisers than by the consent and election of the clergy and people.” Exactly the same words are found in the manuscript *Franco-Saxon Annals*. Hermannus places Rabanus’s death in the same year and on the same day, but assigns him only nine full years of rule. We can explain this difficulty in two ways. The first is to say that the annalists mentioned above used the old reckoning in designating the year in which Rabanus died. For he died on 4 February, and according to the old reckoning this day could be assigned to the end of the year 856, or according to the new reckoning to the beginning of the following year.

But three facts altogether oppose explaining the Fulda and Saxon annals in this manner. First, they followed the new reckoning in assigning the death of Charlemagne, which occurred on 28 January, to the year 814 according to the new method of counting, rather than to 813 according to the old. Second, those same annals record Rabanus’s death at the beginning of the year 856 and consequently the death of Hatto, abbot of Fulda, on 12 April; then, in the following August, they record King Louis’s expedition against the Dalmatians in that same year [Col. 0030A]—whereas they would have assigned it to the year 857 if, according to the old reckoning, they had moved the month of February, in which Rabanus died, back to the end of the year 856. Moreover, even in this way the number of years, one month, and four days attributed to Archbishop Rabanus would not be accurate, but there would be seven, eight, or nine months in addition to the nine years.

A different explanation of this passage, obscurely suggested by Serarius, must therefore be adopted: namely, that the Fulda and Saxon annals defined Rabanus’s first year of episcopacy as the year 847, although his ordination took place in June, and counted that year as a full year for Rabanus; while they began the second year—and the same must be said of the years that followed—in 848. In this way there are found nine years, one month, and four days of Rabanus’s episcopate up to 4 February 856, the time at which those annals place his death.

“But the most blessed archbishop died,” says Trithemius, “at Vinicella (Winfel), a village of his residence on the banks of the Rhine; and his sacred body, as he had commanded while alive, was brought back to Mainz.” That he reached an advanced age is clear from a letter to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, published by Sirmond, in which Rabanus excuses himself from a more extensive refutation of Gottschalk because, as he says, the weakness of his body and the infirmity of old age did not permit it. I therefore believe that he reached nearly seventy years of age—Trithemius gives sixty-eight.

39. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Alban, “in the chapel of Saints Martin and Boniface,” as we read in the brief notice of him that appears after the books *On the Universe* in our manuscript codex no. 270, in these words:

“Rabanus Maurus, born and reborn at Mainz, and a monk at Fulda from childhood, then enclosed in a cell, was finally raised to the archbishopric. His suitable works are found throughout the page of both Testaments, and before the southern gate of the aforesaid city, at Saint Alban’s, the memorial of his tomb is displayed in the chapel of the holy archbishops Martin and Boniface.”

From this monument, copied in our codex four hundred years ago, we learn that Rabanus was born at Mainz, as I said above. Consequently, some have incorrectly separated the third and fourth verses of his epitaph, which he himself composed and which in our codex is preceded by the following title:

**Epitaph of Saint Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of the see of Mainz, buried at Saint Alban’s**

Honest reader, if you wish to know my life,  
You can learn it thus from my mortal time.

In this city indeed I was born—“in this city” is absent from the manuscript—and reborn in the sacred font;  
After this, at Fulda, I learned sacred doctrine.

Having become a monk, I followed the commands of my elders.  
The holy Rule was the standard of my life.

But although I did not always hold it carefully and firmly,  
My cell nevertheless was a pleasant dwelling for me.

But when many years of time had now passed,  
Men gathered together to change the fate of the place.

They dragged me, weak, from my home and brought me to the king,  
Asking me to undertake the office of bishop.

In which there was found neither merit of life nor learning,  
Nor was the shepherd’s work rightly pleasing.  
[Manuscript: *urbe*, “city,” instead of *jure*, “rightly.”]

My spirit was ready, but my weak body delayed;  
I did what I could, and what God had granted.

[Col. 0031A] Now, from the tomb, as I help you, beloved brother,  
Commend me to Christ in your prayers to the Lord,

That the grace of the eternal Judge may save me forever,  
Looking not to merit, but to the work of mercy.

Rabanus is my name; for me the reading  
Of the divine law was always sweet everywhere.

To him, almighty God, grant the heavenly kingdoms,  
And true rest forever in the citadel of heaven.

40. His “sacred body,” according to Trithemius, “remained for 659 years buried in the aforesaid monastery of the holy martyr Alban, in a sarcophagus raised beside the wall of the choir. From the beginning there was also a great gathering of people at his tomb, and many miracles are reported to have occurred there. In the course of time, however, this entirely ceased, and his chapel remained for a long time without honor. Therefore, by the providence of God, who governs all things, for the glory of his name and the perpetual honor of his servant, he ordained and willed that his most holy body should be transferred from Mainz to Saxony in the present year in which we wrote this, namely, 1515 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the third Roman indiction. We have described in a separate treatise how, by whom, when, and for what purpose this translation was carried out.”

That work of Trithemius is no longer extant. In the dedicatory letter prefixed to the *Life of Rabanus*, he attributes the translation to Albert, archbishop of Mainz, addressing him as follows:

“Rabanus, despised at Mainz and almost buried in perpetual oblivion, you raised from the earth in the name of the Just One with the utmost veneration. For this reason the almighty Lord will also exalt your soul with his saints in the heavenly homeland.”

Trithemius speaks more distinctly of the same translation in his book on the *Life of Saint Maximus, Archbishop of Mainz*, in these words:

“When Albert, in the first year of his archiepiscopate at Mainz and the second at Magdeburg, was traveling about Mainz out of love for God and reverence for the saints, he devoutly entered the basilica of the martyr Saint Alban. Seeing there the sacred bodies of the ten bishops mentioned above neglected and without honor, he used an authority no less apostolic than ordinary, and removed from that place the entire body of Saint Rabanus, formerly archbishop, and half of the body of Saint Maximus, with the permission of the canons. Transferring them to Saxony, he placed them in the basilica of Saint Maurice at the town of Halle with the solemn office of a procession, in the year 1515 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the third Roman indiction.” [Col. 0031D]

41. From this it is clear how great an honor was accorded him after his death, since while he was still alive some called him holy or most holy. Among them was Humbert, bishop of Würzburg, in his letter prefixed to the commentary on Judges:

Hail, holy father, rightly blessed throughout the world.  
You are our glory, holy father, rightly so.

Ermanricus likewise, in his book on the *Life of Saint Sol*, speaking of the monastery of Fulda, says that there “by God’s providence the most holy and most accomplished in every art, Abbot Rabanus, shines clearly.”

Amulo, bishop of Lyon, in a letter to Gottschalk, calls him “a good and learned man and a catholic bishop”; Hincmar, in his treatise against the same Gottschalk, calls him “Rabanus, the venerable archbishop, a father zealous in holy religion and a catholic writer.”
