Frodoardus, canon of Reims, calls him “blessed Rabanus” in Book II, chapter 21, of his *History of Reims*. Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, calls him “thoroughly learned in secular knowledge, catholic in faith, and fully instructed in spiritual knowledge” in his sermon on the praise of the holy cross.

William, abbot of the Roman monastery of Saint Paul, mentions him in the *Calendar of Holy Monks*, which he composed in 1372, in these words: “The day before the Nones of February: Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz.”

Finally, in our codex no. 170, copied by hand about five hundred years ago, the *Epitaph of Saint Rabanus* given above is recorded. From all this it is clear that among the ancients Rabanus was regarded as a saint, and that Trithemius was mistaken in placing his death on 27 October. I have preferred to call him blessed rather than saint until the Church supplies more authoritative confirmation, since he is honored with no festal cult in the church of Mainz, as Browerus testifies in his notes on the poems.

Baronius calls him “the shining star of Germany, the summit of theologians”; Bellarmine calls him “equally learned and devout.” I pass over the other praises of other writers.

## CHAPTER X

**Judgment concerning his writings and teaching**

42. It remains to discuss Rabanus’s writings. Three questions must be asked about them: first, which are genuine and which spurious or by other authors; second, which remain unpublished; third, at what time each work was written.

43. Of the works of Rabanus that have been published, only the following are spurious: namely, the three books *On Questions of the Penitential Canons*, which in the printed editions are said to have been written to Heribald; the following three books likewise entitled *On Virtues and Vices*; the *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*; and the *Book on the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, published under his name at Cologne in 1551.

The first and second works are by Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, as the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius correctly observed in the preface to Rabanus’s letter to Heribald. Halitgarius composed five penitential books at the request of Ebbo, archbishop of Reims; they were published by Heinrich Canisius in volume V of the *Ancient Readings*. For Rabanus’s first book *On Questions of the Canons* is Halitgarius’s fifth book; the second is his third; the third is his fourth. Rabanus’s first book *On Vices* is Halitgarius’s first; the second is also Halitgarius’s second; whose the third, attributed to Rabanus, may be, is uncertain.

The *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict* is by Smaragdus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael on the Meuse in the diocese of Verdun, as is clear both from Sigebert’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 118, and from many parchment books that I have seen.

Finally, the book *On the Eucharist* is by Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie.

44. To distinguish easily which of Rabanus’s works have not yet been published in print, it is worth examining what is missing from the works mentioned by Rudolfus in the collection of Pamele; then what, among the works contained in the printed collection, Rudolfus omitted; and finally what further works are still wanting besides those listed by Rudolfus and those found in the collection of Rabanus’s works.

45. Of the works listed by Rudolfus, the following are missing from Pamele’s collection: the unpublished *Commentaries on the Books of Judith and Esther*, copied for us by the hand of Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius; the letter *On Chorepiscopi* to Drogo, bishop of Metz, published through the care of Stephanus Baluzius in the third edition of Petrus de Marca’s books *On the Concord of the Empire*, together with the *Book on the Reverence of Sons toward Fathers and of Subjects toward Kings*, addressed to Emperor Louis, which book Rudolfus calls a *Collectarium*; the *Letter to Notingus, Bishop of Verona, on God’s Foreknowledge and Predestination*; the *Book to Emperor Louis on the Offering of Children according to the Rule of Saint Benedict*; the *Letter of Consolation* to the same; and the *Dialogue on Computation*, recently published in the *Baluzián Miscellanies*.

Of these, the letter to Notingus was published by Sirmond; the book *On the Offering of Children* exists in manuscript in the library of Melk.

46. Conversely, the following works are found in that collection in addition to those listed by Rudolfus: the *Book on Grammar*; the work *On the Universe*; the *Exposition of the Canticles Sung during the Week at Matins*; *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*; the *Book to Thiotmar on the Sacred Orders*; three books to Reginald, or Regimbald, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*; three books to Abbot Bonosus; the *Letter to Humbert, Bishop of Würzburg, on the Degree of Kinship within Which Marriage Is Lawful*; the *Book on the Soul and Virtues* to King Lothair; the *Little Book on the Life of Antichrist*; the *Martyrology*; the *Poems*; the *Glosses*; and *On the Discovery of Languages*. All of these appear to be genuine works of Rabanus. Concerning Rabanus’s German glosses, see volume II of the Imperial Library.

47. Certain letters published by Jacob Sirmond at Paris in 1647 are missing both from Rudolfus’s index and from the aforesaid collection: namely, the *Letter to Hincmar, Bishop of Reims*; another to Count Heberard; Rabanus’s synodal letter, already published in the councils; and the *Letter to Notingus, Bishop of Verona, against Gottschalk*.

Of these, the letters to Notingus and Heberard were reprinted in volume III of Ferdinand Ughelli’s *Sacred Italy*, although he had not seen Sirmond’s edition.

Finally, two important letters are missing from Rudolfus’s index and from Pamele’s collection: one to Egilo, or Eigil, abbot of Prüm, which is believed to have been lost; the other to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, which was brought to light by Petrus Stevartius from a Weingarten codex and recently reprinted by Stephanus Baluzius after Regino’s collection of canons.

There are also two letters to Regimbald, chorepiscopus of Mainz, concerning certain small questions of penance: one published by the same distinguished man in the *Appendix to the Ancient Acts concerning the Frankish Kings’ Capitularies*, order VIII; the other in volume VIII of Labbe’s edition of the councils.

I would not dare pronounce on the remaining minor works attributed to Rabanus by Trithemius, whether they are by Rabanus or not.

To all these Browerus adds an epitaph of Emperor Lothair composed by Rabanus, which he records in Book VIII of the *Trier Annals*.

In addition, some attribute to Rabanus a prophecy concerning the kings of the Franks, which others ascribe to Saint Augustine. Among them is Jacobus Alexander Tenneurius, in the final chapter of *Truth Vindicated*. If we believe this prophecy, “as long as the kings of the Franks endure, who are to hold the Roman Empire, Roman dignity will not wholly perish.” By what authority it is attributed to Rabanus is not yet known to me. Still less should this kind of oracle be attributed to Saint Augustine, although it is included in the appendix to his works in volume IX.

48. Finally, the learned Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius attributes to Rabanus a book, or letter, *Against the Jews*, which he himself printed at Dijon in 1656 together with Alcuin’s *Confession*. But that this letter is not by Rabanus but by Amulo, bishop of Lyon, is explicitly proved by a more recent writer in an appendix to Joannes Dallaeus’s dissertation *On the Author of the Aforesaid Confession*.

This anonymous writer’s arguments are drawn first from the persistent silence of all those who catalogued Rabanus’s works; then from the fact that the author of the letter says that he was already a bishop in the year “846 from the coming of the Lord,” one year before Rabanus’s episcopate; and finally from the fact that he reports having established certain harsher measures against the Jews at an earlier time—something that cannot in any way fit Rabanus, who enacted no decree against the Jews.

Moreover, the author of the letter seems clearly to indicate that, when writing against the Jews, he was following the footsteps of his predecessor, who likewise had written and done much against the Jews. But Otgar, Rabanus’s predecessor, did nothing of this kind in the diocese of Mainz.

On these arguments the author of the appendix rejects the letter as Rabanus’s and insists that it should be restored to Amulo, bishop of Lyon, as its proper parent. For Amulo was ordained bishop in 841 and soon made harsher statutes against the Jews. From Agobard we learn that the Jews in the diocese of Lyon had behaved with unrestrained license; Agobard, Amulo’s predecessor, wrote against those same Jews, and the author of the disputed letter transfers much from his writings into his own.

But—and this is the argument he considers preferable to all conjectures—from Frodoardus, priest of Reims, Book III, chapter 21 of the *History*, he concludes that Amulo wrote an encyclical letter against the Jews. There Hincmar is said to have written “to Amulo of Lyon concerning the dispute he had had with the king and the chief men of the kingdom, and concerning the condition of the Jews in this kingdom.”

But, if I understand correctly, these words say nothing about an encyclical letter by Amulo, although the passage does serve to prove what was stated immediately beforehand: namely, that Amulo enacted statutes against the Jews.

The final argument of the same author should therefore be preferred, drawn from Joannes Trithemius’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Trithemius says that he had read “a distinguished work by Hamulus, bishop of Lyon, to Charles against the Jews,” whose beginning is formed by the words “The detestable [things] of the Jews,” and so forth. This is precisely the beginning of Chiffletius’s letter.

Trithemius therefore saw an ancient codex presenting this letter under Amulo’s name; Chiffletius may have seen another presenting it under Rabanus’s name. But the evidence given above supports the side of Joannes Trithemius.

49. The chronological order in which Rabanus’s individual works appear to have been composed by their author should be set out as follows.

In the thirtieth year of his life he completed the two books *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, which he had begun at the request of his teacher Alcuin. He first dedicated them, through Alcuin, to Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, at whose monastery he had devoted himself to letters; in Alcuin’s person he played with a dedicatory poem. Later he dedicated the same books to Emperor Louis, and then to Pope Gregory IV, although they were delivered not to him but to his successor Sergius in 844 by Ascrichus and Ruodpertus, monks of Fulda. Afterwards he dedicated them to Heberard, count of Italy, who had requested the books from Ascrichus and Ruodpertus as they returned from Rome, as is clear from Rabanus’s letter to him; and finally to the monks of the monastery of Saint-Denis in the Parisian region.

That Alcuin was the person who encouraged Rabanus to write these books appears from Alcuin’s Letter 55, addressed to “Maurus, blessed child of Saint Benedict”—Maurus being Rabanus’s other name, although the printed editions incorrectly read “Benedict.” It contains these words: “The little book which, at my request, you promised to write—I ask you to make your promise firm and to fulfill my joy”; and at the end: “May you prosper happily with your children.”

From this letter I had inferred that Alcuin had lived beyond the year 804, but afterward I corrected the statement in the appendix to the preceding volume, where I had made the assertion in Alcuin’s eulogy.

In Alcuin’s person Rabanus sang Saint Martin the dedicatory poem of these books, in which he expresses his age in the following verses:

But when he had completed six lustra, now attempting to write,  
He composed this book with skill to the praise of Christ.

This date agrees with approximately the year 806, since Rabanus received the diaconate in the year 801, at the age of twenty-five.

After some years he dedicated the same work to Emperor Louis, placing the emperor’s image at the beginning. I infer that this was done some time after the first publication of the work from Rabanus’s words: “For the little book that long ago I composed in prose and verse in honor of the holy Cross, I now, as a suppliant, offer to your serenity.”

Later, at the request, I believe, of Abbot Hilduin, to whom he dedicated his *Commentaries on the Kings*, he also sent the same books to the monks of Saint-Denis and commended them with this poem, which does not appear in the printed editions. It is preceded by the following inscription:

“To the most beloved brothers in Christ established in the monastery of Saint Denis the martyr, Rabanus, the least of the servants of God, wishes eternal salvation in the Lord.”

I have decided to send a gift to the holy martyrs,  
Which long ago I published in ancient verse.

For the praise of Christ, in prose and verse,  
I completed the book with mind and hand together.

Afterward I was pleased to offer it to Emperor Louis,  
And then I wished to send it to the apostolic see,

So that the Roman and apostolic teaching might rightly approve its words and meaning.

And because Saint Denis was once sent from there here  
With his companions, I had given the work to him.

Holy brothers, I ask that you gladly accept it;  
For the author, the least of men, pour forth prayers, I beg.

May almighty God, the gracious creator of all things,  
In his goodness grant forgiveness for his servant’s sin.

May he protect him unharmed and preserve him whole forever,  
[Col. 0036B] So that with a good end he may ascend from here to heaven’s heights.

May Christ save you; may Christ preserve you everywhere.  
As I wish, fare well always and forever.

In the year 819 Rabanus, already a priest, offered the books *On the Instruction of Clerics* to Haistulf, archbishop of Mainz, in the year when the church of Fulda was dedicated, as is clear from the poem prefixed to those books and published among Rabanus’s poems.

Having become abbot in 822, he dedicated the *Commentaries on Matthew* and certain *Homilies* to the same Haistulf, who died in 826.

Around the year 830 he sent the *Exposition of the Octateuch* to Freculf, bishop of Lisieux in Gaul, who had obtained it from him through letters and petitions.

In 834 he wrote to Emperor Louis a *Letter of Consolation* after the misfortune that had befallen him through his sons. Later he wrote the *Collectarium* from the sayings of the divine books, concerning the reverence of sons toward fathers and of subjects toward kings. I have said that this was recently published by the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius.

At nearly the same time he expounded the *Book of Joshua* “at the request of Frideric, bishop of Utrecht on the Rhine,” who was killed in 834. He prefaced it with a dedicatory letter, a fragment of which Henschenius quoted after receiving it from the learned Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, a priest of the Society of Jesus. Our Acnerius received it from him, together with the *Commentary*, divided into three books, which is absent from the printed editions.

A little later, at the request of Humbert, bishop of Würzburg, he explained the *Books of Judges and Ruth*. Then, at the request of Abbot Hilduin, he explained the *Books of Kings*. He presented this exposition to Emperor Louis at Fulda; not long afterward he sent the commentaries on the *Books of Chronicles* to King Louis.

Around the year 836 he dedicated to the Empress Judith, after she had “conquered her enemies to no small extent,” his work on the *Books of Judith and Esther*. Its preface had not yet been published in print; through the kindness of the same learned man, Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, we received it and reproduce it here from the Benignian and Fontanian codices. [See this preface in volume III of our edition of the works of Rabanus Maurus.]

Afterward, before the year 840, he dedicated the exposition of the *Books of Maccabees* to Gerold, archdeacon of the palace of Emperor Louis; then the *Exposition of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus* to Otgar, bishop of Mainz; and he wrote the *Letter to Notingus, Bishop of Verona*, before the death of Emperor Louis.

After the year 840, following the death of Emperor Louis, he offered the *Books on Jeremiah* to Emperor Lothair. Hartmotus, dean of Saint Gall, arranged for them to be copied, according to Ratpert in chapter 9.

At the beginning of 842 he sent the *Collectarium on the Epistles of Paul* to Lupus, afterward abbot of Ferrières, who had recently returned to Gaul from the school of Fulda, as follows from the foregoing. Around the same time he dedicated the *Commentaries on Ezekiel* to Emperor Lothair, and the *Penitential Book* to Archbishop Otgar. In chapter 15 of the latter he mentions the battle of Fontenay, fought between the sons of Emperor Louis in 841.

The *Letter on Chorepiscopi* to Drogo, bishop of Metz, must also be assigned to this period, as must the letter to Regimbald, chorepiscopus of Mainz, concerning certain small questions of penance.

At the same time he explained the *Book of the Prophet Daniel* at the request of friends and later dedicated this work to Louis, king of Germany. To the same king he also dedicated the *Exposition of the Canticles Read throughout the Week at Matins*.

Around the year 844, during the period when he was free from the administration of the abbacy, he composed the twenty-two books *On the Universe* for Hemmo, bishop of Halberstadt. He likewise sent this work, together with the letter still prefixed to it, to King Louis at his request.

[Col. 0037C] In the year 847 the archbishop wrote the *Letter to Count Heberard against Gottschalk*, which in Ughelli’s edition is dated 22 April.

Also in the same year 847 he presented the canons of the Council of Mainz to King Louis, together with a letter.

In the following year, after the synod held against Gottschalk, he wrote a letter about him to Hincmar, bishop of Reims, to whom he sent Gottschalk. Several years later he sent Hincmar another letter concerning the same man, published in print by Sirmond.

I think that Rabanus’s letter to Regimbald, chorepiscopus, concerning penitential acts should also be assigned to this year, in which King Louis is said to have held a public assembly at Mainz according to the *Annals of Fulda*. It was published in volume VIII of the new edition of the councils. In it Rabanus excuses the delay in his reply on the grounds that he had been occupied with receiving King Louis.

Finally, after the year 853 he wrote the *Letter to Egilo, abbot of Prüm*. This letter is mentioned in a letter that he subsequently sent to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre.

We owe our knowledge of the time when both letters were written to the diligence of the most learned Stephanus Baluzius, who published them in a second edition with a careful preface on the matter. There he observed that Egilo, or Eigil, to whom the first of these two letters was written as abbot of Prüm, assumed that dignity in 853, as I shall also demonstrate below in his eulogy.

In the later letter to Heribald—which is cited by Regino, Ivo, and Gratian in their collections of canons under the title “Rabanus’s letter”—a letter to Egilo the abbot is mentioned. Therefore the letter to Heribald, entitled *Penitential Book* by Stevartius, was written some time after the letter to Eigil and was perhaps the last of Rabanus’s works that we possess.

Adam of Bremen, a canon, mentions in chapter 22 of his *Ecclesiastical History* a chapter of Rabanus concerning the ambiguous reputation of Ebbo. This chapter is found at the end of the letter to Heribald.

These are the observations I have been able to make concerning Rabanus’s writings. I leave the others to the diligence of other scholars.

50. It remains for us to examine at this point certain matters in Rabanus’s writings that may seem worthy of notice to some.

One concerns the letter, or penitential book, to Heribald, in which he seems somewhat obscurely to say that the Eucharist is subject to evacuation (*secessus*), and denies that the sacrament contains the same body of Christ that was born of the Virgin Mary. He explicitly asserted the latter in his letter to Abbot Egilo.

Whatever the exact meaning of both passages may be, learned men who have treated of the Eucharist insist that Rabanus was free from every error in this matter.

51. There is another passage in Rabanus, in Book IV of *On the Universe*, chapter 10, which may perhaps likewise be criticized. He says:

“We believe that no catechumen, even if he has died in good works, possesses eternal life, except through martyrdom, where the whole sacrament of baptism is fulfilled.”

Alcuin’s *Confession* attributed to Chiffletius holds the same opinion. I do not know whether Rabanus received this doctrine from that teacher.

Augustine opposes it in his *Questions on Leviticus*, chapter 84, where he proves “that invisible sanctification has been present and beneficial to some without visible sacraments,” using the example of Cornelius and others.

In Book IV of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, after discussing the matter at length, he concludes in chapter 22:

“Baptism is then fulfilled invisibly when the mystery of baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by an exigency of necessity.”

Ambrose agrees in his funeral sermon on the death of the younger Valentinian, where he asserts without hesitation that although Valentinian died before receiving baptism, he received the grace that he had asked for and desired. He writes of him splendidly in these words:

“He who possessed your spirit—how did he not receive your grace? Or if it is troubling that the mysteries were not celebrated solemnly, then let martyrs who were catechumens not be crowned either; for they are not crowned if they are not initiated. But if they are washed in their own blood, then his devotion and his will also wash him.”

Thus, according to Ambrose and Augustine, the will to receive baptism benefits not only catechumens who suffer martyrdom, but also those who sincerely and fervently asked for and desired the grace of this sacrament and were prevented from receiving it not through negligence but through divine dispensation.

Saint Bernard also defended this position forcefully and explicitly in Letter 77, or his treatise to Hugh of Saint-Victor, adducing the testimonies of Augustine and Ambrose against someone who held the contrary view.

Yet I find the opposite in Augustine himself, in Sermon 20 *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 6. Considering why, among two catechumens—one good and one wicked—“the one was led by God’s governance to be baptized, whereas the other, although he had lived well as a catechumen, died by a sudden fall and did not reach baptism,” he gives only this answer:

“Seek merits: you will find nothing but punishment. Seek grace: O the depth of riches!”

From this it appears that Augustine understood the passage to mean that the good catechumen who did not attain the grace of baptism was assigned to punishment, and that good conduct did not profit him for salvation.

This may be what Rabanus and Alcuin taught, although elsewhere, together with Ambrose and Augustine, they admitted that good catechumens who had desired the grace of baptism with great and perfect charity were not harmed by being taken away before receiving the mysteries; but not if their charity was lukewarm, even though they were endowed with good works.

Nevertheless, the Council of Braga, in canon 17, deprives all catechumens who die without baptism’s redemption of sacred offering and the intercessions of the Church.

52. Finally, some blame Rabanus for condemning Gottschalk and his doctrine. Others, on the contrary, approve Rabanus’s action in this matter.

It is clear that he held the correct view concerning predestination from the letters mentioned above. And even if we concede that Gottschalk’s opinion was likewise correct, Rabanus nevertheless rightly restrained him: first, because he rashly usurped the office of preaching in Rabanus’s province; and second, because he was believed to be using the word “predestination” with excessive obstinacy in an unfavorable sense, to the offense of the people. The Fathers use this word more rarely in that sense.

[Col. 0039]

# B. THE LIFE OF RABANUS MAURUS, BY RUDOLFUS, HIS DISCIPLE AND A SCHOLAR

*(In Mabillon, Annals of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, fourth century, part II.)*

## Preliminary Observations

Rudolfus—or Ruodolfus, or Rodulfus—a monk of Fulda and a disciple of Rabanus, wrote the book on the deeds of Rabanus, or Hrabanus, otherwise called Maurus, first a monk, then abbot of Fulda, and finally archbishop of Mainz. He was the same man who committed to writing the *Life of Saint Lioba*, abbess of Bischofsheim, published in the second part of the third century, where we said more about Rudolfus.

It is uncertain whether Hruodolfus the scholastic and chancellor, who in the first year of Emperor Louis wrote several deeds of donation for his monastery during the abbacy of Ratgar, as found in Pistorius on page 524, is the same as this Rudolfus, or whether he was Rudolfus the subdeacon, who later wrote other documents in the eighth year of the same emperor, on page 530, and in the tenth year, on pages 534–535.

Since Rudolfus, the author of this *Life*, was certainly a disciple of Rabanus, I do not think that during the abbacy of Ratgar, when Rabanus was teaching letters at Fulda, Rudolfus had already been called both chancellor and scholastic. It is more likely that he was the same Rudolfus the subdeacon who, in the eighth year of Louis, drew up a charter in place of the priest Althuringus and was therefore not yet chancellor.

He later became a priest and director of the schools after Rabanus, whom he calls his own teacher in the prologues to the present *Life* and to the *Life of Saint Lioba*. He undertook Lioba’s life at the command, as he himself says, of “my revered father and teacher, Rabanus.”

King Louis of Germany calls him his orator, confessor, and director of the schools of Fulda in a charter of donation, a fragment of which Browerus records in chapter 14 of Book III of the *Antiquities of Fulda*.

Ermenricus the levite, a monk of Ellwangen, dedicates the *Life of Saint Sol* to “my lord Ruodolfus, most celebrated in every art, my teacher,” from whom, he acknowledges, he tasted goodness and learning in his youthful years.

Whether Rudolfus completed the whole of Rabanus’s *Life* is uncertain, for it has nowhere appeared in its entirety. It is defective in its enumeration of Rabanus’s works, and no mention is made of his archiepiscopal administration—whether in Serarius’s *History of Mainz*, in Colvenerius at the beginning of Rabanus’s works, in Browerus’s *Antiquities of Fulda* [Col. 0040B], or in Bollandus’s February volume.

## 2.

If John Trithemius had read this work of Rudolf’s, he did not count it among the proper biographies. In the prologue to his Life of Rabanus—which he arranged in three books at the urging of Albert, archbishop of Mainz, in 1515—he writes:

> “Nor is it surprising if I have passed over many of his deeds in silence, since before me I could find no established, reliable, and adequate writer on this very subject; rather, I am compelled to be the first author without a predecessor.”

And below:

> “I confess that many historians have here and there written various tributes of praise to this most blessed and learned man in their works; yet none of them composed his Life in a continuous narrative.”

For this reason Trithemius was moved to write it, and, as I have said, divided it into three books: the first concerns Rabanus’s private life, the second his rule as abbot, and the third his episcopate. In this work Trithemius several times used the testimony of Meginfrid, a monk of Fulda in the twelfth century, from his volume *On the Times of Grace*, hitherto unpublished, in which he frequently mentions Rabanus.

Nevertheless, although Trithemius’s work on Rabanus is not to be despised, it did not seem worth the effort to reprint it, because of the many errors he committed in it—especially since the work is found at the beginning of Rabanus’s *Works* and in the Bollandist February volume, where Godefridus Henschenius illuminated the Life of Rabanus with learned commentaries. It will therefore be enough for us to have Rudolf’s little book, to which we have prefixed, in place of a commentary, a historical eulogy of Rabanus.

## 3.

Rabanus, bishop of Mainz, endowed with a holy life, is the third after Saint Boniface in the succession of the Order of Saint Benedict. From that order came almost all who held that see after Rabanus, down to the twelfth century. Paulus Langius counted thirteen of them, on the basis of his *Chronicle of Citz*. It is therefore not surprising that there were so many monasteries of the Benedictine family in those regions, so that in Trithemius’s time “in the province of Mainz alone” there remained “one hundred and twenty-four abbeys of our order, besides those which have been separated from the order, whose number exceeds ten,” as Trithemius himself testifies in Book I, chapter 2, of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*.

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE

## 1.

Ecclesiastical writers wisely and usefully established the practice of handing down to posterity, through the disclosure afforded by writing, the lives and deeds of righteous men who lived according to the divine commandments. The faithful rightly praise them with great commendation because they did not maliciously pass over these matters in silence; rather, filled with charity, which desires to benefit everyone, and supported by the truth of faith, they set them forth as examples for all who wished to imitate a rightly ordered life.

For if they had not done so, we could in no way have known what the holy patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles, and the other holy martyrs and confessors of Christ had done or taught, or by what signs and virtues they had shone before or after their deaths, unless we learned these things from what had been believed and understood through their writings. They did not publish such accounts in order to seek their own praise, but so that, through examples of this kind, they might stir the minds of all people to correct the depraved habits produced by human presumption and to praise the power of the divine majesty.

Therefore, following their praiseworthy practice according to my ability, I strive to write, insofar as I can, of the virtues and miracles that God has deigned to perform through his saints in recent times. Their sacred ashes, brought into our region, daily serve the faithful as a source of salvation. I believe that I labor neither in vain nor without benefit, both for myself and for many others: for myself, because by God’s grace I trust that I shall receive the reward of my labor together with those whom I have imitated, as they sweat over similar work for the glory of God; and for others, because, once these events are known, they embrace the venerable feasts of the saints with greater faithfulness and, kindled by a greater devotion of mind, rise more joyfully to praise their Creator.

## 2.

In the time of the emperor Louis, who held the empire of the Franks for twenty-seven years after his father, the emperor Charlemagne,

[Note: Not quite complete: nearly eight months are lacking. He succeeded his father, who died on 28 January 814, and ceased to live in the year 840, on 21 May. — BOLL.]

the relics of many saints were brought from the city of Rome into Francia. Some were brought by those who, at the command of their lords, had gone to Rome for that purpose; others were brought by clergy of the Holy Apostolic See and by citizens of the city of Rome. Whether along the roads by which they were carried or in the places where they were received and deposited, the saints’ merit before God was revealed by many great signs of miracles.

It is established, for example, that the relics of Saint Sebastian the martyr, carried from Rome and reverently deposited by Abbot Hilduin in the church of Saint Medard the Confessor at Augusta Suessionum

[Al.: Suessorum]

in the city of Gaul, flourished with such great and unheard-of miracles, surpassing all former generations, that their revelation would exceed belief

[Note: These are almost the words of Einhard. — MAB.]

unless it were certain to all who faithfully believe that God and our Lord Jesus Christ—who is glorious in his saints, wondrous in his majesties, and performs miracles—can accomplish without difficulty everything whatever he wills in heaven and on earth.

The bones also of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter,

[Note: They are celebrated on 2 June. See Einhard’s *History of the Translation of the Relics of Marcellinus and Peter*. Rabanus’s poem on the same translation is extant in volume VI of his *Works*; it is hymn 24. — BOLL.]

of Protus and Hyacinth,

[Note: Einhard discusses the relics of these saints, obtained from Rome and sent to him, in Book IV of the cited *History of the Translation of the Relics of Saints Peter and Marcellinus*. — ID.]

together with the relics of Saint Hermes, shine daily with no lesser glory of miracles in the various healings of the sick. These relics too were transferred from Rome and brought to Abbot Einhard,

[Note: Browerus incorrectly says “by Einhard the abbot.” The relics of Saints Marcellinus and Peter were brought to him from Rome by Ratleius, his notary; the others were brought by another monk of his and by a certain Sabbatinus, a companion of Deusdona, a deacon of the Roman Church, through whose efforts they had been obtained. — ID.]

and are venerated by the faithful with fitting celebration beside the German river Main, in a village formerly called Mullinheim and now called Saligunstat.

[Note: That is, “blessed city.” Trithemius should therefore be corrected: in his abridgment *On the Origin of the Frankish People*, drawn from the fabulous books of Hunibald, he states that this city was founded under Clodius Crinitus by Salagastus, a wise man and philosopher of the Franks and writer of the Salic laws. He adds that Salagastus died in this city, which he himself had named, was burned, and was placed in an urn in the sixteenth year of Clodius. — ID.]

I omit here speaking of their translation and of the miracles that God worked through them, because these matters have been carefully committed to memory.

## 3.

But concerning the bones of the blessed martyr Alexander and of the other saints whose names will be given in their proper places, I believe that it ought to be written and committed to memory how and by whom they were translated, and to what places; and by what signs and virtues they flourished, whether on the journey during which they were carried or in the places where they were deposited. Thus, once an account has been given of their translation and miracles according to the truth of what occurred, these writings may make known the places where they ought to be found for veneration by the faithful.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

## 4.

In that part of Germany inhabited by the Franks who are called Eastern Franks there is a place named Fulda after a nearby river,

[Note: Here the river, after flowing through Buchonia and Hesse, joins the Weser. — ID.]

situated in a great forest which in modern times is called by the inhabitants of those regions Bochonia.

[Note: Also Buchonia, named from the beech trees, which are called *buchen* by the Germans. Thus Candidus, the disciple of the blessed Rabanus, in the Life of Abbot Eigil:

> “Carried from his native shores,  
> He is led into a forest called  
> Buchonia, from the name of the beech.”

— ID.]

Saint Boniface the martyr, sent into Germany as legate by the Apostolic See and ordained bishop of the church of Mainz, obtained this place from Carloman, king of the Franks,

[Note: In the year of Christ 741, after the death of his father Charles Martel, Eastern Francia, together with Thuringia and Swabia, or Alamannia, fell to him, while Burgundy, Provence, and Neustria were left to his brother Pippin. In 747 he embraced the monastic life and ended his life in holiness. — BOLL.]

because it was secluded and very far removed from the crowds of the people. With the authority of Zacharias,

[Note: He governed the Church from 6 December 741 until 15 March 752, the day on which he is commemorated. — ID.]

the supreme pontiff of the Holy Apostolic See, Boniface established there a monastery of monks in the tenth year before his passion, which was the seven-hundred forty-fourth year from the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Note: Carloman was king in power, but not in title. His brother Pippin obtained the royal title in 752, after Childeric, the last of the Merovingians, had been confined to a monastery by the authority of Pope Saint Zacharias. — ID.]

## 5.

The fifth abbot to govern this monastery after the blessed Boniface was Rabanus, my teacher, a very devout man and especially learned in the divine Scriptures. His entire study was devoted to meditation on the law of the Lord and to teaching the truth, and he showed the greatest concern for monastic discipline and the progress of his disciples.

His mind was always intent on arranging whatever pertained to divine worship. Whenever he was permitted to be free from worldly cares—which, insofar as possible, he avoided with all his strength—he either instructed others in sacred letters or nourished himself by reading or dictating the divine Scriptures.

Amid these and his other activities, through which in prayer, vigils, abstinence, and the other marks of virtue he offered himself as a model to his subjects, he constructed the entire monastery with open buildings and suitable dwellings

[Note: See Browerus, *Antiquities of Fulda*, especially Books I, chapters 3 and 4, where he sets forth the beginnings of the monastery’s foundation and construction. — ID.]

[Perhaps: “with suitable buildings”]

and adorned the church with a beautiful variety of different metals and precious vestments. In the cells of the brothers entrusted to him and in many other places belonging to him, where previously there had been none, he built churches with the permission of his bishop. After gathering relics of saints from every source, he had these churches consecrated in their names and honor.

## 6.

There were also estates belonging to the monastery in various provinces. Some had been given by kings, others bestowed by faithful persons out of love for God and veneration of the holy martyr Boniface. He placed some of these under the administration of stewards, while others—especially those in which there were churches—he entrusted to priests

[Note: These priests were monks, whom they already called provosts; see below, no. 13. From this arose the institution of provostships, as they are called. — MAB.]

to manage and organize.

One of these estates was in Italy, where Count Adumar had once given property to Saint Boniface. The man named Addo who administered it, returning from Italy, reported among other things that a certain powerful Italian named Alabingus

[Al.: Halabingus]

had sent word to the abbot that he wished to send him the bones of a certain holy martyr, provided that a suitable place for veneration of the martyr were furnished; and that he intended to grant to that place, by solemn donation, part of the inheritance he possessed in Francia, from which he had originated, so that it might serve the needs of those who would serve there.

When the abbot heard this, he rejoiced greatly in the Lord and was strongly moved by his desire for such relics. He quickly settled the matters for which the priest had come and sent him back to Italy, instructing the aforesaid Alabingus that he must act energetically in transferring the relics of that holy martyr; indeed, because of the various contingencies of events, he must hasten with all possible speed to accomplish it.

He added that he already had a suitable basilica constructed for the performance of the divine offices and everything prepared that the reception and worship of such relics required, and that there was no obstacle on his part preventing him, if he were willing, from fulfilling his promise.

## 7.

When the priest had departed to return to Italy, it happened that a certain deacon of the Roman Church named Deusdona

[Note: Concerning Deusdona and his companion Sabbatinus, Browerus writes in Book III, chapter 13, of *Antiquities of Fulda*: “From the fact that the ancients approve the skill of both men in handling and transporting relics, perhaps rejoicing in the success of their undertaking, anyone can easily understand that, although engaged in such a sacred matter, they were not acting with the best faith or with chaste motives when they approached Einhard. Nevertheless, these men, industrious in a praiseworthy way, also rendered Rabanus energetic assistance here, as Rudolf’s History clearly shows. Whoever compares it with Einhard’s Commentary will immediately feel that a greater light shines from the combined work of both.” — BOLL.]

came into Francia, apparently seeking the king’s assistance for certain personal needs, but in reality intending to give the relics of saints that he carried with him to some religious men in Francia, with whose help he might obtain some relief from his poverty.

After crossing the passes of the Alps and descending to the plains and lowlands in the territory of the Alamanni, he came to a village called Kentibruto, in the district of Turihgawe.

[Note: Browerus notes Zurichgaw and adds: “Thurihgawe, Tuigaw, or Durgow, a tract well known in Alamannia and the regions of the Swiss, between Constance and Zurich.” — ID.]

There, entering a church with the relics, he was kindly received by the priest and gave him a portion of the relics of the blessed martyr Alexander

[Note: Below, in no. 14, he is called a pope, as also in poems 109 and 117 of Rabanus. He is commemorated on 3 May. Anastasius the Librarian writes that his head was brought to Rome by Leo IV. — ID.]

to be placed beneath the altar of the church.

Once this had been done, the saint’s great merit before God began immediately to be revealed through miracles. When the people heard that the relics of saints had been brought there, they began to bring from every direction the weak, the sick, and those afflicted by various troubles, believing that through the prayers of the saints they would recover their former health.

Among them was a woman possessed by an unclean spirit. She entered the basilica, and while the priest was exorcising her according to ecclesiastical custom, the demon answered through her mouth that, if it were expelled from her, it would immediately have to enter another vessel that had been assigned to it in the same region. It identified by name a certain Othmar, whom it was to enter.

The priest, since Othmar lived not far away, immediately sent him a messenger and ordered him, after making confession, to perform penance for his sins, lest by the merit of his crimes he should become the enemy’s

[Note: Colvenerius reads *inimico*, as though the word *obnoxius* were lacking. — BOLL.]

victim. Obeying the command and fleeing with all his heart to the penance that the devil always detests, Othmar escaped the enemy’s snares. The demon, expelled that very day through the power of the holy martyr, left the woman whom it had possessed of sound mind and unharmed.

## 8.

Likewise, a certain woman came to the relics of the saint for the sake of prayer and offered two golden earrings at the altar as a gift. Her servant, who attended her, coveted them after they had been placed on the altar. While she knelt in prayer among the other women who had come, she wished in her heart that she might possess them lawfully.

While she was turning this thought over in her mind during prayer, a strange thing immediately occurred. When the others rose from prayer, she was completely unable to raise herself. Remaining bent over her knees in the posture in which she had knelt for prayer, she was gripped by a kind of stiffness.

The priest asked her the cause of the sin for which she had suffered such sudden contraction of her limbs, and what she had been thinking when she bowed down in prayer. She replied that she could see no other cause of her affliction than her desire for those earrings.

The priest said to her: “If it is the will of Saint Alexander that you possess them as you desired, rise and take them from the altar.”

At his words she immediately recovered her health and rose. She then wished to offer at the altar the cloth she had been wearing around her head, but she could not remove it from her head by any effort.

When the priest saw this, and understood from her recovery that the earrings she had desired had also been divinely granted to the girl, he gave them to her and said: “Receive the gift you desired, and know that it has been given to you freely by God’s saint, not in exchange for any temporal price.”

She gave thanks to God, glorified the merits of Saint Alexander, and returned home joyfully with her mistress.

## 9.

Later it happened that some very poor women, hastening with devout hearts to those holy relics for the sake of prayer, came to the river Turiseo.

[Note: Commonly called the Thur, from which that district was named Turgow. The river flows into the Rhine between Schaffhausen and Rheinfelden; from this Henschenius correctly infers the location of the previously mentioned Kentibruto. — MAB.]

Since they could not cross without a boat and had nothing with which to pay the fare—for they had only five loaves for their journey—the boatman insistently demanded payment from them. At last they offered him four loaves, reserving only one for themselves because of the necessity of food.

But when he still would not agree, they gave him the fifth as well, choosing rather to endure for a time the hunger of their dying bodies than to deprive their souls, which would live forever, of the fruit of holy prayer.

After receiving the fifth loaf, the wretched man ferried the women to the opposite bank. Taking the loaves and the other goods that he had extorted with similar inhumanity, and wishing to return home, he was suddenly stiffened by such rigidity of the nerves that he could not move from the spot where he stood.

Stunned and struck with fear, he began to consider how such a great misfortune had come upon him. At last, accused by his conscience and coming to his senses, he recognized the crime he had committed. Repenting of it, he desired to go for absolution to the relics of the saint, which by then were visited in religious veneration by almost all the inhabitants of that region.

Immediately, by divine mercy, he recovered the ability to walk and set out. He entered the church and placed the loaves before the altar, publicly confessing his crime. When the women received them, he regained complete health and returned home joyfully.

## 10.

Likewise, a certain man from the retinue of Count Gerald, named Perathgarius, son of Theodaldus, was traveling. When he came alongside the church in which the relics of the holy martyr had been placed and wished to pass by, the boy accompanying him urged him to turn aside for a little while to the sacred relics for the sake of prayer.

He replied that he had to hurry at that moment in order to carry out his lord’s mission, but that he would come to pray at a more suitable time.

As he spoke, the horse on which he was riding was suddenly fixed in place by an invisible power and stood motionless. Although he wore it out excessively with his spurs, he could not induce it to walk.

Therefore, confused and terrified with fear, he dismounted from the horse and fulfilled on foot what he had previously disdained to do on horseback. He proceeded to the church and, after devoutly completing his prayer before the relics of the holy martyr, formally donated to the church, for the salvation of his soul, a field belonging to him that adjoined its property. He then continued freely on the journey to which he had been sent.

## 11.

At another time it happened that a certain man from the eastern regions of Alamannia came to the aforesaid relics for the sake of prayer, accompanied by a considerable number of companions and carrying gifts to be offered in the Lord’s sanctuary.

When he had placed them on the altar, they immediately slipped off and fell to the ground. When he placed them on the altar a third time, they nevertheless fell to the ground again.

The priest, understanding from this that some hidden wickedness was present in the mind or actions of the person making the offering, told him to take his things away and return home. He warned him to be concerned for the salvation of his soul and to cleanse his conscience through sincere confession and worthy fruits of penance, so that thereafter his prayers and gifts might be pleasing to God.

## 12.

There was a certain man in the same region named Sigibaldus. One of his servants, among the many people who flocked there to pray, came to the church. He was received by his own brother, a servant of that same church, and stayed with him for several days.

When he was returning, he suddenly became speechless on the road along which he was walking. Those who were with him, recognizing what had happened, brought him to his master and explained the entire sequence of events.

The servant’s master immediately sent him back to the church. Since he was healed and recovered his former health through the merits of Christ’s holy martyr, the master handed him over to serve there permanently at the place where the relics were kept.

Many other miracles are also reported in famous accounts by those who travel to that place as having been divinely performed there. I have not wished to insert them into this work, lest an overly lengthy narrative perhaps produce weariness in its readers.

The events I have recounted I took from a certain little book brought from that place and inserted in the same order in which they had been written, although not in the same words, because they appeared to be certain. In this way, the other events reported in popular speech may be believed more truthfully and known more securely from them.

## 13.

The aforesaid deacon, continuing on the journey he had begun, came into Francia

[Note: Browerus believes that this was Deusdona’s second arrival, mentioned by Einhard at the end of the *History of the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter*. But neither the year nor the month agrees. He is said to have arrived around the middle of August, with the Kalends of September falling on a Sunday—that is, in the year 830, the third year of Pope Gregory III. Here, however, June and the year 835 are indicated. — BOLL.]

and first went to Einhard, whom I mentioned above—for he was familiar with him.

Then, after entrusting the relics of the saints under seal to be preserved there in the church of the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, he went to Mainz. At that time a certain priest from our monks, named Theotmar,

[Note: This is Theotmarus, praised again below in no. 33. Rabanus dedicated to him the book *On the Sacred Orders*, and so forth. — MAB.]

had been sent there by the abbot to Archbishop Otgar

[Note: Rabanus’s predecessor, he became archbishop around the end of 826 or the beginning of the following year, as Serarius observes in Book IV of *The Affairs of Mainz*. Rabanus dedicated to him his Commentary on *Wisdom* and *Ecclesiasticus*, as well as his *Penitential Book*. Rabanus described his praises and epitaph among his poems. — ID.]

for certain matters.

When Theotmar saw the deacon and learned that he was a Roman, he asked why he had traveled so far from his homeland. After hearing the reasons for his journey, he began to urge him to give a portion of the relics which he confessed to possess to his own abbot, knowing that he would undoubtedly be well rewarded by him for this.

The deacon accepted the adviser’s proposal. After making the promise, he dismissed the priest on the understanding that he would return to meet him, on the day then agreed between them, at the place where he had left the relics; and that, if their agreement pleased the abbot, he would receive the relics.

The priest hurried back to the monastery. First he reported the archbishop’s reply to the abbot; then he explained the agreement he had made with the deacon concerning the relics.

When the abbot heard this, he rejoiced greatly. Wishing to test the reliability of the promise without delay, he sent the priest back, together with another priest from our brothers named Artharius, carrying gifts for the deacon as had been promised.

When they arrived at his lodging and presented the gifts, they asked him to hand over the relics he had promised.

He replied: “I have decided to travel with you to the monastery and to offer your abbot not merely a portion of the relics, as I promised, but everything that I now possess from all the relics I have brought into this land, and to entrust myself along with them to his fidelity.”

At that time it was the feast of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter.

[Note: 2 June. — ID.]

Because a great multitude of people had gathered for it, and the deacon suspected some of those with whom he was staying—he feared that through their plotting, fraud, or violence he might lose the relics—it seemed best to them not to leave the place until the feast had ended and the people had returned home.

They sent word to the abbot, announcing the deacon’s intention. Meanwhile, they took care to prepare whatever seemed necessary for their journey and for transporting the sacred relics.

There was also a priest not far from them, one of our brothers, named Authadus

[Boll.: Anthadus],

the provost of the estates belonging to the monastery in those regions. He had been instructed to supply the brothers there with necessities at the appointed times.

They decided to have him summoned, so that, strengthened by fraternal counsel, they might more easily accomplish what they had begun and were striving to complete.

## 14.

When he arrived, and once the solemnity was over and most of the people had already departed, they prepared everything required for their journey. They lifted the small chest in which the sacred relics had been stored and began to carry it with hymns and praises.

People streamed together from every direction along the road, singing divine praises with uplifted voices. Thus, with the Lord prospering their journey, they reached the monastery on the following day with a considerable crowd accompanying the bier.

The brothers came out to meet them with crosses and candles. The abbot awaited their arrival in the church of Saint John the Baptist,

[Note: Browerus notes that this church is now called Johansberg. — BOLL.]

which stood along the route, about nine stades west of the monastery.

Entering it with the sacred relics on the day before the Nones of June, they gave the people who had followed them through the forest from various places, and who now wished to return, time to pray and fulfill their vows.

When this had been done, they lifted the chest and came to the monastery. They entered the basilica of the blessed martyr Boniface with praise and joy and placed the bier containing the sacred ashes beside the altar, on the southern side.

## 15.

On the following day, the deacon Deusdona and his brother, a layman named Theodorus, entered the basilica privately at first light with the abbot and two priests, of whom I was one. They opened the chest and brought out the bones of the individual saints, which had been separately deposited in cushions, giving them to the abbot:

the thigh and foot of Saint Alexander, pope and martyr;

the arm of Felicissimus the deacon;

[Note: He is commemorated on 6 August. Rabanus mentions him in poems 119 and 120. — BOLL.]

the head of Saint Concordia the martyr;

[Note: 13 August. Rabanus, poem 31. — ID.]

a considerable portion of the bones of the holy apostolic

[Boll.: episcopal]

martyrs Fabianus

[Note: Rabanus mentions him in poems 34, 112, 119, 133, 139, 143, and elsewhere. — ID.]

[Al.: Favianus]

and Urbanus;

[Note: 25 May. Rabanus, poems 109, 119, and 129. — ID.]

the foot of the blessed Castulus;

[Note: 26 March. Rabanus, poem 32. — ID.]

a tooth of Saint Sebastian;

[Note: 20 January. Rabanus, poems 33, 115, 139, and 143. — ID.]

bones of Saints Pamphilus, priest and martyr,

[Note: 21 September. — ID.]

Papia,

[Note: 29 January. — ID.]

Maurus, and Victor;

[Note: There are various Saints Victor: twelve are celebrated in January alone. Perhaps this is the companion of Saint Zeno, mentioned below in no. 24. Their feast day is 20 April. Rabanus mentions him in poems 73 and 121. — ID.]

[Note: 23 November. — ID.]

and sizable portions of Saint Felicitas, the mother of seven sons, and of the holy virgins and martyrs Emmerentiana

[Note: 23 January. — ID.]

and Basilla.

[Note: 20 May. Rabanus, poems 35 and 64. — ID.]

Each portion had been separately stored in its own little sack.

After reverently receiving them and kissing them with honor and respect, the abbot placed them back in the chest. A few days later he sent the deacon and his brother back to their homeland, rewarding them, while they promised that, if life and divine favor permitted, they would return to him with other relics of the saints.

## 16.

After they had returned to go back to their homeland, only a very few days passed before the aforesaid abbot, with the authority of Otgar, archbishop of the church of Mainz, brought the bones of the holy martyrs Alexander and Fabianus, with great honor, into the church of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, situated on the northern side of the monastery.

Through Reginbald,

[Note: Rabanus wrote his epitaph. He seems to me to be the Reginbald to whom Rabanus dedicated the book *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, calling him, in the printed editions, “Reginaldus,” a holy priest of God concerned for the flock entrusted to him—namely, for converting pagans and strengthening the faithful. It is of little importance to note that elsewhere this passage reads “through Reginbald the chorepiscopus,” since in that age *coepiscopus* and *chorepiscopus* were used almost interchangeably, although *coepiscopus* often also designated a bishop’s suffragan. Reginbald is mentioned again below in no. 27. — MAB.]

his co-bishop,

[Note: In the usage of that age, *coepiscopus* and *chorepiscopus* meant what is now a bishop’s vicar in pontifical functions, commonly called a suffragan. Browerus shows in his notes on Rabanus’s twelfth poem, using the example of Saint Wigbert and Albuin of Fritzlar, that abbots generally performed this office at that time. The “other co-bishops” mentioned above are those subject to the same archbishop. — BOLL.]

he placed them, enclosed in their lead containers, in a stone chest east of the altar on 29 July. Above it he erected a wooden structure, made with mechanical skill, and decorated it with silver, gold, and stones in a beautiful variety. He also added verses, composed according to metrical rules and written in golden letters, explaining from where, to where, and to whom

[Al.: to what places]

they had been translated. They read as follows:

> The highest pontiffs whom Rome sent here to be honored  
> Had been rulers of the Apostolic See.  
>   
> Christ’s servant Rabanus received them with rejoicing  
> And placed their bones in this chest.  
>   
> Therefore the two Levites, coming from the aforesaid city,  
> Came here, worthy of their honor;  
>   
> The same servant of the Lord, at once standing to meet them,  
> Received them humbly and placed them here together.  
>   
> The martyr Alexander and the martyr Fabianus himself  
> Came here together, each a pious teacher.  
>   
> Disciples of Pope Sixtus and worthy ministers,  
> Felicissimus and Agapitus remain here.  
>   
> All these together sufficiently adorn this hall with their bones  
> —or, according to the variant, with sacred bones—which the Virgin Mother of God also claims through their merits.  
>   
> You also who have entered the temple,  
> Seek these patrons for your aid with poured-out prayer.

[Note: From this it is clear that these verses were composed only in subsequent years, after the relics of Saint Agapitus had been received. — ID.]

The bones of the other saints named above he placed in a chest made of wood after the pattern of the Ark of God’s Covenant, gilded and fitted with its cherubim and carrying poles

[Al.: appearances],

which he had placed in the eastern apse of the basilica of the blessed martyr Boniface. He kept them there until he could prepare a suitable place for their veneration.

With God’s help, he subsequently fulfilled this devoutly and as quickly as he could.

These events took place in the year 835 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction, while our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning. With God the Father and the Holy Spirit, he lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

### 17

But in the following year a certain layman came from the city of Rome into Francia with his companions, named Sabbatinus [Note: [Col. 0050C] About the year 829 he had brought to Einhard at Seligenstadt the relics of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus. ID.], carrying relics with him. [Note: [Col. 0050D] By that time the trafficking—indeed, the revival of the trade—in sacred relics had become so widespread; Augustine and Gregory the Great complain about it. Thus some were hungry for gold, others for relics. Someone once purchased the arm of Saint Augustine the Doctor for one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold, according to William, the monk of Malmesbury. Read Abbot Guibert of Nogent, *On the Relics of the Saints*, book I, chapter 3, § 3. MAB.] Having heard the name of the abbot mentioned above, whose devotion in divine service and in the veneration of the saints was widely proclaimed by fame, he came to him on the eighth day before the Kalends of May and gave him the bones of Saint Quirinus [Note: [Col. 0050D] He is mentioned by Rabanus, poem 121, 127. BOLL.], a martyr who was once bishop in the Pannonian city of Siscia [Note: [Col. 0050D] In others, Syscia, on the river Sava. Ancient writers frequently mention it. ID.], and the bones of blessed Romanus [Note: [Col. 0050D] Augustus. ID.], a soldier who was baptized by blessed Laurence and immediately thereafter attained martyrdom by sentence of death; thirteen bones from the body of Saint Cornelius [Note: [Col. 0050D] 13 September. Rabanus, poem 34, 109, 121, 142. ID.] the pope; ten from the body of Saint Callistus [Note: [Col. 0050D] 14 October. Rabanus, poem 112. ID.] the pope; from the bodies of Saints Nereus and Achilleus [Col. 0051A], sixteen bones; the bones of Saint Turturin [Note: [Col. 0051D] We have not yet found his feast day in any calendars. ID.]; and, of Saint Stacteus [Note: [Col. 0051D] 28 September. ID.], most of the ashes of his body and ten bones. The abbot reverently received all these relics and, with humble devotion, placed them in the chest which, as we said above, had been set beneath two cherubim.

### 18

While these things were taking place, Addo, the abbot’s priest—whom we reported above as having been sent to a certain Alabingus in Italy to obtain the bones of a saint—found and took up the body of blessed Venantius [Note: [Col. 0051D] He was Saint Venantius, a bishop and martyr. He is distinct from the non-bishop who is venerated at Camerino on 18 May and was crowned with martyrdom there. ID.] in the territory of the city of Ariminum and hastened to return to Francia. At first, indeed, he carried it secretly because of fear of the inhabitants. But after he had crossed the Alpine passes and reached the territory of the Bavarians, having become more secure, he placed it upon a bier and, amid crowds of people hastening together from every direction and praising God with a loud voice, carried it to the cell called Suolenhus [Note: [Col. 0051D] That is, “of Solus” or “of the monk Solon.” MAB.—“Solenhoff” is written in the margin, and the cell is commonly called Saint Sola’s. The monastery is situated in the diocese of Eichstätt, by the river Altmühl, and was founded by Saint Sola, Solus, or Sualo, whose feast is celebrated on 10 December. It was subject to the monastery of Fulda; after it had been exempted, blessed Rabanus later recovered it for Fulda by obtaining a diploma from Louis the Pious. See Brower, book II of *The Antiquities of Fulda*, chapter 13. BOLL.], situated in the region of Sualaveldon [Note: [Col. 0052D] Bolland: “Sualavel of the lords.” MAB.—For Brower, Sualeveldoni; in the *Life of Saint Sola*, the district or estate of Sualva; in the diploma of Louis the Pious, Sualefeldt, a district beside the river Altmühl, near which are also Eichstätt and Pappenheim. Not far from it is the monastery of Heidenheim, where Saint Walburga died, likewise in the district of Sualfeld. BOLL.], and honorably placed it in a bier on the southern side of the church altar, just as it had been brought.

At that time the provost of that cell was one of our brothers, named Santharatus. He immediately sent a messenger to the abbot, reporting the entire sequence of events and asking him to reply whether he wished those holy relics to remain where they then were or to have them transferred to the monastery. All the people of that region were asking and earnestly desiring that they might deserve to have the body of the holy martyr there, whose help they felt daily in the healing of various illnesses.

When the abbot heard this, he immediately sent two priest-monks from his own community to the aforesaid brother, ordering them to bring those holy relics to him with all possible speed. For by then the name of Saint Venantius was celebrated throughout almost all those regions because of the wonders and miracles which Christ the Lord and King of Martyrs had deigned to perform through him. I think that a few of the miracles which occurred in that place before those sent by the abbot arrived should be briefly related.

### 19

While the bier containing the sacred bones still stood beside the altar, a woman from that district, who had lost the sight of her eyes six years earlier, asked to be brought there, believing that through the merits and prayers of Saint Venantius the Lord would be reconciled to her. When she had been brought there and had humbly prayed prostrate before the bier, she recovered her sight.

After this, another woman placed her six-year-old son, lame from the womb, before the relics of the holy martyr. When the evening praise had been completed and the others had returned to their homes, she herself spent the night there with the boy. In the morning, she carried him home still weak as he had been, placed him in his bed, and entered her storeroom to give the boy bread. When she came out, she found her son, whom she had left lame in bed, playing in the street with the other children of the place—so completely healthy that no sign of his former infirmity remained.

This clearly shows that the boy was healed through the intercession of Saint Venantius, by the power of him who healed by a word both the ruler’s son and the centurion’s servant, and who, in every place, can most easily accomplish whatever he wills through the presence of his majesty: Jesus Christ our Savior, who is God, blessed above all, forever. Amen.

I learned these two miracles which I have just related from those who were present and testified that they had seen them. The remaining miracles which I shall write down I myself saw with my own eyes, since I was one of those who had been sent to carry the sacred ashes.

### 20

When we had come to the place which, as we said above, is called Suolenhus, everything necessary for transporting the holy relics was quickly prepared. At first light, after the matins office had been completed and the solemnities of Mass celebrated according to custom, amid the great grief and sorrow of those who were to remain there, we lifted up that holy treasure and began to carry it on our journey.

The sky was heavy with very dark clouds, which could quickly have dissolved into a tremendous downpour, unless divine power had prevented it. For it had rained throughout that entire night without interruption, so that it seemed utterly impossible that we could begin that journey on that day. But through the merits of his saint, heavenly grace brought about something quite different from what had been feared. As soon as we began to proceed, the clouds immediately dispersed, the sky became clear, and very little mud was found along the road. The streams, too, which in such great and continual rain as had fallen that night usually swelled, were found to have risen scarcely at all.

As we proceeded through the individual villages, crowds of people came out to meet us. They eagerly helped us both in singing divine praises and in carrying the sacred burden, until we came to the place called Holzkircha [Note: [Col. 0052D] The name of a monastery situated between the Main and the Tauber, in the present county of Wertheim, on the river Abstade. Charlemagne subjected it to the monastery of Fulda; in his charter it is called the monastery of Holtzkiricha, or of Saint Sixtus, said to have been built by the prince Troandus. See Brower, book II of *The Antiquities of Fulda*, chapter 5. MAB.—Blessed Rabanus illustrated it in various verses. BOLL.], situated in Alamannia. There, a very great crowd of both sexes and every age had gathered, and we were received with immense joy.

There was a small oratory there. We wished to enter it and bring in the bier, but because of the great crowds going before us and following behind, we could not do so. Therefore, in the open air, we erected an altar in a higher place, set the bier beside it, and again celebrated the solemnities of Mass. During the celebration, two women who were possessed by unclean spirits began to be tormented; but soon, through the power of Christ and the merits of Saint Venantius, the demons were driven out, and the women were permitted to recover perfect health of mind and body.

### 21

When the celebration of Mass had been completed and the people had returned to their homes, we brought the sacred ashes into the nearby oratory and placed the bier behind the altar. After appointing people to keep watch there and devote themselves to singing divine praises, we ourselves withdrew to our lodging.

That very night, while divine praises were being sung during the nocturnal vigils, a mute woman, through the merits of the holy martyr, had the bond of her tongue loosed and recovered speech. Not long afterward, another woman possessed by an unclean spirit and having a withered arm was so perfectly healed in body and mind, after the demon had been expelled through the prayers of the holy martyr, that on the following day she herself carried the bier with the others.

In the morning, while the solemnities of Mass were being performed, a woman who had been blind for three and a half years recovered her sight. Another, whose right hand had been weak, obtained complete healing through the merits of the saint.

### 22

When we were preparing to move on from there, and at the very moment of our departure a priest was solemnly saying the prayer, one of the clerics who were with us, named Otheri, who had been entrusted with receiving the gifts offered by the people, stole—or, according to another reading, defrauded others of—a portion of the money that had been brought. He suddenly fell and, in the sight of the entire crowd, which had gathered from every direction in countless numbers, was given over to an unclean spirit and began to be tormented.

He remained possessed by the demon until the money which he had hidden in his belt was brought out by those standing around him. Then, through the merits and prayers of the holy martyr of God, he was so perfectly healed that he accompanied the bier from that place in safety, praising God and publicly confessing his crime, until the holy relics were deposited in their appointed place.

Nothing of this kind had ever before been heard or seen in him from infancy until that time; nor, for as long as he lived afterward, was the enemy ever again given power over him.

From there we set out and came to a village called Truthmuntiga. There, beside the sacred ashes placed in the church, four women were freed from unclean spirits during that very night.

### 23

I think that a miracle which is rightly attributed to this holy man of God must not be passed over. Before we reached the aforesaid village, a certain noble matron, having heard that the relics of the holy man of God were being carried through that region, hurried to meet us. She had been on her way to another place, but abandoned the road she had been following. As she did so, she lost her golden brooch, which in the Frankish language is called a *spanga*.

After she had searched for it for a long time with her entire, and by no means small, retinue, without finding it, she resumed the journey she had begun, saying:

“If it pleases our Lord Jesus Christ, whose holy servant’s relics I have humbly come to meet, it will easily happen that the brooch I have lost will be found by someone and restored to me.”

She came, therefore, and after venerating the relics and offering gifts, was returning when an unknown man met her, holding the same brooch in his hand. When she said that it was hers, he replied:

“Take it, for through the prayers of the saint whose relics you have venerated, it has been restored to you.”

And so, having received what belonged to her, the woman continued on her journey, praising and blessing God.

### 24

On the following day, after the solemnities of Mass had first been celebrated early in the morning, we set out with the sacred ashes and came to a place called Hassarodt. There is a monastery there belonging to monks who had gone out with crosses and reliquaries containing the relics of the saints. Singing divine praises, they were waiting for our arrival on the opposite side of the river. [Reading: “on the other side.”] [Note: [Col. 0053D] The river Main, beside which this monastery was situated. MAB.]

When we came to the bridge over the river, we stopped for a short while because of the crowd that had come with us from Alamannia and now wished to return in order to have a place for prayer. At that spot, a considerable portion of the people from the surrounding region came to meet us from the opposite direction. Among them was a woman carrying a fleece of wool. When she stretched out the wool she held in order to offer it as a gift to the bier, the wool vanished like smoke.

When she saw this, frightened and trembling, she began to seek a priest to whom she could confess her sins and from whom she could receive advice for her salvation. When she was asked whether the wool which had vanished from her hands had been stolen, she confessed that she had not stolen it herself but had received it as a gift from one of her companions. When the matter was investigated carefully, it was discovered that the sheep from which the fleece had been taken had been fraudulently stolen from its rightful owner.

Thereupon the crowd which, as we said, had accompanied us from Alamannia venerated and kissed the sacred relics and returned home. The monks who had been waiting for us on the other bank of the river, together with another multitude which had come to meet us there, accompanied us with divine praises to the place where we were similarly received by others who came to meet us. After praying in the same manner as the earlier crowd, they too returned home.

In this way, each day from morning until evening, crowds of people accompanied us and sang “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*), and we proceeded with immense joy.

### 25

As we approached the village called Hamalunburg [Note: [Col. 0054D] Today the town of Amelburg on the Saale. MAB.—For others, Hamelburg, a town known in this age; Brower observes in his chronicle of the abbots of Fulda that its citizens defected from the orthodox faith in the year of Christ 1540. BOLL.], situated on a river named the Sala, formerly a royal estate until, through the generosity of Pippin, king of the Franks, it was solemnly granted to the domain of Saint Boniface the martyr, our brothers who live in the cell called Baugulf’s [Note: [Col. 0055D] Brower discusses this cell of Baugulf in book IV of his chronicle. ID.]—so called because he once lived there—came out to meet us with candles and crosses. With them came a huge crowd of men and women flowing together from every direction.

Among them was a certain lame man from the village I mentioned above. Because of weakness in one leg and foot, he supported himself with two sticks in order to walk. While we paused for a short time and the people who had come out to meet us venerated the sacred relics, he was so perfectly healed, in the sight of the crowd, through the merits of the holy martyr, that thereafter he no longer needed the support of sticks when walking.

### 26

When we, carrying the sacred burden, had come to the river, we found our abbot waiting for our arrival on the opposite bank, together with priests, monks, and a great multitude of people. A boat had indeed been prepared there for our crossing, but it had not been drawn up to the shore at a suitable place. Therefore the boatmen were ordered to bring it toward us, and we went a long way upstream from that place to the bank.

As they hurried to carry out the order, they untied the rope and were preparing to descend into the boat. Suddenly it slipped from their hands and, falling into the river, was carried along by some invisible force against the current until it reached and touched the bank at the place where it was to receive the sacred burden.

After the relics had been transferred, and the solemnities of Mass had been celebrated in the adjoining meadow in the open air because of the multitude, we placed the bier containing the sacred ashes in the oratory that stood in the village. A certain woman had been so bent by a contraction of the nerves that she could not raise herself at all to look toward the sky. In the sight of everyone present, before the relics of the holy man of God, she was instantly freed by divine power from the affliction which had troubled her for many years.

On the following day we set out from there and came to a place called Lihtolvesbah [Lichtesbach], situated in the Buchen Forest, four leagues from the monastery of Fulda [Note: [Col. 0055D] Thus they often inflect the name of the monastery of Fulda, which is also called Volda by Matthew Paris and several others. MAB.]. We were received there by the inhabitants of the forest, a great multitude of whom had come out to meet us. When we had placed the bier in the oratory, a poor woman carried her six-year-old son in her arms and placed him before the relics of the saint. He had been deaf and mute from birth. She spent the night there and, on the following day, carried him home, as the people said, hearing and speaking.

### 27

After we had completed the praises of matins and duly celebrated the solemnities of Mass, we set out while the people sang divine praises.
