When we came within sight of the monastery, behold, our abbot, who had gone ahead of us the previous day to arrange the reception of the holy relics, came to meet us. With him was the entire multitude of our brothers, except those whom age or infirmity prevented from coming out. They carried crosses and candles, as well as the bones of the blessed martyrs Urbanus and Quirinus in reliquaries; I mentioned above that these had recently been brought from Rome.

Reginbaldus, the chorepiscopus, was also with them, together with an innumerable multitude of people who had gathered at the monastery from various places for the greater litanies, which were then held on the Ides of May. [Note: [Col. 0055D] Add “were celebrated,” or something similar. The year was 836, in which Easter fell on 9 April, the Ascension on 18 May, and the first day of the Rogation ceremonies on the Ides of May. BOLL.]

After they had humbly venerated the relics with the greatest devotion, they carried the body of Saint Venantius the martyr, with hymns and praises, into the church of Saint John the Baptist, which, as I have said, is approximately nine stadia from the monastery. [Note: [Col. 0055D] See the diploma of Louis, king of Germany, granted to his faithful secretary Rabanus—so he calls him—in honor of Saint Venantius, in Brower, *The Antiquities of Fulda*, book III, chapter 13. MAB.]

After saying a prayer, Reginbaldus the chorepiscopus placed it in a stone chest in the eastern apse of the church, east of the altar. He also deposited there the ashes of the holy martyrs Urbanus and Quirinus, enclosed separately, each in its own reliquary. There, through their prayers as they faithfully entreated God, benefits are granted to the present day, [Note: [Col. 0056D] Louis the Pious, emperor, testifies that Saint Venantius soon became famous for miracles at this place in the charter for the transfer of the estate of Uresprungen, donated to blessed Rabanus, which Brower prints in book III, chapter 13 of *The Antiquities of Fulda*. It says that “miracles occurred there, celebrated far and wide: the sick were healed, the possessed freed, the paralyzed cured, the blind given sight, and the human race saved from every kind of illness.” BOLL.] to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever.

### 28

The abbot then erected above it a wooden structure, which he suitably adorned with gold and silver. Around it he had metric verses written, explaining the reason for what had been done, as follows:

> The Lord’s Forerunner, who baptized Christ in the waters,  
> Inhabits this hall and sanctifies the house.  
> Four men who have now [alternative: then] recorded Christ’s mighty works in writing  
> Behold, dwell here together.  
> But holy men, illustrious in their sacred order,  
> Exult no less and ennoble the site—  
> Men whom the vigorous love of the servants of the Lord  
> Brought here from different parts of the world.  
> Rome sent Urbanus, Siscia sent Quirinus;  
> This place contains them, having piously received them.  
> The distinguished holy bishop Venantius, too,  
> Came from Ariminum and himself remains here.  
> These too, once received, Rabanus placed by lot  
> [Alternative reading: “Here too, Rabanus placed them by lot”]  
> In this worthy sarcophagus, and composed this inscription,  
> Asking all who enter the church  
> To commend him properly to God in their prayers.

### 29

After this, the relics of the holy bishops Cornelius and Callistus [Note: [Col. 0057C] Sabbatinus had brought other relics of these pontiffs two years earlier; see above, no. 17. BOLL.], and of the holy martyrs Agapitus [Note: [Col. 0057D] Agapitus, Januarius, and Magnus are called below deacons of Pope Sixtus; Vincentus was also their companion. They are commemorated with Saint Sixtus on 6 August. Rabanus discusses Saint Vincentus in poem 120. ID.], Georgius [Note: [Col. 0057D] In poem 34, Rabanus seems to mean the great Georgius, whose feast is celebrated on 23 April. ID.], Vincentus, and Maximus [Note: [Col. 0057D] Perhaps the companion of Saints Tiburtius and Valerianus, with whom he is joined below? ID.], as well as of the holy virgins Caecilia [Note: [Col. 0057D] 22 November. Rabanus, poems 122, 131, 135, 145. ID.], Eugenia [Note: [Col. 0057D] 25 December. Rabanus, poems 114, 122. ID.], Digna and Emerita [Note: [Col. 0057D] These virgins and martyrs are commemorated on 22 September. ID.], and Columbana [Note: [Col. 0057D] We have not yet found her feast day. Whether she is Saint Columba, either of Córdoba or of Sens—the former commemorated on 17 September, the latter on 31 December—or rather some third woman, is unknown to us. ID.], were brought to him.

A certain Italian cleric named Felix brought them in the year 838 from the Incarnation of the Lord [Boll.: 837], on the fifth day of April.

### 30

After his return, when not many days had passed, Theodorus [Note: [Col. 0057D] Einhard often calls him the brother of Deusdona, Luvison, in his *History of the Translation of the Relics of Saints Marcellinus and Peter*, and censures his greed. ID.], the brother of Deusdona, who was mentioned above, came from the city of Rome into Alamannia with a certain companion of his, Sabbatinus. As he had long before promised the abbot, he brought relics of the saints with him—namely, the bones of Saint Quirinus [Note: [Col. 0058D] The same Sabbatinus had brought some of this Saint Quirinus two years earlier. ID.], who had once been bishop in the Pannonian town of Siscia and, in the time of the emperor Diocletian, under the governor Amantius, endured many sufferings for the name of Christ. With a millstone tied to his neck, he was thrown into the river.

When he continued floating on the water for a very long time, he spoke to those watching, telling them not to be frightened by his example. He scarcely obtained from the Lord through prayer that he should be drowned. His body was found and honorably buried by the faithful on the day before the Nones of June.

When the barbarians invaded parts of Pannonia, the Christian people took the body of blessed Quirinus the martyr and fled to Rome. They buried the sacred relics on the Appian Way, at the third milestone from the city, in the church of the apostles Peter and Paul, where they lay for some time, in the place called the Catacombs.

### 31

He also brought the relics of Pope Urbanus and confessor [Note: [Col. 0058D] Rather, martyr, as above, no. 15, where Deusdona gave some of his relics. BOLL.], whose teaching caused many to be crowned with martyrdom in his time; also the bones of Saint Caecilia the virgin, who won her husband and his brother for Christ and made them martyrs, and who herself was afterward martyred. She overcame the fire but was killed by the sword under Almachius, prefect of the city.

He likewise brought the bones of Saints Tiburtius and Valerianus [Note: [Col. 0058D] They are commemorated on 14 April. Rabanus, poems 32, 126, 131. ID.] and Maximus. The first two were beaten with clubs and struck with the sword under the aforesaid Almachius, prefect of the city; the last was beaten with leaden weights until he gave up his spirit.

He also brought the bones of Saints Agapitus, Januarius, and Magnus, deacons of blessed Pope Sixtus, who, as is read in the papal acts, were beheaded with him under Decius [Note: [Col. 0058D] Under the emperor Valerian, according to Rabanus, poem 127. ID.]. He also brought the bones of the deacon Zeno [Note: [Col. 0058D] Various men named Zeno are commemorated. We have not yet found the feast day of this deacon. ID.] and of Hippolytus the martyr [Col. 0058A], who, in the time of the emperor Decius, was bound by the feet to the necks of untamed horses and dragged through a field of thistles, giving up his spirit.

He also brought the sacred relics of Aquila [Note: [Col. 0058D] 8 July. Rabanus, poem 126.] and Priscilla, formerly companions of Paul, as the Acts of the Apostles testify. During the journey on which they were being carried, a great and unheard-of miracle occurred: they appeared to have been drenched with real blood. For so much moisture of a bloody color dripped from the reliquary in which they had been placed that it stained even the clothing of those carrying it and struck the minds of the spectators with the wonder of the event.

### 32

When they arrived, our brother Santhratus received them; we said above that he had been appointed provost of the cell of Solus (no. 18). He promptly arranged to announce their arrival to the abbot. He honorably placed the relics in the place called Holtzkircha on Holy Saturday of Pentecost, five days before the Kalends of June. [Note: [Col. 0058D] Bolland: “on the Kalends of June.” MAB.—Brower incorrectly gives “five days before the Kalends of June.” For in the year mentioned, 838, Pentecost fell on 2 June. Therefore Pentecost Saturday was on the Kalends of June itself. BOLL.]

A great multitude of men and women gathered there. Among them was brought a twelve-year-old girl who had been blind from birth and whose arms and legs were contracted. During the very vigils, through the merits and prayers of the saints, she recovered both the health of her limbs and the use of her eyes.

Two or three days later [Boll.: eight days], a certain blind woman recovered her sight, and the tongue of a man who had been mute from birth was restored to speech. After this, on the third day, a woman who had seen nothing for three continuous years [Note: [Col. 0058D] Perhaps “had seen.” ID.] deserved to receive light through the merits of the saints. On the following day, the contracted hand of another woman was restored to its former health.

### 33

While such things were divinely taking place at the relics of the saints, three priests from among our monks arrived, sent by the abbot. One was called Megingoz, another Oedoltus, and the third Theothmarus—the same man whom I mentioned in the translation of the relics of the blessed martyr Alexander (no. 13).

In accordance with the command they had received, they took the bones of the saints that had been brought and began to carry them with honor and reverence. A great multitude of men and women accompanied them, singing psalms and joyfully chanting divine praises. People also flocked eagerly from the districts and villages, bringing with them those possessed by unclean spirits and those afflicted with various kinds of illness, believing that through the merits and prayers of the saints they would receive the healing they desired.

Among them was brought a possessed woman named Ruodmwi. She belonged to the jurisdiction of Saint Kilian the martyr [Note: [Col. 0059D] That is, as Brower explains, she was from the territory of the Franconian land. Saint Kilian, bishop of Würzburg, is commemorated on 8 July. BOLL.] and lived in a village called Ascbah.

As soon as she came within sight of the reliquary in which the relics of the saints were being carried, she was seized by an unclean spirit and tormented for a long time and severely. But by the grace of God she was so perfectly healed in the sight of the multitude that thereafter she remained safe and sound in mind, praising God, whereas previously she had often suffered from this kind of affliction.

### 34

This occurred on Friday, fourteen days before the Kalends of August.

The abbot, who was greatly concerned for the honor of the saints, sent me and some of the brothers to meet them, ordering that the bones of the holy martyrs Januarius and Magnus should be left in the little monastery called Holtzkircha, situated in the province of Waldsazi, while the relics of the other saints should be brought to him.

We met them in a village called Biscofesheim [Note: [Col. 0059D] The Biscofesheim nunnery was situated there. MAB.]. We spent the night singing praises to God and keeping watch. On the following day, which was Sunday, we reached Holzkircha with the holy relics. After the bier had been placed in the church beside the altar and the solemnities of holy Mass were being celebrated, a woman was cured of a demon.

For while she was being miserably tormented in the sight of the people, an enormous black fly of extraordinary size was seen to fly out of her mouth. After it had emerged, she recovered her soundness of mind and was healed.

### 35

On the following day, leaving there, as we had been ordered, the bones of the holy martyrs Januarius and Magnus, reverently placed in a reliquary behind the altar just as they had been brought, we set out with the other relics of the saints. The brothers and a great multitude of the people of that region followed us.

From every direction the sick and those afflicted by various sufferings were also brought. Among them was a girl named Sclina. On the very road along which we were walking, she was seized by a demon, ran up, and grasped the bier with her teeth. Immediately she became sound in mind. Taking up the banner of the holy cross, she went before the relics of the saints, rejoicing and praising God.

### 36

When we came to the river Main, the nuns from the monastery called Zellinga [Note: [Col. 0059D] This monastery, situated near the village of Retzbach, has long since disappeared, as Brower attests in book II, chapter 10 of *The Antiquities of Fulda*. ID.] came out with crosses and candles and received us. We entered the church with the sacred burden so that the people who had come with us—and who already wished to return—might have a place to pray and fulfill their vows. There we celebrated the solemnities at the sixth hour of the day.

When these had been completed, we came with the entire multitude to the boat. On the opposite bank there was also a considerable crowd waiting for our arrival.

As we were boarding the boat with the sacred bones, a certain maidservant of Mathilda, the abbess of that monastery, named Liobsuind, came crawling on her feet. She had been afflicted by an old disease and was so bent toward the ground that she could not raise herself at all to look toward the sky. She supported herself with her hands on small stools or climbing supports. [Note: [Col. 0060D] Thus it should be read, not *scabellis* as in Bolland. *Scammela* or *scammula* are supports used by crawling people, on which they lean with their hands. ID.]

When she wished to board the boat but could not, one of our brothers, named Gozmundus, lifted her and placed her in the boat. After we had crossed and gone ashore on the other side with the sacred bones, the woman was immediately healed in a wonderful manner through the power of God and the merits of the saints. Without anyone’s assistance, she raised herself and touched the top of the bier with the small supports on which she had previously been leaning.

An innumerable multitude of both sexes and all ages still stood on both sides of the river. Among them was a certain priest, Reginolfus, belonging to Bishop Humbertus (see no. 38). He climbed to a higher place and displayed the woman, now healthy, to the people, who cried out in praise of God, so that the miracle might produce many witnesses and many praisers of God.

Her mistress also testified that the woman had been crippled and rendered helpless by that disease for many years, and had remained so until the time when, through the grace of God and his saints, she was freed from such an affliction.

### 37

From there, with divine help, we set out and arrived at the monastery on the third day, that is, eight days before the Kalends of August. The brothers came out with crosses and candles to meet us on the slope of the mountain called Hurodleichesberg.

A considerable crowd from the inhabitants of the wilderness had gathered there, some accompanying us and others coming out to meet us. We stopped for a short time to give those assembling an opportunity to pray.

Behold, a certain woman who had been bedridden for ten years or more was being carried. When the bearers brought her to the bier and she touched it, she immediately recovered the health of all her limbs. Rejoicing and praising God, she returned home.

The brothers carried the holy relics they had received into the church of the blessed martyr Boniface with hymns and praises. They placed them, together with the reliquary, just as they had been brought, beside the altar of the blessed apostles, and visited them day and night with fitting veneration.

### 38

After these things had taken place and several days had passed, the venerable man Rabanus, the abbot, invited Humbertus [Note: [Col. 0060D] Rabanus dedicated to him his commentary on the books of Judges and Ruth, as well as a letter in which he discusses in which degree of relationship marriage is lawful. BOLL.], bishop of the church of Würzburg, to the monastery which, as was said above, is called Holzkiricha.

Because the place belonged to his diocese, Rabanus, with Humbertus’s authority, reverently placed the bones of the holy martyrs Januarius and Magnus there in a stone chest east of the altar, eight days before the Kalends of November. Above it he erected a wooden structure and decorated it with beautiful workmanship in gold and silver. Around it he had the following metric verses written in gilded letters:

> Behold these men, distinguished and illustrious patrons,  
> Whom Rome, the glory of the world, sent here together.  
> The humble abbot Rabanus received them,  
> And here he duly placed them with Bishop Humbertus.

Here rest the martyr Magnus and Januarius,

Distinguished in office and in sacred merits;

Who, slain by the sword with Bishop Christus,

As deacons, rendered their souls to heaven.

### 39

Accordingly, from the time when their sacred relics were buried there, divine benefits have been granted to the people down to the present day. Through their prayers and merits, the weak and infirm are healed, demons are driven from possessed bodies, and the petitions desired by those who pray faithfully are granted. Of these miracles I have taken care briefly to relate a few that were reported to my knowledge in writing by those who were present and testified that they had seen them.

There is a village one thousand paces south of that monastery, called Gundichenhus. From it came a woman named Adalburg, who, when she had sat down at table with her husband to take food, suddenly became so rigid through a contraction of the nerves that, with her fingernails driven into her palms, she could not at all unfold one finger from another. Seeing this, her husband brought her with all possible speed to the monastery, presenting her to the priests and brothers of that place and begging them to pray to the divine mercy for her recovery. She was accordingly led to the memorial of the martyrs. While the brothers were celebrating the evening office, and she was lying prostrate before the altar in prayer, the use of her right hand was restored. On the following day, around the third hour, having also recovered the health of her left hand, she returned home rejoicing.

### 40

There is also another village not far from the same monastery, called Hohhus. In it a certain girl, while she was engaged in weaving, was suddenly seized by an assault of the evil spirit and became helpless, with her hands contracted. For three continuous days and three nights she raged and shouted, uttering many unknown things as though they were familiar. She called upon Saint Gertrude [Note: evidently the Gertrude honored at Carleburg on 17 March. MAB.] and proclaimed the names of other saints. Among other things, she asserted that Lucia [Note: She is commemorated on 13 December. BOLL.] had descended from heaven and was admonishing her to hasten to Saints Januarius and Magnus the martyrs. She said that she saw the aforesaid saints, and, specifying by name the place where they rested, desired to go there.

When she had been brought there by her parents, she repeated the same account in order to the priests and monks of that place. The girl’s father placed three denarii upon his daughter’s contracted hand and, with his right hand, extended her hand toward the altar together with the offering. When this had been done, immediately, in a wondrous manner through the prayers of the saints, at one and the same moment the denarii fell upon the altar and the girl’s soundness of mind and hand was restored.

### 41

There was also at that time a certain woman in a village called Erlabah, twelve leagues distant from the monastery, who had suffered for ten continuous years from the affliction of an unclean spirit. Her parents brought her in full faith to the memorial of the holy martyrs, while the priest Eberhard stood beside the altar and celebrated Mass. When prayers had been offered for her, she suddenly vomited something unclean and foul; together with the vomit the demon came out, and she was healed and restored to soundness of mind. After confessing her sins, she returned home rejoicing and praising God.

### 42

There was a certain man in that region named Freviricus, from a village called Bettinga. His servant-girl, named Gersuind, suddenly became mute and remained speechless for seven continuous days. On the eighth day she was brought to the memorial of the martyrs and, through their merits, restored to her former health.

For, while the solemnities of Mass were being celebrated publicly in the church and the Gospel reading was being read, with everyone standing in silence and reverence according to custom, she suddenly, as though driven by some force, burst into speech and cried out “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) before all the people. Thus, through the power of God and the merits of the holy martyrs, she recovered the power of speech and returned home.

### 43

It was the feast day of the holy martyrs Januarius and Magnus. All men and women belonging to the jurisdiction of that monastery had been ordered on that day to abstain from rural and servile labor and to dedicate the day to the feast.

It happened in a certain village inhabited by Christian Slavs [Variant: Schavis], that one of them, disregarding the honor due to the saints, went out into the field with his companions. While the others were celebrating the solemn holiday, he reaped the grain and harvest and gathered it into heaps.

Meanwhile the air grew exceedingly dense with clouds, and a violent storm arose. Lightning and winds were driven with great force from every direction; flashes were also terribly frightening, and the bolts darting about inspired mortals with immense dread. A great miracle occurred, as the Lord distinguished between those who honored and those who despised the feasts of his saints.

For all the heaps of grain that the wretched man had reaped and gathered on that day were consumed by heavenly fire, while the others remained unharmed—the heaps that he himself or his fellow villagers had reaped on the previous day. Such fear struck everyone in the surrounding area that thereafter they observed the feasts of the saints with the highest reverence.

### 44

It also happened on the day of the solemnity that a girl from the village of Munbrunnosi, named Selina, daughter of Bernalah, was so completely healed from her daily affliction by an evil spirit that from that day onward the wicked spirit never again attacked her.

By such miracles, and by countless others that, intent on brevity, we omit, our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to make known the merits of his saints Januarius and Magnus, whose bones are known to have been transferred and buried in the manner described above. As for the bodies of the other saints, whether brought at the same time as these or at another time, I shall explain, on the basis of trustworthy accounts, where they were transferred and buried.

### 45

There is a place ten or more leagues north of the monastery of Fulda, called Rathesthorph [Note: In the deed of settlement or agreement concluded in the second year of Louis Augustus between Wolfger, bishop of Würzburg, and Ratgar, abbot of Fulda, mention is made of the monastery of Ratestorf, which was situated in the diocese of Würzburg, whose bishop Humbert later became. A charter concerning the boundaries of Ratesdorf is preserved in Pistorius, *Traditions of Fulda*, p. 514. Rabanus mentions this cell in the preface to his exposition of the *Song of Songs* addressed to King Louis: “Recently,” he says, “when I was summoned to you in the cell of our monastery called Ratestorf, and there was conversation between us about the sacred Scriptures,” etc. MAB.]. It was inhabited by monks but at that time belonged to the aforesaid monastery and to Rabanus the abbot.

There he newly built a beautiful church suited to divine worship, which he tastefully adorned with paintings and a variety of metals. He appropriately supplied it with altars and crosses fashioned in gold and silver, and with vessels of various kinds required for divine worship.

With the authority of Humbert, who had sent the priest Herilolf there as his representative, he brought into it the bones of Saint Cecilia the virgin and of the holy martyrs Tiburtius and Valerian, and placed them in a stone sarcophagus behind the altar, the bones of each being separately enclosed in its own small reliquary. Above it he erected, as was his custom, a wooden structure and adorned it with gold and silver. He also wrote around it, in gilded letters, a metrical inscription explaining the sequence of events, as follows:

After Christ, the King of kings, had victoriously ascended

Above the lofty heavens, almighty judge,

He left here a throng of servants and a faithful people

Who by word and deed would produce abundant gain.

Among them these men, whose bodies rest here,

Were distinguished by the titles of their virtues.

Despising the pomp of the world, they rightly held

The palm of martyrdom and the honor of virginity.

Behold, here rest two brothers whom blessed Cecilia,

By her teaching, won for Christ.

Here is Valerian, the one; Tiburtius, the other,

Illustrious in name, yet more illustrious in merits.

These three persons, coming from the Roman citadel,

Were received by Rabanus, your servant, O Christ.

Desiring them to become his patrons,

He adorned the tomb by skilled workmanship and composed its inscription.

### 46

He also built a very conspicuous church on a lofty mountain, about twelve stadia east of his monastery. At the command of Archbishop Otgar, he had it consecrated by Reginbald, his chorepiscopus, in honor of the blessed apostles, patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, and of all the holy heavenly spirits.

Into it he brought the bones of Saint Felicity [Note: She and the following three saints were discussed above, no. 15. BOLL.], mother of the seven martyred sons, and of Saint Concordia; also those of the holy virgins Basilla, Emmerentiana, Candida [Note: It is uncertain which Candida this was. Was she one of those said to have suffered at Rome and commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 6 June, 29 August, and 1 December? ID.], and Eutropia [Note: Perhaps the sister of Saint Nicasius, bishop of Rheims, who is mentioned below? Their feast is on 14 December. ID.]. To these he added the bones and garments of Saints Aquila and Priscilla, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [Note: Other copies have the fourth day before the Kalends; Brower has the sixth day before the Kalends. In Book II, chapter 12, of the *Antiquities of Fulda* the inscription reads: “In the year of the Lord 808 [read 837], indiction 15, this oratory was dedicated by command of Otgar, archbishop, by Reginbald, chorepiscopus, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in honor of the blessed apostles, patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, and of Saint Felicity, mother of the seven sons,” etc. This church is situated on Mount Saint Peter, adjoining the monastery of Fulda to the east, below, no. 50. MAB.].

Above it he erected, as he had done in the other places, a wooden structure and adorned it with gold and silver. On both sides he wrote verses explaining the course of the event, as follows:

Behold, this place duly holds the buried bones

Of the saints, and at the same time remembers and honors their pious deeds.

Here rest holy Felicity, Concordia, the nurse

Of Hippolytus, Candida, and Eutropia.

Here also rest Aquila and Prisca, Paul’s hosts,

And here remain the virgin Eugenia and Basilla.

Here stands the foster-sister of the virgin Agnes,

Namely Emmerentiana, herself also a holy martyr.

### 47

On the same day he also transferred the bones of the blessed virgin Leuba [Note: Rabanus treats of her in poems 110, 131, 135, and 138. BOLL.], whose Life and deeds I recently comprised in a short book. He placed them in the crypt of the same church, behind the altar, which was dedicated in honor of the holy Mother of God and of the holy virgins of Christ, in a stone chest. He also encased the chest in wood and tastefully adorned it with gold and silver.

### 48

On the following day, through the agency of the aforesaid chorepiscopus, he placed in the church of the blessed martyr Boniface the relics of the holy bishops Cornelius, Callistus, Sixtus [Note: These three were bishops of Rheims; of them, Sixtus and Sinicius—called Sinitius by others and Sinisius by Brower—are commemorated on 1 September. ID.], Sinicius, Nicasius, and Felix [Note: Perhaps the bishop of Rheims. Rabanus treats of him in poem 32; his feast is on 21 February. ID.]; also those of the presbyters Stacteus and Pamphilus; and of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian [Note: 25 October. Rabanus, poem 126. The others were discussed above, nos. 15, 17, 29, and 31. ID.], Nereus and Achilleus, Sebastian, Castulus and Romanus, Papias and Maurus, and Valerian; as well as those of the holy virgins and martyrs of Christ Cecilia, Eugenia, and Anastasia, in the place where the holy body of Boniface had formerly rested.

For there he built a stone tower behind the altar. In the middle of the summit of this tower he enclosed the aforesaid bones of the saints, carefully sealed within a stone chest. Above it he raised a wooden canopy supported by four columns and adorned it with gold and silver. Within this he placed an oblong chest, quadrangular in form, which he likewise adorned with gold, silver, and precious stones, decorating it with suitably executed images of each of the saints. Around it he wrote verses spoken, as it were, by the chest itself, as follows:

Those whom this place names and marks by their images,

Behold, they are illustrious servants of Christ God.

With fearful hearts they reddened themselves with sacred blood;

Having followed Christ, they offered up their souls.

On the adjoining tower he also wrote verses—four on one side and four on the other—composed in elegiac meter, as follows:

For the martyrs of Christ, whose sacred bones rest here,

Humble Rabanus composed this inscription.

Reader, if you desire to know their names,

The chest placed above reveals them to you.

Rome, glory of the world, praise of all things, supreme power,

Once possessed these men as readers and pontiffs.

With them here rest, gathered from various parts of the world,

Servants of Christ, illustrious in virtue.

On the remaining two sides he wrote these verses in Asclepiadic meter:

Most fortunate and blessed are those

Whom Christ the King, rejoicing, from his heavenly citadel

Places among the stars for their holy merits

And grants everlasting life.

You who enter the temple of the Lord with your feet,

I now admonish you, with kindly heart,

To beseech Christ in prayer

To grant you the stars together with the martyrs.

### 49

He also gathered many relics of other saints from various parts of the world and honorably placed them in the oratories—thirty in number—that he built during his administration and had dedicated by the bishops in whose dioceses they were located.

Concerning the locations of these oratories, the persons responsible for their consecration, the times of their consecration, and the names of the saints whose relics adorn them, I shall explain at suitable points to those who wish to know, if life and divine favor permit.

### 50

After that venerable man had nobly governed the monastery entrusted to him for twenty years [Note: In the year 842, as stated above. Trithemius must be corrected here both in the year and especially in the account of his flight to King Louis. BOLL.], he laid down the burden of pastoral care and withdrew to the church that, as I said above, he had built east of the monastery on the mountain [Note: Bollander adds “of Saint Peter”; these words are absent from other printed editions. “On Mount Saint Peter” would be more correct. See no. 46 above. MAB.]. Remaining there and serving God, he devoted himself to heavenly philosophy.

From childhood he had been very zealous in the Scriptures, and, according to the gift bestowed upon him from heaven, he loved the reading of the divine books exceedingly and meditated upon them frequently. Therefore, at the urging of his brothers and friends, he began to write expositions of the divine books, both of the Old and of the New Testament.

For, as he himself testified, at about the thirtieth year of his life [Note: In the year of Christ 815. BOLL.] he first wrote two little books in praise of the holy cross. One was in metrical style, with mystical figures that had long before been indicated in the divine books, so that it might be shown that the passion of Christ and our redemption had been foretold in the figure of the holy cross. In it, an explanation of each figure was also appended in prose. Thus, apart from the title page, it appears to contain twenty-eight figures together with their explanations.

He thought that the following little book should then be composed, and abridged it into twenty-eight chapters, so that in it he might make the expression of the first metrical book clearer.

After this he wrote to Archbishop Heistolf [Note: In other copies, Staistulphus, archbishop of Mainz, who held office from A.D. 814 to 826 and ordained Rabanus as a priest. Rabanus dedicated these earlier books to him in A.D. 819. ID.] three books *On the Instruction of Clerics*. In them he explains the ecclesiastical orders and the various offices performed in the Church, and sets forth the order of learning and the method of proclaiming the word of God.

For him he also wrote a treatise on the Gospel of Matthew, completing it in eight books. At his urging he composed various homilies for the whole year, for different feast days. He also added sermons on various vices and virtues for preaching to the people of God.

### 51

After this, at the request of the bishops—namely Frecholf [Note: Bishop of Lisieux, to whom he dedicated the Pentateuch. ID.], Frideric [Note: Bishop of Utrecht, to whom he dedicated the books on Joshua; Chifflet’s manuscript numbers these as only three books. ID.], and Humbert [Note: To this bishop of Würzburg he presented his studies on Judges and Ruth. ID.]—he wrote twenty-nine books of commentaries on the Octateuch [Bollander: Pentateuch]: four books on Genesis, four on Exodus, seven on Leviticus, four on Numbers, likewise four on Deuteronomy, three books on Joshua [Bollander: four], two on Judges, and one on Ruth.

At the request of the abbot Hilcwin [Note: Abbot of Saint-Denis and chief chaplain of the palace of Louis the Pious. ID.] he also wrote four books of exposition on Samuel and Kings. Likewise, at the urging of the emperor Louis [Note: But the preface placed before it is addressed to Louis, king of Germany, the son of another Louis. ID.], he published four books on Chronicles.

He further wrote one book of exposition on the history of Judith and likewise one on the history of Esther, which he delivered to Judith Augusta. He explained the First Book of Maccabees, at the request of the archdeacon Gerold [Note: Archdeacon of the imperial palace, whose intimate conversation Rabanus says he enjoyed at the palace of the city of the Vangiones—that is, Worms—in the preface. ID.], in two little books, and the following book in one.

He also elucidated the book called Wisdom in three little books, as best he could, at the urging of Archbishop Otgar [Note: He was Rabanus’s predecessor in the archbishopric of Mainz and held office from 826 to 847. Rabanus also dedicated Ecclesiasticus to him. ID.]. Likewise he explained in ten books the book of Jesus son of Sirach, which is called Ecclesiasticus. [Note: He completed it after the death of the emperor Louis the Pious, which occurred on the Kalends of July in the year 840. He presented it to his son, the emperor Lothar. ID.]

He also published twenty books of exposition on the prophet Jeremiah, according to the understanding of the Fathers. At the urging of Lupus [Note: Lupus, a disciple of Rabanus and abbot of Ferrières in France. ID.] the deacon, he composed a collection on the Pauline Epistles, gathering sayings from various works of the holy Fathers and arranging them in order; he completed it in thirty books.

### 52

There are also other minor works of his, which it was necessary for him to write in response to questions put to him by various persons. One of these is *On the Ordination of Co-bishops* [Note: Perhaps *chorepiscoporum*, as Colvenerius noted. This book has not yet been printed. ID.]. On this subject he wrote one book to Archbishop Drogo [Note: Drogo was bishop of Metz, called archbishop because of the honor of the pallium and the dignity of apostolic vicar received from Pope Sergius in the year 844. MAB.—This Drogo was the son of Saint Charlemagne by the concubine Regina, raised in the palace of Louis the Pious, and later bishop of Metz. In A.D. 844 Sergius II appointed him vicar of the Apostolic See in Gaul and Germany. In Sergius’s letter to the bishops beyond the Alps he is called archbishop of Metz, a precedence he had exercised long before under his brother Louis the Pious. He presided at the council held at Thionville in 835 and deposed Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, from his rank. Hincmar should be read in his later work against Gottschalk, chapter 36, where the following signatures appear: “Drogo, archbishop; Hetti, archbishop,” and so forth, concluding with these words: “This document was issued by Drogo, who presided over the synod together with Hetti, bishop of Trier, and Fulco, who had been designated successor to Ebbo in the see of Rheims.” BOLL.].

He also wrote one book to Notingus, bishop of Verona, *On the Foreknowledge and Predestination of God, on Grace and Free Will*, in which he showed what ought rightly to be believed.

He wrote one book to the emperor Louis against those who wished to abolish the offering according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. To him he also sent a consolatory letter after the calamity that had befallen him through his sons and nobles. In it he demonstrated from divine testimonies that a false judgment cannot rightly condemn an innocent man; and finally he urged him to grant pardon for the offenses committed against him.

Afterward, at the same emperor’s urging, he composed a collection of sayings from the divine books. First he proved from divine testimonies that honor toward parents and submission to the authority ordained by God must be observed. Then, in the same work, he added testimonies from divine authority concerning various kinds of virtues and, conversely, vices, demonstrating how God is to be served by each order in the Church. He completed this work in eleven chapters.

In response to questions from Abbot Bonosus—concerning how the mixing of kinship is to be avoided and how the magical art is to be shunned—he composed one book.

He also wrote one little book to Archbishop Otgar, in which he first treated legitimate penance and the hope of pardon. He then added various chapters drawn from the canons of different councils, for correcting human vices and strengthening the institutions of the Christian religion.

Furthermore, at the request of the monk Macarius, he composed one dialogue on the computation of the calendar [Note: Brower notes: “I wish that someone who can would fill in certain omissions in the manuscript.” BOLL.].

[Col. 0067]

## The Second Life of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, by Trithemius

*(From the edition of Georg Colvenerius. The Bollandist notes from the Acts of the Saints are appended to this Life.)*

## Dedication Letter

[Col. 0067]

To the most reverend father in Christ and most illustrious prince and lord, Lord Albert, archbishop of the holy see of Mainz [Note: Elected on 9 March 1514; previously archbishop of Magdeburg and administrator of Halberstadt; afterward admitted among the cardinals by Pope Leo X in 1518; he died on 24 September 1525.] and of the church of Magdeburg; prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire; archchancellor throughout Germany and primate; administrator of the church of Halberstadt; margrave of Brandenburg [Note: Son of John, elector of Brandenburg.]; duke of Stettin, Pomerania, Kashubia, and the Slavs; burgrave of Nuremberg; and prince of Rügen—John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Greater in the suburbs of the city of Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, offers whatever prayer of a sinner can avail before God.

I obeyed your commands, most reverend prelate, and gathered into one volume, from writers of different periods, a truthful and concise account of the Life of your blessed predecessor, Rabanus Maurus Magnentius, formerly archbishop of your sacred see of Mainz and a doctor of the most celebrated reputation and learning.

Nor is it surprising if I have passed over many of his deeds in silence. For I could find no earlier, fixed, sound, and sufficient author on this very subject. I am compelled to be the first author without a predecessor, gathering ears of grain fallen from many different little fields and, as a new reaper, bringing ancient sheaves into the Lord’s storehouses.

From his departure from this world to the Lord down to our own time, six hundred and fifty-nine years are reckoned. This long interval of time has consigned many glorious things done by him to perpetual oblivion.

I admit that many writers of histories have scattered here and there in their works various praises of this most blessed and learned man; yet none of them composed his Life in a continuous narrative. For this reason a very difficult labor confronted me. While I was compelled to investigate through various authors what each had written about Rabanus, I had to arrange individually what I found as gracefully and coherently as I could.

Who in our own times can be found sufficiently capable of causing to live again in literary perpetuity those things that, for so many years, have plainly remained in the oblivion of mortals?

Let the bishops of Germany be ashamed of their innate, if I may put it so, sluggishness. Devoted to vanities, they neglect the honor of God in his saints and, through shameful dissimulation, despise the glory of their homeland.

I grieve over the misfortune of my German nation, whose minds are so fierce that it neither knows how properly to educate its own children nor is accustomed to honor with fitting titles of praise and merit those who strive to show themselves superior to others in character and learning.

From the time when the holy archbishop Rabanus departed to Christ until the beginning of your pontificate, most reverend prelate Albert, there have been, if I remember correctly, fifty archbishops of the church of Mainz [Note: The first of these fifty is Blessed Rabanus; the last is Albert.]. Yet none recalled to mind the memory of Rabanus, that most holy man, and none attempted to make his name known to posterity.

This holy work was reserved for you, most Christian prelate and most eminent prince. To your name belongs the glory of so great a man. Following the example of ancient and most holy bishops, you strive in all things to show yourself a true minister of Christ and, by word and example, an irreproachable bishop of the church entrusted to you.

Blessed, therefore, is the holy church of Mainz under your rule. You reverently raise the sacred bones of the saints from their tombs and make them available for veneration by the faithful; and what the negligence of former times would soon have allowed to dissolve into ashes, you have firmly entrusted to perpetual memory.

Thus all Germans rightly proclaim you their light and immeasurable glory: a supreme worshiper of God, an utterly faithful venerator of his saints, a most steadfast defender of the Catholic religion, a prince of the noblest lineage, and without dispute the most distinguished of all in life and character. For this reason your name must never be spoken without honor.

The Apostolic See, weighing these and still greater accumulated benefits of divine mercy—something that, as far as is recorded, had never before occurred among the Germans—appointed you, a prince young in age but old in character, when you had scarcely reached your twenty-fifth year, as archbishop of the see of Mainz and of the church of Magdeburg and as primate of all the German bishops, after the canonical election of the brothers. In its gracious kindness it granted you the office of consecration, together with the splendor of the pallia of both churches.

Moreover, so that you might rightly appear to have attained the name of threefold greatness, or of a triarch, it appointed you administrator of the distinguished church of Halberstadt and raised the glory of your Highness above all the bishops of Germany.

No one doubts that this was done by divine foreordination, since he carefully considered your life and character, which he had known from your earliest years. For from tender youth divine things were always in your mind, and nothing was sweeter to you than to attend the choirs of clerics singing psalms, to adorn altars with beautiful decoration, and to clothe in the varied and shining splendor of gold and silver the bones of the saints, and likewise of the most blessed martyrs and confessors of Christ.

I have been able to write this about your most religious Highness with all the greater truth and confidence because, after spending more than ten years at the court of the most serene prince Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg and prince-elector of the Empire, your fellow German, I saw and heard you more fully at Ursula of Cölln on the Spree [?] [Note: Berlin, the seat of the elector, is said to have been founded and named around A.D. 1142 by Albert the Bear, prince of Anhalt, just as the neighboring town of Bernau was called Bernavia, Bernavicum, or Bernwaldia. The German word for “bear” is *ber*. The town of Cölln lies beside Berlin, separated from it by the river Spree.].

Since, therefore, prompted by divine mercy, while still a boy becoming a young man, you desired with such piety, charity, and devotion to devote yourself to the most holy ministries of Christ that you inspired wonder not only in your elders but also in all who were worthy to see, hear, or address you, who could deny, unless insane, that before you were born into the world you had been chosen and set apart by divine providence for this ministry of a threefold pontificate? In it you can acquire manifold merits of holiness, while also recalling the mortals entrusted to your care to the paths of justice by your life, teaching, and pastoral authority.

Having received these greatest honors from the supreme providence of God, you act excellently by showing yourself in your deeds to be a true bishop: unlike many prelates, you place heavenly things before earthly things and eternal things before perishable ones.

Therefore all the peoples of Germany will call you blessed, provided—and may the Almighty grant this—that you persevere to the end in the holy purpose you have begun.

You have rivals, do not doubt it, to whom this youthful fervor of your holiness is suspect. If, by God’s mercy, you remain steadfast in it, you will increase the joy of the good and cause no small confusion to those who hate mankind.

But, knowing your devotion to God’s saints, I trust that through their prayers and merits you will remain in the good works you have begun and add better things daily to your worthy pursuits, until at last, made a participant with them, you rejoice without end in heaven—the saints whose name and memory you honor with such desire of mind and ardor of spirit, now diligently serving as a pilgrim prelate on earth.

You raised Rabanus, despised at Mainz and almost buried in everlasting oblivion, from the earth in the name of the just, with the highest reverence. For this the almighty Lord will exalt your soul with his saints in the homeland.

And, so that I might not fail in your holy ministry, I willingly accepted the burden that you recently imposed upon me. With as much diligence as I could, I laboriously gathered the Life of the aforesaid most blessed bishop from the books of various authors into a single volume.

If I have not satisfied your desire, let good will in this poor little man suffice as a meritorious act of obedience. I obeyed your command, did what I could, and dedicated to your most sacred name everything that occurred to me concerning the praises of so great a bishop.

Receive now, therefore, with consecrated hands, most reverend prince, the first fruits of the barren little field of Trithemius, offered with the greatest humility to your pontificate. Since you are the supreme priest of God, kindly separate the chaff from the grain, so that this barren little work of mine on the Life of Saint Rabanus, composed by your command and dedicated to you, may come to light with greater confidence, insofar as under the rod of your pontifical Eminence it shall have been more carefully and thoroughly corrected.

For your Serenity possesses abundant knowledge joined to authority, by which you will be able not only to defend this labor of mine from the injury of detractors but also, when necessary, to correct it with the greatest precision.

Farewell, prince of bishops.

From my monastery, on the sixth day of November, in the year of the Lord 1515.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 0071B]

## Book One

[Col. 0071B]

Rabanus, surnamed Maurus, of the Magnentian family, by nationality an East Frank, by homeland a Buchonian, was born in the town of Fulda on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 788, in the eleventh Roman indiction, which was the twentieth year of King Charles the Great of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0071D] Rather, it was the twenty-ninth year of Charles’s reign and the sixteenth of Hadrian’s pontificate, since this pope was elected on 9 February 772. He succeeded his father Pippin, who died on 24 September 768.], and the seventeenth year of the Roman pontiff Hadrian I. His father, named Ruthard [Note: [Col. 0071D] In the Life of Pope Stephen III, Fulrad the abbot and Rothard the duke are said to have been sent to him by King Pippin. But who will establish that this man was the same as the parent of blessed Rabanus?], born of the Magnentian family, a wealthy and powerful man, served bravely for a long time under the Frankish princes in Germany. His mother was called Aldegundis, a woman of most honorable conduct. From infancy she taught her son to fear God, instructed him in letters, and with no less diligence by example than by word carefully trained his receptive mind [Col. 0071C] for every good work.

Indeed, while the mind of her child was still pliable with the tender weakness of boyhood, that pious mother commendably formed his character according to the integrity of Christ’s teaching. With the wisest judgment she restrained the wanton impulses of childhood, and with unremitting care instructed him, while still almost an infant, to visit the church, listen to God’s words, and frequently attend the divine mysteries. Rabanus was a boy greatly favored by the Lord with gifts both of nature and of grace. These gifts steadily increased in strength with time, until at last they brought him to the summit of the highest perfection. He was teachable in understanding, extraordinarily vigorous in memory, and beautifully proportioned in mind and body; modest and most chaste. In his conduct integrity shone forth, and singular tranquility gleamed in his soul. Yet all these gifts, both of grace and of nature, shone more clearly in him when he had reached manhood, at which time, as a perfect practitioner, he ascended the summit of every virtue.

As far as concerned the visible constitution of the man, he was exceedingly robust in body, of a phlegmatic complexion mixed with blood [Col. 0072B], more stout than thin, strong and large of head, and of pleasingly proportioned form in all his limbs. Since, therefore, the boy of good disposition advanced daily toward better things, and since even then a certain foreboding of his future dignity and holiness shone in him, his pious mother feared that his corruptible body, placed amid a perverse people, might by some circumstance defile his soul, or that his earthly dwelling might weigh down a mind intent on many things (Wis. 9:15). She therefore resolved to hand him over to a monastery, where she had no doubt that he could live more purely. At first, however, this purpose of the mother did not please the father; later, inspired by divine prompting, he approved it. For human counsel is easily changed whenever divine power brings about its impulse, predestined from eternity [Col. 0072C].

At that time the newly founded monastery of Fulda [Note: [Col. 0071D] Begun around the year of Christ 744.] was governed by a most reverend abbot named Bangolfus [Alternative: Baugulfus], a man of great religious devotion and of many virtues in Christ. He succeeded Saint Sturmus [Note: [Col. 0071D] The Fulda Annals report of him under the year 779: “Sturmi, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, died, and Baugulf, a monk of the same monastery, succeeded him”; Saint Sturmus, or Sturmio, died on 16 December and is especially commemorated on 20 April.] as the first abbot of that place and governed it for twenty-five years [Note: [Col. 0072D] Rather, only twenty-two years, from 802 to 817. The Fulda Annals under the year 802 state: “Baugulf, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, relinquished the authority he had held and had Ratgarius as his successor.”], gaining a glorious reputation for holiness among all the Germans. Under the instruction of this renowned abbot, the boy Rabanus, when he was about nine years old, was handed over by his parents and entrusted to the monks to be instructed according to the rule of the holy father Benedict. This solemn entrustment of Rabanus to the monastery took place on the twenty-first day of March, which was solemnized as the feast of that same most holy father Benedict [Col. 0072D], in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 697, in the fifth Roman indiction.

At that time an immense multitude of monks flourished in the aforementioned monastery of Fulda. They led an arduous life for the love of God, abstaining at all times from wine and meat. They did not even take meat broth as food, except for the sick and those utterly weakened, and they did not indulge in the pleasures of this world. Their bread was coarse and rustic; beans, peas, and vegetables were their food, water or beer their drink. They lived by the labor of their hands, like true followers and monks of our father Benedict, since at that time they were not permitted to have secular servants in the monastery. For whatever necessary work arose to be done in the monastery was performed not by secular people but by the hands of the monks.

All the monks then strove to live according to the purity of the monastic rule, in common under the direction of one shepherd, in true poverty, preserving chastity of mind and body inviolate without private possessions, and serving almighty God in the bond of fraternal charity. O [Col. 0073B] happy age, and times abundantly fruitful in the gifts of the Holy Spirit, when those who professed the cloistered life were excellent and wonderfully adorned and endowed with every beauty of virtue!

By divine appointment the boy Rabanus was joined to these men, most holy in life and conduct, in the monastery of Fulda, and was entrusted to a certain venerable elderly monk named Rathgarius, to be imbued with knowledge of letters and holy conduct. From him he was diligently formed in every excellent discipline. The boy also, of good disposition, having obtained a good teacher, and with the help of divine mercy, immediately began well, insofar as his age permitted, the beginnings of a holy life; he progressively advanced it toward what was better and ultimately brought it to a most excellent completion.

After he had completed his sixteenth year [Col. 0073C], that is, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 804 [Note: [Col. 0073D] Browerus maintains that he died in 815, although he survived the relinquishing of his office by thirteen years.], in the twelfth Roman indiction, Baugulf, abbot of Fulda, departed to the Lord in the twenty-fifth year of his rule. After he had been buried with a great reputation for holiness, the aforementioned teacher of Rabanus Maurus, Rahtgarius, succeeded him as the third abbot by the unanimous election of the brothers and governed for sixteen years [Note: [Col. 0074D] Rather, only fifteen years, from 802 to 817, when he is recorded in the same Annals as having been deposed by the brothers], a man of approved religious devotion and great holiness.

He loved Rabanus above all the others with a singular affection, because he knew him to be more ready than anyone else for obedience and indefatigably diligent in reading the divine Scriptures. He saw that Rabanus had been born for arduous tasks and that in time he would benefit many toward salvation by word and example. He also knew that instruction is necessary for shepherds, since a good life without spiritual knowledge of the divine Scriptures is insufficient for the formation of those subject to them. For one who is good only for himself cannot be a useful ruler of others. Therefore Rathgarius by no means judged that the teachable boy should be neglected; enlightened by the divine Spirit, he did not doubt that Rabanus would one day be set over many. Nor was his confidence disappointed, since Rabanus became greater in learning, dignity, and likewise in the merit of holiness than any of his own people could either have thought or imagined.

[Col. 0074A] As soon as he had passed beyond the years of boyhood, he devoted himself entirely to divine service: frequent in church, constant in the choir of those singing psalms, and outstanding in the Lord’s service without any stain of vanity. No monk was more cheerful than he during singing and reading; among them all, no one ever showed himself more ready to obey his elders. He always loved God above all things with the pure elevation of his mind, and whatever he knew to be pleasing to God’s perfectly ordered will, he strove with all his strength to fulfill. Whatever he learned to be contrary to the divine will, he judged should never be admitted into the workshop of his heart.

He kept the eye of his mind pure and clean from the dust of earthly desire, and always lived without offense among his brothers. In [Col. 0074B] holy prayer he was almost continual, and in reading the divine Scriptures he was commendably occupied without interruption. No one saw him idle; no one heard him absorbed in tales or idle conversations, nor did anyone find him wandering through the cloister in the pointless wanderings customary to many. Always devoted in mind to God, he either applied himself to reading the Scriptures, wrote something for the common benefit of the brothers, or else lived alone with himself in his cell.

Nothing was sweeter to him than continual study of the holy Scriptures. Therefore he regarded the solitude of the monastic cell—which many cloistered people find unbearable—as the delights of paradise. For what a stream and water are to fish, the cell is rightly said to be to good and diligent monks. Just as fish cannot live long without water, so monks who frequently roam outside the cell cannot remain in true purity of mind. The cell is a workshop of virtues for monks, while the world, when frequented excessively, is the cause of many vices. The cell is a school of divine knowledge for monks; outside it no instruction in heavenly wisdom is given. Hence the monk who does not love the solitude of his cell does not attain true knowledge of God’s Scriptures.

This our most blessed father, the holy Rabanus, rightly considered, and from his infancy loved the monastic cell. In it he kept his conscience unharmed by the vain works of the world, and attained full knowledge of all writings, both human and divine. The solitude of the cell is compared to the pleasantness of paradise [Col. 0074D]. Dwelling there delightfully, united to himself through continual exercise of divine love, he lived in body and mind quietly with himself in the house of God, devoted in spirit to his Creator, troublesome to none of his brothers, burdensome to none, a weight to none, but welcomed by all good people and sincerely loved in the bond of fraternal charity.

In him was fulfilled that gentle promise of eternal wisdom which is read as having long ago been pronounced through the prophet Jeremiah: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth, for he will sit solitary and be silent, because he will lift himself above himself” (Lam. 3:27 ff.). [Col. 0075A]

These are the banquets of a purified mind, which no one understands unless he receives them, and no one receives them unless he has truly separated himself from every enticement of the flesh for the love of God. For the true joys of the mind and the corruptible pleasures of the belly do not consent to dwell together, since the Savior of all declares that it is impossible to serve two contrary masters.

Blessed, therefore, was this great servant of Christ, Rabanus, who, anticipated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, did not walk in the counsel of the wicked, did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of scoffers; rather, his will was confirmed and established in the law of the Lord, and he meditated on His statutes day and night (Ps. 1:1–2). [Col. 0075B] Blessed, I say, was this man, rightly to be venerated by every generation, who, placed in this mortality, sowed good seed in the blessings of the Lord, from which he now eats the fruit of eternal happiness in heaven. For this reason he is judged worthy of every honor and is to be celebrated in everlasting memory: made an imitator of the Lord’s disciples, he enlightened the whole Church by teaching and conduct, and refuted various errors of heretics by disputation and writing. We shall speak of these more fully below in their proper place.

When, therefore, blessed Magnentius reached the eighteenth year of his age, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 806 [Note: [Col. 0075D] Alcuin died in 804; Rabanus was sent to him in 802.], and was held by an incredible love of the divine Scriptures, and had already equaled or even surpassed all the teachers and masters assigned to him in learning and instruction, [Col. 0075C] yet could not be satisfied with what he had attained through study, but because of the greatness of his desire hastened toward the greater mysteries of sacred learning, he decided to leave temporarily in order to change his place.

For at that time, as afterward, a general course of literary studies had not yet flourished in the monastery of Fulda. The monks, content with a humble understanding of the Scriptures, grave in conduct and imbued with rustic simplicity, did not concern themselves with the higher studies of knowledge. Thus the most blessed young man, unable to satisfy his mind in his own monastery because of his immense desire for the Scriptures and the scarcity of teachers, knew that he had in Rathgarius a favorable shepherd. One day he threw himself at his feet and, with the greatest humility making known what he had in mind, begged the consent of his elder.

The abbot approved the young man’s request, and after taking the advice of the elders gave his petitioner an easy consent. For the prudent elder saw, as was said shortly before, that divine grace shone in him; by its operation he had no doubt that Rabanus would become great. Therefore he gladly granted what was requested [Col. 0076A].

In those days Albinus, also called Alcuin, flourished in the kingdom of the Franks. By nationality an Englishman, by profession a monk [Note: [Col. 0075D] In the Chronicle of Tours he is said to have presided over canons; the ancients are silent concerning his monasticism.], by order a Levite, and by dignity the abbot [Note: [Col. 0075D] At the Roman council held under Leo III in 799, he is called “abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin,” in act 2.] of his monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, he had once been the teacher of King Charles the Great and was most learned in every variety of writing. He was placed in charge of the public schools of monks at Rome among the Gauls and Italians, at Paris, and at Soissons, and wrote much for the common benefit, educating many hearers as extremely learned in every branch of knowledge.

To this venerable man—at that time the custodian and administrator in the city of Rome of the Lateran Church [Note: [Col. 0076D] This is entirely false; the error arose from an incorrect interpretation of a poem prefixed to the work on the Cross.] and presiding over the public schools of monks—Abbot Rathgarius of Fulda [Col. 0076B] sent Rabanus with two other monks, Haimo and Diedo [Note: [Col. 0076D] Rather, he was sent with only one companion, Hatto, not to Rome but to the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours.]. The former later became bishop of Halberstadt, while the latter succeeded Hatto in the abbacy of Fulda by election of the brothers.

Albinus therefore received the monks sent to him from Fulda under the discipline of his instruction, applied every care to them, and spared no labor for their beneficial formation. He nevertheless devoted himself to teaching Rabanus with more eager attention, since he saw that Rabanus was sharper in intellect than the others, and watched over him with singular concern. Rabanus remained with the master Albinus at Rome for six continuous years [Note: [Col. 0076D] But Alcuin died in the second year of Rathgarius’s rule.], as a most diligent hearer and disciple, and devoted tireless study to learning the Scriptures.

In the seven arts which those who teach them call “liberal,” he became most learned. In every field of knowledge, both of divine and human traditions, he had no equal. Indeed, whoever desires to understand more fully how learned he was in grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, poetry and music, astronomy and mathematics, physics and metaphysics, philosophy and theology, and in human as well as divine matters, should carefully read through his volumes, which are both numerous and most elegant.

In disputation he possessed such acumen that he was regarded and recognized as the most famous of all sophists. Thus, like another Augustine, he was the terror and hammer of heretics, whom he all overcame and defeated in easy combat [Col. 0076D]. Yet although he had acquired such a wealth of all knowledge, he was never lifted up into pride, never vainly exalted himself above others in his own judgment, and never even lightly despised those who were simpler and less learned in the Scriptures.

For founded upon true monastic humility, he appeared little in his own eyes [Col. 0077A], and the greater he became, the more he humbled himself. He knew that a monk’s knowledge without true humility of mind is destructive folly, even if he is considered most learned among men. For Scripture says: “A man’s learning is recognized through patience” (Prov. 19). No one deserves truly to be called patient who has not been humble and wholly subjected his will to the command of the Almighty.

Our Rabanus, a true lover of God, who was genuinely humble and patient, humbled his soul before God and men all the more as he advanced further in good studies. Vain ambition for earthly honor did not draw him to study, nor did poverty or want make him a monk diligent in the Scriptures. Rather, the love of God, which conquers all things, inflamed his mind [Col. 0077B] toward the growth of spiritual knowledge.

Nothing is difficult for a good will; nothing is fearful to one who truly loves God. Since he had therefore devoted himself entirely to divine service and sought, desired, or hoped for nothing in this world except God alone and knowledge of the Scriptures, he strove to show himself a worthy minister of Christ, from whom he knew that every perfect gift comes to mortals.

He always kept some book of divine reading in his hands; always, being at one with himself within himself [perhaps *unitus*, “united”], he performed some good work. Neither by day nor by night did he cease investigating the divine Scriptures. For apart from the time required either by unavoidable bodily necessity or by the demands of divine worship, he devoted all the rest [Col. 0077C] to the study of the Scriptures. He considered all time lost that had been spent in any other way than in the praises of God or in sacred reading.

Therefore, whenever he could be free from public activities, he usefully devoted himself to his private pursuits. Always after first offering a prayer, with special devotion of mind toward God, he either read, wrote, or listened to the master Albinus reading in the schools. While he was intent upon these sacred studies and continuously occupied without interruption, the great mercy of God adorned him with the beauty of every virtue. It granted the one who desired it a mind perfected in every respect for understanding the Scriptures, gave him the knowledge of the saints as one who had deserved it well, and brought every good work to completion in him.

At length, after six years had been completed at Rome with the master, with immense progress in learning [Col. 0077D], the blessed servant of God was recalled to the monastery of Fulda, together with Haimo and Diedo, by the command of his shepherd. Although he would much rather have continued the study he had begun for several more years under the direction of his teacher, he nevertheless promptly obeyed his abbot, knowing that obedience surpasses all the virtues of monks and that through it alone the way is opened for those in the cloister to their heavenly homeland.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 812 [Note: [Col. 0077D] This calculation of the years also collapses in light of the statements above.], in the fifth Roman indiction, the blessed Rabanus, then twenty-four years old, returned from Rome with Haimo and Diedo to the monastery of Fulda at his abbot’s command [Col. 0078A], namely, in the eighth year of the aforementioned Rathgarius’s abbacy.

The brothers received him with great joy of charity, honoring in him the manifold gifts of God. For they knew that, not only because of his excellence in knowledge was he a venerable teacher, but much more because of the merit of his life he was rich in every virtue in Christ. During the six years in which he had devoted himself to letters at Rome under the instruction of his abbot, he had made wondrous progress beyond all his contemporaries in every kind of knowledge, human as well as divine. He became the greatest philosopher in every field of learning, a most eloquent poet, and, in the judgment of all, an outstanding theologian.

Finally, he shone with such holiness of virtues and merits throughout all the days of his life, both at Rome and at Fulda, that none of those who lived with him doubted that he had been specially anticipated by the grace of God [Col. 0078B]. Thus he benefited not only himself but showed many the way of salvation by word, writing, and example.

Rathgarius too, the venerable abbot, who, as we said above, loved him more closely than the others, rejoiced at his progress with remarkable affection. He was glad to have such a disciple, already capable of teaching anyone else, and rendered magnificent thanks to almighty God.

Yet, so that Rabanus’s authority among the brothers might be greater through advancement in ecclesiastical rank, he was raised through each degree of sacred ministry, and finally, when he was thirty years old, the abbot promoted him to the dignity of the priestly office [Col. 0078C]. Once consecrated priest, he abandoned nothing of his former humility and neglected nothing of monastic conduct and purity. Rather, subjecting himself to greater humility, he turned his entire mind toward observance of the regular discipline and showed himself most obedient to all his brothers. He was always intent either upon prayer or upon the study of sacred reading.

As was said earlier, the cell was his paradise, and he regarded the choir of his singing brothers as heaven. Because he strove humbly to serve all for the name of Christ, he was rightly loved by everyone. The holy elders loved him as a son; the diligent young men revered him as a teacher of heavenly doctrine. All alike regarded him as an example of the whole monastic religious life and as the supreme lesson of Christian learning.

Abbot Rathgarius, most reverend, rejoiced above all others with a special duty of congratulation, because he saw that the man whom he pursued with singular affection of love possessed such distinguished marks of virtue [Col. 0078D]. And truly he deserved to be loved by all, since he had always loved the Creator of all with a pure affection.

In him was fulfilled that gentle promise of eternal Wisdom which says: “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early will find me. With me,” she says, “are riches and glory, abundant wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my produce than refined silver” (Prov. 8:17).

For Rabanus loved the wisdom of God the Father, whose knowledge is given to believers through faith in the holy Scriptures. He applied himself to reading them all the more frequently as he loved God more sincerely [Col. 0079A]. The fruit of sacred reading was always sweet to his throat; he tasted it in the fervor of the Holy Spirit.

O how truly sweet is the taste of divine love to one who tastes it, by which all the adversities of this world become sweet, and all its allurements grow contemptible to a courageous spirit! Nothing except what is divine is admitted into the affection of the heart where the Creator alone is loved above all things.

Rabanus, of whom we are speaking, was the supreme worker in this sacred workshop. In him the overflowing fullness of spiritual doctrine enlightened the whole Church and instructed many unto righteousness. And so that we may not wander longer in an inverted order, we have judged it worthwhile to return to what was omitted and briefly note what was done concerning Rabanus after his return from the City and before he was ordained a priest.

[Col. 0079B] The memorable abbot Rathgarius, wishing to provide for the benefit of many, established a public school in the monastery of Fulda with the advice of his brothers, and entrusted its direction to Saint Rabanus, who had recently returned from Italy. Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 813, in the sixth Roman indiction, Rabanus, twenty-five years old, was placed in charge of the school of the monastery’s monks and was ordered to maintain among the monks of Fulda the method of teaching he had just learned from Albinus.

As soon as he undertook the office of teaching, he took care in every respect to follow and imitate his teacher Albinus: namely, he first taught the younger monks grammar, and when they appeared capable of greater things, he formed them through more serious disciplines as well.

When the reputation of this new method of instruction had become publicly known among the Germans, several superiors of monasteries, praising this form of teaching, sent some of their monks to Fulda to be instructed in sacred studies under Rabanus’s discipline; others established schools in their own monasteries and placed over them the more learned teachers from the aforementioned monastery.

Within a short time, however, the number of Rabanus’s students increased greatly, and throughout Germany and Gaul the venerable reputation of his learning and holiness spread. As a result, not only abbots and monks but also the nobles of the land placed their sons under Rabanus’s instruction. Since he was most gentle, he carefully trained them all, insofar as each one’s age or intellect permitted [Col. 0080A]: some in grammar, others in rhetoric, and others in the higher writings of divine and human philosophy. Without envy he shared whatever each had requested from him. All whom he admitted to his school for instruction he taught to write whatever arose, not only in prose but also in verse.

He had many distinguished, learned, and most holy hearers. The more outstanding and eminent of them are named individually by Megenfridus in the fourteenth book of *On the Times of Grace*. They are as follows:

Strabus [Note: [Col. 0079D] Walafrid Strabus, abbot of Reichenau], a monk of Fulda, an East Frank by homeland, succeeded his teacher in directing the schools at Fulda. He was most learned in the full range of the Scriptures, practiced in both meter and prose, and composed many works in each genre [Col. 0080B].

Freculfus [Note: [Col. 0079D] He was a disciple of Elizachar], a monk of Fulda, by homeland a Saxon, later bishop of Lisieux in the province of Rouen and an outstanding preacher of the Christian faith. He too composed several small works.

Lutbertus [Note: [Col. 0079D] Also called Lintbertus by others; Trithemius discusses him in the *Hirsau Chronicle*], a monk of Fulda and later the first abbot at Hirsau in the diocese of Speyer, by homeland a Swabian, a teacher outstanding in every variety of Scripture. He was no less distinguished in the merit of his life than in his learning, left behind several memorials of his intellect, and bestowed many benefits upon his good monks.

Hildolfus [Note: [Col. 0079D] Trithemius mentions him nowhere else, not even in the *Hirsau Chronicle*. Is Rudolfus, the author of the earlier Life, to be understood?], a monk of Fulda, an East Frank by homeland, and the first master of the schools at Saint Aurelius in Hirsau. He was a man of most upright conduct and learning and also wrote many useful works.

Ruthardus [Note: [Col. 0079D] He is counted among the saints by Wion, Menardus, and Ferrarius, on 25 October], a monk of Fulda and, after Hildolfus’s death, the second schoolmaster at Hirsau. Since he was most learned, he composed several works.

Bernardus [Note: [Col. 0079D] He is called Brunuart by others], a monk of Fulda and later abbot of Hersfeld, an East Frank by homeland, a man distinguished in wisdom and conduct, produced many works.

Bertholfus, a monk of Fulda, a Thuringian by homeland, was far more learned in both the divine Scriptures and human letters. He too wrote several works.

Joannes, a monk of Fulda, an East Frank by homeland, was an outstanding poet and musician. He wrote several works and was the first among the Germans to compose ecclesiastical chant with varied modulation.

Vingbertus, a monk of Fulda, a Saxon by homeland, was a man of remarkable simplicity and, nevertheless, great learning. He shone with the merit of his life and his virtues.
