Egbertus [Note: [Col. 0079D] There was another Egbertus, two centuries later, who became the twenty-second abbot of Fulda in the year of Christ 1048 and died on 17 November 1058, as Schafnaburgensis and Marianus Scotus write under those years. Lesleus relates the following about him in book five of *On the Affairs of the Scots*, under the eighty-fifth king Machabaeus: “Egbertus, too, abbot of Fulda, flourished at this time. His successor Sigebertus the Scot attained such virtue and piety that, by the unanimous agreement of all, he was declared archbishop of Mainz.” Yet Browerus in book four of the *Antiquities of Fulda* and Ferrarius in book five of *The Affairs of Mainz* show that his successor was not Sigebertus but Sigefridus, who originated among the Germans from the family of Eppstein. Because of Lesleus’s words, Wion assigned Egbertus to the Scots in the appendix to the *Monastic Martyrology*: “Saint Egbertus,” he says, “a Scot, abbot of Fulda, a man distinguished in learning and holiness.” The author of the *English Martyrology* and Camerarius in the *Scottish Menology* cite both men and number Egbertus among the saints: the former on 26 November, the latter on 19 November. Ferrarius follows him in his *General Catalogue of the Saints*, confuses him with the other Egbertus, and conjectures that he lived around the year 690. Would this man not with greater justice be numbered among the saints as a disciple of Rabanus, since he is said to have shone with miracles? Yet we require more solid testimony from the ancients.], a monk of Fulda [Col. 0081A], was a man of admirable life who for a long time voluntarily enclosed himself for Christ and shone with miracles. He composed several works.

Carolus, a monk of Fulda, an East Frank by homeland, was a man of great wisdom and learning. It is said that, after his teacher’s death, he merited the archbishopric of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0081D] This has been refuted above]. He also published several volumes.

Altfridus [Note: [Col. 0082D] We discussed him above], a monk of Fulda, a Saxon by homeland, was distinguished for remarkable holiness and learning and was an outstanding preacher of God’s word. Sent from Fulda as schoolmaster to New Corvey in Saxony, he was later ordained the fourth bishop of the church of Hildesheim.

Meginfridus, the writer of histories, mentions all the distinguished disciples of Rabanus at Fulda listed above and is said to have written various small works. From other monasteries as well he had many distinguished hearers sent to him, men renowned for learning and holiness of life. Since their names are recorded by the aforementioned writer, we have omitted them here for the sake of brevity, lest we cause weariness.

He also took care, this most blessed instructor of monks, to educate his students no less in the fear of God and observance of the commandments than in understanding the Scriptures, knowing that it is written in the holy prophet Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12:3). For it is of little value to educate the understanding of a cloistered man in knowledge unless one also strives, according to one’s ability, to kindle his affections toward the love of God.

In this mode of teaching blessed Rabanus the teacher conspicuously excelled above all others. He first instructed his students in righteousness, repeatedly striving, while they were reading, to persuade them to conform their conduct to the sanctions of the Rule and, above all, always to obey the evangelical precepts. He taught them to despise the world and all the pleasures of the flesh for the love of God, to flee transient vanities and the pomps of the age, and to avoid every desire of an undisciplined will. He admonished them to love God above all things with a pure mind, and carefully impressed upon his disciples that they should remember they would die.

He was so sincere a lover of the monastic way of life that he admitted no one to his school unless he had first examined that person’s mind with the greatest care concerning the integrity of regular observance. Therefore, if he found anyone wandering in mind or body and insufficiently suited to the observance of monastic discipline, he kept him away from access to the mountain of divine Scripture as though he were a brute animal or an unclean beast, saying:

> “It is written: ‘The beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned’” (Exod. 19:12).

“For this reason, brothers, go away, and first learn to compose your minds, so that, with your conduct corrected, you may be worthy to hear the words of God with Moses on the summit of the mountain. For no one profitably apprehends the Scriptures of God by studying them while his soul is still soiled with the dust of vices.”

This form of teaching was always familiar to the holy man: he placed discipline in righteousness before the study of letters, and piety before knowledge of the Scriptures. He was able to persuade others of righteousness and the practice of the virtues all the more easily because he demonstrated them not only in words but also in deeds. He possessed an exceptional gift for teaching and the greatest facility in persuasion. He was sharp in intellect, eloquent in speech, sonorous in voice like a trumpet, and venerable through a certain gravity. Thus, whenever reason required it, he could terrify the wicked by his voice alone, and no less soothe the prostrate by his humility. By the Lord’s generosity he possessed a body suited to the gifts of his soul; in him there was great authority of love, together with a humanity no less marked by gentleness and affability. Using this moderation with the utmost restraint from his youth, he remained tranquil in himself and presented himself to his disciples as a useful and fruitful teacher, as their circumstances required.

According to Meginfridus, there were at that time in the monastery of Fulda 150 monks under the Rule of Saint Benedict, serving almighty God with the highest religious devotion; as stated above, all of them abstained from wine and meat. Of these, at least twelve, said to be exceedingly learned in every branch of scriptural knowledge, were called “Seniors.” The abbot used their counsel in daily necessities, so that there would be no need to weary the entire congregation. Whenever one of these twelve was either sent to another monastery or taken away by death, another of the more learned and holier monks was immediately appointed in his place by the election of the abbot and the Seniors.

This praiseworthy institution of the Seniors lasted for many years—namely, as long as the study of the Scriptures that Saint Rabanus had begun flourished in the monastery of Fulda. The rule of these twelve teachers was that each taught his assigned group, according to the principal arrangement of the master, who was always the thirteenth. For this reason he was appointed over all the lessons, and all the others, after the abbot, were bound to obey him.

As the reputation for holiness and learning of the monks of Fulda, and especially of Saint Rabanus, spread ever farther throughout the entire Frankish realm, many nobles and commoners entrusted their sons to their fellowship to serve the Lord. From among these, the Church later received many bishops and pastors in Germany. For as long as regular observance endured, no one was excluded from the service of God, whether noble or of humble birth; in accordance with the precept of the legislator Benedict, the way was open to all who wished to turn to God with a pure intention.

In the course of time, however, this custom was seen to have been changed, contrary to the intention of the Rule, both in the monastery of Fulda and in many others—after wealth had extinguished religion and luxury, together with the worst kind of ambition, had driven out the study of the Scriptures. At that time the monks’ enthusiasm for the study of the holy Scriptures, which began at Fulda through Saint Rabanus, as we have said above, was extraordinary; within a short time it grew strong throughout nearly all the monasteries of Germany and Gaul. Nor were they content with the Latin and native languages. They judged it necessary for students of divine contemplation to learn and teach Greek, and with labor they also acquired knowledge of Hebrew and Chaldaean.

For Saint Rabanus, a student of Albinus at Rome, had as his teacher a certain Theophilus of Ephesus [Note: What Brower feared concerning Trithemius in his notes on the *Life of Saint Sturmus*—that he had given the reader words which the reader had not asked to receive—we might fear here as well. But from where did Trithemius derive the claim that Rabanus was taught Greek letters at Rome by this Theophilus? Perhaps from Alcuin’s seventy-second letter to him among Alcuin’s Works.], from whom he acquired a sufficient understanding of the language of the Pelasgians—that is, Greek—which, after returning to his homeland, he shared without envy with his own students. Indeed, since he was not only extraordinarily devoted to study but also, without anyone’s dispute, exceedingly learned, he understood very well that no one among the Latins could be found truly educated and accomplished in sacred letters who had not acquired knowledge of the Greek language.

I confirm this all the more confidently because, now that Greek books have been multiplied by the art of printing, I myself, under good teachers, have acquired at least some understanding of this language. For just as a stream comes from a spring, so Latin descends from the Greek language. Whoever despises knowledge of the spring has no real understanding of the force and proper character of the stream from which he drinks.

Rightly, therefore, all Germany together with Gaul in its three divisions venerates this most blessed teacher Rabanus as the unique prince of all learning. From him Roman pontiffs received ecclesiastical discipline, and monks the saving key to the understanding of the Scriptures. Deservedly, I say, all the posterity of the Germans will perpetually resound with the praises of Rabanus, who, after driving out the ancient barbarism, was the first of all to make his nation Latin in language.

For, under the faith of Christ, he was the first of all to teach the Germans to make both the Greek and the Latin languages resound. No one before him, whether born or educated among the Germans, possessing knowledge of Greek, ever composed so many volumes anywhere with such elegance, precision, harmony, and Latinity. If any learned men existed among the Germans in the Frankish realm before him, they were not natives but Greeks, Romans, Gauls, Scots, Britons, or immigrants who had come from elsewhere.

But the most blessed and distinguished teacher of the Christian faith, Rabanus, the unique and first founder of German education and master of learning—who had no predecessor in his own nation as a teacher accomplished in knowledge—was, without doubt, kindled by divine inspiration. What he could not find at home, he commendably sought, found, and learned at Rome, and brought back to the Germans without envy, driving ancient barbarism from his homeland.

He adorned his people with a double ornament: he refined them in conduct toward holiness, and, by infusing into them the elegance of the Roman language, introduced them into the fullness of all knowledge. O teacher worthy of veneration throughout all ages! O prince of letters, to be celebrated forever by all learned men, who led a most holy life in the flesh and poured forth saving instruction upon all the children of the Church! Rightly, I say, he should be commended in the living memory of all, since he not only offered those then living, by his example, nourishment for eternal life but also left salutary instruction to posterity in his writings.

Truly he is worthy that all posterity throughout Germany should celebrate his memory in blessings, through whom such great benefit came to us in mind and body. He always taught the orthodox faith of Christ with the greatest zeal; he was the first among the Germans to render the same sacred Scripture accessible; and, while leading an apostolic life, he refuted the destructive errors of heretics with the utmost firmness and reason.

Finally, as was said above, he was the first among the Germans to maintain a public school for monks, in which he had as students not only cloistered men but also many people living in the world. He turned secular learning toward the service of the divine Scriptures; and, like a second Socrates, transformed philosophy drawn down from heaven into ethics. Therefore, as I remember having said, he fully trained his students in every branch of secular learning, first making them grammarians, dialecticians, rhetoricians, arithmeticians, geometers, astronomers, musicians, and poets, and afterward introducing those who were suitable to the knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

This method of teaching, transmitted by him as a master, continued for many years in the monastery of Fulda and, in the course of time, was transferred with the greatest benefit to many monasteries of Germany. This can easily be confirmed from the writings of the ancients. At that time, apart from the sole order of the holy father Benedict, there were no monasteries of cloistered men throughout Germany: the Cistercians had not yet been instituted, nor the convents of the Mendicant Brothers, nor any other distinct observance; all these arose much later.

Therefore, whenever in this work we mention monks, Benedictines are to be understood, unless another profession is expressly named. For many years this remarkable study of the Scriptures continued in the monasteries of monks, and the sacred order of Benedict produced innumerable men distinguished no less by holiness than by learning.

For we read, as is clearly established by the reckoning of our annals, that from monks professing the order of the holy father Benedict there were, over the course of time, twenty-four pontiffs of the holy Roman Church, 269 cardinals, 1,684 archbishops in the various churches of the world, and 4,512 bishops.

Finally, in the catalogue of the saints, 15,600 are found registered from the same order, besides nuns and innumerable others whose names we do not know.

[Note: On these matters Baronius writes as follows under the year of Christ 494, no. 77: “Since the patriarch Benedict was the most fruitful champion of nearly innumerable most holy and also most learned fathers, in my judgment those who foist upon him offspring whom he did not beget, calling alien births his own, act improperly. I mean those who, through excessive love of the order under which they profess, imprudently and most rashly assert that certain men famous for their reputation, who flourished even before the time of Saint Benedict, were professors of the same Rule. For a second offspring is customarily assigned not to the fertile but to the barren. Among others, Trithemius did this and became the source for later writers who did the same.” Thus Baronius. Yet we produce as saints of this order very many whom Trithemius nowhere mentions.]

These are the fruits of the monks’ salutary study, in which, through Rabanus’s planting, many thousands in every branch of learning and holiness illumine the whole Church. But this holy custom of the monks did not endure to the end, because what had commendably begun in the course of time also shamefully declined with time. For around the year 1100 of the Lord’s Nativity, as various monastic institutions multiplied in the Church of God, the study began to grow lukewarm among our monks and almost died out.

Rabanus Maurus, the distinguished teacher of the monks, after presiding over the schools for five years, set his hand to writing in the thirtieth year of his age. This was the year 818 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the eleventh Roman indiction. His first work was that remarkable book *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*, which he later dedicated to Gregory IV, the supreme pontiff. Concerning it, his teacher Albinus says in the supplication for Maurus:

[Note: Rather, Rabanus himself speaks in the person of his teacher Albinus, who had by then long been dead; and the patron whom he invokes is Saint Martin, not Pope Gregory IV, as was shown above.]

> I taught this boy by the stream of the divine word,  
> through the counsels of ethics and the studies of wisdom.  
> He is indeed a Frank by birth, and an inhabitant  
> of the Buchonian forest, sent here to learn the words of God.  
> For his abbot, the shepherd of the Fulda flock,  
> sent him here, Father, to your dwelling.  
> So that with me he might read the art of scholarly meter  
> and eagerly prepare the sacred Scripture in due form.  
> But when he had completed six lustres, the time had come to write;  
> for the praise of Christ he produced this book with skill.

What and how much he wrote thereafter, and of what kind, the diligent reader will be able to find both at the end of this volume and in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. No German before him composed so many volumes; no one in the Teutonic nation had previously labored through so many useful treatises for the Church, radiant with such beauty and elegance of Latin speech. For he expounded the Old and New Testaments in their entirety in many volumes and splendidly adorned them with brilliant commentaries.

He continued this devotion to writing without interruption from that time until his death, for thirty-nine years. In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 820, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, Rathgarius, the third abbot of Fulda, [Note: A verb is missing here, such as “was deposed,” or something similar. It was stated above that the chronology does not fit. On the Fulda schism under Abbot Rathgarius there is a poem by Rabanus, no. 30. His deposition is discussed at greater length in the *Life of Eigil*, his successor, by Candidus, then a monk of Fulda.] [lacuna: “was deposed,” or something similar] Aegiso, an elderly and religious man, succeeded him as fourth in the order of abbots by the election of the brethren and ruled for five years. Under him blessed Rabanus vigorously continued the office of teaching that he had begun, leading a most religious life in the full practice of every virtue and continually expounding the sacred Scripture for the glory of almighty God, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## BOOK TWO

Up to this point, most reverend bishop and illustrious prince Albert, with the help of the Lord God we have completed the first book on the life of Saint Rabanus, your predecessor. In it we set forth in an open narrative his conversion to monastic institutions, as well as his study and learning in the Scriptures, so that we might commend forever to the memory of posterity the fervor of divine love and fraternal charity with which so great a man began his way of life.

Now, in the following book, which we add as the second, we proceed first to commend in writing the period during which he presided as abbot over the monastery of Fulda, insofar as our very limited strength [perhaps, *se*, “themselves”] can extend, so that we may not deprive the history of its proper order. We do not, however, promise to write everything he did during his abbacy; rather, from among many things we record only a very few, since through the negligence of writers we have been unable to discover what more important matters remained.

In the year 825 of the Lord’s Nativity [Note: Rather, it was the year 822, as was proved above], in the third Roman indiction, Aegiso, the fourth abbot of the monastery of Fulda, died in the fifth year of his administration. He was a religious man in conduct and life and an outstanding lover of the divine Scriptures. After his burial, Rabanus Maurus Magnentius, the renowned teacher and master of the monks, was appointed abbot by the common election of the brethren, fifth in order, in the thirty-seventh year of his age. He presided for twenty-two years, displaying himself as a shepherd of Christ’s sheep, admirable in every holiness of life and always effective in his work.

The first abbot of Fulda instituted by Saint Boniface the archbishop was Saint Sturmus, an Englishman by birth [Note: Others write *Sturmius*, *Sturmio*, and *Sturmis*. His disciple Eigil, the fourth abbot, wrote his life.] [Note: Eigil says in the *Life*: “He sprang from the province of Noricum, begotten and reared by noble and Christian parents.” Brower notes that the Boii are meant, because the Norici migrated into the territory of the Boii. Enough has been said concerning the other abbots.], in the year of the Lord 743, in the eleventh Roman indiction; he presided for thirty-six years. After him Baugolfus was abbot for twenty-five years. Rathgarius succeeded him and ruled for sixteen years. After his death, Aegil was abbot for five years. When he had died, Saint Rabanus, fifth in the order of the brethren, was appointed, as we have said.

Thus, from the foundation of the monastery of Fulda up to Rabanus himself, over eighty-two years, there had been four abbots in succession. Rabanus, therefore, was appointed fifth abbot of the aforesaid monastery in the year already mentioned, which was the tenth year of Louis, king of the Franks, the Pious [Note: It would rather have been the eleventh according to Trithemius, since he succeeded his father Saint Charlemagne on 28 January 814; or else only the first year of Pope Eugenius II, who was created on 19 May 824], the second year of Pope Eugenius II, and the first year of Othgarius, archbishop of Mainz [Note: Seranius writes in Book IV of the *History of Mainz* that throughout this entire year 825 and almost the following year 826 Haistulphus, Othgarius’s predecessor, was still alive, and says that he died on 28 December, the feast of the Holy Innocents, in the year 826. Othgarius would rather have been given as his successor in the year 827. Haistulphus is numbered among the saints in the manuscript *Acts of the Patrons of the City of Mainz*].

He persevered in his former humility and, as he had been accustomed to do, continued his life continually before God in complete purity of mind and body. He loved God above all things with a clean conscience, and for his love despised everything else. He was always mindful of God’s commandments with all his heart and never ceased from the good work. He was so devoted and constant in prayer that no one unfamiliar with his way of life would have thought that he could devote even a moment to reading the Scriptures or labor over any new composition.

Again, in reading the divine Scriptures, in almost daily labor over new volumes, in teaching and forming the monks entrusted to him in piety toward divine worship, observance of regular discipline, and integrity of conduct, and no less in arranging the administration of the household, he was so frequent and diligent that he seemed to have no time at all for prayer. For the love of God, with which he burned wholly aflame, did not permit him to be idle, since, as blessed Gregory most truthfully testifies from experience, the love of God is never idle. Great things are hoped for when it exists; but if it refuses to work, it certainly was never the true love of God.

Blessed Abbot Rabanus, therefore, solicitous for Christ’s sheep and sparing little of the weakness of his nature, devoted to prayer and study all the time he could steal from the duties of household administration. He had a monk named Strabo [Note: This is the same man as Walafridus Strabo, later abbot of Reichenau, as was said above.], a Frank by birth and from the city of Praeapolis [Note: Should *Poapolis* be written? *póa* means “herb,” so that the city of Herbipolis might be understood. We read nothing elsewhere about his birthplace. Trithemius, in Book II *On Illustrious Men*, where he distinguishes Strabo from Walafridus, writes that both were Teutonic by nation, in chapters 35 and 41], a man exceedingly learned in every branch of divine and human letters, skilled through long practice in both verse and prose, and venerable no less for the merit of his life than for his learning in the Scriptures. He placed him over the school of the monks as his successor [Note: We have discussed him above. In his *Hirsau Chronicle* under the year 854, Trithemius proves that Gerungus II, abbot of Hirsau, had been his student at Fulda, and says that he “found a little book by Strabo on arithmetic measurements, prefaced by a letter to this Gerungus beginning as follows: ‘To Gerungus, the most reverend father in merit, a son in age, a disciple in letters, and a teacher in grace, abbot, may he possess the reward of eternal blessedness.’” These are his words, though they present difficulties: for Walafridus Strabo died five years before this Gerungus was made abbot. Browerus failed to notice this; in the same chapter 14 of Book I of the *Antiquities of Fulda* he states both that Strabo was Walafridus and that he died in 849, and from this proves that Gerungus was his disciple].

He ordered him to observe and continue the method of teaching that had been introduced. This Strabo wrote many works in both prose and verse. Finally, Rabanus himself, a most watchful shepherd, did not entirely abandon the task of teaching on account of his abbacy, nor did he cease composing volumes. As a sincere lover of God, whenever he could do so at a suitable time, he resumed the office of teaching as before.

Therefore, so that he might have greater freedom for interior concerns, he appointed capable and suitable administrators of temporal affairs, whose fidelity he could not doubt. He strove to seek the kingdom of God above all things and never involved himself with excessive anxiety in transitory matters. And because he loved God above all things with all his heart, he obtained from him the necessities of this life in great abundance.

Nevertheless, he was extremely solicitous concerning the governance of souls. He took the greatest care to feed the sheep of Christ entrusted to him with the word of salvation, the example of holiness, and the nourishment necessary for their support. Under his governance, the monastery of Fulda grew daily in both possessions and persons, and the reputation for holiness of its monks spread throughout the Frankish realm.

Yet the reputation of Abbot Rabanus for learning and holiness was especially celebrated and glorified in everyone’s speech, not only among the Franks of Germany but also among the Gauls and Italians. The fame of this man moved kings and princes, bishops and every sort of teacher, even those living at a great distance, to venerate him. All admired his incomparable learning and everywhere proclaimed with continual praise the holiness joined to his erudition.

From every part of the Frankish realm—which at that time was one realm—Germans and Gauls flocked eagerly to hear him. They considered themselves blessed if they had been admitted to his familiarity. Many princes, nobles, and citizens also entrusted their sons to Rabanus’s instruction, honoring their teacher with various and magnificent gifts and presents. He taught them with such diligence that scarcely could anything greater be imagined.

He was patient in labor and judged nothing burdensome or difficult if it contributed either to the honor of God or to the benefit of his neighbor. Therefore he did not wish to appear to have been born for himself alone, since he always sought the salvation of others as his own. By God’s providence he was highly suited to the governance of souls, second to none in vigilance, piety, discernment, prudence, action, and learning.

There was no partiality toward persons in him, but only selection according to merit. As soon as he had been appointed abbot, he followed the Rule of the father Benedict in everything, as the teacher of justice, and never rashly departed from it throughout his life. For in that Rule Abbot Benedict gives the abbot this command:

> “A freeborn man is not to be preferred over one who has converted from servitude, unless another reasonable cause exists. For whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ, and under one Lord we bear an equal service in warfare, because with God there is no partiality toward persons. We are distinguished before him only in this respect: whether we are found humble and better than others in good and holy works.”

Saint Abbot Rabanus strove continually to fulfill these and other institutions of monastic perfection, together with the evangelical precepts and counsels, and he showed himself in the monastery to be a faithful minister and representative of Christ.

In his teaching he guarded the apostolic rule in which Paul, the lover of Christ, commanded his disciple, saying: “Reprove, beseech, rebuke” (2 Tim. 4)—that is, with discerning judgment, mingle times with times and gentleness with terrors. He displayed toward the monks subject to him both the harsh feeling of a teacher and the devoted affection of a father. When they were undisciplined and hard of heart, he rebuked them more severely; but the obedient, gentle, and humble he benevolently entreated with paternal affection, so that they might advance toward what was better.

He never concealed the sins of wrongdoers. As soon as vices began to arise, he cut them out by the roots. Those who were more honorable and noble in spirit he corrected gently at the first or second admonition and immediately recalled to soundness of mind by the mildest prayer. But if any wicked, hard-hearted, proud, or disobedient persons appeared, he chastised them more severely not only with words but also with blows and abstinence, knowing that it is written: “A fool is not corrected by words” (Prov. 18). And again: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” [Alt.: “from hell”] (Prov. 23:14).

He was accustomed daily to turn over in his heart, with singular devotion, the meditation on the Lord’s passion, and to give thanks, weeping and groaning, for the innocent death of the Savior. For he is said to have made it a holy custom never to take food unless he had first given thanks and, beginning with the incarnation, passed through in meditation, groaning, and prayer the life, acts, and passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, point by point, up to his ascension into heaven.

As evidence of the truth of this stands his work *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*, in which he unraveled the mysteries of the Lord’s passion with the utmost diligence and devotion. For if he had not deeply sympathized with the suffering Christ, he could never have written such an abundance of praise in memory of his passion. But because he possessed a mind compassionate toward Christ, piety supplied the strength that weakness denied.

Of all spiritual exercises, meditation on the Lord’s passion is the greatest. A monk who persists in it rightly and with sound understanding will quickly discover great progress in his inner way of life. I have placed the monk above the worldly man in this holy meditation because, stripped of secular affairs, he is rightly considered more suited to meditation on the Lord’s passion, life, and death.

Rabanus’s way of life was greatly separated from the world [Col. 0090A]; for this reason he became close to God and was monastically united to himself through the binary in the ternary. No one profitably understands the mystery of the ternary’s relation to the monad in this most holy way of life while still soiled with the dust of vices.

For whoever, purified from the pleasures of the flesh and separated from the empty cares of the world, dwells alone in the house of the Lord, already begins commendably to have the eyes of his mind opened, and loves or fears nothing except God alone. By this most holy kind of purification, blessed Abbot Rabanus was wonderfully enlightened. He feared God above all things and judged it terrible to appear before his sight either guilty or idle in good works.

Therefore, often terrified by the thought of the death that awaited him, and of the one to whom he would one day have to render an account of his stewardship, he carefully reflected on it, knowing that the governance of souls is the art of all arts. He continually turned over in his mind the remembrance of the account he would have to render, knowing clearly that whatever the master of the household might find lacking in usefulness among his sheep would lie as a fault upon the shepherd.

For this reason he resolved with the greatest effort to live in such a way that, insofar as human frailty allowed, he might appear more secure before God when rendering his account. Thus he strove to show himself at all times a true shepherd of Christ’s sheep, no less in deed than in speech. For this reason he showed in his own actions that everything he taught his disciples to be contrary to the good was not to be done.

He strove to show himself pleasing to almighty God in all his actions. He loved God with a pure conscience, a clean heart, and the most fervent desire of charity. He was always rightly ordered in his own conduct and never departed from the paths of righteousness. Toward his subjects also he showed himself properly ordered under vigilant care, seeking their benefit and progress in everything. [The supplied text repeats *quaesivit* (“he sought”).]

He was ardent and fervent in love of neighbor for God’s sake. He was burdensome to no one, injurious to no one, troublesome to no one; harming no one, he benefited everyone. Obediently clinging to the evangelical precepts, he first diligently bestowed upon others the good that, according to the sound judgment of reason, he wished to be done to himself.

He sincerely loved everyone in Christ, anticipated everyone in honor, and took care to benefit all according to his ability. Truly denying himself for the love of Christ, he subjected his own will in everything to the evangelical commandments and monastic institutions. Having put to death destructive desires and the pleasures of the flesh, he took up the Christian weapons of patience and did not lack martyrdom under the order of confession. For he continually afflicted his body severely with fasts, vigils, prayers, disciplines, and other harsh monastic exercises. He always abstained from meat, wine, and every more luxurious food, sustaining the needs of nature as best he could with beans, peas, and vegetables.

He loved fasting as though it were the delights of paradise and always placed nourishment of the soul before the needs of the flesh. Whatever he was able to take away from his own necessities, he immediately decided to distribute for the use of the poor.

For since he was most compassionate toward the poor, both as abbot of Fulda and as archbishop of Mainz, he treated them with such mercy that he seemed to make no provision for the following day. Hence good and God-fearing men called him the father of the needy and the host of the poor.

But those whom an insatiable greed for gold had inflamed with the fires of avarice customarily called him—not compassionate, merciful, or generous, but wasteful, vainglorious, and a squanderer of Christ’s property. Thus virtue always has its haters, who, following the example of the Pharisees and scribes, recklessly twist into an evil and sinister meaning the good that they cannot deny in their neighbor.

Blessed Rabanus suffered many things of this kind from wicked men. Although they could not deny his compassion toward the poor, they did not hesitate, out of a desire for vanity, to attribute it to him, asserting that he gave alms out of love of empty praise rather than for the honor of God.

But the man of God, fighting under the faith of Christ and already burning with the stable firmness of the ray of divine love, paid no attention to the vain chatter of slanderers and did not for that reason cease from the good work he had begun, although he was pressed not only by the detractions of his own people but also by their insults.

Nor is it surprising that in so great a congregation of good men there were also some less perfect or wicked, since among Christ’s twelve apostles one was found to be the betrayer of his teacher, and among the first seven deacons of the Church one proved to be the originator of error bearing his own name.

Nevertheless, the Almighty did not abandon his servant in tribulation. He found him, after being tested in many ways in the furnace of poverty, faithful and almost invincible through the steadfast firmness of his good will. None of those who held the love of God and the study of the sacred Scriptures dear troubled the man of God in any way when he gave alms. But among the monks whom he had appointed ministers and stewards of domestic affairs, some, inflamed by the torches of avarice, opposed the good works of their shepherd.

One of these was a man named Edelhardus, a Frank by birth, excessively concerned with worldly affairs. The father had appointed him chief cellarer of the household. The demands of fairness require that we write the history of his misfortune.

The most compassionate father of the needy ordered by public decree that whenever anyone outside the monastery’s boundaries exchanged this pitiable life for death, his provision of food and drink should, intact and without reduction, be distributed to the poor for thirty consecutive days for the salvation of the deceased’s soul.

It happened, moreover, in the twelfth year of Abbot Rabanus, which was the year 837 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, that several monks in the Fulda monastery, called by the Lord, migrated from this misery to the life to come. Therefore the holy man, sympathizing both with the dead and with the living poor, gave Adelhardus, the steward of the household, a very earnest command, saying to him in the presence of everyone:

“Take the greatest care, brother, to distribute faithfully to each of the poor the provisions of my deceased brothers, full and entire, just as I have ordained for their salvation. If you neglect this, know that your soul will be guilty at God’s strict judgment and will be punished.”

Adelhardus replied that he would gladly carry out his father’s commands. But, O deadly poison, how harmful avarice always is to those living in the cloister: it makes them forgetful of their own salvation and stubborn in pride against monastic purity. Adelhardus, slow to obey, tardy in compassion, and wholly ardent in avarice, neglected the poverty of the poor and, led astray by excessive greed, fraudulently withheld the assistance owed to the dead. Partly out of contempt for the abbot, whose compassion he opposed, and partly through avarice—which was no less destructive than lukewarmness—he was given over to a depraved mind: he either retained altogether the provisions assigned to those resting in the Lord, or distributed them to the poor dishonestly.

But divine justice did not allow such rashness to go unpunished. One day, when he was excessively occupied with external administrative concerns and the hour had grown late, while the others were sleeping and he alone was making his way through the chapter house toward the dormitory, carrying in his hands, as usual, a small lamp, he saw many monks seated there in a circle, clothed in their customary black garments. Seized by great terror, he did not know what to do. It was late at night, and he could not imagine that the community had then assembled together. When he looked more carefully, he recognized that they were the individual shades of the brothers who had recently died, whose assigned stipends he had withheld. Overwhelmed beyond measure, he tried to retreat. But excessive fear, driving his blood violently backward, caused his legs and feet to stiffen so completely that he could not move from the spot.

At once the terrifying shades of the dead spirits rose up violently. Seeing him prostrate in overwhelming fear, they stripped him by a hidden power of his garments, leaving his back bare—not merely as is customary when we administer correction, but his entire body as well—and beat the wretched man, striking him visibly with rods. Their voices joined together in a horrible sound:

“Take [perhaps: ‘Receive’], wretch, the punishment for your avarice that you have deserved; after three days you will receive heavier things, once you have been counted among the dead with us.”

The shades immediately vanished, and Adelhardus remained lying there like a dead man. Around midnight, when the brothers rose for the morning praises, they found the beaten wretch lying in the chapter house, more like a corpse than a living man. He was carried to the infirmary and, with the brothers’ help, eventually returned to consciousness. He disclosed to those listening what he had seen and what evils he had suffered, and foretold that he would die on the third day, according to the word of the spirits who had appeared to him. And lest they think it a dream or merely a mental affliction, he said:

“Look at the wounds and examine the bruises of the blows, for no one could be marked in this way while sleeping, without some violent external force leaving its impression.”

Those standing around gazed upon him, stricken by pitiable severity, and could not restrain their tears. Among them the holy shepherd Rabanus felt an especially abundant affection of charity and devout compassion for the sheep in such peril. Therefore, diligently fulfilling the duty required of an abbot, he exhorted the man, whose strength was already failing, with paternal affection to do penance for his offenses and in no way to despair of God’s mercy. After his salutary admonition had made him contrite and penitent, he fortified him with the Lord’s sacraments and commended him more earnestly to the Lord in prayer as he was dying.

With a great and manifest sign of true contrition, he departed this life on the third day. After his death, the most blessed Abbot Rabanus offered to almighty God the sacrifice of the saving Victim for the remedy of his soul; he imposed fasts and prayers upon himself and the brothers, increased the almsgiving, and mercifully devoted whatever good he could to the man’s salvation.

Then, behold, on the thirtieth day after his death, the deceased appeared visibly and filthy to Rabanus, who was praying in his cell after the morning praises, and he showed to some extent what he was suffering both by his appearance and by the clothing and form he had assumed. The man of God was not at all frightened and said to him:

“How is it with you, brother, and what is now happening to you, since you appear to me so filthy? Tell me, I beg you by the Lord, what benefit have our prayers, chastisements, and fasts brought you?”

The spirit replied:

“Your prayers were pleasing and acceptable to almighty God, and they provided me no small relief from my punishments. But I cannot obtain complete pardon until our brothers, whom I delayed in purgatorial punishments through my greed and negligence while I was in the flesh, have ascended purified into heaven. For the provision that would otherwise have been owed to me also came to them as assistance, just as divine justice ordained. But I beg you, father, let the provisions for the poor be doubled, and I trust that through God’s mercy I shall be freed more quickly.”

The holy man promised to do what the deceased had requested. He doubled the provisions for the needy and continued his prayers. After another thirty days, the deceased appeared once more to the living shepherd in radiant attire; he reported that he had now been freed, and gave thanks to the Lord God and to Rabanus.

From that time the monks of Fulda, struck with fear by this most pitiable story, took careful pains to make satisfaction for the dead and strove to observe their abbot’s commands without contradiction, as though they had come forth from God himself. For since the memory of this event among those who were then living as mortals was utterly indelible, it had struck the minds of all with such fearful dread that they not only distributed in full the provisions owed to their deceased brothers, in their entirety and for the use of the poor, but each person also willingly set aside something daily from his own portion of food and contributed it to the support of the needy.

The blessed Abbot Rabanus also enacted another highly necessary regulation, which, it is said, is still observed in the monastery to the present day. Knowing how dangerous the frequent sight of women is for monks, especially for those who are younger in age and whose senses are still less trained in the fear of the Lord, he permanently prohibited all women from approaching the monastery, on the advice of twelve elders. To give this holy regulation lasting force, he permanently forbade and prohibited passage by the female sex through the city’s northern gate, outside which the monastery is situated.

At the beginning of this regulation, a certain noble matron, overcome by feminine curiosity and scorning the holy abbot’s prohibition, went out through the forbidden city gate with a crowd of attendants and entered the monastery church with presumptuous boldness. Immediately seized by a demon, she began to utter horrifying cries and terrified those standing nearby with overwhelming fear. Her attendants carried her back into the town with her hands bound and, amid tears, entrusted her recovery to the prayers of Rabanus and the monks.

But, by the Lord’s permission, the demon raged against her so cruelly that within a few days she was compelled to die, while the demon continually cried out within her:

“God’s sentence has been given against me, because no one, except death alone, will drive me from this vessel.”

It is established that similar things later happened to several women whom a demon invaded under a similar presumption. Nevertheless, on the feast of Saint Boniface the martyr and on the feast of the dedication, women are permitted to approach only the monastery church—a permission that was entirely denied in the time of blessed Rabanus and for many years thereafter.

After these and many other things had been praiseworthily established and wondrously accomplished by the man of God, no one could doubt his sanctity, since everyone saw such ready divine power attending his command. Accordingly, his name became gloriously famous throughout the entire kingdom of the Franks, and many people from distant regions of the earth, stirred by the reputation of his learning and holiness, flocked daily to see and hear him. Having observed his way of life and conduct, they advanced to better things.

He shone in the Fulda abbey through many virtues and signs, the memory of which the excessive lapse of time has hidden from us and buried in perpetual oblivion. Thus present things are always cheap in the eyes of mortals: no matter how excellently the words or deeds of distinguished men are reported in their own times, people disdain not only to commend them in writing but even refuse to grant their merits praise worthy of them. They eagerly read the magnificent deeds of the ancients and celebrate them with praise, but they deprive men of their own time—even if they are better than those of old—of the recognition due to their merits, despising them as familiar and therefore of lesser value.

Human judgment concerning matters is always so unjust that it marvels at what is unknown and celebrates it with praise, while it treats what is known and present to it as worthless, giving greater credence to uncertain writings from elsewhere than to the knowledge or judgment of its own eyes. Hence many who accomplished great things in this world during their own times suffer injustice and, because of the scarcity or negligence of writers, have obtained no or little remembrance among posterity.

So it was with Rabanus, a most holy abbot: he performed great works in his days, yet did not receive from writers a remembrance worthy of his merits. For the aforementioned author Meginfridus reports in his volume *On the Times of Grace* that this Rabanus, the most blessed abbot, illuminated two blind men by his prayers to God, restored the use of their legs to four lame men, expelled demons from several human bodies, and shone forth through many other miracles. But he did not set out clearly enough in what order these things occurred. Nevertheless, there is no reason to doubt Rabanus’s holiness merely because we have not found his life arranged in sequence by the ancients, since similar things happened to many saints.

If anyone doubts this man’s holiness, let him reread attentively the books that he once published with great labor. He wrote excellent works, for, illuminated by the divine Spirit, he lived purely, holily, and irreproachably amid a crooked nation. Nor could one who taught and wrote such holy things have lived otherwise. Since he was ardent in divine love, no time passed without spiritual exercise, for he had devoted himself wholly to the service of God. He read what was useful, wrote holy things, taught what was right, practiced heavenly things, and meditated continually on divine matters.

This holy manner of life made him rightly venerable to us on earth and rendered him glorious with all God’s saints in heaven. As a young man he began to live for God in the monastery and faithfully continued his good beginnings until death. He was an innocent monk; an abbot always making progress in God; an outstanding archbishop among prelates; a most fervent lover and practitioner of brotherly charity; and he sought the salvation of all with the greatest diligence.

Therefore, kindled by zeal for divine love, he supplied monks from his own community, when requested, to many monasteries then being newly founded, as well as abbots distinguished for their learning. He kept the weaker monks, those less zealous and less perfect in regular observance, with him in the monastery and never ceased daily to compel them toward better things under the rod of discipline. To monasteries newly founded, however, he sent not the weak but the strong—not the lukewarm and worldly, but men perfected and complete in conduct and learning.

In the thirteenth year of his abbatial rule, which was the year 838 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the first Roman indiction, when a certain Count Erlafrid had built from the foundations a new monastery at Calbe, near Hirsau in the diocese of Speyer, in memory of Saint Aurelius the bishop, he sent an embassy to Fulda with letters and petitions from Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, and [perhaps: to] Abbot Rabanus. He asked him for monks and entrusted to his direction the monastery he had built.

Out of reverence for God, the latter granted the petitioner’s request and appointed Lutbert the first abbot of Hirsau. He added to him fifteen monks from his own community, men perfected in every aspect of monastic religion.

To the monastery of New Corbie, which began to be founded in the Saxon region now called Westphalia in the year 822 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, he later sent accomplished monks, learned and most holy men.

**Note:** The ancient author on the construction of the monastery of Corbie in Meibomius and in volume II of the *Writers of France*, Schafnaburgensis in his *Chronicle*, Albertus Crantzius, book I of the *Metropolis*, chapter 19, and others agree on the year. Among them was Saint Altfrid, later the fourth bishop of Hildesheim, who became one of their number and through whom God displayed many signs and miracles to the faithful.

**Note:** This is the Armenian bishop of the Bedicians, a contemporary and contemporary in age of Saint Basil the Great, whom Galesinius, Ferrarius, and others report as being honored on 9 November; Trithemius gives 25 May.

**Note:** On this new Corbie, see Radbert’s *Life of Saint Adalard*, chapter 16, and the *Life of Saint Ansgar*.

**Note:** More precisely, Westphalia. Modern geographers collect much material concerning the origin of this word, as does Werner Rolewinck in book 2, chapter 2, of *On the Site and Customs of the Westphalians*. None of them grants the origin of the name to the Gauls. Concerning these people, the Saxon poet, who lived in the time of Emperor Arnulf down to the year 772, writes:

> But the general division holds the peoples in three groups,
>
> Marked by which Saxony once flourished:
>
> The names now remain; the ancient virtue has departed.
>
> Finally, they call “Westphalians” those dwelling in the western part,
>
> Whose boundary is not far distant from the Rhine
>
> By the river. The lands toward the rising sun
>
> Are inhabited by the Oosterlingi, whom some
>
> Call by another name “Ostphalians”; their borders
>
> The treacherous Slavic people assail where they join their own.
>
> In the region lying between those mentioned
>
> Dwell the Angarii, the third people of the Saxons . . .

Thus they are called Westphalians because they lived in the western part, edge, or boundary of the Saxons; and Ostphalians because they lived in the eastern part. *West* means west, *oost* east, and *palen* boundaries, limits, or frontiers of regions or an empire.

To many other monasteries newly built at that time, the blessed Father sent abbots and monks. For the sake of brevity we have passed over their names in silence, since we are reasonably hastening toward the end of the history.

While the most reverend Abbot Rabanus was living irreproachably according to the monastic rule and instructing many in righteousness by word and example, the adversary of all goodness raged against him. In various ways he labored to weaken and completely overthrow the man’s purpose. Having attacked the holy man through many different means of harm and finding that he could in no way break his steadfastness of mind, he cunningly strove to provoke the minds of his subjects to hatred of their shepherd.

In the fifty-seventh year of his life, therefore, according to Meginfridus, who later became a monk at Fulda, a serious and harmful dissension arose between him and his monks at the devil’s instigation.

**Note:** From this passage we showed above that Trithemius is in error by three years here in reckoning the age. Meginfridus did not state its cause.

**Note:** Rather, as stated in the earlier *Life*, no. 49, Rabanus withdrew to the church of Saint Peter on the hill east of the monastery and completed the books he had begun.

When Louis, king of the Germans, brother of Lothair, emperor and king of Italy, and son of Louis I, heard of this, he sent messengers to Fulda, summoned Rabanus the abbot to him, and restrained the monks’ rashness by royal authority. He received Rabanus with honor and kept him with him at the royal court for nearly two years.

**Note:** It is certain from what has been stated above that he lived privately for five years.

Meanwhile the monks of Fulda, moved to repentance, sent envoys to the king, humbly asking him to return the abbot who had been taken from them. For a reasonable cause, however, the abbot himself refused to do this, and the king absolutely declined to consent. The blessed Abbot Rabanus therefore remained at the royal court for two years, until the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, while the monks mourned in the meantime.

**BOOK THREE**

After the death of the aforementioned Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, who was fifth in the succession of archbishops and died in the year 847 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the tenth Roman indiction, on 21 April, at the monastery of Saint Alban the martyr near Mainz, and was honorably buried in the chapel of Saint Boniface, in the twenty-second year of his episcopate, the blessed Rabanus Maurus Magnentius, abbot of Fulda, was elected archbishop of Mainz through the advancement of King Louis. He succeeded according to the wishes of the nobles and presided for nine years and four months.

**Note:** It is certain from letter 40 of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, to Rabanus that Hatto succeeded the retiring Rabanus at the church of Saint Peter in 842: “I have heard,” he says, “that you have laid down the burden of your administration and are now devoted solely to divine matters, while you have left to our Hatto a care full of toil.” The *Fulda Annals* place Hatto’s death in 856, stating that he died on 12 April. He therefore presided not seven years but about thirteen. Brower supplies further details in his work on Fulda; these Annals shed clearer light on the matter than the manuscript catalogue of the ancient abbots cited in the scholia to Rabanus’s poems, no. 28, where he is said to have ruled for twenty-two years, from 841 to 862.

**Note:** Others give twenty-first, since it is thought that he was ordained at the beginning of the year 827 or at the end of the preceding year.

Hatto, appointed in his place and succeeding him in the abbacy of Fulda, presided for seven years.

Thus Rabanus, in the fifty-ninth year of his life, which was the seventh year of Emperor Lothair, the second year of Pope Leo IV, and likewise the seventh year of Louis, king of the Germans,

**Note:** More precisely, the first: for when Sergius died on 12 April of this year, 847, Leo succeeded on the same day, according to Anastasius the Librarian and Baronius, no. 7.

 and the previously mentioned year from the Lord’s Nativity, was ordained archbishop. He did not diminish the former rigor of his life in anything; rather, as though he were then beginning for the first time to turn to God, he maintained the discipline of regular observance, increased in many respects, until death.

He abstained especially from meat and wine, sought no delicacies, and admitted no pleasures or enticements of weak flesh or of the world. Baths and everything that nourishes the tender body but relaxes the mind he rejected under perpetual condemnation. As a true bishop and fervent minister of Christ, he guarded the flock entrusted to him with the greatest diligence. By word and example, and with the nourishment of this life, he fed and nurtured it with every care he could provide.

The apostolic saying of Paul never departed from his memory:

> “A bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, adorned with virtues, prudent, modest, hospitable, and a teacher of sound knowledge; not given to wine, not violent, but moderate; not quarrelsome, not greedy, and possessing a good testimony even from those outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and the devil’s snare” (1 Timothy 3).

Turning all these matters over frequently in his mind, he omitted nothing that seemed required by the duty of episcopal ministry, but always displayed himself to everyone irreproachable in good works.

As has been said, he was ordained archbishop on 26 June, a day solemnized by the feast of Saints John and Paul the martyrs, at Mainz in the cathedral church, with King Louis and many others present.

**Note:** The *Fulda Annals*: “In the same year, at the command of King Louis, he held a synod at Mainz around the Kalends of October.”

In that same year, at the command of King Louis, he held a synod at Mainz in the monastery of Saint Alban the martyr, around the beginning of October. He summoned to it not only many bishops and abbots from his own province but also many from other regions. With their counsel, he prudently established many measures for the common benefit of the Church.

**Note:** He copied this from the same *Annals*, where it is said that a woman named Thiota came from the regions of Alemannia. Trithemius relates the same story in his *Hirsaugiensis Chronicle* under the year 848.

Around this time a certain woman named Thierda, a false prophetess, came to Mainz from foreign regions. Through her prophecies she had greatly disturbed the parish of Solomon, bishop of Constance. For she publicly proclaimed that she knew, as though divinely revealed to her, the precise day when the end of the age was soon to occur, along with many other things known only to God. She said that the final day of the world was imminent in that same year.

Many people of both sexes, struck by fear, therefore came to her, offered gifts, and commended themselves to her prayers as though to those of some holy woman. More seriously, even men of the sacred order, setting aside ecclesiastical teaching, followed her as though she had been sent from heaven as a teacher.

She was brought before the holy archbishop Rabanus and the other bishops at Saint Alban and carefully questioned about her assertions. She confessed that a certain priest had suggested these things to her and that she had sown such claims among the people for the sake of profit. Therefore, by synodal judgment, she was publicly beaten with whips. She lost, amid the greatest disgrace and manifest confusion, the ministry of preaching that she had irrationally usurped and had presumptuously claimed for herself contrary to ecclesiastical custom. Finally confounded by her own prophecies, she brought them to an end.

**Note:** He was condemned in another synod the following year, as stated above.

**Note:** More precisely, he was also a monk of the monastery of Orbacum, founded by Saint Regulus, archbishop of Rheims, who was buried there, toward the end of the seventh century.

A certain priest named Gotescalcus, a Gaul by nationality and coming from the diocese of Rheims, was also spreading a new and pernicious error concerning God’s predestination.

**Note:** More precisely, from the archiepiscopal province, as we now say, since Orbacum belongs to the diocese of Soissons. Rabanus uses “diocese” for “province” in his synodal letter to King Louis.

For he said that the good, for the life of eternal blessedness, and the wicked, for everlasting death, had both been predestined inevitably by God; that sin could not harm the good, nor conversion to a better way of life benefit the wicked and foreknown, because God’s providence was entirely infallible.

Against him the most blessed archbishop Rabanus entered a broad field of disputation. With God’s help he overcame him before everyone by both the authority of Scripture and the evidence of reason. By the force of his argument he reduced him to such silence that he could advance nothing further in defense of his opinion.

Blessed in all things is God, who through the mouth of his servant Rabanus refuted this most pernicious doctrine of error.

Thus, reasonably convicted, defeated, and confounded by Saint Rabanus in the presence of the bishops, abbots, and all the others who were present, he accepted correction and publicly retracted his error.

**Note:** In Rabanus’s synodal letter to Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, he writes that Gotescalcus “was found incorrigible and ought to be confined, nor should he any longer be allowed to teach error and lead the Christian people astray.” In a final letter to the same man he writes that he “could not be drawn away from his wickedness while present.” Sigebert, under the year 849, says: “He was convicted, but nevertheless persevered in his error.”

**Note:** The archbishop. His proper bishop was Rothardus, or Hrothadus, of Soissons, who also attended the synod of Quierzy. There it is said that “he had usurped priestly rank through Rigbold the chorepiscopus, while he was a monk of the parish of Soissons, without the knowledge of the bishop of his city.”

By the judgment of the holy synod he was sent to his proper bishop Hincmar at Rheims, after first giving an oath of confirmation that he would not return again to the kingdom of Louis—that is, to the German kingdom.

**Note:** By the decree of the synod of Quierzy, “he was stripped of priestly rank, exposed as a wicked man, beaten with rods, and confined in a prison so that he would not harm others.”

Many other useful decrees were also issued at that synod, which are recorded elsewhere.

It must not be passed over in silence how the devil, the enemy and adversary of every good thing, opposed the holy pursuits of Rabanus in everything, day and night, seeking out and watching the paths of his life so that he might either turn him back from his purpose of holiness, expose him to public death, or subject him to personal disgrace. Nor did he cease from his evil beginnings until at last, in a short time, he subverted the souls of many of Rabanus’s subjects.

For when he had scarcely completed two months in the episcopate, he began, at the instigation of the evil spirit, to displease almost all his people greatly. Their rashness then went so far that they secretly plotted his death.

**Note:** More precisely, it is certain from what follows that this occurred in the second year of his archiepiscopate, in 848.

Several members of the clergy of the church of Mainz conspired against him. The holy man had reasonably reproved their vices and disorderly conduct. They also secretly drew many nobles and commoners from the laity into their perverse association and joined them in a plot against their own bishop.

Rabanus was upright, blameless, and just in himself; toward his subjects he was zealous and most vigilant in pastoral care. When he wished to bring the ministers of the Church back to the canonical regulations in accordance with their office, he gravely provoked the minds of the wicked against him.

And unless divine providence, which is never deceived in its ordering, had arranged otherwise, he would scarcely have escaped the hands of the impious. But “there is no counsel against God” (Proverbs 21).

At that same time, while Archbishop Rabanus presided over a synod at Saint Alban, King Louis was holding an assembly of the kingdom’s nobles in the city of Mainz. As Regino testifies in his chronicles, the king publicly convicted Rabanus’s men, who had conspired against their lord, made peace between them and him, and imposed on each a satisfaction proportionate to his offense.

**Note:** Not Regino, who does not mention Rabanus, but the author of the *Fulda Annals*, where the following is recorded under the year 848: “Around the Kalends of October King Louis held a general assembly at Mainz, in which he received, heard, and dismissed the envoys of his brothers and of the Northmen and Slavs. The men of Bishop Rabanus, who were conspiring against their lord, were publicly convicted and reconciled with him.”

In the year 852 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, which was the fifth year of blessed Rabanus’s episcopate, another synod was held at Mainz, at the command of King Louis, in the monastery of Saint Alban the martyr. Rabanus himself presided as archbishop, and almost all the bishops and abbots of eastern Francia, Bavaria, and Saxony appeared in person, together with those from the Rhineland and the Moselle region.

**Note:** The *Fulda Annals* report the following under the year 852: “A synod was also held by the will and command of that most serene prince, King Louis, in the city of Mainz, the metropolis of Germany, with Rabanus, the venerable archbishop of that city, presiding, together with all the bishops and abbots of eastern Francia, Bavaria, and Saxony. They dealt ecclesiastically with the resolution of disputed questions. The king, however, occupied himself with settling public affairs and lawsuits together with the princes and governors of the provinces. After he had approved their synodal decrees by his judgment and had heard and dismissed the embassies of the Bulgarians and Slavs, he returned to Bavaria.” It is certain, however, that the people of the Moselle were outside King Louis’s realm.

Many matters were established at that synod for the common benefit of the Church and for the correction of the conduct of those serving God; King Louis himself confirmed all of them by royal authority. The bishops determined synodal questions in council, while the king, together with the princes, attended in the city to the settling of disputes.

In the year 850 from the Lord’s Nativity, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, which was the third year of Saint Rabanus’s episcopate, an extremely severe famine oppressed the peoples of Germany, especially those living around the Rhine. For one modius of grain was sold at Mainz for ten silver coins, of which twenty-six today make one gold florin.

**Note:** He again copied this from the *Fulda Annals*, where ten silver shekels are mentioned; the rest, concerning the *maldrum*, is Trithemius’s explanation.

**Note:** The same Trithemius praises Rabanus’s charity during this famine in his *Hirsaugiensis Chronicle* under the years 849 and 856.

From this calculation it is clear that one *octale* of grain, called a *maldrum*, cost more than three florins of the Mainz measure in question.

At that time the blessed Archbishop Rabanus was staying in a certain village of his parish called Wincella. It lies on the descent of the Rhine River, approximately three miles to the right of Mainz, and is now called Wunckel by the inhabitants of the region. While residing there, he received daily more than three hundred poor people arriving from various places and sustained them with food, apart from those who were continually eating in his presence.

One day, among others, a certain woman from the village of Crucinacum (which is now a town [Note: [Col. 0101D] of the Lower Palatinate. The name of the place is missing in the Annals of Fulda.]), nearly wasted away by hunger, came with a small infant among the other poor, desiring to be restored. Before she had crossed the threshold of the episcopal residence, she collapsed to the ground from excessive weakness and breathed her last. But the child, drawing the breast of his dead mother—who lay there as though alive—from her bosom and trying to suckle, moved many who witnessed it to tears.

When this was reported to the blessed bishop, he groaned and, overcome by the pain of such compassion, could not restrain his tears. From that day onward he caused mercy toward the needy to be proclaimed throughout the entire region, and increased almsgiving according to his means. To the poor who came from every direction he supplied more abundantly the food necessary for their present life.

The almighty God, regarding this generosity toward the poor as pleasing, is said to have rewarded him with a double benefit: in the present life he repaid him with abundant provision, and, when his soul was finally separated from the body, he continually satisfied it with the delights of eternal happiness in heaven. For he scattered the riches of this life for the love of Christ and gave them to the poor; therefore “his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Psalm 111:9), and “his feast [and his horn] is exalted with all the saints in glory.”

He loved Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, whose minister and bishop he was, above all things. For his honor he showed himself a faithful shepherd of Christ’s sheep: he taught the ignorant, fed the poor, and restored those who had gone astray and been thrown down along the byways of sin to the path of righteousness with fatherly concern. Truly just and holy was he, for he did not pursue gold, nor place his hope in treasures of money (Ecclesiasticus 31:8). All his confidence was in the Lord, for whose love he despised everything else.

Therefore, following the example of the ancient bishops, he entrusted the care of temporal affairs to suitable men, so that, relieved by their service, he might devote himself more intently to spiritual matters. Whatever required episcopal office, however, he administered personally throughout the entire diocese. Whenever he could be free from episcopal duties, he was always devoted to reading the divine Scriptures, meditation, prayer, and contemplation. The practice of holiness that he had learned as a monk in the monastery he continued without interruption even after becoming archbishop, and he never abandoned it.

He was not ashamed to preach the word of God to the people entrusted to him, since he recognized that he had received the ministry of the apostles. Indeed, just as a man who, occupied with worldly business or idleness, does not preach the word of God to the peoples entrusted to him does not deserve to be called an apostle, so one who neglects or sets aside spiritual concerns and cares only for temporal matters is altogether unworthy of episcopal honor.

Thus, passing through villages, towns, and estates, Rabanus, in the manner of the apostles, announced the Gospel of God to the people with several clerics and monks whom he knew to be suitable for this ministry; he rebuked offenders and reconciled penitents to the Lord. He strove with all his strength to reform the conduct of the clergy according to apostolic discipline. For their wholesome guidance he had previously composed, through long night labor, three notable books addressed to Haildolf, the fourth archbishop of Mainz, his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0101D] In the year of Christ 819, when he was not yet abbot.].

Whenever he was free from the public activities of the Church, he maintained a residence either in the aforementioned estate of Wincella near the Rhine, or at Mainz, near the principal church, in the episcopal residence, or indeed on a hill not far from the previously named village, which was called Bisthofeberus after him and on which the monastery of Saint John the Baptist can now be seen constructed.

He also frequently used to stay in the monastery of the holy martyr Alban, which Richolfus, the third archbishop, built on a hill near Mainz in the year of the Lord 796, in the fourth Roman indiction, because of the holiness of life of the monks serving God there [Note: [Col. 0101D] Richolfus occupied the see from 787 to 814. The church of Saint Alban was consecrated on 1 December 805. With the permission of Pope Martin, this monastery of monks was transformed into a collegiate body of canons in 1419. See Ferarius, *Moguntiaca*, book I, chapters 30 and 31, and book IV, under the third archbishop.].

He also often resided in the monastery of the canons of Saint Victor outside Mainz, both because of the mildness of the air and because of the pleasantness of the place and its setting [Note: [Col. 0102D] Wicelius presents “Saint Willibald” in his *Hagiologium* as having “written the Life of Saint Boniface and rewritten it in the place called Saint Victor outside the Walls, where Lullus and Rabanus devoted themselves to prayer”; these details were added by the enlarger of the Life, since Saint Willibald died before Rabanus was born.]. There he composed and wrote certain works for the edification of the faithful; Saint Lullus, formerly archbishop, had also been accustomed to devote himself there to prayer and meditation.

I now think it appropriate to commend to posterity’s memory as many and as useful volumes as possible that this most holy bishop Rabanus wrote, from the thirtieth year of his life until the end of it—nearly thirty-eight years during which he never ceased studying the Scriptures and publishing books [Col. 0102D]. For, as was said above, he was the most learned man in all Germany. In the number, usefulness, eloquence, and elegance of the books he published, he had neither an equal among those who preceded him nor a peer among those he left behind.

This will become more readily evident if we list the titles of his books in order—not in the order in which they were published, but in the arrangement we have assigned them.

Accordingly, he wrote for Frecolfus, bishop of Lisieux in Normandy and formerly his disciple, whom we mentioned above, four books on Genesis; four books on Exodus; four books on Numbers; four books on Leviticus; four books on Deuteronomy; two books on the history of Joshua; two books on the history of Judges; and one book on the history of Ruth. For Hildowin, abbot of Saint-Denis, he wrote several books on the history of the Kings; four books on Chronicles; three books on Ezra [Note: [Col. 0103D] Rather, forty-one, as is clear from our calculation.] and Nehemiah; one book on the history of Tobit; seven books on the history of Judith; one book on the history of Esther; several books on the history of Job; several books on the entire Psalter; several books on the Proverbs of Solomon; several books on Ecclesiastes; several books on the Song of Songs; three books on the Book of Wisdom; ten books on Ecclesiasticus; twenty books on the prophet Isaiah; twenty books on Ezekiel; three books on the prophet Daniel; twelve books on the twelve minor prophets; three books on the history of the Maccabees; eight books on the Gospel of Matthew; three books on the Gospel of Luke; four books on the Gospel of Mark; and several books on the Gospel of John.

For the presbyter Luxus Servatus he wrote twenty-three books on all the epistles of the apostle Paul [Col. 0103C]; several books on the Acts of the Apostles; seven books on the Catholic Epistles; and several books on the Apocalypse of John.

For Pope Gregory IV he composed a laborious and marvelous work, *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*, in two books. For Haimo, bishop of Halberstadt, he wrote twenty-two books *On the Universe* and one book *On Universal Nature*. For Hailfolsus, the fourth archbishop of the Church of Mainz, he wrote three books *On the Instruction, Life, and Conduct of Clerics*. For Bishop Heribert he wrote one book *On Questions of the Canons*, and for Bishop Reginbald one book on the same subject. He wrote one book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*; eight books *On the Divine Offices*; and two books *On the Ecclesiastical Computus*.

As a young man he composed many volumes, *Preparations for the Seven Liberal Arts*; four books of *Epigrams*; and three books *On Metrical Composition*. For Louis, king of Germany, he published many books and letters on various and diverse subjects proposed to him by the king. He also wrote, composed, and delivered many letters, sermons, and homilies, without any fixed number; to mention each of them individually in order would be tedious for readers.

For he is believed to have written many other works that have not yet reached the workshop of our knowledge. These are the writings of the most learned and holy archbishop Rabanus, which I remember having read. For their publication he labored unceasingly for thirty-eight years, as we have said [Note: [Col. 0103D] Rather, forty-one, as is clear from our calculation.]: first as a monk and teacher at Fulda, then as abbot, and finally as archbishop, always for the greatest glory of God and the benefit of the faithful.

He was indeed the most devoted scholar of all the Germans of his age, and easily the universal leader in learning. In wisdom and education he surpassed everyone in his nation and defeated those who preceded him; he had no equal among his successors. From the time when he established a monastic school at Fulda as a training ground, for nearly four hundred years many exceptionally learned monks of the order of the holy father Benedict flourished throughout Europe.

Of these I named many individually in the first book of *Illustrious Men* of our aforesaid order, and I also included not a few in the volume *On Ecclesiastical Writers* some time ago [Col. 0104B]. At that time the proverb proved true which said: “The knowledge of the Scriptures lies hidden in the monks’ cowls.” For in those days the monks were studious and highly learned, applying themselves diligently among the Germans and the Gauls not only to Latin letters but also to Greek letters.
