But when our monks eventually began to prefer the pleasures of the flesh and leisure to the reading of Scripture, knowledge of Greek letters likewise completely declined among both Germans and Gauls. Then new institutions of the Mendicant Brothers arose, bringing with them new methods of study and a certain familiar, plain style of writing.

Rabanus, however, the first among the Germans to be universally learned, profound in knowledge, eloquent and substantial in speech, excelled in life and conduct [Col. 0104C] as a most learned, religious, and holy man. He was truly a worthy, pleasing, and acceptable bishop to God.

In his ministry he kept such diligent watch day and night. Whatever he could do for the honor of God, he never neglected at any time or on any occasion. Throughout the diocese of Mainz he established many churches anew and repaired many old and ruined ones. While presiding as abbot over the monastery of Fulda, he founded several monastic priories and established certain convents of nuns of his order within the boundaries of the Buchonian Forest.

He is also said to have accomplished many other deeds worthy of remembrance and is reported to have shone with various miracles. Since we do not possess certain and manifest testimony to the truth of these matters, we thought it better to remain completely silent than to commit uncertain reports to writing [Col. 0104D].

But what we learned from Meginfrid’s testimony we do not hesitate to commend to posterity through the work of our pen. For the most reverend bishop Rabanus, both during his abbacy at Fulda and during his episcopate in the Church of Mainz, endured many injuries, accusations, slanders, and insults from his rivals, even from his own people, without deserving them; and he was often exposed to danger even to the point of death.

He bore all these things with the greatest patience for the love of God, and whatever adversity occurred against him he humbly attributed to his own sins. Thus he not only always showed himself patient in adversity; what is more meritorious, he willingly endured everything contrary to himself for the love of the Lord [Col. 0105A].

Although he was the gentlest of all the bishops of his time, he never summoned his persecutors and rivals for punishment, nor did he ever seek revenge against them either by word or deed. Founded by the bond of divine charity upon the firm rock, no temptation could separate him from the Lord. He had learned to walk rightly, by living well, in the way of fear and love of the Lord from the tender years of his childhood.

No one saw him moved to anger beyond the moderation of just reason; no one found him disturbed in spirit. Rather, joyful in the testimony of a good conscience, he was always peaceful in mind and, united with God within himself, tranquil at all times.

He remained constant in these exercises of piety. The nearer he felt or believed himself to be to death, the more he distanced his mind from the fleeting and empty pursuits of the world [Col. 0105B]. He devoted himself without interruption to fasts, vigils, prayers, sacred almsgiving, preaching, and other good works, and at all times was profitably occupied in the workshop of divine love.

When the time predetermined from eternity had come, at which the merciful and compassionate Lord had predestined to grant his servant the reward of a good will in eternal happiness, Rabanus was seized by a fever and lay confined to bed. As the illness increased, he finally reached the end.

Forewarned by an angelic vision that the final struggle of this wretched life was approaching, he joyfully fortified his departure with the Lord’s sacraments. Having prudently distributed his books partly to Fulda and partly to the monastery of Saint Alban outside the walls of the city of Mainz [Col. 0105C], he happily departed to the Lord whom he had always loved with his whole heart, amid words of prayer, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 856, in the fourth Roman indiction, in the ninth year of his episcopate.

At his passing, the voices of singing angels were heard saying:

> This saint is deservedly turned into the memory of men,  
> who is led into the joy of the angels,  
> because in this pilgrimage, etc.

The most blessed archbishop Rabanus died at Vinicella, the estate of his residence, on the banks of the Rhine. His sacred body, as he had ordered while alive [Col. 0106A], was carried back to Mainz and honorably buried in the church of the holy martyr Alban. The following epitaph is found written in his memory:

> Honorable reader, if you wish to know my life in the woods,  
> you will thus be able to learn it during mortal time.  
>   
> I was indeed born in a city and reborn in the sacred font;  
> at Fulda, thereafter, I learned holy doctrine.  
>   
> Having become a monk, I followed the commands of the elders;  
> the holy Rule was the standard of life for me.  
>   
> Yet although I did not always keep it carefully or steadfastly,  
> my cell was nevertheless a pleasant dwelling for me.  
>   
> But when several years of time had now passed,  
> men gathered to alter the fate of the place.  
>   
> They dragged me, weak, from my home and took me to the king,  
> asking that I undertake the office of bishop.  
>   
> In this office neither merit of life nor knowledge of doctrine was found,  
> nor was the shepherd’s work rightly pleasing.  
>   
> My spirit was ready, but my weak body was slow.  
> I did what I could, and what God had granted.  
>   
> Now, therefore, dear brother, help me from the tomb,  
> commending me in your prayers to Christ the Lord,  
>   
> so that the grace of the eternal Judge may save me forever,  
> looking not to merit but to the work of piety.  
>   
> For Rabanus was my name; the reading  
> of the divine law was always sweet to me everywhere.  
>   
> May almighty God grant him the heavenly kingdoms  
> and true rest forever in the citadel of heaven.

Such, then, was the end in this world of the life of the most blessed bishop Rabanus. His holy body remained buried for 659 years in the aforementioned monastery of the holy martyr Alban, in a sarcophagus raised beside the wall of the choir.

From the beginning there was also a great gathering of people at his tomb, and many miracles are reported to have occurred there. In the course of time, however, this entirely ceased, and his chapel remained long without honor. Therefore, by the providence of God, who governs all things, for the glory of his name and the perpetual honor of his servant, God ordained that his most holy body be removed from Mainz and transferred to Saxony in the present year, in which we have written this account—namely, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1515, in the third Roman indiction.

How, by whom, when, and to what place this translation was carried out we have described in a separate treatise, to the praise and glory of almighty God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is one God, living and reigning throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0105]

## A SUMMARY OF THE SAME LIFE

[Col. 0105D] Rabanus was born at Fulda, to his father Ruthard and his mother Aldegund, on 2 February in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 788. Book I.

Rabanus became a monk at Fulda in the year of the Lord 797, in the ninth year of his age. Book I.

For the sake of study, the monk Rabanus was sent to Rome in the year of the Lord 806, to Albinus, teacher and master of the monks.

After spending six years in study at Rome, Rabanus returned to Fulda in the year of the Lord 812. Book I. Soon afterward he was appointed teacher of the monks at Fulda.

Rabanus became the fifth abbot of Fulda, serving for twenty-two years, in the year of the Lord 825, in the thirty-sixth year of his age. Book II, at the beginning.

Rabanus became archbishop of Mainz on 26 June in the year of the Lord 847, in the fifty-ninth year of his age, and governed for nine years. Book III.

[Col. 0106D] The works that Rabanus wrote and laboriously composed over thirty-nine consecutive years are listed. The same Book III.

Rabanus, sixth archbishop of Mainz, died at Vinicella on 27 October, in the ninth year of his episcopate, in the fourth month, at the age of sixty-eight years and nine months, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 856. Book III.

Rabanus’s body lay buried in the church for 659 years. At the end of Book III.

Rabanus’s body was transferred honorably to Saxony in August of the year of the Lord 1515.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Apostle at Würzburg, described the translation of Rabanus’s body or bones in a separate book. Completed, with God’s help, on 20 October 915 [Note: [Col. 0105D] It should read 1515. EDIT.].

[Col. 0107]

## TESTIMONIES AND EULOGIES OF DISTINGUISHED WRITERS CONCERNING RABANUS

*(From the edition of Georg Colvenerius.)*

### I. Life of Saint Sola, Priest and Monk

The *Life of Saint Sola*, priest and monk, disciple of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz and martyr, was written while Rabanus himself was still alive; Georg Wicelius includes an abridgment of it in his history of the Saints of the Church of God.

“Some also gave him part of their estate, which he accepted in the fear of God, together with what Lord Charles Augustus graciously granted him, and conveyed it to the distinguished monastery of Fulda, where, by God’s providence, the most holy and highly skilled abbot Rabanus now shines conspicuously in every art.”

### II. Hincmarus, *Against the Heretic Gottschalk on Predestination*

“He also wrote another book” (Hincmarus is speaking of Gottschalk) “against the venerable archbishop Rabanus, a father zealous in the holy religion and a Catholic writer, who had been nourished by the orthodox and great teacher Lord Alcuin, for the benefit of the holy Church, on Alcuin’s abundant Catholic milk, and who had gathered and prepared flowers of the holy authors from the meadow of doctrine. These flowers, spoken by Catholics in a Catholic manner, he either mutilated or corrupted.”

The same Hincmarus, as Flodoardus testifies in book III, chapter 21, of his *History of the Church of Rheims*, where he reviews Hincmarus’s various writings, among other things reports that Hincmarus wrote to Rabanus, bishop of Mainz: “In this letter,” says Flodoardus, “he asserts that this blessed Rabanus was then the only one remaining from the discipleship of blessed Alcuin.”

### III. Frankish Annals from the Year of the Lord’s Incarnation 714 to 883

These annals, by an unknown author, were published from the library of Petrus Pithaeus among twelve contemporary writers and placed first. In the judgment of Petrus Pithaeus, they were written at Mainz during the time of Rabanus Maurus, archbishop; or, as others believe, at Fulda, and for that reason are called the *Annals of Fulda*.

In the year 822, Eigil, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, died and was succeeded by Rabanus.

In the year 844, Rabanus the sophist, second to none among the poets of his time, sent through Ascrihus and Hruodbertus [Note: [Col. 0107D] Baronius, volume X of the *Annals*, in the same year, reads Asericus and Theodbertus], monks of the monastery of Fulda, to Pope Sergius a book that he had composed in a difficult and marvelous poem, *On the Praise of the Holy Cross of Christ*, distinguished by a variety of figures, so that it might be offered to Saint Peter.

In the year 847, Otgarius, bishop of Mainz, died on 21 April. Rabanus was ordained in his place on 26 June. In the same year, at the command of King Louis, he held a synod at Mainz around the Kalends of October.

In the year 850, an extremely severe famine oppressed the peoples of Germany, especially those living near the Rhine. For a single bushel of grain was sold at Mainz for ten shekels of silver. At that time Archbishop Rabanus was staying in an estate of his diocese called Winzella [Col. 0107D]. Receiving the poor who came from various places, he provided food every day for more than three hundred, apart from those who continually ate in his presence.

In the year 856, on the fourth day of February, Rabanus, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, died [Col. 0108A], having held the episcopate for nine years, one month, and four days. Karlus succeeded him, and so forth.

### IV. Lambert of Hersfeld, *On the Deeds of the Germans*

In the year 831, Brun and Raban, abbots, dug the foundation of the church of Saint Wigbert on 10 July, a Monday.

In the year 842, Luithar was expelled from the kingdom, and Raban from the monastery.

In the year 847, Oggarius, archbishop of Mainz, died. Raban, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him, and Waldo assumed the abbacy.

In the year 856, Archbishop Rabanus died, and Charles succeeded him.

### V. Saint Odilo, Abbot of Cluny, in His Sermon *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*

[Col. 0108B] “Rabanus, richly educated in secular knowledge, Catholic in faith, and fully instructed in spiritual knowledge, wove and completed by weaving such a work *On the Praise of the Holy Cross* that nothing more precious to behold, more pleasing to read, sweeter to retain, or more laborious to write can be found.”

### VI. Hermannus Contractus, in His More Extensive *Chronicle*

In the year 822, Eigil, abbot of Fulda, died. Rabanus, a learned man and distinguished expounder of the divine books, succeeded him.

### VII. Marianus Scotus, Monk of Fulda, *Chronicle*, Book III, Year 6

In the year 822, Eigil, abbot of Fulda, died, and Rabanus succeeded him.

In the year 847, Otgarius, archbishop of Mainz, died. Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him, and Hattho became abbot [Col. 0108C].

In the year 856, Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, died, and Charles succeeded him.

### VIII. Honorius of Autun, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*

Rabanus, from being abbot of the monastery of Fulda, became bishop of Mainz. He wrote a marvelous book *On the Mystery of the Holy Cross* and expounded the entire Old and New Testament. He flourished under Louis.

### IX. Sigebert of Gembloux, *Chronicle*

In the year 824, Rabanus the sophist, second to none among the poets of his time, became abbot of Fulda. He discussed many matters from the holy Scriptures and also composed, in a difficult and marvelous poem, a book *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, distinguished by a variety of figures [Col. 0108D], and sent it to Pope Sergius to be offered to Saint Peter.

In the year 827, Rabanus the abbot published a treatise on the Book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus for Archbishop Otgarius.

In the year 848, Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, was ordained archbishop of Mainz. After a synod had been held at Mainz [Col. 0109A], he decreed many things useful to the Church by order of King Louis.

In the year 849, the heretic Gottschalk was reasonably convicted by Archbishop Rabanus, as many thought, but nevertheless persisted in his error.

In the year 851, a severe famine afflicted Germany, so that even a father wished to devour his own son. At that time Archbishop Rabanus showed great benevolence to the poor.

In the year 856, Rabanus, an archbishop distinguished in life and learning, died.

### X. The Same Author, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, Chapter 90

Rabanus, also called Maurus or Magnentius, became archbishop of Mainz from being abbot of Fulda. He wrote a book *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, depicted with marvelous variety, which he sent to Rome to be offered to Saint Peter.

He wrote for Archbishop Otgarius a book on the Books of Solomon’s Wisdom; he wrote on the First Book of the Maccabees, on Ezra, and on Judith; one book *On the Mysteries of the Mass*; one book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*; four books for Abbot Hilduin on the Books of the Kings; one book *On Questions of the Canons* for Bishop Heribald; one book on the same subject for his fellow bishop Reginbald; and other works.

### XI. Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, Book XXIV, Chapter 28

“Rabanus the sophist, second to none among the poets of his time, became abbot of Fulda. He discussed many matters from the holy Scriptures and also composed, in a difficult and marvelous poem, a book *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, distinguished by a variety of figures, and sent it to Pope Sergius to be offered to Saint Peter.

He likewise published treatises on the Book of Wisdom and on Ecclesiasticus for Archbishop Othgarius. Finally, from being abbot of Fulda [Col. 0109C], he was ordained archbishop of Mainz. There, after a synod had been held by order of King Louis, he decreed many things useful to the Church.

“The author therefore wrote two books *On the Praise of the Cross*; one book *On the Instruction of Clerics*; four books on Genesis; four books on Exodus; one book on Numbers; four books on the Kings; four books on Chronicles; seven books on Judith; one book on Esther; four books on the Book of Wisdom; ten books on Ecclesiasticus; one book on Jeremiah; three books on the Books of the Maccabees; eight books on Matthew; and one book on the Acts of the Apostles.

“Besides these he wrote *On the Natures of Things* and many other works. His disciple was Strabo, who took down many things from his dictation and published certain brief commentaries on some books of the Pentateuch. Rabanus’s book *On the Praise of the Cross* is partly metrical and partly in prose.”

### XII. Martin of Troppau, *Chronicle* (Year 816)

At that time Rabanus, a monk of Fulda, flourished—an eminent poet and outstanding in theological learning.

### XIII. Saint Antoninus, *Historical Summary*, Part II, Title 14, Chapter 5

“Rabanus the sophist, second to none among the poets of his time,” says Vincent above, following Sigebertus, “was abbot of Fulda and discussed many matters from the holy Scriptures,” and so forth.

In his time a certain false prophetess, saying that the Day of Judgment was imminent, disturbed Mainz, to such an extent that she even drew some members of the sacred order to herself. Rebuked by the archbishop, she confessed that, at the suggestion of a certain presbyter, she had done this for the sake of profit, and so forth.

As Vincent says above, Rabanus wrote many books: two books *On the Praise of the Cross*, partly metrical and partly in prose; besides these, *On the Natures of Things* and many other works; and also certain letters, such as one of the prologues placed before the Book of the Maccabees.

His disciple was Strabo, who took down many things from his dictation, published certain brief commentaries on some books of the Pentateuch, and to whom certain works on the Bible and mystical expositions are attributed.

These passages are found in the Decretals, from Rabanus’s books, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Before Baptism.” Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*: “Before baptism, the office of catechizing must precede, so that the catechumen may first receive the sacrament of faith,” and so forth.

The same author in the same work, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, “After the one to be baptized…”; likewise in the same distinction, “Afterward”; and in the following chapter, “From this point.” The same author in the same distinction, chapter “From this point again”; likewise in the same distinction, “Afterward II”; likewise in the same distinction, “Then by the priest”; likewise in the same distinction, “After he ascended”: III; likewise, “Let him first be questioned.”

The same Rabanus, writing to Heribald about those who had fallen away—whether they should be promoted or serve in ministries they had received—says in distinction 50: “Concerning these, it seemed…”

The same author, in his commentary on Matthew, on the passage “He handed him over to the torturers,” in *On Penance*, distinction 4:

> “It must be considered that he says ‘the entire debt,’ because not only the sins a person committed after baptism will be reckoned to him for punishment, but also original sins, which had been forgiven him in baptism. What he says in the plural, ‘original sins,’ refers to the various effects of original sin. In itself it is one; and such things are reckoned as forgiven not through their return, but through a certain effect of aggravation, according to Thomas in Book IV.”

The same author in the book *On Ecclesiastical Pressures*, cited in distinction 37, chapter “We read of blessed Jerome.” The same in the same work, cited in distinction 24, question 3, “We are not condemned forever.”

### XIV. Hartmann Schedel, *Chronicle of Chronicles with Illustrations*

Rabanus, a monk of German nationality, abbot of Fulda and afterward archbishop of Mainz, was a highly distinguished theologian [Col. 0110C] and an eminent poet. In this period he was greatly accomplished in both prose and verse. Through the greatness of his talent he published many books, especially the marvelous work *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*.

He also commented on the Book of Chronicles and the Maccabees. He had sufficiently elegant sermons for the people, especially for the solemnity of All Saints, and he sat for ten years, in the year of salvation 846.

Strabo likewise, a most eminent Gaulish monk and a very diligent commentator, was a pupil of the aforesaid Rabanus. In these same times he was not inferior to his teacher, commenting very beautifully on the books of the Bible, writing *On the Offices of the Church* for the emperor Louis, and producing many other works.

### XV. Bartholomew Platina, *Lives of the Pontiffs*, under Gregory IV

Some write that, at the request of Louis, Gregory instituted the solemnity of All Saints on the Kalends of November and that this action was greatly praised in verse and prose by the monk Rabanus, an eminent theologian. In these two forms of expression the learned man was quite capable, especially for that age.

The same Rabanus also commented on the Book of Chronicles and the Maccabees. He had sufficiently elegant sermons for the people, but the one he delivered for the solemnity of All Saints is especially praised.

### XVI. Jacobus Philippus Bergomas, *Supplement to the Supplement of Chronicles*, Book XI, Year of Christ 833

Rabanus, a monk of German nationality and archbishop of Mainz, a highly distinguished theologian and eminent poet, was in this period greatly accomplished in prose and verse, the two modes of expression, and was held in high esteem.

Through the greatness of his talent he commented on and published many books, whose titles are the following, insofar as I was able to discover them. First, he begins four books on Genesis: *In the Beginning*. Four books on Exodus: *Exodus, the Departure*. Likewise, three books on the Epistle to the Ephesians. One book on Leviticus: *The Book That Follows*. One book *On the Instruction of Clerics*. One book on Deuteronomy: *These Are the Words*. Eight books on Matthew: *Therefore the Expectation*.

He also commented on the Books of Chronicles and on the Books of the Maccabees. He had many elegant sermons for the people. Likewise, two books *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*; twenty-two books *On the Universe*; one book *On the Divine Offices*; one book in dialogue *On the Computus*; *On Questions of the Canons*; one book *On the Patriarchs*; and certain other works.

### XVII. Werner Rolewinck, *Fasciculus Temporum*, Year 834

Rabanus, a poet and monk, afterward abbot of Fulda and then archbishop of Mainz, flourished as a great teacher [Col. 0111B] and wrote many works. His disciple Strabo was likewise notable in learning and virtues during the same period.

### XVIII. The Same Author, in the Same Work, Year 844

The feast of All Saints was transferred to the Kalends of November by Gregory IV, and at this time the Gauls and Germans began to celebrate it; there is also a fairly beautiful sermon of Rabanus on the same subject.

### XIX. Johannes Nauclerus, Provost of Tübingen, *Chronicles*, Volume II, Generation 28, at the End

This year was also mournful because of the death of Pope Gregory—Gregory IV—who, among his other distinguished deeds, instituted the feast of All Saints on the Kalends of November. Some think that this was done on Rabanus’s advice.

He was one of Alcuin’s disciples, abbot of Fulda and afterward archbishop of Mainz, distinguished in bound speech no less than in prose. He left many monuments of his talent: commentaries on the remaining books, which we call Chronicles, and on the Maccabees; *The Praise of the Holy Cross*; and many sermons.

### X. Robert Gaguin, Book IV, *On the Deeds of the Franks*
By his (Charlemagne’s) authority the Parisian school—which they call the University—began on this occasion. Claudius and John were brought by ship from Scotland, and Rabanus and Alcuin likewise came as disciples of the venerable Bede. When they had arrived in Gaul, having brought nothing out of their homeland except the liberal disciplines, they loudly proclaimed that they professed wisdom and that they held it for sale. When this was reported to Charles, he summoned them to himself. Once called, they freely acknowledged that they possessed wisdom, and that, if only life and a place were provided for them, they would teach freely those who desired to acquire it. The emperor recognized the men’s honorable purpose, and, after keeping them with him for several days, ordered Claudius—whose name was Clement—to reside in Paris and educate noble youths in the liberal disciplines; but he sent John to Pavia. [Col. 0111D]

### XI. Raphael Volaterranus, *Anthropologia*, Book XIX

Rabanus, an English monk and supreme theologian, eloquent in verse and prose, as Ricobaldus of Ferrara and Ptolemy of Lucca write, was bishop of Meaux, a disciple of Bede, in the time of Louis the Pious and Gregory V. He wrote on the Second Book of Chronicles and on the Maccabees. He also delivered sermons to the people. He made the Parisian school, then first being established, more renowned through his celebrated teaching.

### XXII. John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Rabanus Maurus, the sixth archbishop of Mainz, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fulda of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation from the city of Fulda in Buchonia, once a student of Albinus the Englishman, was a man exceedingly learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly educated in secular literature: a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, and most subtle poet. To speak without envy, neither Italy produced his equal nor Germany his peer. While still young he put on the monastic habit in the monastery of Fulda and made marvelous progress both in character and in learning. Consequently, after being consecrated the fourth abbot of that same monastery, he governed the sheep entrusted to him by word and example for twenty-four years and composed almost innumerable little works on the Scriptures.

At length, offended by the wickedness of his monks, who said that he was too intent upon the Scriptures and neglected temporal matters—for the devil was working in them—they conceived displeasure against him, taking offense at the very thing in which they ought most to have been edified. Therefore, giving place to anger and unwilling to remain longer with ungrateful sheep, he left the monastery and its inhabitants and went to Louis the emperor, son of Charles, with whom he also remained for many days. The monks, however, moved to repentance, sent an embassy to him and begged him to return to the monastery, but they did not obtain their request. [Col. 0112A]

Thus he remained with the emperor until the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz. He was appointed in his place and presided over the aforesaid church of Mainz for nine years. After holding a synod, he established many measures for the benefit of the faithful. While he was still established in the monastery of Fulda, he wrote many volumes, both in verse and in prose, chiefly on the Holy Scriptures, all of which he explained from beginning to end. The following works are reported among his writings. [Col. 0112B]

To Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, whom we mentioned above, he wrote a distinguished work:

- On Genesis, 4 books. “In the beginning,” etc.; “many things were...”
- On Exodus, 4 books. “Exodus is called departure...”
- On Numbers, 4 books. “The Book of Numbers, many...”
- On Leviticus, 4 books. “The following book, that is, Leviticus...”
- On Deuteronomy, 4 books. “The children of Israel encamped...”
- On Joshua, 2 books. “To the most blessed and truly...”
- On Judges, 2 books. “After the death of Joshua...”
- On the Book of Ruth, 1 book. “Therefore, for those examining the history...”
- On Kings, to Hilduin, 4 books. “There was a man,” etc.; “let us say...”
- On Chronicles, 4 books. “Adam,” etc., “the tenth from...”
- On Tobit, 1 book.
- On Ezra and Nehemiah, 3 books.
- On Judith, 7 books. “O Lord, chosen and deservedly...”
- On Esther, 1 book. “The Book of Esther, which these...”
- On Job, 1 book.
- On the Psalms, 1 book.
- On Ecclesiastes, 1 book.
- On Solomon’s Proverbs, 1 book.
- On the Song of Songs.
- On the Book of Wisdom, 3 books. “Love,” etc.; “I admonish...”
- On Ecclesiasticus, 10 books. “Every wise man,” etc.; “therefore, at the beginning...”
- On the Prophet Isaiah, 8 books. “To the most reverend lord,” etc.
- On Jeremiah, 20 books.
- On Ezekiel, 20 books. “And it came to pass,” etc.; “he used...”
- On Daniel, 3 books.
- On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 12 books.
- On the Maccabees, 3 books. “And it came to pass after...”
- On the Gospel of Matthew, 8 books. “Therefore, expectation...”
- On the Gospel of Luke, 3 books.
- On the Gospel of Mark, 4 books.
- On the Gospel of John, 1 book. “Among all the divine histories...”
- On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book.
- On all the Epistles of Paul, 23 books. “To the venerable brother Lupus...”
- On the Catholic Epistles, 7 books.
- On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. [Col. 0112C]

- *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, 2 books. “The King of kings, the Lord, the world...”
- *To Haymo, bishop, On the Universe*, 22 books. “First among the Hebrews...”
- *On Universal Nature*, 1 book. “A discussion of the universe...”
- *On the Instruction of Clerics*, 3 books. “To the reverend lord...” and the remaining words to Haistulf.
- *On the Divine Offices*, 1 book.
- *A Dialogue on Computation*, 1 book. “Because you, venerable father...”
- *To King Louis*, 1 book.
- *To Regenbald, bishop*, 1 book.
- *Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book.
- *On Questions of the Canons*, 1 book.
- *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, 1 book.
- *Sermons*, almost innumerable, 1 book. [Col. 0113A]

He also published many other works that did not come to my notice. He died under the princes Louis and Lothair, in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the ninth year of his episcopate. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Alban near Mainz, not without a reputation for holiness. I read his epitaph, composed in approximately twenty ornamented verses. [Col. 0113B]

> **Note:** In the edition of Trithemius’s *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* printed at Cologne in the workshop of Peter Quentel in 1546, two additions have been made. The first follows the words “To King Louis, one book,” as follows: “He also wrote to King Louis another twenty-two books on the Properties of Words and the Mystical Signification of Things; this work may properly be called a Cornucopia.” [Col. 0113D] The same work is entitled *On the Universe* and *Etymologies*. The second addition appears at the end: “There are also extant in the library of Eberbach some little works of Rabanus: *On Seeing God*, *On Purity of Heart*, and *On Penance*, GEORGIUS COLVENERIUS.” [Col. 0114D]

### XXIII. The same Trithemius, in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers of Germany*

Rabanus Maurus Magnentius, the sixth archbishop of Mainz after Saint Boniface, a Thuringian by birth and from the city of Fulda, a disciple of Albinus, first became a monk of the monastery of Fulda while still a boy of ten. Thereafter he devoted all his study to knowledge of the Scriptures. He became by far the most learned in every branch of both secular learning and the divine Scriptures: a distinguished philosopher, an outstanding poet, an eloquent rhetorician, and a celebrated astronomer and computist. He was skilled in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, and the Church had no one like him in his time.

As his merits increased, in the thirty-fifth year of his age he was elected abbot of the same monastery by the suffrage of all the brothers. Presiding over its government for twenty-four years, he wrote many and almost innumerable volumes. Finally, after the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, he was consecrated bishop of that same church and, sitting in the episcopate for nine years, did much good for the Church. [Col. 0113C]

The following works are reported among his writings: to Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, four books on Genesis; four on Exodus; four on Numbers; four on Leviticus; four on Deuteronomy; two on Joshua; two on Judges; one on Ruth; four on Kings, to Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis; four on Chronicles; three on Ezra and Nehemiah; one on Tobit; seven on Judith; one on Esther; one on Job; one on the Psalms; one on Solomon’s Proverbs; one on Ecclesiastes; one on the Song of Songs; three on the Book of Wisdom; ten on Ecclesiasticus; eight on Isaiah the prophet; twenty on Jeremiah the prophet; twenty on Ezekiel the prophet; three on Daniel the prophet; twelve on the Twelve Minor Prophets; three on the Books of the Maccabees; eight on the Gospel of Matthew; three on the Gospel of Luke; four on the Gospel of Mark; two on the Gospel of John; twenty-three on all the Epistles of Paul; seven on the Catholic Epistles; one on the Acts of the Apostles; and one on the Apocalypse of John. [Col. 0113D]

Also, one book *On Faith in the Most Holy Trinity*; two books *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, a work of marvelous ingenuity; twenty-two books *On the Universe*, or *On Etymologies*, to Haymo, bishop; one book *On Universal Nature*; three books *On the Instruction of Clerics*, to Haistulf, bishop; one book *On the Divine Offices*; one book *On Ecclesiastical Computation*; one book *To the Emperor Louis*; one book *On Questions of the Canons*; one book *To Regenbald, bishop*; one book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*; two books of homilies and sermons for the whole year; and one book of letters to various persons. [Col. 0114A]

He also composed various epigrams and many treatises in humane letters, which have not yet come into our hands. He died under the emperor Lothair, in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the sixty-eighth year of his age, after completing the ninth year of his episcopate. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Alban the Martyr near Mainz, then belonging to the Order of Saint Benedict.

### XXIV. The same, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Book II, chapter 39

Rabanus Maurus Magnentius, formerly abbot of Fulda and the sixth archbishop of Mainz, a German by nation, from the regions of the Franks in the forest called Buchonia, approximately fifteen miles from Mainz toward Thuringia, was once a student and disciple of Albinus. He was exceedingly learned in the divine Scriptures and highly skilled in every branch of secular literature, a philosopher and poet inferior to no one of his time. [Col. 0114B]

While still a boy, he was entrusted by his parents to the monastery of Fulda, in which he progressed so greatly through study that Germany had no teacher like him. Thereafter, as his merits in learning increased, he was elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery with the assent of all the monks. Presiding in that office for twenty-four years, he governed the monastic discipline vigorously.

He wrote many volumes, of which I found only the following: four books to Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, on Genesis; four on Exodus; four on Leviticus; four on Numbers; four on Deuteronomy; two on Joshua; two on Judges; one on Ruth; four on Kings, to Hilduin, abbot; four on Chronicles; three on Ezra and Nehemiah; one on Tobit; one on Solomon’s Proverbs; one on Ecclesiastes; one on the Song of Songs; three on the Book of Wisdom; ten on Ecclesiasticus; eight on Isaiah the prophet; twenty on Jeremiah the prophet; twenty on Ezekiel; three on Daniel; twelve on the Twelve Minor Prophets; three on the Maccabees; eight on the Gospel according to Matthew; three on the Gospel according to Mark; four on the Gospel of Luke; one on the Gospel of John; twenty books on Paul’s Epistles; one on the Acts of the Apostles; seven on the Catholic Epistles; and one on the Apocalypse of John. [Col. 0114C]

While still a monk, at the age of thirty, he wrote a work worthy of admiration, a marvelous poem *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, in two books. The first was composed in meter, the second in prose; afterward he offered them to Saint Peter through the hands of Pope Sergius. [Col. 0114D]

He wrote to Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, twenty-two books *On Etymologies*, or *On the Universe*. He wrote one book *On Universal Nature*; three books to Haistulf, the fourth archbishop of Mainz, *On the Instruction of Clerics*; one book to Heribert, bishop, *On Questions of the Canons*; one book to Regenbald on the same subject; one book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*; one book *On the Divine Offices*; one very useful book *On Ecclesiastical Computation*; one book to King Louis; one book of letters to various persons. [Col. 0115A] He also wrote almost innumerable sermons and homilies.

I myself saw many other books of Rabanus in the library of the monastery of Fulda, especially on the liberal arts; but oblivion has now removed their titles from my memory. Among all the teachers of Germany and Italy, no one surpassed Rabanus in the number and usefulness of his books. For he wrote many volumes that we have not listed here. He was a most diligent scholar, always devoted to reading, and had many highly learned disciples.

In the abbey of Fulda he was the fourth after Saint Sturm, its first abbot; in the archbishopric of Mainz, the sixth. He governed the bishopric for eight years, being exceedingly compassionate toward the poor. During a famine he showed them great kindness and generously supported them all. After holding a synod at Mainz, he established many measures for the benefit of the faithful. He died in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction.

### XXV. The same, in the same work, Book IV, chapter 81

Rabanus Maurus, the fourth abbot of Fulda, a Frank by nation, from the forest called Buchonia, after governing the aforesaid abbey vigorously for twenty-four years, was ordained, following the death of Otgar, as the sixth archbishop of Mainz in his place. He was the most learned man of his time in every field, as the countless volumes he wrote testify; of these we made partial mention in the second book. He died in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the ninth year of his episcopate. [Col. 0115B]

### XXVI. The same, in the *Hirsau Chronicle*, under Lintbert, the first abbot of this monastery

Since this Lintbert, our abbot, was for a long time a student and fellow student of Rabanus of Fulda, a man learned in every respect, it must be believed that he could not have become anything but highly educated. For Rabanus himself, while still a monk, had conducted a public school for monks in the monastery of Fulda, and continued it as abbot. In it he instructed the monks in every way, not only in the sacred Scriptures but also in secular literature. [Col. 0115C]

He educated not only the monks of the monastery of Fulda but also many disciples in every kind of learning who had been sent to him from various other places. In time, many of these were promoted to great dignities. He had as his teacher Albinus, a most reverend monk and disciple of the English monk Bede, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours, formerly the teacher of the emperor Charlemagne. From him Rabanus had absorbed in Gaul what he later taught others in Germany.

Lintbert, at first Rabanus’s fellow student and afterward his disciple, did not neglect as a monk and abbot what he had learned from a good teacher. He was a most devoted cultivator of regular discipline. He taught the monks subject to him, by word, to live according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict; and by conducting himself in the fullness of every virtue, leading the sheep blamelessly as a good shepherd, he displayed the example of good works. [Col. 0115D]

His meditation on the law of the Lord continued day and night without interruption. Praying to the Lord continually, he remained a true disciple of Christ to the end. As the fame of his holiness and learning spread throughout the surrounding region, many noblemen entrusted their sons to his instruction. Many also who appeared distinguished among men in the secular world voluntarily submitted themselves to his discipline for love of the kingdom of heaven. Consequently, the number of brothers soon increased greatly, and the monastery’s temporal substance was enlarged through the offerings of many.

At the same time the monastery of Corvey in Saxony began its existence under the rule of our holy father Benedict. Its foundation was begun in the year of the Lord 822, in the fifteenth indiction. At almost the same time as this monastery of Saint Aurelius, it was completed and began to be inhabited. [Col. 0116A]

At nearly the same time, the monastery of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter at the place called Seligenstadt, in the parish of Mainz, was founded under the rule of our holy father Benedict by the emperor Louis the First, with the cooperation of the venerable Einhard, formerly chancellor and then a monk and first abbot of the same monastery. The bodies of the aforesaid two martyrs, Marcellinus and Peter, were brought from Rome through the emperor’s agency in November of the year of the Lord 828 and honorably placed there.

In the time of Lintbert, first abbot of Saint Aurelius of Hirsau, around the year of the Lord 840, under the most devout emperor Louis and his sons, many celebrated men in our Benedictine order became renowned for holiness and distinguished learning in the Scriptures. Like the stars of heaven, they wonderfully illumined the whole Church by their character and teaching.

Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda, whom we mentioned above, was held in high esteem by everyone at this time because of the integrity of his life and his immeasurable learning. How much he wrote we have shown for the most part both in our book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and in the second book *On Illustrious Men of Our Order*. [Col. 0116B]

Finally, in the year of the Lord 842, which was the fourth year of Abbot Lintbert, he left the monastery of Fulda, provoked by the deceits of certain men, and, taking refuge with Louis, son of the elder Emperor Louis, remained as if an exile until the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, who had expelled him for some reason unknown to me. But five years later, after Otgar’s death, Rabanus was appointed archbishop in his place in the year of the Lord 847, in the tenth indiction. He was elected by the suffrage of all and occupied the see for nine years. He was exceedingly compassionate toward the poor and governed his Church vigorously in character and learning.

### XXVII. Beatus Rhenanus, in his notes on Tertullian’s *On the Crown of the Soldier*

Rabanus Maurus also mentions, in a certain letter to Regenbald, some ceremonies and ecclesiastical regulations instituted after the beginnings of nascent Christianity, undoubtedly without Scripture, as Burchard likewise cites him in the sixth book, which concerns the Sacraments, in these words:

“Therefore, as blessed Ambrose testifies, after churches had been established in every place and the offices ordered, the arrangement of things was made different from what it had been at the beginning. At first, everyone taught and everyone baptized on whatever days and at whatever times opportunity arose. For Philip did not seek a time or a day on which to baptize the eunuch, nor did he introduce a fast. Nor did Paul and Silas delay the time when they were to baptize the jailer with all his household. Nor did Peter have clergy or seek a day when he baptized Cornelius with his entire household. Nor did he himself, but he ordered the brothers who were with him at Cornelius’s house in Joppa. For at that time no one had yet been ordained except the seven deacons. [Col. 0116C]

“Thus, so that the people might grow and multiply, at the beginning everyone was permitted both to evangelize and to baptize and to explain the Scriptures in the church. But when the Church had embraced all places, meeting places were established, and rulers and the other offices were ordered in the churches, so that no one from the clergy who had not been ordained would dare do what he knew had not been entrusted or permitted to him.

“And the Church began to be governed by another order and foresight; for if everyone could do the same things, it would be irrational, and the matter would appear common and utterly worthless. Hence it is that now neither deacons preach among the people, nor do others or laymen baptize, nor are believers immersed on just any day, except when they are ill. [Col. 0116D]

“Therefore the writings of the Apostle do not agree in every respect with the regulation that now exists in the Church, because they were written at the very beginning. Thus he calls the apostle Timothy, whom he himself had appointed, a bishop, because the first presbyters were called bishops, so that when he departed his successor might succeed him. Finally, in Egypt the presbyters confirm if the bishop is not present. [Col. 0117A]

“But because subsequent presbyters began to be found unworthy to hold primacies, the arrangement was changed by prudent foresight, so that not rank but merit would create the bishop, appointed by the judgment of many priests, lest an unworthy man rashly usurp the office and become a scandal to many.”

Thus far Rabanus.

### XXVIII. From the same Rhenanus’s *Admonition on the Doctrines of Tertullian*

Moreover, although in certain Greek collections I have found much concerning confession and penance, drawn partly from the ancient writers Basil, Chrysostom, and Maximus, and partly from the more recent monks Nilus, Climacus, Isaac, and Thalassus, nevertheless I especially approved what I recently copied from an older manuscript: from a little book *On the Remedy of Penance*, attributed to Augustine, and also from material gathered elsewhere by some diligent scholar. For Gratian cites these passages in various places under various titles. [Col. 0117B]

I thought it worthwhile to transfer them here, so that what is found elsewhere either scattered or abridged might here be read together. Indeed, the little book *On the Remedy of Penance* lies hidden among Augustine’s works and is therefore rarely read. Accordingly, these passages have for the most part been taken word for word. It begins as follows:

“Human life,” he says, “however greatly it may excel in the fruitfulness of righteousness, is not lived without the remission of sins,” etc.

### XXIX. The same, after much intervening material

They do not prescribe the measure of time to be spent in penance with sufficient precision for each individual crime, but rather determine that it should be left to the judgment of the bishop. Before the Lord, the measure of time is not so important as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food alone, but rather the mortification of vices. [Col. 0117C]

For this reason they command that the periods of penance be greatly shortened by faith and conduct, and prolonged by negligence. Nevertheless, forms of penance have been imposed for certain faults, according to which other faults must be assessed, since by these same forms it is easy to estimate the punishment and severity of the canons.

These statements were, as it were, spoken by one present in a work divided into three books. The first contained matters concerning penance and penitents, crimes, and judgments. The second dealt chiefly with the accused, accusers, and witnesses, together with the other ecclesiastical regulations pertaining to these matters. The third concerned the orders of priests.

I would gladly purchase these books at a great price, but through the injury of time and human negligence they have been lost. Only this little work survives, which there served in place of a preface, and which I have here reproduced in full for the benefit of students of Christian affairs.

At the end, the author testifies that he followed not only the ecumenical councils but also adopted certain material from the constitutions of provincial synods, over which a metropolitan bishop usually presides. For this reason I would all the more gladly read the books just mentioned. [Col. 0117D]

The constitutions of the provincial synod that Rabanus, archbishop, held at Mainz by command of Louis the Pious Caesar, together with his fellow bishops Samuel, Gozbald, Hebo, Gozbrath, Hemmo, Waldgar, Ansgar, Otgar, Lanto, Salomon, and Gebahart, along with the remaining colleagues—fellow bishops, abbots, monks, priests, and the other ecclesiastical orders—pleased me beyond expression when they recently came into my hands by chance. But they too were not complete, and the very matter I most wanted to know was missing.

From that book, however, I discovered the method for investigating crimes, apparently sent from Rome by Pope Nicholas to Rathald, bishop of the holy Church of Strasbourg.

### XXX. Jacobus Meyerus, in the *Annals of Flanders*

In the year 791, the Parisian school was begun by four highly learned men—Claudius, John, Alcuin, and Rabanus—English by nation and disciples of the venerable Bede. [Col. 0118A]

### XXXI. Sebastian Münster, in the *Cosmography*, Book III, under Mainz

Rabanus, a native of Fulda, elsewhere called Magnentius Maurus, a disciple of the Englishman Bede, a poet and theologian, first an abbot and afterward an archbishop, died in the year 856.

### XXXII. Gaspar Bruschius, in the *Chronology of the Monasteries of Germany*, in the description of Fulda, or the Monastery of Fulda

This monastery possesses, among its other ornaments, a distinguished and incomparable library, first collected and furnished by Rabanus and afterward greatly enlarged and put in order by Hildebert—monks and abbots of Fulda, distinguished for learning and integrity of life. On account of his outstanding virtue and honorable life, Rabanus was finally recalled even to govern the archbishopric of Mainz. You will read more concerning them in the first volume of our *Bishoprics of Germany*. [Col. 0118B]

### XXXIII. The same, under the fifth abbot of the same monastery

Rabanus, surnamed Magnentius Maurus, a native of Fulda, succeeded Eigil in the year of the Lord 825. He was exceedingly learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly educated in secular knowledge. Formerly a disciple of the Englishman Bede and a professor of the Parisian school, he was a philosopher, rhetorician, and astronomer, and second to none among the poets of his time; neither Italy produced his equal nor Germany his peer.

The numerous and great volumes, monuments of his divine talent, bear witness to these qualities. For just as all libraries commend to us the learning of so great a man, so the book *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*, dedicated to the pious emperor Louis, most clearly proves the power of his genius. Although it is wonderfully distinguished by an unchanging [or: inimitable] variety of different figures, the characters of all the figures nevertheless yield a definite meaning, no matter how one turns them. [Col. 0118C]

He enriched the library of Fulda with such a multitude of books that they can scarcely be counted. Finally, when he wished to devote himself wholly to writing divine books, he set aside the administration and withdrew to Mount Saint Peter. There he placed brothers who were rivals in his studies. Explaining all the biblical writings to his disciples, he illumined them with commentaries that survive to this day. [Col. 0118D]

Then, when the number of brothers had increased through the report of his devout manner of life, he decided to dedicate another monastery on the mountain to John the Baptist. Meanwhile, after Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, had died, he was summoned from Mount Saint Peter to the see of Mainz in the year of the Lord 847 by the emperor Louis II.

He died after having held the leadership of the see of Mainz for ten years, with Charles, duke of Aquitaine, as his successor. He was buried at Mainz at Saint Alban, in the chapel of Saint Boniface. That place, however, is now no longer identifiable because of the construction of the new choir; and it is reported that he was afterward transferred to his homeland.

### XXXIV. Guilielmus Eysengrein, in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*

> **Note:** The work was published in the year 1565. [Col. 0117D]

718 years before, namely in the year of Christ 847:

Saint Rabanus, surnamed Magnentius Maurus, a German by nation and a native of Fulda, became archbishop of Mainz from the abbacy of the Benedictine monastery of Fulda. Formerly a student and disciple of Albinus the Englishman, he was a man exceedingly practiced in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular knowledge. He was once a professor of the Parisian school, a philosopher, rhetorician, and astronomer, and second to none among the poets of his time; neither Italy produced his equal nor Germany his peer. [Col. 0119A]

The numerous and great volumes, monuments of his divine talent, bear witness to these qualities. For just as all libraries commend to us the learning of so great a man, so the book *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, dedicated to the pious emperor Louis, most clearly proves how great his genius was. Although it is wonderfully distinguished by an unchanging [or: inimitable] variety of different figures, the characters of all the figures nevertheless yield a definite meaning, no matter how one turns them.

He enriched the library of Fulda with such a multitude of books that they can scarcely be counted. Finally, when he wished to devote himself wholly to writing divine books, he set aside the administration of Fulda and withdrew to Mount Saint Peter. There he placed brothers who were rivals in his studies. Explaining each and every biblical writing to his disciples, he illumined them with commentaries that survive to this day. [Col. 0119B]

He wrote books *On the Universe* to Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt. He also wrote works *On the Instruction of Clerics*, a volume *On the Divine Offices*, and the work *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*. He also delivered sufficiently elegant sermons to the people; but the sermon he composed *On the Feast of All Saints* is especially praised.

He convened a synod at Mainz, in the church of Saint Alban, at which he condemned a certain heretical priest, Gottschalk, and established many measures for the benefit of the Church.

He died in the year of Christ 857, after holding the leadership of the see of Mainz for ten years, with Charles, duke of Aquitaine, as his successor. He was buried at Mainz at Saint Alban, and it is reported that he was afterward transferred to his homeland.

### XXXV. Sixtus of Siena, in the *Holy Library*, Book IV, under Rabanus

Rabanus Magnentius Maurus, the sixth archbishop of Mainz, a German by nation, formerly the fourth abbot of the monastery of Fulda in Buchonia, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a student of Albinus the Englishman, was a man perfected in knowledge of every discipline: rhetorician, poet, astronomer, philosopher, and theologian. Germany had no equal to him in that age. [Col. 0119C]

This man, I say, offended by the wickedness of his monks, who condemned him because, being too intent upon the study of sacred literature, he neglected temporal matters, left the ungrateful men and withdrew to Louis Augustus. He remained with him for several months. The monks earnestly recalled him, having already repented of what they had done, but they did not obtain their request. This occurred by God’s will, for shortly afterward God raised him to the archbishopric of Mainz, to the confusion of those men.

While he was still in his monastery, at the urging of Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, and of the emperors Louis and Lothair, he composed 172 books of commentaries on all the divine Scriptures, according to the literal sense and spiritual understanding. [Col. 0119D] He compiled them in continuous sequence from all the Latin Fathers, from Jerome to Bede, preserving everywhere their statements and meanings. Where he did not find an exposition by the Fathers, he used explanations of his own. At the beginning of the pages he marked both his own name and those of the other interpreters whose opinions he had incorporated into the books, so that the reader might know what came from the Fathers and what from him, and by what judgment each passage should be read.

Besides these works, he also compiled a dictionary of mystical significations for the whole of divine Scripture, exceedingly useful for the spiritual senses of the holy writings. Of these volumes I have read only the works listed below, printed with beginnings that differ for the most part from those noted by Trithemius in his catalogue:

- On Genesis, to Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, 4 books. “The undertaking of great men...”
- On Exodus, to the same, 4 books. “[Among the other Scriptures...”
- On Numbers, to the same, 4 books. “The Book of Numbers...”
- On Deuteronomy, to the same, 4 books. “Therefore, after completing...”
- On Ecclesiasticus, to Otgar, archbishop, 10 books. “Knowing your goodwill...”
- On Jeremiah, to the emperor Lothair, 18 books. “After the little commentaries...”
- On the Lamentations, to the same, 3 books. “The final part of Jeremiah...” [Col. 0120A]

The printers inserted these works into Jerome’s works and sold them under Jerome’s false name. The beginnings of the remaining writings have not yet been seen by us; they may be found in Trithemius. He flourished in the year of the Lord 855.

### XXXVI. From the same book of Sixtus of Siena, under Jerome

In the commentaries on the Lamentations, apart from certain prefaces to Eusebius, partly collected from Jerome’s letter to Paul of Urbica on the interpretation of the Hebrew alphabet and partly from other writings of his, there is nothing that breathes the spirit of Jerome’s genius. [Col. 0120B]

For, apart from the fact that they contain no trace whatsoever of Greek or Hebrew understanding, the structure of the language is everywhere uneven and openly declares that this work is nothing other than a hodgepodge of excerpts, heaped together by a diligent compiler from the statements of various authors and, above all, from the opinions and entire chapters of Gregory.

Nor do I hesitate to affirm that Rabanus Maurus was the compiler who joined this accumulation together. In the works of Rabanus printed at Basel, these three books are found. The printers inserted them into the volumes of Jerome, so that they might publish them more plausibly as Jerome’s writings, enlarged in bulk, and sell them at a higher price. They cut several lines from the beginning of Rabanus’s preface so that the deception would not be detected by blind purchasers.

### XXXVII. From Book V of the same work, note 12

“And it came to pass morning and evening: the second day” (Genesis 1). [Col. 0120C]

Rabanus, bishop of Mainz, in his Commentary on Genesis, investigating why, after the work of the second day, it is not said—as it is concerning the works of the other five days—“God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1), replies, on the authority of the ancient Fathers, that this occurred because the number two is infamous and to be feared on account of the cause of corruption, which first proceeds from it. This, however, is Jerome’s opinion at the beginning of his Commentary on Haggai and in the first volume Against Jovinianus, where he writes as follows:

> “It must be considered according to the Hebrew truth that, when Scripture on the first, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days, after the works of each had been completed, said, ‘And God saw that it was good,’ on the second day it entirely omitted this, leaving us to understand that the number two is not good, since it divides unity and prefigures the bonds of marriage. Hence, in Noah’s ark, all animals that enter in pairs are unclean.”

Nicholas of Lyra, in his Postil on Genesis, rejects this opinion—or rather this fabrication—and prefers to it Rabbi Solomon’s explanation, who says:

> “God did not call the work of the second day good because the work concerning the waters, which was completed afterward on the third day, was not yet perfect, implying that what is not yet perfect is not worthy to be called good.”

Paul of Burgundy, bishop of Burgos, nevertheless refutes Lyra’s refutation of this.

### XXXVIII. Arnoldus Wion, a Belgian of Douai, in Book II of *The Tree of Life*, when discussing the archbishops of Mainz, chapter 26

Blessed Rabanus Magnentius Maurus, a German, of Fulda, a disciple of the Englishman Alcuin, an eminent theologian of Paris, monk and abbot of Fulda, was appointed in 847, in the thirty-second year of his abbatial administration. For nine years he diligently nourished the flock entrusted to him in learning and holiness. He built the monastery of Saint Peter, situated on a high hill outside the city walls. At the council of bishops held at Mainz in the year 848, he condemned the heretic Gottschalk, and by his continual writing wonderfully enlightened the holy Church. He died in 856, on the fourth day of February, and was buried at Fulda. Trithemius, Book IV, chapter 81; Demochares and Belleforest in the places cited, and countless others.

### XXXIX. The same, Book V of *The Tree of Life*, chapter 71

Saint Rabanus, bishop, doctor of the holy Church, and inventor of the exposition of sacred Scripture called *isogrammatic*, that is, “equal-lettered.”

### XL. From the same work

“For he himself was filled, like a river, with wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 47).

Saint Rabanus Magnentius Maurus attained the greatest glory of learning and piety in his own age. Endowed by nature with excellent abilities and exceptionally instructed by learning, he devoted himself above all to pouring out upon as many people as possible the many benefits of his intellect and natural gifts. Believing that he could not suitably accomplish this in Germany, he went to Gaul and soon brought the Parisian Academy—which had previously been begun by English and Scottish monks—to perfection and to the summit of every kind of profound learning.

For after making great progress in philosophy, rhetoric, astronomy, and theology under the English monk Saint Alcuin, he exerted the full strength of his intellect in publicly and privately instructing the young in all these sciences. He consecrated the first part of his youth to the institutions of Benedict. When he became a man, he was unanimously made abbot of Fulda in Germany; finally, elevated to the archbishopric of Mainz, he there completed a glorious death ten years later.

The books he published, filled with exceptional learning, are almost countless. Thus Trithemius did not hesitate to write of him that neither Italy had produced anyone like Rabanus nor Germany anyone equal to him.

While he was still in his monastery, at the urging of Freculf, bishop of Lisieux, and of the monks and also the emperors Louis and Lothair, he composed 178 books of commentaries on all the divine Scriptures, according to both the literal sense and spiritual understanding. He collected them from all the Latin Fathers in continuous sequence from Jerome to Bede, preserving everywhere their words and meanings. In places where he found no exposition by the Fathers, he used explanations of his own. At the head of the pages he marked both his own name and those of the other interpreters, indicating what material came from him and according to what judgment each passage should be read.

The following volumes of these works were printed among the works of Saint Jerome, falsely bearing Jerome’s name, and beginning for the most part with words different from those recorded by Trithemius, namely:

- On Genesis, addressed to Bishop Freculf, Book IV: “The undertaking of great men.”
- On Exodus, addressed to the same, Book IV: “Among the other Scriptures.”
- On Numbers, addressed to the same, Book IV: “The book of Numbers.”
- On Deuteronomy, addressed to the same, Book IV: “Therefore, having passed through…”

All these, together with four other books on Leviticus, were printed at Cologne in 1532, in octavo.

- On Ecclesiasticus, addressed to Archbishop Otgar, Book X: “Knowing the benevolence…”

They were printed at Paris by Simon de Colines in 1544.

- On Jeremiah, addressed to the emperor Lothair, Book XVIII: “After the short commentaries…”

Trithemius, however, cites twenty books on the same Jeremiah. I saw them printed at Basel in 1534, in folio.

- On Lamentations, addressed to the same emperor, Book III: “The final part of Jeremiah.”

We have not yet seen the beginnings of the remaining works. They are given by Trithemius as follows:

- On Leviticus, Book IV: “Of the following book.”

They were printed at Cologne together with the works mentioned above in 1532, in octavo.

- On Joshua, Book VII: “To the most blessed Lord.”
- On Judges, Book II: “After the death of Joshua.”
- On Ruth, Book I: “Therefore, for those who investigate.”
- On Kings, addressed to Hilduin, Book IV: “There was a man, etc.; let us say…”

These are manuscripts at Monte Cassino, written in Lombard script.

- On Chronicles, Book IV: “Adam, etc., the tenth.”
- On Ezra and Nehemiah, Book III.
- On Tobit, Book I.
- On Judith, Book VII: “Lord, chosen and rightly so.”
- On Esther, Book I: “The book of Esther, which…”
- On Job, Book I.
- On the Psalms, Book I.
- On Proverbs, Book I.
- On Ecclesiastes, Book I.
- On the Song of Songs, Book I.
- On the Book of Wisdom, Book III: “Love, etc., admonish…”
- On the prophet Isaiah, Book VIII.
- On Ezekiel, Book XX: “And it happened…”
- On Daniel, Book III.
- On the twelve minor prophets, Book XII.
- On Maccabees, Book III: “And it happened after…”
- On the Gospel of Matthew, Book VIII: “Therefore, the expectation…”
- On the Gospel of Luke, Book III.
- On the Gospel of Mark, Book IV.
- On the Gospel of John, Book I: “Among all the history of God…”
- On all the Epistles of Paul, Book XXIII: “To the venerable brother Lupus.”
- On the canonical Epistles, Book VII.
- On the Acts of the Apostles, Book I.
- On the Apocalypse, Book I.

These are his sacred works. The following are reported concerning his other works.

[Note: According to the judgment of Pamelius himself, this work belongs to Paschasius Radbertus and is extant among his works.]

- On the Body and Blood of the Lord, Book I.
- On the Natures of Things, Book V.
- On the Origin and Conduct of Antichrist, Book I.
- Dictionary of Mystical Meanings, exceedingly useful for understanding the spiritual senses of the books of the saints, Book I.
- On the Virtues, Vices, and Ceremonies of the Ancient Church, Book I.

First printed at Antwerp in 1560, in octavo, together with certain fragments of Charlemagne’s works, edited by Wolfgang Lazius.

- On the Deeds of the Emperors Lothair, Louis, and Charles, the sons of Louis the Pious, in heroic verse.

Several books were extant in manuscript at Vienna, Austria, in the possession of Wolfgang Lazius.

- On the Universe, addressed to Bishop Haymo, Book XXII: “First among the Hebrews…”

Some fragments of these works are in manuscript in the possession of D. Constantius.

- On Universal Nature, Book I: “Of the universe.”
- On the Signs of the Nativity of the Lord, Book I.
- On the Virtues of Numbers, Book I.
- On the Origin of Things, Book I.

I saw this work in manuscript at Monte Cassino, on shelf 10, to the right.

- A Dialogue on Computation, Book I: “Because you, venerable…”
- Book of Penitents, or, as others have it, On the Questions of the Canons, Book I.

Printed at Venice in 1584, in quarto, together with other authors.

- Penitential Canons, addressed to Bishop Regenbald, Book I.
- On the Benedictions of the Patriarchs, Book I.
- A Book of Sermons, almost countless in number.

One of these, on the Feast of All Saints, is read in the Roman Breviary and printed in Alcuin’s Homiliary.

- On the Sacrament of the Eucharist, Book I.

Printed at Cologne in 1551.

- Letters to Various Persons, Book I. [Note: These belong to Rupert of Deutz, the abbot.]
- On the Divine Offices, Book XII.

Often printed at Cologne in octavo and duodecimo.

- The Banquet of God, addressed to the emperor Louis, Book I.

Printed at Basel in 1557.

- On the Christian Faith, Book IV.

Manuscripts exist at Vienna in the Lazius library.

- On the Instruction of Clergy, Book III.

First printed at Pfortzheim in Germany by Thomas Anselm in 1505; afterward at Rome, together with other works of the same kind, in 1590, in folio.

- Book of Revelations, Book I.

A manuscript of this is at Venice, in the possession of Jerome Porro.

He also composed that wondrous and highly ingenious work, in two books, *In Praise of the Holy Cross*, in laborious verse. In it he demonstrates that many mysteries of the Christian faith and many mystical numbers—the numbers of angels, virtues, gifts, beatitudes, elements, times, plagues, months, winds, the books of Moses, the name Adam, and other noble things—can correspond and be adapted to the holy Cross. He links verse to verse so that the figures too may have their own verses, by which different images and varied representations of things are displayed; yet the proper order of the principal poem is neither broken nor interrupted in its course or continuity. Thus the letters themselves usually form a double arrangement.

After each poem there follows a prose passage clearly explaining the astonishing depth of the verses. I would say that I have encountered nothing more laborious or more ingenious than this work. He dedicated it to the apostle Saint Peter and, through the hands of Pope Sergius, to whom he had sent it, presented it to that same Saint Peter.

It was printed at Pfortzheim in Germany by Thomas Anselm in 1513; others give the date as 1503. A manuscript on parchment exists in the Cassinese library, on shelf 10, to the right. He is also said to have written many other works, which I have neither seen nor found cited by the authors.

When I was in Flanders, the most learned and reverend James Pamelius, then a canon of Bruges and afterward bishop of Saint-Omer, a man who rendered excellent service to literary scholarship and was my close friend, was correcting all the works of our Rabanus that he could find, intending afterward to publish them with his own commentaries and notes. I do not know whether his pious plan and undertaking was ever completed.

In the second year of his rule, in the year of Christ 848, at the council held at Mainz, he condemned the heretic Gottschalk. Finally, after having served the whole Church, the monastic order, and sound learning, he departed to the Lord in a great reputation for holiness in the year 856, the ninth year of his episcopate. He was first buried in the monastery of Saint Alban, of the Order of Saint Benedict, near Mainz; afterward he was transferred to Saxony, as Trithemius reports. Trithemius also narrated this translation in Book I and composed his Life in three books.

The following epitaph, composed by Rabanus himself before his death, was affixed to his tomb.

### Rabanus Maurus: Funeral Poem on His Own Life

Honest reader, if you wish to know my life,  
You can learn it thus during mortal time.

I was born in this city and reborn at the sacred font;  
Afterward at Fulda I learned sacred doctrine.

There I became a monk and followed the commands of the elders;  
The holy Rule was the standard of my life.

Although I did not always keep it carefully or steadfastly,  
My cell was nevertheless a pleasant dwelling for me.

But when several years of time had now passed,  
Men gathered to change the affairs of the place.

They drew me, infirm, from my home and took me before the ruler,  
Asking me to undertake the office of bishop.

In that office there was neither merit of life nor learning,  
Nor was the shepherd’s work rightly pleasing.

My spirit was ready, but my weak body was slow;  
I did what I could and what God had granted.

Now from the tomb I ask you, beloved brother: by helping me,  
Commend me to Christ the Lord in your prayers.

May the grace of the eternal Judge save me forever,  
Who looks not upon merit but upon the work of piety.

For Raban is my name, and the reading  
Of the divine law was always sweet to me everywhere.

May almighty God grant him the heavenly kingdoms  
And true rest forever in the citadel of heaven.

Ricobald of Ferrara and Ptolemy of Lucca, because it is written here that Rabanus was a disciple of Bede, thought—and even left it recorded in their writings—that he was an Englishman and also bishop of Meaux. Several other recent writers followed them.

Rabanus himself answers the first opinion when he says in the preceding epitaph:

> “I was born in this city and reborn at the sacred font;  
> At Fulda, etc.”

The second opinion is addressed by Demochares, *On the Sacrifice*, Book II, chapter 19, and Belleforest in Part I of his *Cosmography*. In their enumeration of the bishops of Meaux, they do not name even one Rabanus. These writers therefore appear to have been seriously mistaken and to require no small correction.

Thus far Wion. In Book III of the same work, which contains the monastic martyrology, he places him under the fourth day of February in these words:

> “At Mainz, Saint Rabanus, archbishop and doctor of the Church, who, after a life spent composing books and preaching, departed to Christ renowned for holiness.”

### XLI. Caesar Baronius, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume X, under the year 843

Finally, among Gregory’s monuments one must also count the work that Rabanus Maurus, that shining star of Germany in those times and a thirty-year student of Albinus Flaccus, undertook to compose in metrical style, so that the mysteries and praises of the holy Cross might be sung. He dedicated this distinguished work to Gregory IV, Roman Pontiff, etc.

Further below:

> “Although the book was dedicated by Rabanus to Gregory IV, it is nevertheless certain that it was sent through reliable men to Sergius, his successor. Hence we are led to conjecture that Rabanus wrote the book during the final days of Gregory’s life; but because Gregory was prevented by death, it was sent to his successor, namely in the following year, 844, which was the first year of Pope Sergius II.”

### XLII. The same, under the year 847

Hear what the leading theologian of this age, Rabanus, together with his fellow bishops, decided should be written first, as though upon the very threshold, etc.

### XLIII. The same, under the year 856

Rabanus clearly shone forth like a most brilliant star. His surviving writings, like rays of light, demonstrate the excellence of their author, and Germany, illuminated by them, may boast that it possessed a teacher by no means unequal to the great ones. Trithemius, the same authority cited above, reports of him that, besides the short works written both in verse and in prose, he successfully explained the whole of sacred Scripture from beginning to end—a man thoroughly cultivated in every branch of learning and skilled in the three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

### XLIV. Antonius Possevinus, *Sacred Apparatus*, volume II

Rabanus—whom some incorrectly write *Rabbanus*, and whom Cardinal Baronius rightly calls, after others, the most brilliant star of the Church—was not, as some think, an Englishman, nor was he bishop of Meaux. Concerning his nation or homeland, there is strong testimony in his own epitaph, where these words occur:

> “I was born in this city and reborn at the sacred font  
> At Fulda.”

Demochares, *Books on the Sacrifice of the Mass*, Book II, chapter 19, and Belleforest in the first part of his *Cosmography*, in their catalogue of the bishops of Meaux, mention no Rabanus.

Nevertheless, others had written about him before this, Trithemius afterward, and in our own age Sixtus of Siena. The latter says of him:

> “Rabanus Magnentius Maurus, sixth archbishop of Mainz, a German by nation, etc.”

—as above.

Rabanus himself indeed described his life in elegiac verses. It is read at the beginning of his Commentary on Jeremiah, printed at Basel, although Trithemius also wrote three books on his life and discussed the translation of that same Saint Rabanus from the monastery of Saint Alban, of the Order of Saint Benedict, near Mainz, to Saxony.

But when Sixtus says that he flourished in the year 855, this must be understood in such a way that it is known that he died in 856, whatever those may have thought who assigned his death to the preceding year. This is established by an ancient chronicle published by Pithou, and Cardinal Baronius also accepts it.

Although Sixtus, according to the purpose of his work, listed only a few of his writings as expositions of sacred Scripture, Trithemius and finally Arnoldus Wion indicated many more. We add to these that, in the preceding year—that is, 1603—a manuscript martyrology of the same Rabanus was found in the library of the celebrated monastery of Saint Gall among the Swiss.

The following, therefore, is to be regarded as a complete catalogue, insofar as we can make it. (See this above, column 120, in Arnoldus Wion, from which it was reproduced here word for word.)

There is also a work of Rabanus, *In Praise of the Holy Cross*. Not only James Wimpheling, who was a Catholic, but even the heretical enemies of the Cross were compelled to extol it with praise. Wimpheling, in his preface to the work, speaks as follows:

> “Rabanus the Teutonic composed a wondrous and highly ingenious work, *In Praise of the Holy Cross*, in most laborious verse. In it he demonstrates that many mysteries of the Christian faith and many mystical numbers—the numbers of angels, virtues, gifts, beatitudes, elements, times, plagues, months, winds, the books of Moses, the name Adam, and other noble things—can correspond and be adapted to the holy Cross. He links verse to verse so that the figures too may have their own verses, by which different images are represented; yet the proper order of the principal poem is neither broken nor interrupted in its course or continuity. Thus the letters themselves usually form a double arrangement. After each poem there follows a prose passage clearly explaining the astonishing depth of the verses.”

So he writes.

Nor was there anyone lacking who, speaking of this work, wrote—as Arnoldus Wion did—that the two books of the work, which truly attest that it was exceedingly laborious, contain many mysteries of the Christian faith and many mystical numbers: of angels, virtues, gifts, beatitudes, elements, times, plagues, months, winds, the books of Moses, the name Adam, and other noble things. He demonstrates that their power and dignity can correspond and be adapted to the holy Cross, linking verse to verse so that the figures too may have their own verses, by which diverse images and varied representations of things are displayed. Yet the proper order of the principal poem is neither broken nor interrupted in its course or continuity; thus the letters themselves usually form a double arrangement.
