After each poem there follows a prose passage clearly explaining the astonishing depth of the verses. “I would say,” he writes, “that I have encountered nothing more laborious or more ingenious than this work.” He dedicated it to the apostle Saint Peter and, through the hands of Pope Sergius, to whom he had sent it, presented it to that same Saint Peter. It was printed at Pfortzheim in Germany by Thomas Anselm in 1513; others give the year as 1503. Finally, it was reprinted in 1605. A manuscript on parchment exists in the Cassinese library, on shelf 10, to the right.

Nor was there lacking someone who supplied an example of a figure in the manner in which it was expressed, taken from the first part of Figure 13, entitled “On the Days of Christ’s Conception in the Virgin’s Womb,” represented by four crosses—that is, 236—and by the significance of that number.

I know that James Pamelius, who eventually became bishop of Saint-Omer in Belgium, devoted himself to collecting as many of Rabanus’s works as he could find and publishing them with commentaries or notes of his own, as he had done splendidly with Tertullian and Saint Cyprian. I do not know, however, whether they were ever published. Rabanus himself, at the beginning of his Commentary on Jeremiah, described his life in verse.

### XLV. Robert Bellarmine, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Rabanus Maurus, a German by nation, was abbot of Fulda in the time of the emperor Louis the Pious. He was made bishop of Mainz during the reign of Lothair, Louis’s son. He died in the year of the Lord 856, during the reign of the emperor Louis the Younger. He was a man equally learned and pious. He wrote much both in verse and in prose. He published commentaries on the whole of sacred Scripture of both Testaments. He also published three books *On the Instruction of Clergy*, which exist together with many other works on the same subject, printed at Cologne in 1568.

But above all, in the flower of his age he wrote a wondrous work in prose and verse, *In Praise of the Holy Cross*, addressed to Pope Gregory IV in the year of the Lord 843; after Gregory’s death he sent it to his successor Sergius. This work was published through the efforts of James Wimpheling in 1501.

Among Rabanus’s works is also a commentary on Lamentations, which some attribute to Saint Jerome. It truly belongs to Rabanus, not to Jerome, as we stated above.

## Georgius Colvenerius to the Reader

We do not add more testimonies, since these are sufficient, although others are not lacking: from Fulbert of Chartres, Letter 81; from Gratian, who cites Rabanus in various places in his *Decree*, passages that we have presented as collected by Saint Antoninus; likewise from Peter Lombard, called the Master of the Sentences, in Book IV, distinction 22, section A; from Saint Thomas in the *Summa Theologica*; from Christian Massaeus in his *Chronicle of the World*; from John Aventinus in Book IV of the *Annals of Bavaria*; from John Garetus, *On the Eucharist*, century nine; from Peter Cratepolius in his catalogue of the electors of Mainz; from Conrad Gesner in his *Bibliotheca*; from Israel Spachius; from Papirius Masson, Book II of the *Annals of the Franks*; from Andreas Thenet in his *Images of Illustrious Men*, published in French; and so forth.

Anyone wishing for more should read what two very learned and diligent members of the Society of Jesus, especially skilled in recovering antiquities, have written about Rabanus: the Reverend Father Nicholas Serrarius, in Book IV of *The Affairs of Mainz*, on Rabanus as its sixth archbishop; and the Reverend Father Christopher Browerus, in Book II of the *Annals of Fulda*, chapter 13, and Book III, chapters 13 and 14, where he inserts the whole of the priest Rudolf’s book *On the Life of Rabanus*, and again in Book IV, on the fifth abbot of Fulda.

Only this point concerning Rabanus’s homeland seemed worth adding. Most people think that he was born and reborn at Fulda, on the basis of the epitaph composed by him, which we quoted above. Some, however, read it incorrectly in this form:

> “I was born in a city and reborn at the sacred font;  
> At Fulda I afterward learned sacred doctrine.”

The word *this* (*hac*) has been omitted. I have seen it read in this way in a certain manuscript. Others include the word but punctuate incorrectly as follows:

> “I was born in this city and reborn at the sacred font  
> At Fulda; afterward I learned sacred doctrine.”

This was first printed in this form before Rabanus’s Commentary on the Prophet Jeremiah, at Basel, by Heinrich Petri in 1534. Others followed it, except Baronius in volume X of the *Annals*, under the year 856, and Browerus in the book in which he published Rabanus’s poems on various subjects and illustrated them with learned scholia. Arnoldus Wion also agrees, placing a comma after the word *reborn*. They therefore punctuate it as follows:

> “I was born in this city and reborn at the sacred font:  
> At Fulda I afterward learned sacred doctrine.”

That this is the correct punctuation is proved by the fact that he composed this epitaph while already residing in the city of Mainz and serving as archbishop. Thus he indicates that he was from Mainz by birth, not from Fulda.

The same thing is clearly attested by what is written in his manuscript book *On the Universe*:

> “Rabanus Maurus was born and reborn at Mainz, and from childhood was a monk at Fulda; afterward he was enclosed in a cell, and finally elevated to the archbishopric. His suitable works concern the text of both Testaments, and before the southern gate of the aforesaid city, at Saint Alban’s, the memorial of his tomb is displayed in the chapel of the holy archbishops Martin and Boniface.”

So it is written there.

# A Bibliographical Notice of Rabanus’s Works by Fabricius

*(The Library of Medieval and Late Latin.)*

We shall list the writings of Rabanus Maurus in chronological order, following Henschenius and Mabillon as our guides; we shall also add the volumes of the Cologne edition of 1627 and mark with an asterisk those works that first appeared in Colvenerius’s edition.

1. **On the Praises of the Holy Cross**, 815. Volume I, p. 273. Published separately at Pfortzheim through the efforts of James Wimpheling, by Thomas Anshelm, 1501, folio; Augsburg, 1605; and together with John Valentine Merbitzius’s *Treatise on the Variety of the Human Face*, Dresden, 1676, quarto.

2. **On Clerical Instruction**, 819. Volume VI, p. 1; Cologne, 1532; in the later Paris *Library of the Fathers*, volume X, p. 559; in Melchior Hittorp’s *Writers on the Divine Offices*, Cologne, 1568; Rome, 1591. Baluze published the poem to Archbishop Heistulf, appended to these books, in *Miscellany*, Book IV, p. 553.

3. **Commentary on Matthew**, 822, according to Mabillon. Volume V, p. 1. *“It should be noted,” says Colvenerius in Book VII, chapter 26, and Book VIII, chapters 26 and 28, “that certain passages are missing, as is indicated in the margin there. They were lost through the insolence of the soldiers of Halberstadt at Ursellis in the archbishopric of Mainz, where that volume V was printed in 1622.”*

4. **Homilies.** Volume V, p. 580.

The following works were written when he was already abbot:

5. **Commentary on the Pentateuch**, filling the whole of volume II; previously printed at Cologne in 1532, octavo. Colvenerius’s edition adds, on p. 296, an epitome of the Commentaries on Leviticus by Strabo, Rabanus’s disciple.

6. **On Joshua**, 834. Henschenius published a fragment of the dedicatory letter; Mabillon published the complete letter, p. 41. The commentary itself has not yet appeared.

7. **On Judges and Ruth.** Volume III, p. 1, *p. 36.*

8. **On the Books of Kings and Chronicles.** Volume III, pp. 45, 145. *

9. **On Judith and Esther.** Volume III, pp. 243, 279. * Mabillon calls these unpublished, p. 38, but says that he possesses them transcribed by Peter Francis Chifflet. He gives the preface on p. 42. On p. 263 he adds James Pamelius’s commentary on the Book of Judith. *

10. **On Maccabees**, before 840. Volume IV, p. 380.

11. **On Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus.** Volume III, pp. 362, 344. The latter had previously appeared at Paris in 1544 through Simon de Colines, folio.

The writings composed after he had relinquished the office of abbot are:

12. **A Collection on the Epistles of Paul**, 842. Volume V, p. 169. * On p. 161, James Pamelius’s short commentary on the Epistle to Philemon is prefixed. *

13. **On Ezekiel.** Volume IV, p. 169. *

We now add the remaining works without observing chronological order.

14. **Extracts from Priscian’s Art of Grammar.** Volume I, p. 28. *

15. **On the Universe**, twenty-two books, or *A Work on Etymologies*, addressed to King Louis, 844. Volume I, p. 51. Mabillon examines his distinctive opinion concerning the damnation of catechumens who died before baptism, p. 44.

16. **Commentary on the Songs sung during the week at the morning praises.** Volume III, p. 295.

17. **On Proverbs.** Volume III, p. 323. *

18. **On Jeremiah.** Volume IV, p. 1. Basel, 1534, through Heinrich Petri.

19. **On the Seven Signs of the Nativity of the Lord.** Volume V, p. 746.

20. **Allegories on the Whole of Scripture.** Volume V, p. 749. *

21. **On Sacred Orders, Divine Sacraments, and Priestly Vestments.** Volume VI, p. 50. * In many respects it is the same as Book I *On the Instruction of Clergy*, but the prefixed letter is different, as are certain other passages.

22. **On Ecclesiastical Discipline**, three books. Volume VI, p. 60. * In the first two books are several chapters that correspond to the books *On the Instruction of Clergy*, as is noted in the margin.

23. **On Seeing God, Purity of Heart, and the Manner of Penance.** Volume VI, p. 85. *

24. **On Questions concerning the Penitential Canons.** Volume VI, p. 110. * It first appeared in Peter Steuart’s *Canisian Supplement*, p. 635; afterward in the *New Canisian Treasury*, volume II, part II, p. 293; and also in Baluze’s edition of Regino, p. 465, but under the title *Letter to Heribald, Bishop of Auxerre*, written in 853.

The work was published in 841. The prefixed letter, however, could not have been written in 854, because the author calls himself a bishop. Near the end of chapter 33, the author answers Heribald’s question: “Does the Eucharist pass into the privy?” Mabillon, in the preface to the fourth Benedictine century, Part II, pp. 32ff., counts him among the Stercoranists, whereas Basnage defends him. Consult those authors, as well as our Book VIII, p. 701; we avoid prolixity here.

25. **On Vices and Virtues, on the Satisfaction for Sins and Remedies, or Penances**, three books. Volume VI, p. 125. These, together with no. 24, are attributed by preference to Halitgarius, under whose name they also appear in Canisius and in the *Libraries of the Fathers*. See Mabillon’s *Eulogy of Rabanus*. Add our discussion above in Book VIII, p. 186, and Book III, p. 242. Lazius published them at Antwerp in 1560, octavo, after certain fragments of Charlemagne.

26. **One Book of Penitents**, written after 841. Volume VI, p. 155. It appeared among the *Penitential Canons* of Antonius Augustinus, with notes, Venice, 1584, quarto.

27. **In Which Degree of Kinship Marriage Is Permitted.** Volume VI, p. 165.

28. **On the Marriages of Kinsmen and the Sorceries of Magicians.** Volume VI, p. 166.

29. **On the Soul and the Virtues.** Volume VI, p. 173.

30. **On the Origin, Life, and Conduct of Antichrist.** Volume VI, p. 177. Pfortzheim, through Thomas Anselm, 1505.

31. **Martyrology.** Volume VI, p. 179. First published by Steuart in volume VI; in the new edition, volume II, part II, p. 313. Its prologue, together with the verses to Abbot Grimoald, was published by Canisius in volume IV, p. 326. Another prologue, addressed to Ratleicus, abbot of Seligenstadt, was recovered from the library of Saint Gall by Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 418.

32. **Poems on Various Subjects**, with notes by Christopher Browerus, Mainz, 1617, quarto. Volume VI, p. 202. Du Chesne published the epitaph of the emperor Lothair and the empress Irmentrudis in volume II of the *Writers of the Franks*.

33. **Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict.** Volume VI, p. 246. * This belongs to Abbot Smaragdus, as is attested by Sigebert of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 118, and by the parchment codices to which Mabillon appeals.

34. **Latin-Barbarous Glosses on the Parts of the Human Body**, published by Goldast in volume II of *Alemannic Affairs*. Volume VI, p. 331.

35. **On the Invention of Languages from Hebrew to Theotisc**, published by the same Goldast. Volume VI, p. 333.

These works of Rabanus Maurus, distributed among six volumes, were published through the care of Georgius Colvenerius, chancellor of the Academy of Douai, Cologne, 1627, folio, three volumes.

The following works were published from manuscripts after that time:

1. **Three Letters on Predestination against Gottschalk**, addressed to Noting, bishop of Verona, and Eberhard, duke, published by James Sirmond at Paris in 1647, octavo, and together in the collected works, volume II, p. 985; in Ughelli’s *Sacred Italy*, volume III, new edition, pp. 592–608; and in the first volume, part I, of Gilbert Mauguin’s *Authors on Predestination and Grace*.

2. **Book against the Jews**, published by Peter Francis Chifflet at Dijon in 1656. [Note: Ittigius, *On the Libraries of the Fathers*, p. 684.] Mabillon maintains in his *Burgundian Journey*, p. 10, that it belongs to Agobard. Others, however, attribute it to Amulo of Lyon. Mabillon has more on the subject in his *Eulogy of Rabanus*. Martène and Durand published another genuine book of Rabanus against the Jews in the *Newest Treasury*, volume I, pp. 401, 594.

3. **Two Short Works**, one on chorepiscopi and the other on the reverence of children toward parents and of subjects toward kings, published by Baluze at the end of the works of Peter de Marca, volume I, p. 285. Rudolf calls this book a *Collection*. The former short work is also found in volume V of Hardouin’s *Councils*, p. 1417.

4. **Letter to Reginbald, Chorepiscopus, 848**, and **Short Work on the Ordinations of Chorepiscopi**, in volume VIII of the *Councils*, p. 1845, royal edition; in volume V of Hardouin, p. 1411; and in volume II of Baluze’s *Capitularies*, p. 1378.

5. **Some Poems**, by the same author, in *Miscellany*, volume IV, p. 553.

6. **Book on the Computation of the Fingers**, in the same work, near the beginning of volume I. A fuller manuscript codex, illustrated with the necessary figures, was to be published at Leiden by Frederick Paccus, as our Fabricius noted, through Gabriel du Mont of Rotterdam.

7. **Three Books on Joshua**, published by Martène and Durand in volume IX of the *Most Extensive Collection*, p. 667, although the priest Rudolf, in chapter 9 of the *Life of Rabanus*, mentions four, while Trithemius, in the same Life III.3, mentions only two.

8. **Letter to Egilo on the Eucharist**, in Mabillon, *Benedictine Century IV*, Part II, p. 591.

9. **Short Work on the Passion of the Lord**, published in volume IV, part II, p. 7, of Pez’s *Newest Treasury*.

10. **Latin-Theotisc Glossary**, not, as Lambecius and Nesselius maintain, covering the whole Bible, but extending over many biblical words and also words of other authors. A specimen exists in Lambecius, *On the Vienna Library*, II, p. 415. A larger specimen was published by John Diecmann, superintendent of the churches of Bremen and Verden, who also illustrated it with a not contemptible commentary, Bremen, 1721, quarto. John George Eccard published the complete work in volume II of *Frankish Affairs*, pp. 950–976.

11. **Treatise on the Sacrament of the Eucharist**, consisting of fifty-seven books. It was published from the library of Cuthbert Tunstall, bishop of Durham, at Cologne by John Quentel in 1551, as Olearius reports in *Ecclesiastical Library*, II, p. 112.

12. Mabillon published the verses to Grimald in *Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 326, new edition, p. 419.

13. The longer Synodal Letter was published by Sirmond in 1647. See vol. II of the *Works*, p. 1295; the other, shorter letter to Hincmar of Rheims had previously been published in the volumes of the Councils.

## Unpublished Works

1. Commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, in the Library of Balliol College, Oxford.

2. A book on the Life of Saint Mary Magdalene, in Magdalen College, Oxford.

3. Exposition of Easter and the Paschal Lamb, in Saint Benedict’s College, Cambridge.

4. Explanation of Isaiah, in the library of the monastery of Heilsbronn in Franconia, according to Hocker in the catalogue of that library, p. 14.

5. A book to the Emperor Louis on the Offering of Boys according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Manuscript in the library of Melk.

6. A consolatory letter to the same man. Rudolph mentions these two works in the *Life of Rabanus*.

7. Commentaries on Joshua, Ezra and Nehemiah, Tobit, Job, Ecclesiastes, and the remaining biblical books not listed above.

8. On the deeds of the emperors Lothar, Louis, and Charles, the sons of Louis the Pious, in heroic verse.

9. On the blessings of the patriarchs; letters to various persons; and other works mentioned by Colvenerius at the beginning of volume I. Their titles must nevertheless be carefully compared with the published works, lest something already published long ago be regarded as unpublished.

* In Gocceius’s German *Ephemerides* for April 1751, Rabanus’s *Commentary on Daniel* is announced. They state that Father Ziegelbaur, a Swede of the Order of Saint Benedict, possesses it in manuscript and has already prepared it for publication. In the common interest I ask and beg that this learned man publish it as soon as possible—unless, perhaps, our requests have already anticipated him. As I write this, however, I have just learned that the same religious man has died. I hope that this will not damage the common expectation.

### Treatise on the Sacrament of the Eucharist

The work published at Cologne is altogether identical with the treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which is the genuine work of Saint Paschasius Radbertus. Therefore the English manuscript from which it was published assigns it to Rabanus Maurus only through scribal error. See *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. V, p. 194, and vol. VI, pp. 15–16, preface.

[Col. 0131]

## Catalogue of the Works of Rabanus Maurus Contained in the Six Volumes of Colvenerius’s Edition

### Volume One Contains:

The *Life of Rabanus the Abbot*, published by Rudolph, priest and monk, his disciple. The *Life of the same Rabanus*, written by Johannes Trithemius in three books. An excerpt from Priscian’s *Art of Grammar*. *On the Universe*, in twenty-two books, from an old printed edition. *On the Praises of the Holy Cross*, partly in prose and partly in verse, from the Augsburg printed edition of 1605.

### Volume Two:

Four books on Genesis. Four books on Exodus. Seven books on Leviticus. An epitome of the same Commentary on Leviticus, by his disciple Strabo. Four books on Numbers. Four books on Deuteronomy, all from the Cologne printed edition.

### Volume Three:

[Col. 0131B]

Two books on the Book of Judges. One book on the Book of Ruth. Four books on the four Books of Kings. Four books on the two Books of Chronicles. One book on the Book of Judith, followed by Jacobus Pamelius’s Commentary on the same book. On the Book of Esther. On the Canticles sung at Matins throughout the week. Three books on Solomon’s Proverbs. Three books on the Book of Wisdom. Ten books on Ecclesiasticus, from the Paris printed edition.

### Volume Four:

Thirty books on the prophet Jeremiah, including his Lamentations, from the printed edition. Twenty books on the prophet Ezekiel. On the two Books of Maccabees.

### Volume Five:

[Col. 0131C]

Eight books of Commentary on Matthew.

*(In these, it should be noted that in book VII, chapter 26, and book VIII, chapters 26 and 28, certain passages are missing, as is indicated there in the margin. They were lost through the violence of the soldiers of Halberstadt at Ursellis in the archbishopric of Mainz, where that fifth volume was printed in the year 1022.)*

Thirty books of Rabanus Maurus’s Commentaries on the fourteen Pauline Epistles.

To these we prefixed Jacobus Pamelius’s short commentary on the Epistle of blessed Paul to Philemon.

Rabanus Maurus’s Homilies on the Epistles and Gospels, from Christmas Day to the vigils of Easter, numbering 61, to which many other homilies on the saints and various virtues are added.

Homilies on the Epistles and Gospels from the Easter Vigil to the fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost, both for the Temporal Cycle and for the saints, numbering 91.

A homily on the Gospel, “The Book of the Generation of Jesus Christ.”

On the seven signs of the Nativity of the Lord.

Allegories on Sacred Scripture.

### Volume Six:

[Col. 0132]

Three books *On the Instruction of Clerics and the Ceremonies of the Church*, addressed to Heistulf, archbishop, from the Cologne printed edition.

One book addressed to Giotmar on the sacred orders, the divine sacraments, and priestly vestments. This work is in many respects identical with Rabanus’s first book *On the Instruction of Clerics*, but its prefatory letter is different, and there are some other differences.

Three books addressed to Reginald *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*: the first is on the sacred orders; the second on catechesis and the divine sacraments; the third on the Christian struggle, treating virtues and vices.

In the first two there are several chapters that correspond to the books *On the Instruction of Clerics*, as is noted in the margin.

Three books addressed to Abbot Bonosus: the first on seeing God; the second on purity of heart; the third on the manner of penance.

Three books addressed to Heribald *On Questions Concerning Penitential Canons*: the first contains rules concerning ministers of the Church if they have gone astray, together with letters of Pope Hormisdas, Isidore, and others; the second is on satisfaction for penance; the third on the penances of laypeople.

Three books *On Vices and Virtues, on Satisfaction for Sins and Remedies—in other words, on Penance*.

One book addressed to Archbishop Otgar, *On Penitents*, which is, as it were, a fitting compendium of the preceding works.

“How many generations of kinship make marriage lawful?” A letter to Bishop Humbert, from the Cologne printed edition.

[Col. 0132C]

One book addressed to Bonosus *On the Marriages of Blood Relatives and the Tricks of Magicians*, from the Cologne printed edition.

A short work addressed to King Lothar *On the Soul and the Virtues*, from the Cologne printed edition.

A treatise *On the Origin, Life, and Character of Antichrist*, from the Cologne printed edition.

The *Martyrology of Rabanus Maurus*, from volume VI of Henricus Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*.

Poems on various subjects, edited by Christoph Brower with his scholia, Mainz.

Commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Latin-Barbarian glosses on the parts of the human body, from volume II of the *Alemannic Matters*, published at Frankfurt in 1606.

[Col. 0132D]

Also, *On the Invention of Languages from Hebrew to German*, from the same work.

# The Complete Works of Rabanus Maurus, Abbot—First of Fulda, Later Archbishop of Mainz—Arranged in Chronological Order

## Part One: Works Published by Him While He Was Already Abbot

[Col. 0133]

## (A.D. 815) Two Books on the Praises of the Holy Cross

Marvelous in learning, verse, and prose. In twenty-eight figures or images, many mysteries of the Christian faith and many mystical numbers—the numbers of angels, virtues, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, the eight beatitudes, the four elements, the four seasons of the year, the four Evangelists and the Lamb, the months, winds, the five books of Moses, the name Adam, Alleluia, and Amen, and the power and dignity of other things—are subtly and ingeniously explained as having been brought into the form of a cross.

## Various Encomia on This Work

[Col. 0133]

### Jacobus Wimpfeling of Sélestat to All Lovers of Good Literature: Greetings

[Col. 0133A]

Rabanus the Teuton has woven together, in a most laborious poem, a marvelous and highly ingenious work in praise of the holy cross. In it he demonstrates that many mysteries of the Christian faith and many mystical numbers—the numbers of angels, virtues, gifts, beatitudes, elements, seasons, regions, months, winds, the books of Moses, the name Adam, and other noble things—can correspond and be adapted to the holy cross. He links verse to verse so that the figures too may have their own verses, by which the various images are represented; yet the legitimate order of the principal poem is not broken or interrupted in its course or continuity.

Thus the letters themselves generally form a double arrangement. After each poem there follows a prose explanation, clearly expounding the astonishing profundity of the verses. O splendid work, worthy of every kind of veneration, by which Germany—having produced such a man—is not undeservedly made illustrious and glorious!

Therefore, candid reader, whoever you are and whoever you are truly Christian, make this book especially your own, I beg you: so that you may see its novelty, praise its ingenuity, marvel at its extraordinary vein, be kindled to love the cross and the Crucified One, begin to be devoted to him who suffered for you, and delight yourself in this sweet tree on which the salvation of the world hung, in which all our hope, our refuge, and our medicine are found, and through which we have been saved and liberated. From God’s gift you will doubtless obtain the immortal fruit of your soul.

Farewell, most beloved reader in Christ.

From the hermitage of Saint William, in the suburb of Strasbourg, on the fifth day before the Ides of Sextilis, in the year of our salvation 1501.

### Johannes Reuchlin of Pforzheim, Doctor of Both Laws, to the Printer Thomas Anshelm, in Praise of Rabanus’s *On the Holy Cross*: Encomium

Esteem yourself, O Thomas, and deem Pforzheim blessed,  
for through you Rabanus’s work on the Cross shines forth.

The seeds of writing, scattered throughout the world, return;  
the art that earlier fathers concealed from those to come.

Let the mind that knows not what is shameful draw near:  
here, in the beautiful heaven, lies something more beautiful.

Not the cross of Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus,  
nor the cross of the Ganymedean Bear, will be seen in this book,

but the cross to which the Creator of humankind and God  
was fastened, paying the penalty for our crimes, innocent himself.

This cross of Rabanus shines more brightly than the Constantinian cross,  
once painted as a vision marked with stars.

The bronze image of the serpent, fixed upon the cross,  
could heal; but by this one you will be safer still.

A mottled sequence scatters beautiful strokes  
in various parts, so that its arrangement may indicate the cross.

By this Rabanus easily defeated the painter of Cos, Apelles;  
for you there will be no Parrhasius, no Zeuxis.

Whether you read the book, you will see everything fashioned with manifold art;  
whether you wish to hear it, harmony sings.

Come then, both of you, and raise your titles to lofty heights  
through this single, more splendid book of Rabanus:

Thomas Anshelm, who first gives the pages form through your art;  
and you, Pforzheim, fountain and origin of my work.

City honored by artists, maker of ingenious minds—  
O glory, live as Rabanus’s second mother!

### To the Man of Great Talent and Most Diligent Seeker of Good Things, Brother Nicolaus Keinbos, of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, Parish Priest of Durlach: An Introduction, or Commendation, of the Marvelous Work of Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda, *On the Praises of the Cross*

The work of Rabanus, which you recently sent me, Nicolaus,  
concerning the sacred Cross and the beauty of the cross,

I could not help admiring in many ways,  
nor could I refrain from judging it worthy of extravagant praise.

And rightly so: for what servant of Christ or of the cross  
would not himself strive to praise the cross?

Yet who will think himself capable of speaking worthily  
in verse of the marvelous and saving cross?

[Col. 0135A]

Sense fails in everyone, as do tongue and the power of genius,  
when a mortal attempts to sing of the cross.

Yet that learned Father Rabanus, an excellent author,  
dared to do so, with varied poetic inspiration.

He accomplished the mystery, praise, and glory of the cross,  
and taught that the cross is present in all things.

From the heavenly powers and from the first parent  
he drew the cross through all creatures and elements.

O how great a labor that holy Father undertook!  
How immense a burden he assumed for love of the cross!

He passed sleepless nights in constant wakefulness, beyond doubt,  
so that he might continue the praises of the cross.

All the more do I resent, condemn, marvel at, and lament  
the frivolity of the people of this age:

not only the sluggish, who, flowing in idleness,  
do not sweat and keep vigil worthily for the cross,

but even those who violate, profane, and defile it,  
who despise, dread, and tear the cross apart;

[Col. 0135B]

who, moreover, trample the venerable sign beneath their feet  
and shamefully put to death those marked with the cross.

Their punishment awaits them in the end. Meanwhile,  
it delights us to sing the praises of the cross continually with Rabanus.

Let us return thanks to the Lord; let us acknowledge and give thanks  
to him who frees and blesses us through his own cross.

You too, dear Father Nicolaus, will receive fitting reward  
from heaven and from pious Christians,

you who wear a garment marked with the cross. Therefore you love  
the weapons of the cross, observe them, and strive to enlarge their honor.

You also provide the material by which this work may one day  
come into the light and receive life under your direction.

Rightly, then, you are called KEINBOS, because you live free  
from every crime and take no pleasure in wrongdoing.

For this reason you seek the praises and triumph of the cross  
and cultivate your intelligence through the liberal arts.

Farewell, therefore. May the shadow of the cross defend us,  
receive us beneath its wings, and protect its servants.

[Col. 0135C]

And may the cross, venerable in everlasting glory,  
also protect us forever. Amen.

### Tetrastich by Dodocus the Frenchman, Addressed to Christians

Learn from the infernal powers, you whom the sacred cross alone has redeemed,  
with what devotion the cross deserves to be embraced,

since nowhere have affection, labor, talent, and the power of memory  
been so well scattered and displayed as in this book.

### In Praise of Rabanus’s Poems, by Theodoricus Gresemundus, Doctor of Laws

Rabanus indulged in the stylus, Apelles in panels;  
whatever each painted with his hand breathed forth.

Time, devourer, has scraped away all the panels of the one,  
but the work of the other will live through eternal time.

Painted forms owe their life to poems;  
if the line perishes, the poems do not perish.

### Another Poem by the Same on the Same Subject

[Col. 0135D]

Look upon Rabanus’s verses, turned with marvelous art,  
if you possess a cheerful and inventive mind.

However you read them, meaning rises with the poem,  
for each letter serves in many ways.

And what is more marvelous, each image inhabits  
its own metrical measures. For the poet this involved no labor,

for although these poems are not easily composed,  
they nevertheless flow with effortless grace.

### Elegiac Poem of Johannes Gallinarius of Heidelberg to the Lovers of Christ, That They Read Rabanus’s *Praise of the Holy Cross*

If anyone desires to pass through the triumphal song of Christ’s cross,  
let him direct his steps here with swift stride.

Rabanus is the greatest glory of the Teutonic race;  
in a marvelous poem he has fashioned a noble work.

No work like this has German soil produced, nor Italy,  
nor Tartessus, nor the Rhône, nor the Saône.

[Col. 0136A]

Here no flames of Helen, no wound  
of unhappy Dido, no couches of the descendants of Tantalus resound.

Nor does the poem sound of the burning battles  
of unconquered Mars, nor approve songs composed in Aeaean modes.

Rather, it sings the sacred scars of the triumphant Christ,  
the weapons with which he himself conquered the Stygian ruler,

at which the guilty shades of Erebus, the unspeakable darkness,  
Tartarean Pluto, and Persephone tremble.

### To the Muses, That They Adorn and Encircle Rabanus with a Crown of Every Kind of Fragrant Plant; An Elegy by the Same Johannes Gallinarius of Heidelberg

Bind a maiden laurel around Rabanus’s temples,  
Castalian Muses, and a wreath of Pallas’s foliage.

Let not green ivy be absent, nor the myrtle grove;  
let lilies and purple roses come together.

Cinnamon, thyme, boxwood, narcissus, amomum,  
incense, violets, nard, balsam, myrrh, and thyme—

let terebinth come here, and walnut trees, and rosemary;  
with you, Sylvanus, come here too, O Cyparissus.

[Col. 0136B]

Weave in whatever grows in the gardens of Panchaea,  
whatever Cilicia or the grove of Ida possesses,

whatever the black Indian seeks in the Erythraean seaweed,  
whatever Pactolus or Tagus itself carries.

Let Tmolus also bring his saffron fragrances here,  
and here the honey-bearing mouths of the bees of Hybla bring their honeycombs.

Let the griffins of Hyperborea and the beasts of Caucasus  
bring crystals from the icy summit of Taurus.

Let the white swans bring from the snowy shore amber—
the tears of the Eridanus and of the daughters of Phaethon.

And you, Hamadryads and Nymphs of the meadows,  
pluck every kind of fragrant grass.

Interweave precious gems with woven flowers;  
encircle Rabanus’s temples, Pierian Muses.

### Six Lines by the Same Author

[Col. 0136C]

With Daedalian skill Rabanus guided the threads  
and ordered them to be controlled in labyrinthine fashion.

Though you may be Theseus, relying on Ariadne’s divine aid,  
Daedalus in ingenuity, or Maro himself in verse,

you cannot equal this poet by any art;  
therefore the glory of so great a poet will be greater still.

### In Praise of the Laborious and Extraordinary Poem, by Georgius Symler of Wimpfen, Addressed to Its Maker

How great the name of Rabanus for the land of Mainz—  
a name destined now to possess everlasting honor!

Where the horn-bearing Rhine flows in golden waves  
and cuts its channels through the Belgian waters of the Teutonic shore,

he is our leader and our honor—let posterity imagine greater things—  
a radiant glory to Germans and to nobles.

He has shown what our land and Italy can accomplish  
when he summons the unusual lyre.

Now let the golden rocks of Tarpeian Jupiter be silent,  
and the mechanism called the Pharos of Ptolemy.

Let Crete also be silent, and the inextricable maze  
which they say the hands of Daedalus were able to make.

[Col. 0136D]

Here, in your resonant theater, let wonders be joined together,  
and the ancient fame celebrated for its hot springs.

If you wish to speak of Smyrna’s suspended mass,  
or of Bellerophon’s horse with its weighty rider,

or if you wish to recall the column at Ephesus  
or the column of Rhodes,

this work is rarer than all works of genius.

Beautiful Apollo gave him power over meter,  
for he sang things scarcely imitable by many men.

You may marvel at the plectrum of the Andinian poet,  
but you could not know anything greater than the *Iliad*.

Let Thebes, the civic tombs of Philip,  
Hannibal, and the glory of Venus’s cultivated lyre come forward.

Nothing that has been brought before our Minerva will amount to anything;  
all those things yield individually to these images.

### Four Lines by the Same Author

This chief praise is owed to our poet,  
because he has disclosed a useful work to Christians:

he has painted for all, in rosy blood, the venerable signs  
of the cross and the warfare of the supreme God.

[Col. 0137]

President, ruler, and moderator of the Apostolic See,  
immortal radiance and harbor and breeze to your people,

may you kindly love the lands on your right  
and yourself cherish the gifts offered to you by the author of this unheard-of poem.

[Col. 0138]

He chose a subject more worthy than any other,  
whether it is to be celebrated in prose or in verse.

Say that the poem lives in the image of Apelles’ form,  
as long as golden Rome remains the capital of the earth.

## Albinus’s Intercession for Maurus

[Col. 0137]

[Col. 0137A]

Holy bishop of God, living through the ages by your merits,  
receive with pious mind the cause we bring before you.

When I was the humble guardian and servant  
of this Church, reading the sacred doctrines,

I taught this boy the divine word,  
with ethical instruction and the studies of wisdom.

He is indeed Frankish by birth, an inhabitant of the forests  
of Bochonia, sent here to learn the words of God.

For his abbot, the ruler of the flock at Fulda,  
his father sent him here, to your dwelling,

so that he might study with me the scholarly art of meter  
and prepare himself properly and joyfully in sacred Scripture.

But when he had completed six lustres, and now attempted to write,  
he produced this book with artistic skill in praise of Christ.

Into it he inserted symbolic numbers and figurative images  
in due order, so that he might reveal the gracious gifts of God:

what honor Christ’s Passion would bring to the world,  
and how it would overcome the ancient serpent;

what the holy prophets sang would come to pass,  
and what the writings of the Law properly proclaimed.

[Col. 0137B]

[Col. 0138A]

And because he remembers that he was nourished  
in the distinguished house of this place, behold, he brings you these gifts.

Although they are unworthy and of little value, nevertheless,  
as a gentle patron, receive them, I beg you, in piety,

and return to the Most High the pledge that he himself provided,  
earnestly asking pardon for the craftsman.

He has given as much as he could, not as much as he himself  
was obliged to give, in order to render thanks to God with his mouth.

Pour forth abundant prayers to the powerful Lord  
for the wretched sinner, gracious one, and thus aid your own servant,

who confesses that he has committed many unspeakable deeds,  
as much as a wanton age is accustomed to perpetrate.

Yet firm hope remains: the great goodness of the Thunderer,  
the almighty physician, will save him,

he who by his own blood released the world from its debts  
and washed away many crimes in the sacred font.

Only commend him to Christ through your prayers and sacred merits,  
and thus he will be blessed.

May he pass through the present life safely and be preserved  
for the homeland of the future.

[Col. 0138B]

Protect your own, holy one.

[Col. 0139]

Christ our Savior, protect the supreme pontiff  
and preserve our shepherd safely for all ages:

[Col. 0140]

so that the excellent bishop Gregory may rightly be  
the guardian of the holy Church and the faithful teacher in its court.

## Commendation of the Pope

[Col. 0139A]

Prince of the Apostolic See, golden light of Rome,  
glory and teacher of the people, nourishing love,

you are the head of the Church, the first patriarch throughout the world,  
illustrious in merits and powerful in piety.

Salt of the earth, light of the world, and renowned city of Christ,  
you provide the people a path to perpetual light.

Your tongue has power to open and close heaven;  
though set upon earth, you are the heavenly key-bearer.

You are the renewer, hope, ruler, and honor of your homeland,  
sweet love to all and worthy of God’s love.

The times of this life are now full of dangers:  
peoples stir up wars, and the enemy rages everywhere.

Therefore there is great need that your strong protection  
come to the aid of the wretched, whom the enemy hates.

By pious instructions and sacred prayers, rescue  
the flock entrusted to you, shepherd, from the enemy.

May your praise, reward, and glory remain forever,  
as you hold blessed kingdoms in heaven with Christ,

joined eternally to the apostolic prince Peter,  
whose place on earth you yourself also occupy.

### He Offers a Gift to the Pontiff

[Col. 0140A]

Beloved bishop of God, Pope Gregory, I beg you:  
count me, wretched man, among your own sheep.

Be the true protector of your servant,  
and through your prayers restore him to the eternal Lord,

the one who offers himself entirely and presents these small gifts,  
commending to you both himself and what belongs to him.

Through you, may the holy praise of the cross now stand more acceptably  
before the apostolic prince Peter:

the praise composed for Christ’s honor in ancient times,  
when it pleased me to play with poetic verse.

I truly believe that through you I can seek  
the life which I cannot obtain by my own merits.

May the eternal God, the gentlest creator of the world,  
protect and govern you through long ages,

so that you may be strong, healthy, and prosperous,  
and attain the heavenly kingdoms hereafter and forever.

May he who never sleeps keep you vigilant,  
and restore the merit of your name.

As a watchful shepherd, Gregory, stand attentive  
to your sheep, holy and blessed pope. Farewell.

## On the Image of the Emperor

[Col. 0141] [Col. 0141A]

Lord, King of kings, governing the world by your dominion,  
you who reign by everlasting right and hold the scepter of empire,

you who released the many crimes of our ancestors on the cross,  
when you established the reins of justice:

therefore, O Christ Jesus, you have granted all your servants  
the hope of a blessed life beyond the stars.

[Col. 0142A]

This is now the gift of you, Christ, and of your Father, God.  
Now all the ages rightly marvel at your name,

which long ago was borne upon the head of the beloved  
supreme worshiper of Christ, who properly bears this sign;

and fittingly, let Augustus cultivate the whole world  
by his just throne and by his eager observance of the law.

[Col. 0143A]

For this fruitful work, emerging as the great cosmic wheel turns,  
shows that the world prays for protection through the Emperor’s counsel.

May Augustus purely bear from this place  
a gracious crown of praise.

For divine virtue prepares the right hand by the best art;  
we all ask, Jesus, that your gift grant triumph.

Now may what is gracious and just reign everywhere in justice.  
May he clothe himself in this stone and circle it with a kindly bond,

while the breastplate itself brings forth what is pleasing and prepared.  
May we always desire as our friend the one whom Christ piously protects,

whom no enemy presses with a dart,  
but whom the defender of right shows to be firm and worthy of love.

The emperor possesses a noble adornment,  
and the power of his right hand is sustained by it.

Every favorable omen arises, and the empire remains safe throughout the world.

Behold, all the kingdoms of the Greeks bring gifts through every age,  
and the Persian kingdom gives them, thus surrounding his descendants.

A joyful people, a flourishing race, piously offers its support;  
it delights in producing the Muse, and knows how to love and preserve the shield,

holding the scepters of hope in exile,  
while everywhere it gives the word of faith,

until it drives away its own ages of evil through this power.

[Col. 0144A]

They will hold their rights beautifully; their weapons will be innocent,  
and they will calm and consolidate the arrogance of the earth.

Augustus remains firm and covers the sheepfold,  
as Christ transforms the world with illustrious tribute.

While remembering the trophies of worship and preparing them equally by right,  
he grants that this name be spoken everywhere by devoted lips.

Indeed, it thunders and properly presses upon the breast long cherished;  
there is trembling, and the good fame granted by God increases.

From this the drenched sea of the world advances,  
and casts away unlawful things from its harbor.

By the cross he gives Jesus and follows him.

For this was given to you, O Caesar, ever chaste and pious.  
Now, with generous gaze, terrify the enemy’s camp,

and, driving away hostile fear, grant hope.  
This people, pious and exceedingly grateful, humbly asks this:

that our spirit may go toward forgiveness  
and obey the commands of the Father.

[Col. 0144B]

Long ago I composed a little book in praise of Christ,  
in verse and prose; now, Emperor, I gladly offer it to you,

holy one, whose image goes before it,  
standing armed with faith and showing you victorious everywhere.

## Explanation of the Figure

[Col. 0143]

O Christ the Savior, King of kings and Lord of lords,  
you who govern the world by your own dominion

and, holding an incorruptible scepter, reign over all  
by everlasting right:

you erased the many crimes of our ancestors on the cross  
when you established the reins of justice for the human race,

and granted your faithful the hope of blessed life in heaven  
and the ability to attain it swiftly.

Therefore it is the gift of your most generous Father,  
that is, of the all-powerful Father,

that your ineffable name, once long feared by every age,  
is now borne by the head of the most pious prince

with honorable devotion, and is venerated by all  
with the greatest reverence.

From this it is also shown that by his authority and protection  
the august empire is held firmly,

and that power is removed by just judgment from every miser  
and opponent of Christian religion,

so that the whole world may be governed by the will  
of the religious prince.

For his most abundant distribution of gifts everywhere reveals this,  
summoning the peoples of the earth to praise the revered emperor,

so that all together, by common counsel, may seek his protection.

This is what we, your servants, Christ, gentle Savior,  
humbly ask:

that through the banner of the holy cross  
your most sacred power may imbue his right hand with divine skill

and grant triumph to justice everywhere.

This same power clothes him in a breastplate of faith,  
harder than diamond,

which confers both the most fitting adornment  
and the strongest protection.

Therefore it is necessary that we, together with all Christian people,  
desire the favor of his friendship.

The Lord Christ protects and guards him in such a way  
that no plotter can harm him in any manner

or stain his most just reputation with any crime.  
Rather, the almighty defender, helper of his good zeal and good will,

sets before us in him a steadfastness  
and a pattern of true innocence always worthy of imitation,

and wills that the most noble Caesar possess every fortunate action,  
so that his empire—on land and sea—may remain safe.

For the peoples bring him the most precious gifts of the Greeks,  
and likewise the kingdoms of the Persians;

other peoples too frequently surround him and his offspring  
with their protection,

especially the German nation and the Frankish people,  
from whom his noble lineage derives its origin.

They join in his praises, wishing him life  
and continuing prosperity.

Every exile who in ancient times wandered from his own seat  
hopes, through love of his triumphs, for a swift return,

because, holding the scepters, he scatters the word of faith everywhere  
until he purifies his people from their ancient practice of crimes.

With Christ’s help he will firmly hold the laws of Catholic faith,  
so that he may not cast forth the darts of the word in vain,

but so that they may be powerful weapons of God for every good work  
and, strengthened by faith in Christ, subdue the arrogance of the flesh.

O how firm in faith and steadfast in Christian religion he remains,  
the one who carefully guards at every hour the sheep entrusted to him,

and vigorously demands from all who obey him  
the duty of the Lord’s service and divine worship,

while he shows that the banner of the heavenly King  
must be venerated by all

and sends his teachers everywhere to preach Christ’s Gospel.

They soften the hard-hearted by their words  
and, with divine grace assisting, lead them to receive

the good fragrance of the virtues,  
so that they may despise worldly luxury

and, placing their hope in Christ, desire to share in his sufferings.

Behold, most merciful and most holy emperor,  
I offer you this present gift,

submissive with every devotion.  
You are terrifying to adversaries, pursuing the backs of enemies,

yet gentle toward the devout, mercifully granting pardon  
to those who turn back.

Every people and every nation desires to do your will;  
we, your wretched servants, wish to approach your mercy

with obedient service  
and desire to obey your wishes in all things.

For the little book that I composed long ago  
in honor of the holy cross, in prose and meter,

I now offer humbly to your serenity,  
begging that you, adorned fittingly with the shield of faith,

the breastplate of justice, and the helmet of salvation,  
may deign to fortify us, soldiers of Christ, under your protection

and, with the Lord’s aid, lead us to the harbor of eternal salvation,  
to the increase of your rewards.

The present image of the most serene Emperor Louis contains fifteen verses, written in dactylic tetrameter, as follows:

Jesus Christ, may your sign upon his head  
grant Augustus a gracious helmet,

and make his right hand unconquered.  
May your virtue, Jesus, also grant triumph,

and clothe him in the breastplate of just justice,  
ever pleasing and friendly,

which no enemy may overthrow with a dart.  
But may everything belonging to Caesar remain firm,

and your whole empire through every age.

[Col. 0145B]

[Col. 0146A]

And may his joyful offspring, succeeding him,  
remain in possession of the scepters,

until their ages shall hold their rights,  
and the solid world remain established,

Christ, while it remembers your name everywhere  
and freely preaches the word of the Lord.

In the circle surrounding the head are these two verses in Adonic meter:

You, Christ, crown  
Louis.

The cross held in the right hand contains these verses in Asclepiad meter:

In your cross, Christ, are true victory and salvation;  
you rightly govern all things.

The shield held in the left hand is written in elegiac meter, as follows:

For the shield of faith drives away wicked darts  
and, preparing bright trophies, protects Augustus.

It preserves unharmed forever  
the devoted breast that trusts in the divine gift,

[Col. 0146B]

and drives away the enemy camp.

## The Prologue Begins

[Col. 0146]

The divine law urges us to bring gifts to the Lord and excludes no one, but asks a voluntary offering from all, when the Lord commanded Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they take for me firstfruits; from every person who offers willingly you shall accept them.” Here no room is given for excuse, since readiness of will is sought and necessity is not imposed; rather, the matter is left to each person’s own judgment.

Therefore I, reading this and devoting my mind to it, offered these firstfruits, expended in praise of the holy cross, which is the pillar of the heavenly building, in which, plainly, [Col. 0145C] the house of Christ has been constructed. Before that inner judgment which sees me, I wished to contribute to his praise—not with proud intention but with humble devotion—whatever I can by his grace. For he who judges not according to outward appearance but according to the heart does not measure the quantity of the gift but the extent of the devotion.

Nor do I suppose that I can add any beauty to the holy cross, which by its own radiance illuminates all things. But I proclaim its radiance and perpetual majesty, with whatever praises I can offer, to my fellow servants, so that, reading of it more often and contemplating it attentively, we may continually ponder our redemption in it and ceaselessly give thanks to our Redeemer. Although he needed nothing and possessed, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, an everlasting kingdom, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross.” Once for our sins he also died, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might present us to God and make us a kingdom and priests to God the Father.

Therefore [Col. 0145D] I ask that whoever examines the text of this work not immediately despise and cast it aside because of the lowliness of its craftsman. Rather, if he wishes and is able, let him read it; and, looking upon it with the eye of sound faith and judging it by the authority of the divine Scriptures, let him attribute to him from whom all good comes whatever he finds argued in it in a Catholic and correct manner. If, however, he finds anything expressed less correctly or thoughtlessly, let him attribute it more to my ignorance than to malice. I have always desired, as far as I can, the rectitude of the Catholic faith, and I eagerly continue to learn it; and, insofar as heavenly grace permits, I strive to preserve its rights.

Therefore, to anyone to whom I appear to have erred I humbly suggest that he not delay informing me of my error, either by word of mouth if I am present, or in writing if I am absent. But if, because of the distance between lands or because of some other impossibility, he can do neither, or if it should be established that I have departed from this present life, I beg him to pray to the most merciful Judge for my guilt [Col. 0146B], so that he himself, from whom nothing of human weakness is hidden, may loosen the bonds of my error and, by the grace of his forgiveness, grant me pardon for my sins. I also desire to do this myself for as long as I live in this body: namely, to pour out daily prayers for my own errors and those of others, so that he, in his goodness, may by his grace correct those who err and grant forgiveness to those who have erred.

For the rest, I warn the reader to preserve the order of this composition and not neglect to maintain the figures made in it, lest the value of the work perish [Col. 0146C] and the usefulness of the reading be diminished. To make this easier, I took care to explain the rationale of each figure for him on the following page in prose style, adding at the same time its exposition and the verses inscribed upon it.

If anyone is troubled that, since I decided to write on each page verses of the same number, I have inserted certain marks or points among them, let him understand that I did this not so much from necessity as from choice, so that the sense and expression in them might be clearer. Nor did I do this commonly or frequently, or without the authority of my predecessors. For I do not remember having placed points anywhere in the verses themselves except where there was the pronoun *quae*, or the conjunction *-que*, or the final syllable *-us* of a word. Porphyry did the same; according to his exemplar I learned to scatter the letters, and in some places I marked the letter *m* with a stroke over the vowel preceding it.

I also employed synaloepha, occasionally joining vowels in writing where synaloepha was appropriate, as Titus Lucretius too is found to have done not rarely. I likewise sometimes inserted *v* between *q* and a vowel [Col. 0146D]; similarly, it is demonstrated that *h* is not a letter but a sign of aspiration.

If all writers of metre are granted considerable freedom through metaplasms, figures, tropes, and the other devices in which grammarians allow poets such abundant latitude, why should it not be granted to me? I have taken care to preserve not only definite kinds of metre and proper feet, but also the sequence and number of letters and the arrangement of the figures, with greater diligence.

Above all, I beg everyone who reads this work not to be stirred against me by the goads of envy and attempt to destroy my labor. Let him not, while I have striven to prepare this for the praise of God, strive to erase it and thereby seek to harm himself more than me. And while he cannot bear to hear the glory of the holy cross proclaimed through my humility, let him beware of incurring the displeasure of the crucified King and failing to attain the grace of redemption that is in the cross.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0147]

The swift Muse, rejoicing in her zeal, now desires to speak of the divine power,

And likewise in poetry and in words of address,

Of the gifts of the highest Father, which he generously restored to the world,

And of the holy trophies of the King enthroned on high.

This is the holy cross, filled with the power of the Crucified,

Most suitable for every good, a venerable stock indeed.

I, poor, needy, destitute, with mouth and speech,

Have here attempted, as a servant, to produce this work and to begin it.

Nor does the work trouble me because I do not believe myself

To be worthy of so great a gift; even so, in mind I judge it good.

But God’s abundant goodness is my greatest hope of fulfilling my desire,

For it makes me ready, gladdening me with praise.

He did not despise the rare little coins of the poor woman and widow,

But accepted them, himself, the all-ruling Judge, approving them;

He who rules the world, who alone and singly establishes all things,

[Col. 0147B] Blessed this gift with love, making all things beautiful by his praise.

For it is indeed commanded in the ancient law

That all should give suitable gifts to the temples of the honorable God.

[Col. 0148A] One gave silver, another splendid gifts of gold;

Another contributed gems; another gave dyed

Wood; someone gave oil and costly spices;

And the great house displays many such things, shining everywhere.

Others had brought bristles and the hair of goats;

Nor were these gifts despised when they brought them to God.

Therefore I ask the wealthy man with his money not to wish

To scorn this burden here, since I carry humble things:

Even if he, supported by great ranks, brings immense treasures

To burden the temples of God,

I am not disturbed or troubled by this, nor do I look upon him with an impious face;

Rather, I rejoice and watch his gifts increase for him.

Nor do I wish him to regard my gifts with hatred;

Let him instead know that these, whatever they may be, are God’s.

He himself reproaches God who harshly despises the needy:

[Col. 0148B] This needy man belongs to him, and so does every human being.

See how much I contribute; Jesus, the loving one, has contributed to me;

May his deeds be done piously here, and may he take everything here.

**End of the Preface; the First Book follows.**

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0149]

## FIGURE I. On the image of Christ extending his arms in the form of a cross, and on his names pertaining to the divine or human nature

[Col. 0149]

[Col. 0149] But the offspring of the Lord and Lord of lords everywhere,

With hands extended, teaches that the custom of forming this shape is to be observed [text corrupt/uncertain].

This one the flock justifies and honors, and thus, in the manner of one weary upon the cross,

[Col. 0151A] For Scripture [declares] this one. And I pray to the height of the exalted Jesus,

Let us be joyful; let each person be silent who wickedly doubts [text uncertain].

The eternal Lord is silent—O holy author, here in the world [text uncertain].

Everything is fitting to be handed over to the Most High, because his right hand,

[Col. 0151B] The equal hand of the Lord, or power, and leader and prophet [text uncertain],

Behold, clothed in truth, I shall explain what Christ indicates

For this garment conceals that author—he who closes the fields within his span—

Yet he himself is shown everywhere to this world through his work:

He is its angel, its bridegroom, its devotion to the people,

Its wisdom, teaching, and peaceful guardian,

The mountain, eagle, Paraclete; likewise lion, shepherd, and kid.

[Col. 0152B] Foundation, sheep, and priest who piously returns vows.

Melchizedek the priest, wine and bread also,

Victim is made, well born from the Father without decay;

He who is the starry one, born among the stars before every light-bringer.

Here he was born of a virgin mother, then, at the appointed time,

And to save humanity he went here to the altar of the cross,

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0151]

[Col. 0151B] Behold, by the position of his limbs, the image of the Savior consecrates for us [Col. 0151C] the most health-giving, sweetest, and most beloved form of the holy cross. Thus, believing in his name and obeying his commandments, we may through his passion have hope of eternal life; and whenever we look upon the cross, we may remember him who suffered on it for us, so that he might rescue us from the power of darkness, swallowing death itself, so that we might become heirs of eternal life. He went up into heaven, with angels, powers, and virtues subjected to him.

We are also to recall that we were not redeemed from our vain conduct inherited from our fathers with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of an undefiled and spotless lamb. Thus we may be holy and undefiled in his sight, in love, and through this become partakers of the divine nature, fleeing the corruption of the desire that is in the world. [Col. 0151D]

The names of this same Redeemer are also contained in verses on the page itself. Some arise from the substance of his divinity, while others arise from the dispensation of the humanity he assumed. This was shown so that it might be understood that the same mediator of God and human beings is consubstantial and coequal with the Father in divinity, and connatural and similar to his mother in the humanity he assumed, because he perfectly assumed our entire nature without sin.

The character of these names can easily be recognized from the explanation provided below: whether they belong to his divine or human nature.

Christ is called *Christus* in Greek from *chrisma*, that is, “anointed.” Among the Jews, priests and kings were anointed with sacred anointing in the Old Testament. Therefore Christ is called “anointing,” since he is king and priest: he was anointed not with material oil but with the oil of gladness, that is, the Holy Spirit, above all his companions.

Christ is called *Messias* in Hebrew. *Hiesus* is Hebrew; in Greek, *sōtēr*; in Latin, *salutaris* or *salvator*, “saving” or “savior,” because he came as the bringer of salvation to all nations.

*Emmanuel*, from Hebrew into Latin, means “God with us”: namely, that God, born through a virgin, appeared to human beings in mortal flesh.

He is called “God” because of the substance united with the Father. “Lord” because of the servant-creature. “God and human” because he is Word and flesh.

He is called “Only-begotten” because of the excellence of his divinity, since he has no brothers. “First-born” because of his assumption of humanity, in which, through the adoption of grace, he deigned to have brothers, among whom he would be first-born.

“Consubstantial with the Father” is named from the unity of substance. For substance or essence is called *ousia* in Greek. *Homousion*: the two words joined together sound as “one substance.”

“Beginning,” because all things are from him and because nothing exists before him.

“End,” because at the end of the ages he deigned humbly to be born and die in the flesh; or because whatever we do we refer to him, and when we have reached him we have nothing further to seek.

He is the “mouth of God,” because he is his Word. Just as, instead of “words” made through the tongue, we often say “this language” or “that language,” so “mouth” is used for the Word of God, because words are customarily formed by the mouth.

He is called “Word” because through him the Father created or commanded all things.

“Truth,” because he does not deceive but grants what he promises.

“Life,” because he gives life to all things.

He is called “Image” because of his equal likeness to the Father.

“Figure,” because, taking the form of a servant, he displayed in himself the image and immeasurable greatness of the Father through the likeness of his works and virtues.

He is the “hand of God,” because all things were made through him. Hence also “right hand,” because of the effect of the whole creation, which was formed through him.

“Arm,” because all things are held together by him.

“Power,” because he possesses in himself all the Father’s power and can do all things.

“Wisdom,” because he himself reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom.

“Splendor,” because he makes things manifest.

“Light,” because he illuminates.

“Light,” because he opens the eyes of the heart to contemplate virtue.

“Sun,” because he gives light.

“Dawn,” because he is the source of light and makes us rise to eternal life.

“Fountain,” because he is the origin of things, or because he satisfies those who thirst.

He is also Alpha and Omega, because he is the beginning and the end.

“Paraclete,” that is, advocate, because he intercedes for us with the Father and takes care to remove our faults.

“Bridegroom,” because, descending from heaven, he joined himself to the Church so that the two might be one flesh.

He is called “Angel” because he announces the Father’s will and his own; hence he is read of in the prophet as the “angel of great counsel,” although he is God and Lord of angels.

He is called “Sent” because the Word became flesh.

“Human” because he became incarnate.

“Mediator” because he led us from death to life.

“Prophet” because he revealed future things.

“Priest” because he offered himself as a sacrifice for us.

“Shepherd” because he is the guardian.

“Teacher” because he is the one who reveals.

“Nazarene” from the place. “Nazareus” from merit, that is, “holy” or “pure,” because he committed no sin.

[Col. 0153C] Christ also draws to himself the forms of names from other, lower things, so that he may be understood more easily.

He is called “bread” because he is flesh.

“Vine,” because we have been redeemed by his blood.

“Flower,” because he is chosen.

“Way,” because through him we go to God.

“Door,” because through him we enter to God.

“Mountain,” because he is strong.

“Rock,” because he is the firmness of believers.

“Cornerstone,” because he joins two walls from opposite directions—that is, from circumcision and uncircumcision—into one structure, the Church; or because he makes peace between angels and human beings.

“Stone of stumbling,” because, coming in humility, unbelievers took offense at him, and he became a rock of scandal.

He is called “Foundation” because faith is founded upon him, or because the Catholic Church has been built upon him.

“Lamb,” because of his innocence.

“Sheep,” because of his gentleness.

[Col. 0153D] “Ram,” because of his leadership.

“Kid,” because of the likeness of sinful flesh.

“Calf,” because he was sacrificed [Col. 0154A] for us.

“Lion,” because of kingship and strength.

“Serpent,” because of death and wisdom.

“Worm,” likewise, because he rose again.

“Eagle,” because after the resurrection he returned to the stars.

Nor is it surprising that he is represented by lowly signs, since, although he is the Son coeternal with the Father before the ages, he did not despise the lowliness of our nature but was born in time as the human son. For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

There are therefore five verses written around the outside, encircling the human body’s form. The first begins at the middle finger of the right hand, passes into the index finger, then rises into the thumb and ascends along the right arm, ending at the crown of the head. It is as follows:

> The right hand of the highest God, Jesus, created all things.

[Col. 0154B] The second descends from the head and similarly ends at the middle finger of the left hand:

> Christ will release the world’s debts through blood.

The third begins at the fourth finger of the right hand, which is called the middle finger, and is led beneath the right arm through the little finger, descending along the right side as far as the middle of the belly; then it begins again at the right knee and ends at the root of the foot. Thus:

> Placed upon the cross, he released the tyrant’s bonds.

The fourth begins externally at the root of the right foot, rises between the legs, and reaches the external root of the left foot. Thus:

> The eternal Lord led the blessed to the stars.

[Col. 0154C] The fifth likewise ascends externally from the root of the left foot to the knees, and from the middle of the belly extends along the side and the left arm to the middle finger. Thus:

> God had given from the citadel the crown that brings salvation.

On the garment encircling the thighs are these two elegiac verses:

> In this small garment is concealed the one who contains the stars,  
> And who everywhere encloses the earth within his own span.

In the hair of his head is written: “This is the king of righteousness.”

On the face, chin, breasts, and navel is contained the following: “A just order to God.”

On the crown encircling his head: “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

On the cross placed beside his head are three letters, namely A, M, and [Col. 0154D] Ω, signifying that all things—the beginning, middle, and end—are comprehended by him.

## FIGURE II. On the figure of the cross inscribed within a quadrilateral, and showing that it comprehends all things

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155A]

> O cross, who surpasses all things and rules over Olympus,  
> You receive the heavenly peoples and the glorious  
> Kingdoms of the sky to be governed; the naked ardor

> The songs that the world offers on earth, and the exiled  
> World sanctifies, along with the wind, the sea, and this sun,  
> Exalt you joyfully; with the mountains, the dry  
> Fields sing their song, and by their movement you give songs to the stars.  
> Sunrise and sunset, the north wind, and likewise the south wind and breeze:  
> May you possess the joy of the kingdom, which is light within light,

[Col. 0155B]

> Open the heights of heaven, proclaim the divine power there,  
> Distributing such great gifts of God, who made all things.  
> O cross, which is the blessed flesh of Christ’s triumph,

> For God himself prepared you by the gift of the one who gives life,  
> And raised you up well—[the following wording is corrupt and uncertain].  
> May no rancid deceiver, leader of the wicked, be able to say  
> “Hush,” when he saw the prey rescued from the ether of light;  
> And may he not wish to punish by killing here  
> What had long been cast down.  
> Behold the pious cross of the Lord! What pious Muse

> You shine beautifully in your adornment; glory surrounds you in appearance.  
> The dreadful yew flees; the reed and the pine  
> Humbly bow before your honor; cedar, myrrh, and [uncertain term]  
> Fear the fragrance, as do nard and myrrh, cypress,  
> Mastic, frankincense, gum, amomum, balsam, and bdellium.  
> Overcome by your majesty, they offer you more than their vows.  
> In name you are harsher, in virtue greater; to the devout you grant this  
> [Col. 0156B] As a reward, before the tribunal of Christ.  
> O cross, who, once the people were released, gave them passage from Avernus.

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0157]

[Col. 0157A] This figure rightly proclaims that the cross of Christ embraces all things in its four arms: whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on earth, and whatever is beneath the earth—in short, all visible and invisible things, living and nonliving things. For the four arms of the cross signify four places in which rational creatures dwell: the heavenly, earthly, infernal, and superheavenly realms. The apostle Paul speaks of these when he says that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

Paul’s testimony concerns three; let us also consider the fourth: “Praise the Lord, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.” Again, some are called heavenly and others superheavenly.

Alternatively, the four arms signify the four kinds of the whole creation: being, living, sensing, and understanding, in all of which creation subsists.

Some things merely exist but neither live, sense, nor discern, as stones do.

Others exist and live but neither sense nor discern, as shrubs and all the plants of the earth do.

Others exist, live, and sense but do not discern, as brute animals do; they possess the power of sensation but lack the reason of understanding.

Others exist, live, sense, and discern, as angels and human beings do: they subsist through being, live through life, sense through sensation, and discern through intellect.

There are also four affections of the soul itself, by which living beings employ themselves either for good or for evil. The ancients discovered these with subtlety, and later generations, approving their findings, accepted them: fear, sorrow, desire, and joy.

When these are ordered and fortified by the protection of the holy cross, they prove salutary in religious people, although the folly of certain worldly wise men has judged them to be vices. If that were so, and if only sinners or the lost could possess them at all, they could rightly be called not affections but diseases.

Or, when such movements of the soul are found in holy apostles and prophets, who would be so foolish [Col. 0157C] as to believe them vices? Through these very affections those men pleased God, because they resisted vices more than other human beings.

Thus the apostle Paul speaks in this way about fear: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the charity that is in Christ.”

The same teacher speaks confidently about desire: “I desire to depart and be with Christ.”

And concerning sorrow, which others call grief, the same teacher of the nations says: “I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.”

Writing to the Romans, he also says: “I rejoice in you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.”

The prophet David likewise speaks of fear: “The fear of the Lord is holy and endures forever.” Again: “Fear the Lord, all his saints.”

Concerning sorrow he says: “I was saddened in my exercise.”

Likewise, concerning desire, he says: “My soul desired to long for your ordinances at all times,” and “I desired your salvation, O Lord.”

And concerning joy, the same Psalmist, exhorting God’s saints, says: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; be glad, you righteous, in the Lord.”

Whoever therefore wishes to condemn this fear or grief, this desire or joy [Col. 0158A], condemns the apostle and the prophet themselves. Through such affections they not only pleased God but also exhorted others to the same; and they blamed those who were deprived of them as being among the guilty because they were without feeling.

We therefore sin not by possessing these affections but by using them badly. The existence of human affections indicates their Creator; their quality, however, signifies a good or evil will. The movements that are affections in everyone become virtues in those who use them well, but passions or disturbances—and, as some wish to call them, illnesses—in those who use them badly.

A person uses them well who seeks to do not his own will but God’s, so that he no longer lives for himself but for him who redeemed him through the shedding of his blood on the cross. Such a person can say with the Apostle:

> For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live for God. I have been crucified with Christ. Yet I live—not I, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

All these things therefore belong to the holy cross, because on it Christ, the Creator of all, suffered.

The passion of Christ sustains heaven, rules the world, and pierces Tartarus. Through it angels are strengthened, peoples are redeemed, enemies are crushed, things that subsist are established, living things are given life, sentient things are preserved, and intelligent things are enlightened.

From it, fear arising from punishment liberates the faithful; salutary sorrow cleanses penitents from sins; desire for the good germinates the fruit of virtues; and joy gladdens those who trust in the hope of life.

The author of all things had foreseen this holy structure for himself. He wished it to be built so that in it he might restore and unite all things through Jesus Christ our Lord.

There are also two verses inscribed on the cross itself. The first is:

[Col. 0158C]

> O cross, dedicated to the famous trophy of the Most High,

It descends from the top to the bottom.

The other is:

> O cross, which is the blessed flesh of Christ’s triumph.

It extends from the right to the left of the cross.

There are also four verses around the cross in the quadrilateral. The first, above the cross, is:

> O cross, who surpasses all things and rules over Olympus.

The one below is:

> O cross, who, once the people were released, gave them passage from Avernus.

The one on the right, that is, in the anacrostic, is:

> O cross, leader and broad redemption for the wretched world.

The one on the left, that is, in the telestic, is:

> O cross, holy standard and pious protection for the age.

[Col. 0158D] It should be noted that we placed the letter O, which resembles a circle, in the four corners of the quadrilateral, in the four arms of the cross, and also in the middle of the cross, so that it might be shown that the holy Cross by its power links together all things and joins in the veneration of Christ what is above with what is below.

[Col. 0159]

[Col. 0159A]

> Hail, holy salvation, O joyful passion of Christ;  
> Venerable cross of God, teacher, wisdom, light,  
> Praise of the true one, beloved power, bright philosophy, for these  
> Whom the fields of earth or the summit of Olympus nourish,  
> And for the starry choirs and the bright scepters of day.

> The whole world blesses you, the glorious wing of the heavens.
