> Proclaims you, remembering by the power of God that all the ether  
> Is both ruled and protected by you, provided that you stand as the gracious altar of the divine power.  
> With what shield he rejoices, with what sword the strong one enters  
> The dreadful battles of the dragon, exulting with holy thousands.  
> [Col. 0159B] And as victor he will seek rewards for himself from your praises.  
> For by right, action, order, and destiny  
> He established this cross suspended as such an altar, by which  
> [Col. 0160A] Life itself may openly testify to the council of virtues.  
> Good things, rightly written, rise up in the cross of life.  
> Christ, inclining humbly, led himself toward the Rock of faith, greatly strengthened,  
> Then came from the citadel,  
> And taught by words, leaving examples through deeds;  
> And the Creator completed all things in the sacred, pious cross.  
> This Gabriel, the joyful archangel and herald,  
> Announced clearly to the ear of the Virgin, praying,  
> And, now touching Jesus the Savior, proclaimed the triumph in praise.  
> O Raphael, medicine of God, did this cross give you the power  
> To restore radiance, whose figure you then rightly  
> Showed to the blind man, and which restored light to the world?

> When a new song of the psalm-singers resounded in praise  
> And the angels, as ministers, came rightly to their service.  
> [Col. 0160B] Therefore I ask you, host of heaven, bless Christ,  
> Who saved the world by the cross, giving kingdoms to the blessed,  
> And completed your number in the citadel of heaven.

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0161]

[Col. 0161A] With good reason the orders of the holy angels and the army of the heavenly host correspond to the holy cross in name and number, so that they may praise together the victory of the eternal King and proclaim the greatness of their joy in honorable service. For sacred Gospel text recalls not only that they praised him at the hour of Christ’s birth and afterward ministered to him in the desert, but also plainly relates that they attended him in due service at the time of his passion and resurrection. They ought especially to be believed devoted to this matter because, the more worthily they serve in his army, the more devotedly they praise his triumph.

There are therefore nine orders of angels, as Holy Scripture commends to us: Angels, Archangels, Virtues, Principalities, Powers, Dominations, Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim.

To explain this, let us set down the words of blessed Pope Gregory:

“Nearly all the pages of sacred speech testify that angels and archangels exist. The prophetic books also frequently speak, as is well known, of Cherubim and Seraphim.

The apostle Paul enumerates the names of four orders in his letter to the Ephesians, saying: ‘Above every Principality and Power and Virtue and Dominion.’

Again, writing to the Colossians, he says: ‘Whether Thrones, or Dominations, or Principalities, or Powers.’

He had already described Dominations, Principalities, and Powers when speaking to the Ephesians; but, intending to mention them also to the Colossians, he prefixed Thrones, of which he had not yet said anything to the Ephesians.

When Thrones are joined to the four which he named to the Ephesians—that is, Principalities and [Col. 0161C] Powers, Virtues and Dominations—there are five orders specifically expressed. When Angels and Archangels, Cherubim and Seraphim are added to these, there are unquestionably found to be nine orders of angels.

Thus it is said through the prophet even to that first angel who was created: ‘You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.’

Here it should be noted that the first angel is said to have been made not ‘in the likeness of God’ but ‘the seal of likeness,’ so that, the subtler his nature, the more nearly the image impressed upon him might express likeness.

The passage immediately continues: ‘Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper; chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; sapphire, [Col. 0161D] carbuncle, and emerald.’

Behold, he named nine kinds of stones, because there are plainly nine orders of angels. That first angel was adorned and covered with these orders because, while he was set above all the ranks of angels, he was brighter in comparison with them.”

But let us continue to explain what sacramental meaning this arrangement of the nine orders of angels on the cross conveys to us. This form of the holy cross therefore contains two orders in its lower part, namely angels [Col. 0162A] and archangels; two in the right arm, namely virtues and powers; likewise two in the left arm, namely principalities and dominions; one in the middle, namely thrones; and likewise two in the upper part, namely cherubim and seraphim. These names also fit very well for proclaiming the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ and suitably serve to recount his magnificence and power.

For whom do the angels and archangels, placed in the lowest part of the cross, proclaim, except him who descended from heaven to earth—the Angel of the Great Counsel, sent to announce the message to the meek, so that the stronger one might bind the strong man and plunder his goods? And whom else do the virtues, powers, principalities, and dominions, placed in the arms of the cross, proclaim, except him of whom it is written: “The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly”? And again: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” Likewise: “The principality has been placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace.” And again: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.”

The thrones, therefore, placed in the middle of the cross, indicate whom else as sitting upon them except him to whom, as the Apostle bears witness, it was said: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom”? And the Psalmist says: “You sit upon the thrones, judging equity.”

And whom do the cherubim and seraphim, placed at the summit of the cross, signify, except him of whom the Apostle says: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”? And again: “Our God is a consuming fire.” For *cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” and *seraphim* as “burning” or “kindling.”

Yet we do not proclaim these things about the orders of angels as though we were making them equal to the Only-Begotten. Rather, through the offices and names of the subordinate creature, we reverence the mysteries of his dispensation. For he himself is God and Lord of the angels, begotten before all ages from God the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—who in the final age of the world was born from a virgin mother and assumed human nature in himself, being sent to conquer the ruler of the world, “so that he might strip the principalities and powers, triumphing over them openly in himself.” The Father raised him from the dead and established him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power and virtue and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He subjected all things beneath his feet and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body.

The nine larger letters that form the shape of the cross on this page signify this: **CRVX SALVS**—“The Cross is Salvation.” Each letter has one of the orders of angels assigned to it. This will easily be clear to anyone who knows the letters and is not ignorant of the names of the nine orders.

## FIGURE IV. On the Cherubim and Seraphim written upon the cross, and on their meaning

[Col. 0163]

### [Col. 0163A]

O cherubim, seraphim, now exalt from heaven the name of Jesus;  
For henceforth your fire shines in speech.  

With the divine cross—the true praise of the cross—this is the way, the life.  
Christ is the true fruit of the light, and praise is his companion.  

Then the king conquered sorrow, and now he rejoices everywhere,  
He who is beloved as a seraph; let prayers be made here in celebration.  

O heavenly beings, many in number, exalt the Most High with this praise.  
One altar of wings, by boldness—[the text is uncertain]—for the proclaimed  
Sacredness and honor of the altar are confirmed; and by their vow  
They declare what power there is and what good the king bestows.  

By this counsel Christ, when he burned away iniquity,  
Behold, he endured all things and drove away the powerful with his heel;  
He broke the tightly closed barriers of the shaken serpent,  
Cleansed the ancient deeds, and, in his goodness, gave back  
The kingdoms of Sabaoth in the heights to Adam, who had stood as a sinner.  

### [Col. 0163B]

Those prayers prove that power and divinity were commanded  
To bring blessed aid to him in darkness and in prison,  
To the maker on the cross, the king fastened to the stake.  

Behold, here is the king’s throne; here is the reconciliation of the world,  

[Col. 0164A]

The standard, the sword, the lot of war, the noble insignia.  

This crushes the enemies and breaks the weapons of iniquity;  
It raises up his own and grants the rewards of virtue.  

For from here, exiled fire, know what weapons lay hidden.  
The cherubim stand—those who attend this altar, those who attend the ark.  

Here these banners rightly give a sign, and the prayers sufficiently  
Understand the holy altar; by one sacred power they are also made.  

The anointed vessels that contain the triumph of the endeavor  
Lead these deeds joyfully, blessing them with outstretched rejoicing.  

Behold, little by little they convey the nourishing things on their wings  
And spread them high; with their wings and mouths the seraphim now declare  
That the time is near when bodily luxury must depart,  
And that vices must henceforth be abandoned.  

Here the outstretched arms signify the service of the Savior.  
By these things he himself is drawn and carried, in his lofty judgment,  
While he dispenses them and chooses what is safe, testing  
What he had already recognized and approved everywhere as increased and dear.  

### [Col. 0164B]

The messages of the righteous prophets do not waver concerning the cross.  
The signs of these living creatures do not deceive concerning the cross.

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0165]

### [Col. 0165A]

On this page, therefore, the Lord’s cross can be seen depicted and inscribed, together with the figures of the seraphim and cherubim placed around it. They are introduced here into this work so that it may be shown with what forethought and dispensation divine mercy has always secured salvation for the human race: for God wished the form of our redemption to be seen beforehand even in the angelic spirits themselves through prophetic revelation, and through the prophetic works constructed in the inner courts of the tabernacle and temple—that is, in the cherubim themselves placed beside the ark beyond the veil—he determined to reveal the eternal propitiation to the world.

Accordingly, although many people have interpreted the appearance and position of these creatures, and have written different things in different styles though with no difference of faith, it nevertheless seems to me not inappropriate—without prejudice to the tradition of our predecessors—to understand the creatures themselves, in their physical form, as representing the figure of the holy cross. For they preserve the intervals of the cross according to their spatial arrangement and extend themselves similarly upward and downward, to the right and to the left.

Thus the prophet Isaiah recounts the seraphim, saying:

“I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne, and the things beneath him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it; six wings belonged to one and six wings to the other. With two they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew. One cried to the other and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.’”

What, then, does this arrangement of the six wings of the seraphim prefigure except the image of Christ’s cross? Those wings that covered the upper part of their bodies—that is, the face—must have been raised upward toward the head, and therefore plainly display the upper part of the cross. Those that covered the lowest part, namely the feet, must be understood to have been lowered downward, and therefore signify the lower part of the cross. And what else do the two wings extended for flight signify except the transverse wood of the cross, on which the Lord’s arms and hands were extended? Therefore no wise person doubts that, in the position of the seraphim’s six wings, the sign of the whole cross of Christ is plainly expressed.

They are also rightly interpreted as “walking” or “burning,” because they display the form in which all hostile powers were conquered and the sins of the whole world consumed and destroyed; indeed, they commend to God’s elect that fire which the Lord testified that he wished to send upon the earth and to kindle.

And rightly, with a threefold voice, they exhorted all the elect to praise the holy Trinity: that is, those who lived before the Savior’s coming, those who lived during the presence of his incarnation, and those who are still to be converted to the faith until the end of the world after his ascension into heaven. For one passion of Christ redeemed them all together, both Jews and gentiles.

Furthermore, what else did the cherubim made in the tabernacle or temple display by the extension of their wings except the image of Christ’s cross? Concerning them, the Book of Kings rightly relates that they were made ten cubits high and that they measured ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other. To their likeness the form of the human body can also be compared, whose breadth, when the arms are extended from the fingertips of one hand to the fingertips of the other, is almost as great as its height or length from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head.

These cherubim stood beside the ark and the propitiatory because they displayed to the human race the true propitiation in the incarnation of the Savior. They always held their wings extended in the form of a cross because they duly proclaimed our perpetual redemption in the passion of Christ.

Here too, on the cross, the following verse runs lengthwise from top to bottom:

> Behold the holy citadel of the Cross; behold the sacred structure of salvation.

This one runs across its breadth:

> Behold, here is the king’s throne; here is the reconciliation of the world.

On the seraphim and cherubim elegiac verses are also written. On the seraphim standing above the right arm of the cross are these verses:

> The heavenly seraphim display the signs of Christ’s cross,  
> And by the arrangement of their wings prove that all these things are sacred.

On the one standing above the left arm are these:

> For these companions rejoice, celebrating the Most High with this praise,  
> And proclaim three times the scepters of Sabaoth.

On the cherubim at the right are these verses:

> From here the holy cherubim mark the triumph with their banners;  
> With outstretched wings they indicate the arms extended.

On the one at the left are these:

> They stand beside the ark and cover the sacred coverings,  
> And by their service prove that the things made are propitiatory.

## FIGURE V. On the four tetragonal figures placed around the cross, and on the spiritual building of the house of God

[Col. 0167]

### [Col. 0167A]

O holy cross of God, I pray, impress your signs upon my heart by divine power,  
So that I may rightly sing your glorious triumphs in praise;  
How from heaven you bring covenants down to earthly things,  
Confirm the pact and break the bonds of death.

O apostolic host, and you order of martyrs,  
Whom the summit of Christ’s house has rightly placed in him;  
You have built it, and the nourishing people has been found in its lowest voice.  

Holy, saving cross, inserted into the highest foundation,  
Constructed and fixed by the strength of the Crucified:  
You truly consecrated the human race to life.  

The established column comes forth to display the protective power,  
To raise through itself the eternal form of paradise,  
The chamber of the bridegroom’s covering and of the righteous king.  

Christ, soon by right, by blood, and by the way,  
Raise new trophies in the world, preserving the covenant of the righteous;  
Let it despise what is condemned and conquer deceit through devotion.  

To it belong favor and fear, virtue and victory, the crown.  
Glorious cross of the Lord, foundation and hall of Christ.

### [Col. 0168A]

You are more beautiful than the whole field blooming with flowers,  
Higher than cedar and more precious than Parian marble.  

You join squared stones along a firm path,  
And rightly draw the authority of the patriarchs and the people—  
The earlier foundations—into the whole foundation of the building.  

It knows how first to bind devoted hearts by its teaching;  
The prophet’s words, rightly spoken to the reigning one, have been fulfilled,  
So that they might piously prepare a living hall for the king by his commands,  
Already fashioned for Christ upon the worn pavement.  

For all together ascend to the stars in his name.  
This hall, Jesus, extends toward the joyful northern lightning,  
And the good structure of life grows strong, confirmed by its voice.  

The joining signifies and gives the command to proceed,  
The way by which the guide leads to the possession of the scepters of light.  
The joyful good dwelling of Christ consecrates them to the temple.  

And when the cross increases with these four rocks,  
The very corner completes and leads the house to perfection.

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0169]

### [Col. 0169A]

On this page, therefore, the holy cross extends through the middle, with four quadrangular forms placed around its sides. This is plainly to display the structure of the heavenly building, namely the Church of the living God, which is also his house, the pillar and foundation of truth.

To this house belong the chosen angels, whose likeness is set before us in the future life, as the Lord says:

“Those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they cannot die any more, because they are equal to the angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.”

To this house belongs the mediator himself between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, as he himself testifies when he says:

“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

Explaining this, the Evangelist added:

“But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

The Apostle says of us:

“Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”

If, therefore, he became the temple of God through the humanity he assumed, and we become the temple of God through his indwelling Spirit, it is clear that the material temple built by King Solomon in Jerusalem bore the figure of all of us—and of the Lord himself and of his members, who are us. It represented the Lord as the uniquely chosen and precious cornerstone founded in the foundation, and us as living stones built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, that is, upon the Lord himself.

The Apostle shows this when he says:

“No one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.”

He can rightly be called the foundation of the Lord’s house because, as Peter says:

“There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.”

And again:

“Coming to him, a living stone rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.”

The first stones of this foundation, therefore, suitable for the foundation, may appropriately be understood as the patriarchs and prophets, apostles and martyrs. Whether by preaching, acting, or suffering, they laid the foundations of faith for us; the whole remaining company of the faithful follows their authority in doctrine, their examples in deeds, and their imitation in endurance.

For just as, after the Savior’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, the apostles and martyrs built throughout the whole world the spiritual building of the house of God by preaching Christ and also by dying for Christ, so before his coming in the flesh the patriarchs and prophets in the former people, and in the regions where they lived, always strove to turn the lives of others toward what was better by words and examples, so that through worthy conduct they might deserve to have God as their inhabitant and might perceive that God himself was favorable to them—God under whose dominion they had been placed and whom they recognized as almighty.

It is therefore rightly written in the Book of Kings concerning the construction of that typical temple that the king ordered large stones and precious stones to be taken for the foundation of the temple and squared. The precious stones, then, are holy men distinguished by their merits, who are rightly commanded to be squared and thus placed in the foundation. For every square customarily stands firm, fixed whichever way it is turned. To this figure the hearts of the elect are likened: they have learned to stand so firmly in the steadfastness of faith that no adversity they encounter—not even death itself—can bend them from the uprightness of their position. The Church has received many such teachers not only from Judea but also from the gentiles.

This building is rightly displayed in the holy cross because the whole Catholic Church was founded, perfectly constructed, and dedicated in it—that is, in the passion of Christ. Nor would this building ever reach completion unless the human race were liberated through the Cross, nor would the office of the priest be fittingly fulfilled unless the priest himself became the sacrifice upon the cross.

Upon the cross itself the following verse is written:

> Glorious cross of the Lord, foundation and hall of Christ.

The verses inscribed in the tetragons placed around the cross do not run completely around the perimeter—that is, their final letters do not return by a winding course to their initial letters. Rather, each begins in its upper right corner and descends through the upper left to the lower left in nineteen letters; then, beginning again in the upper right corner with the twentieth letter, it proceeds downward through the lower right and reaches the lower left in seventeen letters. Thus each verse of the four tetragons contains thirty-six letters. This number is that of the plane tetragon, produced by multiplying six by itself, as we shall demonstrate below.

The verse of the tetragon placed beneath the right arm is:

> The praiseworthy deed of the patriarchs signifies you.

The one placed beneath the left arm is:

> And the people of the prophets, commanded by divine utterance.

The verse of the tetragon placed above the right arm of the cross is:

> The apostolic host duly displays your triumphs.

The one above the left arm is:

> And the choir of martyrs, by right, through poured-out blood.

## FIGURE VI. On the four principal virtues, how they pertain to the cross, and how the fruit of all the virtues has been bestowed upon us through it

[Col. 0171]

### [Col. 0171A]

Almighty virtue, supreme wisdom, Christ,  
You who, as the Lord, adorn the whole world in the citadel of the cross,  
And distribute to your saints the holy gifts of salvation:  

For the chariot well fitted to its four sacred horns  
Displays the sequence of the virtues, dedicating the triumph,  
And showing through the blood of the victorious king  
That all their forms advance and bear fruit through devotion in the world.  

Virtue is the disposition of the mind and every moral excellence,  
The nobility of life, reason, and restraint of speech.  
All these things the gracious cross, worthy of praise, gives to the devout,  
Bringing forth each one together according to its pleasing purpose.  

Your holy prudence has instructed the tender world.  
From you, justice, burning rightly, rejoices to despise  
The terror of the devil; blessed love climbs  
Toward holy counsels and removes the mind consumed by deceit.  

### [Col. 0171B]

From there it can also remove carnal force and conflict;  
With all its strength and powerful effort, it looks from here  
Toward glorious things, bearing adversity as it proceeds,  
While restraining the deadly harms of forbidden crimes.

### [Col. 0172A]

Showing that good times can now be celebrated in song,  
That God’s signs can be known, and his commands explained,  
And that light can be sought from here by hope and deed,  
So that raised ears may worthily attend to the best heavenly things,  
Which prepare gifts and shoots of the field:  
From leaves, fruits; and, when the withered branches are pruned,  
They kindle them rightly and bring forth royal dishes.  

Holy devotion therefore sowed these fruits;  
Grace cleansed them, and patience tested them by its art;  
The Father’s gracious law joined the covenant and watered it;  
Goodness brought forth the living grasses of Christ.  

Cultivation consecrated them, and steadfast praise supported all the stalks;  
Virtue now humbly stores up new grain everywhere,  
And modesty nourishes the full grain in the ear;  
Perseverance gives the fruit, and Christ hastens it,  
Ripe and shining in its season.

### [Col. 0172B]

Then through you, O cross, justice, seeing the divine power nearby,  
Will send the sickle and bring the harvest into the barns.

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0173]

### [Col. 0173A]

It is worthy, therefore, to recall in this sacred poem how many and what kinds of fruits the wood of the holy cross brings forth from its shoot. Its fruit is eternal and its root perpetual; its fragrance fills the world and its flavor feeds the faithful; its brilliance surpasses the sun and its whiteness dims the snow; its summit exceeds the heavens, and its lowest part penetrates the underworld; its firmness humbles, its joy exalts, and its exalted power humbles.

For the whole sequence of the virtues has been bestowed upon the world through it and in it, because the perfection of all things was completed in it. In it prudence displays its height, in it justice reveals its solidity, in it fortitude seals its power, and in it temperance praises its restraints.

Here prudence more devotedly grants the acquisition of wisdom and the understanding of truth; here every faithful person receives the gifts of foresight, understanding, and memory. Here justice laid the foundation of faith, and from here it distributes to each person the equity of devotion and religion, and also of grace and retribution. Here fortitude magnificently despises what is pleasant and what is adverse, and from here it sets forth examples of confidence, patience, and perseverance. Here temperance places the reins of discipline upon the insolent impulses of lust and obstinacy, and from here it bestows manifold gifts of chastity, self-restraint, clemency, and sobriety upon those who desire them.

This wood was planted by him of whom the Prophet speaks, comparing him to a tree:

“And he shall be like a tree planted beside channels of waters, which shall give its fruit in its season; its leaf shall not fall, and everything that he does shall prosper.”

The channels of waters are the daily passages of peoples who are failing away. And Truth says concerning himself:

“If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?”

The tree beside channels of waters has both leaves and fruit because the Creator appeared to us in the flesh, offering the shelter of his protection, and raised the human race to life through the resurrection—humanity that was daily going toward death through decay.

Truly this tree gave fruit in its season when, after our Savior had completed his passion and resurrection, he caused the Church, gathered into himself as the true vine throughout the whole breadth of the world, to abound in every virtue. He himself testifies to this, saying:

“I am the vine, and you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.”

The spiritual fruits produced here are enumerated by the Apostle:

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity.”

The spiritual fruit is therefore rightly applied to the holy cross, because the author of all good things was crucified upon it. For, as regards the flesh, when Christ willed to die upon it, the human race received complete salvation. A grain of wheat fell into the earth and produced the glorious harvest of martyrs. One piece of wood bore a man hanging upon it, and the whole world was consecrated to the heavenly kingdom. The insolent Jewish people did not fear to kill the king, and the nations of the whole world received him as Redeemer, because in the seed of Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed.

### [Col. 0174B]

These four figures, therefore, arranged in one form of the cross, contain the names of the four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, from which the whole sequence of virtues proceeds and in which the reasoning of a good life consists.

The figures mentioned are joined according to the form of a triangle but distinguished by various levels. They have been made so that each stands upon two sides, and no one can obtain them except through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

This arrangement of the holy cross also contains, in its four triangles, four verses of thirty-six letters, one in each. The first, placed in the uppermost triangle, begins at the upper right corner and winds through the other corners until it reaches the place from which it began, as follows:

> At the summit of the Lord’s cross supreme prudence stands.

In the lowest triangle this verse begins at the lower right corner and proceeds around the other corners until it returns to the point from which it began:

> Justice commands that it be held on the inclined side.

The triangle on the right contains this verse. It first ascends from the lowest corner and then winds around the others until it returns to its beginning:

> But in the right arm it bears the pledge through fortitude.

The verse of the left triangle begins at the middle corner, first ascending to the other corner and then returning by the circuit to its head:

> While on the left it orders modest laws with restraint.

Thus “modesty,” written by syncope, is used for “temperance,” the species standing for the genus.

## FIGURE VII. On the four elements, the four changes of the seasons, the four regions of the world, and the four quarters of the natural day; how everything is ordered in the cross and sanctified in it

[Col. 0175]

### [Col. 0175A]

Now all things shine with the true light,

They celebrate together so that, for the heavenly Victor,

Behold the nourishing one; and, not [in the uncertain word *vaaharo*],

Let the cross draw all things and crown them piously by sound right:  

### [Col. 0175B]

Let it not disagree with the praise of God, but let it speak honorably  
Of his work with joy: fishes, terrible dragons,  
Hills, groves, mountains, cattle, trees, sand,

### [Col. 0176A]

Together with wild beasts, wasps, worms, and beasts with open jaws;  
Birds, whether peaceful in appearance or savage in mind.  

The heavenly hall of Christ’s worshippers is sown throughout earth.  
To you virtue, bringing light from every direction against the enemies,  
Carries its message; it becomes prayer or water, but, skilled in speech,  
Fame likewise casts away—[the text is uncertain]—the palm  
And gives this message to the fortunate and to all the righteous:  

Rightly sparing the enemy, it allows the foolish to live,  
But justly condemns many whom iniquity has enclosed and increased.  

Therefore it is fitting that mouths praising together should likewise

And you, people whom the earth produces everywhere:  
Shared reason has directed you together to songs.  

The joys of heaven, the heavenly kingdoms and good things,

### [Col. 0176B]

Behold, your Savior has given this to you,  
And he himself, your proper King, ruler, joyful Creator, is Jesus.

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0177]

Almost no one is unaware that the number four is sacred through its perfection; therefore the whole world rightly venerates it transformed into the form of Christ’s cross.

For it is clear that the world consists of four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. The whole globe is also known to be bounded by four regions or angles: east and west, north and south. There are likewise four changes of the seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter; and four quarters of the natural day, namely four periods of six hours, which are distinguished by these beginnings: morning, midday, evening, and midnight.

How, then, this arrangement can suitably be adapted to the cross must be explained. If we wish to look upon the cross standing upright, let us place fire, which is the highest of the elements, at its summit. Let us also assign air and water, which are intermediate among the elements, to the transverse wood of the cross, drawn through the middle of the upright trunk. Let us assign earth, which is the heaviest and occupies the lowest place among created things, to the lower part of the cross.

Just as all these elements mingle with one another through a certain kinship of nature in order to complete the integrity of the world, so they are joined to one another through the four parts of the cross in order to display its perfect form.

If we wish to assign it to the four regions of the world, we must necessarily measure it lying down as follows: assign its first part to the east, its farthest part to the west, its right side to the north, and its left side to the south.

Likewise, the four changes of the seasons and the four parts of the natural day can be united on the cross in the same arrangement, so that one fitting image of the year or day may be displayed in them. Spring and dawn produce, in their proper order, the rising of light and the growing shoots of the earth; therefore they are rightly assigned to the east. Summer and midday are adapted to the south because, while the sun rises in those regions of heaven, it scorches the world with more blazing heat. Autumn and evening are rightly assigned to the west because then the harvest of all the earth’s fruits is completed and the whole span of the day comes to an end. Winter and midnight are likened to the north because then the earth is numb with cold and the time is more suitable for rest than for any work.

Therefore, since everything has been restored through the cross and reborn and improved through Christ’s passion, all things rightly converge in his praise. For he is, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, to whom alone those blessings belong which the three children in the furnace of burning fire sang while exhorting all creatures to praise the Creator:

“Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord,” and so forth.

Of him the Psalmist also says:

“Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all that is in them.”

For, according to the Apostle, “from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be honor and glory for ever and ever.”

The reason why I have depicted the four elements, the four seasons, or the four regions of the world in wheels is that the whole machinery of the world is temporal and is variable or changeable through a certain mixture of the elements and succession of the seasons. Solomon bears witness to this when he says:

“Everything has its season, and all things pass through their appointed times under heaven.”

Now fire dries the air; water makes it more humid. Now the earth is affected by the overflowing of waters; now it is dried by the heat of the sun. Water is naturally mobile and completes a certain circle in its course. Ecclesiastes says:

“All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled; to the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again.”

Fire likewise has a natural movement, by which, when kindled, it always rises toward higher places and seeks a position above the air. Lightning darts about, and the ether flashes with frequent fires. The seasons pass in circles, and the four changes proceed through the circuits of three-month periods. The year also received its name from always turning and returning to itself. The globe of the earth and the rotation of the heavens are said to revolve around lands and seas. The spirit goes round and round and returns to its circles. Five zones hold the heavens, where the oblique order of the constellations turns.

These verses are also written throughout the complete spherical or circular figure, namely thirty-six, a number completed by multiplying six by six and ending in six. The first, in the uppermost circle, is:

> Spring, rising fire, dawn, shine forth in this region.

In the lowest:

> Autumn, west wind, earth, and evening are here.

On the right:

> North, winter, water, and midnight—behold, they are placed in the middle.

On the left is this verse:

> Air, summer, south wind, the summit, and midday are here.

## FIGURE VIII. On the twelve months, the twelve signs, and the twelve winds; on the preaching of the apostles; and on the other mysteries of the number twelve displayed in the cross

[Col. 0179]

### [Col. 0179A]

Christ the Savior, Christ the serene king at the summit,  
Counsel, great power and blessing, light,  
The divine offspring of the Father: surely from here he draws

All who now truly celebrate these rays shine  
With the perpetual lot of light, repeatedly.  
In this radiance the weapons of the prophets shone sufficiently,  

### [Col. 0179B]

And the apostolic flock is adorned with flashing light.

### [Col. 0180A]

By this faith of Christ it shines; by this sun  
The hearts of good people gleam, and by this light their vows increase.  
The righteous, prevailing through mystical signs and goodness,  
Will cast forth the ray, believing the commandments because of him,  
And, when they mark the heavenly laws for the peoples,  
They ascribe to Christ the fellowship that leads to life.  

Christ the king, the divine Lord, supreme in his gift,  
Climbing the lofty strength of the cross, at last in this

And willed that the grateful be gathered there.

Indeed, it itself bestows them.

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0181]

[Col. 0181A] It is of no small importance to understand how suitably and appropriately the number twelve corresponds to the holy cross: there are twelve winds that blow through the world; twelve signs of the zodiac, through which the seven planets proceed in ordered and regular courses; and twelve months, by which the annual cycle is completed. There are also twelve hours of the artificial day, by which the sun illuminates the whole surface of the earth; twelve patriarchs, from whom the entire multitude of the children of Israel was propagated, and which possessed the promised land according to the lots of the twelve tribes; from these patriarchs arose the prophets, heralds of divine birth.

Therefore the Savior himself deigned to assume flesh and be born among human beings. As the light coming into this world, he chose from that very people twelve apostles, [Col. 0181B] illuminating them like the sun of righteousness in the likeness of the hours, and sent them throughout all the regions of the world to preach faith in the Holy Trinity.

In the construction of the heavenly Jerusalem, the mystery of the same number is indicated in many ways. The Apocalypse displays this, where it is written:

> And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem, descending from heaven, from God, having the glory of God; its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal. It had a great and high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written upon them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel. On the east were three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb, and so forth.

The holy Church is signified in this spiritual structure—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem and the city of the great King, whose builder and maker is God. He is both its foundation and its completion, and for our sake he also deigned to become high priest, so that by the sacrifice of his own blood he might at once cleanse and consecrate the walls of that city.

He alone possesses, in his own peace, everything that it contains. Hence, upon the breast of the high priest twelve precious stones, arranged in four rows and inscribed with the names of the twelve patriarchs, were seen to be set, so that it might be beautifully revealed that all the spiritual gifts which each of the saints individually fulfilled in part had been completed together and perfectly in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

John also bears witness to this in the Gospel:

> And the Word, he says, became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

And shortly afterward:

> And from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace, because the law was given through Moses, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

This form of the holy cross therefore has three lines at each of its arms, to demonstrate that, just as on its right and left it has neighboring and adjoining lines running along its straight course, so the supremacy of the four cardinal winds joins other winds to those on the right and left according to their position. Likewise, the four seasons, each consisting of three months and lying between the equinoxes and solstices, are divided according to certain authorities. This will be clear to anyone who diligently wishes to learn the accounts of the Greeks or Egyptians concerning the seasons.

There are two hexameter verses in the cross itself. The first, running lengthwise from the top downward, is:

> On the cross are now the months, the winds, and the twelve signs.

The verse that runs across it is:

> The apostolic flock is adorned with flashing light.

There are also two pentameter verses on the lines adjoining the arms of the cross. One is joined above and below to the length of the cross by a turn, as follows:

> Here the stock, the region, and the work of the world are likewise joined.

The other is joined horizontally to the right and left sides, as follows:

> The holy cross is powerful here to give this good by its renowned path.

## Explanation of the Figure

[Col. 0185]

[Col. 0185A] This figure of the holy cross, written with scattered letters through four hexagons and a unit placed between them, embraces all the days of the year. For the solar year has 365¼ days. Divide these by four: four times ninety-one makes 364, leaving one day and a quarter. Divide that one day by four: four times six hours make twenty-four hours, which is a complete day from sunrise to the next sunrise. Divide the quarter likewise: four times an hour and a half make six hours, which is the annual addition of the leap year. Thus, if the whole year is divided into four parts, each part contains ninety-one days and seven and a half hours. This is the true division of the four changes of season—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—so that each has ninety-one days and seven and a half hours.

It must nevertheless be noted that in this figure the quarter is demonstrated only through the interpretation and examination of the six angles, so that each hour is assigned to one angle. If you inspect the four hexagons at their angles, you will mark twenty-four hours in them; by this full complement of hours the leap day is completed, and this arrangement is not without reason. For if, over four years, the quarter-day portion reaches the sum of one day, the cross displays and represents this correctly in the four hexagons, four times six hours.

The hexagon, therefore, has rightly been divinely ordered for this arrangement, because the number six has great force throughout the sequence of the year. To demonstrate this also, let us set down a passage from the fourth book of Saint Augustine’s *On the Holy Trinity*:

> One year, too, if its twelve complete months are considered, which thirty-day periods complete—for the ancients observed such a month, as the lunar cycle shows—possesses the power of the number six. For whatever six is worth in the first order of numbers, which consists of units and reaches ten, sixty is worth in the second order, which consists of tens and reaches one hundred. The number sixty, therefore, is a sixth part of the days of the year. Accordingly, the numbers of the first order are multiplied by six, as though six were a number of the second order, and six times sixty makes 360 days, which are the complete twelve months.

> But just as the moon’s cycle shows human beings the month, so the year is recognized by the sun’s circuit. Five days and a quarter of a day remain, for the sun to complete its course and bring the year to an end. For four quarters make one day, which must be intercalated after four years have elapsed—what they call a leap year—so that the sequence of the seasons may not be disturbed.

> If we consider those five days and a quarter, the number six again has great force in them. First, as is customary, the whole is reckoned from the part: there are no longer five days but rather six, since the quarter is taken for one day. Then, because within those five days there is a sixth part of a month, while the quarter contains six hours. For the whole day, that is, together with its night, consists of twenty-four hours, of which the fourth part—the quarter of a day—is found to be six hours.

> Thus the number six has great force in the course of the year.

The sequence of days has therefore appropriately been fitted to the holy cross, because through it human hearts have been illuminated. The joining of the hexagons belongs to it, because in it the perfection of things is established. The temporal order of light corresponds to it, because through it humanity finds eternal light. The number ninety, together with the unit, corresponds to it, because through it the angelic order reaches the fullness of its number.

At its middle, too, units from the four sides of the straight hexagon are joined together, because through its majesty all nations from the four regions of the world are united in the unity of faith, and through its completed work the heavenly and earthly creation is joined in one charity. To it belong honor and majesty, through whose mercy all these things have been accomplished; praise and glory for ever and ever.

This form of the holy cross has, along its length through two hexagons, a Sapphic meter, which is a pentameter and hendecasyllabic; its three verses are equal. Each receives these four feet of two syllables: trochee, spondee, trochee, iamb, and the final three-syllable bacchius. After the three verses a dicolon dactylicum is added, that is, a dactyl and a spondee.

The following verses are in the uppermost hexagon:

> Three times a hundred, ten times six,
>
> And once five, the whole
>
> Of time, the annual circuit
>
> Of the cross—behold, this is the day.

The following are in the second:

> But the four sides of the hexagon sufficiently show
>
> Ten times nine,
>
> Each complete, piously, together with the unit,
>
> And above one.

It must be noted that the upper verses, because they draw to themselves the letter C, which is in the middle of the hexagons, have ninety-two letters, while the following verses have ninety-one.

The two hexagons that form the transverse part of the cross are composed in elegiac meter. The first has these verses:

> The holy stock of the cross completes the scepter in a fixed order,
>
> And this is the world’s adornment and the great salvation of humankind.

The second has these:

> Christ holds all things: the abyss, the world, and the lofty heavens.
>
> For here he governs the stars of heaven and all the bolts of day.

## Explanation of the Figure

[Col. 0189]

[Col. 0189A] The present form of the holy cross, written with scattered letters, displays the number seventy. Through it we are informed that all the mysteries contained in this number correspond most appropriately to the honor of the holy cross.

For what else do the seventy years of captivity, which the prophet Jeremiah foretold would come upon the sacrilegious people, signify than the whole duration of this life, which runs its course according to the number seven, the days of the week? Because of the sin of the first human being we have been condemned to it, afflicted with punishments and hardships, and daily subjected to various tribulations and anxieties.

But since the same prophet foretold the end of the captivity after seventy years, this—unless I am mistaken—indicates that at the end of the world our captivity will be completely dissolved, when the last and hostile enemy, death, will be destroyed; when, namely, we shall rejoice without end with Christ, both in the rest of the soul and in the immortality of the body. Therefore this reckoning had to be demonstrated in the form of the holy cross, because through Christ’s passion it brought about for us the effect of this grace.

The prophet’s own words agree with this. He says:

> Thus says the Lord: When seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I will visit you and raise up over you my good word, and I will bring you back to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think concerning you, thoughts of peace and not of affliction, to give you a good end and patience. And you will call upon me, and you will go and worship me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and will not find me; when you seek me with all your heart, I will be found by you, says the Lord. And I will restore your captivity and gather you from all the nations and from all the places to which I drove you, and I will bring you back to the place from which I caused you to be carried away, and so forth.

For what does the prophet mean when he says, “When seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I will visit you and raise up over you my good word,” except what the Apostle says:

> When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

And again:

> In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages.

He said, “When they begin to be fulfilled,” not “when they have been completed,” because Christ was incarnated not at the consummation of the world but in the final age of the world. Through the word of the Gospel he illuminated believers, and through his passion and resurrection he restored the human race.

What he predicts here as a return—when he says, “And I will bring you back to this place,” and shortly afterward adds, “And I will bring you back to the place from which I caused you to be carried away”—may be understood as indicating, in the first statement, the soul’s return to rest, and, in the second, the bodies’ resurrection to glory.

After the death of the saints, therefore, their souls now go to paradise; at the end of the world, receiving their bodies, they will enter the eternal kingdom.

Daniel also numbered seventy weeks up to Christ, when transgression would reach its end and everlasting righteousness would be brought in. But so that these matters may shine forth more clearly, let us now consider the words spoken by the angel to the prophet:

> Seventy weeks, he says, have been shortened for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed, and so forth.

No one doubts that these words designate the incarnation of Christ, who took away the sins of the world, fulfilled the law and the prophets, and was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

Let these weeks, then, be counted in divisions of seven years, beginning from the twentieth year of the reign of King Artaxerxes, when Nehemiah, his cupbearer, obtained from him permission to restore the walls of Jerusalem, the temple having been built long before by permission of Cyrus. These weeks are described as having been shortened—that is, according to the lunar calculation of twelve lunar months. This yields 490 years, which, converted to solar reckoning, make 475 years.

By the time of Christ’s baptism, when the Holy of Holies was anointed and the Holy Spirit descended upon him like a dove, not only had seven weeks and sixty-two weeks been completed, but part of the seventieth week had also begun.

> And after sixty-two weeks, he says, Christ will be killed, and his people, who denied him, will no longer be his.

Christ was not killed immediately after the sixty-two weeks, but at the end of the seventieth week. The reason why Daniel separated this week from the others, so far as we can conjecture, is that he was going to say more about it. For Christ was crucified during it, and by the faithless people he was denied not only in his passion but continuously from the time when John began to preach him.

> He will confirm a covenant with many for one week—

namely, the final one, during which either John the Baptist, or the Lord, or the apostles, by preaching, converted many to the faith.

> And in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease—

that is, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. When Christ’s baptism had begun, the purification by sacrifices gradually began to seem worthless to Christ’s faithful, and rightly so: the closer truth approached, the more the shadow withdrew.

It was also fitting that, when the Savior himself chose to become the lawful sacrifice upon the cross, the victims of animals should cease; and when Christ, the true Lamb of God, was sacrificed for the sins of the whole world, that symbolic lamb should disappear, since it had been killed as a testimony for the liberation of one nation.

Likewise, at the Lord’s command Moses placed seventy elders over the people, to show that only those who understand the law spiritually through the grace of the Holy Spirit are fit to provide instruction to others.

This too was fitting to be shown in the number of the holy cross, because no one was found—in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth—who could open the book, loose its seven seals, and look upon it, except the Lamb standing in the midst of the throne as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes.

He is the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, who holds the key: when he shuts, no one opens; when he opens, no one shuts. He was given as a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to lead out the prisoner from confinement and from the prison house, the one sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

In the figure of the holy cross there are five small spheres, arranged so that together they contain the number seventy, while individually each contains fourteen. Three of these hold one verse in length, beginning at the top and ending at the bottom:

> Pious cross, constructed here, you have overcome the bonds of death.

Likewise, three small spheres across the width hold another verse:

> Great and holy good things, here you have overcome the crimes of the age.

The middle of the cross is common to both verses.

## Explanation of the Figure

[Col. 0193]

[Col. 0193A] Whoever desires to possess complete knowledge of the first law must remember this figure in every respect, repeatedly turn over its construction in his mind, and, comparing earlier things with later ones, recall the Scripture:

> All these things happened to them in figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

And again:

> They serve as an example and shadow of heavenly things.

And likewise:

> The law possesses only a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things.

A shadow does not exist without a true body, but it does not itself express the body’s true and complete form. Therefore, whoever is a lover of truth, if he first sees the shadow, must quickly turn his eyes toward the true body of which it is the shadow, lest, while his gaze remains fixed entirely upon the shadow, he neglect the fruit of truth and lose it.

The law therefore provided drink for those who were thirsty, but without wood it was not drinkable. The Lord showed Moses a piece of wood; when he cast it into the water, it removed all its bitterness. What had previously attracted the thirsty people only by a deceptive appearance, once the wood was put in, refreshed them all with the sweetest drink.

Thus, according to the Apostle, the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good. But, as the same Apostle says, the law is spiritual and must be understood not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed us from the law of sin and death. For what was impossible for the law, weakened as it was through the flesh, God accomplished by sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. By sin he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

It is written in the law:

> Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.

But since no one is justified before God by the law, and all who rely on the works of the law are under a curse, Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us, because it is written:

> Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree.

This was so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

Therefore, since the curse of the law has been destroyed through the cross, and its bitterness has through it been changed into sweetness, it is fitting that the books of the law also be arranged in the likeness of the cross, so that the correspondence of the work may become known in it and the sacramental mystery appear.

At the head—that is, at the summit of the holy cross—let the book of Genesis be placed, because it is the head and first of all the books. It narrates that in the beginning God made heaven and earth, certainly through his co-eternal Son, God the Father’s Word. Of him the Psalmist says:

> By the word of God the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.

The evangelist John says the same:

> All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

At the lower part of the cross, that is, at its foot, let the last of the five books of the law be placed: Deuteronomy, which is interpreted as “renewal of the law.” It signifies the Gospel, in which all that the law brought forth figurally and typologically has been truly and spiritually explained and opened by the mouth of our Savior.

Rightly, therefore, Genesis stands at the head of the cross and Deuteronomy at its end, because the one whom the law narrates as having created all things with the Father at the beginning of time, the Gospel reports as having renewed all things through the cross at the end of time.

Exodus is appropriately placed on the right, since it records the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt and narrates many miracles performed there by the Lord, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words:

> The right hand of the Lord has shown strength.

And again:

> He struck Egypt with its firstborn and brought Israel out from its midst, with a strong hand and an exalted arm.

On the left the book of Numbers is placed, because it describes the left-handed assemblies of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram raising disputes against Moses and Aaron, and being quickly suppressed by the Lord’s power.

Leviticus, standing in the middle of all, occupies the middle of the cross, because it designates the high priest through its many sacrificial rites: he who offered himself as an unblemished sacrifice to God on the altar of the cross, to take away the sins of many, and who, interceding for transgressors, was heard because of his reverence.

Thus, in five quadrangles, the five books of the law are marked by five verses, which correspond to the order of the quadrangles and to the sixth place through six multiplied by itself. For six times six makes the sixth quadrangle in the plane figure, which makes thirty-six.

The verse placed in the upper quadrangle of the cross is:

> Your gracious cross, Genesis, praises your gifts.

The second, placed in the right arm of the quadrangle, is:

> Exodus also sings the song of the crossing with love.

The third, situated in the middle of the cross, is:

> Leviticus, excellent, sings the laws of the priest.

The fourth, written in the left arm, is:

> But Numbers sings the wondrous greatness of triumph.

The last, written in the final quadrangle, that is, at the base of the cross, sounds as follows:

> For Deuteronomy speaks of the joys of renewal.

> And heavenly he remains, whose entire generation is heavenly.
>
> He is lord of the world, of earth, sea, and heaven;
>
> He reigns forever and grants kingdoms to the blessed.
>
> This Adam, the creator of all, will himself justly give
>
> The four regions of the world, as though named from his name:
>
> His light and power everywhere bear witness to the Lord.
>
> Behold: *anatolē* (east), *dysis* (west), *arctos* (north), *mesēmbria* (south)—these
>
> Designate them by art; behold, it is fitting that all things piously
>
> Acknowledge the Lord their creator with blessed praise,
>
> And celebrate Christ, because he truly is himself the Son
>
> Of the highest Father and the true right hand of the Thunderer,
>
> Whose good care is the touch that brings healing and salvation.

## Explanation of the Figure

[Col. 0197]

[Col. 0197A] What this figure and this inscription signify must therefore be understood. The name of the first human being, Adam, has been arranged in the figure and form of the holy cross. From him all nations arose and the entire human race derived its origin. According to the Apostle, he is the form of the one to come, namely Christ. The same Apostle says:

> The first Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.

And shortly afterward:

> The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.

He immediately added the reason why he said this:

> This I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor can corruption possess incorruptibility.

Rightly, therefore, the name Adam is configured in the cross, in which the entire human race is recognized as having been liberated through Christ. No other form more appropriately contains the appearance of our redemption than that in which the regions of the whole world could be comprehended.

This is the holy cross which, when lying down, measures the whole world. Of it the poet says:

> From it he gathers the four regions of the square world.
>
> The radiant East shines from the author’s summit.
>
> The sacred feet are bathed by the star of the West.
>
> The right hand holds the North; the left raises the central axis.
>
> All nature of the Creator lives from his limbs,
>
> And the Lord, fastened to the cross, rules the world everywhere.

This same thing was formerly signified in the name of the first-formed man, namely Adam. In the four letters of this name, [Col. 0197C] the four regions of the world are indicated by their Greek designations. For if east, west, north, and south are expressed in Greek, as Holy Scripture mentions them in many places, you will find *Adam* in the initial letters of the words. The four aforesaid regions of the world are called in Greek *anatolē*, *dysis*, *arktos*, and *mesēmbria*. If you write these four names one beneath another, as though they were four lines, *Adam* is read in their initial letters. Hence it is understood that he was created as lord of the world, and that he signifies the one who was destined to be the Redeemer and Restorer of the whole world on the four-sided cross. Therefore he is also called the second Adam.

The same name also contains within itself the mystery [Col. 0198A] of Christ’s incarnation, if attention is given to the numerical value of the letters of that name according to the Greek system—for the Greeks assign their own numbers to their letters. Thus Α signifies one among the Greeks; Δ, four; the second Α, one; and Μ, forty. Add these four numbers together, and they make forty-six. This is what the Jews are recorded to have answered in the Gospel: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” Understanding this, the Evangelist said: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body,” because our Lord Jesus Christ received a body from Adam, but did not derive sin from Adam; he took from him the bodily temple, not the iniquity that must be expelled from the temple.

The very flesh which he took from Adam—for Mary was from Adam, and the Lord’s flesh was from [Col. 0198B] Mary—the Jews crucified; and he was going to raise that same flesh on the third day, the flesh which they were about to kill on the cross. Thus they destroyed the temple built in forty-six years, and he raised it up in three days.

Let us therefore bless God the almighty Father, who formed us through his Word, coeternal with himself. Let us also bless our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who through the mystery of his incarnation restored us on the cross. Let us bless also the Holy Spirit, who by his grace sealed us, once enlightened, for eternal life: the one and only almighty, eternal, boundless, incomparable, incomprehensible, immortal, invisible God. Let us desire him alone, from whom we shall also receive blessedness; let us love him alone with our whole heart, our whole [Col. 0198C] mind, and our whole strength, in whose love we shall rejoice forever. Let us hasten only toward him, and sigh only for him during this pilgrimage; he will reward us in the heavenly places before the sight of the glory of his majesty, and make us glad without end. To him be glory, honor, power, and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

But here, in the four larger letters of the name *Adam*, a verse of fifty-one letters, written in smaller letters, is composed in this manner and is to be read according to the order of the letters of the name *Adam*:

> Behold, it is fitting that songs in meter and art should hence be for Christ.

[Col. 0199]

[Col. 0199A]

> true honor surrounds it; rejoicing, he speaks of it according to his prayer,

>   
> O beautiful cross, O more beautiful pine, surpassing all  
> the groves; O taller even than the cedars,

**EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE**

[Col. 0201]

[Col. 0201A]

These four crosses, therefore, written by a threefold route, show within themselves, through the sequence of their letters, the number of days in which the Lord’s body, according to the faith of the Church, was formed and fashioned in the virginal womb: namely, that temple which the Savior himself foretold would be destroyed by the Jews and raised up by him in three days. To make this clearer, let us set down a passage from the fourth book of Saint Augustine’s *On the Holy Trinity*, where this is written:

> “Not without reason,” he says, “in the building of the Lord’s body—for in its figure he said that the temple destroyed by the Jews would be raised by him in three days—the number six itself is understood as standing for a year. For they said that the temple had been built in forty-six years; and forty-six times six makes 276, the number of days that completes nine months and six days, which are counted as ten months for women who give birth—not because all reach the sixth day after nine months, but because the very perfection of the Lord’s body is found to have been brought to birth over that many days, as the authority preserved by the Church, received from our predecessors, has handed down. For he is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which day he also suffered. Thus the new tomb in which he was buried, where no dead person had been placed either before or afterward, corresponds to the virgin’s womb in which no mortal seed had been sown. He is traditionally said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. Counting, therefore, from that day up to this one, 276 days are found, containing the number six forty-six times—the number of years in which the temple was built—because in that number of sixes the Lord’s body was perfected: destroyed by the passion of death, it was raised by him in three days. For he was speaking about the temple of his body, as the clearest and strongest testimony of the Gospels declares.”

Thus far Augustine.

Moreover, we must observe how aptly this same number corresponds to the form of the holy cross, in which the temple of the Lord’s body was destroyed by the Jews and prepared by the Lord himself to be raised again. For Christ came for this purpose: to die in the flesh which he had assumed for the redemption of the world; and he died for this purpose: that he might rise again in that same flesh.

Therefore it is pleasing to consider how the aforesaid number, namely 276, divided into four parts, universally expresses the arms of the holy cross and presents the image of the cross in each of its parts. For sixty-nine stands in each arm, which also does not differ from the likeness of the preceding calculation, according to which it was said that the number 276 completes nine months and six days. Just as the numbers nine and six predominated in the whole, and the entire sum was calculated according to their designation, so in the parts the same designation shines forth together with the mystery.

For what is signified by the number nine if not the nine orders of angels? And what by the number six if not the human being, who was created on the sixth day? Both creatures are marked in the figure of the cross, because both are restored by the Savior on the cross, and by both the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation was honored, since on the day of his birth both were summoned to praise and joy. Hence Luke says:

> “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will.”

And shortly afterward:

> “And the shepherds,” he says, “returned, glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.”

[Col. 0202B]

Thus four crosses are painted and written on this page in four places, as follows. The length of each cross, descending from top to bottom and to be read in three separate lines, contains one verse of thirty-nine letters. Likewise, across the breadth, three lines extending from left to right form one verse. Thus the letters in the middle of the cross are common to both verses and express the number nine; those arranged around the arms express sixty.

The following verse of thirty-nine letters is in the length of the upper cross:

> The sacred form of the cross shines in a venerable covering.

Across its breadth is this verse, containing the same number of letters:

> Great honor clothes it; rejoicing, I speak this to the people.

At the end of the cross, in its length, is this verse:

> I am the construction of the sacred body, blessed in art.

Across it is this:

> Radiant in number, by which within it proves that it has gone blessedly.

On the right-hand cross, the following verse is to be read lengthwise:

> Now I shall sing, beseeching Jesus to hide and cleanse the wetness.

Across it is this:

> True salvation is this, the holy blessing of salvation.

On the left-hand cross, the following verse is written lengthwise:

[Col. 0202D]

> Remaining wholly in himself, he holds all things, and himself lives in all.

Across it is this:

> Fountain of goodness, love and piety, true redemption.

[Col. 0203]

[Col. 0204A]
