**EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE**

[Col. 0205]

[Col. 0205A]

This page contains the number of years from the beginning of the world up to the year of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, expressed in the Greek letters arranged in the form of a cross. The number is [V]CCXXXI, according to the authority of the chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome. [Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]

According to their calculation, the years from Adam to the Flood amount to [V]CCXLII; from the Flood to Abraham, 942 years; and from Abraham to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, in which the Lord was baptized in the Jordan by John and announced the way of salvation to the peoples, proving by signs and mighty works that what he said was true, there are [II]XLIV years. All these joined together make [V]CCXXVIII years. Add three years, when in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar the Lord came to his Passion, was crucified by the Jews, and rose again on the third day; the total is [V]CCXXXI years.

If this number is divided according to the letters written above in the cross, a venerable mystery is suggested to us. There are therefore four letters that form the figure of the cross, namely Γ, Ζ, Τ, and Χ; but the last three are placed four times, once in each arm. Γ is placed once in the middle of the cross. If their numerical values are considered, this arrangement shows us gifts of heavenly grace. Γ signifies the number three among the Greeks, Ζ seven, Τ thirty, and Χ one thousand.

What is suggested to us by Γ if not faith in the Trinity? What by Ζ if not the hope of the faithful? What by Τ if not charity? And what by Χ if not eternal blessedness?

Rightly, therefore, faith is shown by Γ, which is the first of these letters and is placed in the middle of the cross, because sound faith is the foundation of good works and the beginning of our salvation. For it is impossible to please God without faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith.”

Hope is also well signified by Ζ, because the whole intention of the faithful pants toward eternal rest, which is signified by the number seven, saying with the Prophet:

> “My soul thirsts for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

Charity, too, is rightly expressed by Τ, which bears the image of the holy cross. In the work of the cross the great charity of God the Father was displayed: he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, as the Savior himself said concerning himself in the Gospel:

> “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

And the Apostle says:

> “God commends his own charity toward us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having been justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.”

Τ therefore signifies the number 300, which is six times fifty. What else is suggested by these numbers than the perfection of charity? The number fifty, on account of Pentecost, signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit; and the number six is perfect. “The charity of God,” as the Apostle says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

Through the letter Χ, therefore, which expresses the number one thousand, eternal blessedness is appropriately signified. For in Scripture the number one thousand is customarily used as a sign of perfection, since it produces a solid square number. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred. This figure is already square, but still flat; let it rise in height and become solid. Multiply one hundred by ten, and one thousand results. By this perfect number the stable, inseparable, and, as it were, squared life of the righteous in heaven is designated, because it is perfect on every side: they enjoy both the boundless joy of souls and the immortality of bodies, when they possess the perfect form of their state—that is, eternity in length, charity in breadth, and divine contemplation in height.

Finally, it is pleasing to say something concerning the characters of the letters themselves, which mark the numbers mentioned and by their arrangement display the figure of the cross.

[Col. 0206A]

Γ, which stands upright and is flat at the top, aptly signifies faith, which ought to be raised upward toward the Lord and to establish the steadfastness of the mind; yet it must be guarded with great humility, lest, wandering everywhere in uncertainty, it fall into error. The Apostle indicates both of these things when he says:

> “Brothers, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and be strengthened.”

And elsewhere:

> “Do not be wiser than you ought to be, but be wise unto sobriety. To each person God has apportioned a measure of faith.”

Ζ, therefore, appropriately signifies hope, which curves its boundaries in the manner of an anchor, showing that we ought to cling immovably to heavenly things through hope, lest the storm of persecution, the whirlwind of temptations, or the allurements of pleasures tear us away from the desire for eternal life. Concerning this the Apostle wrote to the Hebrews:

> “Let us have the strongest consolation, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us. We have this hope as a sure and firm anchor of the soul, reaching even into the interior of the veil, where Jesus, the forerunner, entered for us, having become high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

[Col. 0206B]

The letter Τ, which has the likeness of the cross and is joined together in a twofold form, aptly signifies to us the two commandments of charity. One part rises upward, while another extends across; the part that is raised upward commends to us divine love, so that we may love God our Creator with our whole heart, our whole soul, and our whole mind. The part drawn across the middle, while remaining joined to the upright part, signifies our love for one another, which must be ordered by divine love, so that we may love our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake.

The Apostle John instructs us concerning this:

> “By this we have known the charity of God: that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.”

And again:

> “We have this commandment from God, that whoever loves God should also love his brother.”

Χ, which in Greek is called *chīlē* and signifies “one thousand” in Latin, is written not with straight lines but with enclosing lines when it signifies one thousand. Thus Ω, because it indicates another number, is written with straight lines. We have said that this signifies the perfection of the saints in heaven, and it is written with enclosing lines to show that heavenly joy has no boundary, where the praise of the saints will remain without end. Concerning them the Prophet says:

> “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you.”

Then, according to the prophet Isaiah, the seed of the saints will stand before God like the new heaven and the new earth, and there will be month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath.

Χ is also the first letter of the name of Christ, and this aptly accords with the interpretation. For he is our joy, to whom we say with the Prophet:

> “You will make us glad with joy in your presence,”

and into whom the angels desire to look.

The sequence of these letters, therefore, beginning with Γ—that is, from the middle of the cross—is carried through its four regions. This signifies the marvelous fact that after Christ’s Passion his disciples, beginning from Jerusalem, began to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world and to distribute divine gifts among all nations, so that from every part of the earth the faithful might deserve to reach eternal rewards through the goods of faith, hope, and charity.

There are also two verses written here in the aforesaid numerical signs of the holy cross. The first is to be read lengthwise, from the top of the cross downward, as follows:

> Behold, this form of the cross rightly displays the honor of Jesus.

The second is to be recited across its breadth, in this order:

> Jesus counts this number, by which he suffered in the fields.

The name *Jesus*, which contains the letter Γ in the middle of the cross, is common to both verses, as is clearly shown.

[Col. 0208A]

>   
> Behold the forming hand and the equal number of Herod’s days;  
> in Bethlehem, born of his mother, a wondrous infant;  
> himself born of Mary, a care exceedingly rich for the world;  
> noble also as a boy, an ancient person in the days,  
> who came from Edom, from Bozrah, wearing a bloodstained garment;

>   
> For Matthew, writing well, gave the first account in order.  
> He who confirms the law in his face marked him as a human being,  
> descended from David from the beginning; and when he piously displayed

**EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE**

[Col. 0209]

[Col. 0209A]

Here too the four prophetic animals standing around the Lamb express the likeness of a cross. This is the vision mentioned by Ezekiel and by the Apocalypse of John: Ezekiel writes that they are in the midst of fire or electrum, while John places them in the midst of the throne and around the throne.

Let us first examine Ezekiel’s words concerning them. Among other things, he wrote:

> “The likeness of their faces was the face of a human being and the face of a lion on the right side of the four of them; but the face of an ox was on the left side of the four of them; and the face of an eagle was above the four of them,”

and so forth.

John wrote as follows:

> “In the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. The first living creature was like a lion; the second living creature was like a calf; the third living creature had a face like a human being; and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle.”

Shortly afterward he introduced another vision, saying:

> “And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and in the midst of the elders stood a Lamb as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.”

Since the prophet and the Apostle agree concerning the four living creatures and their four faces, although they differ in certain details which there is no time to discuss individually, let us see what the position of these four creatures signifies—those whom John wrote to be around the throne and the Lamb standing in the middle of the throne.

Does this not signify the Lord’s cross? When it is said that there are four around the throne, I do not think he intends to signify anything other than the four parts—front and back, right and left—as far as the position of a place is concerned; but, apart from location, nothing of this sort can be defined. What else, then, do these four parts signify than the four arms of the cross, if we wish to consider it lying flat?

And what else are we to understand the Lamb, who is in the middle of the throne, to hold except the middle of the cross? He was fastened to it, the one who took away the sins of the world.

These four living creatures signify the four Evangelists, as the authority of the Church has handed down: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. They are rightly written in the form of the holy cross, because all four unanimously bear witness in the books of the holy Gospel to the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection.

Matthew is rightly placed at the bottom and bears the form of a human being, because at the beginning of his Gospel, describing the Savior’s genealogy, he indicates that he assumed flesh from earthly parents.

Mark and Luke, as though already placed higher, signify in him royal power and priestly dignity. The former, namely Mark, has the form of a lion, in whom the voice of a lion roaring in the desert is heard:

> “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

For Amos says:

> “The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice.”

The lion is the king of beasts, which is why Solomon says:

> “As the roaring of a lion, so is the anger of a king.”

And in Genesis the patriarch Jacob said concerning Judah—from whom kings came and from whom Christ assumed flesh:

> “Judah is a lion’s cub; to the prey you have gone up, my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness. Who will rouse him? The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he will be the expectation of the nations.”

The other, namely Luke, bears the likeness of a calf. Beginning with Zechariah the priest, he testifies that the Lord was also born as a human being from a priestly family, when he relates that the angel said to Mary, his mother:

> “And behold, Elizabeth, your kinswoman, has conceived a son in her old age.”

And by tracing the Savior’s genealogy from David through Nathan, he indicates that he is a priest.

John shows in himself the form of an eagle. He rightly stands at the top of the cross; flying toward higher things, he explores the more secret mysteries of Christ’s divinity, and, fixing the eyes of his mind upon the very sun of the Godhead, he began his Gospel at once with Christ’s divinity, as follows:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

The four Gospels written by the four Evangelists therefore signify the four rivers of Paradise proceeding from one source. Just as those rivers, proceeding from one source, watered the whole earth, so the four Gospels, flowing forth from one true source—namely Christ, and whoever drinks from him once will never thirst—and spreading through the mouths of preachers, water the whole world so that it may bring forth the fruits of virtues.

These are the divine chariot: the four wheels, followed by the four living creatures, having four faces and four wings. When the prophet says that one wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures, having four faces, and immediately adds in the plural:

> “Their appearance was like the appearance of the sea, and the likeness of all four of them was one,”

and so forth, this can be applied to the understanding of the present interpretation. For in one wheel four forms of wheels appeared, because the four Gospels agree in one Passion of the Savior. So great was the likeness of the four wheels following the four living creatures that they could truly be believed to be one wheel; and so great is the likeness in the Evangelists’ narration that it is readily recognized as dictated by one Spirit.

The statement that the wheels moved in their four directions and did not turn back when they moved means that the Gospels run teaching through the four regions of the world and will not turn back to deny what they teach, because truth observes the course of uprightness and does not bend into the crookedness of falsehood.

On these four living creatures are written things corresponding to them, signifying their office and authority and what they proclaim concerning the Lord the Savior. On the form of the human being, below, this verse is written:

> Matthew marked this human being in the order of his lineage.

The lion has these words:

> Mark marks the king.

The image of the calf contains this:

> Luke gives the high priest.

But the eagle, standing at the top of the cross, gives forth this verse:

> The high-flying eagle, John, drew the Word from the citadel.

These same four living creatures also hold four scrolls, on which their principal statements are marked; hence the opening portions of the four Gospels are indicated.

The Lamb, standing in the middle, has written on his head and horns:

> The seven Spirits of God.

This signifies the seven horns and the seven eyes. On the rest of his body he also bears the statement of John the Baptist concerning him:

> Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.

On the cross which he carries on his head he displays the Greek name written as **YOS**, which is interpreted as “son,” signifying that this image represents not an ordinary lamb but the Son of God.

**FIGURE XVI. On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet Isaiah enumerates.**

[Col. 0211]

[Col. 0211A]

> Holy Spirit, come, directed from the height,  
> so that you may dedicate to yourself the mind devoted to you  
> and hearts that rightly believe, O prophet’s Spirit, who are also the Spirit of life.  
> Christ promised to send you, promised from the Father,  
> an ancient gift and a new one, praised by the lofty-throned one,
