>   
> To whomever you give yourself, he grasps each mystery  
> with understanding, taught inwardly and weighing all things:  
> how Christ himself, the Wisdom of the Father, gave you to the world  
> as a pledge, wishing you to be the noble bride’s earnest,  
> while you, the Creator Spirit, formed this entire mass.  
> You see its inner parts, and none of it will remain hidden from you  
> unless you immediately search it out.  
> For the unseen creation is before the holy eyes—  
> I know that Isaiah rightly gave him and seven to these highest things [the wording is materially corrupt in the supplied text]—

[Col. 0212A]

> For the Creator says that Christ placed you twice into the meaning of life,  
> giving a clear command concerning the twofold love:  
> that God be praised with the honor of the whole heart,  
> that the gracious one be loved, and that all knowledge be given to love itself.  
> Then that all should embrace the love of their brother:  
> this the holy cross marks by the pattern of God’s beneficent work.  
>   
> For the part raised upward piously commands the love of God;  
> the transverse part gives peace, which he established  
> must be held together with one’s brother—  
> the supreme lover of holy piety, Christ,  
> who was fixed upon the cross as the victim of peace.  
>   
> For love of his friends, the pious arbiter of the world,  
> laying down his beloved life, left examples.  
> Sanctifying this love, which must always be sung,  
> may every harmful fear depart from me through the Spirit.  
> So that the glory of the divine cross, increased with me,  
> may remain in song; you will fill the silent mouth with song  
> and rightly make it sing the heavenly hymn.

**EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE**

[Col. 0213]

[Col. 0213A] It is written in Isaiah: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his stock; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” Thus the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is enumerated by the prophet. It is said to rest most delightfully upon that flower which, in the Song of Songs, says to the bride: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

The Jews say that the shoot and the flower of which the prophet spoke signify the Lord himself, on account of the power of the reigning one and his beauty. We, however, say that the shoot signifies holy Mary, sprung from the stock of Jesse, who had no shrub growing together with her, because she had no husband in a carnal union; but the flower signifies the Lord Jesus, who sprang forth most splendidly from the bark of human nature, because he was born and came forth from a virgin’s womb without the stain of sins. In the chastity of his flesh he also displayed the whiteness of the lily, and in the blood of his passion he showed the redness of the rose.

The Spirit of the Lord therefore rests upon him—that is, he will remain in him in an everlasting dwelling—for in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. For God does not give the Spirit by measure; rather, God the Father anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions, and from his fullness we have all received. How, then, is it written of Christ that he received the Holy Spirit from the Father and gave him? Both natures are revealed in him, namely the human and the divine. He received as man; he gave as God.

We are indeed able to receive this gift according to our limited capacity, but we certainly cannot pour it out upon others. Rather, so that this may occur, we invoke the Lord over them, asking that it be accomplished. But one may ask why the prophet began to count from the spirit of wisdom and ended with the spirit of fear, when the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” This can be resolved as follows.

When the prophet prophesied concerning the flower of the shoot that was to come forth from the root of Jesse—that is, concerning Christ—and understood him to be coeternal with the Father in his divinity, recognizing him as the author of every good and every holiness, indeed of all things, he intended to signify that, with such a fullness of holiness, he descended from heaven all the way to us and poured grace into our nature, that is, into human nature. He therefore begins from the very summit of spiritual gifts and proceeds downward to the lowest point.

For what grace is greater than to behold, according to our capacity, fully and perfectly the almighty Creator, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist, and Wisdom herself, eternal, by whom, through whom, and in whom all things are enlightened? And what grace is lower than to restrain oneself as a human being from sins on account of the punishment of Gehenna? For the one who is afflicted here by punishment has not yet ascended to the higher degrees, because fear contains punishment. But the one who fears is not perfect in love. Nevertheless, human weakness can ascend to higher things only through this fear.

Therefore the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” because a person must first restrain himself from sins through fear, knowing that it is written that God repays each person according to his works, and that the impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. Then, through love of the eternal reward, he should ascend through the remaining degrees.

The second degree is that he should be pious and gentle, holding a right faith and returning no evil for evil, but always returning what is good; not cursing in response to one who curses, but blessing instead.

The third is that he should possess knowledge to choose good and reject evil, to turn away from evil and do good, to seek peace and despise hatred.

The fourth is that he should be strong, walking with a firm step along the path of righteousness, and not allow himself to be corrupted by any prosperity or distressed by any adversity.

The fifth degree is that he should do everything according to true counsel and act obediently in accordance with what divine Scripture teaches: that is, that he should forgive his neighbors their debts, so that God may forgive him his sins; show mercy to another, so that God may have mercy on him; make friends for himself from the mammon of iniquity, so that when it fails they may receive him into the eternal dwellings; sow earthly things, so that he may reap heavenly things; lose his soul for the present in this world, so that he may preserve it for eternal life—and things of this kind.

The sixth is that he should understand God: that is, seek him, contemplate him, and examine him with the full intention of his heart; hasten to uproot immediately every evil thought that comes into his heart; and dash his little ones against the rock, Christ.

But when he has ascended to the seventh degree, that is, to wisdom, he will already present the human being as perfect, and will pass from a servile condition into sonship. He will no longer need anyone to teach him; but, as it is written, “his anointing teaches him about everything.” Delighted with perfect love of God, he will become certain, with the Apostle, that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither power nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to separate him from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The fact that these same seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are counted here twice signifies, without doubt, the two commandments of love, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit; or else the two Testaments, dictated and written through the same Spirit. These have been joined and united in one cross, that is, in the one passion of Christ.

In the cross of Christ, therefore, two things are accomplished. One is that every separation and hostility were dissolved in it, and all things in heaven and on earth were reconciled in it. [Col. 0214C]

I have therefore depicted here a flower-bearing cross in four principal colors—hyacinth-blue, purple, linen-white, and scarlet—in order to display the beauty of that most delightful flower which prophetic speech describes as having arisen from royal stock. Existing more beautiful in form than the sons of men, it wondrously displayed in himself, beyond all others, the beauty of every virtue.

For it is not permissible to believe that any of the saints could have attained to the excellence of his love, since it is established that he alone was born without the stain of sin, and that what grace bestowed upon the others in part, nature supplied to him wholly and completely.

In the hyacinth we understand his heavenly manner of life among human beings; in the purple, the blood of his passion; in the whiteness and linen, the utterly inviolate chastity of his body; and in the scarlet, his extraordinary and perfect love. In all these respects Christ Jesus, born as a human being among human beings, shone serenely, because he was inwardly and outwardly full of the beauty of every adornment. [Col. 0214D]

Jesus the child therefore advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings; and when he had become a man, he was praised by the testimony of the people, who said: “He has done everything well: he has made the deaf hear and the mute speak.” By enlightening the world through his teaching and healing its sick, he destroyed death through death, rose triumphantly in glory, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## FIGURE XVII. On the eight evangelical beatitudes

[Col. 0215]

[Col. 0215A]

Holy, blessed, powerful praise of life, glory of Christ,

Venerable cross of God, prosperous work of the world,

Worthy, good, and pious, because you fastened Christ’s members,

Suspended upon the timber; beneath the shadow of prison

You rescue afflicted peoples, and gave them the kingdom

Set on high; for the long expectation of heaven,

Restored by right to the pious, once blesses those worthy of the crown.

For the good seeds which the pious Judge scattered over the earth

With serene countenance, he multiplied and loved;

And whatever the Teacher prayed while seated upon the mountain’s height,

Bestowing upon his disciples the covenant, the pious treaties of the law—

For then, in a holy and beneficent order,

The Lord began to unfold for the saints the teachings

Of virtue under these titles,

So that the blessed offspring of the Father might confirm them by this doctrine.

Because the cross embraces every good and gives

The best things through itself, teaches, joins them to lovers, and blesses:

[Col. 0215B]

Thus, happy one, trembling with divine ardor, press your heart.

You who are here, act justly; preserve the cold [reading uncertain]

For those who weep, who desire [reading uncertain], for to these above

The omen is directed toward him; [the following lines are textually obscure]

[Col. 0216A]

They will see what counsel and eternal mercy may be,

Consolation—and likewise refreshment, abundant nourishment—

And in the citadel, action does not belong to a lofty mouth,

But sudden heavenly provision is now at hand;

Here it is effective, and this is sufficient, while inward things

Are far away, upon the humble ground which the prostrate worshipper adores.

When he asks not words alone but also gentle conduct,

The All-Holding One always demands this, at this time and every time.

Therefore it is blessedness to dwell in the light of those who desire,

And by this number eight to seek gifts above the difficult heights,

And, rising again in this way, the kingdom—for thus they will proceed by the cross.

The cross is the way, the ladder, the wheel, the homeland, the guide, the gate, the triumph,

The blessed life of meritorious human beings, and the greatest reward.

Behold, twice four times placed, the pious formula of the kingdom

Reveals the holy gifts by which the good merit ascending to heaven.

The almighty Lord of all, powerful over everything,

The Spirit himself desires by these means to ascend to the seat of peace:

[Col. 0216B]

He had raised seven steps among the heavenly stars, so that from there

He might graciously reveal how the good can proceed to the heights of heaven,

Those whom love, reason, light, praise, good virtue,

Glory, lineage, and throne accompany, and to whom the citadel of heaven is added.

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0217]

[Col. 0217A]

The sequence of the eight beatitudes is therefore marked here in the form of the holy cross, so that it may be known to the entire people of the faithful where their salvation had its beginning and where they will find the completion of their perfection: when through Christ’s passion they receive remission of sins, and through his resurrection hope for eternal life and immortality; and when they seek the fullness of heavenly blessedness from no other than the one from whom they have once again received redemption.

These mysteries therefore rightly belong to the holy cross, because, having been liberated through it, they enter into the covenant of faith and the fellowship of the unity of the people. In it redemption from death is intimated; in it the holy conduct of life is displayed; in it the perfection of all virtues is revealed; in it resurrection to eternal life is promised; in it the attainment of eternal life and the acquisition of true happiness are hoped for.

Since, after the enumeration, we have decided to speak about the eight beatitudes in a treatment of spiritual gifts, let us see how these two things correspond to one another, and whether the structure of the holy cross can demonstrate this correspondence within itself.

The blessed Father Augustine, in the book which he chose to call *On the Sermon on the Mount*, makes the following mention of this correspondence, saying:

“It seems to me, therefore, that the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks, also corresponds to these degrees and sentences, but there is a difference in their order. There he began the enumeration with the higher things; here, however, with the lower. For there he begins with the wisdom of God and ends with the fear of God, but the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Therefore, if we count them step by step as ascending, the first there is the fear of God, the second piety, the third knowledge, the fourth strength, the fifth counsel, the sixth understanding, and the seventh wisdom.

“The fear of God corresponds to the humble, of whom it is said here: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’—that is, those who are not puffed up and not proud. Of them the Apostle says: ‘Do not be high-minded, but fear,’ that is, do not be exalted.

“Piety corresponds to the meek. For one who seeks piously honors Holy Scripture and does not criticize what he does not yet understand, and therefore does not resist; this is what it means to be meek. Hence it is said here: ‘Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance.’

“Knowledge corresponds to those who mourn, who have already learned from the Scriptures by what evils they are held bound—things which, in ignorance, they desired as though they were good and useful. Of them it is said here: ‘Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.’

“Strength corresponds to those who hunger and thirst. They labor while desiring joy from true goods and wishing to turn their love away from earthly and bodily things. Of them it is said here: ‘Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.’

“Counsel corresponds to the merciful. For this is the one remedy for escaping from so many evils: that we forgive as we wish to be forgiven, and help others insofar as we can, just as we wish to be helped in what we cannot do. Of them it is said here: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.’

“Understanding of the heart corresponds to the pure in heart, as to an eye that has been cleansed, by which one can perceive what no bodily eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of a human being. Of them it is said here: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’

“Wisdom corresponds to the peacemakers, in whom all things have already been ordered and no rebellious movement exists, but everything obeys the human spirit when it itself obeys God. Of them it is said here: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.’”

A little later he added:

“These things can indeed be fulfilled in this life, just as we believe they were fulfilled in the apostles. But that complete transformation into angelic form which is promised after this life cannot be explained in words. ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.’”

[Col. 0218A]

This eighth sentence, which returns to the beginning and declares the human being perfected, perhaps signifies also circumcision on the eighth day in the Old Testament, and the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath—which is certainly the eighth day and also the first.

The entire sequence of virtues is therefore rightly distributed into degrees, because the whole life of the faithful is raised upward through growth and increase to higher things, until it reaches the summit of perfection, namely love—that love which perfectly casts out fear, through which one merits to have God dwelling within oneself; for “God is love,” and “whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.” This occurs when, the storm of temptations having been calmed, the whole person will be occupied in contemplation of God.

Hence the Psalm says: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.” And elsewhere: “His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.”

This is rightly made known through spiritual gifts, because through the grace of the Holy Spirit every good gift and every perfect gift is granted to us.

These degrees are rightly arranged in the form of the holy cross, because through it one truly ascends to the heavenly kingdom. But since the holy cross has two parts—one that stands upright and another that extends transversely—the eight degrees of the beatitudes have been arranged by us upon it in such a way that one ascends from the bottom to the middle along its upright part, and then the order of ascent is carried across its transverse part. Finally, in its upright section, in the part that rises above the transverse beam, that ascent comes to an end. This will be readily apparent to anyone who properly understands the verses that we have written upon it.

The appropriate arrangement of the parts can also be recognized in the division itself. At the bottom of the upright shaft are placed the poor in spirit; at the top are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. To both groups the kingdom of heaven is promised, because it is through true humility alone that one properly reaches the palm of martyrdom and the heavenly kingdom, and because all adversities are endured with the utmost patience for the sake of righteousness, which is Christ.

Along the transverse section a path extends from the blessed who mourn now to the blessed who are pure in heart. To the first group consolation is promised, and to the second the vision of the Lord; this is rightly understood as one and the same thing. For those truly receive consolation who enjoy the vision of the eternal King without end.

Thus, in the present life, the more the holy men humble themselves outwardly through contempt for themselves, the more abundantly they are nourished inwardly by the revelation of contemplation. Those whom the valley of humility confines outwardly in weeping, the ascent of contemplation raises inwardly.

Therefore, eight octagons, joined together by odd-numbered figures, contain eight verses of thirty-seven letters, containing the eight beatitudes. The first, placed at the base of the cross, has this verse:

> The Lord wills the kingdom of heaven to belong to the blessed poor.

The second, following it, is:

[Col. 0218D]

> And the meek alone to dwell forever in heaven above.

The third octagon in order is the first on the transverse path of the cross, containing this verse:

> Happy are those who weep, for their consolation is on high.

The fourth, next to it, has this verse:

> For eternal refreshment will fill those who hunger for righteousness.

Beside it is the fifth, with this:

> Abundant mercy from above repays the pious in mind.

The sixth is the one that closes the transverse path:

> Serene hearts will see God in the heavenly citadel.

The seventh, standing below in the projecting part of the cross, is this:

> The Lord embraces the peacemakers with the love of offspring.

The highest of all the octagons is inscribed with this verse:

> The afflicted for Christ already looks toward the kingdom of Olympus.

## FIGURE XVIII. On the mystery of the number forty

[Col. 0219]

[Col. 0219A]

Reveal, tongue, the saving triumph of the Lord who conquers:

By figure, hand, lip, voice, syllable, and sense,

The great glory of the Lord’s cross, which calls for praise everywhere—

Above the lofty stars and wherever the abyss reaches,

Where pure light remains, where the dreadful silences

Of perpetual night lie hidden, where night and day in turn

Succeed one another and yield to one another, where the whole world

Slips onward in time, where the appointed order is changeable.

It is scarcely enough to bind this with four; but this page,

Worthy of the cross, binds ten praises along its path,

And at the same time, by sacred art, joins together

Forty complete units, full also of serene light,

Whom mystical power adorns, consecrates, and honors.

This number fittingly bears the figure of the present time,

In which the whole holy Church, under Christ its ruler,

[Col. 0219B]

Piously bears hostile weapons, here opposing the raging enemy,

Standing firm as a conscious warrior;

And by the battles of virtue, with faith’s shield,

Subdues all those vices which are its glory to overcome.

With this shield and with the spear of the word it binds on the breastplate,

[Col. 0220A]

And properly clothes itself in holy righteousness;

It bears this helmet of salvation upon its head.

The emblems of the cross themselves make the forehead bright,

And pour beautiful adornment over the opposing brow.

For on the cross the Savior conquered his savage enemy,

And by this number Christ, in the wilderness, drew from every food

A holy fast of sobriety. He had seized and rescued the human being

From the black throat of the proud robber, whom gluttony

Had dragged into crime and had brought at the same time

A dreadful and savage rage.

Light avarice and vainglory thrust him onward;

Jesus, the Lord, eternal redemption, removed him from the kingdom,

But pressed down the enemy and saved the captive from him.

Generous, humble, meek, and himself sober,

Whose battle is salvation, whose victory is holy,

[Col. 0220B]

Whose throne is on high, whose gaze reaches the lowest places,

The cross is the world’s rejoicing honor; the cross is the world’s elevation.

The cross shall be my song: the bright victory of Christ.

[Col. 0221]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0221A]

The number forty therefore forms the appearance of the cross in this manner and declares the sacramental mystery through an appropriate arrangement. Divided into four sums, it clearly displays ten in each. This pertains to the mystery because, just as the fullness of ten is found in the four sections, so the perfection of the Decalogue is indicated to all the faithful in each of the books of the holy Gospel.

These joined decades, however, make one form of the cross, because the unity of faith and the fellowship of love are concordantly affirmed by the Decalogue of the Law and the majesty of the Gospel.

Moreover, the number ten itself is completed by the number that proceeds from one to four; and, in order to rise to forty, it is multiplied by four. This signifies precisely that the fulfillment of the Law does not occur without the Gospel, nor does evangelical teaching lack the testimony of the Law.

For Christ is the end and perfection of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. He is our peace, who made both one, breaking down the middle wall of partition, the hostility, in his flesh; abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new human being, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself.

Because this number is the sacramental sign of the present laborious time, in which we fight against the devil under the discipline of Christ the King, it also declares the fact that he consecrated forty days through fasting and the humiliation of his soul. The Law and the Prophets are represented by Moses and Elijah, who fasted for forty days; and the Gospel by the Lord’s own fast, during which for forty days he was also tempted by the devil. What else does this prefigure except the entire period of this age, our temptation in the flesh that he graciously took from our mortality?

From the hour of his death until the dawn of his resurrection there are also forty hours, if the ninth hour itself is counted. After the resurrection he likewise chose to remain no more than forty days with his disciples on this earth. During those days he remained mixed with their human manner of life, receiving mortal food with them although he was no longer destined to die, in order through those forty days to signify by his hidden presence that he would fulfill what he had promised when he said: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

The reason that this number signifies this temporal and earthly life is immediately apparent—although there may perhaps be another, more hidden reason—in that the seasons of the years run through four divisions, and the world itself is bounded by four regions, which Scripture sometimes names by the winds: east and west, north and south.

For this world, for this earthly and mortal life of human beings, and to govern us as we labor in temptation, Matthew, receiving Christ the King who came, began with Abraham and enumerated forty persons. Christ came in the flesh from that Hebrew people, for whose distinction from the other nations God had separated Abraham from his land and his kindred. Christ came in the flesh, and from that people he brought the saving cross to the whole world.

In this period of years Isaac was joined to Rebecca, and through the mystery of the same number the Church was joined to Christ. For this number of days twelve men were sent to explore the land of promise; and for the same number of years the unbelievers and detractors were punished in the barren wilderness, because often, through the labor of the present life by which the elect are tested, the reprobate are tormented.

Likewise, according to half of this number—that is, from the age of twenty—the sons of Israel were chosen for the service of the Lord, as the history of the Pentateuch relates. This showed that as soon as the battles of vices began to arise against the saints, the labor of combat was immediately no small one. “Those who belong to Christ,” says the Apostle, “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

According to the position of the holy cross in Solomon’s temple, this number measures the Holy of Holies: twenty cubits in length and twenty cubits in width. This shows that he himself is the Holy of Holies, who was fastened to the shaft of the fourfold cross in order to atone for the sins of the people and sanctify the nations of the whole world, dwelling among them and saving all who believe in him.

The holy cross can therefore rightly be called the Holy of Holies. It is revered and worshiped by all the saints on earth, and it is also considered worthy, as we believe, of every honor from the holy angelic spirits themselves, who rejoice in our redemption. They remember that Christ was exalted because of obedience to the cross and was given the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

The number forty is here enclosed in four triangles, according to the properties of a geometrical figure, containing a verse of forty letters in this form:

> Holy cross, you are the victory of Christ, the eternal King.

[Col. 0223]

## FIGURE XIX. On the number fifty and the mystery revealed in it

[Col. 0223A]

The cross shall be my song; lend your ears, faithful ones.

Praise of the cross flows from the mouth; guide your devoted minds,

You for whom Christ exists, for whom wisdom is a concern,

The eternal light of God, for whom incorruption becomes love.

Here the power of the craftsman resounds, and the work of blessedness;

Here beauty rejoices, here the glory of art is fashioned.

Your honor lives, because its life-giving source shines brightly;

Your palm remains immortal by right in the heavens,

Because Christ is your bright victory everywhere.

He himself is your salvation, and he wrought vengeance in darkness

For you, dying; and justly crushed the wicked,

Killing death by death, while he conquered the realms below.

Hither, hither, sick ones, hasten with swift running; behold,

Yours will be the physician whom the healing cross bore

Upon its lofty timber; it stretched out its arms for your healing.

[Col. 0223B]

Ask to be healed, and spread out both your palms.

By his touch he is able swiftly, here upon this same face,

To restore the pious right hand to the trembling one;

Here is the holy summit of rest, whose power it is

To apply salvation wisely.

[Col. 0224A]

Let the art of healing descend, so that he may recover through physical art [text uncertain].

Let the wounds of fear depart; let blessed signs live again.

This figure of the cross, full of divine grace,

Gives the saving and blessed number fifty:

It signifies forgiveness and the joyful Sabbaths of rest;

It is the sign of the ancient Law given after the festival of unleavened bread;

And after the holy solemnities of Passover

It is itself full of the power of the Paraclete sent everywhere.

Good through the love of peace, it displays the tokens of peace,

Perfect in beauty, perfect in the appearance of honor.

It offers five crosses through its branches, and ten units

It counts as the letter X, always a form suited and friendly to the cross.

There are five books of the Law and ten commandments.

Everything indeed agrees with the cross in word and course:

Law, number, time, mysteries, deeds, and character.

[Col. 0224B]

Let us therefore all praise the cross together in exultation.

Let us here pay our vows to the crucified King,

Who by his own blood released the world from its sins.

[Col. 0225]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0225A]

This page therefore contains the number fifty, expressed in five letters X. These both mark the sum of tens and express the figure of the cross, in whose honor the entire work is composed.

Here it observes the jubilee and is a sign of the true remission granted to the whole world through the cross. Here, after the celebration of the typical Passover, the solemnities of the slain lamb, and the Lord’s passage through Egypt, it bears witness to the most celebrated festival of the Law given on Mount Sinai. And after the true Passover and the sacrifice of Christ the Lamb, it demonstrates the sending of the Paraclete upon the apostles.

Here, after the completion of seven weeks, with one unit added, it indicates the Sabbath of Sabbaths and demonstrates the joys of eternal rest, which is truly one. There the earth of our bodies will truly celebrate its Sabbath, [Col. 0225B] because it will no longer experience any of the losses of the present life or the burdens of labor, but will perform its service in praise of the eternal Trinity, rejoicing that the joy of its incorruption has no end.

It is therefore rightly asked how the number fifty rises from the number forty. The number forty belongs to those called “evenly even” numbers: it is divided into equal parts, and each part can itself be divided into other equal parts; likewise, the parts of the parts are divided, but the process does not proceed all the way to unity. This is equal division.

Thus its half is XX, its fourth part X, its fifth part VIII, its eighth part V, its tenth part IV, its twentieth part II, and its fortieth part I. For one, two, four, five, eight, ten, and twenty together make fifty.

But what else does this increase of the smaller number into the greater signify except our progress? We have already said that the number forty designates this temporal and present life, whereas the number fifty demonstrates the rest of the future homeland and eternal joys.

What else is suggested to us through these two numbers except that, while leading this life in holy conversion, devoting ourselves to prayers, vigils, and fasts, and laboring also in works of mercy and almsgiving, we should hasten with full faith, unwavering hope, and perfect love toward that homeland awaiting us in heaven? There eternal rest is possessed without any labor; there true joy is contained without any sadness; there whatever good we have here received in part will be perfected wholly and completely without end.

Moreover, the number ten signifies knowledge of the Creator and the creature. For the Creator is the Trinity. The number seven, however, indicates the creature because of life and body. For in life there are three things, and therefore God must be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind; while in the body four elements appear most clearly, from which it is constituted.

This number, therefore, rightly appears in the mark of the cross, because through the mediator of God and human beings we have been reconciled and united in it to our Creator and transferred to the eternal Father as adopted sons.

The number of the jubilee is also rightly expressed in the figure of the cross, because its whole meaning is spiritually adapted to the cross. In the jubilee the unjust servitude of the Israelites is released; through the cross the captivity and servitude of the human race—by which it wickedly served sin and idols—is destroyed, and the human being, created in the image of God, is restored to true freedom, in which God alone is served.

In the jubilee, too, the property sold returns to its former owner. In the Lord’s passion, humanity’s former possession—that is, paradise—is restored, which humanity itself had wickedly exchanged through the forbidden fruit, receiving food and losing life.

There the sons of Israel were commanded to abstain from agricultural labor; here the saints of God are granted freedom from earthly desire. The sons of Israel sounded the trumpet throughout their land in the jubilee itself, in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, at the time of atonement. They sanctified the fiftieth year and proclaimed release to all the inhabitants of their land.

The trumpet of preaching was sounded by the apostles and the other preachers of the Gospel, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, interpreting the Law spiritually and teaching throughout the whole world that all who believe in Christ receive repentance and remission of sins through his name.

The Savior himself also displayed this time of true remission when, coming to Nazareth, he read in the synagogue the passage from the prophet Isaiah concerning himself, saying:

> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to set the broken free into release, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.”

Understand the acceptable year and the day of recompense as the whole period of his preaching, during which he lived in the flesh. Then he opened the eyes of the blind through word and miracles to know the truth—the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world—and, dying on the cross, he released captives and the broken into freedom. For, having destroyed the bonds of death, he rose in glory, ascended, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings.

That these testimonies refer to him is attested by the Evangelist Luke, when he adds that the Savior affirmed this very thing to his hearers, saying:

> “He began to say to them: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.’ And all bore witness to him and marveled at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth.”

[Col. 0226D]

Contained in the five X marks is this one verse of fifty letters:

> Five [things] aid in saying sacred things at the apex; and this too is of the cross.

The letters are counted by tens for each individual mark, though this applies to pronunciation. In writing, however, nine letters are assigned to each mark. For the middle letter of each mark is common to both paths: both the one toward the right and the one toward the left.

[Col. 0227]

## FIGURE XX. On the number one hundred and twenty, and its mystical significance

[Col. 0227A]

The outpouring of sacred blood has washed us,

And Christ has cleansed us from every impurity

And wiped away all harmful things. For, having suffered, he bore our stains,

Erasing the written indictment against the world; then the author

Established the imitable light of the Gospel.

He forbids the crime by what is written and rejects every vain thing;

This signifies life, which is expended throughout the whole world;

The light of virtues, by ascent, and the one who rules everywhere,

It indicates, opening the written prayer in which the mystical writings

Show how many gifts of God he offered to all by his word.

But here the character called *lauda* contains one hundred and twenty

Letters—not merely once, but four times over,

Marking great mysteries of faith and great joys

For the faithful, displaying the welcome gifts of healing

And the shared honor which the Spirit, the author,

[Col. 0227B]

As a burning light, had given to the harmonious tongue.

From this the joyful assembly everywhere proclaims the sacred name,

Spreading the net which, as a full dragnet in the abyss

Of the world, draws up the depths and restrains everyone

[Col. 0228A]

With these reins of the cross, so that Christ may everywhere

Worthily commend to humanity the insignia that reveal great gifts,

Adding worthy rewards of the Son [*nati*; reading uncertain].

Behold the Lord of the world, who establishes rewards in action

And multiplies them justly with the heavenly Father,

The ruler reigning and governing all things by his dominion;

He had rightly given the Paraclete as the pledge of salvation,

To govern, preserve, and lead us to the halls of life, and—
Sing devoutly, sing well to Christ,

Nations and tongues, and acknowledge the true king,

And the Father’s power, by which dreadful death and its goads

Have fallen; know the author of all things.

This praise has its summit, brought forth from a true seed:

“This is eternal rest”; this order has been implanted in nature,

That it may preserve only what has been implanted and hope for blessed gifts.

[Col. 0228B] This glory is virtue, and the highest cause of rest;

And this man preserves the laws well; he is free, and he is the one

Who desires the highest goods, rightly regarding lesser things as secondary. [Col. 0229]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0229A] Finally, the form of the holy cross is expressed on this page by the Greek letter lauda, λ [lambda], placed in four positions; among the Greeks it also signifies the number thirty. Since, therefore, it is placed here four times, it produces the number 120, whose sacramental meaning is great. For 120 years before the Flood are read as having been decreed for human beings as a period of repentance; the height of Solomon’s Temple was 120 cubits; and on 120 men the Holy Spirit descended on the day of Pentecost.

Since the same result is produced by four signs, the four Gospels are signified, in each of which the number thirty is found, because faith in the Holy Trinity and the perfection of the commandments are preached most fully in each book of the holy Gospel. Therefore, what was signified when Noah’s ark was being built at God’s command and was prepared, in the likeness of the holy cross, for the salvation of the elect who were to perish in the impious Flood—when a period of repentance was first decreed for human beings in the reckoning of 120 years—what else does it signify except that we can remain unharmed amid the waves of this age only if, working worthily in faith in the Holy Trinity, we obey with devoted minds the teaching of the Gospel?

This too—that the entire height of the Temple was 120 cubits—refers to the same sacrament: the primitive Church in Jerusalem, after the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men. Thus, as the natural progression of number advances from one to fifteen, and the maxima of all the places are gathered into one, they make 120 [the source’s wording is mathematically irregular]. For the things composed of seven and eight are sometimes referred to the meaning of the future life, which is now enacted in the Sabbath-rest of faithful souls but will be completed at the end of the age through the resurrection of immortal bodies.

Therefore the great blessedness of the elect in the future life is appropriately indicated by the number 120; appropriately the third upper room of the Lord’s house is brought to completion in this number, because after the present labors of the faithful and after the future rest received by souls, the complete happiness of the entire Church will be fulfilled in the glory of the resurrection.

[Col. 0230A] To this mystery likewise belongs what we have said: when he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, he sent the Holy Spirit in fiery tongues upon this number of men. Those who had been separated from one another by the diversity of languages he suddenly caused to have a common speech, through the understanding of all tongues, in his praise. For the Church too, when in its own time it rises from death and ascends into heaven in incorruptible flesh, will be fully and perfectly illumined by the gift of the Holy Spirit, when, according to the Apostle’s promise, God will be all in all.

Then there will be complete unification of languages among all, for proclaiming the mighty works of God, because with one mind and voice all will praise the glory of the divine majesty, which they see present. Then that verse of the Psalm will be perfectly fulfilled by which the Holy Spirit, through the prophet, exhorts all nations and urges them to the praise of the Lord, saying:

“Praise the Lord, all nations,
and praise him together, all peoples,
for his mercy toward us has been confirmed,
and the truth of the Lord remains forever.”

Then all who from every nation have been predestined to eternal life, after all scandals have been expelled from the Church of Christ through the ministry of the angels, will be united to their head and all the members will sing one praise harmoniously and perpetually.

It should also be noted that the letter lauda, placed here in four positions, displays the number 120 not only in its single character—thirty for each—but also that each of the verses written within it contains thirty letters. The verse at the upper lauda is:

“The Lord’s passion is life for the whole world.”

This is likewise at the lower one:

“One cross in the field, hope of freedom from wrath.”

This is at the right:

“Joyful light shines, full of divine grace.”

And this at the left:

“With a truthful sign it marks out the rewards of the kingdom.”

[Col. 0231]

## FIGURE XXI. On the number seventy-two and two, with their meanings

[Col. 0231A] Behold, the true law of God must be overcome by blessed lot,

Behold the cross of Christ, by which the world is freed from wrath,

Led to life, reaching the harbor and rest,

After the first inhabitant of the field himself had suffered shipwreck.

Because destructive death conquered through the forbidden wood,

And the savage beast had widely consumed the whole human race,

It pleased him who restored it by the law of the cross

To place this stake, so that through the wood

He might remove it from the jaws of death,

Which the cruel one had swallowed in his drenched belly,

And vomit it out upon the dry ground, paying the penalty due from this point onward.

The savage thief invaded and wickedly seized the dominion;

He wished to mark this in the written teachings

Of the Testaments. God, author of the work of the cross,

Himself foretold it, taught it, and, the Almighty confesses,

Fulfilled it. Therefore the cross shows itself wholly flashing

[Col. 0231B] Into the light; it gives a consecrated path,

Properly revealing to the righteous all things through the air:

It summons nations and peoples to the lofty stars,

Marks those who have been rescued, and knows how to make them joyful

[Col. 0232A] In the adornment of night; from here it leads them upward to the heights of the kingdom.

When the enemy has been expelled, it becomes victorious and is not deceived in its craft,

But, ruling over the human race, performs miracles alone.

Because of its gifts it makes all kingdoms serve it,

Devoted, peaceful, gentle, tranquil, redeemed.

As many tongues as the world possesses, and laws of speech,

By this number it marks the entrance for those who come,

And by this path the Savior opens the way of the disciples.

For, as the world’s mouth is said to vary eight times ninefold,

And so an eighth is piously granted as an addition to the nine blessed orders

Of spirits, that the Creator may duly wish to make up their number

And close the ages at their end.

For the Creator, by suffering, consumed all the world’s sins

In the fire-spouting heat of the cross itself;

Yet from the side of the flesh the divine nature shone forth,

Inscribed, and produced a sober origin.

Indeed he made his law beloved according to the order of the cross,

Rightly making it light, gentle, and rich in the gift of ascent. [Col. 0233]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0233A] This figure, therefore, must be understood to be full of mystery. In it, through four heptagons, the number 72 is displayed; according to its plurality, it is a true opinion that the languages of the nations were divided, and there is no doubt that the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments are contained within its sum.

The Lord himself also designated seventy-two other disciples, apart from the twelve apostles, and sent them two by two before his face into every place and city where he himself was about to come. Thus the number of the designated disciples would correspond to the multitude of the nations and the division of languages, so that all nations might receive the light of faith and deserve to share in Christ’s grace.

Just as the entire world is traversed and illumined in twenty-four hours, so the mystery of illumining the world through the Gospel of the Trinity is intimated in the seventy-two disciples. For twenty-four times three equals seventy-two [the source’s numerical wording is corrupt].

This distribution is appropriately entrusted to the figure of the holy cross, because through it the entire world is glorified by the dispensation of Christ’s sacraments. In its four heptagons it marks this principle of the mystery: in the four books of the holy Gospel, it distributes divine gifts through the four regions of the world. In both its paths—that is, the one that runs upward and the one that runs across—it displays through two heptagons six times six, because it clearly indicates that every perfection comes to us through it, whether in the steadfastness of hope, the breadth of charity, perseverance in good action, or the height of contemplation.

Throughout itself it contains eight multiplied by nine, because it teaches that from all nations God’s elect reach, in the number eight—that is, through the resurrection of bodies—the increase of the nine orders of angels.

O truly good and truly holy cross of Christ! Who can rightly recount you in your entirety, or praise you worthily? You are the devout revealer of heavenly secrets, the sacred guardian of God’s mysteries, and the suitable steward of Christ’s sacraments.

In you the angels behold their joys increased; in you human beings learn the laws of their salvation; in you the underworld receives the just repayment of its deceit.

[Col. 0234A] You are equal toward all, good toward all, just toward all. You renew past things, illumine present things, foretell future things; you seek what has been lost, find what has been sought, guard what has been found, restore what has fallen, strengthen what has been restored in its progress, and direct what has been strengthened onto the way of peace.

You are indeed the victory of the eternal King, the joy of the heavenly army, and the power of earthly beings. You are the remission of sins, the display of mercy, the increase of merits, the remedy of the weak, the aid of those who labor, the refreshment of the weary, the safety of the healthy, the serenity of the peaceful, and the happiness of the fortunate.

You are the cross that heals the sick, the joy that comforts the sorrowful, the health that gladdens those in pain, the upright state of believers, the steadfastness of those who work well, and the blessedness of those who persevere rightly.

Holy, devout, good, just, kind, rational, praiseworthy, venerable, lovable, strong, gentle, mild, wise, patient, powerful.

Whatever, therefore, can worthily be thought in the heart concerning our redemption, and whatever the tongue can rightly say, can all most suitably be adapted to your praise. For whatever is praised in you is attributed to Christ the King, crucified in you; and whatever honor is given to Christ is referred to the reverence of the highest Father, whose only-begotten Son he is. Concerning him Truth itself testifies in the Gospel:

“He who receives me,” he says, “receives him who sent me.”

And again:

“He who despises me despises him who sent me, and he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father.”

For everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father; but whoever confesses the Son also has the Father. Their majesty, power, honor, and glory, together with the Holy Spirit, are one throughout eternal ages.

[Col. 0234C] There is a verse in the upright part of the cross—that is, in the two heptagons descending from the top downward—and it is to be read across the heptagons:

“In the cross the Lord’s law is adorned with flashing light.”

Another is contained in the transverse part, in two heptagons, and is likewise to be read across them:

“Nations and tongues are joined in sacred praise.”

[Col. 0235]

## FIGURE XXII. On the monogram in which the name of Christ is contained

[Col. 0235A] Christ is my love and vow, who gives these devout gifts

Of song; here is the price, here the way, the faithful portion of rest.

Approving all good things by his power, he rightly bestows

Such great and such gifts upon his servants,

And, taking pity, the devout Creator promises that all may obtain

The citadel of heaven and its lofty kingdoms,

If firm hope, faith in the Most High, and holy love desire them here,

And if one, not lost in remembering these beginnings, loves them.

Coming here, he had scattered these gifts throughout the world

In the earlier age, gifts powerful in their fruit,

By dedicating them he taught the world not to rush headlong

Into worse places, giving instruction as master

To know the Gospel and to tame its savage customs.

When God, just in heaven’s citadel,

The author comes to give the righteous the rewards of the Father in heaven,

Then the right hand will receive good gifts for the worthy according to their merits.

[Col. 0236A] This number marks both advents of the healing Lord:

The first, when he restrained the tyrant,

When, having become a man, he restored such great blessings to the world,

And after his baptism uttered worthy teaching to all.

The second, when the just Savior is to come from the highest Father

As judge; and, as man, [the following words are materially uncertain], he will first bring

These holy rewards from here to give them on high, and continually behold

The sacred face of the heavenly one.

Indeed, the true herald announces that those who have been obtained through good merits

Must sing hymns; blessed destiny is accustomed to sing them,

As the serene writings of the Apocalypse have it:

There the shining multitudes bear glory and power,

And every day and throughout the age Alleluia resounds.

[Col. 0237A] Yet what court will not have this one?

And our God and Lord must everywhere be appeased,

So that the writing may help us, as it is the blessedness of the bronze citadel,

When he will appear rejoicing over his servants here, and the blessed crowd,

Losing nothing, will remove the stumbling-blocks through wrath,

So that he may send his devoted servants, the wheat, into the granary.

Blessed is he who has the power and permission to climb heaven, [Col. 0238A]

And wishes rightly to contemplate the joyful face of the Lord Christ;

For him lofty love remains, and every perfection is restored.

Mixed with the angelic choirs, he rejoices everywhere

In praises and strives, singing, to praise Christ.

This devotion never ceases to lay down new songs properly;

For the eternal Queen thus knows joys both then and well. [Col. 0237]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0237A] What, then, this figure is and what it signifies must be explained. It is one of the figures called “notes of meanings”; in a special term the Greeks call this a *chrismon*, invented according to each person’s intention for marking something. But it is assumed by Christians with greater dignity to express the name of Christ, as though the first two letters of his name were contained together in a single monogram, namely X and P.

The reason why it has now been adopted by us in this work is as follows. In it is marked the number of days during which Christ is believed to have preached to the world, as well as the number that, before his second advent—from the time of Antichrist until the end of the world—is explained by the orthodox teachers of the Church according to Daniel’s prophecy.

Thus in the letter P the first number, namely 1,260, which amounts to three and a half years, is found; during that span of time Christ is understood to have preached to the world. For the months of three and a half years—that is, thirty times forty-two—produce 1,260 days. Under this number the holy city is described in the Apocalypse as being trampled by the nations, and the woman as fleeing from the face of the dragon into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God so that she may be nourished there for the same number of days.

This number mystically embraces the whole period of Christianity, as the firm tradition of the Fathers maintains, because Christ—whose body this is—preached in the flesh for only this length of time, during which Christianity either rejoices in hope of eternal things while journeying through the present wilderness, or suffers the distress of persecution from unbelievers or false brothers.

The letter X, therefore, contains the number that Daniel’s prophecy foretold would occur in the time of Antichrist, namely 1,335 days. For it is written there:

“And blessed is he who waits and reaches the 1,335 days.”

Blessed Jerome explains this as follows:

“Blessed,” he says, “is he who, after Antichrist has been killed, waits beyond the 1,290 days—that is, three and a half years—for forty-five days, during which the Lord and Savior will come in his majesty.”

Why there should be a silence of forty-five days after the killing of Antichrist belongs to divine knowledge, unless perhaps we say: the delay of the kingdom of the saints is a test of patience.

But since the explanation given above is clearer, if the letters written in this figure and forming the monogram by their arrangement are written out together with their numerical values in order, let space for this be granted by the pen.

The letters placed in P read:

Ο, ϹΟΤΗΡ, ΙΗϹΥϹ, ΑΛΗΘΙΑ,

namely three names of Christ, which are interpreted in Latin as *Salutaris*, *Salvator*, and *Veritas*—“Saving,” “Savior,” and “Truth.”

The latter two Greek names are written out in their complete sequence of letters, namely ΙΗϹΥϹ and ΑΛΗΘΙΑ. The third, ϹΟΤΗΡ, is marked according to Greek writing by three letters, excluding the article Ο: namely Ϲ, Η, and Ρ. Thus all the letters written in Ρ amount to fifteen.

The first is Ο, marking the number seventy;

the second is Ϲ, signifying two hundred;

the third is Η, with the number eight;

the fourth is Ρ, expressing one hundred;

the fifth is Ι, ten;

the sixth is Η, eight;

the seventh is Ϲ, two hundred;

the eighth is Υ, four hundred;

the ninth is Ϲ, two hundred;

the tenth is Α, one;

the eleventh is Λ, thirty;

the twelfth is Η, eight;

the thirteenth is Θ, nine;

the fourteenth is Ι, ten;

the fifteenth is Α, one.

Added together, these make the number 1,260. Five still remain to complete the number mentioned above; these too can be found in the character Ρ, if Ρ is divided so that its upper part, which contains the image of the letter Δ, signifies the number four, while its lower part, which forms the Latin I, displays the number one according to Latin usage. Thus the thousand, two hundred, and sixty are found in Ρ.

The X, which is the other part of the monogram, likewise contains three names of the Lord, written in eight letters:

ΘΕΟϹ, ΧΡΗϹΤΥϹ, ΙΗϹΥϹ.

The letters are these: Θ, expressing nine; Ϲ, two hundred; Χ, five hundred; Ρ, one hundred; Ϲ, two hundred; Ι, ten; Η, eight; Ϲ, two hundred. Together they make 1,327, and eight still remain; these are increased when the letter Η, situated in the middle of the eight letters and serving as a nail, is added together with the number eight from Ρ.

There are also three verses in the monogram, written in larger letters with smaller letters inside them. The first, beginning from O, runs around through all the larger letters, which above display the figure Δ within Ρ, and contains two Greek names, namely Ο, ϹΟΤΗΡ, ΙΗϹΥϹ, enclosed in nine letters:

“For from this name of Christ the blessed writings rightly shine.”

The second is in the remaining part of Ρ—that is, in the line running straight downward—and contains the name ΑΛΗΘΙΑ, written in six Greek letters:

“This sacred saving writing praises Christ.”

The third, in the letter X, contains eight letters in which three names are marked, namely ΤΗΕΟϹ, ΧΡϹ, ΙΗϹ:

“Christ is man, gentle indeed; here too he is the judge of the world.”

[Col. 0239]

## FIGURE XXIII. On the number twenty-four and its sacramental meaning

[Col. 0239A] Behold, a noble flower shines, painted in the king’s name,

And the signs mark the deeds of the powerful victor:

The joyful horns of the cross, thus formed in a threefold verse,

Which count six single units four times by a distinguished art,

And show that perfect beauty exists in all things

Which the Almighty created and redeemed.

That bright day was when the Creator fashioned all things;

No less brightly shines this day on which the Teacher blessed everything.

Then the good Creator, being good, completed all good things by his deeds;

Now the devout lover, being devout, has blessed all things by his works.

Therefore the sixfold world praises the four regions;

Six shines in numbers, and is itself the first perfect number.

It divides the entire day and binds together

The leap year and the quarter of the year and month.

Here this number is present, raising the times by its sign.

It encompasses the ages at their end and closes the world at its boundary;

Then the ruler gives perpetual life and shining kingdoms

[Col. 0239B] Above the stars to the devout, releasing what is owed, and marking with his face

The devout rewards that Jesus, you know, inscribes.

[Col. 0240A] From the whole world he has gathered into these great gifts

Those upon whom the light of faith shines, and he has implanted living draughts.

True love adorns the righteous and blesses the blessed work.

Therefore this number, placed here, marks from every region of the world

The peoples who are to advance everywhere

To the aid of the cross, to ask Jesus for devout divine powers,

And to learn perfect beauty through perfect teaching,

So that kindly deeds may follow perfect faith.

All these things everywhere testify to the true God:

Perfect things are truly perfect, beautiful, and decorous—

What the vault of heaven turns, what Olympus creates,

What the sea contains, what the earth contains, what the heavenly court contains.

We human beings too, a small part among these things,

Should properly sound the saving cross in song and voice.

Let us sing repeatedly in celebrated song of the love

Of him who made us well, who increased us, and who redeemed us,

Of the love which he himself has already abundantly shown us

By sacred work and protection, persuaded, displayed, commanded, and loved. [Col. 0241]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0241A] Behold, the number six suitably encloses the four horns of the Lord’s cross and displays the complete perfection of the accomplished work, because in it the Creator of all things made the judgment of his consummation when, having received the cup, he said, “It is finished.”

For it is rightly written that it was finished where the human race was liberated. Christ’s passion benefited not only human beings, when they obtained the grace of redemption, but also the heavenly hosts of angels, when in him they attained the fullness of their number.

Four times six makes twenty-four. By this number the circuit of the heavenly sphere is carried around, and the course of the natural day is discerned by the judgment of the revolving stars. By this number the books of the Old Testament are received among the Hebrews into canonical authority, Ruth and Lamentations being counted in place of books. By this number the Levitical tribe was divided by David into lots, and all the sons of Aaron were appointed to minister to God in their turns.

This was fitting, so that the number of the elect priests might foreshadow the eternal priesthood of Christ, who, made priest according to the order of Melchizedek, offered himself as an unblemished sacrifice to God on the altar of the cross—namely, that Lamb who took away the sins of the world. Through the sprinkling of his blood the holy place and the Holy of Holies were cleansed, and through the true expiation the filth of all sins was washed away.

The elders of this same number are described as seated around that most powerful throne from which the Apocalypse says that flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps proceed. They signify the Church, generated through the two Testaments from patriarchs and apostles, which is seen seated around him because of his judicial dignity in Christ.

The Savior says of it, displaying the power of his kingdom:

“And I,” he says, “when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.”

The Savior drew all things to himself when, placed upon the cross, he subjected every power to himself. After rising on the third day, he said to his disciples:

“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

[Col. 0242A] The Apostle testified concerning this:

“Christ,” he says, “became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.”

From this throne, therefore, flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps proceed, because after the Savior’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, his disciples, as Mark writes, went forth and preached everywhere, God working with them and confirming the word through the accompanying signs.

One of them, replying with great authority to the Jews gathered against him, said:

“Let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you healed. This is the stone rejected by you builders, which has become the cornerstone. There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.”

And the teacher of the nations says to the Corinthians:

“I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified,”

and the rest.

Again, he says to the Galatians:

“But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

There are also written in the four triangles around the cross four names of the heavenly victor. The holy cross expands them through its horns in the manner of the leaves of an unfolding lily. Beginning at its center—that is, with the two names Christus and Jesus—it is arranged so that at the top and bottom of the cross are two names in the place of sons, namely Fortis and Virtus, “Strong” and “Power”; and on the right and left are two others, namely Victor and Clarus, “Victor” and “Bright.”

Thus two verses are found written across the cross, from one triangle to another. The text running lengthwise is:

“Strong Christ completed his words, the power.”

Across its breadth:

“Victor Jesus, marking the devout rewards, bright.”

## FIGURE XXIV. On the number one hundred, forty, and four, and its meaning

[Col. 0243A] But now sing a new song, bless Christ,

People, song, beloved of God, most holy order.

Sing—not for others—a song worthy of imitation,

Immortal heavenly glory before this tribunal,

Before four times six elders, and before four

Living creatures of different form, rightly heavenly,

Firstfruits for Christ, the spotless Lamb of the Godhead,

And honors of an undefiled lot to the true God.

You are the companies purchased with the purple of blood.

Sing properly to heaven, from earthly beings, a trophy.

Playing upon harps, you calm the countenance with praise;

Your sacred hand everywhere fills the courts with voices,

Like thunderous voices filling the air with spreading cries,

And as the voice of many waters fills the valleys.

Your tongue is ignorant of deceit and does not know iniquity.

Before the throne of the Lord you know how to speak worthily

Praises and songs, and here, prepared in close ranks,

Through signs which your King does not disdain in his bosom.

For no leader and author except the one has poured out this,

[Col. 0244A] Who, with a scornless utterance, gives splendid gifts in this manner.

From here sing the gifts, you virtuous order and devout ones—

Men in virgin dress, and likewise nursing women,

Infants and old women alike, young and old,

You who here have never been defiled by union with women.

Therefore go now where the Almighty gives rewards to the righteous;

Jesus proceeds where the Lamb of the Virgin goes,

Feeding in the meadows, rejoicing. Following him rightly,

You feed among the lofty stars above, O pastures of the fields.

Now your life receives the rewards of virtue,

Rightly the robe which the Virgin’s unique offspring brought,

And at the end the Lamb will return another with the body.

Ask—I ask you—through the blessed signs of the cross,

O peoples, companies, populace, ranks, crowd, cohorts,

You who hold a place and seats above the stars in the citadel:

May the praise of you and the Lamb, the King and God,

Confer joyful rewards upon us with the saints in heavenly light,

So that we may be permitted to hear your song throughout the ages. [Col. 0245]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0245A] This figure of the holy cross, formed in four pentagons, contains the number 144 letters, written in four verses. According to the multiplication of this number by a thousand, the multitude of the sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel is counted in the Apocalypse, and that number of the whitened ones who stood with the Lamb on Mount Zion is indicated.

First, by the innumerable thousands of the sealed, the multitude of the entire Church is signified, generated from the patriarchs, whether through descent of the flesh or through imitation of faith. For he says: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring.”

The multiplication of twelve by twelve also belongs to the increase of perfection, and the sum is completed by a thousand. This is the solid square number ten, signifying the stable life of the Church.

From the time when the Lord suffered, the power of worldly rule was crushed; and the power of the nations was broken for this purpose, so that the faces of the saints might be freely marked with the sign of faith, which they had resisted.

The sign of faith, therefore, is the cross of Christ, in whose likeness the letter Tau was formed. Concerning it, it is written in Ezekiel:

“And the glory of the Lord of Israel was taken up from the cherub, which was beneath him, to the threshold of the house. And he called the man who was clothed in linen and had the writer’s inkwell at his waist, and said to him: ‘Pass through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in its midst.’

“And he said to them in my hearing: ‘Pass through the city after him and strike; let your eye not spare, and do not show mercy to old man, young man, virgin, child, or women. Kill them to destruction. But do not kill anyone upon whom you see the Tau,’ and the rest.”

Rightly every unrighteous person is killed by the sword of unbelief if he is shown to have neglected to display the sign of faith in himself through good works. And rightly each person is freed through the power of Christ’s cross by doing good works, because he is known to have preserved inviolate until the end the faith of the Lord that he received in baptism by fulfilling Christ’s commandments.

Next, that flock of the whitened ones is counted in the quantity of the same number, and the abundant multitude of holy virginity among the elect is intimated. Nevertheless, everyone of sound understanding must recognize that a finite number is here used for an infinite one, through the secret meaning of the mystery appropriate to the virginal order: whoever loves God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind is also consecrated to him in the integrity of the body, which consists of four elements.

For three times three makes nine, and four times four makes sixteen; sixteen times nine makes 144. Thus, when so perfect a multitude of those established in the stricter way of life is seen with the Lamb on Mount Zion, there is no doubt concerning the other members of the Church.

“And they sang as if a new song before the throne, and before the four living creatures and the elders,” and the rest.

[Col. 0246A] Those sing to God as though on harps who, by the privilege of angelic chastity, make themselves wholly a burnt offering to the Lord. Taking up their cross, they follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and they will sing as though a new song which no one else can sing. For to sing the Lamb’s song uniquely means to rejoice with him forever, before all the faithful, even in the incorruptibility of the flesh.

The other elect, however, can hear this song, although they cannot sing it, because through charity they rejoice in the exalted state of those people, even though they do not rise to their rewards.

The old song was:

“Blessed is he who has offspring in Zion
and household members in Jerusalem.”

And again:

“Grow and multiply and fill the earth.”

The new song is:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth;
break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail,
for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous
than those of her who has a husband.”

And again the same Prophet says:

“And let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree.’ Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast my covenant: ‘I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that will not perish.’”

And again:

“Blessed are the barren who did not give birth,
and the breasts that did not nurse,”

and the rest.

For they have his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads, because the Church, dedicated in the confession of the Holy Trinity, carries on its forehead the emblem of its faith, which through the mystery of the holy cross is painted on the foreheads of Christians and marked by the frequent inscription of the hand.

Behold, each of the four pentagons contains thirty-six letters; but this is not because the number five forms the figure of the pentagon—for thirty-five is the pentagonal number—but it has been placed in this way to intimate a certain sacrament.

The number five therefore signifies the Law, and the number four the Gospel. But when the four pentagons, with the four units attached to them, complete the four horns, then, after Christ’s passion and resurrection have been completed, the Law and the Gospel together have been entrusted to teachers to be preached throughout the breadth of the whole world.

With the fathers of both Testaments given as a single example, the faithful everywhere throughout the world strove to imitate them by preserving chastity; joined to the Lamb, they sang as if a new song upon Mount Zion on their harps.

Therefore we have shown that the four units attached externally to the pentagons form one name in four letters, namely *crux*—“cross”—so that they might both adhere to their pentagons for the completion of the verses and, to display their proper meaning, be joined to one another by one name.

There is also this verse in the upper part of the cross:

“Spotless company, there you sing with your voices.”

And at the bottom is this:

King, where Jesus triumphs, whom the Virgin’s Lamb feeds.

On the right:

> Songs that no one sings with far-spreading utterance.

And on the left:

> Here is your snow-white flock and splendid order.

[Col. 0247A]

> Be present to earthly beings, so that they may now be able  
> To say something worthy of you and fittingly fill

> Indeed, O cross, I have sung of you in this living poem,

> The lofty stars of heaven; nor is anyone sufficient

> I inserted angelic words and interwove them with fitting verses.  
> Indeed, “Amen,” placed in the middle, promises the seals of life;  
> [Col. 0247B] “Alleluia,” surrounding the horns of the cross, completes them,  
> And marks the sacred image with heavenly song.

> And all their gifts, surpass them now in the ardor of hope,  
> [Col. 0248A] So that, infused into their mouths, it may grant the good palm of victory,  
> And that death, which once, livid and savage, harmed  
> The first stock of the human race, may flee away,  
> Having swallowed up the whole offspring and dragged it down  
> Into the depths below.  
> But all of us whom love raises from here into heaven  
> Properly please the sacred face of the Lord with song.  
> For with that song which will be in the heavenly dwellings,  
> Which the righteous sing, they will sing forever in their vows.  
> This pleases rightly if we fulfill the commands of the Thunderer  
> In our minds, our appearance, our deeds, and the utterance of our tongue.  
> For mere speech will not receive these precious rewards of the righteous;  
> rather, true virtue together with good utterance will receive them.  
> A praise that is not good, but a false fabrication of truth,  
> is that which sings great things, desires lofty things,  
> yet deserves little.  
> Therefore, come: faithfully praise Christ in songs,  
> [Col. 0248B] Heavenly peoples and powers, and you mighty  
> Multitudes of the righteous who stand in heaven’s citadel.  
> Sing “Amen” and “Alleluia” to Christ throughout the ages. [Col. 0249]

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIGURE

[Col. 0249A]

Here, then, that praise which the voice of the saints is believed to sing perpetually to God in heaven is imitated in the writing of the holy cross—namely, “Alleluia” and “Amen,” which the apostle and evangelist John writes that he heard in the Apocalypse after the killing and drowning of the great harlot who was seducing all nations by her fornication, and with whom the kings of the earth had fornicated. He says that he heard the voices of many multitudes devoutly singing in heaven and repeating the song several times. For it is written there:

“After this I heard, as it were, the voice of a great multitude in heaven saying: ‘Alleluia: praise and glory and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just, because he has judged the great harlot who corrupted the earth by her prostitution, and has avenged the blood of his servants from her hands.’ And again they said: ‘Alleluia’; and her smoke rises for ever and ever. And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God seated upon the throne, saying: ‘Amen, Alleluia.’ And a voice came forth from the throne, saying: ‘Give praise to our God, all his servants, and you who fear him, small and great.’ And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of great thunderings, saying: ‘Alleluia, because the Lord our almighty God has begun to reign. Let us rejoice and exult and give glory to his name, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself. And it has been granted to her that she clothe herself in fine linen, shining and white; for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints,’” and so forth.

Although all these things are spoken of the future joy of the saints in heaven after the resurrection, the Church already sings them in part, since she has been saved in hope; but then they will be sung perfectly, when the separation has taken place and vengeance has been more openly exacted. After the universal judgment of the Lord, therefore, the righteous will be completely separated from the goats: the impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

For now, the souls of the saints go after death to paradise, and those of the impious to punishment, as the Lord makes clear in the account of the poor man and the rich man. But their bodies await the end of the world. At present, individual white robes are given to the righteous while they receive eternal rest in their souls; then two robes will be given, when their bodies, endowed with immortality, receive an everlasting kingdom together with their souls. Thus the marriage of the Lamb will truly appear when the whole Church is joined to the Lord in the bridal chamber of the heavenly kingdom.
