Thus the devotion of believers increases when it sees the creator of all things fitting and adapting the succession of times so suitably and appropriately to the realities themselves. The figure of the cross, the redemption accomplished upon it, and the salvation bestowed on the faithful through gifts of virtue duly agree in all things with the number, which is full of sacred mysteries.

Finally, the beginning of the book of Genesis most clearly proves and confirms that the Lord renewed the ancient ages and his creation, founded by him in the beginning, through the holy cross at the end of time. For just as God is said to have rested after the works of six days and the creation of humankind, so, in the sixth age of the world, after humanity had been restored through the cross on the sixth day of the week, the Redeemer is shown to have rested in the tomb on the Sabbath.

By divine ordinance, therefore, it was arranged that the number V. CC. XXX. I. should aptly correspond to the figure of the holy cross. Through this it would display the sacrament of Christ’s passion, resist every wickedness of demons and every falsehood of evil men, crush and overcome by its power and justice everyone who by fraud and deceit disparaged the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation; and, once convicted by the truth, it would silence entirely every trickery of philosophers and heretics.

Nor would the deceitful faction of the Jews any longer oppose the Gospel with its terrible and cruel hostility toward Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. Through this it becomes clear that the Creator wills the holy cross to sanctify all the ages of the world in God’s elect, those who existed from the beginning, and to promise the heavenly kingdom. Through our Redeemer this kingdom will be granted to all the faithful who, obeying his word with believing hearts and pure works, have striven to please God.

The form of the holy cross is great consolation for the faithful and provides the material for praise, because it makes us know the goodness of the Creator. He had first formed humankind upright in paradise, and now, unwilling that humanity should perish through the fraud of the ancient enemy, he recovered it through the cross and led it back to paradise. The cross is indeed the stronghold of virtues and remission of sins; it raises from these lowly and perishable things to heavenly and higher things all whom the election of Christ proves worthy, through faith, hope, and charity, of the eternal vision of God.

## CHAPTER XV. On the fifteenth figure, where the Lamb and the four evangelists are depicted

Son of the most high Father, who shatter the dreadful darts of the most wicked enemy, grant me to sing the victory of the holy cross in sweet-sounding song. Indeed, the evangelist John, like a high-flying eagle fixing the gaze of his mind upon the very Sun of justice, recognized the Word of God through true revelation and proclaimed and wrote it in lucid speech.

Divine grace was bestowed upon John above the other evangelists in this respect: while they chiefly wrote the mysteries of the Savior’s incarnation and his humanity, he disclosed in profound speech the mysteries of his divinity—namely, that the maker of all things had taken a human soul and body into himself, and that he who in the beginning was the one God with God the Father would appear visible in the flesh at the end of time.

The figure of the lion signifies him as king; the calf prefigures him as high priest. For, like a lion and as a lion’s cub engaged in combat, he seized an exceedingly rich prey; and, having deigned to become both priest and victim, he granted us eternal salvation and bestowed immense gifts upon those who share in him.

Mark, in the mystery of the seven loaves with which Jesus fed four thousand men, mystically indicates the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which the Savior daily nourishes the evangelical people.

O evangelist Luke, proclaim the most just king as a saving victim—this is what the Catholic faith holds—and resound in your writings the glorious high priest who takes away the sins of the whole world. Though he was the eternal hand of the Creator and consubstantial with the eternal Father, behold, in the days of King Herod he was born at Bethlehem from Mary his mother, a wondrous child sent, namely, for the salvation of the whole world.

He is the noble child who is also described by the prophet as the Ancient of Days; he who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah; he who alone trod the winepress of the cross; and although he was hung upon the cross, the heavenly judge nevertheless sustained the stars. By suffering the cross he sanctified it, glorified it, and enriched it with heavenly blessing.

Thus Matthew, who first wrote the Gospel in Judaea, signifying the human face by the figure, indicated that Christ was born from the stock of David according to humanity. He also demonstrated that Christ was the son of the promise when he placed Abraham at the head of the genealogy, against the hardness and dullness of the hearts of unbelievers who deny that Christ was appointed for the salvation of the nations. For this is the truest sign of the Savior’s coming: the succession of generations descending through the patriarchs and kings of the Jewish people reached all the way to Christ, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of the faithful.

## CHAPTER XVI. [Col. 0280D] On the sixteenth form, where the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are recounted

You, holy Spirit, Paraclete, I humbly beseech: descend upon us savingly from the heavenly throne, dedicate to yourself the devoted mind of your poet, and make his heart rightly believing and faithful. For you too are the Spirit of life, whom Christ, the power and wisdom of God, declares that he will send to his disciples as promised by the Father—the gift, namely, by which he wondrously enriched all his saints before and after his coming, betrothed his bride, the Church, to himself during her pilgrimage in this world, and purchased her at the price of his blood.

To whomever you give understanding, that person fully grasps the divine mysteries through the individual testimonies of both Testaments; taught inwardly, he investigates all things astutely and considers truthfully how Christ, the divine Wisdom, sent you into the world and gave you as pledge or earnest to his bride, while you, coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father and the Son, exist with them as the maker of all things and penetrate all things, and no creature is invisible in your sight.

The prophet Isaiah, inspired by God, distributed you—though you are one and the same—into seven kinds of names because of the diversity of your gifts, and called you the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of God.

Christ our Savior and giver of eternal life showed by deeds and commandments that he gives you twice to his apostles when he established the two commandments of charity: that we should love God with our whole heart and proclaim his praise with complete devotion, assigning all our knowledge and understanding to the truth of his grace, and that we should love our neighbors as ourselves.

For after his resurrection he breathed upon his disciples and commanded them to receive the Holy Spirit; and again, on the day of Pentecost, he sent the same Holy Spirit from heaven upon them, appearing in tongues of fire. This, clearly, the holy cross of God displays to us in its form. Its upright part commends divine love, while its transverse part commends fraternal love. Christ showed us the integrity of this love and instructed us by his example: dying on the cross, he laid down his beloved soul for his friends and taught us to do the same.

Holy God the Spirit, ever praiseworthy and ever to be praised, place this love in me, and let harmful fear and carnal affection withdraw far away, so that the glory of the holy cross, increased and multiplied, may remain with me forever in true profession and worthy praise. For you are the one who fills the mute mouth and rightly makes it resound with heavenly song.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the meaning of the seventeenth figure, where the eight beatitudes are numbered

O holy and blessed, powerful and venerable cross of Christ, praise of the life to come and glory of the Redeemer, you are indeed a beneficent work and life-giving through all the ages from the beginning, gracious and honorable. For when, through the passion, you wearied the members of Christ suspended upon you, you rescued innumerable peoples from the darkness of their sins and mercifully restored by grace the kingdom of heaven that had been taken away through transgression. The goodness of the Creator did not allow those who had long before placed their hope in it to perish, but through you rewarded their good merits by granting them an eternal crown.

The seed of evangelical teaching, which the Savior sowed in the hearts of the disciples, he multiplied according to his will in their works when, sitting on the mountain, he taught them and, beginning with the eight beatitudes, brought forth the most abundant instruction. He plainly indicated a number most suitable to the figure of the holy cross, because the holy cross is the bestower of virtues and the beginning and perfection of our salvation; through it our salvation and resurrection are accomplished.

Thus, whoever you are among the number of the just, as long as you are here, fittingly proclaim divine praise with fear and love. Do works of justice. Forgive your enemy who persecutes you and offer him refreshment. Kindly receive Christ’s poor, who now mourn in the present age, and those who hunger and thirst for righteousness and with all desire breathe after the life to come. They are pierced by divine inspiration and, with their hearts raised above, contemplate who rules all things by eternal counsel and who forgives sins through boundless mercy.

This I, in the Latin tongue, a wretched man, describe; and I desire that it itself be the refreshment of my mind in the present and eternal satisfaction in the future.

No proud person will be justified merely because he displays humility in speech and appearance and, prostrate, worships the heavenly ruler, while his heart inwardly thinks proudly; nor will one who possesses wealth but gives no alms, or who, being sound in body and full of strength, does no works of justice, be justified. For it is certain and plain that the all-holding Creator seeks not words alone but also good deeds and an honorable life at all times.

Therefore whoever truly seeks eternal light and wishes to reach eternal blessedness must proceed toward the heavenly kingdom through the eight evangelical titles in which the forms of true blessedness are expressed. For, once the general resurrection has been accomplished in that number, after judgment has been completed the holy people of God will enter eternal kingship together with Christ.

The cross of Christ is also the way of the just, the ascent to heaven, the wheel drawing us from the lowest places to the highest, the guide and gate of the kingdom, our victory. Through it we shall possess true life and receive an eternal reward. By the number two set four times, enclosing the number eight within itself, it signifies that through the two commandments of charity, which the four holy books of the Gospels commend to us, we can deserve everlasting joys.

The almighty Spirit of the almighty God, who invites us through peace and true charity to the kingdom to come, has also placed an ascent in our hearts through the seven gifts of his grace, to demonstrate that the faithful can rightly ascend to heaven in this way, if they do not neglect to become participants in his grace. He has shown that glory above and the shining crown of the heavenly throne await those whom true charity has illumined here with virtue.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the eighteenth form, where the number forty is placed

Explain now and proclaim in praise, O human being, with the whole affection of your soul and all the senses of your body, the noble triumph of the eternal victor, which the glory of the Lord’s cross extends everywhere, above the lofty stars of heaven and beneath, in the deepest Tartarus of the abyss, where the radiance of eternal light remains and the horror of perpetual night endures; and also throughout all the expanses of the earth, where night and day alternate in their distinct turns, until the end of the world arrives.

Let the mind’s understanding consider this; let the throat resound it with the voice; let the tongue strike it within the palate; let the hand write it in letters; let the lips express it in words; let the figure itself mark it, depicted in metrical work. Although difficult, it nevertheless orderly proclaims the clear praises of the holy cross through the number forty, divided and represented in four decades.

This number, full of venerable mystery and serene with heavenly light, bears among the other sacraments of its meaning the figure of the present time. Through it the holy Church, under Christ her prince, battles bravely and inseparably against spiritual wickedness and against lovers of the world with the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit—that is, the word of God. Confident in the power of her king and conscious of his virtue, she breaks and casts down all the flaming weapons of the ancient enemy.

With the banner of the cross, which the victorious Church carries gloriously, marked upon her forehead, she confounds the forehead of the opposing party and suddenly throws the savage line of the enemies into confusion.

Thus in the holy cross our Savior conquered the ancient enemy. In the number properly and suitably corresponding to its figure—namely, forty—he prolonged the sacred fast in the desert, so that he might first conquer the most deceitful robber, who was tempting him, through patience and humility; and afterward, when the enemy persisted and continued in his wickedness, Christ, by dying, might justly condemn him to eternal death.

For just as that slippery and cunning serpent enticed the first human being into sin through gluttony, avarice, and empty glory, and thus made him subject to death, so, conversely, through suitable remedies our Savior raised the human race to life through abstinence, kindness, and humility. He also, as the author of death and guilty of eternal torments, subjected him victoriously to Tartarus.

The battle of Christ is also our victory, and his triumph is our salvation. He sits in the citadel of heaven and looks upon the lower regions of the earth. His cross is itself the honor of the whole world; it sustains the entire world, and may it itself remain ever venerable to me in song and love. May praise always be in my mouth and perpetual rejoicing in my heart.

## CHAPTER XIX. The nineteenth form, where the meaning of the number fifty is given

[Col. 0283D]

Look with your eyes and see with your mind; hear with your ears and receive with your heart, all you faithful in whom the charity of Christ and love of wisdom burn, who care to reach eternal light and receive incorruption and immortality without end.

I bring forth the praise of Christ’s cross in song. Here the power of the supreme maker is displayed, the beauty of the blessed work is expressed, and the nobility of his art is revealed. Your honor is not a perishable honor but, according to the order of redemption, remains perpetual. Immortal is your palm in heaven, because Christ himself is your victory. Truly existing as our salvation, he turned vengeance against the ancient enemy and, tasting death on the cross, conquered the author of death himself.

Come here, all you sick, and do not be ashamed to complain to him of the troubles of your illness. This is your true physician, whom the holy cross bore upon its outstretched wood. With his hands extended, he invites you to healing, and he quickly grants you complete health.

Reveal to him the wound of your mind, and do not hide the concealed poison in the ulcer of your body. Ask for healing of the heart with devotion, and knock upon the physician through the zeal of good works. His saving hand does not know how to delay through the passage of time but, in the speed of a moment, is able to grant health to all who, beneficially pierced with fear and approaching with reverence, desire to be healed by that true physician. Supreme is his power to accomplish healing, and wise his counsel to grant salvation.

He descended from heavenly and eternal things to lowly and temporal things so that, through divine dispensation, he might restore the nature of things, which had been corrupted; so that the fear of death might depart; and so that the signs of blessedness might again be displayed in humanity through divine gifts.

The form of the holy cross reverently marks for us that the number fifty, inscribed upon its horns, is saving, and properly signifies that it is full of heavenly sacraments. In it the knowledge of the true jubilee—that is, of full remission—is given; in it the rest of the Sabbath is duly celebrated. It is distinguished by the giving of the ancient Law and is more distinguished by the coming of the Spirit Paraclete upon the apostles. It reveals that the author of peace has come and displays, through perfect reconciliation by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the seal of peace between God and human beings.

It is venerable in form, saving in figure, and perfect in the beauty of its sacraments. For the letter X, most suitable to the figure of the holy cross and designating the number ten, placed in two positions after the pattern of the holy cross, signifies the five books of the Law with the ten commandments. What the ancient Law in figure and shadow in a certain way depicted, Christ fulfilled entirely through the cross in the New Testament according to the truth.

Everything most fittingly agrees with the holy cross: the character of the letter, the number marked upon it, the mystery of the Law, the sacrament of time, and the deed laudably accomplished in this. Therefore it is fitting that we all praise the holy cross with rejoicing and continually give thanks to the crucified King, who by his own blood released every debt for the world.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 0284D] On the twentieth form, where the numbers one hundred and twenty are impressed
Behold the devout outpouring of Christ’s blood, and that stream which, while he slept upon the cross, flowed from his side: it cleanses us from every defilement, because the Redeemer himself, by his death, removed every harmful thing from us, when he took away the stain of our sins and erased through his passion the bond that stood against us. For he established the Gospel’s praiseworthy teaching, which, driving away the darkness of sins, forbids every crime and utterly rejects the worship of idols. Teaching an upright life, it commends this to all nations beneath heaven through the power of virtues in its preachers.

[Col. 0285A] After the Savior’s ascension, the apostles, instructed by Truth itself, testified in their preaching of the Gospel that the mysteries of the Old Testament had been fulfilled and made manifest through Christ, and by true assertions confirmed that he himself is the end—or fulfillment—of the Law and the Prophets. Finally, the praiseworthy letter *lambda*, set four times according to its meaning, that is, arranged in the form of a cross, nobly completes the number one hundred and twenty, which is significant both in the age of the Lawgiver and in the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles. It unfolds the mysteries of faith and displays the joys of true blessedness. For just as, through its four characters, the holy cross gathers together one hundred and twenty units into one, so, when the Holy Spirit came, he united the one hundred and twenty believers in the knowledge of all languages. Hence it is clearly and manifestly understood [Col. 0285B] that the holy cross is our true redemption, and that in it our unity truly consists.

When, therefore, the gift of speaking in all languages had been received, the eager assembly of believers spread everywhere the light of divine testimonies, while the multitude of miracles shone forth at the same time. It cast the Gospel’s net into the sea of this world, so that the Lord’s dragnet might draw human beings from the depth of the abyss and fasten them to the solidity of the Lord’s standard. Thus the signs of Christ’s cross might be made manifest to all: how it bestows spiritual gifts upon each of the faithful, and how it causes them faithfully to receive in heaven the rewards that the incarnate Savior promised them. These rewards have been established in increasing measure according to the quality of their merits. Their true guarantor, Christ, the Son of God, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, preserves and truly grants manifold rewards in the heavenly places to each of the worthy—the King of kings, who reigns forever and governs all kingdoms by his own authority. He had given us the Paraclete Spirit, the pledge of our salvation and inheritance, so that, governing us according to his will, he might preserve us until he makes us enter, rejoicing, into the joys of life.

Sing devotedly of life; sing well to the Lord Christ, all nations, tribes, and every language. Acknowledge your true King, the wisdom and power of God the Father, by whose power death was defeated and overthrown, and the memory of death was erased. Acknowledge Jesus, the parent of all things. This praise, because it has sprung from a true and proven root, possesses the end and perfection [Col. 0285D] of eternal rest. For this order has been implanted in our nature: that a person should observe what has been commanded with reverence and trembling, and await perpetual recompense in the future. This also is our glory, this our strength, this the true stability of supreme rest. He rightly observes the laws of religion and properly exercises his judgment who seeks the highest goods above all else and governs intermediate matters rationally.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On the twenty-first figure, in which the number seventy-two is contained

Therefore the true and blameless Law of the Lord, written in the books of the two Testaments, is to be placed in the form of the holy cross. Through it the whole world was released from its deserved wrath and found perpetual life, the harbor of salvation, and eternal rest, after that shipwreck which our first parent brought upon us through the transgression of the divine command.

For because cruel death swallowed the entire human race through the forbidden tree and took it captive by its own right, our Redeemer was pleased to raise the wood of the holy cross upon the earth, so that what that enemy had swallowed through the sin of appetite might, pierced by the point of the life-giving wood, vomit forth through the grace of self-restraint, and might suffer the deserved punishments for having, contrary to every right and law, as a most wicked slave and most deceitful thief, usurped dominion over what belonged to another.

[Col. 0286A] Wishing also to make this known, the God who is the author of all creation and giver of the two Testaments both foretold the saving work of the holy cross through the Law, promised it through the prophets, and declares through his Gospel that he has fulfilled it, so that human beings might recognize their Creator and give thanks to their Redeemer.

Finally, the holy and magnificent cross shows itself entirely sparkling with serene light and demonstrates that it is our way and guide to perpetual life. Therefore, shining with its rays like a lamp, it summons all nations and peoples to the heavenly kingdoms of eternal light, declares that they have been mercifully snatched from the enemy, and thus now makes those placed in the night of this world rejoice through its illumination, afterward raising the deserving from here to the heights of heaven. Nor, therefore, should we fear that any deception might lead someone astray; with the prince of this world cast out, the true victor truly reigns.

[Col. 0286B] Hence also, in preaching his power and dominion, holy preachers shine with miracles, subject the whole world to him, and perfect those redeemed by Christ’s grace into people devoted in heart, peaceful in conduct, meek in patience, and tranquil in their way of life.

Behold how many languages there are among the nations: the holy cross, represented in the number seventy-two, makes this manifest and signifies through it to all peoples an open gate of light. The Savior himself commanded this to be preached through the seventy-two disciples, and the same number also signifies the company of the holy archangels which he promised in heaven after the general resurrection.

For the number eight multiplied by the number nine produces seventy-two. The number eight refers to the time of the resurrection, while the number nine refers to the nine orders of angels. Thus the Catholic faith holds that, at the end of the world—that is, in the eighth age of the world—the saints, rising again, will pass into the fellowship of the angels.

[Col. 0286C] For Christ consumed all the sins of the world in the heat of his passion when, in the flesh, he tasted death itself, and by the power of his divinity freed his elect from the prison of hell. Through his apostles he commanded the light of sobriety and faith to be preached to the human race—namely, his old and new Law, which, because it corresponds to the figure of the holy cross, he demonstrated to all believers to be a light burden and an easy yoke, suitable for leading them to heaven.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### On the twenty-second figure, in which a monogram is depicted

Christ, who is our true Redeemer, in whom all our desire lies, and who by his grace wished me to undertake this work—would that he himself might be the end of my labor and the reward of my song! He delights in every good, because he is the giver of every good.

He therefore exhorts and invites everyone to heavenly gifts, and promises that these can easily be obtained if, despising all the desires of this world, a person seeks them worthily through faith, hope, and charity. These gifts he himself, coming into this world and killing carnal love with the sword of holy separation, had sown through the preachers of his Gospel and had gathered an abundantly peaceful harvest in his field.

[Col. 0287A] The excellent Teacher always taught this, forbidding them to turn toward low and downward things, but urging them rather to rise toward what is lofty; understanding his Gospel, they were to lay aside their habitual savagery of conduct and learn to be gentle and meek, so that, at his second coming, when he arrives in the glory of his Father with his angels to repay each person according to his works, he may find such people as he can reward with eternal recompense because of their good merits.

This number, which the Greek letters form as a monogram, signifies both comings of the Lord and Savior: the first, when, having become human, he cast out the prince of this world after his baptism, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every infirmity among the people; and the second, when that same just judge, the human being Christ Jesus, descends from the throne of God the Father at the command and voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, and the dead who are in Christ rise to glory, according to the proclamation of the holy Gospel and the voices of the prophets.

[Col. 0287B] These testify that the saints will see the Lord’s goodness in the land of the living, when they come and appear before God’s face. Those, therefore, who are of good merit will then bring back to the Lord the talents they have received with profit. Cleansed from every stain of sins—for they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb—they will be found worthy to follow him. They will sing to God a new song, namely the angelic hymn, “Alleluia,” day and night in his holy temple. There will be neither mourning nor any pain there, because the former things have passed away and everything will have become new.

[Col. 0287C] Therefore we must strive to please our God and Lord with full faith, which indeed works through love, so that he may then deign to become our helper and Savior when, according to the Scriptures, he comes for judgment. Fire will go before him and burn his enemies round about; his ministers will come, gather from his kingdom all causes of scandal, and bind the weeds into bundles for burning, while they gather the wheat into the barn of their Lord.

O exceedingly happy soul, to which it is permitted to enter the gates of heaven with an incorruptible body and to behold the author of light with the pure eyes of the heart! Its desire will rightly be fulfilled then, when it remains perfect in every respect and rejoices in eternal joy with the holy angelic spirits in everlasting light, singing praises to Christ and chanting a new song to the Lord in the assembly of the saints. In this devotion it will never afterward know weariness, because it desires perpetually to possess the kingdoms of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On the twenty-third figure, in which the number twenty-four is marked

Behold, a noble flower shines here, painted with the name of the true King, Jesus Christ. The figure of the holy cross represents it with its horns, joyfully displaying the works of Christ.

The number six, which the holy cross marks on each of its horns, arranged in three lines, signifies the perfection of Christ’s passion and our redemption. For just as the number six signifies the perfection of the world’s creation, so, through the number six, Christ—who was crucified on the sixth day—indicates the perfection of the world’s restoration.

That day was bright, on which the Creator completed his work; no less bright is this day, on which the Redeemer sanctified his work by restoring it. Then the Creator completed his creation through his activity; now also he has filled it with heavenly blessing by restoring it.

[Col. 0288A] Finally, to indicate the mystery, the number six was placed at the four horns of the cross and extends toward the four regions of the world, demonstrating the perfection of created things. For this number is itself the first perfect number; it also divides the civil day in half and, placed twice, completes it. It is the sixth part of one month and the sixtieth part of the whole year; it counts a quarter of the leap-year cycle and, together with five additional days, completes the excess. It orders the ages of the world and will bring the course of time to an end when the King of kings comes to forgive the sins of his saints with a peaceful countenance and to grant them the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore, good King Christ Jesus, you know well how to give certain rewards to your servants, whom the true light of faith, illuminating them from the whole world, and the living draught of wisdom, watering them, have led to you, rightly adorning them with the beauty of charity and works of justice.

[Col. 0288B] Finally, the number mentioned above, placed around the cross, indicates the gathering of peoples from the four regions of the world to their Redeemer, imploring his divinity for eternal salvation, so that they may eagerly learn his greatness from the perfect teaching of the Gospel and prove perfect faith by perfect works.

All the works of God are perfect and signify a perfect Creator; by their own beauty they testify to his immeasurable beauty. All things that are in heaven, on earth, and in the sea praise the excellent Craftsman. But we human beings, who are a small part of his creation, should sing to his name a glory that, though not worthy, is nevertheless devoted, and give him thanks for our redemption, because the one who made and multiplied us also freed us by his own blood from the power of the enemy.

[Col. 0288C] In this celebrated song, therefore, let us proclaim the love that he himself has shown toward us: he demonstrated it by his immeasurable compassion in acting for us, made it known by defending us, and commanded us to possess it by exhorting us and showing that it is pleasing to him.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the twenty-fourth form, in which the numbers one hundred, forty, and four are marked

O people beloved by God, most holy order of virgins, bless the Lord Christ, singing to him a new song that is worthy of imitation by all others. Sing the adornment of immortal glory before the throne of the Most High, and before the four living creatures formed with different faces, and before the twenty-four elders seated on twenty-four seats.

You have been taken from among human beings as first fruits for God and the Lamb. Beautiful companies, purchased at the price of his blood, you stand in his camp and sing the most worthy praises of the noblest triumph.

[Col. 0289A] Your hand, sounding the lyres, will make the serene and favorable face of God appear toward earthly beings, filling the courts of the Lord’s house with a mighty cry, thundering in the air like the voice of a great thunderclap and resounding in the valleys like the roar of many waters.

No falsehood has been found in your mouth, nor deceit in your heart. Rather, composing devout songs, you sing worthy praises before God’s throne day and night through the signs of virginity and the chastity of body and soul, which your King loves in you above all else.

For no one else gave you this soul but your leader and Creator, so that, living on earth without reproach, you might afterward receive eternal recompense in heaven.

[Col. 0289B] Therefore, most approved and perfect order of virgins, who, in differing sexes and at unequal ages, lived a heavenly way of life in the world, free from every defilement of fornication and immune from every filth of the devil, sing peaceful praises to God through the service of your mouths, the devotion of your hearts, and the bearing of your bodies.

Behold, your passage to heaven is direct. There eternal reward is prepared for you; there the immaculate Lamb of the Virgin grazes in flowering meadows. Following him wherever he goes, you enjoy pleasant pastures. You already possess individual robes in your souls, with the praise of chastity; you will receive others near the end of the world in immortal bodies, and you will rejoice with a double honor.

[Col. 0289C] Therefore we pray and beseech you, O peoples and ranks of the heavenly army, by the most noble name and most renowned distinction of your beauty, that, where you already reign joyfully with your King, you strive to obtain eternal joys for us also, so that the Lamb, your leader and glory, who rules in heaven’s citadel, may grant us a spacious and desirable place there, where, even if we cannot sing your song, we may at least hear it joyfully throughout the ages.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### On the twenty-fifth figure, in which “Alleluia” and “Amen” are placed

O devout and perpetual praise of the holy cross, which the assembly of the saints continually celebrates in heaven, be present to earthly beings, so that they may be able to speak something about you decently and worthily and proclaim your glory with full voice.

For I have sung you, holy cross, as best I could in metrical form, greatly desiring to satisfy you in this way; but you, surpassing the measure of our powers in dignity, have also surpassed the abundance of our gifts.

[Col. 0290A] Nor is this surprising, since you surpass all things heavenly and earthly together, and no one is sufficient either to satisfy your majesty or to fashion words worthy of your honor.

Therefore I attempted to take certain words from heavenly hymns with which to praise you, words that would also suit your appearance and figure. I arranged those same words on the page of verses, not continuously but in scattered form, and inserted angelic songs, placing “Amen” in the middle of the cross and filling its horns with “Alleluia.” Thus I also marked this sacred image with a heavenly song and indicated its mystery.

For all faithful and just servants of God now triumph over the scepters of the world and despise the splendor of its gifts, openly proclaiming that the hope of eternal things, the ardor of faith resounding through the mouths of the elect, prepares heavenly rewards for their companions and puts to flight the ancient enemy, who inflicted the most savage death upon the human race at the beginning and dragged the whole progeny of our first parents down to the places of hell until Christ’s coming.

[Col. 0290B] But we, whose desire for eternal things raises our minds to heaven, should anticipate the face of the Lord in confession and, properly rejoicing in psalms, strive to find grace in his sight. Let us exult in his praises in the manner required by the order of justice, as the ranks of the saints continually celebrate together in heaven.

This will rightly take place if we strive to fulfill the commands of the Thunderer and endeavor to offer most pleasing praises not only with our tongue but also in thought and deed. For a word of faith spoken only by the mouth, without harmony of mind and action, is not sufficient for salvation. Such praise is not pleasing to God: although it promises great things to him, it merits little, because it is written: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.”

[Col. 0290C] I therefore beseech you, heavenly hosts and spirits of angels, and souls of the righteous, who truly rejoice in the presence of the glory of the divine majesty: just as without ceasing you sing “Alleluia” and perpetual “Amen” to the Lord Christ forever, so strive also to assist our lot by your prayers, so that, through Christ’s grace, we may at last deserve to receive the true blessedness which you already possess perfectly.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On the twenty-sixth figure, in which prophetic sayings are marked

You, therefore, O holy cross of Christ, are nobly honored by the prophets’ oracles: they proclaim your deeds and exalt your powers, because whatever that most sacred people, inspired by the divine Spirit, uttered prophetically concerning Christ’s coming revealed in him the glory of your power, since the Savior appeared in the world for no other reason than to save the human race through you.

Let us therefore see what the prophet and psalmist David said, in case he spoke of you in some especially significant way. For he says: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones.” What, then, is the piercing of hands and feet and the counting of all the bones, except the fastening of Christ’s limbs, stretched out upon you, with nails?

Again David says: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” This plainly signifies what the Evangelist explained concerning Christ, saying: “Afterward, Jesus, knowing that all things had now been completed, so that Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’ A vessel full of vinegar was standing there. They placed a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop and offered it to his mouth.” And elsewhere it is written: “They gave him wine mixed with gall to drink.”

[Col. 0291A] The prophet Isaiah, moreover, prophesying, says: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and the government has been placed upon his shoulder,” and so forth. Again, speaking in the person of Christ, he says: “I gave my body to those who struck me and my cheeks to those who pulled them.” And again: “I did not turn my face away from those who reproached and spat upon me.” And: “The Lord will raise a sign among the nations and will gather the fugitives of Israel,” and so forth.

In all these sayings he expressed both your erection and the reality of Christ’s passion, as well as the savagery of the Jews. Jeremiah, moreover, depicts Christ as an innocent lamb led silently to sacrifice, and says that unbelievers will place wood in his bread. This signifies that the bread of life would be raised upon you and would taste the death of the flesh.

Ezekiel, for his part, asserts that the letter *T*, *tau*, resembling your figure, was placed upon the foreheads of the men who groaned and mourned, for their deliverance from the destroyer’s devastation.

[Col. 0291B] Thus you too, holy cross, were shown by the holy prophets not to be weakness or ignobility, but firm power, supreme praise, and the most trustworthy ship or harbor in lifting up the shipwreck of the whole world.

For Daniel foretold that Christ the Lord would be killed by the faithless and that in this way the guilt of sin would be brought to an end. Hosea describes the killing of death and the salvation of the people; Joel foretold that the stars would be darkened at Christ’s death; Amos that the festivals of the wicked would be turned into mourning and all their songs into lamentation; Obadiah expressed the Jews’ treacheries against the Lord and the salvation of the Church.

Jonah, likewise, prefigured the Lord’s three-day burial by his own example. Micah, calling Christ the mountain of the Lord, foretold the gathering of peoples to him. Nahum promised that the Lord would be an avenger of the impious and a consoler of the devout.

[Col. 0291C] Habakkuk, too, in plain speech testifies that your horns, O holy cross, would shine in Christ’s hands. Zephaniah foretells the Lord’s future coming and describes the day of his resurrection.

Haggai testifies, amid the shaking of heaven and earth, that the Desired One of all nations has come. Zechariah sees Jesus in the filthy garments of our mortality, with wounds fixed in his hands, and many mourning over him as over an Only-Begotten Son.

Malachi, although placed last in the order of the twelve prophets, nevertheless clearly, like the others, describes the Lord of the earth coming to his temple and cleansing his ministers through a searching examination, so that they may offer sacrifices of righteousness.

[Col. 0291D] The holy prophets unanimously foretold that all these gifts of salvation and mighty judgments would be accomplished through you, O holy cross of Christ. The author of all things appointed you for this purpose, and in you he himself completed, without any doubt, everything that had been promised concerning him.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On the twenty-seventh form, in which the sayings of the apostles are placed

The letter of the New Testament bears witness to your rights, O holy cross, no less than the writing of the Old Law, because what the latter promised as future gifts of divine grace, the former teaches to have been completed through the Savior’s incarnation. From this it is especially clear that Christ Jesus is Lord of both Laws, because by his own mouth he had disclosed to the world a twofold abyss, explaining the Law and establishing the Gospel. He refreshed the ancients through the desire of their holy hopes and satisfied later generations through the manifestation of the things themselves—good, truthful, and equitable toward all.

Hence the apostolic assembly spoke most joyfully about your most holy construction and displayed your magnificent deeds in a most salutary account.

For Peter, first in the order of the apostles, drew a powerful example of persuasion from you, saying: “Christ suffered for us, brothers, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps.” And again: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; by whose bruising you have been healed.”

[Col. 0292A] Hence I believe that he who gave his life for the impious and ungrateful inclines the ears of his compassion to the prayers of those devoted and faithful to him. Therefore, if in his honor he deigns to receive some small gift of human art, I wish with the greatest effort to offer him this song, trusting in his goodness that gifts of devout dedication will not displease him if we persevere in the true confession of his name.

The blessed apostle James, moreover, exhorts us here, setting before us the example of Christ’s patience: “Take, brothers, as an example of toil and patience the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Behold, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of Job’s endurance and have seen the Lord’s outcome.”

[Col. 0292B] Here also the beloved John of the Lord summons us to mutual love, bringing Christ into our midst, so that, just as he laid down his life for us, we too might lay down our lives for our brothers.

Judas, servant of Christ and brother of James, likewise demonstrated, through the example of Jesus the successor of Moses, that Jesus Christ led us through the cross out of spiritual Egypt—that is, from the power of darkness—and destroyed the unbelievers.

Paul, therefore, spoke of you not a little but magnificently. He says to his hearers: “For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” He also denied himself any ground for boasting except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world was crucified to him and he to the world.

[Col. 0292C] He affirms that Christ, because of the death of the cross, received power in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.

Behold, holy cross of Christ, how harmoniously the apostolic order proclaims your praises together with the ancient prophets, differing in nothing, since the things they foretold as future, these apostles affirm to have been completed in you. For you, the sign of true harmony, bring all things heavenly and earthly, old and new, to perfection.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### On the twenty-eighth figure, in which the craftsman himself worships the holy cross

Almighty majesty, exalted power, creator of heavenly things and fashioner of earthly things, Lord God Sabaoth, who are the true founder and redeemer of human beings: you are our praise, our strength and glory together with true salvation; you are King of kings, teacher of the ignorant, ruler of the faithful, and master of believers. You are the supreme shepherd and leader, the devout protector of your sheep, holy Savior, author of every good, good guide, straight way, true light, and perpetual life, radiant reward, and gate of eternal salvation.

From you proceed every understanding, voice, word, and fruit of all virtues. Therefore I directed my speech to you at the beginning of this work, and whatever I added in what follows, I wished to bring to your praise.

My heart rises to you; the whole intention of my mind cries out to you. Whatever the tongue of right confession or the hand of good action produces anywhere with the devotion of a pious mind—all of it belongs to your praise.

[Col. 0293A] For all things glorify and bless you, those below and those above. And I, too, the smallest part of your creation, worship you humbly and joyfully as the true Lord, and, saluting your cross submissively and humbly, I say:

O life-giving wood and saving altar, I worship you, praying for the hope of eternal life, so that through you, most holy structure, I may be offered as a sacrifice acceptable to God.

This is my desire; this is the powerful ardor of love; this is what the whole intention of my mind and the voice of my tongue entreat. This is the hunger of my heart and the thirst of my soul: that through the grace of your passion you may receive me, offered to you as your servant, and that your crucifixion may consume everything in me that is opposed to you; may temper carnal heat, extinguish anger, restrain my tongue from wickedness and empty talk, place words of compassion in my mouth, calm every disturbance of mind, and lead me into an upright life.

[Col. 0293B] Therefore, when you come, Lord Jesus, to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, when the flame has consumed your adversaries, all who hate your name, at the last trumpet and in the mighty storm; when, according to your Gospel, the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth mourn over themselves, looking upon him whom they pierced—I beseech you that then the holy cross may rescue me from the avenging flames and defend your own poet from the wrath of the Lamb.

To him I sing this present song. Would that I might continue to chant what is pleasing and honorable to him until the end of my life—I, Rabanus, the least of all your servants and a sinner—with hymns, praises, heart, mouth, hand, and every movement of my body, always remembering with what goodness you, our Creator, created us, and with what compassion you redeemed us when you freed us from the prison of hell and the flame of Gehenna.

[Col. 0293C] And now, good Savior, I beseech you to give me that rest which you promised to give your faithful in the citadel of heaven, where your people truly keep Sabbath, enjoying an everlasting Sabbath.

Meanwhile, as long as I am in this little body, guide me in the straight path of the Catholic faith, sustain me with firm hope, refresh me with your love, so that you yourself may be my refreshment on the way, you whom I desire to possess as my rest in my homeland.

For without any distrust I believe all your promises to be most true; I dread your judgments as perfectly just; I await your gifts as most sweet. Grant that, rejoicing in you, I may remain with you in eternal gladness.

O gracious cross of God, up to this point, as far as I could, I have sung your praise. But because you seek perpetual triumph, which you do not fully and perfectly find amid these mortal things, go to the heavenly ranks of the angels; there your perpetual praise will resound for you throughout all ages.

[Col. 0293]

## (A.D. 819)  
### Three Books of the Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, On the Formation of the Clergy, Addressed to Archbishop Heistulphus

### Epigram of the Same Author to the Brothers of Fulda

[Col. 0293D]

See what the meaning of the Law intended, brothers,  
which rightly commands us to know the words of God.

“Whoever has ears,” it says, “let him hear here  
what the Holy Spirit says to the Churches.”

[Col. 0294D]

The Psalmist likewise agrees with this in corresponding verse,  
ordering the people rightly to attend to the Law of the Lord.

Thus it is always proper for us, brothers,  
to learn the words of God with attentive eyes and ears,

[Col. 0295A]

what it commands in words, what it indicates in deeds themselves,  
which that book contains in its two parts;

what the beloved Bride of Christ signifies by celebrating  
through holy sacraments and various observances.

For you asked me to render these things for you in writing;  
I myself presented them in three small books.

What worship brings, what it announces through its holy steps,  
what the holy Church of God declares through prayer and feasts;

which doctrines it is fitting for all to learn and teach,  
and which mystical sayings of God are appropriate to the various orders.

[Col. 0296A]

Although I cannot gather all these things completely in writing,  
I have nevertheless embraced and set forth many of them here with skill.

I, Rabanus the sinner, now share these gifts of the Thunderer with you,  
receiving them together with you and piously making them common.

I humbly ask you, calling upon the scepters of the Thunderer,  
to commend me to the Lord in your prayers,

so that he in his compassion may grant gifts of salvation  
and, together with you, the blessed kingdoms of heaven to me.

Christ is your guide, Christ your king, Christ your lover.  
May the supreme God always save you in his heavenly citadel.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0295]

[Col. 0295B]

To the most reverend and most religious HEISTULPHUS, archbishop, RABANUS, the least of the servants of God, wishes eternal salvation in Christ.

When you, holy Father, are revered by very many on account of your outstanding piety, and stand honored and beloved among all the faithful as a great source of true faith and sound doctrine, I judged it fitting that I, to whom you have shown an abundance of your benefits, should bring to your veneration some little gift—not indeed worthy, but, as I believe, not unwelcome. I have no fear concerning its value, because a heart rich in goodness esteems the devotion of the giver more highly than the gift. Trusting in this, I have dared to send you, as a gift, a portion of the work that I have composed through study of sacred reading—you whom I know to be most kind and most just—so that, whatever its character, you might receive it, approve it by your sacred judgment, and examine it thoroughly.

For I was compelled to answer the various questions of our brothers, especially those who excelled in the sacred orders. They repeatedly questioned me about their office and about the various observances that are most properly maintained in the Church of God. To some of their questions I replied orally, and to others in writing, according to the opportunity afforded by place and time, following the authority and style of our predecessors. But I could not satisfy them sufficiently in this way. They pressed me most urgently—indeed, they compelled me—to gather all these matters into a single volume, so that they might in some way satisfy their inquiries and find written together in one book what previously had been recorded separately on different sheets, each item according to the question that had been asked.

I agreed with them and did what they requested as far as I could. For I have produced three books on this subject. The first contains an account of the ecclesiastical orders and of priestly clothing. It also treats of the four charisms of the Church—that is, baptism, chrism, the body and blood of the Lord, and the office of the Mass according to the custom of the Roman Church. The second book contains an account of the office of the canonical hours, fasting, confession and penance, the lawful fasts, various festivals, readings and ecclesiastical chant, the Catholic faith, and, conversely, various heresies.

The third book teaches how everything written in the divine books is to be investigated and learned, as well as those matters in the studies and arts of the pagans that it is useful for a churchman to examine. Finally, the book itself explains how those who bear the office of teaching ought to admonish different hearers with different addresses and faithfully instruct them in ecclesiastical doctrine. Since all the matters we have mentioned chiefly belong to the office of clerics, who hold a position of governance in the Church and ought to instruct the people of God in all lawful things, it seemed appropriate to call these books *On the Instruction of Clerics*—that is, concerning the instruction by which they should prepare themselves and those subject to them for divine service.

Therefore I beseech you, holy Father, to accept the work offered to you, and, reading it again with devotion, to examine it carefully. Whatever you find reasonably set forth in it, attribute to the one by whom reason was created; but whatever you find stated thoughtlessly, quickly render corrected through your diligence. For I will always willingly submit myself to your instruction, from whom I remember having received ecclesiastical dignity.

Nevertheless, I trust in the grace of almighty God that I have maintained the Catholic faith and understanding in all things, and that I have not produced these matters as though they came from me, but, relying upon the authority of our predecessors, have followed their footsteps in every respect. I mean Cyprian and Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, John, Damasus, Cassiodorus, and several others. In some places I have inserted their statements in this work just as they were written by them; elsewhere, for the sake of brevity, I have expressed their meaning concisely in my own words. At times, where necessary, I have presented certain matters according to their example but in my own understanding.

In all things, however, if I am not mistaken, I have imitated Catholic truth. If the Lord helps me, I will not allow myself to be separated from it in any way. I trust that you, above all, possess and love this truth; and for that reason I humbly ask your support, so that Truth itself, creator and governor of all things, may deign—although not because of my merits, yet because of your most sacred prayer—to preserve me in itself forever, without any deviation into error.

I wish your Blessedness always to enjoy good health in every respect, holy Father, and to remember us.

# Here Begins the First Book on the Instruction of Clerics

## Chapter I. On the One Church of God

The catholic Church of God, spread and extended throughout the whole world, is glorified and ennobled by the name of Christ. Every person who participates in right faith and is reborn through holy baptism is called a Christian from Christ, and is recognized as a son of God the Father and of the Church his mother.

“Church,” *ekklesia* (ἐκκλησία) in Greek, is rendered in Latin as “convocation” or “assembly,” because it calls everyone to itself. It is called catholic, *katholikos* (καθολικὸς), that is, “universal,” because throughout the whole world there is one Church of Christ, which is both Christ’s bride and his body.

## Chapter II. On the Three Orders of the Church

There are nevertheless three orders in the Church: those who live in the world—that is, laypeople—monks, and clerics.

The first, the lay order, is interpreted as “popular.” For *laos* (λαὸς) in Greek means “people” in Latin. The second is the monastic order, that is, living in solitude, removed from worldly society. For *monas* (μονὰς) in Greek means “singularity,” and *monachos* (μοναχὸς) means “solitary” or “alone.”

The third is the clerical order. *Cleros* (κλῆρος), in Greek, means “lot” or “inheritance.” Our teachers say that clerics were so called from *cleros* because Matthias was chosen by lot, and we read that he was the first whom the apostles ordained (Acts I). In the same way, those whom the leaders of the Churches ordained in those times were selected by lot.

For “inheritance” in Greek is also called *cleronomia* (κληρονομία), and an heir *cleronomos*. Therefore they are called clerics either because they belong to the Lord’s lot, or because they possess the Lord’s portion, as it is written concerning them, with the Lord speaking: “I am their inheritance” (Ezek. XLIV). Hence those who possess God as their inheritance ought to strive to serve God without any impediment from the world, so that they may fittingly say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV).

This order is placed first in the Church because it rightly serves in holy things and dispenses the sacraments to the people. For just as in the Old Testament the tribe of Levi was specially chosen by the Lord above the other tribes to serve him through various offices in the tabernacle—which is the present Church—so that they might serve him day and night in his holy temple, stand before the people in matters pertaining to God, offer gifts and sacrifices to God for their own ignorance and that of the people, judge between the just and the unjust, distinguish between the holy and the profane, and between the polluted and the clean, and teach the people of God all his lawful commands and precepts that he had given them.

## Chapter III. On the Tonsure of Clerics

The tonsure used by the Church arose, I believe, from the Nazareans. They first kept their hair, but afterward, when they had completed their devotion through a life of great continence, they shaved their heads and were commanded to place their hair in the fire of the sacrifice, evidently so that they might consecrate the perfection of their devotion to the Lord.

Following their example, this practice was introduced by the apostles, so that those who are dedicated to the Lord and consecrated to divine worship might, like Nazareans—that is, holy people of God—be renewed by cutting their hair.

This is what the Lord commands the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “You, son of man, take a sharp sword and draw it over your head and your beard” (Ezek. III), evidently because he too served God in the ministry of sanctification and belonged to the priestly line.

We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that those Nazareans, Priscilla and Aquila, were the first to do this, as well as the apostle Paul and certain disciples of Christ, who proved worthy of imitation in this form of devotion.

Among clerics, the tonsure is a certain sign represented on the body but enacted in the soul: namely, that by this sign vices may be cut away in the practice of religion, and that we may strip ourselves of the sins of our flesh as of hair. Then, renewed in our minds, we may shine with fresh locks, stripping off, according to the apostle, the old person with his deeds and putting on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God (Col. III).

This renewal ought to take place in the mind, but it should be demonstrated on the head, where the mind is understood to dwell. As for the fact that, when the upper part of the head has been shaved, a circular crown is left below, I think that the priesthood and kingship of the Church are signified in them.

Among the ancients, the tiara was placed on the heads of priests. Made of fine linen, it was round, like half a sphere; this is signified by the shaved portion of the head. The golden crown, however, is the breadth of a circle that surrounds the heads of kings. Thus both signs are expressed on the heads of clerics, so that what is written by the apostle Peter may also be fulfilled through a certain likeness of the body: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II).

It is asked why, as among the ancient Nazareans, the hair is not now first allowed to grow and then cut. But those who investigate this should consider the difference between that prophetic veil and this revelation of the Gospel, concerning which the Apostle says: “When you have turned to Christ, the veil will be removed” (2 Cor. III).

What, then, did the veil placed between the face of Moses and the sight of the children of Israel signify? In those times, the hair of holy people signified the same thing. For the Apostle also says that hair is a veil. Therefore, the heads of those who are consecrated to the Lord ought no longer to be veiled with hair, but only to be revealed, because what had been hidden in the sacrament of prophecy has now been made clear in the Gospel.

There are also certain teachers who assert, for various reasons, that the apostle Peter first adopted this practice so that he might bear on his head the form and likeness of Christ, when Christ, about to undergo the cross for our redemption, was cruelly crowned by the impious Jewish people with the sharp points of thorns.

They say, further, that it was adopted so that the priests of the Old and New Testaments might be distinguished by tonsure and dress. Finally, they say that the same Apostle and his successors and followers bore among the Roman people the ridiculous mockery of jeering, because the barons of those people also customarily sold conquered enemies of the army under a crown.

But concerning these matters we leave the decision as to what should be accepted to the judgment of the reader. Let us now proceed to the most sacred orders of clerics and set forth their origin and ranks individually.

## Chapter IV. On the Ecclesiastical Orders

There are eight ecclesiastical ranks. Their names are these: doorkeeper, psalmist or lector, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, and bishop.

The beginning of the priesthood in the Old Testament was Aaron, although Melchizedek had previously offered sacrifice, and after him Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. We also read that Noah built an altar and offered a burnt offering upon it to the Lord. But these men did such things of their own free will, not with priestly authority.

Aaron, however, was the first in the Law to receive the priestly name, and the first to offer victims clothed in pontifical vestments, at the Lord’s command, when he spoke to Moses:

“Take Aaron and his sons,” he said, “and bring them to the door of the tabernacle of testimony. When you have washed the father and his sons with water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments: the linen garment, the tunic, the ephod, and the breastpiece, which you shall fasten with a belt. You shall place the tiara on his head and the holy plate upon the tiara, and pour the oil of anointing over his head; by this rite he shall be consecrated. You shall also bring his sons near and clothe them in linen tunics. You shall gird Aaron and his sons with a belt, place mitres upon them, and they shall be my priests by perpetual consecration” (Exod. XXIX).

In this passage we should understand Aaron the priest to have been the high priest, that is, the bishop. His sons prefigured the presbyters, beside whom the Levites ought rightly to have stood, just as they stood beside the high priest. Moses, however, the mediator of this act, signifies Christ.

In the New Testament, after Christ, the priestly order began with Peter. To him first was given the pontificate in the Church of Christ. For Christ the Lord speaks to him in this way:

“You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX).

He therefore first received the power of binding and loosing, and he was the first to bring the people to faith through the power of his preaching. Indeed, the other apostles became his partners in equal honor and authority. They preached the Gospel after being scattered throughout the whole world. When they departed, bishops succeeded them; these were established throughout the world in the seats of the apostles. They are no longer chosen by fleshly descent and blood, as at first according to the order of Aaron, but according to each person’s merit, faith, and teaching, which divine grace has bestowed upon him.

The fact that bishops are ordained by the laying on of hands by their predecessors, the priests of God, is an ancient institution. The holy patriarch Isaac placed his hand upon Jacob’s head and blessed him, and Jacob blessed his sons. Moses also placed his hand upon the head of Joshua son of Nun and gave him the spirit of power and leadership over the people of Israel.

In the same way, our Lord Jesus Christ, the fulfiller of the Law and the Prophets, blessed his apostles through the laying on of hands, as it is written in the Gospel of Luke: “He led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he departed from them, and they returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke XXIV).

In the Acts of the Apostles, by command of the Holy Spirit, the apostles laid hands upon Paul and Barnabas for the episcopate, and they were sent to evangelize (Acts XIII).

Moreover, the fact that a bishop is ordained not by one but by all the bishops of the province is recognized as having been instituted because of heresies, lest the tyrannical authority of one man attempt anything against the faith of the Church. Therefore he is appointed by all who assemble, with no fewer than three present, while the others consent through written testimony.

When he is consecrated, a staff is given to him, so that by its indication he may govern or correct the people subject to him, and sustain the weaknesses of the weak. A ring is also given to him as a sign of pontifical honor or as a seal of secret matters. For there are many things that priests conceal from the senses of the carnal and less discerning, as though under a seal, lest the sacraments of God be revealed to the unworthy.

## Chapter V. On the Threefold Order of Bishops

The order of bishops is threefold: patriarchs, archbishops—who are also metropolitans—and bishops.

“Patriarch,” *patriarchos* (πατριάρχος) in Greek, is interpreted as “father of princes” or “highest of fathers,” because he holds the first, that is, the apostolic, place. Since he exercises the highest honor, he is designated by this name, as in the case of the archbishop, the bishop of Antioch, and the bishop of Alexandria.

“Archbishop,” *archiepiskopos* (ἀρχιεπίσκοπος), is a Greek term meaning “highest” or “chief of bishops.” He holds the apostolic office and presides over the other bishops. He is placed over individual provinces, and by his authority and teaching the other priests are subject to him. Without him, the remaining bishops may do nothing except what has been entrusted to each in his own parish.

The care of the entire province is committed to him. All the ranks described above are called bishops by one and the same name, but they also use particular names to distinguish the powers that each has received individually.

A metropolitan is so called because he presides over the city that is, in a certain sense, the mother of the other cities established in the same province. *Metropolis* (μητρόπολις), therefore, is Greek for “mother of cities.”

The word “episcopate” is derived from the fact that the one placed in charge watches over others, caring for those subject to him. For *skopein* (σκοπεῖν) means “to watch attentively” in Latin. “Bishops,” *episkopoi* (ἐπίσκοποι), therefore, is interpreted in Greek as “watchers” or “overseers” in Latin.

For a “watchman” is the name given to one placed in authority in the Church because he watches over and looks after the conduct and life of the peoples placed under him, and declares to each person his deeds, just as the Lord said to the prophet Ezekiel:

“And you, son of man,” he said, “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Hearing the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not speak so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand,” and so forth (Ezek. XXXIII).

A pontiff is the chief of priests, as though he were the way of those who follow. He is also called the high priest and the chief pontiff. He creates priests and Levites, arranges all the ecclesiastical orders, and shows what each person ought to do.

“Antistes” is likewise so called because he “stands before.” He is first in the order of the Church and has no priest above him.

The word “priest” is composed from Greek and Latin, as though it meant “one who gives what is sacred.” He therefore dispenses the heavenly mysteries, gives baptism to the faithful, distributes the body and blood of Christ, and preaches the word of God. A priest may be called either a bishop or a presbyter.

Bishops hold the place of the apostles in the Church, as we said above. Chorepiscopi, who are vicars of bishops, were established as an example of the seventy elders. They may not order or establish anything more in the Church than is granted to them by the lawful bishops who possess the full seat and governance of the Churches.

Chorepiscopi were ordained for the care of the poor who live in fields and villages, so that they would not lack the comfort of confirmation. They are called chorepiscopi because they belong to the “choir” of priests. They are ordained only by the bishop of the city to which they are attached, just as presbyters are.

## Chapter VI. On Presbyters

The order of presbyters took its beginning, as has been said, from the sons of Aaron. Those who were called priests in the Old Testament are the ones now called presbyters; and the one who was then called the high priest is now called a bishop.

For “presbyter,” *presbyteros* (πρεσβύτερος) in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as “elder.” They are not called presbyters because of age or decrepit old age, but because of the honor, dignity, and teaching of wisdom that they have received, as it is said through Wisdom: “The glory of old men is their gray hair” (Prov. XX), and again: “The gray hair of a person is his prudence.”

Hence among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same. One name referred to dignity, the other to age.

The apostle Paul, writing to Titus, says: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remains to be set right and appoint presbyters in each city, as I instructed you: if anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedience” (Tit. III).

He immediately adds: “For a bishop must be without blame, as God’s steward, not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine, not violent,” and so forth (ibid.).

He also writes to the Philippians about bishops and deacons, although one city could not have several bishops; under the name “bishops,” he included presbyters.

Presbyters are called priests because they give what is sacred, just as bishops do: in the consecration of the divine body and blood, in baptism, and in the office of preaching.

But although they are priests, they do not possess the highest pontifical rank. They neither sign the forehead with chrism nor give the Paraclete Spirit—Scripture in the Acts of the Apostles shows that these duties belong only to bishops—nor can they ordain clerics to the sacred orders, for this is reserved to bishops for the sake of unity and concord.

Presbyters are men of the second rank. Their type was prefigured by the seventy men in the Old Testament, among whom the Lord extended the spirit of Moses, so that, using such assistants among the people, he could easily govern innumerable multitudes.

In the same way, an abundance of the fullness of the fatherly spirit was poured out upon Eleazar and Ithamar, so that the ministry of priests would be sufficient for salutary sacrifices and the sacramental duties of more frequent service.

Likewise, teachers and companions in faith were added to the apostles of Christ. Through these secondary preachers they filled the whole world and spread it through evangelical teaching.

## Chapter VII. On Deacons

The Levites were named from their founder; the Levites arose from the name of Levi. Through them the mysteries of the mystical sacrament were performed in the temple of God.

For the Lord commanded Moses that, after the ordination of Aaron the priest and his sons, the tribe of Levi should again be ordained for the mystery of divine worship, consecrated to the Lord in place of all the firstborn, and should serve Israel before Aaron and his sons, keeping watch in the Lord’s tabernacle day and night. They were to carry the ark, the tabernacle, and all its vessels; they were to encamp around the tabernacle; when the tabernacle moved, they were to take it down, and again they were to take it down, and again set it up (Exod. XXIX).

In Greek they are called deacons, *diakonoi* (διάκονες), and in Latin “ministers,” because just as consecration is found in the priest, so the administration of ministry is found in the deacon.

In the Old Testament they kept watch in the tabernacle of testimony at Aaron’s command and performed all the work of the tabernacle. Nevertheless, they did not approach the vessels of the sanctuary or the altar, as the Lord had commanded Aaron:

“Behold, I have given you your brothers, the Levites, from among the children of Israel, and I have handed them over as a gift to the Lord, so that they may serve in the ministries of his tabernacle. But you and your sons shall guard your priesthood and everything that pertains to the service of the altar and is within the veil; it shall be administered by the priests,” and so forth (Num. XVIII).

From the age of twenty-five and above they entered to minister in the tabernacle of the covenant. When they completed their fiftieth year, they ceased to serve, and became ministers of their brothers in the tabernacle of the covenant, guarding what had been entrusted to them.

In the New Testament, the apostles appointed seven deacons, because of the sacramental significance of that number, for sacred ministry and the service of the altar. We read that they also preached and baptized many people. Thus Saint Stephen disputed against the Jews, and Philip, after baptizing the eunuch, evangelized all the cities until he came to Caesarea; in Samaria he preached and baptized those who were afterward confirmed by the apostles Peter and John.

But they are permitted to baptize only in the presence of bishops or presbyters. Others may not do so unless extreme necessity compels them, especially when the aforementioned ministers are far away.

These are the seven angels whom we read of in the Apocalypse, sounding trumpets. These are the seven golden lampstands. These are the seven voices of thunder (Rev. VIII). They admonish everyone with a clear voice, like heralds, whether in singing psalms or in hearing readings. They cry out that we should have ears attentive to God. They also evangelize.

Without them, the priest has the name but not the office. For just as there is consecration in the priest, so there is the administration of the sacrament in the minister. The priest sanctifies what has been offered; the minister distributes what has been sanctified.

Even priests themselves, because of the danger of presumption, may not take the chalice from the Lord’s table unless it has been handed to them by the deacon.

The Levites offer offerings upon the altars. The Levites arrange the Lord’s table. The Levites cover the ark of the covenant. Not everyone sees the altar of the mysteries, which are covered by the Levites, lest those who ought not see should see, and those who cannot preserve what they receive should take it.

For this reason they stand at the altar dressed in white, so that, reminded by this, they may possess a heavenly life and approach the sacrifices pure and undefiled.

Pope Sylvester, the thirty-fourth pontiff of the Roman Church after Peter, was the first to make them use dalmatics. He also established that their *laena* should be covered with a linen cloak, as is contained in the pontifical records.

## Chapter VIII. On Subdeacons

“Subdeacons,” *hypodiakonoi* (ὑποδιάκονες) in Greek, are what we call subdeacons. They are so called because they are subject to the commands and duties of the Levites.

They themselves receive the offerings of the faithful in the temple of God and carry them to the Levites to be placed upon the altars.

Among the Hebrews they are called Nathinaeans, as the books of Chronicles and Ezra testify; this is interpreted as “those who serve the Lord in humility.”

From their order was Nathanael, who in the Gospel of John, warned by divine revelation, was deemed worthy to confess the Savior. He also proved faithful at the first judgment concerning his divinity, when the Lord bore witness and said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John I).

These men also offer the vessels of the Lord’s body and blood to the deacons at the altar.
