The Fathers decreed concerning them that, since they handle the sacred mysteries, they should be chaste and continent with respect to their wives and free from every carnal impurity, according to what the prophet commands under divine instruction: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII).

When they are ordained, they do not receive the laying on of hands, as priests and Levites do. Instead, they receive only the paten and chalice from the hand of the bishop, and from the archdeacon a cup of water, together with water, a towel, and a hand-towel.

## Chapter IX. On Acolytes

Acolytes, *akolouthoi* (ἀκόλουθοι) in Greek, are called “candle-bearers” in Latin because they carry candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered.

At that time they light and carry the lamps, not to drive away darkness while the sun is shining brightly at the same time, but to display a sign of joy, so that under the symbol of bodily light the light may be revealed of which we read in the Gospel: “That was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I).

Their type was prefigured by those who, at the Lord’s command, lit each day the lamps placed upon the lampstand in the tabernacle.

## Chapter X. On Exorcists

Exorcists, *exorkistai* (ἐξορκίσται), are called in Latin, from the Greek, “those who adjure” or “those who rebuke.”

They invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over catechumens or over those who have an unclean spirit, adjuring the spirit through him to depart from them.

Josephus reports that King Solomon devised and taught his people methods of exorcism—that is, of adjuration—by which unclean spirits, once expelled from a person, did not dare to return again.

The book of the Acts of the Apostles also bears witness concerning them, saying: “But certain of those who went about among the Jews attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus through exorcisms,” and so forth (Acts XIX).

We find that those whom Ezra calls administrators of the temple are now exorcists in the Church of God. Under Ezra there were temple administrators who were descendants of Solomon’s servants. They had the administration of the entire temple under their care, but they did not perform priestly duties or serve in sacred offerings.

The temple administrators had no other responsibility than the repair of the buildings, so that whatever in the structure of the temple had grown old or fallen down might be restored and improved by those administrators from the Lord’s treasuries.

Thus the temple administrators are exorcists among the people of God. For just as a prudent and good administrator knows the amount of his lord’s revenues and the extent of all his property, and keeps with him the original documents of the entire estate, so an exorcist gathers into his diligence the secrets of the whole kingdom of the Lord, committing to memory the mysteries of Scripture, from which he may exercise the gift granted to him by the Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle’s proclamation.

The Apostle mentions exorcists when he says: “Do all possess gifts of healing?”

When they are ordained, these men receive from the hand of the bishop a booklet in which the exorcisms are written. The bishop says to them: “Receive this, commit it to memory, and have the power to lay hands upon the possessed or upon catechumens, so that you may command unclean spirits and cast them out.”

## Chapter XI. On Lectors

Lectors are so called from reading, and psalmists from singing psalms. Lectors proclaim to the people what they should follow. Psalmists sing in order to stir the minds of their hearers to compunction.

Some lectors also pronounce their words so plaintively that they compel certain people to weeping and lamentation. They are likewise called “proclaimers,” because they announce things from afar.

Their voice must be so strong and clear that it fills the ears even of those who are positioned at a great distance.

The order of lectors took its form and beginning from the prophets. Lectors, therefore, are those who preach the word of God, to whom it is said: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Ezek. XXXIII).

When they are ordained, the bishop first speaks to the people about their way of life. Then, before the congregation, he hands them the book of divine writings so that they may announce the word of God.

A lector ought therefore to be steeped in teaching and books and richly equipped with knowledge of meanings and words, so that, speaking distinctly and clearly, he may instruct the hearts of his hearers.

David and Asaph were the leaders or founders of the psalmists, that is, of the singers. After Moses, they were the first to compose and sing psalms.

After Asaph died, his sons were appointed by David to this order. The psalmists held their office by hereditary succession, as did the priestly order. They alone sang continuously in the temple, clothed in white robes, with the choir responding to the voice of one singer.

From this ancient practice the Church took the example of training psalmists, through whose songs the minds of the hearers may be stirred toward the effect of God’s work.

A psalmist ought to be distinguished and excellent both in voice and in skill, so that he may arouse the minds of his hearers through the delight of sweetness.

Those who prove capable in the art of singing are sometimes chosen for this office even without the bishop’s knowledge, by command alone.

## Chapter XII. On Doorkeepers

Doorkeepers are those who in the Law were also called custodians and gatekeepers.

In the Old Testament, among the Hebrews, they were chosen to guard the temple. Appointed in their turns, they guarded all the inner and outer areas of the temple, so that nothing unclean might enter it.

They are called doorkeepers because they preside over the doors of the temple. Holding the key, they guard everything inside on both sides; exercising judgment between good and evil, they receive the faithful and reject the unfaithful.

## Chapter XIII. Who Should Enter the Sacred Order, and in What Sequence

The canons and decrees of Pope Zosimus prescribe that a cleric who approaches the sacred order should spend five years among the lectors or exorcists. After that, he should serve for four years as an acolyte or subdeacon.

He should approach the blessing of the diaconate at no less than twenty-five years of age. After completing five years in that order, if he has ministered blamelessly, he may be advanced to the honor of the presbyterate, but not before the age of thirty, even if he is highly worthy, because our Lord also did not begin to preach before his thirtieth year.

If, from that rank, a more mature life should lead him toward good morals, he may receive the highest pontificate, provided that this law is observed: neither a man married twice, nor a penitent, nor a convert recently come to the faith may be admitted to these ranks.

## Chapter XIV. On Priestly Vestments

Having compared the modern priestly garment with the ancient attire of the Old Testament, let us now proceed, according to the understanding of our predecessors, to explain what it signifies mystically.

## Chapter XV. On the Superhumeral

The first of these garments is the *ephod bad*, which is interpreted as the linen superhumeral. It signifies the purity of good works.

For this reason, when the Lord instructed Moses concerning priestly clothing, he first commanded that the superhumeral be made. Whoever is to be advanced to the priesthood and to the governance of God’s people must first have his works examined, so that, when what is outward and visible to everyone has proved blameless, the integrity of his heart and the sincerity of his faith may then be appropriately scrutinized.

## Chapter XVI. On the *Poder*, That Is, the Linen Tunic
The second is the linen tunic, which in Greek is called *ποδήρης* (*poderēs*), and in Latin *talaris*, because it descends as far as the ankles. Josephus calls it *byssina*, “made of fine linen”; its mystical significance is evident. Since linen or fine linen plainly signifies continence and chastity, priests wear the linen tunic closely fitted when they preserve their commitment to continence not feebly but diligently. It descends to the ankles because the priest must persist in good works until the end of this life, as the Lord commands and promises: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation II).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the belt

The third vestment is the belt, or girdle, which they use so that the tunic itself may not fall loose and impede their walking. This signifies the guarding of the mind. For whoever walks dressed in an ankle-length tunic without a belt allows the tunic to hang loose and, having left the body exposed, gives winds and cold an opportunity to enter; moreover, by hindering his steps, it slows his ability to walk, or even becomes a cause of falling for those who tread upon it.

Therefore priests put on linen so that they may possess chastity; they gird themselves with belts so that this chastity may not be lax and negligent; so that the wind of self-exaltation may not gain access to blow through the mind; so that, as iniquity increases, it may not cause their charity to grow cold; so that the steps of good works may not be hindered by the boasting of their presumption; so that, when the course of the virtues has been obstructed, chastity itself may not become worthless after being stained by the filth of earthly desire; and so that, finally, by growing proud, it may not drive its author to ruin.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the *phanon*

The fourth vestment of the priest is the small napkin or cloth, commonly called the *phanon*. For this reason it is held in their hands whenever the office of the Mass is being performed, so that the people may see them prepared for service at the Lord’s table. Napkins are linen cloths placed at banquets and meals; hence the diminutive *mappula*, as also *mantilia*, now denotes cloths used to cover tables, though, as their name indicates, they were formerly provided for wiping the hands. Priests and ministers of the altar, whose office is to celebrate the divine sacraments, ought therefore to hold small cloths in their hands, so that the spontaneous work may agree with the devotion of the mind and the office, piously entrusted as a divine gift, may be worthily performed.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the *orarium*, that is, the stole

The fifth is what is called the *orarium*, although some call it the stole. The use of this kind of garment has been granted only to those persons to whom the office of preaching has been entrusted. It is fitting that the orators of Christ should also possess an *orarium*, because, while their clothing corresponds to their proper office, they themselves are continually urged on toward the ministry of the word, and the people entrusted to them, seeing this salutary sign, are admonished to hasten more fervently toward meditation on the law.

The *orarium* appropriately covers both the priest’s neck and chest, so that he may thereby be instructed that whatever he utters with his mouth must be considered with the utmost rational reflection. Thus the Apostle’s saying may always be recalled in him: “I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians XIV). And again: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. Lest perhaps, if he should speak rashly and irrationally, he suffer harm” (2 Corinthians VI). Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “The heart of the wise instructs his mouth, and adds grace to his lips” (Proverbs XVI). Likewise: “Whoever guards his mouth guards his soul; whoever is thoughtless in speaking will experience evils” (Proverbs XXI).

## CHAPTER XX. On the dalmatic

The sixth is what is called the dalmatic, named from Dalmatia, a province of Greece, where it was first woven. This garment is made in the form of a cross and is a sign of the Lord’s Passion. The tunic also has purple bands descending from the top to the bottom, both in front and behind, and likewise along each sleeve, so that the minister of the Lord may be reminded, by the appearance of his clothing, of the ministry in which he participates: that through the mystical offering he should commemorate the Lord’s Passion, so that he himself may become an acceptable offering to God.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the chasuble

The seventh priestly vestment is what they call the chasuble. It is named by diminution from *casa*, “house,” because it covers the whole person, like a smaller house. The Greeks call it *planētē* (*πλανήτην*). It is the outermost of all the vestments, and covers and protects all the others within it by its own shelter.

We may therefore understand this garment as charity, which surpasses all virtues and protects and illuminates their beauty by its own covering. For there will be no splendor of the virtues if the radiance of charity has not illumined them. The Apostle demonstrates this when he says:

“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And though I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing. Charity is patient; it is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails,” and so forth (1 Corinthians XIII).

Without this charity, or chasuble, the priest himself ought neither to approach the altar, nor to offer a gift, nor to pour out prayers. Hence Truth itself says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then, coming, you shall offer your gift” (Matthew VI). And again: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone,” and so forth (Mark XI).

Concerning this spiritual garment of the virtues, the Apostle wrote to the Colossians as follows: “Put on, he says, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassion, kindness, humility, modesty, patience,” and so forth (Colossians III). Shortly afterward, concerning the preeminence of charity, he added: “Above all these things, have charity, which is the bond of perfection.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the sandals

Priests also put sandals, or *solci*, on their feet. This type of footwear has been granted to them by evangelical authority, as the Gospel of Mark testifies (Mark XVI), because the footwear has a mystical significance: the foot should be neither covered nor bare before the earth—that is, the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rely upon earthly advantages. For it is written by the Apostle: “And having your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Ephesians VI).

Just as sandals cover part of the foot while leaving part uncovered, so teachers of the Gospel ought partly to conceal and partly to reveal the Gospel—specifically, so that the faithful and devout person may have sufficient instruction, while the unbeliever and contemptuous person may find no material for blasphemy.

This type of footwear also admonishes us to care for our flesh and body in their necessities, but not to fall into the wantonness of lust; concerning these matters the divine law instructs us. For it is written: “You shall not despise your flesh.” And again: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Isaiah LVIII).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the pallium

Above all these vestments, the dignity of the pallium is conferred upon the chief priest—who is called an archbishop—on account of the apostolic office. This type of garment displays the sign of the cross in purple, so that the bishop wearing it may bear a cross on his back and breast, think piously and worthily in his mind about the Passion of the Redeemer, and show the people for whom he entreats the Lord the sign of their redemption.

It is also fitting that the apostolic dignity should make the man apostolic, so that with complete devotion, sound speech, and worthy conduct he may say with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians VI).

These are the things we have briefly said about priestly dress, according to our understanding and in proportion to the modest measure of our talent. We do not prejudice those who might write about the same subject more appropriately and worthily, and discuss it more fully.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the sacraments of the Church

The following discourse ought to set forth and explain the priestly rite concerning the sacraments performed in the Church. The sacraments are baptism and chrism, the body and blood. They are called sacraments because, beneath the covering of bodily things, divine power works the salvation of those same sacraments in a more hidden manner. Hence, from their secret or sacred powers, they are called *sacramenta*, “sacraments.”

They are therefore fruitfully performed within the Church because the Holy Spirit, dwelling in her, secretly brings about the same effect of the sacraments. Thus, whether they are administered within the Church of God by good or by evil ministers, these gifts are neither increased by the merits of the good dispensers nor diminished by those of the evil, because “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” Hence in Greek it is called *μυστήριον* (*mystērion*), because it contains a secret and hidden deposit.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the sacrament of baptism

The first of the sacraments is baptism, because before anyone is anointed with holy chrism or becomes a participant in the body and blood of Christ, he must be cleansed by sacred regeneration and thereafter approach the other rites properly.

Baptism, Greek *βάπτισμα* (*baptisma*), is interpreted in Latin as *tinctio*, “immersion” or “dipping.” It is not called *tinctio* merely because a person is immersed in water, but because there he is changed for the better by the spirit of grace and becomes something very different from what he was.

At first we were foul through the deformity of sins; in the immersion we become beautiful through the whitening of virtues. Hence it is also written in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up as though whitened?” Its mystery is fulfilled in no other way than under the designation of the Trinity—that is, through knowledge of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—when the Lord says to the Apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (the end of Mark).

For just as every word stands on three witnesses, so the ternary number of the divine names confirms the sacrament.

The reason baptism is given through water is this: the Lord wished that the invisible reality should be conferred through a fitting, yet certainly tangible and visible, element, over which the Holy Spirit was also carried in the beginning. For just as oil, by its natural weight, floats above every liquid, so in the beginning the Holy Spirit was carried over the waters.

Just as water cleanses the body externally, so through its mystery the soul is secretly purified by the Holy Spirit. Its sanctification occurs in this way: when God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, having healed the waters, sanctifies them from himself. They receive the power of purification, so that in them flesh and soul stained by transgressions may be cleansed.

Both things must necessarily be applied to the one being baptized: the washing of baptism and the purification of the Holy Spirit, because the Savior says: “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

But before baptism, the ministry of catechizing must reach the person, so that the catechumen may first receive the rudiments of faith. For in the Gospel according to Matthew it is read that after the resurrection the Lord commanded the Apostles to teach and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (the end of Matthew)—that is, first to instill the knowledge of God in them through faith, and then to baptize those who believed for the remission of sins.

This is what is read in Mark: the same Lord placed faith before baptism, when he said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (the end of Mark).

And, as John testifies, Jesus first smeared the eyes of the man born blind with mud made from spittle, and then sent him to the waters of Siloam, because the person to be baptized must first be instructed in faith in the incarnation of Christ and then admitted to baptism already believing, so that he may know whose grace he is sharing in and to whom he is thereafter made debtor.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On catechumens

A catechumen is so called because he is still listening to the teaching of faith, although he has not yet received baptism. For *catechumenus*, Greek *κατηχούμενος* (*katēchoumenos*), is interpreted in Latin as *auditor*, “a hearer.”

Since the first command of exhortation in the law is: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy VI), the person to whom God speaks through the priest, as through Moses, is called a catechumen—that is, a hearer—so that, recognizing the true Lord, he may abandon the various errors of idols.

I think that all those baptized by John with repentance represented the figure of catechumens.

After the catechumens, the second grade is that of the *competentes*. The *competentes* are those who, after instruction in the faith and after a life of continence, hasten to receive the grace of Christ. For this reason they are called *competentes*, that is, “those seeking the grace of Christ.” Catechumens merely listen; they do not yet ask. They are like guests and neighbors of the faithful: from outside they listen to the mysteries and hear about grace, but they are not yet called faithful.

The *competentes*, however, ask and already receive; they are already catechized—that is, formed by instruction in the faith and the sacraments. To them the saving Creed is handed over as a reminder of the faith and a sign of holy confession. Instructed by it, they recognize how they ought now to present themselves for the grace of Christ.

It should be noted that in the Church of the Savior the salvation of little ones, who by reason of age can neither yet renounce the devil nor believe in God, is accomplished through the hearts and mouths of those who carry them. For it is also read in the Gospel that Jesus, seeing the faith of those who brought a paralytic to him for healing, said to him: “Man, your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew IX). Likewise, he raised the widow’s son from the dead, moved by compassion for her.

It is evident that, just as little ones have drawn sins from others—sins that are remitted to them in baptism—so through others they believe unto salvation. Even the mute and deaf, who can neither hear nor profess the faith, are brought by certain Christians for baptism, and are believed to be saved through the faith of those who bring them, because human weakness does not obstruct the grace of almighty God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the order of catechizing

The order of catechizing is as follows. First, the pagan is asked whether he renounces the devil and all his destructive works and deceitful pomp, so that he may first reject error and thus approach the truth. In accordance with the Apostle, he may then put off the old person according to his former way of life, which is corrupted according to the desires of error, renouncing impiety and worldly desires.

Next, the Creed of the apostolic faith is shown to him, and he is asked whether he believes in God the almighty Father; in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord; and in the Holy Spirit—one God in Trinity and unity; whether he confesses that there is one Catholic Church; and whether he believes in the remission of sins and the resurrection of the flesh.

If, therefore, he truly professes belief in all these things, he already begins through faith to put on the new person, who has been created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth. Yet he is fully clothed in this person when he is regenerated through the washing of baptism.

After he has commended himself, through confession of the true faith, to another lordship, and through renunciation of his former possessor has withdrawn himself from his service, the cruel power is breathed out of him, so that through the holy mystery performed by the priest the fleeing evil spirit may yield to the Holy Spirit.

The person is also marked with the sign of the holy cross, both on the forehead and on the heart, so that the apostate devil, recognizing in his former vessel the sign of his own destruction, may henceforth know that it belongs to another.

From then on prayers are said over him, so that he may become a catechumen. Then blessed salt is placed in his mouth, so that, seasoned by typical salt with the salt of wisdom, he may be free from the stench of iniquity and no longer decay through the worms of sin, but may instead be preserved unharmed for receiving greater grace.

Thereafter the devil is exorcised again, so that, recognizing his wickedness and fearing God’s just judgment against him, he may depart from the person and no longer attempt by his art to overthrow him and prevent him from obtaining baptism. Rather, displaying honor toward God his Creator, he should return his work to its Maker.

Afterward his nostrils and ears are touched with saliva, and the Gospel word spoken by Jesus when he healed the deaf and mute is said to him. When Jesus touched the man’s tongue with spittle and put his fingers into his ears, he said: “Ephphatha,” which means, “Be opened” (Mark VII).

This sacrament is performed here so that through the priest’s symbolic saliva and touch, divine wisdom and power may work the salvation of the catechumen. His nostrils are to be opened to receive the fragrance of the knowledge of God; his ears are to be opened to hear God’s commandments and to store them in the innermost sense of his heart.

Next he is fortified with the priestly blessing, so that he may be preserved with the faith he has received until holy baptism. His breast is then anointed with sanctified oil, with invocation of the holy Trinity, so that no hidden remnants of the enemy may remain in him, but that his mind may be strengthened in faith in the holy Trinity. He is also anointed between the shoulders with the same oil, so that he may be protected on every side and strengthened for the performance of good works to the glory of God.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On baptismal immersion and the anointing with chrism

After these things, the font having been consecrated, the catechumen approaches baptism itself and is baptized in the name of the holy Trinity by a threefold immersion.

Rightly so: the person who was created in the image of the holy Trinity is renewed into that same image through invocation of the holy Trinity; and the one who fell into death at the third stage of sin—that is, through consent—may, raised from the font a third time, rise by grace to life.

This threefold immersion can also signify the Lord’s three-day burial, especially when the Apostle says: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be planted together in his resurrection,” and so forth.

Baptism must therefore be completed with invocation of the holy Trinity through a threefold immersion, so that the mystery of baptism may be celebrated according to the distinction of the Persons, while, according to the unity of substance, there may be one baptism. Hence the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism,” and so forth.

After the baptized person has come up from the font, he is immediately signed on the head by a presbyter with sacred chrism, accompanied at the same time by prayer, so that he may become a participant in Christ’s kingdom and may be called a Christian from Christ.

It is also written in the Gospel: “When Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.”

The anointing with chrism rightly follows baptism, because the Holy Spirit, who through that chrism sanctifies believers by the imparting of his power, descended immediately upon the baptized Jesus in the form of a dove. The dove, moreover, prefigured this: the dove that, during the Flood, carried back to the ark a branch of olive with green leaves, signifying that through the anointing with chrism in baptism the Holy Spirit bestows upon the faithful the verdure of heavenly grace.

But we shall speak more fully about this in what follows.

We also read in the *Acts of the Fathers* that Pope Sylvester established in the Roman Church that, just as the power and privilege belong to the bishop alone—namely, that he himself should prepare the sacred chrism and sign the baptized person by the laying on of hands with that chrism, on account of heretical persuasion—so also a presbyter should anoint with the same chrism the baptized person who has been lifted from the water, because of the danger of death during the interval. For it is written by the Apostle: “But you, brothers, are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him,” and so forth.

It is therefore plainly evident that whoever does not belong to Christ cannot become a participant in his kingdom. It is consequently necessary that the baptized person be immediately assisted by the anointing with chrism, so that, receiving participation in the Holy Spirit, he may not remain alien to Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the clothing of the baptized and the Eucharist

After baptism, a white garment is given to the Christian, signifying Christian innocence and purity. After the old stains have been washed away, he must preserve this garment unstained through the discipline of holy conduct, in order to present himself before Christ’s tribunal.

All those reborn are clothed in white garments as a mystery of the Church’s resurrection, just as the Lord himself was transfigured before his disciples, as it is said: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow.” By this splendor, as has been said, he prefigured the future resurrection of the Church.

They therefore use white garments so that, whereas the infancy of their first birth had been darkened by the cloth of ancient error, the clothing of their second generation might display the garment of glory.

After the sacred anointing, his head is covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he bears the diadem of royal and priestly dignity, in accordance with the Apostle: “You are,” he says, “a royal and priestly race, offering yourselves to God as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice,” and so forth.

For in the Old Testament the priests always adorned their heads with a certain mystical veil.

Then the whole preceding sacrament is confirmed in him through the body and blood of the Lord. He ought to receive these so that he may be worthy to have God dwelling within him and may be a member of that head who suffered and rose for us.

Truth itself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” And again: “Unless you eat,” he says, “the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

## CHAPTER XXX. On the episcopal laying on of hands

Finally, through the laying on of hands by the chief priest, the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, is given to him, so that through the Holy Spirit he may be strengthened to preach to others the same gift that he himself received in baptism, having been granted eternal life by grace.

The baptized person is signed with chrism by the priest at the crown of the head, but by the bishop on the forehead. The first anointing signifies the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him, for the dwelling that is to be consecrated to God; the second declares that the sevenfold grace of that same Holy Spirit, with the fullness of holiness, knowledge, and power, comes upon the person.

Then the Holy Spirit himself, after bodies and souls have been cleansed and blessed, willingly descends from the Father, so that by his visitation he may sanctify and illumine his vessel. Now he comes upon the person for this purpose: that he may make him, filled with heavenly gifts and strengthened by his grace, bear fearlessly and boldly before the kings and powers of this age the seal of faith that he received on his forehead, and preach the name of Christ with a free voice.

It is no wonder if a person is anointed twice with the same chrism to receive the Holy Spirit, since the same Spirit was given twice to the Apostles: once on earth, when after his resurrection the Lord breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained”; and once from heaven, when after the Lord’s ascension, on the day of Pentecost, he came upon the Apostles in fiery tongues and granted them to speak in the languages of all nations.

Thus the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God in the Gospel, and the law was written by the finger of God. He is called the finger of God so that his operative power may be signified together with the Father and the Son.

Just as through baptism we die and are reborn in Christ, so we are signed by the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God and the spiritual seal.

It is entirely fitting that through sacred chrism and through the richness of the olive the grace of the Holy Spirit should be bestowed, because it is written in the psalm concerning Christ the Savior that God the Father anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions; and likewise concerning us, that he makes our face glad with oil.

Chrism, Greek *χρίσμα* (*chrisma*), is called in Latin *unctio*, “anointing.” From this name Christ is also called Christ, and through it a person is sanctified after the washing.

For just as in baptism the remission of sins is granted for forgiveness, so through anointing the sanctification of the Spirit is applied for glory. This is drawn from the example of the former anointing by which the ancients were accustomed to be anointed for the priesthood and kingship. Thus Aaron and his sons were anointed by Moses after the washing, so that they might become priests of the Lord. Solomon and the other kings were also poured over with oil from a horn by prophets and priests, so that they might hold the reins of royal government.

While this occurs bodily, it produces a spiritual benefit, just as the grace of baptism itself is a visible act—we are immersed in water—but its spiritual effect is that we are cleansed from transgressions.

Let us therefore examine the nature of oil itself, to see whether anything in it can be understood as corresponding to this meaning. Burning oil gives light; medicinal oil heals; and when poured into water, it makes the water clear. This can well demonstrate the grace of the Holy Spirit.

He illumines souls with the flame of charity and the splendor of wisdom. By the medicine of his mercy he heals the wounds of sins through forgiveness. By the imparting of his power he truly illuminates the waters of baptism, driving away the darkness of sins.

Holy Scripture also bears witness to this. Paul says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” And John says: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light.” And again: “You have an anointing from the Holy Spirit, and you know all things.”

The sayings of the Apostles thus show that through the anointing of the Holy Spirit we possess the light of charity and knowledge.

For the Savior shows in the Gospel that the Holy Spirit is the medicine of sins when through him he gave the Apostles the power to forgive sins, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,” and so forth.

That the grace of the Holy Spirit makes the waters of baptism fruitful and illumines them is indicated by John when he testifies that the Lord himself baptizes in the Holy Spirit, saying: “But the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

For the water of baptism could never beget children of light unless it had first been illumined by the gift of that same Holy Spirit, so that within it he might wondrously produce the birth of spiritual light—the same Spirit who in the beginning, together with the Father and the Son, created it suitable for purification.

The Lord therefore washed us from sins in baptism, anointed us, and sealed us with the Holy Spirit of promise. He gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts, which is truly the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the acquired possession and for the praise of his glory, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

“And because you are,” says the Apostle, “sons of God, he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”

For the confirmation of all holiness, power, and justice rests in him. He is the remission of all sins; he distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil. For “whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.”

He justifies and illumines the saints. He is God; he is the gift of God, because he is given by God. Through him the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each person for the common good: to one, the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of speeches.

All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills. For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, although many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we have all been given to drink of one Spirit.

We read in the Gospel that the Holy Spirit is called by the name of water, when the Lord himself cries out and says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink; whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The Evangelist explained what he meant, for he continued: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive.”

But the water of the sacrament is one thing, and the water that signifies the Holy Spirit is another. The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit is invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what is in the soul; through the latter—that is, through the Holy Spirit—the soul itself is cleansed.

Just as bodily water washes and gives drink to the body, so spiritual water washes and nourishes the spirit.

The Holy Spirit is called sevenfold because of the gifts which, according to the fullness of his divinity, each person, insofar as he is worthy, merits to obtain in particular measure. He is called the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord
But since we have already discussed above, insofar as the Lord has granted us understanding, two sacraments—that is, baptism and chrism—it remains for us now to investigate more carefully the other two, namely, the body and blood of the Lord, to the extent that the Lord may grant it.

First, we must ask why the Lord wished the mysteries of his body and blood to be consecrated in things that can be eaten and consumed, and not rather in things that, preserved with greater honor, could have remained intact for a longer time. Next, why did he wish the same sacrament to be given in food and drink, when people commonly use earthly fruits as terrestrial beings, rather than give it from some other substance which, received in the same way, would refresh them? Yet perhaps an unusual substance would have been revered even by the unlearned as a greater miracle, just as heavenly food, manna, nourished the people of Israel in the wilderness and rained down for all to marvel at.

It may also be asked why, among all the fruits of the earth, he chose above all wheat and wine for this purpose, as though these surpassed all the fruits of the earth in dignity and became more precious than all others. We believe, however, that all these questions can be resolved. For the Lord preferred the sacraments of his body and blood to be received by the mouths of the faithful and reduced to their nourishment, so that through a visible act an invisible effect might be shown. Just as material food externally nourishes and invigorates the body, so also the word of God inwardly nourishes and strengthens the soul, because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” And: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

Therefore Truth itself says: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Christ’s flesh is truly food because it truly feeds and nourishes a human being for eternal life; and his blood is truly drink because it truly satisfies forever the soul that hungers and thirsts for righteousness. Human beings can have temporal life without this food and drink, but they absolutely cannot have eternal life without them, because this food and drink signifies the eternal fellowship of the head and his members.

“He who eats my flesh,” he says, “and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Therefore we must receive his body and blood so that we may remain in him and be members of his body, because “no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III).

As for the fact that he wished these sacraments to be made from the fruits of the earth, the reason is this: since the Son of God himself became human on earth among human beings, and was born from earthly parents, namely, from the stock of Adam—“Truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm IV)—he made a heavenly food from earthly fruits in order to make earth-dwellers citizens of heaven. Just as the invisible God himself appeared as a mortal in visible flesh in order to save mortals, so also, fittingly, he showed them an invisible reality through visible matter, so that in the same reality they might learn both what God became for our sake and what we are to become through him.

The apostle John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John III).

Why he chose bread and wine for this dignity, Scripture explains when it testifies that the Holy Spirit declared Christ to be destined to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Genesis therefore relates that Melchizedek offered bread and wine (Genesis XIV). For it was fitting that the one who had become a priest according to the order of Melchizedek should himself, having become the chief priest, imitate the offering of that same priest, so that Scripture might be proved truthful in its declaration concerning him. Jesus did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, as Truth itself testifies: “How necessary it is,” he says, “that everything written about me in the law, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled.”

For this reason our Lord commended his body and blood in things that are reduced to one substance from many elements—whether from many grains or from unleavened loaves—in order to signify the unity of the saints in charity and to make understood the unity of his body and members, which is the holy Church in his predestined, called, justified, and glorified saints. Of these realities, the first has already taken place, namely, predestination; the second and third both have taken place, are taking place, and will take place, namely, calling and justification; but the fourth belongs to the future in reality, namely, glorification.

This sacrament of that reality—that is, the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is received from the Lord’s table by some for life and by others for destruction; but the reality itself is for life to every human being and for destruction to no one. Whoever becomes a participant in it—that is, whoever is joined as a member to Christ the head in the heavenly kingdom—[does so because] the sacrament is one thing and the power of the sacrament another. The sacrament is received by the mouth; by the power of the sacrament the inner person is satisfied. The sacrament is converted into bodily nourishment; through the power of the sacrament the dignity of eternal life is attained.

In the sacrament, all the faithful who communicate enter into a covenant of fellowship and peace. Through the power of the sacrament, all the members joined and united to their head will rejoice in eternal glory.

Therefore, just as it is converted into us when we eat and drink it, so we are converted into Christ’s body when we live obediently and devoutly. Yet the dignity and power of the sacrament itself—as we said above—is so great that whoever receives it unworthily acquires condemnation for himself rather than salvation. The Apostle shows this when he says: “Whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body” (1 Corinthians XI).

We truly and beneficially receive the body and blood of Christ, therefore, if we do not merely wish to eat and drink Christ’s flesh and blood in the sacrament, but eat and drink unto participation in the Spirit, so that we may remain in the Lord’s body as members and be nourished by his Spirit. The faithful therefore receive Christ’s body rightly and truly if they do not neglect to be Christ’s body, but become Christ’s body, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ. No one lives by the Spirit of Christ unless he is the body of Christ.

For this reason, when the Apostle explains this one bread, he wishes it to be understood as signifying the one body of Christ. “The cup of blessing,” he says, “which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all share in the one bread and the one cup.”

Nor is it permitted to offer anything else in the sacraments except what the Lord himself established and taught us to do by his example. For on the night when he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread and, giving thanks, broke it and said: “This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise, after he had supped, he took the cup, saying: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood; do this whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians XI).

Therefore unleavened bread and wine mixed with water ought to be sanctified as the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, because the Gospel relates that the Lord himself testified concerning these very things. For the Lord himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI). And again: “I am,” he says, “the true vine.” “The bread of God came down from heaven and gives life to the world”; the Father has sealed him, and God sent him into the world. “This is the bread of life; whoever eats this bread will never hunger.”

This bread strengthens the human heart; indeed, it has been produced from the earth, from our nature. This wine makes the human heart glad, and it proceeded from the true vine. For nothing other than wine can be born from a vine.

Therefore, because bread strengthens the body, it is suitably called Christ’s body. Wine, because it produces blood in the flesh, is accordingly referred to Christ’s blood. Although these things are visible once sanctified, through the Holy Spirit they pass into the sacrament of the divine body.

That the sacrificial bread ought to be without leaven is testified by the book of Leviticus, where the Lord is remembered as having commanded the children of Israel through Moses as follows: “Every offering that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven, and no leaven or honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord” (Leviticus VIII).

We therefore believe that the bread which the Lord first consecrated at the mystical supper as the mystery of his body was unleavened, especially since at the time of Passover no one was permitted either to eat leaven or even to have it in his house. The Lord commanded this in the law, as Exodus testifies: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, in the evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses; whoever eats leavened bread, that person shall perish from the assembly of Israel, whether he is a resident alien or a native of the land” (Exodus XII).

And shortly afterward: “You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days; nothing leavened shall be seen among you, nor within all your borders,” and so forth.

Since the people of God were not permitted to have it either in their houses or anywhere within all their borders, it is superfluous to suppose that the Lord sought it outside. What the prohibition against eating it at Passover signifies, the Apostle shows by explaining the meaning of Passover and unleavened bread in the clearest manner: “For our Passover has been sacrificed, Christ; therefore let us feast, not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians XI).

Whoever, therefore, approaches the Lord’s table—where the flesh of the immaculate and undefiled Lamb is sacrificed and where the venerable mysteries of his passion and resurrection are celebrated by the faithful—filled with deceit and malice, and, inflamed by the torches of hatred, envy, greed, or lust, does not fear to receive the Lord’s body, must beware lest, where he ought to receive life, he find the judgment of condemnation, and be driven more fiercely toward punishment than drawn back toward pardon.

For it is written concerning Judas the traitor, who approached the Lord’s table in wickedness and did not fear to take part in the sacred banquet, that after the morsel Satan immediately entered into him, and the Lord said to him: “What you are doing, do quickly.” Then he immediately went out and poured forth the manifest poison of his madness, which he had previously plotted in secret, so that a great crowd, equipped with swords and clubs, torches and weapons, came to seize him as though he were a robber—though he had come willingly to die.

Whoever, therefore, with plots hidden in his mind and with his inmost thoughts polluted by some crime, does not fear to participate in the most sacred offerings of Christ’s mysteries, betrays the Son of Man after the example of Judas—not indeed to the Jews, but to sinners, namely, to his own members, whom he presumes to profane that inestimable and inviolable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

He sells the Lord who, neglecting fear and love of him, is proved to love and pursue earthly and perishable things, indeed even criminal things, in his place.

But wine mixed with water ought to be offered in the sacrament, because the Gospel states that when one of the soldiers opened Jesus’ side with a spear, blood and water immediately came out. That blood was poured out for the remission of sins; that water tempers the saving cup and provides both washing and drink.

Neither of these, therefore, ought to be offered in the sacrifice without the other: neither wine without water nor water without wine. For we must remain in Christ and Christ in us. Saint Cyprian demonstrates this when he says:

“The Lord’s cup is offered mixed with wine, because we see the people signified by the water and Christ’s blood shown by the wine. When water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are united to Christ, and the community of believers is joined and united to the one in whom it believes. This union and conjunction of water and wine is so blended in the Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated from one another; so neither can the Church be divided and separated from Christ,” and so forth.

For, as John testifies, the water signifies the people. It is not permitted to offer either water alone or wine alone, just as one may not offer a grain of wheat alone without the addition of water and its being made into bread. Otherwise such an offering would signify that the head must be separated from the members and would presume either that Christ could suffer without the love of our redemption or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without his passion.

Nor should those be heeded who offer water without wine in the cup. Against them, let us quote a portion of the chapter from the book of the aforementioned martyr Cyprian, in which he discusses the sacrament of the cup.

There he resolves the question of whether the Lord’s cup ought to contain water alone or water mixed with wine. After the beginning of the letter, as he begins to resolve the question proposed, the same martyr says:

“Know that we have been admonished that the Lord’s tradition concerning what is to be offered in the cup must be observed. For we must do nothing other than what the Lord first did for us, so that the cup offered in his remembrance may be offered mixed with wine. For Christ says: ‘I am the true vine.’ Christ’s blood is certainly not water but wine; nor can his blood, by which we have been redeemed and justified, be seen to be in the cup when wine is absent from the cup, by which Christ’s blood is shown and proclaimed according to the sacrament and testimony of all the Scriptures.

“For we find that this same matter was prefigured earlier in Genesis concerning the sacrament of Noah, and that the figure of the Lord’s passion was there displayed: that he drank wine, that he became drunk, that he was uncovered in his house, that he lay naked, with his thighs exposed; that the nakedness of that father was uncovered by the middle son, but covered by the elder and the younger, and the other details, which it is not necessary to pursue now. It is enough to embrace this one point: that we show Noah to have displayed a type of the future Truth, that he drank not water but wine, and thus expressed an image of the Lord’s passion.

“Likewise, in the priest Melchizedek, we see the mystery of the Lord’s sacrament prefigured, as divine Scripture testifies and says: ‘And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine; he was priest of the Most High God, and he blessed Abraham’ (Genesis XIV).

“That Melchizedek bore a type of Christ, the Holy Spirit declares in the Psalms, speaking from the person of the Father to the Son: ‘Before the morning star I begot you; you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’ (Psalm CIX).”

Some say that, unless prevented by some sin, the Eucharist should be received daily. For we ask that this bread be given to us daily, as the Lord commands, saying: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew VI). They approve this, provided that they receive it with reverence, devotion, and humility, and do not do so with proud presumption, trusting in their own righteousness.

But if their crimes are such that they should be removed from the altar as though dead, they must first undertake penance and then receive the saving medicine. “Whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” To receive it unworthily means receiving it at a time when one ought to be separated from the table of the Lord’s body, lest perhaps someone, being barred after a long absence, be separated from Christ’s body.

It is evident that those who touch his body live. Therefore we must fear lest, while someone is separated for a long time from Christ’s body, he remain alienated from salvation, since Christ himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have a share with me, nor life in yourselves” (John VI). Whoever has already ceased from sinning should not cease from communicating.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Office of the Mass

We have, as I think, said enough above about the sacraments. Now let us speak briefly about the office of the Mass, by which the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood are effected, since the order of the subject requires it.

Although there are many kinds of offices, nevertheless that which is performed in sacred and divine matters is especially to be designated by the name “office,” because the greater the dignity of the matter itself, the more prepared and prompt an execution it requires.

“Office” is said from *efficere*, “to effect,” as though it were *efficium*, with one letter changed for the sake of elegant expression.

“Sacrifice” means, as it were, “a sacred thing made,” because it is consecrated by mystical prayer in remembrance of the Lord’s passion; accordingly, at his command, what is sanctified from the fruits of the earth into Christ’s body and the Lord’s blood becomes a sacrament through the invisible working of God’s Spirit. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and cup “Eucharist,” Greek *εὐκαριστία* (*eucharistia*), which is interpreted in Latin as “good grace.” And what is better than the body and blood of Christ?

A sacrament is present in a celebration when, through the performance of an act, something is made to signify something else; this must be received in a holy manner.

The *missa* is the dismissal at the time of the sacrifice, when the catechumens are sent outside, the Levite crying out: “If any catechumen remains, let him go outside.” Hence it is called *missa*, because those known not yet to have been regenerated cannot be present at the sacraments of the altar.

The Mass is also a legation between God and human beings. The priest performs the office of this legation when he offers the people’s vows to God through prayers and supplications. It is fitting that this occur at the time of the sacrifice, when the memory of the passion is celebrated—namely, of Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, who offered himself to the Father for us.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the teacher, first established this manner of sacrifice when, before he was handed over, he entrusted his body and blood to his Apostles, as it is read in the Gospel: “Jesus took bread and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, saying: ‘Take; this is my body.’ And having taken the cup and given thanks, he gave it to them” (Matthew XXVI); and they all drank from it, and so forth.

With blessing and thanksgiving the Lord first dedicated the sacraments of his body and blood and handed them over to the Apostles. From then on, the Apostles imitated this practice and taught their successors to do the same. The whole Church throughout the world now generally observes it.

At the beginning, however, this custom of singing, which is now practiced in the Church before the sacrifice, did not exist; nevertheless, Paul’s Epistles and the holy Gospel were read.

Celestine, the forty-fifth bishop of the Roman Church after Peter, is said to have first established that all 150 psalms should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice.

It is also reported that Pope Telesphorus, the ninth after Peter, established long before this that the hymn “Glory to God in the highest” should be said before the sacrifice. This, however, is now not always done, but only on Sundays and on the feasts of the saints, as Pope Symmachus, the fifty-sixth after Peter, commanded it to be done.

But since we had begun to speak about the celebration of the sacrifice, let us proceed according to the proper arrangement by which the whole order has been instituted.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Order of the Mass

First, in the celebration of the Mass, when the priest enters the altar, an antiphon is sung by the clergy, so that a sound may be heard when he enters the sanctuary in the sight of the Lord, just as in the Old Testament the entrance of the high priest was announced by the sound of bells.

It is therefore fitting that, at the priest’s entrance, divine praise should be heard in the harmony of resounding choirs, so that the ministers’ devout concord may precede the mysteries of the Lord’s celebration and a sacrifice of worthy praise may precede the venerable sacrament of Christ’s body and blood.

A choir is a multitude gathered for sacred purposes. It is called a choir because at the beginning they stood around the altars in the form of a crown and thus sang the psalms. Hence the book of Ecclesiasticus also speaks of a priest standing before the altar, with a crown of brothers around him.

Others have said that *chorus* comes from concord, which consists in charity, or from the harmony of sound.

When one person sings, it is called in Greek *monodia* (*μονῳδία*), in Latin *sicinium*. When two sing, it is called *bicinium*; when many sing, it is called a choir.

The Greek word *antiphona* (*ἀντίφωνη*) means “reciprocal voice”; it is so called because two choirs sing the psalms alternately.

After the priest’s entrance to the altar, litanies are conducted by the clergy, so that a general prayer may precede the priest’s particular prayer. The priest’s prayer follows; and first greeting the people with a peaceful salutation, he receives from them the response of peace, so that true concord and pure devotion of charity may more readily obtain what they ask from the one who sees hearts and judges inner thoughts.

Then the lector reads the canonical lesson, so that the minds of the hearers, instructed by it, may rise with greater attentiveness to what follows.

After this, the cantor sings the responsory, in order to provoke compunction and make the minds of the listeners gentle. It is called a responsory because, when one person has finished, another responds.

The difference between responsories and antiphons is that in responsories one person sings the verse, whereas in antiphons the choirs alternate in the verses. The Greeks are said to have discovered antiphons first, and the Italians responsories.

Some call this responsory a gradual because it is sung beside the steps of the reading desk.

After the responsory, the Alleluia is sung, so that it may lift the people’s minds toward heavenly things and raise them to divine contemplation.

“Alleluia” is the interpretation of two words, namely, “praise of God,” and it is Hebrew. *Ia* is one of the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

Likewise, “amen” is Hebrew, and the faithful people respond with it to every prayer or blessing of the priest. *Amen* may also be translated into Latin as “truly,” “faithfully,” or “let it be.” Jerome bears witness to this in the Psalter, where he says: “Let it be, let it be”; in Hebrew it reads, “Amen, amen.”

These two words, however—namely, “amen” and “alleluia”—may not be transferred entirely into the language of the Greeks, Latins, or barbarians, nor announced in another language. Although they can be interpreted, the Apostles preserved their antiquity in their proper language because of their greater sacred authority.

They are such sacred names that John also relates in the Apocalypse that, by revelation of the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of the heavenly host, like the sound of many waters and of mighty thunder, saying “Amen and Alleluia” (Apocalypse XIX). Therefore both words ought to be spoken on earth as they resound in heaven.

Then the Gospel is recited by the deacon with the greatest authority in the hearing of the people, so that the teaching of the one toward whom all attention burns may be heard there, and so that his power may be understood through the Gospel, since the most holy mystery of his body is then celebrated.

Thereupon offerings are presented by the people, and the offertory is sung by the clergy. It takes its name from the act itself, as though it were “the song of those offering.”

A corporal cloth is placed over the altar. It signifies the linen in which the Savior’s body was wrapped. It ought to be woven from pure linen, not from silk or purple cloth, nor from dyed fabric, as we find instituted by Pope Sylvester. For the Gospel states that the Savior’s body was wrapped in a clean shroud by Joseph, and that after the Lord’s resurrection the head-cloth was found not lying with the linen wrappings but wrapped separately.

At that time the sacred vessels—the chalice and paten—are also placed upon the altar. In a certain way they have the form of the Lord’s tomb: just as Christ’s body, anointed with spices, was placed in a new tomb through the pious service of the faithful, so now his mystical body, seasoned with the ointments of sacred prayer, is administered in sacred vessels through the ministry of priests for the faithful to receive.

Afterward the Mass is sung by the priest. Having spoken to the people about lifting their hearts to God and exhorted them to give thanks to the Lord, he fills his mouth with praises and asks that God the almighty Father, whom the heavenly powers serve, by his grace command human confessions to be joined to their voices.

This supplication is immediately followed by praise composed of angelic and human songs:

“Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of your glory,” and so forth.

Then the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood takes place, together with a powerful prayer to God, during which the Lord’s Prayer is also sung.

After the point has been reached at which they are to communicate and receive the body, they give one another the kiss of peace, singing:

“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us,”

so that, receiving the sacrament of peace, they may deserve to be joined, with all sins forgiven, to the number of the children of God.

After Communion, and after the song of the same name, the priest gives a blessing to the people. The deacon then proclaims that the office of the Mass has been completed and gives permission to depart.

The Roman Church holds this order as handed down by the Apostles and by apostolic men, and throughout almost the whole of the West all the churches preserve the same tradition.

But since we have explained the sacred orders, the four sacraments, and the office of the Mass, we judge that this book should here be brought to an end. In what follows, if the Lord grants it, we shall report more fully on the remaining offices and observances.

## Addition Concerning the Mass

Anastasius, a Roman by nationality and son of Maximus—as is recorded in the episcopal acts—established that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests and the rest of the people should not sit but stand.

Then a prayer for his own sins and for the remission of the people, so that he may be worthy to approach the altar and touch the offerings, lest what happened to the men of Beth-shemesh, who rashly touched the ark of the Lord, happen to him also (1 Kings V).

After receiving the offerings, the priest returns to the altar, washes his hands, and cleanses them from contact with ordinary hands and earthly bread. From the offering the priest makes two crosses beside the chalice, to teach that Christ was taken down from the cross and crucified for the sake of the two peoples.

The elevation by the priest and deacon of Christ’s body and blood signifies his elevation upon the cross for the salvation of the whole world.

The cloth spread over the altar shows the Lord’s body stretched out upon the cross. Upon it, the consecrated body and blood of the Lord are placed, which we eat. The water and wine in the chalice show the sacraments that flowed from the Lord’s side on the cross, by which we have been given to drink.

The placing of bread into the wine is observed and performed in various ways among different people. The Italians first place a portion of the holy bread into the chalice and afterward say, “The peace of the Lord”; others reserve the placing until the peace has been celebrated and the bread broken.

The Romans, when they say, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you,” place the Lord’s body—the portion of the offering—into the chalice.

The body itself shows before our eyes the one who was crucified for us. It touches the four sides of the chalice because through it he joins the human race from the four regions of the world into the unity of one body and brings it into the peace of the catholic and apostolic Church.

With these words he places the Lord’s body into the chalice:

“May this commixture of the body and blood of the Lord, received by us, bring salvation of mind and body unto eternal life.”

Then the people make peace, so that it may be shown that we are members of the one who was crucified for us and rose again.

After peace has been made, the priest breaks the offering from the right side, leaving one portion upon the altar, and places the remaining offerings upon the paten held by the deacon.

By the portion of the offering placed into the chalice, he shows Christ’s body, which has already risen from the dead.

By the portion eaten by the priest and the people, he shows that after the resurrection Christ still walked on earth with his disciples and offered himself as food.

By the portion left upon the altar, he signifies that Christ lies in the tomb and was abandoned by the disciples during the passion.

It is asked at what point the office of the Mass begins and, if someone should happen not to attend the entire office, where he ought to be present at the beginning of the Mass. It seems to us that the Mass is called by that name from the point at which the priest begins to offer sacrifice to God up to the final blessing, when the Levite cries out and says: “Go, the dismissal has taken place.”

# BOOK TWO

## CHAPTER I. On the Offices and Prayers of the Canonical Hours

The office of the Mass, which we composed in the preceding book, pertains for the most part solely to the priest, who has been granted permission to sacrifice and to consecrate the venerable mysteries.

But since this office has been placed first because of its reverence and dignity, let us now explain, in due order, the other offices of the day and night hours, at which, at fixed intervals, it is fitting for all the churches generally, without distinction, to offer prayers and supplications to the Lord.

Prayer is called a petition, for *orare* means “to ask,” just as *exorare* means “to obtain through entreaty.”

Prayer is determined by place and time. By place, because we are forbidden by Christ to pray everywhere publicly or in the streets in the manner of the Pharisees; rather, we should pray where opportunity permits or necessity requires.

This is not contrary to what the Apostle says when he writes to Timothy: “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or dispute,” and so forth (1 Timothy II). Nor is it contrary to what the Psalmist says: “In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul” (Psalm CII).

These words, however, refer to the inner realities by which we ought always to pray to and bless God. Therefore the person who prays to God in every place is the one who strives everywhere, through acts of charity and good works, to raise pure hands of the heart to God.

Prayer is also determined by time, because the Church continually observes the canonical hours established by the Fathers for prayer. These hours, as though statues of the obligation of entreaty, may in no way be neglected: they are the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours, evening, and the others that are likewise observed.

Nor does what the Psalmist says confuse this arrangement: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII). And the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing,” and so forth (1 Thessalonians V).

To bless God at all times means always to praise him through a worthy manner of life; and to pray without ceasing means to do everything for the glory of God, as the same Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians X).

The aforesaid hours have therefore been set apart especially for prayer, so that, if we should happen to be detained by some task, the appointed time itself may remind us of our duty.

These times are found established in the divine Scriptures. In the Old Testament, it was commanded that incense be burned to the Lord every day, morning and evening. David says: “In the evening, morning, and at noon, I shall declare and proclaim, and he will hear my voice” (Psalm CX). And again: “Seven times a day I have praised you.”

The holy prophet Daniel also went up to his upper room at the third, sixth, and ninth hours of the day to entreat the Lord; with his hands extended toward heaven, he prayed to God for himself and for the people of Israel.

## CHAPTER II. On the Celebration of Matins

David the prophet first testified concerning the antiquity of Matins, saying: “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the light” (Psalm CX). And again: “In the morning I shall meditate on you.” And again: “My eyes have anticipated you at dawn, that I might meditate on your words.”

Prayer is offered at dawn so that Christ’s resurrection may be celebrated. At the morning watch, the Lord, leading Israel through the Red Sea, drowned Pharaoh and the Egyptians in it; and at the morning hour Christ, rising from death and saving his people, condemned the devil and his followers to eternal captivity.

As the morning light shone, our Lord and Savior rose from the underworld. Then the light that had set for sinners when Christ died began to rise for the faithful.

At that same time, moreover, the hope of the future resurrection is believed to be granted, when the righteous and all who have died this temporal death will rise and awaken as from the sleep of slumber.

## CHAPTER III. On the Office of the First Hour

The celebration of the first hour takes place because, at the rising of day, when the sun first appears from the east, we ought to ask that the Sun of Righteousness rise, so that, walking in his light, we may escape the darkness of sins and the snares of death.

This accords with what Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John XII). And again: “Whoever walks in the day does not stumble” (John X).

## CHAPTER IV. On the Celebration of the Third Hour
[Col. 0327B] The office of the third hour is performed for this reason: at the third hour Christ’s Passion began, when the Lord was then crucified by the tongues of the Jews; and after his resurrection, at the third hour on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. At its proper place and number, as proof of the venerable Trinity, the Spirit Paraclete descended to earth, to fulfill the grace that Christ promised.

## CHAPTER V. On the office of the sixth hour

At the sixth hour Christ ascended the altar of the cross, offering himself to the eternal Father so that he might free us from the power of the enemy and from everlasting death. Therefore it is fitting that at that hour he should find us praying and entreating him in his praises—the hour at which, through his [Col. 0327C] Passion, he restored us to eternal life.

## CHAPTER VI. On the office of the ninth hour

The ninth hour is consecrated for this reason: at it the Lord, making petition for his enemies, commended his spirit into the hands of the Father. Accordingly, all the faithful ought to commend themselves to God with devout prayer, since at that hour they recognize that he commended his own soul to his Father, so that, united with his body, they may be able to enter with him into the everlasting kingdom.

It is also worthy of consideration that throughout all these intervals of time the number three shines forth as sufficiently venerable, admonishing us that, after the course of three hours, as we perform each of these offices, we should celebrate the Holy Trinity with sacred praises. [Col. 0327D] The apostles themselves are also read to have observed the prescribed times of these offices. Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles that Peter, on the day when he experienced the vision of the vessel containing the various creatures, went up at the sixth hour for the sake of prayer (Acts 10). Likewise: “Peter and John,” it says, “were going up into the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer” (Acts 3).

## CHAPTER VII. On the celebration of evening prayer

The evening office takes place at the setting of the daylight, and its solemn celebration derives from the Old Testament. Indeed, at this time it was customary for the sacrifices of the ancients to be offered and burned, and for spices and incense to be placed upon the altar, as we said above. The witness to this is that hymn-singing man, [Col. 0328A] who exercised both royal and priestly office, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting of my hands like the evening sacrifice.”

In the New Testament also, at that time our Lord and Savior, while the apostles were dining, first entrusted to them the mystery of his body and blood, so that the time itself might signify the evening of the world. Therefore, in honor and remembrance of such great mysteries, it is fitting for us at these times to be present before God’s sight and to raise our voices, offering him the sacrifice of our prayers in his worship and rejoicing together in his praises.

Evening is called *vesper* from the star called Vesper, which rises when the sun declines; concerning it the prophet says: “And he causes evening to be brought forth over the children of men” (Job 38).

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0328B] On Compline
