We also find examples of the celebration of Compline among the Fathers, the prophet David saying: “If I ascend into the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Psalm 131).

Who would not be astonished at such devotion of mind in the love of God, if he did not entirely forbid himself sleep, without which human bodies necessarily grow weak, until the king and prophet should find in his heart a place and temple to be built for the Lord? This ought powerfully to admonish us that, if we ourselves wish to be the Lord’s place and his dwelling, and desire to be regarded as his temple, we should imitate the examples of the saints as far as we can, lest what is written be said of us: “They slept their sleep, and found nothing,” and what follows.

Around the eleventh hour, that is, at the end of the day, when the time of this office occurs, we believe that the Savior’s body was placed in the tomb. Accordingly, the solemn celebration of this course also ought to be observed, and we ought earnestly to ask that he who at this hour entered the rest of the tomb may deign to grant us eternal rest in heaven.

## CHAPTER IX. On the nocturnal celebration of the vigils

The celebration of the nightly vigils is also an ancient institution; devotion to the vigils is a familiar good among all the saints. Isaiah also cries out [Col. 0328D] to God, saying: “By night my spirit watches for you, O Lord, because your commandments are light upon the earth.”

David too, consecrated by royal and prophetic anointing, sings thus: “At midnight I arose to give thanks to you, because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118).

At this time, the destroying angel passed through and struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians. Therefore we too ought to keep awake, lest we be involved in the danger of the Egyptians. The Savior also affirmed in the Gospel that he would come during these same hours. Thus, stirring his hearers to watchfulness, he said: “Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke 12). “Watch, therefore, for you do not know when the Lord will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning, lest, [Col. 0329A] when he comes, he find you sleeping” (Mark 13).

And so that it might not be thought that this command was given only to the apostles, he immediately added: “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch.”

Indeed, he taught vigils not only by words but also confirmed them by example, for the Gospel testifies that Jesus spent the night in prayer to God. Paul and Silas also, while held in the public prison, are remembered to have prayed and sung a hymn at about midnight, bound as they were, with everyone listening (Acts 19). Then, when an earthquake suddenly occurred, the foundations of the prison were shaken, the door opened of its own accord, and everyone’s bonds were loosed.

Therefore, during these hours we ought to maintain regularity in psalmody and prayer in the holy offices, and await our end with confidence—even if it should come while we are engaged in such an activity.

There is, however, a certain kind [Col. 0329B] of heretics who regard sacred vigils as superfluous and spiritually fruitless. They say that God’s ordinances are being violated, since God made the night for rest just as he made the day for work. These heretics are called in Greek *nystages*, νυσταγεῖς, that is, “sleep-lovers” or “drowsy ones.”

This, however, is the catholic order of divine celebrations, which is steadfastly observed by the whole Church of Christ.

## CHAPTER X. On the other prescribed prayers

There are also other prescribed prayers that are owed without any admonition, such as the prayer we say before beginning any work, asking for the Lord’s help. For it is not fitting for a Christian to begin any undertaking on his own presumption before taking care to call upon the Lord for assistance, since he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

When humbly called upon, he deigns to help us, as it is written concerning him: “He will call upon me, and I will answer him; I am with him in trouble, I will rescue him and glorify him,” and what follows (Psalm 90).

Nor is it permitted to take food before prayer has been inserted, for the refreshments of the spirit must come first, before those of the flesh, since heavenly things come before earthly things. Likewise, it is fitting to pray after food, so that thanks may be returned to the Lord for his gifts, and so that what the Psalmist says may be fulfilled in this matter: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him” (Psalm 21).

## CHAPTER XI. [Col. 0329D] On private prayers

To offer private prayers frequently and sincerely is both good and praiseworthy, because the examples of many Fathers urge us to do so. The Lord himself also deigned to teach us this by his instruction, saying: “But when you pray, enter your room, and after shutting the door pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6).

This should not be done with a loud voice, but with concentration of heart and compunction expressed through tears, because we believe that in this way we are heard by the Lord, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping,” and what follows (Psalm 6). Likewise: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” [Col. 0330A] (Psalm 5).

For the Truth himself taught us to pray constantly and insistently when he said: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7).

And to commend the same matter more forcefully by an example, he brought forward the parable of a man who asked his friend, shut inside a room, for three loaves of bread. Making a comparison between bread and a stone, a fish and a serpent, an egg and a scorpion, he finally concluded the account in this way: “If you, then,” he said, “although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XII. On the fourfold form of prayers

The Apostle distinguished the form of prayers in a fourfold manner, saying: “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Timothy 8). We must not doubt that these were divided by the Apostle in this way for a reason.

For it cannot be believed that the Holy Spirit spoke anything through the Apostle casually or without purpose. Therefore, we must first investigate what is signified by supplication, prayer, petition, and thanksgiving; then we must inquire whether these four forms are to be taken up equally by every person who prays, or whether one person ought to offer supplications to God, another prayers, another petitions, and another thanksgivings.

Each person should apply himself according to the measure of his own age—that is, according to the stage at which each mind advances through devotion and diligence. Supplications, therefore, are implorations or petitions for sins, by which each person, pierced with remorse for sins either present or past, begs for pardon.

Prayers are those by which we offer or vow something to God. For example, we pray when, renouncing this world, its actions, and its worldly way of life, we promise that we shall serve the Lord with such wholehearted devotion. We pray when we promise that we shall continually offer the purest chastity of body or steadfast patience; or when we vow to uproot completely from our heart the roots of anger or of sorrow that produces death.

In third place come petitions, which we customarily utter for others as well, while we are established in spiritual fervor—whether asking for our dear ones or for the peace of the whole world. In the words of the Apostle, we supplicate “for all people, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority.”

In fourth place come thanksgivings, which the mind offers either when it recalls God’s past benefits, or when it embraces those of the present, or when it foresees what and how great are the things God has prepared in the future for those who love him. Through unspeakable transports, the mind returns thanks to the Lord. With this intention, more abundant prayers are sometimes poured forth, when, gazing with pure eyes upon the rewards that have been set in the future, our spirit is stirred to pour out thanksgiving with immense joy.

## CHAPTER XIII. [Col. 0331A] How compunction arises from these forms

From these four forms, occasions for abundant supplications are also accustomed to arise. From the form of supplication, which is born from compunction for sins; from the state of prayer, which flows from confidence in one’s offerings and in the fulfillment of future things, through purity of conscience; from petition, which proceeds from the ardor of charity; and from thanksgiving, which is generated by consideration of his benefits, greatness, and loving-kindness—we very often vow most fervent prayers, and unknown ones come forth.

Thus it is also established that all the forms mentioned above are found useful and necessary for all people, so that in one and the same person they may produce varied and pure, fervent movements of supplication: now of supplication, now of prayer, now of petition, and now of thanksgiving.

The first seems especially to belong to those who are still tormented by the sting and memory of their vices. The second belongs to those who, already advancing in spiritual progress and aspiring to virtue, stand at a certain elevation of mind. The third belongs to those who, fulfilling the vows of their own perfection through their works, are moved by charity to intercede also for others out of consideration for their weakness.

The fourth belongs to those who, having already driven the thorn of a guilty conscience from their hearts, recall with the purest mind the Lord’s singular acts of generosity and mercy—whether those he granted in the past, bestows in the present, or prepares in the future—and are carried with a most fervent heart into that fiery prayer which the mouths of human beings can neither comprehend nor express.

Sometimes, however, the mind that advances toward that true disposition of purity and begins to take root in it conceives all these things together and at once. Sweeping through them all like a certain incomprehensible and fiercely consuming flame, it sends them forth to God ineffably, conceiving in the moment of that hour and pouring out in supplication as much as it cannot merely utter with its mouth, but cannot even recall at another time with its own mind.

## CHAPTER XIV. On exomologesis, that is, confession

*Exomologesis*—ἐξομολόγῆσις—is called by a Greek word that is interpreted in Latin as *confessio*, “confession.” This term has a double meaning. For confession is understood either as praise, as in: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth”; or as the disclosure of sins, when each person confesses to God his sins, so that they may be forgiven by him whose mercy is unfailing.

Thus the Greek word *exomologesis* expresses and denotes our confessing our offense to the Lord—not, indeed, as though he were ignorant, since nothing is hidden from his knowledge. Hence Wisdom says: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28).

Confession is, properly speaking, an avowed recognition of a matter that was previously unknown. Someone had considered it useful and pleasant to act, commit adultery, or steal; but once he recognizes that these things make him liable to eternal damnation, having come to know them, he confesses his error.

Confession of error is a declaration of the intention to cease. One must therefore cease from sins: while confession is made, confession precedes and forgiveness follows. Otherwise, the person who recognizes his sin but does not confess what he has recognized is outside the way. The Psalmist instructed us concerning him, saying: “Reveal your way to the Lord,” and so forth (Psalm 36). He also testifies that he himself did this, saying: “I said: I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord,” and so forth.

The Apostle James likewise exhorts us to do the same, saying: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another,” and so forth (James 5).

Thus *exomologesis* is a discipline of prostrating oneself and humbling oneself before people: bending the body in a poor garment and with meager food, in sackcloth and ashes, darkening it with filth, casting down the spirit through grief, and changing through sorrowful treatment those things by which one has sinned.

## CHAPTER XV. On litanies

Litanies—λιτανείᾳ—are called by a Greek name; in Latin they are called *rogationes*, “supplications” or “petitions.” The difference between litanies and *exomologesis* is that *exomologesis* is performed solely through confession of sins, whereas litanies are appointed for entreating the Lord and obtaining some mercy from him.

The name *supplication* is retained in a certain manner from pagan custom. Among them, festivals were either regular or specially proclaimed. The proclaimed ones were so called because the ancient poverty of the Romans offered sacrifices from contributions, or from certain goods of condemned persons. Hence punishments are called supplications, which were made from goods derived from the punishment of those who had suffered it. Sacred things were made from the possessions of accursed persons.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the distinction of the Lord’s Prayer

In the evangelist Matthew, the Lord’s Prayer appears to contain seven petitions. In three of them eternal things are requested, and in the remaining four temporal things, which nevertheless are necessary for attaining eternal things.

For what we say—“Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven and on earth”—they rightly understood as things that must be retained altogether, without end, in spirit and body. They begin here and increase in us as much as we progress; but in the other life, as we hope, they will be possessed perfectly and forever.

But when we say: “Give us today our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil,” who does not see that these petitions pertain to the needs of the present life?

In that eternal life where we hope always to be, the sanctification of God’s name, his kingdom, and his will will remain perfectly and immortally in our spirit and body. Daily bread, however, is so called because here it is necessary, in whatever measure it must be supplied to soul and body—whether it is understood spiritually, bodily, or in both ways.

Here also is the forgiveness that we request, where there is the entire remission of sins. Here are the temptations that entice or compel us to sin; here, finally, is the evil from which we desire to be delivered. There, however, none of these things exists.

The evangelist Luke, in the Lord’s Prayer, included not seven but five petitions. He did not thereby disagree with Matthew, but by his brevity he indicated how the seven are to be understood. God’s name is sanctified in the spirit, while God’s kingdom will come in the resurrection of the flesh.

Thus Luke shows that the third petition is, in a certain sense, a repetition of the two preceding ones. By placing it earlier, he made this more readily understood. He then adds three others: concerning daily bread, the remission of sins, and the avoidance of temptation.

But what Matthew placed last—“But deliver us from evil”—Luke did not include, so that we might understand it as belonging to what was said above about temptation. For he says “but deliver,” not “and deliver,” as though demonstrating that the petition is: “Do not do this, but do that.” Thus each person may know that he is delivered from evil precisely in that he is not led into temptation.

This prayer, although it appears to contain the whole fullness of perfection, since it was either initiated or established by the authority of the Lord himself, nevertheless advances his household to that higher state mentioned above and leads them by a more elevated step to that fiery prayer known and experienced by very few—or rather, as I said earlier, ineffable prayer.

Our Lord likewise represented this state in the form of those supplications that he is described as having poured forth either alone, withdrawing onto the mountain, or silently; and when he was engaged in the agony of prayer, he poured out drops of blood in an incomparable example of concentration.

For whoever wishes his prayer to fly to the Lord should give it two wings: fasting and almsgiving. Then it will rise swiftly and be heard.

Fasting, therefore, together with prayer, overcomes all the enemy’s power and drives away all his insolence. The Lord showed this in the Gospel when the apostles complained that they could not cure an epileptic; he answered them: “This kind cannot be driven out except by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17).

The book of the Acts of the Apostles also confirms that almsgiving assists and strengthens prayer, when it reports that the angel said to the centurion Cornelius: “Cornelius, your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended into the sight of the Lord” (Acts 10).

But we shall speak first about fasting and afterward about almsgiving. For who would not praise moderation, remembering that the first human being fell through the appetite of the stomach? Who would not proclaim fasting, knowing that our first parent, the protoplast, was conquered through eating, while the Savior conquered the devil through fasting?

## CHAPTER XVII. On fasting

Fasting is a holy thing, a heavenly work, the gate of the kingdom, and an image of the life to come. Whoever practices it in holiness is joined to God, separated from the world, and made spiritual. Through it [Col. 0334A] vices are overthrown, the flesh is humbled, and the devil’s temptations are conquered.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What is the difference between fasting and a station?

Fasting is moderation in food and abstinence from nourishment. Its name is derived from a certain part of the entrails that is always thin and empty, commonly called the *jejunum*. Hence the name *jejunium* is derived, because through hunger its entrails remain empty and drained.

Fasting is also called a station. “Station” takes its name from military practice, because no joy that comes upon a camp breaks the soldiers’ station. Joy administers discipline more freely, while sorrow administers it more anxiously.

Some distinguish between fasting and a station. Fasting is abstinence on any day indiscriminately, not imposed by law but undertaken according to one’s own will. A station is the observance of appointed days or times.

Of days: Wednesday and Friday, on which fasting was commanded according to the ancient law. Concerning this station, the man in the Gospel said: “I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke 18), that is, on the fourth and sixth days of the week.

Of times: those established at fixed periods by legal or prophetic institutions—for example, the fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth; or, as in the Gospel, those days on which the bridegroom was taken away; or the observance of Lent, which throughout the world is kept by apostolic institution around the time of the Lord’s Passion.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months

[Col. 0334C]

The fast of the fourth month is in July, on the seventeenth day of that month, when Moses, descending from the mountain, broke the tablets of the Law. On that same day Nebuchadnezzar first destroyed the walls of the city of Jerusalem.

The day of the fast of the fifth month is in August, when, because of the scouts sent into the Holy Land, sedition arose in the camp of the Hebrews, and it came about that they wandered laboriously through the wilderness for forty years, and that within those forty years they all perished in the desert.

Indeed, in that month the Temple was also overturned and burned by Nebuchadnezzar, and much later by Caesar Titus; and it was ploughed up as a reproach to the ruined nation.

The day of the fast of the seventh month is in the seventh month, called September, [Col. 0334D] in which Goliath was killed and the rest who were in Jerusalem were slain, as Jeremiah says (Jeremiah 36).

The day of the fast of the tenth month is in the tenth month, which among us is called December. At that time all those carried away to Babylon learned that the Temple had been destroyed in the fifth month, and they mourned and fasted.

The most blessed Jerome wrote this in his commentaries on Zechariah. But since these fasts were celebrated more in the Old Testament than in the New, so that we might not seem to have passed them over entirely, since they are mentioned in the prophet Zechariah, we have briefly noted them and proceed to explain the fasts of the New Testament.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 0335A] On the Lenten fast

The first fast is the fast of Lent, which originated in the ancient books from the fasts of Moses and Elijah, and from the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days. In this way he demonstrated that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets.

In the person of Moses, the Law is understood; in the person of Elijah, the prophets. Between them Christ appeared in glory upon the mountain, so that it might more clearly stand forth what the Apostle says concerning him: “Bearing testimony from the Law and the Prophets.”

In what part of the year could the observance of Lent have been established more appropriately than adjacent and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion, since it signifies this laborious life? This life also requires self-restraint, so that we may fast from the allurements of the world itself, living on manna alone—that is, on heavenly and spiritual commandments.

This life is represented by the number forty because ten is the perfection of our blessedness. The creature, however, is represented by the number seven, since it clings to the Creator; in this the unity of the Trinity is proclaimed throughout the temporal world.

And because the world is described by the four winds, is raised up from the four elements, and is varied by the four cycles of the seasons, ten multiplied by four is completed in forty. By this number it is shown that we must abstain and fast from every temporal pleasure and live chastely and continently. Yet another mystery of the sacrament is also expressed in the fact that these same fasts are celebrated for forty days.

For the Mosaic Law generally commanded the whole people [Col. 0335C] to offer tithes and firstfruits to the Lord God. Thus, when by this teaching we are admonished to refer the beginnings of our pleasures and the completions of our works to God’s grace, the total of these legal tithes is nevertheless fulfilled in the reckoning of the forty days.

The entire duration of the year is tithed in the number of thirty-six days. For when the Sundays are subtracted from Lent, on which fasts are relaxed, we come together to the church on these days as though offering the tithes of the entire year, and we offer the work of our actions to God as a sacrifice of jubilation.

According to our Cassianus, those who are perfect are in a certain way not bound by the law of this Lent, nor are they content with submission to this small canon. The leaders of the churches established it especially for those who are entangled throughout the whole year in pleasures and secular business, so that they might dedicate to the Lord, as a kind of legal tithe, at least this portion of the days of their life—days whose entire harvest they had been about to devour as though they were fruits.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the fast after Pentecost

The second fast is begun, according to the canons, on another day after Pentecost, in accordance with what Moses also says: “At the beginning of the month you shall regularly make seven weeks for yourselves” (Exodus 34).

Many complete this fast by the authority of the Gospel after the Lord’s Ascension, understanding historically that saying of the Lord in which he says: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Mark 2).

They say that after the Lord’s resurrection, during the forty days in which he is later read to have lived with his disciples, there ought to be neither fasting nor mourning, because we are in joy. But after that period was completed, when Christ flew up into heaven and withdrew his bodily presence, then a fast ought to be proclaimed, so that through humility of heart and abstinence of the flesh we might deserve to receive from heaven the promised Holy Spirit.

But, as we said, it was rightly and regularly established by the Fathers that this should begin after Pentecost, so that, rejoicing in God’s praises, we might await the coming of the promised Holy Spirit; and then, renewed by his grace and inflamed by the spiritual heaven, devote ourselves to abstinence and fasting.

The words of Luke agree with this. He relates that the Lord, about to ascend into heaven, commanded his disciples: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24).

Nevertheless, if any monks or clerics wish to fast, they should not be forbidden, since Antony, Paul, and the other ancient Fathers are read to have abstained during these days in the desert and not to have relaxed their abstinence except on Sunday.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the fast before the Lord’s Nativity, observed in the ninth and tenth months

The third fast is observed in November. That it was instituted or begun by divine authority is shown by the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah, when the Lord said to him:

“Take the scroll of the book and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and against every nation; perhaps each person may turn back from his evil way, and I will be merciful toward their iniquity.”

So Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Lord that he had spoken to him in the scroll of a book. And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying:

“Enter and read from the scroll that you wrote from my mouth the words of the Lord in the hearing of the people, in the house of the Lord, on the day of fasting. Perhaps their prayer may fall into the sight of the Lord, and each person may turn back from his evil way, for great is the anger and indignation that the Lord has spoken against this people.”

And Baruch son of Neriah did everything that Jeremiah the prophet had commanded, reading the words from the scroll in the house of the Lord. And it happened that in the ninth month they proclaimed a fast in the sight of the Lord for all the people in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 36).

By this authority of divine Scripture, therefore, the Church adopted the custom and celebrates a universal fast according to this observance. This fast, however, beginning in the ninth month, extends into the tenth; that is, it reaches up to the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

Accordingly, by an appropriate arrangement, the leaders of the Church established the Lenten fast at this point, so that before the day of the Lord’s Nativity we might chastise ourselves through fasting and abstinence, in order that we might be able to receive the coming Redeemer with a worthy manner of life, [Col. 0337A] just as before the time of his resurrection we afflict our flesh so that we may deserve to attain the grace of the resurrection that takes place through him.

Let this suffice concerning the three Lents.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the other prescribed fasts

Besides these, there are also prescribed times of fasting, such as every Friday, on which the faithful fast because of the Lord’s Passion, and Saturday, which many regard as consecrated by fasting because Christ lay in the tomb on that day. We find this established in the decrees of Pope Innocent: namely, so that the Jews might not be given cause for rejoicing over what Christ removed by dying.

For it is certainly established that during these two days the apostles were both in mourning and, because of fear of the Jews, concealed themselves. There is no doubt that they also fasted during those two days. This practice must therefore be maintained every week, because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated.

But if they think that one should fast on Saturday alone, then Sunday and Friday, too, will necessarily have to be observed only once at Easter.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the fast of the four Saturdays, during which twelve readings and sacred ordinations take place
There are also four Saturdays, one in each of four months, on which special fasts have been established and more extensive offices of prayers and readings are celebrated in the Church: namely, in the month of March, on the first Saturday; in the fourth month, that is, June; also in the seventh month, that is, September, on the third Saturday; and on the fourth Saturday of the tenth month, that is, December.

The first of these is celebrated in springtime, in accordance with the observance of Lent, when among the Jews the month of new produce was observed. The second is during the fast after Pentecost, in summertime, when among the Jews the days of firstfruits were kept according to the commandment of the Law—that is, when the first loaves made from the crops were offered to God—and the lawful observance of that day was celebrated.

The third is in the seventh month, namely in autumn, which throughout the Law had been dedicated to God by various solemnities. In that month was the Day of Atonement, as the Lord says to Moses:

“On the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a Day of Atonement, and it shall be most solemn and shall be called holy; you shall afflict your souls on it and offer a burnt offering to the Lord. You shall do no work during this day, because it is a Day of Propitiation, so that the Lord your God may be propitiated for you,” and so forth.

During that month there were also the ten days of the Feast of Booths, that is, of Tabernacles. For on the fifteenth day of that month the ancients celebrated the solemn feasts of Tabernacles, continuing the same solemnity for seven days. The Book of Ezra indeed records that the ancients observed this fast. For after the children of Israel had returned to Jerusalem and made for themselves great rejoicing over the Tabernacles, they then assembled in fasting, wearing sackcloth, with earth upon them; they stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. They rose to stand, and they read from the scroll of the law of the Lord their God four times during the day and four times during the night; they confessed and worshiped the Lord their God.

The fourth is the fast of the Saturday in the tenth month before the Lord’s Nativity, when the saving advent of the coming Savior is proclaimed in the sacred readings, so that all the faithful, instructed by this religious observance and strengthened by the medicine of holy prayers together with the sacred fast, may joyfully await the Redeemer’s birth.

Before these four Saturdays, the established fasts are always observed in the same week on Wednesday and Friday, as the prescribed canon of prayers and readings at the solemn celebration of Mass on those weekdays indicates, and as the examples of the Fathers who came before confirm.

That sacred ordinations ought to be performed on these days is testified by the decrees of Pope Gelasius, in which the following is written:

“Ordinations of presbyters and deacons ought not to be performed except at fixed times and on fixed days, namely during the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and also at the beginning and midpoint of Lent; they should know that these are to be celebrated toward evening, on the Saturday fast.”

The offices of these four Saturdays are commonly called “the twelve readings,” because, together with the readings that are read and the psalms that are read, the number twelve is completed. They may be called blessings, because they are counted among the canonical Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XXV. On private fasts

Moreover, each person is permitted to adopt whatever measure of fasting he wishes, or to extend his abstinence from food, provided above all that the regulation of the established fasts mentioned above is observed—those which the holy and apostolic Church universally keeps.

Everyone must also observe those fasts which the bishop proper to each Church commonly commands all to undertake, whether for affliction or for thanksgiving. For whoever neglects to keep the fasts that have been established and commanded commits sin; but whoever, after completing the established fasts, adds a private fast beyond them will receive his own reward.

For we read that some of the saints extended their fasts for two days, or three days, or even an entire week. Many abstained from drinking wine or any fermented drink and from eating anything except dry bread and vegetables; others abstained from all meat; others abstained so severely that they did not even use bread as food, but sustained their bodies with a few dried figs.

There are also many other kinds of abstinence. But above all, anyone who wishes to abstain from some food or drink must take care that his mind is not defiled by a hidden thought, so that, deceived by superstitious judgment, he condemns some creature of God, saying or thinking that one thing is permitted and another not, that one thing is clean and another unclean.

Let anyone troubled by such a thought of this world consider that the Apostle said: “Every creature of God is clean, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; and it is evil for a person to eat through causing offense” (1 Tim. IV; Rom. XIV).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the origin of the two-day and three-day fast

I think that the custom of fasting for two days was taken from the fact that the apostles fasted during those two days on which the Lord suffered and was buried.

The practice of fasting for three days was therefore derived from the example of the Ninevites, who, having condemned their former vices, devoted themselves entirely for three days to fasting and repentance.

Only the fast of one who fasts from food in such a way that he abstains from sins is acceptable to God. But the fast of one who fasts only with his stomach will be rejected before God, who said through the prophet:

“Behold, on the days of your fast your own will is found, and you exact all your debts. Behold, you fast for quarrels and disputes, and you strike wickedly with your fist. Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this the kind of fast that I have chosen, for a person to afflict his soul for a day?” (Isa. LVIII).

And afterward:

“Is this not rather the fast that I have chosen? Undo the bonds of wickedness; release the burdens that oppress; set free those who are broken and oppressed, and break every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, and your health shall quickly arise,” and so forth (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On eating meat and drinking wine

Meat and wine were granted for human use after the Flood. For at the beginning this had not been permitted, except only what is written: “I have given you every fruit-bearing tree and every plant producing seed for food.”

Afterward, through Noah, all animals were given for food, and permission to drink wine was also granted. But after Christ—who is the beginning and the end—appeared, what he had suspended at the beginning he withdrew again at the end of the ages, speaking through his Apostle: “It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine” (Rom. XIV). And again: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (ibid.).

Meat is therefore not forbidden because meats are evil, but because their feasts produce the wantonness of the flesh. For food is the fuel and nourishment of all vices. “Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God,” as it is written, “will destroy both the one and the other.”

We may certainly eat fish, because the Lord ate it after his resurrection. For neither the Savior nor the apostles forbade this. I believe that the eating of birds was also permitted by the Fathers for this reason: they were created from the same element as fish. For in the rule of the monks we do not find that the eating of any other meats was prohibited to them except that of four-footed animals.

### Addition

Only four-footed animals, not flying creatures, were forbidden to monks. It is said that in the time of Louis the Pious this was changed, so that they were permitted to use blood in every dish, because of the excessive consumption of birds in which they engaged, to the detriment of others as well.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the different kinds of almsgiving

Almsgiving—ἐλεημοσύνη, a Greek word—is interpreted in Latin as “a work of mercy.” It was so called, I think, because the misery of human weakness strikes the heart or mind.

But among human beings, in whom various emotions arise in the mind, such an affection may exist; whereas it must not be understood in this way of God, who by nature is always kind and merciful. For nothing temporal can occur there where eternity remains fixed without any change in itself. When God is called merciful, he should be understood to be pious and compassionate; these names seem rather to reveal the character of his very nature.

There are also many forms of almsgiving, although some think that this word ought to be confined to the administration of aid to the poor.

A person performs almsgiving when he corrects someone who is sinning and persisting in evil deeds, whether by admonition or by discipline. Nor should the person who regularly strives to restrain another from sins and vices, whether by excommunication or by blows, be thought to act without mercy, because he shows mercy not according to the other’s will but according to that person’s welfare.

A person performs almsgiving when he leads someone who has gone astray back to the way of truth. A person performs almsgiving when he teaches the unlearned, when he preaches the word of God to his neighbors. A person performs almsgiving when he does not cease to share temporal goods with his brothers—that is, with other human beings. A person performs almsgiving when he supplies food and clothing to those in need, receives guests, visits the sick, provides from his goods for those confined in prison or afflicted by tribulations, and does not cease to rescue those destined for death and punishment.

All the good works that every righteous person performs in this present life can be included under this one name—not only those performed for other people, but also those we can perform for ourselves, as it is written: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Eccli. XXX).

Therefore, when we turn ourselves from sins to good works, from pride to humility, from lust to continence, from spite and envy to charity and love, from anger and contention to gentleness and patience, from gluttony to moderation, from greed to generosity, from worldly sadness to spiritual joy, and from temporal sloth to good diligence, what else are we doing but bestowing alms upon ourselves, when we have mercy on ourselves so that through disobedience to God’s commandments we may not be condemned to eternal punishments?

For what, says the Savior himself, will it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a person give for his soul? And so forth (Mark VIII).

The person who first practices the art of mercy well and in an orderly manner, by not allowing himself to lack good works, holy conduct, and the fruits of virtue, and then does not cease to help his neighbors wherever he can, whether in spiritual or bodily matters, exercises this art properly.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On repentance

Job first provided an example for penitents when, after bereavement and affliction, he still took up the lament of repentance in self-reproach, even in sackcloth and ashes, saying: “Therefore I repent in dust and ashes.”

After him David offered us a model of repentance. Having fallen through a grave wound, as soon as he heard his sin from the prophet, he immediately repented and healed his guilt by confessing his repentance.

Thus the Ninevites and many others confessed their sins, did penance, and were displeased with what they had been; they were pleased with what they were made by God.

Repentance is the medicine of a wound and the hope of salvation. Through it sinners are saved; through it the Lord is moved to mercy. It is not measured by length of time but by the depth of grief and tears.

The word repentance, *poenitentia*, derives from punishment, *poena*, by which the soul is tortured and the flesh is mortified. It is called *poenitentia*, as though it meant “punishing,” because a person punishes by punishment what he has wrongly committed.

Those who perform penance therefore grow their hair and beard, in order to display the abundance of crimes by which the sinner’s head is burdened. Hair is understood as a figure for vices, as it is written: “Each person is bound by the crimes of his sins.” For a man to grow his hair long, as the Apostle says, is a disgrace to him (1 Cor. XI). Penitents therefore assume this disgrace in proportion to their sins.

Their prostration in sackcloth signifies that they keep the memory of their sins. Sackcloth represents the remembrance of sins, because of the goats that will be placed on the left. Therefore we penitents prostrate ourselves in sackcloth as though saying: “My sin is always before me.”

Their being sprinkled with ashes signifies either that they should remember that they are ash and dust, or that they have become dust—that is, that they have become impious. Hence those transgressors, the first human beings, having departed from God and offended the Creator by evil deeds, returned to the dust from which they had been taken.

It is therefore fitting that the penitent mourns his sin in sackcloth and ashes: in sackcloth the harshness and pricking of sins are shown, while in ashes the dust of the dead is displayed. For this reason we perform penance in both, so that by the prickling of sackcloth we may recognize the vices we have committed through guilt, and by the embers of ashes may weigh the sentence of death to which we have come by sinning.

The Catholic Church faithfully binds the remedy of repentance to the hope of forgiveness and prescribes it to be practiced. After the one sacrament of baptism—which is commended by a unique tradition and which the Church carefully forbids to be repeated—it substitutes the aid of repentance as a medicinal remedy. Everyone ought to acknowledge that he needs this remedy for the daily excesses of human weakness, without which we cannot exist in this life, while preserving the proper dignity of each case.

Thus, before God as witness, this should be done by priests and Levites; by others, it should be done solemnly before God in the presence of a priest, so that fruitful confession may cover what rash desire or neglect arising from ignorance is observed to have brought about. Just as we believe that all iniquities are forgiven in baptism, and that through martyrdom no sin is counted against anyone, so by the fruitful compunction of repentance we confess that all sins are erased.

For the tears of penitents are reckoned before God in place of baptism. Therefore, however great and serious their offenses may be, one must not despair of God’s mercy toward them.

In the practice of repentance, as stated above, the measure of time is not so much to be considered as the measure of grief. “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”

Nevertheless, just as great as the mind’s inclination toward evil was in sin, so great must its devotion be in the act of repentance.

There are two kinds of penitential lamentation: either when we mourn what we have done wrongly, or when we fail to do what we ought to have done. The person truly performs repentance who neither neglects to repent of past deeds nor commits deeds that will require repentance.

But whoever continually sheds tears and nevertheless does not cease sinning has lamentation but not cleansing.

If some people are converted to repentance by the grace of God, they should not be disturbed if, after amendment, their abandoned vices again assail their hearts, provided that such thoughts cannot harm their good conduct because they do not break out into consent or action.

To endure thoughts of vices without completing the vices themselves is not condemnation but testing; it is not an occasion for entering into danger but rather for increasing virtue.

Even if someone ceases to be evil through repentance near the end of his life, he ought not to despair because he is at the final limit of life. For God does not consider what we were previously, but what we are near the end of life. By his end he either justifies or condemns each person, as it is written: “He himself judges the ends of the earth.” And elsewhere: “He himself considers the end of all things.”

Therefore we do not doubt that a person may be justified near the end of life through the compunction of repentance. But because this rarely happens, one must fear that, while the hoped-for confession is postponed until the end, death may arrive before repentance.

For this reason, although conversion at the very end is good, conversion undertaken long before the end is better, so that we may pass more securely from this life.

## CHAPTER XXX. On satisfaction and reconciliation

Satisfaction is to remove the causes and suggestions of sins and not to repeat the sin thereafter.

Reconciliation, on the other hand, is what is administered after the completion of repentance. For just as we are reconciled to God when we first turn away from paganism, so we are reconciled when, after sinning, we return through repentance.

The repentance of those whose sins are public ought to be public, for the periods determined at the bishop’s discretion for penitents according to the difference among their sins. Their reconciliation likewise ought to be public and performed by the bishop, or by presbyters at the bishop’s command, as the canons of the African Council testify. There it is written:

“If the public and notorious crime of any penitent has disturbed the whole Church, hands shall be imposed on him before the apse.”

The sins of those whose offenses are hidden and have been revealed by their spontaneous confession to a presbyter alone or to a bishop should therefore receive hidden penance, according to the judgment of the presbyter or bishop to whom they confessed, lest the weak in the Church be scandalized when they see punishments whose causes they entirely do not know.

The decrees of Pope Innocent indicate at what time reconciliation ought to take place after repentance. There it is found written:

“Concerning penitents who perform penance either for graver offenses or for lesser ones, if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter.”

As for judging the weight of offenses, it belongs to the priest to determine this, attending to the penitent’s confession and to the correction of his weeping and tears; he should then order him to be released when he sees that satisfactory satisfaction has been made.

If someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he should be released before Easter, lest he depart from the world without communion.

Above all, then, one must take care that repentance and reconciliation are not denied to those at the point of death, lest they perish in despair. For the mercy of almighty God can aid anyone who turns to him at any time, and can raise up one endangered beneath the burden of sins.

Would the thief hanging at Christ’s right hand have lost his reward if the repentance of a single hour had not helped him? While suffering punishment, he repented and, by the profession of a single statement, earned—as God promised—a dwelling in paradise.

The true conversion to God of those placed at the end of life should therefore be judged more by the mind than by the time, as the prophet declares elsewhere: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Nativity of the Lord

The day of the Lord’s Nativity was established by the Fathers as a solemn festival of vows because on it Christ wished to be born bodily for the redemption of the world, coming forth from the Virgin’s womb, although he was in the Father’s dominion.

The reason for his assumption of flesh is this: after that first parent, deceived by empty hope through the devil’s envy, fell, he immediately, as an exile and one who had been ruined, transmitted the root of malice and sin to his entire race. The whole human race was increasingly growing toward evil, with crimes spread everywhere and, what is worse, with the worship of every kind of idol.

Therefore, wishing to bring sin to an end, God addressed the world through the Word, the Law, the prophets, signs, afflictions, and wonders. But when the world, even after being admonished in this way, did not recognize its errors, God sent his Son to put on flesh, appear to all, and heal sinners.

He came in human form because he could not be known by human beings through himself. In order to be seen, the Word became flesh by assuming flesh, not by being changed into flesh. He assumed humanity and did not lose divinity: thus the same one is both God and human being, equal to the Father in the nature of God and made mortal in the nature of humanity—among us, for us, from us—remaining what he was and assuming what he was not, so that he might free what he had made.

This, then, is the great solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity. This is the new and glorious festival of this day: the coming of God to human beings.

The day is called the Nativity because Christ was born on it. We customarily observe it with a festive solemnity as the year’s cycle returns, so that the memory of Christ’s birth may be recalled.

Christ was also born in Bethlehem and raised in Nazareth, so that the event of the things themselves might be made evident through the names of the places.

It was therefore fitting that he should be born in Bethlehem, because heavenly food came from heaven to earth. Bethlehem is called “house of bread.” And the Savior said of himself: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John VI).

Bethlehem is therefore truly the house of bread, because Christ the human being graciously chose to be born there: the bread of life, of which whoever eats will live forever.

For this reason also, we believe that the custom arose in the Church of celebrating the solemn rites of Mass on the night on which Christ is believed to have been born, so that the faithful might receive the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood at the hour when they knew that he had mercifully been born among human beings.

Pope Telesphorus is nevertheless read to have first established this celebration among the Romans.

The reason he was raised in Nazareth was that, since Nazareth is interpreted as “flower” or “purity,” it might be a sign of his eternal purity. The nurse of that flower flourishes, the one who, rising from the branch of the root of Jesse, would possess the sevenfold Spirit and, distinguished by perpetual purity, would rightly be called a Nazarene, that is, “pure.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Epiphany of the Lord

The apostolic men therefore marked the feast of the Epiphany with solemn celebration, because on it the Savior was revealed by a star, when the Magi worshiped Christ lying in the manger and offered him fitting gifts of the Trinity—gold, frankincense, and myrrh—as king, God, and one destined to suffer.

They therefore consecrated this day with annual celebration so that the world might acknowledge the Lord whom the heavenly elements revealed.

On that same day the same Jesus is also washed in the Jordan’s waters; and when heaven is divided, the testimony of the descending Holy Spirit declares him to be the Son of God.

The name of this day derives from the fact that he appeared to the nations, and it is called Epiphany. For Epiphany, in Greek ἐπιφάνεια, means “appearance” or “manifestation.”

This day therefore received this name for three reasons: either because Christ was then manifested to the peoples in his baptism; or because on that day he was revealed to the Magi by the rising of the star; or because by the first sign, when water was changed into wine, he was manifested to many.

It should nevertheless be known that, although Christ’s baptism by John is believed to have taken place on that day, canonical authority contradicts the celebration of universal baptism on it.

The Roman Church therefore preserves only the time of Easter and Pentecost for this purpose, as was decreed by the apostles and apostolic men. These two seasons are shown to be suitable for this purpose by the resurrection of Christ our Lord from the dead and by the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the primitive Church.

“For all of us,” says the Apostle, “who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death,” and so forth (Rom. VI).

And the Savior, about to ascend into heaven, said to the apostles: “John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts I).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Purification

The time of the Purification of the Lord’s mother is celebrated forty days after his birth, because this period was established by the precept of the Law for women who had given birth, during which they were to be purified.

For it is written in the Book of Leviticus that the Lord commanded Israel through Moses that a woman who gave birth to a male child conceived from seed should be unclean for seven days, and that the infant should be circumcised on the eighth day. She herself was then to remain thirty-four days in the blood of her purification. She was not to touch anything holy or enter the sanctuary until the days of her cleansing had been fulfilled.

But if she gave birth to a female child, she was to be unclean for two weeks and remain for forty-three days in the blood of her purification.

When the days of her cleansing had been fulfilled, she was to bring, for a son or daughter, a yearling lamb as a burnt offering and a young pigeon or turtledove as a sin offering. If she could not offer a lamb, she was to take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a burnt offering and the other as a sin offering. The priest was to pray for her, and thus she would be cleansed (Lev. XII).

This is why this festival was established in the Church: it was evident that the Lord’s mother was purified according to the Law on this day. This was not because she needed any legal purification, since she bore the Lord of the Law, but because Jesus did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

The Lord’s mother therefore came to the temple according to the Law, bringing the child with her and carrying the offerings that the Law prescribed, so that she might differ in nothing from the Fathers and might first show in herself what is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Eccli. III).

She encountered the aged Simeon, Anna, a widow of many years, and the other persons who were present for this sacred ministry. The sacred text of the Gospel clearly demonstrates that they blessed and glorified God and prophesied many things about him.

For this reason the same festival is called Hypapante, ὑπαντή, because the persons mentioned above came to the temple to meet Christ with devoted heart and service. For in Greek, *hypantao*, ὑπαντάω, means in Latin “I meet.”

This festival of the Purification occurs at the beginning of February. The month was called February from Februus, that is, Pluto, who was believed by the pagans to possess power over purification; among the Romans it was customary in that month to purify the city so that due offerings might be paid to the spirits of the dead.

Christian religion rightly changed this custom of purification. In the same month, on the day of holy Mary, the entire people, together with the priests and ministers, proceeds through the churches and suitable places of the city with hymns and devout melodies, and all carry in their hands the burning candles distributed by the pontiff—not for the five-year purification of an earthly empire, but in perpetual memory of the heavenly kingdom. Then, according to the parable of the wise virgins, all the elect, coming with lamps shining with good works to meet their bridegroom and king, will immediately enter with him into the wedding feast of the heavenly city.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima

There are various opinions concerning Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Quadragesima, and why the Sundays before the Lenten fast are called by these names. This is especially so because the Sunday called Septuagesima is not found to be the seventieth day before Easter, whereas the Sunday called Sexagesima does not contain a full sixty-day number extending to Easter.

Some simply state that this is the custom of the Church and that the rite of this religious observance has been established by Roman authority.

Others say that the expression should be understood by synecdoche as referring to the whole, namely, that where a greater number of days is found than the actual lesser number—as with Septuagesima and Sexagesima—a part should be understood from the whole. But where there is a lesser number, as with Quadragesima, the whole should be understood from the part.

Others, following—I know not whose authority—assert that the Eastern peoples customarily fast for nine weeks, the Greeks for eight, and the Latins for seven, and that for this reason Alleluia should not be sung at all in the Church during all these periods.

Others, whose reasoning seems to me more commendable than the rest, say that it is called Septuagesima because of the ten weeks that extend from that very day until the close of Easter, when the white garments are removed from the newly baptized.

Accordingly, we read in the Apostle: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses,” and thus it continued until the final periods of the Law given through Moses, reaching into the times of Christ our God (Rom. V).

Sexagesima, moreover, can be so called because there are sixty days until the middle of Easter, which occurs on the Wednesday of Easter week.

Quinquagesima is rightly so called because that number brings it to the holy day of the Resurrection.

The number forty is placed there because its Sunday coincides with the mystical Passover of the Hebrews, which our Lord Jesus Christ celebrated with his disciples and which we call the Lord’s Supper.

We have set all these explanations down here just as we have found them in the statements or writings of others, giving the reader the opportunity to retain any explanation he may discover that has been investigated more truthfully and reasonably.

It should nevertheless be noted that Pope Telesphorus, mentioned above, established that among the Romans the fast should begin at Quinquagesima, so that for seven weeks before Easter we might chastise the body with fasts. Since we wish to relax from fasts in joy during the other seven weeks after Easter until Pentecost, we should spend the first Quinquagesima in the fullness of our sins, so as to merit mercy, and devote ourselves in the second to praises and prayers, striving to reach the promised grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Palm Sunday

Palm Sunday is celebrated because on it our Lord and Savior, as the prophet sang, is said to have sat upon a colt while proceeding toward Jerusalem.

Then, as he advanced, the multitude of the peoples came to meet him with palm branches and cried out: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (Matt. XXI).

The palm branches signified the victory by which the Lord was to overcome death by dying, and by the trophy of the cross was to triumph over the devil, the prince of death.

In the colt on which he came to Jerusalem while seated, he indicated the simple hearts of the Gentiles, whom, by presiding over and governing them, he was leading to the vision of peace.

On this day the Symbol is handed over to the candidates for baptism, because of the nearness of the solemnity of the Lord’s Easter, so that those who hasten to receive the grace of God may recognize the faith that they profess.

The common people call this day “Capitular,” because it is then customary to wash the heads of the children who are to be anointed, lest they should approach the anointing with heads soiled by the observance of Lent.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Lord’s Supper

The Lord’s Supper takes place on the Thursday of the final week of Lent, when our Lord and Savior, after completing that typological Passover and passing over to the true Passover, first handed on to the apostles the mystery of his body and blood.

After the heavenly sacraments, the deceitful and treacherous disciple received his price from the Jews and sold Christ’s blood.

On that same day the Savior rose from the supper and washed the disciples’ feet, in order to commend the example of humility that he had come to teach, as he himself subsequently explained. He did this especially so that by the deed he might teach what he had previously warned the disciples to observe.

Hence, on that same day, the altars, walls, and floors of the church are washed, and the vessels consecrated to the Lord are purified.

On that day the holy chrism is also prepared, because two days before Easter Mary is said to have anointed the Lord’s head and feet with ointment.

Therefore the Lord said to his disciples: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matt. XXVI).

On the same day also, as we showed above, penitents are reconciled. Since it was on the very day on which the Lord first instituted the sacraments of his body and blood and handed them on to his disciples to receive, penitents ought to be restored so that they might receive them again—at the time when Christ’s blood was poured out for the remission of all sins.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Good Friday
Parasceve, that is, the sixth day of the week, is held in solemn observance because on that day Christ fulfilled the mystery of the cross, for which he had come into this world: so that we who had been struck by the wood in Adam might again be healed through the mystery of the wood. For the sake of this triumph, human weakness offers Christ an annual celebration throughout the world, because he deigned by the blood of his passion to redeem the age and, by conquering death through the cross, to absolve the sin of the world. Yet the injury of that cross was not suffered by the substance of divinity, but only by the nature of the humanity he had assumed. The passion was suffered by the body; divinity, untouched by injury, remained beyond it.

A threefold reason for the Lord’s passion is discerned. The first reason is that Christ should be given as redemption for the guilt of the world: namely, so that the serpent might vomit forth those whom it had swallowed and lose the prey it held—not defeated by power, but by justice; not by domination, but by reason. The second reason is that he might provide a pattern of life for those who would follow. Christ ascended the cross to offer us an example of passion and resurrection: of passion, to strengthen patience; of resurrection, to awaken hope; so that he might show us two lives in the flesh, one laborious and the other blessed—the laborious life that we must endure, and the blessed life that we must hope for.

The third reason for the cross he assumed was that the proud and inflated wisdom of the world might be humbled and collapse through the apparently foolish preaching of the cross, so that it might be evident how much wiser than human beings is what is foolish in God, and how much stronger than all human strength is what is weak in God.

The apostle Paul teaches that we ought to have the eyes of our heart enlightened, so as to understand what are the breadth, length, height, and depth of the cross. The breadth of the cross is the transverse wood on which the hands are extended. Its length extends downward from the breadth to the earth. Its height reaches upward from the transverse beam to the head. Its depth is the part fixed into the earth and hidden.

It is said to a human being: “Take up your cross and follow me.” When the flesh is crucified, when our members upon the earth are put to death—sexual immorality, impurity, lust, and the rest—and when the outward person is corrupted so that the inward person may be renewed day by day, this is the passion of the cross. These things are indeed good works, yet they are still laborious, and their reward is rest. Therefore it is said: “Rejoicing in hope,” so that, while considering the rest to come, we may work with cheerfulness amid our labors.

The breadth of the cross, in the transverse wood where the hands are fixed, signifies this cheerfulness. For by the hands work is understood; by breadth, the cheerfulness of the worker, since sadness causes narrowness. Further, by the height of the cross, to which the head is joined, the expectation of heavenly reward is sanctified by the exalted justice of God, so that good works may be understood to be performed not for the sake of earthly and temporal benefits from God, but rather for the sake of what faith, working through love, hopes for from above.

The length, by which the whole body is extended, signifies endurance itself, so that we may remain patient. Hence those who endure are called long-suffering. By the depth, that is, by the part of the wood fixed secretly in the hidden earth, from which everything that projects above arises, the inscrutable judgments of God are signified. By these judgments, through a hidden will, a human being is called to participate in so great a grace of God.

On this day, therefore, the altars of the churches are stripped of their coverings and left bare, because on it Christ is read to have been stripped of his garments, and the Gospel proclaims that the veil of the Temple was torn when Christ was killed. On this day lamps are not lit in the church, because, when the Redeemer was crucified, the heavenly bodies were darkened.

On this day the bishops of the holy congregations, because they discharge the embassy entrusted to them, plead the cause of the human race before the divine mercy. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray: first, for the condition of the entire Church of Christ; then, that faith may prevail over unbelievers, and that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed from the Jews, the light of truth may appear; that heretics may come to their senses through acceptance of the catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and finally, that, when catechumens have been led to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them. For on this day the blood of Christ was poured out for the redemption of all these.

That these things are not asked of the Lord in vain is shown by the effect of the things themselves: God deigns to draw many people from every kind of error, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them into the kingdom of the Son of his love, making vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. All this is perceived to be the work of God’s divine action, so that thanksgiving and confession of praise may always be rendered to God, who accomplishes these things, for the enlightenment or correction of such people.

On this day the bishop, clergy, and entire people venerate the image of the cross, because the passion of the Redeemer is honored by the faithful with fitting praise at the hour of their redemption. On this day the sacraments are not celebrated at all. Rather, after the service of readings and prayers and the veneration of the holy cross, they receive again the Eucharist consecrated at the Lord’s Supper. For, as Pope Innocent bears witness, because during those two days in which the Savior was crucified and buried the apostles and lovers of Christ, overcome with grief, abstained from all food, the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments are not celebrated during those two days. Instead, the holy night of the resurrection is awaited, and on it the sacrifice is offered with special gladness and joy.

On this day Vespers is celebrated in silence, so that due reverence may be offered to the repose of the Lord’s burial.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Holy Easter Saturday

The veneration of Easter Saturday is celebrated because on that same day the Lord rested in the tomb. Hence, suitably, in the Hebrew language *sabbath* is interpreted as “rest”: either because God rested on that day, when the world had been completed, or because on it the Lord and our Redeemer rested in the tomb.

This day lies between the Lord’s death and resurrection, signifying a kind of rest for souls from all labor and every affliction after death. Through this rest there is passage, by the resurrection of the flesh, to that life which our Lord deigned to foreshadow by his resurrection.

On this day we ought to remain in complete silence and tranquility, and with prayer and psalmody await the holy hour of the resurrection, lest worldly concern trouble us more and earthly affairs disturb us more than spiritual pursuits and salutary concern for our souls occupy us.

As this day inclines toward evening, the appointed celebration of the Lord’s night is begun in the Church. First, according to the institution of Pope Zosimus, while the archdeacon blesses the candle, the celebration appropriately begins with the consecration of the Paschal light, which has brought us the brightness of eternal light.

Then the order of readings from the Old Testament and prayers is carried out, so that it may become known with what expectation, from the beginning of the world, our salvation was foretold through patriarchs and prophets—a salvation completed in the passion and resurrection of our Savior.

Then litanies are conducted, so that the fellowship, remembrance, and prayer of the saints may help us attain the joys to come. These are followed by the sacrament of baptism, and the flock of those made white ascends from the font. Whoever wishes to know with what authority and reasoning the baptism of this season is commended to us should read the decrees of Pope Leo, and will find the answer there.

After baptism and the litanies comes the holy celebration of the Mass and participation in the body and blood of the Lord. Of any member of the faithful who abstains from participation on this night, I do not know how to call him a Christian—except those who, excommunicated for capital crimes, are undergoing repentance.

It should also be noted that we read in Jerome that in the Eastern churches it is customary on this night for the faithful not to leave the church before midnight, waiting for that hour in the sacred vigils, of which it is written: “At midnight there was a cry made,” and so forth (Matthew XXV).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Lord’s Pascha

The Paschal sacrament, which is now most clearly celebrated as a mystery concerning our Savior, was first enacted figuratively in the Old Testament, when, after the lamb had been killed, the people of God celebrated Pascha in Egypt. Its figure was fulfilled in truth in Christ, who was led like a sheep to slaughter. When our doorposts are marked with his blood—that is, when our foreheads are marked with the sign of the cross—we are freed from the danger of this age as from Egyptian captivity.

We celebrate the day of his Paschal resurrection not only because he rose from the dead on that day, but also because of the other sacraments signified through it. For, as the Apostle says, “He died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (Romans IV), the passage from death to life was consecrated in the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

The very word *Pascha* is not Greek but Hebrew. It is not derived from passion, because *paschein*, πάσχειν, is the Greek word for “to suffer”; rather, it was called *Pascha* from the Hebrew word for “passage.” The Evangelist expressed this especially when the Lord celebrated Pascha with his disciples: “When Jesus had seen,” he says, “that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII).

The passage, therefore, from this mortal life to another, immortal life—that is, from death to life—is commended in the Lord’s passion and resurrection. This passage is now enacted by us through faith, which is given to us for the remission of sins, when through baptism we are buried together with Christ, as though passing from the dead from worse things to better, from bodily things to spiritual things, and from the conduct of this life to the hope of the resurrection and glory to come.

Because of the beginning of the new life into which we pass, and because of the new person whom we are commanded to put on and the old person whom we are commanded to put off, cleansing out the old leaven so that we may be a new lump—for “Christ our Pascha has been sacrificed”—the first month among the months of the year was assigned to this celebration. It is also called the month of new things.

Because now the third period of the whole age has appeared, the Lord’s resurrection lasts three days. The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace, where the sacrament that had been hidden in prophetic enigma has now been revealed.

This is also signified by the lunar reckoning. Since the number seven commonly appears in Scripture as mystical and indicative of a certain perfection, Pascha is celebrated in the third week of the moon—that is, on whichever day occurs between the fifteenth and the twenty-first. This is so not only because it is the third period, since the third week is beginning, but also because of that turning of the moon. For at that time it turns from lower things toward higher things.

From the moon, therefore, we take a likeness for ourselves: we are to pass from visible things to invisible, from bodily things to spiritual sacraments, so that we may die more and more to this age, our life being hidden with Christ, and turn all the light of our devotion, which had been directed toward lower things, toward higher things—namely, toward the eternal contemplation of unchanging truth.

Pascha is observed up to the twenty-first day because of the number seven, by which the totality of things is often signified. This number is also attributed to the Church because of its likeness to totality; hence the apostle John writes in the Apocalypse to seven churches.

The Church, while still established in this mortal flesh, is often called “the moon” in Scripture because of this mutability.

The reason the annual day of Pascha does not return to the same day of the year, as, for example, the day on which the Lord is believed to have been born does, is the Lord’s day and the moon. It is clear on what day the Lord was crucified, was in the tomb, and rose again. The observance of those days was added by the Council of Nicaea, and the entire Christian world was persuaded that Pascha ought to be celebrated in such a way that we should await not only the Paschal moon but also the Lord’s day, on which he rose from the dead.

Hence Pascha does not return to the same day of the year. The Jews observe only the month of new things and the moon; our fathers judged that a day should also be added, so that our festival might be distinguished from the Jewish festival.

The beginning of the first month is to be observed from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the day of the Nones of April. The fourteenth moon of Pascha is to be sought from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April through the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. The Lord’s day of Pascha, moreover, extends from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the seventh day before the Kalends of May, and this from the fifteenth through the twenty-first day of the moon.

It can never happen, therefore, that the fourteenth moon of the first month occurs before the spring equinox, which falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, because the lesser light must follow the greater light in its fullness, not precede it.

Since in the Old Testament the Paschal season was commanded to be observed by three indications—namely, after the equinox, in the first month, and in its third week, that is, from the evening of the fourteenth moon, which is the beginning of the fifteenth, until the evening that is the end of the twenty-first—there is a fourth rule imposed upon us for this observance from the time of the Lord’s resurrection. When, after the equinox has passed, we see the fourteenth moon of the first month rise in the evening, we must not immediately hasten to celebrate Pascha, but must await the Lord’s day and celebrate Pascha appropriately on it.

If it could happen that the fourteenth moon fell on the Sabbath every year, the timing of our Paschal observance would differ in nothing from that of the Law. For we too, following the commands of the Law, would always slaughter and eat the flesh of the immaculate lamb on the evening of the fourteenth moon of the first month, sprinkling its blood on our doorposts to repel the destroyer—that is, celebrating the solemn rites of the baptismal and Paschal Masses. We would overcome spiritual Egypt, and at dawn, on the fifteenth moon of that same month, enter the first day of Unleavened Bread. We would complete with due reverence the seven appointed days of that celebration, from the morning of the fifteenth day through the evening of the twenty-first day of that month—that is, from the Lord’s Pascha through the eighth Sunday of Pascha.

But because the same lunar day moves through different days of the week, it happens that, since we are taught to preserve the Lord’s day as the beginning of Pascha because of the resurrection of our Redeemer, our festival sometimes begins on the seventh day after the beginning of the legal Unleavened Bread. At other times, however, it happens that our Paschal solemnity includes within itself one of the legal days of Pascha, and often all of them.
