It should nevertheless be noted that there is this difference between the Pascha and the Unleavened Bread of the Law: the single day on which it was necessary to kill the lamb, and the following night in which the Lord struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians while passing over, freeing the houses of the children of Israel marked with the lamb’s blood (Exodus XII), was called Pascha. The following seven days, from the fifteenth through the twenty-first of the same month, were properly called the days of Unleavened Bread.

The Church also imitates this custom of the Law in a worthy manner. It principally observes one night of the passage of the Lord’s resurrection from the dead, in which he triumphed over the impious and deigned to save the faithful; then it adds seven other days in a fitting celebration in memory of that same resurrection of the Lord. We call these seven days the “White Days,” because those who are baptized on the holy night wear white garments throughout the entire week.

At that time, especially when the white garments are removed from the baptized, it is fitting for them to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands by the bishop—for in baptism they have received remission of all sins—and throughout the seven days they customarily attend the holy sacrifices in the evangelical garment of purity and with the lights of heavenly brightness.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Ascension of the Lord

The solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension is celebrated because on that same day, after victory over the world and return from hell, Christ is remembered to have ascended into heaven, as it is written: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm LXVII).

This festival is celebrated in the recurring cycle of the years so that the humanity of the flesh he assumed, ascending to the right hand of the Father, may be recalled. We believe that his body is in heaven as it was when he ascended, and the angelic voice also bears witness to this, saying: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I)—that is, in the same appearance and substance of flesh. To that flesh he gave immortality; he did not remove its nature.

The right hand of the Father, at which the same Son is believed to sit, is not bodily—for it is impious to think this about God—but the right hand of the Father is perpetual blessedness, which is promised to the saints in the resurrection, that is, to the whole Church, which is Christ’s body. Likewise, his left hand is understood as the misery and perpetual punishment that will be given to the impious.

Before this day of the Lord’s Ascension, it is customary for the churches of the West to undertake a fast for the three preceding days and to conduct litanies, and this appropriately. For if we believe that Christ ascended into heaven at this time, it is fitting that before the day of his Ascension we should devote ourselves to fasting and prayers, chastising our flesh and carrying his cross within ourselves, so that we may be worthy to follow him.

“For whoever,” he says, “wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX). Therefore, just as we carry the likeness of his cross in our hands, so let us also carry in our flesh the likeness of his passion. “Those who belong to Christ,” the Apostle says, “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians V).

Thus it will come about that, where Christ ascended in glory after his resurrection, we too may rise from the dead and ascend there, in incorruptible flesh, by his grace, as the same Apostle says: “For if,” he says, “we have been grafted into the likeness of his death, we shall also be joined to his resurrection” (Romans VI).

## CHAPTER XLI. On Pentecost

The beginning and origin of the festival of Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day, must be traced somewhat further back. The day of Pentecost began when the voice of God thundered from above on Mount Sinai and was heard, and the Law was given to Moses.

In the New Testament, Pentecost began when Christ displayed the coming of the Holy Spirit which he had promised, and said that he would not come unless he himself had ascended into heaven. Finally, when Christ had entered the gate of heaven, after ten intervening days the place suddenly trembled while the apostles were praying. As the Holy Spirit descended upon them, they were set aflame, so that they spoke of the mighty works of God in the tongues of all nations.

The coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven upon the apostles transmitted to later generations a solemnity expressed in a variety of languages; for this reason Pentecost is celebrated, and the day itself is held in distinction.

This festival corresponds to the festival of the Law. There, after the lamb had been sacrificed and fifty days had intervened, the written Law was given to Moses by the finger of God. Here, after Christ had been killed—he who was led like a sheep to slaughter—the true Pascha is celebrated, and after fifty days the Holy Spirit is given. He is the finger of God, bestowed upon the one hundred and twenty disciples who were constituted according to the number of the Mosaic age.

This festival also contains another sacrament. It consists of seven weeks. The weeks of days produce this same Pentecost, in which the remission of sin occurs through the Holy Spirit. The weeks of years produce the fiftieth year, which among the Hebrews is called the jubilee. In it likewise there is remission for the land, freedom for slaves, and restoration of possessions that had been acquired for a price.

For seven multiplied by seven produces the number fifty, when the unit is added—a unit which the authority of our predecessors teaches was anticipated as a figure of the age to come. It is always both the eighth and the first; indeed, it is always the one, which is every day.

For the sabbath-rest of souls must necessarily arrive and be completed there where a portion is given to those who are eight, as someone, expounding the words of Solomon, wisely explained (Ecclesiastes XI).

For this reason all the days of the fifty-day period after the Lord’s resurrection are celebrated with abstinence dissolved and replaced by pure joy, because they figure the future resurrection, where there will no longer be labor but the rest of joy. Therefore the knees are not bent in prayer during these days, because, as one of the wise men says, the bending of the knees is a sign of repentance and mourning.

For the same reason we observe throughout those days the same solemnity that we observe on the Lord’s day. Our predecessors handed down that on the Lord’s day neither fasting should be undertaken nor the knees bent, out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection.

During these holy days the teachers of the Church decreed that “Alleluia” should continually be sung in the Church because of the joy of the resurrection. Since, from the Sunday of Septuagesima throughout the entire period of fasting until Pascha, we must devote ourselves to repentance and the mortification of our bodies and must abstain from this praise—although the praise of God is absent from the Church at no time—so during the days of the Paschal solemnity, indeed throughout the entire fifty-day period until Pentecost, and on the Lord’s days, when it is fitting for us to rejoice and to be released from fasting, we ought to repeat it continually in song.

The time before Pascha therefore signifies the fasting of the present life, because on account of our sins we are afflicted daily with punishments and hardships. The time of the Paschal fifty-day period signifies the future resurrection of our bodies, that is, eternal life in heaven, because our Head rose at that time.

Therefore the heavenly song “Alleluia,” which the apostle John recalls in the Apocalypse as being sung in heaven by a great multitude of saints, ought to be repeated at the time when we desire our immortality, celebrating the glorification of our Savior. We should desire this: that, although placed in a foreign land, we cannot worthily sing the Lord’s song on earth, we may reach the land of the living, where, rejoicing without end, we may sing a new song to the Lord without cessation forever.

On Holy Pentecost Saturday, as on Holy Easter Saturday, baptism is celebrated, with readings from the Old Testament recited beforehand, prayers and litanies first completed, and the holy celebration of the Mass following.

Holy Pentecost Saturday is also rightly venerated with a celebration similar to Holy Easter Saturday, because the only-begotten Son of God did not wish there to be any separation between himself and the Holy Spirit in the faith of believers or in the power of works. There is no diversity in nature, as he says: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John IV).

And again: “The Paraclete, however, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything I have said to you” (ibid.).

And again: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth” (John XVI).

Since Christ is truth and the Holy Spirit is truth, and the name “Paraclete” is proper to both, the festival is not dissimilar where there is always one sacrament.

## CHAPTER XLII. [Col. 0355D] On the Lord’s Day

The apostles established the Lord’s day as a religious solemnity because on it our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is called the Lord’s day so that on it, abstaining from earthly works and the enticements of the world, we may devote ourselves solely to divine worship, giving this day honor and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection, which we possess in it.

For just as the Lord Jesus Christ himself, our Savior, rose from the dead on the third day, so we hope that we too shall rise on the last day. Hence on the Lord’s day we pray standing, which is a sign of the future resurrection.

The whole Church does this. It is found on pilgrimage in mortality, awaiting at the end of the age what was foreshadowed in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn from the dead.

We read that the Sabbath was celebrated physically in rest by the former people, so that it might be a figure of rest; hence *sabbath* is interpreted as “rest.” The Lord’s day, however, was declared not to the Jews but to Christians through the Lord’s resurrection, and from that time it began to possess its own festival.

It is the first day, which is found after the seventh as the eighth. Hence in Ecclesiastes, with reference to the two Testaments, it is said: “To seven, likewise to eight.”

At first it was handed down that only the Sabbath should be celebrated, because previously there was rest for the dead, whereas there was no resurrection of anyone until Christ the Lord, who, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him.

After such a resurrection had taken place in the Lord’s body, so that he might go before as the Head of the Church in what the body of the Church hoped for at the end, the eighth day, which is also the first, succeeded in the festival.

It is evident that this day too is solemn in the holy Scriptures. It is the first day of the world; on it the elements of the world were formed; on it the angels were created; on it Christ also rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the apostles; and on it manna was first given from heaven in the wilderness.

For the Lord says: “For six days you shall gather manna, but on the sixth day you shall gather twice as much” (Exodus XVI). The sixth day is Parasceve, which is placed before the Sabbath. The Sabbath, however, is the eighth day, and it is followed by the Lord’s day, on which manna first came from heaven.

Let the Jews therefore understand that already then our Lord’s day was preferred to the Jewish Sabbath; already then it was indicated that on their Sabbath no grace of God descended to them from heaven, but that he first rained it upon them on our Lord’s day.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Festivals of the Saints

The ancient fathers decreed that the festivals of the apostles and the solemnities in honor of the martyrs should be celebrated as a mystery of veneration (Augustine, *On the City of God*), either to arouse imitation, or so that we might be joined to their merits and assisted by their prayers. This is done, however, in such a way that we establish altars not to any martyr but to the God of the martyrs, even though they are in the memorials of the martyrs.

For which bishop, standing at an altar in the places where the bodies of the saints rest, has ever said: “We offer to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian”? What is offered is offered to God, who crowned the martyrs, at the memorials of those whom he crowned. Through love for them, a greater affection arises to sharpen charity, both toward those whom we could imitate and toward the one through whose help we are able to do so.

We honor the martyrs, therefore, with that worship of love and fellowship with which holy people of God are honored in this life. We perceive their hearts to have been prepared for such suffering on behalf of the truth of the Gospel. We honor them with greater devotion because, after all uncertainties have been overcome, they are safer; and with more confident praise because they are already victorious in the happier life, whereas in this life we are still fighting.

But that worship which in Greek is called *latreia*, λατρεία, cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word. Properly, it is a certain service owed to divinity. We neither worship nor teach that anyone should worship any being except the one God.

Since the offering of sacrifice belongs to this worship, and since *idolatry* is the name for those who offer this even to idols, we in no way offer or command anything of this kind to be offered either to any martyr, any holy soul, or any angel. Whoever falls into this error should be corrected by sound doctrine, whether so that he may be corrected or so that he may be warned away from it. For the holy, whether human beings or angels, do not wish to have offered to them what they know is owed to God alone.

This was evident in Paul and Barnabas when the Lycaonians, moved by the miracles performed through them, wished to sacrifice to them as gods (Acts XIV). They tore their garments, confessing and persuading that they were not gods, and prohibited these things from being done to them.

It was also evident in the angels, as we read in the Apocalypse, when an angel prevented himself from being worshiped and said to the one worshiping him: “I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers; worship God” (Apocalypse XIX).

It is rightly written, therefore, that the human being was forbidden by an angel to worship the angel, but was commanded to worship the one God under whom both the angel and the human being were fellow servants.

Let there not, then, be for us that worship of divine religion directed toward angels or martyrs, because they are not regarded as beings who seek for themselves honors belonging to God. They themselves do not wish to be worshiped in God’s place; rather, they wish us to worship the one whose illumination makes them rejoice.

Martyrs, therefore, are to be honored for imitation, not adored as an act of religion; honored with love, not with servitude.

It should also be noted that Felix, the Roman pope, the twenty-seventh after Saint Peter, is read to have established that Masses should be celebrated above the memorials of martyrs. Nevertheless, the blessed Pope Gregory, the sixty-sixth pope of the city of Rome, established that Masses should be celebrated above the body.

Certain festivals are called *natales*, “birthdays,” and rightly so. Just as someone is customarily said to be born when, proceeding from the womb of his mother, he comes forth into this light, so he can most properly be called born when, released from the bonds of the flesh, he is raised to eternal light.

Thus the ecclesiastical custom arose of calling the days of the blessed martyrs or confessors of Christ who have departed from the world their “birthdays,” and of calling their solemnities not funerals but birthdays.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Offering Sacrifices for the Dead

We believe that the offering of sacrifice for the rest of the faithful departed, or praying for them, was handed down by the apostles, because this practice is observed throughout the entire world.

The Catholic Church holds this everywhere. If it did not believe that sins are remitted to the faithful departed, it would not make almsgiving or offer sacrifice for their particular benefit.

For when it also says, “Whoever has sinned against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew XII), it demonstrates that certain sins are to be forgiven there and that certain others are to be cleansed by purgatorial fire.

Therefore, as Saint Gregory relates in the books of the *Dialogues*, and as the teacher Bede relates in the *Deeds of the Angels*, it has frequently been shown by example or revealed in visions that sacrifices offered for the dead greatly benefit their souls.

In one place Saint Augustine also said that the souls of the dead are undoubtedly relieved by the piety of their living relatives when sacrifice is offered for them or alms are given, provided that each person prepared some merit for himself while he was still living in the body, on account of which these things may benefit him.

For they do not benefit everyone, except according to the difference in the life each person led in the body. For the very good, they are acts of thanksgiving; for those who were neither very good nor very evil, they are acts of propitiation; and for the very evil, even if they provide no assistance for the dead, they are nevertheless consolations for the living.

For those whom such offerings benefit, they benefit either so that their remission may be complete or at least so that their condemnation itself may become more bearable.

## CHAPTER XLV. [Col. 0358B] On the Encaenia, and the Origin of That Entire Observance
Annual festivals of the dedication of churches are celebrated according to the custom of the ancients, as we read in the Gospel, where it says: “Now the Dedication took place in Jerusalem” (John X). For the *encaenia* were festivals of the dedication of the temple. In Greek, *kainon* (καινὸν) means “new.” Whatever, therefore, is dedicated as something new is called an *encaenium*. The Jews solemnly celebrated the day on which Solomon’s temple was dedicated, as the Book of Kings and Chronicles relate, and that day was kept as a feast among them. This observance evidently fell into disuse among those who lacked both worship and a temple.

Christians, however, preserve that custom of the fathers, in whom the glory appears to have been transferred. For the fact that, at the dedication of a temple, on the night preceding the day of dedication, the relics of the saints are placed in a bier and guarded by vigils in a tent demonstrates what else but that the Ark of the Covenant, together with the holy things that were in it, was kept in the Mosaic tabernacle before the building of the temple, under the watch of the Levites. And when, at the time of the dedication, a multitude is summoned from every direction and the bier containing the relics of the saints is carried by priests from the tent to the temple, what else does this signify but what the Book of Chronicles relates: “All the men of Israel came to King Solomon on the solemn day, and the Levites carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, together with all the furnishings of the tabernacle, and the priests brought it into its place” (II Chronicles V), that is, into the sanctuary of the temple, the Holy of Holies?

But when the bishop, together with the priests carrying the bier, and with all the clergy and the rest of the people singing praise and litanies, circles it three times outside before entering the temple, what else does this signify but that, at the coming of the Lord and his saints—which takes place through his invocation, as he himself said, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew XVIII)—all the pride and power of the devil, if any has been lurking in the house, should fall and be scattered, and that, according to the prophet, “The Lord alone will be exalted on that day, and the name of that place will henceforth be called ‘The Lord’” (ibid.)?

We also read in Joshua that the priests and Levites, together with all Israel, went around the city of Jericho with the ark of the Lord, and that, when the priests sounded the trumpets and all the people shouted, the walls of the city suddenly collapsed. This plainly signifies that, at the sound of the preaching and praise of the Lord, after the Savior’s coming, worldly pride fell and the kingdom of the devil was destroyed.

The twelve lamps placed inside beside the walls of the temple express the number twelve, that is, the apostles and patriarchs, which the apostle John also records in the Apocalypse as being prominent in the structure of the heavenly Jerusalem.

The fact that the altar is anointed with chrism after the sprinkling of water was done in imitation of the patriarch Jacob, who, after that terrible vision, raised up a stone as a pillar, poured oil over it, and called the place “the house of God” (Genesis XXVIII). We also read in Exodus that Moses made the holy oil of anointing and anointed with it the tabernacle of the testimony, the ark of the covenant, the table with its vessels, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense and the altar of burnt offering, and all the furnishings belonging to their worship; and likewise Aaron and his sons, so that they might perform the priesthood of the Lord.

He blesses these things so that the objects to be sacrificed may be smeared with the sacred ointment of chrism, to show that all sanctification consists in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power has been mingled with the holy chrism in order to bestow sanctification.

The fact that incense is then placed by the bishop upon the altar signifies that the priest’s prayer ought to be pure upon it, so that he may say to the Lord with the prophet: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm CXL).

That the relics of the saints are placed beneath the altar-table signifies that the saints have seats and rest beneath the throne of God. John also testifies to this in the Apocalypse when he says: “I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony that they held, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not avenge and judge the blood of those who dwell on the earth?’ And individual white robes were given to them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who were to be killed as they had been, should be completed” (Revelation VI).

When the dedication of the temple and altar has been completed, the bishop and clergy put on other vestments and solemnly celebrate the celebration of the holy Masses. This too has been preserved from ancient usage, because we read in Chronicles that, after the ark had been placed in its position—that is, in the Holy of Holies—and the priests had gone out from the sanctuary, all the priests were sanctified, as were the Levites and the singers, those under Asaph, those under Heman, and those under Jeduthun; their sons and brothers, clothed in linen, resounded with cymbals, psalteries, and lyres, standing on the eastern side of the altar, and so forth (II Chronicles V).

And again: “The king and all the people were sacrificing victims before the Lord.” A little later: “The king and all the people dedicated the house of God. The priests stood at their offices,” and so forth (II Chronicles VII).

In this respect our practice is superior to that ancient dedication: there, many thousands of oxen and sheep were slaughtered; here, the body of that Lamb is sacrificed who took away the sins of the world. There, a multitude of trumpets, cymbals, and other musical instruments resounded; here, the jubilant song that proceeds from a devout heart sounds sweetly through human voices.

As far as truth surpasses shadow, so far does our sacrifice surpass the legal victim; and as far as the sensible surpasses the insensible, so far does praise uttered by the human voice from a pure heart surpass the empty breath of trumpets and the striking of cymbals.

But because all those things happened to them in figure, while we, with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of the Lord, we observe that custom of the ancients, transferred into our religion, all the more fittingly because it is more truly fulfilled.

All festivals, because of the variety of religious observances, and the various times established in honor of the martyrs, were instituted by prudent men so that perhaps infrequent gatherings of the people might not diminish faith in Christ. Therefore certain days were appointed so that all might come together as one, and so that, through seeing one another, faith might grow and greater joy arise.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the festivals of the ancients, and from what source festivals or holidays derive their names

The following were feast days under the Old Law: the Day of Unleavened Bread and Passover, when, at the full moon, the leaven having been removed, the lamb was sacrificed. The Day of Pentecost, on which the Law was given to Moses on the summit of Mount Sinai, and on which the first loaves of the grain harvest were offered as the bread of the Presence.

The days of Sabbaths, on which rest was observed and on which it was not permitted to gather manna in the desert.

The days of the New Moons, the celebration of the new moon. The Jews always kept a feast at the beginning of the months, that is, at the first moon. They did this at the beginning of the month because, when the moon wanes, time comes to an end, and when it is born again, time begins again.

The Day of Trumpets was the beginning of the seventh month, when the Jews, celebrating the solemnity, sounded the trumpet more extensively and offered more sacrifices on that day than during the individual months.

In this month, on the tenth day of the month, was the Day of Propitiation, or Atonement, when the bishop entered the Holy of Holies once a year. While the people prayed outside, he alone prayed within, offering incense to the Lord on the altar of incense both for his own ignorance and for that of the people.

In this month also occurred the very celebrated days of the Feast of Booths, that is, of Tabernacles. From the fifteenth day of that month they lived for seven days in shelters, taking for themselves palm branches, branches of trees with dense foliage, and willows from the torrent; and they rejoiced before the Lord their God in commemoration of their departure from Egypt, because the Lord had made them dwell in tabernacles when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.

The fast days of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months were celebrated among them for the reasons we mentioned above when we were discussing fasting.

They are called *festi*—“feast days”—because on them *ius fatur*, that is, “the law is spoken,” while *nefasti* are those on which it is not spoken.

Likewise, *feriae*—holidays—are named from *fari*, “to speak.” For this reason Pope Sylvester I established among the Romans that the names of the days, which they had previously called according to the names of their gods—namely, the day of the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Venus, Saturn—should henceforth be called *feriae*: the first holiday, second holiday, third holiday, fourth holiday, fifth holiday, and sixth holiday. For at the beginning of Genesis it is written that God spoke on each day: on the first, “Let there be light”; on the second, “Let there be a firmament”; on the third, “Let the earth produce green vegetation”; and so forth.

He commanded that the Sabbath should still be called by the ancient term of the Law, and that the first holiday should be called the Lord’s Day, because on it the Lord rose again.

The same pope established that the rest of the Sabbath should rather be transferred to the Lord’s Day, so that on that day we might be free from earthly works in order to praise God, according to what is written: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm XLVI).

In accordance with this custom, the holy Church commands us to be free on the birthdays of the saints—that is, to devote ourselves to celebrating the praises of God. But whoever wishes to abstain from farming on these days in order to devote himself to overeating and drunkenness, or to spend his time in empty amusements, should recognize that he sins more through such leisure than if he were occupied with some useful work. Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “Woe to those who linger over wine and apply themselves to drinking cups” (Proverbs XXIII); and again: “The servant who is intelligent is acceptable to the king, but the useless man will endure wrath” (Proverbs XIV).

But since we have already spoken above, according to the understanding of the ancients, about the more distinguished festivals, for the instruction of those who serve God in the Church and preside over the people, let us now also speak about the origin of chant, the readings, and the authority of the Creed.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the canticle

Moses is read as having been the first of all to establish the canticle, when, after Egypt had been struck with ten plagues and Pharaoh had been drowned, he came out with the people through the unfamiliar paths of the sea toward the desert, rejoicing and saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exodus XV).

The same author later composed in Deuteronomy a canticle foretelling future events. Then Deborah also, a woman of no little distinction, is found to have exercised this mystery in the Book of Judges. Afterward, many—not only men but also women—filled with the divine Spirit, are recorded to have sung the mysteries of God.

A canticle is a human voice; a psalm, however, is what is sung to the psaltery.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the psalms

The Church declares that Moses first introduced the practice of psalmody, and that the prophet David did so in a great mystery. From childhood specially chosen by the Lord for this office, he deserved to become the leader of the singers and the treasury of psalms.

For this reason the Church frequently uses his psalter together with the melody of sweet songs, so that minds may be more easily bent toward compunction.

The primitive Church sang psalms in such a way that the singer’s voice resounded with only a slight inflection, so that it was closer to ordinary speech than to singing.

The custom of singing was instituted in the Church for the sake of the carnal, not the spiritual, so that those who are not moved to compunction by words might be moved by the sweetness of melody.

Thus the most blessed Augustine, in his book of Confessions, approves the custom of singing in the Church, saying that “through the pleasures of the ears, the weaker mind rises toward the effect of devotion.” For our minds are moved more religiously and ardently toward the flame of devotion by the sacred words themselves when they are sung than when they are not sung. All our emotions are stirred more powerfully by the diversity or novelty of sounds, through some hidden familiarity, when something is sung with a sweet and artful voice.

The psalmist ought to be distinguished and illustrious both in voice and in skill, so that he may stir the minds of his hearers through the pleasure of sweetness.

His voice should not be harsh, hoarse, or discordant, but musical, sweet, clear, and high-pitched; it should possess a sound and melody suited to holy religion—not one that cries out with tragic technique, but one that demonstrates Christian simplicity in the very modulation, and not one that smells of musical affectation or theatrical art, but one that produces rather compunction in its hearers.

A perfect voice is high, clear, and sweet: high, so that it may reach the heights; clear, so that it may fill the ears; sweet, so that it may delight the minds of the hearers. If any of these qualities is lacking, the voice will not be perfect.

For in ancient times singers abstained from food on the day before they were to sing, taking only pale legumes for the sake of the voice; hence singers were commonly called *fabarii*, “bean-eaters.” If such a practice was observed among pagans merely for the preservation of the voice, how much more ought Christians, who are concerned not so much with the voice as with virtue itself, to abstain from every enticement of pleasure?

## CHAPTER XLIX. On hymns

It is clear that the same prophet David was the first to compose and sing hymns, and that other prophets did so afterward. Later, the three boys placed in the furnace, having summoned every creature, sang a hymn to the Creator of all things.

Thus, in singing hymns and psalms, we possess not only the example of the prophets but also that of the Lord himself and of the apostles, together with useful instructions on this matter for moving the mind devoutly and inflaming the feeling of divine love.

Some hymns are divine; others are composed by human ingenuity.

Hilary, a Gallic bishop born at Poitiers and distinguished for his eloquence, first flourished in the composition of hymns. After him, Bishop Ambrose, a man of great glory in Christ and a most renowned teacher in the Church, is known to have flourished abundantly in this kind of composition. Hence hymns are called “Ambrosian” after him, because they first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan in his time; thereafter devotion to this practice was observed throughout the Churches of the West.

All songs that are spoken in praise of God are called hymns.

## CHAPTER L. On antiphons

The Greeks were the first to compose antiphons, with two choirs singing alternately, like two seraphim and two Testaments crying out to one another.

Among the Latins, the same most blessed Ambrose was the first to institute antiphons, imitating the example of the Greeks. From then on, their use increased throughout all the regions of the West.

## CHAPTER LI. On responsories

Responsories were discovered by the Italians long ago and were called by this name because, when one person sings, the choir answers by resounding in return.

Previously each person performed this alone; now sometimes one, sometimes two or three sing together, while the choir responds for the most part.

## CHAPTER LII. On readings

The Jewish tradition holds that the recitation of readings is an ancient institution. They too make use of readings from the Law and the Prophets on appointed and fixed days, preserving this practice from the institution of the fathers.

A reading is no small edification for those who hear it. Therefore, when psalmody is taking place, all should sing; when prayer is being offered, all should pray; when a reading is being read, all should listen equally in silence.

Even if someone arrives while the reading is being celebrated, he should simply adore God and, having marked his forehead, attentively lend his ear. There is an appointed time for prayer when we all pray; and when he wishes, he may pray privately under the pretext of prayer.

Do not miss the reading, because not everyone can always have it ready at hand, whereas the opportunity for prayer is readily available. Nor should you think that little benefit arises from hearing the reading. Prayer itself becomes richer when the mind, marked by the reading it has just heard, runs through images of divine things.

For Mary, the sister of Martha, who sat at Jesus’ feet and listened intently to his word while her sister was neglected, is affirmed by the Lord’s voice to have chosen the good portion for herself (Luke X).

Therefore the deacon also admonishes the people to silence in a clear voice, so that, whether psalmody is taking place or a reading is being pronounced, unity may be preserved by all, and what is preached to all may be heard equally by all.

Whoever wishes to perform his office decently and properly must be imbued with instruction and books, and richly adorned with knowledge of meanings and words. He must understand, in the divisions of sentences, where the connection ends, where the statement still hangs unfinished, and where the final sentence closes. Thus, being well prepared, he will possess the force of delivery, so as to move the minds and understanding of everyone toward comprehension.

The various kinds of delivery should be distinguished, and the proper emotions of the sentences expressed: sometimes with the voice of one simply indicating, sometimes grieving, sometimes indignant, sometimes rebuking, sometimes exhorting, sometimes showing pity, sometimes asking a question, and in similar ways according to the character of the particular delivery.

There are many passages in the Scriptures which, unless they are delivered in their proper manner, turn into the opposite meaning, as in the Apostle’s words: “Who will accuse God’s elect? God, who justifies” (Romans VIII). If this is spoken as though it were a statement of weakness, without preserving its proper manner of delivery, great perversity results.

It must therefore be pronounced so that an inquiry comes first and a question follows. The ancients said that the difference between an inquiry and a question is that many answers can be given to an inquiry, whereas to a question the answer is either “no” or “yes.”

Thus, after the inquiry in which we say, “Who will accuse God’s elect?” what follows should be uttered in the tone of one asking a question: “God, who justifies,” so that the unspoken answer may be “No.”

Likewise, let us ask: “Who is the one who condemns?” And again let us put the question: “Christ Jesus, who died, indeed rather who rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us?”—so that everywhere the unspoken answer may be “No.”

But in the passage where he says: “What then shall we say? Because the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness,” unless, after the inquiry “What then shall we say?”, the answer is supplied—“Because the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness” (Romans IX)—the following text will not cohere.

There are many other passages that likewise require their own proper manner of delivery.

Furthermore, the reader must know the force of accents, so that he may know on which syllable the voice of the speaker should be extended, because there are many words that can be distinguished by the accent alone in pronunciation, lest their meaning be misunderstood. These matters, however, must be learned from grammarians.

The reader’s voice should be simple and clear, suited to every kind of delivery, full of vigorous male substance, avoiding a rustic and somewhat uncultivated sound. It should be neither low nor excessively high, neither broken nor delicate, and should sound nothing feminine. It should contain no inflated or breathless words, should not growl in the throat, resound through the emptiness of the mouth, or be uttered harshly with growling or gaping lips. Rather, it should be pronounced closely, evenly, gently, and clearly, so that each letter is expressed with its own sound and every word is adorned with its proper accent, and so that the sentence is not broken for the sake of display.

Nor should the reader have an immodest movement of the body, but rather an appearance of gravity. The reader should attend to the ears and heart, not to the eyes, lest he make spectators rather than hearers of those before him.

There is an ancient opinion that readers took especial care of their voices for the sake of delivery, so that they could be heard amid the tumult. Hence readers were formerly called heralds or criers.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the books of the two Testaments

In the churches of Christ, readings are pronounced from the Holy Scriptures. The same sacred Scripture consists of the Old Law and the New.

The Old Law is that which was first given to the Jews through Moses and the prophets, and it is called the Old Testament. It is called a testament because it was written and duly sealed by trustworthy witnesses, namely, the prophets.

The New Law is the Gospel, which is called the New Testament and which was given through Christ, the very Son of God, and his apostles.

The Old Law is like a root; the New is like fruit arising from the root. For one comes from the Law to the Gospel. Indeed, Christ, who has been manifested here, was previously foretold in the Law. Rather, he himself spoke in the prophets, as it is written: “I who was speaking—behold, I am here,” setting forth the Law like a pedagogue for children, while granting the Gospel, the perfect instruction of life, to all who have reached maturity.

Therefore, in the former, earthly goods were promised to those who worked; here, under grace, the heavenly kingdom is granted to those who live by faith.

The Gospel is called “good news,” and truly it is good news, so that those who receive it may be called sons of God.

These, then, are the books of the Old Testament which the leaders of the Churches have handed down to be read and received with love of instruction and devotion.

The first are the five books of the Law, that is, of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

These are followed by fifteen historical books: Joshua son of Nun and Judges, one book each, together with Ruth; four books of Kings; two of Chronicles; one each of Tobit, Esther, and Judith; two of Ezra; and two of Maccabees.

In addition to these there are sixteen prophetic books: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, one book each, together with one book for each of the twelve prophets. These are the prophetic books.

After these there are eight books in verse, written among the Hebrews in different meters: the Book of Job, the Book of Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

Thus the books of the Old Testament number forty-five.

The first books of the New Testament are the four Gospels, of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. These are followed by the fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul, to which are added the seven canonical Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude.

There are also the Acts of the twelve apostles. The seal of all these books is the Apocalypse of John, which is the revelation of Jesus Christ and which concludes all the books both in time and in order.

These are the seventy-two canonical books. For this reason Moses chose seventy elders to prophesy, and for this reason our Lord Jesus also commanded seventy-two disciples to preach. And since seventy-two languages were spread throughout the world, the Holy Spirit fittingly provided that there should be as many books as there were nations, so that peoples and nations might be built up for the completion of the grace of faith.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the writers of the sacred books

According to the tradition of the Hebrews, the following are regarded as the writers of the Old Testament.

Moses first wrote the Pentateuch. Joshua son of Nun published his book. Samuel wrote Judges, Ruth, and the first part of Samuel; David wrote the remainder of Samuel to the end.

Jeremiah composed the whole of *Malachim*—“Kings”—for previously it had been scattered through the histories of the individual kings.

The Hebrews think that Moses wrote the Book of Job; others think that one of the prophets did so.

The Psalter was written by ten prophets: Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Jeduthun, Heman, and the sons of Korah, namely Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. Some also say that Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah wrote it.

Solomon wrote Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

Isaiah wrote his own book, and likewise Jeremiah wrote his, together with his Lamentations.

The wise men of the Synagogue wrote Ezekiel, Daniel, Chronicles, and Esther.

Ezra wrote his own book.

After the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans and the Jews had entered Jerusalem, the same Ezra, inspired by the divine Spirit, restored all these books and corrected all the volumes of the prophets that had been corrupted by the nations. He established the whole Testament in twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there are letters.

After Ezra, the first translation from Hebrew into Greek was produced by the Seventy Interpreters under Ptolemy, king of Egypt and successor of Alexander, who was devoted to reading and gathered the books of all nations.

This king sent many gifts to the temple and asked Eleazar, who was the high priest, that elders from the twelve tribes of Israel be sent to interpret all their books. So that he might assess the reliability of the interpretation, he gave each of those who had been appointed a separate cell and, having assigned the task to all of them, ordered them to interpret all the Scriptures.

When they had completed this task over seventy days, he gathered together all their interpretations, which they had produced separately in different cells, with none of them approaching another. They were found to have translated all the books through the Holy Spirit in such a way that they agreed not only in understanding but even in wording.

This was the first true and divine translation.

The Churches of all nations first began to study these books and, translating them from Greek into Latin, the earliest guardians of the Churches handed them down.

After this, Aquila produced a second edition; Theodotion and Symmachus produced a third and fourth, both being Jewish proselytes. Origen discovered a fifth and sixth edition and compared them with the other editions mentioned above.

These, then, are the translators who rendered the Holy Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek—five in number, as they are counted.

As for the number of Latin translators who rendered them from Greek into our language, Saint Augustine says that it is unlimited. “For,” he says, “if, in the earliest times of the faith, a Greek codex came into someone’s hands and he sensed that he possessed even a little knowledge of both languages, he immediately dared to translate it. Hence there came to be so innumerable translators among the Latins.”

From Hebrew into Latin, however, only the presbyter Jerome translated the Holy Scriptures. All the Churches everywhere generally use his edition because it is more venerable in its meanings and clearer in its words.

Solomon is shown to have written the Book of Wisdom by those testimonies in which one reads: “You chose me, he says, as king for your people, and you said that I should build a temple for your holy name, in the city of your holy dwelling” (Wisdom IX).

The Hebrews, as one of their wise men records, received this work among the canonical Scriptures. But after they seized and killed Christ, they remembered the book’s most explicit testimonies about Christ, in which it says: “The ungodly said among themselves: ‘Let us seize the righteous man, because he is useless to us and opposed to our works, and he promises to possess the knowledge of God and calls himself the Son of God’” (Wisdom II).

And below: “For if he is truly the Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his adversaries.” And then: “So that we may know his reverence and test his patience, let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (ibid.).

After comparing the texts, they removed it from the prophetic books, lest our people reproach them for such an open sacrilege, and they forbade it to be read among them.

The Book of Ecclesiasticus was composed by Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem, grandson of Jesus the priest, whom Zechariah mentions. Among the Latins this book is prefaced with the title of Solomon, because of the similarity of its language.

Moreover, it is by no means established who wrote the books of Judith, Tobit, or Maccabees.

As for the New Testament, the four evangelists each wrote one of the four Gospel books. Only Matthew is said to have written in the Hebrew language; the others wrote in Greek.

The apostle Paul wrote his Epistles. Of these, he wrote nine to seven churches and the others to his disciples Timothy, Titus, and Philemon.

As for the Epistle to the Hebrews, its authorship is uncertain to most Latins because of the difference in its language. Some suspect that Barnabas composed it; others that it was written by Clement.

Peter wrote two Epistles in his own name, which are called Catholic. Some do not believe that the second of these is his, because of the difference in style and language.

James wrote his Epistle, which some likewise deny to be his, thinking that it was dictated by another under his name.

John published three Epistles. Some assert that only the first is his; the other two are thought to belong to a certain presbyter named John, whose second tomb, according to Jerome’s opinion, is shown at Ephesus.

Jude published his Epistle.

Luke composed the Acts of the Apostles from what he heard or saw.

The evangelist John wrote the Apocalypse at the same time that he is said to have been exiled to the island of Patmos because of preaching the Gospel.

These are the writers of the sacred books, speaking by divine inspiration and dispensing heavenly instructions in the Church for our education.

The author of these Scriptures is believed to be the Holy Spirit. For he himself wrote who dictated to his prophets what was to be written.

## CHAPTER LV. On blessings

That blessing is given to the people by priests is revealed and confirmed by the ancient blessing through Moses, by which he is commanded to bless the people under the sacrament of a threefold invocation.

For the Lord says to Moses: “Thus you shall bless my people, and I will bless them. May the Lord bless you and keep you” (Numbers VI); “may the Lord illuminate his face upon you and have mercy on you” (Psalm LXVII); “and may the Lord turn his countenance toward you and grant you peace” (Numbers VI).

Hence the Church also has the practice of administering multiple blessings for various things.

Oil is blessed on apostolic authority as a medicine for the sick, as the apostle James commands in this way: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, so that they may pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (James V).

Salt and water are blessed for various uses of the faithful: for sick people, against the enemy’s illusion, for the health of cattle, for removing diseases, and so forth. Thus we read that Alexander, the seventh bishop of the city of Rome after Peter and a martyr, established that water for sprinkling should be blessed with salt in human dwellings.

For there is no other element that purifies everything in this world as water does, and none that gives life to all things. Therefore, when we are baptized in Christ, through it we are reborn, so that, having been purified, we may be given life. At the time of his Passion, water flowed from Christ’s side together with blood, to show that the sacrament of all sanctification and purity derives its power from this.

The fact that sanctified salt is mixed with water arose from divine authority, because God commanded through Elisha that it be thrown into the spring so that the barrenness of the waters of Jericho might be healed.

Thus the nature of salt is near and closely joined to the nature of water, because both possess the same gentleness, and both have the same function and meaning.

Water cleanses filth; salt drives away corruption. Water provides brightness; salt supplies purity. Water signifies the drink of wisdom, and salt indicates the taste of prudence. The authority of the sacred books sufficiently attests this, and their many testimonies make it clear.

A wondrous effect of divine action takes place here: through the mouths of the priests, God himself blesses, and through their visible ministry divine power invisibly effects the sacrament.

The priest’s devout intention prays for the health of human beings, and the devotion of divine mercy grants it. Thus it happens that the charity which offers supplication in the priest itself obtains complete health from the Lord.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Creed
Our forebears relate that the Symbol was instituted in the following manner. After the ascension of our Lord and Savior to the Father, when, following the coming of the Holy Spirit, his disciples, aflame, were speaking in the languages of all nations—so that no foreign people, and no barbarous language, would seem inaccessible or impassable to them—the Lord gave them the command to go to each nation in turn to preach the word of God.

As they were therefore about to depart from one another, they first established together a rule for their future preaching, lest, departing quickly from one another, they should preach something diverse or discordant to those who were being invited to the faith of Christ. Thus, all gathered as one and filled with the Holy Spirit, by contributing a brief statement of their preaching they composed into one what each had thought, and they decreed that this should be given as a rule to believers.

They wished to call this the *Symbol* for many and most fitting reasons. For *symbol*—in Greek, σύμβολον—can mean both “sign” and “contribution,” that is, something that several people contribute into one. This is what the apostles did: in those words, each contributed into one what he had understood.

It is called a “sign” or “token” because at that time, as the Apostle Paul says and as is reported in the Acts of the Apostles, many pretended to be apostles of Christ, indeed naming Christ, but not proclaiming him along the complete lines of tradition. They therefore established this token, by which the one who preached the true Christ according to the apostolic writings could be recognized.

The Symbol is also a sign by which God is recognized; believers receive it for this reason, so that they may know how to prepare themselves for the contests of faith against the devil. It contains few words, but all the mysteries. For it has been briefly compiled by the apostles from the whole of Scripture, so that, since many believers do not know letters, or since those who do know them cannot read the Scriptures because of the preoccupations of the world, they may retain this in their hearts and possess sufficient saving knowledge.

It is a brief word of faith, also foretold long ago by the prophet: “For the Lord will make a brief word upon the earth.”

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Rule of Faith

This, then, is the most certain faith after the apostolic Symbol, which our teachers have handed down: that we confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one essence, of the same power and eternity, one invisible God; yet, while the distinct property of each Person is preserved, the Trinity must neither be divided substantially nor altogether confused personally.

We are to confess the Father as unbegotten, the Son as only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit as neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. The Son proceeds from the Father by being born, whereas the Holy Spirit proceeds without being born. The Son himself, perfect, took a human being from the Virgin, without sin, so that he might mercifully restore, by his own will, the one whom he had created solely through goodness and who had fallen voluntarily.

We confess that he was truly crucified, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven in that same flesh, now glorified, in which he is expected to come for the judgment of the living and the dead. We confess also that one Christ bore, in a single Person, the divine and human substances, perfect in both: for the integrity of the two substances neither multiplied the Person, nor did the unity of the Person confuse the two substances. For neither excluded the other, since each preserved its own integrity inviolate.

The salutary authority of the New and Old Testaments commends this, the former truthfully fulfilled through prophecy, the latter through history. We are not to hold, with pagans or heretics, any opinion concerning God or the creature of the world in those matters in which they disagree with the truth.

Rather, the divine utterances of both Testaments proclaim that we are to believe only this: that God created neither humanity nor the universe under any compulsion; that there is no visible or invisible substance at all except either God himself or something created good by the good God; that God is supremely and immutably good, while the creature is good in a lower and mutable manner; that the origin of souls is uncertain; and that the nature of angels and of souls is not part of the divine substance, but a creature of God made from nothing, and therefore incorporeal because it was created in the image of God.

We are to hold also to the piety of conduct, without which faith in divine worship lies idle and grows numb, but with which the integrity of divine worship is brought to completion; and that each person should love God for God’s sake, and his neighbor in God, so that by attaining perfection he may arrive at the goal.

Nor can one person be defiled by another’s sin where there is no consent of a shared will. Lawful marriages are not to be considered condemnable, although offspring born from them are also believed to be subject to original sin; nevertheless, the integrity of faithful virgins and those who practice continence is taught to be preferable to them by right.

The one baptism of the Trinity must not be repeated—which would be impious. Nor should anyone suppose that, because of the diversity of the ministers who administer it, each recipient must make confession to a different one; rather, baptism is bestowed by the singular power of the one of whom we read: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit”; and, “I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1).

Nor should we think that we have no need of the remedies of repentance for the daily offenses of human frailty, without which we cannot exist in this life. Rather, through the fruitful compunction of repentance we must confess that all sins are wiped away, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Psalm 31).

No one is joined to Christ the Head by his own powers, but through divine grace, and is established in the unity of the Church by perseverance in unbroken peace. Nor should anything good be attributed to the judgment of human will; rather, the entire number of the elect is acquired according to the purpose of God’s will.

Temporal goods, common to the good and the wicked, are created by God and, by his dispensation, either granted or denied to each person. In each believer, it is not possession but use of these goods that is either to be condemned or approved.

The certain and eternal goods, however, only the good can attain in the future. We believe that the Church, now formed by the pledge of these goods, possesses here the first fruits of the Spirit and will possess perfection in the future; here she is sustained in hope, and afterward nourished in reality; here she sees through a mirror in an enigma, but in the future face to face, when she has been brought through faith to direct vision.

Until this is perfected, so that we may enjoy the eternal goods of the highest God, we must enjoy them in such a way that we do not harm our neighbors.

We must also possess this hope of resurrection: that, in the same order and form in which the Lord himself rose from the dead, we too shall rise, in the same body in which we are and in which we live. We shall not change our nature or sex, but shall merely lay aside frailty and vices.

Satan himself, together with his angels and worshipers, is to be condemned to eternal fire; he is not, as some sacrilegiously arrange matters, to be restored to his former—that is, angelic—rank, from which he fell through his own wickedness.

This is the integrity of the faith of catholic tradition. If any one element of it is rejected, the entire credulity of the faith is lost.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On Various Heresies

Every soul that fears God must therefore beware lest, falling away from the catholic faith and abandoning the teaching of truth, it fall into the errors of heretics, since this is the most certain kind of death. To make this easier to avoid, we have set out in this book all the sects arising from the errors of heretics and schismatics that we find recorded by catholic teachers, together with their founders or followers.

“Heresy,” in Greek αἵρεσις, is called after “choice,” because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him—for example, the Peripatetics, Academics, Epicureans, and Stoics among philosophers—or like others who, conceiving a perverse doctrine, withdrew from the Church according to their own judgment.

Thus heresies are named by the Greek term derived from “choice,” because each person, according to his own judgment, chooses for himself whatever he wishes either to establish or to accept. We, however, may introduce nothing according to our own judgment, nor may we choose what someone else has introduced according to his own judgment. We have the apostles of God as our authorities: they too did not choose to introduce anything from their own judgment, but faithfully handed on to the nations the discipline they had received from Christ.

A “sect” is named from “following” and “holding,” for we call sects the dispositions of minds and institutions concerning a discipline faithfully proposed, which people follow by holding to them, forming opinions about religious worship that differ greatly from those of others.

“Schism” takes its name from the rending of minds. A schismatic believes with the same worship and the same rite as the others, but takes pleasure only in the division of the assembly. Schism occurs when they say: “We are just people; we sanctify the unclean,” and other similar things.

“Superstition” is so called because it is an excessive or superimposed observance. Others say it comes from old men, because, having survived for many years, they become delirious and err with age.

Among the Jews, these were the heresies: the Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Marbonites, Genists, and Meristae.

The Pharisees and Sadducees are opposed to one another. For “Pharisees” is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “divided,” because they give precedence to the righteousness of the traditions and observances which they call *deuteras* (“second things”). Hence they are also called “divided” from the people, as though by their righteousness.

“Sadducees” is interpreted as “just,” for they claim for themselves what they are not. They deny the resurrection of the body and preach that the soul perishes with the body. They do not believe that there is either a spirit or angels. They accept only the five books of the Law and reject the prophecies of the prophets.

The Essenes say that the one who taught them complete abstinence is himself the Christ.

The Marbonites say that the one who taught them to keep sabbath in everything is himself the Christ.

The Genists are so called because they boast that they are of the lineage of Abraham. For when the people of God came into Babylonia, many abandoned their wives and attached themselves to Babylonian women. Certain others, content only with Israelite wives, or born from such wives, separated themselves from the whole people when they returned from Babylonia and adopted this name as a boast.

The Meristae are so called because they divide the Scriptures, not believing all the prophets, and saying that different prophets spoke through different spirits. For *meros*, μέρος in Greek, means “part” in Latin.

The Samaritans are so called because they observe the Law alone, for they do not accept the prophets.

The Hemerobaptists are so called because they wash their garments and bodies every day.

Some heretics who withdrew from the Church are named after their founders; others are named after the causes that they chose and established.

The Simonians are named after Simon, an expert in magical discipline, whom Peter cursed in the Acts of the Apostles because he had wished to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit from the apostles with money. They say that creation was made not by God but by some higher power.

The Menandrians are named after Menander the magician, a disciple of Simon. They assert that the world was made not by God but by angels.

The Basilidians are named after Basilides, who, among his other blasphemies, denies that Jesus suffered.

The Nicolaitans are named after Nicolas, a deacon of the Church of Jerusalem, who was appointed together with Stephen and the others by Peter. Because of his wife’s beauty, he abandoned her and said that anyone who wished might use her. Such a practice was turned into fornication, so that marriages were exchanged among them.

The Gnostics wished to be called by this name because of the excellence of their knowledge. They say that the soul is the nature of God and fabricate in their doctrines a good God and an evil God.

The Carpocratians are named after a certain Carpocrates, who said that Christ was merely a human being and was born from both sexes.

The Cerinthians are named after a certain Cerinthus. Among other practices, they observe circumcision and preach that, for a thousand years after the resurrection, they will live in the pleasure of the flesh. Hence in Greek they are called *chiliasts*, χιλιασταί, and in Latin *milliasts*.

The Nazaraeans are so called because, although they confess Christ—who is called after the village of Nazareth—to be the Son of God, they nevertheless observe all the commandments of the old Law.

The Ophites are named after a serpent. For “serpent” is called ὄφις in Greek. They worship the serpent, saying that it introduced the knowledge of virtue in paradise.

The Valentinians are named after a certain Valentinus, a follower of Plato, who introduced certain *aeons*—αἰῶνες, that is, ages—into the origin of God the Creator. He also asserted that Christ took no bodily substance from the Virgin, but passed through her as through a conduit.

Apelles was also the founder of the Apellites. He made some glorious angel the creator and superior god, and affirmed that the God of the Law of Israel was a fiery being. The Apellites, whose founder was Apelles, said that Christ appeared not as God in reality, but as a human being in appearance.

The Archontiacs are named after rulers. They maintain that the universe which God created is the work of archangels.

The Adamites are so called because they imitate Adam’s nakedness. Hence they were naked, and naked men and women come together among them.

The Cainites are so called because they worship Cain.

The Sethians took their name from Adam’s son, who was called Seth, saying that he is the Christ.

The Melchisedechians are so called because they consider Melchizedek, the priest of God, not to have been a human being but a power of God.

Those who worship angels are called Angels.

The Apostolics adopted this name because, possessing nothing of their own, they refuse altogether to receive those who make use of any worldly possession.

The Cerdo­nians are named after a certain Cerdon, who asserted two contrary principles.

The Marcionists are named after Marcion, a Stoic philosopher, who followed Cerdon’s doctrine and asserted one good God and another just God, as though there were two principles of the Creator and of goodness.

The Arroterites are named after their offering. For they offer bread and cheese, saying that the first human beings made an offering from the fruits of the earth and the fruits of sheep.

The Aquarians are so called because they offer only water in the sacramental cup.

The Severians arose from Severus. They do not drink wine, and they do not accept the Old Testament or the resurrection.

The Tatianists are named after a certain Tatian, who was also called an Encratite because he abominated meat.

The Alogi are called as though they were “without the Word”; for *logos*, λόγος in Greek, means “word.” They do not believe that God is the Word, rejecting the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse.

The Cataphrygians received their name from the province of Phrygia, because their founders arose there.

Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla were their leaders. They assert that the coming of the Holy Spirit was given not to the apostles but to themselves.

The Cathari called themselves by this name because of their supposed purity. Boasting of their own merits, they deny pardon for sins to penitents; if widows marry, they condemn them as adulteresses; and they proclaim themselves purer than others. If they wished to understand their own name, they should call themselves “worldly” rather than “pure.”

The Pauliani arose from Paul of Samosata, who said that Christ did not always exist but took his beginning from Mary.

The Hermogenians are named after a certain Hermogenes, who, introducing uncreated matter, compared it with the uncreated God and asserted that it was the mother of the elements and a goddess. The Apostle condemns such people as servants of the elements.

The Manichaeans arose from a certain Persian named Manes. He introduced two natures and substances, namely, a good one and an evil one, and asserted that souls flowed from God as from some source. He rejected the Old Testament and accepted the New only in part.

The Canoniani are called in Latin “without law.”

The Anthropomorphites are so called because, with rustic simplicity, they suppose that God has human limbs, as is written in the divine Scriptures. For *anthropos*, ἄνθρωπος in Greek, is translated into Latin as “human being.” They do not understand the Lord’s statement: “God is spirit.” For he is incorporeal; he is neither distinguished by limbs nor measured by bodily mass.

The Heraclites arose from their founder Heraclitus. They receive only monks, reject marriages, and do not believe that the kingdoms of heaven contain little children.

The Novatians arose from Novatus, a presbyter of the city of Rome, who, attempting to seize the priestly chair against Cornelius, established a heresy, refusing to receive apostates and rebaptizing those who had already been baptized.

The Montanist heretics are so called because they hid in the mountains during the time of persecution, on which occasion they separated themselves from the body of the catholic Church.

The Ebionites are named after Ebion, or after poverty. They think that Christ was made just merely through moral progress. Hence they are appropriately called Ebionites because of their poverty of understanding. They are half-Jews and hold the Gospel in such a way that they observe the Law carnally. The Apostle is found writing against them in the Epistle to the Galatians.

The Photinians are named after Photinus, a bishop of Sirmium in Gaul-Greece, who revived the heresy of the Ebionites and asserted that Christ had been conceived by Mary through marital intercourse with Joseph.

The Aeriani are named after a certain Aerius. They disdain to offer sacrifice for the dead.

The Ethians are named after Aetius; they are also called Eunomians after a certain Eunomius, a dialectician and disciple of Aetius, by whose name they became better known. They assert that the Son is unlike the Father and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son, and they also say that no sin is imputed to those who remain in the faith.

The Origenians arose from their founder Origen. They say that the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son. They also say that souls sinned at the beginning of the world and, because of the diversity of their sins, deserved different bodies as though they were bonds, from heaven down to earth; and that for this reason the world was made.

The Noetians are named after a certain Noetius, who said that Christ is the same as the Father and the Holy Spirit. They understand the Trinity in the names of its functions, not in its Persons; hence they are also called Patripassians, because they say that the Father suffered.

The Sabellians are said to have sprung from the same Noetius, whose disciple they report Sabellius to have been. They became especially known by his name and are therefore called Sabellians. They assert one Person of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Arians arose from Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, who, failing to acknowledge the Son as co-eternal with the Father, asserted different substances within the Trinity, contrary to what the Lord says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10).

The Macedonians are named after Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople. They deny that the Holy Spirit is God.

The Apollinarists are named after Apollinaris. They say that Christ assumed only a body without a soul.

The Antidicomarites are so called because they contradict Mary’s virginity, asserting that after Christ was born she had intercourse with her husband.

The Metangismonites received this name because *angos*, ἄγγος in Greek, means “vessel.” They assert that the Son is in the Father as a smaller vessel within a larger vessel.

The Patricians are named after a certain Patricius, who says that the substance of human flesh was created by the devil.

The Colinthians are named after a certain Colinthus, who says that God does not make evil, contrary to what is written: “I am the Lord, creating evil” (Isaiah 45).

The Florians are named after Florinus, who, on the contrary, says that God created evils, contrary to what is written: “God made all things good.”

The Donatists are named after a certain Donatus of Africa, who, coming from Numidia, deceived almost the whole of Africa by his persuasion. He asserted that the Son is lesser than the Father and the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son, and he rebaptized Catholics.

The Bonosians are reported to have arisen from a certain bishop Bonosus, who asserts that Christ is the adopted Son of God, not his true Son.

The Circumcellions are so called because they are rural people, whom they call Cothopites, and because they hold the teaching of the aforementioned heresy. Out of love for martyrdom they kill themselves, so that, violently departing from this life, they may be called martyrs.

The Priscillianists are named after Priscillian, who in Spain composed a doctrine mingled from the errors of the Gnostics and Manichaeans.

The Luciferians arose from Lucifer, bishop of Sirmium. When the catholic bishops who had consented to the perfidy of the Arians during the persecution of Constantius were later corrected and chose to return to the catholic Church, the Church received them in her maternal bosom, condemning what they had believed—or what they had pretended to believe—as a mother received Peter after his weeping denial.

They proudly rejected this motherly charity and refused to receive those men; they withdrew from communion with the Church and, together with Lucifer himself, their founder—he who rose like the morning star—deserved to fall.

The Jovinianists are named after a certain monk Jovinian, who asserted that there is no difference between marriage and virginity and no distinction between those who practice abstinence and those who simply feast.

The Elvidians are named after Elvidius, who says that after Christ was born Mary bore other sons from her husband Joseph.

The Paterniani arose from a certain Paternus, who supposes that the lower parts of the body were made by the devil.

The Arabians are so called because they arose in Arabia. They say that the soul dies with the body and that both will rise again at the end.

The Tertullianists are named after Tertullian, a presbyter of the African province and the city of Carthage. They preach that the soul is immortal but corporeal, and they think that the souls of sinful human beings are changed into demons after death.

The Tessarodecadites are so called because they insist that Easter should be observed with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon. For *tessara* means “four,” and *deca* means “ten.”

The Nyctares are named from sleep because they reject night watches, saying that they are a superstition and that they violate God’s ordinances, since he appointed the night for rest.

The Pelagians arose from the monk Pelagius. They place free will before divine grace, saying that the will is sufficient to fulfill the divine commands.

The Nestorians are named after Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who asserted that the blessed virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being, so that he made one person of the flesh and another of the divinity. He did not believe in one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but preached separately and distinctly one Son of God and another son of man.

The Eutychians are named after Eutyches, an abbot of Constantinople, who, after the assumption of humanity, denied that Christ existed from two natures, asserting that there was in him only the divine nature.

The Acephali are called “headless,” that is, heretics without a head whom they follow; for none of them is found to have a founder from whom they arose. They are opponents of the three chapters of Chalcedon, deny the distinct property of two substances in Christ, and preach one nature in his Person.

The Theodosians and Gaianites are named after Theodosius and Gaianus, who, in Alexandria during the reign of the emperor Justinian, were ordained bishops on the same day by the choice of a perverse populace. Following the errors of Eutyches and Dioscorus, they reject the Council of Chalcedon. They assert one nature in Christ from two: the Theodosians contend that it is corruptible, while the Gaianites contend that it is incorruptible.

The Gnoites and Tritheists arose from the Theodosians. The Gnoites are named from ignorance because they add this to the perversity from which they arose: that the divinity of Christ does not know future things, which are written concerning the last day and hour. They do not remember Christ’s Person speaking in Isaiah: “The day of judgment is in my heart” (Isaiah 63).

The Tritheists are so called because, just as they assert three Persons in the Trinity, so they also assert three gods, contrary to what is written: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God.”

There are also other heresies without founders and without names. Some of them think that God is three-formed; others say that Christ’s divinity is capable of suffering; others assign a beginning in time to the Son’s birth from the Father; others do not believe that the liberation of human beings in the underworld was accomplished by Christ’s descent; others deny that the soul is the image of God; others think that souls are changed into demons and into whatever animals; others disagree about the state of the world; others imagine innumerable worlds; others make water co-eternal with God; others walk barefoot; others do not eat with human beings.
