These are the heresies that arose against the catholic faith and were condemned in advance by the apostles, the holy Fathers, or councils. Some of them differ from one another in many errors, yet under a common name they conspire against the Church of God. Anyone, however, who understands Holy Scripture in a way different from what the meaning of the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, demands may be called a heretic, even if he has not withdrawn from the Church.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I. What Those Who Wish to Enter the Sacred Order Should Know and Possess

Ecclesiastical instruction explains, through many kinds of discourse, how the most holy order of the clergy ought to be trained for divine service. For those who occupy a kind of summit and hold the helm of governance in the Church ought especially to possess fullness of knowledge, uprightness of life, and perfection of learning.

They may not be ignorant of any of the matters with which they must instruct either themselves or those subject to them: namely, knowledge of the sacred Scriptures; the pure truth of histories; the modes of figurative expressions; the meaning of mystical realities; the usefulness of all disciplines; the dignity of life in upright conduct; elegance in the delivery of speech; discernment in presenting doctrines; and the differences among remedies corresponding to the variety of illnesses.

Whoever does not know these things cannot properly arrange the benefit not only of others but even of himself. It is therefore necessary that the future ruler of the people, while he has leisure, first prepare for himself the weapons by which he may afterward bravely overcome his enemies and suitably defend the flock entrusted to him.

It is disgraceful for anyone first to wish to learn when he ought, having been appointed pastor, to teach; and it is dangerous for one to undertake the burden of teaching who, unsupported by the protection of knowledge, is unable to bear it. No art should be presumed to be taught unless it has first been learned through diligent study.

With what presumption, then, is pastoral teaching undertaken by the unskilled, when the governance of souls is the art of arts? Who does not know that the wounds of thoughts are more hidden than wounds of the entrails? And yet often those who have in no way learned spiritual precepts do not fear to claim that they are physicians of the heart, while those who do not know the power of medicines are ashamed to appear physicians of the body.

For there are some within the holy Church who, moved solely by ambition for honor, seek the height of rank and, as Truth bears witness, desire the first greetings in the marketplace, the first places at banquets, and the chief seats in assemblies. They are all the less able to administer worthily the office of pastoral care entrusted to them, the more they have reached the school of humility through mere exaltation.

Against such people the Lord complains through the prophet, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become rulers, and I did not know them” (Hosea 8). They reign from themselves and not according to the judgment of the supreme ruler when, supported by no virtues and not called by God, but inflamed by their own desire, they seize the summit of government rather than attain it.

Yet the inner Judge advances them and does not know them, because those whom he tolerates by permission he certainly does not know through the judgment of rejection.

The ignorance of pastors is therefore rebuked by the voice of Truth when it is said through the prophet: “The shepherds themselves had no understanding; those who held the law did not know me” (Isaiah 56). Truth complains that it is not known by them and declares that it does not know the leadership of the ignorant, because those who do not know the things of the Lord are not known by the Lord, as Paul bears witness when he says: “If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14).

This excessive ignorance of pastors often corresponds to the merits of their subjects. Although the latter lack the light of knowledge because their own fault demands it, it is nevertheless brought about by strict judgment that, through their ignorance, even those who follow them should stumble.

For this reason Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matthew 15).

There are also some who investigate spiritual precepts with diligent care, but trample through their manner of living what they penetrate by understanding. They suddenly teach what they have learned not through practice but through study, and by their conduct oppose what they preach in words. Thus it happens that when the shepherd walks over precipitous places, the flock follows him to destruction.

For this reason the Lord complains through the prophet against the contemptible conduct of pastors, saying: “When you yourselves drank the clearest water, you muddied what remained with your feet; and my sheep fed on what had been trampled by your feet, and drank what your feet had muddied” (Ezekiel 34).

Pastors drink the clearest water when they rightly draw in the streams of truth. But to muddy that same water with their feet is to corrupt the studies of holy meditation through evil living. The sheep drink water muddied by their feet when subjects do not follow the words they hear but imitate only the examples of depravity that they see.

Again the Lord says through the prophet: “They became a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 44). No one harms the Church more than one who acts perversely while bearing the name or rank of holiness.

The unworthy would flee the burden of so great a guilt if they carefully considered the sentence of Truth, which says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be fastened around his neck and he be cast into the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18).

The millstone turned by a donkey signifies the circuit and labor of secular life, while the depth of the sea signifies final damnation. Therefore, whoever, led astray by the appearance of holiness, destroys others either by word or example would certainly have been better off if earthly actions, under an external form, had bound him to death, rather than that sacred offices should display him to others as an example to imitate in guilt. For if he alone fell, the punishment of hell would somehow torment him more tolerably.

But since both are necessary—that a good life illuminate wisdom and that a good life commend wisdom—we shall arrange both matters in this book, if the Lord permits: namely, what those who now serve the Lord in the sacred orders of the Church, or who will serve him in the future, need to know concerning the learning required in the mind, the sobriety of life required by example, and the virtue and discernment required in teaching, so that life may not disagree with prudence, nor speech dissent from discipline.

## CHAPTER II. On the Excellence of the Sacred Scriptures and to What All Knowledge Must Be Referred

The foundation, stability, and perfection of prudence is knowledge of the sacred Scriptures. This knowledge flows from that unchangeable and eternal Wisdom which came forth from the mouth of the Most High—namely, the firstborn before every creature—and through the distributions of the Holy Spirit shines, by means of the vessels of Scripture, as an unfailing light through lanterns upon the whole world.

If anything else may rightly be counted as wisdom, it is derived from the one source of the Church’s wisdom and looks back to its origin. Whatever truth is found by anyone is recognized as true through Truth itself, and whatever good is found anywhere is discovered to be good through Goodness. Likewise, whatever wisdom anyone investigates is understood to be wise through Wisdom.

The truths and wisdom found in the books of the wise men of this age are not to be attributed to anyone other than Truth and Wisdom. These things were not first established by those in whose words they are read; rather, they investigated realities that have existed eternally, insofar as Truth and Wisdom themselves—the teachers and illuminators of all things—granted them the ability to investigate.

Therefore everything must be referred to one end: both whatever useful things are found in the books of the nations and whatever salutary things are found in the sacred Scriptures. In this way we may arrive at perfect knowledge of Truth and Wisdom, by which the highest good is perceived and held.

When the highest good has been attained and possessed, everyone truly becomes blessed when he enjoys the highest Wisdom fully and perfectly for eternity. For without this Wisdom no one can become blessed, as Truth and Wisdom themselves, Christ, testify when speaking to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

Consequently, the Holy Spirit is also understood here, who is the consubstantial love of the Father and the Son, as it were, of both together.

Knowledge of God will therefore be perfect when death is no more. Blessedness will then also be complete, when God’s glorification is supreme.

But here and now God is glorified in a certain manner, when he is proclaimed throughout the whole breadth of the world through the faith of believers and the manifestation of the sacred Scriptures. For now we see him through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face; now we know in part, but then we shall know even as we are known.

## CHAPTER III. By What Obscurities Holy Scripture Is Enveloped, and That It Is Not Permitted to Anyone to Read It Rashly
Therefore divine Scripture, by which such great maladies of human wills are remedied, was disseminated throughout the world from one perfect language, through which it could suitably be spread across the earth, and was extended far and wide through the various languages of translators, so that it might become known among the nations for their salvation. [Col. 0380B] Those who read it seek nothing else than to discover the thoughts and will of those by whom it was written, and through them the will of God, according to which we believe such men spoke. But those who read rashly are deceived by many and manifold obscurities and ambiguities, thinking one thing instead of another; and in certain passages, when they cannot discover what they may even falsely suspect, they cast so dense a darkness over some obscure statements that they obscure everything. I do not doubt that all this has been divinely provided, in order to subdue pride through labor and to renew an understanding that grows weary of what it easily investigates, since things discovered without difficulty usually become worthless to it.

For there are very many difficult passages in the divine books because of figurative expressions; there are also many passages remarkable because of the greatness of the matters treated. Therefore they must be investigated both with the acuity of understanding and intelligence, and, once understood according to their worth, held in reverence. No one doubts that things are more readily learned through comparisons, and that what has been sought with some difficulty is found with much greater pleasure. Those who do not find at all what they seek suffer from hunger; those who do not seek because they have everything at hand languish from satiety. In both cases, however, weakness must be avoided.

Thus the Holy Spirit has magnificently and beneficially medicated the holy Scriptures: in their clearer passages they meet hunger, while in their more obscure passages they wipe away satiety. Almost nothing, however, is drawn from those obscurities that is not found stated most plainly elsewhere.

## CHAPTER IV. On the stages of wisdom and charity

[Col. 0380D] Above all, anyone who desires to reach the summit of wisdom must be turned toward the fear of God, in order to learn what his will is and what he commands us to desire and avoid. This fear must necessarily impress upon the mind thoughts of our mortality and future death and, as though our flesh were nailed down, must fasten every movement of pride to the wood of the cross.

Next, it is necessary to become gentle through piety and not to contradict divine Scripture—whether it is understood and strikes at some of our faults, or is not understood, as though we might be able to know and perceive better—but rather to think and believe that what is written there, even if it remains hidden, is better and truer than what we can know by ourselves.

After these two stages, fear and [Col. 0381A] piety, one comes to the third stage, that of knowledge, which I have now decided to discuss. In this stage every student of the divine Scriptures exercises himself. Nothing else is found anywhere in them to be loved except God for God’s sake and one’s neighbor for God’s sake: God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind; one’s neighbor as oneself—that is, so that the love of one’s neighbor, just as also the love of oneself, may be referred to God.

Therefore, whoever seems to himself to have understood the holy Scriptures, or any part of them, in such a way that by that understanding he does not build up this double love of God and neighbor, has not yet understood as he ought to understand. Thus there are three things in the service of which all knowledge and prophecy labor: faith, hope, and charity. Hope succeeds faith, and blessedness succeeds hope; but charity will rather increase when those things pass away.

Since, then, there are four things to be loved—one above us, namely God; a second, which is ourselves, namely the soul created in the image of God; a third, which is beside us, namely another human being; and a fourth, which is beneath us, namely the body—no commands needed to be given concerning the second and fourth. However much charity may stir a person, the love of himself and the love of his own body nevertheless remain to him. It remained, therefore, for us to receive commands concerning what is above us and what is beside us.

“You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth. Every human being, insofar as he is human, is to be loved for God’s sake; God, however, is to be loved for his own sake. Moreover, each person ought to love God more than himself; likewise, another human being is to be loved more than our own body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake. Another human being can enjoy God together with us, whereas the body cannot, because the body lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God.

All human beings, however, are to be loved equally. But since we cannot benefit everyone, we should chiefly care for those who, by the opportunities of place, time, or any other circumstances, are more closely joined to us, as though by a kind of lot. Nevertheless, we ought to wish that all human beings should love God with us, and everything by which we either help them or are helped by them must be referred to that one end.

Charity is rightly joined to knowledge, because the fruit of knowledge consists solely in charity. “Knowledge puffs up,” says the Apostle, “but charity builds up” (I Cor. VIII). If, then, what puffs up is to be desired, how much more what builds up, so that, when we know the will of God, we may love to obey God and so reach God.

For this knowledge makes a person one of good hope, not boasting but mourning. By this disposition he obtains, through persistent prayers, the consolation of divine assistance, lest he be broken by despair; and he begins to be in the fourth stage, namely, that of fortitude.

Righteousness is sought and thirsted for. By this disposition a person is often drawn away from every deadly delight in passing things, and, turning away from them, turns toward the love of eternal things—namely, the unchangeable unity and that same Trinity—which he will have seen shining from afar as much as he can, and will have perceived that, because of the weakness of his sight, he cannot endure that light. In the fifth stage, therefore, namely, in the [Col. 0382A] counsel of mercy, he purifies the soul that is somehow tumultuous and clamorous against itself because of the stains conceived from the desire for inferior things.

Here he exercises himself diligently in the love of his neighbor and is perfected in it. When, already full of hope and sound in his strength, he reaches the love of a friend, he ascends to the sixth stage. There he now purifies the very eye by which God can be seen by those who die to this world; for they see him insofar as they die to this world, whereas insofar as they live for this world they do not see him. And so, although the appearance of that light has already begun to seem more certain, not only more bearable but also more delightful, it is nevertheless still said to be seen in a riddle and through a mirror, because in this life, while we are pilgrims, we walk more by faith than by sight, although our manner of life is in heaven.

In this stage he so purifies the eye of the heart that he does not even prefer himself to the truth, so that he may compare his neighbor [with the truth], and therefore not even himself, because neither does he compare with it the one whom he loves as himself. This holy person will therefore have a heart so simple and purified that he will neither be turned away from the truth by a desire to please human beings, nor out of regard for avoiding any inconveniences of his own that oppose this life.

Such a son ascends to wisdom, which is the final and seventh stage, in which he is pacified and enjoys it in tranquility. For “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord”: from that beginning one ascends and arrives at wisdom itself through these stages.

## CHAPTER V. That whoever reaches the fullness of wisdom reaches the perfection of charity

Whoever, therefore, reaches the summit of wisdom must reach the height of charity, because no one is perfectly wise except one who loves rightly. When someone strives to reach the fullness of wisdom through the stages mentioned above, he does nothing other than reach the perfection of charity; and to the extent that he is perfected in wisdom, he is perfected in charity.

For we said earlier that true blessedness consists in the perfect contemplation of wisdom. We say the same of charity, because the highest blessedness consists in the perfect love of charity. God, the Creator of all things, who is our blessedness, is equally named with respect to both, as it is written of him in the Book of Wisdom: “The artificer of all things taught me wisdom. For in her is a spirit of understanding, holy, unique,” and so forth (Wis. VII).

And the Apostle John says: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (I John IV). The Savior, wishing wisdom and charity to be understood as one, said to the Father in the Gospel: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me, and I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John XVII).

Whoever, therefore, perceives the full knowledge of God possesses in himself at the same time the perfect love of God; and, enjoying both, he will possess eternal blessedness when he has attained the highest good.

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 0383A] On the method of reading the holy Scriptures

Having thus briefly laid these matters before us, let us return our consideration to that third stage, namely, knowledge, concerning which we have undertaken to discuss and treat what the Lord has suggested. The most diligent investigator of the divine Scriptures will therefore be one who first reads them all and becomes acquainted with them—not yet necessarily through understanding, but already through reading—at least those called canonical. Let him read the others with confidence once instructed in the faith of truth, lest they take hold of a weak mind and, deceiving it with dangerous falsehoods and fantasies, prejudge something against sound understanding.

In the canonical Scriptures, let him follow the very great authority of the Catholic Churches, among which are certainly those that have deserved to possess apostolic sees and to receive apostolic letters. He should follow this method in the canonical Scriptures: he should prefer those books accepted by all the Catholic Churches to those not accepted by some; and among those not accepted by all, he should prefer those accepted by the greater and more authoritative Churches to those held by Churches of lesser and lower authority. If he should find some books held by a greater number and others by more authoritative Churches—although this cannot in fact be found—I think they should nevertheless be held to have equal authority.

The entire canon of Scripture, in which we say that this consideration is to be exercised, is contained in these books. In brief, there are forty-five books of the Old Testament and twenty-seven of the New, making seventy-two in all. Since I described their names, order, and authority as fully as I could in the preceding book, I do not think it necessary to repeat them.

## CHAPTER VII. On the canon of the Hebrews, and how among them the order of the divine Scriptures is divided into three parts

It should nevertheless be noted that the Hebrews, with Ezra as author, receive the Old Testament as twenty-two books, according to the number of their letters, dividing them into three orders: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa.

The first order, that of the Law, consists of five books. The first is *Bresith*, which is Genesis. The second is *Ellesmot*, which is Exodus. The third is *Vaiicra*, which is Leviticus. The fourth is *Vaiedabbet*, which is Numbers. The fifth is *Ellehadabarim*, which is Deuteronomy.

These are the five books of Moses, which the Hebrews call *Thorath* and the Latins call the Law. Properly speaking, however, the Law is what was given through Moses.

The second order is that of the Prophets, containing eight books. The first is *Josue bennun*, called in Latin *Jesus Nave*. The second is *Sophthim*, which is Judges. The third is Samuel, which is First Kings. The fourth is *Malachim*, which is Second Kings. The fifth is Isaiah. The sixth is Jeremiah. The seventh is Ezekiel. The eighth is *Thereasar*, which is called the book of the Twelve Prophets. Because these books are joined together on account of their small size, they are counted as one.

The third order is that of the Hagiographa—that is, of those who write holy things. It contains nine books. The first is Job; the second, the Psalter, which is divided into five sections; the third, *Massoth*, which is the Proverbs of Solomon; the fourth, *Coheleth*, which is Ecclesiastes; the fifth, *Sirhasirim*, which is the Song of Songs; the sixth, Daniel; the seventh, *Dibrehaiomim*, which is “Words of Days,” that is, Paralipomenon; the eighth, Ezra; the ninth, Esther.

These, taken together—five, eight, and nine—make twenty-two, as stated above. Some, however, add Ruth and *Cinoth*, which is called in Latin the Lamentation of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa, making twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament, corresponding to the twenty-four elders who stand before the presence of God.

These are the books that possess canonical authority among the Hebrews.

Among us there is a fourth order of the Old Testament: those books that are not in the Hebrew canon. The first is the Book of Wisdom, the second Ecclesiasticus, the third Tobit, the fourth [Col. 0384B] Judith, the fifth and sixth the Books of Maccabees. Although the Jews separate these among the apocrypha, the Church of Christ honors and proclaims them among the divine books.

In the New Testament there are two orders. The first is the Gospel order, containing Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second is the Apostolic order, containing the Epistles of the apostles Peter, James, John, Jude, and Paul, the book of the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse.

In all these books, those who fear God and have been made gentle by piety seek the will of God. The first observance of this work and labor is, as we have said, to know these books; and if not yet through understanding, then at least through reading either to commit them to memory or not to leave them wholly unknown.

Next, those matters plainly set forth in them—whether precepts for living or rules for believing—must be investigated with greater skill and diligence. Each person finds more of them according to the capacity of his understanding. In the things plainly set forth in Scripture are found all that pertains to faith, moral conduct, hope, and charity. Once familiarity has been acquired with the language of the divine Scriptures themselves, one must proceed to open and examine what is obscure, so that examples may be taken from the clearer passages to illuminate the more obscure expressions, and so that certain testimonies of definite statements may remove doubt from uncertain matters. In this work memory is of the greatest value; if memory is lacking, these instructions cannot be given.

## CHAPTER VIII. From what it results that what is written is not understood

[Col. 0384D] What is written is not understood for two reasons: either it is concealed by unknown signs or by ambiguous signs.

Signs are either proper or transferred. They are called proper when they are employed to signify the things for which they were established, as when we say “ox” while intending the animal that all speakers of the Latin language call by this name.

They are transferred when the things themselves that we signify by proper words are used to signify something else. Thus we say “ox,” and by these two syllables we understand the animal commonly called by that name; but again, through that animal we understand the evangelist whom Scripture signified, as the Apostle explains when he says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain” [Col. 0385A] (I Cor. IX).

Among proper signs belong words, which have acquired among human beings the supreme power of signifying whatever one wishes to express, in whatever manner it is conceived in the mind. But because they pass away immediately when the air is struck, and remain no longer than they sound, signs of words were established through letters. Thus voices are displayed to the eyes, not in themselves, but through certain signs of their own.

These signs could not therefore be common to all nations, because of a certain sin of human dissension, when each person seizes supremacy for himself. The sign of that pride is the tower raised toward heaven, where impious human beings deserved to possess not only differing minds but also discordant voices.

But by the merciful provision of God it was arranged that the divine Scripture, which was first written in that original language in which the first human beings spoke, should be conveyed from that language to human knowledge through the various services of translators, lest human misery, wasting away from hunger for the word of God, should perish forever without remedy. Nevertheless, the order established especially by the canon of these Scriptures was preserved in the three languages that were dedicated on the cross of our Redeemer and Savior—namely, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—in order to signify the faith of the holy Trinity, and so that the faith of the holy Trinity might be principally commended, in threefold division, to the human race divided among the three parts of the world. Thus every people and nation might draw salutary understanding to itself with the aid of its own language, by interpreting and expressing in its own words the same canonical meaning.

But since we stated earlier that understanding was held back either by unknown signs or by ambiguous signs, so that what was written might not easily be understood, we shall speak of ambiguous signs later; for now we are dealing with the unknown.

We have resolved, if the Lord wills, to set down, in an ordered and arranged manner, as much as we can, whatever is necessary for us to learn concerning the two kinds of signs mentioned above. It was therefore appropriate first to discuss unknown proper signs, in which the root and beginning of learning consist; then unknown transferred signs, in which the subtlety and usefulness of reading are found; and afterward ambiguous signs, both proper and transferred. When these have been fully clarified and discovered according to the truth, the firmness and completeness of reading are produced.

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 0385D] On unknown signs

There are two forms of unknown signs, insofar as words are concerned. Either an unknown word causes the reader to hesitate, or an unknown expression does so.

If these come from other languages, they must either be sought from speakers of those languages, or the language itself must be learned, if there is both leisure and ability for study, or the comparison of a great many translators must be consulted.

If we are ignorant of certain words and expressions of our own language, that is, Latin, they become known through the habit of reading and hearing. Nothing should be committed to memory more carefully than those kinds of words and expressions that we do not know, so that, when someone more learned appears, we may ask him about them; or so that, when a passage quickly reveals through what precedes, what follows, or both what force and meaning the unknown matter has, we may readily notice and learn it with the aid of memory.

Anyone who wishes to be skilled in proper signs—that is, insofar as language is concerned—should strive both to know the precise force of words and to understand the proper manner of expressions. Whoever wishes to do so can learn this to a considerable degree from grammarians and rhetoricians.

## CHAPTER X. On unknown transferred signs

With transferred signs, if some unknown matters happen to cause the reader to hesitate, they must be investigated partly through knowledge of languages and partly through knowledge of things.

Something in the name *Siloa* certainly contributes to the comparison and undoubtedly intimates some hidden meaning: it was at the pool of Siloam that the Lord commanded the man whose eyes he had joined with mud made from spittle to wash his face. Yet if the evangelist had not interpreted this name, though it belongs to an unknown language, a great meaning would remain concealed.

Likewise, many Hebrew names that were not interpreted by the authors of those same books must undoubtedly possess considerable force and usefulness for resolving the riddles of Scripture, if someone can interpret them. Certain learned men who knew that language conferred no small benefit on later generations by interpreting separately all such words from the Scriptures: what *Adam* means, what *Eve* means, what *Abraham* means, what *Moses* means; and likewise the names of places—what *Jerusalem* means, or *Zion*, or *Jericho*, or *Lebanon*, or *Jordan*, and whatever other names in that language are unknown to us. Once these have been disclosed and interpreted, many figurative expressions in Scripture are revealed.

Ignorance of things, however, makes figurative expressions obscure when we do not know the natures of animals, stones, plants, or other things that are often introduced in Scripture for the sake of some comparison.

For example, how greatly it illuminates the meaning in which the Lord commands us to be as wise as serpents to know the familiar fact that the serpent exposes its entire body to those who strike it, protecting its head. Thus, in place of our head, which is Christ, we should offer our body to our persecutors, lest Christian faith be killed in us if, sparing the body, we deny God.

Or consider the serpent’s being said to receive new clothing after, while constricted by the narrowness of a cave, it has shed its old skin. How well this corresponds to imitating the serpent’s cunning and putting off the old person, as the Apostle says, so that we may put on the new (Col. III), and to the Lord’s saying that we should enter through the narrow gate (Matt. VII).

Just as knowledge of the nature of the serpent illuminates many comparisons that Scripture customarily draws from this creature, so ignorance of certain animals—which Scripture likewise mentions frequently through comparisons—greatly hinders the interpreter. The same applies to stones, plants, and whatever is held by roots.

Knowledge of the carbuncle, which shines in darkness, illuminates many obscure passages of the books wherever it is introduced by way of comparison; and ignorance of the beryl or diamond often closes the doors of understanding. For no other reason is it easy to understand that perpetual peace is signified by the olive branch brought by the returning dove to the ark, except that we know both that the gentle touch of oil is not easily corrupted by another liquid and that the tree itself continually puts forth leaves.

Many, however, through ignorance of hyssop, because they do not know its power either for cleansing the lungs or for penetrating rocks with its roots, although it is a short and low-growing herb, cannot discover at all why it is said: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. L).

Ignorance of numbers and of musical matters also causes many things placed figuratively and musically in Scripture not to be understood. We shall explain these more fully when we discuss the individual disciplines; for now we are about to speak of ambiguous signs.

## CHAPTER XI. [Col. 0387B] How ambiguous signs are constituted

Ambiguity in Scripture is found either in proper words or in transferred words.

When proper words make Scripture ambiguous, one must first see whether we have incorrectly divided or pronounced the sentence. When careful attention foresees uncertainty concerning how something should be divided or pronounced, one should consult the rule of faith learned from the clearer passages of Scripture and from the authority of the Church.

If both, or even all, of the possible divisions of the ambiguity sound according to the faith, then the text of the discourse itself must be consulted through the preceding and following portions that have placed the ambiguity in the middle. We must see which of the several meanings that present themselves the text supports and allows to be joined with it.

Consider examples. The heretical division of the sentence, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I), produces this meaning: “The Word was this in the beginning with God,” and refuses to confess that the Word was God. This must be refuted by the rule of faith, which prescribes to us the equality of the Trinity, so that we say, “And God was the Word,” and then add, “This was in the beginning with God.”

But the ambiguity arising from the division of the sentence does not resist the faith on either side and must therefore be judged by the text itself, where the Apostle says: “And what I shall choose I do not know. I am compelled by two alternatives: having the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I).

It is uncertain whether the phrase “having the desire to depart” should be joined to “I am compelled by two alternatives,” or whether the words should be understood as: “I am compelled by two alternatives, having the desire to depart and be with Christ.” But since what follows is “for that is much better,” it appears that he says he has the desire for the better of the two: although compelled by two alternatives, he has the desire for one and the necessity of the other—namely, the desire to be with Christ and the necessity of remaining in the flesh.

This ambiguity is settled by the following word, *enim* (“for”). Because translators removed that particle, they were led to the interpretation according to which he seemed not only to be compelled by two alternatives but also to have the desire for both.

The sentence should therefore be divided as follows: “And what I shall choose I do not know; I am compelled by two alternatives,” followed by “having the desire to depart and be with Christ.” And as though someone asked why he has the desire for this rather than the other, he says: “For that is much better.” Why, then, is he compelled by two alternatives? Because there is a necessity of remaining, which he adds in this way: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.”

Where neither the rule of faith nor the text of the discourse itself can resolve an ambiguity, there is no harm in taking care to divide the sentence according to any of the meanings that present themselves.

Such is the passage in the Letter to the Corinthians: “Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (II Cor. VII). It is uncertain whether “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit” should be understood according to the meaning, “so that she may be holy in body and spirit,” or whether it should be understood as, “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh,” so that the sense is different: “And [the] spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God—take us” (*capite nos*, sic). [Col. 0388B] Such ambiguities of division therefore lie within the reader’s power.

Everything we have said concerning ambiguous divisions must also be observed in ambiguous pronunciations. Unless these are confused by the reader’s excessive carelessness, they are corrected either by the rules of faith or by the connection of the preceding or following discourse. If neither of these is applied for correction, they will nevertheless remain doubtful, so that, however the reader pronounces the sentence, he is not at fault.

How the words spoken by Nathanael should be pronounced—“Can anything good come from Nazareth?” (John I)—whether affirmatively, so that only “From Nazareth?” belongs to the question, or whether the entire sentence is asked with doubt, I do not see how it can be distinguished. Both meanings, however, do not impede the faith.

## CHAPTER XII. On ambiguities in proper words

Ambiguity in proper words, insofar as the books of the divine Scriptures are concerned, can therefore be found only very rarely and with great difficulty—an ambiguity that is not resolved either by the context itself, through which the writer’s intention is recognized, by comparison of translators, or by examination of the earlier language.

For in the passage that is written, “My bone is not hidden from you, which you made in secret,” it is not clear to the reader whether *os* should be pronounced with a shortened vowel or a lengthened one. If shortened, it is understood from the word for “bone” (*ossa*); but if lengthened, it is understood as the singular of the word for “mouth” (*ora*). Such matters, however, are judged by examining the earlier language, for in Greek the word is not στόμα (*stoma*, “mouth”) but ὀστέον (*osteon*, “bone”).

Likewise, in the Apostle’s words, “What I proclaim to you, as I proclaimed before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (II Cor. XIII), if he had said only “what I proclaim to you” and had not added “as I proclaimed before,” it would be uncertain whether the middle syllable of *praedico* (“I proclaim”) should be lengthened or shortened. But now it is clear that it should be lengthened; for he did not say *sicut praedicavi* (“as I proclaimed”) but *sicut praedixi* (“as I foretold”).

But since, as we have said, such words are rare—words that do not readily admit of resolution—let us turn our attention to ambiguities in transferred words, which require no small degree of care and diligence.

At the outset, one must beware of taking a figurative expression literally. This is the point of the Apostle’s saying: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III). No death of the soul can more appropriately be named than when what surpasses the beasts in the soul—namely, understanding—is subjected to the flesh by following the letter alone.

Whoever follows the letter holds transferred words as though they were proper words and does not refer what is signified by the proper word to another meaning. This is the soul’s miserable slavery: to take signs for things and to be unable to raise the eye of the mind above bodily creation to draw in eternal light.

This slavery, however, differed greatly among the Jewish people from the practice of the other nations, since the Jews were so subjected to temporal things that one God alone was commended to them in everything. The nations, on the other hand, possessed handmade images as gods; and whenever some of them attempted to interpret those images as signs, they referred them to the worship and veneration of a created thing. But Christ, coming with the light of his truth, truly freed all who believe in him from both forms of slavery.

## CHAPTER XIII. The method for discovering whether an expression is proper or transferred

To this rule of caution—by which we take care not to follow a figurative, that is, transferred, expression as though it were proper—another must also be added: we must not wish to take a proper expression as though it were figurative.

The proper method for discovering whether an expression is proper or figurative must therefore be demonstrated. It is this above all: whatever in divine speech cannot properly be referred either to moral uprightness or to the truth of faith should be recognized as figurative.

Moral uprightness pertains to loving God and one’s neighbor; the truth of faith pertains to knowing God and one’s neighbor. Each person’s hope lies in his own conscience, according to how he perceives himself progressing in the love and knowledge of God and neighbor.

Scripture commands nothing except charity and condemns nothing except desire, and in this way it shapes human conduct. By charity I mean the movement of the soul toward enjoying God for his own sake, and enjoying oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. By desire I mean the movement of the soul toward enjoying oneself, one’s neighbor, or any bodily thing not for God’s sake.

What uncontrolled desire does in order to corrupt its own soul and body is called *flagitium* (“shameful vice”); what it does in order to harm another is called *facinus* (“crime”). These are the two kinds of all sins, but shameful vices come first. When they have emptied the soul and brought it to a kind of poverty, one rushes into crimes, either to remove obstacles to shameful vice or to seek aids to it.

Likewise, what charity does for its own benefit is called *utilitas* (“usefulness”); what it does to benefit one’s neighbor is called *beneficentia* (“beneficence”). Here usefulness comes first, because no one can benefit another from what he does not possess.

The more the kingdom of desire is destroyed, the more charity increases. Therefore, whatever is read in the holy Scriptures that is harsh or seemingly cruel in deed or word, whether spoken in the person of God or of his saints, serves to destroy the kingdom of desire.

If it sounds plainly as it stands, it should not be referred to another meaning as though it had been spoken figuratively, as in the Apostle’s words: “You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works,” and so forth (Rom. II).

Thus, in figurative expressions, the rule should be this: what is read must be examined carefully for as long as necessary, until interpretation leads to the kingdom of charity. If it already sounds proper in this sense, it should not be considered a figurative expression.

If an expression is a command forbidding shameful vice or crime, or commanding usefulness or beneficence, it is not figurative. But if it seems to command shameful vice or crime, or to forbid usefulness or beneficence, it is figurative.

“Unless you eat,” he says, “the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VII). This seems to command a crime or shameful vice. It is therefore figurative: it commands participation in the Lord’s passion and the sweet and beneficial remembrance that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

Scripture says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Rom. XII). Here, without any doubt, it commands beneficence. But what follows—“For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head”—might seem to command the crime of malevolence.

Do not, therefore, suppose that this is spoken figuratively in a harmful sense. Since it can be interpreted in two ways, one toward doing harm and the other toward conferring a benefit, charity should recall you rather to beneficence, so that you may understand the burning coals to be the burning sighs of repentance by which the pride of the person who grieves that he was an enemy of the one who comes to the aid of his misery is healed.

Likewise, when the Lord says, “Whoever loves his life will lose it” (Matt. X), we must not think that he forbids the usefulness by which each person ought to preserve his life. Rather, it is spoken figuratively: “let him lose his life,” that is, let him destroy and lose the use he now makes of it—the perverse and disordered use by which he is inclined toward temporal things and therefore does not seek eternal things.

It is written: “Give to the merciful, and do not receive a sinner.” The latter part of this statement seems to forbid beneficence. Understand, therefore, that “sinner” is figuratively placed for “sin,” so that you should not receive his sin.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the various meanings of words, which consist in contrariety and difference
Since things appear similar in many ways, let us not suppose that what some thing signifies by likeness in one place must always signify the same thing. For the Lord used leaven in condemnation when he said, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Luke XII); and in praise when he said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a woman who hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Luke XIII). The careful observation of this variation has two forms. For things signify one thing and another either by signifying opposites or by signifying different things.

They signify opposites when the same thing is set forth figuratively now in a good sense, now in an evil one, as in the example of the leaven just mentioned. The lion likewise signifies Christ where it is said, “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V). It also signifies the devil, where it is written, “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (I Peter V). The serpent has a good meaning in, “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. X); but an evil one in, “The serpent deceived Eve by his cunning” (II Cor. XII). Bread has a good meaning in, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI); and an evil one in, “Bread eaten secretly is sweet” (Prov. IX). And so with very many other things.

The examples I have mentioned have an entirely unambiguous meaning, since examples ought to be drawn only from what is clear. There are, however, passages where it is uncertain in which sense they should be understood, such as: “The cup in the Lord’s hand is full of unmixed wine with mixture” (Ps. LXXIV). For it is uncertain whether this signifies the Lord’s wrath, not extending to the final punishment—that is, to the dregs—or rather the grace of the Scriptures passing from the Jews to the Gentile nation, because he inclined it from this to that, while among the Jews there remain the observances that they understand carnally, since its dregs have not been drained away.

When the same thing is not used with an opposite meaning but nevertheless has a different signification, the following is an example: water signifies the people, as we read in the Apocalypse; and it signifies the Holy Spirit, whence comes the passage, “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII). If water is understood to signify still other things according to the places in which it occurs, then, where it is set forth more clearly, one must learn how it is to be understood in obscure passages. For what is said to God, “Take hold of weapons and shield, and rise up to help me” (Ps. XXXIV), cannot be better understood than from the passage where we read, “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. V).

## CHAPTER XV. That there is no danger in a variety of interpretations of the same words of Scripture, provided that the sense itself accords with the truth

When from the same words of Scripture not one thing but two or more meanings are understood, even if what the writer intended remains hidden, there is no danger, provided that each of those meanings can be shown from other passages of the holy Scriptures to accord with the truth. Yet the person who searches the divine utterances must strive to arrive at the intention of the author, through whom the Holy Spirit produced that Scripture. Whether he achieves this, or extracts from those words another meaning that does not conflict with sound faith, provided that he has testimony for it from any other passage of the divine utterances, the result is legitimate.

For that author may perhaps have seen in the same words that meaning which we are seeking to understand; and certainly the Spirit of God, who worked these things through him, foresaw without doubt that the same meaning would occur to the reader or hearer—or rather, he provided that it should occur because it was supported by the truth itself. For what could have been provided more generously and abundantly by divine providence in the divine utterances than that the same words should be understood in several ways, with other passages no less divine bearing witness to and confirming those interpretations?

But when such a meaning is extracted that cannot be made clear by certain testimonies of the holy Scriptures, it remains for it to be shown manifest through a reasoned explanation, even if the person whose words we seek to understand perhaps did not perceive that meaning.

Yet this practice is dangerous. For one proceeds much more safely through the divine Scriptures if, when we wish to investigate obscure expressions used figuratively, we ensure that either the result contains nothing controversial, or, if it does, that the matter is settled by witnesses drawn from that same Scripture wherever they are found and brought to bear.

But what has now been said about signs is sufficient. Whoever desires fuller knowledge of these matters should seek it in the books of Saint Augustine *On Christian Doctrine*, from which we have excerpted this material, and will find it there. I shall now explain, as far as I am able, what benefit those who read the canonical Scriptures may derive from the subjects practiced in pagan learning and called the liberal arts.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the two kinds of pagan learning, and on those established by human beings

There are two kinds of learning practiced even in pagan customs: one concerns things established by human beings; the other concerns things they have observed as already accomplished or as established by divine action.

That which derives from human institutions is partly superstitious and partly not. Everything established by human beings that pertains to making and worshiping idols, or to worshiping a creature or any part of creation as God, or to consultations and certain agreements of signs arranged and allied with demons, is superstitious. Such are the devices of the magical arts, which poets are accustomed to mention rather than teach. The books of diviners and augurs belong to this category, though with something like a more licensed vanity.

To this category also belong all amulets and remedies that even the medical art rejects—whether incantations, certain marks called characters, or objects hung up and tied on—not because of some natural power by which they might regulate the body, but for the sake of certain hidden or manifest signs.

Nor should those who are called astrologers—because of their consideration of birth dates, though now commonly called mathematicians—be separated from this pernicious superstition. For although they pursue, and sometimes even investigate, the true position of the stars at the moment of a person’s birth, they nevertheless go seriously astray when they attempt to predict from this either our actions or the outcomes of our actions; and they sell ignorant people a pitiable slavery.

The useful and necessary institutions of human beings with one another include every distinction in dress and bodily adornment that has been adopted for distinguishing the sexes or honors; countless kinds of signs, without which human society could either not be conducted at all or could be conducted only with less convenience; and the systems belonging to each city and people in weights and measures, and in the striking and valuation of coins; along with other things of this kind. If these had not been human institutions, they would not vary among different peoples, nor would they be changed within individual peoples at the discretion of their rulers.

This entire part of human institutions, which contributes to the necessary uses of life, is by no means to be avoided by a Christian. Rather, it should be observed and retained in memory to the extent that is sufficient.

The forms of letters also belong to this category. They have been established according to human choice, yet they are not common to all peoples: one nation has Hebrew letters, another Greek, another Latin, and other peoples likewise have formed letters for themselves according to the particular character of their language.

## CHAPTER XVII. What human beings investigated as divinely established

Those things that human beings have transmitted not by establishing them, but by investigating what happened in past times or what was established by divine action, wherever they are learned, should not be regarded as human institutions. Some of these concern the bodily senses, while others concern the mind’s reason.

Of those that touch the bodily senses, we either believe what has been narrated, perceive what has been demonstrated, or infer what we have experienced.

Whatever indicates the order of past events—that is, what is called history—helps us greatly in understanding the holy books, even if it is learned outside the Church through elementary instruction. We are often asked about Olympiads and the names of consuls. Ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born and of that in which he suffered has caused some to go astray, so that they thought the Lord suffered at the age of forty-six because the Jews said that the temple had been built for that number of years, and the temple bore the image of the Lord’s body.

We retain, on the authority of the Gospel, that he was baptized at about thirty years of age. Although from the very text describing his actions one may observe how many years he afterward lived in this life, nevertheless, lest the darkness of doubt arise from another source, the matter is gathered more clearly and certainly from the history of the nations when it is compared with the Gospel.

Then it will be seen that it was not said without purpose that the temple was built over forty years. Since that number cannot be referred to the Lord’s age, it may be referred to the more hidden instruction concerning the human body, which the only Son of God did not disdain to assume for us—the one through whom all things were made.

It is one thing to narrate what has been done, and another to teach what should be done. History faithfully and usefully narrates deeds; but the books of diviners and writings of similar kinds aim to teach what should be done or observed, with the boldness of an adviser, not the reliability of a witness.

There is also a kind of narration similar to demonstration, by which not past events but present realities are indicated to those who do not know them. Such are the writings concerning the situation of places and the natures of animals, trees, herbs, stones, and other bodies. We discussed this category above and explained that this knowledge is useful for solving the riddles of Scripture, not for employing such things as remedies for particular signs or as devices of some superstition.

The knowledge of the stars, however, is not narration but demonstration. Scripture mentions very few of them. Yet, besides demonstrating present realities, it also possesses something resembling a narration of past events, since from the present position and movement of the stars one may regularly retrace their former configurations. It likewise contains regular conjectures about future events—not suspicious or idle ones, but rare and certain ones—not so that we may attempt to draw from them anything concerning our fates and fortunes, as in the follies of astrologers, but insofar as they concern the stars themselves.

For just as someone who calculates the moon, having observed what day of its cycle it is today, can say what day it was in any past year and what day it will be in any future year, so those skilled in calculation customarily give answers concerning each of the stars.

As for the other arts by which something is made, or by which something remains after the craftsman’s work has produced it—such as a house or a bench—or which provide some service to the God who is at work—such as medicine, agriculture, and navigation—all these arts make use of experiments concerning the past in order to form conjectures about the future. No craftsman in any of these arts moves his limbs while working without joining the memory of past events to the expectation of future ones.

We have mentioned these matters for no other reason than that we may not be wholly ignorant of what Scripture wishes to convey when it inserts figurative expressions drawn from these arts.

There remain those things that concern not the bodily senses but the mind’s reason, where the disciplines of disputation and number prevail.

The discipline of disputation is of great value for penetrating and resolving every kind of question found in the holy writings. One must beware there only of the desire to quarrel and of a certain childish display aimed at deceiving an opponent. We shall discuss this more fully when we treat of dialectic and rhetoric.

As for the discipline of number, it is clear even to the most sluggish mind that it was not established by human beings but rather investigated and discovered. For just as Virgil wished the first syllable of *Italia* to be pronounced short, and it thereby became short, no one can bring it about, whenever he wishes, that three times three should not be nine, or that they should not produce a square figure, or that they should not be threefold in relation to the number three, one and a half times in relation to six, and twice in relation to no number, because intelligible numbers do not have a half.

Whether numbers are considered in themselves, or are applied to the laws of figures, sounds, or movements, they possess unchangeable rules. They were not established in any way by human beings, but discovered through the intelligence of the ingenious.

Yet whoever loves all these things so much that he wishes to boast of them among the unlearned, rather than seek the source of the truths he has merely perceived to be true, and the source of certain things that are not only true but also unchangeable—things whose unchangeability he has grasped—and who, proceeding from the appearance of bodies to the human mind, finds that mind itself changeable, now learned and now unlearned, yet established between the unchangeable truth above it and all other changeable things below it, and fails to turn everything toward the praise and love of the one God, from whom he knows all things to derive: such a person may appear learned, but can in no way be wise.

Up to this point I have spoken generally and in combination about pagan disciplines. From here onward I shall speak separately about each.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the art of grammar and its branches

The first of the liberal arts is grammar, the second rhetoric, the third dialectic, the fourth arithmetic, the fifth geometry, the sixth music, and the seventh astronomy. Grammar derives its name from letters, as the sound derived from that word shows.

Its definition is as follows: Grammar is the science of interpreting poets and historians, and the method of writing and speaking correctly.

This is both the origin and the foundation of the liberal arts. It is therefore fitting to read this school of the Lord, because the knowledge of speaking correctly and the method of writing correctly reside in it. How can anyone recognize the force of articulated speech or the power of letters and syllables if he has not first learned these things through grammar? Or how can he know the distinctions of metrical feet, accents, and pauses if he has not first acquired their knowledge through this discipline? Or how can he know the rules governing the parts of speech, the beauty of figures, the force of tropes, the logic of etymologies, and the correctness of orthography if he has not first made the art of grammar known to himself?

Whoever does not enjoy engaging in a vain battle of words but desires to possess knowledge of correct speech and skill in writing learns this art without blame—or rather, with praise. For grammar is the judge of all scribes: wherever it sees an error, it reproves it, and wherever things have been well expressed, it approves them by its judgment.

All the figures that secular learning has set down in writing are found repeatedly in the sacred books. Anyone who reads the divine books carefully will discover that our authors used tropes too, and used them more extensively and abundantly than can be imagined or believed. The names of some of these tropes, not merely examples of them all, are also found in the divine books—for example, allegory, enigma, and parable.

Knowledge of all these things is necessary for dissolving the ambiguities of Scripture, because if a passage is understood according to the literal propriety of its words, the result is absurd. One must ask whether what we do not understand may have been expressed through one trope or another; in this way many things that lay hidden have been discovered.

It is also worthwhile to know the principles of meter learned through the art of grammar, because among the Hebrews, as blessed Jerome testifies, the Psalter now moves in iambic meter, now resounds in Alcaic meter, now swells in Sapphic meter, and now proceeds in half-feet. Deuteronomy, the song of Isaiah, and likewise Solomon and Job, as Josephus and Origen write, proceed among their own people in hexameter and pentameter verses.

For this reason, although this method is common to pagans, it should not be despised; it should be learned thoroughly to the extent that is sufficient. Many Christian men have composed distinguished books through this art and have thereby labored to please God, including Juvencus, Sedulius, Arator, Alcimus, Clement, Paulinus, Fortunatus, and many others.

If we wish to read the poems and books of the pagans for the sake of the flower of eloquence, we should observe the figure of the captive woman described in Deuteronomy. The Lord is said to have commanded that if an Israelite wished to take her as a wife, he should shave her head, cut her nails, and remove her hair; and, once she had been purified, she could then enter the embrace of marriage.

If we understand this according to the letter, is it not ridiculous? Accordingly, we too are accustomed—and ought—to do this when we read pagan poets and when books of secular wisdom come into our hands. If we find anything useful in them, we convert it to our own doctrine; but whatever is superfluous concerning idols, love, or care for worldly affairs, we scrape away, shave it, and cut it off with the sharpest iron, as one cuts the nails.

Above all, however, we must beware that this liberty of ours does not become a stumbling block to the weak: that a brother weak in knowledge should not perish because of our knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died—if he sees us reclining in an idol’s temple.

## CHAPTER XIX. On rhetoric

Rhetoric is, as the teachers transmit it, the science of speaking well in secular literature and in civil questions. Although this definition may seem to belong to worldly wisdom, it is nevertheless not foreign to ecclesiastical discipline.

Whatever an orator and preacher of divine law expresses eloquently and appropriately in teaching, or whatever he sets forth suitably and elegantly in writing, accords with the skill of this art. Nor should the person who studies this art at the appropriate age, and observes its precepts in writing and in delivering a speech, be thought to sin. Indeed, he does a good work if he learns it fully for the purpose of becoming capable of preaching the word of God.

Since through the art of rhetoric both truths and falsehoods may be recommended, who would dare to say that the truth should stand defenseless against falsehood among its own defenders? Would the people who attempt to persuade others of false things know how to make their hearer favorable, attentive, or receptive through an introduction, while those defending the truth would not? Would the former narrate falsehoods briefly, clearly, and plausibly, while the latter would state truths in such a way that hearing them became tiresome, understanding them impossible, and believing them finally undesirable? Would the former attack the truth with deceptive arguments and assert falsehood, while the latter could neither defend the truth nor refute falsehood? Would the former, moving and driving the minds of their hearers into error, terrify, sadden, cheer, and make them shudder passionately through their speech, while the latter would be sluggish and cold, sleeping on behalf of the truth? Who could be so foolish as to think this wise?

Since eloquence is thus placed in the middle as a power greatly capable of persuading people either to what is wrong or to what is right, why should it not be acquired through the zeal of good people so that it may serve the truth, if the wicked usurp it for the purposes of iniquity and error in obtaining perverse and empty causes?

Whatever observations and precepts belong to this matter, when joined to the most skillful practice of a well-trained tongue in many words and verbal ornaments, produce what is called fluency or eloquence. These matters should be learned by those who can master them quickly, after setting aside an appropriate period of time and at a suitable age.

Even the leading Roman authorities on eloquence were not reluctant to say that anyone who cannot quickly master this art will never be able to master it at all. But we do not value it so highly that we wish the mature—or even the advanced—years of human beings to be spent in learning it. It is enough that this should be the concern of the young, and not of all those whom we wish to educate for the usefulness of the Church, but only of those who have not yet been occupied by some more urgent necessity, which must undoubtedly take precedence over this matter.

For if a sharp and fervent intellect is lacking, eloquence is more easily acquired by reading and hearing eloquent speakers than by following the precepts of eloquence. Nor should there be a lack of ecclesiastical writings, even apart from the canon, which have been beneficially placed in the citadel of authority. By reading them a person may absorb their content; and even if he does not deliberately pursue this, but merely attends to the matters expressed in them, he is also imbued, while occupied with them, by the eloquence in which they are expressed—especially when practice is added in writing, composing, and finally speaking what accords with the rule of piety and faith.

What has now been said about rhetoric is sufficient, since shortly afterward we shall reserve a fuller demonstration of its rules in the art of speaking.

## CHAPTER XX. On dialectic

Dialectic is the rational discipline of seeking, defining, and discussing, and it is capable of distinguishing truth from falsehood. This, then, is the discipline of disciplines. It teaches how to teach; it teaches how to learn; within it reason itself demonstrates and reveals what it is, what it wants, and what it sees. It alone knows how to know, and it not only wishes to make people knowledgeable but is also able to do so.

Through it, when we reason, we learn what we are and whence we are. Through it we understand what a good maker is and what a good thing made is; what the Creator is and what a creature is. Through it we investigate truth and detect falsehood; through it we argue and discover what follows, what does not follow, and what is contradictory in the nature of things; what is true, what is probable, and what is completely false in debates.

In this discipline we seek each thing intelligently, define it truthfully, and discuss it prudently. Therefore clerics ought to know this most noble art and to keep its rules constantly in mind, so that through it they may recognize subtly the cunning of heretics and refute their statements by the poisoned conclusions of syllogisms.

There are many things called sophisms—false conclusions of arguments—which often imitate the truth so closely that they deceive not only the slow-witted but even intelligent people who are insufficiently attentive.

Someone once proposed the following to a person with whom he was speaking: “What I am, you are not.” The other agreed. This was true in part, or at least because the first man was more crafty while the other was simple. Then the first added, “But I am a human being.” When he had obtained agreement to this as well, he concluded: “Therefore you are not a human being.”

I believe Scripture detests this kind of deceptive conclusion in the passage where it says, “The one who speaks sophistically is hateful” (Ecclus. XXXVII). Nevertheless, speech may also be called sophistic when it is not deceptive but pursues verbal ornaments more abundantly than dignity permits.

There are also true connections of reasoning that contain false propositions, propositions that follow from the error of the person with whom one is dealing. A good and learned person introduces these in order that the one whose error follows from them may be ashamed and abandon that same error. If he wishes to remain in it, he must also be compelled to hold the things he condemns.

The Apostle was not asserting truths when he said, “Neither has Christ been raised,” and, “Our faith is empty, and our preaching is empty” (I Cor. XV). These statements are entirely false, because Christ has been raised, and the preaching of those who announced this was not empty, nor was the faith of those who believed it.

But because what follows is false, what precedes must also be false. The preceding proposition was that there is no resurrection of the dead—the claim made by those whose error the Apostle wished to destroy. The preceding statement, that there is no resurrection of the dead, necessarily entails the following statement: “Neither has Christ been raised.” But what follows is false, for Christ has been raised; therefore what precedes is false. What precedes is that there is no resurrection of the dead; therefore there is a resurrection of the dead.

The whole argument is briefly expressed as follows: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised; but Christ has been raised; therefore there is a resurrection of the dead.”

Since there are valid connections not only of true propositions but also of false ones, it is easy to learn the truth of connections even in those schools that exist outside the Church. The truth of the propositions themselves, however, must be investigated in the sacred ecclesiastical books.

The truth of connections itself was not established by human beings but observed and noted by them, so that they could either learn or teach it. For it exists in the order of things as something perpetual and divinely established, as do the things created by God the author.

But since we have now spoken about logic, we shall next speak about mathematics.

## CHAPTER XXI. On mathematics

Mathematics is what we may call in Latin *doctrinal science*: it considers quantity abstracted from matter. Abstract quantity is what we separate in thought from matter or from other accidents, such as even and odd, or other things of this kind that we treat in reasoning alone.

It is divided into arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. We shall discuss each of these in order.

## CHAPTER XXII. On arithmetic

Arithmetic is the discipline of numerable quantity considered in itself. It is the discipline of numbers. The Greeks call number *arithmon* (ἄριθμον). The writers of secular literature therefore wished it to be first among the mathematical disciplines, because no other discipline indicates what it is. Music, geometry, and astronomy, which follow, depend upon its assistance in order to exist and endure.

We ought to know that Josephus, the most learned of the Hebrews, says in the ninth section of the first book of his *Antiquities* that Abraham was the first to transmit arithmetic and astronomy to the Egyptians. Receiving the seeds of these disciplines, they—being people of exceptionally keen intelligence—cultivated the remaining disciplines more broadly for themselves.

Our holy fathers rightly urge the most diligent students to read these subjects, because through them the appetite is largely drawn away from bodily things, and they cause us to desire what, with the Lord’s help, we can behold with the heart alone.

Accordingly, the theory of number must not be despised. Its great importance shines clearly for those who carefully observe how often it appears in the holy Scriptures. It was not said without reason in praise of God, “You have ordered all things by measure and number and weight” (Wisdom XI).

Each number is so defined by its own properties that none can be equal to any other. Therefore they are unequal and different from one another; each individual number is finite, while all numbers together are infinite.

Nor will those who have Plato commending God with great authority as the maker of the world through numbers dare to despise numbers or claim that they do not belong to the knowledge of God. Among us also the Prophet says of God, “He brings forth the age in due number.” And the Savior says in the Gospel, “All the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. X).

Although numbers present themselves to the sight as if they were certain bodily images, when the composition, order, or division of the number six is considered, a stronger and more powerful reasoning from above does not inwardly assent to those appearances. That reasoning contains the force of number, through which it is faithfully said that what is called one in numbers cannot be divided into any parts, whereas all bodies can be divided into innumerable parts; and that heaven and earth, which were made according to the number six, would pass away more easily than it could come about that the number six should not be completed by its parts.

Therefore we cannot say that the number six is perfect because God completed all his works in six days. Rather, God completed his works in six days because the number six is perfect. Even if those works did not exist, the number six would still be perfect; but unless it were perfect, those works would not have been perfected according to it.

Ignorance of numbers also causes many things placed figuratively and mystically in Scripture to remain unintelligible. The mind—or, as I may put it, the intellect—cannot help wondering what is meant by the fact that Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for forty days. The figurative knot of this action cannot be untied without knowledge and consideration of this number.

For forty contains four times ten, as if the knowledge of all things were woven into time. The cycles of both day and year are completed through the number four: the daily cycle through the hours of morning, midday, evening, and night; the yearly cycle through the months of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

From the delight of temporal things, then, while we live within time, we must abstain and fast for the sake of the eternity in which we wish to live, although through the courses of time the teaching itself concerning the despising of temporal things and the desiring of eternal things is conveyed to us.

The number ten signifies the knowledge of the Creator and the creature. The Creator is represented by the Trinity, while the number seven indicates the creature because of life and body. In the Trinity there are three persons; hence God is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind. In the body, on the other hand, four elements are most clearly apparent, and the body consists of them.

Thus, when this ten is conveyed to us temporally—that is, when it is multiplied by four—it signifies living chastely and continently in relation to temporal things, which is to fast for forty days.

This is the Law, whose representative is Moses. This is prophecy, whose representative is Elijah. This is what the Lord himself teaches: as one bearing testimony from the Law and the Prophets, he appeared between them on the mountain, with three disciples looking on in wonder.

Next it is asked how the number fifty arises from the number forty—a number made especially sacred in our religion because of Pentecost—and how, when multiplied by three, it refers to the mystery of the most purified Church: whether because of the three periods before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, or because of the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, with the Trinity itself added in a more exalted way. It then reaches the one hundred and fifty-three fish that the nets cast to the right side caught after the Lord’s resurrection.

In many other forms of numbers, various hidden meanings are placed in the sacred books on account of likeness; because of ignorance of numbers, these meanings remain closed to readers.

Therefore those who wish to attain knowledge of sacred Scripture must study this art attentively. Once they have learned it, they will more easily understand from it the mystical numbers in the divine books.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On geometry

Now let us come to geometry, which is the contemplative description of forms and also the customary [variant: visual] demonstration of philosophers. As they proclaim in celebrated praises, they testify that their Jupiter practices geometry in his own works.

I do not know whether this should be counted as praise or blame, when they paint what they claim Jupiter does in heaven with colored powder on the ground. But if the matter is beneficially applied to the Creator and almighty God, it may perhaps accord with the truth.
