For the geometer—if one may speak in this way—is the holy Divinity, since he grants diverse forms and patterns to his creation, which he continues even now to bring into existence. He distributes the courses of the stars by his venerable power, makes moving things run along appointed lines, and establishes fixed things in a determinate place.

Whatever is well ordered and composed can be related to the qualities of this discipline.

In Latin, geometry is called *the measurement of the earth*, and it is defined as follows: Geometry is the discipline of immovable magnitude and forms.

According to the various forms of this discipline, some say that Egypt was first divided among its own rulers; the masters of this discipline were formerly called surveyors. Varro, however, the most learned of the Latins, reports that the origin of the name arose as follows. At first, human beings, by measuring lands and setting boundaries, provided the wandering peoples with the benefits of peace. Then they divided the entire cycle of the year according to the number of months; hence the months themselves were named because they measure the year.

After these things had been discovered, eager minds were challenged to learn about invisible things. They began to inquire how far the moon was from the earth, how far the sun itself was from the moon, and how great a distance extended from the earth to the summit of heaven. Varro reports that the most skilled geometers succeeded in determining these matters.

He also says that the measurement of the whole earth was gathered by a credible method. This is why the discipline itself came to be called geometry, a name it has preserved through the long ages.

This discipline was observed in the construction of the tabernacle and the temple, where provision was made for linear measurement, the circle, the sphere, and the hemisphere, as well as quadrangular and other forms. Knowledge of all these things greatly assists the interpreter in attaining spiritual understanding.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On music
Music is the discipline that speaks about numbers which are related to something, that is, those found in sounds: double, triple, quadruple, and similar ratios that are spoken of relationally. This discipline is so noble and so useful that anyone who lacks it cannot properly fulfill ecclesiastical office. For whatever is suitably pronounced in the readings, and whatever is sweetly modulated from the psalms in church, is regulated by knowledge of this discipline; and not only through it do we read and chant in church, but through it we rightly fulfill the whole service of God.

The discipline of music is therefore diffused through all the activities of our life in this way: first, if we obey the Creator’s commands and serve Him with pure minds according to the rules He has established. Whatever we say, or whatever inwardly moves us through the pulses of our veins, is shown to be joined by musical rhythms to the powers of harmony. For music is the science of good modulation. If we conduct ourselves well, we are proved always to be joined to such a discipline; but when we commit iniquities, we do not have music.

Heaven and earth also, and everything that is carried out in them under the dispensation from above, are nothing other than musical discipline, since Pythagoras testifies that this world was formed through music and can be governed through it. This discipline is also deeply interwoven with the Christian religion; hence ignorance of certain musical matters closes off and conceals no small number of things. For one man has not ineptly disclosed certain figures of realities concerning the difference between the psaltery and the cithara; and among learned men the ten-stringed psaltery is reasonably asked about, whether it possesses some law of music that compels that number of strings, or whether, if it does not, the number itself should thereby be understood as more sacred—either because of the Decalogue of the Law, in which case, if one asks about that number, it must refer only to the Creator and the creature, or because of the ten itself that has been set forth.

The number of years mentioned in the Gospel for the building of the temple—namely, forty-six—also sounds, I do not know what, of music; and when it is referred to the construction of the Lord’s body, on account of which the temple was mentioned, it compels certain heretics to confess that the Son of God was clothed not falsely but truly in a human body. Thus we find both number and music honorably set forth in many places in the holy Scriptures.

For we must not listen to the errors of pagan superstitions, who invented the nine Muses as daughters of Jupiter and Memory. Varro refutes them; I do not know whether anyone among them could be more learned or more inquisitive about such matters. For he says that a certain city—I do not remember its name—commissioned three craftsmen to make three statues each of the Muses, intending to place the gift in the temple of Apollo, so that it might buy from whichever craftsman had fashioned the more beautiful ones. It happened that those craftsmen all executed their works equally beautifully, and the city approved all nine and bought all nine, in order to dedicate them in the temple of Apollo. He says that the poet Hesiod later supplied them with names.

Jupiter, then, did not beget nine Muses; rather, three craftsmen created three each. That city had commissioned three sets of statues not because it had seen the Muses in dreams, or because they had displayed themselves in such a number before the eyes of any of those men, but because it was easy to observe that every sound—the material of songs—is by nature threefold. For it is produced either by the voice, as with those who sing through the throat or with an organ; or by breath, as with trumpets and pipes; or by striking, as with citharas and drums, and with any other instruments that produce sound by being struck.

But whether what Varro reported is so or not, we nevertheless ought not to flee music because of the superstition of the profane, if we can seize from it anything useful for understanding the holy Scriptures. Nor should we turn to their theatrical trifles if we discuss anything concerning citharas and organs that may be useful for grasping spiritual realities. For neither ought we to have refrained from learning letters because they say that Mercury is their god; nor, because they dedicated temples to Justice and Virtue, and preferred to worship in stones what ought to be carried in the heart, should justice and virtue therefore be avoided by us. Rather, whoever is a good and true Christian should understand that his God is wherever he finds truth.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Astronomy

Astronomy, then, remains; as someone has said, it is a subject worthy of the religious and a great torment to the curious. If we investigate it with a chaste and moderate mind, it also suffuses our senses with great love, as the ancients say. For what is it like to ascend in spirit to the heavens, to examine that entire celestial structure by investigative reasoning, and by the sublimity of contemplative thought to gather in some measure what the mysteries of such vast magnitude have veiled?

For the world itself, as some say, is reputed to be gathered into a spherical roundness, so that by the circuit of its circumference it might contain the various forms of things. Hence Seneca composed a book in a philosophical discussion consistent with this view, entitled *On the Form of the World*.

Astronomy is so called—the term means “law of the stars”—because the stars cannot in any way either remain or move otherwise than as they have been arranged by their Creator—unless perhaps they are changed by the will of divinity when some miracle occurs. Thus we read that Joshua son of Nun commanded the sun to stand still at Gibeon (Josh. X); that in the time of King Hezekiah it turned back ten steps (IV Kings XX); and that during the Lord’s Passion the sun was darkened for three hours (Luke XXIII), along with similar events. They are called miracles for this reason: that admirable things occur contrary to the ordinary course of events.

The stars fixed in heaven, astronomers say, are carried along; the planets, however—that is, the wandering stars—move, yet complete their courses according to a definite ordering. Astronomy, then, as has already been said, is the discipline that contemplates the courses and forms of the heavenly bodies and investigates, by searching reason, all the arrangements and relationships of the stars both among themselves and with respect to the earth.

There is, however, some difference between astronomy and astrology, although both belong to one discipline. Astronomy includes the revolution of the heavens, the risings and settings, and the movements of the stars, as well as the reason why they are so called. Astrology, however, is partly natural and partly superstitious. It is natural when it examines the courses of the sun and moon and of the stars, and certain questions concerning times. It is superstitious when it follows the practices of the astrologers, who draw omens from the stars and also distribute the twelve signs of heaven among the several members of the soul or body, attempting to predict human births and deaths from the course of the stars.

This part of astrology, which by natural inquiry examines the courses of the sun, moon, and stars and carefully investigates the fixed divisions of time, ought to be learned by the clergy of the Lord with diligent care. Thus, through certain conjectures based on rules and through established and true assessments of arguments, the clergy may not only investigate truthfully the courses of past years but also learn faithfully to reason about future times, so that they may know how to communicate to themselves the beginnings of the Paschal feast and the fixed dates of all solemnities and celebrations that must be observed, and may duly announce to God’s people what is to be celebrated.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Books of the Philosophers

Behold, concerning the seven liberal arts of the philosophers and the usefulness for which Catholics should learn them, we have said enough above, as I think. We add this further point: if the philosophers themselves—especially the Platonists—who are so called, have perhaps said anything true and suited to our faith in their systems or writings, they not only need not be feared, but, as though they were unjust possessors, their possessions must also be claimed for our use.

For just as the Egyptians possessed not only idols and heavy burdens that the people of Israel would detest and flee, but also vessels and ornaments of gold and silver, and clothing, which that people, as it went out of Egypt, secretly claimed for a better use—not on its own authority, but by command and instruction, with the Egyptians unknowingly lending those things that they used as goods—so all the teachings of the pagans contain not only fabricated and superstitious inventions and heavy burdens of needless labor, which each one of us, going out from the fellowship of the pagans under Christ’s leadership, ought to abhor and avoid, but also the liberal disciplines of which we have just spoken, which are more suited to the use of truth, and certain highly useful moral precepts. Moreover, among them are found certain truths concerning the worship of the one God.

These truths are like their gold and silver: they did not themselves institute them, but dug them out, as it were, from certain veins of divine providence, which is infused everywhere. They use them perversely and unjustly in the service of demons; but when the Christian separates himself in spirit from their wretched fellowship, he ought to take them away from them for the proper use of preaching the Gospel.

Their clothing also—that is, human institutions, but nevertheless those suited to human society, without which we cannot live in this life—may be accepted and possessed in order to be converted to Christian use. For what else did many of our good and faithful men do? Do we not see how laden with gold, silver, and clothing they came out of Egypt—Cyprian, [Col. 0404D] that most gentle teacher and most blessed martyr? How much Lactantius? How much Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary? How much countless grammarians [Alternative reading: Greeks]? The most faithful servant of God, Moses, had himself done this earlier, and it is written of him that he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts VII).

The superstitious custom of the pagans—especially in those times when, shaking off Christ’s yoke, it persecuted Christians—would never have lent these disciplines that it considered useful if it had suspected that they would be converted to the worship of the one God, by which the empty worship of idols would be destroyed. Yet they gave their gold, silver, and clothing to the people of God as they went out of Egypt, not knowing how what they gave would be returned to the service of Christ.

For what happened in Exodus was undoubtedly a figure, prefiguring this event—though I say this without prejudice to another or an equal or better interpretation. But the student of the divine Scriptures, instructed in this way, when he begins to approach their investigation, should never cease to ponder the apostolic saying: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (I Cor. VIII).

He therefore understands that, even if he comes out of Egypt rich, he cannot be saved unless he has undergone the Passover. Our Passover, however, is Christ sacrificed; and Christ’s sacrifice teaches us nothing more than what He Himself cries out, as though addressing those whom He sees laboring in Egypt under Pharaoh: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Acquisition and Practice of Virtues

Meanwhile, while he desires to attain spiritual knowledge through attentive meditation, it is necessary for him to seek an abundance of virtues through continual practice, lest, while he wishes to be rich in one thing and neglects to seek the riches of another, he lose the fruit of true wealth; and lest not only should it happen to him that he does not possess the usefulness of the things he has sought, but also that, as an unjust possessor, he should pay the Lord penalties for them. For Truth Himself says to His servants: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few” (Luke XII).

[Col. 0405C] What benefit, then, will it be for people to gather immense riches and make no use of them, when the person who is content with his poverty and rejoices in his labor is much better than one who, possessing riches, consumes his entire life in want? Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “Better is the poor man who is sufficient for himself than the glorious man who lacks bread” (Prov. XII).

Holy rusticity benefits only itself; and as much as it builds by the merit of life, so much does it harm if it is not also able to resist those who oppose it. But between two imperfect things, I choose holy rusticity over sinful eloquence, because Wisdom says: “Better is the poor man who walks in his simplicity than the rich man who follows crooked paths; but the one who keeps the law is a wise son” (Prov. XIX).

Certainly, the person who studies wisdom ought to study virtue, so that he may usefully put into practice what he wisely understands in his mind; and whatever good he commands others to do by his words, he should first teach them must be done by his own works. Thus, by doing and teaching the commandments of God, he will be called great in the kingdom of heaven; but least, if he teaches and violates in action one of God’s least commandments.

“For everyone,” says the Savior, “who comes to me and hears my words and does them is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid its foundations upon rock. When a flood occurred, the river struck that house but could not move it, because it had been founded upon rock. But the one who hears and does not act is like a man building his house upon the sand without a foundation. The river struck it, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great” (Luke VI).

Every Catholic ought to devote equal attention to all the virtues, so that, nobly adorned within and without, he may be worthy of the eternal King’s banquet and, carried in a spiritual chariot, ascend to his eternal homeland.

He ought to devote himself to prudence, so that he may provide prudently, understand truly, and retain in memory what he has understood. He ought to devote himself to justice, so that he may become religious, pious, and humble; so that he may preserve grace and retribution, observance and truth; and so that he may keep a pact, an equitable judgment, and the law.

He ought to devote himself to fortitude, so that he may possess magnificence and confidence, patience and perseverance. He ought to devote himself to temperance, so that he may become continent, merciful, and moderate; and above all these things, so that he may be a faithful executor of peace and love, which is the bond of perfection.

A man of God perfectly adorned with these kinds of virtues and illumined by the light of wisdom can rightly and suitably perform the service and worthily fulfill the office of an orator in the Church. The ancient definition affirms that an orator must be a good man skilled in speaking.

If this definition was observed in the orators of the pagans, it is much more fitting that it be observed in the orators of Christ, whose speech—and indeed whose whole life—must be a teaching of virtue. But since we have already said much about the method of discovering what is to be understood in the Scriptures, with the Lord’s help we shall say a little about expressing what has been understood, so that in this final book we may close the whole work.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What the Catholic Teacher Ought to Do in Speaking

The interpreter and teacher of the divine Scriptures, defender of the true faith and conqueror of error, ought both to teach good things and to unteach evil ones. In this work he should reconcile the alienated by his speech, raise up the negligent, and make known to those who do not know what they ought to do and what they ought to seek.

When he has found—or himself made—his hearers well disposed, attentive, and teachable, the remaining tasks are to be carried out as the case demands. If those listening are to be taught, this should be done by narration, provided that the matter under discussion requires it to be made known. To make doubtful matters certain, one must reason by adducing proofs.

But when the hearers need to be moved rather than taught, so that they do not grow sluggish in acting upon what they already know and may give their assent to matters they acknowledge to be true, greater powers of speech are necessary. Entreaties and rebukes, exhortations and challenges, and whatever else is effective in stirring the emotions are then required.

Nearly everyone does all these things in what he undertakes through speech. But some do them bluntly, awkwardly, and coldly; others sharply, ornamentally, and vehemently. The person who should now approach the work of which we are speaking is one who can discuss or speak wisely, even if he cannot speak eloquently, so that, even if he cannot speak eloquently, he may nevertheless benefit his hearers wisely, though less than he could by speaking eloquently.

But the person who overflows with foolish eloquence is all the more to be avoided because the hearer takes greater pleasure in him in matters that are useless to hear and assumes that the person he hears speaking eloquently is also speaking truthfully.

This principle did not escape those who thought that the art of rhetoric ought to be taught. For they acknowledged that wisdom without eloquence benefits states little, while eloquence without wisdom usually does immense harm and never benefits.

A person speaks wisely in greater or lesser measure according to how much or how little he progresses in the holy Scriptures. I do not mean in reading and memorizing them extensively, but in understanding them well and diligently investigating their meaning. For there are people who read them and neglect them: they read in order to retain them, but neglect them in order not to understand them.

Those who retain fewer of their words but see their meaning with the eyes of their own hearts are unquestionably to be preferred to such people. Yet better than both is the one who can recite them whenever he wishes and understands them as he ought.

For the person who ought to speak wisely, even if he cannot speak eloquently, it is especially necessary to retain the words of the Scriptures. The poorer he sees himself in his own words, the richer he ought to be in these, so that what he says in his own words he may establish by theirs.

Furthermore, the person who wishes to speak not only wisely but also eloquently—for he will certainly benefit more if he can do both—I instruct to devote himself much more to reading or hearing eloquent speakers and practicing by imitating them than to teachers of the rhetorical art, provided that those who are read or heard are praised with truthful commendation as having spoken, or as speaking, not only eloquently but also wisely.

Those who speak eloquently are heard pleasantly; those who speak wisely are heard profitably. There are therefore ecclesiastical men who have expounded the divine utterances not only wisely but also eloquently. There is not enough time to read them, rather than they lack anything that could serve those who study and devote themselves to such matters.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the Authors of the Canonical Books Were Both Wise and Eloquent

Here someone may perhaps ask whether our authors—whose divinely inspired writings established the canon for us with saving authority—should be called merely wise or also eloquent. This question is very easily resolved for me and for those who share my judgment.

For wherever I understand them, I can imagine nothing wiser than they are, nor anything more eloquent; and I dare to say that all who rightly understand what they say also understand that they ought not to have spoken otherwise.

Just as there is one kind of eloquence more fitting for youth and another for old age, so speech cannot be called eloquence if it does not suit the person speaking. Wherever I do not understand them, their eloquence appears less to me; nevertheless, I do not doubt that it is of the same quality as where I do understand them.

They spoke in such a way that later generations, who would rightly understand and expound them, might find in the Church of God another grace—different, certainly, yet subsequent to the first. Their interpreters, therefore, ought not to speak as though they were putting themselves forward to be interpreted with similar authority. Rather, in all their speech they should labor first and foremost to be understood, using as much clarity of expression as they can, so that either the person who does not understand is extremely slow, or the obstacle lies in the difficulty and subtlety of the matters we wish to explain and demonstrate, not in our manner of speaking, which makes what we say impossible or difficult to understand.

There are some matters that are either not understood or scarcely understood, even though they are expressed in the speaker’s very clear language. Such matters should be brought before the people either rarely, if some urgent necessity requires it, or never at all.

## CHAPTER XXX. That One Ought to Use Simple Speech for the Common People

Although good teachers have, or ought to have, such concern for teaching that a word which is excessively obscure or ambiguous cannot be Latin, nevertheless it should be spoken according to the usage of the common people, so that ambiguity and obscurity are avoided. It should not be spoken as the learned speak, but rather as the unlearned usually speak.

For what benefit is there in correctness of expression when it is not followed by the hearer’s understanding, since those for whose understanding we speak do not understand? Therefore, the teacher will avoid all words that do not teach; and if he can use in their place words that are understood while remaining correct, he will choose those. But if he cannot—either because such words do not exist or because they do not occur to him at the moment—he will use even less correct words, provided that the matter itself is taught and learned correctly.

This principle must be followed not only in conversations, whether they take place with one person or with several, but much more among the people when a sermon is delivered, so that we may be understood. In conversations each person has the opportunity to ask questions. But when everyone is silent so that one person may be heard and all turn their faces attentively toward him, it is neither customary nor seemly for each person to ask about what he has not understood. Therefore, the speaker’s care ought especially to assist the person who remains silent.

The eager crowd usually indicates by its movement whether it has understood. Until it gives that indication, what is being discussed must be treated with varied forms of speech—something those who deliver material prepared and memorized word for word cannot control. As soon as it becomes clear that the matter has been understood, the speech should either be brought to an end or move on to something else. For just as the person who brings what must be understood out of obscurity is pleasing, so the person who repeats what is already known is burdensome.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Best Manner of Speaking and What the Preacher Ought to Observe in Speaking

The best manner of speaking is one in which the hearer hears the truth and understands what he hears. It is a mark of good minds to love truth in words, not words themselves.

What good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can, when we seek nothing except that what is closed may be opened?

A certain eloquent man therefore spoke—and spoke truly—when he said that the eloquent person ought to speak in such a way as to teach, delight, and move. Then he added: “Teaching is a matter of necessity, delighting of pleasantness, and moving of victory.”

Of these three, the first—that is, the necessity of teaching—is established in the matters we discuss; the other two lie in the manner in which we speak. Let eloquence in teaching be precisely this: not to make pleasing what was horrifying, or to make happen what was burdensome, but to make apparent what was hidden.

If he also wishes to delight or move the person to whom he speaks, he will not accomplish this in just any manner of speaking, but it matters how he speaks in order to accomplish it. Just as the hearer must be delighted so that he may remain attentive, so he must be moved so that he may act.

He is delighted if you speak pleasantly; he is moved if he loves what you promise, fears what you threaten, hates what you condemn, embraces what you commend, grieves over what you magnify as grievous, rejoices when you proclaim what ought to bring joy, pities those whom, by your words, you place before his eyes as deserving pity, and flees those whom you present with warnings as people to be avoided. Whatever else can be accomplished by elevated eloquence to move the minds of hearers should be used not merely so that they may know what ought to be done, but so that they may do what they already know ought to be done.

Therefore, when the ecclesiastical speaker urges something that ought to be done, he must not only teach in order to instruct and delight in order to attract, but also move in order to prevail.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Threefold Manner of Speaking, Which the Roman Teacher of Eloquence Distinguished in This Way

The same Roman authority on eloquence seems to have intended these three aims—teaching, delighting, and moving—to correspond to those other three when he likewise says: “He will be eloquent, then, who can speak of small matters in a restrained manner, of middling matters in a moderate manner, and of great matters in an elevated manner.”

It is as though he added those three aims and explained one and the same statement in this way: “He will be eloquent, then, who, in order to teach, can speak of small matters in a restrained manner; in order to delight, of middling matters in a moderate manner; and in order to move, of great matters in an elevated manner.”

These three modes, as he described them, can be displayed in forensic cases, but not here—that is, in ecclesiastical questions, in which the speech of the person we wish to instruct is engaged.

In forensic cases, matters are called small when judgment is to be made concerning money; great when the safety and life of people are at stake; and when nothing is to be judged and nothing is being done to induce anyone to act or decide, but the hearer is merely to be delighted, matters were called intermediate and therefore middling—in other words, moderate. For he gave them their name from moderate modes; we use “middling” for “small” only by an abuse of language, not properly.

In our matters, however, since everything we say—especially what we say to the people from a higher position—must be referred to the salvation of human beings, not temporal but eternal, and since eternal destruction must also be avoided, everything we say is great. So much so that even concerning the acquisition or loss of money, the matters spoken of by an ecclesiastical teacher ought not to seem small, whether the sum of money is great or small.

For the justice that we ought to preserve even in small amounts of money is not small, since the Lord says: “The one who is faithful in the least is faithful also in much” (Luke XVI). The least thing is therefore the least thing; but to be faithful in the least is great.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. When the Restrained, Moderate, and Elevated Modes Are to Be Used

Nevertheless, although this teacher ought to be a speaker of great matters, he ought not always to speak of them in an elevated manner. He should speak in a restrained manner when something is being taught, and in a moderate manner when something is being blamed or praised. But when something must be done and we are speaking to those who ought to do it but do not wish to do so, then great matters must be spoken of in an elevated manner, suitably for moving their minds.

Sometimes one and the same great matter is spoken of in a restrained manner when it is being taught, in a moderate manner when it is being preached, and in an elevated manner when a mind turned away from it is impelled to turn toward it.

For what is greater than God Himself? Is He therefore not spoken of? Or when someone teaches the unity of the Trinity, ought he to proceed in any manner other than restrained discussion, so that a matter difficult to discern may, as far as possible, be understood? Are ornaments rather than proofs being sought here? Must the hearer be moved to do something, or should he instead be instructed so that he may learn?

Furthermore, when God is praised—whether He Himself or His works—what a beautiful and splendid form of speech rises before the person who can praise Him as much as he can, whom no one praises adequately and no one praises in any manner whatsoever!

But if He is not worshiped, or if idols, demons, or any creature are worshiped with Him or in His place, how great an evil this is—and in order that people may be turned away from it, it must certainly be spoken of in an elevated manner.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Examples in the Apostle of the Three Modes Mentioned Above

An example of restrained speech is found in the Apostle Paul, to recall something more clearly, when he says to the Galatians:

“Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, have you not read the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants,” and so forth (Gal. IV).

Likewise, when he reasons and says:

“Brothers, I speak according to human standards. Yet no one annuls or adds provisions to a ratified human covenant. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, ‘And to offsprings,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘And to your offspring,’ who is Christ.

“Now this is what I mean: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not invalidate a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to abolish the promise. For if the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through the promise.

“And because the thought of the hearer might raise the objection, ‘Why then was the law given, if the inheritance does not come from it?’ he raised the question himself and said, as though asking: ‘What, then, is the law?’ Then he answered: ‘It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator,’” and so forth.

It therefore belongs to the duty of teaching not only to open what is closed and loosen the knots of questions, but also, while this is being done, to anticipate other questions that may arise, lest what we say be disapproved or refuted by them—provided that their solution also presents itself at the same time, so that we do not raise an issue we cannot remove.

It happens, however, that when questions arising within a question are examined and resolved, and still other questions arise within those questions, the mind’s attention is extended into such a length of reasoning that, unless memory is exceptionally strong and vigorous, the disputant cannot return to the point from which the discussion began.

It is very good, however, that whatever can be contradicted should be refuted if it arises, lest it arise where no one is present to answer it, or arise before someone who is present but silent and depart less fully healed.

In those apostolic words the mode of speech is moderate:

“Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters” (I Tim. V).

And in these:

“I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. XII).

Nearly the whole passage of that exhortation has a moderate manner of speaking. Its most beautiful features are those in which particular things are fittingly assigned to particular persons, as though what is owed were being returned to each:

“Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the rule of faith; whether ministry, in ministering; whether one teaches, in teaching; whether one exhorts, in exhortation; one who gives, in simplicity; one who presides, in diligence; one who shows mercy, in cheerfulness,” and so forth.

A little later he says:

“Render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is owed; revenue to whom revenue; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor” (ibid.).

These statements, poured out in separate members, are also enclosed by the very period formed by the joining of two members:

“Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. XIII).

The elevated manner of speaking differs chiefly from this moderate manner in that it is not so much adorned with verbal ornament as it is violent with the emotions of the soul. It can include nearly all those ornaments, but if it does not possess them, it does not seek them. It is borne along by its own force; if beauty of expression happens to appear, it seizes it through the force of the subject rather than adopting it out of concern for elegance.

For its purpose is served if suitable words are selected not by the skill of the mouth, but follow the ardor of the heart. If a brave man is armed with a sword adorned with gold and jewels and is intensely focused on battle, he does what he does with those weapons not because they are precious but because they are weapons.

The Apostle acts so that all things may be endured patiently, with the consolation of God’s gifts, for the sake of the ministry of the Gospel. This is a great matter, and it is treated in an elevated manner, nor are ornaments of speech lacking:

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. We give no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything we commend ourselves as God’s ministers, in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities,” and so forth, which it would take too long to pursue (II Cor. VI).

Likewise he says to the Romans that the persecutions of this world are overcome by love, through certain hope in God’s help (Rom. VIII). He speaks both in an elevated and an ornate manner:

“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to His purpose as saints; because those whom He foreknew He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers,” and so forth, in what follows in the same chapter.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How These Three Modes Ought to Be Mixed with One Another
It matters, indeed, which kind is inserted into or employed alongside which other kind at particular and necessary points. For when a discourse is prolonged in one kind, it holds the listener’s attention less effectively. But when there is a transition from one kind to another, even if the speaker wanders somewhat farther, the discourse proceeds more fittingly.

In the grand style, therefore, the openings ought always—or almost always—to be in the restrained style. It lies within the power of the eloquent speaker to say in a subdued manner certain things that could have been said grandly, so that what is said grandly may, by comparison with those subdued passages, become still grander, and may be rendered brighter, as it were, by their shadows. Whenever, in whatever style, certain knots of questions must be untied, acumen is required; and this the restrained style properly claims for itself. Accordingly, this style must also be used in the other two styles whenever such matters arise in them. Thus, whenever something must be praised or blamed, where neither anyone’s condemnation nor liberation nor assent to any action is required, whichever other style the matter occurs in, the moderate style must be employed and inserted.

In the grand style, therefore, the other two styles find their proper places, and likewise in the restrained style. The moderate style, however, does not always, but does sometimes, need the restrained style—if, as I have said, a question arises whose knot must be untied; or when certain matters that could have been embellished are deliberately left unembellished, so that they may provide certain other matters, as it were, with more prominent places among the embellishments.

The restrained style of speaking teaches silent hearers; the moderate style, through its delightfulness, arouses the acclamations of its hearers; but the grand style generally presses down their voices by its weight, while drawing out their tears. And whence does this arise, unless because truth, when so demonstrated, so defended, and so rendered unconquerable, gives delight?

This teacher and speaker of ours, therefore, ought to take the greatest care that he be heard not only intelligently, but also willingly and obediently. He should accomplish this through words, so that truth may be revealed, truth may please, and truth may move. For even charity itself, which is the goal and fulfillment of the commandment, can in no way be right if the things loved are not true but false. Just as a person whose body is beautiful but whose soul is deformed is more to be pitied than if he had a deformed body, so those who eloquently proclaim what is false are more deserving of pity than if they expressed such things poorly.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. What it means to speak wisely and eloquently; and that one does not speak what belongs to another when one proclaims through one’s life what has been uttered by another.

What, then, is it to speak not only eloquently but also wisely, except to apply words that are sufficient in the restrained style, brilliant in the moderate style, and forceful in the grand style, to true matters that ought to be heard? But whoever cannot do both should speak wisely without speaking eloquently rather than speak eloquently while speaking foolishly.

If he cannot even do this, let him conduct himself in such a way that he not only gains a reward for himself, but also provides an example to others, so that his manner of life may be, as it were, an abundance of speech and a model for living. There are, certainly, some who can deliver words well but cannot think what they should deliver. If such people take from others something written wisely and eloquently, commit it to memory, and present it to the people, when they occupy that office they do not act improperly. For in this way—which is certainly useful—many become preachers of the truth. Nor are there many teachers merely because, if all are teachers of one and the same subject, they all say the same thing, provided there are no divisions among them.

Nor should such men be deterred by the words of the prophet Jeremiah, through whom God rebukes those who steal his words, each one from his neighbor (Jeremiah XXIV). Those who steal seize what belongs to another; but the word of God is not alien to those who obey him. Rather, he speaks alien things who, although he speaks well, lives badly. Whoever speaks good things seems to have devised them by his own intelligence, but they are alien to his conduct. God therefore said that those steal his words who wish to appear good by speaking what belongs to God, while they are evil in doing what belongs to themselves.

But when good and faithful people provide this service to other good and faithful people, both are speaking what is their own. The God to whom the words belong is their God, and they make their own those things that they were not able to compose themselves, but according to which they live in an orderly manner.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On distinguishing doctrines according to the character of the hearers.

It is also fitting that every Catholic teacher should know how to win over the hearer of his discourse, so that, by understanding through the method described above the modes and forms of speech, he may, by distributing them well, find the fruit of his preaching and its praise. When a discourse displays perfection in itself, the speaker must weigh the character of his hearers, because, as Gregory Nazianzen of revered memory taught, the same exhortation is not suitable for everyone, since not everyone is held by the same quality of character.

Often things that benefit some offend others, because frequently the plants that nourish certain animals kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses but provokes puppies; a medicine that lessens one person’s illness strengthens another; and bread that reinforces the life of the strong kills the little ones. The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the character of their hearers, so that each thing may suit each person, and so that it may never depart from the art of common edification.

For what are the attentive minds of hearers except, so to speak, certain strings stretched across a lyre? When the musician touches them, so that they may produce a song that is not discordant with itself, he strikes them differently; and for this reason the strings produce harmonious music, because although they are struck by one plectrum, they are not struck with the same force. Therefore every teacher, so that he may build everyone up in the one virtue of charity, must touch the hearts of his hearers with carefully considered teaching, though not with one identical exhortation. (Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Book III.)

Men must be admonished in one way and women in another, because serious burdens are appropriate to men according to their sex, while lighter ones should be imposed on women: great tasks should exercise the former, while the latter should be won over by being gently drawn toward lighter things. Young people must be admonished in one way and the elderly in another: severity of admonition generally directs the young toward perfection, while gentle pleading prepares the elderly for better works.

The poor must be admonished in one way and the rich in another: to the poor we must offer the comfort of consolation against tribulation; to the rich we must bring fear against pride. Yet the character of a person’s conduct often changes the outward condition of his station, so that a rich person may be humble and a poor person proud. Therefore the tongue of the preacher must immediately adapt itself to the life of the hearer, so that it may strike pride in the poor more sternly, since even poverty imposed upon him does not humble him, and may soothe the humility of the rich more gently, since even the abundance that supports them does not exalt them.

The cheerful must be admonished in one way and the sorrowful in another: to the cheerful must be brought the sadness that follows punishment; to the sorrowful, the joys promised by the kingdom. Subordinates must be admonished in one way and superiors in another: the former, so that subjection may not crush them; the latter, so that their higher position may not inflate them. The former must not fulfill less than they are commanded; the latter must not command more than is rightly fulfilled.

Slaves must be admonished in one way and masters in another: slaves, so that they may always consider the humility of their condition; masters, so that they may not lose the memory of the nature in which they were created equal with their slaves. The former must be admonished to know that they are servants of their masters; the latter, to recognize that they are fellow servants of servants.

The wise of this world must be admonished in one way and the dull in another: the wise must be admonished not to neglect knowing what they know; the dull, to desire to know what they do not know. The former must abandon foolish wisdom and learn the wisdom of God, which is not foolish; the latter must hasten more nearly toward true wisdom from what is thought to be foolishness.

The shameless must be admonished in one way and the modest in another: only harsh reproach restrains the former from the vice of shamelessness, while a moderate exhortation generally guides the latter toward what is better. The former do not recognize that they are committing wrong unless they are rebuked by many; for the latter, it is generally enough for conversion that the teacher gently recalls their wrongdoing to their memory.

The insolent must be admonished in one way and the fainthearted in another. The former, because they presume greatly upon themselves, disdain others by reproaching them; the latter, because they are excessively aware of their own weakness, often fall into despair.

The impatient must be admonished in one way and the patient in another. It must be said to the impatient that, because they neglect to restrain their spirit, they are carried through many precipices of wrongdoing that they do not even desire. For anger drives the mind where desire does not draw it, and, once agitated, it acts as though unaware of what it is doing, while later, knowingly, it grieves over it. The patient, on the other hand, must be told to strive to love those whom they must endure, lest, if love does not follow patience, the virtue displayed become a worse fault through hatred.

The benevolent must be admonished in one way and the envious in another. The benevolent must be admonished to rejoice in the goods of others in such a way that they also desire to possess goods of their own; to praise the deeds of their neighbors by loving them in such a way that they may also multiply those deeds by imitating them. They gain no reward for themselves if they do not imitate, insofar as they can, the things they love.

The envious must be admonished to consider how great is the blindness and misery of those who are weakened by another’s advancement and waste away at another’s rejoicing, becoming worse through the improvement of their neighbor.

The simple must be admonished in one way and the impure in another. The simple should be praised so that they may strive never to speak falsely, but they should also be admonished to understand that they must sometimes keep silent about the truth, so that they may join prudence to the goodness of simplicity. Thus they may possess the security of simplicity without losing the vigilance of prudence.

The impure, on the other hand, must be admonished to recognize how serious is the labor of duplicity that they sustain together with their guilt. For because they fear being discovered, they are always seeking wicked defenses.

The healthy must be admonished in one way and the sick in another. The healthy must be admonished not to despise the opportunity of earning salvation forever, lest, if they are unwilling to please God when they can, they later be unable to do so when they wish. The sick, on the other hand, must be admonished to recognize themselves as children of God, since the scourges of discipline chastise them. For if he did not intend to give an inheritance to those whom he corrects, he would not take care to educate them through hardships.

Those who fear scourges and therefore live innocently must be admonished in one way; those who have persisted in wrongdoing so stubbornly that even scourges do not correct them must be admonished in another. It must be said to those who do good because they fear the evils of punishment that they possess no freedom of spirit. For if they did not fear punishment, they would undoubtedly commit wrongdoing. Hence it is clearer than daylight that innocence is lost before God, since one sins in desire before his eyes.

The wicked whom not even scourges restrain from their wrongdoing must be struck with a sharper denunciation, in proportion to the greater insensibility with which they have remained hardened.

The excessively silent must be admonished in one way, and those who are occupied with excessive talk in another. The excessively silent must be shown that, while they carelessly flee certain vices, they become secretly entangled in worse ones. For often, because they restrain their tongue too excessively, they tolerate more serious loquacity in their heart. Those occupied with excessive talk, on the other hand, must be admonished to watch carefully how far they are falling away from the state of uprightness as they dissipate themselves through their many words.

For the rest, see Gregory in the place mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Which forms of virtue are opposed to the individual forms of vice.

Each preacher can express these matters with greater appropriateness in proportion as he more truly knows how to distinguish the forms of virtue and, conversely, those of vice, so that, knowing how to set each against its counterpart, he may find a suitable medicine for every wound.

Among the virtues there are certain forms that proceed in a manner from other forms, like branches from trees. Since they are generated from one root of virtue, the most beautiful foliage is borne upon one trunk of that same root. Conversely, among vices there are certain poisonous shoots from which that entire multitude of destructive wickednesses is generated. Just as among virtues some proceed from others, like precious offspring from their progenitors, so among vices certain utterly wicked offspring proceed from the most filthy mothers.

But since the wars between virtues and vices are enduring, let us explain, as far as we can, who are the leaders of each kind of wickedness and who are their particular companions, while also showing which virtue properly wages war against which vice. For we cannot otherwise avoid the fiery darts of vices unless we know how to set suitable shields of virtue against them. Defended by these, and with Christ reigning over us, we may overcome that insolent army together with its leaders.

The vices that tempt us and serve the pride that reigns invisibly against us proceed in part like commanders and in part like an army that follows. For not all faults enter the heart in the same way. When the greater vices, though few, precede the neglected mind, countless lesser ones pour into it in a swarm.

Pride itself, the queen of vices, when it has fully seized the conquered heart, immediately drags it to be ravaged by the seven principal vices, as by its own commanders. These commanders are followed by an army, because from them, without doubt, arise the troublesome multitudes of vices.

Pride is indeed the root of all evil, concerning which Scripture testifies: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus X). Its first offspring—the seven principal vices—spring from this poisonous root: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust.

Because our Redeemer grieved that we had been taken captive by these seven vices of pride, he came full of the Spirit of the sevenfold grace to wage the spiritual battle of liberation. Yet each of these has its own army against us.

From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations. From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in one’s neighbor’s adversity, and distress at his prosperity. From anger arise strife, swelling of the mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sadness arise malice, resentment, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness regarding the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward unlawful things.

From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardness of heart against mercy. From gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, impurity, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding. From lust arise blindness of mind, thoughtlessness, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present world, and dread or despair of the future.

Having enumerated these seven filthy things of pride, which lead the army of vices against us, let us see what are the commanders and ranks of the army of virtues that Christ, the author of humility, provides for us to fight against the cohorts of vices. Let us set commanders of virtues against the individual commanders of vices, and armies against armies.

Against the commander of vainglory, therefore, we must set the commander humility, which chiefly produces in a person self-contempt and contempt for transitory things. Against its companions we must set their opposing companions: against disobedience, obedience; against boasting, humble confession; against hypocrisy, simplicity; against quarrelsomeness, innocence; against obstinacy, submission; against discord, peace; against presumptuous innovations, fear of God and honor for the Fathers.

Against the commander of envy we must set the commander benevolence. Against its companions we must set their opposites: against hatred, true love; against whispering, truthful speech; against detraction, pious praise; against rejoicing in one’s neighbor’s adversity, compassion for his affliction; against rejoicing in his prosperity, gladness at his well-being.

The commander opposed to anger is the commander gentleness. Against its companions we must set the companions of gentleness: against swelling of mind, calmness of spirit; against insult, kindness; against shouting, gravity of speech; against indignation, sweetness of character; against blasphemy, purity of mouth.

Against the commander of sadness stands the commander spiritual joy; against its army stands the army of spiritual joy: against malice, goodness; against resentment, mildness; against faintheartedness, patience; against despair, perseverance; against sluggishness regarding the commandments, spiritual zeal; against wandering of the mind toward unlawful things, concentration upon divine reading.

Opposed to the commander of avarice is the commander generosity. Against its ranks we must set the corresponding ranks: against betrayal, unfeigned faith; against fraud, sincerity; against deceit, truth; against perjury, refusal to swear; against restlessness, tranquility; against violence, patience; against hardness, mercy.

Opposed to the commander of gluttony—that is, of dreadful voracity—is the commander abstinence. Against its cohorts we must set their opposites: against foolish merriment, modesty; against buffoonery, disciplined speech; against impurity, sobriety; against excessive talk, silence; against dullness of understanding, eagerness to learn wisdom; against sleepiness, vigilance.

Against the commander of lust and its people stands the commander chastity with its people: against blindness of mind, contemplation of God; against thoughtlessness, foresight; against inconstancy, steadfastness; against rashness, self-control; against self-love, the mortification of the desires of one’s flesh; against hatred of God, perfect love of God.

These, then, are the things that the ruler of souls ought to know and that he must preserve in the diversity of his preaching, so that he may carefully weigh the weaknesses of each person and set suitable medicines against their wounds.

Yet while it requires great diligence to serve each person with an exhortation suited to each matter, and while it is exceedingly laborious to instruct every individual concerning his own concerns with the proper exercise of discernment, it is far more laborious to admonish countless hearers, afflicted by different passions, at one and the same time, with one voice and a common exhortation.

There the voice must be regulated with such great skill that, although the vices of the hearers are different and suitable remedies are found for each, those remedies may nevertheless not conflict with one another. The voice must pass through the midst of the various passions in a single course, but, like a two-edged sword, cut into the swellings of carnal thoughts from opposite sides.

Thus humility must be preached to the proud without increasing the fear of the timid; austerity must be infused into the timid without increasing the unrestrained conduct of the proud; concern for good works must be urged without increasing the license for excessive activity in the restless; restraint must be imposed upon the restless without making secure sluggishness arise in the idle; anger must be extinguished in the impatient without increasing negligence in the mild and gentle; the gentle must be kindled to zeal without adding fuel to the fire of the angry; generosity in giving must be instilled into the stingy without loosening the reins of outpouring in the prodigal; frugality must be preached to the prodigal without recalling the self-controlled to luxury; virginity must be praised to the continent without making the fruitfulness of the flesh despised among married people.

Good things must be preached in such a way that evil things are not thereby commanded indirectly; the highest goods must be praised so that the final goods are not despaired of; the final goods must be nourished so that, while they are believed sufficient, there may be no failure to strive toward the highest.

The preacher must therefore take care that sorrow arising from time is wiped away in such a way that joy arising from mixture (*conspersio*) is not increased; and that joy arising from mixture is restrained in such a way that sorrow arising from time does not increase. Thus sudden fear arising in one person must be suppressed without allowing long-nurtured rashness to grow; and long-arising rashness in another must be suppressed without allowing fear impressed by mixture to prevail.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That the ability to preach ought to be requested from the Lord.

If he is able to do these things, and insofar as he is able, let him have no doubt that he can do them more through the piety of his prayers than through the ability of an orator, so that, by praying for himself and for those to whom he is about to speak, he may be an orator before he becomes a speaker.

When the very hour of speaking has arrived, before he brings forth the tongue that will speak, let him raise his thirsting soul to God, so that he may belch forth what he has drunk or pour out what has filled him.

Since, concerning each matter that must be treated according to faith and love, there are many things that can be said and many ways in which those who know these matters can say them, who knows what it is useful for us to say at the present moment, or what it is useful for the hearers to hear through us, except the one who sees the hearts of all? And who makes it possible for us to say what ought to be said and in the manner in which it ought to be said, except the one in whose hand are both we and our words?

Accordingly, let the one who teaches learn all the things that must be taught, and acquire the faculty of speech—which he wishes both to know and to teach—in the manner appropriate to an ecclesiastical man.

At the moment of speaking itself, let him rather think that what suits a good mind is what the Lord says: “Do not consider how or what you are to speak; for it will be given you in that hour what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X).

If, then, the Holy Spirit speaks in those who are handed over to persecutors for Christ’s sake, why should he not also speak in those who impart Christ to learners? Whoever says that people should not be instructed about what or how they are to teach, on the grounds that the Holy Spirit makes them teachers, could also say that we ought not to pray for what the Lord says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew VI).

Whether he is about to speak immediately before the people or before any others, or whether he is about to dictate what is to be said before the people or read by those who wish or are able to read it, let him pray that God may put a good word into his mouth.

If Queen Esther prayed before speaking to the king for the temporal safety of her people, asking that God place a fitting word in her mouth, how much more ought the one who labors in teaching and speech for the eternal salvation of human beings to pray that he may receive such a gift?

Those who are going to say things that they have received from others should, before receiving them, pray for those from whom they receive them, so that what they wish to receive through those people may be granted to them. After receiving them, they should pray that they themselves may present them well, and that those to whom they present them may receive them. After the successful conclusion of their speech, they should give thanks to the same one from whom they do not doubt that they received it, so that whoever boasts may boast in the one in whose hand are both we and our words.

---

**(A.D. 819.) THE BOOK OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE OFFERING OF CHILDREN**

*(Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, Appendix to Volume II.)*

## HERE BEGINS THE LITTLE WORK OF RABANUS MAURUS AGAINST THOSE WHO OPPOSE THE INSTITUTIONS OF BLESSED FATHER BENEDICT.

If anyone examines Sacred Scripture, which heavenly Wisdom bestowed upon the human race through good and divinely inspired men, he will find that it deals with us with nothing other than the destruction of unbelief and greed and the building up of faith and love, so that, renouncing the devil and his pomp and works, we may faithfully serve the one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, through faith, hope, and love.

Therefore those people are to be wondered at—or rather pitied—who, neglecting what they professed in infancy and what they renounced at the beginning of their lives, place something else before it as though it possessed a more eminent and greater dignity.

There are, then, certain people who learned the sacred writings from their cradles and were nourished for so long by the nourishment of the holy Church that, once sufficiently educated, they were advanced to the heights of the sacred orders. Yet, ungrateful for so great a gift, they hold opinions contrary to the faith of the orthodox Fathers and daily attack the mother of all the faithful with the weapons of their wickedness. They pretend this to be honorable and strive to commend it to everyone as true, although neither the patriarchs nor the prophets ever possessed such a practice in the Old Testament, nor did the apostles and evangelists ever make it customary in the New.

Thus their madness will become known to all, since they agree in no respect either with the earlier or with the later true worshipers of God.

For the shameless craftsmen of wicked doctrines, with pomp, say that parents may not hand over their small children to the service of God, and that it is not fitting for a free man to make his freeborn son a servant. In this way they attempt to impose human law upon God and to subject every human will and dominion to human enactments.

They do not recall what the Apostle says: “Whether slaves or free, we are all one in Christ.” And again: “For he who was called as a free man is Christ’s servant”; and: “He who was called as a slave is the Lord’s freedman.” Especially since the holy Fathers also regarded it as a great honor to be called servants of God.

Thus Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called servants of the Most High God. Hence Moses and the prophets, and hence Job and David, are honorably recorded under the name of servants of God. The Lord himself says to Satan concerning Job: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth?” And concerning David: “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him.”

Perhaps, however, these founders of new doctrines reply to this that they do not contradict the proposition that the entire human race is subject to divine servitude, but that they do not wish anyone to hand over his son to monastic discipline and to the observance of a regular order. As though they were exempt because they object not to the genus but to the species, even though the species is referred to the genus and the genus cannot exist without the diversity of its species.

Who among heretics or schismatics ever entirely rejected and denied the whole Christian religion? That is properly the act of unbelievers. But because such people mingled falsehoods with truths and refused to follow the rule of truth in every respect, they were cast out of the holy Church and wholly deprived of communion.

For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” Hence the Apostle James says: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all.” Hence Paul also says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.” And John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us. But this happened so that it might be made clear that not all are of us.”

And again he says: “Everyone who does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God; whoever remains in the doctrine has both the Son and the Father. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works.”

Therefore whoever, with blasphemous speech, introduces criticism of or diminishment into any part of the Christian religion and sound doctrine—which the holy Church honorably preserves as received from the apostles and prophets and from the Lord himself—should know that he has been entirely deprived of unity with the body of Christ and cannot merit forgiveness for his error or access to the heavenly kingdom except through worthy repentance. For, according to the Savior’s declaration, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

Whoever remains in the bond of unity will ascend together with the Head to the kingdom; but whoever loves separation must be plunged together with the author of error and instigator of dissension, the devil, into the lowest depths of hell and the abysses of Tartarus, because God is not a God of dissension but of peace.

But since we have undertaken the task of writing against those who say that parents may not dedicate their freeborn children to the service of God, and also against those who, making light of the vow that they have made to God, unworthily cast aside the holy service that they professed as though they could abandon it without guilt; and since they despise and condemn monastic discipline, ordered according to the rules of the holy Fathers, as though it had been established by human invention rather than divine authority, we shall first demonstrate, by testimonies from Sacred Scripture and examples of the holy Fathers, that a Christian may consecrate his offspring to God. Next, we shall show that a vow made to God cannot be abandoned without great guilt. Finally, we shall show that the monastic life was established not by human reasoning but by divine authority.

Our purpose is that those who place greater confidence in their own sects than in the writings of the divine books may, at least when overcome by the truth itself, repent and, abandoning their error, cease deceiving themselves and dragging others with them to destruction.

Accordingly, near the beginning of the Book of Genesis, where Sacred Scripture recounts the first sons of the first-created man, it continues in these words:

“Now Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer. And it came to pass after many days that Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth. Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. And the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look.”

Behold: at the beginning of the human race, God immediately approved the offering of firstborn creatures, brought forth from an innocent heart and from the richness of love, more than the pursuit of earthly cultivation, in which human ingenuity excels.

And lest you should perhaps say that the Lord delights in the offering of brute animals, hear the Apostle say: “Does God care for oxen? Or is this written rather for our sake?” Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks, because all the beasts of the forests are mine, the animals on the mountains and the oxen.” And shortly afterward he says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.” And again: “The sacrifice of praise,” he says, “will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show them the salvation of God.”

When Cain killed Abel out of envy, Adam again knew his wife, and she bore him a son whom she called Seth, saying: “God has appointed for me another offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.”

Seth also had a son, whom he called Enos. Concerning him Scripture not without reason continues: “He began to call upon the name of the Lord.” Just as it showed that the offering of Abel, Adam’s son, was pleasing to God, so it also expressed the devotion of his grandson, Enos, in praise of God when it said: “He began to call upon the name of the Lord.”

For it does not say, “He was diligent and skilled in the exercise of earthly labor.” Rather, it extols as a great honor of praise what it knew to be more pleasing to the Lord, saying: “He began to call upon the name of the Lord.”

He therefore rightly calls upon the name of the Lord who unites a devoted heart, the service of the mouth, and the zeal of good works for the glorification of the Lord. Such a person can rightly say with the Psalmist: “My vows are upon me, O God; I will repay them with praises to you.”

Similarly, Enoch and Noah hold the chief place in this title of praise because they feared and loved the Lord and walked in the steps of good works according to his commandments. Scripture says that God took the former away so that he would not have to endure the affliction of sinners for a longer time; and it records that, while the world was perishing in the flood, he preserved the latter in the ark together with his offspring, in order to restore the human race.

His firstborn, Shem, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, was a priest of the Most High God. In what follows, Scripture calls him Melchizedek; he offered bread and wine, and that Priest is said to have existed according to his order. To him the ancestral voice says in the Psalms: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Abraham, then, was the unique model of faith, obedience, and true piety. At the Lord’s command he went out from his land and from his kindred and lived as a stranger in the land that the Lord had promised to give him and to his offspring after him.

This man is described as having offered his son Isaac, from whom he had received the promise, at the Lord’s command, in the place that God had shown him. There he built an altar and arranged wood upon it. When he had bound his beloved son, he placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood, stretched out his hand, and seized the sword to sacrifice his son.

But the angel of the Lord stopped him, saying: “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him. Now I know that you fear God, and you have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake.”

And shortly afterward Scripture continues its account of the same man, saying:

“By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son, I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore. Your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because you obeyed my voice.”

What do the presumptuous defenders of so-called genuine liberty, and the empty talkers against the Lord, answer to these things? Do they perhaps say that this patriarch acted unjustly because, at the Lord’s command, he was offering his only son and heir, born of a free woman? Or do they accuse the Lord of impiety because he compelled his faithful worshiper to commit parricide? Or is not the opinion of those who place worldly and temporal law above the divine and eternal law—which rules all things and orders everything by its own will—far more unjust? For if what the eternal God commands to be done is not permitted, how can what utter vanity teaches be permitted? For it is written: “Every living human being is altogether vanity.” Although he walks in the image of God, he will nevertheless be troubled in vain.

Thus the same Lord who at that time, by his oracle, commanded the patriarch to offer his son as a burnt offering now, in his Gospel, commands the ecclesiastical people to hand over their offspring for holy service; and he who then praised pious obedience for the sake of his love now approves holy devotion in his love. For the one who then said in the law to the priest that he should not tear his garment, should not enter at all for any dead person, should not defile himself even for his father or mother, and should not go out from the sanctuary lest he pollute the sanctuary of the Lord—for the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him—now himself says in the Gospel to the Christian: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; and if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna.” And again: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me; and whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” And again: “If anyone,” he says, “wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.” And again: “Everyone who leaves house, brothers, sisters, mother, father, wife, children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

Finally, faithful Isaac, worshiper of God and most devoted executor of his father’s will, was a type of the one of whom the Apostle says: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross.” For this reason he carried the wood with which he was to be made a burnt offering of himself, so that he might portray Christ carrying the cross to accomplish the sacrament of his passion. [Col. 0424A] He dug many wells in order to find living water, teaching us to meditate attentively on the sacred Scriptures until we receive divine wisdom. Thus by his patience and obedience he reproves those who proudly resist their father’s vow, lest the effect of divine service be fulfilled in them.

Likewise Jacob, a simple man dwelling in tents, offers us an example of the greatest humility and gentleness, so that, if we wish to inherit the paternal blessing, we may remain in the tents of our simplicity and, subject in all things to the mother Church, submit ourselves more to rules than, together with ruddy and hairy Esau, serve the vain affairs of the world.

Why should I enumerate individually the deeds of each of the patriarchs, to establish the power of paternal authority in handing over their sons for the service of God, when the Lord himself commanded in the law that Israel consecrate all the firstborn to him, saying to Moses: “Sanctify to me every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of human beings and of animals; for all are mine.” And again, when he wished to choose the Levites in place of the firstborn for the service of the tabernacle, he spoke to Moses as follows: “Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and you shall purify them.” And shortly afterward: “You shall bring,” he says, “the Levites before the tabernacle of the covenant, after summoning the whole assembly of the children of Israel. When the Levites are before the Lord, the children of Israel shall place their hands upon them, and Aaron shall offer the Levites as a gift before the Lord from the children of Israel, so that they may serve in his ministry. You shall consecrate them as an offering to the Lord, for they have been given to me as a gift by the children of Israel. In place of all the firstborn who open every womb in Israel, I have taken them. For every firstborn among the children of Israel is mine, both human and animal.
