From the day on which I struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified them to myself; and I took the Levites in place of all the firstborn of the children of Israel, and I gave them as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people, to serve me for Israel in the tabernacle of the covenant and to pray for them, so that there may be no plague among the people.”

Behold, the Lord demands every firstborn from those who ought to obey his laws—not only human firstborn, but also the firstborn of animals—in order to show that we are obliged to offer to him not only what is ours, but also ourselves.

And lest you be able properly to raise any complaint and say that it is not lawful for just anyone to offer his son, equally free, for the service of God, he commands the whole people to offer one entire tribe out of the twelve to the tabernacle of the covenant and there to consecrate it as an offering to the Lord for his service. Which then seems to have greater authority: the children of Israel in offering their brothers, the Levites, who after their offering, by the Lord’s decree, were denied every share in earthly inheritance and possession among the other tribes; or a father with his own son, still of tender age and not yet, according to the law, existing in his own right or power, when he has decreed that, stripped of all worldly cares, business, and possessions according to the statutes of the holy Rule, the boy should be made wholly subject to God alone for his service? For it is one thing for an equal to be handed over to an equal, and another for an inferior to be subjected by a superior to someone else. Among equals contradiction often arises, lest one party surpass or be forced to serve the other; but between a superior and an inferior there is no rational basis for the younger not to submit entirely to the command of the elder.

If the Lord’s authority is just both over the greater and over the lesser, why do these empty murmurers and composers of unjust complaints not cease to detract from the laws of God and to speak wickedness against the one who created heaven and earth and everything in them, rules them, and orders them according to his will? Especially since, reproving such people through the Psalmist, the Holy Spirit speaks as follows: “Do not lift up your horn on high, and do not speak injustice against God; for neither from the east nor from the desert mountains—for God is judge.” Let them also remember the judgment which the Apostle Jude set forth in his Epistle, saying: “Certain men have slipped in, who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly men who turn the grace of our God into debauchery and deny the only ruler, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

To these, shortly afterward in the same Epistle, he adds a threat, saying: “Woe to them, for they have gone in the way of Cain, have poured themselves out in the error of Balaam, and have perished in the contradiction of Korah. These are stains in their feasts, feasting without fear, feeding themselves; clouds without water, carried about by winds; autumn trees, fruitless, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own confusions; wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever.”

They go in the way of Cain who, out of envy of better people, assume for themselves the name of teachers, by which those people are honored. They perish in the error of Balaam who, out of love for earthly advantages, attack the truth they themselves know. They perish in the contradiction of Korah, who descended alive into the underworld, whoever, driven by desire for an undeserved primacy, separates himself from the unity of holy Church; although they know and foresee how much evil they are committing, they nevertheless descend to Tartarus.

Indeed, the Lord rebuked Cain while he was contemplating fratricide, but envy did not allow him to be saved. The Lord forbade Balaam, who was journeying against the people of God, but love of money prevented him from obeying. Moses sought to calm Korah in his pride while the Lord was speaking through him, but the arrogance burning within Korah made him incurable. Thus, certainly thus, act the heretics who disdain being corrected by the rebuke of holy Church. Rather, they strive to kill their brothers with the sword of evil teaching, like Cain; to deceive them by wicked counsel, like Balaam; and to rise up against Catholic teachers, like Korah—to their own destruction.

These few examples from among the many deeds of those fathers whom the Pentateuch of Moses recounts at length are sufficient to establish that the offering by parents of their sons is valid and lawful. Now let us bring forward in writing those matters concerning the times of the Judges and Kings that come to mind, to confirm the same point.

It is read in the Book of Judges that Jephthah the Gileadite, a very brave man, when he had decided to wage war against the Ammonites in order to rescue Israel from their power, after the spirit of God had come upon him, made a vow to the Lord, saying: “If you deliver the children of Ammon into my hands, whoever is the first to come out of the doors of my house and meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, I will offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord.”

Jephthah then went against the children of Ammon to fight them, and the Lord delivered them into his hands. He struck them from Aner as far as Minnith—twenty cities—and as far as Abel, which is planted with vineyards, with a very great slaughter. And the children of Ammon were humbled before the children of Israel.

When Jephthah returned to his house at Mizpah, his only daughter met him with tambourines and dances, for he had no other children. When he saw her, he tore his garments and said: “Alas, my daughter! You have deceived me, and you yourself have been deceived. For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot do otherwise.” She answered him: “My father, if you have opened your mouth to the Lord, do to me whatever you promised, since the Lord has granted you vengeance and victory over your enemies.” And she said to her father: “Grant me this one thing that I ask of you: let me go for two months, that I may wander over the mountains and mourn my virginity with my companions.” He answered her: “Go.” And he let her go for two months. When she had gone with her companions and associates, she mourned her virginity in the mountains. At the end of two months she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed; and she had not known a man.

What do my friends, whose entire speech is directed toward disparaging our order, answer to this? Who is so foolish and perverse as to call Jephthah sacrilegious because he offered his daughter on account of the vow that he had made to God, when Scripture says that he did this after the spirit of God had come upon him—especially since the Apostle Paul, in the Epistle that he wrote to the Hebrews, counts him among the saints?

If it was permitted to the fathers of that time to offer a son or daughter to God by the sword, why is it not permitted now for people of this age to consecrate their offspring spiritually to God and present a living, holy, God-pleasing sacrifice, rationally devoted to the service of Christ? But if Abraham’s offering pleased God, and Jephthah’s deed obtained for him the merit of holiness, why should we not believe that a spiritual offering established through evangelical teaching pleases God all the more? For the Apostle James testifies concerning Abraham, saying: “Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar?” You see that faith cooperated with his works. For by his works faith was perfected, and the Scripture was fulfilled which says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.”

And concerning Jephthah, after the vow that he made to God, it is written: “Jephthah went against the children of Ammon to fight them, whom the Lord delivered into his hands.” Behold: Abraham, by offering his son, earned the friendship of God; Jephthah, by making a vow to God, obtained victory over his enemies. What follows from this except that those who despise the offering to God and abominate such a deed of the holy fathers are called, and are, enemies of God, and for this reason are not only unable to rule over their spiritual enemies but, deservedly because of their perversity, are entirely subjected to them? For it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world is made an enemy of God.” Nothing can please God except what is good; and what is good for the one who does it earns the merit of holiness.

The praiseworthy deed of Hannah also proves this, as the Book of Samuel records. For since she is described as barren and was therefore mocked by her rival—namely, the other wife of her husband Elkanah—she turned to entreat the Lord. Her hope did not disappoint her; rather, she obtained the result of her petition. For it is written:

“When Hannah was bitter in spirit, she prayed to the Lord, weeping profusely, and made a vow, saying: ‘Lord of hosts, if you will look upon the affliction of your handmaid and remember me, and do not forget your servant, but give your handmaid a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head.’”

And shortly afterward: “Elkanah,” it says, “knew Hannah his wife, and the Lord remembered her.” After the passage of days, Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, because she had asked him of the Lord.

Her husband Elkanah and all his household went up to offer the solemn sacrifice and fulfill his vow. “But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband: ‘I will not go until the child is weaned; then I will bring him, that he may appear before the Lord and remain there continually.’ And Elkanah her husband said to her: ‘Do what seems good to you, and remain until you have weaned him; and may the Lord fulfill his word.’ So the woman remained and nursed her son until she took him from the breast. After she had weaned him, she brought him with her, together with three calves, three measures of flour, and a jar of wine, and brought him to the house of the Lord at Shiloh.

“Now the child was still very young. They sacrificed a calf and presented the boy to Eli. And she said: ‘I beg you, my lord—as surely as your soul lives, my lord—I am that woman who stood before you here, praying to the Lord for this child. I prayed, and the Lord granted me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore I too have lent him to the Lord for all the days for which he has been lent to the Lord.’”

I should like to know what these haters and opponents of regular offering would say about this offering, which is almost identical with the regular offering established by blessed Father Benedict in his Rule. For just as there he commands parents to offer infant children to God beside the altar, with an offering and a petition, so here this holy and prophetic woman solemnly offered her infant son to the Lord before the priest Eli in the tabernacle, together with an offering of flour and the other items mentioned in the Book of Kings.

Do they think that Hannah did this because she was driven by a spirit of arrogance, and that, as though she possessed authority over herself, she first made a vow to God before the child had even been conceived, without her husband’s counsel or command? Then, after his birth, although with her husband’s consent, she nevertheless confidently offered him to the Lord herself and carefully explained the entire order of her vow to the priest Eli there.

Who would dare say that the Lord is unjust, since, on account of this woman’s merit of faith and the outcome of her great devotion, he granted her the grace of his Holy Spirit? For if the deed of this offering had displeased him, he would certainly not, after the offering had been performed, have bestowed upon her the gift of the Holy Spirit, through which she was able to prophesy concerning the future mystery of Christ’s coming, the transformation of the former priesthood and the earlier law, as well as the rejection of the unbelieving people and the calling of the nations to faith.

After the parents of blessed Samuel had worshiped the Lord at Shiloh, Hannah prayed and said: “My heart has rejoiced in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God,” and so forth.

On the other hand, if worldly law alone ought to rule in divine worship, so that no one were permitted to transgress it in the service of Christ, how would the author of all goodness and the most vigilant guardian of justice—of whom it is written, “The Lord is just and has loved justice; his countenance beholds equity”—not confirm this by his own testimony and provide everyone with a manifest judgment of his will?

Therefore let these empty talkers and detractors cease at last to disparage the Christian religion and to tear with a poisonous tooth the grace of Christ, which has been distributed in various gifts to the holy mother Church. For, as Scripture testifies, “The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue.”

But since many examples of this kind can be found in the Old Testament, and in the New Testament likewise there are not a few testimonies of this sort, let our discourse not proceed beyond measure. Leaving aside the examples from the Old Testament, let us bring forward examples from the New.

For the holy Gospel relates that the parents of the Savior presented the child Jesus in the temple to the Lord, together with an offering prescribed for them according to the law, so that the giver of the law might confirm and establish it by his own example and show that he was altogether not displeased by the offering and devotion of the faithful in his Church.

If Jesus wished to be brought by his parents to the temple and there to have a sacrifice offered to God on his behalf, who is there who would dare to criticize the offering of parents in their children and forbid them to present their children as a living sacrifice to God? For, as Scripture testifies, not only the faith of those offered but also that of those offering them was acceptable to God. Hence, too, in holy Church the baptism of infants is accomplished through the faith and profession of their parents.

Some people brought a paralytic to Jesus, “and when he saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you. Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.’” The faith of the centurion obtained salvation for his servant; and the son of the royal official returned to his former health when his father believed the words of Jesus. At the request of the ruler of the synagogue, the Lord raised his daughter from the dead; and, when requested, the same Lord freed Peter’s mother-in-law from a fever.

When the people of the land of Gennesaret learned of Jesus’ arrival, they sent throughout that whole region and brought to him all who were ill. They begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and all who touched it were healed. The Canaanite woman pleaded with the Lord for her demon-possessed daughter and obtained salvation for her from him.

People brought infants to Jesus so that he might touch them. But the disciples rebuked those who brought them. When he saw this, he was indignant and said to them: “Let the little children come to me, and do not forbid them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. Amen I say to you: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it.” And embracing them and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them.

Let those who disparage the offering of infants hear these things and understand that their endeavor is directed toward iniquity, and that they strive in vain by objecting to the smallness of the children’s age, as though parents were not permitted to offer their infant children to God and bind them to his service.

If Truth itself was indignant when his still-carnal disciples, not yet enlightened or strengthened by his passion, resurrection, and the coming of the Holy Spirit, rebuked those bringing infants, what do these people think they deserve? The Church has now been spread throughout the world and the truth has been made manifest everywhere, yet they still, with hearts blinded by earthly desire, hold opinions contrary to the Catholic faith and introduce new sects into the Church as the end of the world approaches.

For while they ought by this time to be teachers, they again need someone to teach them what are the first elements of the beginning of the words of God. Why do they not fear the judgment of Paul, who says:

“Anyone who annuls the law of Moses is put to death without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as unclean the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay.’ And again: ‘The Lord will judge his people.’ It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God.”

It has always been the custom of good teachers to win people for God through words and examples, to strive to rescue from the kingdom of the devil all whom they can, and to convert them to the service of God. Hence the teacher of the nations says to the Corinthians:

“Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might win more. I became weak to the weak, that I might win the weak; I became all things to all, that I might save all. I do everything for the sake of the Gospel, so that I may become a partaker of it.”

And again he says: “In all things we suffer affliction, but are not crushed; we are perplexed, but not abandoned; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but do not perish; always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies.” And elsewhere: “I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with heavenly glory.”

For this reason very many, through the grace of God and through the diligence of good teachers, both from among the Jews and from among the nations, were converted to the faith of Christ. Thus it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when Peter preached, about three thousand souls were added in one day to the number of believers. “For the word of the Lord grew, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem increased greatly.” A large crowd of priests also obeyed the faith.

Likewise, when Paul and Barnabas were preaching in Antioch, a great number of believers were converted to the Lord, so that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with his whole household; and many of the Corinthians, hearing, believed and were baptized. Hence the same Apostle Paul boasts that he had filled the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum.

On the other hand, certain people now, paying attention to spirits of error and to teachings of demons speaking lies in hypocrisy, their consciences seared as with a branding iron, forbid some people to withdraw from worldly pomp and earthly desire and to join themselves to those who despise the world and serve God under regular discipline.

Let these people beware lest the Lord’s judgment directed in the Gospel against the Pharisees and teachers of the law apply to them. Truth itself says: “Woe to you Pharisees, who love the first seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace; woe to you, for you are like tombs that do not appear, and people walk over them without knowing it.” And again: “Woe to you, teachers of the law, who have the key of knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering.”

Hence Peter wrote in his Epistle, saying:

“God knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust for punishment on the day of judgment—especially those who follow the flesh in unclean desire and despise authority, bold and self-willed, not afraid to introduce sects, blasphemers, luxuriating in their pleasures and reveling in their banquets, enticing unstable souls, possessing a heart trained in greed. They are children of the curse. They have abandoned the straight way and gone astray; they have followed the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the reward of iniquity but had a rebuke for his madness: a speechless beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly.

“These are waterless springs and clouds driven by storms, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved. Speaking arrogantly of vanity, they entice, by the desires of the flesh and by debauchery, those who barely escape, who live in error. They promise them freedom, although they themselves are slaves of corruption; for by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved. For if, after escaping the pollutions of the world through knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their later condition has become worse for them than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.”

Although these things are perceived by the bodily ears, they do not apply the inner ears that the Savior requires in the Gospel, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” Thus they do not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them, and who, with perverse intention, strive to diminish or utterly overturn the monastic way of life.

When they hear that the regular offering of young children must be confirmed by suitable witnesses, because they do not dare openly to oppose and resist the truth, they seek indirectly how they may accomplish by this wicked action what they devise with perverse intent. They argue subtly and adopt this as a device of their error, by which they may more easily deceive those who comply with and obey them.

They claim that no one may summon witnesses to confirm the truth of the Christian religion except from his own people. For example, they say that concerning a Saxon no one from among the Franks or Romans, or from any other nation, may be a witness—even if he is noble by birth and regarded as honorable in conduct among his own people—unless he is a Saxon. They say that the law of his nation cannot tolerate a person of another nation being summoned as a witness to invalidate the law of his own liberty.

As though those who profess the service of Christ lose the liberty and nobility of their lineage, when in fact those are freer who serve the one God than those who are shown to serve various vices and sins. They devise this argument for no other reason than to make the monastic way of life and regular discipline hateful to people, saying that those who become monks become slaves. They do not understand that they are fighting against the Lord when they say that devotion to his service is a burden imposed upon nature, since there is no better or greater power than to serve God, whom love serves well.

If truth is to be sought from witnesses, the faithfulness and integrity of the witnesses must be required. And how are suitable witnesses found unless the person making the selection considers the matter carefully, so that not only nobility of lineage but also steadfastness of mind is approved in them? From the beginning, prudent people sought witnesses in this way; above all, they valued the discovery of truth rather than the invention of falsehood.

But if anyone must consider distinctions of persons and the status of nations, and witnesses are to be approved so that each person accepts no witnesses except those of his own nation, how did the nations receive the testimony of the Jews in the faith of Christ, although the Jews were not like them in religion or nation? For all the Apostles and prophets were Jews. Or how did the Jews choose to receive the testimony of the nations, who were not their equals in rite or dignity?

For Luke the evangelist was from Antioch, a physician by profession, and, as it is written, a Syrian by nationality. He composed his Gospel more from hearing than from seeing; nevertheless, believers both from the Jews and from the nations receive it equally and include it among the four Gospels. For God does not show partiality to a person, but in every nation and condition whoever fears the Lord and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.

Since these things are so, what reason is there, whether according to God or according to human beings, for those who are inferior in virtue and dignity to despise their superiors and more eminent persons, and, rejecting them as unworthy of all honor, cast them away—although they ought to be subject to them?

Who does not know that, under this region of the world, the Franks possessed the Christian faith and religion before the Saxons, whom they later subjected to their rule by arms? Having become their superiors, they drew them away from the worship of idols and converted them to the faith of Christ, treating them as lords—or rather with paternal affection. But now certain leading men born from that very nation according to the flesh ungratefully despise them and, contrary to the law of heaven and the law of the forum, indignantly reject them so that they may not be witnesses to the truth.

Yet neither human nor divine reason in any way dictates that this should happen, nor has such an order ever existed throughout the four-cornered world. Histories relate that all Asia, organized under one hundred and twenty satraps, obeyed the laws of the Persians. Likewise, all nations were subjected to Roman rule, in census and in sentiment, according to the decrees of the emperors, through the various provinces in their respective times; and being enrolled as a Roman citizen was regarded among all nations as a great dignity and honor.

But it is not surprising that those who hold opinions contrary to the divine laws do not properly keep the covenants of human agreements. For, wandering and leading others into error, they become guilty before God and blameworthy before human beings.

Finally, truth, which reigns everywhere, conquers all things. Although it has many enemies, it nevertheless, as victor, will overcome all its foes with eternal victory. Its holy Church, most faithful observer and guardian of the truth, founded upon the firm solidity of the rock, accepts no fellowship with the faithless. Hence the gates of hell will not prevail against it.

There is also no small multitude of monks belonging to this Church. Devotedly serving their Creator, they gather their flocks in nearly every part of the world, build dwellings, and strive to offer an acceptable service to the one almighty God. Instituted according to the norm of apostolic tradition, possessing nothing as private property, they live in common, seek their food by their own hands, and desire in all things to obey the authority of their spiritual father. They despise no one and disdain no one.

Every sex, every age, and every condition is regarded among them as capable of the service of God. Therefore they receive infants, welcome young people, and do not reject the old or the infirm. Among them the adolescent consecrated to God in childhood has a place; there the young man, salutarily contrite for his sins, finds a remedy for his salvation; there the old or decrepit person does not lose the labor of the eleventh hour, nor does one who has converted late lose his reward.

Through this community our David also gathered and restored those whom the world had despised and cast away because of their crimes or bodily infirmity, and made them leaders of his journey. Hence we find many described in the Conferences of the Fathers and in their Lives who, prompted by the Spirit of God, entered upon the monastic vocation; and many who handed over their own sons to be brought up for the service of God.

Blessed Pope Gregory also recorded that this was done by the venerable Father Benedict, whose Life he himself wrote and whose Rule of instruction he wonderfully praises, in the books of the Dialogues, saying:

“When the holy man was increasing in virtues and signs before the Lord in that same solitude, many were gathered by him in that place for the service of almighty God, so that, with the help of almighty Jesus Christ our Lord, he built twelve monasteries there. In these he appointed twelve monks under established superiors, while he kept a few with himself, whom he judged better suited to be instructed in his presence.

“At that time, noble and religious people of the city of Rome also began to come to him and to give him their sons to be brought up for almighty God. Then Equitius entrusted to him his son Maurus, a child of good promise, and the patrician Tertullus entrusted his son Placidus. Of these, the younger Maurus, since he excelled in good conduct, began to be an assistant to his teacher; Placidus, however, was still of childish character and age.”

Indeed, holy Gregory, who held the episcopate of the Apostolic See and was regarded as the most distinguished in the order of pontiffs, and who is celebrated throughout almost the whole world among the foremost teachers of the Church and is worthy of every veneration—how could he, in describing the deeds of the holy man, record as proper the offering of boys to be brought up for the service of almighty God, if that offering were not valid but instead were to be regarded as contrary to the truth and to divine authority?

For one who is blameworthy in his actions is not holy; nor is one worthy of praise who is found to be contrary to the divine laws. Therefore let those whose judgment and speech disagree with the divine constitutions and the examples of the holy Fathers beware lest, corrupted by earthly desire and made detestable in their pleasures, they diminish the merit of holiness for themselves and lose their reward.

For, as Paul testifies: “God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap; because whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.”

But now, believing that what we have briefly excerpted from the sacred Scriptures is sufficient to confirm the regular offering to the prudent and sound-minded, let us now show, by a few testimonies from the same Scripture, how necessary it is to fulfill the vow that is vowed to God.

The Lord speaks through Moses in the Law, saying: “If any man vows a vow to the Lord, or binds himself by an oath, he shall not make his word void, but shall fulfill everything that he promised.” And again: “When you have vowed a vow to the Lord your God,” he says, “you shall not delay in paying it, because the Lord your God will require it of you; and if you delay, it will be reckoned to you as sin. If you are unwilling to promise, you will be without sin; but whatever has once gone forth from your lips, you shall observe and do as you promised the Lord your God: you have spoken from your own will, from your mouth.”

For the Psalmist likewise exhorts us, saying: “Vow and pay to the Lord your God, all who bring offerings in his presence.” Confirming this by his own example, he says elsewhere: “I shall pay my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people, in your midst, Jerusalem.” And again: “Thus I shall sing a psalm,” he says, “to your name, O God, forever and ever, that I may pay my vows day by day.”

Hence Ecclesiastes also says: “If you have vowed anything to the Lord, do not delay in paying it; for an unfaithful promise displeases him. Whatever you vow, pay it. It is much better not to vow than, after vowing, not to fulfill your promises.”

The Savior likewise expressed this very point in the Gospel by means of a comparison, saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” And again: “Whoever is on the roof, with his possessions in the house, must not come down to take them; and likewise whoever is in the field. Remember Lot’s wife. Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will restore it to life.”

Hence also the teacher of the nations, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, admonishes us, saying: “Therefore, brothers, do not abandon your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need patience, so that, by doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come and will not delay. But my righteous one lives by faith. And if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him.”

Hence also the shepherd of the Church exhorts us, saying: “With the loins of your mind girded, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace that is being offered to you at the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Therefore the apostle John, instructing us by salutary exhortation in his Epistle, says: “Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what you have accomplished, but may receive a full reward.”

By these and similar testimonies of Scripture we are instructed not to neglect paying the vow that we make to God, because the Lord will not hold that person innocent who is not afraid to lie to him. But, alas, certain people, treating as insignificant the covenant they made with God, as though it could be abandoned without danger, cast it away altogether in ingratitude; and, desiring the friendship of this world, are not afraid to become enemies of God. For whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God.

Since they had freely chosen to pursue what is more perfect, and for that reason consecrated their souls to God by making a vow, so that they might please in all things him whom they had undertaken to serve exclusively, they gradually relapse through negligence into vices. Against the Gospel, they suppose that they can serve both the world and God, although the Savior plainly says: “No one can serve two masters, that is, God and mammon.”

Such people are deceived and stand under condemnation, because they have made their first faith void. Unless they are converted again and strive with all their strength to restore what they destroyed, they will not be able to attain salvation.

But since there are certain people who, while professing the monastic life, contradict the constitutions of the holy Rule, and, despising it, murmur and whisper among themselves that the rule’s ordinance is superfluous and unnecessary, and rests more upon human invention than upon divine authority, we shall first demonstrate—following the understanding of those who, imbued with Catholic truth, have written most fully about the origin and nature of this order—that the monastic way of life was instituted by God through the words and deeds of the holy Fathers. Then we shall add testimonies from the divine canon appropriate to this discipline, so that those who have long served this error may at least, once overcome by truth revealed in every respect, be ashamed to continue their empty chatter.

Thus the discipline of the cenobites took its beginning from the time of the apostles’ preaching. For such was the whole multitude of believers in Jerusalem, which is described in the Acts of the Apostles as follows: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them. They sold their possessions and goods and distributed them to everyone, according as each had need.”

And again: “There was no needy person among them. For all who owned fields or houses sold them, brought the money from what they had sold, and laid it at the apostles’ feet. It was distributed to each according as each had need.”

Such, then, was the whole Church at that time—such as it is now difficult to find even a very few in monasteries. But after the apostles’ departure the multitude of believers began to grow lukewarm, especially that multitude which came to the faith of Christ from foreign peoples and diverse nations. From these the apostles, because of their rudimentary faith and their ingrained pagan customs, required nothing more than that they abstain from sacrifices offered to idols, from fornication, from things strangled, and from blood.

When this liberty, which had been granted to the nations because of the weakness of their initial belief, began gradually to contaminate even the perfection of that Church which was established at Jerusalem, and when the fervor of that first faith grew cold as the number of natives and newcomers increased daily, not only those who had come to the faith of Christ but also those who were leaders of the Church were released from that strictness.

Some, judging that what they saw conceded to the nations because of their weakness was also permitted to them, believed that they would suffer no loss if they followed the faith and confession of Christ together with their possessions and resources. But those in whom the apostolic fervor still remained, remembering that former perfection, withdrew from their cities and from the company of those who thought that a more relaxed way of life could be tolerated by themselves or by the Church of God.

They began frequently to live in suburban and more secluded places, and privately and individually to practice what they remembered had been instituted generally by the apostles throughout the whole body of the Church. Thus the discipline of those disciples whom we have mentioned, who had separated themselves from the contagion of the others, gradually grew strong.

As time passed, they were separated from the crowds of believers to such an extent that they abstained from marriage and withdrew themselves from the company of their parents and from the society of this world. They were called monks, or *monozantes*, that is, “solitary ones,” from the strictness of the solitary life.

Consequently, because of their common association and fellowship, their cells and lodgings were called monasteries, or cenobia. This, then, was the one most ancient kind of monks—not only the earliest in time but also the first—which continued alone for many years, down to the age of Abbots Paul and Antony. Even now we see traces of it remaining in strict monasteries.

From this ancient number and, so to speak, most fruitful root, the flowers and fruits of the holy anchorites subsequently came forth. We know that the leaders of this profession were those whom we mentioned shortly before, namely Saint Paul and Antony. They did not seek the solitude of the desert because of cowardice or from the disease of impatience, but from a desire for higher progress and divine contemplation, although it is said that the former entered the desert under the pressure of necessity, while avoiding the plots of his relatives during a time of persecution.

Thus from the discipline we have described there arose another kind of perfection, whose followers are rightly called anchorites, that is, “those who withdraw.” They were not content with the victory by which they had trampled underfoot the Devil’s hidden snares among human beings; desiring to engage all adversaries in open battle and manifest conflict, they did not fear to penetrate the vast retreats of the desert, in imitation of Saint John the Baptist, who remained in the wilderness throughout his life; and also of Elijah and Elisha, and of those whom the apostles recall in these words:

“They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, distressed, afflicted, destitute—men of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and caverns of the earth.”

Of these the Lord also speaks figuratively to Job: “Who is it that set the wild ass free and loosed its bonds? He made its dwelling in the desert and its shelters in the salt land, mocking the multitude of the city and not hearing the complaint of the taskmaster. He considered the mountains of its pasture, and it searches after every green thing.”

It is also written in the Psalms: “Let those who have been redeemed by the Lord speak, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy.” And shortly afterward: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a dry land; they found no road to a city in which they might dwell. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. And they cried to the Lord when they were in distress, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

Jeremiah also describes them in this way: “Blessed is the one who has borne the yoke from his youth. He will sit alone and keep silent, because he has lifted himself above himself.”

They also fulfill in feeling and deed what the Psalmist says: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have kept vigil and become like a solitary sparrow on the roof.”

Therefore those who think that the monastic discipline should be despised ought first to consider the virtue of this rule and way of life. If they see that it agrees with the laws of God, let them cease to persecute it with hatred and stop tearing it apart with blasphemous speech. For the one who, through envy, proves treacherously hostile to the gifts of God will not go unpunished.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter.”

The purpose of a monk is to renounce the world and its pleasures; to devote himself to continence, quiet, obedience, and humility; to endure patiently the tribulations and hardships of the present life; and above all to seek the reward of heavenly grace.

Let us therefore consider whether these things are confirmed by divine testimonies. For the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple. And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

And again he says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.”

Hence, when a rich man anxiously asked about his salvation, Truth itself answered him, saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me.”

He also said to the apostles: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ The nations seek all these things. For your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man.

“Amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy. Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted.”

Isaiah shows what work must follow, saying: “The work of righteousness will be peace, and the service of righteousness will be quietness and security forever.”

Jeremiah likewise says: “It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of the Lord; it is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He will sit alone and keep silent, because he has lifted himself above himself; he will put his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope. He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches, because the Lord will not reject forever. He who loved to move his feet and did not rest did not please the Lord.”

Hence Paul says to the Thessalonians: “We ask you, brothers, to abound more and more, and to strive to live quietly, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we commanded you, and to walk honorably toward those who are outside, desiring nothing from anyone.”

Concerning humility, gentleness, and obedience, the Savior himself instructs us in the Gospel, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart. Therefore everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the earth.”

And again he says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father.”

Hence the Apostle says: “Christ became obedient for us to the Father unto death, even death on a cross,” and so forth.

In the Book of Kings, Samuel likewise said to Saul the sinful king: “Does the Lord desire holocausts and sacrifices, rather than that the voice of the Lord should be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry.”

Concerning endurance of tribulation and patience, Truth itself says to the disciples: “In the world you will have affliction, but be confident: I have overcome the world. In your patience you will possess your souls.”

And because prayer and fasting are the work of monks, the same Mediator between God and human beings commends and approves them. When the apostles reproached him because a demon-possessed man had not been healed by them, he answered: “This kind can come out by nothing except prayer and fasting.”

Behold the order and life of monks, which the Lord himself confirms by his sayings, and by the writings of his prophets and apostles. Who, then, would dare to criticize it, except one who is insane in speech and heart and therefore opposed to the laws of God?

It is not, therefore, a light crime or a minor sin to wish to make Truth a liar and to portray the Lord as unjust, when one strives to condemn what he himself praises. But if this adversary of ours should still persist in the wickedness he has once conceived, and should say that people can be saved without a monk’s vow, we do not deny this; but we do not dare to disparage the path of perfection.

Thus, as best we could, we have tasted a few things from among many. But if he finds our writings tedious, let him hear what blessed Jerome thought, in the book he wrote against Vigilantius, who attacked monks with a similar blasphemy:

“But when you assert,” he says, “that those who use their own possessions and gradually distribute the produce of their estates to the poor do better than those who sell their possessions and give everything away at once, the answer will come to them not from me but from the Lord: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me.’

“He speaks to the one who wishes to be perfect, the one who, together with the apostles, leaves his father, his little boat, and his net. The man whom you praise is in the second or third degree, and we also accept him, provided that we know that the first degree must be preferred to the second and third.

“Do not, by your cunning and zeal, frighten monks away with the craft of a viperous tongue and its most savage bite. You argue about them and say: ‘If everyone shuts himself away and lives in solitude, who will celebrate the churches? Who will win secular people? Who will be able to restrain sinners and compel them to virtue?’ In this way, if everyone is foolish with you, who will be able to be wise?

“Virginity, too, should not be approved: if everyone is a virgin, there will be no married women; the human race will perish; infants will not cry in their cradles; midwives will beg without payment; and in the harshest cold the solitary and stiff Dormitantius will remain awake in bed.

“Virtue is renowned, but it is not sought by many. Would that all were what the few are, of whom it is said: ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’; the prisons would be empty.

“A monk’s office is not that of a teacher, but of one who mourns—whether mourning for himself or for the world—and who fearfully awaits the Lord’s coming. Knowing his weakness and the fragile vessel he carries, he fears offending, lest he stumble and fall and be shattered.

“Therefore he avoids the sight of women, especially young women, and is so strict with himself that he fears even what is safe.

“‘Why,’ you will say, ‘do you go into the desert?’ Obviously so that I may not hear you, may not see you, may not be stirred by your fury, may not endure your battles; so that the eye of a harlot may not capture me, and a most beautiful form may not lead me into forbidden embraces.

“You will reply: ‘This is not fighting but fleeing. Stand in the battle line; armed, resist your adversary, so that after you have conquered you may be crowned.’

“I confess my weakness: I do not wish to hope for victory through battle, lest I lose another victory. If I flee, I have avoided the sword; but if I stand, I must either conquer or fall. Why abandon certainties and pursue uncertainties? I must avoid it either with my shield or with my feet.

“You who fight may be overcome or may conquer. When I flee, I am not conquered in the thing from which I flee; rather, I flee so that I may not be conquered. There is no safety in sleeping near a serpent. It may happen that it will not bite me; nevertheless, it may happen that someday it will bite.”

There are, moreover, other holy and orthodox Fathers whose understanding and judgment on this matter are the same: they affirm that the rule of regular discipline was instituted and founded by God through apostolic teaching.

But since it would exceed the proper length of a book if I wished to heap up in this little work the many statements of these men, let what has been said suffice for the sober reader. Whoever seeks more and greater things, and finds our writings tedious, should read the numerous volumes of the Catholic teachers; and, I believe, will see that their understanding does not differ from that of this present little work.

**Explicit.**

[Col. 0439]

**(A.D. 819.) Four Books of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, of Commentaries on Genesis.**

**Bishop Freculphus to Abbot Maurus**

[Col. 0439C]

Freculphus, the least of bishops, sends greetings in Christ, the Son of God, to the venerable Abbot Maurus and fellow priest.

Your charity’s goodwill knows, my most beloved, that although I had no merits to support me, I undertook pastoral care on the western shore of the Ocean. There I found a people suffering from hunger for the word of salvation, but entirely unaware of their want. They did not hunger for spiritual food, whose sweetness they had not yet tasted; I judged that they should first be nourished with milk, not solid food.

Therefore, with the Lord’s approval, they now desire to touch the food, and, although still little ones, they ask that bread be given to them. But, so that it may be broken for them and healthfully conveyed into their innermost parts without danger of choking, we need your assistance, especially concerning the Pentateuch.

Accordingly, we humbly ask that you elucidate these books of the Lawgiver through your concise labor, so that, by searching out and comparing the labors of earlier interpreters, and, like bees, gathering honey-bearing flowers from blooming and pleasant meadows into a hive, you may not neglect to offer us a honeycomb with fragrant honey.

We therefore earnestly request that this work be made concise, so that first the literal sense and then the spiritual understanding may be carefully revealed with its length cut short; and that the names of the individual authors from whom you have extracted the present opinions be written at the head of the pages.

In addition, we earnestly ask that whatever the Holy Spirit—who once spoke through men devoted to God, and still speaks and will speak—may inspire in your benevolent and devoted mind, you conceal under no silence. Rather, mark separately the first letter of your name, so that we may be able to rejoice all the more in the gift that is likewise your own.

When we have tasted these preliminary offerings, have been sprinkled with their fragrance, and refreshed by their nourishment, our west will be turned into the east, and the region adjoining the western pole will become Judea; our Britons will be neighbors to the Israelites.

Therefore, if you attempt to put forward excuses, so as not to undertake a work of such magnitude and labor, and if you try to answer, “Why do you not read through the books yourself, by your own sweat, the books from which you command these things to be made, gathering whatever passages you like by extracting them?”—then let the vigilance of your charity attend to this: we have no abundance of books with which to do these things.

Even if the smallness of our dull understanding were vigorous, in the bishopric entrusted to our insignificance I did not find even the canonical books of the New and Old Testament, much less their expositions. Nor is this unknown to your prudence: food is taken much more agreeably by a hungry man when it has been sensibly seasoned by someone at the proper time with the fragrance of precious spices than when it is gathered through sluggish labor.

When the hour of eating has already arrived, various ingredients are then first ground in a mortar and cooked by fire, and, only half-cooked, are set before the anxious hungry man; whatever has been prepared prematurely does not provide an agreeable taste to those who eat it.

Therefore, since I have confidence in both your affection and your obedience, I confidently command that which my insignificance enjoins upon your fraternity: apply yourself as quickly as possible to the study of so great a work.

Fare well, brother, and remember us constantly.

**Rabanus to Freculphus**

[Col. 0441]

[Col. 0441B]

To the most reverend and holy Father Freculphus, by God’s gift bishop, Rabanus, a sinner in Christ, sends greetings.

From ancient times it has been the practice of great men, by writing to one another, to provoke one another’s studies and exercise one another’s talents. Although you have decided to do this in the present age after their example, you are nevertheless to be wondered at for not seeking a suitable person for this undertaking, since you have chosen for this office a man so insignificant and incapable that neither the resources of knowledge nor the powers of eloquence provide him with strength for it.

This is especially so since I am more accustomed to rural labor in the desert—to seeking my livelihood with my own hands—than to composing books with urban eloquence.

For you have imposed on me a task beyond my strength: to arrange in one volume, after reading everywhere the sayings of the holy Fathers, both the literal sense and the spiritual understanding of the Pentateuch of Moses, and to undertake by my own labor to clarify whatever I did not find explained by others.

But you know better than I how far these things exceed my capacity. Living in a most difficult place, and occupied with the care of the Lord’s flock so that it may lack nothing necessary, I have been unable either to read through the sayings of others or to devise things of my own.

Nevertheless, because I do not dare to deny your charity anything, and do not wish to be disobedient to your holiness, I devoted myself more strictly to this work, so far as I was able, considering not what would be useful to me but what would be useful to others.

I did as you requested. I read, as far as I was able, the books of the holy Fathers in which I thought something concerning the sayings of the Law had been expressed, and I inserted each passage according to the suitability of its place, as seemed sufficient to me, with their names written beforehand on the page.

If divine grace has deigned to elucidate anything through me, unworthy as I am, I inserted it in the necessary places together with a mark bearing my own name, so that the reader might know what he had from the tradition of the Fathers and what he might find expounded from our own small resources—although in rustic language, yet, as I believe, with Catholic understanding.

Therefore, most holy brother, I earnestly beg you to reread with pious intention the work that you extracted from me by your excessive insistence, and to examine it carefully. Wherever correction is needed, do not delay to make this known to me with brotherly affection, so that whatever, detained by various occupations, I may perhaps have said carelessly, I may strive to correct when admonished by you.

Thus both the one who sows may rejoice together with the one who reaps, and both may gather an everlasting fruit.

Read, therefore, the books of the ancients, apply yourself attentively to meditation on the Law of God, and diligently carry out the ministry of a teacher, as has been enjoined upon you.

First, from the book of Genesis, through the creation of invisible things, meditate upon the effect of invisible things; from the structure of the bodily world, seek a spiritual understanding. Then, through the historical generation of the Fathers, learn the mystical fecundity of the holy Church. Instructed sufficiently in moral understanding, consider our pilgrimage in this world through the patriarchs’ migration from place to place, to whom an inheritance is promised not in the present life but in the future, because “the God of gods will be seen in Zion.”

For the rest, I ask you to receive the work entrusted to you with the disposition in which it has been sent to you, and to adapt it both to your own needs and to those of your people. If any of your relatives should take pleasure in it, do not refuse to provide it to him, so that the affection of your love and the fruit of our labor may, if it is God’s will, benefit many, and so that we may receive a reward for the talent we have spent rather than suffer loss for our stinginess by keeping it buried in the earth.

May divine grace preserve your blessedness in good health at all times, holy Father. Remember us.

[Col. 0443]

## The Commentaries on Genesis Begin. Book One.

### Chapter One

#### On the Creation of Heaven and Earth

**(Chapter I.)** “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

**(Bede.)** The Greek philosophers discussed the nature of things at great length, but among them no fixed and stable account is found, since each later account always overthrows the one before it.

**(Ambrose.)** Some people—Plato and his disciples, for example—asserted three principles of all things: God, the exemplar, and matter. They maintained that these were incorruptible, uncreated, and without beginning, and that God was not the creator of matter but its craftsman.

Aristotle, however, thought that there were two principles, matter and form, together with a third, which is called the operative principle, whose function would be suitably to accomplish whatever it had decided to undertake.

From this it came about that they believed the parts of the world to be gods, although there is considerable dispute among them even about the world itself. Pythagoras asserts that there is one world; others say that there are innumerable worlds, as Democritus writes, to whom antiquity has accorded great authority in physical matters.

Aristotle makes a practice of saying that the world has always existed and will always exist. Plato, on the other hand, presumes to assert that it has not always existed but will always exist. Very many others testify in their writings that it has neither always existed nor will always exist.

Therefore, foreseeing by the divine Spirit that these errors of human beings would arise, and perhaps had already begun, holy Moses says at the beginning of his account: “In the beginning God made,” and so forth. This statement embraces the beginning of things, the author of the world, and the creation of matter, so that you might know that God existed before the beginning of the world, or that he himself is the beginning of all things: “In the beginning,” he says.

How fitting is the order, by which he first asserted what they were accustomed to deny, so that they might recognize that the world has a beginning and not suppose that it existed without a beginning. He appropriately added “made,” so that no delay in making would be imagined, and so that human beings might understand that the maker was incorporeal: he completed so great a work in a brief and tiny moment of action, so that the effect of his will preceded any sense of time.

No one saw the one who was working, but they recognized what had been worked. Where, then, was there delay, when we read that “he spoke, and they were made”?

He needed neither the use of art nor the assistance of power, because in a moment of his will he fulfilled the majesty of so great an operation. He made things that did not exist come into existence so quickly that neither the will preceded the operation nor the operation the will.

You marvel at the work and seek the maker: who gave a beginning to so great a work, who made it so quickly? He immediately adds, saying: “God made heaven and earth.”

You have heard the author; you ought not to doubt. Who could doubt that God made these things? Through the prophet he speaks: “Who measured the waters in his hand, and heaven with a span, and enclosed the whole earth in his hand? Who set the mountains on a scale and the rocks in a balance?” (Isaiah XLVI.)

Elsewhere we also read of him: “He holds the circle of the earth, and made the earth as though it were nothing” (Isaiah XL).

Jeremiah says: “Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from the earth and from the things that are under heaven. The Lord made the earth by his power, established the world by his wisdom, and stretched out heaven by his understanding, and the multitude of water in heaven” (Jeremiah X).

“Beginning” refers either to time, number, or foundation.

It refers to time if you wish to say: At what time did God make heaven and earth? That is, at the beginning of the world, when it began to be made.

It refers to number if you understand it in this way: “At first he made heaven and earth, then hills, regions, uninhabitable boundaries, fruit-bearing trees, day, night, and the kinds of living creatures.”

**(Bede.)** If you refer “beginning” to foundation, just as in the construction of a house the beginning is the foundation, so you read that the foundation is the beginning of the earth, when Wisdom says: “When he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was beside him, arranging” (Wisdom VIII).

The will of God, therefore, is the foundation of all things.

At the beginning of time, then, God made heaven and earth. Time began with this world, not before the world; a day is a portion of time, not its beginning.

God, however, whose hand is omnipotent, did not need the delay of time to complete his work, because, as it is written: “He has done whatever he willed” (Psalm CXIII).

Therefore it is rightly said that “in the beginning God created heaven and earth,” so that it may plainly be understood that both were made by him at once, although human speech cannot say that both were made at once.

The prophet says: “At the beginning you founded the earth, Lord” (Psalm CI); here, however, the Lord is said to have created heaven and earth in the beginning.

From this it is clearly gathered that the making of both elements was completed together, and with such speed of divine power that not even the first moment of the world’s birth had yet passed.

It may also be understood, without implausibility, that in the beginning God made heaven and earth in his only-begotten Son. When the Jews asked him what they ought to believe concerning him, he answered: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John VIII), because, as the Apostle says, “all things were created in heaven and on earth in him” (Colossians I).

But each person must carefully take care to devote himself to allegorical meanings in such a way that, by allegorizing, he does not abandon the manifest faith of the historical account.

What heaven was, and what kind of heaven was made with the earth in the beginning, is indicated by the words that follow, when it is said:

But the earth was formless and empty, and darkness was over the face of the abyss. Why, then, did he introduce this matter concerning the earth while passing over heaven, unless he wished nothing of this kind to be understood about heaven? For this is the heaven above, which, withdrawn from every condition of this changeable world, remains forever at rest in the presence of the glory of God. As for our heaven, in which the luminaries necessary to this age have been placed, Scripture declares below how and when it was made.

That heaven above, therefore, which is inaccessible to the sight of all mortals [Col. 0445B], was not created formless and empty like the earth, which in its first creation produced no green shoots or living creatures. Indeed, it was immediately filled with its inhabitants when it was created—that is, with the most blessed hosts of angels. The Creator himself testifies that they were created in the beginning together with heaven and earth, and that soon afterward they jointly proclaimed their own creation and that of the whole primordial creation to the praise of the Creator. Speaking to his holy servant Job, he says: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38). And a little later: “When the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (ibid.). The morning stars are, of course, the same angels whom he calls the sons of God, clearly distinguishing them from the holy human beings who were to be created later and who, like evening stars, were to set through the death of the flesh after confessing the praise of God [Col. 0445C].

One of these morning stars, because of his contempt for the praise offered together with his fellow angels, deserved to hear: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn! You have fallen upon the earth, you who wounded the nations, who said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne’” (Isaiah 14). In explaining this passage, Saint Jerome also mentions the heaven above, writing as follows:

> “Either he was saying these things before he had fallen from heaven, or after he had fallen from heaven. But if he was still situated in heaven, how does he say, ‘I shall ascend into heaven’? Yet because we read, ‘The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord’ (Psalm 113), while he was in heaven—that is, in the firmament—he desired to ascend into the heaven where the Lord’s throne is, not in humility but in pride. If, however, he speaks these words after he had fallen from heaven, we should understand them as words of arrogance: although he has been hurled down, he does not rest but still promises himself great things—not to be among the stars but above the stars of God.”

It is rightly said, therefore, that the heaven of heaven was not created formless or empty; nor is any place said to remain there for darkness or the abyss, since the Lord God illuminates it, and the Lamb is its lamp [Col. 0445D].

And rightly was the earth formless and empty, since it was still entirely covered by the abyss—that is, by an immense depth of waters. Darkness was rightly over the face of the abyss, since the light that would dispel it had not yet been created. We must not listen to those who, in criticizing God, say that he created darkness before light, because God did not make any darkness in the water or the air; rather, in the distinct order of his providence, he first created the waters together with heaven and earth, and afterward, when he willed, adorned them with the grace of light. We see him doing the same even now, both in the water itself and in the air, through the daily rising and setting of the sun [Col. 0446A].

For it is not lawful to believe that the waters were made by anyone other than God. Although Scripture does not state this openly here, it nevertheless clearly signifies it when it indicates that the waters were illuminated by God and ordered at his command. The psalm says plainly: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord, because he spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 148).

Here it should be noted that, together with heaven, two elements of this world—water and earth—are explicitly said to have been made in the beginning. Yet it is clear that the other two were included within them: fire, namely, in iron and stones, which even then lay concealed, created in the bowels of the earth; and air in the earth itself. We know that air is mixed with the earth because, when the earth has been moistened and receives the warmth of the sun, it immediately exhales abundant vapors. Fire, too, implanted in the interior of the earth, is revealed by hot springs. When these run through certain metals deep below the waters, they flow out upon the surface of the earth not merely warm but boiling [Col. 0446B].

These elements were not, as some argue, formlessly mixed together. Rather, they were then such as they are now, bounded on every side within their proper limits; the earth as a whole was like what still remains in part beneath the lowest depths of the sea. The waters covered its entire surface to such a height that they reached even those regions where they still remain in part above the foundation of heaven and do not cease, together with the heavens of heavens, to praise the name of God the Creator [Col. 0446C].

Moreover, so formless was that matter from which Scripture testifies that the world was made that it says in praise of God: “You who made the world from formless matter” (Wisdom 11). For everything that we see in the world together with the waters and the earth either took the beginning of its nature from them or came into being from nothing. The earth itself and the waters themselves were therefore called “formless matter,” because before they came into the light there was nothing from which they might possess beauty.

What is there, moreover, that is incongruous if the beginnings of the world’s matter were dark, so that, when light was added, what had been made might be rendered more beautiful, and so that the disposition of a person making progress, which was to come afterward, might be signified in this way, as the Apostle explains when he says: “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4). Hence elsewhere he says: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5)—in him, namely, who, when darkness was over the face of the abyss, said: “Let there be light,” and there was light [Col. 0446D].

“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

We must not childishly suppose that the Creator Spirit, of whom it is written, “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1), was physically borne over the things that were to be created. Rather, we should understand that he excelled the creatures by divine power, possessing in his own authority the time when he would illuminate the abyss of waters, when he would separate them into one place so that the dry land might appear, and when and how he would arrange the remaining creatures according to his will—like a craftsman whose will is accustomed to govern the materials that are to be fashioned [Col. 0447A].

This also pertains to the distinction of the heaven above, in which, once everything had been perfectly arranged, the presence of the Holy Spirit immediately illuminated all things. He did not [alternative reading: “these”], as in the lower—that is, the creatures of this world—intend to bring the beginnings of a good creation to perfection in time. For this reason Moses also mentioned the higher world so briefly: he had undertaken to speak for the instruction of the human race about this world, in which humanity was made. He thought it sufficient to comprehend the whole state and adornment of spiritual and invisible creation under the single name of heaven, which he said had been made in the beginning [Col. 0447B].

But he would describe the bodily, visible, and corruptible creation more fully and in order. Omitting what is higher to seek and more difficult for human beings to investigate, he would propose for human consideration rather those things that had been commanded or promised by God. Thus he also deliberately remained completely silent about the fall of the rebellious angel and his companions, since this belongs to the state of that invisible and spiritual creation.

Concerning this higher and invisible creation, Saint Ambrose says in the second book of his *Hexameron*:

> “For we believe that if anything existed before the establishment of this sensible and corruptible world, it was certainly in light. Neither the dignity of the angels, nor all the heavenly host, nor whatever is named or unnameable, nor any rational power, nor ministering spirit could dwell in darkness; rather, in light and joy it possessed an appearance fitting for itself.”

When at the beginning he declared that God—that is, the Father in the Son—had made heaven and earth, he rightly also introduced mention of the Holy Spirit by adding: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” thereby signifying that the power of the whole Trinity cooperated in the creation of the world.

## CHAPTER II. Where light is first commanded to come into being

“And God said: ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” [Col. 0447D].

It is fitting that the adornment of the world should begin with light, since God himself is the true light and dwells in inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6). The angels created in the heavens of heavens had already begun to enjoy the blessed vision of that light. Appropriately, therefore, he also gave this age, as it was being adorned, the first grace of material light, so that there might be something by which the other things he created could be seen.

When God is said to have spoken—whether that light should come into being or anything else—we must not think that he did so in our manner, through the bodily sound of a voice. We must understand more profoundly that God “spoke” in order that a creature might come into being because he made all things through his Word, that is, through his only-begotten Son. The evangelist John states this more clearly:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him” (John 1).

What John says—that all things were made through the Word of God—is what Moses says when he writes: “God said, ‘Let there be light’”; “He said, ‘Let there be a firmament’”; “He said” concerning the rest of creation. The psalm likewise adds the person of the Holy Spirit: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32) [Col. 0448A].

If it is asked in what places light came into being at God’s command, while the abyss still covered the whole extent of the earth, it is plainly evident that the first light shone in the upper regions of that same earth, which divine light commonly illuminates through the sun even now.

Nor should it seem surprising to us that, by divine action, light could shine upon the waters, since it is well known that human activity often illuminates them. Sailors, when submerged in the depths of the sea, release oil from their mouths and thereby make the water clear and luminous for themselves. If a human being can accomplish such things through the oil of his mouth, how great a light must God be believed capable of creating through the breath of his mouth—especially since the waters at the beginning must be believed to have been much more rarefied than those we now see on earth, before they were gathered into one place so that the dry land might appear [Col. 0448B].

“And God saw that the light was good.”

He did not suddenly see light as something previously unknown and praise it after learning that it was good. Rather, he declared that the light—which he knew he would make worthy of praise—once made, was worthy of praise and admiration by human beings.

But because the infusion of light did not drive away all the darkness of the world—for it belongs to the heavenly age to enjoy a fixed and perpetual light—but illuminated one part of it while leaving another dark, the text rightly adds [Col. 0448C]:

“And he divided the light from the darkness.”

He divided them not only by their quality but also by the distance between their places: spreading the light through the upper part of the world, where human habitation was to be, while allowing its lower regions to remain in their ancient darkness.

“And he called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.”

The text says that he “called” them because he distinguished and ordered everything in such a way that they could both be discerned and receive names. Thus we say that a householder “built this house,” meaning that he caused it to be built; many similar expressions are found throughout the books of divine Scripture [Col. 0448D].

This is said for the sake of our understanding. For in what language did God call the light “Day” and the darkness “Night”—Hebrew, Greek, Latin, or some other language? And when it is said that he called everything else, one might ask in what language he called it. But with God there is pure understanding, without the noise and diversity of languages.

“And there was evening and there was morning, one day.”

There was evening—that is, the light gradually set after the full span of the day’s length and passed beneath the lower regions of the world, as now happens at night through the customary course of the sun. There was also morning, when that same light gradually returned above the lands and began another day. Thus one day was completed, namely, twenty-four hours [Col. 0449A].

In commending this expression, Scripture carefully instructs us to say that the light which had been created passed over the lower regions of the world in its setting. For if it did not do this, but instead gradually disappeared altogether when evening came and again gradually rose in the created world at morning, then it would not say that one complete day consisted of the morning of the following day, but rather of the evening of the first day.

For this reason it preferred to speak of evening and morning rather than of night and day, to indicate that the course then belonged to the primordial light, corresponding to what now takes place through the course of the sun by day and by night. The sole difference is that, after the creation of the stars, night too is filled with its own light, although less than that of day; during those first three days, however, it remained entirely dark and obscure [Col. 0449B].

For in every respect it was fitting that a day beginning with light should be extended to the morning of the following day, so that it might be indicated that the works of him who is the true light, and in whom there is no darkness at all, begin with light and are all completed in light.
