## CHAPTER III. The firmament made on the second day, and the division of the waters above and below the firmament

“And God said: ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.’ And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament. And it was so. And God called the firmament Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day” [Col. 0449C].

Here the creation of our heaven, in which the stars are fixed, is described. It is evidently established in the midst of the waters. We see the waters beneath it in the air and upon the earth. That waters are above it, we learn not only from the authority of this Scripture but also from the words of the prophet, who says: “Stretching out the heavens like a skin, covering its upper regions with waters” (Psalm 103).

It is therefore evident that the starry heaven was established in the midst of the waters. Nor is there anything to prevent us from believing that it was made from waters. We know how great are the solidity, transparency, and purity of crystal, which is certainly produced from the congealing of water. What, then, prevents us from believing that the same arranger of natures solidified the substance of the waters into the firmament of heaven [Col. 0449D]?

If someone is troubled by the question of how waters—whose nature is always to flow and descend toward the lower regions—can remain above heaven, since heaven appears to be round in form, let him remember what Scripture says of God: “Who binds up the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth all at once below” (Job 26). Let him understand that he who binds the waters below heaven for a time, whenever he wills, so that they do not all fall together—waters supported not by the foundation of some firmer substance but held merely by the vapors of clouds—could also suspend waters above the round sphere of heaven so that they would never fall, not with vaporous thinness but with icy solidity.

But even if he wished liquid waters to remain there, would this be a greater miracle than the fact that he “hung the mass of the earth upon nothing,” as Scripture says? (ibid.) For when the waves, whether of the Red Sea or of the Jordan River, are raised up high like walls and fixed in place for the passage of the Israelite people, do they not plainly show that waters can also remain fixed above the revolving roundness of heaven [Col. 0450A]?

Whatever those waters may be like, holy Scripture has left no one room to doubt that they are there.

What it means when God says, “Let this creature” or “that creature” come into being has already been explained. He said that it should come into being when, in his coeternal Word—namely, his only-begotten Son—he ordained all that was to be created. When, therefore, we hear, “God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters,’” we should understand that the Word of God contained the decree that it should come into being. In that Word God foresaw, before all time, whatever he made outwardly in time [Col. 0450B].

When, therefore, we hear, “And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament; and it was so,” we should understand that the creation and arrangement of heaven and the waters did not exceed the boundaries prescribed for them in the Word of God, in accordance with the psalmist’s words: “He established a command, and it shall not pass away” (Psalm 48).

The same should be understood of the creatures said to have been made during the following four days.

When we hear added, “And God saw that it was good,” we should understand that, in the goodness of his Spirit, the work did not please him as something learned to be good only after it had been made. Rather, it pleased him in that goodness in which he willed it to remain where he had willed it to come into being [Col. 0450C].

It should be noted that this addition—“And God saw that it was good”—is not found at this point in the Hebrew text. It is remarkable that, among all the things God is said to have created, this confirmation of divine vision is omitted only here, that is, in the works of the second day. Yet these works are shown, together with the others he made, to have been good in God’s sight when the text later says: “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.”

Unless perhaps, as some of the Fathers explain, Scripture wished us to understand that the number two is not good, because it divides from unity and prefigures the bonds of marriage. Hence in Noah’s ark all the animals that enter in pairs are unclean, while an odd number is shown to be clean.

Concerning the matters explained thus far—that is, the creation of the first and second days—the history of Saint Clement reports that the apostle Peter spoke as follows [Col. 0450D]:

> “In the beginning, when God had made heaven and earth as one house, the shadow produced from the bodies of the world gave darkness from itself to the things enclosed within. But when the will of God introduced light, those darknesses that had been produced from the shadow of the bodies were immediately swallowed up. Then the light was assigned to the day, and the darkness to the night.
>
> “Now the water that was within the world, in the midst of the space between that first heaven and earth, was stretched out as if congealed like frost and solidified as crystal. By such a firmament the spaces between heaven and earth were enclosed, as it were, in the middle; and the Creator called that firmament ‘heaven,’ naming it with the name of the earlier heaven.
>
> “Thus, although the whole structure of the world had been one house, he divided it into two regions. The reason for this division was that the upper region might provide a dwelling for angels, and the lower region for human beings” [Col. 0451A].

I have wished to insert these few words into our work so that the reader may recognize how closely they agree with the understanding of the Fathers.

## CHAPTER IV. Where the separation of the waters from the earth is commanded, and the earth is made to sprout on the third day

“And God said: ‘Let the waters that are beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear’” [Col. 0451B].

The waters that had filled all the space between heaven and earth are withdrawn and gathered into one place, so that the light which during the preceding two days had brightly illuminated the waters might shine more brightly in the pure air, and so that the earth which had been hidden might appear. Covered by the waters, it had remained muddy and weak; when the waters withdrew, it became dry and suitable for receiving plants.

If someone asks where the waters that had covered all parts of the earth up to heaven were gathered, he should know that the earth itself could have subsided widely and at the Creator’s command provided other regions as hollows into which the converging waters might be received. Thus the dry land could appear in those regions from which the moisture had departed, making them dry.

It may also reasonably be believed, as we mentioned above, that the primordial waters were more rarefied, like a mist covering the lands, but that they were thickened by being gathered together, so that they could be contained in the places assigned to them while the dry land appeared in the remaining regions [Col. 0451C].

Although there are many seas, the text rightly says that the waters were gathered into one place, because all these waters are joined by an unbroken and continuous stream to the great Ocean and sea. But if certain lakes appear to be enclosed within themselves, people say that these too are pierced by hidden caverns through which they send their channels toward the sea. Diggers of wells prove the same thing, since the whole earth is filled with flowing waters through invisible veins, and these draw their origin from the sea.

“And God called the dry land Earth, and the gatherings of waters he called Seas.”

Earlier, to distinguish it from the waters, he called the whole more solid part of the world “earth,” when he said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth; but the earth was formless and empty.” Now, however, as the world begins to take shape and the face of the earth appears when the waters retreat to their proper place, the portion that could be dry received the name “earth,” in distinction from the part that was still oppressed by the waters [Col. 0451D].

The Latin word *terra* is so called because it is “trodden” by the feet of living creatures. The gatherings of waters are called “seas”—*proxima sui parte* [uncertain; alternative reading: *pro maxima*, “for the greater part”]. Among the Hebrews too, all gatherings of waters—whether salty or fresh—are said to be called seas.

Appropriately, therefore, the text first said that all the waters were gathered into one place because of the continuity of all the waters on earth; now it names their gatherings in the plural and says that these are called seas in the plural, clearly because of their many inlets, which also receive different names according to the names of their regions [Col. 0452A].

“And God saw that it was good.”

The earth had not yet sprouted, nor had either the earth or the waters themselves produced living creatures, and yet God is said to have seen that it was good when the dry land appeared as the waters withdrew. The evaluator of the universe, foreseeing what was to come, praises as though already complete what was still only the beginning of the first work.

Nor is this surprising in the sight of him for whom the perfection of things lies not in the completion of the work but in the predestination of his will.

“And he said: ‘Let the earth bring forth green grass, producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.’ And it was so. And the earth brought forth green grass, producing seed according to its kind, and trees producing fruit, each having seed according to its species. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening and there was morning, the third day” [Col. 0452B].

From these words of God it is clear that the world received its complete adornment in springtime. For it is then that green grasses commonly appear upon the earth and fruit-bearing trees stand.

At the same time, it should be noted that the first shoots of the grasses and trees did not come forth from seed but from the earth. At the one command of the Creator, the earth—which had appeared dry—was suddenly adorned with grasses and clothed with flowering groves; and immediately each of these produced from itself the fruits and seeds proper to its own growth [Col. 0452C].

For it was necessary that every form of thing should first come forth perfect at the Lord’s command, just as the human being himself, for whose sake all things were made on earth, must be believed to have been formed in a perfect—that is, youthful—age.

## CHAPTER V. Where the luminaries are commanded to be made, and are made on the fourth day

“And God said: ‘Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven’” [Col. 0452D].

In a wholly fitting order, the world proceeds from formless matter toward an appropriate form. After God had created, before any day of this age, heaven, earth, and water—that is, the higher and spiritual world with its inhabitants, together with the formless matter of this entire world—in accordance with what is written, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18), he made light on the first day of this age, so that it might render the other creatures capable of visible form.

On the second day he solidified the firmament of heaven in the midst of the waters, namely, the upper part of this world. On the third day he assigned the sea and the lands in the lower regions their proper boundaries, and, as the water withdrew, spread the air through its appointed places.

It was therefore necessary that the elements should receive the progress of a more extensive adornment in the same order in which they had been created: on the fourth day heaven was to be distinguished by the luminaries; on the fifth, the air and sea were to be filled with their living creatures; on the sixth, the earth was to be filled with its living creatures.

The fact that on the third day the earth was clothed with grasses and trees does not belong to its adornment, properly speaking, but rather, so to speak, to the surface of its form.

“And God said: ‘Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, to divide the day from the night’” [Col. 0453A].

This division is explained more clearly in what follows: the sun is to illuminate the day, while the moon and stars illuminate the night.

When the stars were made, this was added to the increase of the primordial light, so that night too might become luminous—illuminated either by the splendor of the moon, by that of the stars, or by both—whereas until then it had known nothing except its ancient darkness.

For even if night often appears dark and blind to us, because the air nearest the earth is obscured by cloudy storms, those upper regions which are reckoned under the name “ether,” extending from this turbulent air up to the starry heaven, are always made bright by the radiance of the stars as they move around.

The stars that arose also brought this gift of divine generosity to the world, together with an increase of light: through them the distinction of passing times could also be recognized. Hence the text continues:

“And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years.”

Before the stars were made, there was nothing by which the order of times could be marked. There was no means of recognizing the hour of midday before

> “The fiery sun climbed to the middle of heaven;”

nor was there any means of marking the other hours of day and night, until the stars divided the celestial pole among themselves by equal allotment, by day and by night [Col. 0453B].

The luminaries are therefore for signs, seasons, days, and years—not because time began with their creation. Time plainly began at the beginning, when God made heaven and earth, and days and years are known to have originated when God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. Rather, it is because by their risings and settings the order of times, days, and years is marked [Col. 0453C].

That entire preceding three-day period had passed without any distinct progression of its course and without any measurement whatever in hours. The primordial light still filling everything in general had no fixed point of origin such as it now receives from the sun; nowhere had more intense rays yet shone, and no more distant shadow had cooled beneath a rock or tree.

Apart from the marking of time, however, the luminaries are signs necessary for the uses of this life. Sailors observe them for navigation, as do travelers in the sandy deserts of Ethiopia, where, at the slightest impulse of wind, all traces of travelers’ footsteps are immediately smoothed away once they have been made.

For this reason those traveling in such regions need the signs of the stars by night and by day no less than those who sail upon the sea. They are also signs because we sometimes foresee from their observation what sort of weather is to come [Col. 0453D].

“That they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth. And it was so.”

The luminaries always shine in the firmament of heaven, as we have said, and fill the places near them with bright light; but at appropriate times they illuminate the earth.

At times a cloudy atmosphere prevents the light of the moon, when it is small, or of the stars from appearing upon the earth. The rising sun also prevents the moon and stars from illuminating the earth with their greater light. Hence it received its Latin name, because it alone shines upon the earth during the day, dimming the stars together with the moon.

“And God made two great luminaries.”

We may understand “great luminaries” not so much by comparison with other things as by their own function, just as we speak of a great heaven or a great sea. The sun is great because it fills the globe of the earth with its heat, and the moon because of its light. Wherever they are in the heavens, they illuminate everything and are equally visible to all [Col. 0454A].

An evident proof of their greatness is that their size appears the same to all people throughout the world. For if one appeared smaller to those at a distance and shone larger to those standing nearby, that would reveal its smallness.

“The greater luminary to rule the day, and the lesser luminary to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven.”

The greater luminary is the sun, not only by virtue of the size or form of its body, whatever that may be, but also because of the magnitude of its light, since it is believed to illuminate both the lesser luminary and the stars. It is also greater in the power of its heat, because when it rises it warms the world, whereas during the days before its creation there had been no heat at all [Col. 0454B].

As for the fact that the moon is seen to be equal in size to the sun, they say this happens because the sun travels much farther from the earth and at a greater height than the moon. Consequently, its actual size cannot at all be discerned by us who live on earth. For things placed farther away generally appear smaller.

“And the lesser luminary,” he says, “to rule the night; and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven.”

Although it sometimes happens that the moon is seen by day throughout the month, and occasionally even that the stars appear larger by day, it is nevertheless entirely certain that they bring some consolation of light not to the day but only to the night [Col. 0454C].

“To shine upon the earth and to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness.”

These words can be understood both of the great luminaries and of the stars, with this distinction: “to rule the day” applies especially to the sun, while “and the night” refers to the moon and stars.

The statement that follows—“and to divide the light from the darkness”—applies equally to all the heavenly bodies. Wherever they travel, they carry light with them; wherever they are absent, they leave everything dark.

If someone asks what the daylight could have been like before the creation of the stars, it is not unreasonable to believe that it was like what we see every day as morning approaches, when the sun is about to rise but has not yet appeared above the earth. At that time the day is bright with the dim rays of the stars, but the risen sun does not yet shine forth [Col. 0454D].

Therefore at that time there could have been no distinction of seasons except between day and night, and rightly, once the stars had been made, it was said: “Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years.”

The changes of the seasons began to be distinguished when, on the fourth day of the world’s birth, the sun emerged from the middle of the East and consecrated the spring equinox by its rising. Advancing daily toward the high summits of heaven, and then gradually descending from the solstitial height toward the lowest regions, it soon returned from the lowest and wintry places to the equinoctial circles. Through four clearly distinguished seasons and appointed days, it completed the span of the year.

The full moon appearing in the evening also established, by its first rising, the times that were to be observed for the celebration of Passover [Col. 0455A]. This is the very time that not only that ancient people of God but also we observe today as the beginning of the celebration of Passover: after the day of the equinox has passed, when the full moon—that is, the fourteenth moon—has appeared in the face of heaven in the evening.

Soon afterward, when the Lord’s day arrives, the appropriate time for celebrating the Lord’s resurrection will be at hand, and the prophet’s words will also be fulfilled literally: “He made the moon for seasons; the sun knows its setting” (Psalm 103).

The stars too, apart from what we have mentioned above—that by their appearance they indicate what the coming condition of the air will be, and by their course they show which watch of the night it is—are for signs and seasons. Some, coming into the sky, mark the summer seasons; others mark the winter.

They are also for days: some accompany the sun in the spring days, others in the autumn. They are also for years: those, for example, that now rise in the morning at the spring equinox come into the face of heaven every year at that same equinox; those that now rise in the evening or morning at the solstice always rise at the same hours at that time [Col. 0455B].

There are also certain stars which astronomers call planets, that is, “wanderers.” Through their revolutions they make longer years, returning to the same place in the heavens. The star called Saturn is said to complete its circuit of heaven and return to the same places among the stars once every thirty years; Jupiter, once every twelve years; Mars, once every two solar years.

The moon too makes a common year when it has completed twelve periods of its course—that is, 354 days. In order that its cycle might agree with the solar year, the reckoners added a thirteenth month every second or third year. They call it an embolismic year, and the year then consists of 384 days [Col. 0455C].

“And God saw that it was good.”

Holy Scripture necessarily repeats many times that God saw the things he made to be good, so that the piety of the faithful might thereby be instructed not to judge visible and invisible creation according to human understanding—which is often offended even by good things whose causes and order it does not know—but to believe and yield to God as he praises his work.

The more reverently someone believes God before understanding, the more easily he comes to know something by advancing in understanding.

God therefore saw that the things he had made were good because the things he had chosen to be made pleased him as they came into being, and, once made, pleased him as they remained—each thing according to the measure of existence or continuance that so great a maker had ordained for it.

And there was evening and morning, the fourth day. This was that memorable evening on which the people of God in Egypt offered the lamb in celebration of the Passover; and this was the morning which they saw first after the yoke of long servitude had been shaken off, when they had begun the journey of freedom. For it is written, the Lord saying to Moses:

“This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. On the tenth day of this month, each man shall take a lamb for his family and household, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening,” and so forth (Exod. XII).

On that evening, moreover, in order to complete the sacramental observances of the legal Passover, our Lord, after eating the lamb, symbolically initiated the mysteries of his body and blood, which were to be celebrated for us. When that morning dawned, he redeemed us by his blood, like an immaculate Lamb, and freed us from slavery to demonic domination. This day, occurring under the fullest moon, came forth in the creation of the world as the fourth day. But at the time of the Lord’s Passion, by the higher grace of the sacrament, it fell on the fifth day of the week, so that the Lord, crucified on the sixth day, might rest in the tomb on the Sabbath itself, consecrate the first day of the week by his resurrection, and grant us also faith and hope that, on the day on which light was made, we might rise from the dead and enter everlasting light.

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 0456B] Where the animals are commanded to be brought forth from the waters on the fifth day, and the animals themselves are blessed

God also said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature possessing a living soul, and the flying creature above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.”

After the face of heaven had been adorned with the luminaries on the fourth day, the lower regions of the world—namely, water and air—were consequently adorned on the fifth with those things that are moved by the breath of life. These elements too are joined to one another and to heaven by a certain kinship, as it were. They are joined to one another because the nature of water is close to the quality of air. Hence it is proved that the air grows rich through their exhalations, so that it both gathers clouds and can support the flight of birds, as Scripture testifies: “Suddenly the air will be compressed into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away” (Job XXXVII). Indeed, even on clear nights it produces dew, whose drops are found in the grass in the morning. [Col. 0456C]

Air is joined to heaven in this way because it is so near to it that it sometimes even receives its name, as when Scripture calls them “birds of heaven” which plainly fly in the air. The Lord himself speaks to the crowds who had not recognized the time of his coming from the manifestation of his mighty works, saying: “When you see a cloud rising from the west, you immediately say, ‘A storm is coming.’ And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be heat.’ And so it happens. Hypocrites, you know how to discern the appearance of heaven and earth; how is it that you do not discern this time?” (Luke XII). Here it is clear that by “the appearance of heaven” he means no other than the changing condition of the air.

God therefore said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature possessing a living soul, and the flying creature above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.” [Col. 0456D] And lest someone suppose that, because there are aquatic animals that move not by crawling but by swimming or walking on feet, or that among the flying creatures there are some that have wings yet are entirely incapable of flight, some class of flying or aquatic animals had been omitted from the Lord’s words, the text carefully adds:

“And God created the great sea creatures, and every living and moving soul, which the waters were to bring forth according to their kinds, and every flying creature according to its kind.”

No kind, therefore, was excluded, since together with the great sea creatures every living soul was created—those which the waters had brought forth in their various kinds, namely, creeping things, swimming things, and flying things; [Col. 0457A] and also those which, being suited to no mode of locomotion, cling fixedly to rocks, such as the many kinds of shellfish. As for what is said, “And the flying creature above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven,” nothing contrary to the truth of reason is implied. For although an immense expanse intervenes, birds nevertheless fly beneath the starry heaven, and they fly above the earth, just as we human beings, placed on earth, are truly and rightly said to be established beneath heaven and beneath the sun. Scripture bears witness when it says: “There were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven” (Acts II); and: “What more does a man have from all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. I).

According to another translation, some are troubled by the wording: “And the flying creatures according to the firmament,” that is, “near the firmament of heaven.” But [Col. 0457B] it should be understood that the birds are said to fly according to the firmament of heaven because the term also indicates the ether—that is, that upper region of air which extends from this turbulent and dark place in which the birds fly all the way to the stars, and which is reasonably believed to be wholly calm and full of light. For Scripture also says that the seven wandering stars, which are said to be borne along in this region of the ether, were placed in the firmament of heaven. Therefore birds are rightly said to fly beside the firmament of heaven, because these turbulent regions of air that support the flight of birds are, as I have said, near the ether. Nor is it surprising that the ether is called the firmament of heaven, since the air is called heaven, as we explained above.

Nor should it be passed over that, when God was said to have created every living soul, the phrase “and moving” was added, evidently to distinguish it from man, whom he was going to make in his own image and likeness, so that, if he kept God’s commandments, he might live in perpetual unchangeableness and blessedness. For the other animals were made at their first creation in such a way that either some would serve as food for others, or, wasting away through old age, they would perish.

And God saw that it was good; and he blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea. And let the birds multiply upon the earth.” And there was evening and morning, the fifth day.

When he said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea,” this pertains to both classes of animals made from the waters, namely, fish and birds. For just as all fish can live only in the waters, so there are many birds which, although they sometimes rest on land and propagate their offspring there, nevertheless feed not from the earth but from the sea, and use marine haunts more willingly than terrestrial ones. But what he adds—“And let the birds multiply upon the earth”—refers to both classes of birds: those that feed from the waters and those that feed from the land. For even those birds that cannot live without water, and that often remain beneath the depths of the waters for much of the year like fish, are accustomed to come out onto the land, especially when they are laying eggs and nourishing their young.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 0458A] Where the animals are commanded to be brought forth from the earth on the sixth day, and the Lord commands that man be made, who, immediately after being made, is blessed by the Lord himself

God also said: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds.” And it was so.

After heaven had been illuminated by the stars, after the air had been filled with flying creatures—air which, because of its proximity, as we have said, deserved the name of heaven—and after the waters had been enriched with their own animals, waters which are themselves joined to the air by a great kinship of nature, since from them he took both animals and rains, snows, hail, and other things of this sort—it followed that the earth too should be filled with its own animals, namely, those generated from it. For the earth itself has a special kinship with the waters, since without their moisture and irrigation it can not only fail to bear fruit but cannot even remain firm, as Peter testifies when he says: “The heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water, established by the word of God” (2 Pet. III).

God therefore commands the earth to bring forth cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth, because the name “beasts” plainly includes everything that rages with its mouth or claws, except serpents. Under the name “creeping things of the earth,” serpents too are included. Under the name “cattle,” the animals that serve human use are designated. Where, then, is the creation of the other four-footed creatures described—for example, deer, roe-deer, buffaloes, boars, and the rest of their kind? Perhaps we may say that, because of the savagery of their untamed disposition, they were counted among the beasts, according to the ancient translation, in which it is written: “Let the earth bring forth every living soul according to its kind, four-footed creatures, creeping things, and beasts of the earth.” There is no question at all that under the name “four-footed creatures” everything is included that the earth brought forth, apart from beasts and creeping things, whether animals under human care or those that are wild and untamed.

And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and cattle and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind.

The change in the wording should be noted. Above it was said that God commanded the earth to bring forth cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth; now, with the order changed, God is said to have made the beasts of the earth, and cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth. It should be understood that he made everything he wished more quickly than words could say, and that it makes no difference which creatures human speech names first in its ordering, since divine power created them all together.

When the text continues:

“And God saw that it was good,” it is reasonably asked why here too there is not added what was said concerning the animals produced by the waters: “And he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth.” Or perhaps, what God commended when he spoke of the first living creature, he left us to understand also concerning the second? This is especially possible because he was going to add several other things to the works of this day. But concerning man, once made, he carefully repeated this, saying: “And God blessed them, and said: Increase and [Col. 0459A] multiply, and fill the earth,” lest anyone should think that sin belonged to honorable marriage, or that the marriage bed could be compared with defilement and fornication.

Once the earthly dwelling had been made and adorned, it remained that the one for whose sake all things had been prepared—the inhabitant and lord of creation—should himself be created. The text continues and says:

“Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Now it becomes clearer why it was said of the herbs and trees created, of the fish and birds, and also of the terrestrial animals, that each should be made according to its kind and species. But in the future creation of man, who was to correspond not only to his own kind and species but also to be made in the image and likeness of his Creator, this testimony is given because of the nobility of his creation: God did not say, as with the other creatures, “Let man be made,” and man was made; nor, “Let the earth bring forth man,” and the earth brought forth man. Rather, before he was made, the words “Let us make” are used, so that, because a rational creature was being created, he might appear to have been made as if with deliberation, formed from the earth as if through purposeful design, and raised up by the Creator’s breathing through the power of the life-giving spirit. Thus he was to exist not merely through the voice of command but through the dignity of the work, since he was made in the image of the Creator.

When it says, “Let us make him in our image and likeness,” the unity of the holy Trinity is openly commended. Indeed, the same undivided Trinity had already been mystically intimated in the preceding formation of things, when it was said: “And God said, ‘Let there be …’ And God made … And God saw that it was good.” [Col. 0459C] But now this same truth is intimated more clearly when it says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And rightly so: until the one who was to be taught existed, the preaching of the Godhead lay hidden in the depths. But when the creation of man began to be anticipated, faith was revealed and the doctrine of truth shone forth distinctly.

In the words “Let us make,” the work of the three persons is shown to be one. In the words that follow, “in our image and likeness,” the one and equal substance of the same holy Trinity is indicated. For how could there be one image and likeness if the Son were less than the Father, or the Holy Spirit less than the Son, or if the glory of the whole Trinity were not consubstantial and of the same power? Or how could the words “Let us make” be spoken if there were not a cooperating power of three persons in one Godhead?

For God could not have said to the angels, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” since no reason whatsoever permits us to believe that the image or likeness of God and of the angels is one and the same.

The Apostle testifies in what respect man was made in the image and likeness of God, when he diligently admonishes us to recover in ourselves, through the grace of the same Creator, what we lost in our first parent. “Be renewed,” he says, “in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Eph. IV).

Adam, therefore, the new man, was created from the earth according to God, so that he might be righteous, holy, and true, humbly subject to and clinging to the grace of his Creator, who exists eternally and perfectly righteous, holy, and true. Because Adam corrupted by sin this most beautiful newness of the divine image in himself and generated from himself a corrupted offspring of the human race, the second Adam came—that is, the Lord himself and our Creator, born of a Virgin—created incorruptibly and unchangeably in the image of God, that is, free from every sin and full of every grace and truth, so that by his example and gifts he might restore his image and likeness in us.

He is truly the new man created according to God, since he took from Adam the true substance of flesh, yet drew from him none of the stain of vice. To follow his example according to our capacity, to cling to his gifts, and to obey his commandments [Col. 0460B]—this is to recover in the new man the image of God that we lost in the old man.

[Let us therefore reform in ourselves, in the new man and according to our capacity, the image of God which we lost in the old man—that is, insofar as we are able, let us follow his example, cling to his gifts, and obey his commandments, and so forth.]

Man was therefore created in the image of God not according to the body but according to the understanding of the mind, although even in the body he possesses a certain characteristic that indicates this: he was made standing upright, so that by this very fact he might be admonished not to pursue earthly things, as cattle do, whose every pleasure comes from the earth. Hence all creatures are naturally prone and prostrate upon their bellies, according to what one of the poets said with great beauty and truth (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I):

> While all the other animals gaze downward toward the earth,  
> He gave to man an elevated face, and commanded him to look upon heaven  
> And raise his upright countenance toward the stars.

His body therefore corresponds to his rational soul, not in the lines and shapes of its limbs, but rather in the fact that it is raised toward heaven, to put on the things that are above in the body of the world, just as the rational soul ought to be raised toward those things that excel most in spiritual nature, so that it may think on the things above, not on those upon the earth (Col. III).

Well is it added:

“And let him rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and the beasts of the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.”

For man was made in the image of God especially in this respect: he surpasses irrational animals because he was created capable of reason, through which he could rightly govern all created things in the world and enjoy knowledge of the one who created everything. If, placed in this honor, he does not understand how to act well, he will be compared with those same senseless animals over which he was set, as the Psalmist also testifies:

“And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him.”

What he had said earlier, “in his own image,” he repeated for confirmation by adding, “in the image of God he created him,” so that he might more carefully impress upon us what kind of beings we were made by God and fix more firmly in our minds the form of the image of God that we are to receive [“inculcate”]. Thus we who walk in the image of God should not be troubled in vain by storing up treasures in the uncertainty of riches, but should rather await the Lord, thirsting for the time when we shall come and appear before his face, certain that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

What is now said, “In the image of God he created him,” whereas above we read, “Let us make him in our image,” signifies that this plurality of persons does not mean that we are to believe in several gods. Rather, because of the Trinity it was said, “in our image”; and because of the unity, “in the image of God”—so that we may acknowledge one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“Male and female he created them.”

In what follows, God’s making of the first-formed man and woman, and how he made them, will be explained more fully. But for the sake of brevity they are now mentioned as having been created, so that the work of the sixth day and the dedication of the seventh may be explained along with the rest; then, with the passage of time allowing greater freedom, this and other matters worthy of narration, which had been omitted, may be discussed.

God created one male and one female at the beginning—not like the other animals, which he created not singly but in greater numbers within each kind—so that by this means he might bind the human race to one another by a closer bond of love, since it would remember that the whole race had arisen from one parent.

For this reason, when holy Scripture had said, “And God created man in his own image; in the likeness of God he created him,” and immediately added, “Male and female he created them,” it did not wish to add, “He created them in the image of God.” The woman too was created in the image of God, insofar as she also possessed a rational mind; but Scripture did not think it necessary to add this concerning her, since, for the sake of the unity of their union, it left the point to be understood in her—and indeed indicated that it should be understood concerning the whole human race born from them. Every human being, insofar as he makes use of reason, still possesses the image of God in himself.

Hence John says: “He was the true light which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John I). This is the light of which the Psalmist glorifies the Lord, saying: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV).

It is fitting that here the creation of male and female is mentioned, even though the manner of that creation has not yet been related, so that there may be an appropriate place for the account of the divine blessing. Concerning this the text continues:

“And he blessed them, and said: Increase and multiply, [Col. 0461D] and fill the earth and subdue it.”

This multiplication of human beings and filling of the earth could be accomplished only through the union of male and female. If the human race grows and multiplies by the blessing of God, how great a curse do those deserve who forbid marriage and condemn the arrangement of the heavenly decree as though it had been devised by the devil?

Marriage, therefore, is not to be condemned—the marriage which the grace from above instituted for the propagation of the human race and the filling of the earth. Rather, virginity is to be honored and deserves the greater blessing: after the earth has been filled with human beings, virginity desires, in purity of mind and body alike, to follow the Lamb wherever he goes—that is, the Lord Jesus in the heavenly places—and to sing the new song which no one else can sing to him.

For our God and Lord, who at the beginning of the world formed woman from the side of man, thereby teaching that the earth was to be filled through their mutual union, himself, at the end of the age, took a man from the flesh of a Virgin, free from every defilement and perfect in the fullness of divinity, in order to show that he loved the glory of virginity more than marriage.

“And rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and all the animals upon the earth.”

It is reasonably asked what benefit man received from ruling over the fish, birds, and all the animals of the earth, or for what uses and consolations these creatures were made for man, if he had never sinned, since—as the following words of Scripture make clear—in the first creation he was granted for food not these creatures but only the fruits of herbs [Col. 0462B] and trees.

Perhaps it should be said that God knew man would sin and, through sin, become mortal, although he himself had created him immortal. Therefore, from the beginning he established for man those consolations by which a mortal being could protect his frailty: food from these creatures, perhaps, or clothing, or assistance in labor and travel.

Nor is it an unworthy question why man does not even now rule over all the animals. After he himself refused to be subject to his Creator, he lost dominion over those creatures which his Creator had subjected to his authority. Indeed, as a testimony to the first creation, we read that birds have offered their service to holy men humbly serving God, that the jaws of beasts have been restrained, and that the venom of serpents has been unable to cause harm.

## CHAPTER VIII. Where Adam received authority over food

God said: “Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees that contain within themselves the seed of their own kind, so that they may be food for you, and for all the animals of the earth, and every bird, and everything that moves upon the earth and possesses a living soul, for food.”

Here it is already clear that before man’s guilt the earth produced nothing harmful: no poisonous herb and no barren tree, since it is expressly said that every herb and all trees were given as food to human beings, birds, and all the animals of the earth. It is clear also that the birds did not live by seizing weaker birds, that the wolf did not prowl around the sheepfolds seeking an ambush, and that dust was not the serpent’s bread; rather, all creatures fed harmoniously on green herbs and the fruits of trees.

A question naturally arises among these matters that should not be passed over: how was man made immortal above the other animals, while nevertheless receiving with them the common nourishment of the earth? We should understand here that there is one kind of immortality of the flesh, which we received in Adam at the first creation, and another which we hope to receive in the resurrection through Christ.

Adam was made immortal in such a way that he could avoid death if he did not sin, but if he sinned, he would die. The children of the resurrection, however, will be immortal when they are equal to the angels of God, so that they can neither die nor sin thereafter. [Col. 0463A] Therefore our flesh after the resurrection will need no nourishment from food, since it will suffer no weakness from hunger, weariness, or any other infirmity.

Adam’s flesh before sin was created immortal in such a way that, supported by the means of temporal nourishment, it might remain free from death and pain until, through bodily growth, he reached the age appointed by the Creator. Then, after a numerous offspring of this kind had been created, he would, by the Creator’s command, also take from the tree of life, through which he would become perfectly immortal and no longer require the supports of bodily food.

Thus the flesh of the first human beings was created both immortal and incorruptible, so that by observing God’s commandments they might preserve this same immortality and incorruptibility. Among those commandments was that they should eat from the trees of paradise that had been granted to them and refrain from eating from the tree that had been forbidden. Through these foods they were to preserve the gifts of immortality implanted in them, lest by touching the forbidden tree they should encounter the ruin of death.

In the end, our flesh will likewise be incorruptible and immortal, in likeness to the angelic exaltation, so that it will remain in the same state and have no need of bodily food, since in spiritual life there will be no one who can experience need. When angels are said to have eaten with the patriarchs, they did so not from necessity but from kindness, so that by acting in this way they might more graciously accommodate themselves to the human beings to whom they appeared. The Lord too ate with his disciples after the resurrection, not from the necessity of nourishment but to show that he had truly received flesh after death.

[Col. 0463C] “And it was so”—that is, so that man might rule over all things created on the earth and in the waters, and receive, together with the birds of heaven and the animals of the earth, the ability and authority to eat the fruits of the earth.

And God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good.

Since it had been said individually of each of God’s works that he saw it to be good, it was rightly stated in conclusion, when everything had been completed, with the addition that he saw everything he had made, and it was very good. But it is reasonably asked why, concerning the man who had been made, the individual statement “And God saw that it was good” was not also added, but his making was rather reserved for universal praise among the rest. Was it because God, who knew that man would sin and would not remain in the perfection of his image, wished to say that he was good not individually but together with the others, as if hinting at what would happen? [Col. 0463D]

Man, therefore, before sin, was good in his own kind; but Scripture omitted saying this so that it might instead say something that would foretell a future event. For God is the best Creator of natures but the most just arranger of sinners, so that even if some things, considered individually, become deformed through wrongdoing, the universe as a whole may nevertheless always remain beautiful.

And there was evening and morning, the sixth day.

## CHAPTER II

Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment. The number six is evidently perfect, because it is completed by its own parts: the sixth, namely one; the third, which is two; and the half, which is three. For one, two, and three make six. This is a property that you will find nowhere among the numbers counted by units except here, nor among the numbers counted by tens except in the number twenty-eight. Thus in six days God completed all the adornment of heaven and earth, so that, because he established everything by measure, number, and weight, he might also teach through the number in which he worked that his works are perfect.

## CHAPTER IX. The completion of the world on the seventh day

And God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made.

In another translation it is said: “For God completed on the sixth day the works that he had made.” This raises no difficulty at all, since a clear account shows what things were made on it. But it is reasonably asked how our edition, which descends from the source of the Hebrew truth, can say that God completed his work on the seventh day, when no new creation is mentioned on that day. Perhaps we should say that he made the seventh day itself at that time and completed his work in making it, since by that act he completed the measure and number of the days, through whose cycle all subsequent ages would continue until the end. For in the revolution of time, the eighth day is reckoned as the same as the first.

God therefore completed on the seventh day the work that he had made because on it he brought to an end the total number of the days he had made, adding that seventh day, which he wished to be and to be called the Sabbath, since he endowed it with a mystical blessing and sanctification surpassing the others, as what follows teaches.

Hence the day of judgment and the consummation of the age, because it is to come after the seventh day, is called the eighth in Scripture, as though only seven days had preceded it. For it is said in the title of a psalm: “For the end; with hymns, a psalm of David, for the eighth.” The whole text of the following psalm shows that this was written concerning the day of judgment, in which the Prophet, fearing the anger of the coming Judge, cries out: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and so forth (Ps. VI).

The day of the Lord’s resurrection, too, although it was to come after so many thousands of days, was nevertheless called the eighth in the title of another psalm, because it followed the seventh and became the first day of the following week—that is, the very day on which in the beginning God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made. The psalm itself proves that it was written about the Lord’s resurrection, for the one who speaks in it says: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Ps. XI). [Col. 0464D]

It may also rightly be understood that God completed on the seventh day the work he had made in that he blessed and sanctified that day itself. For blessing and sanctification are not no work at all; nor should Solomon be said to have done no work when he dedicated the temple he had made. Indeed, it is an extraordinary work of God when he glorifies eternally through blessing and sanctification the things he has made.

Finally, concerning this work that he performs in the eternal Sabbath day, he himself says in the parable of the faithful servants: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them” (Luke XII). The one who girds himself, who prepares a place at table, who passes by, and who ministers is certainly working. Yet through all these words nothing else is intimated than that the Lord eternally blesses and sanctifies his saints—that is, after the good works which he has granted, he rewards them with the vision of his glory.

And on the seventh day he rested from all his work that he had done.

God did not rest, as though tired from excessive labor, in the manner of human weakness, once the structure of the world had been completed. Rather, he is said to have rested from all his work because he ceased to establish any new creation. Scripture often uses the word “rest” to indicate the cessation of an action or speech. Thus, concerning the living creatures in the Apocalypse, it says: “And they had no rest day or night, saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty’” (Rev. IV), meaning: “They did not cease always to sing this.” For the greatest and only rest of the saints in heaven is to proclaim with unwearied voice the praise of the supreme Trinity, who is God.

It may, however, be understood more profoundly that God rested from all his works in the sense that he did not need those works as something in which to rest, since his rest in himself, without beginning or end, is always true. Rather, he made the works for the sake of his goodness alone, so that they might rest in him. This is more easily understood by remembering that human need compels us above all to devote ourselves to daily labors so that we may find rest in our works, as the Lord said to man: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Gen. III).

God, however, who before the creation of the world eternally possessed perfect rest in himself, after creating the world likewise rested not in the works he had made but from all the works he had made, since he had no need to rest in his creatures. Rather, while he himself always rests perfectly in himself, he grants rest to rational creatures, blessed by that good which he himself is to himself.

And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it—that blessing and sanctification, namely, which he later more fully made known to his people in the Law, saying: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work” (Exod. 20). And shortly afterward: “For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all that is in them, and he rested on the seventh day; therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (ibid.).

[Col. 0465D]

This blessing and sanctification of the seventh day was undoubtedly made as a type of a greater blessing and sanctification. For just as, through the frequent—indeed daily—sacrifices prescribed in the Law, the blood of the Lord’s Passion, which was to be poured out once for the salvation of the world, was signified, so also, through the rest of the seventh day, which was always accustomed to be celebrated after the works of the six days, that great Sabbath day was prefigured on which the Lord was once to rest in the tomb, when all his works had been completed and perfected on the sixth day—works by which he was restoring the world, which he had completed on the sixth day and which had already been lost.

[Col. 0466A]

On that day also, as though recalling the ancient work, he openly declared that he had now completed the salvation of the world. For when he had received vinegar, he said: “It is finished.” And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (Matt. 27). This sanctification and blessing of the seventh day, and the rest on that day after his very good works, also signified that each of us, after the good works which he himself works in us, both to will and to accomplish, is moving toward the rest of heavenly life, in which we may enjoy his eternal sanctification and blessing.

(Greg.) Hence it is rightly not written that this seventh day had an evening, since it clearly signifies our perpetual rest in it. Finally, the number seven is understood as the summit of perfection. To say nothing of the arguments drawn from human reason concerning the number seven—which assert that it is perfect for this reason, that it arises from the first number that can be divided and the first number that cannot be divided—

[Col. 0466B]

—we know with complete certainty that Holy Scripture customarily uses the number seven to signify perfection. Thus it also asserts that on the seventh day the Lord rested from his works. Hence, too, the seventh day was given to human beings for rest, that is, as the Sabbath. Hence the jubilee year, in which complete rest is expressed, is completed in seven weeks and fulfilled by the addition of one unit of our union. Hence also twelve apostles were chosen to be filled with the perfection of the sevenfold grace.

For from the number three one rises to the number twelve. The number three, multiplied by its component parts, tends toward twelve. Whether four are multiplied by three or three by four,

[Col. 0466C]

three is turned into twelve. Therefore the holy apostles, who were sent to preach the Trinity in the four parts of the world, were chosen as twelve, so that by their number also they might display the perfection which they were to proclaim by life and voice.

“And he blessed,” it says, “the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which he had created”—that is, once the adornment of the world had been completed, he ceased from establishing any further new kinds of things. Nor should what he himself says be judged contrary to this statement: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5).

[Col. 0466D]

He was responding, plainly, to those who complained that, because of the rest of God commended from ancient times by the authority of this Scripture, the Sabbath was not being observed by him. For on the seventh day he had ceased from creating the kinds of creatures, since thereafter he did not create any new kinds. From then until now, however, he has continued to work in governing those same kinds which were then established—not so that on the seventh day his power ceased even for a moment from governing heaven and earth and all the things which he had made; otherwise they would immediately fall apart.

## CHAPTER 10. Allegorical Exposition of the Work of the Six Days

Up to this point, it is sufficient to have spoken of the beginning of the newly arising world according to the literal sense.

(Isidor.) According to the allegorical sense, however, it may be understood in this way: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” The Beginning is Christ,

[Col. 0467A]

as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who am also speaking to you” (John 8). In this Beginning, therefore, God made heaven—that is, spiritual people who meditate upon and seek heavenly things. In him he also made carnal people, who have not yet laid aside the earthly human being.

“Now the earth was formless and empty.” The earth of our flesh was formless and empty before it received the form of teaching. “And darkness was over the face of the abyss,” because the blindness of sins and the profound darkness of ignorance covered our hearts. But the Spirit of God was already moving over our dark and unstable heart as over the waters; in him we might subsist and rest, by his breath we might be quickened, and by his [uncertain printed reading: *uno*] we might be washed.

And God said: “Let there be light”—that is, let the illumination of faith appear. On the first day he gave the light of faith, because faith is first in conversion.

[Col. 0467B]

Hence the first commandment itself is: “The Lord your God is one God.” On account of this faith the Lord himself also willed to appear visibly in the world.

Already then, according to the grace of his presence, God divided the righteous—that is, the children of God and of light—from sinners as from darkness, calling the former “day” and the latter “night.” For those who are called righteous by the name of light—hear the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Then, on the second day, God established the firmament—that is, the solidity of the holy Scriptures. In the Church, the firmament is understood as the divine Scriptures, because “heaven will be folded up like a book.” And he divided the waters above this firmament—that is, the heavenly peoples of the angels,

[Col. 0467C]

because they do not need to receive this firmament in order that, by reading the Law, they may hear the word of God. They always see and love him. But he placed the firmament of his Law above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that, by receiving it, they might learn how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the waters above and the waters below.

After this, on the third day, he gathered together the lower, false waters—that is, unbelieving people, who are shaken by the storm of desires and the waves of carnal temptations and in themselves are enclosed, as it were, in bitterness. He separated dry land from them: namely, the people thirsting for the fountain of faith. Then he fixed the boundaries of the proud and restrained them, lest with the turbulent waves of their iniquities they disturb the dry land—that is, the soul thirsting for God—

[Col. 0467D]

and lest they prevent it from producing the fruits of good works according to its kind. It loves its neighbor by providing assistance in bodily necessities; it has within itself seed according to likeness, so that from its own weakness it may suffer with others in order to help those in need. It also produces a tree strong in its timber and fruitful—that is, a benefaction for rescuing one who suffers injustice from the hand of the powerful, and for providing the shelter of protection with the strong support of righteous judgment.

Then, on the fourth day, the luminaries fixed in the firmament of the Law appeared: the evangelists and teachers, joined to the Holy Scriptures by their exposition and displaying the light of wisdom to all those below.

[Col. 0468A]

At the same time there also appeared the remaining multitude of shining stars—that is, the variety and multitude of virtues in the Church—which, shining amid the obscurity of this life as in the night, divide in this firmament of Scripture sensible things from intelligible things, as between the light of the perfect and the darkness of the little ones. They also exist as signs of virtues and miracles.

They are also for seasons and years, because preachers live and pass away at their appointed times; but “the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40). Why did the earth first put forth vegetation and only afterward were the luminaries made, unless because illumination by the light comes after good works, for contemplating the beauty of heavenly virtue?

Among these things, on the fifth day, creeping things with living souls were made: namely, human beings renewed to life through the sacrament of baptism. Birds were also made—that is, holy souls flying toward heavenly things.

After this, on the sixth day, the earth produces a living soul,

[Col. 0468B]

when our flesh, abstaining from dead works, brings forth living shoots of virtue according to its kind—that is, living by imitating the saints, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me” (Phil. 3). We live according to our kind when, in good works, we imitate holy men as our neighbors.

Then the earth produces beasts: people powerful in worldly affairs, or people characterized by the ferocity of pride. Likewise, it produces cattle: the faithful who live in the simplicity of life. It produces also harmless serpents—that is, holy men who, by the liveliness of their cunning, distinguish good from evil and, insofar as is lawful, investigate earthly things by creeping through them, so that they may understand eternal things. These are not the venomous serpents who place themselves amid the earthly desires of this world.

After this God made human beings in his image:

[Col. 0468C]

namely, the perfect man, who practices righteousness not by imitating merely one or another of the holy men, but by contemplatively gazing upon the truth itself, so that he may understand and follow that in whose image he was made according to truth.

This man also receives authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the cattle, the wild beasts, and the creeping things, because everyone who has become spiritual and has been made like God “judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2).

What follows—“Male and female he made them”—shows the spiritual and the obedient in the Church. For just as the woman is subject to the man, so the less perfect person obeys the spiritual and perfect man, as the Apostle says:

[Col. 0468D]

“We ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who labor among you and preside over you in the Lord” (1 Thess. 4).

They are told: “Increase and multiply,” whether in languages or in degrees of spiritual understanding, so that by the understanding of reason they may rule over all carnal disturbances, as over irrational animals.

Every seed-bearing plant and every fruit-bearing tree, which was given to human beings for food, signifies the faithful who share their offerings with the needs of the saints. Hence the Apostle says: “If the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (1 Cor. 9). These are the fruitful trees.

In these stages, as in certain days, evening is the completion of each individual work, and morning is the beginning of the works that follow.

[Col. 0469A]

After these works of the six days, therefore—works that are very good—a person established in the spiritual paradise hopes for rest of mind. By this paradise the blessed life is signified, where there is a fountain of wisdom divided into the four parts of the virtues, where the grace of the tree of life is enjoyed [the reading *edati* is uncertain, as printed], and where useful disciplines of conduct are gathered like fruit from trees.

Paradise is the life of the blessed. The four rivers are the four virtues. Its trees are all useful disciplines; the fruits of the trees are the conduct of the godly. The tree of life is wisdom itself, the mother of all good things, concerning which Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and whoever holds her fast is blessed” (Prov. 3). The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the transgression of the commandment through experience.

Up to this point, the work of the six days has been explained as it is spiritually understood in the Church.

[Col. 0469B]

Next it must be set forth what it signifies figuratively concerning the ages of the world.

God completed all his works in six days and rested on the seventh. The six ages of the human race in this world, through the succession of times, signify the works of God. The first extends from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the transmigration to Babylon; the fifth thereafter up to the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now unfolding, until the world comes to an end, when the Most High comes to judgment. The seventh is understood as the rest of the saints, which has no evening, because no end will ever close it.

Let us proceed briefly through all these ages of the world and, retracing the order of the times, distinguish their mystical differences.

[Col. 0469C]

In the first age, the human being was made like light in paradise. In that age God divided the children of God, under the name of light, from the children of human beings, as from darkness. The evening of this day was the Flood.

The second age was made like a firmament between water and water: namely, that ark which floated between the rain and the seas. Its evening was the confusion of languages.

The third age was made when, through Abraham, he separated his people from the nations, distinguishing them like dry land from the waters, so that it might bring forth the shoot of herbs and trees—that is, the saints and the fruit of the Holy Scriptures. Its evening was the sin and wickedness of the most evil king Saul.

Then the fourth age began with David, when God established the luminaries in the firmament of heaven:

[Col. 0469D]

that is, the splendor of the kingdom like the excellence of the sun; and, in the form of the moon, the obedient one, like the Synagogue; and its princes as the stars. The evening of this age occurred in the sins of the kings, on account of which that people deserved to be carried captive to Babylon.

In the fifth age, that is, in the transmigration to Babylon, animals were made, as it were, in the waters, and birds of heaven, because at that time the Jews began to live among the nations as in the sea; nor did they have a fixed place, like flying birds. The evening of this day, as it were, was the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, when they were so blinded that they could not even recognize the Lord Jesus.

The sixth age begins with the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0470A]

For just as on that sixth day the first man, Adam, was formed from the clay of the earth in the image of God, so in this sixth age of the world the second Adam, that is, Christ, was born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary: the former a living soul, the latter a life-giving spirit.

And just as on that day a living soul was made, so in this age the desire for eternal life arises. And just as on that sixth day the earth produced the kinds of serpents and wild beasts, so in this sixth age of the world the Church brought forth nations desiring eternal life.

(Aug.) The same meaning was revealed by the vessel shown to Peter (Acts 10). And just as on that day male and female were created, so in this age of the world Christ and the Church are manifested.

And just as on that day the human being was placed over cattle, serpents, and the birds of heaven, so Christ in this age is placed over Gentiles, peoples, and nations, so that they may be governed by him—whether they are devoted to carnal desire like cattle, darkened by earthly curiosity like serpents,

[Col. 0470B]

or lifted up by pride like birds.

And just as on that day the human being and the animals that were with him were fed with seed-bearing plants, fruit-bearing trees, and green plants, so in this age the spiritual person, who is a good minister of Jesus Christ, is spiritually nourished together with that people by the food of the Holy Scriptures and by divine Law, for conceiving the fruitfulness of reasonings and words.

These are like seed-bearing plants, partly for the usefulness of moral conversion, like fruit-bearing trees; partly for the strengthening of faith, hope, and charity unto eternal life, like green plants, which do not wither under the heat of tribulations.

[Col. 0470C]

Thus he is nourished by spiritual foods and by these provisions so that he may understand many things. But the carnal person, that is, the little one in Christ, like God’s cattle, believes many things which he is not yet able to understand. Nevertheless, they all possess the same foods.

May the evening of this age not find us. For it is the age of which the Lord says: “Do you suppose that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18). After this evening there will be morning, when the Lord himself will come in charity. Then those to whom it was said, “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5), will rest with Christ from all their works. Such people perform works that are very good. After such works, rest is to be hoped for on the seventh day, which has no evening.

From here follows a recapitulation of all creation.

[Col. 0470D]

## CHAPTER 11. Recapitulation of the Whole Creation and Its Mystical Interpretation

“These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created.”

By this conclusion Holy Scripture addresses those who assert that the world has always existed without a beginning, or who indeed think that it was made by God, but from matter which God did not make and which, without a beginning, was coeternal with the Creator.

For it says “the generations of heaven and earth,” meaning the order of the divine establishment by which their adornment, through the works of the six days, reached the perfection described above, in accordance with what the Creator himself said in the Decalogue of his Law:

[Col. 0471A]

“For in six days God made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all that is in them” (Exod. 20).

What follows, however—

“In the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose in the earth, and every plant of the region before it germinated”—

should in no way be considered contrary to the statement of God already mentioned. It should rather be understood plainly that here Scripture uses “day” for the whole period in which the primordial creation was formed.

For heaven was not made, or illuminated by the stars, and earth separated from the waters and planted with trees and herbs, all in any one of the six days. Scripture, according to its customary manner, uses “day” for a period, just as the Apostle, when he says, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (1 Cor. 6),

[Col. 0471B]

signifies not one particular day but the whole period in which we labor in the present life for eternal salvation.

The prophet likewise speaks not of one particular day but of a lengthy period of divine grace: “On that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book” (Isa. 29).

Otherwise, it is difficult to understand how the Lord made heaven and earth, every shrub of the field, and every plant of the region in one day, unless perhaps we say that every creature was made together in unformed matter, according to what is written: “Because he lives forever, he created all things together” (Ecclus. 18).

(Greg.) The substance of things was indeed created together, but it was not formed together according to its species. What existed together according to the substance of matter did not appear together according to the form of its species.

When heaven and earth are described as having been made together, spiritual and bodily things are indicated as having been made together; whatever arises from heaven and whatever the earth produces are likewise indicated as having been made together.

[Col. 0471C]

Hence it was also written above: “God created human beings in his image; in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” Eve is not yet described as having been made, and yet the human being is already said to be male and female. But because a female was undoubtedly going to proceed from Adam’s side, she is already counted in him according to substance, from whom she was to be produced according to form.

We may consider this even in the smallest things, so that from the smallest we may weigh the greater. When grass is created, its fruit and its seed are not yet visible in it. Yet fruit and seed are present in it even when they do not appear, since they are evidently together in the substance of the root, although they do not emerge together through the increase of time.

This creation of matter, however, he made before every day of this world, when “in the beginning he created heaven and earth.” Although “the earth was formless and empty, and darkness was over the abyss,” nevertheless within the nature of the earth and the abyss—that is, of the waters—things that were later to be produced by the Creator’s work were hidden, already created together, as it were, through a seminal substance.

[Col. 0471D]

Therefore, if we say this, the previously mentioned question returns, so that we understand the designation “day” to have been used as a signification of time—namely, of that time in which God created all these things together in the beginning.

“In the day,” it says, “when the Lord God created heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose in the earth, and every plant of the region before it germinated.”

If we understand the “day” of which he speaks as designating that time when all things were made together before every day of this world, the meaning is readily apparent: every plant and tree was made causally within the substance of the earth itself before they visibly arose or germinated from the earth.

But if, as we more appropriately judge, we take the designation “day” as signifying that period in which this world was made and adorned through the six days, we can understand that Scripture now wished to explain more clearly what it had said above: “The earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit according to its kind.”

If we understand the “day” of which he speaks as designating that time when all things were made together before every day of this world, the meaning is readily apparent: every plant and tree was made causally within the substance of the earth itself before they visibly arose or germinated from the earth.

[Col. 0472A]

But if, as we more appropriately judge, we take the designation “day” as signifying that period in which this world was made and adorned through the six days, we can understand that Scripture now wished to explain more clearly what it had said above: “The earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit according to its kind.”
