For the earth did not produce these things at the beginning of creation in the manner in which it now produces fruit spontaneously when it has received water according to God’s arrangement. Rather, through the Creator’s altogether more marvelous work, before any fruits grew or germinated from the earth, all the fields and hills were suddenly covered with herbs and trees of suitable height and stature, spreading branches, shady foliage, and an abundance of fruits.

[Col. 0472B]

They did not arise gradually from the earth, germinating and growing through successive increases, but received these features by being brought forth from it in an already developed state.

The words that follow also seem to support this interpretation:

“For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no human being to work the earth; but a fountain was rising from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.”

Who does not see that this could not be said of the first creation of the earth, when it was still formless and empty and darkness was over the face of the abyss? Was there any need to report that rain had not descended upon the earth at a time when the earth itself could not yet receive rain, nor the air release it, since the waters still filled all the places of both?

[Col. 0472C]

Nor could a fountain rise from the earth to water it while the whole earth was covered by the abyss.

Hence, if I am not mistaken, it remains to be understood that when it is said above, “In the day when the Lord God created heaven and earth,” the name “day” refers to the period of the first six days, during which all the creation of the world was formed.

It is rightly recalled there that God had not rained upon the earth and that there was no human being to work the earth, so that we may understand how far the earth’s first germination differed from the present one. Now, through the watering of rains, the earth germinates spontaneously, and through human industry and cultivation many things are sown and produced in gardens and groves.

But the first creation of herbs and trees was accomplished in a very different way. By the new command of the supreme Craftsman, the earth, appearing as dry land, was suddenly filled far and wide, without rain and without human labor, with many kinds of fruits.

[Col. 0472D]

“But a fountain,” it says, “was rising from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.”

Before speaking of this fountain and its rising from the earth, let us first observe that the first germination of the earth, which the preceding statement mentions, took place at God’s command without any watering of the waters. The irrigation of this fountain, whatever its nature, came afterward, when the earth had been clothed with herbs and trees.

This is also proved by the very words of Scripture. After saying, with a verb in the perfect past tense, that “the Lord God created heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field and every plant of the region,” it immediately added, with a verb in the pluperfect: “For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no human being to work the earth.” It shows that before the creation of the shrubs and plants God had not sent rain.

What happened afterward it immediately added with a verb in the imperfect past tense, saying: “For a fountain was rising from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” By the form of the verb it indicates that this did not happen once but repeatedly, since it does not say “it rose” but “it was rising.”

[Col. 0473A]

Therefore, when the fountain is said to have risen from the earth and watered its whole surface, it is rightly asked in what manner it rose. Nor is there any obstacle to believing that it rose and returned at intervals in order to water the earth, just as to this day the Nile annually rises to water the plains of Egypt; just as the Jordan once watered the land of the Pentapolis, concerning which Scripture says that “the whole region was watered like the paradise of the Lord” (Gen. 13), and like Egypt, before God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.

As Saint Augustine testifies, the remarkable alternation of certain springs is also reported: at a fixed interval of years they overflow in such a way as to water the entire region, while at another time they provide sufficient water for drinking from deep wells.

Why, then, is it incredible—as the same author says—if the whole earth was watered from one head of the abyss, flowing and receding by alternating changes?

[Col. 0473B]

If, he says, Scripture wished to call “fountain” the magnitude of the abyss, except for that part which is called the sea and which surrounds the lands with evident breadth and bitter waves; if it meant the single part that the earth encloses in hidden recesses, from which all the springs are distributed through different channels and veins and burst forth in their respective places; if it called this a fountain rather than fountains because of the unity of its nature, and if it rose from the earth through innumerable passages of caves and fissures, watering the whole face of the earth after being scattered everywhere like strands of hair—not continuously in the manner of a sea or pond, but as we see waters flow through the beds of rivers and the bends of streams, flooding the neighboring areas when they overflow—who would not accept this, except one troubled by a contentious spirit?

The words can also be understood to mean that the whole face of the earth was watered in the same way that a whole garment is said to be colored, even if the coloring is not continuous but occurs in spots. This is especially plausible because, at that time, in the newness of the earth, it is credible that many places, though not all, were flat, so that the streams bursting forth could be dispersed and spread more widely.

[Col. 0473C]

Therefore, concerning the magnitude and multiplicity of this fountain—which either had one eruption from elsewhere, or was called one fountain because of some hidden unity in the earth’s boundaries, from which all the waters on earth spring, whether great or small, and which rose from the earth through all its dispersions and watered the whole face of the earth; or, as is more credible, because Scripture does not say “one fountain was rising from the earth” but “a fountain was rising,” using the singular for the plural—we should understand that many fountains watered their own places or regions throughout the earth.

The same usage occurs when “soldier” is said while many are understood, or when “locust” and “frog” are spoken of in the plagues with which the Egyptians were struck, although there was an innumerable multitude of locusts and frogs. Let us not labor over this any longer.

[Col. 0473D]

When it had been said that God created the herbs and shrubs before rain descended and before there was a human being to work the earth, the creation of the human being is appropriately introduced, and it is said:

> The Lord God therefore formed the human being from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.

Here the making of the human being is described at greater length. He was indeed made on the sixth day, but there his creation was mentioned briefly, whereas here it is explained more fully. He was made, namely, with respect to the substance of body and soul: the body was formed from clay, while the soul was created from nothing by God’s breathing; and the female was formed from the side of the sleeping man.

In this statement, the poverty of a carnal understanding must be avoided, lest we suppose that God formed the human body from clay with bodily hands, or breathed through a throat or lips into the face of the one he had formed so that he might live and possess the breath of life.

[Col. 0474A]

When the prophet says, “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Job 10), he speaks more figuratively than literally—that is, according to the custom by which human beings ordinarily work. God is spirit, and his simple substance is not composed of the outlines of bodily limbs, unless this is believed by the unlearned.

God therefore formed the human being from clay, the one whom by his word he had commanded to be made from clay.

“He breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul,” when he created for him the substance of soul and spirit in which he would live. For God’s breathing into the human face is rightly understood in the same way as the earlier statement, “God called the light day”: the latter is put for “he caused it to be called by human beings,” and the former for “he created for him the breath by which he would live.”

[Col. 0474B]

God is rightly said to have breathed into the human face so that the human being might become a living soul, because all the bodily senses, through which the spirit implanted within him observes external things, are more active in the face—namely, sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. This is because the anterior part of the brain, from which all the senses are distributed, is located toward the forehead.

The sense of touch, which is diffused throughout the whole body, also shows that it has its pathway from this same anterior part of the brain; the pathway leads backward through the crown and neck to the marrow of the spine.

This statement also agrees with what was said above: “He created him in the image of God; male and female he created them.”

[Col. 0474C]

“He created him in the image of God” is rightly understood to refer only to the soul; while the addition “male and female” refers only to the body.

We must not listen to those who think that the soul is a part of God. For if the human soul were a part of God, it could not be deceived either by itself or by anyone else; it could not be compelled by any necessity either to do or to suffer evil; nor could it change at all for better or for worse.

That breath of God which gave life to the human being was made by him, not from him. For neither is a human being’s breath a part of the human being, nor does a human being make it from himself; rather, it is taken from and expelled as aerial breath.

[Col. 0474D]

God, however, was able to create from nothing a living and rational being, which a human being cannot do. Nevertheless, some think that the first human being was not then animated when God breathed into his face and he became a living soul, but that he then received the Holy Spirit.

Whichever of these alternatives may be shown to be more credible, there can nevertheless be no legitimate doubt that the soul is not a part of God, nor created or brought forth from his substance and nature, but made from nothing.

(Isidor.) Mystically, the passage is understood in this way:

“These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, in the day when the Lord made heaven and earth, and the rest.”

According to prophecy, the name “day” signifies the whole time of this life, in which heaven and earth were made—that is, in which visible creatures are arranged, governed, and exist.

But what does it mean that, after naming heaven and earth, he added the shrub of the field and the plant of the region, while saying nothing of the other things that are in heaven and earth, or even in the sea? It means that by the shrub of the field an invisible creature is understood, such as the soul.

It is called a shrub because of the vigor of life, and a plant because of that same life, which never withers. Then he adds: “Before it was upon the earth.” This is understood to mean before the soul sinned. Once soiled by earthly desires, as though born upon the earth or existing upon the earth, it is rightly described in this way.

Hence he adds: “For the Lord had not yet rained upon the earth,” as though he were saying plainly: Before the soul sinned, the Lord had not yet granted the rain of teaching from the clouds of the Scriptures to water the soul. Nor had the Lord, on account of the human being who is earth, assumed the cloud of our flesh, through which he poured out the most abundant rain of the holy Gospel.

[Col. 0475A]

What he added—“And there was no human being to work the earth”—means that no human being worked in the virgin from whom Christ was born. For he is the stone cut from the mountain without hands: that is, without intercourse and human seed, cut from the virginal womb as from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh.

“But a fountain was rising from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” The earth is most rightly understood as the Virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother, concerning whom it is written: “Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45). The Holy Spirit watered this earth; in the Gospel he is signified by the name of fountain and water.

“God therefore formed the human being from the clay of the earth”—that is, Christ became man, according to what the Apostle says, “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1), as though from the clay of the earth.

[Col. 0475B]

“And he breathed into his face the breath of life”—namely, the infusion of the Holy Spirit, who worked the human being Christ.

“And the human being became a living soul”—so that he who was perfect God might also be believed to be perfect human being.

## CHAPTER 12. The Planting of Paradise and the Division of the Four Rivers, in Which the Human Being Was Appointed by God as Cultivator and Guardian
But the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the human being whom he had formed. God must indeed be understood to have planted paradise from that beginning when, after removing the waters that covered the whole earth, he commanded it to produce grasses and fruit-bearing trees; yet it was in this paradise that he placed the human being on the sixth day, on which he had also formed him. Nor should there be any doubt that the paradise in which the first human being was placed—although it bears the figure of the Church of the present or future age—must, in the literal sense, be understood as a place of great beauty, shaded by fruitful groves, both extensive and made fertile by a great spring.

Whereas our edition, translated from the Hebrew truth, reads “from the beginning,” the ancient translation has “toward the east.” Hence some wish to understand that paradise is located in the eastern part of the world, although separated from all the regions now inhabited by the human race by an immense intervening distance of either ocean or land. For this reason even the waters of the Flood, which covered the entire surface of our world to a great depth, could not reach it. But whether it is there or elsewhere, God knows; nevertheless, we cannot doubt that this place was and is earthly. Finally, in the words that follow, Scripture explains more fully how God planted it, saying:

“And the Lord God brought forth from the soil every tree that is beautiful to look at and good for food; also the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” This is understood to have occurred on the same day on which, at God’s command, the earth also produced the other fruit-bearing trees. It is repeated here, however, so that we might know what kind of place paradise was, especially because specific mention had to be made of the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. In the one there was a sign of the obedience that human beings owed to God; in the other, the sacrament of eternal life, which they would merit through that obedience.

The tree of life was so called because, as we have said, it had received from God the power by which anyone who ate from it would have his body established in lasting health and would never be changed for the worse by illness or age, nor fall into decay. Yet this occurred bodily in such a way that it was also a figure of a spiritual sacrament, namely of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom it is said in praise of Wisdom: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her.” And in the Apocalypse of Saint John he says: “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. II).

This plainly means: “To the one who conquers the temptation of the ancient serpent, by whom Adam was conquered, I will give what I would have given to Adam had he conquered, so that he may be restored forever by the present vision of Christ’s glory and therefore may be touched by no assault of death.” This Lord Christ, the power and wisdom of God the Father, is in the paradise of the heavenly kingdom, which he also deigned to promise, together with the other saints, to the thief who confessed him on the cross.

We must next consider the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. This tree too was plainly visible and corporeal, like the other trees. There can be no doubt that it was a tree; but we must inquire why it received this name. As I consider the matter carefully, I cannot say how pleasing I find the view that the tree was not subject to being eaten. For he who had made all things in paradise very good had not established anything evil there; rather, the evil for the human being lay in transgressing the commandment.

It was necessary that the human being, placed under the Lord God, should be prohibited from something, so that obedience itself might be the virtue by which he pleased his Lord. Indeed, we may most truthfully say that obedience alone is the virtue of every rational creature acting under God’s authority. The first and greatest fault of pride would be to wish to use one’s own power for one’s downfall; the name of this fault is disobedience. The human being therefore would have had no basis for thinking and feeling that he had a lord, unless something had been commanded him.

Thus the tree itself was not evil, but it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, if the human being ate from it on account of the prohibition, the transgression of the commandment would take place in connection with it. Through the experience of punishment, he would learn what the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience were. Accordingly, this too must be understood not as spoken figuratively, but as referring truly to a certain tree, which received its name not from its fruit or apple, whatever grew upon it, but from what was to follow when it was touched contrary to the prohibition.

“And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise”—that is, those beautiful and fruitful trees which shaded the whole land of that region. We should believe that this took place in the same arrangement by which the Nile irrigates the flat land of Egypt in the region where we live. Hence the statement we cited above concerning the land of Sodom, which was wholly irrigated like the paradise of the Lord and like Egypt. And the Lord and creator of all things, in his provident ordering, clearly wished our world to possess some likeness of that homeland for the possession of which we were created in our first parent, so that he might admonish us, through a nearby example, to seek our return to it—especially through that river which is known to flow from paradise.

For the Nile, which irrigates Egypt, is itself the Gihon, which is subsequently said to proceed from paradise. Likewise, after overthrowing those same cities of Sodom, which were once irrigated like the paradise of the Lord, he set them forth as an example of those who will act impiously, so that, having in the world the clearest traces of the destruction of the wicked, we might flee their eternal torments more vigilantly.

“And from there it is divided into four heads. The name of the first is Pishon.” It is established, on the testimony of the most reliable authorities, that the sources of all these rivers said to go out from paradise are known in our world: that of the Pishon, which is now called the Ganges, in the regions of the Caucasus Mountains; that of the Nile, which Scripture, as we have said, calls the Gihon, not far from Mount Atlas, which is Africa’s farthest western boundary; and the Tigris and Euphrates in Armenia.

We should therefore believe that, because paradise itself is most remote from human knowledge, the four branches of water divide there; but that the rivers whose sources are said to be known emerge elsewhere beneath the earth, after passing through the long stretches of intervening regions, in places where they are said to be known as though those were their sources. For who does not know that some waters commonly do this? It is known, however, where they do not run beneath the earth for a long time. Indeed, historians report that these same rivers—the Tigris, Euphrates, and Nile—are swallowed up by the earth in many places and, after an intervening distance, emerge again and resume their customary course. This too should be understood as something the Lord did to indicate the course by which these waters come to us from paradise through the earth’s more hidden hollows and longer channels.

Pishon is interpreted as “change of mouth” or “mouth of the pupil.” This is appropriate, since it plainly displays in our world a different—indeed, much poorer—appearance than the grace it possesses in paradise.

“It is the one that circles the whole land of Havilah.” This is the region of India, bearing that name because after the Flood it was possessed by Havilah, the son of Joktan, who was a son of Heber, the patriarch of the Hebrews. Josephus also reports that Havilah, together with his brothers, possessed the region from the river Cephene and the territory of India as far as the place called Hieria.

“Where gold is born, and the gold of that land is excellent.” Pliny the Elder also relates that the regions of India abound in veins of gold more than other lands. Hence their islands received the names χρυσά and ἀργυρά—“golden” and “silver”—from the abundance of gold or silver.

“And there bdellium and the onyx stone are found.” Bdellium is, as the same Pliny says, an aromatic tree, black in color, the size of an olive, with a leaf like the oak and a fruit like the wild fig; its nature is that of gum. Its tear is bright, somewhat whitish, smooth, and thick, with the consistency of wax; it is easily softened, bitter to the taste, and of pleasant odor, though it becomes more fragrant when soaked in wine. The Book of Numbers also mentions it: “The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance was like the appearance of bdellium” (Num. I), that is, bright and somewhat whitish.

The onyx is a precious stone, so called because it contains a mixed whiteness resembling a human fingernail. For the Greeks call a fingernail ὄνυξ, onyx. Arabia also produces it, but the Indian variety has fiery sparks surrounded by white bands. The Arabian variety, however, is black with shining bands.

The ancient translation has “carbuncle and prasinus stone” in place of these. A carbuncle is, as its name itself indicates, a stone of fiery color, which is said to illuminate even the darkness of night. A prasinus is a stone of green appearance. It received its Greek name from the leek, which they call πράσον.

“And the name of the second river is Gihon: it is the one that circles the whole land of Ethiopia,” and it is interpreted as “breast” or “precipice.”

“The name of the third river is Tigris: it flows toward the Assyrians.” It is also called Tigris because of its speed, running with the extreme swiftness of a wild beast.

“The fourth river is the Euphrates.” Euphrates is interpreted as “fruit-bearing” or “growing.” For this reason he does not say where the Euphrates flows or what lands it circles, because, flowing nearby in the land of promise, it could easily be known by the people of Israel, who were situated there and would read these words.

Since through the waters of rebirth our return to the heavenly things is opened to us, it is entirely fitting to the dispensation of divine mercy that the very element by which we are led back to our heavenly homeland should be shared by us with paradise, where the first human being was placed. And just as grace, invisibly renewing us, prepares our entrance into the heavenly kingdom, so also the water by which he renews us should invisibly spring forth from paradise through the earth’s channels into our world.

Therefore, if “the Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John III), it was likewise fitting that the water which sanctifies those whom the Spirit wills should come to us from paradise by unknown routes and return to places unknown to us, although it is clear that it has its origin in the paradise of delight.

“But the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.” Paradise is the Church, for this is how we read of her in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister” (Song IV). Paradise is planted “from the beginning” because the catholic Church is understood to have been founded by Christ, who is the beginning of all things (Isidore).

The river flowing out from paradise bears the image of Christ flowing from the Father’s fountain, who waters his Church with the word of preaching and the gift of baptism. Of this the prophet fittingly says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river, springing up over the thirsty land” (Isa. XLIV).

The fact that the earth is watered by the four rivers flowing out from paradise contains the solid structure of our mind: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. For the whole edifice of good works rises upon these four virtues. (Gregory.) Thus the four rivers of paradise water the earth because, when the heart is infused with these four virtues, it is restrained from every heat of carnal desire.

Allegorically as well, the four rivers of paradise are the four Gospels sent forth for the preaching of all nations. The fruit-bearing trees are all the saints; their fruits are their works; and the tree of life is certainly the Holy of Holies, Christ, toward whom anyone who stretches out his hand will live forever. (Isidore.) The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the free choice of the will, placed in the midst of us for distinguishing good and evil; whoever tastes from it after abandoning God’s grace will die the death.

So the Lord God took the human being whom he had formed and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it. This seems to refer to the place where it was said above: “There was no human being to work the ground.” But in explaining this word as well, let us set forth the words of the holy Father Augustine:

“What was he to work, or what was he to guard?” he says. “Did the Lord perhaps intend the first human being to perform agriculture? Or is it not believable that before sin he condemned him to labor? We would certainly think so, unless we saw that some people cultivate the soil with such delight of spirit that it is a great punishment for them to be called away from it to something else.

“Whatever delight agriculture possesses, it was surely much greater then, when nothing adverse happened either to the earth or to the sky. It was not a distressing labor but a joyful exercise of the will, when the things God had created produced more happily and abundantly through the assistance of human work. Thus the Creator himself was praised more fully, for he had given the soul, placed in an animal body, both the reason and the capacity to work—to the extent that was sufficient for a willing mind, not to the extent that bodily necessity compelled an unwilling one.

“‘To work it and guard it,’ he says: he was to guard that same paradise for himself, lest he admit anything by which he might deserve to be expelled from it. Finally, he receives a command so that he may have the means of guarding paradise for himself—that is, by keeping the command he may not be cast out of it.

“For anyone is rightly said not to have guarded his property if he acted in such a way as to lose it, even if it remains safe for another who either found it or deserved to receive it.”

There is another sense in these words, which I think should rightly be preferred: that God himself was to work and guard the human being. For just as a human being works the soil not to make it soil but to make it cultivated and fruitful, so God, all the more, works the human being whom he himself created to be human, so that he may be just and so that the human being may not depart from him through pride.

Thus he placed the human being in the paradise of delight, and so forth: he was to work it so that he might be good and blessed, and guard it so that he might be secure, humbly submitting himself to God’s dominion and protection.

## CHAPTER XIII. Where God gave Adam the commandment in paradise, and Adam bestowed names on all living creatures

“And he commanded him, saying: ‘You may eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.’” We must not believe that anything evil was naturally present in that tree, as we have also explained above. Rather, the human being was prohibited from a tree that was not evil, so that the keeping of the commandment itself would be good for him and its transgression evil.

In the end, the sinner desired nothing other than not to be under God’s dominion, when he committed the act in which he ought to have attended solely to the command of the one who ruled, so that it would not be committed. If that command alone had been heeded, what else would have been loved but God’s will? What else would have been placed above the human will but God’s will?

Nor can it happen that one’s own will does not fall upon a human being with the weight of a great ruin if, by exalting it, he places it above the will of his superior. The human being experienced this when he despised God’s command, and through this experience learned what difference there was between good and evil: the good of obedience, and the evil of disobedience, pride, defiance, perverse imitation of God, and harmful freedom.

The tree in which this occurred received its name from the event itself, as has already been said. The commandment that Christ received figuratively, we receive in him, because every Christian, not inappropriately, bears the person of Christ, as the Lord himself says: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me” (Matt. XXV).

(Isidore.) Thus it is said: “You shall eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.” We are commanded to enjoy every tree of paradise, by which spiritual delights are signified. “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, self-control, chastity” (Gal. V), as the Apostle says.

And we must not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil planted in the midst of paradise—that is, we must not become proud of the nature of our free choice, which is placed in the middle, lest, deceived by the knowledge gained through experience, we discover evil.

“For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death.” He did not say: “If you eat, you will be mortal.” Rather, he says: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death.” The human being died in soul when he sinned, because God, who is the life of the soul, departed from him. As a consequence of this death, bodily death also followed when the soul, which is its life, departed from the body.

That death occurred to the first human being when he reached the end of the present life, though not until a considerable time after he ate what had been forbidden. It can also be understood that the death of which he died was inflicted upon him on the day on which he sinned—the death that the Apostle laments when he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner human being, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched human that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. XII.)

It would not have been enough for him to say: “Who will deliver me from this mortal body?” Rather, he says, “from this body of death.” Likewise he says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin.” There too he does not say “mortal,” although it is certainly mortal because it will die.

We must not believe that those bodies were such from the beginning. Although they were not yet spiritual but animal bodies, they were nevertheless not dead—that is, they were not necessarily destined to die. This occurred on the day on which they touched the tree contrary to the prohibition.

(Isidore.) Mystically, however, God took the human being and placed him in paradise: that is, God assumed flesh and became the head of the Church. He placed him there “to work it and guard it,” meaning that, by the Father’s will, he might fill the Church from all the nations, and that the saying of the Lord might be fulfilled: “I guarded them in your name; those whom you gave me I have kept” (John XVII).

We must carefully consider that good things cannot benefit us if the evils that creep in are not avoided. Every good deed that is performed is lost if it is not carefully guarded in humility. Hence it is also rightly said of our first parent: “The Lord placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it.” Whoever does the good that is commanded is working; but he loses what he has worked for when what is forbidden is stolen from him.

Therefore we must always do good works and also carefully guard ourselves in our thoughts even amid those good works, lest the good things that elevate the mind become things that serve not the Creator but our exaltation.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the making of the woman from Adam’s rib

“Then the Lord God said: ‘It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself.’” This speech of God must be understood to have been made not through a bodily voice sent outward into the air, but ineffably through the inward reason of the divine will, by which all things were created. This agrees with what we taught above, where it is written: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.”

If anyone asks for what purpose this helper ought to have been made, let him hear the response of Saint Augustine, whose words we have often previously set forth without naming him. “Nothing else,” he says, “reasonably suggests itself except that it was for the procreation of children, just as assistance is given to seed in the earth so that a shoot may arise from both sides.”

This too had been stated in the first creation of things: “Male and female he made them, and he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule it.’” This purpose in the constitution and union of male and female, and this blessing, did not cease even after the human being’s sin and punishment.

Indeed, it is according to this that the earth is now filled with human beings who rule it. Although it is recorded that they came together and begot children after they had been expelled from paradise, I do not see what could have prevented them from having honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage bed even in paradise.

With God granting this to those who lived faithfully and justly and served him with equal obedience and holiness, children could have been generated from their seed without any troubled heat of lust and without any labor or pain of childbirth—not so that children would succeed parents who were dying, but so that, while those who had begotten them remained in some fixed condition of bodily form, and while they and their offspring drew bodily vigor from the tree of life planted there, those who were born would also be brought to the same condition.

Then, when the appointed number had been completed, if all lived justly and obediently, that transformation would take place: without any death, animal bodies would be changed into another quality, because they would serve the spirit governing them at every command, and would live by the spirit alone, without any support from bodily food. They would then be called spiritual bodies.

For if Enoch and Elijah, who did not die in Adam but bear in the flesh the propagation of death, are believed also to be destined to return to this life in order to pay that debt and, though this has been delayed so long, to die, are now in another life, where before the resurrection of the flesh, before the animal body is changed into a spiritual one, they do not fail through illness or old age, how much more justly and reasonably would this have been granted to those first human beings, living without any sin of their own or of their parents, so that, after children had been born, they might pass into a better condition? Thus, when the age had ended, they and all the posterity of the saints could be changed into an angelic form—not through the death of the flesh, but through the power of God—and with far greater happiness.

When the Lord God had formed from the soil all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of heaven, he brought them to Adam. If anyone is troubled that he did not say, “Having formed from the soil all the living creatures of the earth and from the waters all the birds of heaven,” but seems to say that both kinds were formed from the earth—“The Lord God,” he says, “having formed from the soil all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of heaven”—let him see that this can be understood in two ways.

Either Scripture is now silent about where he formed the birds of heaven, because it may occur to us, even without its saying so, that God did not form both kinds from the earth; rather, we are to understand that he formed only the living creatures of the earth and the birds of heaven, while Scripture remains silent about their origin.

Or “earth” may have been used universally to include the waters as well, just as it is used in the psalm where, after the praises of the heavenly beings have been completed, the discourse turns to the earth and says: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps, and so forth” (Ps. CXLIX). It does not then say: “Praise the Lord from the waters.” For all the deeps are there, and yet they praise the Lord from the earth.

There too are the reptiles and winged birds, which likewise praise God from the earth according to this universal use of the word “earth.” In accordance with this same usage, it is also said of the whole world: “God, who made heaven and earth.” Whether what was created was made from dry land or from water, it is truthfully understood to have been created from the earth.

“He brought them,” he says, “to Adam, to see what he would call them.” We must not think carnally that God brought the living creatures of the earth or the birds to Adam in the way a shepherd usually drives his flock from one place to another. Rather, we should understand that just as divine power created these creatures from the waters or the earth when it willed, so by the hidden impulse of its power it brought them to the human being to be seen when it willed.

In the same way, all kinds of birds and four-footed animals are read to have come to Noah’s ark and entered it, not gathered by human hands but moved by God. The creatures themselves did not know why they were coming, while the human being, instructed and commanded by God, knew and received them as they came into the ark.

“For whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name.” “And Adam gave names to all the living creatures of the earth, all the birds of heaven, and all the beasts of the earth.” It is clear that Adam gave names to the living creatures of the earth and the birds of heaven in the language in which the whole human race spoke until the building of the tower at which languages were divided.

But when, at the destruction of the tower, God gave each nation its own distinct language, then the names of living creatures, as well as those of other things, must also be believed to have been distinguished according to each people’s manner of speech. It is nevertheless also clear that later, among the various peoples, human beings gave names according to their own preference to many things or living creatures that happened to appear new to them; even now they commonly distinguish them in this way.

Finally, Scripture says nothing about fish being brought to Adam so that he might give them names. Yet it is believable that, as they gradually came to be known, different names were given to them by all peoples according to the diversity of nations.

The first language of the human race appears to have been Hebrew, because all the names of human beings that we read in Genesis up to the division of languages are clearly in that language.

The reason why all the living creatures of the earth and the birds of heaven were brought to Adam, so that he might see what he would call them and give them names, was that God might thereby demonstrate to the human being how much better he was than all irrational living creatures. It is evident from this that the human being is better than cattle by reason itself, because only reason, which is superior, can distinguish them and discern them by name.

Spiritually, however, “Let us make him a helper like himself” means that, in the human being assumed, the Church was joined to God. Adam gave names to all the living creatures and birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, signifying the nations that would be saved in the Church and that, through Christ, would receive a name they had not previously possessed, as it is written: “I will call my servants by another name.”

But no helper like Adam himself was found for Adam. Although each person may be faithful or just, no one can be equated with Christ. For Moses says: “Who is like you among the gods, Lord?” And David says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV). No one could free the human race from death and overcome death itself except Christ, as the Apocalypse says: “No one was found worthy, either in heaven or on earth or under the earth, to open the book” (Rev. V).

So the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam. When he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs, filled its place with flesh, and the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman.

The fact that the woman was made from the man’s side should be understood to have occurred in order to commend the power of that union. But what happened while Adam slept, namely that flesh was supplied in place of the bone that had been removed, was done for the sake of a deeper mystery.

It signified that from Christ’s side, when he was put to sleep in death on the cross, the sacraments of salvation would come forth—namely, blood and water—from which the Church, his bride, would be formed.

For if the creation of the woman had not been intended as a figure of so great a sacrament, why did Adam need to sleep so that God might take from him the rib from which he would make the woman, when he could have done the same while Adam was awake and without pain?

Why was it necessary that, when the bone taken from the man’s side was fashioned into a woman, not bone but flesh should be supplied in place of the bone? It was because this signified that Christ would be weak for the sake of the Church, while the Church would become strong through him.

For the sake of the same mystery Scripture also used a figurative word: it did not say “made,” “formed,” or “created,” as it had with all the works above, but said, “The Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman”—not as though it were a human body, but as though it were a house. “That house is us,” if we hold firmly to the confidence and glory of hope to the end.

For it was fitting that the origin of the human race should proceed with God’s cooperation, so that the redemption of the race, which was to come at the end of the age through the same creator, might be attested by harmonious figures.

(Gregory.) It must also be understood that we never reach the summit of contemplation unless we cease from the oppression of outward cares. We never look upon ourselves so as to know that one thing in us is rational and governs, while another is animal and governed, unless, returning to the secret of silence, we are put to sleep away from every disturbance outside us.

Adam sleeping rightly foreshadowed this silence of ours. From his side a woman then proceeded; and whoever is carried away toward understanding inward realities closes the eyes of his mind to visible things. Then, within himself, he distinguishes what ought to rule with manly strength from what can submit in weakness, so that within him there is one element able to govern like a man and another, like a woman, that is governed.

“And he brought her to Adam. And Adam said: ‘This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.’” Since Adam, when all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds had been brought to him, had found none among them like himself, he rightly recognized and exclaimed when he saw that a helper like himself had now been made and brought to him: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”

“This now,” because earlier, after seeing the other living creatures, he had not seen one like himself. “Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” because he knew that the other creatures he had seen, which possessed bone and flesh and which he had distinguished by name, had been made not from his substance but from the earth or the waters.

Just as he had given names to the other creatures brought to him, it remained for him to give a name to the one whom he recognized as like himself and created from his own body.

“This one,” he said, “shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.” Just as the Latin etymology corresponds in these names, since virago, “woman,” is named from vir, “man,” so too does the Hebrew correspond: in that language, a man is called *’îš*, and a woman, derived from this name, is called *’iššâ*. That *’îš* means “man” in Hebrew is also attested by the name Israel, which is interpreted as “a man seeing God.”

This also agrees most fittingly with the mysteries of Christ and the Church: Adam wished the woman created from his flesh to become a participant in his name, because our Lord Jesus Christ likewise gave the Church, whom he redeemed by the price of his body and blood and adopted as his bride, a share in his name. Thus she is called Christian from Christ and obtains eternal salvation from Jesus, that is, from the Savior.

Nor should we pass over the fact that the sleep—or “ecstasy,” that is, an “excess of mind,” as the ancient translation has it—which the Lord sent upon Adam is rightly understood, as Saint Augustine says, to have been sent for this purpose: that Adam’s mind might, through ecstasy, become a participant, as it were, in the angelic court and, entering into the sanctuary of God, understand the last things.

Finally, awakening as though filled with prophecy, when he saw the woman brought to him, he immediately uttered the great mystery that the Apostle commended: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man,” and what follows:

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

Although Scripture itself testifies that these words belonged to the first human being, the Lord nevertheless declared in the Gospel that God had spoken them. For he says: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’?” (Matt. XIX).

By this we understand that, because the ecstasy had preceded in Adam, he was able to speak this as a prophet under divine inspiration.

If Christ therefore clung to the Church so that the two might be one flesh, how did he leave his father, and how did he leave his mother? Because, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II).

This is what it means that he “left his father”: not that he deserted or departed from the Father, but that he did not appear to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father.

How did he leave his mother? By leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, and cleaving to the Church, which he gathered from all nations, so that through the peace of the new covenant the two might be one flesh. For although he is God with God the Father, through the flesh he became our participant, so that we might be the body of that head.

“Now both were naked, Adam namely and his wife, and they were not ashamed”—and rightly so. For what could cause shame when they had not yet felt any law in their members warring against the law of their minds? This was the punishment for sin that followed after the transgression, when disobedience seized what had been prohibited and justice punished what had been committed.

Before this occurred, they were naked, as it was said, and were not ashamed. There was no movement in the body that required modesty; they thought nothing needed to be covered because they had felt nothing that needed to be restrained.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the serpent’s suggestion and the seduction of Adam and his wife
### CHAPTER III

But the serpent was more crafty than all the animals of the earth that the Lord God had made. This serpent may be called more crafty than all the animals, not on account of its irrational soul but because of the spirit already inhabiting it—that is, the diabolical spirit. For however much the transgressing angels were cast down from their heavenly seats on account of their perversity and pride, they are nevertheless by nature superior to all the animals of the earth because of the eminence of reason. What wonder, then, if the devil, now filling the serpent by his impulse and mingling his spirit with it, in the manner in which prophets are accustomed to be filled by demons, had made it the craftiest of all the animals of the earth? Or, as another edition says, “the wisest of all the beasts,” according to the living, irrational soul of living creatures?

(Augustine.) If, then, it is asked why God permitted the human being to be tempted, when he knew that he would consent to the tempter, the true answer is this: it would not have been a matter of great praise for the human being if he could live rightly for the reason that no one urged him to live wrongly, since by nature he possessed the ability, and by his own power the will, not to consent to the one urging him—though aided by him who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Prov. III). Nor should it be thought that this tempter would have overthrown the human being if a certain exaltation had not first arisen in the human soul that needed to be restrained, so that through the humiliation of sin he might learn how falsely he had presumed upon himself. For it was said most truly: “Before ruin the spirit is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. XVI).

Some people are disturbed by this temptation of the first human being, because God permitted it to occur, as though they did not now see the entire human race being ceaselessly tempted by the devil’s snares. Why does God permit this also? Is it because the human being is tested so that virtue may be exercised, and because it is a more glorious victory not to have consented when tempted than not to have been able to be tempted? But if it is asked why the devil was permitted to tempt chiefly through the serpent, this was done for the sake of signification—not because the devil wished to signify something for our instruction, but because, since he could not approach to tempt unless permitted, could he do anything other than what he was permitted to do? Whatever, therefore, that serpent signified must be attributed to the providence under which the devil himself indeed has the desire to harm, but no power except what is granted—whether for overthrowing and destroying the vessels of wrath, or for humbling or testing the vessels of mercy.

The serpent did not, therefore, understand the sounds of the words that came from it to the woman. For one must not believe that its soul had been transformed into a rational nature, since even human beings, whose nature is rational, when a demon speaks within them in that condition for which an exorcist is required, do not know what they are saying; how much less would that serpent have understood the sounds of the words which the devil was producing in that way through it and from it—he who would not have understood a speaking human being if he heard him free from diabolical possession?

Then he said to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman replied: “We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat from it and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.”

The serpent first questioned her, and the woman answered, so that her transgression would be inexcusable: in no way could it be said that the woman had forgotten what God had commanded. For the crafty enemy of the human race does not cease to do daily what he did in paradise. He strives to tear the words of God from human hearts and to implant in them the flattering deceits of his fictitious promises. Every day he makes light of what God threatens and invites people to believe what he falsely promises. For he falsely promises temporal things in order to diminish in human minds the punishments that God threatens as eternal.

When he promises the glory of the present life, what else does he say than, “Taste, and you will be like gods”? It is as though he openly said: “Touch temporal desire and appear exalted in this world.” And when he tries to remove fear of the divine judgment from the heart, what else does he say than what he said to the first human beings: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” But because, by divine gift, the human being who had lost righteousness receives it again—the righteousness that he lost after having first been created—he now exercises himself more vigorously against the blandishments of crafty persuasion. Experience has taught him how much he ought to obey the command; and the one whom guilt once drove toward punishment is now restrained from guilt by his punishment. The more he fears committing sin, the more, compelled by punishment, he himself condemns what he has committed.

But the serpent said to the woman: “You will certainly not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

What is meant here except that they were persuaded not to wish to be under God, but rather to possess power without God, so that they would not observe his law—as though he begrudged them the ability to govern themselves? They would no longer need his eternal light, but would use their own, relying, as it were, upon their own eyes to distinguish good and evil, which he had forbidden.

In these words we should note with what art of wickedness the devil tempted the human being from the beginning. He not only taught him disobedience and contempt for his Creator, as though the Creator begrudged him something, but also proposed that he believe in a plurality of gods, saying, “You will be like gods,” so that, even if he could not perhaps draw them into disobedience, he might nevertheless corrupt the chastity of the faith by which they worshiped the one God. If he could draw them into disobedience, he would be victorious in both respects.

How could the woman have believed by these words that she had been forbidden by God to do something good and useful, unless there had already been in her mind that love of self-determination and a certain proud presumption about herself which that temptation was intended to expose and humble? Finally, not content with the serpent’s words, she looked at the tree.

And she saw, as Scripture says, that it was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance. Not believing that she could die from it, I think she supposed that God had said, “If you eat, you will die,” for some symbolic reason. And therefore “she took of its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband,” perhaps also with some persuasive word that Scripture has left unstated, indicating that it was to be understood. Or perhaps the man no longer needed persuasion, since he saw that she had not died from eating that food?

The ancient enemy rose against the first human being, our ancestor, in three temptations, for he tempted him by gluttony, vainglory, and avarice; and by tempting him he overcame him, because through consent he subjected him to himself. He tempted him by gluttony when he displayed the forbidden fruit of the tree and persuaded him to eat it. He tempted him by vainglory when he said, “You will be like gods.” And certainly he tempted him by avarice when he said, “Knowing good and evil.” For avarice concerns not only money but also exalted status. It is rightly called avarice when someone seeks elevation beyond measure. If the seizure of honor did not belong to the avarice of status, Paul would never have said of the only-begotten Son: “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. II). Thus the devil drew our ancestor into pride by stirring him toward the avarice of exalted status.

But by the same means by which he cast down the first human being, he himself succumbed when he tempted the second human being. He tempted him through gluttony when he said, “Command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matt. IV). He tempted him through vainglory when he said, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (ibid.). He tempted him through the avarice of exalted status when he displayed all the kingdoms of the world, saying, “All these I will give you if you fall down and worship me” (ibid.). But he was defeated by the second human being by the same means by which he boasted that he had defeated the first, so that, captured at the very entrance, he might depart from our hearts by the very entrance through which he had entered and held us.

The man ate, and the eyes of both were opened—but opened to what, except to desire one another? Opened to the punishment of sin, with death conceived in the flesh itself? The body was now not merely an animal body—which, if they had preserved obedience, could have been changed without death into a better and spiritual condition—but also a body of death, in which the law in the members would resist the law of the mind.

For they had not been created with closed eyes, wandering blind and groping about in the paradise of delights. The same is meant in the Gospel when it says of the two men, one of whom was Cleopas, that when the Lord broke bread for them, their eyes were opened and they recognized him (Luke, last chapter)—the one whom they had not recognized along the way. They were certainly not walking with closed eyes, but were unable to recognize him. Thus the eyes of the first human beings were opened to what previously had not been accessible to them, although they had been open to other things.

That serpent, “wiser than all the beasts,” indicates the devil, who is called a serpent because he moves about in the winding course of his cunning. But why did he deceive through the woman and not through the man? Because our reason cannot be led into sin unless it is preceded by carnal pleasure, through the impulse of weakness; and that pleasure ought rather to obey reason as a ruling man. This takes place in every individual within a certain hidden and secret marriage.

We understand the serpent as suggestion, the woman as the animal sense of the body, and the man as reason. Therefore, when an evil suggestion arises, it speaks as a serpent. But if thought alone takes pleasure in that suggestion, and no consent to carry out the deed follows because reason restrains it, the woman alone seems to have eaten the forbidden thing. But if the mind itself also decides that the sin should be committed, then the man has been deceived, and the woman seems to have given the man food.

To consent to enticement is to eat from the forbidden tree. Then the human being is rightly expelled from blessed life as from paradise, and sin is imputed to him even if the act does not follow; for although there is no guilt in deeds, the conscience is nevertheless held guilty in its confession.

This is according to the anagogical sense. According to metaphor, however, this crafty serpent may signify the cunning of heretics. Some of them promise, with excessive eloquence and subtlety, an opening into the knowledge of hidden things and of good and evil, and display it as something to be discerned in the human being himself, as in the tree planted in the middle of paradise.

Against this serpent the Apostle cries out when he says: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (II Cor. XI). Our carnal desire is deceived by the words of this serpent; and through it Adam was deceived—not Christ, but the Christian.

This serpent therefore says to the woman: “Why did God command you to eat from every tree of paradise?” So also the curious desire of heretics, and so wicked preachers, kindle the hearts of carnal hearers to love the deceit of error, saying: “Why have you fled from possessing the knowledge that lies hidden? Always seek new things; attain the knowledge of good and evil.” Hence that woman in Solomon, representing the type of heretics, says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. IX).

Then the same serpent added: “On whatever day you eat, your eyes will immediately be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” So all heretics generally profess a claim to divinity; they deceive by promising knowledge and reproach those whom they find believing simply. And because they persuade people toward all carnal things, they try to lead them toward what is like the opening of the carnal eyes, so that the inner eye may be darkened.

The woman therefore saw that the tree was good. She took its fruit and ate. The woman ate before the man because carnal people are more easily persuaded to sin, while spiritual people are not so quickly deceived. And she gave it to her husband, and he ate, because after the pleasure of our carnal desire, our reason also is subjected to sin, and thus we turn over certain slippery things in our thoughts.

We must be vigilant, because we ought not look upon what we are not permitted to desire. To preserve a pure mind in thought from the wantonness of its pleasure, the eyes—as a kind of robbers—must be lowered away from sin. For Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree if she had not first looked upon it carelessly. We should therefore consider with what restraint we must limit our sight with regard to forbidden things, we who live according to moral discipline, if even the mother of the living came to death through her eyes.

For this reason, also, the prophet says in the voice of the Jews concerning one who, by looking at outward things, lost his inward possessions without desiring what was good: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. III). In desiring visible things, he lost invisible virtues. Thus the one who lost his inner fruit through outward sight suffered the plunder of his heart through the bodily eye.

Therefore, to guard the purity of the heart, we must also maintain discipline over our outward senses. However strong the mind may be in virtue, however firm it may be in seriousness, the carnal senses nevertheless make a childish clamor outwardly. Unless they are restrained by the weight of inner seriousness and by a kind of youthful strength, they drag the unarmed mind toward everything unstable and trivial.

In our first ancestor we learned that we commit every wickedness of sin in three ways: by suggestion, by pleasure, and by consent. The first is carried out through the enemy, the second through the flesh, and the third through the spirit. The adversary suggests what is wicked; the flesh submits itself to pleasure; and finally the spirit, overcome by pleasure, consents.

Thus the serpent suggested what was wicked; Eve, as the flesh, submitted herself to pleasure; and Adam, like the spirit, overcome by suggestion and pleasure, consented. We recognize suggestion in sin; we are overcome by pleasure; and through consent we are also bound. Therefore we should cry out with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII), so that we may hear the consolation that follows: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

Again, sin is committed in the heart in four ways and brought to completion in action in four ways. In the heart, it is committed through suggestion, pleasure, consent, and the boldness of self-defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, pleasure through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and boldness through pride.

Sin is likewise brought to completion in action through the same four ways. First, the hidden fault is committed; afterward the guilt is openly revealed even before the eyes of human beings, without shame; then it is made habitual; and finally it is nourished either by the deceptions of false hope or by the obstinacy of miserable despair.

### CHAPTER XVI. Where Adam and Eve Saw That They Were Naked

When they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made loincloths for themselves. The rational soul was ashamed of the beastlike movement in the members of its flesh and struck them with shame—not only because it perceived there something it had never before perceived, but also because that shameful movement arose from the transgression of the commandment.

There it perceived with what grace it had previously been clothed, when in its nakedness it suffered nothing indecent. Finally, in their disturbance they ran to the fig leaves, which they perhaps first found in their confusion, and sewed loincloths— that is, coverings for the waist. Because they had abandoned what had been a source of glory, they covered what had become a source of shame.

Nor do I think that they had considered that their itching members should now be covered by those leaves because such leaves were suitable for that purpose. Rather, by a hidden impulse they were driven to this in their disturbance, so that even for those who did not know it, their punishment might signify something: the deed would convict the sinner and instruct the reader of the written account.

Blessed Ambrose briefly but clearly explained the mystery of this tree, under which Nathanael also saw the Lord still situated. He said:

“Blessed are those who tie their horses beneath the vine and the olive tree, consecrating the labor of their journeys to peace and joy, lest the fig tree—that is, the itching of the world’s seductive pleasures—still cast its shadow: lowly in height, frail for labor, soft for use, barren in fruit.”

And elsewhere he says:

“What is more serious,” he says, “is that Adam girded himself with this interpretation in the place where he ought rather to have girded himself with the fruit of chastity. For in the loins with which we gird ourselves, certain seeds of generation are said to exist. Adam therefore wrongly girded himself there with useless leaves, where he signified not the future fruit of generation but certain future sins.”

“When they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves and covered themselves,” because those who embrace the harshness of the world, who are plowed by the itch of carnal pleasure, and who, deceived by heretical perversity and stripped of the grace of God, gather coverings of lies like fig leaves, make girdles for themselves out of wickedness when they lie about the Lord or the Church.

And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the paradise at the breeze after midday, Adam and his wife hid themselves. Such people, who had fallen away from the light of truth, were fittingly visited after midday. Hence the Lord ascended the cross at midday and, having promised the thief a dwelling in paradise, gave up his spirit after midday—that is, at the ninth hour—so that at the very hour when the first human being had touched the tree of transgression, the second human being might ascend the tree of redemption; and at the hour of the day when he had expelled the transgressors from paradise, he might bring the confessor into paradise.

“He hid himself,” it says, “Adam and his wife from the face of the Lord God, in the middle of the tree of paradise.”

(Bede.) When God turns his face away inwardly, we should not be surprised that things occur which resemble madness through excessive shame and fear. That hidden impulse also continued, so that they unknowingly did things that would signify something to their descendants, who would one day know these things, for whose sake they were written.

Those who sin hide from the face of God because they render themselves unworthy of the sight of divine mercy. They hide from the face of God—not so that the inward judge may fail to see their conscience, but so that they themselves may never behold the glory of his face except by repenting.

### CHAPTER XVII. Where the Lord Speaks to Adam in Paradise after His Transgression

And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: “Where are you?” He did not ask because he was ignorant, but by reproving him he admonished him to consider where God was not. For since he had eaten from the forbidden tree, he had already died the death of the soul, since God, its life, had abandoned it.

This also surely has a symbolic significance: just as the commandment was given to the man, through whom it would come to the woman, so the man is questioned first. The commandment came from the Lord through the man to the woman, but sin came from the devil through the woman to the man.

And God called Adam: “Where are you?” Here he shows that God does not despise those who fall away from faith or good works into his lies and their own desires, but still calls them to return through repentance, because he does not desire the death of the sinner but that he should turn and live. Therefore there is no need for any sinners to despair, since even the ungodly are summoned to hope for pardon.

He said: “I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” It is sufficiently probable that God was accustomed to appear to those first human beings in human form, through a creature suited to such an action. He had never permitted them to notice their nakedness, lifting their attention toward heavenly things, until after sin they had felt the shameful movement in their members under the penalty imposed upon their members.

They were therefore affected as human beings are accustomed to be affected beneath the eyes of other human beings. Such an emotion was the punishment of sin: they wished to hide from one whom nothing can escape. For what already caused them shame in relation to themselves—and for which they had made loincloths—they were much more ashamed to be seen in that condition by the one who, as though in a familiar manner, brought human eyes through a visible creature in order to see them.

The Lord, wishing also to punish sinners by questioning them according to the manner of justice, imposed an additional penalty beyond the punishment that had already compelled them to feel shame: “Who told you,” he said, “that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” For death, conceived because of God’s sentence, by which he had threatened them in this way, caused the members to be perceived with desire, where it is [or: they are] said to have been opened eyes, and what caused shame followed.

And Adam said: “The woman whom you gave to be my companion gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.” Pride never says, “I have sinned.” It has the deformity of confusion but does not possess the humility of confession.

These things were written so that we might understand why those questions too were surely asked: namely, so that we might observe how people struggle with pride even today, striving to attribute whatever evil they have done to the Creator, while wishing whatever good they have done to be attributed to themselves.

“The woman,” he says, “whom you gave as my companion gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate,” as though she had been given for this purpose, rather than so that she herself would obey the man and both would obey God.

And the Lord God said to the woman: “Why have you done this?” She replied: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” She too does not confess her sin, but attributes it to another—with a different sex but equal arrogance.

“The serpent,” she says, “deceived me, and I ate,” as though the serpent’s persuasion ought to have been preferred to God’s command; and she also attributes the cause of her guilt to the Creator, who created the serpent in paradise through which she was deceived.

The marks of true humility are for each person to recognize his own iniquity and, once recognized, to disclose it by verbal confession. In contrast, it is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and to defend the sin committed by denying it, and then to multiply it by defending what has been exposed.

From the fall of the first human being we derive these additions to wickedness, since from that fall we drew the very root of guilt. For when he had touched the forbidden tree, he hid himself from the face of the Lord among the trees of paradise. In that hiding, because he could not remain hidden from God, the effect of concealment is not described but the emotion is indicated.

When the Lord reproved Adam and his wife because they had eaten from the forbidden tree, they immediately replied: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” They were questioned for this purpose: so that by confessing they might erase the sin they had committed by transgressing.

The serpent, however, that persuader who was not to be recalled to forgiveness, was not questioned about its guilt. The human being was asked where he was so that he might look upon the guilt he had committed and, by confessing, recognize how far he was from the face of his Creator.

But both chose the consolations of self-defense rather than confession. When the man tried to excuse his sin through the woman, and the woman through the serpent, they increased the guilt that they attempted indirectly to protect. Adam touched the Lord by suggesting that he himself had been the author of their sin because he had made the woman; Eve referred the guilt to the Lord because he had placed the serpent in paradise.

They had heard through the mouth of the deceiving devil, “You will be like gods.” Since they could not become like God in divinity, they tried, to complete their error, to make God like themselves in guilt. Thus, while they attempted to defend their guilt, they added to it, so that upon examination their guilt became more atrocious than it had been when committed.

Therefore even now the branches of the human race draw bitterness from this root, so that whenever someone is reproved for his vice, he hides himself beneath words of defense as beneath certain leaves of trees and flees from the face of his Creator into dark retreats of excuse, because he does not wish what he has done to be known.

In this concealment he does not hide himself from the Lord but hides the Lord from himself. He acts so that he may not see the one who sees everything, not so that he himself may not be seen.

In contrast, for any sinner the beginning of illumination is the humility of confession, because the person who is not ashamed to confess the evil he has done has already refused to spare himself. The one who could have excused himself by defending himself most quickly defends himself by accusing himself.

Thus, when Lazarus had died and was weighed down by a great mass, the Lord does not say, “Come back to life,” but, “Come out.” In that resurrection, which took place in his body, it is signified how we are raised in the heart, when the dead man is told, “Come out.” The human being who has died in sin and has already been buried beneath the weight of evil habit, lying hidden within his own conscience through wickedness, comes out from himself through confession.

“To the dead man it is said, ‘Come out,’” so that he may be urged to leave the excuse and concealment of sin and come out into self-accusation with his own mouth. Hence the prophet David, reviving from the death of so great a crime, came out, as it were, at the Lord’s voice when, reproved by Nathan, he accused himself of what he had done.

### CHAPTER XVIII. Where Judgment Is Pronounced upon the Serpent

And the Lord said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all the animals and beasts of the earth.”

The serpent was not asked why it had done this. It may be understood that it had not done it by its own nature and will, but that the devil had acted through it and by means of it—the devil who had already been destined for the fire because of the sin of his ungodliness and pride. Therefore what is now said to the serpent, and is certainly also referred to the one who acted through the serpent, is expressed figuratively. For in these words that tempter is described as he would be toward the human race.

“You will walk upon your breast, and you will eat earth all the days of your life,” and so forth. The serpent walks upon its breast because all the devil’s steps are wickedness and deceit. By the breast he indicates the craftiness and subtlety of his thoughts, by which he creeps toward those whom he wishes to deceive.

For this reason the ancient translation has: “You will crawl upon your breast and belly.” He crawls upon his breast when he suggests wicked thoughts to earthly human beings whom he desires to make his members. He crawls upon his belly when, after overcoming them through gluttony, he stirs them to the heat of lust.

Everything that crawls drags its body along the earth. The body of the devil is all the reprobate. He crawls upon his breast and belly when through wicked thoughts or the enticements of feasting and luxury he presses people down toward the lowest things.

He devours the earth when he feeds upon and delights in the error of sinners and drags those whom he deceives toward destruction. For just as the saints are often indicated by the name “heavens,” so those who set their minds on earthly things are indicated by the name “earth.”

The same is said later to Adam: “You are earth, and you will go into earth,” which our translation has as: “You are dust, and you will return to dust.”

As a sign of this devouring, that spiritual serpent itself—the irrational serpent that the devil used as his instrument to deceive the human being—is now commanded to eat material earth, although earlier it had been permitted, together with the other animals of the earth, to feed on the herbs and fruits of the trees.
