“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.”

The seed of the woman is the whole human race. The seed of the devil is the transgressing angels, who were corrupted by imitating his pride and rebellion. His seed is wicked suggestion; the seed of the woman is the fruit of good works by which wicked suggestion is resisted.

How greatly the enmity of this serpent and its seed would assail the human race, and how greatly all the elect exert themselves against that enmity by right living, is clearer than the sun to all the faithful.

A sign of this enmity also appears in the nature of the irrational serpent, because it is always hostile to all animals and beasts of the earth on account of the universal plague of poison implanted in it. This must be understood as having been implanted in it from the time of this curse, and not before.

“She will crush your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel.”

The woman crushes the serpent’s head when the holy Church, having immediately detected the devil’s snares and poisonous persuasions, drives them away and, as though trampling upon them, reduces them to nothing. She crushes the serpent’s head when she resists the pride by which Eve was deceived, humbling herself under the powerful hand of God. For the beginning of every sin is pride.

And the serpent lies in wait for the woman’s heel because the devil, like a roaring lion, circles around the Church, seeking whom he may devour and seeking how he may turn aside the steps of our good action. He lies in wait for the heel when he strives to seize us at the end of the present life.

Since the heel is the end of the body, it is not improperly understood as signifying the end of our life. Both meanings are also figuratively announced by the condition of the serpent itself, which is commonly crushed by all who can do so and nevertheless does not cease to lie in wait for the feet of human beings in order to strike them.

(Isidore.) Some have understood the words, “I will put enmity between you and the woman,” as referring to the Virgin from whom the Lord was born. At that time the Lord was promised as one who would be born from her to overcome the enemy and destroy death, of which the enemy was the author, as it is written in David: “From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. CIX).

They also understand the words that follow—“She will crush your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel”—as referring to the fruit of Mary’s womb, which is Christ. That is: “You will trip him so that he may die; but after conquering you, he will rise again and crush your head,” which is death.

David likewise said, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC). By the asp he meant death, by the basilisk sin, by the lion Antichrist, and by the dragon the devil.

### CHAPTER XIX. Where Corruption Is Imposed upon the Woman and Also upon Adam

He also said to the woman: “I will multiply your troubles and your conceptions; in pain you will bear children.”

These words of God addressed to the woman are likewise understood much more fittingly in a figurative and prophetic sense. Nevertheless, since the woman had not yet given birth, and the pain and groaning of childbirth come only from the body of death [or: of the dying body], which was conceived through the transgression of the commandment, this punishment is also referred to the literal meaning.

Likewise, in what follows—“You will be under your husband’s power, and he will rule over you”—although it is not fitting to believe that the woman was made before sin in any other way than so that the man would rule her and she would live under his authority, it may rightly be understood that a kind of servitude is signified, one that belongs more to a condition than to love. Thus even the form of servitude by which human beings later began to be servants of other human beings is found to have arisen from the punishment of sin.

The Apostle indeed said: “Through love serve one another” (Gal. V), but he never said, “Rule over one another.” Husband and wife can therefore serve one another through love, but the Apostle does not permit a woman to rule over a man.

God’s sentence assigned this to the man; and the woman earned a husband as her lord not by nature but by guilt. Yet unless this is observed, nature will be further corrupted and guilt increased.

Figuratively, however, these words apply to the Church, the spouse of Christ. Her troubles are multiplied in this life after the guilt of transgression so that, chastened, she may reach eternal life. Her conceptions are also multiplied, as she strives to beget spiritual offspring for God by preaching and living rightly.

Therefore she says to that offspring through the distinguished preacher: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV). She bears children in pain when, in anxious concern, she fears that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, their minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ.

She acts under the man’s authority because she serves the Lord in fear and rejoices in him not in security but with trembling. If she had never sinned, she would be joined to him only in the embrace of love.

“And he will rule over you”: he restrains her carnal movements and advances her toward the redemption of heavenly life through the continual exercise of higher instruction. If she had never fallen away, she would always reign with him in shared freedom.

In the moral sense, what does the punishment of the woman signify when it is said to her, “In pain you will bear children,” except that carnal pleasure, which had struggled painfully against the formation of a good habit, suffers pain at the beginning when it wishes to overcome an evil habit, and thus, through a better habit, gives birth to a good work as to a child?

But when he added, “Your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you,” this signifies that carnal pleasure, which had struggled painfully against the formation of a good habit, becomes more cautious after being disciplined by those very pains; to prevent itself from falling, it obeys reason and willingly serves as though reason were a commanding husband.

And to Adam he said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat from it,’ cursed is the earth in your work. In labors you shall eat from it all the days of your life; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth,” and so forth. Who does not know that these are the labors of the human race upon the earth—labors that would not exist if the happiness that had been in paradise had been preserved? For because of the human being’s sin, the earth was cursed so that it might bring forth thorns, not so that it itself might feel punishment, since it is without sensation, but so that it might continually place the guilt of human sin before human eyes, warning them at some point to turn away from sins and convert to God’s commandments. Poisonous plants, too, were created for the punishment or discipline of mortals; and all this happened because of sin, since we became mortal because of sin. Through fruitless trees also an insult is directed at human beings, so that they may understand how shameful it is to be without the fruit of good works in God’s field, that is, in the Church, and may fear lest God abandon them, since they themselves also abandon fruitless trees in their fields and apply no cultivation to them. Before sin, therefore, it is not written that the earth produced anything except grass for fodder and fruit-bearing trees; but after sin we see many things both dreadful and fruitless growing, for the reason we have mentioned.

Mystically, however, the earth that is said to have been cursed because of Adam’s transgression is best understood as our flesh, which now brings forth thorns and thistles for us, because, propagated through the desire of the flesh, we suffer from that very flesh the pricks and incitements of vices. Since the divine voice teaches that the dart of the curse is to be punished by a severe vengeance, so much so that it even closes the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, what does it mean that now, when the human being sins, the divine voice imposes in the earth’s curse what the human being is forbidden to do? But it must be understood that Sacred Scripture speaks of a curse in two ways: one, namely, which it approves, and another which it condemns. A curse is uttered in one way by the judgment of justice, and in another by the resentment of vengeance. The curse pronounced by the judgment of justice was uttered when the first human being sinned, when he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work.” A curse is pronounced by the judgment of justice when it is said to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you.” Again, because a curse is pronounced not by a just judgment but by resentful vengeance, we are warned by Paul’s preaching, where he says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII). And again the Truth says: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God.” God, therefore, is said to curse, and yet the human being is forbidden to curse, because what the human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only with the scrutiny and power of justice.

Even holy men, when they pronounce a sentence of cursing, do not utter it from a desire for vengeance, but it bursts forth from the scrutiny of justice. Within themselves they perceive God’s subtle judgment, and they recognize that the evils arising outwardly ought to be struck by a curse; and in cursing they do not sin because they do not disagree with the inward judgment. Hence Peter hurled a sentence of cursing at Simon, who had offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts VIII). By saying not “is,” but “may it be,” he indicated that he had spoken these words not in the indicative but in the optative mood. Hence Elijah said to the two companies of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven now and consume you” (IV Kings VII). The outcome of the matter showed how greatly the sentence of both was strengthened by the reasoning of truth. Simon perished in eternal destruction, and fire descending from above consumed the two companies of fifty. The power that followed therefore testifies with what intention a sentence of cursing is uttered. For when the innocence of the one who curses remains, yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even unto destruction, it is inferred from the outcome on both sides that the sentence was hurled against the guilty by the good and inward Judge.

“By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Here understand as that bread the one who said: “I am the bread of life who came down from heaven” (John VI). We eat this bread by the sweat of our face, because we ascend to the sight of the divine majesty only through the labor of necessary affliction.

The first human being was created in such a way that, while time continued, he himself would not pass away with time. He stood amid the passing moments, for he was by no means advancing toward the end of life through the increase of days. He stood all the more robustly the more firmly he clung to the One who always stands. But when he touched what was forbidden, immediately, having offended the Creator, he began to move along with time. Hence it was said to him: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” Having lost the state of immortality, the course of mortality swallowed him up; and while he was drawn from youth to old age, and from old age to death, by passing away he learned what he had been when standing. Because we are born from his stock, we retain the bitterness of the root, as it were, in a young shoot. Since we derive our origin from him, we receive his course by being born, so that in the very daily moment in which we live we continually pass away from life, and the span of life from which we are thought to grow diminishes for us from that very source. Infancy passes into childhood, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age into death; and in the course of the present life it is driven toward loss by its very increases. It continually declines from the point at which it believes it is progressing toward an extension of life. We cannot have a fixed condition here, where we live only temporarily; indeed, our very living each day is a passing from life. The first human being could not have possessed this decline before his guilt, because time passed while he himself stood. But after he sinned, he placed himself, as it were, upon a slippery course of temporality; and because he ate the forbidden food, he immediately discovered the decline of his former state.

And he called his wife’s name Eve, because she is the mother of all the living. Adam, by divine inspiration, evidently gave this name to his wife, and it most aptly corresponds to his holy Church, in whose unity alone—the unity called Catholic—the door of life stands open to all.

The Lord God also made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them. This too was done for the sake of a sign. For by such clothing the Lord indicates that they had already been made mortal. Skins, which are taken only from dead animals, contain a figure of death. Thus, when the human being desired to be God against the commandment—not through legitimate imitation, but through illicit pride—he was cast down to the mortality of beasts.

They themselves had indeed made loincloths for themselves from fig leaves, with which to cover their nakedness; but the Lord made tunics of skins for them and clothed their whole bodies. They had lost through transgression the glory of innocence and had held out to themselves a veil of excuse by which they might transfer their guilt to the Creator; but the Creator himself, by the sentence of a just judgment, removed their state of unchangeable life and changed them in soul and body alike through the punishment of mortality.

The Gospel parable (Luke XV) relates that the merciful father, when his prodigal son returned to him through repentance, ordered, among other gifts, that the first robe be brought out and that he be clothed in it. This mystically indicates that the elect will receive in Christ, at the end of the age, the garment of immortality that they lost in Adam at the beginning of the world—and indeed with a greater grace. Adam was made immortal in such a way that he could avoid death if he kept the commandment; but the children of the resurrection will be immortal in such a way that they can neither ever die nor be affected by fear of death. Concerning the reception of this robe the Apostle says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (I Cor. XV). Where he says “put on,” he clearly signifies that the nakedness has been removed—the nakedness that Adam and Eve recognized in themselves after the sin and were ashamed of.

And he said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.” Concerning this, Saint Augustine says:

“Howsoever and by whatever means this may have been said, nevertheless, when God said, ‘one of us,’ it must be understood in no other way than that the plural number is taken on account of the Trinity, just as it had been said: ‘Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness’; and as the Lord also says of himself and the Father: ‘We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him’ (John XIV). Thus what the proud man had desired was turned back upon his head, with the very outcome of his desire suggested by the serpent: ‘You shall be like gods.’ ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘Adam has become like one of us.’ These are God’s words, spoken not so much to mock him as to deter the others for whose sake these things were written, lest they become proud in the same way. ‘He has become,’ he says, ‘like one of us, knowing good and evil.’ What else should be understood than that an example intended to inspire fear has been set forth? He not only failed to become what he had wanted to become, but did not even preserve what he had been made.

“Elsewhere concerning this he says: ‘These are not the words of God confessing, but rather of one reproaching him: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us,” just as the Apostle says: “Give me this injury” (II Cor. XII), clearly intending the opposite to be understood.’”

“Now, therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever,” the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight, to work the earth from which he had been taken. The preceding words are God’s; this deed followed because of those very words. Since he had been alienated from life—not only from the life which, if he had kept the commandment, he would have received together with the angels, but also from the life he had led in paradise in a certain blessed condition of body—he had necessarily to be separated from the tree of life. Either that blessed bodily condition was sustained by the tree through an invisible power arising from a visible thing, or the tree contained a visible sacrament of invisible wisdom. He had to be alienated from it, whether because he was already going to die or because he was to be treated as excommunicated, just as in this paradise, that is, in the Church, ecclesiastical discipline customarily removes people from the visible sacraments of the altar.

## CHAPTER XX. The Expulsion of the First Parents from Paradise

“And he expelled Adam, and placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to guard the way to the tree of life.” The ancient translation has this passage as follows: “And he expelled Adam, and placed him opposite the paradise of delight; and he appointed the cherubim and a flaming rhomphaia,” and so forth. If we follow that version, we must also believe that this was done for the sake of signification; nevertheless, it was done so that, opposite the paradise in which blessed life was also spiritually signified, the sinner might dwell in misery.

As for the statement that God placed the cherubim and the flaming sword before the paradise of delight, this must certainly be understood as having been done through heavenly powers in the visible paradise, so that through angelic ministry a certain fiery guard might be present there. Yet it cannot be doubted that this was not done without also signifying something concerning the spiritual paradise. The guard is rightly affirmed to be turning, because a time would eventually come when it could also be removed.

It was removed when Enoch was taken away from sinners; removed when Elijah was carried off in a fiery chariot; removed for all the elect when, after the Lord had been baptized, the heavens were opened to him; likewise removed for individual elect persons when they are washed in the baptismal font; and removed more perfectly for those same people when, released from the bonds of the flesh, each in his own time ascends to the glory of the heavenly paradise.

Again, since *cherubim* is interpreted as “the multitude of knowledge,” or “knowledge multiplied,” it is rightly said that the cherubim and the flaming sword were placed to guard the way to the tree of life. For through heavenly knowledge of discipline and through the labor of temporal afflictions, the return to our heavenly homeland is opened to us, from which we departed through the folly of transgression and through the desire for carnal pleasures.

It is also fitting that he does not simply speak of a flame, but says that a flaming sword was placed before paradise, so that he might indicate that the enticements of temporal desire must be struck within us by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI), if we desire to penetrate to the tree of life, which is the Lord Christ. He appropriately reports that the same sword is turning, to indicate mystically that this sword is not always necessary for us, but that, as it is written, “there is a time for war, a time for peace.” It is a time of war when, in the pursuit of this life, we fight against the powers of the air and also against the vices of our mind and body; a time of peace when we are crowned with perfect victory.

Having briefly explained these matters concerning the creation of the world and the establishment of the human being in paradise, historically and spiritually, according to the statements and understanding of our forebears, we have judged that the first book of this work should end here, so that we may consider at the beginning of the following book the remaining things that Sacred Scripture records after Adam’s expulsion from paradise.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0501]

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the Two Brothers, Cain and Abel, and the Figure Each of Them Represented

**(Chap. IV.)** “Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived and bore Cain, saying: ‘I have acquired a man through God.’” Cain is interpreted as “acquisition” or “possession,” that is, *κτῆσις* (*ktēsis*). Thus, expressing his etymology, she says: *canithi*, that is, “I have acquired a man through God.”

Again she bore his brother Abel. Abel is interpreted as “mourning,” or “vanity,” or “vapor,” or “wretched.”

Now Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer. After many days it happened that Cain brought an offering to the Lord from the fruits of the earth; Abel, however, brought from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat portions. And the Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look.

How could Cain have known that God had accepted his brother’s offerings and rejected his own, unless that interpretation is true which Theodotion gives: “And the Lord kindled over Abel and his sacrifice, but over Cain and over his sacrifice he did not kindle”? We read that fire customarily came down from heaven to consume a sacrifice both at the dedication of the temple under Solomon and when Elijah built an altar on Mount Carmel. The almighty God does not accept a gift from the hand when it is brought forth by a heart bound by wickedness. The one who wishes to offer a gift to God must first cleanse his mind, because everything given to God is weighed according to the mind of the giver.

Cain was very angry, and his face fell. And the Lord said to him: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do evil, your sin will immediately be present at the door. Yet its desire will be under you, and you will rule over it.”

Necessity compels us to linger longer over individual points. For here too the sense in the Hebrew differs greatly from that in the translators of the Septuagint. God says to Cain: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will it not be forgiven you? But if you do not do well, your sin will sit before the doors, and its association will be toward you; but you rule over it.”

What does he mean by saying, “Why are you angry, and, tortured by envy and resentment against your brother, do you lower your face to the earth? If you do well, will not every offense be forgiven you?” Or, as Theodotion says, “Will it not be acceptable?”—that is, “I will accept your gift, as I accepted your brother’s gift.” But if you do evil, your sin will immediately sit before the entrance, and you will be accompanied by such a doorkeeper. Yet because you possess free will, I warn you not to let sin rule over you, but to rule over sin.

As for what is read in the Septuagint—“The Lord said to Cain: Why have you become sorrowful, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?”—because it is not clear why or from where this was said, the obscurity has produced many interpretations, as each interpreter of the divine Scriptures tries to explain it according to the rule of faith.

Sacrifice is rightly offered to the true God, to whom alone sacrifice must be offered; but it is not rightly divided when the places, times, or things themselves that are offered are not rightly distinguished; or when the one who offers and the one to whom it is offered are not distinguished; or when the circumstances in which what has been offered is distributed for eating are not distinguished. Thus we may understand “division” here as “discernment.” The offering may be made where it ought not to be, or something may be offered there that ought to be offered elsewhere; it may be offered when it ought not to be, or something may be offered then that ought to be offered at another time; something may be offered that ought never and nowhere to have been offered; a person may keep for himself the better portions of the same kind of things rather than those he offers to God; or an irreligious person, or anyone who ought not to be made a participant, may be made a participant in what has been offered.

Which of these displeased God in Cain cannot easily be discovered. But since the Apostle John, speaking of these brothers, says: “Not like Cain, who was from the evil one and killed his brother. And for what reason did he kill him? Because his works were evil, but his brother’s righteous” (I John III), it may be understood that the Lord did not look upon his offering because he was dividing it wrongly in this very respect: he was giving God something of his, but giving himself to himself.

All who do not follow God’s will but their own do this—that is, those who come not with an upright but with a perverse heart. They nevertheless offer God a gift by which they think he can be bought off, so that he may not assist in healing their depraved desires but in fulfilling them. This is characteristic of the earthly city: to worship a god or gods whose assistance may enable one to rule in earthly victories and peace, not from the charity of serving others but from the desire to dominate. The good use the world in order to enjoy God; the wicked, by contrast, wish to use God in order to enjoy the world, although they do not believe that he either exists or takes care of human affairs.

“And Cain said to Abel his brother”—the words spoken by the Lord are understood. It is therefore superfluous that the following is found in the Samaritan and our volume: “Let us go out into the field.”

And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him, and so forth. The birth of Adam’s two sons bears a likeness to the two peoples who were to come to faith at different times, equal in their works but unequal in their love before God.

Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer. But just as Cain’s sacrifice from the fruits of the earth is rejected, whereas Abel’s sacrifice from the sheep and their fat is accepted, so the faith of the New Testament, praising God through the grace of innocence, is preferred to the earthly works of the Old Testament.

God said to Cain: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” For even if the Jews formerly performed those right actions rightly, they are nevertheless guilty of unbelief because, when Christ came, they did not distinguish the time of the New Testament from the time of the Old Testament.

For if Cain had obeyed God when he said, “Be still; its desire will be under you, and you will rule over it,” he would have turned his sin toward himself, attributing it to himself and trusting in God. Thus, aided by the grace of forgiveness, he himself would have ruled over his sin; he would not have been ruled by it and, as sin’s servant, killed his innocent brother.

So also the Jews, in whom this figure was enacted, if they had ceased from their agitation and recognized the time of salvation through grace for the forgiveness of sins, would have heard Christ saying: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” Then they would have turned their sin toward themselves in confession, as it is written in the Psalm, where the prophet says: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. XI). And, while they were still in mortal bodies, they would have ruled over that sin as free through the hope of grace.

But now, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, lifted up by works of the law rather than humbled by their sins, they did not cease; instead, they stumbled over the stone of stumbling and burned with anger against Christ. Seeing that his works were acceptable to God, they grieved.

**(Gregory.)** Tropologically, an offering is made rightly when something is done with a right intention; but it is not divided rightly if what is done piously is not also examined with subtle discernment. To divide offerings rightly means to weigh all our good efforts carefully through discernment. Whoever neglects to do this sins even when offering rightly. Often, while we fail to distinguish carefully what we do with good zeal, we do not know how it will be judged without end; and sometimes what is thought to be a cause of virtue becomes a charge of guilt. We therefore offer rightly when we perform a good work with good zeal; but we do not divide rightly if we postpone exercising discernment in a good work.

Thus, after these events, Abel, the younger by birth, is killed by his elder brother. Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, the elder people. The former in a field, the latter at the place of Calvary.

**(Isidore.)** God asks Cain—not as one ignorant and seeking information from the one who knows, but as a judge questioning the guilty man whom he is to punish—where his brother is. He replied that he did not know and that he was not his brother’s keeper. To this day, what do the Jews reply when, with the voice of God—that is, of the holy Scriptures—we question them about Christ? They answer that they do not know Christ. Cain’s false ignorance is the Jews’ false denial. They would in some sense have been guardians of Christ if they had been willing to accept and guard the Christian faith.

God said to Cain: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.” Thus the divine voice accuses the Jews in the holy Scriptures. The blood of Christ has a great voice in the earth when, having received it, all nations respond, “Amen.” This is the clear voice, the voice of blood, which the blood itself expresses through the mouths of the faithful redeemed by that same blood.

God says to Cain: “You shall be cursed upon the earth, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand.” Why is Cain cursed in his sin, whereas in Adam’s sin the earth is cursed? Because Cain knew of the condemnation of the first transgression and was not afraid to add the crime of fratricide to original sin; therefore he was considered worthy of a greater curse.

The unbelieving Jewish people are cursed by the earth—that is, by the Church, which opened its mouth in the confession of sins to receive the blood of Christ, poured out for the forgiveness of all sins—from the hand of the persecutor who refused to be under grace but chose to be under the law. Thus he was cursed by the Church; that is, the Apostle’s testimony answered that he was cursed by the Church: “For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse of the law” (Heb. VI).

“When you work it, it shall not give you its fruits.” For in the very earth that Christ bore—that is, in his flesh—they worked our salvation by crucifying Christ, who died for our sins. Yet that earth did not give them its power, because they were not justified by the power of his resurrection, who rose for our justification. And although he was crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God.

This, then, is the power of that earth, which it did not reveal to the impious and unbelieving. Hence, when he rose, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified, just as Cain, working the earth, did not see the grain that was to be sown.

“Wandering and fugitive,” or, as it is written in the Septuagint, “You shall be groaning and trembling in the earth.” Now, who does not see, who does not recognize, throughout the whole earth wherever that people has been dispersed, how it is wandering among the nations and fugitive from Jerusalem; how it groans in grief over the loss of its kingdom and trembles with fear among innumerable Christian peoples? Therefore Cain replied:

“My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve forgiveness. Behold, today you drive me from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden; and I shall be wandering and fugitive on the earth. Therefore everyone who finds me will kill me.”

He said this in despair. After Cain had killed his brother, the Lord questioned him: “Where is Abel your brother?” He had insolently replied: “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” Therefore, condemned by a curse to live groaning and trembling upon the earth, he wished to beg for forgiveness; but, heaping sin upon sin, he considered his offense so great that God could not forgive it. Finally he answered the Lord: “My cause is greater than that I should be forgiven,” that is, “I have sinned more than I deserve to be absolved.” “Behold, you drive me from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden; and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth. And it shall happen that everyone who finds me will kill me.” “I am driven,” he says, “from your sight; and, unable to bear even the light because of the consciousness of my crime, I shall hide myself so as to lie concealed. And everyone who finds me will kill me, while, from the trembling of my body and the agitation of my deranged mind, he recognizes that I am one who deserves to be killed.”

**(Isidore.)** Allegorically, the Jewish people truly wanders and flees, groaning, lest, after losing even its earthly kingdom, it should be killed by this visible death. Cain says that this is a greater cause than the fact that our earth does not give him its power, lest he die spiritually. For he thinks according to the flesh and hides himself from the face of God—that is, he does not consider it serious to have God angry with him; but he fears that he may be found and killed. He thinks according to the flesh, like one working the earth whose power he does not receive. To think according to the flesh is death. Not understanding this, he grieves over the loss of his kingdom and trembles at bodily death. But what did God answer him?

“By no means will it be so; but whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “shall pay seven acts of vengeance.” The number seven is very often accustomed to be placed in Sacred Scripture for the fullness of any matter, as though he had said that the one who, even when warned by the severity of so great a condemnation, did not wish to restrain his hands from shedding blood, was to be punished by an exceedingly grave vengeance.

But God, unwilling to end his torment by a quick death, and not handing him over to the punishment by which he had condemned himself, said: “Not so”—that is, “You will not die in the way you imagine and take death as a remedy. Rather, you will live until the seventh generation and will be tormented by the fire of your conscience, so that whoever kills you will, according to a twofold interpretation, either free you in the seventh generation or free you from great torment.” This does not mean that the one who struck Cain was to be subjected to seven acts of vengeance, but that he pays the seven acts of vengeance that continued against Cain for so long, inflicting death on one who had been left alive for punishment.

This is the opinion of our forebears: they believe that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation. Adam begot Cain; Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Irad; Irad begot Mahuiael; Mahuiael begot Matusael; Matusael begot Lamech, who, being seventh from Adam, killed Cain—not intentionally, as is written in a certain Hebrew volume. Later he himself confesses: “I have killed a man in my wound, and a young man in my bruise; for Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, but Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

A Hebrew told me that, in their apocryphal books, seventy-seven souls are found to have descended from Lamech, and that vengeance was exacted from Lamech in this number because his line continued until the cataclysm of the waters. Others speculate variously about Cain’s seven acts of vengeance. They say that his first sin was that he did not divide rightly; the second, that he envied his brother; the third, that he acted deceitfully when he said, “Let us go out into the field”; the fourth, that he killed him; the fifth, that he shamelessly denied it, saying, “I do not know”; the sixth, that he condemned himself: “My guilt is greater than that I should be forgiven”; the seventh, that, although condemned, he did not repent, unlike the Ninevites and King Hezekiah of Judah, who delayed the death hanging over them with tears, so that those who had been condemned might not perish but might obtain God’s mercy by repenting.

They say that the most merciful God therefore postponed his punishment for seven generations, so that, compelled at least by his very evils and by the sorrow of a long life, he might repent and deserve to be absolved. According to the mystical interpretation, then, the Lord’s answer to Cain can be transferred in this way to the Jews, who tremble because of the loss of their temporal kingdom: “It will not happen as you say. The race of the impious and carnal Jews will not perish by bodily death. Whoever destroys them in this way shall pay seven acts of vengeance”—that is, shall remove from them the seven acts of vengeance by which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s killing, throughout the whole period that revolves in the number seven, the number of days. This is shown especially by the fact that the Jewish nation has not perished, as faithful Christians can see, but has deserved only dispersion, according to what Scripture says: “Do not kill them, lest they forget your law. Scatter them by your power, and bring them down” (Ps. LVIII).

The Lord placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. This sign was evidently that he should always live trembling and groaning, wandering and fugitive, never daring to have a quiet dwelling anywhere in the world. Perhaps for this reason he built a city in which he could be safe.

This is truly remarkable: all the nations that were subjected by the Romans passed over into the Roman religious system and accepted those sacrileges to be observed and celebrated; but the Jewish nation, whether under pagan kings or under Christian ones, did not lose the sign of its law and circumcision, by which it is distinguished from the other nations and peoples. Moreover, every emperor or king who found them in his kingdom bearing that sign did not kill them.

Cain therefore went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Naid. What the Septuagint translated as *Naid* is called *nod* in Hebrew and is interpreted as *σαλευόμενος* (*saleuomenos*), that is, “unstable,” “wavering,” and “of uncertain dwelling.” Naid is therefore not a land, as many of our people think; rather, the sentence of God is fulfilled, that he wandered here and there, wandering and fugitive.

Against this evil the Lord is petitioned in the Psalm: “Do not let my feet be moved, and let the hands of sinners not move me” (Ps. XXXV). Now the Jews, and all who are obstinate in various errors and resist the truth, go out from the face of God—that is, from the mercy of his love or from participation in his light—and dwell as fugitives in the land of agitation, that is, in carnal disturbance, opposed to the delight of God. This is opposed to Eden, which is interpreted as “delight,” that is, the planted paradise.

Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch, and Cain built a city.

**(Augustine.)** It is asked how Cain could establish a city, since a city is established for some multitude of human beings, whereas only two parents and two sons are reported to have existed, and one of the sons was killed by the other. Another is said to have been born in the place of the one who was killed.

Is the question raised because readers think that at that time there were only those human beings whom divine Scripture mentions, and do not notice that those two who were first created, and even those whom they begot, lived long enough to beget many others? Adam himself did not beget only those whose names are recorded, since Scripture, speaking of him, concludes by saying that he begot sons and daughters. Therefore, since they lived many more years than the Israelites spent in Egypt, who does not see how many people could have been born to fill that city, if the Hebrews could multiply so greatly in a much shorter time?

**(Isidore.)** What, then, does it signify that the offspring of the impious built a city at the very beginning of the world, unless you understand that the impious are founded in this life, whereas the holy are guests and pilgrims? Hence Abel, as a pilgrim on earth, did not establish a city—the Christian people did not establish one. The city of the saints is above, although here it gives birth to citizens among whom it lives as a pilgrim until the time of its kingdom arrives.

And he named it after his son Enoch. This son, in whose name Enoch was founded—that is, the earthly Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “possession”—signifies this city, and that it has both a beginning and an end on earth, where nothing more than what is visible is hoped for. (Gregory.) While the wicked neglect to pass in their hearts toward eternal things and do not perceive that all present things are fleeting, they fix their minds upon love of the present life and, as though it were a long dwelling-place, build a foundation for themselves in it, because they are not made firm in eternal realities through desire. Hence the first, Cain, is also described as having built a city, so that it might plainly be shown that he set his foundation upon earth who was alienated from the solidity of the eternal homeland. For, being a stranger to what is above, he laid his foundation in what is below, because he placed the dwelling-place of his heart in earthly pleasure. Hence also in his line Enoch, whose name is interpreted as “dedication,” is born first; but in the lineage of the elect Enoch is remembered as having been the seventh, [Col. 0508B] because the reprobate dedicate themselves by building themselves up in this present life, which comes first, whereas the elect await the dedication of their building at the end of time, that is, in the seventh [generation]. For you may see very many people thinking only about temporal things, seeking honors, longing for things to be acquired, and desiring nothing beyond this life. What, then, do these men dedicate in the first generation except themselves? And you may see the elect seeking none of the glory of the present life, willingly enduring poverty, and patiently suffering the world’s evils, so that they may be crowned at the end. Thus Enoch is born for the elect in the seventh generation, because they seek the dedication of their joy in the glory of the final recompense.

## CHAPTER II. On the sons of Lamech, who displayed music and the art of working iron and bronze, and on Lamech’s vengeance

Moreover, Enoch begot Irad, and Irad begot Maviael; and Maviael begot Matusael; and Matusael begot Lamech, who took two wives: the name of one was Ada, and the name of the other Sella. Ada bore Jahel, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and of shepherds; and the name of his brother was Jubal: he was the father of those who play the lyre and the organ. Concerning him Josephus, the Jewish historian, reports as follows: “Jubal,” he says, “cultivated music and praised the psaltery and the lyre; and lest the things that seemed to have been discovered by him should slip away from human memory, or perish before they came to be known, since Adam had foretold the destruction of all things, one destruction by the force of fire and another by the power and mass of waters, he made two pillars, one of bricks and the other of stones, and inscribed upon both whatever he had discovered. Thus, if the brick structure were destroyed by rains, the stone one, remaining, would enable people to learn what had been written; and likewise, because he had set up the other, brick pillar, it would preserve this one from the violence of fires, even if the stone one were dissolved. This stone pillar, nevertheless, remains to this day in the land of Syria. But Tubalcain, who was born from the other wife, excelling all in strength, practiced the arts of war becomingly.” (Isidore.) From these [arts] he also developed things that pertain to bodily desire, and he was the first to invent the art of working iron. It should be noted, however, that in the offspring of Seth no female born there is expressly named, whereas a female is mentioned only in the offspring of Cain: [Col. 0509A] this signifies that the earthly city will have carnal generations until its end, generations that arise from the union of husbands and wives.

And Lamech said to his wives, Ada and Sella: “Hear my voice; wives of Lamech, listen to my speech, for I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise. Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times sevenfold.” (Albinus.) Because the sin of homicide is read as having been punished in the seventh generation by the Flood, whereas the crime of adultery—which Lamech was the first of all to commit with two wives—was to be expiated only by the blood of Christ, who, according to the Gospel of Luke, came into the world in the seventy-seventh generation (Isidore); therefore, from Adam to Christ seventy-seven generations are found, in which the sin of Lamech, that is, of the whole world, was loosed by the shedding of Christ’s blood. Indeed, among the Jewish people also, because of the killing of Christ, seventy-seven acts of vengeance have been established, according to that saying of the Gospel in which it was said to the apostle Peter: “Not only seven times, but also seventy times seven, if he repents, is a brother to be forgiven” (Matthew 18); that is, the Jew who returns after the seventy-seven established acts of vengeance is to be received into Christ’s forgiveness.

Adam also knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, saying: “The Lord has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.” (Jerome.) Seth is properly called θέσις, that is, “placing,” because God placed him in Abel’s place; therefore he is called Seth, that is, “placing.” Seth, as some think, is interpreted as “resurrection,” and he is Christ; and his son Enos is interpreted as “man,” who began to invoke the name of the Lord. Although many of the Hebrews think otherwise: that at that time idols were first fashioned in the name of the Lord and in his likeness. (Isidore.) What, then, is understood by the statement that Enos is said to invoke the name of the Lord, except that every human being who is a child of resurrection lives in confession of God for as long as he is a pilgrim on earth? Likewise, through those two men, Abel—whose name is interpreted as “mourning”—and his brother Seth—whose name is interpreted as “resurrection”—the death of Christ and his life from the dead are prefigured. Therefore, to put it more briefly: Abel is mourning, Seth resurrection, and Enos man, because after mourning comes resurrection, and from resurrection comes the man who invokes God.

## CHAPTER III. How Adam again received sons, and the end of his life

### (CHAP. V.)

This is the book of the generation of Adam: on the day when God created man, he made him in the likeness of God; male and female he created them; and he blessed them and called their name Adam on the day when they were created. (Jerome.) “And he called,” it says, “their name Adam,” that is, “man.” The name “man,” however, applies equally to male and female.

Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and begot a son according to his likeness and image. Note that Adam was made in the image and likeness of God, whereas human beings were made in the likeness of Adam.

And the days of Adam after he begot Seth were eight hundred years, and he begot sons and daughters. And all the time that Adam lived was nine hundred and thirty years, and he died. Seth also lived one hundred and five years and begot Enos. Likewise, Enos begot Cainan; Cainan begot Malaleel; Malaleel begot Jareth; Jareth begot Enoch, and so forth. (Isidore.) This Enoch, the seventh from Adam, who pleased God and was taken away, signifies the seventh rest, to which everyone is referred who, as on the sixth day—that is, in the sixth age of the world—is formed through the coming of Christ. For after the six ages of the world have passed, after judgment has also taken place and heaven and earth have been renewed, the saints are transferred into the life of perpetual immortality. The fact that the number ten is indicated through Seth, from Adam to Noah, signifies the completion of the commandments in the works of the Church. If Noah’s three sons are added to this number, with the rejected one placed in the middle, the number twelve is completed. This number is prominent in the number of the patriarchs and apostles, because it is formed from the two parts of seven multiplied by one another; for three times four, or four times three, produces it. But the fact that the offspring of Adam through Cain ends with the number ten indicates the transgression of the commandments, or sin. For since Lamech is found written as the seventh from Adam, three sons and one daughter are added to him so that the number eleven may be completed, by which sin is demonstrated. That number is also closed by a female, from whose sex the beginning of sin was committed, through which we all die—namely, so that the pleasure of the flesh, which resists the spirit, might follow. Hence Lamech’s daughter herself, Noema, is interpreted as “pleasure.” Adam is interpreted as “man,” or “earthly,” or “native,” or “red earth.” The interpretation of these same names signifies the same thing. Seth likewise is interpreted as “placing,” or “resurrection,” as we have said; Enos is interpreted as “man”; Cainan as “lamentation,” or “their placing”; Malaleel as “praising God”; Jareth as “strengthening”; Enoch as “dedication”; Mathusala as “sending forth of death”; Lamech as “humbled”; Noah as “rest.” Thus a man proceeding from red earth, rising from sins, and added to the assembly of believers, will be a man invoking God and lamenting former sins; through patience he possesses his soul; and thus, rightly praising God, he is strengthened by the Spirit of God; he is dedicated to eternal life; and, having conquered death and subjected himself to God, he possesses everlasting rest.

## CHAPTER IV. On Mathusala and Lamech

### (CHAP. V.)

Mathusala also lived one hundred and eighty-seven years and begot Lamech, and so forth. It should be noted, however, that in the Seventy Translators this passage reads as follows: “And Mathusala lived one hundred and sixty-seven years and begot Lamech. And Mathusala lived after he begot Lamech eight hundred and two years, and begot sons and daughters; and all the days of Mathusala that he lived were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.” [Col. 0511A] This is a famous question, discussed and debated by all the churches: according to a careful calculation, Mathusala appears to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. For when Mathusala was one hundred and sixty-seven years old, he begot Lamech; and again, when Lamech was one hundred and eighty-eight years old, he begot Noah; and together, up to the day of Noah’s birth, Mathusala’s years of life amount to three hundred and fifty-five. In Noah’s six-hundredth year, however, the Flood occurred; and thus, when the calculation is made in parts, it is proved that the Flood occurred in Mathusala’s nine-hundred-and-fifty-fifth year. Since he is said to have lived more than nine hundred and sixty-nine years, there is no doubt that he lived fourteen years after the Flood. And how is it true that only eight persons were saved in the ark? It therefore remains that, as in many other passages, there is also an error in the number here. Indeed, I find it written in the Hebrew and Samaritan books as follows: “And Mathusala lived one hundred and eighty-seven years and begot Lamech; and Mathusala lived after he begot Lamech seven hundred and eighty-two years, and begot sons and daughters; and all the days of Mathusala were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died. And Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and begot Noah.” Thus, from the day of Mathusala’s birth to the day of Noah’s birth there are three hundred and sixty-nine years. Add to these Noah’s six hundred years, because the Flood occurred in the six-hundredth year of his life, and so Mathusala died in the nine-hundred-and-sixty-ninth year of his life, in the very year in which the Flood began. (Isidore.) For according to the Seventy, years of Mathusala are counted beyond the Flood, so that, since Christ alone is he whose life experiences no age, it might appear that even among those ancient men the Flood was not experienced.

Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and begot a son; and he called his name Noah, saying: “This one will comfort us from our works and from the labors of our hands, on the earth which the Lord has cursed.” (Jerome.) Noah is interpreted as “rest.” Therefore, because under him all the former works ceased through the Flood, he was called “rest.” Through all his actions Noah signifies Christ. For Noah, as we have said, is interpreted as “rest.” The Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11). Noah alone is found righteous among that people, and seven persons are granted to him because of his righteousness. Christ alone is righteous and perfect, and the seven churches, because of the sevenfold Spirit illuminating them, are granted to him as one Church.

## CHAPTER V. On the giants, and on the one hundred and twenty years granted by God to human beings for repentance

### (CHAP. VI.)

When human beings had begun to multiply upon the earth and had begotten children, the sons of God, seeing the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they had chosen. The Hebrew word *elohim* is common in number, and “God” and “gods” are alike called by it. For this reason Aquila dared to say, in the plural number, “sons of gods,” understanding gods to mean saints or angels. “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Psalm 81). (Augustine.) Hence Symmachus, following this interpretation, also says: “The sons of the mighty, seeing the daughters of men,” and so forth. But this raises the question how giants, born from intercourse with women, could have intercourse with them if they were not human beings but angels. As for the giants—that is, those of extraordinary size and strength—I think there is no reason for wonder that they could have been born from human beings, since after the Flood some such people are also reported to have existed; and in our own times, too, certain human bodies have been extraordinarily huge, not only those of men but also those of women. Therefore it is more credible that righteous men were called the sons of God and, having fallen through desire, sinned with women than that angels, who do not possess flesh, could have descended to that sin; although many people say so much about certain demons who are wicked toward women that it is not easy to reach a final judgment on this matter. (Albinus.) Scripture wished to call the daughters of men the offspring of Ham, and the sons of God the descendants of Seth: the former impious through their father’s curse, the latter religious through their ancestral blessing. But after the sons of Seth, overcome by desire, entered into marriages with the daughters of Ham, from such a union were begotten men of immense body, proud in strength and uncultivated in character, whom Scripture calls giants.

[Col. 0512C] And God said: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.” (Jerome.) In Hebrew it is written: “My spirit shall not judge these men forever, because they are flesh”; that is, because the human condition is fragile, I will not preserve them for eternal punishments, but here I will repay them what they deserve. Thus it is not God’s severity, as it reads in our books, but his clemency that is expressed, since the sinner is punished here for his crime. Hence, too, the angry God says to certain people: “I will not visit their daughters when they have committed fornication, nor their brides when they have committed adultery” (Hosea 4). And in another place: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges. Nevertheless, I will not remove my mercy from them” (Psalm 88). Moreover, lest he seem cruel in that he had not granted sinners a place for repentance, he added: “But their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”; that is, they would have one hundred and twenty years in which to perform repentance. Human life, therefore, was not shortened to one hundred and twenty years, as many mistakenly think; rather, one hundred and twenty years were granted to that generation for repentance. Indeed, we find that after the Flood Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years, and others more than two or three hundred years. But because they had scorned repentance, God did not wish to await the appointed time; instead, shortening the period by twenty years, he brought on the Flood in the hundredth year assigned for repentance.

[Col. 0513A] And God saw that the wickedness of human beings was great on the earth and that every inclination of their heart was directed toward evil at all times; and it repented him that he had made man on the earth, and he was touched by inward grief of heart. “I will destroy,” he said, “the man whom I created from the face of the earth, from man to living creatures, from creeping things to the birds of the sky; for it repents me that I made them.” What does it mean when it is said of God, “It repents me that I made man,” and again, “He was touched by inward grief of heart”? Can repentance or grief of heart occur in God? God’s anger is not a disturbance of his mind, but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted upon sin; and his thought and reconsideration concerning the changing of things is an unchanging plan. God does not repent or grieve over his action as a human being does, for his decision concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. Rather, Holy Scripture uses familiar words that we can understand and adapts itself to our smallness, so that through things we know we may come to know things unknown.

## CHAPTER VI. On Noah and the construction of his ark

Noah was a righteous and perfect man in his generations; he walked with God. (Albinus.) If no one is without sin, how can anyone be perfect? Here some are called perfect not as the saints will be perfected in that immortality in which they will be made equal to the angels of God, but as people can be perfect in this pilgrimage. Hence Scripture significantly says, “in his generation,” to show that he was righteous not according to consummate righteousness but according to the righteousness of his generation; [Col. 0513C] and this is what is said in Hebrew: “Noah was a righteous and perfect man in his generations; he walked with God,” that is, he followed his footsteps.

And he begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Shem is interpreted as “name” or “named.” Ham is interpreted as “cunning”; Japheth is interpreted as “breadth.”

But the earth was corrupt before God, and it was filled with iniquity. And when God saw that the earth was corrupt. (For all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth.) The earth, however, is called corrupt because all flesh, that is, every human being, had corrupted its way by sinning; that is, he had led the entire period of his life in sins. Since only human beings sinned, all flesh is said to have corrupted its way, because all flesh was created on account of humanity.

[Col. 0513D] He said to Noah: “The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them together with the earth.” What does God’s statement, “The end of all flesh has come before me,” mean except that by “all flesh” he signified the entire race of mortals apart from those who were to be saved in the ark? They were preserved as the seedbed of a second generation. “And I will destroy them,” he says, “together with the earth.” How were they destroyed together with the earth, when the earth remained afterward? For teachers relate that the earth’s vigor and fertility were far less after the Flood than before it; and for this reason permission was given to human beings to eat meat, whereas before the Flood they had lived solely on the fruits of the earth.

[Col. 0514A] “Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood; you shall make small compartments in the ark.” What, then, is the smoothed wood from which the ark is commanded to be made, except strong, unbreakable, and well-fitted wood? Another translation says “squared,” so that the ark would not be broken apart either by the force of winds or by the flooding of waters. This ark was divided within by small compartments because of the various species and kinds of animals.

“And you shall coat it with bitumen inside and outside; and so you shall make it.” Bitumen is an extremely hot and powerful adhesive, whose property is that wood smeared with it can be eaten neither by worms nor dissolved by the heat of the sun or by the flooding of waters. Concerning this bitumen the historian Pliny reports as follows (Book II, chapter 104): “Several lakes of bitumen are said to be found, as in Commagene, where a lake at the city of Samosata emits burning mud—which they call *maltha*—with which they usually protect walls, because, clinging upon contact, it pulls back those who flee. There is also one in the Pentapolis, where the Dead Sea or the Lake of Salt is said to be situated; whatever living things you try to immerse in it immediately spring back, and however forcefully they are thrown in, they are at once cast out. Nor is it moved by winds, since the bitumen resists whirlwinds and causes all the water to stand still; nor does it permit navigation, because everything without life sinks into the depths and it supports no material except what is made bright with bitumen. They say that a lighted lamp floats upon it but, when its flame is extinguished, sinks. There are also wells of bitumen in the regions of Babylon, and the sons of Adam used it in place of mortar in the construction of the tower, because against the nature of water it is exceedingly firm.”

“The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits; its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. You shall make a window in the ark and finish its top within one cubit.” The question is often asked what figure or shape the ark had. For from this account it appears to rise from its base with four corners, and, as these were gradually drawn inward toward the top, it was narrowed to the space of one cubit. The text thus reports that its foundations were three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty in height, but that it was narrowed toward the peak so that its length and breadth at the top were one cubit. In truth, no form could have been given to the ark more suitable and fitting than for it to spread the torrents of rain from above like a narrow roof and to stand upon the waters below with square stability, so that it could not be tilted or sunk by the force of winds, the violence of waves, or the agitation of the animals inside.

Therefore the window is commanded to be made at the top of the ark so that Noah would have a place from which he could send out birds to investigate whether the earth was dry.

“And you shall place the door of the ark in its side below; you shall make it with a lower and a third story.” How, then, the ark was two-storied and three-storied, some of the teachers assert as follows: it was two-storied in its lower parts and three-storied in its upper parts, so that we understand there to have been five divisions of habitation in it. Its lower places were assigned to dung and filth, lest the animals, and especially the human beings, should be troubled by the foul stench; the upper and adjoining chamber was assigned to preserving food for the animals. They therefore report that the lower parts, which are called two-storied, were divided for these purposes, while the upper parts, which are called three-storied, were assigned first as a dwelling for beasts, or for wilder animals, or for serpents. Above these, they say, were stalls suitable for gentler creatures; and above all, in the highest place, a seat was established for human beings, so that, just as humanity excels the animals in honor and wisdom, so also it might surpass them all in position. Thus five dwellings are understood to have been in it: first, the dung-room; second, the storeroom; third, for wild animals; fourth, for tame animals; fifth, for human beings.

They likewise report concerning the door built in the side of the ark that it was placed where the lower parts called two-storied were beneath it, while the parts called three-storied were above the level of the door. From there all the animals entered and were separated into their respective places with suitable arrangement, according to what we have said above.

(Isidore.) The fact that Noah was delivered through water and wood can be understood allegorically in this way: wood and water signify the cross and baptism. Just as he and his household were saved through water and wood, so the household of Christ is healed through baptism and the passion of the cross. Noah constructed the ark from incorruptible wood; the Church is built by Christ from human beings who will live forever. For this ark signifies the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world. The fact that the same ark is commanded to be made from squared wood signifies on every side the stable life of the saints, prepared for every good work. For in whatever direction you turn a square, it stands firmly.

The wood of the ark is joined with bitumen inside and outside, so that, in the joining of unity, the endurance of charity may be signified, lest, when scandals test the Church, whether from those who are inside or from those who are outside, the brotherly bond yield and the bond of peace be dissolved. For bitumen is an extremely hot and powerful adhesive, as was said above, signifying the ardor of love, with the great force of strength, for holding together spiritual fellowship and enduring all things.

The ark is three hundred cubits long, so that it is completed by six times fifty, just as the whole period of this world extends through six ages. In all of them Christ never ceases to be proclaimed: in the first five he was foretold through prophecy, and in the sixth he was made widely known through the Gospel. These three hundred cubits can also signify the wood of the passion of the cross. For the numerical value of that letter displays the sign of the cross, through which, having become companions in Christ’s passion, we attain the length of eternal life through baptism.

The fact that its breadth is expanded to fifty cubits signifies the breadth of charity among the faithful, as the Apostle says: “Our heart has been enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6). Through what, except spiritual charity? For this reason he says again: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5). For on the fiftieth day after his resurrection Christ sent the Holy Spirit, who enlarged the hearts of believers.

The fact that its height rises to thirty cubits, a number which the ark’s length of three hundred cubits contains ten times, signifies that Christ is our height. At the age of thirty he consecrated the teaching of the Gospel, testifying that he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. The heart of the Law is recognized in the Ten Commandments; hence the ark’s length is completed by ten times thirty. Thus Noah himself is counted as the tenth from Adam.

The fact that the ark is six times as long as it is high and ten times as long as it is broad displays the form of the human body, in which Christ appeared. For the length of the body, from the crown of the head to the feet, is six times its breadth from one side to the other, and ten times its height, whose measure is from the back to the belly, as if you were measuring a person lying on his back or face down. He is six times as long from head to feet as he is broad from right to left or from left to right, and ten times as long as he is high from the ground. Hence the ark was made three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty in height.

Likewise, the same ark, gathered together into one cubit, is finished above, just as the Church, the body of Christ, gathered into unity, is raised up and perfected. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 10). The fact that its entrance is made in the side signifies that no one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the remission of sins, which flowed from Christ’s opened side.

The lower parts of the ark are constructed as two-storied and three-storied, just as the Church is gathered from all nations either through a twofold multitude, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision, or through a threefold division, on account of Noah’s three sons, whose descendants filled the whole world. For this reason these lower parts of the ark are so called, because in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations. At the top, however, everything is brought together into one, and this diversity no longer exists, because Christ is all and in all, completing us above in one cubit through heavenly unity.

(Gregory.) Accordingly, the Church as a whole is rightly signified by the ark. It is still broad in its many carnal members and narrow in its few spiritual ones; and because it is gathered toward one man who is without sin, it is, as it were, completed in one cubit. For we see many within the bosom of that same holy Church rising up in pride, dissolving in the pleasure of the flesh, longing to acquire earthly things, crossing the seas at the command of greed, serving anger, devoting themselves to quarrels, and injuring those neighbors whom they are able to harm. But because holy Church still tolerates them so that they may be converted, the beasts dwell, as it were, below in the breadth of the ark.

We see others who no longer seek what belongs to others, bear injury inflicted upon them with equanimity, are content with their own possessions, and live humbly; but because these are already few, the ark becomes narrow.

We see still others who even abandon what they possess, devote no attention to earthly things, love their enemies, subdue the flesh from every pleasure, restrain all impulses under the judgment of reason, and are lifted up on the wing of contemplation through heavenly desire. But because such people are exceedingly rare, the ark is already drawn toward the cubit, where human beings and birds are contained.

Yet let it be asked whether any of them can exist without sin, and none is found. Who, then, is a human being without sin except the one who was not conceived in sins? Thus the ark is completed in one cubit, because there is one author and redeemer of the holy Church who is without sin, toward whom and through whom all those who acknowledge themselves to be sinners make progress. The text continues:

“And you shall enter the ark, you and your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you. And of all living creatures of every kind of flesh, you shall bring two of each into the ark, so that they may live with you, male and female, and so forth.” (Albinus.) [Col. 0517B] What does it mean that here he commands two of all living creatures to be brought into the ark, and in the following passage two and two, seven and seven, male and female? Should we understand that four of the unclean animals and fourteen of the clean animals were to be brought in? Certainly not: “two and two” refers not to four but to male and female. For of the unclean there were only two, and of the clean only seven. He therefore placed the unclean in an even number, but the clean in an odd number, so that Noah would have animals from among the clean from which to offer sacrifices. Thus there were more clean than unclean, because of the future use of the human race, for whom the clean animals were destined, so that there might be more that were beneficial than harmful.

“Of the birds according to their kind, of cattle according to their kind, and of every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind, two of each shall enter with you, so that they may live.” It is often asked whether the ark is described as having sufficient capacity to carry so many animals, together with the compartments suitable for them and their food. (Augustine.) Origen solves this question by means of the geometric cubit, asserting that a geometric cubit is equal to six of our cubits. If we therefore understand the cubits to have been that great, there is no question that the ark had sufficient capacity to contain all those things.

It is likewise asked whether an ark so large could have been built in one hundred years by four men, namely Noah and his three sons. But if they could not have built it, it would not have been difficult to employ other builders, although, after receiving payment for their work, they may not have cared whether Noah built it wisely or foolishly; and for this reason they did not enter it, because they did not believe what he had believed.

The statement that all the animals entered the ark was not fulfilled by Noah gathering them, but by God’s command. For just as it was said in the first creation that God brought the animals to Adam so that he might see what he would call them, so, compelled by divine impulse, the animals came of their own accord to Noah’s ark in the number predetermined. It is likewise asked about the smallest beasts—not only such as mice and geckos, but also such as locusts, beetles, flies, and even fleas—whether there were more of them in that ark than the number prescribed when God gave this command.

Those whom these matters trouble should first be warned that the statement “those that creep upon the earth” is to be understood in such a way that it was not necessary to preserve in the ark creatures that can live in water—not only when submerged, like fish, but also while floating upon it, like many waterfowl. Moreover, when it says, “There shall be male and female,” it plainly means that they were brought in for the restoration of their kind. Consequently, it was not necessary for those creatures to be there that can be born without intercourse from various things or from the decay of things; or, if they were there, as they commonly are in houses, they could have been present without any fixed number. Or, if the sacred mystery being enacted, and the figure of so great a matter, could not otherwise be fulfilled in actual fact except that all creatures unable by their nature to live in water should be present in that definite number, this was not the concern of that man or of those men, but of God. For Noah did not catch them and bring them in; he merely allowed them to come and enter. This is the force of the statement, “They entered to you”: not, of course, by human action, but by God’s impulse.

“Therefore you shall take with you from all foods that can be eaten, and you shall store them with you, and they shall be food both for you and for them.” It also usually troubles some people what kinds of food the animals that are thought to eat only meat could have had there: whether, in addition to the prescribed number, there were animals included whose necessity for feeding others compelled their inclusion without violating the command, or whether—and this is more credible—there could have been foods besides meat that would suit them all. For we know how many animals for which meat is food also eat fruits and apples, especially figs and chestnuts. And what is surprising if that wise and righteous man, divinely warned also about what suited each creature, found and stored suitable nourishment for every kind without meat? What is there that hunger could not compel a creature to eat? Or what could God not make pleasant and wholesome, since by divine power he could even grant them to live without food?

## CHAPTER VII. On the entry of the living creatures into the ark and on the Flood
## (CHAP. VII)

All the birds and every winged creature entered two by two into the ark to Noah, of every kind of flesh in which there was the breath of life; and those that entered were male and female. From every kind of flesh they entered, just as God had commanded him.

**(Albinus.)** Hence some think it should be asked what ought to be thought concerning animals whose nature cannot live always in dry places or always in water, such as otters and sea-calves, and many kinds of birds that seek their food in the waters but sleep, nourish their young, and rest on dry land. For divine power could have softened or adapted either aspect of their nature until the Flood had passed, so that they could live either only in water or only on dry land—unless perhaps places had been prepared for them outside the ark, in some part of it, from which they could both live in the waters and rest on dry land.

[Col. 0519A] And the Lord shut him in from outside. For this was without doubt a divine work, so that the waters might not enter through the opening, which human hands had not fortified.

And the Flood was upon the earth for forty days; the waters increased and lifted the ark high above the earth; they rose exceedingly and covered everything over the surface of the earth. The ark was carried upon the waters, and the waters prevailed greatly over the earth. All the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered. The water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains that it had covered.

Some maintain that these events did not actually happen, but are only figures signifying other things. First, they suppose that so great a Flood could not have occurred; and likewise that there could not have been another such flood in the upper regions, so that, as the waters rose, they would have overtopped the highest mountains by fifteen cubits.
