They argue this on account of the summit of Mount Olympus, above which, they claim, clouds cannot gather, since it is already so close to heaven that the denser air in which winds, mists, and rains are generated is not found there.

They do not consider that the densest of all the elements, earth, might have existed there. Or do they perhaps deny that the summit of a mountain is earth? Why, then, do they insist that earth could be raised as high as those regions of heaven, but that water could not be raised there, when these measurers and weighers of the elements declare that water is above and lighter than earth? What reason, then, do they offer for saying that heavier, lower earth invaded the region of the calmer heaven for so many years, while lighter and higher water was not permitted to do so, at least [Col. 0519C] for a short time?

## (CHAP. VIII)

But God remembered Noah and all the animals and all the beasts that were with him in the ark, and he brought a spirit over the earth; the waters subsided. The fountains of the abyss and the sluices of heaven were closed, and the rains from heaven were stopped.

This spirit may rightly be understood as the one of which it was said: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” Then it was borne over them so that, when the waters had been gathered into their place, the earth might appear; now it is said to have been brought forth so that, when the waters of the Flood had been removed, it might reveal the face of the earth. The word “spirit” may also be understood as “wind,” in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “And the storm-wind stood” (Psalm 106), whose repeated blasts might have forced the water to withdraw.

And the waters returned from the earth, going and coming, [Col. 0519D] and after one hundred and fifty days they began to diminish. Where did the waters return when it is said, “The waters returned from the earth, going and coming”? According to the literal sense, it appears that all the courses of rivers and streams return through the hidden veins of the earth to the womb of the abyss, in accordance with Solomon’s words: “To the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” (Ecclesiastes 1).

And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia. Josephus, the Jewish historian, mentions this place, saying:

> The Armenians call this place the Place of Descent. There, even to the present day, the inhabitants display the remains of the ark after it was dismantled.

All who have written barbarian histories likewise preserve the memory of this Flood and of the ark. One of them is Berossus the Chaldean. In relating the Flood, he spoke as follows:

> It is said that the ship which came to Armenia, near the mountain of the Cordyaeans, still survives in part, and that some people gather bitumen from it, which they chiefly use for purification.

Jerome of Egypt also mentions these matters; he is known to have written the antiquities of Phoenicia. Manasseas of Damascus likewise says the following about them in the ninety-sixth book of his *Histories*:

> There is also a lofty mountain above Mount Mummad in Armenia, called Paris. It is said that many fugitives were saved there at the time of the Flood, and that someone who had been carried there in the ark was preserved for a long time on the summit of the mountain by the remains of wood that had been saved.  
> [The wording “in the summit” is materially uncertain in the supplied text.]

## CHAPTER VIII. Noah’s Departure from the Ark, His Sacrifice, and His Blessing

In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains appeared. When forty days had passed, Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent out a raven. It went out and did not return until the waters had dried up from the earth. He also sent out a dove after it, to see whether the waters had already ceased from the face of the earth. Since it found no place where its foot could rest, it returned to him in the ark, for the waters were still over the whole earth.

A question commonly arises whether the raven died, or whether it could have lived in some way; for surely, if there had been land on which it could rest, the dove too could have found a resting place for its feet. Hence many infer that the raven could perch upon a corpse, something which the dove naturally avoids.

Another question is how the dove could find no place to rest if, as the sequence of the narrative seems to indicate, the tops of the mountains had already been uncovered. This question can be resolved either by recapitulation, so that what is narrated later is understood to have happened earlier, or, preferably, by supposing that the waters had not yet dried up.

**(Isidore.)** Mystically, the fact that all kinds of animals are enclosed in the ark signifies that a gathering from all nations and peoples takes place in the Church. The same is signified by the sheet shown to Peter, in which there were clean and unclean animals (Acts 10), just as good and evil are found in the mysteries of the Church.

That the clean animals were seven and the unclean two does not mean that there are fewer evil people than good people, [Col. 0520D] but that the good preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Holy Scripture commends the Holy Spirit in a sevenfold operation: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge, piety, and fear of God. Hence that number of fifty days, pertaining to the coming of the Holy Spirit, is completed in seven times seven—which makes forty-nine—with one added. Therefore it is said: “Striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4).

The evil are shown by the number two to be prone to schisms and, in a certain sense, divisible. That Noah himself is counted as the eighth together with his companions signifies that in Christ the hope of our resurrection appeared, because on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the Sabbath—he was the first to rise from the dead. That day is the third after the Passion, but in the number of days that revolve throughout all time it is both the eighth and the first.

The fact that the Flood occurred seven days after Noah entered the ark shows that we are baptized in the hope of the future rest, which was signified by the seventh day. The fact that, apart from the ark, all flesh that the earth sustained was destroyed by the Flood indicates that outside the fellowship of the Church the water of baptism, although it is the same water, not only does not bring salvation but rather brings destruction.

That it rained for forty days and forty nights signifies that all guilt for sins is admitted through the ten commandments of the Law throughout the whole world, which is contained in four parts. For ten multiplied by four makes forty. Alternatively, that guilt which belongs to the days and is contracted through prosperity, or that which belongs to the nights and is contracted through adversity, is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly baptism.

When the Lord spoke to Noah and commanded him to make an ark, Noah was five hundred years old; he was entering his six hundredth year when he entered it. From this it is understood that the ark was built over one hundred years. What else do these one hundred years seem to signify here but the successive ages of the world? Thus this sixth age, signified by the period from the completion of five hundred years to six hundred, builds the Church through the manifestation of the Gospel.

Therefore, whoever takes thought for his life should be like squared timber, prepared for every good work, and should enter the holy structure. The second month of Noah’s six-hundredth year, in which he entered the ark, likewise signifies the same sixth age. Two months are concluded by the number sixty; from the number six come the names sixty, six hundred, six thousand, sixty thousand, six hundred thousand, six hundred times, and whatever thereafter arises in larger sums through infinite increases according to the same numerical progression.

The mention of the twenty-seventh day of the month also pertains to the significance of squareness, which has already been expounded through the squared timber. Here it is made clearer, because the Trinity perfects us, prepared for every good work—that is, in a certain sense squared—in the memory by which we remember God, in the understanding by which we know him, and in the will by which we love him. Three times three, and that again three times, make twenty-seven, which is the square of the number three.

The fact that the ark came to rest, that is, rested, in the seventh month returns us to the signification of that seventh rest, because the perfected rest there. The number of that same square is repeated there as well. For on the twenty-seventh day of the second month this mystery was commended, and again on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month the same commendation was confirmed when the ark rested. What is promised in hope is displayed in reality.

Since that seventh rest is joined with the eighth resurrection, this signifies that rest does not end with the resurrection of the body—the rest that receives the saints after this life—but rather that it takes up the whole human being, no longer in hope but already in reality, renewed on every side in the perfect and immortal salvation of spirit and body, as a gift of eternal life.

Because the seventh rest is joined with the eighth resurrection, this is a profound mystery in the sacrament of regeneration, that is, in baptism: the water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains, exceeding their height. Eight and seven make fifteen; eight signifies resurrection, and seven signifies rest.

Thus this sacrament of resurrection and rest surpasses all the wisdom of the proud, so that by no height of their knowledge can they investigate the rest of the resurrection. And because seventy is named from seven and eighty from eight, when the two numbers are joined, the water was raised for one hundred and fifty days, commending and confirming for us that same height of baptism, in the consecration of the new person, so that the faith of rest and resurrection might be maintained.

That after forty days the raven sent out did not return—whether it was caught by the waters or enticed by some floating corpse—signifies people who are utterly wicked in the uncleanness of desire and, for this reason, excessively intent upon the things that are outside in this world. Such people are either rebaptized or are led astray and held by those whom baptism outside the ark, that is, outside the Church, has destroyed.

That the dove, when sent out, found no rest and returned shows that through the New Testament rest has not been promised to the saints in this world. For it was sent out after forty days, and that number signifies the life lived in this world.

Then, after seven days, it was sent out again and, through that sevenfold spiritual operation, brought back a fruitful olive branch in its beak. This signified that some who have been baptized even outside the Church, if the richness of charity has not been lacking in them, may at a later time be brought into the fellowship of unity in the dove’s mouth, as though in the kiss of peace.

But when it was sent out again after another seven days and did not return, this signifies the end of the world, when the rest of the saints will exist—not still in the sacrament of hope by which the Church is joined together in this present time, as long as it drinks what flowed from Christ’s side, but already in the perfection of our salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that in the clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we may need no bodily ministries.

That in the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life, that is, after six hundred years had been completed, the roof of the ark was opened signifies that, when the sixth age of the world has ended, the hidden mystery and promise will be revealed.

Why is it said that the earth dried on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, as though the need for baptism had already ended? It is because the fifty-seventh day—the twenty-seventh day of the second month is that day—expresses the time of the resurrection, when the sacrament of baptism is completed. This number, through the joining of spirit and body, contains seven times eight, with one added on account of the bond of unity.

Why do those who entered the ark separately come out joined together? For it had been said that Noah, his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons entered the ark separately: the men were mentioned separately, and the women separately. It is because in this present time the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Galatians 5).

Afterward, however, Noah and his wife, his sons and the wives of his sons, come out together: males and females joined together. This signifies that at the end of the world and in the resurrection of the righteous, the body will cling to the spirit in complete and perfect peace, with no need for changeability or opposing desire.

Noah built an altar to the Lord; and taking from all the clean cattle and clean birds, he offered burnt offerings upon the altar to the Lord. And the Lord smelled the pleasing fragrance and said to him: “I will never again curse the earth on account of human beings.”

What does it mean that the Lord says, “I will not again add to cursing the earth because of human deeds, for the mind of human beings is inclined toward evil from youth”? “Therefore I will not again,” he says, “strike every living creature as I have done.” Then he added what, according to the abundance of his goodness, he grants to unworthy human beings.

Is the indulgence of the New Testament symbolized here, while the punishment of the past pertains to the Old Testament—that is, the former to the severity of the Law and the latter to the goodness of grace?

“For the sense and thought of the human heart,” he says, “are inclined toward evil from its adolescence.” The evil of corruption, which each of us has taken from the beginning of our carnal desires, exercises itself as we advance in age; and unless the hand of divine fear restrains it swiftly, guilt suddenly swallows up all the goodness of created nature [Col. 0523C] into the abyss. Therefore let no one claim victory over his own thoughts, since the Apostle says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

## (CHAP. IX)

“Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth; and let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth.”

For powerful men, the consideration of humility and the equality of our condition is of great value. By nature all human beings are equal; but, through an administrative ordering, it has come about that some appear to be placed over others. If, therefore, we press down in our minds what has been added temporally, we more quickly discover what we are by nature.

Often power accepted with eagerness does harm and deceives a person through proud thoughts. The swelling of exaltation must therefore be pressed down by the hand of the deepest humility. If the mind descends within itself from the summit of its height, it will more quickly find the level ground of natural equality.

For, as we have already said, nature gave birth to all human beings as equals; but, through the varying order of merits, a hidden dispensation places some below others. The very diversity that arose from fault has rightly been ordered by divine judgments, so that, since not everyone walks equally along the path of life, one may be governed by another.

When holy men preside, they consider not the power of rank in themselves but the equality of condition; nor do they rejoice to rule over people, but to benefit them. They know that our ancient fathers are remembered as shepherds of flocks rather than kings of human beings.

Hence, when after the Flood the Lord said to Noah and his sons, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth,” he added: “And let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth” (Genesis 9).

Human beings are naturally placed over irrational animals, but not over other human beings. Therefore it is said that they should be feared by animals, and not by other human beings, because it is against nature to act proudly and to wish to be feared by one’s equal.

All who preside, therefore, ought to weigh not the power of rank in themselves but the equality of condition. For, as we have said, our ancient fathers are remembered as shepherds of flocks, not kings of human beings. Nevertheless, it is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects when they discover that the latter have no fear of God, so that at least through human fear they may fear to sin—those who do not fear divine judgments.

Superiors should never grow proud because of the fear they have sought, since in seeking it they pursue not their own glory but the righteousness of their subjects. When they demand fear from those who live perversely, they rule them as though they were not human beings but animals; for insofar as their subjects are bestial, they ought also to lie prostrate in fear.

“Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you, as the green plants.”

The question is asked why the eating of meat was granted to human beings after the Flood and not before. It is thought to have been because of the infertility of the earth and the frailty of humanity.

“I have given you everything, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood.”

When they are commanded to eat flesh except with blood, this is so that the former life may not remain, as though suffocated, in the conscience, but may have something like an outpouring through confession.

“For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast, and from the hand of human beings; from the hand of each person and of his brother I will require the life of the human being.”

**(Augustine.)** What does it mean when he says, “From the hand of a human being, his brother, I will require the life of a human being”? Did he intend every human being to be understood as the brother of every other human being according to the kinship derived from one ancestor?

Mystically, the fact that all animals are given to them as food signifies that in the calling of the nations to faith there is no distinction, just as Peter is told concerning the sheet: “Kill and eat.”

“I will place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.”

The covenant that God established between himself and human beings and every living creature, so that he would not destroy it by a Flood—the bow that appears in the clouds and never shines except from the sun—signifies that those do not perish in the Flood who recognize Christ in the prophets and in all the divine Scriptures, as in the clouds of God.

Almighty God placed the bow between himself and human beings as a sign, so that he would not again destroy the world by a Flood. Hence in that same bow the color of water and of fire is shown together: in part it is blue, and in part red, so that it may bear witness to both judgments, one that is to come and the other that has already occurred; namely, that the world will be consumed by the judgment of fire, while it was not destroyed by the water of the Flood.

## CHAPTER IX. Noah’s Planting of the Vineyard, His Nakedness, and Ham’s Mockery

[Col. 0525A]

Noah, a farmer, began to cultivate the land, and he planted a vineyard. After drinking wine, he became drunk; and, having been stripped, he lay naked in his tent. When Ham, the father of Canaan, saw that his father’s private parts had been exposed, he went out and told his two brothers, and so forth.

**(Augustine.)** It is asked why Ham, who sinned in the offense against his father, was cursed not in himself but in his son Canaan. Was it not because it was in some way prophesied that the sons of Israel, who would come from the seed of Shem, were to receive the land of Canaan after the Canaanites had been expelled and defeated?

**(Isidore.)** Now, as for the fact that after the Flood Noah became drunk from the wine of the vineyard he had planted and lay naked in his house, who would not recognize this as a figure of Christ? He became drunk when he suffered; he was stripped when he was crucified; and this occurred in his house—that is, among his own people and among the members of his own blood, namely, the Jews. Then the mortality of his flesh was exposed.

When Ham saw this nakedness—that is, Christ’s Passion—he mocked it; and when the Jews saw Christ’s death, they derided it. Shem and Japheth, however, like two peoples believing from circumcision and uncircumcision, having learned of their father’s nakedness, which signifies the Savior’s Passion, took a garment, placed it upon their backs, and entered backward; thus they covered their father’s nakedness and did not see the private parts they covered.

In a certain manner we cover Christ’s Passion with a veil—that is, we honor it as a sacrament—and, by explaining the meaning of that mystery, we cover the Jews’ disparagement. The garment signifies the sacrament; the back signifies memory of past events, because the Church celebrates Christ’s Passion as something completed and does not still look forward to it as future.

**(Gregory.)** Morally, we say that we turn away from what we reject. What, then, does it mean that the sons, with a cloak thrown over their backs, come backward and cover their father’s private parts, except that good subjects are displeased by the faults of their superiors, yet nevertheless conceal those faults from others?

**(Isidore.)** They carry the covering backward because, while judging the deed and honoring the office of teaching, they do not wish it to be seen that they are covering it. Ham, the middle of the brothers—that is, the impious Jewish people—is in the middle because it held neither the primacy of the apostles nor the last place among the nations in believing. It saw the nakedness of its father because it consented to the death of the Lord and Savior.

Afterward he told his brothers outside. Through him what had been secret in prophecy was made manifest; therefore he becomes the servant of his brothers. For what else is that people today but a kind of archive-keeper for Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony supporting the Church’s claim, so that we may honor through sacrament what they announce to us through the letter?

After this, the two who honored their father’s nakedness are blessed.

“Blessed,” he says, “is the Lord God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

Shem, the elder, is the one from whom the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles were born. Japheth, however, is the father of the nations; his name is also interpreted as “enlargement.” The people from the nations have been enlarged into a vast multitude, and they were to dwell with the prophets and apostles.

Indeed, in accordance with Noah’s prophetic blessing, we see that Japheth’s dwelling has passed into the tent of Shem—that is, into the house of the Law and the Prophets—and that the Church is justified there: younger in the age of time, but greater according to the law of grace.

Ham, whose name is interpreted as “crafty,” is the middle son, distinguished from both. He neither remains among the first fruits of the Israelites nor in the fullness of the nations. He signifies not only the crafty kind of Jews but also heretics, crafty not through the spirit of wisdom but through impatience, by which the beginnings of heretics commonly boil over and disturb the peace of the saints.

All who glory in the Christian name yet live wickedly also appear to bear his figure. They proclaim Christ’s Passion, which was signified by that man’s nakedness, by making a good confession, but dishonor it by their evil conduct. Of such people it was said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Luke 6).

Therefore Ham too was cursed in his son, as in his fruit, that is, in his work. Accordingly, his son Canaan is appropriately interpreted as “their movement.” What else is this than their work?

Likewise, the fact that when Ham sinned his descendants were condemned signifies that the reprobate sin here, but afterward—that is, in the future—they receive the sentence of condemnation. The Jewish people, too, which crucified the Lord, transmitted the punishment of its condemnation even to its children. For they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27).

[Col. 0526C] And all the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years.

Behold, Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the Flood. From this it is clear that the one hundred and twenty years, as we said above, were given to that generation for repentance and were not established as the limit of mortal life.

## CHAPTER X. The Generations of the Sons of Noah

After Noah’s two sons had been blessed and his middle son cursed, their generations are subsequently set forth. From them seventy-two nations arose: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem.

## (CHAP. X)

The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, and Meshech.

**(Jerome.)** Seven sons were born to Japheth, the son of Noah. They occupied the land in Asia from Mount Amanus and the mountains of Taurus in Coele-Syria and Cilicia as far as the river Tanais; in Europe, as far as Gadara, leaving their names to places and peoples. Later, many of these names were changed, while the rest remain as they were.

They were Gomer, that is, the Galatians; Magog, that is, the Scythians; Madai, that is, the Medes; Javan, that is, the Ionians, who are also Greeks, whence the Ionian Sea; Tubal, that is, the Iberians, who are also Spaniards, from whom Celtiberia derives its name, although some suspect that Italians are meant; and Meshech, that is, the Cappadocians, among whom a city called Mazecha is still known today.

The translators of the Septuagint, moreover, consider the Caphtorim to be Cappadocians and Thiras to be Thracians; their name has not been preserved without considerable alteration.

I know that someone has recently connected Gog and Magog, both from the present passage and from Ezekiel, with the history of the Goths who have lately been raging through our land. Whether this is true will be shown by the outcome of the war itself. Certainly, educated writers of earlier times have generally called all Goths Getae rather than Gog and Magog.

These seven nations that I have said came from the stock of Japheth dwell in the northern region.

The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The Greeks call the Ashkenazim Rheginians; Riphath the Paphlagonians; and Togarmah the Phrygians.

The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. From these the islands of the nations were divided among their lands, each according to its language, its kinship, and its nation.

From the Ionians, that is, the Greeks, came the Elishaeans, who are called Aeolians. Hence the fifth language of Greece is called Aeolic; they call it **πέμπτη διάλεκτος**, “the fifth dialect.”

Josephus considers Tarshish to be the Cilicians, saying that the aspirated letter θ was corruptly changed by later generations into τ. Hence their chief city is called Tarsus, famous for the apostle Paul.

The Kittim are the Citians, from whom the city in Cyprus is still called Citium. Dodanim are the Rhodians; this is how the translators of the Septuagint rendered the name.

Let us read the books of Varro *On Antiquities*, those of Sinnius Capito, the Greek author Phlegon, and the other highly learned men, and we shall see that nearly all the islands and the shores of the whole world, together with lands near the sea, were occupied by Greek settlers. As we said above, from the mountains of Amanus and Taurus they possessed all the maritime regions as far as the British Ocean.

The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.

Cush is still called Ethiopia by the Hebrews; Mizraim is Egypt; Put is Libya, from whom the river in Mauretania is still called Put, as is the entire region around it, the land of Put. Many Greek and Latin writers bear witness to this. Why the ancient name of Libya remained only in one part of that climate, while the rest of the land was called Africa, is not a matter for this place or time.

Canaan, moreover, obtained the land that the Jews later occupied after expelling the Canaanites.

The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca.

Seba is the ancestor of the Sabaeans, concerning whom Virgil says:

> “And for the Sabaeans alone the branch is rich in incense.”

And elsewhere:

> “A hundred altars of the Sabaeans glow with incense.”

Havilah refers to the Gaetuli, who adjoin the desert in the more remote part of Africa. Sabtah is the ancestor of the Sabatheni, who are now called Astabari. Raamah and Sabteca gradually lost their ancient names, and it is unknown what names they now bear in place of the old ones.

The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan.

This Sheba is written with the letter *sin*; the earlier Sheba, from whom we said the Sabaeans were named, was written differently, with *samekh*. Sheba is therefore now interpreted as Arabia. For in the seventy-first Psalm, where we read, “The kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall offer gifts,” the Hebrew has “the kings of Sheba and Sheba”: the first name is written with *sin*, the second with *samekh*. Dedan is a people of Ethiopia in the western region.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Nimrod the Giant and the Confusion of Tongues in the Building of the Tower

Now Cush begot Nimrod; he was the first to become mighty on earth. He was a powerful hunter before the Lord. From this came the proverb: “Like Nimrod, a powerful hunter before the Lord.” The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar. Asshur went out from that land.

**(Isidore.)** Nimrod, the son of Cush, was the first among men after the Flood to seize tyranny through a novel desire for dominion; and he reigned in Babylon, which was called Babel because the languages were confused there, and whose name means “confusion.” This same Nimrod was the originator of the tower’s construction. Since he strove beyond his nature to penetrate the heights of heaven, he is not inappropriately compared with the devil, who, swelling with the thought of his heart, wished to exalt himself above the stars—that is, purposing to make himself equal to God above every power of the angels—when he says: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14). And what is signified by his being called a hunter except a deceiver of earthborn souls, capturing people for death?

**(Jerome.)** He also reigned in Erech, that is, Edessa; in Accad, now called Nisibis; and in Calneh, which was later, after a change of name, called Seleucia after King Seleucus, or certainly is now called **Κτησιφὼν**, Ctesiphon.

“Asshur went out from that land and built Nineveh and the city of Rehoboth.” From this land sprang up the Assyrian empire; from the name of Ninus, son of Belus, they founded the great city of Ninus, which the Hebrews call Nineveh, and to whose destruction or repentance the whole prophecy of Jonah pertains. When it says “Nineveh and the city of Rehoboth,” we should not suppose that these are two cities; but since *Rehoboth* means “streets,” it should be read: “and he built Nineveh and the streets of the city.”

Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Laabim, Nephthuim, Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and Caphtorim. Except for the Laabim, from whom the Libyans were later named and who were previously called Phuteans, and the Casluhim, who were later called Philistines and whom we corruptly call Palestinians, the remaining six nations are unknown to us, because they were overthrown in the Ethiopian war and came to the oblivion of their former names. They occupied the land from Gaza to the furthest boundaries of Egypt.

Canaan begot his firstborn, Sidon, and the Hittite, Jebusite, Amorite, Girgashite, Hivite, Arkite, Sinite, Arvadite, Zemarite, and Hamathite. Sidon was the firstborn of Canaan, from whom the Phoenician city is called Sidon. Then came the Arkite, who founded the town of Arca opposite Tripoli, situated at the foot of Lebanon. Not far from it was another city named Sin, later destroyed through the changing fortunes of wars, so that only its ancient name remained for the place. The Arvadites are those who occupied the island of Aradus, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait. The Zemarites are those to whom belonged Edessa, the famous city of Coele-Syria. Hamath, down to our time, is called by Syrians and Hebrews as it had been called among the ancients. The Macedonians who ruled in the East after Alexander named it Epiphania. Some think that Antioch is so called. Others, though not correctly, console their opinion with a seemingly plausible name: they think that Hamath is the first stopping-place from Antioch for travellers proceeding to Edessa, and that it is the same as what the ancients called Hamath.

The boundary of the Canaanites was from Sidon, as one goes toward Gerar, as far as Gaza; and, as one goes toward Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha. Since the other cities—Sidon, Gerar, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—are known to everyone, this alone seems worth noting: Lasha itself is what is now called Callirrhoe, where hot waters bursting forth flow into the Dead Sea.

The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Lud, Arphaxad, and Aram. These occupy the part of Asia from the Euphrates River as far as the Indian Ocean. Elam, from whom come the Elamites, is the beginning of Persia. Asshur has already been mentioned as the founder of the city of Ninus. Arphaxad is the ancestor of the Chaldeans; Ludim (Lud), of Lydia; and Aram, of the Syrians, whose chief city is Damascus.

The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Uz, founder of Trachonitis [Col. 0529C] and Damascus, held dominion between Palestine and Coele-Syria. From him the Seventy Translators, in the Book of Job, where the Hebrew reads “the land of Uz,” translated the region of Ausitis, or rather Ussitis. Hul was the ancestor of the Armenians; Gether of the Acarnanians, or Carians. Mash, for whom the Seventy Translators read Mosoch, is the ancestor of those who are now called Maeonians.

Arphaxad begot Shelah, and Shelah begot Eber. Eber had two sons: the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; and the name of his brother was Joktan. Eber, from whom the Hebrews are named, gave his son Peleg a name derived from prophecy: it means “division,” because in his days the languages were divided at Babylon.

Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. I have not been able to discover the later names of these peoples; but since they are far from us, either they are still called by their original names or it is not known which names have been altered. They occupied the whole region of India from the river Coepher, which is called Hieira.

Now the earth had one language and the same expressions. “The whole earth had one language,” he says. How can this be understood, when it was stated above that the sons of Noah, or the sons of his sons, had been distributed throughout the earth according to their tribes, nations, and languages, unless he is later recalling by recapitulation what had occurred earlier? Yet the obscurity arises because he joins these statements together in such a manner that the narrative seems to proceed as though it were describing events that happened afterward.

When they journeyed from the East, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. One said to his neighbor, “Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire.” They used bricks for stone and bitumen for mortar, and they said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven; and let us make our name famous before we are scattered throughout all the lands,” and so forth.

This tower signifies the pride of the present world, or the impious doctrines of heretics. After they had been moved away from the East—that is, from the true light—they came to the plain of Shinar, which means “shaking of teeth.” [Col. 0530B] Immediately, in opposition to God, they built a tower of their impiety and, with criminal boldness, fashioned the pride of their doctrines, wishing by illicit curiosity to penetrate the heights of heaven itself. But just as those people were divided from one language into many through pride, so heretics, separated from the unity of faith and confession, are divided among themselves by the diversity of their errors, as though by the discord of languages. Those whom the destructive agreement of an exalted conspiracy arms against God are again divided when discord among their doctrines intervenes and sudden confusion arises. The Trinity itself, which they offend, condemns them; it scatters them when it says:

“Come, let us confuse their languages,” namely, in the variety of error or schism. God’s descending is to inspect a human act or to draw near to their thoughts. [Col. 0530C] But when he said “Let us descend” in the plural and then again used the singular, “The Lord confused the language of the whole earth,” he wished to show, through the distinction of persons and the unity of operation, the holy Trinity in the divine majesty. So also, at the beginning of the creation of humanity, it is said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” and again, “The Lord made man in his likeness,” so that the Trinity may be believed to exist in persons and unity in power.

If anyone asks in which family the language first given to Adam remained, let him know that it is credible that it remained in the family of Eber, from whom the Hebrews are named, among that portion of humanity in which God’s portion remained, and in which Christ was to be born. For it was fitting that salvation should first be proclaimed to the world in that language through which death had first entered the world. The title written on the Savior’s cross also shows that this was the first of all languages.

Again, if anyone is troubled by what is written above, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works” (Gen. I), and wonders how such diversity of languages could suddenly appear, let him understand that in this division of languages the Creator did not create something new, but divided modes and forms of speech among different kinds of languages. Hence, in the languages of different nations, we find the same syllables and letters of the same force joined together in different ways. Often, too, the same names or words signify one thing in one language and something else in another. Where we say in the Psalm, “with an iron rod” (Psal. II), the Greek has [Col. 0531A] ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ. Thus, in Latin, *sidera* does not mean “iron,” as it does in Greek, but “stars.”

## CHAPTER XII. On the generation of Abram and his departure from the land of the Chaldeans

These are the generations of Terah: Terah begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran begot Lot. Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans. In the passage which, according to the Seventy, we read as “in the region of the Chaldeans,” the Hebrew has *Ur Casdim*, that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.”

The Hebrews, taking this as an occasion, transmit a story of the following kind: Abram was cast into the fire because he refused to worship the fire revered by the Chaldeans; and, delivered by God’s help, he fled from the fire of idolatry. [Col. 0531B] This is what is written later, namely, that Terah went out with his offspring from the region of the Chaldeans. In the Hebrew, however, it reads “from the burning of the Chaldeans.” This, they say, is also the meaning of the statement, “Haran died before Terah his father, in the land of his birth, in the fire of the Chaldeans”: because he refused to worship the fire, he was consumed by fire. The Lord later says to Abram, “I am the one who brought you out of the fire of the Chaldeans.”

Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah. The father of Milcah was also the father of Iscah. Haran, son of Terah and brother of Abram and Nahor, had two daughters, Milcah and Sarai, also called Iscah, *δυώνυμον*, “having two names.” Of these, Nahor took Milcah as his wife and Abram took Sarai; for at that time marriage between uncles and their brothers’ daughters had not yet been prohibited by law, just as among the earliest human beings marriages had even been contracted between brothers and sisters.

Terah therefore took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Abram, and led them out of Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. They came as far as Haran and settled there. All the days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran.

(Aug.) It is rightly asked how this should be understood. Terah, when he was seventy years old, begot Abram; afterward he remained with all his household in Haran, lived two hundred and five years in Haran, and died there. Then the Lord told Abram to leave Haran, and he departed from there when he was seventy-five years old, as is shown later. This can be understood only if, by recapitulation, the Lord is shown to have spoken to Abram while Terah was still alive, and Abram, while his father was still living, left Haran at the Lord’s command when he was seventy-five years old—that is, in the one hundred and forty-fifth year of his father’s life, if his father’s lifetime was two hundred and five years. Thus it was written, “The years of Terah’s life were two hundred and five in Haran,” because there he completed all the years of his entire life.

The problem is therefore resolved through recapitulation; it would remain insoluble if we understood that the Lord spoke to Abram to leave Haran only after Terah’s death. Abram could not still have been seventy-five years old when his father had already died, since his father had begotten him in the seventieth year of his own life. Abram would have been one hundred and thirty-five years old at his father’s death if his father’s whole lifetime had been two hundred and five years.

If this recapitulation is observed in Scripture, it resolves many questions that may appear insoluble. According also to the explanation of the earlier questions, and through the same recapitulation—although some solve this question differently—the years of Abraham’s life may be reckoned from the time when he was delivered from the fire of the Chaldeans, into which he was cast to be burned because he refused to worship that fire according to the superstition of the Chaldeans. Though this is not recorded in Scripture, it is transmitted in Jewish tradition.

The matter can also be resolved in this way: when Scripture says that Terah, being seventy years old, begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran, it does not necessarily mean that he begot all three in the same seventieth year of his life. Rather, Scripture mentioned the year in which he began to beget children. It is possible, therefore, that Abram was born later; but because of his distinction, since he is highly commended in Scripture, he was named first. Thus the prophet named the younger first: “Jacob I loved, Esau I hated” (Matt. I). Likewise, in Chronicles, although Judah was fourth in birth order, he is named first because the Jewish people received their name from him on account of the royal tribe.

More conveniently, several solutions can be found by which difficult questions may be resolved. The account of Stephen concerning this matter (Acts VII) must certainly be considered, since the difficulty of these interpretations should not be allowed to conflict with him.

That account does compel us to understand that God did not speak to Abraham, as the narrative in Genesis seems to say, after Terah’s death, telling him to depart from his kindred and his father’s house. Rather, God spoke to him while he was in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran, after he had already departed from the land of the Chaldeans; thus God’s word is understood to have come to him during that journey.

But what Stephen afterward says—“Then Abram went out from the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran, and from there, after his father had died, he placed him in this land”—creates considerable difficulty for this exposition [or, “question”] based on recapitulation. [Col. 0532D] It seems that Abram had received the Lord’s command, spoken to him on his journey through Mesopotamia, after he had gone out from the land of the Chaldeans and was going to Haran; and that he obediently fulfilled this command after his father’s death, when it is said, “And he settled in Haran; and from there, after his father had died, he brought him into this land.”

The question therefore remains: if, as the Book of Genesis clearly says, Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran, how can this be true? Unless perhaps Stephen’s statement, “Then Abram went out from the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran,” is not to be understood in this way: “Then he went out” after the Lord had spoken to him. For he was already in Mesopotamia, as was stated above, when he heard that command from the Lord. Stephen may have wished to join together the rule of recapitulation and say at the same time: “He went out from the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran.”

In the intervening period—that is, between his departure from the land of the Chaldeans and his settlement in Haran—God spoke to him. Then, in what Stephen adds, “And from there, after his father had died, he brought him into this land,” we must observe that he did not say, “After his father had died, he departed from Haran,” but “From there he brought him into this land.” Thus, after his settlement in Haran, he was brought into the land of Canaan—not because he was brought into the land of Canaan only after his father’s death, but so that the order of the words may be understood as follows: “He settled in Haran; and from there he brought him into this land after his father had died.”

Abram was then understood to have been settled and established in the land of Canaan when he received there the grandson whose entire offspring was destined to reign there, through the inheritance promised and granted by God. From Abram himself Ishmael was born of Hagar. Others were born of Keturah, but the inheritance of that land did not belong to them. From Isaac was born Esau, who was likewise excluded from that inheritance. From Jacob, Isaac’s son, all the sons who were born—that is, his entire offspring—belonged to that inheritance.

Abram was therefore settled and established in that land because he lived until the birth of Jacob. If this is correctly understood, the question is resolved according to the principle of recapitulation, although the other solutions should not be despised.

## (CHAPTER XII)

The Lord said to Abram: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I will show you; [Col. 0533C] and I will make you into a great nation.”

(Isid.) Who else went out in Abram from his own land and kindred in order to become wealthy among foreigners and to be made into a great nation, except Christ, who, having left the land and kindred of the Jews, now excels, as we see, among the peoples of the nations?

But we too, following Christ’s example, must go out from our land—that is, from the possessions of this world and earthly riches—and from our kindred, that is, from our former manner of life, conduct, and vices, which cling to us from our birth and are joined to us by a kind of affinity and blood relationship. We must also depart from our father’s house, that is, from every memory of the world, so that by renouncing it we may increase among God’s people and, when the time comes, be led into the land of the heavenly promise.

[Col. 0533D] “And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

Two promises are given to Abraham. One is the promise that his offspring will possess the land of Canaan, when God says, “Go into the land that I will show you, and I will make you into a great nation.” The other is far more excellent: it concerns not carnal but spiritual offspring, through which he is the father not of the single Israelite nation but of all the nations that follow the footsteps of his faith. This began to be promised in the words, “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

[Col. 0534A] Abraham therefore departed as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.

The Jewish tradition mentioned above should therefore not be despised: namely, that Terah went out with his sons from the fire of the Chaldeans, and that Abram, surrounded by the Babylonian conflagration because he refused to worship it, was delivered by God’s help. From that time, they say, the days of his life and the period of his age were reckoned, from the time when he confessed the Lord and rejected the idols of the Chaldeans.

It is also possible that, since Scripture has left the matter uncertain, Terah had departed from Chaldea only a few years earlier and had come to Haran shortly before his death; or certainly that he came to Haran immediately after the persecution and remained there for a longer period.

The Lord appeared to Abram and said to him, “To your offspring I will give this land.” He built there an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him, and so forth.

When Abram arrived in the land of Canaan, which was then inhabited by the Canaanite, the Lord is described as having appeared to him. Abram built an altar to him because, rejecting the idols of the nations, he was a worshiper of the one God.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Abram’s descent into Egypt and what then happened there concerning his wife Sarai

Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there, for a famine had prevailed in the land. When he was near entering Egypt, he said to his wife Sarai: “I know that you are a beautiful woman. When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘She is his wife,’ and they will kill me but preserve you. Say, therefore, I beg you, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you, and my life may be spared for your sake.”

(Albin.) It is asked whether it was appropriate for Abram, such a holy man, to conceal that Sarai was his wife, and why he did not rather place his hope in God, so that he would not be killed by the king. This deed shows that a person ought not to tempt the Lord his God when he has something he can do through reasonable counsel. Abram did what he could for the sake of his life. What he could not do, he entrusted to the one in whom he hoped; to him also he entrusted the chastity of his wife. His faith and hope did not fail him.

Pharaoh, terrified by God and afflicted with many troubles on her account, learned by divine revelation that she was Abram’s wife and restored her unharmed and with honor to her husband. Could God not have driven away the death that Abram feared and protected him with his wife during that journey, so that no one would desire his wife, beautiful though she was, and so that he himself would not be killed on her account? God could certainly have done this.

(Aug.) Who would be so foolish as to deny it? But if Abram, when questioned, had identified her as his wife, he would have entrusted two things requiring protection to God: his own life and his wife’s chastity. Sound doctrine teaches that, when a person has something he can do, he should not tempt the Lord his God.

For could the Savior himself not have protected his disciples? Yet he said to them, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. x). He first provided an example of this conduct. Although he had the power to lay down his life, and would not lay it down except when he wished, nevertheless, as an infant, he fled to Egypt, carried by his parents. He also went up to the feast not openly but secretly, although on other occasions he spoke publicly to the Jews who were angry and listening with the greatest hostility. They were nevertheless unable to lay hands on him, because his hour had not yet come—not an hour whose necessity forced him to die, but an hour whose appointed opportunity allowed him to be killed.

By teaching and rebuking openly, yet not allowing the rage of his enemies to have any power over him, he demonstrated God’s power. But by fleeing and hiding he also instructed human weakness, so that a person may not dare to tempt God when there is something he can do to escape what ought to be avoided.

The Apostle Paul likewise had not despaired of divine help and protection, nor had he lost faith, when he was lowered in a basket through a wall in order to escape the hands of his enemies (II Cor. XI). He did not flee because he failed to believe in God; rather, he would have tempted God if he had refused to flee when he was able to flee in this way.

When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was exceedingly beautiful. They reported this to Pharaoh’s princes, and they praised her before him. The woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house. Abram was treated well on her account, and he acquired sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants, households, and camels.

Although the bodies of holy women are not defiled by force but by the will, and Sarai could be excused on the grounds that, in a time of famine, alone in a foreign land before a king, and with her husband’s acquiescence, she was unable to resist, the shameful necessity may also be excused in another way. According to the Book of Esther, every woman who pleased the king among the ancients was anointed for six months with oil of myrrh, and for six months with various perfumes and women’s treatments; only then did she enter the king’s presence. It is therefore possible that after Sarai had pleased the king, while her entry to the king was being prepared for a year, and while Pharaoh was giving Abram many gifts, Pharaoh was struck by the Lord, with Sarai still untouched by his intercourse.

## (CHAPTER XIII)

Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and everything that belonged to him, and Lot with him, toward the southern region. Abram was very rich in silver and gold. He returned by the route on which he had come, from the south toward Bethel, and so forth.

He is beautifully said to have gone up after being delivered from Egypt. But the following statement seems to conflict with this interpretation: how could he have become exceedingly rich when he departed from Egypt? The difficulty is resolved by the Hebrew truth, in which it is written, “Abram was exceedingly heavy,” that is, Βαρὺς σφόδρα, “very heavy.” He was weighed down by the burden of Egypt. Although his wealth may appear to consist of livestock, gold, and silver, if these were Egyptian possessions they were nevertheless a burden to a holy man.

Accordingly, Abram did not, as we read in the Seventy, go from the place where he had come through the wilderness as far as Bethel. Rather, as it is written in the Hebrew, he went on his journey through the Negeb as far as Bethel. He departed from Egypt not in order to enter the wilderness that he had left behind with Egypt, but to come through the south, which is opposite the north, to the house of God, where he pitched his tabernacle between Bethel and Hai.

Bethel is a small town twelve miles from Aelia, on the right as one travels toward Neapolis. It was previously called Luz, that is, Almond-tree, and it fell by lot to the tribe of Benjamin. Hai is a city in the tribe of Judah, set apart for the priests. Bethel is interpreted as “house of God,” while Hai means “eye” or “fountain.”

It is fitting that Abram is said to have pitched his tabernacle on the mountain between Bethel and Hai and to have built an altar to God there. For holy men, after withdrawing from the prince of this world and from the pleasures of the age, washed in the fountain of sacred baptism and proceeding cautiously and thoughtfully through the course of the present life, offer to God on the altar of right faith the sacrifice of praise and good works. Thus they advance happily toward the house of God, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the quarrel between Abram’s and Lot’s shepherds, and on the promise by which God promised Abram the land of Canaan as a possession

Abram said to Lot: “Let there be no quarrel, I beg you, between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers. Behold, the whole land is before you; depart from me, I beg you. If you go to the left, I will take the right; if you choose the right, I will go to the left.”

In a figurative sense, blessed Abram, wishing to avoid discord between his shepherds and Lot’s shepherds and therefore choosing that they should separate from one another, warns us to place nothing before charity and concord. We should always be ready to persevere in peace and love, whether through prosperity, signified by the right hand, or through adversity, expressed by the left.

Lot lifted up his eyes and saw all the region around the Jordan, which was entirely watered before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the Lord and like Egypt as one approaches Zoar.

(Aug.) The land of Sodom and Gomorrah is compared, before its destruction, with the garden of the Lord because it was well watered, and with the land of Egypt because the Nile irrigates it. This sufficiently shows, as I think, that the garden planted by God, where he placed Adam, is what must be understood by “the garden of God.” I do not see what other garden of God could be meant. And certainly, if the trees in paradise were to be understood as virtues of the soul, as some think, and no bodily paradise with genuine kinds of trees had been established on earth, Scripture would not have said of this land, “like the garden of God.”

Lot chose for himself the region around the Jordan and departed toward the East. They separated from one another. Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot dwelt in the towns around the Jordan and settled in Sodom.

Allegorically, Lot’s shepherds, who chose the plain of the land of Sodom and a place of pleasure, may represent the multitude of heretics. Devoted to the pleasures of the present life and bound by the chains of error, they turn away from the path of truth and reject fellowship with Christ and the unity of the Catholic faith. The name Lot aptly expresses this, for it is interpreted as “bound” or “turning aside.”

The men of Sodom were evil and sinners exceedingly in the sight of God. The words “in the sight of God” have been added here unnecessarily by the Seventy Translators. The people of Sodom were plainly evil and sinful in the judgment of everyone. But that person is called a sinner “in the sight of God” who may appear righteous to human beings, just as it is said in praise of Zechariah and Elizabeth that both were righteous in the sight of God (Luke I), and as the Psalm says, “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psal. CXLII).

The Lord said to Abram after Lot had separated from him: “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north and the south, toward the east and the west. All the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever, and I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth. If anyone can count the dust of the earth, he will also be able to count your offspring.”

He set out the four regions of the world: east and west, north and south. Historically, possession of the land of Palestine is promised to him and to his offspring, that is, to the Israelite people. In some copies, however, the text is found as follows: “Lift up your eyes toward the north and the south, toward the east and the sea,” and so forth. “The sea” is used for “the west,” because the region of Palestine is situated so that the sea lies on its western side.

Mystically, the inheritance of all nations is promised to Abraham’s offspring, which is Christ. He extends his Church throughout the length and breadth of the world. The Father says to him, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psal. II). The Psalmist likewise says, “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psal. LXXII).

## CHAPTER XV. How four kings fought against five kings of the Sodomites and plundered Lot, and how Abram brought back the spoils with Lot

## (CHAPTER XIV)

At that time Amraphel, king of Shinar; Arioch, king of Pontus; Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites; and Tidal, king of nations, waged war against Bera, king of Sodom; Birsha, king of Gomorrah; Shinab, king of Admah; Shemeber, king of Zeboiim; and the king of Bela, which is Zoar.

All these gathered in the wooded valley, which is now the Salt Sea. *Bela* in the Hebrew language means “devouring.” The Hebrews therefore relate that this same place is called *Salisa* elsewhere in Scripture and is again described as μόσχον τριετίζουσαν, that is, “a three-year-old calf,” because it was swallowed up by an earthquake on the third occasion. From the time when Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim were overthrown by divine fire, it has been called the little one. For Zoar means “little” in translation, and in the Syrian language it is called Zoara.

The Valley of Salt, in which, as is written in this same book, there had previously been wells of bitumen, was turned into the Dead Sea after God’s anger and the rain of sulfur.

They struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, and the Zuzim with them, and the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in the mountains of Seir as far as the plain of Paran, which is in the wilderness. They turned back and came to the spring of Misphat, which is Kadesh; and they struck the whole region of the Amalekites and the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar.

Another edition reads as follows: “They cut down the giants at Ashteroth-karnaim, and the strong nations with them, and the Ommim in the city of Sabe.” Before reaching Sodom, the four kings who had set out from Babylon killed the giants, that is, the Rephaim, and all the strong men of Arabia; they also killed the Zuzim in Ham and the Emim in the city of Shaveh, which is still so called today.

The Zuzim and Emim are interpreted as “terrible” and “dreadful.” For this reason the Seventy, translating the sense rather than the word literally, rendered it “very strong nations.” Returning, they came to the spring of Judgment, that is, Kadesh. This is said by anticipation, because it was called by that name only later. It denotes the place near the rock called the Spring of Judgment, because there God judged the people.

They struck the whole region of the Amalekites and the Amorite who lived in Hazazon-tamar. This is the town now called Engaddi, fertile in balsam and palms. In our language, Hazazon-tamar means “city of palms,” for *tamar* means “palm.”

It should be known that, where the text shortly afterward reads, “And they drew up their battle line against them in the Valley of Salt,” the Hebrew has, “in the Valley of Siddim,” which Aquila and Theodotion translated as “pleasant groves.”

They took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah. The Seventy have: “They took all the cavalry of Sodom and Gomorrah.” Instead of “cavalry,” the Hebrew has *rekhush*, that is, “possessions.”

The one who had escaped reported it to Abram the traveler. He was dwelling by the oak of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner, who had made a covenant with Abram. Where we have translated “traveler,” the Hebrew text has *ibri*, which means “one who crosses over.”

Where it says “by the oak of Mamre the Amorite,” the Hebrew reads more accurately, “by the oak of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of”—not Aunan, as the Seventy translated, but Aner. This shows that Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner were Amorites and brothers, and that they were Abram’s allies.

Abram pursued them as far as Dan, the town of Phoenicia now called Paneas. Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan. The other is called Jor, which is interpreted as ῥεῖθρον, that is, “stream.” When these two springs, which are not far from one another, unite into a single stream, it is thereafter called the Jordan.

When Abram heard that his brother Lot had been captured, he counted the three hundred and eighteen trained servants born in his household and pursued them as far as Dan, and so forth. By “trained servants” he means young men ready for war and unmarried, of whom he later says, “Except those things which the young men ate.”

He brought back all the possessions, and Lot his brother with his possessions, together with the women and the people.

Mystically, the four kings who overcame the five kings may signify opposing powers that conquer and bring under their dominion carnal persons who abuse the five senses of the body through vices.

Amraphel, whose name is interpreted as “he said, ‘Let him fall,’” and who is king of Shinar—interpreted as “shaking of teeth” or “their stench”—may signify heresy. It tends toward a certain downfall and pours forth, through deceptive words, a foul understanding.

Arioth, whose name is interpreted as “drunk” or “drunkenness,” figuratively represents the folly of the pagans. Drunk with iniquity and blind in heart, they worship the creature instead of the Creator and are entirely entangled in the enticements of the world.

Chedorlaomer, whose name is interpreted as “a kind of beautiful sheaf,” and who is king of Elam, that is, of the world or the globe, not improperly expresses hypocrisy. Although hypocrisy is vain and destructive, it appears in the present to be attractive to the ignorant crowd because of its pleasing outward appearance; but in the future, when the true light comes, its true nature will be revealed.

Tidal, who is said to mean “knowing the yoke” or “explorer,” and who is king of the nations, can appropriately be transferred to signify greed. Clever and crafty, greed subjects many to its dominion.

Such kings first conquer Bera, whose name signifies “evil” or “creature,” and who is king of Sodom, interpreted as “blindness” or “a silent animal.” They persuade those who persist in ancient wickedness to follow, like animals, the blindness of lust.

They also conquer Birsha, that is, the king “established in distress,” king of Gomorrah, which means “a swelling and rebellious people.” They overwhelm and overthrow those who are distressed by anxiety over present things and do not fear to commit the crime of plunder.

They conquer Shinab, king of Admah, that is, of the earth, when they urge those who think only of carnal things and do not consider heavenly matters to remain in the luxury of pleasures, so that in their deeds they say, according to the prophetic word, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (I Cor. XV).

They conquer Shemeber, whose name is interpreted as “there is destruction,” king of Zeboiim, that is, “a girdle of mourning,” when through anger and envy they deceive the unwary. Hence it is written, “Anger kills the foolish, and envy slays the little ones” (Job V).

The spiritual wickednesses likewise conquer the fifth king, that is, the king of Bela, when they cast the fainthearted and fearful into despair. For Bela is interpreted as “precipitation” or “swallowing.” The ancient enemy strives and labors at nothing more than, after deceiving people through the fall of sin, to cast them into despair so that they cannot recover themselves, and thus destroy them.

But what did Abraham’s victory over the four kings signify? He, the father of faith, overcame them through a mystery. It signifies that if our faith is strengthened by the principal Spirit, it subjects our body, which consists of four elements, to the Word of God.

(Isid.) Just as Abraham became victorious over those kings, so faith, victorious for the soul, triumphs over the outward human being. The fact that he defeated hostile kings not by a multitude or the strength of legions but with only three hundred and eighteen companions was already foreshadowed in the mystery of the cross. The Greek letter τ, whose numerical value is three hundred, represents this mystery: the passion of Christ would free us from the dominion of carnal perception, which had previously overcome us after taking us captive through various vices.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Melchizedek and Abram’s tithe
But Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine—for he was priest of God Most High—blessed him and said:

“Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands,” and so forth. (Jerome.)

We shall set forth what the Hebrews think about this. They say that he was Shem, the son of Noah; and, reckoning the years of his life, they demonstrate that he lived until the time of Isaac, and that all Noah’s firstborn descendants were priests until Aaron exercised the priesthood. Moreover, Salem is said to be the city of Jerusalem, which was formerly called Salem.

As for Melchizedek, the blessed Apostle, when he mentions him in the Letter to the Hebrews (chapter VII) as being “without father and without mother,” refers him to Christ, and through Christ to the Church of the Gentiles. For all the glory of the head is referred to the members: although uncircumcised, he blessed Abraham, who was circumcised; and in Abraham he blessed Levi, and through Levi, Aaron, from whom the priesthood would later descend. From this he wishes it to be understood that the priesthood of the Church, which possesses uncircumcision, blessed in Abraham the circumcised priesthood of the Synagogue.

But when he says, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109), our mystery is signified by the word “order”: not through Aaron, by the sacrifice of irrational victims, but through the offering of bread and wine—that is, the body and blood of the Lord Jesus. (Isidore.)

Now the great patriarch gave all the tithes of his substance to Melchizedek the priest after receiving the blessing, knowing spiritually that a better priesthood would one day exist among the people of the Gentiles than the Levitical priesthood, which was to arise in Israel from him. It was also to come about that the priesthood of the Church possessing uncircumcision would bless, in circumcised Abraham, the priesthood of the Synagogue.

For who is greater: the one who blesses, or the one who is blessed? Hence the priests born from Abraham’s seed blessed their brothers—that is, the people of Israel—and these gave them tithes according to the command of the Law, truly treating them as their greater and more eminent superiors.

The very name Melchizedek is interpreted as “king of peace” or “king of righteousness,” which is rightly referred to Christ, as has been said above. For he is the king of peace, because through him we are reconciled to God; he is the king of righteousness, because he will come to distinguish the holy from the ungodly. He is likewise both priest and king: as priest, he offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father for the redemption of all; as the true king, he rules his people in the present age and will judge them in the age to come.

## CHAPTER XVII. Where God appeared to Abraham a third time and promised him a son; and concerning Abraham’s sacrifice

**(Chapter XV.)** After these things had taken place, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying:

“Do not be afraid, Abram; I am your protector, and your reward is exceedingly great.”

And Abram said:

“Lord God, what will you give me? I shall go away without children, and the son of the steward of my house, this Damascus Eliezer, will be my heir.”

Abram added:

“You have given me no offspring, and behold, my household servant will be my heir,” and so forth.

(Jerome.) What he says means this: “I shall die without children, and the son of my steward or bailiff, who manages everything and distributes provisions to the household, and whose name is Damascus Eliezer, will be my heir.” Eliezer is interpreted as “My God is my helper.” They say that Damascus was both founded and named from him.

Immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying:

“This man shall not be your heir; but one who will come forth from your own body, he shall be your heir.”

And he led him outside and said to him:

“Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can.”

And he said to him:

“So shall your offspring be.”

Abram believed the Lord, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

There is a twofold figure of his promised offspring: one in the likeness of the sand of the sea, and the other in the likeness of the stars of heaven. Therefore, when God led Abram outside, he showed him the stars of heaven, saying:

“Thus will I make your offspring”—that is, the Christian people, whose father you remain in faith—“thus will I make it shine with the light of the resurrection.”

Then he showed him the sand of the sea and said:

“Thus shall your offspring be in multitude.”

That is: the nation of the Jews will indeed be numerous, but barren and unfruitful like the sand of the sea.

After this, when the Lord promised him that he would become possessor of the promise, he asked for a sign by which he might recognize it—not as though he doubted whether it would happen, but inquiring how it would happen. The Lord proposed the following likeness to him:

“Take,” he said, “for me a heifer three years old, a she-goat three years old, and a ram three years old; also a turtledove and a pigeon.”

So Abram took all these, divided them down the middle, and placed the two halves opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds. Birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.

When the sun was setting, terror fell upon Abram, and a great and dark horror fell upon him. A smoking furnace and a flaming torch appeared, passing between the divided pieces, and it was said to him:

“Know with certainty that your offspring will be foreigners in a land not their own; they will serve and be afflicted,” and so forth.

Thus the manner of Abraham’s promised offspring was established, and this is its figure. The heifer signified the people placed under the yoke of the Law; the she-goat, the same people destined to become sinful; and the ram, the same people also destined to rule well.

The animals are said to be three because, through the divisions of time—from Adam to Noah, from Noah onward to Abram, and from Abram onward to David—that people grew as though passing through a third age.

The turtledove and the pigeon signify spiritual peoples, undivided children of the promise and heirs of the future kingdom. Their age is left unstated because, meditating on eternal things, they have passed beyond temporal desires.

But what does it mean that those three animals are divided, with their parts set opposite one another, except that the carnal are divided both among the ancient people and now among themselves? The birds, however, are not divided because spiritual people are undivided: they do not contemplate schism, nor are they led astray by heretics. Peace is always within them, whether they withdraw from the crowds like the turtledove, or dwell among them like the pigeon; yet both birds possess simplicity and innocence.

The birds of prey descending upon the bodies that had been divided signify unclean spirits seeking some nourishment for themselves from the division of carnal people. But the fact that Abram, sitting near them, drove them away signified that, through the merits of the saints, many carnal people would at the end of the world be freed from their afflictions.

The terror that fell upon Abram around sunset, and the great dark horror, signify the great disturbance that will come upon the saints from Antichrist near the end of this age. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel:

“For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning” (Matthew 24).

Therefore, what follows—when the sun had gone down, a dark gloom arose, and a smoking furnace and a flaming torch appeared, passing between the divided pieces—signifies the day of judgment that will come after the end of the world, when the peoples of the saints and of the wicked will be separated by fire. (Gregory.)

Tropologically, thoughts arising from earthly things often touch the hearts of the righteous with their delights. But when they are quickly driven away by the hand of holy discernment, care is promptly taken lest the gloom of temptation cover the face of the heart, which had already been touched by unlawful pleasure.

For intrusive thoughts often force themselves upon the very sacrifice of our prayer, and can seize or defile what we offer to God as pleasing to him. But, following Abraham’s example, while we offer a burnt offering to God upon the altar of the heart, let us guard it from unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts seize what our mind hopes to offer usefully to God.

(Isidore.) What was said to Abram—“Know with certainty that your offspring will be foreigners in a land not their own, and they will reduce them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years”—was most clearly prophesied concerning the people of Israel, who were to serve in Egypt. This does not mean that they served under the Egyptians for four hundred years, but that this number was completed in that affliction, reckoned from the time when these things were promised to Abraham.

“But you shall go to your fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they shall return here.”

(Jerome.) Why does God say to Abram that the children of Israel would return from the land of Egypt in the fourth generation, when afterward Moses writes, “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt” (Exodus 3)? Unless this is explained, the statements appear contradictory.

The children of Israel therefore left Egypt in the fourth generation. Let us review the genealogy of Levi: Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; Amram begot Aaron; Aaron begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Phinehas. Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi; Eleazar, in turn, departed from Egypt with his father Aaron. From Kohath to Eleazar, four generations are counted, although some wish to begin with Amram and proceed to Phinehas, as we have proceeded to Eleazar.

If, however, you wish to demonstrate by an unequal number how, according to Exodus, the children of Israel left the land of Egypt in the fifth generation, let the order of the tribe of Judah be counted for you.
