Judah begot Perez; Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon.

Perez entered Egypt with his father Judah. Nahshon is described as the prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and his son Salmon entered the promised land. Count from Perez to Nahshon, and you will find five generations, although some, as we showed in the tribe of Levi, begin with Hezron and proceed as far as Salmon.

“On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.”

Thus it is not from the great river of Egypt—that is, the Nile—but from the stream which divides Egypt and Palestine, where the city of Rhinocorura is situated.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the union of Hagar, Sarai’s maidservant, with Abram, and Hagar’s flight

**(Chapter XVI.)** Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had not borne him children. But, having an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar, she said to her husband:

“Behold, the Lord has closed me off so that I may not give birth. Go in to my maidservant; perhaps at least through her I may receive children.”

(Albinus.) How can Abram be defended from the charge of adultery, since, while his lawful wife was alive, he joined himself to his maidservant, unless it is because the Gospel law of one wife had not yet been promulgated? He also had a promise from the Lord that his offspring would be multiplied, but he did not yet know from which wife, since afterward he was told that he would have a son by Sarai.

Therefore his intention to propagate offspring was pious, because his intention in intercourse was not lustful. Sarai likewise wished to have through her maidservant the offspring which she could not have from herself. Both consented to the act, because both knew that Sarai was barren.

And he went in to her. But when she saw that she had conceived, she despised her mistress. Sarai said to Abram:

“You act unjustly toward me. I gave my maidservant into your embrace; and when she saw that she had conceived, she holds me in contempt. May the Lord judge between me and you.”

Abram answered her:

“Behold, your maidservant is in your hand; deal with her as you please.”

When Sarai afflicted her, she fled. The angel of the Lord found her beside a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Assur in the desert, and said to her:

“Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?”

As an Egyptian on the road to Assur—which leads through the wilderness to Egypt—she was hastening to go to Egypt, where the angel of the Lord found her. And the angel of the Lord said to her:

“Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand.”

And again:

“I will multiply your offspring exceedingly, and it shall not be numbered because of its multitude.”

And thereafter:

“Behold, you have conceived and shall bear a son; you shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your affliction. He will be a wild man: his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand will be against him; and he will pitch his tents opposite all his brothers.”

Another edition has it this way:

“He will be a rustic man; his hand will be over all, and everyone’s hand will be over him, and he will dwell opposite all his brothers.”

In place of “rustic,” the Hebrew has *phere*, which is interpreted as “wild ass.” It signifies that his offspring would dwell in the wilderness—that is, the wandering Saracens, with uncertain settlements. They attack all the nations adjoining the desert on its borders, while being attacked by everyone.

Mystically, these two women—namely Sarai and Hagar—signify, according to the Apostle’s interpretation, the two covenants. Hagar signifies the Old Law, which in the Synagogue nourished the Jewish people subject to slavery. Sarai signifies evangelical grace, which brought forth the Christian people into the freedom of faith.

Thus the children of the maidservant, the Jews, were multiplied and could not be numbered because of their multitude. Concerning them it was written above that they would be multiplied like the sand of the sea.

“He will be a wild man, and his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand will be against him; and he will pitch his tents opposite all his brothers,” because that people, in its ferocity, is rival and hostile to all good things, especially when, stirred by envy, it persecutes the Christian people throughout the world. Scattered far and wide, wandering about and engaging in commerce, and always existing in uncertain settlements, it is a burden to everyone.

Nevertheless, I have read in a certain treatise that Sarai, Abram’s wife, was interpreted as the primitive Church, while the Egyptian maidservant signified the Church from the Gentiles. After conceiving the word of faith, this Church despised the barrenness of the Synagogue. The angel’s command that Hagar return to her mistress Sarai and humble herself under her hands signified that apostolic teaching warned the Gentiles not to become proud against the Jewish people.

Hence the Apostle says:

“Do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root bears you” (Romans 11).

And again:

“If God,” he says, “did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either” (ibid.).

The phrase “wild man” might indirectly be understood to mean one who fights against demons and heretics and resists vices. But we leave these matters to the judgment of the reader.

Hagar called upon the name of the Lord who spoke to her:

“You are the God who saw me.”

For she said:

“Surely here I have seen the back of the one who sees me.”

It was rightly said that she called upon the name of the Lord, “You are the God who saw me,” because he freely comes to the aid of the wretched and consoles the humble in their tribulation. Hence the Psalmist says:

“You, Lord, see labor and consider grief. To you the poor is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Psalm 9).

And what follows—“Surely here I have seen the back of the one who sees me”—well corresponds to that saying which the Lord spoke to Moses when he had asked that his majesty be shown to him:

“You cannot see my face and live. For man shall not see my face and live.”

And the Lord said:

“Behold, there is a place beside me; you shall stand upon the rock. As soon as my majesty passes by, I will place you in the cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I have passed by. Then I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back. For my face shall not appear to you.”

Therefore it is not without reason that no one can see the face—that is, the very manifestation of God’s wisdom—and live. This is the form whose contemplation is longed for by everyone who desires to love God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind. In order to contemplate it, such a person also builds up his neighbor, insofar as he can, through that love with which he loves him as himself.

By the “back” of the Lord we may understand his incarnation, which at the end of time he assumed from the Virgin. In the present we contemplate it through faith and love, desiring it; in the future life we shall enjoy its eternal contemplation.

Therefore she called that well “the well of the living one who sees me.” To this day Hagar’s well is shown in the desert of Arabia, between Kadesh and Barad.

Typically, this well signifies the Old and New Law, which our Creator—who is the life of the living and the hope of the dying—gave to mortals out of loving compassion, so that, instructed and corrected from their vices through it, they might become worthy to enjoy his perpetual vision in heaven.

And Hagar bore Abram a son, and he called his name Ishmael. The name is an allusion: Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing of God,” just as the angel said above to Hagar:

“You shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard my affliction.”

## CHAPTER XIX. God’s covenant made with Abram; the Lord promises that he will become the father of nations and gives him the name Abraham

**(Chapter XVII.)** When he had begun to be ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him and said:

“I am God Almighty; walk before me and be perfect. I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.”

Abram fell facedown. And God said to him:

“I am he, and I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall be the father of many nations. No longer shall your name be called Abram, but you shall be called Abraham, because I have appointed you the father of many nations.”

It should be noted that wherever we read “testament” in the Greek language, the Hebrew has “covenant” or “agreement,” that is, *berith*. The Hebrews say that God added the letter *he* to Abram’s and Sarai’s names from his own name, which among them is the τετραγράμματον—that is, the “four-letter name.”

At first he was called Abram, which is interpreted as “exalted father”; afterward he was called Abraham, which is rendered “father of many.” The word “nations,” which follows, is not contained in the name but is understood.

Nor should it be considered strange that, although among the Greeks and among us an *a* appears to have been added, we have said that the Hebrew letter *he* was added. It is a peculiarity of that language to write with *he* but read with *a*. Conversely, they often pronounce the letter *a* as *e*.

“And I will give you and your offspring after you the land of your sojourning, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession,” and so forth.

(Augustine.) The question is how he could call it everlasting, since it was given to the Israelites only temporarily. Was it called everlasting with reference to this age, so that it was derived from the Greek word αἰών (*aion*), which signifies an age, and αἰώνιον (*aionion*), as though in Latin one could say “secular”?  Or are we compelled to understand something here according to the spiritual promise, so that it is called everlasting because it signifies something eternal?

“Therefore you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you and your offspring after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, so that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you. An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in the household or purchased, shall be circumcised; and whoever is not of your stock shall be circumcised. My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. Any male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

Even then, because of the future sojourn, so that his offspring would not mingle among the nations, God made a covenant with Abraham and gave him circumcision as a sign, in these words:

“Every male among you shall be circumcised. An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you; both one born in the household and one purchased shall be circumcised. But the male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

But what else does circumcision signify except the renewal of nature through baptism after the stripping away of the old man? And who is the eighth day except Christ, who, when the week was complete—that is, after the Sabbath—rose again?

The fact that he commands not only sons but also slaves, household servants, and purchased servants to be circumcised testifies that the grace of redemption pertains to all.

There the names of the parents are changed, so that everything might resound with newness. Abram, as he was previously called, is interpreted as “exalted father”; Abraham means “father of many.” By this name it was foretold that many nations would follow the traces of his faith.

But what does this mean:

“The male who is not circumcised on the eighth day shall perish from the people, because he has broken my covenant”?

Why should the soul of an uncircumcised infant perish, when the infant itself did not break God’s covenant, but those who neglected to circumcise it did? It signifies that infants have broken God’s covenant in the first man not by their own deeds but by their origin, in whom all sinned.

All are born sinful, not personally but originally. Unless regeneration frees a person, his soul will perish from his people, because he has broken God’s covenant when, originally, he too sinned in Adam.

For this reason Abraham’s circumcision was first commended, so that he might be under the Law, just as Adam was, lest he eat from the tree, and so that it might be proved whether he would fulfill this command or not.

(Albinus.) He believes that he will have a son through whose birth blessing will come to all nations, and among whose descendants a unique pattern of chastity and sobriety would remain. Therefore he received the sign of faith on that part of the body from which a son of faith, not of flesh, was to be born.

He was not made more deformed by the cutting away of a bodily part, but more glorious through faith in God. Thus to lose something for God is gain, not loss. In receiving the sign of his faith, Abraham was not disfigured but improved.

For if Adam had kept God’s covenant, Abraham would not have received this covenant. But because Adam first acknowledged the guilt of disobedience in this member, it was fitting that Abraham should receive in this member the sign of obedience a second time, so that it might be shown that the obedient would eventually beget children for life, whereas the transgressors of old had begotten children for death.

And the Lord said to Abraham:

“You shall not call the name of your wife Sarai, but Sarah. I will bless her, and from her I will give you a son; I will bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of peoples shall arise from him.”

Here the promise concerning the calling of the Gentiles in Isaac, the son of promise, is now made clear—that is, by grace, not by nature. For he was born from an aged father and a barren mother. And because this was to occur not through the generation represented by Ishmael but through regeneration, circumcision was commanded at the very time when a son was promised from Sarah, who prefigured the Church, not at the time of Ishmael, who represented the Jews.

Those are mistaken who think that Sarah was first written with one *r* and that another *r* was later added, and who, because *r* among the Greeks represents the number one hundred, imagine many foolish things about her name. However one wishes to alter the name, the explanation must be Hebrew, not Greek, since the name itself is Hebrew. No one, when calling someone by a name in one language, derives the etymology of the name from another language.

Sarai was therefore first written with *sin*, *resh*, and *yod*. When the *yod*—that is, the element *i*—was removed, a letter read as *a* was added, and she was called Saraa. The reason for this change of name is that previously she was called “my princess,” the mistress of one household only; afterward she was called simply “princess,” that is, ἄρχουσα (*archousa*). For she was now to become the princess of all nations.

Some very badly suppose that she was formerly called “leprous” and afterward “princess,” although leprosy is called *zaraath*. In our language the words may appear somewhat similar, but in Hebrew they are entirely different. It is written with [letters materially uncertain in the supplied text], which plainly differ greatly from the three letters with which Sarah is written.

And Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart:

“Shall a son be born to one who is a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”

Since shortly afterward it says, “You shall call his name Isaac,” there is a difference of opinion, but there is one etymology for why he was called Isaac. For the name is interpreted as “laughter.”

Some say that he was called “laughter” because Sarah laughed, but this is false. Others say that it was because Abraham laughed, and this we approve. For only after his son Isaac was named from Abraham’s laughter do we read that Sarah laughed.

It should be known that four persons in the Old Testament were called by their names, without any veil of concealment, before they were born: Ishmael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josiah. Read the Scriptures.

And he said to God:

“If only Ishmael might live before you!”

And God said to Abraham:

“Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his offspring after him.

“I have also heard you concerning Ishmael. Behold, I will bless him and increase him and multiply him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time in the following year.”

Finally, concerning Ishmael, who represents the Jewish people, it was rightly said that he would be increased and multiplied exceedingly and would beget twelve princes, since the multitude of the carnal Jews, born from the twelve patriarchs, was divided into twelve tribes.

The Lord’s covenant with Isaac is the covenant with the people of believers, whom the mother Church brought forth through faith and baptism. An everlasting covenant was established with them because possession of eternal life is promised only to the one who, with his head Christ, will always possess the kingdom of heaven.

The following year, in which Sarah bore Isaac, signifies the times of regeneration, in which Christ’s blood was shed and the human race was restored to life.

## CHAPTER XX. The circumcision of Abraham and his son Ishmael, and of all the household servants of his house

When the speech of the one speaking with him had ended, God departed from Abraham. Abraham took Ishmael his son, all the household servants of his house, all those whom he had purchased, and every male among the men of his household, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins on that very day, as God had commanded him.

Since we have now come to these passages, I wish to inquire whether Almighty God, who holds dominion over heaven and earth, when he wished to establish a covenant with a holy man, placed the substance of so great a matter in this: that the foreskin of his flesh, and also the future offspring begotten from him, should be circumcised.

“For it shall be,” he says, “my covenant upon your flesh.”

This was contained in the matter: the Lord of heaven and earth was granting the gifts of an eternal covenant to the one man whom he alone had chosen from among all mortals.

These are the only things in which the teachers and doctors of the Synagogue place the glory of the saints. Hear, therefore, how Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, instructs the Church of Christ in faith and truth concerning the mystery of circumcision.

“Beware,” he says, speaking of the Jews who are mutilated in the flesh, “of the concision. For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit and do not put confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3).

This is one statement of Paul concerning circumcision. Hear another:

“For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, with circumcision of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter” (Romans 2).

Does not such circumcision appear more worthy to be spoken of among the saints and friends of God than the cutting away of the flesh?

But perhaps the novelty of this teaching will frighten not only the Jews but also some of our brothers. For Paul seems to presume something impossible when he introduces circumcision of the heart. How could a member be circumcised that is covered by the inward organs and hidden even from the sight of men?

But you, O people of God, a people chosen for acquisition, to declare the virtues of the Lord, receive the worthy circumcision of the word of God in your ears, on your lips, in your heart, in the foreskin of your flesh, and in all your members altogether.

Let your ears be circumcised according to the word of God, so that they may not receive the voice of the slanderer, and so that they may not hear the words of the malicious and blasphemous, nor open the mind to false accusations. Let them be stopped and closed, so that they may not hear judgments of bloodshed or open themselves to immodest songs and theatrical sounds. Let them receive nothing obscene; let them turn away from every spectacle of corruption.

This is the circumcision by which the Church of Christ circumcises the ears of her little ones. These, I believe, are the ears that the Lord sought in his hearers when he said:

“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8).

For no one can hear the pure words of wisdom and truth with uncircumcised and unclean ears.

Let us come, if you wish, also to the circumcision of the lips. I think that he is uncircumcised in his lips who has not yet ceased from foolish speech and buffoonery; who disparages good people; who accuses his neighbors; who incites quarrels; who stirs up slanders; who sets brothers against one another by speaking falsely; who utters vain, foolish, worldly, immodest, shameful, insulting, insolent, blasphemous words, and all the rest that is unworthy of a Christian.

But if someone restrains his mouth from all these things, orders his speech with judgment, represses verbosity, controls his tongue, and moderates his words, he is rightly called circumcised in his lips.

Those also who speak iniquity on high and stretch their tongues to heaven, as heretics do, must be called uncircumcised and unclean in their lips. But circumcised and clean is the one who always speaks the word of God and delivers sound doctrine fortified by evangelical and apostolic rules.

In this way, therefore, circumcision of the lips is also given in the Church of God.

Now, according to our promise, let us see how circumcision of the flesh ought also to be received. No one doubts that the member on which the foreskin is found serves the natural functions of intercourse and generation.

Therefore, if someone is not excessive in his movements concerning this matter, does not exceed the limits established by the laws, knows no woman other than his lawful wife, and engages even with her only for the sake of offspring and at the proper and lawful times, he is to be called circumcised in the foreskin of his flesh.

But whoever rushes into every form of wantonness, hangs upon diverse and unlawful embraces, and is carried without restraint into every whirlpool of lust, is uncircumcised in the foreskin of his flesh.

The Church of Christ, strengthened by the grace of the one who was crucified for her, abstains not only from unlawful and abominable beds but also from those that are permitted and lawful. Like a virgin bride of Christ, she flourishes with chaste and modest virgins, in whom true circumcision of the foreskin of the flesh has taken place, and in whose flesh the covenant of God—truly the eternal covenant—is preserved.

It remains to describe circumcision of the heart. If someone burns with obscene desires and shameful passions and, to put it briefly, commits adultery in his heart, he is uncircumcised in heart.

Likewise, whoever retains heretical thoughts in his mind and arranges blasphemous assertions against the knowledge of Christ in his heart is uncircumcised in heart.

But whoever preserves pure faith in the sincerity of conscience is circumcised in heart. Of him it can be said:

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

I also dare, by analogy, to add these things to the prophetic words: just as the ears, lips, heart, and foreskin of the flesh ought to be circumcised according to what we have said above, so perhaps our hands also need circumcision, as do our feet, sight, smell, and touch.

For, if the man of God is to be perfect in all things, all his members must be circumcised. The hands must be circumcised from robbery, theft, and murder, and opened only for the works of God.

The feet must be circumcised, so that they may not be swift to shed blood and may not enter the assembly of the wicked, but may walk only for the sake of God’s commandments.

The eye must also be circumcised, so that it may not covet what belongs to another and may not look upon a woman in order to desire her. For the one whose gaze wanders lustfully and inquisitively over the forms of women is uncircumcised in his eyes.

If someone, whether eating or drinking, eats and drinks for the glory of God, as the Apostle commanded (1 Corinthians 10), he is circumcised in taste. But of the one whose god is his belly and who serves the pleasures of the throat, I would say that his taste is uncircumcised.

If someone receives the good fragrance of Christ and seeks the fragrance of sweetness in works of mercy, his sense of smell is circumcised. But whoever walks saturated with the finest perfumes is to be called uncircumcised in smell.

Likewise, each of the members, if it serves the duties of God’s commandments, must be called circumcised. But if the members luxuriate beyond the laws divinely prescribed for them, they must be considered uncircumcised.

## CHAPTER XXI. Where three men appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre as he sat at the entrance of his tent
### (Chapter XVIII) The Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the very heat of the day. When he had raised his eyes, three men appeared to him standing near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the entrance of his tent, bowed to the ground, and said: “Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant; but let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest beneath the tree,” etc.

*(Isidore V.)* It must be noted that Abraham bears three figures in himself. First, that of the Savior, when, having left his kindred, he came into this world. Second, that of the Father, when he sacrificed his only son. Third—and this is the figure he bears in this passage—that of the saints, who received Christ’s coming with joy.

Abraham’s tent, moreover, represented Jerusalem itself, where the prophets and apostles dwelt for a time. Thus, when the Lord first came, he was received by believers but suspended upon the wood by unbelievers.

In the three men who came to him, the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ is proclaimed, accompanied by two angels, whom many understand as Moses and Elijah: one, the ancient lawgiver, who indicated his coming through that same Law; the other, who is to come at the end of the world, to announce Christ’s second coming and to preach his Gospel to the Jews. Hence, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, these two—Moses and Elijah—were seen with him by the apostles.

But when Abraham saw the three, he adored one, namely the Lord and Savior, whose coming he had already awaited. In accordance with this, the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII). At that time he beheld the mystery of the sacrament that was to come.

Therefore he washed their feet, to signify the purification that would take place at the end in the washing; for feet signify the final things. He also prepared a banquet, namely a fattened calf. This young, fattened calf is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is also the Lord’s calf, sacrificed for the salvation of believers upon the tree of the cross. He is the calf of the Lord’s body who, in the Gospel, is killed for the sinful son.

He also set before them butter and milk together with the flesh of the calf. Our Apostle announces that milk represented the ancient Law, saying: “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, nor indeed are you able even now” (1 Cor. III). He had handed on to them the commandment of the Law as milk pressed from the breasts of the two tablets—that is, the testament of faith. Because of the infancy of their understanding, they were not yet able to receive the solid and robust food of evangelical teaching.

But the richest and fattest butter is the testimony of the Gospels, which, like oil, is given to the faithful as a sign. Thus Abraham set the calf, together with milk and butter, before them because the body of the Lord, which is the calf, cannot exist without the milk of the Law, nor the milk of the Law without butter—that is, without the testimony of the Gospel.

The three measures from which Sarah made ash-baked loaves signified the image of the three sons of Noah, from whom the whole human race was born. Those who believe in the divine Trinity were to be kneaded through the water of baptism and through the Church, of which Sarah was an image, and brought together into one bread, the body of Christ. These are the three measures that the woman in the Gospel is known to have leavened.

The loaves were unleavened because the unity of believers ought to be without the leaven of malice, without the sickness of wickedness, and without the heat of perverse teaching. They were ash-baked so that, through repentance for past sins and having been cooked by the vapor of the Holy Spirit, believers might become acceptable, like food pleasing to God.

Their sitting beneath the tree was a sign of the Lord’s Passion, whose preachers they are. When God promises the barren Sarah a son, saying, “About this time I will come,” he does not refer to a time or season, but to the character of his coming, when through the promised son a faithful people was to be born.

This is the barren Sarah to whom the Lord says through the prophet: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. XLV).

Sarah’s laughter is a prophecy. Her laughter has a twofold meaning: either that Christ would be laughter to unbelievers, or that he would laugh at all his enemies in his judgment. Hence the one who was born of Sarah received the name of Laughter. For Isaac is interpreted from the Hebrew language into Latin as “laughter.”

*(Gregory.)* Finally, according to the moral interpretation, we must consider with what great discernment and moderation the care of the flesh ought to be restrained, so that it may serve and not be driven headlong; so that, instead of conquering like a mistress, it may be subdued to authority and serve like a maidservant; so that it may be present when commanded and, rejected at the mind’s nod, leap away; so that it may scarcely appear behind the back of holy understanding and never stand opposed to the face of upright thought.

Sacred history aptly conveys this to us when it records that Abraham met three angels. He himself went out to meet those who were coming outside the entrance, whereas Sarah remained behind the entrance. What, then, is indicated to us by Abraham’s going out to meet them, except that our understanding—like a man and master of the spiritual household—ought to pass beyond the barriers of the flesh in the knowledge of the Trinity and, as though leaving the door of its lowly dwelling, go forth?

But the care of the flesh, like a woman, ought not to appear outside; it should be ashamed to look upon display, and, as though behind the man, under the discernment of the spirit, attend only to what is necessary. It should not expose itself brazenly, but regulate itself modestly.

It must also be noted that God sometimes speaks through angels by means of images and bodies temporarily assumed from the air before bodily eyes, just as Abraham was now able not only to see three men, but also to receive them into his earthly dwelling and to set food before them for their use.

For unless angels temporarily assumed bodies from the air when certain inward matters are announced to us, they would certainly not appear to our outward eyes, nor would they take food with Abraham unless, because of us, they bore something solid from the heavenly element.

Nor is it surprising that those who were received there are at one moment called angels and at another the Lord, because they are expressed by the term “angels” insofar as they were ministering outwardly, while the designation “Lord” shows that the one who presided inwardly over them was present. Thus, through the one term, the authority of the presiding ruler is made clear, and through the other, the service of the minister.

*(Augustine.)* From the historical standpoint, one may ask why the Lord reproves Sarah when Abraham laughed. The reason is that Abraham’s laughter was one of wonder and joy, whereas Sarah’s was one of doubt; and this could be distinguished by him who knows human hearts.

Sarah denied it, saying, “I did not laugh,” because she was afraid. How did they understand that the one who was speaking was God, when Sarah even dared to deny that she had laughed, as though he could be ignorant of it—unless perhaps Sarah thought they were men, while Abraham understood that he was God?

Yet Abraham himself, by performing those human services that could be necessary only for weak flesh, seems—unless this is astonishing—to have first thought that they were men. Perhaps, however, he understood that God was speaking through them because certain signs of divine majesty were present and visible, just as Scripture often testifies that God appeared through men.

But the question arises again: if this is so, how did they later discover that they were angels? Perhaps it was when, while they watched, they ascended into heaven.

### CHAPTER XXII. On the Sodomites and Lot’s hospitality

When the men had therefore risen from there, they directed their eyes toward Sodom, and Abraham walked along with them, escorting them. The Lord said: “Can I conceal from Abraham what I am about to do, since he is to become a great and exceedingly powerful nation, and all the nations of the earth are to be blessed in him? For I know that he will command his sons and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord and to do justice and judgment, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham everything he has spoken to him.”

The Lord rightly reveals the secrets of his counsel to Abraham, of whom he was certain that he would be a faithful executor of his will and commandments. From him, moreover, was to be born in the flesh the one in whom, as the Apostle bears witness, “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II).

The Lord also promises Abraham not only rewards, but the righteousness of his sons’ obedience, so that the promised rewards might likewise be fulfilled in them. Again, Isaac is promised as one who will become a great nation, and it is said that all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him. By these words two things were promised to him: the Jewish race according to the flesh, and all nations according to faith.

Then the Lord said:

“The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

If we understand these words not as those of one who doubts which of two outcomes will occur, but as those of one who is angry and threatening, there is no difficulty. God speaks to human beings in Scripture according to human custom, and those who believe that God is immutable know how to understand his anger without supposing disturbance in him.

We also customarily speak threateningly in this way: “Let us see whether I will not do this to you,” or, “Let us see whether I will not do this to him,” or, “If I cannot do this to you.” Likewise, “I shall know”—that is, “I shall test whether I cannot do what is being said in a threat, not in ignorance.” The appearance is that of an angry disposition, but disturbance does not befall God.

The manner of human speech is both customary and suited to human weakness, to which God adapts his speech. Sin accompanied by a voice is guilt in action; but sin accompanied by an outcry is guilt joined to license.

What are we taught by this example except that we must never be too hasty in pronouncing sentence; that we must not rashly judge matters not investigated; that any evils we hear about should not immediately move us; and that we should not believe statements made indiscriminately without proof?

We would certainly fear committing such a fault if we considered more carefully the actions of our Creator. For, in order to restrain us from a hasty pronouncement of judgment, although all things are naked and open to his eyes, he nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely on hearsay. He says: “I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

Why, then, does the omnipotent Lord, who knows all things, appear to doubt before the investigation, unless to set before us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe human evils before proving them?

And behold: through the angels he descends to learn the evils, and immediately strikes the criminals. That patient and gentle one, of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge with tranquillity” (Wis. XII), and of whom it is again written, “The Lord is patient, but he repays” (Sir. V), finding them involved in so great a crime, seems to have set aside his patience and did not wish to await the final day of judgment for vengeance. Instead, he anticipated the day of judgment by the fire of judgment.

Behold the evil that he was slow to believe when he heard it, yet punished without delay when he discovered it to be true, so that he might give us an example: greater crimes are to be believed slowly when they are heard, but punished more quickly when they are truthfully recognized.

They turned from there and went toward Sodom, while Abraham still stood before the Lord. Approaching, he said: “Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? If there are fifty righteous in the city, will they perish together? Will you not spare that place for the sake of the fifty righteous who are in it?”—and so forth.

What does it signify that the Lord said that Sodom would be spared if from fifty righteous persons down to ten they were found within it? Clearly, he established the number fifty as a sign of repentance, in case they should turn and be saved; for the number fifty is always related to repentance. Hence David also wrote a penitential psalm in that number.

Therefore, when God sees the life of sinners and that they do not at all wish to return to repentance, which the number fifty prefigures, he immediately restrains the heat of immoderate lust by the fire of Gehenna.

He said that Sodom would not perish if there were as many as ten righteous because, if he finds the name of Christ in anyone through the keeping of the Ten Commandments, that person does not perish; for the figure of the number ten demonstrates the cross of Christ.

And that there were five cities consumed by fiery rains signifies, unless I am mistaken, that all who have indulged lustfully in the five senses of their bodies will be consumed in that future judgment by [fire].

*(Augustine.)* It is customary to ask whether what God said concerning Sodom—that he would not destroy the place if even ten righteous persons were found there—was a special judgment concerning that city, or whether it should be understood generally of all places: that God spares every place in which even ten righteous persons are found.

In considering this question, we are not compelled to accept it as applying to every place. Nevertheless, it could also have been said in this way concerning Sodom because God knew that there were not even ten righteous persons there. Thus he answered Abraham in order to signify that so many could not be found there, thereby emphasizing the magnitude of their wickedness.

For God had no necessity to spare such wicked people lest he destroy the righteous with them, since, after rescuing the righteous from there, he could inflict upon the wicked the punishments they deserved.

Something similar occurs in Jeremiah, where he says: “Go through the streets of Jerusalem, and see, and search in its squares, and learn whether you find a man doing justice and seeking faithfulness, and I will be merciful toward their sins” (Jer. V)—that is, “Find even one, and I will spare the rest,” to emphasize and demonstrate that not even one could be found there.

The Lord departed after he ceased speaking with Abraham, and he returned to his place.

### (Chapter XIX)

Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the city gate. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them; he bowed face down to the ground and said: “I beg you, Lord, turn aside into the house of your servant and remain there,” etc.

The fact that Lot went out to meet the angels and bowed before them seems to show that he understood that they were angels. Yet, when he invited them to refresh their bodies with what is necessary for mortals, he seems to have thought that they were human beings.

The question is therefore resolved in the same way as it was concerning the three who came to Abraham: certain signs made it apparent that they had been sent by God, while they were nevertheless believed to be human beings. For this is also stated in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where Scripture speaks of the goodness of hospitality: “Through it some, without knowing it, received angels as guests” (Heb. XI).

Before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded the house, from boy to old man, all the people together. They called Lot and said to him: “Where are the men who came in to you during the night? Bring them out here, so that we may know them.”

Lot went out to them, closing the door behind him, and said: “Do not, I beg you, my brothers; do not do this evil. I have two daughters who have not yet known a man,” etc.

Since Lot wished to prostitute his daughters in exchange for the safety of his male guests, so that the Sodomites would not inflict such an outrage upon them, it is rightly asked whether one crime—or any sin—may be admitted as compensation, so that we do something evil to prevent another from doing something more serious, or whether this should instead be attributed to Lot’s agitation rather than to deliberation, since he said it.

This compensation is admitted only with extreme danger. If it is attributed to human agitation and to a mind shaken by so great an evil, it is in no way to be imitated.

They also pressed Lot with the greatest violence. They were already close to breaking down the doors, and behold, the men stretched out their hands, brought Lot inside to them, and shut the door. They struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door.

In the end, they struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness. The Greeks have ἀορασία, which signifies more precisely—if one may put it so—“non-seeing,” by which one is made to see not everything, but not to see what there is no need to see.

For it is rightly asked how they could have failed while searching for the door if they had been struck with such blindness that they saw absolutely nothing. In that case, disturbed by their misfortune, they would no longer have searched for the door.

Those who were searching for Elisha were struck by this same ἀορασία. The same condition affected those who, after the resurrection, walked with the Lord on the road but did not recognize him, although that word is not used there; the reality itself is understood.

Mystically, what is signified by Lot being brought back inside the house and protected when evil men oppose him, except that every righteous person, while enduring the attacks of the wicked, returns to his mind and remains undaunted?

The Sodomite men cannot find the door of Lot’s house because corruptors of minds discover no avenue of accusation against the life of the righteous. Struck with blindness, they circle the house while examining the righteous person’s deeds and words out of envy. But because a strong and praiseworthy action from every side confronts them in the life of the righteous, they wander about touching nothing but the wall.

### CHAPTER XXIII. On Lot’s departure from Sodom and the intercourse of his two daughters with him

Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were to take his daughters, and said: “Rise, depart from this place, because the Lord is going to destroy this city.” But he appeared to them to be speaking in jest.

Scripture says that he spoke to his sons-in-law who were to take his daughters. Since Lot’s two daughters are later said to have been virgins—those about whom he had earlier said to the Sodomites, “Behold, I have two daughters who have not known a man”—and Scripture now mentions that he had sons-in-law, some think that those who had husbands remained in Sodom, while those who were virgins went out with their father.

Since Scripture does not say this, the Hebrew truth must be set out, where it is written: “Lot went out and spoke to the betrothed men who were to take his daughters.” His virgin daughters, therefore, had not yet been joined in marriage.

When morning came, the angels urged him, saying: “Rise, take your wife and your two daughters whom you have, lest you too perish in the wickedness of the city.”

When he hesitated, they seized his hand, and the hand of his wife and of his two daughters, because the Lord was sparing him. They led him out and placed him beyond the city. There they spoke to him, saying: “Save your life; do not look behind you, and do not remain anywhere in the surrounding region. Save yourself on the mountain, lest you perish as well.”

*(Isidore.)* Lot, Abraham’s brother, righteous and hospitable in Sodom, who deserved to escape safely from that conflagration which was an image of the future judgment, prefigured the body of Christ. This body now groans among the wicked and ungodly in all the saints; it does not consent to their deeds, and at the end of the world it will be freed from their association, while they are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.

Lot said to them: “I beg you, my lord, because your servant has found favor before you and you have magnified the mercy you have shown me by saving my life. I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest evil overtake me and I die. There is this city nearby, to which I can flee, and I will be saved in it. Is it not small, and will my life not live?”

He said to him: “Behold, I have also accepted your request in this matter, so that I will not destroy the city about which you have spoken. Hurry and save yourself there, because I cannot do anything until you enter it.” Therefore the name of that city was called Segor.

What, then, does it signify that Lot, fleeing burning Sodom, came to Segor and did not climb to the mountains, except that Sodom—which is interpreted as “blindness”—expresses worldly desires, while the height of the mountains is the contemplation of the perfect?

Since there are many righteous people who flee the allurements of the world but, placed in active life, cannot attain the summit of contemplation, this is what is signified: Lot did indeed leave Sodom, but he did not reach the mountains. A condemnable life is abandoned, but the height of contemplation is not yet grasped with precision.

For this reason Lot says to the angel: “There is this city nearby, to which I can flee, a small one, and I will be saved in it. Is it not small, and will my life live in it?”

It is called “nearby,” yet it is declared safe for salvation, because the active life is neither completely separated from worldly cares nor alien to the joy of eternal salvation.

In another interpretation, fleeing burning Sodom means avoiding the unlawful fires of the flesh. The height of the mountains is the purity of the continent. Or, certainly, those are as though on a mountain who remain attached even to carnal intercourse but are not dissolved by any bodily pleasure beyond the legitimate union required for the begetting of offspring.

To stand on the mountain is not to seek the fruit of propagation in the flesh. To stand on the mountain is not to cling carnally.

But since there are many who abandon the sins of the flesh yet, living in marriage, preserve only the rights of what is properly due, Lot did leave Sodom but did not immediately reach the mountains. A condemnable life has already been abandoned, but the height of conjugal continence is not yet grasped with precision.

In the middle lies the city of Segor, which saves the fugitive and the weak: namely, when spouses join themselves to one another through incontinence, they flee the collapse of sin and yet are saved through pardon.

They find, as it were, a small city in which they are defended from the fires, because this married life is not remarkable in virtues, but is nevertheless safe from punishments. Hence Lot says to the angel: “There is this city nearby, to which I can flee, a small one, and I will be saved in it. Is it not small, and will my life live in it?”

It is therefore called “nearby,” yet is declared safe for salvation, because married life is neither far removed from the world nor alien to the joy of salvation.

Spouses preserve their life in this active state as though in a small city when they intercede for one another through continual prayers. Hence the same Lot is rightly told by the angel: “Behold, I have also accepted your request in this matter, so that I will not destroy the city about which you have spoken.” For when supplication is poured out before God, such a married life is not condemned.

Paul also gave instruction concerning this prayer, saying: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. VII).

The sun rose over the earth, and Lot entered Segor. Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven. He overthrew these cities and the whole surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and everything green that grew from the earth.

*(Gregory.)* What is expressed by sulfur except the stench of the flesh? And what by fire except the burning of carnal desire? When the Lord therefore determined to punish the sins of the flesh committed by the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, he revealed the stain of their crime in the very character of their punishment.

Sulfur has a stench; fire has heat. Those who had burned with perverse desires from the stench of the flesh deserved to perish together by sulfur and fire, so that through a just punishment they might learn what they had done through an unjust desire.

His wife looked behind her and was changed into a pillar of salt. His wife represented those people who, called by the grace of God, look back and strive to return to the things they had left behind. Concerning them the Lord himself says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke VI).

Thus he is forbidden to look behind him, showing that those who, regenerated by grace, desire to escape the final judgment must not return to their former life.

But the fact that she looked back, remained behind, and was changed into salt provides an example for the seasoning of the faithful, through which others may be saved. Christ himself did not leave this unmentioned, saying: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVIII)—that is, so that he might season us as with salt, so that we would not neglect these things like fools but guard against them as prudent people. She herself gave this warning when she was changed into a pillar of salt.

When the Lord overthrew the cities of that region, he remembered Abraham and rescued Lot from the destruction of the cities in which he had lived. Scripture commends Lot as having been delivered chiefly through Abraham’s merits, so that we may understand that Lot was called righteous in a certain sense, especially because he worshiped the one true God and, by comparison with the crimes of the Sodomites, could not be bent toward a similar life while living among them.

Lot went up from Segor and lived on the mountain; his two daughters were also with him. For he had been afraid to remain in Segor, and he lived in a cave, he and his two daughters.

It is asked why, when he first preferred Segor to the mountain as a place of flight and wished it to be preserved as his dwelling, he now moved again from Segor to the mountain.

We shall answer that the Hebrew conjecture concerning Segor is true: it had frequently been buried by earthquakes, first being called Bale and later Salisa. Lot was afraid and said: “If, while the other cities were still standing, this one was often overthrown, how much less will it be able to escape now in the common ruin?” This fear also gave occasion for the beginning of intercourse with his daughters.

But since he had seen the other cities destroyed and this one standing, and had himself been rescued by God’s aid, he certainly ought not to have doubted what he had heard had been granted to him.

The elder daughter said to the younger: “Our father is old, and no man remains in the land who can come in to us according to the custom of the whole earth. Come, let us make our father drunk with wine, and let us sleep with him, so that we may preserve offspring from our father.”

What is said in defense of the daughters—that they thought the human race had perished and therefore slept with their father—does not excuse the father.

Indeed, the Hebrews mark what follows, “And he did not know when she lay down and when she rose,” with a point above it, as though it were incredible, since nature does not permit anyone to have intercourse unknowingly.

The two daughters of Lot conceived by their father. The elder gave birth to a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to the present day. The younger also gave birth to a son and called his name Ammon, that is, “son of my people.” He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.

Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” and the whole name has an etymological meaning. Ammon, for which the reason for the name is given as “son of my kindred,” or, as is better in Hebrew, “son of my people,” is formed in such a way that part of the sense is conveyed by the name and part by the word itself. For Ammi, from which the Ammonites are named, means “my people.”

In Lot himself, when his daughters slept with him, something other than his rescue from Sodom was represented figuratively. At that time Lot seemed to bear the figure of the future Law. Certain people begotten from it and placed under the Law, by understanding it wrongly, in a certain manner make it drunk and, by using it unlawfully, produce works of unbelief.

“For the Law is good,” says the Apostle, “if one uses it lawfully” (1 Tim. I).

### CHAPTER XXIV. On Abraham’s journey in Gerar and on Abimelech, king of the Philistines

### (Chapter XX)

Abraham departed from there for the southern land and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur. He lived as a sojourner in Gerar. Concerning Sarah his wife he said: “She is my sister.”

Therefore Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for her and took her. But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: “Behold, you are going to die because of the woman whom you have taken; for she has a husband.”

Abimelech had not touched her, and he said: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation? Did he not himself say to me, ‘She is my sister,’ and did she herself not say, ‘He is my brother’? In the simplicity of my heart and the purity of my hands I have done this.”

It is customary to ask how, even at that age, Abraham feared that he would be endangered because of Sarah’s beauty. But the power of her beauty, which could still be loved, is more wondrous than the question is difficult.

God said to him: “I know that you acted with a simple heart, and therefore I guarded you so that you would not sin against me, and I did not allow you to touch her. Now, therefore, return the wife to her husband, because he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live. But if you are unwilling to return her, know that you will certainly die, you and everything that belongs to you.”

When God said to Abimelech concerning Sarah, “I spared you so that you would not sin against me,” and warned him that she was Abraham’s wife, although he thought her to be his sister, this must be observed and noted: God is sinned against when such acts are committed as people think should be treated lightly, as though they concerned the flesh of sin.

When he said to him, “Behold, you will die,” this too must be noted: God speaks as though predicting something that will certainly happen, although he says it as a warning, so that a person may guard against sin by abstaining from it.

Abimelech also called Abraham and said to him: “What have you done to us? What have we done wrong against you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin? You have done to us things that you ought not to have done.”

Again he complained, saying: “What did you see that made you do this?”

Abraham answered: “I thought to myself: Perhaps there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife. Besides, she is truly my sister, the daughter of my father but not the daughter of my mother, and I took her as my wife.”

Indeed, she is truly his sister through his father and not through his mother—that is, the daughter of his brother Haran, not the daughter of his sister.

But since the Hebrew reads, “She is truly my sister, the daughter of my father but not the daughter of my mother,” and sounds more as though Sarah had been Abraham’s sister, we say in his defense that at that time such marriages had not yet been prohibited by law.

*(Isidore.)* Next comes the history of Abimelech, when Abraham took his wife Sarah and called her his sister so that, if he were killed, she would not be possessed as a captive by foreigners. He was confident in God, who would not permit her to be violated, just as he had not permitted it earlier by Pharaoh.

Thus Abimelech, warned in a dream, did not defile her through intercourse but restored her untouched to her husband.

Nevertheless, I wish to know whom that man represented at that time, and whose wife she is who, during this sojourn and among foreigners, is not permitted to be polluted or stained, so that she may be without stain or wrinkle for her husband.

The Church rightly lives for the glory of Christ, so that her beauty may be an honor to her husband, just as Abraham was honored among foreigners because of Sarah’s beauty. When he is told in the Song of Songs, “O most beautiful among women,” kings rightly offer gifts to her beauty, just as King Abimelech offered gifts to Sarah, admiring in her the beauty of a form that he could love.

The holy Church is also, secretly, the wife of the Lord Jesus Christ. For secretly and inwardly—that is, through a spiritual mystery—the human soul clings to the Word of God, so that the two may be one flesh. The Apostle commends this great mystery of marriage in Christ and in the Church (Eph. V).

Therefore the earthly kingdom of this world, whose figure was borne by the kings who were not permitted to pollute Sarah, did not experience the Church as Christ’s wife, except when it attempted to violate her.

By the divine testimony manifested through the faith of the martyrs, that kingdom yielded; corrected in its later kings, it honored her with a gift, although in its earlier rulers it had been unable to subject her to its corruption.

What was then represented in the same king, first and afterward, was fulfilled in this kingdom through its earlier and later kings.

When the Church is said to be Christ’s sister from his father but not from his mother, the kinship of heavenly grace—which will remain forever—is commended, not earthly generation, which will be abolished.

According to this grace, we will no longer belong to a mortal race, having received the power to be called and to be children of God. For we received this grace not from the synagogue, the mother of Christ according to the flesh, but from God the Father.

Christ taught us to deny and not acknowledge this earthly kinship when he called us into another life, where no one dies, saying to the disciples: “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XXIII).

The reason why it is concealed from foreigners whose wife the Church is, while it is not concealed that she is his sister, readily presents itself. It is hidden and difficult to understand how the human soul is joined or united to the Word of God—or, what can be said better and more appropriately, how he is God while she is a creature.

Accordingly, Christ and the Church are called bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife, because Christ Jesus and all the saints are truly brothers by kinship of divine grace, not by earthly blood relationship—that is, from the father but not from the mother. This is expressed more graciously and heard more intelligibly.

For all the saints are brothers among themselves through the same grace, but the bridegroom is not one of them through the fellowship of the others.

When Abimelech said to Sarah:

“Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. Let this be for you a covering of the eyes, for all who are with you and wherever you go. Remember that you have been exposed,”

he was speaking, as it were, in jest, because she had pretended that her brother was her husband. He urges her to remember this in the future, lest thereafter, through pretense, she incur disgrace by being exposed.

### BOOK THREE

*[Col. 0561]*
# Chapter One. On the Birth of Isaac and the Expulsion of Hagar with Ishmael

Since the second book of the exposition of Genesis began at the point where, after Adam’s expulsion from paradise, the first-created man is described as having known his wife in this misery of mortal life, and since it was brought down to the end in [Col. 0561C] the history of Abimelech, in which Sarah is praised, I consider it appropriate that the third book should begin at the place where the son of promise was granted to Abraham the patriarch. His person prefigured the one who would dissolve the bonds of original sin, restore the human race by his grace to its former dignity, from which it had long been stripped, and recall its inhabitant to paradise.

## (Genesis 21)

“The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised, and fulfilled what he had spoken. She conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold to her. And Abraham called the name of his son whom Sarah bore to him Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth [Col. 0561D] day, as God had commanded him.”

The type and figure of circumcision is manifold. For, according to the Apostle (Romans 4), it is both the sign of the righteousness of Abraham’s faith and of his offspring, and an indication that those who belong to this offspring and this faith [*offspring through faith*] are to be chastened away from every pollution of flesh and spirit. It is also a prophecy of the Savior who was to be born from this offspring: in the present he would cleanse us through baptism from every pollution of deadly action, and in the future, through the resurrection, would free us forever from every corruption of death itself.

That the number eight corresponds to the glory of the resurrection is clear to almost everyone. For the Lord rose on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day, the Sabbath—and we too shall rise, as though in the eighth age, after the six ages of this world and the seventh Sabbath of souls, which is now being spent meanwhile in the other [Col. 0562B] life: then we shall be utterly pure, stripped of all the vices and corruptions of carnal desire, in which lust especially reigns.

“Thus the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.”

**(Augustine.)** It is rightly asked why Abraham made a feast neither on the day [Col. 0562C] his son was born nor on the day he was circumcised, but on the day he was weaned. Unless this is referred to some spiritual meaning, there is no solution to the question. The point is that great spiritual joy ought to occur when a person has become a new spiritual human being—that is, no longer such as the Apostle describes when he says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, and even now you are still unable, for you are still carnal” (1 Corinthians 3).

“When Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with Isaac, she said to Abraham: ‘Drive out this slave woman and her son. For the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.’”

The Hebrews explain this in two ways: either that he had played at idolatry, according to [Col. 0562D] what is written elsewhere, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32), or that, as though older than Isaac, he had claimed the rights of the firstborn against him through joking and play. Sarah could not tolerate this when she heard it, and this is confirmed by her own words:

“Abraham took this very hard because of his son. God said to him: ‘Let it not seem harsh to you concerning the boy and concerning your slave woman. Everything that Sarah has said to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac shall your offspring be called. But I will also make the son of the slave woman into a great nation, because he is your offspring.’”

Since Sarah said, “Drive out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac,” it is asked why Abraham was saddened when this was a prophecy which he ought surely to have [Col. 0563A] understood better than Sarah. It should therefore be understood either that Sarah spoke this by revelation, because it had first been revealed to her, while Abraham, whom the Lord afterward instructed concerning it, was moved by paternal affection for his son; or that both of them had previously been unaware of what this meant, and that it was spoken prophetically through Sarah without her knowing it, when she had been stirred by a woman’s anger against the slave woman’s arrogance.

It should also be noted that Ishmael is called Abraham’s offspring by God because of what the Apostle teaches should be understood from the words, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called”: not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise, are counted as offspring. Thus this properly applies to Isaac, who was not the child of the flesh but the child of the promise, when the promise is made concerning all the nations.

“So Abraham rose early, took bread and a skin [Col. 0563B] of water, placed it on her shoulder, handed over the child, and sent her away. When she had departed, she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water in the skin had been consumed, she cast the child beneath one of the trees that was there, and went away. She sat opposite him at a distance, as far as a bow can shoot—for she said, ‘I shall not see the death of the child.’ And sitting opposite him, she raised her voice and wept. But the Lord heard the voice of the child, and so forth.”

**(Jerome.)** In the Hebrew, after what is written, “I shall not see the death of my child,” the text reads that Hagar herself sat opposite the child, raised her voice, and wept, and that God heard the voice of the little one. While the mother was weeping and pitiably awaiting her son’s death, God heard the child, concerning whom he had promised Abraham, saying, “I will also make the son of your slave woman into a great nation.”

**(Augustine.)** Otherwise, the mother too is lamenting not her own death but that of her son. God therefore spared her for whom the weeping had taken place.

It is often asked how, when the boy was more than fifteen years old, she could have cast him beneath a tree and gone as far away as an arrow can shoot, so that she would not see him dying. For the wording appears to mean that she carried him and cast him down. But it must be understood that he was cast down, not because she had carried him there, but as one casts down a person in the imagination, as though he were about to die. For when it is written, “I have been cast away from before your eyes” (Psalm 30), the speaker was not being carried. It is also ordinary speech to say that someone is cast away from another when he is removed from the company of someone with whom he had been, so that he may not be seen by him or remain with him.

It should therefore be understood that Scripture has left unstated that the mother departed from her son in such a way that the boy did not know [Col. 0563D] where she had gone, and that she hid among the wooded growth so as not to see her son wasting away from thirst. But while he was still at that age, what is surprising if, after not seeing his mother for some time and supposing her lost, he wept in the place where he had been left alone?

When it is subsequently said, “Take up the child,” this does not mean that he was to be lifted from the ground as though he were lying there, but that she was to join him and thereafter hold him by the hand as her companion, as people of any age commonly do when walking together.

The question therefore remains why Sarah had earlier wished her husband to receive a son from the slave woman, or why now she ordered the slave woman to be expelled from the household with her son. She did not do this because she was inflamed by jealousy, but because she was compelled by the mystery of prophecy.

**(Isidore.)** According to the Apostle [Col. 0564A] (Galatians 4), Hagar gave birth in slavery to a carnal people, whereas Sarah, the free woman, gave birth to a people who are not according to the flesh but are called into freedom—the freedom with which Christ has set them free.

By this mystery, therefore, it was signified that the former people, generated in the bondage of hearts (*pectorūm*; reading uncertain), would not remain forever in Sarah’s house—that is, in the Church—nor be heir or partner with the worshipers of Christ, nor possess the kingdom of heavenly glory together with the noble son, that is, the faithful people.

When Abraham expelled Hagar from his house, he took bread and a skin of water, gave them to Hagar, placed the child on her shoulders, and sent her away. When Hagar went out, she wandered in the wilderness. After casting her son, who was dying of thirst, beneath a tree, an angel of the Lord appeared to her, showed her a spring of water, and gave her son drink.

What, then, does it signify that [Col. 0564B] Hagar, when she went out, placed the child on her shoulders, except that the sinful and foolish people burdened the neck of their mother, the synagogue, when they said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27)?

The bread signified that the old priesthood carried with it the bread of the Presence, as it is written, so that it might eat it. The skin of water, which failed, signifies the Jewish purification that was destined to fail, or their carnal teaching enclosed in a dead skin—that is, in the flesh of the old human being, condemned by the sentence of transgression. It provides neither refreshment nor satisfaction for thirst, but, heated and lukewarm, produces vomiting.

That Hagar wanders in the wilderness with her son signifies that the synagogue, expelled from its land together with its people, wanders throughout the whole world without priesthood or sacrifice, utterly ignorant of the way that is [Col. 0564C] Christ.

That her son perishes from thirst shows that the people possess no spiritual purification. That she cast her son, dying of thirst, beneath a tree, and then, with the angel showing the way, saw a spring, signified that certain people from that nation would seek refuge beneath the shadow of the wood of the cross.

That the boy cries out weeping, that God hears him, and that, with the angel showing the way, he sees a spring signifies those Jews who are converted to Christ: they weep over their former errors, and their prayers are heard; when the eyes of their hearts are opened, they see the spring of living water—that is, through Christ the Son of God, who says, “I am the spring of living water; let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John 4). Hence Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing of God” or “God hears.”

This angel is a likeness of Elijah, through whom this people is to believe, as it is said through [Col. 0564D] Malachi: “Behold, I will send you Elijah, who will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” (Malachi 4).

But when the angel of the Lord immediately called to Hagar, saying:

“Rise and take the child, for I will make him into a great nation,”

this signified either that a numerous people of the Jews would rule in this world, or that those among them who believed in Christ would attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

Moreover, because Scripture first calls the same angel who speaks to Hagar an angel and afterward calls him God, he must be believed to have been the Son of God. He is the one who always spoke through the Law and the Prophets. He is called an angel because of his obedience to the Father’s will, but God according to [Col. 0565A] the nature of the Father, because he himself is truly God, just as the Father is.

# Chapter II. On Abraham’s Oath and His Covenant with Abimelech

At that time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, said to Abraham: “God is with you in everything that you do. Therefore swear by the Lord that you will not harm me, my descendants, or my lineage. But according to the mercy that I have shown you, you shall deal with me and with the land in which you have lived as a foreigner.”

Abraham replied: “I will swear.”

And Abraham reproached Abimelech concerning the well of water which his servants had seized by force. Abimelech answered: “I did not know who had done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have heard of it only today.”

Abraham then took sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them made a covenant. [Col. 0565B] Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs from the flock. Abimelech said to him: “What do these seven ewe lambs mean, which you have set apart?” He replied: “You shall receive these seven ewe lambs from my hand, so that they may be a testimony for me that I dug this well.”

Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there the two of them swore an oath and made a covenant concerning the well of the oath.

**(Augustine.)** It may be asked when Abraham made this covenant with Abimelech, and the well he dug was called the well of the oath, and how this agrees with the truth. For Hagar, after she had been expelled from Abraham’s household with her son, wandered near the well of the oath, as the text says, although afterward the well is said to have been made by Abraham in the valley. There Abimelech and Abraham swore an oath—something which had certainly not yet happened when [Col. 0565C] Hagar and her son were expelled from Abraham’s household.

How, then, was she wandering near the well of the oath? Should we understand that it had already been made, and that what Abraham did with Abimelech was later mentioned by recapitulation? Perhaps the one who wrote the book much later called the region in which the mother wandered with her son the region of the well of the oath, as though he were saying: “She wandered in that region where the well of the oath was made,” even though the well was made afterward, but long before the time of the writer.

The well was called this when the book was written, retaining the ancient name Abraham had given it. But if this is the well that Hagar saw with her eyes, nothing remains except to resolve the question by recapitulation.

Nor should it trouble us that Hagar did not know of the well [Col. 0565D] Abraham had dug, if it had been dug before she was expelled. It could very well have happened that, for the sake of his livestock, he dug a well far from the house in which he lived with his people, and that she did not know of it.

There are two reasons why it was called by this name: either because Abimelech received seven ewe lambs from Abraham’s hand—for the number seven is called *sabe*—or because they swore there, since an oath is likewise called *sabe*.

It should also be noted, both from the earlier passages and from the present one, that Isaac was not born at the oak of Mamre, or in the Plain of Mamre, as it is found in the Hebrew, but at Gerar, where Beersheba is located even to this day. Not long before our time, this province was called [Col. 0566A] Salutaris, having been formed from a division of the province of Palestine.

Scripture bears witness to this when it says: “And Abraham lived in the land of the Philistines for many days.”

“Abraham planted a grove at Beersheba and called upon the name of the Lord, the eternal God; and he lived as a resident alien in the land of the Philistines for many days.”

It may be asked how Abraham planted a field near the well of the oath if, in that land, as Stephen says (Acts 7), he had received no inheritance, not even enough for a footstep. But the inheritance should be understood as that which God was going to give by his gift, not what had been purchased at a price.

The area around the well is understood to have belonged to that purchase agreement, in which the seven ewe lambs had been given when Abimelech and Abraham also swore to one another.

# Chapter III. On God’s Testing of Abraham Concerning His Son and the Offering of the Ram in Place of the Son

## Genesis 22

“After these things God tested Abraham and said to him: ‘Abraham, Abraham!’ He answered: ‘Here I am.’”

It is commonly asked how this can be true when James says in his Epistle (chapter 1) that God tempts no one. The answer is that in the language of Scripture “he tempts” is often said in place of “he tests.”

The temptation of which James speaks is understood only as that by which a person becomes entangled in sin. Hence the Apostle says: “Lest the tempter should have tempted you” (1 Thessalonians 3).

Elsewhere too it is written: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13). Here also the expression “to know” is used as though it said, “to make you know,” since the strength of a person’s love for God is hidden from him unless it becomes known to him through [Col. 0566C] experience.

“He said to him: ‘Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision, and offer him to me as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I will show you.’”

The Hebrews say that this was the mountain on which the Temple was later built, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, as it is written in Chronicles: “They began to build the Temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, on Mount Moriah” (2 Chronicles 3). It is therefore interpreted as “illuminating” and “shining,” because there is the *dabir*—that is, the oracle of God—as well as the Law and the Holy Spirit, who teaches human beings the truth and inspires the prophets.
