“Thus Abraham rose during the night, saddled his [Col. 0566D] donkey, and took with him two young men and his son Isaac. When he had cut the wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place that God had commanded him. On the third day he lifted up his eyes and saw the place from a distance, and he said to his young men: ‘Wait here with the donkey. I and the boy will hurry there; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you,’ and so forth.”

It should be noted that from Gerar to Mount Moriah—that is, to the site of the Temple—is a three-day journey, and consequently the text says that he arrived there on the third day. Some people are therefore mistaken in thinking that Abraham was living at that time by the oak of Mamre, since from there to Mount Moriah is scarcely a full day’s journey.

“So they went on together and came to the place [Col. 0567A] that God had shown him. There he built an altar and arranged the wood upon it. When he had bound his son Isaac, he placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood. He stretched out his hand and seized the sword to sacrifice his son. And behold, the angel of the Lord called to him from heaven, saying: ‘Abraham, Abraham!’ He answered: ‘Here I am.’ He said to him: ‘Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him. Now I know that you fear God, and that you have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake.’”

This question too is resolved through a similar expression. “Now I know that you fear God” means, “Now I have made you know.” The same kind of expression appears clearly in what follows, where it is said:

“Abraham called the name of that place, ‘The Lord saw,’ so that it is said [Col. 0567B] to this day: ‘On the mountain the Lord appeared.’”

“He saw” is used in place of “he appeared”—that is, “he saw” in place of “he caused himself to be seen.” The effective agent is named for the effect produced, as when we speak of “sluggish cold,” meaning cold that makes people sluggish.

“And you did not spare,” he says, “your beloved son for my sake.” Did Abraham fail to spare his son for the sake of the angel and not for the sake of God? Either the name “angel” signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who is unquestionably God and who is expressly called by the prophet “the angel of great counsel” (Isaiah 9), or God was in the angel, and the angel spoke in the person of God, as also often occurs in the prophets.

This seems even clearer in what follows:

“And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from [Col. 0567C] heaven: ‘By myself I have sworn,’ says the Lord.”

For it is not easily found that the Lord Christ calls the Father “Lord” as though he were his Lord, especially at that time, before he had assumed flesh. According to the fact that he took the form of a servant, however, this does not seem inappropriate. In prophecy of this future reality it is said in the Psalm: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son” (Psalm 2).

Nor do we easily find in the Gospel itself that Christ calls God the Father his Lord, although we find him calling God his God in the passage where he says: “I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 16).

As for what is written, “The Lord said to my Lord” (Psalm 109), [Col. 0567D] it refers to the one who was speaking: “The Lord said to my Lord”—that is, the Father said it to the Son. Likewise, “The Lord rained from the Lord” means that the one who wrote it said that the Lord of the one Lord—that is, our Lord from our Lord—rained, the Son from the Father.

“Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among the thorns. He took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.”

It should be noted that, according to Aquila’s translation, we have *vepretum* or *spinetum*—a thorny thicket. If we interpret the force of the word, Aquila used the Greek word *συχνεῶν* (*sychneōn*) to signify dense and intertwined shrubs.

Symmachus, led to the same opinion, says: “And a ram appeared afterward, held by its horns in a net.”

But in this particular passage, the Septuagint and Theodotion seem [Col. 0568A] to have translated better, preserving the name *Sabech*: “In the thicket of Sabech by its horns.” For *συχνεῶν*, or “net,” which Aquila used—and which Symmachus writes with the letter sigma, *s*—these translators instead used the letter samekh. From this it is clear that *sabech* does not mean dense plants or shrubs woven together in the manner of a net, but is the name of a shrub, which is called this in Hebrew.

“He called the name of that place, ‘The Lord sees.’ Hence it is said to this day: ‘On the mountain the Lord will see.’”

Where the text here has “sees,” the Hebrew has “will be seen.” Among the Hebrews this became a proverb, so that whenever they are in [Col. 0568B] distress and wish to be raised up by the Lord’s help, they say: “On the mountain the Lord will see”—that is, just as he had mercy on Abraham, so he will have mercy on us.

**(Isidore.)** Hence, even now, they customarily blow the horn as a sign of the ram that was given.

Come, now, let us see what lies hidden beneath the mystery of this sacrament. When Abraham led his only-begotten son to be sacrificed, he represented the person of God the Father. But what does it mean that he was an old man? God does not grow old; rather, the pronouncement concerning Christ had already in some sense grown old when Christ was born.

It began with Adam, where it was said: “And the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2). That great sacrament concerns Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5). The sixth age of the world had been completed, [Col. 0568C], and this is signified by Abraham’s old age, because the sacrament of God was already ancient and long-standing. Sarah’s old age likewise signifies the people of God—that is, the multitude of prophets—because, at the end of the ages, Christ was born from that people of holy souls.

Her barrenness indicates that in this world people are saved in hope, and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born. The Church of the fathers brought him forth at the end of the ages through the wondrous grace of God, not through natural fertility.

We must now examine what the mystery of the subsequent history prefigured symbolically. Who, then, did Abraham represent in that sacrifice, as has been said, except the exalted Father? And whom did Isaac represent except Christ?

For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a sacrifice to God, so the Lord delivered his only-begotten Son for us all. And just as Isaac himself carried the wood upon which he was to be placed, so Christ carried upon his shoulders [Col. 0568D] the wood of his cross, on which he was to be crucified.

The two servants who were left behind and not brought to the place of sacrifice signified the Jews. Although they lived as servants and understood in a carnal manner, they did not understand Christ’s humility. Therefore, because they did not understand Christ’s passion, they did not reach the place of sacrifice.

Why were there two servants? Because that people was to be divided into two parts. This happened when Solomon sinned, when the same people was divided with respect to the realm, not through an error of impiety. The prophets repeatedly say to them: “Israel the apostate and Judah the transgressor” (Jeremiah 3).

The donkey signifies the senseless folly [Col. 0569A] of the Jews. This senseless folly carried all the mysteries, yet did not know what it was carrying.

As for what was said to them, “Wait here with the donkey,” and, “After we have worshiped, we shall return to you,” listen to the Apostle: “A blindness in part has happened to Israel” (Romans 11).

What is this blindness? “Wait here with the donkey,” until, he says, “the fullness of the nations should enter.” That is, “After we have worshiped”: once the sacrifice of the Lord’s cross has been fulfilled and proclaimed among the nations, “the fullness of the nations should enter” (ibid.).

What does “we shall return to you” mean? “And thus all Israel shall be saved.”

The three-day period in which they came to the place of sacrifice signifies the three ages of the world: one before the Law, another under the Law, and the third under grace. Before the Law extends from Adam to Moses; under the Law, from Moses [Col. 0569B] to John. From then onward, beginning with the Lord and continuing through whatever remains, is the third day of grace. In this third age, as though after three days, the mystery of Christ’s sacrifice was completed.

Then, after his feet have been bound, he is placed upon the altar, and the Lord is suspended on the wood and fastened to the cross.

But what was prefigured in Isaac was transferred to the ram. Why? Because Christ is the sheep. He is himself the Son; he is himself the Lamb. He is the Son because he was born, and the ram because he was sacrificed.

But what does it mean that the ram was caught in the thorns? The cross has horns, for two pieces of wood are joined together and produce the form of a cross. Hence it is written of him: “Horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3).

The ram caught by its horns signifies Christ crucified. The thorns are spines. The spines signify the wicked and sinners [Col. 0569C] who suspended the Lord upon the cross.

Thus the Lord was suspended among the thorns of Jewish sinners, as he says through Jeremiah: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins.”

Others have understood this ram, caught by its horns in the thorns, as Christ himself before he was sacrificed, crowned with thorns by the Jews.

After the sacrifice had been completed, it is said to Abraham:

“In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed.”

When did this happen except when that ram says: “They pierced my hands and my feet, and counted all my bones”? (Psalm 21.)

When that sacrifice was fulfilled in the Psalms, it was then said in the same Psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations.”

After Abraham had offered the ram in place of his son Isaac [Col. 0569D], he called the name of that place “The Lord saw,” meaning “The Lord caused himself to be seen,” certainly through the incarnation.

# Chapter IV. On the Birth of Rebecca and on the Death and Burial of Sarah, Abraham’s Wife

After these things Abraham was told that Melcha also had borne sons to his brother Nachor: Hus the firstborn, and Bez his brother; Camuel, father of the Syrians; Cased and Azau; Phildas, Jedlaph, and Bathuel, from whom Rebecca was born. Melcha bore these eight sons to Nachor, Abraham’s brother. [Col. 0570A]

**(Augustine.)** Among those who reported to Abraham that Milcah had borne eight sons, Kemuel is also named as the father of the Syrians. Those who brought the report could not, of course, have announced him as the father of the Syrians. The Syrian people was propagated much later from his lineage. Rather, this is said from the perspective of the writer, because the person who wrote the account narrated these events after all those intervening times, just as we said earlier concerning the well of the oath.

## Genesis 23

“Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years and died in the city of Arbee, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn and weep for her.”

The phrase found here in certain copies, “which is in the valley,” is not found in the authoritative manuscripts. The name of the city, Arboc, was also gradually corrupted by copyists and readers. For it must not be supposed that the Septuagint [Col. 0570B] translators rendered the name of a Hebrew city in a barbarous and corrupt form, and differently from the way it is called in its own language.

*Arboc* means nothing at all; the name is *Arbee*, that is, “four,” because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried there, as well as Adam himself, the first head of the human race, as is shown more clearly in the Book of Joshua.

“When he had risen from the funeral rites, he spoke to the sons of Heth, saying: ‘I am a resident alien and a sojourner among you. Give me the right of a burial place among you, so that I may bury my dead.’ The sons of Heth answered: ‘Hear us, my lord. You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the chosen graves of our people. No one will be able to prevent you from burying your dead in his tomb.’ Abraham rose and worshiped the people of the land, namely the sons of Heth.”

**(Augustine.)** It is asked how this agrees with the commandment, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” [Col. 0570C] (Deuteronomy 6), when Abraham honored a certain people of the nations so greatly that he even worshiped them.

It should be observed that the commandment does not say, “You shall worship the Lord your God alone,” as it says, “And him alone shall you serve.” The latter expression is *λατρεύσεις* (*latreuseis*) in Greek. Such service is owed to God alone. Hence idolaters are condemned: they offer idols the kind of service that is owed to God.

Nor should it trouble us that elsewhere an angel forbids a human being to worship him and instructs him instead to worship the Lord (Revelation 19). The angel had appeared in such a form that he could be worshiped as God, and therefore the worshiper had to be corrected.

“Abraham worshiped before the people [Col. 0570D] of the land and spoke to Ephron in the presence of the assembled people: ‘Please listen to me. I will give money for the field; accept it from me, and then I will bury my dead there.’ Ephron answered: ‘My lord, listen to me. The land that you request is worth four hundred shekels of silver. That is the price between me and you. But what is that? Bury your dead.’”

When Abraham heard this, he weighed out the money that Ephron had requested in the hearing of the sons of Heth.

In the Hebrew, as we have set it down here, his name is first written *Ephron*, and afterward *Ephran*. Once he had been overcome by the price and had sold the burial place and accepted the silver—although Abraham compelled him to do so—the letter *waw*, which among them is read as *o*, was removed from his name. Instead of *Ephron*, he was called *Ephran*. Scripture thereby indicates that he was not of complete and perfect virtue, since he had been able to sell the memorials of the dead.

Therefore those who sell burial places should know that, even when they are not compelled to accept a price but extort it from those who are unwilling, their name is changed and something [Col. 0571A] of their merit perishes. Even the one who accepts payment unwillingly is secretly censured.

“So the field formerly belonging to Ephron was confirmed to Abraham—the field in which there was the double cave facing Mamre, both the field and the cave, together with all its trees within all its boundaries round about—as a possession.”

**(Gregory.)** What does Abraham’s double burial place signify for us except that every perfect preacher hides his soul, dead to [Col. 0571B] the desires of the present life, beneath the protection of good works and contemplation? Thus carnal desire lies concealed beneath an active and contemplative life, as though insensible, although previously it lived mortally by experiencing the desires of the world.

Hence the outstanding preacher says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3).

The active life is a tomb, because it protects the dead from wicked works. But the contemplative life buries more perfectly, because it completely separates a person from all actions.

Whoever has already subdued the insults of the flesh within himself still needs to exercise his mind through the practices of holy action. And whoever has already expanded his mind through holy works still needs to extend it to the innermost secrets of contemplation.

For a preacher [Col. 0571C] is not perfect if, on account of his devotion to contemplation, he neglects what must be done, or if, because of his zeal for action, he postpones what must be contemplated.

# Chapter V. On Rebecca’s Betrothal through Abraham’s Servant

## Genesis 24

“Abraham was old and advanced in years, and the Lord had blessed him in everything. He said to the senior servant of his household, who was in charge of all that he possessed: ‘Place your hand beneath my thigh, so that I may bind you by an oath before the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell, but that you will go to my land and my kindred and take a wife from there for my son Isaac,’ and so forth.”

The Hebrews report that he swore by his sanctification—that is, by his [Col. 0571D] circumcision. We, however, say that he swore by Abraham’s offspring, that is, by Christ, who was to be born from him, according to the evangelist Matthew, who says: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1).

“So he departed and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor. When he had made the camels lie down outside the town beside the well of water, in the evening, at the time when women usually go out to draw water, he said: ‘Lord God of my master Abraham, meet me, I pray, today, and show mercy to my master Abraham. Behold, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the inhabitants of this city will come out to draw water. Let the girl to whom I say, “Bend your [Col. 0572A] jar so that I may drink,” and who answers, “Drink, and I will also give your camels water,” be the one whom you have prepared for your servant. By this I shall know that you have shown mercy to my master.’”

**(Augustine.)** It must be asked how unlawful divinations differ from that request for a sign which Abraham’s servant made when he asked God to show him that she was to be his master Isaac’s future wife: he would ask her for a drink, and she would say to him, “Drink, and I will water your camels also until they have finished drinking.”

It is one thing to ask for something extraordinary, so that the miracle itself may be a sign; it is another to observe ordinary events which occur without anything miraculous in them, but which diviners interpret through superstitious folly.

Yet even the request for something extraordinary, by which what someone wishes to know may be signified, is not a small [Col. 0572B] question. It belongs to the matter concerning those who, by doing this improperly, are said to tempt the Lord.

For when the Lord himself was tempted by the devil, he cited the testimony of Scripture: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6). The devil was suggesting to him, as though he were merely human, that he test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much power he possessed with God. Such a thing is done wrongly when it is done in this manner.

This is why what Gideon did, when the danger of battle was imminent, is distinguished: his inquiry was consultation rather than a temptation of God.

For this reason Ahaz is afraid to ask for a sign from Isaiah (chapter 7), lest he appear to tempt God, even though the Lord urges him through the prophet to do so—perhaps because he thought that the prophet himself was testing whether he remembered the commandment forbidding the tempting of God.

[Col. 0572C] The man brought out two golden earrings, weighing two shekels, and two bracelets, weighing ten shekels; and he said to her, “Whose daughter are you? Tell me. Is there room in your father’s house for us to lodge?” She replied, “I am the daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.” *Bace*, which in this passage is written in place of *didrachma*, is half an ounce. A *secel*, which in Latin speech is corruptly called a *siclus*, has the weight of an ounce.

“I am Abraham’s servant,” he said, “and the Lord has greatly blessed my master, and he has become great. He has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys. And Sarah, my master’s wife, bore my master a son in his old age, and he gave him everything that he possessed. And my master adjured me, saying: [Col. 0572D] ‘You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell; but you shall go to my father’s house and take a wife for my son from my kindred.’”

(Augustine.) Abraham’s servant, recounting what had been commanded him by his master, says that he told him: “You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell in their land, but you shall go to my father’s house and to my tribe, and from there take a wife for my son,” and so forth. If the commands are read as they were given to him, the meaning is found to be the same, but the words are neither all identical nor expressed in precisely the same way. I thought this should be pointed out on account of foolish and uneducated people who malign the Evangelists because in certain words they do not agree in every respect, although in events [Col. 0573A] and meanings they differ in no way at all. Certainly, one man wrote this book, and when Abraham or Rebekah gave the commands, he could have set down what I have just mentioned in that form if he judged it relevant, since the truth of the narrative requires only that the meaning of the events and statements—on account of which the words are spoken—be made sufficiently clear.

What the Latin manuscripts have is: “As Abraham’s servant recounted what his master had commanded him: ‘Then you will be innocent of my oath,’ or ‘of my swearing.’” The Greeks have: “of my curse,” for *ὅρκος* means “an oath,” while *ἄρα* means “a curse.” Hence also one is called *κατάρατος*, “cursed,” or *ἐπικατάρατος*. Accordingly, the question arises how that oath can be understood as a curse, unless it is because the person who acts contrary to the oath is cursed. Therefore, [Col. 0573B] “if you are showing mercy and truth toward my master, tell me.” Those two qualities that are constantly mentioned in the other holy Scriptures, and especially in the Psalms—mercy and justice—for “mercy and truth” have the same force, have here already begun to appear.

## CHAPTER VI. On Rebecca’s Arrival at Isaac

Laban and Bethuel replied: “This matter has proceeded from the Lord; we cannot say anything else to you apart from his will. Behold, Rebecca is before you; take her and depart, and let her be the wife of your master’s son, as the Lord has spoken.”

The question is: When did the Lord speak, unless either he knew Abraham to be a prophet and they recognized as prophetically spoken by the Lord what had been spoken through him, or they called that sign which his servant recounted to them the Lord’s speech? The latter is more clearly expressed concerning Rebecca. For what Abraham had said was not spoken specifically about Rebecca, but about some woman from his tribe or kindred; and this would have released the servant from his oath if he had not obtained such a woman—something that is certainly not said when a prophecy is given, for a prophecy ought to be definite.

So they sent her away, together with her nurse, Abraham’s servant, and his companions, and they invoked prosperity upon their sister, saying: “You are our sister; may you grow into thousands upon thousands, and may your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.” What her brothers said to Rebecca as she departed—“You are our sister; may you become thousands upon thousands, [Col. 0573D] and may your offspring possess the inheritance of the cities of your enemies”—was not prophecy, nor did they utter so great a wish out of vanity; rather, what God had promised to Abraham could not remain hidden from them.

At that same time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “of the Living One who sees.” He was dwelling in the southern land and had gone out to meditate in the field, with the day already declining. The southern land signifies Gerar, from which he had once been taken by his father for sacrifice. But where it says, “He went out to exercise himself in the field”—which in Greek is *ἀδολεσχῆσα*—the Hebrew reads: “Isaac went out to speak in the field as evening was falling.” This signifies that, just as the Lord alone prayed on the mountain, so Isaac, who was a type of the Lord, went out from the house like a righteous man for prayer and offered spiritual sacrifices to God either at the ninth hour or before sunset.

When he lifted his eyes, he saw camels approaching from a distance. Rebecca, too, seeing Isaac, dismounted from her camel and said to the servant, “Who is that man coming across the field to meet us?” He said to her, “That is my master.” Then she quickly took her cloak and covered herself; or, according to another edition, “she took a *theristrum* and covered herself.” A *theristrum* is called a cloak; it is also the type of Arabian garment, still worn today, with which the women of that region veil themselves.

Let us now consider spiritually what this servant of Abraham, whom Abraham sent to betroth Rebecca, and what the events that follow in the same story signify. What does it mean that Abraham orders the servant to place his hand beneath his thigh and swear by the God of heaven, unless it signifies that the flesh of the one who would descend through that limb was to be both Abraham’s son according to humanity and Lord according to divinity? Thus the servant is told: “Place your hand beneath my thigh and swear by the God of heaven,” as though he were being told plainly: “Touch my son and swear by my Lord.” Therefore he is ordered to place his hand not upon the thigh but beneath the thigh, because from that thigh the one who would descend was to come—a man indeed, but one who would come above all human beings.

What does it mean that Isaac is forbidden to take a wife for his beloved son from the daughters of the Canaanites, except that no rejected souls are joined to him of whom it is written, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III)? But the servant is ordered to bring a wife for the son from his own kindred, because the one holy Church of the elect was to be joined to the only-begotten Son, whom the only-begotten himself, by predestination and foreknowledge, did not regard as foreign.

Who, then, is the servant who is sent to bring the wife, except the order of the prophets, the apostles, and all teachers? When they bring the word of preaching to good minds, they become, as it were, stewards arranging for each soul to be joined to the only-begotten Son. As he went, he carried with him all his master’s good things, because in what they say about the Lord they display within themselves the riches of virtues; and they draw their hearers to follow God all the more quickly insofar as they show in themselves what they proclaim.

The same servant stood beside the spring and, according to the sentence already determined, proposed which girl should be chosen, because holy preachers examine the streams of sacred speech and from them determine to whom they should entrust the words of their preaching and from which hearers they may derive confidence in its certainty.

He asked for a drink, because every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer. But Rebecca offered him a drink, because the holy Church of the elect satisfies the desire of its preachers through the strength of its faith. For she who confessed the God whom she had heard offered her preacher the water of refreshment and cooled his soul.

It should be noted that she placed the pitcher from her shoulder upon her arms, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from good works; or, certainly, she offered water because she did not remain empty in what she believed. For immediately she hastened to proclaim what she had heard, and by teaching she produced many preachers from herself.

The water in the pitcher is knowledge of preaching in due measure, because the holy Church takes care not to think beyond what one ought to think, but to think with sobriety. The pitcher of water upon the arm is the doctrine of preaching expressed in action. It offers drink not only to the servant’s companions but also to the camels, which preach the word of life not only to the prudent but also to the foolish, in accordance with Paul’s words: “I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. I).

Or, certainly, water is also given to beasts when provision is made for how care of the flesh should be exercised, so that it is not indulged for pleasure but is not denied in necessities, as it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” [Col. 0575B] (Rom. XIII). For the one who forbade care of it in desires undoubtedly permits it in necessity, in accordance with what is said again: “No one ever hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. V).

The servant gave Rebecca earrings and bracelets, because every preacher adorns both the hearing of the holy Church through obedience and its hands through the merit of good works. The earrings are of two shekels, while the bracelets are of ten shekels, because the first virtue of obedience is love. This love is distinguished in two commandments, so that God and one’s neighbor may be loved; and upright action is perfected through the completion of the Decalogue, so that once good deeds have begun, no evil deeds are committed thereafter.

Rebecca declared that there was ample room in her father’s house for lodging, because the holy Church showed that it had learned the law of nature from the earlier people and received the words of preaching in the broad bosom of charity. For the teacher, the heart of the hearer is an ample place for lodging, namely, the breadth of goodness. Hence it is said to certain people: “Make room for us: we have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (2 Cor. VI). It is as though it were said openly: “Make a spacious place in your mind for receiving doctrine, but remain narrow in thinking about carnal things.”

She indicated that she had an abundance of straw and hay, because the holy Church, hearing the words of life, repaid earthly support to its preachers. When Paul regarded this as almost nothing, he said: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” [Col. 0575D] (1 Cor. IX).

Rebecca’s brother was Laban. He hurried out, looked at his sister’s earrings and bracelets, and invited the servant inside, because there are carnal people associated with the faithful who, when they see the gifts of spiritual persons, are held in admiration and, even if not as far as works, at least in their minds admit the word of preaching far enough to receive the faith. Since they often see good people shining with miracles, they do not reject what they hear about eternity, although they do not follow the holy Church of the elect in their conduct and remain in carnal activity.

Laban offered straw, hay, bread, and water, but the servant refused to accept them until he had first secured the matter of the marriage, because there are many who are prepared to sustain their teachers with temporal support, but holy preachers do not wish to receive temporal things unless they first obtain eternal things. If they find no fruit in souls, they disdain to accept support for their bodies, nor do they wash their feet with water, because no consolation relieves their desire for their labor.

But as soon as the servant had secured the matter of his master’s marriage, he brought out vessels of gold and silver and garments, which he gave to Rebecca, because the teachers of the holy Church provide as many ornaments as they have taught virtues. She who had previously received earrings and bracelets now receives vessels of gold and silver and garments, because the holy Church, which earlier receives faith, obedience, and action, grows and afterward becomes strong even in spiritual gifts; filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues, it increases as its gifts are enlarged.

The servant offered gifts to her mother and brothers, because the Gentiles, from the time when the Church came to the faith, grew in temporal glory after her conversion, as we also see now: Christians everywhere suffer affliction, while various Gentiles glory in earthly power. Her brothers, too, receive gifts, because those who verbally hold the faith within her but live carnally, not following their profession in their conduct, are customarily honored kindly by the faithful because they appear to be faithful.

Her mother and brothers therefore receive gifts but remain excluded from the lot of the inheritance, because whether unbelievers or carnal people held within the profession of faith, they do not attain the portion of the eternal inheritance, although they temporarily obtain the glory of heavenly generosity.

Rebecca followed the man with her maidens, because the holy Church has with it souls of lesser merit as companions, souls that in certain respects do not possess the throne of contemplation through the ascent of the mind. Such souls are like Rebecca’s maidens, because they follow in conduct but do not at all ascend to the throne of contemplation.

The servant, too, had some people in his company, because among the holy prophets there were some who lived well but did not possess the spirit of prophecy. Among the blessed apostles there were many who maintained a virtuous life but did not bring forth words of preaching.

The servant hastens back to his master, because holy preachers, when through preaching they have won the life of their hearers, immediately give thanks to the one from whose gift they received this, attributing nothing in that work to themselves but everything to its author.

At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “of the Living One who sees.” Who is the Living One who sees except almighty God, of whom it is written, “I live forever, says the Lord,” and of whom it is said again, “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV)?

The well of the Living One who sees is the depth of sacred Scripture, which almighty God has provided for the watering of our minds. What is the road that leads to the well of the Living One who sees except the humility of the suffering of the only-begotten Son, through which what the streams of sacred Scripture had previously spoken secretly was opened to us?

For unless the only-begotten Son of God had become incarnate, been tempted, seized, struck with blows, mocked with spitting, crucified, and killed, the depth of this well—that is, of sacred Scripture—would not have been opened to us. What, then, did the humility of his suffering become for the faithful except the key to opening, through which we find the well of God’s mysteries and draw the water of knowledge from the depths?

The pages of sacred speech speak of his incarnation, suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension. Because we know that these things have occurred, we now understand what we have heard. These things could previously have been read, but because they had not yet come to pass, they could not be understood. Hence it is said through John: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, so as to open the book and break its seven seals” (Rev. V). He opened the book and broke its seals who, by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending to heaven, disclosed to us the secrets of sacred Scripture.

It should also be noted that it does not say, “He was walking along the road that leads to the well,” but “he was walking back and forth.” For the person who treads the road on which he walks by going and returning walks back and forth. The Lord walked back and forth in the humility of his suffering, because he endured, at different times, insults in words from the Jews, false testimony against himself, slaps, spitting, the cross, and the crown of thorns. To have walked back and forth in the humility of suffering is to have endured so many adversities and insults, repeating them in different forms.

Isaac dwells in the southern land when Rebecca comes, because the only-begotten Lord and our Redeemer, when the Church comes to him, dwells in the minds of those born from the Jews who were held not by the coldness of sluggishness but by the fervor of charity. From that people came the prophetess Anna and Simeon, who took the Lord into his arms (Luke II).

He had gone out to meditate in the field, because the field is understood as the world. The Lord himself explains this, saying: “The field is the world” (Matt. XIII). He went out in this way because he deigned to appear visibly, as it is written: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones.”

Young men trained in the use of arms customarily practice with them. Isaac therefore went out to meditate in the field, because our Redeemer, presenting an example of humility to those who follow him, displayed in himself, through the practice of endurance and his suffering, examples of patience. The practice of arms is the repeated experience of sufferings. He who endured the blows of hands, the lance, and the cross allowed his suffering to be repeated even unto death.

We call sufferings weapons because through them we are freed from the hidden adversary, as the Lord himself says: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI). He went out to meditate in the field when the day was already declining, because he undertook the practice of suffering near the end of the world, as he speaks through the Psalmist of the expression of his crucifixion: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL).

What does it mean that Rebecca is brought to Isaac on the back of a camel, except that, as we have already said, Rebecca signifies the Church, while the camel on which she rides signifies the Gentile people, devoted through their twisted movements and burdens to the worship of idols? For those who invented gods for themselves to worship had, as it were, a burden growing upon their backs that they would carry.

Rebecca therefore comes to Isaac carried on the back of a camel, because the Church, hastening from the Gentiles, is found amid the twisted and vicious practices of its former life. When she saw Isaac, she descended from the camel, because the more subtly the holy Church recognizes its Redeemer, the more humbly it abandons the pursuits of carnal life and opposes within itself the strength of vice. Isaac having been seen, she descended, because once the Lord was known, the Gentiles abandoned their way and sought the depths of humility instead of the heights of pride.

What does it mean that Isaac saw Rebecca seated upon the camel, except that the Redeemer saw the Church coming from the Gentiles while it was still supported by vices and attached not yet to spiritual but to animal impulses?

Nor should it trouble us that the servant, too, came with camels carrying his master’s riches, because holy preachers themselves, although they already excel in understanding and living in the knowledge and proclamation of higher things, nevertheless still feel within themselves the opposition of the flesh. They see another law in their members resisting the law of their mind and leading them captive in the law of sin (Rom. VII).

They carry riches on camels because, lest the greatness of revelations exalt them, a thorn in their flesh is given to them. They have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be God’s and not from them [Col. 0578C]. Those who speak heavenly things through the flesh, while still experiencing within the flesh the opposition arising from vice—what else do they do but carry riches upon the crooked backs of camels?

When Rebecca saw Isaac, she asked the servant who that man was and recognized him, because every day the holy Church learns through the words of the prophets and apostles what it ought to believe about its Redeemer. She immediately covered herself with a cloak, because the more subtly she penetrates the mysteries of her Savior, the more deeply she is ashamed of her former life; and because she acted perversely, she grows embarrassed.

She took care to cover herself with a cloak because, when she saw the Lord, she was ashamed of the weakness of her conduct. She who had previously been carried freely upon the camel, after descending, is then covered by shame. Hence, to that Church converted from its former pride, the apostolic voice says, as to Rebecca descending from the camel and drawing a cloak over herself: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI).

Isaac brought her into his mother’s tent and took her as his wife, because in place of the Synagogue, from which he was born according to the flesh, the Lord chose the holy Church and joined it to himself in love and contemplation. She who had previously been near to him by kindred—that is, known through predestination—afterward became joined to him as a wife in continuing love.

He loved her so greatly that he moderated the grief that had come from his mother’s death, because through the gain of the holy Church our Redeemer wiped away the sorrow that could have arisen from the destruction of the Synagogue. When Rebecca is joined to him, grief over his mother’s death is cut off, because when the holy Church, coming from the Gentiles, is led to the throne of contemplation, Judah is regarded as nothing.

If we take care to interpret their names, Isaac means “laughter,” while Rebecca means “patience.” Laughter arises from joy, whereas patience arises from tribulation. Although the holy Church is suspended in contemplation of heavenly joy, it still has to endure the sadness arising from the burden of mortal flesh.

Isaac and Rebecca are joined—that is, laughter and patience are mingled—because in the holy Church there comes to pass what is written: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII), so that prosperity from contemplation may gladden it, while adversity from tribulation may still disturb it.

## CHAPTER VII. On Keturah, Abraham’s Wife

(Gen. XXV.) Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah, and she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. From Midian came Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.

*Keturah* is interpreted in Hebrew as “joined” or “united.” For this reason the Hebrews suspect that, with her name changed, she was the same Hagar who, after Sarah’s death, passed from being a concubine to being a wife. It seems to excuse the age of the already decrepit Abraham, lest, as an old man, he be accused of indulging in new marriages after the death of his aged wife.

Leaving aside what is uncertain, we say this: according to the historical accounts of the Hebrews, the sons born to Abraham from Keturah occupied *Τρωγλοδύτις*—Troglodytis—and Arabia, now called *Εὐδαίμων*—Eudaimon—as far as the boundaries of the Red Sea. It is said that one of Abraham’s descendants, called Apher, led an army against Libya and settled there after defeating the enemies; his descendants, from the name of their ancestor, called the region Africa.

When it says, “The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim,” they think that Asshurim is translated as “merchants,” Letushim as “those who forge bronze and iron,” and Leummim as *φύλαρχος*, that is, “a leader of many tribes and peoples.” Others maintain that the Syrians were called Asshurim from this man, and that many regions of India were occupied by Abraham’s sons from Keturah.

(Isidore.) What does it mean that Abraham took Keturah as his wife after Sarah’s death? Was it because of lack of continence, when he was already advanced in age? Far be it. Or was it for the begetting of children, when offspring as numerous as the stars of heaven had been promised to him through his son Isaac? No. What, then, does this Keturah signify, except that just as Hagar and Ishmael signified the carnal people of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her sons signified heretics, who think that they belong to the New Testament?

Yet both are called concubines, while Sarah alone is always called a wife, as it is written: “For my dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song VI).

[Col. 0580A] Abraham gave everything that he possessed to his son Isaac. But to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts and separated them from his son Isaac, and so forth. What does this signify except that certain gifts are also given to the sons of concubines, that is, to carnal people? But they do not attain the promised kingdom—neither heretics nor Jews—because they pursue carnal gains. There is no heir except Isaac, because it is not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise who are reckoned as offspring.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Abraham’s Death and the Descendants of Ishmael

“Abraham died in a good old age, old and full of days, and was gathered to his people,” and so forth.

The addition in the Septuagint translators, “And Abraham died failing” or “growing weak,” is incorrect, because it is not fitting for Abraham to fail and diminish. What we have rendered, “in a good old age, old and full,” is also written in the Greek manuscripts as “full of days.” Although this seems to explain the meaning, namely, that he ended his life full of the works of the daylight, it is more suitable to the allegorical interpretation if *full* is simply retained.

“These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, in their names and in their generations.” Ishmael’s firstborn was Nebaioth, then Kedar, and the others, up to the passage that says: “And they dwelt from Havilah as far as Shur, which is opposite Egypt as one goes toward Assyria. He died in the presence of all his brothers,” and so forth.

Twelve sons were born to Ishmael. The firstborn was Nebaioth, from whom the entire region extending from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabataea to this day; it is a part of Arabia. Their families, towns, villages, fortified settlements, and tribes are also known by this name.

From one of them, Kedar, the desert is named; another region is called Dumah; Tema lies to the south; and Kedemah lies toward the east. But at the end of this chapter, where according to the Septuagint we read, “He dwelt opposite all his brothers,” the reading we have given is more accurate: “He died in the presence of all his brothers,” that is, he died in the hands of all his sons, with his children surviving and none having been taken by death before him.

That brothers may be called sons is also shown by Jacob in his words to Laban: “What is my sin, that you pursued me, and that you searched through all my possessions? What have you found among all the possessions of your house? Let it be placed before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between us.” For we cannot believe that, as Scripture relates, Jacob had any brothers with him apart from his children.

## CHAPTER IX. On Rebecca’s Conception and the Birth of Her Two Sons

Isaac entreated the Lord on behalf of his wife, because she was barren. He heard him and granted conception to Rebecca. “But the children struggled within her,” and so forth.

In place of “they moved” or “they struggled,” the Septuagint translators wrote *ἐσκίρτων*, that is, “they played” or “they kicked.” Aquila translated it: “The sons were being crushed in her womb,” while Symmachus rendered it *δι’ ἐπλέον*, that is, “they were carried along on the surface like a ship.”

(Gregory.) Those things that holy men accomplish by praying are so predestined that they are obtained through prayers. Even the predestination of the eternal kingdom has been arranged by almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may merit to receive what almighty God determined before the ages to give them.

Whether this is so can readily be proved. Certainly, we know that the Lord said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.” He had also said to him: “I have appointed you the father of many nations.” Again he promised him, saying: “I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore.”

From this it is plainly evident that almighty God had predestined the multiplication of Abraham’s offspring through Isaac. Yet it is written: “Isaac entreated the Lord on behalf of his wife, because she was barren. He heard him and granted conception to Rebecca.” If, then, the multiplication of Abraham’s race through Isaac was predestined, why did he marry a barren wife? It is clearly evident that predestination is fulfilled through prayers, since the one through whom God had predestined to multiply Abraham’s offspring obtained through prayer the ability to have children.

Rebecca went to inquire of the Lord, who answered: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your womb; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

(Augustine.) The question arises where she went, since at that time there were neither prophets nor priests according to the order of the tabernacle or the temple of the Lord. It is therefore worth asking where she went, unless perhaps it was to the place where Abraham had established an altar. But Scripture is entirely silent about how answers were given there—whether through some priest, which is incredible, since if there had been one, Scripture would not have failed to name him, nor would it have made no mention at all of priests there.

Or perhaps, after binding their desires through prayer, they slept in that place so that they might be warned through a dream? Or was Melchizedek still alive, whose excellence was so great that some have doubted whether he was a human being or an angel? Or were there at that time other such men of God, through whom God could be consulted?

Whatever the answer may be, and even if there is something else that has escaped me and that I have perhaps failed to mention, Scripture nevertheless cannot lie when it says that Rebecca went to inquire of the Lord and that the Lord answered her.

In what the Lord answered Rebecca—“Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your belly; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger”—the response is found to have been fulfilled in historical fact, when the people of Israel, that is, Jacob, the younger son, overcame the Idumeans, that is, the nation descended from Esau, and made them tributary under David. This continued for a long time, until the king under whom the Idumeans rebelled, and the Idumeans removed the yoke of the Israelites from their neck, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaac himself, when he blessed the younger in place of the elder.

For he said this to the elder when he afterward blessed him also.

The time for giving birth had arrived, and behold, twins were found in her womb. The first to come out was red and entirely hairy like a hide, and his name was called Esau. Where we have rendered “hairy,” the Hebrew has *Sear*, from which also comes *Esau*, just as elsewhere we read *Seir*, that is, “hairy.”

Immediately the other came out, holding his brother’s heel with his hand; therefore he called him Jacob.

(Isidore.) The figurative meaning of this event is known even to the Jews themselves, though they do not believe it: how the people of the Church overcame the people of the Synagogue, and how the Jewish people, formerly the greater, became subject in time to the lesser people of the Christians.

The same can be said of each of us: there are two nations and two peoples within us, namely, of vices and virtues; one is lesser and the other greater. The wicked are always more numerous than the good, and vices outnumber virtues. Yet within us, too, by the grace of God, one people overcomes the other, and the greater serves the lesser. The flesh serves the spirit, and vices yield to virtues.

Esau comes out first, red and entirely like a hairy hide; then his brother Jacob comes out, with his hand clasped around Esau’s heel. Why is the one entirely red and hairy, except because the earlier people were stained by the blood of the prophets and of Christ and surrounded by the squalor of sin and wickedness? The younger held his heel because, mystically, the younger was to overcome the greater people.

Isaac was sixty years old when the children were born to him. When they had grown, Esau became a man skilled in hunting and a man of the field, while Jacob was a simple man dwelling in tents, and so forth.

(Augustine.) What is called *ἄπλαστος* in Greek has been translated by the Latins as “simple.” Properly, however, *ἄπλαστος* means “not feigned.” Hence some Latin translators rendered it “without deceit,” saying: “Jacob was without deceit, dwelling in a house,” so that a great question arises concerning how he obtained the blessing by deceit, since he was without deceit. But Scripture prefaced this in order to signify something great. For this especially compels us to understand spiritual things in that passage: the one who committed deceit was without deceit.

(Gregory.) What is signified by Esau’s hunting except the life of those who, trusting in interior pleasures, follow the flesh? He is also described as a man of the field, because lovers of this age inhabit outward things all the more as they abandon their inner selves in guilt.

Jacob, however, is said to be a simple man dwelling in tents or in a house, because everyone who refuses to be scattered among external cares remains simple in thought and dwells within the habitation of his own conscience.

(Ambrose.) To dwell in tents or in a house is to confine oneself within the secret places of the mind and not dissipate oneself outwardly through desires, lest, while they yearn outwardly for many things, people depart from themselves through thoughts that have been alienated.

## CHAPTER X. On Esau’s Selling His Birthright to Jacob

Jacob cooked a stew. When Esau came to him from the field, weary, he said: “Give me some of this red stew, for I am exceedingly weary.” For this reason his name was called Edom. In the Hebrew language, red or ruddy is called *Edom*. Therefore, because he sold his birthright for red food, he received the name of the ruddy one, that is, Edom.

Jacob said to him, “Sell me your birthright.” He replied, “Behold, I am dying; what good will the birthright do me?” Jacob said, “Swear it to me, then.” Esau swore to him and sold his birthright. Thus, having received bread and a dish of lentils, he ate and drank and went away, thinking little of the fact that he had sold his birthright.

(Isidore.) The fact that this Esau sold his birthright for food to his younger brother, and afterward was deprived of the paternal blessing promised to him, signifies that same Israelite people who, as the Book of Exodus indicates, was called the firstborn son by God. For the profits of the present age, it not only lost the honor of its primacy but also did not deserve to obtain the prepared reward of the heavenly kingdom. The Lord reproaches it in a certain sense when he says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 22).

The birthright itself was the priestly garment in which the elder sons, clothed with their father’s blessing, offered victims to God like high priests. The Jews were deprived of this gift through their desire for earthly love, together with the future glory of the kingdom.

It must be understood that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the proper time for eating; sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more luxurious foods; sometimes it demands that what is to be eaten be prepared with greater care; sometimes it agrees both in the quality of the food and in the timing, but exceeds the proper measure of refreshment in the quantity consumed. Sometimes, moreover, what it desires is contemptible, yet in the very heat of its immense desire it sins more grievously.

We show these occasions of vice more clearly if we establish them by more evident examples. Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father’s mouth because the appointed time for eating was anticipated in the tasting of honey. The people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, scorning manna, they asked for meat, which they considered more luxurious. The first sin of the sons of Eli arose because, at their request, the priest’s servant wanted to take from the sacrifice not the meat cooked according to the ancient custom, but raw meat, which he could present with greater care. And when it is said to Jerusalem, “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, satiety of bread, and abundance” (Ezekiel 16), it is plainly shown that she lost salvation for this reason: together with the vice of pride, her mind exceeded the measure of moderate refreshment.

From this Esau lost the glory of the firstborn, because in the great heat of desire he longed for a desirable food, namely lentils, which he preferred even to his sold birthright; the intensity of his appetite made this clear. For it is not the food but the appetite that is at fault. Thus we often consume more luxurious foods without guilt, while we taste more contemptible foods without escaping the guilt of conscience.

This Esau, whom we have mentioned, lost his primacy through lentils, while Elijah preserved his bodily strength in the wilderness by eating meat. Therefore the ancient enemy, understanding that the cause of condemnation is not food but desire for food, subjected the first man to himself not through meat but through an apple, and tempted the second not through meat but through bread.

Hence Adam’s sin is often committed even when what is consumed is contemptible and worthless. Nor did Adam alone receive a command of prohibition, so that he might abstain from the forbidden apple. When God declares certain foods contrary to our health, he forbids us from them, as though he were present; and when, desiring what is harmful, we touch it, what else are we tasting but forbidden things? Therefore we should take what the necessity of nature requires, not what the lust for eating suggests, lest, even if this moderate discernment should look ahead less cautiously, someone turn into the abyss of illicit desire.

## CHAPTER XI. On Isaac’s journey to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, where he pretended that Rebekah, his wife, was his sister; and on the wells that Isaac dug

[Col. 0584B]

(CHAPTER 26.) A famine arose in the land, after the barrenness that had occurred in the days of Abraham. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar. The Lord appeared to him and said: “Do not go down into Egypt, but remain in the land that I shall tell you, and dwell there as a stranger; I will be with you and bless you. For I will give all these regions to you and to your offspring, fulfilling the oath that I swore to your father Abraham. I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven,” and so forth.

(Augustine.) In the passage that says, “There was a famine in the land, after the famine that had previously occurred in the time of Abraham. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar,” the question arises when this happened: whether afterward, when Esau sold his birthright for lentils—for this account begins after that narrative—or whether, as commonly happens, the narrator returned to it by recapitulation when, proceeding from the account of his sons, he reached the passage in which the lentils were mentioned.

It is troubling that the same Abimelech appears—the one who had also desired Sarah—for his groomsman and commander of the army, who are mentioned there, are also mentioned here. Could he have remained alive? When he became Abraham’s friend, Isaac had not yet been born, although he had already been promised. Let us suppose that the event occurred a year before Isaac was born. Then Isaac fathered sons when he was sixty years old, and they were young men when Esau sold his birthright. Let us suppose that they were about twenty years old; Isaac’s age at the time of this event involving his sons would therefore have been about eighty. If we assume that Abimelech was a young man when he desired Isaac’s mother and became Abraham’s friend, he could by then have been nearly a hundred years old, if Isaac went to that land because of the famine after the event involving his sons.

Therefore no necessity compels us to think that Isaac’s sojourn at Gerar was narrated by recapitulation. But since Isaac is said to have remained there for a long time, to have dug wells, to have disputed over them, and to have been enriched with money, it would be surprising if these matters were not mentioned by recapitulation. They had been passed over so that the narrative might first proceed from his sons to the passage about the lentils.

Accordingly, what is written about Isaac—“The Lord blessed him, and the man became great and continued advancing until he became exceedingly great”—is shown by what follows to have been spoken according to earthly prosperity. The narrator sets out his riches, by which he became great; and Abimelech, moved by this, feared that Isaac’s presence there might be hostile to him.

Although these things signify something spiritual, nevertheless, according to the events as they occurred, the statement “The Lord blessed him” was placed beforehand so that we might understand with sound faith that even these temporal gifts can neither be given nor hoped for, when they are sought by the weaker, except from the one God. Thus the person who is faithful in the least may also be faithful in the greatest, and the one who is found faithful in unrighteous mammon may deserve to receive what is true, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Luke 16).

For similar things are said about Abraham, namely, that God’s gifts came to him. Thus this narrative greatly builds up sound faith in those who understand it devoutly, even if no allegorical meaning could be drawn from these matters.

What does it mean that, when a famine arose in the land, Isaac went by the command and blessing of the Lord to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar, and there, out of fear, pretended that Rebekah his wife was his sister, whom the foreign king recognized as Isaac’s wife only when he saw him playing with her? What does it mean, in the mystery of Christ and the Church, that so great a patriarch played with his wife, and that their marriage became known in this way?

Anyone who carefully observes the secret of her husband in the holy Scriptures, lest he sin against the Church by narrating something, clearly sees that he temporarily concealed his majesty—the majesty by which, in the form of God, he is equal to the Father—in the form of a servant, so that human weakness might be capable of receiving him; and in this way he adapted himself suitably to the path of marriage.

For what is absurd—or rather, what is unfittingly adapted to the proclamation of future things—if God’s prophet played at something carnal in order to win the affection of his wife, since the Word of God itself became flesh in order to dwell among us? (John 1.) After this Scripture relates that—

After the Lord had blessed Isaac and he had become exceedingly great, Isaac undertook the work and began to dig the wells that his father Abraham’s servants had dug. But the Philistines, envying him, had stopped them up, filling them with earth, and so forth.

Who is this Isaac except our Savior? When he descended into this ravine of Gerar, he first of all wished to dig the wells that his father’s servants had dug. Moses had dug the well of the Law; David, Solomon, and the prophets had dug it as well. They wrote the books of the Old Testament, but the Jews had filled them with an earthly and sordid understanding. When Isaac wished to cleanse their mouth, to show that whatever the Law and the prophets said, they said about him, the Philistines—namely, the Jews, alienated from the kingdom of God—quarreled with him.

But he departed from them. He cannot remain with those who do not want water in the wells but earth, and he says to them: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23).

Isaac therefore dug a new well—or rather, Isaac’s servants dug it. Isaac’s servants are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; Peter and James; Jude and the apostle Paul. All of them dug the well of the New Testament and found living water, which becomes a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.

Yet those who set their minds on earthly things still contend over these matters. They neither allow new things to be established nor old things to be cleansed; they oppose the Gospel wells and resist the apostles. And because they oppose everything in their quarrels, it is said to them: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, from now on we shall go to the Gentiles” (Acts 18).

After this Isaac dug a third well and called the name of that place Rehoboth, saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us and caused us to increase upon the earth.”

Isaac was truly enlarged: he filled the whole earth with the knowledge of the Trinity and established the breadth of the Church throughout the world. Formerly God was known only in Judea and was named in Israel (Psalm 75); now “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

For Isaac’s servants went out through the whole earth, dug wells, and showed water to everyone, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

But why is it that Isaac called the wells of Abraham, which he reopened, by the same names as his father did? Is it not because among us Moses is still called Moses, and each of the prophets is called by his own name? Their names are not changed, as though the names of the wells themselves had been altered.

This is the mystical meaning. Morally, however, Isaac is described as digging wells among a foreign people, by which example we learn that, placed in the misery of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts. As long as the water of true understanding answers us, the hand of our inquiry should never grow sluggish in draining the earth of the heart.

Yet the Allophyli, lying in wait, fill these wells, because unclean spirits, when they see us digging diligently, raise up against us thoughts cast in by temptations. Often, when we devote ourselves to sacred words, we endure the snares of evil spirits more severely, because they sprinkle the dust of earthly thoughts over our minds, so that they may darken the eyes of our attention away from the light of inner vision.

We also recognize this as signified by Isaac’s work and the wickedness of the Allophyli: they filled with heaps of earth the wells that Isaac had dug.

We ourselves—indeed, we ourselves—dig wells when we penetrate the deep meanings hidden in Scripture. Yet the Allophyli secretly fill them when, as we strive toward higher things, unclean spirits thrust earthly thoughts upon us and, as it were, take away the water of divine knowledge that we have found.

The Psalmist expressed this when he said: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Psalm 118). He plainly indicated that he could not investigate God’s commandments while he endured the snares of evil spirits in his mind.

## CHAPTER XII. On God’s manifestation to Isaac, who built an altar there

[Col. 0587A]

Isaac went up from that place to Beersheba. The Lord appeared to him that very night and said: “I am the God of Abraham your father; do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your offspring for the sake of my servant Abraham.”

Therefore he built an altar there, invoked the name of the Lord, and spread out his tent. He ordered his servants to dig a well. When Abimelech, Ochozath his friend, and Phicol the commander of his army came from Gerar to that place, and so forth.

In place of Ochozath the groomsman, the Hebrew has “the company of his friends,” so that it signifies not so much a single man as a crowd of friends who had come with the king, among whom was Phicol, his army’s commander.

Behold, on that very day Isaac’s servants came and announced to him concerning the well they had dug, saying: “We have found water.” Therefore he called it Abundance, and the name of the city was called Beersheba to the present day, and so forth.

I do not know how it is that in the Septuagint interpreters the passage reads as follows: “And Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug, and they said to him: We have not found water.” And it says that he called its name “Oath,” because they had not found water. Conversely, in the Hebrew—which Aquila and Symmachus also follow—the meaning is that they found water, and therefore the well itself was called “Saturation,” while the city was called Beersheba, that is, “the well of saturation.”

Although above we asserted that Beersheba was so called either from the word for oath or from the number seven of the sheep—for *sabe* means “seven”—nevertheless, now, because water was found, Isaac, alluding to the name of the city that was already so called, altered the letter slightly. In place of the harsh Hebrew *sin*, with which *sabe* begins, he put the Greek sigma, that is, the Hebrew *samech*.

Otherwise, according to the law of allegory, after so many wells, at the end of his virtues, it is altogether unfitting that Isaac should not have found water.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Isaac’s old age and Jacob’s blessing

(CHAPTER 27.) Isaac grew old, and his eyes became dim so that he could not see. He called Esau his elder son and said to him: “My son.” He replied: “Here I am.” His father said to him: “You see that I have grown old and do not know the day of my death. Take your weapons, your quiver and bow, and go out. When you have caught something in the hunt, prepare me a dish from it, as you know I like, and bring it to me to eat, so that my soul may bless you before I die,” and so forth.

(Isidore.) The words of Hippolytus the martyr, as Jerome, a man of outstanding knowledge and learning, repeated them, should be placed here.

“Isaac,” he says, “bears the image of God the Father; Rebekah, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the earlier people and of the devil; Jacob, of the Church and of Christ. Isaac’s old age indicates the consummation of the world. The dimness of his eyes signifies that faith has perished from the world and that the light of religion has been neglected before him.

“The fact that the elder son is called signifies the acceptance of the Law by the Jews. The fact that the father loves food and the catch signifies human beings saved from error, whom every righteous person hunts through teaching. The word of God is the blessing of promise and the hope of the future kingdom, in which the saints will reign with Christ and celebrate the true Sabbath.

“Rebekah, full of the Holy Spirit and knowing what she had heard before she gave birth—that the elder would serve the younger—represents here the form of the Holy Spirit. She knew what would happen in Christ and anticipated it in Jacob.

“She speaks to her son:

“‘Go to the flock and bring me from there two excellent young goats.’

“This prefigures the Savior’s coming in the flesh, through which he would especially liberate those who were held subject to sins. For throughout all the Scriptures young goats are understood as sinners.

“The command to offer two signifies the assumption of two peoples; the fact that they are tender and good signifies souls that are teachable and innocent.

“Esau’s garment is the faith and Scriptures of the Hebrews, which were first given to them, and afterward the people of the Gentiles was clothed in them. The skins wrapped around his arms are the sins of both peoples, which Christ, by the extension of his hands, fastened with himself to the cross. For in his own body he endured not his own sins but the sins of others.

“The fact that Isaac asks Jacob why he has come so quickly expresses his wonder at the swift faith of believers in the churches. The fact that pleasing foods are offered signifies the sacrifice pleasing to God, the salvation of sinners. Finally, the blessing that follows and the enjoyment of its fragrance openly proclaim the power of the resurrection and of the kingdom.

“For he is blessed in this manner:

“‘Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field.’

“The field is filled with the fragrance of the name of Christ. His blessing comes from the dew of heaven, that is, from the rain of divine words, and from the richness of the earth, that is, from the gathering of the peoples. The abundance of grain and wine signifies the multitude whom he gathers through the mystery of his body and blood.

“The peoples from the nations converted to him serve him; the tribes—that is, the people from the circumcision—worship him. He is the Lord of his brothers, because he rules over the Jewish people. The sons of his mother worship him, because he himself was born from her according to the flesh. Whoever curses him is cursed; whoever blesses him will be filled with blessings.

“Christ, I say, our Christ, is blessed from the mouth of the ignorant father—that is, he is truly proclaimed. Yet another is thought to be blessed by the Jews, the one whom they, wandering in error, await.

“Behold, Isaac was suddenly alarmed at the blessing promised to the elder, and recognized that he had blessed one man in place of another. Yet when the mystery was revealed to him, he was not angered; rather, he confirmed the blessing in his son, saying: ‘I blessed him, and he is blessed.’

“This is Isaac’s first blessing, which was given to the younger people, the Christians. Nevertheless, the elder son was not entirely despised, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved. The prophecy of this second blessing is:

“‘In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be.’

“In the richness of the earth—namely, in the fertility of possessions and the power of the kingdom, which existed among that people—and in the dew of heaven shall your blessing be, that is, in the words of God. For the oracles of God and the covenants of the Law were entrusted to them.

“‘You shall live by the sword,’ because that people, devoted to bloodshed, inflicted death upon Christ and the prophets. ‘You shall serve your younger brother,’ namely, the Christian people. A time will come when you will shake off and loosen the yoke from your necks, when, converted to the grace of Christ through acknowledgment of the faith, you will lay down the burden of the Law. Then you will no longer serve the younger people but will be called their brother through faith.”

In another way: What does it mean that Isaac desires to eat from the hunt of his elder son, except that almighty God desired to be nourished by the good work of the Jewish people? But while he delayed, Rebekah substituted the younger son, because while the Jewish people sought good works outwardly, maternal grace brought in the Gentile people so that it might offer the almighty Father the food of good work and receive the blessing of the elder brother.

The Gentile people offered those same foods from domestic animals, because, not seeking to please God through outward sacrifices, it says through the voice of the Prophet: “With me are your vows, O God, which I will repay with praises to you” (Psalm 55).

What does it mean that Jacob covered his hands, arms, and neck with the skins of young goats, except that a young goat was customarily offered for sin, and that the Gentile people, not ashamed to confess itself a sinner, slaughtered the sins of the flesh within itself?

What does it mean that he was clothed in the garments of his elder brother, except that he was clothed in good works through the precepts of sacred Scripture, which had been given to the elder people? The younger uses in the house what the elder, going outside, left behind. The Jewish people could not possess these things because it attended only to the letter in them.

And what does it mean that Isaac did not recognize the same son whom he blessed, except what the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning the Gentile people: “A people whom I did not know will serve me” (Psalm 17)?

What does it mean that he did not see the one who was present, yet saw what would happen to him in the future, except that almighty God, when he foretold through his prophets that grace would be granted to the Gentiles, did not see them in the present by grace, because at that time he left them in error; yet, because he would one day gather them, he foresaw them through the grace of blessing?

Therefore it is said in the blessing to the same Jacob, who bears the figure of the Gentile people: “Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field, which the Lord God has blessed.” As Truth says in the Gospel: “The field is this world” (Matthew 13). And because the people of the elect spread throughout the whole world gives off the fragrance of virtues, the scent of faith is the scent of a full field.

For the blossom of the grapevine has one fragrance, because the virtue and reputation of preachers who intoxicate the minds of their hearers are great.

The blossom of the olive has another, because the work of mercy is sweet; like oil, it refreshes and gives light.

The blossom of the rose has another, because its fragrance is wondrous: it shines red and gives off scent from the blood of martyrs.

The blossom of the lily has another, because the life of the flesh is white with the incorruption of virginity.

The blossom of the violet has another, because the virtue of the humble is great. By their desire to occupy the lowest places, they do not raise themselves from earth to high things through humility, yet they preserve the purple of the heavenly kingdom in their minds.

The ear of grain has another fragrance when it is brought to maturity, because the perfection of good works is prepared for the satisfaction of those who hunger for righteousness.

Therefore, because the Gentile people is scattered throughout the world in its elect, and because, through the virtues it practices, it fills all who understand with the fragrance of a good reputation, it is rightly said: “The scent of my son is like the scent of a full field.”

But because it does not possess these virtues from itself, he adds: “Which the Lord God has blessed.”

And because the same people of the elect rises through some to contemplation, while through others it grows rich only in the works of the active life, the blessing rightly adds: “May God give you from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth an abundance.”

For dew comes gently from above and falls subtly. We receive something from the dew of heaven whenever, through the infusion of inward contemplation, we perceive something slight from above. But when we perform good works through the body, we are enriched by the richness of the earth.

What does it mean that Esau returns late to his father, except that the Jewish people returns late to appease the Lord?
