To it also it is said in the blessing: “A time will come when your yoke will be loosed from your neck,” because the Jewish people will be freed from slavery to sin at the end, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; thus all Israel would be saved” (Romans 11).

Esau therefore always hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him, and he said in his heart: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and I will kill my brother Jacob.”

This was reported to Rebekah. She sent for and called her son Jacob and said to him: “Behold, your brother Esau is threatening to kill you. Now therefore, my son, listen to my voice: rise and flee to my brother Laban in Haran. You shall live with him a few days, until your brother’s fury subsides and his anger ceases, and he forgets what you have done to him. Afterward I will send for you and bring you back from there,” and so forth.

(Augustine.) How were Esau’s words announced or reported to Rebekah—those in which he threatened to kill his brother—when Scripture says that he spoke this in his own thought? This can only mean that everything was divinely revealed to her. Hence it belongs to a great mystery that she wanted her younger son to be blessed in place of the elder.

Thus Esau, stirred by the goads of envy after his father’s blessing, deceitfully plotted the death of his brother Jacob.

(Isidore.) The Jewish people likewise premeditated this against Christ. It not only handed the Lord over to the cross and the gallows but also persecuted those who believed in him to the shedding of blood.

(CHAPTER 28.) Isaac therefore called Jacob, blessed him, and commanded him, saying: “Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. But go and depart to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bathuel, your mother’s father, and take for yourself a wife from the daughters of Laban, your maternal uncle.”

(Augustine.) The Latin manuscripts have Isaac saying to his son, “Go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bathuel, your mother’s father, and take for yourself a wife from there.” The Greek manuscripts do not have “go,” but “flee,” that is, *apódrathi* (ἀπόδραθι). Hence it is understood that Isaac also knew what his son Esau had said in his thoughts about his brother.

“May almighty God bless you, make you grow, and multiply you, so that you may become groups of peoples. May he give you the blessing of Abraham, and to your offspring after you, so that you may possess the land of your pilgrimage, which he promised to your grandfather.”

When Isaac had sent him away, Jacob departed and came to Mesopotamia of Syria, to Laban son of Bathuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah his mother, and so forth.

Jacob, fleeing from his brother’s plots, left his ancestral home and parents and went to a distant region to take a wife for himself.

(Isidore.) In the same way Christ, having left his parents according to the flesh—that is, the people of Israel—and his homeland—that is, Jerusalem—and the whole region of Judea, went among the Gentiles and took the Church from them, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “I will call the one who was not my people, my people, and the one who was not beloved, beloved; and in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Romans 9).

## CHAPTER XIV. On Jacob’s vision while he was going to Mesopotamia, and on his vow

Jacob therefore departed from Beersheba and went toward Haran. When he came to a certain place and wanted to rest there after sunset, he took one of the stones lying there, placed it beneath his head, and slept in that same place.

He saw in a dream a ladder standing upon the earth, whose top touched heaven, and angels of God ascending and descending upon it. The Lord was leaning upon the ladder and said to him: “I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. I will give to you and to your offspring the land on which you sleep,” and so forth.

(Isidore.) As Jacob went to Mesopotamia, he came to the place now called Bethel. He placed a large stone beneath his head, and while sleeping saw a ladder propped up and leaning against heaven, with angels of God ascending and descending upon it. When he saw this, he awoke and anointed the stone, saying: “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven.” Having said this, he departed.

This sleep of Jacob is the death or passion of Christ. The stone beneath his head, which is in a certain sense named specifically, signifies Christ, who was also anointed. For “the head of a man is Christ.” Who does not know that Christ is named from anointing? The house of God signifies that Christ was born there, in Bethlehem. The gate of heaven signifies that there he descended to earth and there again ascended to heaven. The raising up of the stone is the resurrection of Christ.

Moreover, the ladder is Christ, who said: “I am the way” (John 14). Upon it angels ascended and descended. These signify the evangelists, preachers of Christ: they ascend when, in order to understand his most exalted divinity, they rise above the whole of creation and find him as “the Word in the beginning with God,” through whom all things were made (John 1); they descend when they find him made of a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law.

That ladder extends from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit, because through progress the carnal become spiritual, as though ascending. And in order to nourish them with milk, the spiritual themselves also descend in a certain way, when they cannot speak to them as spiritual people but as carnal people.

He is above in his head and below in his body, that is, the Church. We therefore understand him to be the ladder, because he said: “I am the way.” One ascends to him in order that he may be understood in the heights; one descends to him so that the little one may be nourished by his showers. Through him alone people raise themselves up, so that they may await him in exaltation; through him they also humble themselves, so that they may proclaim him with exaltation and moderation.

Tropologically, to sleep on a journey is to rest in the love of temporal things amid the transience of the present life.

(Gregory.) To sleep on a journey is, in the course of passing days, to close the eyes of the mind to the desire for visible things—eyes that the deceiver opened for the first human beings when he said: “For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened.” Shortly afterward it is added: “She took from its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband, who ate; and the eyes of both were opened.”

Guilt opened the eyes of desire, which innocence had kept closed. To see angels ascending and descending is to contemplate the citizens of the heavenly homeland: how greatly they cling to their Creator above themselves through love, and with how much compassion of charity they stoop down to our weaknesses.

It must also be carefully noted that the one who places his head upon a stone sees angels while sleeping. Those who cease from exterior works penetrate interior things, because with an attentive mind—the ruling principle in a human being—they pursue the imitation of their Redeemer.

To place one’s head upon a stone is to cling in mind to Christ. Those who have withdrawn from the activity of the present life but are not carried upward by any love toward higher things can sleep, but they cannot see angels, because they disdain to keep their head upon the stone.

There are some who flee the activities of the world but exercise themselves in no virtues. They sleep in torpor, not through discipline; and therefore they do not see interior things, because they have placed their head not upon a stone but upon the earth.

It often happens to such people that, the more securely they withdraw from external activities, the more widely they gather within themselves the noise of impure thoughts. Thus, under the guise of Judea, the soul is lamented by the prophet when, sunk in idle repose, it is said: “Its enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lamentations 1).

For by the command of the Law one ceases from external work on the Sabbath. Therefore enemies mock the Sabbaths when evil spirits drag the very leisure of one’s vocation toward unlawful thoughts, so that each soul, the more it believes that it is serving God because it has withdrawn from external activities, serves their tyranny all the more through unlawful thinking.

But holy men, because they are lulled to sleep with respect to the works of the world not through torpor but through virtue, sleep more laboriously than they could remain awake. In abandoning the activities of this age, they overcome them and fight against themselves daily in a vigorous struggle: lest the mind grow torpid through negligence; lest, subdued by leisure and polluted by desire, it grow cold; lest they serve their very good desires more than is proper; lest, under the appearance of discernment and restraint, they grow weak in perfection.

They do these things, withdraw themselves completely from the restless desire of this world, abandon the noise of earthly activities, and, intent upon virtues through the discipline of quiet, sleep while remaining awake.

For no one is led to contemplate interior things unless he diligently withdraws from those things that entangle him outwardly. Hence Truth itself said: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6). Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2). Through the prophet the Lord likewise admonishes us, saying: “Be still and see that I am God” (Psalm 45).

But when the Lord spoke to Jacob, leaning upon the ladder, and said to him: “I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth. You shall spread abroad toward the west and the east, the north and the south, and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your offspring,” and so forth, this mystically signifies a command of divinity directed to the humanity of Christ. The land of the Church is promised to him and to his offspring, that is, to the Christian people, forever.

The Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2).

In another interpretation, the west in this passage signifies the setting of vices and sins; the east, the light of faith or the rising of good works; the north, the restraint of pleasure and the mortification of desires. The south appropriately signifies the brightness of wisdom and the fervor of charity.

In this way the power of the true Jacob is extended: that is, the kingdom of Christ is spread among unbelievers—through the setting of vices and sins, the rising of faith and good works, abstinence from pleasures, meditation on wisdom, and the fervor of love.

And it is rightly added:

When Jacob awoke from sleep, he said: “Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” And, fearing, he said: “How awe-inspiring is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.” These words pertain to prophecy, because there the tabernacle was to be established, [Col. 0593D] which God founded among human beings in his first people. We should understand “the gate of heaven” as meaning that from there access is provided for believers to attain the kingdom of heaven. Spiritually, whoever, after the torpor of inertia, properly awakens and truly rises again through the practice of good works undoubtedly understands that in the Church there is the surpassing grace of God and the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. When Jacob set up the stone that he had placed beneath his head, made it into a monument, and poured oil over it, he did not do anything resembling idolatry. He neither then nor afterward repeatedly worshiped the stone or sacrificed to it; rather, it was an unmistakable sign established in prophecy, [Col. 0594A] pertaining to anointing. Hence Christ’s name was derived from *chrism*.

And he called the name of the city Bethel, which previously was called Luza. Now he gives the place a name and calls it Bethel, “house of God”; previously that place was called Luza, which means “nut” or “almond.” Hence some people absurdly think that the Hebrew word *ulam* is the name of the city, although *ulam* means “previously.” The order of the reading, therefore, is: “And he called the name of that place Bethel, and previously Luza was the name of the ancient city.” All Scripture is full of the word *ulam*, or *elam*, which means nothing other than “before” or “previously,” or “vestibule,” “threshold,” or “doorposts.”

He also made a vow, saying: “If my God is with me and guards me on the way by which I walk, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and if I return safely to my father’s house, then the Lord shall be my God, and this stone which I have raised as a monument shall be called the house of God,” etc. (Augustine.) The vow he made—if he prospered on his journey and on his return—and the tithes he promised to the future house of God in that place are a prophecy of the house of God. When he returned, he consecrated himself to God there, not calling that stone God, but calling it the house of God—that is, because the house of God was to be established in that place.

## CHAPTER XV. Jacob’s arrival in Mesopotamia, where he recognized Rachel beside the well

**(CHAP. XXIX.)** Jacob therefore departed and came to the land of the East. He saw a well in the field, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it. For the animals were watered from it, and its mouth was closed by a large stone, etc. (Isidore.) Figuratively, the peoples of the righteous are signified by sheep, as in the saying in the Gospel: “He will set the sheep at his right hand” (Matt. 25). The shepherds, however, are the prophets who, purified by the Holy Spirit until the coming of the Lord, governed the people of Israel. The stone placed over the well prefigured the Lord; the well signified the grace of the Holy Spirit, which was to come through Christ’s preaching to the Church from the Gentiles. That grace was covered over, since Christ had not yet come and become human. Alternatively, the well signifies baptism, and the field signifies this world. The fact that three flocks of sheep are said to lie beside the well signifies that those who belong to the reception of faith in the holy Trinity seek the grace of baptism in humility. The stone, because it closed the mouth of the well, suggests the hardness of unbelief; once this has been cast away, human beings can properly receive baptism. The shepherds are the teachers of the Church, because, after Jacob removed the stone, they watered the flocks. When Christ removes all unbelief from the hearts of those whom he has predestined to belong to the sacrament of baptism, believers are properly washed in the water of purification. Likewise, the water of the well signifies knowledge of the Old Testament. The stone closed it because the letter of the Law concealed its spiritual meaning; but when Christ came, the stone was removed, since through the preaching of the New Testament the shadow of the Law was excluded and the truth of the Gospel was revealed.

[Col. 0595A] They were still speaking, and behold, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she herself was tending the flock. When Jacob saw her and knew that she was his cousin, and that the sheep belonged to his uncle Laban, he removed the stone with which the well was closed. After watering the flock, he kissed her; then he raised his voice and wept, and told her that he was her father’s brother and the son of Rebekah, etc. (Augustine.) The fact that Rachel came with her father’s sheep, and that Scripture says that when Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, he approached and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well, should prompt us to notice that Scripture has omitted something that we must understand, rather than to raise any difficulty. It is understood that those with whom Jacob was first speaking were asked who the woman was who was coming with the sheep, and they themselves said that she was Laban’s daughter. Jacob did not know her, but Scripture, omitting their question and their answer, wished us to understand what is written:

“Jacob kissed Rachel and, crying out with his voice, wept. He told her that he was her father’s brother and that he was the son of Rebekah.” It was indeed customary, especially in the simplicity of the ancients, for relatives to kiss one another, and this still occurs in many places. But one may ask how she accepted a kiss from a stranger. Later, however, Jacob indicated his relationship to her. We should therefore understand either that he had already heard who she was and rushed confidently to kiss her, or that Scripture afterward narrated by recapitulation what had happened earlier—that is, that Jacob had indicated who he was. The same occurs when Scripture later says how God established him in paradise, although it had already been said that he planted paradise and placed there the human being whom he had formed. Many things are likewise understood as having been stated by recapitulation.

## CHAPTER XVI. Jacob’s servitude, by which he served Laban for his two daughters, and the mystical significance of those daughters

Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the younger was called Rachel. Leah, however, was weak-eyed, while Rachel was beautiful in face and pleasing in appearance. Jacob loved her and said: “I will serve you for Rachel, your younger daughter, for seven years.” Laban replied: “It is better that I give her to you than to another man; stay with me.” [Col. 0595D] Jacob therefore served for Rachel for seven years, and they seemed to him like a few days because of the greatness of his love. Then he said to Laban: “Give me my wife, since the time has been completed for me to go in to her.” Laban, having summoned many groups of friends to a banquet, held the wedding; in the evening he brought his daughter Leah to him, giving his daughter a maidservant named Zilpah, etc.

Concerning what is written—that Jacob served for Rachel for seven years, and they seemed in his sight like a few days because he loved her—it must be asked how this was said, since even a short period usually seems long to lovers. It was said, then, with reference to the labor of servitude, which love made easy and light.

What else is signified in Jacob’s two wives, Leah and Rachel, except the active and contemplative life? Leah is interpreted as “laboring,” while Rachel means “sheep,” or “beginning of sight.” The active life is laborious, because it sweats in its work. The contemplative life, however, is simple and longs only to see the Beginning—namely, him who said: “I am the Beginning, and for this reason I speak to you” (John 8). Blessed Jacob had desired Rachel, but he received Leah during the night, because everyone who turns to the Lord desires the contemplative life and seeks the repose of the eternal homeland; nevertheless, one must first work in the night of the present life, doing whatever good one can and sweating in labor—that is, receiving Leah—so that afterward one may rest in Rachel’s embrace, beholding the Beginning.

Rachel was seeing and barren, whereas Leah was weak-eyed but fertile. Rachel was beautiful and unproductive because the mind that seeks leisure through contemplation sees more but produces fewer children for God. When, however, it turns toward the labor of preaching, it sees less but bears more. The contemplative life is therefore beautiful in the mind; but while it desires to rest in silence, it does not produce children through preaching. It sees and does not give birth, because, through its devotion to repose, it burns less intensely to gather others, and, however much it sees inwardly, it is not sufficient to disclose what it sees to others by preaching. Leah, however, is weak-eyed and fertile, because the active life, while occupied in work, sees less; but while it kindles those nearby to imitation, now by word and now by example, it produces many children in good works. Even if it cannot hold the mind in contemplation, nevertheless, from what it does outwardly it can generate followers. After Leah’s embrace, therefore, Jacob reached Rachel. This plainly signifies that everyone is first joined to the active life for fruitfulness and afterward joined to the contemplative life for repose.

When morning came, Jacob saw Leah and said to his father-in-law: “What is this that you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?” Laban replied: “It is not customary in our place to give the younger daughter in marriage before the elder. Complete the week of this union, and I will give you this one also for the service by which you will serve me for another seven years.” Jacob accepted the arrangement. After the week had passed, he married Rachel, to whom her father had given a maidservant named Bilhah, etc. It was not therefore, as some wrongly suppose, after another seven years that Jacob took Rachel as his wife, but after the seven days of the first wife’s wedding. For what follows is: “And he went in to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served him for another seven years.”

## CHAPTER XVII. The generation of Jacob’s sons from his four wives

When the Lord saw that Leah was despised, he opened her womb, while her sister remained barren. She conceived and bore a son, and called his name Reuben, etc. For the sake of brevity in reading, I wish to give together the etymologies of the names of all the patriarchs. (Jerome.) “And she called his name,” he says, “Reuben, saying: ‘Because the Lord has seen my humiliation.’” Reuben is interpreted as “son of vision.”

[Col. 0597A] “And she conceived,” he says, “another son and said: ‘Because the Lord has heard me, since my husband hated me, he has given me this one also’; and she called his name Simeon.” She gave Simeon his name from the fact that she had been heard. Simeon, indeed, means “hearing.”

Concerning the third, the text continues:

“And she conceived again and bore a son, and said: ‘Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons’; therefore she called his name Levi.” Where we read, “My husband will be with me,” Aquila translated, “My husband will be joined to me.” In Hebrew this is said to be *ilaue* [Hebrew form unclear in the supplied text], and Hebrew teachers translate it otherwise, saying, “My husband will follow me,” that is: “I have no doubt of my husband’s love for me. He will be my companion in this life, and his affection will lead and follow me even to death; for I have borne him three sons.”

“And she conceived and bore a son and said: ‘Now on account of this I will confess to the Lord’; and for this reason she called his name Judah.” Judah is called “confession”; the name was certainly derived from the confession of the confessor. Here, however, “confession” is understood as thanksgiving or praise, as frequently in the Psalms and the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11)—that is, “I give you thanks,” or “I will glorify you.”

**(CHAP. XXX.)** “And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son, and Rachel said: ‘God has judged me, and has heard my voice, and has given me a son’; therefore she called his name Dan.” She expressed the reason for the name, giving the son of the maidservant the name of judgment because the Lord had judged her. Dan means “judgment.”

“And she conceived again, and Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, bore a second son to Jacob. Rachel said: ‘God has made me dwell with my sister, and I have prevailed’; and she called his name Naphtali.” Here the Law gives the reason for Naphtali’s name quite differently from the form written in the book of Hebrew names. Hence Aquila says: “God has made me live together with my sister, and I have lived together with her” [Greek: *Synanestrepse me ho Theos, kai synanestrephēn*]. In Hebrew it is written *naphthule Elohim napthaleti* [Hebrew form as supplied]. Thus, from “conversation” or “comparison”—for the word can signify either comparison or conversation—she gave the name Naphtali to her son.

What follows is:

“And Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, bore Jacob a son, and Leah said: ‘In fortune’; and she called his name Gad.” Where we have “in fortune,” and in Greek it is said *en tychē* (“in fortune”), which can also be called “outcome,” the Hebrew has *bagad* [Hebrew form as supplied]. Aquila interprets this as “the binding has come,” while we can say “in readiness for battle.” For *ba* can sound both as the preposition “in” and as “he has come.” Thus, from the outcome or readiness for battle—called *gad*—Zilpah’s son was named Gad.

It continues:

“And Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, bore a second son to Jacob, and Leah said: ‘I am blessed, because women call me blessed’; and she called his name Asher.” The word “riches,” that is, *ploutos* [Greek: “wealth”], has been wrongly added, since the etymology of the name Asher is made clear by the authority of Scripture, which says: “Because women call me blessed,” and because she is called blessed by everyone, she called her son blessed. Asher therefore means not “riches,” but “blessed,” at least in the present passage. Elsewhere, because of the ambiguity of the word, riches can also be called by this name.

“And God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son. Leah said: ‘God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband’; and she called his name Issachar.” The translators of the Septuagint gave the etymology of the name: “There is a reward.” It should not therefore be thought, as many wrongly read by adding a pronoun, that the text says “he is a reward”; rather, the whole name means “there is a reward.” For *ies* [Hebrew form as supplied] means “there is,” and *sachar* [Hebrew form as supplied] means “reward.” This was because he had purchased from Rachel the entrance of her husband to her, which she was owed, in exchange for Reuben’s mandrakes.

It continues:

[Col. 0598B] “And Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son, and Leah said: ‘God has endowed me with a good endowment. From now on my husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons’; and she called his name Zebulun.” Where we have “he will dwell with me,” the Septuagint translated “he will love me.” In Hebrew it is *Isboleni*, and the sense is: “Because I have borne Jacob six sons, I am now secure; for my husband will dwell with me.” Hence my son should also be called “dwelling.” The book of Names therefore interprets Zebulun wrongly and violently as “the waves of night.”

“After this she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah.” This is translated as “cause,” which in Greek they call more expressively *dikēn* [Greek: “judgment” or “legal cause”]. For she became the cause of the dispute at Shechem.

After the children, the names of the parents should be set down. Leah is interpreted as “the laboring woman.” Rachel means “sheep”; her son Joseph, because his mother wished another to be added to her, is called “increase.”

Now we must ask what the four wives of Jacob signified; two of them were free women and two were maidservants. We have seen the Apostle understand the free woman and the maidservant whom Abraham had as the two Testaments. There, however, what is said appears more easily because there is one of each, whereas here there are two and two. Moreover, there the son of the maidservant is disinherited; here the sons of the maidservants receive the promised land together with the sons of the free women. Without doubt, therefore, something is signified, although Jacob’s two free wives are thought to pertain to the New Testament, in which we have been called to freedom. They are not two without reason, however, since two lives are proclaimed to us in the body of Christ: one temporal, in which we labor, and the other eternal, in which we shall contemplate the love of God.

Leah is interpreted as “the laboring woman.” Rachel, however, means “beginning of sight,” or “word.” The activity of this life, in which we live by faith, is laborious in its works, and uncertain as to the outcome by which it will reach the benefit of those for whom we wish to care. This is Leah, Jacob’s first wife; consequently she is also said to have had weak eyes. The thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our foresight is uncertain. The hope of eternal contemplation of God, possessing a sure understanding of the truth, is Rachel. Hence she is said to be beautiful in face and fair in appearance. Every devout and diligent person loves her, and for her sake serves the grace of God, by which our sins, even if they are like scarlet, will be made white as snow. Laban, indeed, is interpreted as “whitening,” and Jacob served him for Rachel.

No one turns under the grace of the remission of sins to serve righteousness except in order to live peacefully in the Word, from whom the Beginning—who is God—is seen. Therefore one serves for Rachel, not for Leah. Who could love so greatly the labor of action and suffering in works of righteousness? Who would seek that life for its own sake? Jacob did not love Leah either, but embraced her only because she had been substituted for him in the night, using her in the generation of children and experiencing her fertility. The Lord, because she could not be loved for her own sake, first made her bearable so that one might reach Rachel, and afterward commended her because of her children.

Thus every servant of God, established under the grace of the whitening of his sins, loves and meditates in his conduct on nothing other than the teaching of wisdom. Many think that they will receive this immediately once they have exercised themselves in the seven commandments of the Law, which concern love of neighbor, so that no one may harm another: “Honor your father and your mother. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not kill. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20).

When these commandments have been observed, and once, through various temptations and the endurance of labor—as through the night of this world—the desire for the love of teaching has clung to a person, Leah is unexpectedly joined to him instead of Rachel, and he endures her so that he may reach Rachel, if he continues steadfastly to love her after receiving the other seven commandments, as though it were said to him: “Serve another seven years for Rachel, so that you may be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungry and thirsty for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and peacemaking.”

A person would wish, if it were possible, to reach immediately the delights of beautiful contemplation without any endurance of the labor that must be embraced in action and suffering. But this cannot happen in the land of mortals. This is what is signified by what was said to Jacob: “It is not customary in this place for the younger to be given before the elder.” For the one who is earlier in time is not improperly called “elder.” Labor in good works comes earlier in human education than the repose of contemplation.

We must therefore strive toward one point, while referring to many things on its account. Jacob’s two wives are free women; both are daughters of the remission of sins—that is, of the whitening represented by Laban. Nevertheless, one is loved and the other endured. The one who is endured is the one who first and more abundantly bears children, so that, if she is not loved for her own sake, she may at least be loved for the sake of her children.

The labor of the righteous has its greatest fruit in those whom it generates for the kingdom of God amid many tribulations and temptations, preaching the Gospel to those who are in abundant labors, in blows beyond measure, and in frequent deaths. For their sake they have struggles outside and fears within, and they call them their joy and crown. They are born to them more easily and abundantly through that word of faith by which they preach Christ crucified.

Rachel, radiant in appearance, is carried beyond herself toward God in her mind. She sees in the Beginning the Word, God with God, and wishes to give birth but cannot, because “who shall declare his generation?” Therefore she longs for the leisure of contemplation, so that she may behold the ineffable divinity. She wishes to be free from every occupation, and therefore she is barren, because she does not come to the aid of others amid various pressures.

But because she sometimes burns with the desire to bear children—for she wishes to teach what she knows—she sees her sister overflowing with children through the labor of action and grieves that people run more readily to the virtue by which their needs are served than to that by which something divine is learned. This grief appears to be represented in what is written: “Rachel was jealous of her sister.”

Since pure understanding of spiritual substance cannot be expressed in words produced by flesh, wisdom’s teaching has chosen to convey divine things through every kind of bodily likeness. Thus Rachel chose to receive children from her husband through her maidservant rather than remain entirely without children. For Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, is interpreted as “ancient” or “grown old.” From the old life, devoted to bodily senses, bodily images are conceived, even when something is heard about the spiritual and unchangeable substance of the Godhead.

Leah also receives children from her maidservant, inflamed by the desire to have a greater number of offspring. We find that Zilpah, her maidservant, is interpreted as “mouth.” Accordingly, this maidservant represents those whose mouth was present in the preaching of the evangelical faith, but whose heart was not. Of them it is written: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). Of them the Apostle says: “You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. 2).

Nevertheless, so that through this condition the free wife Jacob, the laboring one, might receive children as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord says: “Do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23). Hence the Apostle says: “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and I shall continue to rejoice” (Phil. 1), as though she also rejoices when the maidservant gives birth to a more numerous offspring.

There is, however, a certain child of Leah born through Rachel’s benefit, when Rachel allows her sister to lie with her husband on the night when he is to sleep with her in due course, after receiving from Leah’s son some mandrakes. What should be said about the mandrake? I have discovered that it is a beautiful and sweet-smelling plant, but bland in taste. Therefore I understand the mandrake fruit to represent popular good reputation.

Hence the Apostle says: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3). Although such people have little discernment, they nevertheless often repay the labor of those who care for them with the splendor of praise and the fragrance of a good reputation. Nor do those who are first in the Church attain this popular glory unless they are engaged in the dangers and labor of active life. For this reason Leah’s son found the mandrake fruits when he went out into the field—that is, when he walked honorably among those who are outside.

That teaching of wisdom, however, which is far removed from the noise of the crowd and fixes itself in sweet delight upon the contemplation of truth, would not attain even a small measure of popular glory except through those who preside amid the crowds, acting and persuading. While these active and busy people, through whom the welfare of the multitude is administered and whose authority is dear to the people, bear witness to the life pursued for the sake of seeking and contemplating truth, the mandrake fruits come, as it were idly, through Leah to Rachel. They come to Leah herself through her firstborn son—that is, through the honor of her fertility, in which lies the entire fruit of laborious action exposed to danger amid the contests of temptations.

Many people who possess good intelligence and burn with zeal, although they may be capable of governing peoples, nevertheless avoid this because of its turbulent occupations and are carried with their whole heart into the leisure of teaching, as into the embraces of beautiful Rachel. Since it is good that this life too, becoming more widely known, should earn popular glory, it is unjust for it to obtain that glory if it keeps its lover—who is suited and capable of administering ecclesiastical responsibilities—in leisure and does not assign him to the governance of the common good. Therefore Leah said to her sister:

“Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband, and do you also wish to take my son’s mandrakes?” By the one husband she signifies all those who, although capable and worthy of being entrusted with the governance of the Church for the administration of the sacrament of faith, are inflamed by devotion to teaching and by the investigation and contemplation of wisdom, and withdraw from all the burdens of action, wishing to remain in the leisure of learning or teaching.

Thus it was said: “Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband, and do you also wish to take my son’s mandrakes?” As though she were saying: “Is it a small matter that the life of scholars keeps in leisure people necessary for the labor of governing affairs, and does it also seek popular glory?”

Therefore, so that Rachel might obtain it justly, she gives her husband to her sister for that night. This means that those suited to the governance of peoples through their laborious virtue, even if they have chosen to devote themselves to knowledge, must undergo the experience of temptations and also accept the burden of responsibilities for the common good, lest the teaching of wisdom to which they had decided to devote themselves be blasphemed, and lest it fail to acquire a good reputation among inexperienced peoples—something signified by those fruits and necessary for the exhortation of learners.

But they are compelled by considerable force to undertake this responsibility. This is signified by the fact that, when Jacob came from the field, Leah went out to meet him, detained him, and said: “You shall come in to me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” As though she were saying: “Do you wish to confer a good reputation on the teaching that you love? Do not flee from dutiful labor.”

Anyone who observes these things being done in the Church sees them and recognizes through examples what we understand in books. Who does not see this happening throughout the whole world? People come from the works of the world and go into the leisure of learning and contemplating truth, as into Rachel’s embrace; then ecclesiastical necessity receives them from the side and appoints them to labor, as though Leah were saying: “You shall come in to me.”

Through those who administer this mystery of God, generating children of faith in the night of this world, that life is also praised by the peoples—a life for love of which they were converted and abandoned their worldly hope, and from whose profession they were taken up to the merciful governance of the people. In all their labors they act so that the profession by which they were converted may be glorified more widely and more clearly, because it has given such rulers to the people. They do not refuse Leah’s night so that Rachel may enjoy fruits that are sweet-smelling and brightly shining.

At times Rachel herself, through God’s mercy, gives birth independently, although only with great difficulty, because it is exceedingly rare for the words “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1), or anything piously and wisely said about this matter, to be grasped, even in part, without the phantasm of bodily thought, and in a salutary way.

In another sense, the martyr Victorinus and the others interpreted Leah and Rachel as figures of the Church and the Synagogue. They thought that Leah, the elder, represented the Synagogue, because she first bore the people of God. She is also said to be afflicted in her eyes, because the Law given through Moses was covered over and sealed. Rachel, however, younger and beautiful, at first barren and afterward fertile, is a likeness of the Church: younger because she came later in time; beautiful because she is holy in body and spirit. Her eyes are beautiful because she was deemed worthy to perceive the Gospel. She remained barren until the Synagogue had produced its people.

Why did Jacob serve for Rachel, while Leah the elder was substituted for her, except because the Lord, in order to take up the Church, first joined the Synagogue to himself? Jacob’s service for seven years for the two wives therefore signifies the time of the present life, since it unfolds through seven days. In this life the Lord took the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father’s will even unto death. He served for all, and our Lord says: “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20). Jacob fed sheep, and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10). Jacob took for himself, as the profit of his wages, a flock of various colors; Christ gathered to himself the diversity of the nations. Jacob cut three rods, stripped them of their bark, and placed them in the water troughs so that his sheep would multiply at the sight of them. Our Lord, in the water of baptism, set before the faithful people the names of the three Persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that whoever fully perceives this may become a sheep of God. How this matter should be understood according to the historical account must not be passed over.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Jacob’s servitude, by which he served Laban for his own flocks

Jacob therefore asked his father-in-law to allow him to return to his relatives with his wives and children. Laban persuaded him to remain with him for some time and said to him:

What shall I give you? He replied: I want nothing. But if you do what I ask, I will pasture and guard your flocks again. Go through all your flocks and separate every speckled sheep, every sheep with variegated fleece, and whatever is tawny, [Col. 0603A] spotted, or parti-colored, whether among the sheep or among the goats, shall be my wages. And tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me, when the appointed time comes before you, and so forth.

Among the Greek interpreters the meaning has become very confused, and to this present day I have been unable to find anyone among our writers who explained clearly what is being said in this passage. “Do you wish,” he says, “Jacob, to serve me for another seven years? Do what I ask. Separate all the discolored and variegated sheep and goats, and hand them over to your sons. Again, from both flocks give me the white and black animals—that is, those of a single color. If, then, anything variegated is born from the white and black animals, which are of one color, it will be mine. But if anything of one color is born, it will be yours. I am asking for nothing difficult. Nature itself works in your favor: white animals are born from white ones, and black from black ones. [Col. 0603B] My righteousness will be with me, while God looks upon my humility and labor.”

Laban readily seized upon the option he had been given. Doing as Jacob requested, he separated by a journey of three days Jacob from his sons, so that no deception might arise from the proximity of the animals. Jacob therefore devised a new stratagem and, by a natural art, opposed the nature of white and black animals. Taking three rods—of poplar, almond, and pomegranate, although the Septuagint has storax, walnut, and plane—he stripped them of bark in part and produced a variegated color in the rods: wherever he had left the bark on the rod, the original color remained; wherever he had removed the bark, a white color was exposed.

Jacob therefore kept watch. [Col. 0603C] At the time when the animals were mounted and, after the heat of the day, eagerly went to drink, he placed the discolored rods in the troughs. When the rams and he-goats were admitted, he caused the sheep and goats, in their very eagerness to drink, to be mounted by them, so that, from their twofold desire—both eagerly drinking and being mounted by the males—they might conceive such offspring as the shadows of the rams and he-goats mounting above them appeared in the mirror of the water. For the color of the images was also variegated because of the rods placed in the troughs.

It is not surprising that this is said to be the nature of women at conception: whatever they have seen or conceived in their minds during the final heat of pleasure in which they conceive, they produce offspring resembling it. The same thing is even said to occur among herds of mares in Spain; and Quintilian, in the controversy in which a [Col. 0603D] matron is accused because she gave birth to an Ethiopian, argues in her defense that conception has the nature described above. It is also found written in the books of the ancient and most skilled physician Hippocrates that a certain woman was about to be punished on suspicion of adultery, since she had given birth to an exceptionally beautiful child unlike either parent and unlike the family, unless the physician just mentioned had resolved the question by advising them to investigate whether there might be some such picture in the bedroom. When one was found, the woman was freed from suspicion.

(Aug.) But as for what usefulness the joining of rods from three different kinds of trees contributed to the matter Jacob undertook—namely, the multiplication of various animals—it is not at all apparent. Nor does it make any difference for this purpose whether the rods were varied from wood of one kind or whether several kinds of wood were used, [Col. 0604A] since only variety of color is in question. This therefore compels us to investigate the prophecy and some figurative meaning in the matter. Without doubt Jacob did this as a prophet, and therefore he should not be accused of fraud. We must believe that he did such a thing only because of its spiritual significance.

After the variegated and discolored lambs and kids had been born from the white and single-colored flocks, Jacob separated them and kept them far from the original flock. Whenever single-colored animals were born—that is, white or black—he handed them over to Laban’s sons. He placed the rods that he had discolored [stripped of bark] in the troughs where the water was poured out and where the animals came to drink, opposite the animals, so that they might conceive [Col. 0604B] when they came to drink. And the animals conceived opposite Jacob’s rods, which he had placed before them in the troughs for conception. But he did not place them before the late-breeding sheep, and the late-born became Laban’s, while the early-born became Jacob’s.

This is not found in the Septuagint interpreters. Instead of “late-born” and “early-born,” they translated something else—I do not know what—which has no bearing on the meaning. What Scripture says is this: Jacob, prudent and shrewd, preserved justice and equality even in his new method. If all the animals had produced variegated lambs and kids, there would have been some suspicion of deception, and Laban, openly hostile to the matter, would have opposed it. He therefore regulated everything in such a way that he himself received the fruit of his labor while Laban was not completely stripped of his possessions.

Whenever the sheep and goats [Col. 0604C] were mounted in the early season—for the spring offspring is better—he placed the rods before them, so that variegated offspring might be born. But whenever the sheep and goats sought a male late in the season, he did not place the rods before their eyes, so that single-colored animals might be born. Whatever was born first belonged to him, because it was discolored and variegated; whatever came later belonged to Laban. For animals of a single color were born, whether black or white.

In the passage where it is written that they conceived at the rods, the Hebrew has *yehammenna*, . I cannot express the force of the Hebrew word except by circumlocution. *Yehammenna* properly refers to the final heat during intercourse, by which the entire body is shaken and which is near the end of the pleasure being consummated.

(Greg.) This deed can also be understood in another way according to the mystical sense. [Col. 0604D] The meaning of sacred eloquence must be weighed between the text and the mystery with such balance that, with the scales of both sides properly regulated, neither is it pressed down by the weight of excessive scrutiny nor, on the other hand, left empty by the torpor of negligence. Many of its statements are pregnant with such a conception of allegories that whoever tries to hold them to history alone is deprived of their knowledge through his own negligence. Others, however, serve exterior commands in such a way that if someone desires to penetrate them more subtly, he finds nothing within, but also conceals from himself what they say outwardly. Hence it is rightly said through historical narration by means of signification:

“Jacob took green rods of poplar and almond [Col. 0605A] and from plane trees, stripped them of bark in part,” and so forth.

What does it mean to place green rods of poplar and almond and plane before the eyes of the flocks, except to offer the lives and teachings of the ancient Fathers as examples to the peoples through the sequence of Scripture? Since these are straight according to the test of reason, they are called rods. He removes the bark from them in part, so that in what is stripped the inner whiteness may appear; and he preserves the bark in part, so that they may remain outwardly in the truth as they were. The color of the rods becomes variegated when the bark is partly removed and partly retained.

The teachings of the preaching Fathers are therefore placed before the eyes of our consideration like variegated rods. When we often avoid the literal meaning, we remove the bark, as it were; [Col. 0605B] and when we often follow the literal meaning, we preserve the bark, as it were. When the bark of the letter is removed from them, the inner whiteness is revealed allegorically; and when the bark is left, the green examples of outward understanding are displayed.

Jacob rightly placed these rods in the water troughs, because our Redeemer fixed them in the books of sacred knowledge by which we are inwardly watered. The rams who look upon them mate with the sheep, because our rational spirits, when fixed upon their meaning, produce offspring of works corresponding to the examples of those who preceded them, which they see in the words of instruction with which they are joined. The offspring has a different color in good works because sometimes, with the bark of the letter removed, they consider inward things more sharply, while at other times, with the covering of history [Col. 0605C] preserved, they form themselves well in outward matters.

And the man became exceedingly rich. He possessed many flocks, female servants, male servants, camels, and donkeys.

## CHAPTER XIX. Jacob’s return from Mesopotamia with his wives and children, and the agreement Laban made with Jacob

### (CHAP. XXXI.)

After he heard the words of Laban’s sons, who said, “Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father, and from his property he has acquired his wealth and become famous,” he also observed Laban’s face, that it was not [Col. 0605D] toward him as it had been yesterday and the day before. The Lord said to him especially: “Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you.”

He sent for Rachel and Leah and summoned them to the field where he was pasturing the flocks. He said to them: “I see that your father’s face is not toward me as it was yesterday and the day before. Yet the God of my father has been with me, and you yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength. But your father has deceived me and changed my wages ten times,” and so forth.

“And your father,” he said, “has deceived me and changed my wages ten times; yet God did not permit him to harm me. If he said, ‘The variegated animals shall be your wages,’ every animal was born variegated; and if he said, ‘The single-colored animals shall be your wages,’ every animal was born single-colored.”

For what we have rendered as “he changed my wages ten times,” the Septuagint interpreters put “ten lambs,” led by I know not what opinion, although the Hebrew word *monim*, , denotes a number rather than lambs. [Col. 0606A] The following context also proves that this is the more appropriate meaning: Laban continually changed the arrangement after each birth.

If he saw variegated animals being born, after the birth he would say, “I want variegated animals to be born to me in the future.” When Jacob heard this, he would not place the rods in the troughs, so that the animals would produce single-colored offspring for him in the future. Again, when he saw single-colored animals being born, he would say that they ought to become his portion. And why say more? As many as ten times, Laban changed the arrangement concerning Jacob’s animals, and whatever he had proposed should be born was turned into the opposite color.

So that no one may think ten periods of giving birth within six years incredible, read Virgil, where it is said:

> Twice-pregnant flocks.

[Col. 0606B] It is traditionally reported that the nature of the Italian sheep and that of Mesopotamia are the same.

Rachel and Leah answered: “Do we still have any portion or inheritance in our father’s house? Has he not treated us like foreigners, sold us, and consumed our price? But God has taken our father’s wealth and given it to us and to our children. Therefore do everything that the Lord has commanded you.”

Jacob then arose, placed his children and wives upon camels, and departed. He took all his property, his flocks, and everything he had acquired in Mesopotamia, and went to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.

At that time Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s idols, and so forth. Where we now read “idols,” the Hebrew has *teraphim*, [Col. 0606C] , written there; Aquila interprets it as *morphōmata* (μορφώματα), that is, “figures” or “images.” This is mentioned so that we may know what *teraphim* means in the Book of Judges.

Laban was told on the third day that Jacob had fled. Taking his brothers with him, he pursued him for seven days and caught up with him on Mount Gilead, and so forth. This does not mean that the mountain was called Gilead at that time, but, by anticipation—as we have often said—it is called by the name by which it was later to be known.

“You did not allow me,” Laban said to Jacob, “to kiss my sons and daughters,” and so forth. Laban calls Jacob’s sons and daughters his own according to the usage of sacred Scripture, which calls sons or brothers one’s relatives, as will be shown below, where it is written: “Jacob said to his brothers, ‘Gather stones,’” calling them sons by the name of brothers. Likewise, in the Gospel, the sons of Mary, the Lord’s maternal aunt, are called the Lord’s brothers. [Col. 0606D]

After the long servitude that Jacob endured with his father-in-law for the sake of his wives and wages, God commanded him to return to his homeland.

(Isid.) Then, without his father-in-law’s knowledge, he hastened away with his wives and his company. Laban, however, pursued him in fury to Mount Gilead and searched for the idols that Rachel had stolen, but did not find them.

What, then, does this signify figuratively? Let us say. Although Laban previously represented another person, he now represents the type of the devil. For Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” “Whitening” is not inappropriately understood as the devil, because although he is dark by merit, he transforms [Col. 0607A] himself into an angel of light.

Jacob served him—that is, in part the Jewish people among the reprobate, from whose flesh the Lord came incarnate. Laban can also represent this world, which pursues Jacob in fury because it attempts, by persecution, to oppress the elect, who are members of our Redeemer.

Jacob took away Laban’s daughter—that is, the daughter either of the world or of the devil—when Christ joined the Church to himself. He took her from her father’s house as well, because through the Prophet he says to her: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV).

What else is designated by the idols except greed? Hence Paul also says: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Galatians). Laban therefore came to Jacob and did not find the idol, because when the devil displayed the treasures of the world, he found no trace of earthly desire in our [Col. 0607B] Redeemer. But the things Jacob did not have Rachel covered while sitting.

Through Rachel, whose name means “sheep of God,” the Church is represented. To sit means to seek the humility of repentance, as it is written: “Rise after you have sat” (Ps. CXXVI). Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting, because the holy Church, following Christ, covers the vice of earthly desire through the humility of repentance. Concerning this covering of sins the Prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI).

Rachel, then, signified us: we press down the idols by sitting when, through repentance, we condemn the sins of greed. This impurity of greed does not chiefly befall those who run manfully, to whom it is said, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XX), [Col. 0607C] but rather those who, walking with an effeminate step, are weakened by the blandishments of the world.

Hence the following words of that same Rachel occur there: “According to the custom of women, it has now happened to me,” that is, she made it known that she was experiencing something womanly.

Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar, and so forth. It must be carefully observed how they set up such pillars as witnesses to various matters—not to worship them as gods, but so that they might signify something through them.

Jacob said to his brothers: “Let us gather stones.” When the stones had been gathered, they made a heap and ate there upon it. Laban called it “Heap of Witness,” and Jacob called it “Heap of the Witness.”

In the Hebrew language, “heap” is *gal*, ; *ed*, , means “witness.” Again, [Col. 0607D] in the Syriac language, “heap” is called *igar*, and “witness” *saadutha*, .

Jacob therefore called the heap of witness—that is, Gilead—in the Hebrew language. Laban, however, called it by the name of his own people, [Col. 0608A] *igar saadutha*, that is, “heap of witness.” For he was a Syrian and had changed the ancient language of his ancestors into the language of the province in which he lived.

Laban said: “This mound shall be a witness between me and you today.” Therefore its name was also called Gilead, that is, “mound of witness.”

It should nevertheless be noted that Laban and Jacob gave somewhat different names to the heap of stones they had set up between them. Thus it is found written in some copies that Laban called it “Heap of Witness,” while Jacob called it “Heap of the Witness.” Those who know both the Syriac and Hebrew languages say that this arose from the peculiarities of each language. It often happens that what is expressed in one language by a single word cannot be said by a single word in another, and each thing is named through a closeness of meaning. For afterward it is said: “Therefore its name was called Heap of the Witness.” This is placed midway because it suited both parties: the one who had said “Heap of Witness” and the one who had said “Heap of the Witness.”

(Isid.) Mystically, among the faithful—both Jews and Gentiles—the prominent stone is a witness in the likeness of Christ, and the heap of stones is the multitude of believers.

“May the Lord look upon us and judge between us when we have departed from one another. If you afflict my daughters, and if you bring other wives in addition to them, no one is a witness to our words [Col. 0608B] except God, who is present and sees.”

(Aug.) What does Laban mean when he says, “No one is a witness to our words,” unless perhaps he means that there was no outsider? Or does he refer to the testimony of God, whom they ought to regard as being with them in such a way that there was no one else whom they could add to his testimony?

Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac—that is, by the fear with which he feared God. He had commended this fear earlier as well when he said: “The God of my father Abraham and the Fear of my father Isaac.”

Laban, rising during the night, kissed his sons and daughters, blessed them, and returned to his own place.

The fact that Laban and Jacob both began traveling along the road that leads across the river toward the promised land, but that neither of them reached the appointed [Col. 0608C] place—for Laban stopped after taking the road—can aptly signify two peoples attempting, through baptism, to go toward the land of the Church. But while Jacob proceeded there, Laban turned back, because, while the sons of light hasten through baptism toward their future homeland by advancing in virtue, the reprobate fall backward from the undertaking they began and return to their former filth.

Hence it follows:

### (CHAP. XXXII.)

Jacob also went on the road he had begun, and the angels of God met him. When he saw them, he said: “These are the camps of God.” And he called the name of that place Mahanaim, , that is, “camps.”

(Aug.) There is no doubt that the camp of God Jacob saw on the road was a multitude of angels. In Scripture they are called the army of heaven. Where we have “camps,” the Hebrew has *mahanaim*, [Col. 0608D] so that whenever the word is translated in another passage, we may know which place it signifies. It is beautifully fitting that, as he was going to meet his hostile brother, he was received by choirs of accompanying angels.

## CHAPTER XX. Jacob’s sending gifts to his brother Esau, and his struggle with the man by whom he was blessed

Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau, to the land of Seir, the region of Edom. He commanded them, saying: “Thus you shall speak to my lord Esau: ‘Your brother Jacob says this: I have lived as a foreigner with Laban, and I have remained there until the present day. I have oxen and donkeys, sheep and servants, and female servants. Now I am sending a delegation to my lord, so that I may find favor in [Col. 0609A] your sight.’”

The messengers returned to Jacob, saying: “We came to your brother Esau, and behold, he is hastening to meet you with four hundred men.”

Jacob was greatly afraid and, terrified, divided the people who were with him, as well as the flocks, sheep, oxen, and camels, into two companies, saying: “If Esau comes to one company and strikes it, the other company that remains will be saved.”

When the report reached him that his brother Jacob was coming to meet him with four hundred men, he was indeed troubled and confused in mind, because he was very afraid. It seemed to the disturbed man that his multitude should be arranged in two camps.

Here one may ask how he retained faith in God’s promises when he said: “If my brother Esau comes to the first camp and destroys it, the second will be preserved for safety.” Yet this too could happen: Esau might overthrow his camp, and then God [Col. 0609B] might be present after that affliction and deliver him and fulfill what he had promised.

We are also instructed by this example that, although we believe in God, we should nevertheless do what human beings must do as a safeguard for salvation, lest, by neglecting such measures, we seem to tempt God.

After this, we should consider what Jacob himself says:

“God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, Lord, who said to me, ‘Return to the land of your kindred, and I will do good to you’: you are sufficient for me against all the righteousness and all the truth that you have shown your servant. For with this staff of mine I crossed this Jordan. But now I have become two camps. Deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, because I [Col. 0609C] fear him, lest when he comes he strike me and the mothers with their children. Yet you said: ‘I will do good to you, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because of its multitude.’”

In these words both human weakness and faithful devotion are plainly evident.

The gifts went ahead of him, but he himself remained that night in the camp. When he rose early, he took his two wives and their two maidservants, together with eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. The Jabbok is a river that flows between Ammaus—that is, Philadelphia—and Gerasa, at its fourth milestone and beyond. It joins the river Jordan.

After crossing this stream, Jacob wrestled against the one who had appeared to him, and he was called Israel. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0609D] Having sent across everything that belonged to him, he remained alone; and behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it immediately withered. He said to him: “Let me go, for dawn has risen.” He replied: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” He therefore said: “What is your name?” He answered: “Jacob.” But he said: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, because if you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against human beings?”

Jacob asked him: “Tell me by what name you are called.” He replied: “Why do you ask my name?” And he blessed him there. Jacob called the name of that place Phanuel, saying: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and [Col. 0610A] my soul has been saved.”

The name is derived from Israel and signifies “prince.” The meaning, then, is this: “Your name shall not be called Supplanter”—that is, Jacob—but “your name shall be called Prince with God”—that is, Israel. For just as I am a prince, so you too, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince.

“If you were able to fight with me, who am God—or an angel, since many interpret the matter differently—how much more will you prevail against human beings?” That is, against Esau, whom you ought not to fear.

But the interpretation found later in the Book of Names—that Israel means “a man seeing God” or “a mind seeing God”—which has been worn smooth by nearly everyone’s usage, seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truthfully as forcefully.

Israel is written with these letters: *iod*, ; *sin*, ; *res*, ; *aleph*, ; *lamed*, ; and it is interpreted as “prince God” or “upright God.”

But “a man seeing God” is written with these letters. “Man” is written with three letters: *aleph*, ; *iod*, ; *sin*, ; so that it is pronounced *ais*, . “Seeing” is written with three letters: [Col. 0610B] *res*, *aleph*, *he*, so that it is pronounced *rahe*, . Then *el*, , consists of two letters, *aleph* and *lamed*, and is interpreted as “God” or “strong.”

Although, then, those who translated Israel as “a man” or “a mind seeing God” possess great authority and eloquence, and their shadow weighs upon us, we should follow the authority of Scripture and of the angel—or God—who himself called him Israel, rather than that of any secular eloquence.

There is also what follows:

“And he blessed him there, and Jacob called the name of that place ‘Face of God,’ saying: ‘For I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved.’”

(Isid.) In Hebrew this is called *Phanuel*, [Col. 0610C] , so that we may know that it is the same place which, in the other books of sacred Scripture, is read as *Phanuel*, exactly as it is written in Hebrew.

Here the image of the Lord’s mystery was principally prefigured. For that man most clearly bore the type of Christ. Jacob prevailed over him because he wished him to do so, in order to represent the mystery of the Lord’s passion. Jacob was seen in the type of the Jews—that is, in the offspring of his body—to have prevailed over God, and to have entered into a struggle with his flesh as with one who was weak, becoming strong in his passion, just as it is written when they said, “Crucify him” (Matt. XXVII). Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from the same angel whom he had overcome as victor. The giving of this name was itself certainly a blessing.

Israel is interpreted as “seeing God,” which will be the final reward of all the saints.

[Col. 0610D] That same angel touched the breadth of his thigh and made him lame. Thus the same Jacob was both blessed and lame: blessed in those from that people who believed in Christ, and lame in the unbelievers.

For in the sinew of the thigh there is health, and in the multitude of the offspring there is the race. Many among the descendants, degenerating from the faith of their fathers and deviating from the commands of their creator, limp in the error of their seed. Of them it was prophetically foretold: “They have limped from his paths” (Ps. XVII).

(Greg.) Yet that people, after its strength had been touched, not only limps but also grows numb, so that it is no longer able to generate sons.

The same matter can also usefully be understood according to the tropological sense. [Col. 0611A] There is a great struggle of the mind in the contemplative life when it raises itself toward heavenly things, when it stretches its spirit toward spiritual realities, when it attempts to pass beyond everything that is seen bodily, when it contracts and expands itself, and when at times it conquers and overcomes the resisting darkness of its blindness and partially and subtly touches something of the unbounded light.

Yet immediately it is struck back upon itself, and from the light toward which it passed by breathing deeply, it returns with a sigh to the darkness of its own blindness. Sacred history aptly signifies this when it narrates blessed Jacob wrestling with the angel.

When he was returning to his parents, he found an angel on the road, with whom he engaged in a great struggle. Whoever struggles in wrestling [Col. 0611B] sometimes finds himself superior to the one with whom he contends and sometimes inferior.

The angel therefore designates the Lord, while Jacob, who contends with the angel, expresses the soul of every perfect man engaged in contemplation. For when the soul strives to contemplate God, it is placed in a kind of contest: at one moment it seems to overflow, because by understanding and feeling it tastes something of the unbounded [Col. 0611C] light; at another it falls short, because after tasting it, it again fails.

The angel is, as it were, overcome when God is apprehended by the innermost understanding. But it should be noted that the same angel, once overcome, touched Jacob’s thigh-sinew, immediately made it wither, and caused Jacob to limp on one foot for a time. For when almighty God is already known through desire and understanding, he dries up in us every pleasure of the flesh.

Previously we seemed to seek God while relying, as it were, on two feet, while also holding on to the world. After the sweetness of God has been recognized, one foot remains sound in us while the other limps, because it is necessary that, as love of the world is weakened, the love of God alone should grow strong in us.

If, then, we hold fast to the angel, we limp on one foot, because as the strength of inward love increases in us, the strength of the flesh is undoubtedly weakened. Everyone who limps on one foot leans only upon the foot that remains sound. Likewise, when earthly desire has been dried up in someone, he supports himself with all his strength on the single foot of the love of God and stands upon it, because he carries suspended above the earth the foot of love for the world, which he had been accustomed to place upon the ground.

[Col. 0611D] Therefore, if we too return to our own parents—that is, to our spiritual fathers—let us hold fast to the angel on the road, so that we may apprehend God through inward sweetness.

The sweetness of the contemplative life is exceedingly lovely. It lifts the mind above itself, desires heavenly things, shows that earthly things ought to be despised, opens spiritual realities to the eyes of the mind, and conceals bodily things. Hence it says well in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V). The heart being awake, a person sleeps who, by progressing inwardly through contemplation, rests from evil outward works.

Finally, when the same patriarch added that he had seen God face to face, although earlier he had said that a man had wrestled with him, this signifies that the same God [Col. 0612A] was going to become man and wrestle with the people of Jacob.

(Greg.) The Truth itself says: “No one has ever seen my face.” How, then, does Jacob testify, saying: “I have seen the Lord face to face”? (Exod. XXXIII.)

When the inner eye of the human mind has been purified and the rust of every vice has been burned away by the fire of tribulation, then, with the eyes of the heart cleansed, the joy of the heavenly homeland is opened. First we purify by grieving over what we have done; afterward, through joy, we contemplate more clearly what we seek.

At first, the darkness of evils is uncovered from the sharpness of the mind by sorrow’s burning. Then, when the heart suddenly flashes with radiance, it is illumined by the unbounded light. By this vision, however imperfect, it is absorbed into the joy of a certain security; and, as though carried beyond itself after the failure of the present [Col. 0612B] life, it is somehow renewed in a kind of newness.

There the mind is sprinkled from the immeasurable fountain of infusion with the dew from above. There it sees that it is not sufficient for what it has been carried away to contemplate; and by sensing the truth it sees, because it does not see how great the truth itself is.

The more closely it approaches that truth, the farther away it considers itself to be, because unless it desired the truth in some fashion, it would not perceive that it cannot desire it fully. When the soul’s effort is directed toward it, the radiance of its immensity flashing around it strikes the soul back.

For the truth itself fills all things and surrounds all things. Therefore our mind cannot expand so as to comprehend an unbounded substance, because the boundary of its own poverty constricts it. Hence it quickly falls back upon itself and, having glimpsed what are like footprints of the truth, is recalled to its own image.

This vision produced by contemplation is not solid and lasting, but, as I might say, a kind of imitation of vision; nevertheless it is called the face of God. Because we recognize someone by his face, we appropriately call the knowledge of God [Col. 0612C] his face.

Thus, after Jacob had wrestled with the angel, he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face,” as though he were saying: “I have come to know God, because he himself has deigned to know me.” Paul testifies that this knowledge will be complete at the end when he says: “Then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Cor. XIII).

## CHAPTER XXI. Esau’s meeting with Jacob

### (CHAP. XXXIII.)

Jacob lifted his eyes and saw [Col. 0612D] Esau coming, with four hundred men accompanying him. He divided the children of Leah and Rachel and of both maidservants. He placed each maidservant and her children first, Leah and her children second, and Rachel and Joseph last. He himself went ahead and bowed to the ground seven times until he approached his brother, and so forth.

He did not, as many suppose, make three companies, but two. Thus, where we have “he divided,” Aquila has *hēmísusen* (ἡμίσυσεν), that is, “he divided in half,” so that he made one group of the maidservants with their children and another of Leah and Rachel, who were free, with their children. He arranged for the maidservants to go first and the free women second. He himself went ahead of both flocks to meet his brother and bow down before him.

[Col. 0613A] Esau said: “What are these companies that I encountered?” He answered: “So that I might find favor before my lord.” He said: “I have very much, my brother; let what is yours be yours.” Jacob said: “Do not do so, I beg you. But if I have found favor in your eyes, accept this little gift from my hands. For I have seen your face as though I were seeing the face of God,” and so forth.

(Aug.) What does Jacob mean when he says to his brother, “For this reason I have seen your face as one sees the face of God”? Did the words of a fearful and troubled mind erupt into such flattery? Or can they be understood as having been spoken without sin, according to some interpretation?

Perhaps, since the gods of the nations are also called gods, though they are demons, these words should not be held against a man of God. [Col. 0613B] Even if these fraternal words were spoken with a kindly intention—for the fear itself had passed after the brother’s favorable reception—he could have spoken in this way, just as Moses is called a god to Pharaoh, according to what the Apostle says: “And if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—for indeed there are many gods and many lords” (1 Cor. VIII).

This is especially so because the expression in Greek is written without the article, and the article is ordinarily used very clearly to signify the one true God. For he did not say *prosōpon tou Theou* (πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ), “the face of God,” but *prosōpon Theou* (πρόσωπον Θεοῦ), “a face of God.” Those who are accustomed to hear and understand Greek easily perceive the difference between these expressions.

At his brother’s urging, he reluctantly consented and said: “Let us go together; I shall be your companion on the journey.” And Jacob said: “You know, my lord, that I have tender little ones, and sheep and cattle with young beside me; if I make them labor too much in traveling, all the flocks will die in one day. Let my lord go on ahead of his servant, and I shall follow gradually in his footsteps, as I see that my little ones are able, until I come to my lord at Seir.” The question is whether Jacob deceitfully promised his brother that, following the feet of his people on the journey and delaying for their sake, he would come to him at Seir. For, as Scripture subsequently relates, he did not do this, but went by the route that led him to his own people. Or perhaps he had made the promise sincerely but later chose another course after reconsidering the matter?

Accordingly, Esau returned that day by the route from which he had come to Seir, while Jacob came to Succoth.
