There, after building a house and fixing his tents, he called the name of that place Succoth, that is, “tents.” Where we have “tents,” the Hebrew reads *Succoth*. To this day there is a city across the Jordan bearing this name, in the region of Scythopolis.

And he crossed over to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, after returning from Mesopotamia of Syria, and he dwelt beside the town, etc. A question arises: how can the city of Shechem be called Salem, when Jerusalem, in which Melchizedek reigned, was previously called Salem? Either, then, both cities have one and the same name—which we can also find in the case of several places in Judea, so that the same name belongs to a city or place in different tribes—or else we must say that this Salem, which is now used for Shechem, is here interpreted as “completed” or “perfect,” while the one later called Jerusalem is translated in our language as “peaceful.” For both meanings are expressed by this name, with only a slight change of accent. The Hebrews relate that Jacob’s lame thigh recovered and was healed there; for this reason the same city received the name signifying “healed” and “perfect.”

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Concerning the abduction of Dinah, the daughter of Leah, by Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, and concerning vengeance for the outrage

**(CHAP. XXXIV.)** Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite and prince of that land, saw her, he fell in love with her and seized her, and slept with her, violating the virgin by force; and his soul was joined to her, and he soothed her grief with flattering words, etc.

**(Albin.)** Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign region when each mind, neglecting its own pursuits and attending to the affairs of others, wanders outside its proper habit and order. Shechem, the prince of the land, oppresses her, because the devil corrupts the mind when he finds it occupied with outward concerns. “And his soul was joined to her,” because he regards as united to himself the one whom he has bound to him through iniquity. And because, when the mind recovers from guilt, it is distressed and strives to lament what it has done, while the corrupter brings empty hopes and false assurances before its eyes in order to remove the benefit of sorrow, the text rightly adds: “And he soothed her grief with flattering words.”

For sometimes he speaks of the more serious deeds of others, sometimes of the offense as though it were nothing, sometimes of God’s mercy, and sometimes promises that there will still be time afterward for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led along by these things, it is held back from the purpose of repentance, so that it receives no good then because nothing evil now causes it sorrow; and then it is more fully overwhelmed by punishments, since even in its sins it rejoices. After Scripture has related the covenant that Hamor and his son Shechem made with the sons of Jacob, it continues concerning circumcision, saying:

“All agreed, and all the males were circumcised. And behold, on the third day, when the pain of the wounds is most severe, two sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, took their swords, entered the city confidently, and, after killing all the males, slew Hamor and Shechem together, taking their sister Dinah from Shechem’s house. When they had gone out, the other sons of Jacob fell upon the slain, plundered the city in vengeance for the outrage, and laid waste their sheep, herds, donkeys, and everything that was in the fields and houses; they also led away the children and wives as captives.”

After these things had been boldly carried out, Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: “You have troubled me and made me hateful to the Canaanites and Perizzites who inhabit this land,” and so forth. Since shortly before, when Jacob was speaking with his brother Esau, he had indicated that his sons were infants—called *paides* (παῖδες) in Greek—it may be asked how they could have perpetrated so great a slaughter and plundered the city, killing its inhabitants, though they were suffering from circumcision, on behalf of their sister Dinah.

It must be understood that Jacob had lived there for a long time, until his daughter had become a young woman and his sons young men. For it is written: “And he dwelt beside the town, and bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tents from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred lambs; and, having erected an altar there, he invoked upon it the mighty God of Israel. Now Dinah, the daughter of Leah, went out to see the women of that region.”

These words therefore show that Jacob did not remain there merely in passing, as a traveler usually does, but bought a field, established a tent, and built an altar; consequently, he lived there for a considerable time. When his daughter had reached the age at which she could already have friends, she wished to become acquainted with the daughters of the townspeople. Thus the exceedingly bloody slaughter and plunder were carried out on her account; and, as I think, the question now presents no difficulty. Jacob had a considerable multitude with him, since he had become very wealthy; but his sons are named in this deed because they were its leaders and authors.

After these things had been boldly carried out, Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: “You have troubled me and made me hateful to the Canaanites and Perizzites who inhabit this land. We are few, while they are gathered together; they will strike me, and I shall be destroyed, I and my household.” Because of the wars of the many who might rise up against him, he called himself few in number—not because he had fewer men than would have been sufficient to conquer that city.

And the sons of Jacob answered: “Should they have treated our sister like a prostitute?” The zeal shown by Jacob’s sons in avenging the outrage against their sister morally admonishes pastors of the faithful to care for the souls entrusted to them, lest they be violated either by bodily sin or by spiritual fornication, and to be ready always, according to the Apostle (II Cor. X), to avenge every disobedience that resists the truth, striking the violator with the sword of excommunication, so that he may not escape unpunished for so great a crime.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Where God speaks to Jacob and commands him to destroy the idols

**(CHAP. XXXV.)** Meanwhile the Lord spoke to Jacob: “Rise and go up to Bethel, and dwell there; make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother Esau.”

**(Augustine.)** Why did he not say, “Make there an altar for me, who appeared to you,” but instead says, “Make there an altar to the God who appeared to you”? Did the Son appear there, and does God the Father say this? Or is it to be counted among some category of expression?

Jacob, having summoned all his household, said: “Cast away the foreign gods that are among you, and cleanse yourselves, and change your garments. Rise, and let us go up to Bethel, that we may make there an altar to the Lord, who heard me in the day of my distress and was my companion on the journey.”

So they gave him all the foreign gods they had, together with the earrings that were in their ears. But he buried them beneath the terebinth that is behind the city of Shechem. Since it is said that they gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands and the earrings that were in their ears, the question arises why the earrings, if they were ornaments, belonged to idolatry. Unless we are to understand that they were amulets of the foreign gods. For Scripture testifies that Rebecca received earrings from Abraham’s servant; this would not have happened if it had been forbidden to possess earrings as ornaments. Therefore those earrings that were given along with the idols were, as stated, amulets of the idols.

When they had departed, the terror of God fell upon all the surrounding cities, and they did not dare pursue those who were withdrawing. Let us begin to observe how God works in human minds. From whom did the fear of God arise in those cities, except from him who was protecting his promises in Jacob and his sons?

Jacob therefore came to Luzan, which is in the land of Canaan and is surnamed Bethel, he and all the people with him. He built an altar there and called the name of the place “House of God,” for God had appeared to him there when he was fleeing from his brother. Here it is most clearly demonstrated that Bethel was not Luz itself, as stated above, but Luzan, that is, “Almond-city,” as it had previously been called.

At that time Deborah, Rebecca’s nurse, died and was buried at the foot of Bethel beneath an oak. If Rebecca’s nurse, named Deborah, died—as the translators of the Septuagint also rendered it—and the Hebrew word itself is *meneket*, “nurse,” we cannot know why they used the word “property” there and “nurse” here.

God appeared again to Jacob after he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, and blessed him, saying: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” And he called him Israel. Previously, a name is by no means imposed upon him by the angel; rather, it is foretold that it will be imposed by God. What is promised there as future is therefore shown here to have been fulfilled.

But since he had once said to Jacob, “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name,” the question arises why Jacob is afterward found called by the same name, as we frequently find throughout the holy Scriptures. Surely this name is rightly understood to belong to that promise in which God will be seen in a manner unlike that in which he was previously seen by the patriarchs; where the old name will no longer remain, because nothing of old age will remain even in the body itself, and the vision of God will be the supreme reward.

And he said to him: “I am the Lord Almighty. Increase and multiply; nations and peoples of nations shall come from you; kings shall go forth from your loins. And the land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I shall give to you and to your seed after you.” And he withdrew from him.

This promise concerns Jacob’s spiritual seed, as was already said concerning Abraham. For all who supplant vices, lay aside the old man with his deeds, and keep the eyes of their minds intent upon seeing God properly belong to Jacob, whose faith and deeds they imitate. “Kings shall go forth from his loins,” that is, the saints, who are truly called kings because they truly rule themselves and those subject to them according to God’s will. They are brought to fruitfulness from his spiritual seed—that is, through imitation of his faith in good works.

He then erected a stone monument in the place where God had spoken to him, pouring libations upon it and pouring oil upon it, and calling the name of that place Bethel. Was this done again in this place after what had already been done, or is the earlier event being recalled again? Whichever of these is the case, Jacob poured a libation upon the stone, not to the stone. He therefore did not act as idolaters customarily do, setting up altars before stones and pouring libations to stones as though they were gods.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Concerning Rachel’s death from the difficulty of childbirth, and also concerning Isaac’s death and burial

After he had departed from there, he came in springtime to the land that leads to Ephrath. While Rachel was giving birth there, she began to be in danger because of the difficulty of the delivery. The midwife said to her: “Do not fear, for you shall have this son also.” As her soul was departing because of the pain and death was already approaching, she called the name of her son Ben-oni, that is, “son of my sorrow.” But his father called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.”

Ephrath and Bethlehem are names of the same city, with corresponding interpretations, since the one is translated “fruitful” and the other “house of bread,” on account of that bread which says that it descended from heaven. And when her soul was departing—for she was dying—she called his name “son of my sorrow,” but his father called his name Benjamin. In Hebrew the entire resemblance is audible. “Son of my sorrow,” the name given by the dying mother, is called *Ben-oni*; but “son of the right hand,” that is, of strength, the name Jacob changed it to, was called Benjamin.

Hence those who think that Benjamin means “son of days” are mistaken. For “right hand” is called *yamin* and ends in the letter *n*, whereas “days” are called *yamim* and end in the letter *m*. But what does it mean that, when Rachel gave birth to this same Benjamin, she called his name “son of my sorrow,” except that she prophetically indicated that Paul would arise from that tribe, afflicting the sons of the Church by the persecution of his time?

Alternatively, through Benjamin earthly Jerusalem was prefigured. Jerusalem lies in the territory of that same Benjamin, whose people caused their mother grievous sorrow by shedding the blood of the prophets and, moreover, by crying out with impious voices for the death of Christ: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

So Rachel died and was buried on the road that leads to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Jacob erected a monument over her grave; this is the monument of Rachel’s tomb to the present day. After departing from there, he pitched his tent beyond the Tower of the Flock. Israel journeyed on and spread his tent beyond the Tower of Eder.

The Hebrews wish this to be the place where the Temple was later built, and they say that the Tower of Eder signifies the Tower of the Flock—that is, of the congregation and assembly. The prophet Micah also testifies to this when he says: “And you, Tower of the Flock, misty daughter of Zion,” etc. (Mic. IV). At that time Jacob had his tents beyond the place where the Temple was later built.

But if we follow the order of the road, it is the place of the shepherds near Bethlehem, where either the flock of angels sang at the Lord’s birth, or Jacob pastured his sheep and gave the place its name, or—and this is more truly the case—a future mystery was then already being revealed by a kind of prophecy.

While he was living in that region, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine; and this did not escape her notice.

**(Isidore.)** This crime of incest would not have been written down unless it foretold the future perversity of the people. Yet in the one who committed it, it is also understood as a disgrace; in Scripture, however, it is a prophecy of future events. For what is signified by Reuben the firstborn except Israel, the firstborn people through circumcision? He defiled the bed of the concubine—that is, he repeatedly stained the law of the Old Testament by transgression.

That the concubine signifies the law of the Old Testament Paul teaches when he says: “Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman” (Gal. IV). These two are the two Testaments. In this figure Hagar, who was a concubine, is placed in the role of the Old Testament. For there is one perfect woman, the dove of her mother, the chaste virgin, bride, and queen, who through the Gospel is joined to Christ the King in the Church.

Now Jacob had twelve sons. The sons of Leah were Reuben, the firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, were Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, were Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria.

**(Augustine.)** The question arises how the twelve sons of Israel who were born to him can be counted, and how it can be said, “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria,” when Benjamin was born much later, after they had already passed Bethel and were approaching Bethlehem.

The question must be resolved in this way: after the twelve sons had been enumerated, the statement “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria” is understood to have been made even though, among all the many people, only one was not born there. Nevertheless, he received there the cause of his birth, since his mother was joined to his father there. There is no easier solution to this question than to understand it as a case of synecdoche.

He also came to his father Isaac at Mamre, the city of Arba. This is Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac dwelt as sojourners. For Arba the Septuagint has “plain,” although Hebron is situated on a mountain. The same city is also called Mamre, having been so named in ancient times after Abraham’s friend.

And the days of Isaac were completed: one hundred and eighty years. Consumed by age, he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### Concerning the descendants of Esau

**(CHAP. XXXVI.)** These are the generations of Esau, who is Edom. Esau took wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah, the daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon the Hivite; and Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.

The fact that, after the account of Isaac’s death, Scripture relates which wives Esau had taken and which children they had borne must be understood as a recapitulation. For this did not begin after Isaac’s death, since Esau and Jacob were already one hundred and twenty years old. Isaac had begotten them when he was sixty, and lived for all the years of his life to the age of one hundred and eighty.

Adah bore Eliphaz. This is the Eliphaz whom Scripture mentions in the Book of Job.

Esau took his wives, sons, daughters, all the members of his household, his possessions, cattle, and everything he could possess in the land of Canaan, and went to another region, withdrawing from his brother Jacob. For they were exceedingly wealthy and could not dwell together; the land of their sojourning could not support them because of the multitude of their flocks. Esau dwelt on Mount Seir; he is Edom.

The question is how Scripture can say that, after the death of his father Isaac, Esau departed from the land of Canaan and dwelt on Mount Seir, when, upon Jacob’s arrival from Mesopotamia, his brother is already said to have been dwelling there.

It is therefore easy to consider what may have happened without believing that Scripture was mistaken or deceptive: namely, that after his brother had departed for Mesopotamia, Esau did not wish to live with his parents, either because of the resentment in which he grieved that he had been deprived of the blessing, or for some reason of his own, or because of his wives, whom he saw were hateful to his parents, or for some other cause; and that he began to dwell on Mount Seir.

Then, after his brother Jacob’s return and the reconciliation between them, Esau himself returned to his parents. When they had buried their father together—for that land, as Scripture says, could not contain them because they had become very wealthy—he departed again for Seir and there propagated the nation of the Idumaeans.

These are the sons of Esau and their chiefs. He is Edom. These are the sons of Seir the Horite, inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.

Esau, Edom, and Seir are one man’s name, and why he is called by different names has been stated above. As for what follows—“and the Horites inhabiting the land,” and the rest—after enumerating the sons of Esau, Scripture goes back and explains who had been chiefs in the land of Edom before Esau, namely, men of the race of the Horites, whose name in our language means “free.”

Let us read Deuteronomy carefully. There it is written more clearly how the sons of Esau came, killed the Horites, and possessed their land as an inheritance. These are the Horite chiefs, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.

The sons of Lotan were Hori and Heman. Lotan had a sister named Timna. These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, etc.

This is the Timna of whom it is written: “Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau; from her Amalek was born.” The Horites are mentioned because Esau’s firstborn had taken a concubine from among their daughters. As for the statement “Theman, Kenaz, Amalek,” and the rest, we should know that names were later given to regions of the Idumaeans from these men.

These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon, and so forth.

In another edition it is read as follows: “This is Anah, who found *haiemim* in the wilderness while pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon.”

Many and varied discussions of this chapter are found among the Hebrews. Among the Greeks and among our own writers there is silence on the matter.

Some think that *yamim* means “seas”—for the same letters are used to write “seas” as are used for the word now written here—and they maintain that, while pasturing his father’s donkeys, Anah found in the wilderness collections of water that, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, are called “seas”; that is, he discovered a pool, the finding of which in the desert would be difficult.

Some think that the expression means “hot springs,” following the usage of the Punic language, which is closely related to Hebrew. Others believe that he allowed wild asses to mate with female asses and discovered this kind of intercourse, from which exceptionally swift asses were born, called *yamim*. Most think that he was the first to cause herds of mares to be mounted by asses in the wilderness, so that new animals contrary to nature—mules—might be born from them.

Aquila translated this passage as follows: “This is Anah, who found ‘with the *simeim*’ (σὺν τοῦ σιμεῒμ).” Symmachus likewise has: “Who found ‘the *simeiu*’ (τοὺς σιμεῒυ).” This interpretation indicates the plural number. The Septuagint and Theodotion, however, translated it alike, saying: “*τὸν ἰαμείν*,” which indicates the singular number.

The kings who reigned in the land of Edom before the children of Israel had a king were these: Bela, son of Beor; and the name of his city was Dinhabah.

The statement, “These are the kings who reigned in Edom before a king reigned in Israel,” should not be understood as though all the kings up to the time when the kings of Israel began to reign—whose first was Saul—had been named. For many ruled there up to the time of Saul, since even during the period of the Judges, which preceded the kings, there were rulers.

But of the many, Moses could mention only those who had lived before his own death. Nor is it surprising that, when one counts from Abraham through Esau, the father of the Edomite nation, through Reuel, Esau’s son, through Zerah, Reuel’s son, and through Jobab, Zerah’s son—Jobab being succeeded in the kingdom by Balak, who is recorded as the first king in the land of Edom—more generations are found up to the last king whom Moses could name than are counted from Abraham through Jacob to Moses.

For in the former line nearly twelve generations are found, while in the latter there are about seven up to Moses. It could have happened that more are named there because, dying sooner, they succeeded one another more rapidly.

Thus, in another genealogical order, Matthew counts forty-two generations from Abraham to Joseph, while Luke, counting the generations in a different order—not through Solomon, as Matthew does, but through Nathan—records fifty-five from Abraham to Joseph. In the line in which more are counted, they died sooner than in the line in which fewer are counted.

And lest anyone be troubled by the fact that Balak, son of Beor, is numbered among the kings of Edom, and from the similarity of the name suppose him to be the Balak who resisted Moses when he was leading the people of Israel, let him know that that Balak was a Moabite, not an Idumaean. He was the son of Zippor, not the son of Beor. But there was also at that time a son of Beor named Balaam, not Balak; it was Balaam whom that same Balak hired to curse the people of Israel.

Bela died, and Jacob, son of Zerah of Bozrah, reigned in his place, etc. Some suspect that this man was Job, as was added at the end of Job’s book. The Hebrews, however, assert that he was descended from the line of Nahor, as was stated above.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### Concerning Joseph’s dream

**(CHAP. XXXVII.)** When Joseph was sixteen years old, he was pasturing the flock with his brothers while still a boy.

How Isaac’s death could have found Joseph, his grandson, seventeen years old—as Scripture seems to relate in sequence—is difficult to discover, however one turns the matter. I do not wish to say that it cannot be discovered, lest perhaps I overlook what another has not overlooked.

For if Joseph was seventeen years old after the death of his grandfather Isaac, when his brothers sold him into Egypt, then undoubtedly his father Jacob was one hundred and twenty years old in the seventeenth year of his son Joseph. Yet Isaac had begotten them when he was sixty years old, as it is written. Isaac therefore lived another one hundred and twenty years, since he died at one hundred and eighty.

Accordingly, he left his sons when he was one hundred and twenty years old, and Joseph when Joseph was seventeen. But Joseph was thirty years old when he appeared before Pharaoh; seven years of abundance and two years of famine followed, until his father came to him with his brothers. Joseph was therefore thirty-nine years old when Jacob entered Egypt.

At that time Jacob was one hundred and thirty years old, as he himself says to Pharaoh. Yet Jacob was one hundred and twenty when Joseph was seventeen. This cannot possibly be true. For if Jacob was one hundred and twenty in Joseph’s seventeenth year, then in Joseph’s thirty-ninth year Jacob would necessarily have been not one hundred and thirty but one hundred and forty-two years old.

But if Joseph was not yet seventeen on the day of Isaac’s death, and reached the age of seventeen some time after his grandfather’s death—in that year, as Scripture testifies, he was sold into Egypt by his brothers—then his father should have been more than one hundred and forty-two years old when he followed his son into Egypt.

After Scripture had related the final year of Isaac’s life, one hundred and eighty, and his death and burial, it then recounted how Esau had departed from his brother in the land of Canaan for Mount Seir, and it continued with the account of the kings and chiefs of the nation that Esau established or propagated.

After this, it introduced the account of Joseph by saying: “Jacob dwelt in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing sheep with his brothers.”

Then the reason for his dreams is related: how he became hateful to his brothers and was sold. Either, therefore, he came into Egypt in that same seventeenth year, or even somewhat older; and in either case the question remains.

For if he was seventeen after his grandfather’s death, when his father was one hundred and twenty, then in Joseph’s thirty-ninth year, when Jacob came into Egypt, Jacob should have been one hundred and forty-two years old. But Jacob was then one hundred and thirty. Therefore, if Joseph was sold into Egypt at seventeen, he was sold twelve years before his grandfather’s death.

He could not have been seventeen except twelve years before Isaac’s death, when Jacob, his father, was one hundred and eight. If we add to these the twenty-two years that Joseph spent in Egypt before his father’s arrival, Joseph’s age becomes thirty-nine and Jacob’s one hundred and thirty; and there is no problem.

But because Scripture related these events after Isaac’s death, it is thought that Joseph was seventeen after the death of that same grandfather. Therefore, let us understand that, when Scripture was speaking of Jacob and his sons, it passed over in silence the life of Isaac, as though he were a very old man; yet Joseph began to be seventeen while Isaac was still alive.

He was with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives, and he reported to his father an exceedingly grave accusation against his brothers. Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he had begotten him in his old age. And he made him a many-colored tunic.

Joseph, one of the twelve sons of Jacob, whom his father loved more than the other sons, prefigured Christ the Lord, whom God the Father, born according to the flesh, placed above the other brothers descended from Abraham.

**(Isidore.)** Hence it is also said there: “Jacob loved him because he had begotten him in his old age.” As the world grew old, the Son of God, shining forth through the birth of the Virgin Mary, came late, as the son of old age according to the mystery of the body he assumed, though he had always existed beforehand with the Father.

“He made him,” it says, “a many-colored tunic,” that is, a variegated one. In place of “many-colored tunic,” Aquila translated *ἀστραγάλειον* tunic, that is, a long tunic. Symmachus has “a tunic with sleeves,” either because it descended to the ankles and was marked with marvelous variety by the craftsman’s hands, or because it had sleeves. For the ancients used short tunics more often.

The many-colored tunic that his father made for him signified, according to allegory, the diversity of peoples gathered from all nations into the body of Christ.

Again, in another way: Joseph, who is described as having remained righteous among his eleven brothers until the end, is said alone to have had a long tunic. What, then, is the long tunic except a completed action? For just as a tunic extending downward covers the body to the ankle, so a good action protects us before the eyes of God to the end of life.

Hence Moses commands that the tail of the sacrificial animal be offered on the altar, so that whatever good we begin may also be completed with a persevering end.

When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his sons, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him. The brothers of Christ according to his fleshly birth were the Jews, from whose lineage the humanity of the Redeemer himself was assumed.

But because they saw that a greater grace of virtues was being manifested in him, bearing witness to the Father’s exceptional love, they envied him and could not speak to him with a peaceful mind. They repeatedly attacked him with plots and blasphemously claimed that he cast out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.

It happened also that he reported a dream he had seen to his brothers, and this became the cause and seed of greater hatred. He said to them: “Hear the dream I saw. I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf, as though rising up, stood upright, while your sheaves surrounded it and worshiped my sheaf.”

His brothers answered him: “Will you be our king, or shall we be subject to your authority?” Thus the dreams and the words provided fuel for envy and hatred.

He saw another dream as well and, recounting it to his brothers, said: “I saw in a dream what seemed to be the sun, the moon, and eleven stars worshiping me.”

When he had related it to his father and brothers, his father rebuked him and said: “What does this dream that you saw mean? Shall I, your mother, and your brothers come and worship you upon the earth?”

Unless the statement is understood as referring to some mystery, how can it be understood of Joseph’s mother, who was already dead? Nor should we think that it was fulfilled in Egypt when he was exalted, since his father did not worship him when he came to him in Egypt, and his mother, who had long been dead, could not do so.

In the person of Christ, however, it can readily be understood even of the dead, according to what the Apostle says (Phil. II): “He bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.”

**(Isidore.)** The dream in which the sheaves of his brothers worshiped his sheaf is what was spiritually fulfilled in Christ: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI), offering the fruit of good works through faith.

He is the one whom the sun, the moon, and the stars worship. Of the sun it is said: “Praise him, sun and moon, and all stars” (Ps. CXLVIII). The excellence of the saints worships him under the name of the sun, the brightness of the Church under the image of the moon, and the multitude of all peoples under the figure of the stars.

Hence his father also rebuked him, saying:

“Shall I, your mother, and your brothers worship you?” This rebuke signifies the hardness of the people of Israel, who, although they recognize that Christ was born from them, refuse to worship him.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Concerning Jacob’s sending Joseph to his brothers where they were pasturing the sheep, and his being sold by them to the Midianites

When his brothers were staying at Shechem, pasturing their father’s flocks, Israel said to him: “Your brothers are pasturing the sheep at Shechem. Come, I shall send you to them.” When he answered, “I am ready,” he said: “Go and see whether all is well with your brothers and the flocks, and report to me what is happening,” etc.

Jacob sends his son Joseph to care for his brothers, and God the Father sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, weakened by sins. He was sent by that Father of whom it is written: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII). He was sent “to see whether the sheep were well,” and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV).

Joseph therefore found his brothers at Dothan. Dothan is interpreted as “defection.” Truly they were in great defection, since they were contemplating fratricide.

When they saw Joseph, their brother, from a distance, they planned to kill him. And the Jews, seeing the true Joseph, the Lord Jesus Christ, all formed one counsel to crucify him, saying: “Crucify him” (Matt. XXVII).

“A most wicked beast devoured him”—that is, the Jewish beast killed him; concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. X).

Immediately, therefore, when he reached his brothers, they stripped him of his long, variegated tunic and threw him into a cistern that had no water; then they sat down to eat bread. Joseph’s brothers stripped him of his variegated and long tunic; the Jews, through the death of the cross, stripped Christ of his bodily garment. The variegated tunic signifies one adorned with a diversity of all virtues. They then sprinkled the tunic with the blood of a kid, because by accusing with false testimonies the one who forgives the sins of all, they made him odious as a sinner. Then he is thrown into the cistern, that is, into a pit; and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell.

They saw Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels carrying spices, balm, and myrrh on their way to Egypt. (Augustine.) It is asked why Scripture calls the Ishmaelites, to whom Joseph was sold by his brothers, also Midianites, since Ishmael was the son of Abraham by Hagar, whereas the Midianites were descended from Keturah. Is it because Scripture had said of Abraham that he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines—namely, Hagar and Keturah—and separated them from his son Isaac toward the land of the East, so that they are to be understood as having become one nation?

Judah therefore said to his brothers: “What profit is it to us if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites, and that our hands not be defiled, for he is our brother and our flesh.” His brothers agreed with his words; and when the Midianite merchants passed by, they drew him out of the cistern and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They brought him into Egypt, and so forth. In place of “twenty pieces of silver,” which the Septuagint has rendered as “twenty gold pieces,” the Hebrew truth has “pieces of silver.” For the Lord ought not to have been sold for a cheaper metal than Joseph. He was lifted from the cistern and sold to the Ishmaelites—that is, to the nations; and Christ, after emerging from hell, is purchased by all nations through the commerce of faith. Joseph was sold through Judah’s counsel for twenty pieces of silver; Christ, through the counsel of Judas Iscariot, was sold for thirty pieces of silver.

They took his tunic and dipped it in the blood of the kid they had killed, sending men to carry it to their father and say: “We found this; see whether it is your son’s tunic or not.” When his father recognized it, he said: “It is my son’s tunic. A most savage beast has eaten him; a beast has devoured Joseph.” Having torn his garments, he put on sackcloth and mourned his son for a long time. (Isidore.) Jacob, lamenting the loss of his descendants, mourned as a father for a lost son; as a prophet, he wept over the destruction of the Jews. Hence he tore his garment, which we read was done by the high priest at the Lord’s Passion. The veil of the Temple also was torn, to show prophetically both that his people had been stripped bare and that the kingdom had been divided.

When all his children had gathered to lessen their father’s grief, he refused to accept consolation and said: “I shall go down to my son, mourning, into hell.” (Augustine.) There is often a major question concerning how “hell” is to be understood: whether only the wicked descend there, or whether the good dead also customarily descend. If only the wicked do so, how does this man say that he wishes to descend to his son in mourning? He does not believe that his son is in the punishments of hell. Or are these the words of a troubled and grieving man, exaggerating his misfortunes even further?

While he persisted in weeping, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and commander of the soldiers. In many places Scripture mentions archimagiri—that is, chief cooks—instead of commanders of the army. Joseph was therefore sold to the commander of the army of fighting men, not to Petephre, as it is written in Latin, but to Potiphar, the eunuch. Here the question is raised how he is later said to have had a wife. For the Hebrews relate that Joseph was purchased by this man, on account of his extraordinary beauty, for a shameful service; and that, after the Lord had dried up his male organs, he was later chosen, according to the custom of the hierophants, for the priesthood of Heliopolis. They say that Aseneth was this man’s daughter, whom Joseph later took as his wife.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT  
## Concerning Judah and his wife and sons, and also concerning his intercourse with Tamar, his daughter-in-law

### (CHAPTER XXXVIII)

At that time Judah, departing from his brothers, turned aside to a man of Adullam named Hirah. He saw there the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua; and, having taken her as his wife, he went in to her. She conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er. Again conceiving, she bore a son and named him Onan. She bore a third also, whom she called Shelah. After his birth she ceased bearing, and so forth. (Augustine.) It is asked when these events could have taken place. For if they occurred after Joseph came into Egypt, how could all this have happened within approximately twenty-two years—for after that much time, it is reckoned, they came to the same Joseph, their brother, in Egypt with their father—and how could Judah and all his sons have reached an age at which they could take wives? For Tamar, his daughter-in-law, after her firstborn husband had died, he gave to another son; when that son also had died, he waited for the third to grow up; and when he had grown up, he did not give her to him, fearing that he too might die. Thus it happened that she offered herself to her father-in-law. How, then, all these events could have occurred within so few years is rightly perplexing, unless perhaps Scripture, as it often does by recapitulation, intends us to understand that this began several years before Joseph was sold, since it is placed in such a way that it is said: “It came to pass at that time.” Yet it is asked how old Judah could have been when Joseph was seventeen years old and sold, given that Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, could at most have preceded his brother Joseph by five or six years. Scripture clearly says that Joseph was thirty years old when he became known to Pharaoh. If, then, he is believed to have been sold in the seventeenth year of his age, he had spent thirteen years in Egypt unknown to Pharaoh. Seven years of abundance were added to these, making twenty years. Two more are added, because Jacob entered Egypt with his sons in the second year of the famine; thus twenty-two years are found during which Joseph was absent from his father and brothers. During this interval, how could all that is related concerning Judah’s wife, sons, and daughter-in-law have happened? It is difficult to investigate, unless perhaps we believe—and this too could have happened—that as soon as Judah began to grow into manhood, he fell in love with the woman whom he married, before Joseph had been sold into Egypt.

When many days had passed, Judah’s wife died. After mourning and receiving consolation, he went up to the shearers of his sheep, he and Hirah the Adullamite, the shepherd of the flock, to Timnah. In place of “shepherd,” the Hebrew reads “friend”; but the word is ambiguous, because both names are written with the same letters. In fact, the friend is read *ree*, and the shepherd *roae*.

It was reported to Tamar that her father-in-law was going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. She removed the garments of her widowhood, took a veil, changed her clothing, and sat at the crossroads of the road leading to Timnah, because Shelah had grown up and she had not been given to him as a husband. This indicates that even in the time of the patriarchs widows had their own distinctive garments, and not the same garments as married women.

When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute. For she had covered her face so that she would not be recognized. Going in to her, he said: “Allow me to have intercourse with you.” For he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She replied: “What will you give me, so that you may enjoy my intercourse?” He said: “I will send you a kid from the flock.” Again she said: “I will consent to what you wish, if you give me a pledge until you send what you promise.” Judah said: “What do you want me to give you as a pledge?” She answered: “Your ring, your bracelet, and the staff that you hold in your hand.” Thus the woman conceived from a single intercourse, and she arose and departed. In Judah’s deed, the sincerity of justice is not evident, but the faithfulness of his promise is. For if he had preserved justice by preserving chastity, he would not have gone in, as he supposed, to a prostitute; nevertheless, he did not refuse to send the woman what he had promised, through his shepherd, in accordance with the faithfulness of his promise.

After three months, they reported to Judah: “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has committed fornication, and now her womb appears to be swelling.” Judah said: “Bring her out, so that she may be burned.” When she was being led out to punishment, she sent to her father-in-law, saying: “I conceived by the man to whom these things belong. Recognize whose ring, bracelet, and staff these are.” When he recognized the objects, he said: “She is more righteous than I am, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.” Yet he did not know her again thereafter. Judah acknowledged this and said: “She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.” The Hebrew has: “She has been justified by me”—not because she was righteous, but because, in comparison with him, she had done the lesser wrong: she was not wandering into disgrace but seeking children.

When the time of delivery came, twins appeared in her womb. During the actual birth one extended a hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it, saying: “This one will come out first.” But when he withdrew his hand, the other came out. The woman said: “Why has a breach been made for you?” For this reason she called his name Perez. Instead of “breach,” Aquila and Symmachus rendered “division,” which in Hebrew is called *Perez*. Because he divided the membrane of the afterbirth, he received the name “division.” Hence the Pharisees, who had separated themselves from the people as though they were righteous, were called “the divided.”

Afterward his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, and she called him Zerah. This name is interpreted as “rising” or “dawn.” Thus, either because he appeared first, or because many righteous men came from him, as is contained in the Book of Chronicles, he was called Zerah, that is, “rising.”

(Isidore.) Let us now consider what Judah’s deed signified, according to allegory, concerning future events. In Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, the Jewish people are understood, to whom kings from the tribe of Judah were owed as husbands. Her name is rightly interpreted as “bitterness,” for she gave the Lord a cup of gall. The two kinds of rulers who did not act rightly among the people were signified by Judah’s two sons: one who harmed them, and another who benefited them in nothing. One of them was wicked, or guilty, before God; the other spilled his seed upon the ground so as not to give seed for Tamar’s fruitfulness. There are no more than two kinds of useless men for the human race: one consisting of those who harm, and the other of those unwilling to do good—and who, if they possess anything good in this earthly life, lose it, as though spilling it upon the ground. Since the one who harms is worse than the one who does no good, the first is therefore called “the wicked,” and the second “the one who spilled upon the ground.”

The name of the elder, who is called Er, is interpreted as “leathery,” like the garments with which the first human beings were clothed in punishment for their condemnation when they were sent out of paradise. The name of the younger, who is called Onan, is interpreted as “their sorrow.” Whose sorrow, if not that of those who benefit no one, although they possess the means by which they could benefit others, and yet waste it upon the earth? The loss of life, signified by the skin, is a greater evil than the failure to help, signified by “their sorrow.” Yet God is said to have killed both of them, signifying that he took the kingdom away from men of this kind.

The third son of Judah, because he was not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which kings of the Jewish people ceased to come from the tribe of Judah. He was indeed Judah’s son, but Tamar did not take him as her husband, because it was still the same tribe of Judah, but no one in the Jewish people now reigned. Hence his name, Shelah, is interpreted as “his division.”

Holy and righteous men do not belong to this interpretation. Although they existed at that time, they belong to the New Testament; through prophecy they were knowingly useful, as David was. When Judea had already begun to have no kings from the tribe of Judah, Herod the Great is not to be counted among its kings as Tamar’s husband, for he was a foreigner. He was not joined to her by that sacrament of mystical anointing as by a marital covenant; rather, as an outsider, he ruled over her, having received that power from the Romans and Caesar. The same applies to his sons, the tetrarchs, one of whom was Herod, called by his father’s name, who agreed with Pilate in the Lord’s Passion.

These foreigners were so entirely not reckoned as belonging to that mystical kingdom of the Jews that the Jews themselves publicly cried out, gnashing their teeth against Christ: “We have no king but Caesar” (Matthew 27). This was not true except in the sense of that universal dominion. Caesar of the Romans was indeed a king, but not properly the king of the Jews; nevertheless, in order to deny Christ and continue worshiping this ruler, they condemned themselves by such an utterance.

At that time, when the kingdom from the tribe of Judah had already failed, Christ, the true Savior and our Lord, had to come—one who would not harm but would greatly benefit. For this had been prophesied: “The prince shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49). By this time, every form of Jewish authority had also failed, as had the mystical anointing by which they were called “christs,” that is, anointed ones, according to Daniel’s prophecy. Then he came for whom the expectation of the nations had been reserved, and the Holy of Holies was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Psalm 44).

He was born in the time of Herod the Great, but he suffered under Herod the lesser, the tetrarch. Judah himself therefore bore the figure of this one who was coming to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel, when he went to shear his sheep at Timnah, which is interpreted as “failing.” For the rulers from Judah had already failed, as had all Jewish authority and anointing, until he came for whom it had been reserved.

He came with his shepherd, the Adullamite named Hirah. “Adullamite” is interpreted as “testimony in water.” Plainly, the Lord came with this testimony, possessing testimony greater than John’s, yet he used this testimony in water on account of the weak sheep. For Hirah, the name of that shepherd, is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” John certainly saw his brother: his brother according to the seed of Abraham, according to the kinship of Mary, his mother, and Elizabeth, John’s mother; and he saw him as his own Lord and God, because, as John himself says, he received from his fullness (John 1). He truly saw him, and therefore no one born of women arose greater than he, because of all who foretold Christ, he saw him—something many righteous men and prophets desired to see but did not see (Matthew 13). He greeted him from the womb and recognized him more perfectly through the dove; and therefore, as an Adullamite, he truly bore testimony in water.

The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to relieve them of the burdens of sins—so that, in the Church’s praise in the Song of Songs, their teeth might be like a flock of shorn sheep (Song of Songs 4).

Then Tamar changes her clothing, for her name is also interpreted as “one who changes.” Tamar changes her clothing and changes her name, and from Synagogue becomes Church; yet the name of bitterness remains wholly in her—not the bitterness in which she gave the Lord gall, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. Judah in Latin means “confession.” Therefore bitterness must be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be prefigured.

Through this repentance the Church, established among all the nations, is made fruitful. For Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and repentance and forgiveness of sins had to be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. The prostitute’s clothing itself signifies the confession of sins. Tamar represents the Church called from the nations, sitting in this clothing at the gate of Ena, or Enahim, which is interpreted as “spring.” For she ran like a deer to reach the springs of water (Psalm 41), coming to the seed of Abraham. She conceived without his knowing her, because it was prophesied concerning him: “The people whom I did not know served me” (Psalm 17).

In secret she received the ring, necklace, and staff: calling is signified by the ring, justification is adorned by the necklace, and glorification is exalted by the staff. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8). But these things, as I have said, take place in secret, where the conception of holy fruitfulness also occurs.

The promised kid is sent to her as though to a prostitute: the kid signifies the reproach of sin, sent through the same Adullamite, as though he were rebuking and saying: “Brood of vipers” (Matthew 3). Yet the reproach of sin did not find her, because she had been changed by the bitterness of confession.

Afterward, through the public tokens of the ring, necklace, and staff, she overcame the rash Judaizing Jews, whose role Judah himself was then representing—those who say today that this people is not Christ’s and that we do not possess the seed of Abraham. But when the most certain proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification are brought forth, they will undoubtedly blush and be confounded, and will confess that we have been justified more than they have. For the Church declares that she has the pledges with her.

She is accused by the Jews as though she were an adulteress against the Law; but she displays the staff, the sign of the Passion; the necklace, the lawful ordinances of the Law; and the ring, the pledge of immortality.

When Scripture presents Tamar suffering and bearing twins in her womb, the first of whom, called Zerah, extended his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it, but then, when he withdrew his hand inward, the later child, called Perez, extended his hand and came out first, this fittingly signifies that Israel extended its hand toward the works of the Law, but withdrew it stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself. Afterward the people of the nations burst forth, so that those who were last would be first, and those who were first would be last.

# BOOK FOUR

## [Column 0629]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### Concerning Joseph’s descent into Egypt and the lust of his mistress, who wished to sleep with him

### [Column 0629C]

### (CHAPTER XXXIX)

Joseph, therefore, was brought into Egypt. Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and commander of the army, an Egyptian man, bought him from the hands of the Ishmaelites by whom he had been brought there. Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch, took possession of him. (Augustine.) Scripture returns to the point from which it had digressed, so that it might relate what was arranged above. Thus Joseph descended into Egypt, and Christ into the world. A eunuch bought him—that is, a people chaste in evangelical disciplines.

The Lord was with him, and he was a man who prospered in all things. He lived in the house of his master, who knew very well that the Lord was with him and that everything he did was directed by him. Joseph found favor in the sight of his master and ministered to him. The master set him over everything, and he governed the house entrusted to him and all that had been committed to him. The Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house because of Joseph and multiplied all his possessions, both in the buildings and in the fields; and he knew nothing else except the bread which he ate.

(Gregory.) Often some people, puffed up with human wisdom, observe that divine judgments oppose their desires. They try to resist them by crafty schemes; and, seeking to bend the force of heavenly providence toward their own wishes, they persist in ingenious plans and search out subtler counsels. Yet they carry out God’s will precisely from the point at which they strive to alter it. While attempting to resist the counsel of almighty God, they serve it, because what human effort foolishly throws against him often works suitably for his design, as it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (Job 5).

He catches the wise in their craftiness when human actions, even while resisting his counsels, serve them appropriately. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Psalm 93).

We can demonstrate this more clearly if we bring forward a few examples from the events themselves. Joseph had seen a dream in which the sheaves of his brothers bowed down before his sheaf. He had seen another dream in which the sun and moon, together with the other stars, worshiped him. Because he piously reported these dreams to his brothers, their hearts were immediately struck by envy and fear of his future domination.

When they saw him coming toward them, turning to wickedness they said: “Here comes the dreamer. Come, let us kill him, and let us see what his dreams will profit him.” Fearing that they would be subjected to his rule, they put the dreamer into a pit and sold him to passing Ishmaelites.

Brought into Egypt, subjected to slavery, condemned on an accusation of lust, helped because of his charity, rescued through the judgment of prophecy, and placed over all Egypt, he prudently gathered grain through heavenly wisdom and forestalled the danger of future need. When famine raged throughout the world, he was concerned with preparing food and sent Jacob’s sons to Egypt. They found Joseph, whom they did not recognize, placed in charge of the distribution of grain; and, in order to deserve to receive food, they were compelled to worship its distributor with their necks bowed to the ground.

Let us therefore consider the order of what happened; let us consider how divine power catches human thoughts in the very midst of their planning. Joseph had been sold by them so that he would not be worshiped; but he was worshiped precisely because he had been sold. They dared to act cleverly so that God’s plan might be changed, but by resisting they served the divine judgment from which they had tried to escape. They were compelled to carry out God’s will precisely where they had cunningly plotted to alter it.

Thus the divine plan is fulfilled while it is avoided, and human wisdom is caught while it resists. The brothers feared that Joseph would rise above them, but by taking precautions against what had been divinely ordained, they brought it about that he came. Human wisdom was therefore caught in itself: in the very point at which it resisted God’s will by intention, it served its fulfillment.

For the just and merciful God, arranging the actions of mortals, graciously grants some things and permits others in anger; and he tolerates what he permits in such a way that he turns it to the use of his plan. Thus, in a wondrous manner, what is done without God’s will is not contrary to God’s will, because, when evil deeds are turned to a good use, even what resists his plan serves his plan.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 111). His works are great in this way: through everything human beings do, his will is sought. For often it is accomplished precisely where it is thought to be thwarted.

Again he says: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 135). Solomon says: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against God” (Proverbs 21).

It remains, therefore, that in everything we do we should seek the force of the heavenly will. Once it is known, our action ought devotedly to serve it and follow it as the guide of its journey, lest, even unwillingly, it serve that will while proudly rejecting it. The force of heavenly counsel cannot be avoided; but the one who restrains himself beneath its commands tempers it for himself with great strength, and lightens its burdens for himself by willingly carrying them upon the shoulder of a submissive heart.

Joseph was handsome in face and pleasing in appearance.

After many days, his mistress cast her eyes upon Joseph and said: “Sleep with me.” He did not consent to the wicked deed but said to her: “Behold, my master, having entrusted everything to me, does not know what he has in his house. There is nothing that is not in my power or that he has not handed over to me, except you, who are his wife. How, then, can I do this great evil and sin against my God?” With words of this kind the woman harassed the young man day after day, but he refused the adultery.

(Gregory.) Whoever, raised up by the successes of this world, feels himself tempted by the goadings of lust while the joy of his heart flatters him, should recall Joseph’s deed and preserve himself in the citadel of chastity. When he saw his mistress urging him to lose his purity, he said:

“Behold, my master, having entrusted everything to me, does not know what he has in his house. There is nothing that is not in my power or that he has not handed over to me, except you, who are his wife. How, then, can I do this great evil and sin against my God?”

These words show that he suddenly brought to mind the good things he had acquired, overcame the evil that was assaulting him, and, because he remembered the grace he had received, broke the force of the approaching sin. When slippery pleasure tempts a person amid prosperity, prosperity itself must be set against the sting of temptation, so that we may be ashamed to commit wrong precisely because we remember that we have received gratuitous goods from God. We should turn the grace of external gifts into weapons of virtue, keeping before our eyes what we have received and subduing what entices us.

Because pleasure itself arises from prosperity, consideration of that same prosperity must be brought to bear, so that our enemy may die from the very source from which he arises.

It happened one day that Joseph entered the house and was doing some work without witnesses. She seized the edge of his garment and said: “Sleep with me.” But he left the cloak in her hand, fled, and went outside.

When the adulterous woman wished to misuse Joseph, he left his cloak and fled outside. So when the Synagogue, believing the Lord to be merely a man, wished to bind him in an adulterous embrace, he left the covering of its letter before its eyes, stripped himself of it, and presented himself visibly to the nations so that they might recognize the power of his divinity. Hence Paul says: “To this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts” (2 Corinthians 3).

That adulterous woman retained the cloak for herself and lost naked the one whom she had held wrongly. Therefore he who, coming from the Synagogue, appeared conspicuous to the faith of the nations, according to the saying of blessed Job, came forth naked from his mother’s womb.

When the woman saw the garment in her hands and realized that she had been scorned, she called the men of her household and said to them: “See, he has brought in a Hebrew man to mock us. He came in to me to sleep with me. When I cried out and he heard my voice, he left the cloak that I was holding and fled outside.”

As evidence of her accusation, she showed the retained cloak to her husband when he returned home and said: “The Hebrew servant whom you brought to us came in to me to mock me. When he saw me cry out, he left his cloak and fled outside.”

When he heard this, her master, excessively credulous toward his wife’s words, became very angry. He handed Joseph over to prison, where the king’s prisoners were kept, and so forth.

Joseph was handsome in face and pleasing in appearance. So David also says concerning Christ: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips” (Psalm 44).

(Isidore.) “But the woman,” he says, “cast her eyes upon him so that she might commit adultery with him.” This woman was a figure of the Synagogue, as we said above, which often, as it is written, committed adultery after foreign gods. In the same way she wished to retain Christ in the crime of her adultery, so that he would deny that he was God and observe the precepts of the Pharisees and scribes rather than those of the Law, which were like her husband.

But Christ, not consenting to the adultery of illicit teaching, had the garment of his body seized by the hand of the adulterous Synagogue. He stripped off his flesh and, free from death, ascended into heaven. When the prostitute could not hold him, she slandered him, saying that he blasphemed the Temple of the Lord and was said to be a transgressor of the Law. But neither prison frightened him nor the underworld held him; and even when he descended there as though to be punished, he freed others from that place.

# CHAPTER TWO  
### Concerning Pharaoh’s two eunuchs who sinned, and whose dreams Joseph interpreted while he was in prison

### (CHAPTER XL)

After these events it happened that two eunuchs offended their master, Pharaoh, the king of Egypt: the royal cupbearer and the baker. Pharaoh became angry with them—for one was in charge of the cupbearers and the other of the bakers—and sent them to the prison of the commander of the soldiers, where Joseph was also confined.

The keeper of the prison handed them over to Joseph, and he ministered to them. In Hebrew the text has *maske*, the word that we previously read in the name of Abraham’s servant, whom we may call, in ordinary speech, a cupbearer. This office should not be considered lowly, since among barbarian kings even to the present day it is a position of the highest dignity to offer the king his cup. Poets also write of Ganymede and Jupiter that he assigned his beloved to this office.

The chief cupbearer first related his dream: “I saw before me a vine in which there were three branches. It gradually grew into buds, and after the flowers, the grapes ripened. Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. I therefore took the grapes, pressed them into the cup that I was holding, and handed the cup to Pharaoh.”

“And behold,” he said, “there was a vine before me, and on the vine there were three shoots, and it itself was putting forth three shoots.” The Hebrew term signifies three shoots and three branches, or tendrils; they are called *sarigim* by the Hebrews.

When the chief of the bakers saw that he had interpreted the dream intelligently, he said: “I too saw a dream: I had three baskets of flour upon my head; and in the uppermost basket I was carrying all the foods made by the baker’s craft, and birds were eating from it.”

(Augustine.) Where the Latin books have “three baskets of flour,” the Greeks have *chondriton* (χόνδριτον), which those who use that language interpret as loaves of coarse or household bread. But the question arises how Pharaoh could have had household bread among his foods. For he says that in the upper basket there was everything from which Pharaoh ate, made by the work of bakers. It must be understood that this basket itself also contained household bread, because the text had said “three baskets,” *chondriton*, and that, on top of it, there were items of every kind made by the baker’s craft in that upper basket.

After this, the third day was Pharaoh’s birthday. He held a great feast for his servants and, during the meal, remembered the chief of the cupbearers and the chief of the bakers. He restored one to his office, so that he might offer the king his cup; but he hanged the other on a gallows, so that the truth of the interpreter might be proved.

(Isidore.) The two eunuchs whom Joseph found bound in prison after they had been taken from the king’s household mystically represent two peoples, believers and unbelievers. They are called eunuchs because they received a chaste rule of discipline. “The words of the Lord are chaste” (Psalm 12).

Accordingly, after the third light, when the Lord had risen from the dead, and when the obscurities of the Law had been revealed as Joseph revealed the dreams, the people of believers were released from sins and, freed from the prison of hell, restored to the service of the divine Law.

But the unbelieving and impious Jewish people, because it did not believe in the tree of salvation, was hanged upon the tree of transgression. This is what happened to the other eunuch, who represented the image of the Jews.

# CHAPTER THREE  
### Concerning Pharaoh’s dream and Joseph’s interpretation

### (CHAPTER XLI)

After two years Pharaoh saw a dream. He thought that he was standing beside the river, and from it there came up seven cows, beautiful and exceedingly fat, feeding in marshy places. Another seven emerged from the river, ugly and wasted with thinness, and fed on the riverbank itself in green places. They devoured the others, whose appearance and bodily condition had been remarkable.

Pharaoh awoke, slept again, and saw another dream. Seven ears of grain were sprouting on a single stalk, full and beautiful. Another seven ears, thin and scorched by blight, were springing up and devouring all the beauty of the first ones.

After waking from his sleep, when morning came, he was terrified with fear. He sent for the Egyptian diviners and all the wise men, summoned them, and told them the dream; but there was no one who could interpret it.

(Augustine.) Pharaoh thought that he was standing beside the river, just as Abraham’s servant said: “Behold, I am standing beside the spring of water” (Genesis 24). If this expression is understood in the Psalm where it is written, “He founded the earth upon the waters” (Psalm 23), people are not forced to imagine that the earth floated upon the water like a ship. According to this expression, it is rightly understood that the earth is higher than the water. It is raised higher than the waters in the places where terrestrial animals live.

Furthermore, Pharaoh relates his dream, and Joseph interprets it.

(Isidore.) But what do the seven years shown in the seven full ears of grain, or in the seven fat cows, signify except the seven gifts of spiritual charisms, through which the abundance of faith overflows with generous devotion? By contrast, the barren and thin ears signify the frequent famines of truth and justice in the last times.

# CHAPTER FOUR  
### Concerning Joseph’s appointment by Pharaoh as ruler of Egypt
Pharaoh said again to Joseph: “See, I have appointed you over the whole land of Egypt.” And he took the ring from his hand and put it on Joseph’s hand; he clothed him in a linen garment and placed a golden chain around his neck. He made him mount his second chariot, with the herald proclaiming that all should bend the knee before him and should know that he had been appointed over the whole land of Egypt. In place of this, Aquila translated: “And he cried out before him, ‘For genuflection.’” Symmachus, interpreting the Hebrew expression itself, said: “And he cried out to him, *abrech*.” Hence it seems to me that what should be understood is not so much “herald” or “genuflection,” which may be taken as referring to the salutation or worship offered to Joseph, as what the Hebrews report when they say that “tender father” is translated by this expression. For *ab* means “father,” and *rech* means “delicate” or “most tender.” Scripture thus indicates that, in wisdom, he was indeed the father of all, but in age he was a very tender young man and child.

(Isid.) Behold Joseph, who had assumed the type of Christ, was deemed worthy of a chariot; a herald went before him, and Pharaoh appointed him over the whole land of Egypt. Likewise, after our Lord had been sold by Judah, as Joseph was by his brothers, and had risen from the prison of the underworld, he mounted the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is written: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold” (Psalm 67). He received from the Father authority to preach, as the apostle Paul says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians 2). He also received the ring—that is, the high priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are marked with the sign of salvation; and the figure of the eternal King is impressed upon our foreheads and hearts through the sign of the cross. He is clothed in a linen garment—that is, in holy flesh whiter than linen, and in the garment of immortality. He also received a golden chain—that is, good understanding. A herald goes before him: either John the Baptist, who, going before him, proclaimed: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matthew 3), or he will have another herald, the angel’s trumpet, for he himself said: “He will come with the trumpet of an angel.”

The king also said to Joseph: “I am Pharaoh. Without your authority no one shall move hand or foot throughout the whole land of Egypt.” And he changed his name and called him in the Egyptian language “Savior of the world.” What could be clearer concerning Christ, when under the figure of Joseph the Savior is shown to be not merely the savior of one land, Egypt, but of the whole world?

(Hieron.) Although this name sounds in Hebrew as “discoverer of hidden things,” nevertheless, since it is given in Egyptian, it ought to be explained according to that language. For in the Egyptian tongue *saphanath phaanecha*, or, as the Septuagint wished to translate it, Ψονθομφανήχ (*Psonthomphanech*), is interpreted as “Savior of the world,” because he had delivered the world from the impending destruction of famine.

He also gave him as wife Aseneth, the daughter of Potiphar, priest of Heliopolis. It should be noted that he received as wife the daughter of his former master and purchaser, who at that time was high priest of Heliopolis. For it was not lawful for the priests of that idol to be anything but eunuchs, thereby confirming the true Hebrew suspicion concerning him that we mentioned earlier. Thus Christ received a wife from the Gentiles—that is, the Church—from whom he begot two sons, that is, two peoples gathered from the Jews and from the Gentiles.

He was thirty years old when he stood in the presence of Pharaoh the king. “Joseph,” it says, “was thirty years old when he stood in the presence of Pharaoh the king”; and Christ is likewise read to have been of that age when, under the type of Pharaoh, he appeared revealed in the sight of the world.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Joseph’s gathering wheat into granaries during the time of abundance, to alleviate the famine of the future.

Joseph went through all the regions of Egypt. Seven years of abundance came, and the crops were gathered into sheaves and stored in the granaries of Egypt. Every abundance of grain was also stored in the individual cities. So great was the quantity of wheat that it equaled the sand of the sea, and its abundance exceeded all measure.

(Aug.) “And Joseph gathered wheat, like the sand of the sea, very much, until it could not be counted, for there was no number.” It is said, “there was no number,” because that abundance exceeded every customary designation of number, and no name could be found for it. For how could it be that a number did not exist for any multitude, however great but finite? Nevertheless, this could also have been said by hyperbole.

Joseph gathered all the abundance of grain for seven years—that is, storing the grain of the saints’ faith in his granaries through the seven spiritual gifts, as though through seven years. Thus, when the seven years of scarcity began—that is, when the iniquity of the seven capital sins under the Antichrist arrives, when there is a famine of faith and salvation—the saints and the faithful together may possess an abundant harvest of righteousness, so that their faith may not fail, weakened by the scarcity of the word.

Joseph’s two sons were born before the famine arrived; Aseneth, the daughter of Potiphar, priest of Heliopolis, bore them to him. He called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, saying: “God has made me forget all my labors and my father’s household.” He called the second Ephraim, saying: “God has made me grow in the land of my poverty.” Observe the question that will shortly be raised concerning Joseph: before the time of famine, when Jacob entered Egypt, he had only two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. He called Manasseh by a name derived from his having forgotten his labors—for this is how “forgetfulness” is expressed in Hebrew—and Ephraim because God had increased him, since from this word “increase” is transferred into our language.

After the seven years of abundance that had occurred in Egypt had passed, the seven years of scarcity that Joseph had foretold began to come, and famine prevailed throughout the whole world. There was famine throughout the entire land of Egypt. When it was suffering hunger, the people cried out to Pharaoh, asking for food. He answered them: “Go to Joseph, and whatever he tells you, do.” The famine increased daily throughout the whole land. Joseph opened all the granaries and sold grain to the Egyptians, for famine had also oppressed them. All the provinces came to Egypt to buy food and lessen the evil of scarcity.

Joseph saved Egypt from the shortage of grain, and Christ delivers the world from hunger for the word of God. For Christ opened his granaries throughout the whole world, and by distributing his grain he subjected all things. If Joseph’s brothers had not sold him, Egypt would have perished; if the Jews had not crucified Christ, the world would have perished. Joseph, therefore, is interpreted as “increase” or “enlargement.” But in that Joseph, enlargement came only to Egypt; in our Joseph, the whole world was deemed worthy to receive increase. The former distributed wheat; our Joseph distributed the word of God. “Their sound has gone out through all the earth” (Psalm 18).

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Jacob’s sending his sons into Egypt during the famine to buy wheat; after recognizing them, Joseph called them spies, yet sent them home with grain and their money.

[Column 0637C] (CHAPTER 42.) When Jacob heard that food was being sold in Egypt, he said to his sons: “Why are you neglecting this? I have heard that wheat is being sold in Egypt. Go down and buy what we need, so that we may live and not be consumed by scarcity.”

Jacob said to his sons: “There is grain in Egypt.” God and the Father says: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Hosea 11). Accordingly, the ten older sons descend—that is, the Jews, as though established under the Decalogue of the Law and its number. Although he recognized them, they did not recognize him. The Hebrews are recognized by Christ, but they themselves do not recognize him.

Joseph’s ten brothers therefore went down to Egypt to buy grain, while Benjamin was kept at home by Jacob, who had said to his brothers: “Lest he suffer any harm on the journey.” They entered the land of Egypt with the others who were going to buy grain. There was famine in the land of Canaan, and Joseph was governor of Egypt; at his command grain was sold to the peoples. When his brothers had bowed before him and he had recognized them, he spoke harshly to them as though they were strangers, asking: “Where have you come from?” They answered: “From the land of Canaan, to buy the necessities of food.” Yet although he himself recognized his brothers, he was not recognized by them.

Remembering the dreams that he had once seen, he said: “You are spies. You have come to see the weaker parts of the land.”

(Aug.) When Joseph remembered his dreams, which he himself had seen—for his brothers had bowed before him—something more exalted must be sought in those dreams. For they cannot be fulfilled in the same way concerning his father and mother, who were already dead, as regards the sun and moon; yet when he had seen them, he had heard his father, who was still living, rebuke him.
