Joseph’s brothers bow before him, and the whole assembly of the saints worships Christ and honors him with divine worship. The perfection of the saints is signified under the name of the sun, while the beauty of the Church is expressed by the likeness of the moon. Thus all in the Church, both older and younger, both perfect and still less perfect, rejoice to worship Christ the Lord, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 71).

They said: “It is not so, my lord, but your servants have come to buy food. We are all sons of one man. We have come peaceably, and your servants are not plotting any evil.”

He answered them: “It is otherwise. You have come to examine the weaker parts of this land.”

They said: “We, your servants, are ten brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father; another no longer exists.”

He said: “This is what I said: You are spies. Now I shall test you. By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not leave this place until your youngest brother comes,” and so forth.

What does it mean that Joseph, a man so wise and praised not only among human beings but also by Scripture itself as a witness, swears by the life of Pharaoh that his brothers will not leave Egypt unless their younger brother comes? Or was Pharaoh’s safety of little value even to a good and faithful man, to whom Joseph preserved faith in all things as to his original master? How much more would he preserve it for the one who had placed him in such great honor, if he preserved it for the one who possessed him as a purchased slave? But if he did not care about Pharaoh’s safety, should he not nevertheless have avoided perjury for the sake of any man’s safety? Or is it not perjury? For he held one of them until Benjamin came, and what he had said came true: “You shall not leave this place until your brother comes.” What was said could indeed have applied to all of them. For how could Benjamin have come unless some of them had returned to bring him?

But what follows presses the question more forcefully, where he again swore, saying:

“Send one of yourselves and bring your brother, but you shall remain bound until your words become clear, whether you are telling the truth or not. Otherwise, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies.” That is: if you are not telling the truth, you are spies. He inserted an oath into this sentence because, if they had not spoken the truth, they would be spies and therefore worthy of the punishment of spies. Yet he knew that they were speaking the truth. For no one is perjured if he says to someone whom he knows to be entirely chaste: “If you committed this adultery of which you are accused, God condemns you,” and adds an oath to these words; he is swearing entirely truthfully. The condition lies in the words “if you did it,” although he is certain that the person did not do it.

But someone may say: “It is true that if he committed adultery, God condemns him.” Yet how is this true—“If you are not telling the truth, you are spies”—when, even if they are lying, they are not spies? The point is that this is what he meant by saying: “You are spies,” as though he had said: “You are worthy of the punishment of spies; you are judged and treated as spies because of your lie.” The use of “are” for “are considered” or “will be judged” is taught by countless similar expressions. Thus Elijah says: “Whoever answers by fire, he shall be God” (1 Kings 18). He will not then become God, but will then be regarded as God.

They said to one another: “We rightly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother. We saw the anguish of his soul when he begged us, and we did not listen. Therefore this tribulation has come upon us.”

One of them, Reuben, answered: “Did I not tell you: ‘Do not sin against the boy,’ and you did not listen to me? Behold, his blood is being required.”

They did not know that Joseph understood, because he was speaking to them through an interpreter.

What is the meaning of the fact that, while the sons of Israel were repenting within themselves and speaking about their brother Joseph—saying that they had treated him badly and that this was being repaid to them by divine judgment, since they saw themselves in danger—the Scripture adds and says: “They themselves did not know that Joseph was listening, for there was an interpreter between them”? This must be understood as meaning that they thought he could not hear because they saw an interpreter between them who was not reporting to him any of the things they were saying. They thought that no other reason existed for the interpreter’s presence than that Joseph did not know their language; nor did they suppose that the interpreter was concerned to tell him what they were saying among themselves rather than addressing him.

He returned and spoke to them. He took Simeon and bound him in their presence, and ordered his servants to fill their sacks with grain and to put each man’s money back in his sack, adding provisions for the journey. They did so. Carrying the grain on their donkeys, they departed.

What does it signify that Joseph’s brothers gave money in exchange for grain, but after receiving the grain they had bought, received their own money back, except that our Joseph does not seek what belongs to us, but seeks us? He gives his gifts freely and made us richer through our purchase, because Christ is not bought with money but with grace.

They came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan and told him everything that had happened to them, saying: “The lord of the land spoke harshly to us and thought that we were spies in the province,” and so forth.

It is asked why Joseph, a very gentle and holy man, wished to treat his brothers in this way by delaying his revelation, when he could quickly have helped them by making his identity known. He did not do this for the sake of vengeance, to repay the evil that had been done to him, but to test their disposition, so that he might discover whether they would persecute their maternal brother with the same impulse with which they had sold him into foreign lands.

Father Jacob said: “You have deprived me of my children. Joseph no longer exists, Simeon is held in chains, and now you will take Benjamin? All these evils have fallen upon me.”

Reuben answered him: “Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Place him in my hand, and I will restore him to you.”

But he said: “My son shall not go down with you. His brother is dead, and he alone remains. If some misfortune happens to him in the land to which you are going, you will bring my gray hairs down to the underworld in sorrow.”

It is asked whether he says this because he will go down to the underworld in sorrow, or whether he would have descended there in dying even if sorrow were absent. The question of the underworld is a great one, and what Scripture thinks about it must be carefully observed wherever it may happen to be mentioned.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Joseph’s brothers’ second journey into Egypt, together with Benjamin, and their testing.

(CHAPTER 43.) Israel their father said to them: “If it must be so, do what you wish. Take some of the best produce of the land in your vessels and carry gifts to the man: a little resin, honey, storax, stacte, terebinth resin, and almonds. Take double the money with you, and carry back the money that you found in your sacks, lest it happened by mistake. Take your brother also and go to the man. May my almighty God make him favorable to you, and may he send back with you your brother whom he holds in chains, and this Benjamin also. As for me, I shall be like one bereaved, without children.”

“Carry gifts to the man,” he says: “some resin and honey, incense and stacte, terebinth resin and nuts”—or, as Aquila and Symmachus translated it, “almonds.” We have included this passage so that we may know that where our manuscripts have “incense,” the Hebrew has *nechotha*, which Aquila translated as *storax*. Hence the “house of *nechotha*” read in Isaiah is most clearly understood as a storehouse of incense or storax, because various spices were stored there.

They approached the doors and spoke to the steward: “We beg you, lord, to listen to us. We came down previously to buy food. After we had bought it and reached the lodging place, we opened our sacks and found the money in the mouths of our sacks. We have now brought it back with the same weight. But we have brought other silver as well, to buy what we need. We do not know who put the former money in our bags.”

He answered: “Peace be with you; do not be afraid. Your God, and the God of your fathers, gave you treasures in your sacks. As for the money that you gave me, I have it tested and accounted for.”

What they hear from the head of the household—“Your God, and the God of your fathers, gave you treasures in your sacks; but I have your silver, tested”—appears to be a lie, but it must be believed to signify something. The silver that is both given and not diminished, and that is called genuine, clearly signifies what we read elsewhere: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11), that is, perfectly purified.

Joseph then entered his house. They presented gifts to him, holding them in their hands, and bowed prostrate on the ground. He kindly greeted them in return and asked: “Is your old father well, of whom you told me? Is he still alive?”

They answered: “Your servant our father is safe; he is still alive.” And they bowed and worshiped him.

Joseph lifted his eyes and saw Benjamin, his maternal brother, and said: “Is this your youngest brother, of whom you told me?” And again he said: “May God have mercy on you, my son.”

He hurried away, because his emotions had been stirred over his brother and his tears were breaking forth. He entered a private room and wept.

A good disposition is always inclined toward compassion. Thus we can observe in Joseph an abundance of virtues. He was chaste when he rejected his mistress’s immorality; wise when, through careful investigation, he tested the disposition of his brothers to determine how they felt toward their maternal brother; just when he applied discipline to those who had sinned; and pious when he received the penitent.

After washing his face again, he went out, restrained himself, and said: “Set out the bread.” When it had been served, Joseph sat separately, the brothers separately, and the Egyptians who were eating with them separately. For it is unlawful for Egyptians to eat with Hebrews, and they consider such a meal profane. Accordingly, Joseph’s food was set separately, as though he were a foreigner; the brothers’ separately, as though they were foreigners by nationality; and the Egyptians’ likewise separately, as though they were natives who thought it profane to dine with foreigners.

They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his age, and they were exceedingly astonished when they received their portions from him. Benjamin’s portion was greater, exceeding the others by five parts. They drank and became merry with him.

Joseph commanded the steward of his house: “Fill their sacks with as much grain as they can hold, and put each man’s money at the top of his sack. Put my silver cup, and the price that he gave for the wheat, into the mouth of the youngest man’s sack.”

It was done. When morning came, they were sent away with their donkeys.

From this passage drunkards often seek support for their case—not on account of those sons of Israel, but on account of Joseph, who is commended as exceptionally wise. Yet anyone who pays close attention will find that this expression is also often used in Scripture for satiety. Thus we read: “You visited the earth and intoxicated it; you multiplied it and enriched it” (Psalm 64), where the expression is used in praise of blessing and refers to God’s gift. It is evident that this intoxication signifies fullness. For to be intoxicated in the way drunkards are intoxicated is useful neither to the earth, which is corrupted by more moisture than is sufficient for its saturation, nor to the life of drunkards, who do not fill themselves with satiety but are submerged in a flood.

(CHAPTER 44.) Then Joseph summoned the steward of his house and said: “Rise, pursue the men, and when you have caught them say: ‘Why have you repaid good with evil? The cup that you stole is the very one from which my lord drinks and in which he practices divination. You have done a very wicked thing,’” and so forth.

(Isid.) In the mystical sense, Joseph’s seeing his little brother signifies that the Lord Jesus saw Paul when light shone around him (Acts 9). He is called “little” because he did not yet possess the mature age of faith in the flesh. Hence he is also read to have been a young man when he guarded the garments of those who stoned Stephen (Acts 7). Joseph wept, and Paul’s blindness (Acts 7) is Christ’s weeping. He washes his face in order to restore to Paul the light he had lost. Christ washes his face when Paul is baptized, through whom the Lord Jesus would be seen by many.

Then the silver cup is placed in the sack of the youngest alone. What does it mean that Joseph’s cup was found in Benjamin’s sack, except that in Paul’s body the eloquence of heavenly teaching already shone forth, since he had been learned in the Law? But because he was not yet subject to it, the cup was inside the sack: doctrine within the Law, a lamp beneath a bushel. Nevertheless, Ananias was sent (Acts 9) and laid his hands upon Paul; he loosened the purse, and when the purse was loosened, the silver shone forth. As the scales fell away, like certain bonds of the sack, and the sack was opened—that is, the veil of the Law was removed—Paul obtained the grace of freedom, and with the face of the word unveiled, he preached the Gospel.

Joseph’s brothers, having been apprehended, returned to the town. Judah entered first with his brothers to Joseph, for Joseph had not yet left the place, and they all fell together before him upon the ground.

He said to them: “Why did you wish to act in this way? Do you not know that no one is like me in the art of divination?”

(Aug.) It is often asked what this means. Since it was not said seriously but in jest, as the outcome showed, it should not be considered a lie. Lies are seriously uttered by liars, not in jest. When things that are not true are said as a joke, they are not counted as lies.

But Joseph’s action is more troubling: he repeatedly mocked his brothers until he revealed who he was, and held them in such suspense. Although something is often the more pleasant to read the more unexpected it is to those involved, nevertheless, given the gravity of his wisdom, he would neither have done this nor would Scripture have preserved it—with its great authority of holiness and such profound intention of prophesying future events—unless something important were signified by this apparent game.

It seems to me that we should not carelessly consider how Joseph held his brothers in such great misery and confusion for as long as he wished, prolonging the delay as much as he wished. He was not truly making them wretched, since he was already contemplating the outcome of their future joy. Everything he did to delay their happiness he did in order that the same delay might increase it, as though their sufferings throughout the time of their distress were not worthy to be compared with the future glory of exultation that would be revealed in them once they recognized the brother whom they thought they had lost.

Judah said to him: “What shall we answer my lord, or what shall we say, or how can we justly defend ourselves? God has found the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are all my lord’s servants, both we and the one in whose possession the cup was found,” and so forth.

Many things in Judah’s account are stated differently from the way Joseph had dealt with them, although he was speaking before Joseph. In particular, nothing is said about the accusation that they were spies. Whether this was intentionally omitted or resulted from the confusion of the moment is not clear. Likewise, they said that Joseph himself had questioned them about their father and brother and that they had given him the information in response. It is surprising whether this account can even be made to agree with the facts so as to be regarded as truthful. Yet if it contains some falsehoods, they could have arisen through forgetfulness rather than through a willingness to lie before him—especially before one who, unlike someone ignorant of the facts, knew even the things they were recounting, and who inserted them into their account in order to move his compassion.

## CHAPTER VIII. Where Joseph recognizes his brothers and sends them back to their father to bring him and his whole household to Egypt.

(CHAPTER 45.) Joseph said: “I am your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Do not be afraid, and do not let it seem harsh to you that you sold me into these regions, for God sent me before you for your preservation. It is now two years since the famine began in the land, and five years still remain in which there will be neither plowing nor harvesting. God sent me ahead so that you might be preserved upon the earth and might have food for your survival. I was sent here not by your plan but by the will of God, who made me like a father to Pharaoh, lord of his entire household, and ruler throughout all the land of Egypt.”

What does Joseph mean when he says: “God sent me ahead so that you might be preserved upon the earth and might have food for your survival”? In certain other copies it is read: “For God sent me before you so that your remnants might remain upon the earth and so that your remnant might be nourished.” This is strange, for it does not entirely fit for us to understand Jacob and his sons as “remnants” or “a remnant,” since they are all unharmed.

Or perhaps it signifies, through a deep and hidden mystery, what the Apostle says: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans 9), because the prophet had foretold: “And if the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved” (Isaiah 10; Hosea 1). For this reason Christ was killed by the Jews and handed over to the Gentiles, as Joseph was handed over to the Egyptians by his brothers, so that the remnant of Israel might also be saved. Hence the Apostle says: “For I too am an Israelite,” and “so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved” (Romans 11)—that is, from the remnant of Israel according to the flesh and from the fullness of the Gentiles who, according to the spirit, are Israel through faith in Christ.

Or, if the Israelite people still awaited the fullness of faith from which the remnant came—the remnant in which the apostles were then also saved—this signifies that fullness of Israel’s deliverance by which they were freed from Egypt through Moses.

The report was heard and spread through the royal court: “Joseph’s brothers have come.” Pharaoh and his entire household rejoiced. He said to Joseph that he should command his brothers: “Load your beasts, go to the land of Canaan, take from there your father and your kindred, and come to me. I will give you all the good things of Egypt, so that you may eat the marrow of the land. Command them also to take wagons from the land of Egypt for transporting their little ones and their wives. Say: ‘Take your father and hurry, coming as quickly as possible. Do not leave anything of your possessions behind, because all the wealth of Egypt shall be yours.’”

These words that Pharaoh spoke concerning Jacob and his sons signify the joy of the Gentile people at the conversion of the Jews. Without doubt, the devotion of the Church of the Gentiles is great, because the Israelite people will come to faith in Christ. If they are converted and become participants in Christ’s faith, he promises them the spiritual riches of virtues and the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that no one who receives it perfectly will suffer want of goodness.

The sons of Israel did as they had been commanded. Joseph gave them wagons according to Pharaoh’s order and provisions for the journey. He ordered that two garments be brought for each man. To Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five excellent garments. He sent the same amount of money and clothing to his father, adding ten male donkeys to carry all the riches of Egypt and ten female donkeys carrying grain for the journey and loaves of bread.

(Isid.) Three hundred pieces of silver and five excellent garments were given to Benjamin. Whoever preaches the Trinity or the cross of Christ receives three hundred pieces of silver from Christ. Hence Paul says: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2).

He receives five garments—that is, the manifold disciplines of all wisdom and of all the senses. Paul therefore surpasses them, and his portion of merits abounds beyond theirs. Nevertheless, the brothers—that is, the other preachers—also have their own grace: two garments, namely, that they confess Christ to be both God and man, according to what Proverbs says: “All his household are clothed with double garments” (Proverbs, final chapter), that is, with mystical and moral understanding.

Gifts are also sent to the father. The Son honors the Father; Christ invites his people to promised gifts. Those donkeys carry these gifts: the Gentiles, once useless and laboring, now useful, carry gifts in the type of Christ. In the Gospel they carry the giver of gifts.

Joseph sent his brothers away and said to them as they departed: “Do not quarrel on the way.” They went up from Egypt, came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, and announced to him: “Joseph is alive, and he rules over the whole land of Egypt,” and so forth.

Joseph sent his brothers away, and they announced to their father: “Joseph is alive, and he is lord over the whole land of Egypt.”

Jacob was terrified—that is, the unbelieving people. But after it learns of Christ’s deeds, its spirit will revive, and the one who seemed dead will be given life by faith in Christ’s resurrection. He is therefore summoned by his sons—that is, by Peter, Paul, and John—and the Jewish people are invited to grace. Judah, whose name is interpreted as “confession,” meets him, because confession now goes before those whom unbelief formerly possessed. Thus the true Joseph, Christ, meets him. He receives the aged people of the latter times—the Jewish people—not according to their merits but according to the election of his grace. He places his hand over their eyes and removes their blindness. Yet he delayed removing their blindness so that the one who previously could not believe might be the last to believe.

Hence the Apostle says: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Romans 11).

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Jacob’s descent into Egypt.

(CHAPTER 46.) Jacob rose from the Well of the Oath. His sons carried him, together with their little ones and wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to transport the old man, and they carried all that he possessed in the land of Canaan. He came into Egypt with all his offspring: his sons and grandsons, his daughters, and his entire progeny together.

It should be noted that when Jacob’s daughters and his entire progeny are here read to have entered Egypt together with Jacob, the plural “daughters” is not used because Jacob had more than one daughter named Dinah. Rather, the plural number is used for the singular, just as the singular is sometimes used for the plural.

All the souls who entered Egypt with Jacob and who came forth from his loins, apart from the wives of his sons, numbered sixty-six.

When Scripture says that Leah bore so many souls, or that so many souls came forth from Jacob’s loins, we must consider what answer should be given to those who try to confirm by this testimony that souls are propagated from parents together with bodies. No one doubts that “souls” is used for human beings, with the part signifying the whole.

But how can we separate the very part by which the whole is recalled—that is, the soul, by whose name the entire human being is signified—from the statement “They came forth from his loins,” so that we understand only flesh to have been born from him, although only souls are named? The forms of expression used throughout Scripture must be investigated.

The sons of Joseph who were born to him in the land of Egypt were two persons. All the persons of the house of Jacob who entered Egypt numbered seventy-five. There is no doubt that, apart from Joseph and his sons, the sixty-six persons who came forth from Jacob’s loins entered Egypt. For the number found in the Hebrew books is confirmed by counting them one by one in this way. But where we read in the Septuagint, “The sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were nine persons,” we should know that the Hebrew has “two” instead of “nine.” Ephraim and Manasseh were born in Egypt to Aseneth, the daughter of Pothipherah, before Jacob entered Egypt and before the time of famine began [Col. 0645D]. But also the passage we read above—“The sons of Manasseh whom his Syrian concubine bore to him were Machir; and Machir begot Gilead. The sons of Ephraim, the brother of Manasseh, were Suthalaam and Ethaam. The sons of Suthalaam were Edem”—has been added. For what we read later is described as having occurred beforehand. At the time when Jacob entered Egypt, Ephraim and Manasseh were not of an age to have been able to beget sons. Thus it is clear that all the persons who entered Egypt from Jacob’s loins numbered seventy: sixty-six entered afterward and found in Egypt three persons—namely, Joseph [Col. 0646A] and his two sons—and Jacob himself was the seventieth.

To prevent us from appearing to speak against the authority of Scripture, the Septuagint translators also rendered in Deuteronomy that Israel entered Egypt with seventy persons. Therefore, if anyone opposes our interpretation, he will make Scripture contradict itself. For the same Septuagint translators who here said that seventy-five persons, including Joseph and his descendants, entered Egypt by anticipation, stated in Deuteronomy that only seventy entered. If, on the other hand, this is opposed by the passage in Acts of the Apostles where Stephen, in his speech, is said to have told the people that seventy-five persons entered Egypt (chapter 7), the answer is easy. Saint Luke, who was the actual author of the history, ought not, when sending his book among the Gentiles, to write in Acts of the Apostles anything contrary to the Scripture that had already been circulated among the Gentiles. At that time, the authority of the Septuagint translators was certainly held in greater esteem than that of Luke, who was regarded among the nations as unknown, insignificant, and not very trustworthy. We should generally observe that whenever the holy Apostles or apostolic men speak to the peoples, they usually make use of testimonies that had already been circulated among the Gentiles, although many maintain that Luke the evangelist, as a proselyte, did not know Hebrew letters.

He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to inform him and to meet him in Goshen. When he had arrived there, Joseph harnessed his chariot and went up to meet his father at the same place. When he saw him, he fell upon his neck and wept in his embrace. The father said to Joseph: “Now I shall die happily, because I have seen your face and leave you alive.”

He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph so that he might meet him at the city of Heroum, in the land of Rameses. According to the edition of the Septuagint translators, this passage is read in this way. The Hebrew has neither “the city of Heroum” nor “the land of Rameses,” but only “Goshen.” Some Jews assert that Goshen is now called the Thebaid. They also maintain that the passage which follows—“He gave them the best land in Egypt, in Rameses, as a possession”—refers to the district once called Arsinoites.

He spoke to his brothers and to his whole paternal household: “I will go up and announce to Pharaoh, and I will say to him: ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. They are shepherds, men who care for flocks, and they have brought with them their sheep, cattle, and everything they were able to possess.’”

(Aug.) The patriarchs are commended for having been from childhood keepers of livestock, both for their parents and deservedly in themselves. For this is unquestionably just servitude and just dominion: livestock serve human beings, and human beings rule over livestock. Thus it was said when humanity was created: “Let us make man in our image and likeness; and let him have power over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and all the animals that are upon the earth” (Genesis 1). This indicates that reason ought to rule irrational life.

Human servitude to human beings, however, was brought about either by iniquity or by adversity. By iniquity, as it is said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Genesis 9). By adversity, as happened to Joseph himself, so that, after being sold by his brothers, he became the servant of a foreigner. Thus wars made the first servants, to whom this name was given in the Latin language. A man who, having been defeated by another in war, could rightfully have been killed was called a servant because he had been spared. Hence also the term *mancipia*, as though they had been taken by hand.

There is also a natural order among human beings, whereby women serve men and children their parents, because here too there is justice: the weaker reason serves the stronger. This, then, is the clear justice underlying dominion and servitude: those who excel in reason should excel in dominion. When this order is disturbed in the present world by human iniquity or by the differences belonging to bodily nature, the just endure temporal perversity, destined at the end to possess perfectly ordered and everlasting happiness [Col. 0647A].

“When he summons you and says, ‘What is your occupation?’ you shall answer: ‘We are shepherds, your servants from our childhood until now, both we and our fathers.’ You shall say this so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, because all shepherds of sheep are detestable to the Egyptians. For every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians.”

With good reason every shepherd of livestock is an abomination to the Egyptians, in whom there is a figure of the present age, in which iniquity abounds. For a righteous man is an abomination to the unrighteous [Col. 0647C].

Jacob and his sons came into Egypt to Joseph. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, heard this and said to Joseph: “Your father and your brothers have come to you. Behold, the land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best land.”

This repetition does not concern an omitted matter to which the narrative often returns by recapitulation; rather, it is entirely explicit. Scripture had already said how Joseph’s brothers came before Pharaoh and what he said to them and heard from them. But now it has repeated the matter as though from the beginning, in order to continue the narrative from the words that Pharaoh spoke only to Joseph. In all the Greek manuscripts written by more careful scribes, some passages bear obeli, indicating those things that are not found in the Hebrew but are found in the Septuagint. Some bear asterisks, indicating those things that the Hebrews have but the Septuagint does not [Col. 0647D].

## CHAPTER X. How Joseph placed his father Jacob before Pharaoh, who, through Joseph, gave him the best land of Goshen

**(Chapter 47.)** After this Joseph brought his father before the king and set him in his presence. Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and Pharaoh asked him: “How many are the days of the years of your life?” Jacob replied: “The days of the years of my life that I inhabit”—for this is what the Greeks have, whereas the Latins have “I spend,” or “I possess,” or something similar—“are one hundred and thirty years. They are few and evil, and they have not reached the days of the years of my fathers in which they dwelt.”

What did Jacob mean when he said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my life which I inhabit” (for this is what the Greek has), whereas the Latin books have “I spend,” “I possess,” or something else? Did he say “which I inhabit” because he was born in a land that the people had not yet received as an inheritance through the divine promise, and, living there, was therefore in a foreign land—not only when he was wandering, as in Mesopotamia, but also when he was in the land where he had been born? Or should it rather be understood according to what the Apostle says: “As long as we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5)?

According to this, the statement in the psalm is also understood: “I am a sojourner in the land and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Psalm 119). For again, speaking of those same days of his life, he says: “They did not reach the days of the years of my fathers, which they inhabited.” Here he intended nothing other than what the Latin books have, namely, “which they lived”; and therefore he indicated that this life is a sojourning upon the earth, that is, a dwelling in pilgrimage. But I believe that this applies to the saints, to whom the Lord promises another, eternal homeland.

Accordingly, we must consider how it is said of the wicked: “They will inhabit and hide; they themselves will watch my heel” (Psalm 55). This is more appropriately understood of those who inhabit in order to hide—that is, to lie in wait for their children—and do not remain in the house forever [Col. 0648B].

Joseph gave his father and his brothers a possession in Egypt, in the best soil of the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded; and he fed them and his entire paternal household, providing food for each one.

It must be asked whether the land of Rameses itself was Goshen. They had requested Goshen, and Pharaoh had commanded that it be given to them (ibid.). Joseph gave his parents and brothers the best land of Goshen and provided them with food, because famine had oppressed the land.

So also the Lord, choosing the best land for his parents—that is, for the patriarchs and prophets, from whom Christ descends according to the flesh—or for all the saints, of whom he says in the Gospel, “These are my brothers, who do the will of my Father” (Luke 8)—gives them the land of promise, namely, the kingdom of God, concerning which the Prophet says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26).

(Aug.) “Joseph measured out grain for his father,” and yet his father neither worshiped him when he saw him nor when he received grain from him. How, then, shall we think that Joseph’s dream was fulfilled at this point, and not rather that it contained a prophecy of something greater? [Col. 0648D]

For there was no bread throughout the whole world, and famine had oppressed the land, especially Egypt and Canaan. From these regions he gathered all the money in exchange for grain and deposited it in the king’s treasury. Scripture has taken the opportunity here also to commend the faithfulness of God’s servant.

When the purchasers’ money had run out, all Egypt came to Joseph, saying: “Give us bread. Why should we die before you, since our money has failed?” He answered them: “Bring your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for them, if you have no money.” When they had brought them, he gave them food in exchange for their horses, sheep, oxen, and asses, and sustained them that year in exchange for their livestock.

They came also in the second year and said to him: “We will not conceal from our lord that, since our money has failed, our livestock has also failed. You are not unaware that, apart from our bodies and our land, we have nothing. Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? We and our land shall belong to you. Buy us into royal servitude, and provide seed, lest, when the cultivator perishes, the land be reduced to desolation.”

It may be asked: Since Joseph had gathered the grain by which human beings lived, on what did the livestock live, when such a great famine was increasing? This is especially puzzling because Joseph’s brothers had said to Pharaoh: “There are no pastures for the livestock of your servants’ children; for famine has grown severe in the land of Canaan,” and they had mentioned that they had come because of this lack of pasture. Therefore, if pasture had failed in the land of Canaan because of that famine, why had it not failed in Egypt, since the same famine was then intensifying everywhere?

Or, as those who know the places report, could pasture have remained available in the many marshes of Egypt even during a famine of grain, grain being what ordinarily comes from the inundation of the Nile? Indeed, those marshes are said to produce pasture more abundantly when the water of the Nile rises less [Col. 0649B].

## CHAPTER XI. How Joseph acquired the whole land of Egypt as Pharaoh’s possession

Joseph therefore bought all the land of Egypt, as each person sold his possessions because of the severity of the famine [Col. 0649C]. He subjected it to Pharaoh, together with all its peoples, from the remotest borders of Egypt to its farthest limits, except the land of the priests, which had been granted to them by the king. They were also supplied with fixed provisions from the public storehouses, and for this reason they were not compelled to sell their possessions, and so forth.

In the fact that Joseph bought all the land of Egypt, subjected it to Pharaoh, and subjected all its peoples to him, he cannot be accused of injustice or iniquity—especially since his fidelity is thereby commended. He showed favor to no individual, but, according to the purchaser’s price, fairly balanced the royal provision against the needs of the needy.

Mystically, however, this signifies that all who are in spiritual Egypt and pursue the riches of Egypt are slaves. There is now no free Egyptian. The carnal person is sold under sin. Pharaoh subjects such people to himself; and perhaps for this reason it is said elsewhere: “I am the Lord your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery” (Exodus 13; Deuteronomy 5, 6, 7).

Therefore the Apostle commands the faithful, saying: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Romans 6). And again: “Do you not know,” he says, “that to whomever you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?” (ibid.)

It is written that the Hebrews were forcibly reduced to servitude. Pharaoh, however, easily reduced the Egyptian people to slavery. For they sold themselves. The steward is therefore not at fault when what is deserved is distributed according to merit [Col. 0650A]. Paul did the same when he handed over to Satan the man who was unworthy of the fellowship of the saints (1 Corinthians 5). Let no one therefore say that Paul acted harshly when he expelled a man from the Church, so that, once expelled, he might learn not to blaspheme.

A person’s will is wicked when, loving earthly things, he abandons heavenly things and, because of greed, subjects himself to the devil. But the Lord’s judgment is just when he abandons to his own choice the one who, scorning better things, has chosen worse, so that he may fall and be overthrown by the desires of the weak.

As for the statement that the priests were not compelled to sell their possessions because fixed provisions were supplied to them from the public storehouses, this signifies that the land of the Church, whose true priests they are, is free from worldly approach, because it is continually nourished by the word of God and will suffer no loss from spiritual famine [Col. 0650B].

In another sense, Joseph’s purchase, by which he bought the land of Egypt with grain, signifies that Christ redeems the whole world by his teaching and by the price of his blood.

And when it says:

“Take seed and sow the fields, so that you may have crops. You shall give the king one-fifth; I leave the remaining four parts to you for seed, for food for your households and for your children,”

it commands the taking of seed—that is, the word of God—and the sowing of fields, namely, one’s own bodies, which, plowed by the evangelical plow and sown with spiritual seed, produce the fruits of virtues.

By the fifth part given to kings, the tribute of the five senses, which must be paid to Christ the true King, is signified. The remaining four parts are permitted to the possessors for seed and food, because the use of the active life is granted to each person, so that he may sow works of virtue and reap the fruit of righteousness unto eternal life. This is truly bestowed upon us by our Savior.

Therefore the Egyptians say to Joseph: “Our salvation is in your hand,” because it is evident that the salvation of the world has been placed in Christ’s power [Col. 0650C].

## CHAPTER XII. How Jacob bound Joseph by an oath concerning his burial

Israel therefore dwelt in Egypt, that is, in the land of Goshen, and possessed it. He increased and multiplied exceedingly, and lived there seventeen years. All the days of his life were one hundred and forty-seven years [Col. 0650D].

When he saw that the day of his death was approaching, he called his son Joseph and said to him: “If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand beneath my thigh and show me mercy and truth: do not bury me in Egypt, but let me sleep with my fathers. Carry me away from this land and bury me in the burial place of my ancestors.”

As he was about to die, Jacob said to his son Joseph: “If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand beneath my thigh and show me mercy and truth.” By this oath he binds his son as Abraham bound his servant: Abraham charged his servant with finding a wife for his son; Jacob commends the burial of his own body.

In both cases, however, those two things are named which are of great importance and weight throughout the Scriptures wherever they are found scattered: mercy and justice, or mercy and judgment, or mercy and truth. For in one place it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24). These two qualities are therefore greatly commended and must be greatly considered.

Abraham’s servant had said: “You will show mercy and justice to my lord.” So Jacob says to his son: “So that you may show me mercy and truth.”

But what does it mean that so great a man was so concerned to commend his body, asking that he not be buried in Egypt but in the land of Canaan beside his fathers? It seems strange and almost absurd, and not consistent with the excellence of a prophetic mind, if we judge it by human custom. But if mysteries are sought in all these things, the one who discovers them will find a joy worthy of greater wonder [Col. 0651B].

It is beyond doubt that the corpses of the dead signify sins in the Law, since people are commanded, after contracting them or any kind of contact with them, to be purified as from uncleanness. Hence the statement: “Whoever is baptized because of the dead and again touches him, what benefit does his washing provide? So also the one who fasts over his sins and afterward goes out and commits the same things” (Ecclesiasticus 34).

The burial of the dead therefore signifies the remission of sins, corresponding to the statement: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31). Where, then, were the symbolic corpses of the patriarchs to be buried except in that land where the one was crucified through whose blood the remission of sins was accomplished? The deaths of the patriarchs prefigured the sins of human beings.

They say that from the place called Abraham’s, where these bodies lie, the place where the Lord was crucified is nearly thirty miles away. Thus even the number itself may be understood to signify the one who appeared in baptism at about thirty years of age.

And if anything else concerning so great a matter can be understood either in this way or in a more exalted manner, we should nevertheless not think that such great men of God took such care for the burial of their bodies without reason. For the security of the faithful is—and ought to be—that wherever their bodies are buried, or even if, through the rage of enemies, they are left unburied or, at their enemies’ will, torn apart and consumed, their resurrection will for that reason be neither less complete nor less glorious [Col. 0651D].

Joseph answered him: “I will do what you have commanded.” He said: “Then swear.” When he had sworn, Israel worshiped God, turning toward the head of the bed.

This holy and God-devoted man, weighed down by old age, had his bed placed in such a way that his posture while lying down was readily prepared for prayer.

(Aug.) Some Latin books have: “And he worshiped upon the *suver* of his staff” [OCR reading uncertain; evidently *super*, “above/upon”]. Others, more correctly, have: “He worshiped upon the head of his staff,” that is, at the head or tip, or above the tip. The Greek word deceives them: it is written with the same letters whether it means “his” or “his own,” but the accents differ, and those who understand such matters do not disregard them in manuscripts [Col. 0652A]. They are important for a significant distinction, although the word meaning “his own” could also have one additional letter if it were not αὐτοῦ (*autou*, “his”) but ἑαυτοῦ (*heautou*, “his own”).

Accordingly, it is rightly asked what the statement means. It is easy to understand that the old man, who carried a staff in the manner in which people of that age customarily carry a walking stick, bent himself toward the Lord in worship and did so over the tip of his own staff, which he held in such a way that, bending his head over it, he worshiped God.

What, then, does “he worshiped upon the tip of his [Joseph’s] staff” mean? Or was the staff Joseph’s, that is, his son’s? Or perhaps Joseph had taken the staff from him when the son swore the oath; and while Jacob was holding it, after the words of the oath had been spoken and before it had been returned, he immediately worshiped God? It was not shameful for him to carry for a short time the emblem of his son’s authority, since a great event to come was prefigured there [Col. 0652B].

## CHAPTER XIII. How Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons

**(Chapter 48.)** When these things had been completed, Joseph was informed that his father was ill. He took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and proceeded to him. Someone said to the old man: “Behold, your son Joseph is coming to you.” Strengthened, he sat upon the bed. When Joseph had entered, Jacob said: “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz, in the land of Canaan, and blessed me. He said: ‘I will increase and multiply you, and I will make you into assemblies of peoples.’”

Here also Jacob recalls the promises of God made to him. He says that God told him: “I will make you into congregations of nations.” By these words he signifies more the calling of the faithful than the propagation of carnal descent [Col. 0652C].

“Your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came here to you shall be mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be counted as Reuben and Simeon. But the children whom you beget after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the names of their brothers in their inheritances.”

If anyone doubted that seventy persons of the sons of Israel entered Egypt, and that Joseph at the time Jacob entered had not nine sons but only two, the present chapter confirms it. Jacob himself says that Joseph had two sons, not nine.

When he says, “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine like Reuben and Simeon,” he means: just as Reuben and Simeon will be two tribes and will be called by their own names, so Ephraim and Manasseh will be two tribes, will produce two peoples, and will inherit the land of promise just as my sons do.

But the other children, he says, whom you beget after my death—thereby showing that they had not yet been born at that time—will be yours, and in their inheritance they will be called by the name of their brothers. “They shall not,” he says, “receive land separately, nor shall they have their own allotments, as the other tribes do; rather, they will be mingled among the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh as additions to the people” [Col. 0652D].

“When I was coming from Mesopotamia, Rachel died in the land of Canaan, on the very journey. It was springtime, and I was entering Ephrathah; I buried her beside the road to Ephrathah, which is also called Bethlehem.”

Why did Jacob wish to tell his son Joseph, as though Joseph did not know, where and when he had buried his mother, when Joseph himself had been present with his brothers? Even if he had been so young that he could neither take care of nor retain the matter in his mind, what compelled Jacob to mention it now, unless perhaps it was relevant to recall that Joseph’s mother had been buried where Christ was to be born? [Col. 0653A]

When he saw his sons, he said to Joseph: “Who are these?” He answered: “They are my sons, whom God has given me in this place.” Jacob said: “Bring them to me, so that I may bless them.” Israel’s eyes were dim with extreme old age, and he could not see clearly. Joseph brought them near him; Jacob kissed and embraced them and said to his son: “I was not deprived of seeing your face; indeed, God has shown me your offspring.”

When Joseph had taken them from his father’s lap, he bowed with his face to the ground and placed Ephraim at his right hand—that is, at Israel’s left—and Manasseh at his left, that is, at his father’s right. He brought both of them close to him. Israel stretched out his right hand and placed it upon the head of Ephraim, the younger brother, and his left hand upon the head of Manasseh, who was the elder, crossing his hands. He blessed Joseph’s son, and so forth.

(Aug.) Israel blessed his grandsons in such a way that he placed his right hand upon the younger and his left upon the elder. When his son Joseph wished to correct him as though he were mistaken and did not understand, Israel answered:

“I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people, and he shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations” [Col. 0653C].

This must be understood of Christ insofar as the statement made concerning Jacob himself and his brother also applies: “The elder shall serve the younger.” By doing this prophetically, Israel signified something: the later people that would come through Christ, by spiritual rebirth, would surpass the earlier people, who boasted in the carnal generation of their fathers.

(Isid.) The elder son of Joseph, Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” represents the Jews, who forgot their God, who made them. The younger represents Christians; his name conveys fruitfulness, which is proper to the younger people, who are the body of Christ and have been made fruitful throughout the breadth of the world.

When Jacob wished to bless them, Joseph placed Ephraim on the left and Manasseh on the right. But Jacob, crossing his hands and prefiguring the mystery of the cross, transferred his right hand to the younger and placed his left upon the elder. Thus the likeness of the cross marked upon their heads prefigured scandal for the Jews and future glory for Christians. Through the mystery of the cross, the elder was made left-handed from the right, and the younger right-handed from the left, because, while the Jews were falling into our deserts, we obtained their grace. By this sacramental sign, the younger people of the nations was placed before the elder people of the Jews. Hence the same patriarch says: “He too shall become a people, but he shall be exalted” [Col. 0653D].

## CHAPTER XIV. Jacob’s prophecy in which he foretold the return of the sons of Israel

He said to his son Joseph: “Behold, I am dying, and God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow.”

Here he calls the bow and sword justice, by which he, a pilgrim and stranger, deserved to be delivered from danger after the killing of Shechem and Hamor. For, as we read above, he feared that the neighboring towns and fortified places would rise against him because of the destruction of the allied city; but the Lord did not allow them to harm him.

Or it may certainly be understood in this way: “I will give you Shechem, which I bought through my strength,” that is, with my money, which I acquired through much labor and sweat. When he says “beyond your brothers,” he indicates that he gave it to the tribe of Joseph without casting lots. Joseph was indeed buried in that same place, and his mausoleum can still be seen there.

In another edition it is read as follows: “I have given you Shechem as a distinguished portion beyond your brothers, more than to your brothers, which I took from the hands of the Amorites with my sword and my arrow.”

According to Greek and Latin usage, *Sichima* is declined; in Hebrew it is called *Shechem*, as the evangelist John also testifies (John 4), although an error has become established whereby it is incorrectly read as *Sychar*. It is now Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans.

Since *Shechem* in Hebrew is translated as “shoulder,” Jacob made an elegant allusion to the name when he said: “I will give you one shoulder” [Col. 0654C].

Nevertheless, it may reasonably be asked how this can agree with the literal sense. Jacob bought that possession for one hundred lambs; he did not acquire it by the right of military victory. Or was it because his sons conquered the city of Salem belonging to the Shechemites, so that it could become his by the right of war, since the war against those who had first inflicted such an outrage by violating his daughter might be regarded as just?

Why, then, did he not give that land to the men who had perpetrated this deed—that is, to his elder sons? Furthermore, if he was now boasting of that victory and giving the land to his son Joseph, why had he been displeased with the sons who committed the deed? And why, when he blessed them even now, did he recall it reproachfully among their deeds?

Clearly, then, a prophetic mystery lies concealed here. Joseph also prefigured Christ in a special way, and that land is given to him where Jacob had destroyed and buried foreign gods. Thus Christ is understood to be destined to possess the nations that renounce the gods of their fathers and believe in him [Col. 0654D].

When these things had been completed, Jacob called his sons to bless them. Speaking in a mystical order, as one truly aware of future events, he told them what would happen in the last times. Yet these words must also be understood historically, in relation to the division of the land of promise and how it would be divided among their descendants; and allegorically they must certainly be understood in a true sense as a prophecy of Christ and the Church. But first the foundations of the history must be laid, so that the summit of allegory may be more suitably placed upon the earlier structure [Col. 0655A].

“Gather together and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.”

(Orig.) Perhaps you ask why those who gather together are called “sons of Jacob,” whereas the one who blesses them is called “Israel.” See whether this may perhaps signify that they had not yet advanced so far as to equal Israel in merit, and therefore are called sons of Jacob as inferiors, while the one who was already perfect and, conscious of future blessings, bestowed them, is called Israel.

## CHAPTER XV. The blessings of the twelve patriarchs with which their father Jacob blessed them

**(Chapter 49.)** “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my grief; foremost in gifts, greater in authority. You have poured yourself out like water; you shall not excel, because you climbed into your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

The meaning is this: “You are my firstborn, greater in children, and according to the order of your birth and the inheritance rightfully due to the firstborn, you ought to receive the priesthood and kingship.” This is shown by the bearing of burdens and by mighty strength.

But because you sinned, you poured yourself out in the impulse of desire like water that cannot be held in a vessel. Therefore I command you not to sin again, but to remain among your brothers, paying the penalty of your sin because you lost the rank of the firstborn.

(Ambr.) The firstborn is the beginning of every grief, because the parents’ innermost feelings are first stirred on his behalf [Col. 0655B].

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of warring iniquity. Let my soul not enter their counsel, and let my glory not be in their assembly, because in their fury they killed a man, and in their will they undermined a wall.”

This signifies that the killing of Shechem and Hamor, allied men, was not done according to Jacob’s counsel, and that they shed innocent blood contrary to the law of peace and friendship. Carried away by a kind of fury and cruelty, they demolished the walls of a foreign city. Hence it follows:

“Cursed be their fury, because it was insolent; and their anger, because it was harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

Levi did not receive a separate inheritance, but throughout all the tribes he had only a few cities in which to dwell. Concerning Simeon, it is written in the book of Joshua that he too did not obtain a separate allotment, but received something from the tribe of Judah. In Chronicles it is written more explicitly that, when he had multiplied and had no place of possession, he went out into the wilderness.

Some interpret the Septuagint reading—“In their fury they killed men, and in their desire they hamstrung a bull”—prophetically: the men killed were the apostles, and the bull hamstrung was Christ [Col. 0655D].

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies. The sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub. You have gone up to the prey, my son—or, as it is written in the Hebrew, ‘You have gone up from captivity, my son.’ You have lain down and rested like a lion, and like a lioness. Who will rouse him?”

Because Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is rightly written: “Judah, your brothers shall confess to you,” or “shall praise you.” Although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, according to the literal sense it signifies that kings are generated from David’s line and that all the tribes worship him. For he does not say, “the sons of your mother,” but “the sons of your father.”

The statement that follows—“You have gone up to the prey, my son”—shows that he would lead the people into captivity; and according to the more sacred understanding, that he ascended on high and led captivity captive. Or, as I think better, captivity signifies the passion, while ascent signifies the resurrection [Col. 0656A].

“Tying his colt to the vine, and his she-ass to the vine.”

This evidently signifies that he would join the colt of the she-ass upon which Jesus sat—that is, the people of the Gentiles—to the vine of the apostles who are from the Jews. To the vine, or, as the Hebrew has, to the *soreq*, that is, the choice vine, he would bind the she-ass upon which he sat, the Church gathered from the nations.

When he says “my son,” he addresses Judah directly, indicating that Christ would accomplish all these things. The statement that follows is:

“The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

This signifies that rulers would not fail from the tribe of Judah until the time when Christ was born. Sent by the Father, he is the expectation of the nations.

Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, and at the anchorage of ships, extending as far as Sidon. Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent; he bent his shoulder to bear burdens and became subject to tribute. Since above he had said of Zebulun that it would possess the shores of the Great Sea and would reach Sidon and the other Phoenician cities, he now returns to the inland province, and by his blessing makes Issachar, who is to possess the most beautiful region of Galilee beside Naphtali, its inhabitant. He calls him a bony or strong ass, and says that he has a shoulder suited for carrying, because he labored greatly in working the land and transporting to the sea the things that grew within his borders, also carrying tribute to kings. The Hebrews say that this signifies metaphorically that, meditating on the Holy Scriptures day and night, he devoted himself to labor; and therefore all the tribes serve him, as though carrying gifts to their teacher.

Dan shall judge his people, as will each of the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s heels, so that its rider may fall backward. I shall await your salvation, O Lord. Samson, the judge of Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. Thus he says that, now seeing in the spirit Samson the Nazirite growing his hair and triumphing after slaughtering his enemies, he will allow no one to pass through the land of Israel, like a serpent or a basilisk blocking the roads; and even if some rash man, trusting in his own strength as though in the speed of a horse, should wish to ravage it like a bandit, he will not escape. He speaks throughout by the metaphor of the serpent and the horseman. But when I saw your Nazirite so strong—who himself also died because of a prostitute and, in dying, killed our enemies—I thought, O God, that he was your Christ, your Son. Yet because he died and did not rise again, and Israel was once more led into captivity, another Savior of the world and of my race must be awaited, so that the one to whom it has been reserved may come: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.”

Gad, girded, shall wage war before him, and he himself shall be girded behind. This signifies that, returning after fourteen years to the sons whom he had dismissed across the Jordan into their inheritance, before Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, he encountered a great battle against the neighboring nations and, after defeating the enemies, fought valiantly. Read the Book of Jesus son of Nave and Chronicles.

Naphtali is a released deer, giving beautiful words; or, “Naphtali is a watered field.” This signifies either that warm springs arise in that very tribe, or that it is watered by the flow of the Jordan above the Lake of Gennesaret. The Hebrews, however, wish a watered field and beautiful words to be prophesied because of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the law. The released deer indicates seasonal crops and the speed of a more fertile land. But it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, because the Savior taught especially there, as is also written in the Gospel.

Joseph is a growing son, a growing son and beautiful in appearance. Daughters ran upon the wall, but they embittered him and quarreled with him; they envied him, bearing javelins. His bow rested in the strong one, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosed by the hands of mighty Jacob. From there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel.

O Joseph, who are so called because the Lord increased you for me, or because you were destined to become greater among your brothers—for Ephraim was indeed the strongest tribe, as we read in the Books of Kings and Chronicles—O, I say, my son Joseph, who are so beautiful that a whole crowd of the girls of Egypt looks upon you from walls, towers, and windows: your brothers envied you and provoked you to anger, bearing arrows of jealousy and wounded by the javelins of resentment. But you placed your bow and your weapons of war in God, who is a strong defender; and your bonds, with which your brothers had bound you, were loosed and broken by him, so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might arise, strong and steadfast, invincible like a harder stone, and ruling the ten tribes of Israel.

Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will devour prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils. Although the prophecy is most clearly about the apostle Paul, it is evident to everyone that in his youth he persecuted the Church and in his old age became a preacher of the Gospel. The Hebrews, however, explain it as follows: The altar on which sacrifices were offered, and at whose base the blood of the victims was poured, was located in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This, they say, signifies that the priests sacrifice victims in the morning, and in the evening divide among themselves what the people, according to the law, have bestowed upon them. They apply the interpretation of the bloodthirsty, ravenous wolf to the altar, and the division of the spoils to the priests, who, serving the altar, live from the altar. What has been said is sufficient to show how these things are to be understood historically. We shall next explain how these blessings of the patriarchs are to be understood mystically.

“Reuben, my firstborn,” and so forth. In Reuben he appears to have shown the person of the former people, to whom the Lord also says through the prophet: “Israel is my firstborn.” For, in accordance with what was owed to the firstborn, the priesthood and the kingship belonged to him. He adds: “You are my strength,” certainly because from that people came the foundation of faith, and from that people came the power of God, who is Christ.

But how is he himself the beginning of sorrows, unless by continually inflicting injury upon God the Father, turning his back toward him and not his face? He is “first in gifts,” because the oracles of God were given to them first, and to them first were given the legislation, the covenant, or the promise. He is “greater in dominion,” certainly because of the magnitude of his strength, since that same people reigned in this world more abundantly than the others.

But he was poured out like water by sinning against Christ, like water that cannot be contained in a vessel, poured out in the rush of pleasure. Therefore he adds: “You shall no longer increase,” because after this people was scattered throughout the whole world, it was greatly diminished and reduced.

But why did he deserve such things? He adds: “Because you went up to your father’s bed.” This is not to be understood, as the Jews understand it, as referring to his intercourse with his father’s concubine Bilhah. The prophecy was announcing future events, not what had already happened, since the patriarch himself says: “I announce to you what will happen in the last days.” Therefore what he foretold as future must not be referred to the past. He was preaching the Lord’s passion and the audacity of the firstborn people, because it went up to the bed of God the Father and defiled his couch when it seized and hung upon the cross the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity dwelt, and stained it with iron.

After this he turns to Simeon and Levi, saying:

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of iniquity for warfare.” By Simeon and Levi are understood the scribes and the priests of the Jewish people. The scribes of the Jews were from Simeon, while from the tribe of Levi came the chief priests, of whom it is written that they took counsel to hand Jesus over to death (Matthew 26). Concerning this counsel the patriarch, who already saw God in his mind, says: “Let my soul not enter their counsel,” and so forth. For even at that time this holy patriarch shuddered to see the counsels of such great crimes that the Jews were to commit in the last days.

It follows: “For in their anger they killed a man,” that is, Christ, in accordance with what Isaiah says (Isaiah 59; Wisdom 2): “Woe to their soul, because their thought is a counsel of evil,” saying against themselves: “Let us bind the just man, because he is useless to us.”

“And in their pain they dug through a wall,” when with a lance they pierced that spiritual and most powerful fortress which protects Israel. “Cursed be their anger, because it was stubborn,” namely, in perpetrating so great a crime, when, inflamed with fury and wrath, they offered Christ to Pontius Pilate, saying to him: “Crucify, crucify,” and: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (Matthew 27).

“And their indignation, because it was hard,” when they asked for the robber Barabbas and demanded that the prince of life be crucified. “I shall divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Here two things are named: division and dispersion. This is because some of them believed in the Lord, while others remained in unbelief. They are called divided because some are separated from them and come to the faith. They are scattered, however, because, after their homeland and temple were overthrown, the unbelieving people are dispersed throughout the world.

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” Through this Judah the true confessor, Christ, is expressed, who was born from his tribe according to the flesh. His brothers shall praise him—namely, the apostles and all his coheirs, who through adoption have been made sons of God the Father and, by grace, brothers of Christ, whose Lord he is by nature.

“Your hands shall be on the necks of your enemies.” By the same hands and by the same trophy of the cross he both protected his own and bent down his enemies and hostile powers, in accordance with what the Father also promises him, saying: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 109).

“Your father’s sons shall adore you,” because many of the sons of Jacob shall adore him, having been saved through the choice of grace.

“Judah is a lion’s cub,” because by being born he became a little one, as it is written: “A little one has been born for us” (Isaiah 9).

“To the prey, my son, you have gone up”—that is, ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples, and those whom the opposing lion had attacked you rescued by dying. Then, returning from the underworld and ascending on high, you led captivity captive.

“Lying down, you rested like a lion.” Most plainly, Christ reclined in his passion when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit; or when, secure in the tomb, he rested as though in a sleep of the body. But why like a lion and like a lion’s cub? In his sleep he was a lion who fulfilled this not by necessity but by power, in accordance with what he himself had said: “I have power to lay down my life, and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down myself” (John 10).

But when he added, “and like a lion’s cub,” he died from the place from which he was also born. Natural philosophers write of a lion’s cub that, once born, it sleeps for three days and three nights. Then, at its father’s growl or roar, the place of its den is said to tremble, as though shaken, and the sleeping cub is roused. This is very appropriately applied to Christ’s death in the passion: lying for three days and three nights in the chamber of the tomb, he fulfilled the sleep of death.

Therefore Christ rested well like a lion, who not only did not fear the bitterness of death but also, in death itself, conquered death’s dominion. Again, he rested well like a lion’s cub, because he rose on the third day. Hence what follows concerning his resurrection: “Who shall rouse him?” That is, no human being except himself, in accordance with what he said of his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up” (Matthew 16).

“A ruler shall not fail from the people of Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” This passage most clearly refers to Judah. For so long there was an unbroken succession of kings from his seed among the Jews, until Christ was born for the redemption of the world. The histories of the Jews prove this, showing that the first foreign king to rule among the Jewish people was Herod, at the time when Christ was born. If the Jews think that Christ has not come, then the kingdom of the Jews from the tribe of Judah remains to this day, so that there has not failed a king from the Jewish people until he should come to whom it has been reserved.

But the one who was to be sent benefited not only the Jews. Therefore it follows: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” “Binding his colt to the vine,” he joined to the vine of the apostles, who are from the Jews, the people from the nations upon whom the burden of the law had never yet been imposed. For “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5).

“And to the vine, O my son, his she-ass.” He says: “I am the true vine” (John 15). To this vine, therefore, he binds his she-ass, upon which he sits—the Church gathered from the nations. He bound it to the vine of his body by the bond of love and by the connection of evangelical discipline, so that, living in imitation of him, it might become the heir of God and coheir of Christ.

Others interpret this she-ass as the Synagogue, slow-footed and weighed down by the heavy burden of the law.

“He washed his robe in wine,” or “his flesh in the blood of the passion”; or the holy Church in that wine which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.

“And his cloak in the blood of the grape.” The nations are the cloak, which he joined to his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe them all as a garment” (Isaiah 49). Christ cleansed them in the blood of the grape when he hung like a cluster upon the wood of the cross. Then blood and water flowed from his side. The water washed us, but the blood redeemed us.

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” The eyes of Christ are the apostles and evangelists, who provide the light of knowledge to the whole body of the Church. They are proved more beautiful than wine because their teaching surpasses the austerity of the old wine, that is, the tradition of the ancient law. For the evangelical commandments are far clearer than the precepts of the Old Testament.

“And his teeth whiter than milk.” The teeth are the holy preachers, who cut people away from errors and, as though chewing them, transfer them into the body of Christ. By the name of milk is signified the teaching of the law, which nourished the carnal people like infants with a cup of milk. The teachers of the Church have become whiter than this, because they chew and distribute the strong and solid food of the word. Concerning them the Apostle says in his Letter to the Hebrews (chapter 5): “But solid food is for the mature.”

He rightly says “whiter than milk.” All who are mature, and who, explaining the nourishment of the Scriptures, supply to the body of the Church the subtle and minute understanding called spiritual, ought to be white and pure, free from every stain.

“Issachar is a strong ass.” Issachar, which is interpreted as “reward,” refers to the people of the nations, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood. This Issachar is written to be a strong ass because formerly the gentile people were like a brutish and lustful animal, existing without any reason. But now it is strong, submitting the hidden things of the mind to our Savior and subjecting its neck to the dominion of the Redeemer, bearing the yoke of evangelical discipline.

“Lying down between the boundaries, he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent.” To lie down between the boundaries is to rest while awaiting the end of the world, seeking nothing of the things now occurring in between but desiring the final things. The strong ass saw rest and an excellent land when the simple gentile people raised themselves to the strength of good works because they were making their way toward the homeland of eternal life.

Therefore he also adds: “He bent his shoulder to bear,” because, desiring to reach the promised rest, he willingly bears all the burdens of the commandments. Hence he became “subject to tribute,” that is, offering to his king and Christ the good gifts of faith and good works.

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, and at the anchorage of ships.” Zebulun, whose name is interpreted as “dwelling of strength,” signifies the Church, exceedingly strong for every endurance of suffering. It dwells on the shore of the sea and at the anchorage of ships, so that it might be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger. Established against all the storms of the world with immovable and unshaken firmness, it awaits the shipwreck of the Jews and the tempests of heretics, who are also carried about by every wind of doctrine.

Although it is battered by their waves, it breaks the waves itself and is not broken. It does not fall amid any storms of heresies, nor does it yield when shaken by any wind of schisms. It extends as far as Sidon, that is, it reaches the nations. It is also read in the Gospel that some of the apostles were taken from there and that the Lord often taught in those places, as it is written: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness saw a great light” (Isaiah 9).

“Dan shall judge his people, as will each of the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path,” and so forth. Some say that these words foretell that the Antichrist will come from this tribe. Others declare that these things are written about Judas, by whom Christ was betrayed, and wish the rider and the horse to signify the Lord together with the flesh he assumed. They understand his falling backward as his returning to the earth from which he was taken.

But because he rose on the third day, he therefore says: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord,” as in David: “You will not leave my soul in the underworld” (Psalm 15). Some interpret these words in this way. Others, however, transfer this prophecy to the Antichrist. They maintain that the Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because in this passage Dan is asserted to be both a serpent and one who bites.

Therefore, not without reason, when the Israelite people were receiving their lands in the division of the camps, Dan first pitched its camp toward the north, signifying the one who said in his heart: “I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” (Psalm 14). Concerning him the prophet also says: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jeremiah 8).
