He is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent, for κέρατα in Greek means “horns”; and this serpent is said to be horned, through which the coming of the Antichrist is aptly asserted. For against the life of the faithful he will arm himself not only with the poisonous bite of his preaching but also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Thus he becomes a serpent on the road because he urges those whom he spares, as though flattering them, to walk in the broadness of the present life. But he bites on the road because he destroys with the poison of his error those to whom he grants freedom.

Again he becomes a horned serpent on the path because, when he finds the faithful constraining themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he not only obstructs them by the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also presses them with the terror of power; after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of power amid the anguish of persecution.

In this passage the horse signifies the world, which through its arrogance foams along the course of passing times. And because the Antichrist strives to seize the world’s final things, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s heels. To bite the horse’s heels is to reach the extremities of the age by striking them.

“So that its rider may fall backward.” The rider of the horse is anyone who is exalted in the dignities of the world. He is said to fall backward, and not forward, as Saul is remembered to have fallen. To fall forward is, in this life, for each person to recognize his own sins and mourn them in repentance. To fall backward, where one does not see, is to depart suddenly from this life and not know to what punishments one is being led.

And because Judea, captured by the snares of its error, awaits the Antichrist in place of Christ, Jacob, in the same passage, rightly changes suddenly into the voice of the elect, saying: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord.” That is, I do not believe faithfully in the Antichrist, as the unbelievers do, but in Christ, who will come for our redemption.

“Gad, girded, shall wage war before him.” This girded Gad expresses the person of Christ, who at his first coming, in the humility of his incarnation, comes forth to fight before the coming of the Antichrist, girded most powerfully with the sword of his word around his thigh. With it he divided friends—that is, son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law—in accordance with what is read in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10).

But when he says, “and he himself shall be girded behind,” the glory of our Lord in his second reign is shown. When the Antichrist comes, Christ will again return behind him—that is, proceeding after his footsteps in his coming, in order to kill him with the sword of his mouth.

Hence Gad is also rightly interpreted as “raider,” because afterward, that is, near his feet, he will leap out like a raider with a swift and unexpected coming against the Antichrist’s open assault. Thus the Apostle exclaims: “For the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5).

Christ, therefore, is written as fighting against the Antichrist both before and behind: before him in the hidden coming of humility, and after him openly in the glory of majesty.

Moses also plainly shows that this prophecy of the patriarch refers especially to Christ. For he says: “Blessed, he says, is Gad in breadth. He rested like a lion; he seized the arm and the crown of the head, and he saw his principality.”

Let them recognize, then, who rested like a lion except Christ in his tomb. Who broke the crown and arms of the powerful except our Redeemer, who humbled the strength and arrogance of the exalted? Who saw his principality except the one to whom dominion, honor, and kingship were given?

“Asher’s bread is rich, and he shall provide delicacies for kings.” Asher, whose name signifies “riches,” is likewise Christ, whose height is the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Romans 11), who for our sake became poor although he was rich, whose bread became rich—namely, his flesh, which is the food of the saints. If anyone eats it, he will not die forever.

He will also provide delicacies of wisdom for kings—that is, for those who rule their own minds well, who dominate their vices, who chastise their bodies and bring them into subjection.

Naphtali, which is interpreted as “expansion,” signifies the apostles and holy preachers, whose teaching has spread throughout the breadth of the whole world. From this tribe came the apostles, who are the leaders of the Churches, and the leaders of Zebulun and the leaders of Naphtali; these certainly refer to the persons of the apostles. They are “the sons of those who have been shaken out” (Psalm 67), that is, of the prophets, who, placed in the hand of mighty God and shaken out like arrows, reached to the ends of the earth.

Therefore Naphtali is rightly written here as a released deer, since the apostles and preachers, leaping forth swiftly like deer, rise above the entanglements of this world. Thus, meditating on lofty and exalted things, they give beautiful words—that is, they preach the teaching of the Lord and Savior to all the nations.

“Joseph is a growing son.” This prophecy, after the Lord’s passion, assumed the likeness of the Father’s voice, because the Father addresses Christ, returning to heaven after his victory, saying: “Joseph is a growing son, a growing son,” certainly among the nations. When he had left the people because of the unbelief of the Synagogue, he enlarged for himself an innumerable people of the Church from all the nations. David also sang this, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm 21).

“A growing son and beautiful in appearance.” His beauty surpasses all others, in accordance with what is sung of him in the Psalms: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44).

“Daughters ran upon the wall”—that is, the nations or Churches that believed in Christ. Inflamed by love of Christ’s beauty, they run upon the solidity of faith as upon a wall, so that they may behold the true bridegroom through contemplation and be joined and cling to him by the kiss of charity.

“But they rebuked him,” when, slandering the holy Lord with false testimonies, the peoples of the Synagogue plotted to oppress him. “They envied him, bearing javelins.” No one, indeed, shot arrows or any weapon of injury at Joseph, but this was specifically fulfilled in Christ.

“His bow rested in the strong one.” Christ placed his bow and weapons of war in God, who is a strong defender; by his power all the wickedness of the faithless will be struck down. “The bonds of his arms were loosed,” the bonds with which his brothers had bound him and led him to Pilate, or with which they crucified him, suspended on the wood. For they were torn apart by the hand of Jacob—that is, by the hand of the almighty God of Jacob—from whose thigh the Lord himself, the good shepherd, went forth, the stone and firmness of those who believe in Israel.

“The God of your father will be your helper.” Who helped the Son except God the Father alone, who said: “Jacob is my servant; let my soul receive him”?

“And the Almighty will bless you with blessings of heaven above, with blessings of the abyss lying below.” He subjected everything to him: heavenly things through the blessing of heaven above, and earthly things through the blessing of the abyss lying below, so that he might rule over all angels and human beings.

“With blessings of the breasts,” that is, either of the two Testaments, in one of which he was announced and in the other revealed; or with the blessings of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed, because through them the holy Virgin gave the Lord the drink of milk. Hence that woman in the Gospel says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11).

“With blessings of the breasts and of the womb.” Here too the womb of the same mother is blessed—namely, the virginal womb that gave birth to Christ the Lord for us. Concerning it the prophet Jeremiah says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1).

“The blessings of your father were strengthened by the blessings of his fathers.” The blessings, he says, of your heavenly Father, which were given to you from the height of heaven and of the abyss, were strengthened—that is, prevailed—over the blessings of your fathers. For the blessing of the Almighty Father in the Son prevailed beyond the entire merit of the holy patriarchs or prophets, so that none of the saints is equal to him.

“Until the desire of the eternal hills should come.” These hills are the saints who, prophesying Christ’s coming, awaited his incarnation with great desire. Concerning them the Lord says: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see” (Luke 10). These saints are called hills because of the excellence of their holiness. They are also called eternal because they attain eternal life and do not perish with the world but are believed to be eternal.

“May they come upon the head of Joseph.” All these blessings are placed upon the head of Christ, which he received when he became incarnate.

“And upon the crown of the Nazirite,” of whom it is written: “He shall be called a Nazirite” (Matthew 2), that is, holy to God.

“Among his brothers,” because he is the head, exalted above all the saints, whom he also calls his brothers in the Psalms.

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will devour prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils.” With these words the apostle Paul is designated, descended from the stock of Benjamin. In the morning he seized prey—that is, at the beginning he devastated as many believers as he could. In the evening, however, he divided the spoils, because afterward he became faithful and distributed the sacred oracles to his hearers with remarkable discernment.

We read of one of the teachers referring to the city of Jerusalem what is written about Benjamin. “Benjamin,” he says, “is interpreted as ‘son of sorrow.’ By lot he received that place in which earthly Jerusalem stands, which has now been rejected and cast aside because of its unbelief. For it is signified in its sons under the person of Benjamin. Just as Benjamin receives the final blessing, so that same people will be saved last, after the fullness of the nations has entered.”

He says: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf”—a wolf, certainly, because that people shed the blood of the prophets and the righteous. It is called ravenous because of its greed. It became ravenous through great hunger for the word of God and deprivation, because it too violently seizes the kingdom of God.

“This one devours prey in the morning.” That morning is believed to be the time when it received the law. At that time the first illumination of the world with the knowledge of God was given. It devours in the morning because it consumes and still meditates upon the law that it received in the morning, although, by following the law of righteousness, it has not reached the law of faith.

“But in the evening he divides the spoils.” The evening is the final time, when it will be converted. Then it will divide the food; then it will understand that the letter must be divided from the spirit; and then it will recognize that “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” Since, therefore, already illuminated by the grace of God, it begins in the law to divide and separate spiritual things from carnal ones, it is said to divide the food in the evening—something it had not previously done, though it meditated on the law throughout the day.

But it is asked why Jacob made all those whom he begot from free women and slave women sons and heirs with equal honor, unless to show that Christ the Lord bestows heavenly rewards upon all the nations that are reconciled to his body through faith, with all being held in equal honor and glory. There is no distinction whether one is a Jew or a Greek, a barbarian or a Scythian, a slave or free (Romans 10; Colossians 3), because Christ is all and in all.

For this reason our Savior and Lord assumed the form of a servant and served both free and slave, so that he might bestow an equal gift of heavenly blessings upon all who believe in him, and so that, in his presence, no one might be preferred because he is nobler according to the flesh. Whoever wins the Lord’s approval through faith is not darkened by any stain of carnal birth.

That this would indeed happen is also signified through the prophet, when the Lord says: “In the last days I shall pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2).

“All these are the twelve tribes of Israel.” When their father had spoken these things to them, he blessed each one with his own blessing and commanded them, saying:

“I am being gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the double cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham purchased, together with the field, from Ephron the Hittite as a burial possession. There they buried him and Sarah his wife; and there Isaac was buried with Rebecca his wife. There also Leah lies buried.”

(Augustine.) We must consider how Scripture speaks when it repeatedly says of the dead: “He was gathered to his fathers,” or: “He was gathered to his people.” For here it is said of Jacob, already dead but not yet buried, and it is not immediately apparent to what people he is gathered. From him arose the earlier people called Israel. Those who preceded him are named as so few righteous people that we hesitate to call them a people. For if it had said, “He was gathered to his fathers,” no question would arise.

Or is the people not only the people of holy human beings, but also the people of the angels of that city? Hence it is said to the Hebrews: “But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of God, Jerusalem, and thousands of exultant angels” (Hebrews 12). Those who become pleasing to God after this life are joined to this people. They are then said to be gathered in, when no anxiety of temptations and no danger of sins remains. Observing this, Scripture says: “Before death, praise no one” (Ecclesiasticus 11).

**CHAPTER XVI. On the death of Jacob and the mourning of the Egyptians at his funeral.**
Having finished the instructions with which he was instructing his sons, he gathered his feet upon the bed and died; and he was gathered to his people (chap. L). When Joseph saw this, he fell upon his father’s face, weeping and kissing him. He ordered his physicians, his servants, to embalm his father with spices. When they had fulfilled his command, forty days passed. For this was the customary period for embalming corpses. [Col. 0666C] And Egypt mourned him for seventy days.

The forty days of burial which Scripture mentions perhaps signify something of repentance, by which sins are buried. For it was not without reason that forty days of fasting were also appointed: during that period Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted, and the Church calls its principal observance of fasting “Lent” (*Quadragesima*). Hence, in Hebrew, they report that it is written concerning the Ninevites in the prophet Jonah: “Forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah III), so that through all those days—clearly suited to the humiliation of the penitent—it might be understood that they mourned their sins in fasting and obtained the mercy of God.

Yet it must not be thought that this number applies only to the mourning of penitents; otherwise the Lord would not have spent forty days with his disciples after the resurrection, entering and going out with them, and eating and drinking. Those days were certainly days of great joy. Nor should the Seventy Interpreters, whom the Church customarily reads, be thought to have erred by not saying, “Forty days,” but rather, “Three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” For, endowed with greater authority than belongs to the office of translators, and by the prophetic Spirit—by which they are also affirmed to have spoken in unison in their translations, a great miracle—they set down “three days,” although they were not unaware that the Hebrew books read “forty days.” Thus, in the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ, sins were to be understood as dissolved and abolished, concerning which it was said: “He was delivered up for our offenses, and rose again for our justification” (Romans IV). The Lord’s glorification is understood in his resurrection and ascension into heaven.

Hence, although he gave the one and the same Holy Spirit twice, he gave him first after he had risen and again after he had ascended into heaven. And because he rose after three days but ascended after forty days, the Hebrew books signify one of these events—the later one—by the number of days; while the Seventy wished to commemorate the other, the three-day period, which also pertained to the same matter, not out of servile submission to translation but by prophetic authority.

Let us not therefore say that one of these is false, nor quarrel on behalf of some translators against others, since those who translate from the Hebrew prove to us that what they translate is written in this way, [Col. 0667A] while the authority of the Seventy Translators—commended by so great a divinely wrought miracle and strengthened in the Churches by such great antiquity—stands equally firm.

When the period of mourning had been completed, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh’s household: “If I have found favor in your sight, speak in Pharaoh’s hearing, because my father adjured me, saying: ‘Behold, I am dying. You shall bury me in my tomb, which I dug for myself in the land of Canaan. I will therefore go up and bury my father, and return.’” Pharaoh said to him: “Go up and bury your father, as you were adjured.”

When he went up, all the elders of Pharaoh’s household went with him, as did all the elders of Egypt, Joseph’s household with his brothers, except for the little ones and the flocks and herds which they had left in the land of Goshen. He also had chariots and horsemen in his company, and a very large multitude gathered.

Joseph instructed the powerful men of Egypt to say to Pharaoh on his behalf: “My father adjured me, saying: ‘In the tomb which I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me.’” One may ask how this can be true, since these words of his father, when he gave instructions about his burial, are not recorded. But we must refer the words to the sense, as we likewise pointed out above concerning similarly repeated words or narratives. Words ought to serve the expression and communication of the will.

Nowhere earlier in Scripture is it written that Jacob dug a tomb for himself; but unless this had happened while they were in those same lands, Scripture would not now say: “And they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan.” There, celebrating the funeral rites [Col. 0667D] with great and vehement mourning, they completed seven days, and so forth.

What does it mean that, when they were going to bury Jacob, Scripture says: “And they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan”? For they passed beyond the place where the dead man was to be buried by more than fifty thousand [units of distance], as those who know the region report. That is roughly the distance from the place where the patriarchs were buried, including Jacob, to this place where they are said to have arrived. After they had mourned and lamented there with great grief, they returned to the place they had passed, crossing the Jordan again.

Unless perhaps someone should say that, to avoid certain enemies, they came with the body through the wilderness, by the route along which the people of Israel were also led by Moses after being liberated from Egypt. By that route one makes a considerable circuit and comes by way of the Jordan to *Abrahamium*—the place of Abraham—where the bodies of the patriarchs are located, that is, to the land of Canaan.

But how it came about that they proceeded so far eastward beyond those places and then came to them by way of the Jordan must be believed to have occurred for the sake of a sign: Israel was later to come to those lands through his sons by way of the Jordan. “And he mourned his father for seven days.”

I do not know whether Scripture records that a nine-day mourning was ever celebrated for any of the saints—the observance which the Latins call a *novendial*. Therefore, it seems to me that Christians who maintain this number in mourning for their dead should be forbidden to do so, since it belongs more properly to pagan custom. The seventh day, however, has authority in Scripture. Thus it is written elsewhere: “The mourning for the dead is seven days; but for the fool, all the days of his life” (Ecclesiasticus XXII).

The number seven, because of the mystery of the Sabbath, is especially a sign of rest. Thus it is rightly offered to the dead as though they were resting. Yet the Egyptians multiplied this number tenfold in Jacob’s mourning, for they mourned him for seventy days.

## CHAPTER XVII. Joseph’s brothers, after their father’s death and burial, ask him not to remember the wrongs they had done to him

Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and the entire company after his father had been buried. After he had died, his brothers were afraid, and spoke with one another: “Perhaps he will remember the injury he suffered and repay us for all the evil that we did.” They sent word to him:

“Your father commanded us, before he died, to say these things to you in his words: ‘I ask you to forget the crime of your brothers, and the sin and wickedness which they committed against you.’ We too ask you to forgive this iniquity to the servant of God, your father.”

When Joseph heard this, he wept. His brothers came to him, and, falling prostrate, worshiped upon the ground, saying: “We are your servants.” He answered them: “Do not be afraid. Can we resist God’s will? You intended evil against me, but God turned it into good, so that he might exalt me, as you now see, and save many peoples. Do not be afraid: I will feed you and your little ones.” He consoled them and spoke to them gently and kindly.

And he dwelt in Egypt with his entire father’s household. He lived one hundred and ten years, and saw the sons of Ephraim to the third generation. The sons also of Machir, son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees.

Since Scripture says that Joseph lived to see these sons of sons, or grandsons of sons, how does it join them to those seventy-five persons with whom it says Jacob entered Egypt, when Joseph lived to old age and saw them born? When Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph was young; and when his father died, he left him at approximately fifty-six years of age. It is therefore clear that, for the sake of a certain mystery, Scripture wished to commend that number—namely, seventy-five. [Col. 0669A]

But if someone demands how it can also be true according to the historical account that Jacob entered Egypt with seventy-five souls, his entry must not be understood as occurring on the one day when he arrived. Rather, because Jacob is often named in his sons—that is, in his descendants—and because it is clear that through Joseph he entered Egypt, his entry must be understood as lasting as long as Joseph lived, since through him it came about that Jacob entered.

Throughout that entire period, all those who are mentioned could be born and live, so that the seventy-five souls might be completed, up to the grandsons of Benjamin. For Scripture says: “These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria” (Genesis XXXV). Speaking also of those who had not yet been born, because their parents, from whom they were born, had been born there, it asserts that they were born there, since the cause of their being born arose there—namely, their parents, whom Leah bore there.

Thus, because Jacob had in Joseph the cause of entering Egypt, the whole period during which Joseph lived in Egypt was Jacob’s entry into Egypt through his offspring, which was propagated while Joseph was alive, and through whom it came about that he entered.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Joseph adjures his brothers that, when they depart from Egypt, they carry his bones with them after his death

Joseph said to his brothers: “After my death God will visit you, and will bring you up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” And after he had adjured them and said, “God will visit you; carry my bones with you from this place,” he died when he had completed one hundred and ten years of life. He was embalmed with spices and placed in a coffin in Egypt.

Joseph, therefore, who, like his father Jacob, desired the promised land with his whole mind and detested dwelling in Egypt, instructs us morally that, as long as we are in this world, we should always desire to enter the land of the living and wish to rest there. This is rightly accomplished if we imitate the number of his years in our conduct.

After completing one hundred and ten years of his life, therefore, he died. Let us also strive, through observance of the Decalogue, to reach the eternal blessedness signified by the number one hundred. [Col. 0670B]

Joseph himself was also embalmed with spices and placed in a coffin in Egypt. A coffin (*loculus*) is a receptacle in which something is entrusted for preservation. O blessed soul, which, seasoned with the spices of the virtues, dwelling in this little body, is preserved day by day through progress for eternal life! Without doubt, if seasoned with such a preparation and guarded in faith, hope, and charity, through the grace of Christ it will deserve to reach the vision of divine contemplation. Its attainment is perfect joy, which the Psalmist, beholding it with the eyes of faith, says:

“You will fill me, Lord, with joy in your presence; delights are in your right hand forever” (Psalm CV). Amen.

[Col. 0669]

## (A.D. 820.) THE BOOK OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON COMPUTATION

(Baluze, *Sacred Miscellanies*, vol. II.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0669B]

Rabanus, a sinner in Christ, sends greetings to his beloved brother Marcharius, a monk. [Col. 0669C]

We read in the Proverbs: “Wisdom is better than all the most precious things, and nothing desirable can be compared with it.” Therefore, dearest brother, I give thanks to God, who inspired you with love for it. Possession of wisdom despises the riches of the world, and it has made you splendid through its radiance and beneficial to those near you.

You therefore asked me to apply my pen to certain questions on computation and to the answers—less than fully developed—which you had brought to me, composed, I do not know by whom, and to make them clearer for you. I did what I could, but not in the order in which I found them set down there, because their confused sequence removed the power of understanding and introduced weariness into the reading.

I therefore added most of what seemed more necessary to me, and endeavored to arrange the order within the subjects themselves. It also happened, while I was striving for brevity and yet wishing to disclose the truth of the matters themselves, that I could not avoid the length of a single book.

I composed, from the numbers and divisions of time, a certain dialogue and dedicated it to you by name. In it I prefaced those matters which seemed necessary to me with the title of “student” when they were to be asked, and with that of “teacher” when they were to be answered. I took care to unravel these matters not only through my own reasoning but also from the sayings of the ancients and the judgments of the holy Fathers.

Therefore, dearest brother, as you read this, know that I have not devoted myself to difficulty of wording or obscurity of meaning. Rather, I have gathered whatever was plain and easy, and have labored, in what I inserted from my own resources, to clarify the truth itself rather than to mock the ignorance of others.

For I prefer myself to no one. To those who seek rightly and properly preserve the Catholic faith, I promise, according to my ability, to be a companion and to place myself beneath them as a junior. May divine grace grant me this: that, as long as I live, I may be a servant of Christ’s servants, a hearer of those who teach well, and a small helper of those who labor well.

May the majesty of Christ preserve your affection now and forever, holy brother, mindful of us. I ask you, as soon as you can, to complete the copy of this book which I sent you to transcribe, and to return it to me. Farewell.

Here ends the prologue.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

Since I have often heard you, revered teacher, discussing numbers and demonstrating the discipline of this art to your students, I beg you not to begrudge us, who are already of more mature age, a little work by which we may rouse our sluggishness and acquire at least some knowledge of numbers.

## CHAPTER I. The power of numbers

**TEACHER.** You ask well, dear brother, because you desire knowledge of this discipline, which is clearly the teacher of all disciplines. For the science of numbers is not to be despised, since its great mystery shines forth in many passages of the holy Scriptures.

Nor was it said without reason in praise of God: “You have made all things in measure and number and weight.” Through number we are instructed so that we may not be confused. Take number away from all things, and all things perish. Remove calculation from the world, and everything is enveloped in blind ignorance. Those who do not know the science of calculation can scarcely be distinguished from the other animals.

But since you have challenged me to explain its power and nature, begin by asking about those matters concerning which you wish to be instructed; and I will follow you by answering, insofar as the Lord grants.

**STUDENT.** From where, then, did this science of numbers first proceed?

**TEACHER.** From God, of course. For all wisdom is from the Lord God, from whom all things exist.

**STUDENT.** Tell me, then: when was this science first discovered?

**TEACHER.** From the time when creatures were made—that is, from the origin of the world. For then number first became known to things, as we read in Genesis: “And there was evening and morning, one day.” When it spoke of evening and morning, it was speaking of night and day. It displayed the science of number when it said: “One day,” “the second day,” and “the third day,” and so on up to the seventh.

God likewise signified number when he spoke of the sun and moon: “Let them be for signs and seasons and days and years.” When he said “days,” “seasons,” and “years,” he was speaking of number. For who can understand days, seasons, and years except through number?

Hence Boethius said (*Arithmetic*, book I, chapter 2):

> “All things whatsoever that were constructed from the first nature of things appear to have been established through the principle of numbers. For this was the principal pattern in the mind of the Creator. From this the multiplicity of the four elements was ordered; from this the changes of the seasons; from this the movements of the stars and the turning of heaven are understood. The very nature of numbers has established the entire course of the stars and the whole science of astronomy. Thus we determine risings and settings; thus we observe the slowness and speed of wandering stars; thus we recognize eclipses and the moon’s manifold changes.”

## CHAPTER II. From where the name “number” is derived

**STUDENT.** Explain to me the name of number and its etymology.

**TEACHER.** The name of number is established among each people according to the character of its language. Among the Latins, however, *numerus* seems to have derived its name from *nummus* and *rivus*. Either it took its name from a stream of coins—that is, from the multitude of the tribute paid to kings or emperors—or from *nummus*.

Hence Isidore says: “The coin (*nummus*) gave number (*numerus*) its name, and from its frequent use bestowed the word” (*Etymologies*, book III, chapter 3).

Or it may derive from Numeria. Thus Augustine says: “Number is named from a certain goddess Numeria, whose priests carried gifts with their faces turned backward, and, after presenting the offerings, proceeded backward.”

**STUDENT.** How is number defined?

**TEACHER.** Isidore therefore defined it as follows: “Number is a multitude constituted from units. For we say that one is the seed of number, not a number” (ibid.).

It is also written elsewhere: “One is not a number, but numbers increase from it.”

Nevertheless, Donatus also counted one as a number, saying: “Number is singular, as in ‘this teacher.’”

Augustine likewise says: “Number is a collection of a singular body, sound, and signification.”

## CHAPTER III. The various kinds of numbers

**STUDENT.** How many kinds of numbers are there?

**TEACHER.** Number has many kinds. Yet they all arise from one origin. For numbers are either cardinal, such as one, two, three, four, five, six, and the rest in this order; or ordinal, such as first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and so forth; or adverbial, such as once, twice, three times, four times, five times, six times, and so on; or distributive, such as one each, two each, three each, four each, five each, six each, and so forth; or multiplicative in the sense of proportion, such as single, double, triple, quadruple, and so on; or declarative, such as alone, the other, or another.

Moreover, let us turn to the other numbers. There are also multiplicative numbers, such as single, double, triple, quadruple, and so forth. There are likewise forms expressed adverbially, such as singly, doubly, triply, and so on.

There are other kinds of derived numbers, derived from those above: singular, dual, ternary, quaternary, and the rest in the same manner.

There are also *assis*, *dussis* or *dipondius*, *tresis*, *quadrassis*, *quinquis*, *sexis*, *septusis*, *octusis*, *nonusis*, *decus* or *decusis*, *vicesis*, *tricesis*, *quadragesis*, *quinquagesis*, *sexagesis*, *septuagesis*, *octagesis*, *nonagesis*, and *centusis*. After this number, Varro testifies, numbers are not compounded with *as*.

There are also the names of unciae: *deunx*, *dextans*, *dodrans*, *bessis*, *septunx*, *quincunx*, *triens*, *quadrans*, *sextans*, *sexcunx*, *sextula*, and *libra*. [Col. 0673A] From these are derived *bilibris*, *trilibris*, *quadrilibris*, and similar forms.

There are also forms derived from *annus*, such as *anniculus* or *annus*, *biennis*, *triennis*, *quadriennis*, and similar words; *biennium*, *triennium*, *quadriennium*, and similar forms; *bimus*, *trimus*, *quadrimus*, and similar forms.

There are *bipes*, *tripes*, *quadrupes*, *decempes*, and *decempeda*, and similar forms; *biceps*, *triceps*, *quadriceps*, *centiceps*, and similar forms; *bifariam*, *trifariam*, *quatrifariam*, and similar forms; *biduum*, *triduum*, *quatriduum*, and similar forms; *bicorpor*, *tricorpor*, and similar forms; *bipatens*, *tripatens*, and similar forms; *bilinguis*, *trilinguis*, and similar forms; *bivium*, *trivium*, and similar forms; *bifidus*, *trifidus*, *quadrifidus*, and similar forms; *bisulcus*, *trisulcus*, and similar forms.

There are *geminus*, *tergeminus*, *centumgeminus*, and similar forms; *unimanus*, *centimanus*, and similar forms; *uniformis*, *biformis*, *triformis*, [Col. 0673B] and the rest.

There are *duumvir*, *triumvir*, *quinquevir*, *septemvir*, *decemvir*, *centumvir*, and similar forms; *bigae*, *trigae*, *quadrigae*, and similar forms; *bijugus*. Hence Virgil writes in book V:

> “With a contest of two-horse chariots  
> they seized the plain.”

There are also coins called *bigati*. Likewise *trijugus*, *quadrijugus*, and similar forms; *triangulum*, *quadrangulum*, *quinquangulum*, *sexangulum*, and similar forms.

## CHAPTER IV. The demonstration of number

**STUDENT.** How, then, is number demonstrated?

**TEACHER.** In two ways.

**STUDENT.** How?

**TEACHER.** Numbers are either marked by letters or expressed by the bending of the fingers.

## CHAPTER V. How numbers are marked by letters

**STUDENT.** First tell me about notation by letters.

**TEACHER.** Numbers are marked by seven letters: I, V, X, L, C, D, M. These either signify numbers when placed alone—for example, I one, V five, X ten, L fifty, C one hundred, D five hundred, M one thousand—or when combined with others: V and I signify six; X and I, eleven; X and L, forty; L and X, sixty. X is placed before C when they signify ninety. D and C signify six hundred.

They may also be multiplied by themselves. Thus I doubled signifies two, tripled three, quadrupled four; X doubled, twenty, tripled, thirty; C doubled, two hundred, tripled, three hundred, quadrupled, four hundred.

Among the Latins, no sign is multiplied by itself more than four times, either alone or in combination with others: for example, I with V, when it signifies seven, eight, or nine; X with L, when it signifies seventy or eighty; and C with D, when it represents seven hundred, eight hundred, or nine hundred.

## CHAPTER VI. How numbers are signified by the fingers

**STUDENT.** How, then, are numbers expressed by bending the fingers?

**TEACHER.** Three fingers of the left hand—the little finger, ring finger, and middle finger—contain the numbers from one through nine. Two fingers of the same hand—the index finger and thumb—contain the numbers from X through XC.

Likewise, two fingers of the right hand—the thumb and index finger—contain the numbers from C through nine hundred. Three fingers of the same hand—the little finger, middle finger, and ring finger—contain the numbers from one thousand through nine thousand.

The left hand, by the various joints of the body, contains the numbers from ten thousand through ninety thousand. Conversely, the right hand contains the numbers from one hundred thousand through nine hundred thousand by the joints and arrangements of the limbs.

**STUDENT.** I ask you, then, to explain all these things to me in detail.

**TEACHER.** When you say “one,” bend the smallest finger of the left hand and press it against the middle joint of the palm. When you say “two,” bend the second finger from the smallest and place it in the same position. When you say “three,” bend the third in the same way. When you say “four,” raise the little finger again. When you say “five,” likewise raise the second finger from the smallest. When you say “six,” raise the third finger as well, leaving only the middle finger—the one called the ring finger—fixed in the middle of the palm.

When you say “seven,” place only the little finger, with the others meanwhile raised, upon the root of the palm. Beside it, when you say “eight,” place the ring finger; when you say “nine,” place the middle finger opposite it.

When you say “ten,” place the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb. When you say “twenty,” insert the tip of the thumb between the middle joints of the index and middle fingers. When you say “thirty,” join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace.

When you say “forty,” pass the inner side of the thumb over the side or back of the index finger, with both fingers raised. When you say “fifty,” bend the thumb at its outer joint like the Greek letter gamma and incline it toward the palm.

When you say “sixty,” carefully encircle the bent thumb described above with the bent index finger, from the front. When you say “seventy,” cover the bent index finger as above by inserting the thumb, with only the nail of the thumb raised across the middle joint of the index finger.

When you say “eighty,” cover the bent index finger as above by extending the thumb lengthwise, inserting its nail into the middle joint of the index finger. When you say “ninety,” insert the nail of the bent index finger into the root of the raised thumb.

This applies up to ninety on the left hand. For one hundred, make on the right hand what you made for ten on the left; for two hundred on the right, what you made for twenty on the left; for three hundred on the right, what you made for thirty on the left; and similarly for the rest up to four hundred.

For one thousand on the right hand, do what you did for one on the left; for two thousand on the right, what you did for two on the left; for three thousand on the right, what you did for three on the left; and so on up to VIV.

When you say ten thousand, place the left hand palm-up at the middle of the chest, with only the fingers raised toward the neck. When you say twenty thousand, lay the same hand broadly extended upon the chest. When you say thirty thousand, place the same hand palm-down but raised, and insert the thumb into the cartilage at the middle of the chest.

When you say forty thousand, place the same hand upright at the navel, palm-up. When you say fifty thousand, place the thumb of the same palm-down but raised hand upon the navel. When you say sixty thousand, grasp the left thigh from above with the same palm-down hand.

When you say seventy thousand, place the same palm-up hand upon the thigh. When you say eighty thousand, place the same palm-down hand upon the thigh. When you say ninety thousand, grasp the loins with the same hand, turning the thumb toward the groin.

As for one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand up to nine hundred thousand, you will complete them in the same order on the right side of the body.

When you say ten times one hundred thousand, interlace both hands, inserting the fingers of one into the other.

There is also another method of calculation proceeding by joints. How it especially pertains to the computation of Easter will be explained more suitably when we reach that subject in due order.

## CHAPTER VII. The Greek signs adapted to numbers

**STUDENT.** What do you say about the Greek method of calculation? I have heard that they mark numbers with their own letters.

**TEACHER.** It is as you say. Having expended the whole character of their alphabet on numerical figures, they depict the three additional numbers with individual signs, following almost the same order of numerical formation as the order of writing their alphabet, in this way:

α = 1, β = 2, γ = 3, δ = 4, ε = 5, ς = 6, ζ = 7, η = 8, θ = 9, ι = 10, κ = 20, λ = 30, μ = 40, ν = 50, ξ = 60, ο = 70, π = 80, [sign omitted in the supplied text] = 90, ρ = 100, σ = 200, τ = 300, υ = 400, φ = 500, χ = 600, ψ = 700, ω = 800, [sign omitted in the supplied text] = 900.

For this reason, having soon learned to signify numbers with their fingers, they know how to prefix letters to these signs at the same time without any intervening delay.

## CHAPTER VIII. The forms and divisions of unciae

**STUDENT.** I ask you to explain what calculators call *unciae*.

**TEACHER.** There is also a considerable discussion concerning the division of unciae, which is no less suited to calculating periods of time and other things than money. Since history and holy Scripture themselves use these terms here and there, we have taken care to attach their names and forms briefly.

A *libra*, or *as* or *assis*: twelve unciae.  
A *deunx* or *iabus*: eleven unciae.  
A *decunx* or *dextans*: ten unciae.  
A *dodrans* or *doras*: nine unciae.  
A *bes* or *bisse*: eight unciae.  
A *septunx* or *septus*: seven unciae.  
A *semis*: six unciae.  
A *quincunx* or *cincus*: five unciae.  
A *triens* or *treas*: four unciae.  
A *quadrans* or *quadras*: three unciae.  
A *sextans* or *sextas*: two unciae.  
A *secunx* or *sescuncia*: one and a half unciae.  
An *uncia*: twenty-four *scripuli*.  
A *semiuncia*: twelve *scripuli*.  
Two *sextulae*, or *scesclae*: eight *scripuli*, that is, one-third of an uncia.  
A *sicilicus*: six *scripuli*.  
A *sextula* or *scescle*: four *scripuli*.  
Half a *sextula* or *scescle*: two *scripuli*.  
A *scripulus*: six *siliquae*.

[Col. 0676A] These terms or symbols of weights apply not only to measuring money but also to measuring any bodies or periods of time. Thus, whether you wish to divide one hour, a whole day, a month, a year, or some other greater or smaller period of time into twelve parts, the twelfth part itself is an uncia; the remaining eleven are called a *deunx*.

If you divide it into six parts, the sixth part is called a *sextans*, while the remaining parts are called a *dextans* or, as some say, a *distans*. If you divide it into four, the fourth part receives the name *quadrans*, while the remaining three are called a *dodrans*. If you wish to divide something by three, you will call the third part a *triens* and the two remaining parts a *bes*. If by two, the half is called a *semis*. And so with the rest.

## CHAPTER IX. Time

[Col. 0676B]

**STUDENT.** I gladly accept these things. Since we must discuss the divisions and reckoning of time, tell me first what time is.

**TEACHER.** Time is the unstable movement of the world and the course of passing things.

**STUDENT.** From where is the word “time” derived?

**TEACHER.** From *temperamentum*—either because each of those periods is separately regulated, or because all the courses of mortal life are regulated by moments, hours, days, months, years, centuries, and ages.

## CHAPTER X. The threefold distinction of time

**STUDENT.** How is the reckoning of time constituted?

**TEACHER.** The computation of time is distinguished in a threefold manner. It proceeds either by nature, by custom, or by authority.

**STUDENT.** How, then, does the course and reckoning of time consist by nature?

**TEACHER.** Nature as guide has disclosed that the solar year is completed in 365 days and a quarter, while the lunar year ends, if it is a common year, after 354 days, and, if embolismic, after 374 days. It has also disclosed that the entire course of the moon is contained in a nineteen-year cycle, and that the other wandering stars likewise revolve through the zodiac, each in its own periods.

**STUDENT.** How does it proceed by custom?

**TEACHER.** Human custom established that a month should be reckoned as thirty days, although this accords neither with the course of the sun nor with that of the moon. For careful investigation has established that the moon has twelve hours less than this, allowing for the intercalation, while the sun has ten and a half hours more.

**STUDENT.** And how by authority?

**TEACHER.** Authority is divided in two ways, since it is either human authority or divine authority.

**STUDENT.** How are periods of time ordered by human authority?

**TEACHER.** It was established by human beings that Olympiads should be celebrated in cycles of four years, nundines in cycles of eight days, and indictions in cycles of fifteen years. The Greeks, Egyptians, and Romans each decreed according to their own understanding that the day, which is composed of quarters, should be intercalated in February or August.

**STUDENT.** And how by divine authority?

**TEACHER.** The Lord commanded in the Law that the Sabbath should be observed on the seventh day, that in the seventh year one should rest from agricultural labor, and that the fiftieth year should be called the Jubilee. For although barbarian peoples are also shown to have weeks, it is not hidden that they borrowed them from the people of God.

**STUDENT.** How many divisions of time are there?

**TEACHER.** Fourteen.

**STUDENT.** What are they?

**TEACHER.** Atom, momentary instant, moment, part, minute, point, hour, quarter, day, month, change or period, year, century, and age.

## CHAPTER XI. The indivisible atom

**STUDENT.** Tell me first about these—that is, what is an atom?

**TEACHER.** Philosophers call atoms certain exceedingly small parts of bodies in the world, so small that they are not easily visible and do not admit of division. Hence they are called *atoms*. For in Greek *tomos* means division, whereas *atomos* means indivisible.

Indeed, they fly and are carried here and there like the finest dust which, entering through windows, is dispersed by the rays of the sun.

**STUDENT.** Since I have heard you say that atoms exist not only in time but also in bodies, explain to me how many kinds of atoms there are.

**TEACHER.** There are five kinds of atoms: an atom in a body, an atom in the sun, an atom in speech, an atom in number, and an atom in time.

**STUDENT.** I ask you to explain each of these to me.

**TEACHER.** An atom in a body exists when you divide some body into parts, and those parts into other parts, and continue doing this until you reach such tiny elements that, because of their smallness, they cannot in any way be divided.

An atom in the sun is that exceedingly fine dust which we said is driven about by the rays of the sun.

An atom in speech is the smallest portion, such as a letter. For when you divide any part of speech into syllables, and then divide the syllable into letters, the letter alone has nothing into which it can be dissolved.

An atom in number is one. If you divide some number—for example, eight into two fours, four into two pairs, and then the pairs into single units—only the unit remains indivisible.

Finally, an atom in time, the subject with which we began to speak, is constituted as follows. When, dividing larger periods of time—such as a day or an hour—by points or other smaller parts, you reach a particle so small that, because of its minuteness, it has no duration capable of being divided in any way, such as the swiftest blink of the eye, know that these are an atom.

An atom is therefore one three-hundred-seventy-sixth part of an *ostentum*.

## CHAPTER XII. The *ostentum*

[Col. 0677D]

**STUDENT.** What is an *ostentum*?

**TEACHER.** The sixtieth part of an hour, containing 376 atoms.

## CHAPTER XIII. The moment

**STUDENT.** What is a moment?

**TEACHER.** A fixed passage of the sun through the sky. Measured forty times in this way, it produces a complete hour.

**STUDENT.** From where is the word “moment” derived?

**TEACHER.** From the swift movement of the stars, when something is perceived to give way and succeed itself within the briefest intervals. One moment therefore contains one and a half *ostenta*, and also 564 atoms.

## CHAPTER XIV. The parts

**STUDENT.** What are called “parts” in computation?

**TEACHER.** The parts are so called from the division of the zodiacal circle, which they divide into thirty days for each month. Each part contains two moments and two parts of a moment, four *ostenta*, and 1,504 atoms.

## CHAPTER XV. The minute
STUDENT. What is a minute?  
MASTER. A tenth part of an hour.

STUDENT. From where is “minute” derived?  
MASTER. From a smaller interval, as though one said “a lesser moment,” because it counts less than the larger unit contains. A minute therefore contains one and a half parts, four moments, six ostenta, and [Note: [Col. 0678A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [V]CCLVI atoms.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Point

[Col. 0678B] STUDENT. What is a point?  
MASTER. A quarter of an hour.

STUDENT. From where is it called a point?  
MASTER. From the small passage of a point that occurs on a clock. For “point” is derived from *pungere*, “to prick,” because it is marked on clocks by certain punctuations indicating a fixed designation. A point contains two and a half minutes, three and a half parts, and a quarter of one part; ten moments, fifteen ostenta, and [V]DCXL atoms. Thus four points make one hour.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Hour

STUDENT. What is an hour?  
MASTER. A fixed limit of time. For an hour is the twelfth part of a day, as the Lord himself attests when he says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble.” Although here, allegorically, he called himself the day and the disciples, who were to be enlightened by him, the hours, he nevertheless expressed the ordinary day according to the customary human manner of reckoning.

STUDENT. From where did the hour receive its name?  
MASTER. From the clock. Just as the clock took its name from the hour, so the name *hora*, descending from Greek, is interpreted as “series,” or “shadow,” or even “end.” Hence we speak of the edges or boundaries of the sea, rivers, and garments as their *orae*.

STUDENT. Is the word for the hour of time written in the same way as the word for the edge of the other things you mentioned?  
MASTER. They are distinguished by aspiration alone. For the hour of time is written with aspiration, whereas those other meanings are written without aspiration.

STUDENT. What subdivisions does an hour have?  
MASTER. It has four points according to solar reckoning, but in certain lunar reckonings five points, as we shall show below. It also has ten minutes, fifteen parts, forty moments, sixty ostenta, and [XXII]DLX atoms.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Quarter

STUDENT. What is a quarter?  
MASTER. A quarter, or *quadras*, is a fourth part of a pound, containing three ounces, as we showed above. Whatever you measure in bodies or in times, you should call its fourth part a quarter, and the remaining three parts a three-quarter measure. For this reason the fourth part of a day is called a quarter. Four quarters make a complete day. For a day together with its night has twenty-four hours.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Day

[Col. 0679A] STUDENT. What is a day?  
MASTER. Air illuminated by the sun, taking its name from the fact that it separates and divides darkness. For God said in the beginning: “Let there be light,” and there was light. And he divided the light from the darkness; he called the light day, and the darkness he called night.

STUDENT. In what ways is “day” used?  
MASTER. Naturally and commonly.

STUDENT. How naturally?  
MASTER. The natural and proper day is from sunrise until the sun rises again. This day has twenty-four hours.

STUDENT. How many divisions does the natural day have?  
MASTER. The principal division of this day has two spans, namely daytime and nighttime. Moreover, every day is subdivided by hours, points, and the other smaller units. The natural day contains twenty-four hours, ninety-six points, CCXL minutes, CCCLX parts, DCCCCLX moments, [I]CCCCXL ostenta, and [DXLI] plus CCCCXL atoms.

STUDENT. Who demonstrates that the term “day” includes night together with day?  
MASTER. Divine Scripture demonstrates it, where we read: “And there was evening and morning, one day,” with “evening” indicating the night and “morning” indicating the time of light.

STUDENT. Since you have explained the natural day, I ask you also to describe the common day.  
MASTER. The common, or artificial, day comprises all the time of light above the earth, from sunrise to sunset. Conversely, night is the absence of light above the earth. For all the time during which the sun returns from sunset to sunrise is called night.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Parts of the Day

STUDENT. What subdivisions does the common, or artificial, day have?  
MASTER. Three.

STUDENT. Which?  
MASTER. Morning, midday, and late day.

STUDENT. What is morning?  
MASTER. Morning is the first part of the day, namely from sunrise to the fourth hour.

STUDENT. From where is “morning” derived?  
MASTER. According to some, *mane* is derived from *manus*. The ancients called *manus* “good”; for what is better than light? Or perhaps *mane* is derived from *manes*, that is, the gods of the underworld. For the pagans believed that when the sun withdrew, the gods of the underworld had drawn it to themselves.

STUDENT. What is midday?  
MASTER. The middle part of the day, from the fifth hour to the eighth hour.

STUDENT. From where did “midday” derive its name?  
MASTER. It is called *meridies*, as though meaning “middle of the day.” Or it is called *meridies* as though meaning “pure day.” For in the whole day nothing is purer than midday. The ancients called what was pure *merum*.

STUDENT. What is late day?  
MASTER. The final part of the day, extending from the ninth hour to sunset.

STUDENT. Why is it called late day?  
MASTER. From *supprimere*, “to suppress.” At that time the sun, as though suppressing its course, inclines toward sunset.

STUDENT. According to what are these three spans of the artificial day ordered?  
MASTER. According to the course of the sun. Morning is from sunrise until the sun rises to the height of heaven; midday is when the sun runs through the middle height of heaven; and late day is when the sun descends from the height of heaven toward sunset.

STUDENT. Since you have explained one span of the natural day sufficiently for me, I ask you to explain its other span, which is night.  
MASTER. I shall do as you ask. But, following your usual custom, proceed by asking questions.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Night

STUDENT. What is night?  
MASTER. The absence of the sun, with the earth covered by shadow, until it returns from sunset to sunrise.

STUDENT. From where is night so called?  
MASTER. Either because it harms sight and human activities, or because thieves and robbers find in it an opportunity to harm others.

STUDENT. For what reason was night made?  
MASTER. For the moderation of human labor, so that bodies might have rest, and so that certain animals unable to endure the sun might have an opportunity to seek nourishment.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Parts of the Night

[Col. 0680B] STUDENT. How many parts does night have?  
MASTER. Seven.

STUDENT. Which?  
MASTER. Twilight, evening, the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn.

STUDENT. Explain the properties of each of these in turn.  
MASTER. Twilight is uncertain light. For we call *creperum* “uncertain,” that is, between light and darkness.

Evening is named from the star that appears at that time, concerning which the poet says:

> Before day, Vesper will set it beneath the closed Olympus.

The time of silence is when everything falls silent, that is, is quiet.

The dead of night is midnight, as though it were “inactive,” when everything is resting in the sleep of repose and there is no time for action.

Cockcrow is when the roosters raise their song.

Morning is the interval between the withdrawal of darkness and the arrival of dawn.

Dawn is as though it were the small light of day already beginning. These periods, together with dawn, extend until sunrise.

STUDENT. Of these parts of the natural day, which comes first in time, night or day?  
MASTER. Without doubt, day came first from the beginning of the world until Christ’s resurrection; but from Christ’s resurrection until the day of judgment, it does not come first. For the divine authority that, in Genesis, decreed for fallen humanity—cast from the light of paradise into this valley of tears—that the day should be reckoned from morning with the following evening until the next morning, established in the Gospel that, for those withdrawing from the darkness of sins toward the true light, the whole day should begin from evening and thus be completed with the following day, ending in the evening.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Where the Day Begins or Ends, and Where the First Day of the World Occurred

STUDENT. Where does the natural day properly receive its beginning and its end?  
MASTER. According to the preference of different peoples, the natural day is said to begin in different ways.

STUDENT. How so?  
MASTER. The Hebrews, Chaldaeans, and Persians, following the course of the day according to the order of the first creation, begin from morning and bring it around to morning, placing the time of shadows after the light. The Egyptians, by contrast, reckon from sunset to sunset. The Romans reckon from the middle of the night to the middle of the night. The Athenians preferred to count their days from midday to midday.

STUDENT. In what place, precisely, did the first day of the world occur?  
MASTER. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which we believe light was first formed; and thus those first three days passed without any measurement in hours, since the stars had not yet been made. Finally, on the fourth morning—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—the sun and the stars were created to serve as signs, seasons, days, and years.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Week

STUDENT. What is a week?  
MASTER. The course of seven days.

STUDENT. From where is “week” derived?  
MASTER. The week received its name from the number seven. For *hebdomada* in Greek is *septimana* in Latin, because it contains seven mornings—that is, seven days.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Kinds of Weeks

STUDENT. Is the week uniform in its kinds or many-formed?  
MASTER. It is certainly many-formed, because by the authority of Holy Scripture it is distinguished into many kinds.

STUDENT. How so?  
MASTER. The first and unique week, from which the others take their form, is exalted by divine activity: for the Lord completed the adornment of the world in six days and rested from his works on the seventh.

After the example of this divine week, a second week was commanded for human observance, as the Lord says: “For six days you shall labor and do all your work. But on the seventh day, the Sabbath of the Lord your God, you shall do no work,” and so forth.

The third kind of week is observed in the celebration of Pentecost, completed by seven weeks of days and one day—that is, by fifty days. On that day Moses received the law from the Lord on the mountain, and Christ sent from heaven the grace of the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire.

The fourth was the week of the seventh month, which was almost entirely devoted to splendid solemnities, when the Day of Atonement and the feast of Tabernacles were celebrated according to the law.

The fifth week is that of the seventh year, during which the people, by command of the law, abstained entirely from agricultural labor, as the Lord says: “For six years you shall sow your field; in the seventh you shall cease.”

The sixth is the week of the Jubilee, that is, of remission. It is formed by seven weeks of years, that is, forty-nine years. When this period was complete—that is, when the fiftieth year finally began—the trumpets sounded more loudly, and the ancient possession returned to everyone according to the law.

The seventh kind of week is the one used by the prophet Daniel. Following the manner of the law, it comprises each week in seven years, but by a new method shortens those years by assigning twelve lunar months to each. It does not add the embolismic months—which ordinarily accrue from the eleven epact days of the years—one in the third or second year according to the ancestral law; rather, when they have increased to the number twelve, it inserts them all together as a complete year.

STUDENT. If these seven kinds of weeks signify anything mystical, I ask you to say what it is.  
MASTER. Therefore, if I am not mistaken, all these kinds look toward one end: they admonish us, after the perfection of good works, to hope for perpetual rest in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Naming of the Days

STUDENT. Now state the correct and authoritative naming of the days of the week.  
MASTER. In ancient times the week was reckoned in this way among the people of God: First of the Sabbath, or One of the Sabbath, or of the Sabbaths; Second of the Sabbath; Third of the Sabbath; Fourth of the Sabbath; Fifth of the Sabbath; Sixth of the Sabbath; Seventh of the Sabbath, or the Sabbath.

This does not mean that all could be days of sabbaths—that is, days of rest—but that, from the day of rest which stood out as unique in its worship and name, the first, second, third, and the others were each designated according to their order.

STUDENT. From where, then, did the names now used by modern people arise?  
MASTER. From the ancient superstition of the pagans. When the pagans learned the observance of the week from the people of Israel, they immediately diverted it to the honor of their own gods: dedicating the first day to the Sun, the second to the Moon, the third to Mars, the fourth to Mercury, the fifth to Jupiter, the sixth to Venus, and the seventh to Saturn. Thus they consecrated their days to the same monsters as the wandering stars.

For they imagined that they received spirit from the Sun, body from the Moon, heat from Mars, wisdom and speech from Mercury, moderation from Jupiter, pleasure from Venus, and sluggishness from Saturn. Consequently, they surrendered themselves to such great error, choosing to serve the creature rather than the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Weekdays

STUDENT. But if there is any remedy for this error, tell me.  
MASTER. One has indeed been found. For Pope Sylvester taught the clergy to use the weekday names. He called the first day, on which light was made in the beginning and Christ’s resurrection was celebrated, Sunday, according to the ancient custom. Then he retained from the Old Scripture the second weekday, third weekday, fourth weekday, fifth weekday, and sixth weekday, adding the Sabbath of his own accord.

STUDENT. From where is *feria* derived?  
MASTER. From *fari*, “to speak.” Therefore Sunday, on which God said, “Let there be light,” may be called the first weekday. The remaining weekdays are then numbered from the first.

STUDENT. How many hours does a week contain?  
MASTER. CLXVII.

STUDENT. How many points?  
MASTER. DCLXII.

STUDENT. How many minutes?  
MASTER. [Note: [Col. 0682D] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [ID]CLXXX.

STUDENT. How many parts?  
MASTER. [II]DXX.

STUDENT. How many moments?  
MASTER. [III]DCCXX.

STUDENT. How many ostenta?  
MASTER. [X]LXXX.

STUDENT. How many atoms?  
MASTER. [III] thousand thousands and [D]CC[XC]. DCCCC.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Months

STUDENT. What is a month?  
MASTER. The lunar circuit through the zodiac.

STUDENT. From where is “month” derived?  
MASTER. From the moon, which is called *mene* in Greek. Among the Greeks, too, months are called *menes*. Likewise among the Hebrews, as Jerome testifies, one month, which they call *Jare*, gave its name to the months. Hence Jesus son of Sirach, speaking of the moon, says: “The month is according to its name.”

STUDENT. Does a month belong to the sun or to the moon?  
MASTER. To both, but more properly to the moon. Therefore I think it should be defined more correctly as the circuit and renewal of lunar light, from one new moon to the next.

A solar month, however, is the sun’s passage through the twelfth part of the zodiac—that is, the circle of the zodiac—which is completed in thirty days and ten and a half hours, being twenty-two and a half hours longer than a lunar month. For a solar month, when the whole year is divided equally into twelve parts, contains thirty days, ten hours, and a half.

A lunar month naturally contains twenty-nine days and twelve hours. But because this reckoning was difficult, the ancient Romans decreed that some solar months should have thirty-one days, some thirty, and one twenty-eight. They wished six lunar months to have thirty days and the other six twenty-nine.

STUDENT. Which solar months have thirty-one days?  
MASTER. Seven: January, March, May, July, August, October, and December.

STUDENT. Which have thirty?  
MASTER. Four: April, June, September, and November. February alone has twenty-eight days.

STUDENT. Which lunar months, as you say, have thirty days?  
MASTER. The lunar months of January and March, May and July, September and November.

STUDENT. Which have twenty-nine?  
MASTER. All the rest.

STUDENT. Who are said to have first discovered the reckoning of the months?  
MASTER. If I am not mistaken, the Chaldaeans, from whom the entire discipline of astrology began. From them, as Josephus testifies, the patriarch Abraham learned and came to know God through the revolutions of the heavenly bodies; and, having soon understood that discipline more truly, he brought it to the Egyptians while he was an exile among them.

Although Scripture does not openly say so, it should not be believed that the ancients who lived before the flood were entirely without knowledge of this art, since many of them are recorded as having pleased God, such as righteous Abel, Enoch, who walked with God and was taken away, and Noah, who was a perfect man in his generations.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Months of the Hebrews

STUDENT. Who are said to have first observed months?  
MASTER. The Hebrews, to whom the Lawgiver said concerning the month of Passover: “Let this month be for you the beginning of months among the months of the year.”

STUDENT. How do the Hebrews name their months, and in what order do they count them?  
MASTER. The Hebrews, who reckon their months according to the course of the moon, call the first month, in which they celebrate Passover, Nisan; the second they call Jar; the third, Sivan; the fourth, Thamul; the fifth, Alo; the sixth, Elul; the seventh, Theseri; the eighth, Maresuan; the ninth, Kasleu; the tenth, Tebet; the eleventh, Sabath; and the twelfth, Adar.

Because of the lunar cycle, which consists of twenty-nine and a half days, they alternate months of thirty and twenty-nine days and, after the completion of the second or third year, intercalate an additional month, which is formed from the eleven epact days of the years.

STUDENT. To which Roman month should we most correctly assign the first Hebrew month?  
MASTER. April, because in it the Paschal moon either ends or, beginning in it, runs for the greater part of the month.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Months of the Egyptians

STUDENT. How do the Egyptians, who are known to have learned astrology from Abraham, reckon their months?  
MASTER. According to the course of the sun, assigning thirty days to each month.

STUDENT. What do they call them?  
MASTER. They call the first month, which they begin in autumn, that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, Thoth; the second, Faovi; the third, Athyr; the fourth, Choeac; the fifth, Thubi; the sixth, Methir; the seventh, Famenoth; the eighth, Farmuthi; the ninth, Pachom; the tenth, Pauni; the eleventh, Epifi; and the twelfth, Mesori.

They end this month on the tenth day before the Kalends of September and call the remaining five days epagomenal, intercalary, or added days. To these they also attach, every fourth year, the sixth day that is formed from the quarter-days. Consequently, their first years begin on the third day before the Kalends of September after the leap year, while the others begin on the fourth day before those same Kalends.

Nor, after the intercalated quarter-day, can they in any way bring their reckoning of the moon or the observance of their festivals into harmony with the course of our year before the time of our intercalation, which occurs on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Months of the Greeks

STUDENT. Since you have spoken of the months of the Hebrews and Egyptians, it remains for you to speak of the Greek and Roman months, which are known to have received the liberal disciplines from the Greeks.  
MASTER. The sequence of the Greek and Roman months is nearly the same, except that the Greeks observe no division of Kalends, Nones, and Ides in their months, just as the Egyptians do not; rather, they count simply by a number running from beginning to end.

The Greeks arranged a fixed cycle within the twelve months of the revolving year. Most of them, beginning their year from the Kalends of December, mark their months with the same number of days as the Romans.

Among them December itself is called Apileos; January, Eudynios; February, Peritios; March, Distros; April, Xanthicos; May, Artemisios; June, Desios; July, Panemos; August, Loos; September, Gorpieos; October, Hyperberetheos; and November, Dios.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Months of the Romans

STUDENT. By what authorities were the Roman months arranged?  
MASTER. Romulus first arranged ten months among them, some of thirty days and others of thirty-one. Beginning with March, he placed December last.

But since this number agreed neither with the course of the sun nor with the calculations of the moon, Numa Pompilius followed. He added fifty days so that the year might extend to CCCLIV days, the length he believed was completed by twelve lunar cycles.

After adding those fifty days, he added six more, taken from the six months that had thirty days—that is, one from each. He divided the resulting fifty-six days equally into two new months, and of the two he called the first January and wished it to be the first month of the year; he named the second February.

A little later Numa added one day, in honor of the odd number, and gave it to January. But when this arrangement still did not seem fixed in relation to the course of the stars, Gaius Julius Caesar finally imitated the Egyptians and established the year according to the number of the sun, as it is observed today. He added ten days to the former reckoning so that the year would comprise CCCLXV days, the period in which the sun itself traverses the zodiac.

And so that the quarter would not be lost, he decreed that every fourth year the priests responsible for the months and days should intercalate one day, in the month and place where the month had also been intercalated among the ancients—that is, before the last five days of February. He judged that this should be called the leap day.

STUDENT. Explain in how many ways the names of the months are formed and from where they originated.  
MASTER. Months are named in four ways: from idols, from things, from kings, and from numbers.

STUDENT. In how many ways is January named?  
MASTER. January received its name in two ways: from an idol and from a thing.

From an idol, that is, from Janus with two faces, the image of Janus, king of the Epirotes, who, by a devised stratagem, committed himself to fire and thereby won victory for the Romans. The image of Janus had two faces because they worshiped him as a man on one side and as a woman on the other. Hence they called January the month of the two-headed day, looking back toward the end of the past year and forward toward the beginning of the future year.

January is also named from a thing, because it is the door of the year, that is, its beginning.

STUDENT. From where is February named?  
MASTER. From an idol and from a thing.

STUDENT. How so?  
MASTER. From the idol Februus, that is, Pluto, whom the pagans believed to have power over purifications, February received its name. For in that month the Roman state had to be purified, when the prescribed commands—that is, sacrifices—were offered to the spirits of the dead.

Or February was named from *febris*, that is, from cold, because of the month’s cold season.

STUDENT. From where, then, is March named?  
MASTER. From the idol Mars, who was believed to be the father of Romulus and the founder of the Roman race. Or it received its name from a thing, namely from males. For at that time all living creatures of the earth desire males for the pleasure of intercourse.

STUDENT. In what ways is April named?  
MASTER. In two ways. From an idol, namely Venus, who is said to have been the mother of Aeneas. *Aphron* in Greek means “foam.” Venus was believed to have arisen from it, and among the Greeks she was called *Afrilis* or *Afronia*.

It is also named from a thing, from “opening,” as though from little openings. In this month, when clouds, frosts, and winter storms have been removed, the sky, the earth, and the sea open themselves to sailors, farmers, and astrologers. Trees and herbs, and also all living creatures, begin to open themselves toward producing offspring.

STUDENT. In how many ways is May named?  
MASTER. In two ways: from the idol Maius, whom they wished to be Jupiter, as though preeminent in majesty; or from Maia, the mother of Mercury. It is also named from a thing, from the maiores, the elders of the Romans, whom Romulus decided should give it this name.

STUDENT. From where does June receive its name?  
MASTER. From Juno, daughter of Saturn and sister of Jupiter. Or from the iuniores, the younger men of Rome, who defended the republic by arms.

STUDENT. From where did July receive its name?  
MASTER. From Julius Caesar, because Gaius Julius Caesar, who first seized imperial power among the Romans, was created on the fourth day before the Ides of July. Previously, when the months were counted from March, it was called Quintilis, taking its name from the number five.

STUDENT. From where did August receive its name?  
MASTER. From Octavian Caesar Augustus, who on the Kalends of this month defeated Antony and Cleopatra and consolidated the power of the Roman people. Since he had assumed the name Augustus from this event, he wished, by decree of the Senate, that the month should bear this name in his memory.

STUDENT. From where is September named?  
MASTER. From a number, because it is the seventh month from March.

STUDENT. From where do you judge October, November, and December to have been named?  
MASTER. Similarly from a number and from rain, because at these times rains threaten the earth.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Kalends, Nones, and Ides

STUDENT. I ask you, then, to explain the Kalends, Nones, and Ides.  
MASTER. I shall do so.

The Kalends derived their name from Greek, because *kalo* is a Greek verb meaning “I call.” In ancient times, responsibility was assigned to the lesser pontiff to observe the first appearance of the new moon and report it to the king of sacrifices.

After the king and the lesser pontiff had celebrated the sacrifice, the same pontiff, having called (*calata*) the people to the Capitol beside the Curia Calabra, which is close to the hut of Romulus, announced how many days remained from the Kalends to the Nones. When five remained, he proclaimed it by repeating the word *calo* five times; when seven remained, he repeated it seven times. They decided to call the first of those days that were proclaimed by calling the Kalends.

From this the curia to which they were summoned received the name Calabra, and the assembly received its name because the whole people were called into it.

The lesser pontiff announced by calling the number of days remaining until the Nones because, after the new moon, the country people were required to gather in the city on the day of the Nones, to receive from the king of sacred rites the reasons for the festivals and to learn what had to be done in that month.

Hence some think that the Nones were so called as the beginning of a new observance, or because from that day eight days were always counted to the Ides.

It was decided to call the day that divides the month the Ides. In the Etruscan language *induere* means “to divide.” Hence *vidua* may mean “very divided,” that is, greatly separated; or *vidua*, “separated from a husband.”

Some think that the Ides were named by a Greek word from a form called *idea* among the Greeks, because on that day the moon displays its full form.

STUDENT. How many hours does a month have?  
MASTER. A proper month, which has thirty days, contains DCCXX hours.

STUDENT. How many points?
