MASTER. [Note: [Col. 0687A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [II]DCCCLXXX.

STUDENT. How many minutes?  
MASTER. [VII]CC.

STUDENT. How many moments?  
MASTER. [XXVII]DCCCDCCC.

STUDENT. How many ostenta?  
MASTER. [XL]I and CC.

STUDENT. How many atoms?  
MASTER. One hundred and sixty times one hundred thousand, and [CCXLIII]CC.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Four Changes of the Seasons

STUDENT. I would like to hear from you what the change that you counted in the sequence of times signifies.  
MASTER. The changes, which some call seasons, are four: winter, spring, summer, and autumn.

STUDENT. From where are they called changes?  
MASTER. Because they yield and succeed one another in turn.

STUDENT. From where are these same periods called seasons?  
MASTER. Because, compared with one another according to a certain similarity of their qualities, they revolve and preserve the tempering necessary for earthly fruits to be born and ripened.

STUDENT. How so?  
MASTER. Winter, since the sun is farther away, is cold and moist. Spring, when the sun returns above the earth, is moist and warm. Summer, when the sun burns above it, is hot and dry. Autumn, when the sun descends toward lower regions, is dry and cold.

Thus, as each embraces what surrounds it with a moderate balance, everything is enclosed together like a sphere. The elements of the world are likewise distinguished by these qualities, which are individually different but joined to one another in mutual association: earth is dry and cold; water, cold and moist; air, moist and warm; fire, warm and dry. Therefore earth is compared with autumn, water with winter, air with spring, and fire with summer.

STUDENT. From where is spring named?  
MASTER. Because in it all things *vernant*, that is, grow green.

STUDENT. From where is summer named?  
MASTER. From the heat that is present in it for ripening fruits.

STUDENT. From where is autumn named?  
MASTER. From the autumnal gathering of the fruits collected in it.

STUDENT. From where is winter named?  
MASTER. From cold. Moreover, winter is interpreted by learned men as sterility.

STUDENT. Where does each of these seasons receive its beginning?  
MASTER. Isidore, bishop of Seville, said that winter begins on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, spring on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, summer on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, and autumn on the tenth day before the Kalends of September.

The Greeks and Romans, whose authority in such disciplines we are accustomed to follow rather than that of the Spaniards, decree that winter begins on the seventh day before the Ides of November, spring on the seventh day before the Ides of February, summer on the seventh day before the Ides of May, and autumn on the seventh day before the Ides of August. They mark the beginnings of winter and summer by the evening or morning rising and setting of the Pleiades; likewise, they establish the beginning of spring and autumn when the Pleiades rise and set approximately in the middle of the day or night.

Pliny the Second also judged in Book II of his *Natural History* that the seasons should be distinguished in the same way. The holy man Anatolius, a member of the Church, says likewise in his *Paschal Work*:

> You should not be unaware that the boundaries of the four seasons mentioned above, although they approach the Kalends of the following months, each nevertheless retains the middle of its season—that is, of spring, summer, autumn, and winter—and the beginnings of the seasons do not start from the point at which the Kalends of the months begin. Rather, each season must begin in such a way that the vernal equinox divides the season from the first day of spring, the summer solstice divides summer, the autumnal equinox divides autumn, and the winter solstice likewise divides winter.

STUDENT. Do these four seasons therefore have equal length?  
MASTER. They do. According to an equal division, each receives three months, ninety-one days, and seven and a half hours.

STUDENT. How, then, does each season measure out according to hours and the other subdivisions?  
MASTER. Each season contains, according to the reckoning of hours, [Note: [Col. 0688A] Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.] [VII]CXC and one and a half hours; according to points, [VIII]DCCLXVI; according to minutes, [XXI]DXXXV; according to moments, [LXXXV]LX; according to ostenta, [CXXXI]XX; and atoms, four hundred and ninety times one hundred thousand and [DX]LC.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Years

STUDENT. What is a year?  
MASTER. The circuit and return of the sun through twelve months.

STUDENT. From where is “year” derived?  
MASTER. From renewing all things that have passed according to the natural order. Or the year received its name from the circuit of time, because the ancients used *annus* for “around,” as Cato says in the *Origins*: “the year is a boundary,” that is, “a boundary around.” And *ambire* means “to go around.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. How Many Kinds of Years There Are
DISC. How many kinds of years are there?

MAG. Seventeen.

DISC. How so?

MAG. For the Moon has five kinds of year, while the Sun has three. There are also the years of the individual planets—that is, of the wandering stars—named from the stars whom they serve. There is the year of the weeks; there is the seventh year of rest according to the Law; there is also the year of the Jubilee; and there is the year of all the planets, which is called the great year.

DISC. I ask you to explain these according to their individual kinds.

MAG. The first lunar type is when the Moon, traversing the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, returns to the sign from which it departed. The second is longer by two days and four hours. The third, completed in twelve such months—that is, in 304 days—is called the common year. The fourth, called in Greek *embolismus*—that is, an intercalation—has thirteen months, or 384 days. The fifth occurs when, after nineteen years and after the lunar leap has passed, the Moon returns to the same ages.

The sixth year is the solar year, when the Sun returns to the same places among the stars after 365 days and six hours. The seventh is likewise solar: when twice six is inserted in the fourth year, there are 366 days. The eighth is likewise solar, when the Sun completes the cycle of the concurrent numbers in twenty-eight years.

The ninth year is reckoned according to the star called Mercury, and is completed in 339 days. The tenth year is reckoned according to the star called Venus, and is completed in 348 days. The eleventh is the year according to the star called Mars, which is completed after two years. The twelfth year is according to the star called Jupiter, and is completed after twelve years. The thirteenth year is according to the star called Saturn, and is completed after thirty years.

The fourteenth year is according to the weeks of the whole year—that is, fifty-two—and has 364 days. The fifteenth is the year of rest of the seventh year according to the Law, in which the people of God were commanded to abstain from agricultural labor. The sixteenth year is the kind of year called the Jubilee, which is the year of remission, and is completed in fifty years. The seventeenth year is the one called the great year, the year of the planets, when all the stars return to the place where they were first established; it is completed in 532 years.

DISC. How many hours, then, does the solar year contain, which consists of 365 days and a quarter?

MAG. IXDCCLXVI.

DISC. How many points?

MAG. [XXXV]CXC.

DISC. How many minutes?

MAG. [LXXXVII]DCLX.

DISC. How many moments?

MAG. [CCCL]DCXL.

DISC. How many portents (*ostenta*)?

MAG. [DXXV]DCCCCLX.

DISC. How many atoms?

MAG. Ten times nineteen times one hundred times one hundred thousand, and four thousand thousands, and [DCCCCXXXI]LX.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the planets and the origin of their names

DISC. Since, in speaking of the solar and lunar years, you added the years of the five planets, I ask you not to begrudge an explanation of the nature of those stars.

MAG. There are seven planets, which are carried in a contrary course against the world: the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Thus, while the heavenly sphere inclines from east to west, they turn back toward the east through the zodiac; and, as seemed right to the wise men of this world, they regulate the speed of the heavens, lest it be hurled forward by the excessive rotation of its course.

DISC. Why is the Sun so called?

MAG. Because it alone shines among all the stars. For when the Sun rises, the other stars immediately conceal their rays; and, as some think, by its appearance it grants to the Moon and all the stars the ability to shine, since they gleam not by their own light but by light borrowed from the Sun. Hence the poet says:

> “And the shining sphere of the Moon and the Titanian stars  
> An inner spirit nourishes.”

DISC. Why is the Moon so called?

MAG. The Moon is called *luna*, as though *lucina*, with the middle syllable removed. Of it Virgil says:

> “... Chaste Lucina, favor me.”

It received its name by derivation from the light of the Sun, because it receives light from him and gives back what it has received.

DISC. Why are the stars called *stellae*?

MAG. From *stare*, “to stand,” because they always stand fixed in the heavens and do not fall. For what we see sliding from heaven like stars are not stars, but little fires fallen from the ether. This happens when the wind, seeking the higher regions, draws the ethereal fire along with it; the fire, dragged in its course, imitates falling stars. Stars cannot fall. They are immobile, as was said above, and are carried fixed together with the heavens.

DISC. If the stars are fixed in heaven, as you assert, why are the planets so called?

MAG. The planets alone are not fixed like the others, but are carried through the air. They are called planets from *apo tēs planēs* [ἀπὸ τῆς πλάνης], that is, “from wandering.” For sometimes they move toward the south, sometimes toward the north; very often against the world, and sometimes with the world. These motions are called retrograde, anomalous, contrary-moving, and stationary.

DISC. How so?

MAG. A star’s retrogradation occurs when it performs its motion and at the same time appears to move backward. They are called anomalous when they add or subtract small intervals. They are contrary-moving, or advancing, when they appear to perform their customary motion and nevertheless advance in some way contrary to custom. They are called stationary because, although a star is always moving, it nevertheless appears to stand still in certain places.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the course of the planets through the zodiacal belt, and the nature of the zodiacal belt

DISC. Since I have heard you say that the passage of the planets occurs in the zodiac, I ask you to explain the nature of the zodiac itself and their course.

MAG. I shall do so. The zodiac, or “sign-bearing” circle, is an oblique circle consisting of twelve signs, through which the wandering stars are carried; and nothing else is inhabited on earth except what lies beneath them. The remaining regions are desolate around the poles.

The sign-bearing circle is 365 parts and a quarter of one part long along the circuit of heaven, and twelve parts wide across it. The star of Venus alone exceeds it by two parts. The Moon also wanders through its entire width, but does not exceed it at all. The star of Mercury ranges most widely within it, though out of the twelve parts—for there are twelve parts in its width, as we have said—it traverses no more than eight, and not equally: two in its middle, four above it, and two below.

The Sun is carried in the middle, between two parts, in an unequal, winding course like that of a dragon. The star of Mars extends four parts in the middle; Jupiter, two in the middle and two above it; Saturn, two, like the Sun.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the twelve signs

DISC. I should like you to explain from where the signs of the zodiac derived their names.

MAG. The twelve signs took their names either from the causes associated with the year or from the fables of the pagans. They assign the Ram to the month of March because of Ammonian Jupiter; hence they also fashion the horns of a ram on his statue. They assign the Bull to April because of the same Jupiter, since he was fabled to have been changed into a bull.

They assign Castor and Pollux to May, because of their distinguished virtue. They assign the Crab to June, when the Sun returns toward the lower regions, because the Crab is accustomed, when driven, to direct its course backward. They assign the Lion, whom Hercules killed, to July, because of the force of the heat. They assign the Virgin to August, because then the earth, exhausted by heat, produces nothing. They assign the Balance to September because of the equality of day and night.

They take the Scorpion and the Archer, fashioned with horses’ legs, for October and November, because of the seasonal “flows” of those months. They assign Capricorn to December because of Jupiter’s nurse, the goat, whose lower extremities are painted like those of a fish, since the end of that month is rainy. They assign Aquarius to January and the Fish to February because these are rainy months.

Each sign is reckoned as thirty parts, three decades of ten each, because the Sun traverses it in thirty days and ten and a half hours, always beginning from the middle of the month—that is, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends. Hence some of the ancients thought that a sign belonged to the following month, since each sign extends as far as the middle of that month, and that it should be assigned to it, as the poet who sang of this in heroic verses said:

> “You see the Ram freezing the April Kalends;  
> May marvels at the horns of Agenor’s Bull,”

and so forth in the same manner.

These signs are of such great extent that they cannot rise, set, or move from their position in less than a period of two hours.

## CHAPTER XL. Demonstration of the signs through the Sun’s course

DISC. I should indeed like you to give me some information about this.

MAG. Knowledge of these signs is better acquired from someone speaking and pointing with his finger than from someone writing, because they become recognizable through the stars arranged within them. They cannot be fully described except by someone who possesses the discipline of astronomy and knows how to disclose and point out the positions of the stars.

Nevertheless, an inquisitive investigator of these signs can acquire some knowledge of them if he carefully observes the Sun’s and Moon’s courses through them, their entries and departures. For the Sun remains in each sign for thirty days, ten hours, and a half, and then enters another sign, which he similarly traverses in thirty days, ten hours, and a half before entering a third. Thus he makes the sign that he had previously left recognizable by the stars appearing in the east before the rising of dawn.

Three signs are always full of daylight around the Sun: the one he has most recently left, the one in which he is present, and the one into which he is about to enter. The Moon likewise displays the signs by her course. For she passes through each sign in two days, half an hour, and two-thirds of an hour. If a calculator accurately learns the computation made from her passage through the signs, he will be able to infer their positions from her condition.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Moon’s course through the signs

DISC. I should like you to explain that computation to me.

MAG. Every day the Moon advances four points, whether, while waxing, she moves farther from the Sun, or, while waning, becomes nearer to the Sun than she was the previous day. Each sign has ten points—that is, two hours, as we also noted above. For five points of the Moon make one hour.

Therefore, if you wish to know in which sign the Moon is, take whatever lunar day you wish—for example, the fifth—and multiply it by four: the result is twenty. Divide by ten: twice ten. Thus the fifth Moon is always two signs distant from the Sun.

Again, take the eighth Moon and multiply it by four: the result is thirty-two. Divide by ten: three times ten, with two remaining. Thus the eighth Moon is always separated from the Sun by three signs and two points.

Understand the two points as six parts—that is, as the distance the Sun traverses in the zodiac in six days. A point indeed contains three parts, because each sign has ten points and thirty parts.

And lest you perhaps fall into suspicion that the computation is misleading, consider the diameter of heaven, where no one doubts that the fifteenth Moon is located. Multiply fifteen by four: the result is sixty. Divide by ten: six times ten. Thus the fifteenth Moon is always separated from the Sun by six signs—that is, by half the heavenly sphere—whether you look before or behind.

Finally, when the lunar orb is fullest, you see it opposite the Sun: the Moon is low while the Sun is high, and the Moon is high while the Sun is low. For when the Moon is full while the Sun occupies the summer circle, she occupies the winter circle; when she is full while the Sun is on the opposite side, she is shown by the longest night to be ascending the solstitial circle. But when the Sun holds one equinox, the Moon at full holds the other. As many parts as the Sun has traversed beyond the equinox or solstice that he had most recently passed, so many parts the full Moon is seen to have entered in the opposite equinox or solstice.

[Note: [Col. 0691D] See Cotelerius, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. II, p. 550.]

DISC. After how many days will the Sun ascend that part of heaven to which the third Moon will arrive?

MAG. In a full month and six days.

## CHAPTER XLII. A computation for investigating the Moon’s course

DISC. Show me how.

MAG. The Sun completes one part of his zodiac every day. We should understand the parts of the zodiac as nothing other than the Sun’s daily advances in heaven. The Moon, however, completes thirteen parts of that same zodiac each day—that is, four points and one part.

Since the Moon completes thirteen parts while the Sun completes one, it follows—as we explained above—that in her daily advance she is separated from the Sun by no more than four points, or twelve parts. Let him therefore place the Moon wherever he wishes to begin his computation—for example, the first Moon on the Kalends of January. Once she has passed through that first night and day, she occupies the place in heaven that the Sun will occupy after completing the thirteenth day of that month.

When it is the second Moon, multiply two by four: the result is eight. Then, to proceed from points to parts, multiply eight by three: the result is twenty-four. Therefore, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, the second Moon occupies that part of heaven which the Sun will occupy after completing the twenty-fourth day from that point.

When it is the third Moon, multiply three by four: the result is twelve. Divide by ten: one ten, with two points remaining—that is, six parts. Therefore, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, the fourth Moon occupies that part of heaven which the Sun will occupy after a whole month and six days: after the sixth day following the third day before the Nones of January, that is, after the day completing the third day before the Nones of February.

To reach the total, take the thirtieth Moon, which then occurs on the third day before the Kalends of February. Multiply it by four: the result is 120. Divide by ten: twelve times ten. The thirtieth Moon moves through that part of heaven which the Sun will occupy after twelve months have been completed—that is, after the entire annual cycle has passed.

It should be noted that the ten and a half hours which lie outside the thirty parts of each sign are disregarded in the computation because they do not amount to a full part of twenty-four hours; they are nevertheless included within the aforesaid number of twelve months.

## CHAPTER XLIII. A computation of the number of hours during which the Moon shines

DISC. I should like you to explain by some computation how I can determine for how many hours the Moon shines during each night of her age.

MAG. If you wish to know for how many hours any Moon shines, take the age of the Moon about which you are asking. Multiply it by four, because the first Moon shines for four points. This number is added daily from the second Moon up to the full Moon; thereafter it is subtracted at equal intervals as the Moon diminishes. Thus the first and the thirtieth Moon shine for the same amount of time, as do the second and the twenty-ninth.

Therefore, if you wish to know, for example, how many hours the fifth Moon shines, multiply five by four: the result is twenty. Divide by five: four times five, the result being twenty. The fifth Moon shines for four hours. The twenty-fifth Moon does so likewise.

Again, if you wish to know how many hours the tenth Moon shines, multiply ten by four: the result is forty. Divide by five: eight times five, the result being forty. The tenth Moon shines for eight hours. The twentieth Moon does so likewise.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the magnitude of the Sun or Moon

DISC. I should like you to say something about the magnitude of the Sun and Moon.

MAG. They say that the Sun’s fire is nourished by water, and that the Sun is much larger than the Moon, while the Moon is larger than the earth; hence she also appears to all people to be of one and the same size. The fact that the Sun appears to be only a cubit in size is caused by the great distance of his height. Otherwise he would appear larger when rising to the Indians and when setting to the Britons.

Since the Sun is fiery by nature, he also increases his heat by his excessive motion. By his varying course he divides days and months, seasons and years, and, by approaching or withdrawing according to the seasons, distributes the temper of the air, lest, if he always remained in the same places, one region be consumed by heat and another by cold.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the nature and position of the Moon

They say that the Moon neither diminishes nor grows, but that, illuminated by the Sun, she gradually turns toward us the bright part that she has toward him, either by withdrawing from him or by approaching him; and that, as the day increases, the new Moon is seen lying on her back, as it were above the Sun, with its northern side turned toward its rising.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the eclipse of the Sun or Moon

DISC. I ask you to explain the cause of the loss of light of either star.

MAG. They say that the Sun is hidden from us by the intervention of the Moon, and the Moon by the interposition of the earth. But an eclipse of the Sun can occur only at the very last or the very first Moon, which they call the conjunction; an eclipse of the Moon, only at the full Moon. It is not possible for the whole Sun to be taken away from the earth when the Moon intervenes, if the earth is larger than the Moon. In every year, however, eclipses of both stars occur on appointed days and hours beneath the earth, although, when they occur above, they are not always visible everywhere—sometimes because of clouds, and more often because the globe of the earth obstructs them through the convexities of the world.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Where an eclipse does not occur, and why

The inhabitants of the East do not perceive evening eclipses of the Sun and Moon, nor do those living in the West perceive morning eclipses, because of the intervening globe of the earth. For neither night nor day, although the same night or day exists simultaneously over the whole world, brings night to one side of the globe or day through its circuit.

In the time of Alexander the Great, the Moon was eclipsed in Arabia at the second hour of the night, while in Sicily she was rising at that same time. The eclipse of the Sun that occurred during the consulship of Hispanius and Frontegius, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, was perceived in Campania between the seventh and eighth hours of the day, and in Armenia between the tenth and eleventh.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the appearance and nature of the planets

DISC. Tell me what colors the planets have, so that I may perhaps recognize them by this means, and whether they change colors or not.

MAG. Each has its own color: Saturn is white, Jupiter bright, Mars fiery; Lucifer joyful, Vesper radiant, Mercury gleaming, the Moon gentle, and the Sun fiery when he rises, later shining brightly.

But the principle of color is modified by altitude. For the planets take on the likeness of the regions of air into which they descend; and, as they approach, the circle of another atmospheric current tinges them: a colder current with pallor, a hotter one with redness, a windy one with a gloomy appearance. The Sun, the junctions of the apses, and the outermost orbits produce blackness and darkness.

DISC. In what place, or in which signs, are they at present?

MAG. At present—that is, in the year 820 of the Lord’s incarnation, in July, on the ninth day of the month—the Sun is in the twenty-third part of Cancer, the Moon in the ninth part of Taurus, Saturn’s star in the sign of Aries, Jupiter’s in Libra, and Mars’ in Pisces. The stars of Venus and Mercury, since they are now near the Sun in the daylight, are not visible, and therefore it cannot be seen in which sign they remain.

DISC. I ask you briefly to enumerate the other stars that are outside the zodiac, and to explain which are on its right-hand side and which on its left.

MAG. If you were content with an account only of the planets’ course, I should think that enough had already been said to you. But since, in your excessive curiosity, you proceed to inquire into the other signs that stand throughout the entire circuit of the heavenly sphere, I think it necessary first to explain briefly the position and nature of that sphere according to the opinion of our predecessors, and then to answer your question concerning the others.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the nature of heaven

DISC. Would that you would do so!

MAG. Heaven is of a subtle and fiery nature, round, and gathered at equal distances on every side from the center of the earth. Hence the wise men of the world have said that its middle and convex surface, wherever it is seen, revolves every day with indescribable speed, so that it would fall if the counter-course of the planets did not restrain it. They relied on the evidence of the stars, which always circle around in a fixed course, while those in the northern regions complete shorter circuits around the pole.

The extreme points of the axis around which the sphere revolves are called the poles; they waste away in icy cold. One of them rises toward the northern region and is called the Boreal pole; the other, bending toward the south and opposite the earth, is called the southern pole. Holy Scripture calls the inner regions of the south by the name “the South.”

In this sphere, the wise men have said, there are five circles.

## CHAPTER L. On the five circles of the world

The first is the northern circle, uninhabitable because of the cold; its stars never set for us. The second is the solstitial circle, on the side of the sign-bearing circle, highest for us toward the northern region, temperate and habitable. The third is the equinoctial circle, passing through the middle circuit of the zodiacal sphere, torrid and uninhabitable. The fourth is the wintry circle, toward the southern pole from the lowest part of the sign-bearing circle, temperate and habitable. The fifth is the southern circle, around the southern pole, which is covered by the earth, cold and uninhabitable.

The three middle circles distinguish the unequal lengths of the seasons, when the Sun occupies one at the solstice, another at the equinox, and the third in winter. The outermost circles are always deprived of the Sun. Hence, one day’s voyage northward from the island of Thyle, a frozen sea is found.

## CHAPTER LI. On those signs of the stars that are outside the zodiac

DISC. I approve and gratefully accept this. But, concerning the position of the stars, as you promised me, I ask you to explain it.

MAG. There are signs outside those that lie in the zodiac, as Aratus’ *Phaenomena* testifies, thirty in number. The horoscope separates some toward the north and others toward the south.

DISC. Which are those toward the north?

MAG. First, the two Bears: namely, Helice, also called the Great Bear, and Phoenice or Cynosura, also called the Little Bear. Then the Dragon, which contains both Bears, turning its head above Helice and encircling the tail of Phoenice.

Next comes Hercules, said to be resting on the Serpent with bent knee, his club cast aside and covered with a lion’s hide. Then the Crown, with nine stars placed in a circle. Then the Serpent-Bearer, also called Asclepius, standing above the Scorpion and holding a serpent in his hands.

Likewise Arcas, also called Boötes, is said to be the guardian of the wagon. He precedes the Great Bear, which itself follows him. Cepheus and the Eagle are then distinguished by their bright stars, as are Cassiopeia and Andromeda. Next Perseus and the Charioteer shine, along with his Kids. Bellerophon and the Dolphin, the Swan and the Balance, and the Triangle above the head of the Ram are also conspicuous in their places by their brilliance.

DISC. Which are those that the zodiac excludes toward the south?

MAG. Orion, of course, and the Little Dog; the Hare and the Argo; the Whale and Eurus, also called Euridanus. Beneath it lies the bright star called Canopus, which touches the ship’s tiller. There is the Great Fish, also called the South Wind; the Altar; the Centaur with the beast that he holds in his hand; the Serpent, upon whose tail they say the Crow sits, and in whose middle they place the Urn.

The last of all is Anticanus, situated beneath the Twins; it is therefore called Anticanus because it is opposite the Dog.

What astonishing folly among the nations: the stars that God created for the honor of his name and established in the heavens, they have attributed to wicked human beings and to brute animals created on earth.

Besides all these, there is also the Milky Circle, a whiter figure running through the middle of the vault of heaven. People commonly say that it shines in this way from the brilliance of the Sun running through it. But this is futile, since the Sun never touches it except in the region of Sagittarius or Gemini, where the sign-bearing circle encloses the white circle.

DISC. Of what use, then, will these stars be to readers, and in what way do they assist the computist?

MAG. They greatly assist the calculator in determining the hours of the night. They are also extremely useful to travelers and sailors, who observe their colors and courses and infer from them the coming storm or calm.

## CHAPTER LII. On comets

DISC. I have heard certain stars called comets, but you passed over them when counting the stars.

MAG. I did not pass over them through forgetfulness, but in order to preserve the order and speak of them separately, since their nature and course differ from those of the other stars.

Comets are stars crowned with flames, appearing suddenly and portending a change of kingdom, pestilence, wars, winds, and heat. Some are extended like the wandering stars; others remain motionless. Almost all are observed beneath the northern region, in some unspecified part of it, but especially in the white region that has received the name of the Milky Circle. The shortest period during which they are visible is recorded as seven days, the longest as eighty.

At times, even the wandering stars and other stars are scattered and acquire hair. But a comet is never in the setting part of the sky.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the solstices and equinoxes

DISC. Since you have said enough about the position and reckoning of the stars, I think it necessary that you should still speak about the greatest lights, namely the Sun and Moon, and show where the proper place of the equinox and solstice is.

MAG. Most people reckon two solstices, namely the eighth day before the Kalends of January and of July. Likewise there are two equinoxes, namely the eighth day before the Kalends of April and of October, in the eighth parts, that is, of Capricorn and Cancer, Aries and Libra.

But because, as we learned in the Paschal calculation, the vernal equinox is specially marked on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April by the judgment of all Easterners, and especially of the Egyptians, who are known to be most skilled in calculation, we think that the other three turning-points of the seasons also ought to be marked somewhat earlier than popular writings state.

For, to speak briefly about the vernal equinox—which the origin of the world teaches to be the beginning of the aforesaid four annual changes—the rule of ecclesiastical observance, confirmed by the Council of Nicaea, holds that the day of Pascha is to be sought from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April until the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Likewise, the rule of Catholic institution has commanded that Pascha not be celebrated before the passing of the vernal equinox. Therefore, whoever thinks that the equinox falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of April must necessarily either say that it is permissible to celebrate Pascha before the equinox, or deny that it is permissible to celebrate Pascha before the seventh day before the Kalends of April; and must also maintain that the Pascha which the Lord celebrated with his disciples on the day before he suffered either was not on the ninth day before the Kalends of April or was before the equinox.

For not only the institution of our own time but also the legal and Mosaic institution decrees that the feast of Pascha is not to be celebrated before this equinox has passed. As Anatolius testifies, Philo and Josephus clearly teach this, as did their predecessors Agathobulus and Aristobulus of Paneas, instructed by him. Aristobulus was one of the seventy elders sent by the high priests to King Ptolemy to translate the books of the Hebrews into Greek; when they set before the king many things from the traditions of Moses and he questioned them, they answered. Thus, when they expounded the questions of Exodus, they said that Pascha must not be sacrificed before the vernal equinox had passed.

Therefore, to preserve the rule of truth, we must say openly both that Pascha is not to be sacrificed before the equinox and the defeat of darkness, and that this equinox is truly to be assigned to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, as we are taught not only by paternal authority but also by astronomical consideration. By like reasoning, the other three boundaries of the seasons of this kind should be marked some days before the eighth day before the Kalends of the following months.

Accordingly, as we spoke above about the alternations, so now we speak of these four limits. From the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, which is the vernal equinox, to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, there are ninety-one days. From the twelfth day before the Kalends of July to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October there are likewise ninety-one days. From the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January there are likewise ninety-one days. From the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April there are likewise ninety-one days. Altogether these make 363 days, and one day of the annual cycle remains, together with six hours, which are shown to accrue each year because of the calculation of the leap day. If these are divided into four parts and added to the preceding portions, each portion will have ninety-one days, seven hours, and half an hour.

But it should be noted that the equinoctial day is equal throughout the world. With the varying increase of daylight, however, the longest day at Meroë comprises twelve equinoctial hours and eight parts of one hour; at Alexandria, fourteen hours; in Italy, fifteen; and in Britain, seventeen. There, bright summer nights undoubtedly testify to what reason compels us to believe: on the days of the solstice, when the Sun approaches nearer to the pole of the world, lands lying beneath a narrow circuit of light have continuous days for six months, and, conversely, nights at the winter solstice when the Sun has withdrawn. Pytheas of Massilia writes that this occurs on the island of Thule, six days’ voyage north of Britain.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the leap day in the course of the Sun and Moon

DISC. I ask you to explain and set forth to me the calculation of the leap day.

MAG. The leap day is produced from the calculation of the quarter-day over four years, when the Sun returns to the sign from which it departed not in 365 days but with an additional fourth part of a day. For example, if the rising Sun should now enter the equinoctial place of heaven, in the following year he will return to it at midday, in the third year in the evening, in the fourth at midnight, and in the fifth again at sunrise; this necessarily indicates that a day must be added, lest, if it should not be added, after sixty-five years the vernal equinox occur on the winter day. The Egyptians insert this after their year is completed, that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September; the Romans insert it on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, whence it also received its name.

In a shorter and more common explanation, the leap day is produced by the Sun’s delay in not returning completely to the same line after 365 days. If, for example, at the vernal equinox—which according to the Egyptians occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—you carefully observe him rising from the middle of the east, you will find that in the following year, on the same day, he rises somewhat lower; and in the third, fourth, and fifth years you will find that same diminution to increase to such an extent that, unless you add a day beforehand, he will rise from the middle of the east when about to make the equinox on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, preserving the same delay in his other risings.

DISC. Must we observe the calculation of the quarter-day in the Moon’s course?

MAG. Certainly we must. For if you refuse to allow for the Moon’s quarter-day, but in a leap year assign to February the lunar month of the same length as you had previously been accustomed to assign, it will certainly happen that the fourteenth Paschal Moon of that year arrives one day earlier than it ought. Consequently the Paschal calculation will waver, the whole course of the year will soon totter, and the ever-inviolable order of the nineteen-year cycle will be increasingly disturbed and overturned.

Therefore, just as the calculation of the quarter-day directs us to add one day to the solar year in the fourth year, which we call leap year, so we must add one day to the lunar year and assign it to the Moon of February, whether it happens to end before or after the intercalated quarter-day. Thus, the Moon of February, which in other years has twenty-nine days, is reckoned as having thirty in a leap year; and that year, if it is common, is completed with 355 days, but, if embolismic, with 385.

Thus it comes about that in one and the same line, the sixth day before the Kalends of March, the number is doubled both for the Sun and for the Moon. As, for example, in the present year we place the sixth and seventh feria there, so in the same place we should place the sixth and seventh Moon. Always be watchful in this practice, so that when we have made the Moon of February have thirty days in a leap year, on the days of the Kalends of March, except only in the eleventh year of the nineteen-year cycle, the Moon retains the age which it had previously been accustomed to retain.

But by what and how great portions of time this same lunar quarter-day increases requires a more extensive investigation. For, along with the quarter-day itself, the frequent interruption of embolisms and the leap make it impossible for the whole measure of the Moon’s course to be determined exactly.

## CHAPTER LV. A computation for finding the leap year

DISC. I should like you to give me some computation by which I might know whether a leap year, or a year in preparation for the leap day, is occurring.

MAG. If you wish to know this, take however many years have elapsed from the incarnation of the Lord—for example, 820 at present. Divide these by four, because the leap day intervenes after four years have been completed. Four times 200 are 800; four times 5 are 20. Since nothing remains, it is a leap year. If one remains, it is the first year of preparation for the leap day; if two, the second; if three, the third.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the lunar leap.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Lunar Leap

**DISCIPLE.** I ask you to set forth for me an explanation of the lunar leap in the same way as you did concerning the bissextile year.

**MASTER.** The position and the earlier hour of the moon’s illumination produce the lunar leap over nineteen years. For although some people, reckoning each lunar month as twenty-nine and a half days, always alternate their illuminations between midday and midnight, they are not seeking in this the truth of nature but the convenience of calculation. For if you inquire into nature, the moon of the first month—which now becomes illuminated at midday—and that of the second—which now becomes illuminated at midnight—will in the following year be illuminated an hour, ten moments, half a moment, and a nineteenth part of half a moment before midday or midnight.

Yet this distinction does not tend toward the fixed end of an embolismic or common year, but toward an equal division of nineteen years. Thus, over nineteen years, the lunar illumination, anticipating itself, loses the span of one day, and causes the final year of the nineteen-year cycle to be reckoned as having 383 days. If you neglect to make this adjustment for fifteen nineteen-year cycles, the fifteenth moon will meet you where the first is thought to be.

**DISCIPLE.** How much does the lunar leap increase in one year?

**MASTER.** One hour, one point, and a nineteenth part of one point; or, as you may express it otherwise, an hour, ten moments, half a moment, and a nineteenth of half a moment, as we showed above.

**DISCIPLE.** How much in one lunar month?

**MASTER.** Fifty-three moments and five instants. Therefore, in each month, four moments and five instants are lacking for a lunation to reach the full measure of twenty-nine days and twelve hours. In half a lunar month, two moments, two instants, and half an instant are lacking.

**DISCIPLE.** Where, then, is the position of this leap?

**MASTER.** Some think that it should be restored on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, because of the origin of the ordering of the stars: the moon of the month of March, which on that day becomes twenty-nine days old, then passes into newness. But others think that this should rather be done in the moon of the month of November, so that, once these hindrances have been settled together with the end of the preceding year, they may thereafter enter the new year with an unimpeded calculation, following, evidently, the example of the Egyptians, who are said to do this in the penultimate month of their year, which is our July. But whether you do it here, there, or elsewhere, it is necessary, unless I am mistaken, to reckon three months of twenty-nine days each in that place.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Nineteen-Year Cycle

**DISCIPLE.** I would like to hear from you the account of the nineteen-year cycle, which produces the lunar leap and regulates the moon’s course, and to infer it by calculation.

**MASTER.** The Council of Nicaea established the nineteen-year cycle because of the fourteen Paschal moons, since each moon returns to the same point through an unerring course after nineteen years. The cycle is divided into an ogdoad and an hendecad—that is, into eight and eleven years. For eight lunar years exceed the same number of solar years by only two days: one of these is used to complete the hendecad, while the other is consumed by the leap. Otherwise, the solar hendecad would exceed the lunar hendecad by one day.

Although some people try by force to make up these days through the bissextile days of the eight years, the bissextile day is customarily added to the sun in the month of February and does not prejudice the moon’s future reckoning; nor do they add a bissextile day to the hendecad. To put it more plainly: the two lunar days that remain in the ogdoad will complete the two days that are lacking in the hendecad.

## CHAPTER LVIII. A Calculation for Discovering Which Year of the Nineteen-Year Cycle It Is

If, then, you wish to discover by calculation which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take however many years have elapsed since the incarnation of the Lord and always add one. Divide these by nineteen. What remains is the year of the nineteen-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is the nineteenth year.

For example, since at present there are 820 years, add one to them, because the Lord was incarnate in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle; the result is 821. Divide this by nineteen: forty times nineteen gives 760; three times nineteen gives 57. Added to the preceding number, these produce 817. Since four years of the original number remain, it is the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle.

## CHAPTER LIX. On Common Years and Embolismic Years

**DISCIPLE.** I await your explanation of common years and embolisms.

**MASTER.** The same cycle is divided into embolismic and common years, which are known to have been observed also on the authority of the ancient Hebrews. There are twelve common years, that is, years of 354 days. There are seven embolismic years, that is, years containing 384 days.

The first and second years are common; the third is embolismic; the fourth and fifth are common; the sixth is embolismic; the seventh is common; the eighth is embolismic; the ninth and tenth are common; the eleventh is embolismic; the twelfth and thirteenth are common; the fourteenth is embolismic; the fifteenth and sixteenth are common; the seventeenth is embolismic; the eighteenth is common; and the nineteenth is embolismic.

Both kinds of year, as was also said above, begin from the beginning of the first month, which the Hebrews call Nisan—that is, from the illumination of the Paschal moon. The beginning of this month must be observed according to the following rule: the Paschal fourteenth moon must never precede the spring equinox, but must occur either at the equinox itself—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—or after it has passed.

The reason for the embolisms, as Dionysius says, is thought to be that they make up the losses of the common years, so that the lunar course may keep pace with solar time. For although the moon traverses the solar year through each of its months, it cannot complete its full measure within twelve of its own months. Consequently, in common years the moon is seen to fall short of the solar year by eleven days. In embolismic years, however, the moon appears to exceed that same solar year by nineteen days.

The Hebrews, who knew and observed only lunar months according to the Law, completed the twelve months of common years according to the moon’s natural course, with months of thirty and twenty-nine days, and in the third or second year, wherever it was necessary, they added a thirteenth month of thirty days at the end of the year as an embolism.

The Romans, however, who have unequal months, did not wish to insert embolisms at one fixed place, but rather wherever they might find a vacant and suitable place between the Kalends in the middle periods of the year. They therefore said that the first embolismic moon was born on the fourth day before the Nones of December, the second on the fourth day before the Nones of September, the third on the day before the Nones of March, the fourth on the day before the Nones of December, the fifth on the fourth day before the Nones of November, the sixth on the fourth day before the Nones of August, and the seventh on the third day before the Nones of March.

## CHAPTER LX. On the Ogdoad and the Hendecad

**DISCIPLE.** Since you briefly mentioned the ogdoad and the hendecad above, I ask you to explain more fully for what purpose this division was first made.

**MASTER.** It was made because in the eighth and, evidently, the eleventh year the Paschal moon reaches the highest limits of its birth, and each of these years is preceded, contrary to the customary arrangement of embolisms, by one common year.

Or perhaps it was because the ancients thought that eight solar years were equal in number of days to an equal number of lunar years. This was discovered by the more learned teachers of a later age to be impossible unless eleven years were added. As an indication, therefore, of both observations, the entire revolution of the moon has been arranged in ogdoads and hendecads.

The Greeks of old—whom the most ancient Romans are said to have imitated—when they still reckoned years according to the moon’s course, after completing eight common years in the same manner, intercalated three embolismic months together. For if you calculate eight times eleven and a quarter, you will obtain ninety days, that is, three months. Yet by this reasoning they could not attain the fixed truth, as will be clear to anyone who properly calculates and accurately considers the number of the ogdoad or hendecad.

The number itself must therefore be examined, and it must be seen how many days eight solar years contain, excluding bissextile days: [II]DCCCCXX.

**[Note: Square brackets surrounding Roman numerals indicate that they should be multiplied by 1,000. In Migne, this is represented by a line printed above the relevant letters.]**

Eight times 365 makes [II]DCCCCXX. Now observe how many days the lunar years contain. Eight times 354 makes [II]DCCCXXXII. Add the ninety days of the three embolismic months: the total is IIDCCCCXXII. But the two days lacking in the solar ogdoad, as we showed above, are expected to be supplied by the addition of two bissextile days.

Let us examine the hendecad of each star, to see whether the sun perhaps seeks help there from the bissextile day. For eleven times 365 makes [IIII]XV. Likewise, eleven times 354 makes IIIDCCCXCIV. Add the 120 days of the embolismic months: the result is [IIII]XIV. Subtract one day for the leap: thirteen remain.

See, then, whether the solar hendecad requires the assistance of the bissextile year, so that, by adding two or three days, it might be sufficient to compensate for the lunar hendecad. Therefore, the two days by which the solar ogdoad is less than the lunar ogdoad are not supplied by the intercalation of two bissextile days; rather, they are supplied by adding the two days by which its hendecad exceeds the lunar hendecad.

Nor does it matter that we said the lunar leap—which some place at the beginning of the ogdoad—should be placed in the hendecad. Wherever you insert it, the proposed question will be resolved with the same result.

The nineteen-year cycle has 228 solar months and 235 lunar months, and, excluding bissextile days, [III]DCCCCXXXV days. This appears as follows. Nineteen times 365 makes [VI]DCCCCXXXV. Likewise, nineteen times 354 makes [VI]DCCXXVI. Add the 210 days of the seven embolismic months: the result is [VI]DCCCCXXXVI. Subtract one day of the lunar leap, and you will prove that the solar and lunar courses enclose the nineteen-year cycle in one and the same number of days.

The solar ogdoad likewise has 96 months, while the lunar ogdoad has 99. The solar hendecad has 132 months, while the lunar hendecad has 136. The number of days has been stated above.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Years of the Lord’s Incarnation

**DISCIPLE.** Since you have begun to explain the account of the nineteen-year cycle, I ask you to give me its complete explanation through all its stages. First, tell me what the first line contains.

**MASTER.** In the first line of the nineteen-year cycle, the order of the times is set out, which the Greek calculators observed from the years of the emperor Diocletian. But the venerable abbot Dionysius of Rome, endowed with no ordinary knowledge of both languages, Greek and Latin, when writing the Paschal cycles, did not wish—as he himself testifies—to attach to them the memory of an impious persecutor. Rather, he chose to mark the times by the years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be better known to us and the cause of the restoration of humanity—that is, the passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more clearly.

By placing the 532nd year of the Lord’s incarnation at the head of his first cycle, he plainly taught that its second year was the year in which the mystery of that same holy incarnation began.

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, was the reason for composing this cycle?

**MASTER.** It was composed because of the conjunction of the sun and moon. Since the lunar cycle is nineteen years, while the solar cycle is completed in twenty-eight years, multiplying the two by one another produces a total of 532 years. When this period is repeated, the entire order of the solar and lunar recurrence revolves back upon its own tracks, restoring the same year of the nineteen-year lunar cycle, the same lunar epacts, the same concurrent days of the sun, the same fourteenth moon, the same day of the Lord’s Pascha, and the same moon in its proper order.

Thus, because the 533rd year from the Lord’s incarnation was completed in the second year of the cycle that Dionysius first wrote, the sequence of the Lord’s years makes clear that this was the year in which, according to the conjunction of the stars, he deigned to become incarnate. For this second year of the nineteen-year cycle is the eighteenth year of the lunar cycle; it has eleven epacts, five concurrent days of the week, and the fourteenth moon on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Everything at that time was very similar.

And if someone at that time had celebrated Pascha on Sunday according to the custom now observed by the churches, that very day would have fallen, as it is marked here, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, and would have had the fourteenth moon. Finally, Dionysius himself silently shows us in a certain way what we are saying in the Paschal calculations that he wrote: when giving the method for discovering which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, he orders that the years of the Lord be taken and that one be added before they are divided by nineteen, signifying that, when the Lord became incarnate, one year of the nineteen-year cycle had already been completed.

**DISCIPLE.** How many years from the Lord’s incarnation are there at present?

**MASTER.** Eight hundred and twenty.

## CHAPTER LXII. A Calculation for Discovering the Years of the Lord

**DISCIPLE.** Prove by calculation what you have said.

**MASTER.** If you wish to know how many years have elapsed since the Lord’s incarnation, find, through the cycles, the indiction-years that have been completed since his incarnation. Calculate fifty-three times fifteen: the result is 795. Add twelve regular years, because when the Lord’s incarnation took place, twelve years remained in the cycle of indictions in which the Lord became incarnate. With these twelve added to the number mentioned above, the total is 807.

Add whichever indiction you wish—for example, the thirteenth indiction of the present year—and the result is 820. This is the number of the Lord’s years in the present year. When you reach the completion of the cycle, that is, the fifteenth indiction, remember always to add one, because you are seeking the years of the Lord through the cycles of indictions; in this way you will find the Lord’s years without any error.

## CHAPTER LXIII. How Many Years Have Passed Since the Lord’s Passion

**DISCIPLE.** How many years have passed since the Lord’s passion?

**MASTER.** Seven hundred and eighty-seven. For, unless I am mistaken, the faith of the Church holds that the Lord lived in the flesh a little more than thirty-three years until the time of his passion: he was baptized when he was thirty years old, as the evangelist Luke testifies, and preached for three and a half years after his baptism, as John indicates not only in his Gospel by mentioning the recurring time of Passover, but also in his Apocalypse, and Daniel prophetically designates in his visions.

Since, therefore, as we mentioned above, the Paschal cycle revolves in 532 years, add to these thirty-three, or rather thirty-four, in order to reach the very year in which the Lord suffered. The total is 566. This, then, is the year of the Lord’s passion and resurrection from the dead. For just as the 533rd year corresponds to the first in all the courses of the sun and moon, so the 566th corresponds to the thirty-fourth.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Where the Lord’s Passion Was First Celebrated

**DISCIPLE.** In what month and on what day of the month is it believed that he was crucified, and where was his resurrection first celebrated?

**MASTER.** This has been reported differently by the Fathers. For the widespread opinion of many ecclesiastical teachers is that he rose on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as the blessed Jerome testifies in his *Martyrology*, saying: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the Lord was crucified at Jerusalem.” And on the sixth day before the Kalends of April: “The resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was celebrated at Jerusalem.”

Augustine likewise says in the fourth book of his work *On the Holy Trinity*: “For he is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which he also suffered. Thus the womb of the Virgin, in which no mortal was sown, corresponds to the new tomb in which he was buried, where no dead person had been placed either before or afterward.”

But Theophilus of Caesarea, an ancient teacher who lived near the apostolic age, wrote in the synodal letter that he composed together with the other bishops of Palestine against those who celebrated Pascha with the Jews on the fourteenth moon, as follows:

“Is it not impious that the mystery of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s passion, should be excluded beyond the boundary? For the Lord suffered from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, on the night when he was handed over to the Jews, and rose from the dead from the eighth day before the Kalends of April. How will three days be excluded beyond the boundary?”

It was established in that synod that Pascha should be observed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. In the same book it is written above:

“For the Gauls, on whatever day the eighth day before the Kalends of April occurred when Christ’s resurrection was said to have taken place, always celebrated Pascha.”

Therefore, when the cycles of the blessed Dionysius have been opened, if you find that, in the 566th year from the Lord’s incarnation, the fourteenth moon occurs on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on a Thursday, and that the Sunday of Pascha falls on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, with the seventeenth moon, give thanks to God, because, just as he promised, he has granted you to find what you sought.

For no Catholic may doubt that the Lord ascended the cross on the fifteenth moon, on a Friday, and rose from the dead on the first day of the week, that is, on Sunday; otherwise he would appear equally incredulous toward the Law, which commanded the Paschal lamb to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month at evening, and toward the Gospel, which declares that the Lord was seized by the Jews on that same evening, crucified and buried on Friday morning, and rose on the first day of the week.

But if you cannot find the year you sought in the place where you thought you would find it, attribute the blame either to the negligence of the chroniclers or, rather, to your own slowness, taking the greatest care not to appear, by defending the writings of the chroniclers, to attack the inviolate testimony of the Law or the Gospel.

## CHAPTER LXV. The Number of Years from the Beginning of the World to the Lord’s Coming

**DISCIPLE.** How many years are there from the beginning of the world to Christ’s coming?

**MASTER.** According to the Hebrew truth, 3,957 years; according to the Septuagint translators, 5,199 years.

All the years from the creation of the first man to the seventh year of the emperor Louis are reckoned as 3,777 according to the Hebrew truth, and 6,019 according to the Septuagint.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On the Indictions

**DISCIPLE.** What is contained in the second stage of the nineteen-year cycle?

**MASTER.** The indictions, which return always to their own tracks in a cycle of fifteen years.

**DISCIPLE.** From where did these indictions first arise, and for what reason were they arranged?

**MASTER.** We learn from the ancient diligence of the Romans that they were instituted to prevent an error that might arise concerning the reckoning of time. For if, for example, an emperor died in the middle of the year, whether in life or in rule, it could happen that one historian assigned that same year to the reign of that ruler because he had ruled for part of it, while another historian thought that the year should rather be assigned in its title to the ruler’s successor, because he too held part of the year in his reign.

But, so that error might not grow in the reckoning of time through such disagreement, they established indictions, by which both writers—and indeed the whole population—could preserve the course of time with great ease. For ease of calculation also, they decided that there should be fifteen of them, so that the state of the elapsed time could be more briefly recalled through a very simple number, one especially convenient for multiplication.

Some, however, think that because in former times Rome was purified in the republic on account of the census conducted every fifth year, the indictions were established as a record of the third purification and census. The indictions begin on the eighth day before the Kalends of October and end there as well.

## CHAPTER LXVII. A Calculation Concerning the Indictions

**DISCIPLE.** I want you to compose for me a calculation for finding these indictions.

**MASTER.** If you wish to discover by calculation which indiction it is, take however many years of the Lord there have been—for example, at present 820. Add three regular years, because when the Lord’s incarnation took place, three years of the indiction cycle then current had already preceded it. With these added to the previous number, the total is 823 years.

Divide these by fifteen. Fifty-four times fifteen makes 810, leaving thirteen. The thirteenth indiction is therefore in the present year.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the Lunar Epacts

**DISCIPLE.** I think the time has now come for you to speak about the lunar epacts.

**MASTER.** Indeed it has, because the third line of the aforementioned cycle contains the lunar epacts, which customarily increase annually in relation to the sun’s course by eleven days. They are called epacts from the Greek word meaning “additions,” because, as we said, they accumulate by an increase of eleven days each year; or certainly because twelve are added throughout the year for discovering what the age of the moon is at the Kalends.

In the complete revolution of the year, each moon has its own addition of eleven days. For example, if today, as I write this, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, the moon is seven days old, after one year it will be eighteen days old on those same Kalends, and after two years twenty-nine days old. The same moon does not return here as it is now until the nineteen-year cycle has been completed.

Properly speaking, the epacts marked in the nineteen-year cycle indicate the age of the moon on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, where the Paschal feast begins. We must always observe the following rule of adjustment: whenever they have a number lower than sixteen, they indicate that the Paschal moon is to be preferred; whenever they have a number higher than sixteen, they show that Pascha must be sought in the following moon. For the fullness of the Paschal moon ought not to precede the equinox but, as was ordered at the beginning of creation, should rather follow it.

## CHAPTER LXIX. A Calculation Concerning the Epacts

**DISCIPLE.** State the calculation for finding these epacts.

**MASTER.** If you wish to discover what the epacts are, take however many years of the Lord there have been—for example, in the present year, the fourteenth indiction, 820. Divide by nineteen. Forty-three times nineteen makes 817, leaving three. Multiply this by eleven, because the epacts increase by eleven in the nineteen-year number. The result is thirty-three. Subtract thirty, leaving three. There are three epacts in the present year.

When the number of the Lord’s years admits of an exact division, there are no epacts.

## CHAPTER LXX. On the Lunar Rules

**DISCIPLE.** From where did those numbers associated with the lunar epacts for each month originate?

**MASTER.** From consideration of the moon, which in the year when there are no epacts must necessarily have a certain age at the Kalends of the months.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which there are no epacts, there is no moon on the Kalends of January; on the Kalends of February it is ten days old; on the Kalends of March, nine; on the Kalends of April, ten; on the Kalends of May, eleven; on the Kalends of June, twelve; on the Kalends of July, thirteen; on the Kalends of August, fourteen; on the Kalends of September, sixteen; on the Kalends of October, seventeen; on the Kalends of November, eighteen; and on the Kalends of December, eighteen.

Take these numbers as the regular numbers for the individual months. By adding the annual epacts to them, you will discover without error the age of the moon at each set of Kalends.

Thus, if you wish to know the moon’s age on the Kalends of January in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, take the nine regular units and add the eleven epacts: the result is twenty; the moon is twenty days old. If you wish to know the moon’s age on the Kalends of June in the third year, take the twelve regular units and add the twenty-two epacts of that year: the result is thirty-four. Subtract thirty, leaving four; the moon is four days old on the Kalends in question.

**DISCIPLE.** Does this fixed rule of calculation remain valid throughout the entire nineteen-year cycle?

**MASTER.** It remains valid except in three years, in which this calculation cannot preserve the consistency of its sequence: namely, the eighth, eleventh, and nineteenth years. The reason for changing it is the varied and scattered insertion of the embolisms throughout the year.

Thus, in the eighth year, the moon of the Kalends of May is reckoned, according to the calculation, as twenty-eight days old. But because an embolism is inserted in the month of March, it is shown to be twenty-seven days old. Likewise, on the Kalends of July the moon could, according to the calculation, be thirty days old; but because of the addition of the day brought by the excess of the embolism, it becomes twenty-nine days old.

Similarly, in the eleventh year, because the embolismic moon is illuminated on the day before the Nones of December, it causes the moon on the Kalends of March to be twenty-eight days old, although the calculation of the rule shows it then to be twenty-nine.

Likewise, in the nineteenth year, because the embolismic moon begins on the third day before the Nones of March, it compels the moon on the Kalends of May to be reckoned as twenty-eight days old, although according to the calculation of the rule it is said to be twenty-nine.

It should be noted, however, that some begin this calculation from September, assigning five regular units to September, five to October, seven to November, seven to December, and so forth, as we set them out above. They do this with complete reason, on the authority of the Egyptians, imitating in their calculation the beginning of the year of those from whom the origin of calculation was taken.

But to others it seems much more suitable and convenient that, insofar as the necessity of the calculation does not prevent it, the calculation should begin from the beginning of the year among the Romans as well, and proceed to the end of the year in a fixed and unimpaired order.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the Concurrent Days, That Is, the Solar Epacts

**DISCIPLE.** Since you have already spoken about the lunar epacts, the order requires you to speak about the solar epacts.

**MASTER.** In the fourth stage of the nineteen-year cycle the solar epacts are marked, that is, the concurrent days of the week. They increase by an addition of one day each year, and by two days in the bissextile year, until they reach the number seven. Their cycle consists of four times seven years, that is, twenty-eight years.

For the cycle cannot be completed before the bissextile day, which normally recurs every fourth year, has touched all the days of the week: Sunday, Friday, Wednesday, Monday, Saturday, Thursday, and Tuesday—for it passes through them in this order.

The course of this cycle is such that the concurrent days in the bissextile year are the same as those five years earlier, and those that will occur six years later. The concurrent days that occur in the first year after the bissextile year are the same as those that had passed eleven years earlier and will return after six years. Those that occur in the second year after the bissextile year had likewise occurred seven years earlier and return after eleven years. Those that occur in the third year after the bissextile year had passed six years earlier and return after five years. This order of distinctions embraces all the days of the revolving years.

**DISCIPLE.** Does this cycle of solar epacts in any way regulate the nineteen-year cycles?

**MASTER.** It does. For the nature of this solar cycle, which is completed in twenty-eight years, causes twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles to have to be completed before the same entire course of Paschal observance returns to itself. Thus every year of this cycle establishes the beginning of a nineteen-year cycle, and each year of the nineteen-year cycle in turn reaches the beginning of this one. Consequently, the entire sequence of Paschal observance is completed only after 532 years.

## CHAPTER LXXII. A Calculation Concerning the Solar Epacts

**DISCIPLE.** If there is a calculation for the solar epacts, I ask you to set it forth.

**MASTER.** If you wish to discover by calculation what the additions of the sun are—that is, the concurrent days of the week—take however many years have elapsed since the Lord’s incarnation, for example, at present 820, in the thirteenth indiction, and always add a fourth part of the years that have elapsed—that is, now 205—because a bissextile day is always added in the fourth year. Nor will the division by seven be correct unless the bissextile day is added.

With these added, the total is 1,025. Add four to this number as well, because there were four concurrent days in the year when the Lord became incarnate; the result is 1,029. Divide the whole number by seven: seven times 100 gives 700; forty times seven gives 280; seven times seven gives 49. Join these numbers—that is, 700, 280, and 49—and the result is 1,029. Since nothing remains, there are seven concurrent days.

Whenever something remains, that number will show how many concurrent days belong to that year.

**DISCIPLE.** From where do these concurrent days arise?

**MASTER.** From the number that remains in the solar year beyond fifty-two weeks. For the solar year ends on the same day on which it begins, unless a bissextile day occurs. If it is a bissextile year, it ends on the second day. For example, the present year began with Sunday; and because a bissextile day occurs, it will end with Monday.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the Solar Rules

**DISCIPLE.** From where, then, do the so-called regular numbers, which are added to the solar epacts, arise?

**MASTER.** They arise from the number that exceeds seven. January has two regular units, February five, March five, April one, May three, June six, July one, August four, September seven, October two, November five, and December seven.

These regular numbers indicate specifically which day of the week falls on the Kalends of each month in the year to which seven concurrent days have been assigned. In other years, add to the regular numbers of each month however many concurrent days have been assigned to the present year. In this way you will always find the day of the Kalends without error.

Remember only this: when, in the approaching bissextile year, one of the concurrent days must be omitted, use for January and February the number that you are going to omit; but on the first Kalends of March begin to calculate according to the number contained in the solar cycle.

Thus, when you wish to find the day of the Kalends—for example, the Kalends of January—you say: January has two; add the concurrent days of the week assigned to the year being calculated—for example, three; the result is five. The Kalends of January therefore begin on Thursday.

Likewise, in a year that has six concurrent days, take the five regular units of March and add six concurrent days: the result is eleven. Subtract seven, leaving four; the Kalends of March fall on Wednesday.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. A Calculation Concerning the Course of the Sun and Moon through the Days of the Year
DISC. Does any other method for calculating the solar epacts exist?

MAG. They propose this as a method: whatever weekday fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, that many concurrent days will there be in each year. But this is an old method, discovered not only for determining the moon or weekday of the Kalends, but also of any days whatever between the Kalends—sometimes more difficult to learn, yet handed down to us on the authority of our predecessors. [Col. 0709D]

If, then, you wish to know what lunar day falls on this or that day, count the days from the beginning of January up to the day you are investigating. When you have determined that number, add the lunar day that fell on the Kalends of January; divide the whole by fifty-nine; and if more than thirty remain, subtract thirty. Whatever remains is the lunar day of the date you seek.

Likewise, if you wish to know what weekday falls on this or that day, count the days from the Kalends of January up to the day you are investigating. When you have determined that number, add the weekday that fell on the Kalends of January; and, if it is a leap year, remember also to add the leap day after it has passed. Divide the whole by seven, and whatever remains reveals the day of the week wherever you are making the inquiry. [Col. 0710A]

This method runs so easily and without labor if you are accustomed to recite from memory the number of the individual months according to their Kalends, Nones, and Ides, as follows:

- January: on the Kalends, 366; on the Nones, 6; on the Ides, 13.
- February: on the Kalends, 32; on the Nones, 36; on the Ides, 44.
- March: on the Kalends, 60; on the Nones, 66; on the Ides, 74.
- April: on the Kalends, 91; on the Nones, 95; on the Ides, 103.
- May: on the Kalends, 121; on the Nones, 126; on the Ides, 125. [The printed figure is inconsistent; translated as supplied.]
- June: on the Kalends, 152; on the Nones, 153; on the Ides, 164.
- July: on the Kalends, 182; on the Nones, 188; on the Ides, 193.
- August: on the Kalends, 213; on the Nones, 217; on the Ides, 225.
- September: on the Kalends, 244; on the Nones, 248; on the Ides, 256.
- October: on the Kalends, 244; on the Nones, 280; on the Ides, 288. [The printed figure for the Kalends is anomalous; translated as supplied.]
- November: on the Kalends, 305; on the Nones, 309; on the Ides, 307.
- December: on the Kalends, 335; on the Nones, 339; on the Ides, 347.

[Col. 0710B]

If, for example, you wish to know what lunar day falls on the Kalends of August in the present year, say: “August on the Kalends, 213.” Add the leap day, because this year was a leap year. Also add the thirteenth lunar day, which fell on the Kalends of January: the total is 227. Subtract one, because you counted the day of the Kalends of January twice—once at the beginning of the days of the year and once in the illumination of the month of January—and the total is 225. Divide by 59: three times 59 is 177; 48 remain. Cut off 20, leaving 10 and 8. Subtract the leap day that you added in the lunar reckoning of February, and 17 remain. Thus the seventeenth lunar day falls on the Kalends of August in the present year. [Col. 0710C]

Likewise, if you wish to know what weekday falls on those Kalends, say: “August on the Kalends, 213.” Subtract one and add the weekday that fell on the Kalends of January, namely, the first. Add also the leap day, making 214. Divide the whole by seven: thirty times seven is 210, and four remain. It is therefore the fourth weekday on the Kalends of August.

## CHAPTER LXXV  
### Another method, using the days of the month, for the same matter

They also add another method, using the days of the month according to both the sun and the moon, as follows. [Col. 0710D]

If you wish to know what weekday falls on whatever day you choose to investigate, take the elapsed days of that month and always subtract one. Add also the number indicating what weekday fell on the Kalends of that month. Divide the whole by seven, and whatever remains will be the weekday of the day you are investigating; the same applies to the moon.

If you wish to know what lunar day falls on each present day, add together the epacts that fell on the Kalends of whatever month you choose and the days of that month up to the particular day in question. Always omit one—that is, the day of the Kalends—because you counted it with the epacts and must not count it again among the days of the month. If that month is supposed to have a thirtieth lunar day, omit thirty; or, if it normally has a twenty-ninth lunar day, omit twenty-nine. Whatever number remains is the complete epact for that day. [Col. 0711A]

But if the number of epacts running on the Kalends of the months and days, together with the number of months, has not yet reached thirty or twenty-nine, whatever number there is will be the lunar day then current.

## CHAPTER LXXVI  
### The return and manual reckoning of both the solar and lunar epacts
