DISC. Since you have already said a good deal about the solar and lunar epacts, it remains for you to explain how they correspond in the manual reckoning made on the joints of the fingers. [Col. 0711B]

MAG. Some people, to shorten their calculations, transfer the cycles of both heavenly bodies—the solar cycle and the lunar cycle—to the joints of the fingers. Since the human hand has nineteen joints, including the nails, they assign one year to each of these. They begin the lunar cycle on the inside of the left hand, at the base of the thumb, and complete it on the inside of the little finger’s nail.

Likewise, since the two hands have twenty-eight joints, excluding the nails, they assign one year to each of these, beginning with the little finger of the left hand and finishing on the thumb of the right. They do not, as in the lunar cycle, work through the fingers one by one in order; rather, for the reckoning of the quarter, they mark each four-year period across four fingers, so that the three joints of the two smallest fingers contain the same number of leap years, and likewise the three joints of the fingers next to the smallest set out the same number of leap years following those; in the same way, the second and third fingers each embrace their corresponding years in equal proportion. Finally, the seventh leap year claims, together with the three years following it, two joints on each thumb. [Col. 0711C]

Whether one chooses to arrange this for oneself in this manner or in another, the hands will nevertheless readily contain the cycles of both heavenly bodies. But the innumerable details of this discipline, as of the other arts, are better conveyed through the address of a living voice than through the work of a stylus making written marks.

## CHAPTER LXXVII  
### The lunar cycle

DISC. I wish, and eagerly desire, to hear from you an explanation of the lunar cycle.

MAG. The lunar cycle is therefore enclosed in the fifth section of the nineteen-year cycle. It begins with its fourth year and is completed in its third year; it is properly Roman and pertains to the month of January. For just as each year of the nineteen-year cycle begins with the paschal month and ends there, on account of the legal observance of the Hebrews, so this cycle, according to Roman institution, begins with the moon of the month of January and ends there. [Col. 0711D]

Like the other cycle, it has first and second common years, a third embolismic year, fourth and fifth common years, a sixth embolismic year, a seventh common year, and an eighth embolismic year. The hendecad of the lunar cycle, like the nineteen-year cycle, contains seven common years and four embolisms.

Common years have twelve lunar months, that is, 354 days; embolismic years have thirteen months, namely, 384 days—except only for the seventeenth year of this cycle, which is the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which one day is omitted on account of the lunar leap.

It should be noted that the first year of the lunar cycle begins in the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle because it then has the first lunar day on the Kalends of January. Beginning in different places during the other years, it finally returns to the same place after nineteen years. [Col. 0712A]

## CHAPTER LXXVIII  
### The calculation of the lunar cycle

DISC. Set out the calculation of this cycle.

MAG. If you wish to know which year of the lunar cycle is current, take the years of the Lord—for example, 820. Subtract two, because when the Lord was incarnate, two years remained of the lunar cycle. After subtracting two, 818 remain. Divide this by nineteen: forty times nineteen is 760; three times nineteen is 57; joined to the preceding total, these make 817, and one remains. It is therefore the first year of the lunar cycle. Whenever nothing remains, it is the nineteenth year.

## CHAPTER LXXIX  
### The calculation of the lunar day on the Kalends of January

But if you wish to know what lunar day fell on the Kalends of January—for example, in the present year, the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle and the first of the lunar cycle—take the first lunar cycle-year and multiply it by eleven. Eleven times one makes eleven. Add one regular, that is, the day of the Kalends of January, making twelve. The twelfth lunar day therefore fell on the Kalends of January.

Likewise, if you wish to know what lunar day falls on the Kalends of January in the fifth lunar year, multiply five by eleven, making fifty-five. Always add one regular, making fifty-six. Divide by thirty; twenty-six remain. The twenty-sixth lunar day therefore falls on the Kalends of January in the fifth year of the lunar cycle. [Col. 0712C]

Likewise, take seven and multiply it by eleven, making eighty-eight. Add one regular and divide by thirty; twenty-nine remain. The twenty-ninth lunar day therefore falls on the aforesaid Kalends in the eighth year of the lunar cycle. [Col. 0712D]

Only remember that in the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth years of the cycle just mentioned, you must add not one regular, as in the other years, but two. In this way you will find the lunar day of the Kalends of January without error.

## CHAPTER LXXX  
### The fourteenth paschal moon

DISC. Now, if I am not mistaken, the place and order of the discussion require you to speak about the fourteenth lunar day of Easter, which demonstrates our Easter. [Col. 0713A]

MAG. It is as you say. The sixth position of the aforesaid cycle encompasses the fourteenth lunar days of the first month, on which the ancients celebrated Easter according to the law of Moses; and these days demonstrate to Christians, each year and without any ambiguity, the day of the Lord’s Easter. For after the fourteenth lunar day comes Sunday, which is the Sunday of the paschal resurrection.

This fourteenth lunar day first displays its evening course on earth at the equinox—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—and finally on the twentieth day thereafter, that is, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. The course of the legal time for observing Easter is contained within these limits over nineteen years. [Col. 0713B]

If it could happen that the fourteenth lunar day fell every year on the same Saturday, the time of our paschal observance would differ in no respect from the legal observance. For then, in accordance with the commands of the law, we too would always sacrifice in the evening of the fourteenth lunar day of the first month, eat the flesh of the sacrificed lamb, and sprinkle its blood on our doorposts to repel the destroyer—that is, celebrating the solemn rites of baptism and the paschal Masses. We would overcome the spiritual Egypt and, when morning dawned on the fifteenth lunar day of that month, enter the first day of Unleavened Bread. We would also complete, with due reverence, the seven legally prescribed days of that celebration, from the morning of the fifteenth day of the month until the evening of the twenty-first—that is, from Easter Sunday to the eighth Sunday of Easter.

But since the same lunar day falls on different weekdays, our festival sometimes begins on the seventh day after the beginning of the legal Unleavened Bread, although we are taught to reserve its beginning for Easter Sunday on account of the resurrection of our Redeemer. Nevertheless, it never happens that our paschal solemnity does not include at least one of the legal days of Easter, and often it includes all of them. [Col. 0713C]

## CHAPTER LXXXI  
### The calculation of the same fourteenth lunar day

DISC. When you were explaining the reckoning of the fourteenth lunar day, I expected you to establish and confirm it by calculations. [Col. 0713D]

MAG. There are, in fact, many calculations for this purpose. First, however, every skilled calculator must retain in memory the fourteenth lunar days of the first month, just as he does the annual lunar epacts.

If someone also wishes to discover these by calculation, let him determine how many lunar epacts there are in whatever year he wishes to calculate. If there are fourteen or fifteen, let him know that the fourteenth lunar day falls on the eleventh or twelfth day before the Kalends of April, respectively. For, as has often been said, the eleventh day before the aforementioned Kalends is the proper place for all the epacts. [Col. 0714A]

But if the epacts are fewer, let him allow them to increase day by day until they complete the number fourteen; there, he may be confident that he has the fourteenth paschal moon. If, on the other hand, he has more than fifteen epacts, let him allow them to increase by days up to thirty, that is, to the limit of the month itself. Beginning in this way from the new moon and proceeding in order up to the fourteenth, he will properly find the day suitable for the paschal observance.

It should also be noted that the fourteenth lunar day, if the year is common, always returns eleven days earlier; but if it is embolismic, it returns nineteen days later than it did in the preceding year—except only in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which, because of the lunar leap, it usually traverses its yearly course in twelve days.

The birth of the fourteenth moon must therefore be sought from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the Nones of April, which marks the beginning of the new moons of the first month. From the twelfth day before the Kalends of April through the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, whichever fourteenth moon occurs is the one that leads to the celebration of holy Easter. [Col. 0714B]

## CHAPTER LXXXII  
### Another calculation

There is also another way by which the paschal limit may be found. March has thirty-six regulars, and April has thirty-five. If you wish to find the limit in March or April, subtract from the regulars of whichever of the two months you are using the epact that runs in that year. If you have more than thirty, subtract thirty as well; however many remain, that many days into the month will be the paschal limit. [Col. 0714C]

For example, in the present year the paschal limit was the fourth day before the Nones of April. April has thirty-five regulars. Subtract the epact for this year, namely three, and thirty-two remain. Cut off thirty, leaving two: the second day of April was the paschal limit.

Likewise, in the coming year, when the paschal limit will be the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, you will infer it by this calculation: March has thirty-six regulars; subtract the epact of that year, namely fourteen, and twenty-two remain. The twenty-second day of March will therefore be the paschal limit in the coming year. [Col. 0714D]

If you also wish to determine the weekday on which the paschal limit falls, take the regulars assigned to those months, and you will find it without error. March has four regulars, while April has seven. Add the appropriate regular to the number of days in the month up to the paschal limit, and add the concurrent day as well. Divide the whole by seven, and whatever remains is the weekday; if nothing remains, it is Saturday. [Col. 0715A]

For example, in the present year, take the two days of April, add the seven regulars of that month and the seventh concurrent day of the present year: the total is sixteen. Divide by seven: twice seven is fourteen, and two remain. The paschal limit this year was therefore the second weekday.

Likewise, in the coming year, take the twenty-two days of March that extend to the paschal limit; add four regulars and the one concurrent day belonging to that year. The total is twenty-seven. Divide by seven: three times seven is twenty-one, and six remain. The paschal limit in the coming year will therefore be the sixth weekday.

DISC. Is there a calculation by which it can be known whether the paschal limit falls in March or in April?

MAG. You can recognize this very easily from the epacts, whose proper place is the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, and determine whether the fourteenth moon falls in March or in April. If you have more than fifteen epacts or fewer than five, the fourteenth moon is assigned to the aforesaid Kalends of April. If, however, you have fewer than fifteen or more than five, it belongs to March. [Col. 0715B]

DISC. I should like you to explain where the regulars you said March has—thirty-six, and April thirty-five—come from.

MAG. They come from the authority of the Egyptians, who add five days after the end of the last month; they call these days *epagomenoi*. Thus these five days are added to the number of days contained in each of the two months: to March, which contains thirty-one, and to April, which contains thirty. When the epact of the year in question is subtracted, a definite number remains that indicates the paschal limit.

For example, in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, when thirty is the number of epacts, subtract thirty from the regulars of April; five remain. The fifth day of that month is the paschal limit. [Col. 0715C]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII  
### Another calculation concerning the paschal limits, the beginning of the moon of the first month, and the limits of Lent, and how they correspond to one another

Just as the Sunday of the paschal feast is regulated according to the fourteenth lunar day of the first month, so the beginning of Lent is regulated and observed according to the moon of the month of March. [Col. 0715D]

Whatever Sunday follows the fourteenth lunar day of the first month will undoubtedly be the Sunday of the paschal feast. Likewise, whatever Sunday follows the second lunar day of the month of March will be the beginning of Lent. [Col. 0716A]

Just as the paschal fourteenth moon has nineteen solar-day limits among the two months over the course of nineteen years—namely, the Nones of April, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and so forth—so the beginning of the moon of the first month will likewise move through nineteen solar days, namely, the tenth day before the Kalends of April, the fourth day before the Ides of March, and so forth.

The second moon of the month of March, by which the beginning of Lent is regulated, likewise has as many limits over nineteen days: the eighth day before the Kalends of March, the third day before the Ides of February, and so forth.

In the order in which the nineteen paschal limits are written, the nineteen limits of the beginning of the moon of the first month and the nineteen limits of the second moon correspond and agree with one another in lunar day, weekday, and regulars. For just as the paschal moon has nineteen regulars, which, when joined with the concurrent day of any current year, indicate the weekday of the paschal fourteenth moon, so those same regulars, placed over the limits of the beginning and joined with the concurrent day of any current year, indicate the weekday of the second moon at the beginning of Lent. [Col. 0716B]

It should nevertheless be noted that when the Lenten limit falls before the sixth day before the Kalends of March, and a leap year occurs in that same year, it does not observe the prescribed locations of the limits, because of the leap day in the moon, which we said must be added to February. For this reason it must be transferred to the following day, so that it may agree with the paschal limit in weekday.

For example, in the present year the Lenten limit, which is written as the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, was transferred to the Kalends of March because of the leap day that we inserted into the lunar reckoning of February on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March. [Col. 0716C]

These Lenten limits, the beginning of the moon of the first month, the paschal limits and their regulars, and the limits of the Rogations—which fall on the twenty-first lunar day of May and are used to find the age of the moon at the time of the litanies and the Lord’s Ascension—are all very readily available. The diagram set out below demonstrates all these matters most clearly through its columns.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV  
### Another calculation of the same matter, expressed in verses

Someone has brought together in verses the regulars written above, along with the paschal limits, so that they might more easily be recognized together in recitation: [Col. 0719A]

> The Nones of April know five.  
>
> The eighth before the Kalends draws out two.  
>
> The Ides of April likewise [know] six.  
>
> The ninths of the fourth [month] [know] a double-as (*dipondium*, two asses).  
>
> The eleventh encompass five.  
>
> The fourth before the Ides takes three.  
>
> The third before the Kalends is marked by six.  
>
> The fourteenth lies upon fours.  
>
> The seventh before the Ides chooses seven.  
>
> The sixth before the Kalends assigns three.  
>
> Tens, sevenths: *danamassi* [uncertain].  
>
> The day before the Nones, moreover, [gives] four.  
>
> The ninths are marked by seven.  
>
> The day before the Ides is displayed by five.  
>
> The Kalends of April expresses one.  
>
> The twelfth, skillfully, [is marked] by four.  
>
> We hope for the fifth form by two.  
>
> The fourth before the Kalends conjectures five.

When these regulars have been added to the concurrent days of the present year, and the entire sum has been divided by seven, whatever number remains will be the weekday at the paschal limit. But if the whole number divides evenly by seven, that paschal limit will fall on Saturday. [Col. 0719B]

Know that the same regulars apply to the Lenten limits, the days of the beginning of the moon of the first month, and the paschal limit. There is an equal reckoning and an equal observance between the beginning of the moon of the first month, the fourteenth paschal moon, and the beginning of Lent.

For just as the beginning of the moon of the first month runs through twenty-nine days—that is, from the Nones of March to the second day before the Nones of April—so the first moon of the first month varies from the eighth day before the Ides of March to the Nones of April.

And just as the fourteenth paschal moon runs through twenty-nine days—that is, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—so the beginning of the moon of Lent also varies through twenty-nine days, namely, from the Nones of February to the third day before the Nones of March. [Col. 0719C]

The Lenten limit, however, begins with the seventh day before the Ides of February and extends to the Nones of March. There are twenty-nine days between these two limits.

Likewise, the limits of the Rogations run through twenty-nine days, namely, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May to the ninth day before the Kalends of June. [Col. 0719D]

## CHAPTER LXXXV  
### A calculation for finding the beginning of the first month

DISC. If any further calculation concerning the paschal limit remains, please do not hesitate to explain it.

MAG. There is the following calculation concerning the beginning of the first month. If you wish to recognize the beginning of the first month—that is, where the beginning of the paschal moon lies—determine how many epacts there are on the Kalends of January in the year you are investigating. Then, beginning from the end, subtract backward through the month of March as many days as the lunar age was. Wherever you arrive, there you will find the beginning of the first month. [Col. 0720A]

There are three embolisms excepted: the last embolism of the ogdoad, the first embolism of the hendecad, and the last embolism of the hendecad. In the last embolism of the ogdoad, the beginning of the first month is found on the Nones of April. In the first of the hendecad, it is found on the fourth day before the Nones of April. In the final embolism of the hendecad, the beginning of the first month is found on the second day before the Nones of April.

This observance never fails.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI  
### Easter Sunday

DISC. I greatly desire you to give a full account of our Easter. For, as I think, we rightly retain the reckoning of the fourteenth lunar day belonging to the ancient Easter of the Jews, if we faithfully and with fitting religious observance celebrate the true Easter, according to the Apostle, in which Christ was sacrificed. [Col. 0720B]

MAG. It is as you say, because Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The seventh position of the nineteen-year cycle therefore contains Easter Sunday, which took its beginning from the Sunday of our Savior’s resurrection from the dead.

In the Old Testament, the time of Easter was commanded to be observed by three indications: after the equinox, in the first month, and during its third week—that is, from the evening of the fourteenth day to the evening of the twenty-first day. A fourth rule has been imposed upon us in the observance of the Lord’s resurrection: after the equinox has passed, when we see the fourteenth moon of the first month rise in the evening, we must not immediately rush to celebrate Easter. Instead, we must await the Sunday on which he himself, by rising, deigned to make Easter—that is, the passage from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, and from punishment to glory—and then celebrate the appropriate rites of Easter on that day. [Col. 0720C]

If someone objects that the Lawgiver established not the observance of the equinox, but only the first month and its third week, let him know that although the equinox is not named explicitly, nevertheless, by commanding Easter to be celebrated at the full moon of the first month, he fully indicates the passage of the equinox. For it is beyond doubt that the moon which, at its first passage after the equinox, displays its full disk is the moon of the first month.

Whenever we have the Sunday arriving immediately after the fifteenth lunar day, our paschal time differs in nothing from the rule, even though we celebrate the solemn rites of the same Easter with other kinds of sacramental observance.

But whenever that Sunday occurs on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day thereafter, even then we do not abolish the law or the prophets; rather, we fulfill the sacraments of evangelical grace. For, as Theophilus, the venerable bishop of Alexandria, writes, our Savior too was handed over on the fourteenth lunar day—that is, on the fifth day after the Sabbath—and was crucified on the fifteenth, then rose on the third day—that is, on the seventeenth lunar day, which was then found to be Sunday—as we learn from the testimony of the Gospels, we have a basis by which we may rightly celebrate Easter even when a postponement has followed because of an intervening necessity. [Col. 0720D]

Thus, if the fourteenth lunar day of the first month falls on Saturday, or if it falls on some other day of the following week before Saturday, we celebrate Easter without hesitation. But if it falls on Sunday, we must postpone it entirely to the following week, for the reasons we have stated. [Col. 0721A]

First, we must not, when the thirteenth lunar day falls on Saturday, break the fast, since that would be improper and was not commanded by the law—especially since the light of the moon still appears imperfect in its own sphere. Further, we must not be forced to fast when the fourteenth lunar day is established on Sunday, thereby doing something improper and unlawful. For this practice properly belongs to the custom of the Manichaeans. [Col. 0721B]

Since, therefore, we must neither fast when the fourteenth lunar day falls on Sunday nor break the fast when the thirteenth falls on Saturday, we necessarily assert that Easter must be postponed to the following week, as I explained shortly above—yet without any transgression concerning the paschal calculation resulting from this postponement. Just as the number ten includes the first, so whenever the fourteenth lunar day falls on Sunday, because fasting is not permitted on that day, it is necessary to defer Easter to the following week. No diminution of Easter appears to result from this, since the following days themselves include the remaining days. [Col. 0721C]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII  
### The opinion of various persons concerning when the Sunday of the Lord’s resurrection was first celebrated

DISC. I should like to know with certainty when the day of the Lord’s resurrection was first celebrated.

MAG. It is reported in various ways. As we mentioned above, some assert that the resurrection of the Lord occurred on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, others on the sixth, and some on the fifth day before those Kalends. [Col. 0721D]

It should be noted that if the Lord’s resurrection occurred on the eighth day before the aforementioned Kalends, as the more ancient writers recorded, the fifth year of the nineteen-year cycle was then in progress; it had seven concurrent days and the fourteenth lunar day, as it always does, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

But if the Lord rose on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, it was the thirteenth year of the aforesaid cycle, having five concurrent days and the fourteenth lunar day, as it always does, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

If, however, Christ’s resurrection was celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends mentioned above, the second year of the nineteen-year cycle was in progress; it had four concurrent days and the thirteenth lunar day, as it always does, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. [Col. 0722A]

All these matters are revealed by the unambiguous course of the seventeenth lunar day and of the day on which the sacred mysteries of the resurrection first took place, namely, Sunday. The greatest care must be taken, however, lest by affirming, as some do, that this event occurred on the sixteenth lunar day, we incur not only the unavoidable loss of our calculation but also the gravest danger to the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII  
### A calculation for finding Easter Sunday

DISC. Is there a calculation for Easter Sunday, just as you showed there is for the fourteenth lunar day?

MAG. They propose the following calculation. As many days before the day preceding the Ides of April as Easter falls, so many days before the Kalends of March will be the beginning of Lent. And as many days after the day preceding the Ides of April as Easter falls, so many days after the Kalends of March will the beginning of Lent be.

If Easter falls on the day preceding the Ides of April, the beginning of Lent will fall on the Kalends of March. As many days before the Kalends of April as Easter falls, so many days before the twelfth day before the Kalends of March will be the beginning of Lent. And as many days after the Kalends of April as Easter falls, so many days after the twelfth day before the Kalends of March will the beginning of Lent be. [Col. 0722B]

DISC. Within how many days can we celebrate Easter?

MAG. Thirty-four or thirty-five—that is, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the seventh day before the Kalends of May. This occurs in the nineteen-year cycle because of the correspondence of the epacts.

These thirty-five days arise from the fact that common years proceed through 354 days, while embolismic years extend to 384. In common years Easter may not be celebrated before the 354th day, but it may be celebrated after it. In an embolismic year, however, it ought not to be celebrated before the 384th day, but it ought to be celebrated after it. This number of days must therefore be observed in the celebration of Easter in both common and embolismic years. [Col. 0722C]

## CHAPTER LXXXIX  
### The moon of Easter Sunday

DISC. Now, if I am not mistaken, the order of the discussion requires you to speak of the final course of the nineteen-year cycle.

MAG. The final limit of the cycle mentioned above reveals the lunar days of Easter Sunday, which, because the same Sunday varies in its occurrence, are enclosed within an interval of seven days, namely, from the fifteenth through the twenty-first. [Col. 0722D]

These days are clearly fixed by the frequent testimony of the law, where the Lord says: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening. For seven days no leaven will be found in your houses.”

The rule concerning this first month and its seven days of Unleavened Bread is now as follows: whichever fifteenth lunar day occurs after the equinox is understood to belong to the first month. And whichever of the seven days—that is, from the fifteenth through the twenty-first—first receives Sunday is to be presented as suitable for the joys of the paschal feast.

## CHAPTER XC  
### A calculation for finding that lunar day

If you wish to recognize on what lunar day the feast of Easter occurs, and Easter is celebrated in the month of March, count the months from September—that is, from the beginning of the year according to the Egyptians, whose reckoning Dionysius follows here—through February. According to the ancient Romans, these are six months. [Col. 0723A]

Always add two regulars to them, making eight. Add the epacts, that is, the lunar additions. For example, in the coming year, the fourteenth year of the indiction, add fourteen, making twenty-two. Add also the days of March up to Easter Sunday, which falls on the ninth day before the Kalends of April; the total is forty-six. Subtract thirty, leaving sixteen. The sixteenth lunar day will therefore fall on Easter, that is, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, when the Lord’s resurrection is celebrated.

But if you wish to understand what lunar day Easter falls on whenever it is celebrated in April, count the months from September through March. For, as some think, whenever Easter is celebrated in April, March is the end of the year. [Col. 0723B]

When Easter is found in March, March is then called the first month. From September through March, therefore, there are seven months. Always add two regulars to these, making eight. Add the lunar epacts of the current year—for example, in this year they are three, making twelve—and add the days of April up to Easter, namely, the sixth day before the Ides of April. The total is twenty. The twentieth lunar day therefore fell this year on the day of the Lord’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XCI  
### Another calculation

It should be noted that whatever the age of the paschal moon, if you subtract twelve from it, the lunar age at the beginning of Lent will result.

For example, if the paschal moon is the fifteenth, subtract twelve from fifteen, leaving three. The third lunar day is therefore the lunar day at the beginning of Lent in the year in which the fifteenth lunar day falls on Easter Sunday, and the same applies in the other cases.

## CHAPTER XCII  
### The difference between Easter and Unleavened Bread
**DISC.** Since you have adequately explained the reckoning of both Paschas—namely, that Pascha which, according to the Law, is observed on the fourteenth day of the moon, and on the following Sunday in commemoration of the Lord’s resurrection—I ask you to explain what distinction there is between Pascha and Unleavened Bread.

**MASTER.** According to the wording of the Law, one feast is Pascha and another is the solemnity of Unleavened Bread. There is one day of Pascha—that is, of the Passover—namely, the fourteenth day of the first month, on which, at evening, the lamb was commanded to be sacrificed. During the night immediately following, the Lord passed through, striking down the firstborn of the Egyptians and freeing the houses of the children of Israel that had been marked with the lamb’s blood. The following seven days, namely from the fifteenth through the twenty-first of that same month, are properly called the days of Unleavened Bread, as the books of the Law testify.

Josephus likewise writes in the fourteenth book of his *Antiquities*:

> “On the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month the lamb is sacrificed. On the fifteenth the festival of Unleavened Bread follows, and it is celebrated for seven days. On the second day of Unleavened Bread, which is the sixteenth, they offer the firstfruits of the crops that they reap.”

[Col. 0724A] The custom of these legal rites is even now imitated, not without honor, by the practice of the Church. She observes above all one night of the Lord’s Passover—that is, of his resurrection from the dead—during which, triumphing over the wicked, he deigned to save the faithful. At its rising, the blood of the Lord, the spotless Lamb, cleanses his people, washed in the font of regeneration, from every sin. She then adds seven further days in a fitting festival, in memory of that same resurrection of the Lord.

Yet because the very day of Pascha is also commanded to be purified from leaven, this passage of the Gospel sometimes calls it the first day of Unleavened Bread. It says:

> “And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they were sacrificing the Pascha, the disciples say to him, ‘Where do you wish us to go and prepare for you to eat the Pascha?’”

Likewise, it calls the fifteenth day of the first month—the day on which the seven days of Unleavened Bread begin—the day of Pascha, because of its proximity to it, when it says:

> “But that they might eat the Pascha.”

This is not because the Gospel text contradicts the Law, but because it wished to impress upon us more vividly, through an association of terms, the sacrament that was fitting. Without prejudice to more subtle investigation, we may understand that each of us has celebrated the mystical solemnities of Pascha on the day of baptism: we escaped the spiritual destroyer through the sign of the precious blood and passed through spiritual darkness.

Throughout the whole period of life that we subsequently spend in this pilgrimage, let us celebrate the seven days of Unleavened Bread. As the Apostle teaches, during them we must feast not on the leaven of malice and wickedness, but on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. [Col. 0724C] Since, in baptism, we must hold fast to sincerity and truth if we are to pass from Satan’s power into the portion of the lot of the saints, and since throughout the entire period of our pilgrimage—symbolized by the number seven—we are commanded by daily progress to pass over to better things, we are understood both to eat unleavened bread spiritually at Pascha and to celebrate Pascha spiritually during the days of Unleavened Bread.

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the mystical meaning of Pascha

**DISCIPLE.** Since you have said something about the mystery of Pascha, I ask you to say whether anything further remains.

**MASTER.** Certainly. Aurelius Augustine has related many things on this subject in his letter on Pascha to Januarius. Because of the brevity of our discussion, however, we think it sufficient merely to recall them here, without setting them out fully. First, Pascha is celebrated after the equinox—that is, after the victory of light over the shadow of night. This signifies that we rightly celebrate Pascha after Christ’s victory over death.

It is celebrated in the month of new things, that is, in the newness of life, and in hope of our immortality and resurrection. It is celebrated at the full moon, or after the full moon—that is, in the fullness of faith or understanding, and after the recognition of God’s grace or mysteries.

It is celebrated in the third week of that month—that is, in the third age of this world: after the patriarchs before the Law, after the prophets under the Law, and at the beginning of grace and the New Testament. In this period we venerate Christ’s triumph, since he rose from the dead on the third day.

[Col. 0725A] The fact that Pascha is rightly celebrated when the orb of the moon has drawn its light from the lower regions to the higher signifies that we ought to turn the whole intention of our mind away from the ambition for visible things toward love of invisible things, and contemplate Christ not as still fighting on earth, but as already reigning in heaven.

We celebrate holy Pascha on the Lord’s Day, on which light was first created, Christ also rose, and which prefigures our resurrection. This reminds us, through the light of faith and good works, to desire to share daily in Christ’s sufferings and to possess heavenly glory with him.

The fact that we celebrate this most holy solemnity for seven days signifies that the grace of the Holy Spirit has enlightened the whole Catholic Church. This grace was manifested after Christ’s resurrection and bestowed upon the apostles and the other faithful. Let it suffice that we have recalled these matters briefly. Whoever wishes to know them more fully should read the letter mentioned above; there he will find them.

## CHAPTER XCIV. On the great paschal cycle

The great Paschal cycle is completed in 532 years, through the multiplication of the solar and lunar cycles by one another. Whether nineteen is multiplied by twenty-eight, or twenty-eight by nineteen, the result is 532.

Thus this same great cycle contains twenty-eight nineteen-year lunar cycles and nineteen solar cycles, which are ordinarily completed in twenty-eight years. It has 19 times 7 leap days, that is, 133; twenty-eight times 228 solar months, that is, 6,384; and twenty-eight times 235 lunar months, that is, 6,580 days.

Excluding the twenty-eight leap days, the total is 194,180; with the leap days added, it is 194,317. When this cycle has completed the aforesaid total of months and days in their proper order, it immediately turns back upon itself and continually restores everything pertaining to the course of the sun or moon in the same sequence in which it had passed.

Only let the years of the Lord’s incarnation advance along their appointed course and the indictions likewise proceed in order: nothing alters the course of the heavenly bodies, and therefore nothing alters the order of the paschal reckoning.

## CHAPTER XCV. On the ages

**DISCIPLE.** Since you have explained fully, insofar as the brevity of our dialogue allowed, the divisions of time and the method of reckoning, it remains for you briefly to speak about the age, which you placed after the year in the sequence of times.

**MASTER.** Ages consist of generations. They are called *ages* because they follow one another. As some pass away, others succeed them.

Some call this period the fiftieth year, which the Hebrews call the jubilee. For this reason, the Hebrew slave who, because of his love for his wife and children, is commanded to serve his master after his ear has been pierced or has been subjected to servitude, is ordered to serve “for an age,” that is, until the fiftieth year.

[Col. 0726A] Sometimes, however, we find *age* used in the prophetic books to mean eternity, as in the Psalmist’s words:

> “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever,”

and:

> “His praise remains forever and ever.”

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the ages

**DISCIPLE.** Now, as I close the little book of our discussion, explain where the word *age* comes from, what it signifies, and what it contains, so that you may at last be released from the goad of my questioning and from the obligation of answering me.

**MASTER.** I shall do so. Would that you might at least then cease from your importunity and allow me to keep my pen at rest for a while.

*Age* is generally used for one year, as in annals; for seven years, as in the case of a human being; for a hundred years; and for any period of time. Hence *age* is also called a period constituted from many ages. The word is derived as though from *aevitas*, that is, “likeness of an age.” For *aevum* is perpetual age, whose beginning and end are unknown.

The Greeks call these periods *aeons*; among them the word is sometimes used for an age and sometimes for eternity. From them the term has also been derived into Latin.

The word *age* is properly used in two ways. It signifies either the stages of a human being’s temporal life, such as infancy, youth, and old age, or the course of the world, so that there are six most famous ages, which the books of commentators frequently mention.

Since we have already given a preliminary account of both kinds of age, we shall now speak of both together.

### I

The first age of this world extends from Adam to Noah. According to the Hebrew truth, it contains 1,656 years; according to the Seventy Interpreters, 2,242 years. According to both editions, the generations number ten. This age was wiped out by the universal Flood.

Just as forgetfulness commonly submerges the first age of every human being, so who is there who remembers his own infancy?

### II

The second age extends from Noah to Abraham. According to the Hebrew authority, it comprises ten generations and 292 years; according to the Seventy Interpreters, it contains 1,072 years and eleven generations.

This was, as it were, the childhood of the people of God. For this reason the Hebrew language was discovered—that is, it was named from childhood. A human being begins to know how to speak after infancy, which is so called because he cannot yet speak.

### III

The third age extends from Abraham to David. According to both authorities, it comprises fourteen generations and 942 years.

This was, as it were, a kind of adolescence for the people of God, since it is at that age that a human being begins to be capable of procreation. For this reason the evangelist Matthew took the beginning of his genealogy from Abraham, who was also appointed father of the nations when he received his changed name.

### IV

The fourth age extends from David to the Babylonian captivity. According to the Hebrew truth, it contains 473 years; according to the Septuagint translation, twelve more. According to both books, the generations number seventeen, although the evangelist Matthew, for the sake of a particular mystery, gives them as fourteen.

In this age, as in the period of youth, the time of kings began among the people of God. For among human beings this is usually the age suited to governing a kingdom.

### V

The fifth age, resembling old age, extends from the Babylonian captivity to the coming of the Lord and Savior in the flesh. It likewise contains fourteen generations and extends over 589 years. In it, as though exhausted by burdensome old age, the Hebrew people are shaken by increasingly frequent afflictions.

[Col. 0728A]

### VI

The sixth age, which is now in progress, has no fixed sequence of generations or periods. Like an age in decrepitude, it is destined to be consumed by the death of the entire world.

Those who have conquered these ages of the world, filled with distress and labors, have done so through a blessed death.

### VII

They have already entered upon the seventh age, that of perpetual Sabbath.

### VIII

They await the eighth age, that of the blessed resurrection, in which they will reign forever with the Lord.

May he graciously grant that we too may happily reach it by his grace—the one who created all times and remains eternally in everlasting eternity, the triune and one almighty God, who is blessed forever. Amen.

---

# (A.D. 822–826.) THE EIGHT BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON MATTHEW BY THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

## PREFACE TO HAISTULPH, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

To the most blessed and deservedly venerable Lord, and to the Father most beloved in sincere charity before the Lord, Haistulph, archbishop, Rabanus, an unworthy priest, wishes eternal peace in Christ.

Mindful of that command which Wisdom once delivered through a vessel suited to her purpose, saying, “With your whole soul fear God, and honor his priests; give the gift of your hands and offer the sacrifice of sanctification, the firstfruits of holy things” (Ecclus. 7), I resolved, holy Father, to send to your holiness the work that, by the gift of divine grace and not without labor, I had completed as an exposition of the holy Gospel according to Matthew.

My purpose is that, once it has been approved by your holy judgment, you may, if you deem it worthy of reading, hand it on to the brothers placed under your governance. I do not present it as absolutely necessary, since many writers have preceded me on this path, but as something perhaps more convenient, because I have gathered the thoughts and opinions of many into one work. Thus a poor reader who does not possess a large supply of books, or who is not permitted to search out the profound meanings of the Fathers in many volumes, may at least find here enough to meet his need.

Many indeed produced treatises on Matthew’s Gospel before us. Origen, as Jerome testifies [Note: [Col. 0727D] In the proem to the Commentaries on Matthew], left twenty-two [twenty-five] volumes on this subject, as well as an equal number of his homilies and a form of commentary arranged in brief sections. There are also commentaries by Theophilus, bishop of Antioch; by Hippolytus the martyr; by Theodore of Heraclea; by Apollinaris of Laodicea [and Apollinarius of Laodicea]; and by Didymus of Alexandria. Among the Latins there are Hilary of Poitiers, Victorinus, and Fortunatianus.

The blessed Jerome mentioned above also wrote a commentary on this Gospel at the request of Eusebius. To speak briefly about his work, however, he set aside the authority of the ancients, whom he had neither the opportunity to read nor the freedom to follow, and briefly arranged a historical interpretation, occasionally adding flowers of spiritual understanding, while reserving a complete work for the future.

I have not said this to disparage him. I greatly admire his ability and the zeal he showed in interpreting and explaining the divine books. Rather, I have said it to demonstrate the reason that compelled us to undertake the present work.

When the brothers who intended to read the Gospel with us complained that they did not have as full and adequate an exposition of Matthew as they had of the other evangelists—works they had for reading by the labor of the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, the venerable Father Augustine, and Bede, servant of the Lord—our smallness was compelled by their requests to undertake this work. We relied not so much on our own strength or ability as on divine assistance and fraternal charity, which believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things (1 Cor. 13).

To this charity alone I yielded, taking no account of the empty talk of detractors and mockers, who may perhaps attribute our labor more to presumption than to piety. This is not surprising, since they are more ready to tear apart the works of others than to compose little works of their own.

Since no one can escape the slander and envious attacks of such people except one who writes nothing at all, I prefer to let their empty complaint pass by my deaf ear rather than, lying idle and numb, neglect the grace of Christ. Desiring to please him alone, we regard the empty mutterings of men as nothing.

Accordingly, I gathered from here and there the most distinguished and worthy craftsmen of sacred learning and carefully examined what they had thought and said in their works on the words of blessed Matthew. I mean Cyprian and Eusebius; Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Fulgentius, Victorinus, Fortunatianus, Orosius, Leo, Gregory of Nazianzus, Pope Gregory of Rome, John Chrysostom, and the other Fathers, whose names are written in the book of life (Phil. 4).

Attentive to their writings, insofar as the countless restraints of monastic service allowed me, and for the nourishment of the little ones—a task that imposes no small burden upon us and interferes with reading—I took care, acting simultaneously as my own dictating author, secretary, and copyist, to commit to notebooks what they had explained, sometimes in their very words, and sometimes, for the sake of brevity, in my own.

Because it would have been laborious to insert their names at every point and identify individually what had been said by each author, I thought it convenient to print, at a distance and in the margin, the initial letters of their names. By means of these letters I indicate, one by one, where each of the Fathers begins and where the speech I have transferred ends. I have been concerned above all that I should not be accused of stealing the words of my predecessors and presenting them as my own.

I earnestly beg, and by the Lord entreat, those who read this work that, if they should consider these little writings of ours, whatever their quality, worthy of being copied, they also remember to attach the signs of the names as they find them in our exemplar.

In addition to these materials, I have appended here and there, without harming others, certain indications of my own labor—things that the author of light deigned to disclose to me—by means of notes bearing my name and surname wherever it seemed appropriate. I divided the whole work into eight books, observing especially, wherever I could, that I should place the ends of the books where the evangelist reported that the Lord’s discourses had been completed.

I also arranged two series of chapters throughout the books. One is the series that I found titled under Matthew’s name in the Gospel itself; the other is a new series that I composed to place before this work. To prevent them from confusing the reader, I distinguished them by colors, writing the first in black ink and the second in red.

I included the former so that if someone, while reading the Gospel, should encounter a statement whose allegorical meaning he wished to know but did not understand, he might note the chapter written in the margin beside that statement, then immediately return to the commentary, turn through the book, and seek there the chapter that I had previously marked in the Gospel. In this way he will find without delay what he desired.

The following series of chapters, which is scattered through the volume in red ink, corresponds to the preliminary page placed at the beginning of this work. For the sake of making consultation and discovery easier, we have carefully arranged that page for the reader, distinguishing each chapter individually, so that he may find in the book, by means of their indications, whatever has been listed there in advance.

[Note: As is our custom, we have prefixed to each chapter its summary. EDITOR.]

We have taken pains to prepare everything for the benefit of the brothers and the convenience of readers, wishing that it may contribute to the improvement of many.

If anyone despises this labor of ours as superfluous because many have treated these matters more fully and perfectly, let him read what he chooses and refresh himself at the abundant banquets of noble teachers. Let him leave our work, poor though it may be, to those who cannot digest the food of the perfect—those whose stomach, filled with rich dishes, does not disdain the vegetables of the garden, but is accustomed to eat food made from legumes.

Yet let him know that the common proverb is true: for a thirsty person, a small drink of pure water is more useful than the most generous cup of spiced wine for one who is nauseated.

Furthermore, most beloved of bishops, I ask your reverence that, if you judge the present work worthy of being possessed, you order it to be copied from the exemplar that I have sent you, and have the copy carefully checked. Thus the copyist’s fault will not be reckoned as the error of the one who dictated it; rather, “the one who sows and the one who reaps” may rejoice together (John 4), and together gather fruit for eternal life.

May the grace of the heavenly Protector deign to preserve your holy fatherhood, which prays for us, and always strengthen it for the defense of his holy Church.

---

# HERE BEGIN THE COMMENTARIES ON MATTHEW. BOOK ONE

## PROEM

As I am about to write an exposition of the Gospel of blessed Matthew, I have judged it appropriate first to explain briefly why this evangelist began to write this Gospel, in what language, and in what order. Thus those who undertake to read this work may immediately find at its beginning who wrote the holy Gospel and for whom he wrote it.

Historical accounts relate that this Matthew, apostle and evangelist—who also took the surname Levi from the tribe—was chosen by Christ from among the publicans and transferred from sin. He first evangelized the Jews. But when he was preparing to pass over to the nations, he composed the Gospel first in his native language, that is, in Hebrew letters, for the sake of those who had believed from the circumcision. He left it with them as a memorial, departing from them in order to preach to the nations.

It should be observed that whenever this evangelist, whether in his own person or in that of the Lord and Savior, uses testimonies from the Old Scripture, he does not follow the authority of the translators of the Septuagint, but the Hebrew text. Two such examples are:

> “Out of Egypt I called my son,”

and:

> “He will be called a Nazaraean.”

**(Augustine.)** Matthew is understood to have presented the Lord’s incarnation according to the royal lineage, and to have followed for the most part his deeds and words according to human present life. Therefore, at the beginning of his Gospel, he begins in this way:

## CHAPTER ONE. Christ’s genealogy is enumerated and divided into three groups of fourteen; the betrothal of his mother is also related

### [I.] The book of the generation of Jesus Christ

**(Augustine.)** By this opening he clearly shows that he has undertaken to narrate Christ’s generation according to the flesh. According to this generation Christ is the Son of Man, as he very often also calls himself, commending to us that he mercifully deigned to be for us.

That heavenly and eternal generation, according to which he is the only-begotten Son of God before every creature, because all things were made through him, is so ineffable that the prophet Isaiah’s words are understood to have been spoken of it:

> “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53)

Yet this prophetic statement may also appropriately be understood of his temporal birth, by which the Word became flesh, and the virgin, made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, bore a son while remaining a virgin, so that the incongruous structure of sacred edification may not fail to hold together.

Accordingly, Matthew, answering in the first book of the New Testament to the first book of the old Law—where it is written, “This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth” (Gen. 2), and again, “This is the book of the generation of Adam” (Gen. 5)—with the beginning of the human race corrupted through transgression, sets the new Adam against the old Adam, through whom the whole world was corrupted.

In the new Adam all things have been restored, both those in heaven and those on earth. Matthew thus makes it clear that he has written the fleshly generation of the one who would receive his chosen into the adoption of the children of God.

Why did he call it “the book of the generation,” when the generation occupies only a small part of the book? The explanation is that he followed the custom of his people. It is the custom of the Hebrews to name volumes from their beginnings, as with Genesis, Exodus, and the other legal books.

By saying “of Jesus Christ,” he expresses in him royal and priestly dignity. Jesus, who bore the prophetic significance of this name, was the first after Moses to exercise leadership among the people of Israel, and he led the children of Israel into the promised land. Aaron, consecrated with mystical oil, was the first priest under the Law.

Our Savior, therefore, whom God anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. 44), is also King. Of him the prophet says:

> “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isa. 9).

And the angel, demonstrating the power of his kingdom, said to Mary:

> “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1).

He is also Priest, of whom the Psalmist says:

> “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

### The son of David, the son of Abraham

**(Jerome.)** The order is reversed, but necessarily so. If he had placed Abraham first and David afterward, he would have had to repeat Abraham in order to complete the sequence of the genealogy.

He called him the son of these two alone, passing over the others, because the promise concerning Christ was made only to them. To Abraham it was said:

> “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22),

and that seed is Christ. To David:

> “I will place the fruit of your womb upon your throne” (Ps. 131).

### Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob

Matthew therefore sets out Christ’s human generation, recalling the ancestors from the very beginning of the promise of Christ, namely from Abraham, and leading them to Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born.

**(Maurus.)** Mystically, he also shows how, from the darkness of paganism—as though from Egyptian slavery—through forty-two men, as though through stations bearing that same number, one comes to the Virgin Mary, flowing with the full flood of the Holy Spirit, as though to an intelligible Jordan, under the leadership of the Lord Jesus Christ, like Joshua son of Nun.

He testifies that Christ himself was born from Mary. Christ was placed at the end of the genealogy like a hook at the head of a net and was sent by the Father into the sea of this world. He killed the crooked dragon, caught on the hook, by being killed; and by dying he put to death the death of the human race.

For this reason, as though by a doubled cord—namely, by repeating each individual name—the order of the genealogy is woven in the likeness of a net, until one comes from its beginning, that is, from Abraham, to the hook, that is, to Christ. Of him it is said to holy Job:

> “Will you draw out Leviathan with your hook, or pierce his jaw with a ring?” (Job 40)

**(Gregory.)** He was caught on the hook of Christ’s incarnation, because when he desired the bait of the flesh in him, he was pierced by the barb of divinity.

### Judah begot Perez and Zerah from Tamar

**(Jerome.)** It should be noted that none of the holy women is included in the Savior’s genealogy, but only women whom Scripture reproves, so that the one who had come because of sinners might, by being born from sinful women, wipe away the sins of all. Consequently, Ruth the Moabite is also included below, as is Bathsheba [Bersabea], the wife of Uriah.

**(Maurus.)** At the level of inner meaning, the Church coming to the Lord from the error of paganism is prefigured in all these four women. Previously alien, full of disgrace, and barren, she was joined to Christ as a legitimate matron and bears to God more adopted sons than the Synagogue, which formerly seemed to have the Lord as its own husband.

*Tamar* is interpreted as “bitterness,” “one who changes,” or “palm tree.” All these meanings rightly apply to the holy Church. She was formerly bitter in idolatry and shameful conduct, but now she is sweet through tears of compunction and devotion to pious labor.

She is rightly called “one who changes,” because she has been changed from sinful to righteous and from hated to beloved. She is appropriately compared to a palm tree because of the contest of labors and the reward of victory. Of her the Psalmist rightly says:

> “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91).

*Rahab* is interpreted as “breadth,” “hunger,” or “impetus.” What is proclaimed in this except the nobility of the holy Church? To her it is also said through Isaiah:

> “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. For you will spread out to the right and to the left, and your seed will inherit the nations” (Isa. 54).

She has a hunger—not a hunger for bread or a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of God (Amos 8) and doing his will. From her an impetus goes forth, because the speed of preaching, as the Holy Spirit breathes upon it, is directed throughout the breadth of the whole world. Hence it is rightly said through Ezekiel:

> “Where the impetus of the Spirit was, there they went; and when they walked, they did not turn back” (Ezek. 1).

Finally, Ruth, whose name is interpreted as “seeing,” “hastening,” or “determining,” rightly signifies the Church, which contemplates the Lord in purity of heart and, according to the Psalmist, hastens to offer her hands to God (Ps. 67). She “determines,” that is, she resolves to persist firmly in faith and love of God.

Thus Paul says:

> “For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

[Note: From the version of blessed Jerome according to the Hebrew truth.]

*Bersabea*, whose name is interpreted as “well of satiety” or “seventh well,” signifies the abundance of the grace of the Holy Spirit that takes place in the Church.

By the spiritual gift, that is, the sevenfold gift, the Church has become a well of satiety, because in her there has arisen a fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 4).

### Nahshon begot Salmon

**(Jerome.)** This is Nahshon, prince of the tribe of Judah, as we read in Numbers (Num. 2).

### Jesse begot David the king

He says “David the king,” not because David alone among the men in this genealogy was a king—for all those listed from him to the Babylonian captivity reigned—but because David was the first king from the tribe of Judah through which the line of the genealogy proceeds.

### David the king begot Solomon from her who had been Uriah’s wife

**(Maur.)** It is asked why, when the three other foreign women are named by their proper names, Bathsheba alone is not named, but is mentioned only as the wife of Uriah.

The reason is thought to be this: although the three women written above had been guilty of crimes, in the births of the sons through whom the genealogy proceeds they deserved not merely not to be blamed but even to be praised.

This woman, however, after committing both adultery and murder, bore a son to King David in a marriage so culpable that she deserved not to be named in the Savior’s genealogy. The name of her husband, Uriah—that is, of a just man—is nevertheless given, so that the enormity of the crime might also be recalled, since the man who was killed because of his wife is brought back to memory.

Mystically, David signifies Christ. His name is interpreted as “strong of hand” and “desirable.” And what is stronger than the lion who conquered, the one from the tribe of Judah, the root of David?

Scripture shows how he is desirable when it says:

> “Behold, the one desired by all the nations will come” (Rev. 5).

Peter also says:

> “Into whom the angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1).

Uriah, whose name is interpreted as “my light is God,” signifies the devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light and dares to say to God, “My light is God,” and, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

All those whom God’s grace frees had been handed over to him in this most wicked marriage, so that the Church might be joined as a bride without spot or wrinkle to her own Savior.

### Joram begot Uzziah, and Uzziah begot Jonathan

**(Jerome.)** In the Fourth Book of Kings we read that Ahaziah was begotten from Joram. After Ahaziah’s death, Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash, the son of her brother, and rescued him from the slaughter that Athaliah was carrying out.

Her son Amaziah succeeded him in the kingdom; after him his son Azariah reigned, who is also called Uzziah; and his son Jonathan succeeded him.

You see, therefore, that according to the historical account there were three kings in the middle whom this evangelist omitted. Joram did not beget Uzziah but Ahaziah, followed by the others whom we have listed.

But because the evangelist’s purpose was to place three groups of fourteen in different periods of time, and because Joram had impiously mixed his lineage with Jezebel’s, his memory is removed as far as the third generation, so that it would not be placed in the line of the holy birth.

**(Hilary.)** It had also been said through the prophet that no one from the house of Ahab would sit on the throne of the kingdom of Israel except in the fourth generation. Once, therefore, the stain of the foreign family had been cleansed and three generations had been passed over, the royal origin is counted in the fourth generation of those who follow.

And after the Babylonian captivity, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel.

(Hieron.) If we wish to place Jeconiah at the end of the first group of fourteen, the next will contain not fourteen but thirteen. Let us therefore understand that the first Jeconiah is the same person as Jehoiakim, while the second—that is, Jehoiachin—is the son, not the father. The former is written with κ and μ, the latter with χ and ν; this distinction became confused among the Greeks and Latins through scribal error and the passage of time. The blessed Jerome, following the historical account, explains the matter in this way.

The venerable Father Augustine, however, says the following in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* (Book II, chapter 4):

“One of those ancestors is counted twice, namely Jeconiah, from whom there was a certain turning aside toward foreign nations, when the migration to Babylon took place. Now, when a sequence turns aside from its straight course and, in order to proceed in another direction, forms something like an angle, the thing situated at the angle is counted twice: once at the end of the former sequence and again at the beginning of the deviation itself. [Col. 0735B] This already prefigured Christ, who would in some manner migrate from circumcision to uncircumcision, as from Jerusalem to Babylon, and would become, for both sides believing in him, a kind of cornerstone. Thus God was then preparing, in figurative form, things that would later come in reality. For Jeconiah himself, at the point where this angle was prefigured, is interpreted as ‘the preparation of God.’

“Thus there are no longer forty-two generations—the number produced by three times fourteen—but, because one is counted twice, forty-one generations, if we also count Christ himself, who, like a king, presides over this temporal and earthly ordering of our life as over the number forty.”

Jacob begot Joseph.

(Hieron.) Julian Augustus brought this passage against us as an instance of disagreement among the Evangelists: why Matthew the Evangelist called Joseph the son of Jacob, while Luke called him the son of Heli. He did not understand the custom of the Scriptures, namely, that one man may be his father according to nature and another according to the law. We know that this was commanded through Moses at the Lord’s order: if a brother or relative died without children, another was to take his wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother or relative.

(Aug.) There was also an ancient custom of adoption among that people of God, by which men made their own as sons those whom they had not themselves begotten. For, apart from the fact that Pharaoh’s daughter adopted Moses—she was, after all, a foreigner—Jacob himself plainly adopted the grandsons born to Joseph, saying:

“Now therefore your two sons, who were born to you before I came to you, are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine as Reuben and Simeon. But if you beget any afterward, they shall be yours” (Gen. 48).

Hence it also happened that there were twelve tribes of Israel, apart from the tribe of Levi, which served the temple. Including Levi there were thirteen, although Jacob had had twelve sons. From this it is understood that Luke received as Joseph’s father not the man by whom he was begotten, but the man by whom he had been adopted. In his Gospel Luke recalls Joseph’s ancestors upward until he reaches David.

How the explanation of this matter is established is shown by the historian Africanus, who wrote to a certain Aristides concerning the disagreement among the Gospels, saying as follows [Note: [Col. 0735D] See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 6; and Nicephorus, Book I, chapter 11.]:

“It is therefore incumbent upon us to show how Joseph is said, according to Matthew, to have had Jacob as his father—Jacob being descended through Solomon—while according to Luke he had Heli, who was descended through Nathan. These two men themselves, that is, Jacob and Heli, who were two brothers, each having a different father—one Mathan, the other Matthat [Melchi]—and coming from different lines, also appear to have been Joseph’s grandfathers.

“The explanation is as follows. Mathan and Matthat, at different times but from one and the same woman, named Estha, each begot a son. Mathan, who descended through Solomon, had first taken her as his wife and, after leaving one son named Jacob, died. After his death, since the law does not forbid a widow to marry another man, Matthat, who traced his lineage through Nathan and belonged to the same tribe, though not to the same family, took Mathan’s widow as his wife. By her he too had a son named Heli.

“Thus Jacob and Heli, though of different paternal lines, became uterine brothers. One of them, Jacob, took the wife of his brother Heli, who had died childless, in obedience to the command of the law, and begot Joseph, who according to natural generation was his own son. Hence it is written: ‘Jacob begot Joseph.’ According to the legal requirement, however, Joseph became the son of Heli, whose wife Jacob, because he was his brother, had taken in order to raise up offspring for him.

“Thus we find both a rare and an intact genealogy: the one which Matthew enumerates, saying, ‘Jacob begot Joseph,’ and the one which Luke, with proper care, sets forth by saying that Joseph ‘was thought to be the son of Joseph, who was Heli.’ By the same distinction Luke indicated clearly that this was a legal succession, established—as it were by adoption—in relation to the dead, rather than by natural generation. For this reason he carefully avoided saying that anyone begot another in such successions. He therefore proceeds not downward but upward, all the way to Adam and ultimately to God.

“These things were not suddenly discovered by us, nor invented without any authorities. They were handed down by the relatives of our Savior according to the flesh, either from their zeal to display so great a lineage or from their desire to teach what had truly taken place.”

Africanus presents these words exactly, except that he put *Melchi* in place of *Matthat*, perhaps because his manuscript read it that way, or because the historical work from which he learned these things found that the same Matthat had two names.

The husband of Mary.

(Hieron.) When you hear “husband,” you should not immediately suspect marriage; remember the custom of the Scriptures, in which betrothed women are called wives.

From whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.

(MAUR.) He fittingly wrote not *de quibus* (“from whom,” plural) but *de qua* (“from whom,” singular), thereby showing that he was born from the virgin alone, without marital seed. When he first says, “From whom Jesus was born,” and then follows with, “who is called Christ,” he first places the proper name, Jesus, which was given by the angel before his conception (Luke 1). Then he appropriately adds what had previously appeared symbolically in priests and kings, namely, “Christ,” so that the one in whom these two mystical names came together might be distinguished from the others who had gone before as figures of him, bearing the same names separately. [Note: [Col. 0737D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 1.]

Those earlier men were called christs only for the brief period of this life. In order to preserve the image of the true Christ, they were consecrated by a certain mystical composition of the anointing oil, yet were anointed with the liquid substance of the material ordinarily used among us [or: “with the liquid of the oil”]. But this true Christ, who had come from heaven, and to whom all the preceding events had been directed, did not receive anointing acquired through human resources. In a new and singular manner he was infused and anointed by the paternal Spirit, and thereby became Christ, just as the prophet Isaiah had foretold of him many ages earlier, speaking in the person of Christ himself:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor, to preach release to captives and sight to the blind” (Isa. 61; Luke 4).

Isaiah alone did not foretell these things through divine oracles. David too, inspired in like manner, bears witness concerning Christ, addressing Christ himself:

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44).

In these words he first clearly designates him as God. Second, by the scepter of uprightness, he recalls the royal scepter in him. Finally, he indicates how Christ became Christ, saying that God was anointed by God—not with ordinary oil, but with the oil of gladness—and not like his companions, that is, those who had gone before as his image, but above his companions. In the sacred books, the oil of gladness is mystically understood to signify the Holy Spirit.

David also marks his priesthood elsewhere with secret words, speaking as though in the person of the Father and pronouncing concerning the Son:

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

Melchizedek is reported in the divine books to have been a priest of the Most High God (Gen. 14), but he was not anointed with ordinary oil, nor did he receive the priesthood by succession of descent, as was customary among the Hebrews. Therefore Christ is said to be a priest according to his order: he is consecrated not by the liquid of oil but by the power of the heavenly Spirit.

Finally, although many among the Hebrews had previously been solemnly anointed with oil consecrated for this purpose, and through it had been appointed kings, prophets, or even high priests, none of them could give his name to a people, disciples, or followers and call those disciples Christians. This was possible only for the one who is the true Christ, anointed not with human oil but with the paternal Spirit. He caused the peoples who followed him, and the whole nation of his name throughout the world, to be called Christians forever, after the name of the true Christ (Acts 11).

(MAUR.) It must also be noted that the ancestors of Christ, who are counted in his genealogy, were assumed by the Evangelist not without a profound mystery, especially since the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them as a figure” (1 Cor. 10). Just as they preceded Christ’s human birth in time, so too they bore witness to him through prefiguration. There is not one of them who does not signify Christ’s incarnation either by his name or by his deed, and demonstrate that he is the one who was prefigured in the patriarchs, promised in the prophets, and proclaimed by the Apostles.

Abraham, whose name is interpreted as “father of many,” or “father seeing the people”—whom does this name signify except the one concerning whom it was promised:

“In your seed all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22)?

And Isaiah says:

“If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isa. 53).

And again:

“O Lord, our Father and our Redeemer, from everlasting is your name. Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not recognize us” (Isa. 63).

How Abraham also signified the Savior by his actions is attested by the fact that, at the Lord’s command, he left his land and his kindred (Gen. 12), so that he might become wealthy among foreigners and become a great nation. We now see this truly fulfilled, when Christ, having left the land and kindred of the Jews, prevails, as we see, among the nations (Gen. 14).

The fact that Abraham defeated four kings with his three hundred and eighteen household servants and liberated Lot signifies nothing other than that Christ, through the cross—which the letter tau represents, containing the number three hundred—freed us from the domination of carnal understanding, which had previously overcome us, held captive by various vices.

Isaac, whose name is interpreted as “laughter” or “joy,” signifies the one of whom the angel said to the shepherds:

“I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke 2).

The Truth himself also says to his disciples:

“Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16).

And again:

“Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full” (ibid.).

How Isaac signifies Christ by his actions would take too long to enumerate in full, since nearly all his deeds narrated by Scripture correspond to the mystery of Christ. Such is the event in which he himself carried the wood to the altar where he was to be sacrificed (Gen. 22), just as Christ carried the cross of his passion in his own body. And when, as a type of the Church, he took Rebecca as his wife, and she bore him twins (Gen. 25), this signifies that the Church, through the baptismal font, bears two peoples to Christ.

Jacob, whose name is interpreted as “supplanter” or “one who supplants,” signifies him of whom the Psalmist says:

“You have supplanted all who rise up against me; beneath me” (Ps. 17).

By the erection and anointing of the stone, and by his dream (Gen. 28), Jacob signifies Christ’s passion and resurrection, him whom God anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

Bethel, where Jacob saw the vision, signifies the Church, which truly is the house of God, because it is the house of the bread that came down from heaven (John 6), and the gate of heaven, because there the Son of God descended to earth and holy men ascend to heaven.

Judah is interpreted as “confessing” or “glorifying,” and signifies the one who said in the Gospel:

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11).

The Psalmist also says:

“God is glorious in his saints” (Ps. 67),

that is, Christ in his members.

Phares, “division” or “he divided,” points to the one who says in the Gospel:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty. All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,” and so forth (Matt. 25).

The Apostle also says:

“The word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts” (Heb. 4).

Zerah is interpreted as “rising” or “sunrise,” and Zechariah says:
