“The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1).

Elsewhere it is written:

“Behold, the man whose name is Dayspring” (Zech. 6).

Hezron, “he saw an arrow,” or “his court,” denotes the one of whom it is said:

“The arrows of the mighty are sharp” (Ps. 119).

The arrows of Christ are the commandments of the Gospel, or the judgments of the one who avenges. The court signifies the abundance of grace and the breadth of charity, by which the Truth himself invites all to him, saying:

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11).

Aram is said to mean “chosen” or “excluded.” The prophet speaks from the person of the Father to the Son:

“Behold my servant, my chosen one; I have given my Spirit upon him” (Isa. 42).

Who is this chosen servant except the one who from childhood rejected evil and chose what is good? (Isa. 7.) The Psalmist also says:

“The Lord is exalted above all nations,” and so forth (Ps. 112).

Amminadab, whose name is interpreted as “my willing people,” signifies the one who said:

“No one takes my life from me; I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John 10).

He is the head of that people concerning whom the Psalmist speaks to the Lord in these words:

“I will sacrifice to you willingly, and I will confess your name, O Lord, because it is good” (Ps. 53).

Nahshon, “serpentine” or “divination,” prefigures the one who said in the Gospel:

“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3).

Here “divination” should be understood as prophecy or revelation, whose prophecy extends over the three periods of prophecy: the past, as in, “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8); the present, as in, “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9); and the future, as in, “They will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22), and, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

Salmon, whose name is interpreted as “sense” or “sensible,” not improperly figures Christ, whom the Apostle called the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1), and who is rightly called “sensible.” For in the Gospel he is recorded as saying:

“Someone touched me, for I perceived power going out from me” (Luke 8).

And again:

“Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9.)

He is truly sensible, since he sees thoughts as deeds and future things as present, as it is written of him who made the things that are to come.

Boaz, whose name is interpreted as “in whom there is strength,” “strength in him,” or “in strength,” can appropriately be applied to Christ, because he is the arm of the Lord, of whom the prophet says:

“Behold, the Lord will come in strength, and his arm will rule” (Isa. 40).

He himself says in the Gospel:

“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12).

For all human strength ends in death. But the Word who became flesh was made stronger through weakness, more alive through death, and higher through humility.

Obed, that is, “serving,” signifies the one who says of himself:

“The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20).

And the Apostle says:

“Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2).

Jesse is interpreted as “libation of the islands.” The islands are the Churches from the nations, situated in the sea of this world and daily battered by the waves of persecution. Concerning these islands Isaiah says:

“Glorify the Lord in the teachings; glorify the name of the Lord God of Israel in the islands of the sea” (Isa. 24).

The libation of the islands is therefore the sacrifice of the body and blood of the Lord, which the holy Church customarily offers daily to God with prayers and praises, rightly commemorating the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

David, “desirable” or “strong of hand,” unquestionably signifies Christ, concerning whom the Psalmist says:

“You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44),

and again:

“The Lord is strong; the Lord is mighty in battle” (Ps. 23).

How his deeds signify the deeds of the Lord, the interpreters of the holy Scriptures adequately explain.

Solomon, king and son of a king, whose name in Latin means “peaceful” or “he will be at peace,” denotes the one concerning whom the Prophet prays:

“O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71).

A little later he says:

“In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted; and he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (ibid.).

It is well known that many of Solomon’s deeds, and especially his building of the temple for the Lord with every care and diligence, bear the figure of our Savior and of the Church.

Rehoboam is interpreted as “the impulse of my people,” and signifies the swift gathering of peoples to the faith of Christ after his incarnation. Foreseeing this in the Spirit, the Prophet says:

“All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord, and will glorify your name” (Ps. 85).

Abijah, translated into our language as “father the Lord,” shows the one of whom the prophet says:

“A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and the government is upon his shoulder. His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace,” and so forth (Isa. 9).

Asa, “taking” or “lifting up,” signifies the one of whom John says:

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

The prophet Ezekiel, speaking in the person of the Lord concerning the gathering of the nations, says:

“I will take you from among the nations, and gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land, says the Lord God” (Ezek. 36).

Jehoshaphat, “he himself judging,” or better, “the Lord will judge,” can be interpreted in a way especially suited to the one of whom it is written:

“He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness” (Ps. 9).

And again:

“The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.”

The Truth himself also says of himself:

“The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

Joram: “Where is the exalted one?” or “Who is exalted?”—but more appropriately, “he will be exalted.” Whom does he signify except the one of whom Isaiah says:

“Thus says the exalted and lofty one, who inhabits eternity, whose name is holy: I dwell in the exalted and holy place, and also with the contrite and humble in spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble and the heart of the contrite” (Isa. 57)?

The Psalmist also says:

“Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth?” (Ps. 112.)

The Lord himself says in the Gospel:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

Uzziah, that is, “the strength of the Lord” or “the Lord’s strong one,” is the one of whom the Savior himself says in the Gospel:

“When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, everything he possesses is in peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11).

For he cast out the ruler of this world, because:

“The right hand of the Lord has done a mighty deed, and the Lord has become our strength and our praise for salvation” (Ps. 117).

Jotham, “completed” or “perfect,” signifies the one of whom the Apostle says:

“Having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him” (Heb. 5).

He himself also says in the Gospel:

“A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10).

But everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher (Luke 6).

Ahaz, that is, “containing” or “comprehending,” is truly the one who said:

“All things that the Father has are mine” (John 16).

And again:

“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

He is the hand of God, containing all things, of which the prophet says:

“He measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth in a handful” (Isa. 40).

Hezekiah, interpreted as “the Lord has strengthened” or “the strength of the Lord,” points to the one who says to his disciples:

“In the world you will have trouble; but take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16).

And according to Daniel:

“A stone cut from the mountain without hands” (Dan. 2) crushed the clay, iron, bronze, silver, and gold.

Manasseh, “forgetful,” bears by his name the type of the one in whose person the prophet Ezekiel said:

“If the wicked person repents of all his sins that he has committed, keeps all my commandments, and practices judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of his sins that he has committed shall be remembered” (Ezek. 18; 33).

In the Gospel he himself says to the paralytic:

“Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven” (Matt. 9).

Amon, “faithful” or “nourishing,” is the one of whom the Psalmist says:

“The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144).

He is called faithful because his promises are always true and, whichever of the two directions they take, are equally to be hoped for and feared.

How he is “nourishing,” he himself shows when he says to the sinful city:

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23.)

Josiah, whose name is interpreted as “where is the incense of the Lord,” “in whom is the incense of the Lord,” or “the salvation of the Lord,” signifies the one of whom it is written in the Gospel that he withdrew alone to the mountain to pray (Matt. 14; Luke 9).

And again it says of him:

“He entered into agony, and he prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22).

That incense signifies prayer the Psalmist confirms, saying:

“Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140).

Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Lord, shows who is the salvation of the Lord:

“The earth will be worn out like a garment, and its inhabitants will perish in the same way; but my salvation will be forever” (Isa. 51).

He is the one who, as the angel bears witness, will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1).

Jeconiah, “preparing” or “preparation,” signifies the one of whom Isaiah says:

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills, and all the nations will flow toward it” (Isa. 2).

He himself says to his disciples in the Gospel:

“If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (John 14).

It must be noted, however, that if Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin are distinguished—that is, father and son—the former is called “the Lord’s resurrection,” and the latter “the Lord’s preparation.” Both names fit Christ well, because he is the one who, according to the sayings of the prophets and according to his own promise, rose from the dead on the third day, caused us to rise from the death of sins, and, on the day of judgment, raising all his elect together, invites them to the eternal kingdom, saying:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

Shealtiel is translated into Latin as “God is my petition,” and this is suited to none more fittingly than to our Redeemer, who, asking the Father for his disciples, spoke as follows:

“Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are” (John 17).

And to show the effect of his petition, he added shortly afterward:

“I ask not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, so that they too may be one in us” (John 17).

Zerubbabel is interpreted as “he himself is the master of Babylon,” that is, “the master of confusion.” And what better signifies this world than Babylon? After the sin of the first human being, the world was entangled and confused in various idolatries and in the errors of human life. But when our Redeemer came and assumed dominion over it, to whom the Father said:

“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2),

it was immediately converted to the worship of the one God and to works of righteousness, and began to live in ordered fashion, whereas previously it had been accustomed to wander through the winding paths of error.

Abiud, interpreted as “my father is this one” or “this one is my father,” most aptly represents the one of whom it is written in the Psalm, in the person of the Father:

“He will call upon me: ‘You are my Father’; and I will make him the firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (Ps. 88).

Eliakim, whose name in Latin means “the resurrection of God,” “God raising up,” or “God will raise up,” symbolically designates the one who says in the Gospel:

“I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live” (John 11).

And again:

“This is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6).

Azor, that is, “access” or “approach,” clearly signifies the one who said:

“He who sent me is with me; he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John 8).

And again:

“My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5).

The Psalmist, speaking in the person of his incarnation, says:

“Behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul.”

Zadok is also said to mean “justified,” and expresses the one of whom the Prophet says:

“The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity” (Ps. 10).

Isaiah speaks of Christ in the person of God the Father:

“The righteous one himself will justify many of my servants, and he himself will bear their iniquities” (Isa. 53).

Achim, that is, “this is my brother,” signifies the one who willed to share in our weakness, so that he might have brothers to whom he could say to the Father:

“I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. 21).

In the Gospel he himself says concerning his faithful:

“Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12).

Eliud is interpreted as “this is my God.” Without doubt it demonstrates the one concerning whom it is written in the song of Exodus:

“This is my God, and I will glorify him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him” (Exod. 15).

Isaiah says to him:

“Truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, Savior” (Isa. 45).

And Thomas, touching the places of his nails after his resurrection, exclaimed to him:

“My God and my Lord!” (John 20.)

Eleazar is said to mean “my God is helper.” The Prophet speaks from the human aspect of Christ to the Father:

“I will love you, O Lord, my strength; the Lord is my foundation, my refuge, and my deliverer. My God, my helper, and I will hope in him” (Ps. 17).

Matham, “gift,” “giving,” or “given,” signifies Christ in this respect. He is called “gift” because grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1), and he himself says in the Gospel:

“God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3).

He is “giving” because he is God:

“Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

He is “given” because he is human:

“Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isa. 8; Heb. 2).

Joseph, “he added” or “adding,” clearly demonstrates the one who says to his faithful:

“I have come so that they may have life, and have it abundantly” (John 10).

And again:

“I am the good shepherd; I know my sheep, and my sheep know me” (ibid.).

A little later he adds:

“I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd” (ibid.).

Mary is also interpreted as “star of the sea” or “bitter sea,” and this name aptly suits the mother of the Savior. She is rightly called the star of the sea because, for this world darkened by the darkness of unbelief and sins, she brought forth the true light, concerning which John says:

“That was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1).

She may also rightly be called the bitter sea, because she made the pleasures and wanton indulgence of this world—which are properly called the sea, that is, bitterness, since they drag those who follow them toward the perpetual bitterness of Gehenna—grow bitter through her example, teaching abstinence from the enticements of this age.

For when marriage had been instituted from the beginning of the world and the whole world had pursued its desires, she determined in her heart to preserve her virginity, to mortify the desires of the flesh within herself, and to maintain a heavenly way of life on earth, so that in all things she might please the one whom she had proved herself willing to serve.

It should also be known that in the Syriac language Mary is called “Lady.” She is rightly called Lady who was worthy to give birth to the Lord of heaven and earth, as that noble poet also says in her praise:

You are enthroned upon the highest throne, happy Queen;

And, Virgin white as milk, you are surrounded by snow-white choirs.

And Sedulius speaks thus in his *Paschal Song*:

You possess a mother’s joys together with the honor of virginity;

No woman like you has ever been seen before, nor will one like you follow;

Alone, without example, you pleased Christ, O woman.

Having thus completed the genealogy of the Savior, we have briefly noted, with testimonies from the divine books, what each person mystically signified through the interpretation of his proper name. Let us now proceed to explain the other things that the same Evangelist said in continuation concerning this same genealogy.

## [II]

“All the generations, then,” he says, “from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the Babylonian captivity, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian captivity to Christ, fourteen generations.”

**(MAUR.)** The rationale of these divisions will be clear if the first group of fourteen begins with Abraham and ends with David; the second begins with David—that is, after David, with Solomon—and ends with the first Jeconiah, that is, his father, who is called Jehoiakim among the Hebrews; and the third, beginning with the second Jeconiah, that is, the son of Jehoiakim, who is called Jehoiachin in Hebrew, extends to Christ, so that Christ himself is included in the enumeration.

The fact that fourteen are placed in the whole genealogy historically distinguishes three periods of the Hebrew people. In the first, they lived under patriarchs, priests, and judges, before the kings; in the second, under kings, prophets, and priests; and in the third, under rulers, prophets, and priests after the kings. Mystically, however, the perfect and those filled with divine grace have been reduced to a single number. For ten refers to the Decalogue, four to the Gospel, and three to faith in the Trinity. All these things correspond to the same mystery: just as three sets of four tens, or four sets of ten threes, agree numerically, so the Law and the Gospel cooperate in the faith of the holy Trinity, and through the Law and the Gospel faith in the holy Trinity is proclaimed.

It is not an insignificant matter to investigate what this number also signifies, in which the genealogy is contained. The number forty, then, appropriately represents the present age, because the seasons proceed in fourfold cycles and the world itself is bounded by four regions. Forty consists of four times ten. The ten itself is completed by the number progressing from one to four.

In this present life, which daily slips away through the passage of time, we must be ruled by Christ according to the laborious discipline by which God chastises every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12). Matthew therefore testifies through this number that Christ the King has come, with the addition of the number two, which may aptly signify the two Testaments. Through them Christ the Lord rules his universal Church and grants it the judgments of his will, clearly revealing through them what displeases him in evil and what pleases him in good.

We may likewise understand in the number two the two commandments of charity, since, according to the Savior’s judgment, “on these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22). Nor is that discipline useful in the present age unless the fervor of charity is preserved within it.

We may also explain the aforesaid number as belonging to the present time of the Church, in which, with the Lord cooperating, it labors in hope of the future Sabbath. Seven times six makes forty-two. Few would doubt that six refers to works and seven to rest. Hence the people saved from the land of Egypt properly remain forty years in the desert; but because they are diligently exercised in the hope of entering rest, they make seven camps of six, that is, forty-two camps, along the most difficult road. At the last of these, when they accepted Jesus as their leader, the Jordan was immediately opened, and, after conquering their enemies, they entered the dwellings promised long before.

So also the Lord Jesus, in the forty-second generation after the world, through Abraham’s faith, dispersed the darkness of the ancient age, and, coming in the flesh, opened for us through the washing of baptism the gates of heaven. We too, after completing the course of virtues, in which we patiently await what we do not see, shall, under the mystery of this same number, as has been said, cross the dried-up river of death under Christ’s leadership and attain the promised kingdoms of the heavenly homeland.

**(August.)** But because Matthew wished to signify one who descended in order to share our mortality, he therefore recounted the generations from Abraham down to Joseph and to the birth of Christ himself, proceeding downward from the beginning of his Gospel. Luke, however, does not narrate the generations from the beginning of his Gospel, but from Christ’s baptism; nor does he proceed downward, but upward, assigning him rather as a priest engaged in the expiation of sins, at the point where the voice from heaven declared him and where John bore witness to him, saying: “Behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). Ascending, he passes to Abraham and reaches God, to whom, cleansed and expiated, we are reconciled.

Appropriately, he himself adopted the origin of adoption, because through adoption we become children of God by believing in the Son of God. Through carnal generation, however, the Son of God became, for our sake, the son of man. He demonstrated sufficiently that he did not call Joseph the son of Heli because he had been begotten by him, but because he had been adopted by him, since he also called Adam the son of God, although Adam was made by God; yet, through the grace that he later lost by sinning, he had been established in Paradise as a son.

Accordingly, in Matthew’s generations the Lord Christ’s assumption of our sins is signified; in Luke’s generations, the abolition of our sins by the Lord Christ is signified. For this reason the former recounts them while descending, the latter while ascending. What the Apostle says—“God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8)—is the assumption of sins; what he adds—“in order to condemn sin in the flesh because of sin” (ibid.)—is the expiation of sins.

Therefore Matthew descends from David through Solomon, in whose mother David sinned; Luke, however, ascends to David through Nathan, the prophet through whom God expiated his sin. [Note: On this passage consult Augustine, *Retractations*, book II, chapter 16, where he says that he ought to have written “through the prophet of whose name,” etc.] The number that Luke follows also most certainly indicates the abolition of sins. Since no iniquity of Christ—who had none—is joined to the iniquities of human beings, which he assumed in his flesh, the number in Matthew, excluding Christ, is forty. But because he joins us, cleansed from every sin, to the justice of himself and of the Father, so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled—“He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6)—in Luke’s number both Christ, from whom the enumeration begins, and God, whom it reaches, are included, and the number becomes seventy-seven. By this number the complete remission and abolition of all sins are signified, which the Lord himself also clearly expressed through the mystery of this number when he said that the sinner must be forgiven not merely seven times, but seventy-seven times (Matthew 18).

Nor is it without reason that this number pertains to the cleansing of all sins, if it is examined more carefully. Ten, as the number of justice, is shown in the ten commandments of the Law. Sin, moreover, is transgression of the Law; and transgression of the number ten is appropriately represented by eleven. Hence the curtains of goats’ hair were commanded to be made eleven in the tabernacle (Exodus 26). Who would doubt that goats’ hair belongs to the signification of sin? And so, because the whole of time revolves through the number seven of the days, when eleven is multiplied seven times all sins arrive at the number seventy-seven. In this number there is also complete remission of sins, our Priest’s flesh expiating us—from whom this number now begins—and reconciling us to God, whom this number now reaches, through the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove in this baptism, where this number is mentioned (Matthew 3).

**(Beda.)** Christ, therefore, by beginning his baptism at the age of thirty, signifies that he will expiate the filth of the whole Church. The mystical kinship of these numbers also declares this, since thirty, calculated through its equal parts, produces an additional twelve—the number of the patriarchs and apostles—and thus makes forty-two. Its parts are: thirtieth, one; fifteenth, two; tenth, three; sixth, five; fifth, six; third, ten; half, fifteen. Joined together, these complete forty-two.

Here, as we have said, it is mystically indicated that the whole perfection of the Church consists in faith in Christ and grace: first recognized by the patriarchs, it was more widely proclaimed by the voice of the apostles. Just as, among forty-two, there is no part that is not contained among the equal parts of the number thirty, so there is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved.

The number thirty, therefore, through its parts completes the forty-second, because the Lord now protects the Church laboring in time through the mysteries of his baptism and, when its labors are ended, leads it eternally to rest.

Nor is it surprising that Luke placed more successions from David to Christ, while Matthew placed fewer—Luke forty-two, Matthew forty-four—since we acknowledge that the genealogy proceeded through different persons. Some may have lived to an advanced age, while men of another generation may have died prematurely; for we see many old men living with their grandsons, while other men die immediately after their sons are born.

After enumerating the generations, Matthew continues as follows.

## [III]

“Now the generation of Christ was thus.”

This sentence may be understood in two ways. It may refer to the genealogy enumerated above, which the Evangelist began at the head of his Gospel in this manner: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham,” and, proceeding through the generations of each person, continued to Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. When the series of generations had been completed, he said, as though recalling it: “Now the generation of Christ was thus,” as if he were saying: “Thus the order of Christ’s human generation through his parents reached even to God.”

Or the sentence may be joined to what follows concerning the betrothal of his mother: how, before she was joined to her husband, she was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit. This makes clear how Christ’s generation differs from that of others: whereas others were born through the customary union of man and woman, he, as the Son of God, was born into the world through a Virgin.

**(Hieron.)** If anyone thinks it should be asked why, since Joseph was not the father of the Lord and Savior, the order of the genealogy was carried down to Joseph, let him know first that it is not the custom of the Scriptures to weave women into genealogical lists. Moreover, Joseph and Mary belonged to one tribe, which is why, according to the Law, he was obliged to take her as a relative; and they were counted together at Bethlehem as descended from one stock.

[Col. 0748B] “When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph.”

The reason why the Savior was conceived not from an unmarried virgin but from a betrothed woman is this. First, so that Mary’s lineage might be shown through Joseph’s genealogy; second, so that she would not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress; third, so that, when she fled into Egypt, she would have the comfort of a husband. Ignatius added a fourth reason for his being conceived by a betrothed woman: as he says, so that the birth would be concealed from the devil, who would think that he had been born not from a virgin but from a wife.

“Before they came together, she was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit.”

**(MAUR.)** How this happened, in what order, and in what city the conception took place—matters that Matthew omitted here—Luke explained sufficiently. After mentioning John’s conception, he narrates as follows: “In the sixth month,” he says, “the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee whose name was Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary. And the angel entered to her and said: ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women,’” and so forth (Luke 1)—the things that follow concerning her conception, the coming of the Holy Spirit upon her, and the overshadowing of the power of the Most High. What the angel, according to Luke, promised would happen, Matthew narrates as having been fulfilled.

“She was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit”—that is, she was found in this condition by no one other than Joseph, who, by marital right, already knew nearly everything about his future wife; therefore he immediately detected the swelling of her womb with a curious gaze.

When he says, “before they came together,” the word “come together” does not indicate sexual intercourse itself, but the time of the nuptials, which ordinarily precede it, when she who had previously been betrothed begins to be a wife. Thus “before they came together” means before they properly celebrated the marriage rites, she was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit. After this, according to the order mentioned, they came together when Joseph, at the angel’s command, took his wife; but they did not have intercourse, since it follows: “and he did not know her.”

“Joseph, her husband, being a just man and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly.”

It is written that whoever joins himself to a fornicator becomes one body, and the Law commands that not only the guilty but also those who know of crimes are liable to sin. How, then, can Joseph be called just while concealing his wife’s crime?

Joseph was just with that justice which is justice before the Lord, which is not separated from mercy, which is formed from simplicity of mind, which agrees with grace and proceeds from faith.

**(Orig.)** Not with that which among human beings is falsely called justice, which is either pretended under the influence of human favor or exercised without discrimination from cruelty of spirit. He was therefore just in word, just in deed, just in the fulfillment of the Law, and just at the beginning of grace.

He wished to dismiss her because he recognized in her the power of the mystery and a certain magnificent sacrament, and considered himself unworthy to approach it. For he had also read in Isaiah that a virgin from the house of David would conceive and give birth to the Lord; and he knew that Mary derived her lineage from that same house. Therefore he did not doubt that this prophecy was to be fulfilled in her.

Thus, humbling himself before so great and ineffable a reality, he sought to withdraw far away, just as blessed Peter, humbling himself before the Lord, said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5).

**(Beda.)** But if he had dismissed her secretly in this way, and had not taken her as his wife, while she, though betrothed, gave birth, there would surely have been few who would think her a virgin rather than a prostitute. Therefore Joseph’s plan was suddenly changed by a better counsel, so that, in order to preserve Mary’s reputation, he would take her as his wife after celebrating the wedding feast and guard her chastely forever. For the Lord preferred that some should remain ignorant of the manner of his generation rather than that his mother’s chastity should be dishonored.

“While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying…”

**(Greg.)** It should be known that divine speech is distinguished in two ways: either the Lord himself speaks, or his words are formed for us through an angelic creature. When he speaks by himself, however, only the inner power of inspiration is opened to us. The heart is taught by his word without words or syllables: it opens the sense of hearing but knows no sound. Thus it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit said to Philip: “Join yourself to the chariot.” And when Cornelius had sent devout soldiers to summon Peter, Peter undoubtedly heard in his mind from the Spirit: “Behold, three men are seeking you” (Acts 10).

When the Lord makes his will known through an angel, he sometimes reveals it in words without any image, as when the Lord said: “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 11), and immediately the response was given: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again.”

Sometimes he reveals it through things without words, as when Ezekiel saw the appearance of electrum in the midst of fire (Ezekiel 1), signifying the incarnation of Christ. Electrum is made from a mixture of gold and silver. In this mixture the silver is made brighter, yet the radiance of the gold is tempered.

What, then, is represented by electrum if not the Mediator between God and human beings? By joining the divine and human natures in himself, he made the human nature brighter through divinity and tempered the divine nature to our sight through humanity.

Sometimes he reveals it through things together with words, indicating through certain movements what he narrates in speech. For what does it mean that, after the human being’s sin, the Lord in Paradise no longer stands but walks, except that, when guilt intervened, he demonstrated that he had moved away from the human heart, and thus revealed their wickedness to blind minds not only through the words with which he rebuked them but also through things?

Sometimes he reveals it through images shown to the eyes of the heart, as Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder resting on heaven (Genesis 28), and Peter, carried away in ecstasy, saw a sheet full of reptiles and quadrupeds (Acts 10).

Sometimes he assumes images that appear for a time before bodily eyes, as Abraham not only saw three men but also received them into his house and fed them (Genesis 18).

Sometimes he speaks through heavenly substances, as it is written that, when the Lord was baptized, a voice sounded from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3).

Sometimes he speaks through earthly substances, as when, rebuking Balaam, he formed human speech in the mouth of a she-ass (Numbers 22).

Sometimes the Lord speaks through angels by means of earthly and heavenly substances together, as before Moses he joined fire and a bush, signifying that he would be the teacher of that people, which would receive the flame of the Law and yet would not entirely avoid the thorn of sin; or signifying that from that people would come one who, in the fire of divinity, would receive the pains of our flesh like the thorns of a bush, while preserving the unconsumed substance of our humanity even within the flame of divinity.

Sometimes, moreover, through angels the Lord secretly infuses the power of his inspiration into human hearts. Hence Zechariah says: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zechariah 2). By saying that the angel spoke to him and yet in him, he plainly shows that the one who spoke the word to him was not externally present in bodily form. Hence shortly afterward he adds: “And behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out.”

**(MAUR.)** How the angel appeared to Joseph is shown by the words “in a dream,” that is, in the way Jacob saw the ladder—namely, through an image shown to the eyes of the heart. What the same angel, appearing to him, said is shown when the text continues:

“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife.”

Joseph is called the son of David so that Mary too might be shown to be of David’s stock, in accordance with what is written: “No one may be joined to a wife except from his own tribe.”

“Do not be afraid,” he says, “to take Mary as your wife.” Do not fear, tremble, or be troubled; but safely and confidently take as your wife the woman assigned to you according to the commandment of the Law, and according to the custom and union of marriage, though she is far removed from such a union. Why he ought not to fear taking her is shown when he says:

“For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

These words teach both the manner of her conception and the dignity of the Father, since she conceived by the Holy Spirit and was to give birth to Christ. Yet it is not permissible to say that Christ is the son of the Holy Spirit, because, according to both divine and human substance, he is the only Son of God the almighty Father.

**(Aug.)** For our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is God, is the one through whom all things were made (John 1); insofar as he is human, he too was made, as the Apostle says: “He was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1). But although the whole Trinity made that creature whom the Virgin conceived and bore—though it belonged solely to the person of the Son, for the works of the Trinity are not separable—why is only the Holy Spirit named in its making?

Since something may be born from something else without thereby being its son, and not everyone who is called a son is born from the one whose son he is called, the manner in which Christ was born from the Holy Spirit—not as a son—and from the Virgin Mary—as a son—indicates to us the grace of God. Through this grace, without any preceding merits, a human being, at the very beginning of his nature, when he began to exist, was joined to the Word God in such unity of person that the same one was both Son of God and son of man, and son of man and Son of God. Thus, in assuming human nature, grace itself became, in a certain way, natural to that human being, so that he could admit no sin.

This grace had to be signified through the Holy Spirit because he is properly God in such a way that he is also called the gift of God.

“She will give birth to a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.”

It is as though he said: “The Virgin will give birth, and you will call him Jesus”—that is, you will call him by what he already was, by what had been named before the ages. You will not give him a name or establish a designation for him from yourself; rather, name and call him with exultation Jesus, that is, Savior. Testify that he is the Savior, and that he did not begin to save in time, but that he is already the most ancient Savior.

“For he himself will save his people from their sins.”

**(Hieron.)** Jesus is called *Savior* in the Hebrew language. The Evangelist therefore indicated the etymology of the name when he said: “You shall call his name Savior, because he himself will save his people.” Two remarkable things are signified by this word: that Christ was God and Lord even before the incarnation, and that his people were already then announced as destined to be saved by him.

**(MAUR.)** It is not that faithless people, namely, carnal Israel, of whom it is written: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1), and of whom Isaiah says in the person of Christ: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted me” (Romans 10).

Rather, it is that people of whom the Lord says through the prophet: “I will call ‘my people’ those who were not my people, and her who had not obtained mercy, ‘having obtained mercy.’ And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God” (Romans 9). For “those whom he foreknew and predestined, he called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8).

Therefore it was said: “He himself will save his people from their sins,” so that he might truly be God. For it belongs to God’s power to save from sin or to forgive sins. This Son of God, therefore, possessing his own people, came to free and save them from their sins, as has been said—whether from the Jews or from the nations—a multitude of faithful and believing people, redeeming them all with his blood and liberating them from the power of death by his death.

“Now all this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and give birth to a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,’ which is translated ‘God with us.’”

“All this took place”—what does “all” mean? It means that the angel was sent to the Virgin; that the Virgin herself was betrothed to her relative; that she was preserved chaste; that the angel appeared to Joseph in a dream; that he was commanded to take Mary and call the child’s name Jesus—and for what purpose? So that the Virgin might give birth to the salvation of the whole world and remain an untouched virgin forever.

“So that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled,” he says.

**(Beda.)** The Evangelist adds to the virginal birth an example from prophetic speech, so that the miracle of so great a majesty might be believed with greater certainty, since he himself not only believed that it had happened but also recalled that it had been foretold by the prophet.

It is customary for this Evangelist, Matthew, to confirm everything he narrates with prophetic testimonies. As we said above, he wrote his Gospel especially for those who believed from among the Jews but nevertheless could not, although reborn in Christ, be torn away from the ceremonies of the Law. Therefore he strove to raise them from the carnal understanding of the Law and the Prophets to the spiritual understanding that concerns Christ, so that they might receive the sacraments of Christian faith with greater security when they recognized that these things were natural and corresponded to what the prophets had foretold.

“Behold,” he says. The very word “behold” expresses amazement at the greatness of so great a mystery, so that all, as though awakened from sleep, might become alert to what is being said.

**(Hieron.)** “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb and give birth to a son.” In place of what the Evangelist Matthew says, “shall have in the womb,” the prophet has written “shall receive in the womb.” But because the prophet foretells the future, he signifies what is to happen and writes “shall receive”; the Evangelist, however, because he narrates history not as future but as past, changed “shall receive” and wrote “shall have,” for one who has something will certainly not be about to receive it.

It follows: “And they shall call his name Emmanuel, which is translated ‘God with us.’”

**(Orig.)** First the angels call his name, singing and rejoicing at his birth, as they welcome among human beings the God of all and King of peace. Then the apostles, proclaiming to all nations the dominion and power of the only-begotten Son of God. After them, the holy martyrs, resisting fire and swords even unto death. Finally, all believers, remembering and praising this same name until the consummation of the age.

**(Beda.)** The name of the Savior, by which the prophet calls him “God with us,” signifies both natures in his one person. He who was born before the ages from the Father as God became, in the fullness of time, Emmanuel—that is, “God with us”—in his mother’s womb, because he deigned to assume the weakness of our nature into the unity of his person, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

“Joseph rose from sleep and did as the angel of the Lord commanded him, and he took his wife, and he did not know her.”

He took her as his wife for the reasons stated above; and he did not know her in the conjugal act because of the mysteries he had learned.

“Until she gave birth to her firstborn son.”

**(Aug.)** At times the word “until” is used in sacred writings to indicate conjunction, by which either “and” or “that” may be expressed. Thus it is written, “until she gave birth to her firstborn son,” that is, “and she gave birth to her firstborn son.”

**(Hilar.)** Mary is therefore said to be known after the birth, that is, she passes into the designation of wife; but she is known, not joined sexually.

**(RAB.)** No one should therefore understand this as though Joseph knew her after the birth of her son, as the Helvidians most perversely assert. They say that those whom Scripture calls the Lord’s brothers were born from her, taking as support for their error the fact that the Lord is called “firstborn.”

But, as Catholic piety teaches, we should understand that the parents of our Savior were always distinguished by inviolate virginity, and that their relatives, not their children, are called the Lord’s brothers according to the customary usage of the Scriptures. For this reason the Evangelist did not trouble to say whether he knew her after the birth of the Son of God, because he thought that no one would have any doubt about it.

Indeed, no one should doubt that righteous spouses, who remained in the chastity of virginity and to whom it was granted by singular grace that the Son of God should be born, could in no way thereafter violate the rights of chastity or defile the most holy temple of God with the seed of their corruption.

It should also be noted that, contrary to the opinion of heretics, “firstborn” does not refer only to those who are followed by other brothers, but, according to the authority of the Scriptures, to all who first open the womb, whether brothers follow them or none follow them.

Nevertheless, the Lord may be understood to be called “firstborn” for a special reason, in accordance with what John says of him in the Apocalypse: “He is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1). The Apostle Paul likewise says: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8).

He is called “the firstborn of the dead” because, although he became incarnate after many brothers, he rose first of all from the dead and opened to believers the way from death to heavenly life.

He is “the firstborn among many brothers” because “to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1). He is rightly called their firstborn because he surpasses in dignity all the adopted children, including those who preceded the time of his incarnation by birth.

Indeed, they can most truthfully testify with John: “He who comes after us was made before us”—that is, he was indeed born in the world after us, but by the merit of his virtue and kingdom he is rightly called the firstborn of us all.

He may also appropriately be called firstborn in the divine birth itself, because before the Father begot any creature by making it, the Father begot the Son, coeternal with himself; before the eternal Father begot any adopted children for himself by redeeming them through the word of truth, he begot the Word, coeternal with himself.

Hence the Word himself—the Son, namely, the power and Wisdom of God—says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

Mary therefore gave birth to her firstborn son, that is, the son of her substance. She gave birth to him who, as God from God, had been born before every creature and who, in the humanity in which he was created, rightly surpassed every creature.

It follows:

“And he called his name Jesus.”

This does not mean that he gave him this name immediately after the birth—that is, Jesus—even though angelic or prophetic oracles had foretold it before his conception. Rather, as Luke clearly indicates in his Gospel, it refers to the definite time prescribed by the Law.

“When the eight days were completed,” he says, “so that the child might be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2).

Jesus, in Hebrew, is interpreted in Latin as *Salutaris*, “saving,” or *Salvator*, “Savior,” as stated above. It is clear that the prophets’ calling upon this name was utterly certain. Hence those words were sung with great longing for his vision: “My soul rejoiced in the Lord, and it will rejoice in his salvation” (Psalm 34); “My soul fainted for your salvation” (Psalm 118); and “But I will rejoice in the Lord; I will exult in God my Jesus” (Habakkuk 3).

And especially: “Save me in your name” (Psalm 53). It is as though he said: “Glorify in saving me the glory of your name, by which you are called Savior.”

Jesus, then, is the name of the Son who was born from the Virgin. As the angel explains, it signifies that he himself will save his people from their sins. He who saves from sins—that is, from the corruptions of mind and body that result from sins—will also save them forever from death itself.

# CHAPTER II  
## On Christ’s Birth in Bethlehem of Judah and the Magi; on the Flight into Egypt and the Slaughter of the Infants, etc.

### [I]

“Now when Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of Herod the king…”

**(MAUR.)** Matthew and Luke agree concerning the Lord’s birth in Bethlehem; but Luke explains how and for what reason Joseph and Mary came there, while Matthew passes over it.

Luke also narrates in order how the angel announced to the shepherds that he had been born and laid in a manger; how a multitude of the heavenly host appeared with the angel, praising the Lord; how the shepherds came and found true what the angel had announced to them; and how Jesus received his name on the day of his circumcision. Matthew is silent about these things.

Conversely, Luke is silent about the magi who came from the East to Herod, led by a star, seeking the King who had been born; about the gifts they offered; and about their return. Matthew recounts these things.

The Lord Jesus was therefore born in the city called Bethlehem of Judah, to distinguish it from another Bethlehem located in Galilee, in the tribe of Zebulun; and he was born under King Herod, who was the first foreigner to be king among the Jewish people. Until that time, the ruling power had always been held by men of their own nation, in accordance with what the patriarch Jacob had once foretold to them: “The scepter,” he says, “shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49).

This Herod was the son of a certain Antipater. On his father’s side he derived his lineage from the Idumaeans, while on his mother’s side he traced his ancestry to the Arabs. He received from the Romans and from Augustus the authority to rule the Jews, after Hyrcanus, their high priest, had been captured and carried away by the Parthians.

It should also be noted that, just as Abraham, to whom Christ was promised, was born in the forty-second year of Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians, so Christ was born after the forty-second year of Augustus Caesar, who first held universal sovereignty.

This too is not without mystery: the birth of the patriarch and of our Savior agrees in number, as does the order of the genealogy enumerated between them by the Evangelist Matthew.

It should not burden the reader if the remarkable events that occurred in the time of Augustus as testimony to the coming of our Savior are briefly recalled.

For when, after his uncle Gaius Caesar had been killed, he was returning from Apollonia and entering the City at approximately the third hour of the day, suddenly, under a bright, pure, and cloudless sky, a circle resembling a rainbow surrounded the orb of the sun, as though it were showing that he alone was the one and most powerful and most illustrious person in the whole world—during whose time he was destined to come who would proclaim faith in the Holy Trinity, he who alone had made and governed both that sun and the entire world. But the fact that Augustus returned thirty thousand slaves to their masters, while crucifying six thousand whose masters could not be identified, signifies that at that time he was destined to come whose service all who rightly devoted themselves to him, and who, by worthy works in the faith of the Holy Trinity, fulfilled the Law’s Decalogue, would live eternally by the grace of their Lord; whereas those who, scorning his dominion, wandered astray by entangling themselves in various vices throughout the six ages of this world would all be punished with everlasting torment.

But when Augustus entered the City, the senate decreed that his tribunician power should remain with him perpetually; and in those days, across the Tiber, oil flowed from the earth in a spring beside a tavern for hire, pouring in a most abundant stream throughout the entire day. What could be signified in this more clearly than that, when Christ entered the world—of whom it is written, “Let the earth bring forth the Savior, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end”—throughout the whole day, that is, throughout the entire period of the Roman Empire, indeed until the end of the world, Christians would be made by Christ, anointed ones from the Anointed One, and would flow forth abundantly and unceasingly from the tavern for hire, that is, from the hospitable and generous Church?

That Augustus had also distributed his legions for the protection of the whole world, and, celebrating a triumph, had decreed that all the debts owed by peoples should be remitted, with even written records abolished, signifies that Christ, born at that time, distributed the world among his preachers to guard it against unbelief, and commanded that repentance and the forgiveness of sins be preached in his name to all nations.

But when the aforementioned Caesar, returning victorious from the East, entered the City in triumph on the fifth day before the Ides of January, and then, for the first time, closed the gates of Janus after all civil wars had been calmed and ended; when on that day Augustus was first hailed by that name—which, previously inviolable and unusual, and lawfully used only by the lords of the world, signifies the summit of imperial power—and from that day the supreme control of affairs and powers began to belong to one man and remained with him, a condition which the Greeks call μοναρχία, “monarchy”: no believer is unaware that this is the very day which we observe as Epiphany, that is, the appearance or manifestation of the Lord’s sacrament.

And what else does this demonstrate than that Augustus had indeed been predestined, through the hidden ordering of events, for the service of preparing for him, so that, on the day when he who was shortly afterward to be manifested to the world checked idolatry by closing the temples of idols and offered true peace to all lands together with unity of religion, Augustus himself might display a sign of peace and assume a name of power?

Therefore, the eclipse of the sun and the severe famine that occurred at that time in the Roman Empire testify to the coming of the Sun of righteousness and the Bread of life. And rightly at that time the worldly sun suffered an eclipse and there was a shortage of bodily food, when the true Light came, which enlightens every person coming into this world, and when that food and drink was given from heaven, of which whoever has tasted will neither hunger nor thirst forever.

Thus, when 5,199 years had been completed from the beginning of the world, Caesar Augustus, by God’s arrangement, brought all the nations of the world into one peace, from East to West, from North to South, and throughout the entire circuit of the Ocean. When a mime, in a theatrical performance, offered him the title “lord,” and everyone, rejoicing, approved it as though it had been rightly spoken of him, he rejected it and restrained the practice by a most severe edict. And rightly so, because at that same time—that is, in that same year—the true Lord, Christ, was born, and this peace served his coming.

At his birth, while people listened, the rejoicing angels sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” After this birth had been celebrated in Bethlehem, Matthew adds an account of the arrival of the magi, saying:

> Behold, magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?”

Magi are those who philosophize about individual matters, but custom and ordinary speech often use “magi” to mean sorcerers. Among their own people, however, they are regarded differently, since they are philosophers of the Chaldeans; and for knowledge of this art, even the kings and princes of that nation undertake everything. Hence, at the birth of the Lord and Savior, they were the first to understand his rising, and, coming to holy Bethlehem, they adored the child, with the star above pointing the way, just as they said when they came to Jerusalem:

> For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to adore him.

This star arose in the East to the confusion of the Jews, so that they might learn Christ’s birth from the Gentiles. Balaam, whose successors they were, had known beforehand by prophecy that it would arise, as is written in Numbers. For among other things he says:

> A star shall arise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up from Israel. (Num. XXIV)

The magi therefore seek the king born among Israel especially because they had heard from Balaam that he would be born from Israel.

(Fulgentius.) The new star revealed that a new man had arrived. With what rays, and with how great a light, do we believe that star of the Lord then shone among the stars of old! As much as it surpassed them in splendor, so much did it lead the way in its service. Like the eye of the whole world, it renewed the ancient sight of the darkened world.

[Col. 0757B]

(Gregory.) But we must ask why, when the Redeemer was born, an angel appeared to the shepherds in Judea, while the magi from the East were led to adore him not by an angel but by a star. The reason is that the Jews, as creatures endowed with reason, ought to have been preached to by a rational creature, namely an angel; whereas the Gentiles, because they did not know how to use reason, were led to acknowledge the Lord not by a voice but by signs. Hence Paul also says: “Prophecy is for believers, not for unbelievers; but signs are for unbelievers, not for believers” (I Cor. XIV).

It should also be noted that, when our Redeemer had already reached mature age, the apostles preached him to those same Gentiles, while the star announced him to the Gentiles as a little child, not yet speaking through the functions of a human body. For the order of reason required that, once the Lord was speaking, speaking preachers should make him known to us, while, before he spoke, mute elements should preach him.

[Col. 0757C]

When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. When the King of heaven was born, the king of earth was troubled, because earthly eminence is confounded when heavenly majesty is revealed.

(Fulgentius.) Herod is troubled in vain by suspicions, agitated by falsehoods for no purpose, inflamed by the goads of envy, and therefore attempts to kill the King who has been born. This disturbance is empty and this thought wholly vain. The King who has been born did not come to overcome kings by fighting, but wonderfully to subjugate them by dying. He was not born so that he might succeed Herod, but so that the world might faithfully believe in him. He came not to fight while alive, but to triumph when killed. He did not come to gather an army for himself from other nations by means of gold, but to pour out his precious blood for the salvation of the nations.

When the text says that, with Herod troubled, all Jerusalem was troubled together with him, we may believe either that this occurred through the favor of flattery, so that the members might agree with their wicked head, as it is written: “The friends of the rich are many, and many are the rescuers of the deceived rich man. He spoke proudly, and they justified him” (Prov. XIV); or that it happened through hatred of heart, because they had read in Balaam’s prophecy: “From Jacob shall come one who will rule and destroy the remaining cities.”

And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born. The verb “gathering” reveals the diligence of the inquirer. For he gathered them to test whether they possessed knowledge of the Law and could discover, in the divinely written Testament, the birth of the heavenly King that had been foretold; and perhaps also to see whether news of such a birth would make them joyful or sorrowful. He calls him “Christ” because he knew that, according to Jewish custom, kings were anointed with oil.

But they said to him, “In Bethlehem of Judah.” For thus it is written through the prophet:

> And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah. For from you shall go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel. (Mic. V)

They use Micah’s testimony, and are thereby accused of excessive forgetfulness because they do not use the same words as the prophet. For the prophet says:

> And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are by no means little among the thousands of Judah. From you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.

(Leo.) What people were more blind, more estranged from the light, than those priests and scribes of the Israelites? When the magi asked, and Herod inquired where Christ was to be born according to the testimony of the Scriptures, they answered from the prophetic utterance that was indicated by the star from heaven. The star could certainly have led the magi, bypassing Jerusalem, directly to the child’s cradle by its sign—as it did afterward—unless it had been necessary to expose the hardness of the Jews, so that the Savior’s birth might become known not only through the guidance of the star but also through the Jews’ own declaration. For when questioned by Herod, they identified the place of his birth, which they had learned from the authority of Scripture.

(Gregory.) And they produce the testimony by which Bethlehem is shown to be honored through the birth of the new ruler, so that their very knowledge might become for them a testimony of condemnation, and for us an aid to faith.

Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. He sent them to Bethlehem and said: “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and adore him.”

(Maurus.) Herod’s mind and his actions correspond, because he displays outwardly in his deed the envy that he held in his heart. He secretly calls the magi, having dismissed the scribes and priests, because he was concealing his inward distress. He carefully learned from them the time of the star because he was plotting the Savior’s death in his mind. By his face and words he pretended that he wished to adore the one whom, in his envious thought, he was planning to kill. All hypocrites bear his character.

[Col. 0758D]

(Leo.) For while they seek the Lord falsely, they never deserve to find him. You are disturbed by needless fear, Herod, and in vain you attempt to rage against a child whom you suspect. Your royal power cannot contain Christ, nor is the Lord of the world confined by the narrow limits of your scepter. The one whom you do not want to reign in Judea reigns everywhere. You yourself would reign more happily if you submitted to his rule. Why do you not sincerely do what you promise with deceitful falsity? Go with the magi, and, by humbly adoring the true King, honor him.

When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood above the place where the child was. “It came,” he says, “and stood where the child was.” Did it not seem to speak and cry aloud: “Here, here is the child whose birth I testified to from heaven! Here is that great King who has come to join an earthly kingdom to heavenly authority”?

Truly this star is the servant of the Lord’s birth. It obeyed the Chaldeans with such devoted service that, in their search for Christ, it not only warned them from heaven but also gave them guidance on earth. This star had never appeared before, because the child now created it and appointed it to go before the magi as they came to him; once its service was completed, it immediately ceased to exist.

When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.

(Maurus.) The magi rejoiced not only because they had seen the star and learned that a king had been born, but also because it was leading them to the one for whom they were already burning with desire. Hence it is written: “They rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” Indeed, they had reason to rejoice with exceedingly great joy, since they had deserved to reach the child of the heavenly King and to behold him both with bodily eyes and with the sight of faith—the one who came to free the whole world from the darkness of sins and unbelief.

And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down, they adored him. When he says “entering the house,” he means the lodging, namely the one mentioned by Luke in his Gospel (Luke II). They found the child with Mary his mother. Why does he call him a child when he was still an infant? Because an age need not be assigned to one who is always perfect.

It is asked why Joseph is not said to have been found by the magi together with the child and Mary. This was so that no opportunity for an evil suspicion might be given to the Gentiles, who, at the Savior’s birth, immediately sent their first offerings to adore him. Thus, falling down, they adore the Word in the flesh, wisdom in infancy, power in weakness, and the Lord of majesty in the reality of a human being. And so that they might reveal the sacrament of their faith and understanding, they proclaimed through their gifts what they believed in their hearts. Hence it follows:

And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Behold, the three magi came together on one journey to adore him, because in the one Christ Jesus, who is the way of all believers, the inseparable Trinity was to be adored by them. They bring him gifts which prove to be not so much gifts as mysteries: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

Through these kinds of gifts, therefore, the divine majesty, royal power, and human mortality of one and the same Christ are signified. Frankincense belongs to sacrifice, gold to tribute, and myrrh to the burial of the dead. Holy faith does not cease to offer all these things truly to Christ, while believing in him as one and the same true Lord, true King, and true man, so that it may truly recognize him as having died for us.

In the offering of frankincense, Arius is confounded, since he insists that sacrifice ought to be offered to the Father alone. In the offering of myrrh, Manichaeus is confounded, since he does not believe that Christ truly died for our salvation. In the gold, both are confounded together. For Manichaeus does not believe that the one born from David according to the flesh is king, while Arius attempts to assign natural servitude to the only-begotten God. Therefore, neither will experience the King by whom he is ruled through faith, but rather the King by whom he will be punished for the crime of unbelief, because one denies the truth of his divinity and the other the truth of his flesh.

Nestorius is also confounded by these gifts, since he attempts to divide Christ into two persons, although he sees that the magi offered the same gifts humbly not one set to God and another to man, but to the one God-man. Let him not be divided in persons who is not found divided in gifts. For this reason he is honored by these gifts as one and the same, so that he may be recognized as one and the same God and man.

This offering of the magi also confounds the madness of Eutyches, who does not want both true natures to be proclaimed in Christ. It removes the truth of these gifts when he insists on proclaiming one nature in Christ.

Another meaning may also be understood in the gold, frankincense, and myrrh, since these mystical gifts are filled with heavenly mysteries. In gold is shown the precious redemption of our captivity. In frankincense are revealed both the superstition of demons, which is to cease, and the future worship of true religion. In myrrh, by which lifeless bodies are ordinarily preserved, the restoration of our flesh and the resurrection of the dead are prefigured.

Again, wisdom is signified by gold, as Solomon bears witness, saying: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI). By frankincense, which is burned for God, the power of prayer is expressed, as the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.” Through myrrh, the mortification of our flesh is symbolized. Hence holy Church says of her workers who contend for the Lord unto death: “My hands dripped with myrrh” (Song V).

When the King is born, therefore, we offer gold if we shine in his sight with the splendor of heavenly wisdom. We offer frankincense if, through holy zeal for our works, we burn the thoughts of the flesh upon the altar of the heart, so that by heavenly desire we may give off a fragrance pleasing to God. We offer myrrh if we mortify the vices of the flesh through abstinence.

As we have said, myrrh is used so that dead flesh may not decay. For dead flesh to decay is for this mortal body to serve the corruption of lust. We therefore offer myrrh to God when, through the seasoning of continence, we preserve this mortal body from the corruption of lust.

Mystically, the three magi signify the Gentile people descended from the three sons of Noah and coming to faith in Christ from the three parts of the world. The star signifies the prophetic word, which truly demonstrates the Lord’s birth. Herod bears the type of the devil, who, having learned of the Savior’s birth, persecutes him, preparing temporal death for his members.

The magi depart from Herod when the nations withdraw from idolatry and arrive at the house in which Christ is, namely the Catholic Church. Entering it through baptism and true faith, they find Christ with his mother—that is, with the holy Church, which, remaining a virgin, gives birth daily to children for God the Father—while Joseph is set aside, that is, the Jewish people are excluded on account of their unbelief.

Opening their treasures, they offer him three gifts, namely physics, ethics, and logic; or history, tropology, and allegory; or the faith of the Holy Trinity. The gifts closed within the treasures signify faith stored up in the heart. The gifts brought forth from opened treasures signify faith made manifest by confession of the mouth and proof through works.

But since, after receiving faith and recognizing the truth, no one is permitted to turn back and relapse into unbelief, the following sentence signifies this when it adds:

And having received an answer in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way. The magi therefore offered gifts to the Lord, and in turn received gifts from him. They return by another way because they were not to be mixed with the unbelief of the Jews.

In what they do after being warned, they plainly indicate to us what we should do. Our country is Paradise, and after coming to know Jesus we are forbidden to return there by the way by which we came. For we departed from our country through pride, disobedience, pursuit of visible things, and the tasting of forbidden food; but it is necessary that we return to it through weeping, obedience, contempt for visible things, and the restraining of the appetite of the flesh. We return to our country by another way when, having departed from the joy of Paradise through pleasures, we are recalled to it through lamentation.

When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you; for Herod is going to seek the child in order to destroy him.”

(Augustine.) Here Matthew omits what Luke relates about Christ: that, after the days of Mary’s purification had been fulfilled, they brought him to Jerusalem; and he omits what Simeon and Anna said about him in the temple after they had recognized him when they were filled with the Holy Spirit.

The aforementioned evangelist is silent about all these matters when he says that, having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, the magi went back to their own country by another way. He immediately adds: “When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph.” After the magi’s departure, the period of purification was completed; and when he was brought to Jerusalem, everything that Luke records as having happened there at that time was accomplished. Then, afterward, Joseph, warned by the angel’s appearance, fled into Egypt with the child and his mother. Thus the Evangelist continues:

[II.] He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt; and he remained there until the death of Herod.

(Hilary.) Joseph is warned by the angel to transfer Jesus to Egypt—Egypt, of course, full of idols and worshiping images of gods of every kind. After the persecution by the Jews and the assent of the profane people to his destruction, Christ passes to the nations devoted to utterly empty religions; leaving Judea, he is brought to be worshiped by the ignorant world.

When Joseph took the child and his mother in order to depart for Egypt, he took them by night and in darkness. But when he returned, neither night nor darkness is mentioned in the Gospel. For when the true Light departed, those who hated the Light itself remained in their ancient darkness; but when the Light returned, all who were worthy were illumined by its perpetual radiance.

The fact that the Lord himself, so that he would not be killed by Herod, was taken by his parents into Egypt signifies that the elect will often be driven from their own homes or even condemned to exile. At the same time an example is given to believers, so that they may not hesitate, when circumstances require, to evade the rage of persecutors by fleeing, remembering that God and their Lord himself did this.

For the one who was going to command his own people, “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. XX), first did what he had commanded, fleeing as a human being, as a man on earth—he whom, shortly before, the star had shown to the magi from heaven.

[Col. 0762B]

So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: “Out of Egypt I called my Son.” This sentence is absent from the edition of the Seventy translators, but according to the Hebrew truth it is found written in the prophet Hosea. And in the Book of Numbers it is written, Balaam saying: “From Egypt he called him; his glory is like that of a unicorn.”

[III.] Then Herod, seeing how he had been mocked by the magi, became exceedingly angry, and sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its territory, from two years old and under.

(Augustine.) It is therefore plausible that, after the magi reported nothing to Herod, he could have believed that they had been deceived by the appearance of a deceptive star, and, after they had not found the one whom they had supposed to have been born, had been ashamed to return to him; and that, his fear thus removed, he had ceased searching for and pursuing the child.

But when, after his mother’s purification, they had come with him to Jerusalem, and the events had taken place in the temple which Luke relates, the words of Simeon and Anna, who prophesied about him, would, once those who had heard them began to proclaim them, have recalled the king’s mind to its former intention. Joseph, therefore, warned in a dream, fled into Egypt with the infant and his mother.

Afterward, when the matters said and done in the temple had become widely known, Herod realized that he had been deceived by the magi. Desiring then to bring about Christ’s death, he killed many infants, as Matthew relates, in Bethlehem and throughout all its territory, from two years old and under. For the cruelty of his heart, blazing up through envy and rage, observed no limit in anything, but sought to surpass everyone in wickedness. Not content with the devastation of Bethlehem alone, he also devastated all its surrounding territory, and showed no mercy even toward the smallest age; instead, he killed them all together, from the child of one night old to the child of two years. Hence it follows:

According to the time which he had carefully learned from the magi. As stated above, the utterly impure tyrant, full of every deceit and wickedness, had carefully learned from the magi the time of the star that had appeared to them because he was planning to kill the child who had been born.
