Nevertheless, it is not apparent whether he carried out this great slaughter of children after one year from the Lord’s birth or after two years. Unless perhaps we say that, after one full year and four days of the following year had elapsed from the Lord’s birth—which is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of January—he ordered the children to be killed on the fifth day before those same Kalends, when the day of their passion is venerated by the holy and apostolic Church.

Thus the exceedingly crafty king may have ordered all children up to two years old to be killed, so that the one whom he had long before resolved to kill could in no way escape amid such a multitude of slain children. For the wicked and subtle king could reason that it was possible for the God-King who was being born, and whom the stars of heaven served, to appear before everyone at a stronger age—that is, as a child of approximately one or two years—and, if he wished, again to conceal the age of his nature in the smallness of his body. For this reason, under this limitation of time, he killed all whom the first and second years contained.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, who said:

> A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and much wailing; Rachel weeping for her children refused to be consoled, because they are not.

Benjamin was born from Rachel, and Bethlehem is not in Benjamin’s tribe.

(Hieronymus.) It is therefore asked how Rachel could mourn the children of Judah, that is, of Bethlehem, as though they were her own. We shall answer briefly that Rachel was buried near Bethlehem in Ephrathah, as the inscription of her monument, which remains to this day, testifies, west of the city beyond the road that leads to Hebron; and that Bethlehem received a mother’s name from the earthly lodging of her little body.

Or it may be because Judah and Benjamin were two neighboring tribes. Since Herod had commanded that boys be killed not only in Bethlehem but also throughout all its surrounding territory, we may understand, under the occasion of Bethlehem, that many from Benjamin were also slain.

The fact that Rachel weeps for her children and did not accept consolation may be understood in two ways: either because she considered them dead forever, or because she did not wish to be consoled for those whom she knew would live.

As for the phrase “in Ramah,” we should not think that it is the name of the place near Gibeah; rather, Ramah means “high.” The meaning, then, is: “A voice was heard on high,” that is, dispersed far and wide.

(Hilary.) Rachel was Jacob’s wife. She was barren for a long time, but she lost none of the children she bore. Yet she prefigured the Church. Therefore it is not the voice and wailing of that Rachel who felt no grief at the loss of children that is heard, but of the Church, long barren and now fruitful.

Her wailing is heard from her children not because she grieved that they had been killed, but because she was herself being killed by those whom she had wished to retain as her firstborn children. Finally, she refused to be consoled because she grieved. For these who were thought to have died were not lost; they were being carried forward into eternity through the glory of martyrdom. Consolation was due for something lost, not for something increased.

After Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.”

Many fall into error through ignorance of the historical account, supposing that this is the same Herod by whom the Lord was mocked during his Passion. That Herod, therefore, who later became friends with Pilate, was the son of this Herod, whose death is now reported; and he was the brother of Archelaus, who, by the will of his father Herod, with Caesar Augustus also adjudicating, became the successor to the kingdom of the Jews.

This Herod, of whom the Gospel speaks, died in the thirty-seventh year of his reign, which was the forty-fourth year of Caesar Augustus, according to the authority of the Chronicles.

For those who sought the child’s life had died.

(Hieronymus.) From this passage we understand that not only Herod but also the priests and scribes had already been plotting the Lord’s death at that time. Josephus also records that Herod killed some of the leaders of the Jews before his own death; and deservedly so, since, for those with whom he had shortly before plotted the death of the Innocents, he himself became the cause of death when he died.

He rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. He does not say, “He took his son and his wife,” but “the child and his mother,” as a foster father rather than a husband.

But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there; and, being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee.

(Maurus.) This Archelaus, who succeeded his father Herod in the kingdom, ruled Judea for nine years. The Jews accused him before Augustus because of the intolerable savagery of his character, and he died in perpetual exile at Vienne, a city of Gaul.

To make the kingdom of Judea less powerful, Augustus arranged to divide it into tetrarchies, which he caused four brothers of Archelaus to hold: Herod, Antipater, Lysanias, and Philip, as the historians of the period report.

(Augustine.) If anyone is troubled by how Matthew can say that the parents of the child Jesus went into Galilee for this reason—that they did not wish to go into Judea because they feared Archelaus—when they seem rather to have gone into Galilee because their city was Nazareth of Galilee, as Luke does not fail to mention, the matter should be understood as follows.

When the angel said to Joseph in a dream in Egypt, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel,” Joseph first understood this as an order to proceed into Judea. For the land of Israel could initially be understood in that way. But after he learned that Herod’s son Archelaus was reigning there, he did not wish to expose himself to that danger, since “the land of Israel” could also be understood so as to include Galilee, because the people of Israel inhabited that region as well.

The question can also be resolved in another way. The parents of Christ may have thought that, given what they had learned through the angelic responses, the child could not be housed anywhere except in Jerusalem, where the Lord’s temple was; and therefore, on returning from Egypt, they would have gone there and lived there, unless the presence of Archelaus frightened them away. For they had not been divinely commanded to live there, so that they ought to disregard what they feared concerning Archelaus.

### [III.] [Cols. 0765B–0766D]

“And coming, he dwelt in the city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He shall be called a Nazarene.’”

**(Jerome.)** If he had set down a definite example from the Scriptures, he would never have said “what had been spoken through the prophets,” but simply “what had been spoken through the prophet.” By now calling the prophets in the plural, he shows that he has taken from the Scriptures not the words but the meaning. *Nazarene* is interpreted as “holy.” Now every Scripture commemorates that the Lord would be holy.

We may also explain it another way: even in the same words, according to the Hebrew truth, it is written in Isaiah: “A branch shall go out from the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11).

Allegorically, the death of the innocent children prefigures the passion of all Christ’s martyrs, who are little and innocent—that is, humble, free from every deceit of wickedness—and who suffered persecution not only in Bethlehem, that is, in Judea, from which the Church’s origin began, but also throughout all the regions of that same Church, across the whole world, at the hands of impious and utterly wicked persecutors, whose type was represented by the exceedingly cruel Herod.

These children were killed at the age of two, that is, perfected in doctrine and conduct. Their being killed, while Christ, whom they sought, escaped alive, indicates that the bodies of the righteous can indeed be put to death by the wicked, but that Christ, on whose account the whole persecution rages, cannot in any way be taken from them, whether they are alive or slain.

That, in accordance with Jeremiah’s prophecy, “a voice was heard in Rama”—that is, “on high”—“of lamentation and much wailing” clearly proclaims the mourning of the holy Church, by which she groans over the unjust death of her members. This mourning does not, as her enemies chatter, vanish into nothing, but rises even to the throne of the heavenly Judge, just as it is written concerning the blood of Abel, the first martyr.

But when Rachel is said to weep for her children and to refuse consolation because they are no more, this signifies that the Church indeed mourns the removal of the saints from this world, but does not wish to be consoled in such a way that those who conquered the world by death should return again to endure with her the struggles of the world. For they are not to be recalled again into the world, from whose sorrows they have escaped once and for all, to be crowned with Christ.

And appropriately Rachel—whose name is said to mean “sheep” or “one seeing God”—is shown to signify the Church, whose entire attention is devoted to keeping watch so that she may deserve to see God. She herself is also the hundredth sheep whom the Good Shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine sheep of the angelic powers in heaven, went to seek on earth; and, having found her, placed her upon his shoulders and thus carried her back to the flock.

That Herod died not long after the children were killed for the Lord, and that Joseph, warned by an angel, brought the Lord and his mother back to the land of Israel, signifies that all the persecutions which were to be stirred up against the Church would be avenged by the death of the persecutors themselves. Once those persecutors had been punished, peace would again be restored to the Church, and the saints who had remained hidden would return to their own places.

We may also understand more particularly Herod’s hatred, by which he sought to destroy Jesus, as referring to the persecutions that took place in Judea in the time of the apostles. When envy grew stronger, almost all the preachers were expelled from the province and scattered far and wide among the nations to preach. Thus it came about that the Gentiles—symbolized by Egypt—which had previously been darkened by sins, received the light of the word.

For this is what it means that the child Jesus was carried into Egypt by Joseph and his mother: that the faith in the Lord’s incarnation and the fellowship of the Church were entrusted to the Gentiles through holy teachers.

That they remained in Egypt until Herod’s death figuratively indicates that the faith of Christ would remain among the Gentiles until their full number entered, and thus all Israel would be saved.

Herod’s death signifies the end of the malicious intention by which Judea now rages against the Church. The killing of the children signifies the death of those humble in spirit whom the Jews, after driving Christ away from themselves, desire to destroy.

But that Jesus returns to the land of Israel after Herod’s death announces the end of the world, when, with Enoch and Elijah preaching, the Jews will receive the faith of the truth after the flame of their present envy has been put to rest.

And appropriately, when he leaves Judea, he is said to flee, and this is said to occur at night; but when he returns, there is no mention not only of flight but even of night. For those whom, because of the darkness of their sins, he once left as persecutors, he will at last revisit when they seek him because of the light of faith.

Although Herod had been condemned, Joseph, fearing to go into Judea because of Archelaus, Herod’s son, who held the metropolitan city there, withdrew, at the angel’s warning, into Nazareth of Galilee. This designates the final times of the present Church, when, amid the persecution by which that people now ceaselessly persecutes Christians as far as it is able, a fiercer persecution by the Antichrist will arise against some.

Many will indeed be converted from unbelief by the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, while the rest, stirred up by the Antichrist, will fight against the faith with all their determination.

The part of Judea in which Archelaus reigned therefore represents the faithless followers of the Antichrist. Nazareth of Galilee, however, to which the Lord is transferred, signifies the peace of that same people, which at that time will receive the faith of Christ.

Accordingly, *Galilee* is appropriately interpreted as “migration accomplished,” and *Nazareth* as “flower” or “its shoot.” For the more ardently the holy Church migrates from the things she sees on earth in order to attain the heavenly things, the more abundantly she flourishes and produces the growth of spiritual virtues.

## CHAPTER III [Cols. 0767A–0775A]  
### On the preaching of John the Baptist and the baptism of Christ

### [I.]

“In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea and saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’”

**(Augustine.)** By the words “in those days,” he does not indicate only the days of Jesus’ childhood, but comprehends all the days from his birth up to the time when John began to preach and baptize. At that time Christ is found to have reached youthful maturity.

For Christ and John were of the same age, and Christ is reported to have been about thirty years old when he was baptized by John. Luke, however, expressed the very time of John’s preaching and baptism more distinctly by reference to earthly rulers, saying:

“In the twelfth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene, the word of the Lord came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness, and he went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Luke 3).

The herald of truth therefore teaches repentance in the wilderness of Judea. For those especially needed it from whom, because of sin, the Lord had withdrawn farther away, so that they had become a wilderness.

Later, when they sinned and heaped new murders upon the ancient slaughter of the prophets, he said to them: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke 13).

Therefore the kingdom of heaven is said to draw near to those who repent. For what, because of the pride and transgression of our first parent, had withdrawn farther away, when death and hell drew near, has through Christ’s humility and obedience, with hell set aside, been brought close to those who turn away from sins.

This is said in comparison with the ancient law, under which earthly goods were promised to those who obeyed it. Here, however, not the fertility of the earth but the kingdom of heaven is described as present for those who act well.

John the Baptist was the first to preach the kingdom of heaven, so that as the Lord’s forerunner he might be honored by this privilege.

“For this is he of whom it was spoken through the prophet Isaiah, who said: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’”

When the same John was questioned, according to another evangelist, about who he was, he replied: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1).

He was therefore called “a voice” by the prophet because he preceded the Word. A voice ordinarily occurs between two words: one incorporeal, belonging to the soul, and the other corporeal, belonging to the mouth.

So John came between Christ’s divine birth—of which it is said, “In the beginning was the Word”—and his human birth, of which it is written: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

He also cries in the wilderness because he announces the consolation of redemption to Judea, which had been abandoned and forsaken.

What he was to cry out he makes clear when he adds: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

Everyone who preaches right faith and good works does nothing other than prepare a way for the Lord who is coming into the hearts of his hearers, so that the power of grace may penetrate them and the light of truth illuminate them, and so that he may make straight paths for God by forming pure thoughts in the mind through the word of good preaching.

“John himself had clothing made of camel’s hair, and a leather belt around his waist; his food was locusts and wild honey.”

**(Jerome.)** Behold, the poverty of food and clothing is praised in John, whereas the practice of these things is reproved in the rich.

“He had,” he says, “hair,” not wool, because one thing indicates austere clothing and another the softer luxury of finery.

The leather belt, with which Elijah also was girded, is a symbol of mortification.

As for what follows—“His food was locusts and wild honey”—it suits an inhabitant of the wilderness, so that he might satisfy not the pleasures of food but the needs of human flesh. He sought neither delicacies nourished by herds nor honeycombs carefully tended, but, content with meager fare, lived on tiny flying creatures and honey found in the trunks of trees.

His clothing and food may also appropriately express, by their symbolism, the quality of his inner way of life. Because he used austere clothing, the Lord likewise testified in his praise, saying to the Jews: “What did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Luke 7).

For John did not indulge the life of sinners with flattering words, but rebuked it with the force of harsh denunciation, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?”

He had a belt around his waist because he crucified his flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians 5). We have learned from the Apostle that this belongs to those who are Jesus Christ’s.

He ate locusts and wild honey because his preaching tasted sweet to the crowds. The people thought, and everyone reasoned in his heart about him, that perhaps he was the Christ; but this expectation quickly reached its end when his hearers understood that he was not Christ himself but Christ’s forerunner and prophet.

**(Maurus.)** In honey there is sweetness; in locusts there is a swift flight, but one that quickly falls.

Nor should it be passed over that in the statements of Arculf, bishop of Gaul, who related many things about the holy places, we find that there was a very small species of locust in the wilderness of Judea, on which John the Baptist fed, and which still appears there. Their small, thin bodies are about the size of a finger and can easily be caught in the grass; when cooked in oil, they provide poor people with food.

The same man likewise reports that in the same wilderness there are trees with broad, rounded leaves, white like milk and of honeyed taste. Their nature is so fragile that they can be rubbed apart by hand and eaten. He says that this is what is called “wild honey” in the Gospel.

There also, he says, a spring with clear water is shown, from which Saint John drank; it is protected by a stone roof coated with lime.

Mystically, John preaching in the wilderness of Judea signifies Christ preaching in the wilderness of this world, either through himself or through his teachers, who are rightly called “the voice of one crying” because of the strength of their preaching.

For it is written of him in the Gospel: “Jesus, saying these things, cried out: ‘Let anyone who has ears to hear, hear’” (Luke 8). And again: “On the last and greatest day of the feast Jesus stood and cried out, saying: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’” (John 7).

He himself also commanded his disciples, saying: “What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10).

A cry occurs in three ways: when someone speaks to those who are far away, to the deaf, or out of indignation. All three conditions applied to the human race.

They were far away, for it is written: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Psalm 118). And the prophet speaks to such people, saying: “Hear, you who are far away, says the Lord” (Isaiah 33).

They were deaf, and to them Isaiah says: “Deaf ones, hear”; and: “Who among you will hear this, will pay attention, and listen to what is to come?” (Isaiah 42).

They deserved anger, and of them the prophet says: “The Lord, mighty, will go forth like a warrior; he will stir up zeal, he will shout and cry out; he will prevail against his enemies” (Exodus 15). And again: “They provoked me,” he says, “with foreign gods, and in my wrath I will drive them out” (Deuteronomy 32).

He therefore prepared a way for the Lord when he began to preach and say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

And: “He appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two before his face into every place and city where he himself was about to come” (Luke 10).

The camel’s hair also signifies the Gentiles who would believe in the Lord. Rescued from the error of unbelief and from the power of sins, they were incorporated into Christ’s garment. Hence the prophet says: “You shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Ezekiel 16).

The leather belt, made from the hide of a dead animal after its flesh and blood have been scraped away, likewise signifies the Gentiles who have been drawn away from the fellowship of the dead—that is, sinful human beings—and no longer serve flesh and blood.

They truly gird Christ’s loins because they faithfully believe in his incarnation.

The locusts, which are driven by the wind over the crops and cut down the ears of grain, signify the Jews. Previously they held the law but did not understand its spiritual mysteries; now, moved by the Holy Spirit, they follow the spiritual meaning, leaving behind the empty straw of the letter, so that they may deserve to become food for the Lord.

The honey is the sweetness of the spiritual meaning, found in the leaves of the trees. When it is stored in the hearts of the faithful through the ministry of teachers, Christ’s body is sweetly nourished.

### [II.]

“Then people went out to him from Jerusalem, and all Judea, and the whole region around the Jordan, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.”

It is fitting that those who were to be baptized are said to go out to the prophet. Unless someone withdraws from unbelief, goes out from the fellowship of the faithless, and renounces the devil’s pomp and the world’s allurements, he cannot obtain saving baptism.

Therefore it appropriately follows: “And they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.”

For *Jordan* in the Hebrew language is said to mean “their descent.” They were rightly baptized in the Jordan who had descended from the pride of life and the deeds of the old person to the humility of true confession and the correction of their conduct.

For each person rightly receives baptism when, through confession of sins, he has withdrawn from pride and, by professing a better life, has utterly forbidden his former way of living.

An example was thus already being given to those who desired to receive baptism: they were to confess their sins and promise a better life.

So also after the Lord’s ascension, when Paul was preaching in Ephesus, many believers came, confessing and declaring their deeds (Acts 19), so that, having renounced their former life, they might deserve to be renewed in Christ.

For this reason, when animals of various kinds had been shown to blessed Peter on a heavenly sheet, he was told: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10). This plainly means: Kill unbelievers with respect to what they previously were, by renouncing crimes and promising a devout religion; then, having been imbued with the mysteries of the Christian faith, transform them into members of the holy Church.

“When he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: ‘Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?’”

The Pharisees and Sadducees belonged to the heretical groups among the Jews, but they nevertheless held contrary opinions among themselves, as is said in the Acts of the Apostles.

For *Pharisees* is translated from Hebrew into Latin as “separated,” because they preferred to the people a righteousness based on traditions and observances, which they call *deuteroses*—“second teachings.” Hence they are called “separated” from the people, as though by a private righteousness.

*Sadducees*, however, is interpreted as “righteous.” They claim for themselves what they are not: they deny the resurrection of the body and teach that the soul perishes with the body. They accept only the five books of the law and reject the prophecies of the prophets.

John rebukes such people when they come to his baptism because they especially needed repentance and correction.

The coming wrath is the mind’s apprehension of the final punishment. The sinner cannot escape it then if he does not now turn to the lamentation of repentance.

It should also be noted that evil offspring, imitating the deeds of evil parents, are called “brood of vipers.” By envying the good and persecuting them, repaying some with evil, and following in all these things the ways of their former carnal ancestors, they are like poisonous children born from poisonous parents.

But because we are entangled in sins and in the practice of evil habits, let him tell us what we must do so that we may be able to flee from the coming wrath.

“Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance.”

**(Gregory.)** Here observe that he does not merely urge the production of the fruit of repentance, but of fruit worthy of repentance.

For producing fruit is one thing, and producing fruit worthy of repentance is another. The fruit of a good work should not be equal for one who has sinned less and one who has sinned more, or for one who has fallen into no crimes and one who has fallen into some.

By saying, therefore, “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” each person’s conscience is challenged to seek greater profits in good works through repentance in proportion to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through guilt.

But the Jews did not wish to acknowledge themselves as sinners because they descended from Abraham’s stock. To them he rightly says:

“And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

**(Maurus.)** Because the herald of truth wished to urge them to produce fruit worthy of repentance, he summoned them to humility and strove to cut away every swelling of arrogance. All arrogance is an abomination before the Lord.

The Jews boasted because of the nobility of their lineage and said: “We are Abraham’s offspring and have never been slaves to anyone” (John 7).

But because they did not possess deeds worthy of so great a father, the prophet placed stones before them.

For what were the stones but the hearts of the Gentiles? They were invisible to the understanding of almighty God, just as it is said to certain Jews: “I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh” (Ezekiel 1).

Nor were the Gentiles signified without reason by the name “stones,” since they worshiped stones. Hence it is written: “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them.”

From these stones, then, children were raised up for Abraham. When the hard hearts of the Gentiles believed in Abraham’s offspring—that is, in Christ—they became children of the one to whose offspring they were joined.

Therefore the same Gentiles are told: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Galatians 3).

If, then, through faith in Christ we already are Abraham’s offspring, the Jews, because of their unbelief, have ceased to be Abraham’s children.

“Already the ax is placed at the root of the trees.”

The tree is this world’s entire human race. The ax is our Redeemer, who consists, as it were, of a handle and iron: he is held by his humanity but cuts by his divinity.

This ax has already been placed at the root of the tree. For although he waits patiently, what he is going to do is nevertheless visible.

The preaching of the Gospel word can also be understood by the name “ax.” For according to the Apostle: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts” (Hebrews 4).

The prophet Jeremiah likewise compares the word of the Lord to an ax cutting rock (Jeremiah 46).

Alternatively, the ax signifies the sentence of the Most High Judge, which has been placed at the roots of the trees—that is, at the end of the kingdom of the Jewish people—in order to cut off from the land of the living those who refused to believe in Christ.

“Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

There are four kinds of trees in the various classes of wood. One is entirely dry; another is green but without fruit; the third is green and fruitful but poisonous; the fourth is green and produces good fruit.

In these four differences among trees, four kinds of people are represented: pagans, hypocrites, heretics, and faithful Christian believers.

Pagans are compared to dry trees, since they are destined for eternal burning.

Hypocrites are like green wood that remains without fruit, because they display simulated piety outwardly but lack its fruit.

Heretics are compared to green and fruitful trees that are nevertheless poisonous. Although they appear to produce fruit through preaching or writing, they offer those who taste it not life-giving but deadly food.

Good Catholics are rightly likened to green wood producing good fruit, because they diligently remain green in the holy religion and do not cease to bear the fruits of good works.

**(Gregory.)** Thus every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire, because every perverse person who here disdains to produce the fruit of good works will quickly encounter the burning of Gehenna, which has been prepared for him.

It should also be noted that he says the ax is placed not beside the branches but at the root. When the children of the wicked are taken away, what else are they than the branches of a fruitless tree being cut off? But when the entire offspring is taken away together with its parent, the fruitless tree has been cut down at the root, so that no source remains from which a perverse offspring might grow again.

“I indeed baptize you in water for repentance. But he who is coming after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.”

John baptizes not with the Spirit but with water. Since he cannot release sins, he washes the bodies of those being baptized with water, but does not cleanse the mind through forgiveness.

Why, then, does he baptize if baptism through him does not remit sins? He does so in order to preserve the order of his forerunning: just as by being born he preceded the One who was to be born, so by baptizing he might precede the Lord who was to baptize. And just as by preaching he became Christ’s forerunner, so by baptizing he might also become his forerunner through an imitation of the sacrament.

**(Bede.)** For this reason John baptized with water: so that all whom he could persuade to repent and believe in Christ might be separated by the sign of his baptism from the crowd of unbelievers and impenitent people, and directed toward seeking Christ’s baptism.

“He who is coming after me,” he says—that is, for preaching and baptizing—“is stronger than I,” because he surpasses me in dignity.

He is strong who baptizes for the confession of sins, but stronger who baptizes for their remission.

He is strong who is worthy to possess the Holy Spirit, but stronger who is able to bestow him.

He is strong than whom no one born of women is greater, but stronger is he to whom everything has been subjected beneath his feet, after he was made a little lower than the angels (Hebrews 2).

He is strong who first came to preach the kingdom of heaven, but stronger is he who alone was able to give it.

“Whose sandals,” he says, “I am not worthy to carry.”

The other evangelists wrote: “Whose sandal-thong I am not worthy to untie.”

**(Augustine.)** John the Baptist could have said both things, either one at one time and the other at another, or both together. He might have said: “I am not worthy to untie the sandal-thong, nor to carry his sandals,” so that one evangelist reported one statement and the others another, while all narrated the truth.

John’s words about the Lord’s sandals intend nothing other than to express Christ’s excellence and John’s humility.

If an allegory is sought here, the sandal may signify the Lord’s incarnation.

**(Maurus.)** For who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? When the incarnate Lord came, he appeared, as it were, wearing sandals, since in his divinity he assumed a body subject to our mortality.

But because people thought John was the Christ—and John himself denies this by subjecting himself to such great power—he confesses that he is unworthy to have taken flesh from a virgin without the seed of a man.

This dignity and power belong not to a servant but to the Lord, not to a creature but to the Creator. For this reason he does not wish to be regarded by anyone as the Christ, but as his forerunner.

**(Gregory.)** Since the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate the mystery of this incarnation—for it cannot in any way investigate how the Word becomes embodied, how the supreme life-giving Spirit is given life within a mother’s womb, or how the One who has no beginning exists and is conceived—John therefore said, according to the other evangelists, that he was not worthy to untie the thong of his sandal.

The sandal-thong is therefore the bond of the mystery. John cannot untie the thong of his sandal because even he, who recognized the incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. Among the ancients there was a custom that if a man did not wish to take as his wife the woman who was properly his, the man who came to her as bridegroom by right of kinship would untie his sandal.

What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be, if not the Bridegroom of the holy Church? The same John says of him: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3).

But because John did not wish to be considered the bridegroom, but rather the friend of the bridegroom, he rightly declares himself unworthy to untie the thong of his sandal, as though he were saying openly: “I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s feet, because I do not presumptuously claim for myself the name of bridegroom.”

“He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

**(Bede.)** This means both by the cleansing of sanctification and by the testing of tribulation.

The same Holy Spirit may also be understood as signified by the name “fire,” because he kindles through love and illuminates through the wisdom with which he fills hearts.

Therefore those to whom it was said, “John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1), received the same baptism of the Spirit in the appearance of fire.

Some explain this to mean that in the present we are baptized in the Spirit and in the future in fire: just as we are now reborn through water and the Spirit for the redemption of all sins, so then, before the final judgment, we will be cleansed by the baptism of purifying fire from certain lighter sins that have clung to us as we depart this life.

The Apostle says: “If anyone builds upon this foundation—gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw—the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone’s work that he has built upon the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3).

Although this can also be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, if anyone accepts it as referring to the fire of future purification, he must carefully consider that the Apostle said that the person can be saved through fire—not one who builds iron, bronze, or lead upon Christ’s foundation, that is, greater and harder sins, already insoluble at that time, but one who builds linen, hay, or straw, that is, minimal and very light sins, which the fire can easily consume.

This must nevertheless be understood: even there, no one will obtain purification from the smallest sins unless, while still placed in this life, he earns it through good works so that he may obtain it there.

“His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor.”

By the winnowing fork—that is, by the open discrimination of a just examination—the present Church is signified by the threshing floor.

Within it, unquestionably—and this is sufficiently grievous—many are called but few are chosen: a few grains are destined for the heavenly dwelling places, in comparison with the weeds that are to be consigned to everlasting flames.

The cleansing of this threshing floor is carried out now individually, whenever a perverse person is either expelled from the Church by priestly correction for manifest sins or condemned after death by divine severity for hidden sins.

It will be completed universally at the end, when the Son of Man will send his angels and “they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling” (Matthew 13).

The Lord therefore has the winnowing fork in his hand—that is, he holds the distinction of judgment in his power. For the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son.

“And he will gather his wheat into the barn, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

The Lord himself likewise brought the parable of the good seed, into which the enemy sowed weeds, to this conclusion, saying: “At the time of harvest I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn” (Matthew 13).

He was clearly teaching that the impious and sinners would be handed over to the fire of Gehenna, while the saints would be crowned with heavenly glory.

There is, however, this difference between chaff and weeds: chaff comes from no other seed than that of wheat, although it degenerates from the nobility of the good root; weeds, on the other hand, not only tear away the fruit by their nature but are produced from an entirely different origin.

The chaff, therefore, consists of those who are instructed in the same mysteries of faith as the elect but dissent from their solid perfection either through the frivolity of their works or through the emptiness of their unbelief.

The weeds, however, are those who do not even deign to hear the words of the faith. For this reason they are separated from the lot, work, and profession of the good alike.

Thus in the field of this world there is one fruit belonging to the elect and two belonging to the reprobate. Everything the enemy sows is subject to the flames, and, what is more grievous, many things sown by the good sower perish—some snatched away by birds, some dried up by the sun, some choked by thorns, and some finally turned into chaff.

Only the wheat of the elect, created from good soil and proved worthy through patience, will be stored in the barn of heavenly life.

Likewise, according to another parable, it is not only the fish that avoid the nets of apostolic faith and remain hidden in the lowest waters of sins; many are also drawn as far as the shore of final judgment among the good, and then, because of the guilt of their wickedness, deserve to be cast into the outer darkness.

He calls the fire of Gehenna unquenchable in two senses: because it cannot itself ever be extinguished and because it will never extinguish those whom it torments, but will punish them with what I may call immortal death.

This is in contrast to that most holy fire with which he previously said Christ’s elect would be baptized.

Concerning this the Psalmist says: “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested” (Psalm 45).

And shortly afterward: “We were not burned forever, but we passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment. I will enter your house with burnt offerings”—that is, after overcoming the anguish of afflictions, I will enter the courts of your kingdom with thanksgiving.

### III.

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.

**Maurus.** By the words “Then Jesus came,” he means, at the time when John was preaching and baptizing, namely, in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Jesus himself was thirty years old. He thereby shows that this was the proper and mature age for those who think that every age is suitable either for the priesthood or for teaching: Jesus was baptized at thirty, and only then began to perform signs and to teach. For at twelve years of age he questioned people on earth, while by his divinity he teaches the angels in heaven. So Joseph, who figuratively preserved the Egyptians from famine for eighty years, assumed the reins of royal government at thirty, after washing away the filth of his prison. David likewise began, at the same age, the kingdom which, at seventy—that is, at the age worthy of perpetual rest—he would complete. Ezekiel too, at thirty, when the heavens were opened to him, obtained the gifts of prophecy. And because through faith adversity must be endured patiently and rewards must be hoped for sublimely, the height of the ark or temple, and the length of the tabernacle, are measured at thirty cubits.

“Then,” he says, “Jesus came into the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.”

**Jerome.** The Savior received baptism from John for three reasons. First, because, having been born as a human being, he was to fulfill all the righteousness and humility of the Law; second, so that by his own baptism he might confirm John’s baptism; third, so that, sanctifying the waters of the Jordan by the descent of the dove, he might reveal the coming of the Holy Spirit in the washing of believers.

**Bede.** The Son of God came to be baptized by a human being—not from the anxious necessity of washing away any sin of his own, since he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth, but by a merciful dispensation, in order to wash away all the filth of our sins. For “we all offend in many things,” and if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. The Creator of the waters came to be baptized in the waters themselves, so that he might signify to us, who are conceived in iniquities and born in transgressions, the mystery of the second birth, which is celebrated through water and the Spirit. He who was clean from every defilement graciously consented to be washed in the waters of the Jordan, in order to sanctify the streams of water for washing away all the filth of our crimes.

But John forbade him, saying, “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” He was astonished that one should come to him to be baptized in water who had no fault for baptism to cleanse—indeed, who by the grace of his Spirit would remove from believers the whole guilt of the world. Hence it is rightly understood that what John says here, “I ought to be baptized by you,” is equivalent to what he is reported to have said in the Gospel according to John when Jesus came to him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” For we must all be baptized by him who came into the world for the purpose of taking away the sins of the world.

John himself ought to have been baptized by him—that is, cleansed from the contagion of original sin. Although he was not inferior to any of those born of women, yet, as one born of a woman, he was not free from the blemish of guilt. Therefore, together with the other children of women, he needed to be washed by him who, born of a Virgin, appeared as God in the flesh. Since it is written, “What is man, that he should be undefiled, and that one born of woman should appear clean?” (Job 25:4), the holy man rightly feared to baptize the Lord: although born of a woman, he was not free from the stain of guilt, whereas he knew that the Lord, born of a virgin, possessed absolutely no stain of sin.

But because true humility is that which is never without obedience as its companion, the office he had at first refused he afterward fulfilled humbly. For it follows:

But Jesus answered and said to him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him. That is, only then did he release him, consent, and permit himself to be baptized by him, when he understood that all righteousness had to be fulfilled in this order.

“Let it be so now,” he says: allow me now to be baptized by you in water, as I have commanded, so that afterward you may be baptized by me in the Spirit, as you desire. Thus it is fitting for us to offer an example of the fulfillment of all righteousness, so that the faithful may learn that no human being can become perfectly righteous without the water of baptism, and that the life-giving rite of regeneration is necessary for all, even for those who live innocently and justly, when they understand that I, who was conceived and born through the work of the Holy Spirit, underwent—or rather, consecrated for them—the washing of the second birth.

Let no person of rank disdain to be baptized for the remission of sins by my humble servants, remembering that the Lord, who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and can forgive sins, subjected his head to be baptized in water by the hands of a servant.

### IV.

But when Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.

This too belongs to the fulfillment of all righteousness: when the Lord had been baptized, the heavens were opened to him and the Spirit descended upon him, so that our faith might thereby be confirmed through the mystery of sacred baptism—that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened to us and the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed.

Should we really believe that the heavenly mysteries first became open to the Lord at that time? Catholic faith holds that, no less during the time when he lived among human beings than afterward and before, the Son of God remained in the bosom of God the Father and occupied his heavenly throne. Nor should we believe that he received the gifts of the Holy Spirit from the age of thirty, when he was baptized, since from his first conception he had always been full of the Holy Spirit.

These mysteries were also enacted for us, who are his members. Because the Lord consecrated the washing of baptism for us through the immersion of his most holy body, he also showed us that, after baptism has been received, the entrance to heaven is opened and the Holy Spirit is given. There is also a highly appropriate contrast here. The first Adam, deceived by an unclean spirit through the serpent, lost the joys of the heavenly kingdom. The second Adam, glorified by the Holy Spirit through the dove, opened the lights of that same kingdom and showed that the flashing flame which, after the expulsion of the first Adam, the cherub guardian had placed across the entrance to paradise was to be extinguished through the water of the washing of rebirth.

Thus, from the place where the first man departed, defeated by the enemy together with his wife, the second Adam might return victorious over the enemy with the holy Church, his bride.

The Spirit of reconciliation rightly appeared in a dove, a very simple bird, so that through the likeness of this creature he might show the simplicity of his own nature—for “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit”—and might teach that the one upon whom he descended would be gentle, mild, and a herald and minister of heavenly mercy toward the world. At the same time he admonished all who were to be renewed by grace to enter as simple and pure in heart.

Accordingly it is written: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart; for wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:1–4).

Since the dove is set before us so that we may learn the simplicity pleasing to God, let us examine its nature more carefully, so that from each example of its innocence we may take instruction for a more disciplined life.

It is free from the malice of gall. “Let all bitterness, anger, and indignation be removed from us, together with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). It harms no one with its beak or claws, not even the smallest birds or worms, with which almost all smaller birds feed themselves and their young. Let us see to it that our teeth are not weapons and arrows (Psalm 56:5), lest, biting and devouring one another, we consume one another (Galatians 5:15).

Let us restrain our hands from robbery: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one in need” (Ephesians 4:28). The dove is also often said to feed the young of others as though they were its own; it feeds itself on the fruits of the earth and on seed.

Let us hear the Apostle: “It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine” (Romans 14:21). And the Apostle Peter says: “Supply virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, perseverance in self-control, godliness in perseverance, and brotherly love in godliness” (2 Peter 1:5–7).

It has a groan in place of a song. Let us be miserable, mourn, and weep before the Lord who made us. Let our laughter be turned into mourning and our joy into sorrow. For “blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4).

It is accustomed to sit upon the waters, so that, foreseeing in the water the shadow of the approaching hawk, it may avoid being seized. Let us also diligently attend upon the streams of the purifying Scriptures, so that, instructed by their mirrors, we may be able to recognize and avoid the snares of the wicked enemy.

It is enough to have recalled these seven examples of virtue from the nature of the dove—and perhaps rightly so, since the grace of the Holy Spirit, who descended in the dove, is sevenfold.

**Gregory.** But it must be asked why the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove in our Redeemer himself, the mediator between God and human beings, but in the disciples in the form of fire.

Certainly the only-begotten Son of God is the Judge of the human race. But who could endure his justice if, before gathering us through gentleness, he had wished to examine our faults through the zeal of righteousness? Therefore, having become human for human beings, he showed himself gentle toward human beings. He did not wish to strike sinners, but to gather them. He first wished to correct them gently, so that afterward he might have people whom he could save in judgment.

The Spirit therefore ought to appear over him in the form of a dove, because he did not come to strike sins, even with zeal, but still to tolerate them through gentleness. Conversely, the Holy Spirit ought to be shown over the disciples in fire, so that the spiritual fervor might kindle those who were simply human and therefore sinners against themselves, and so that they might punish through repentance in themselves the sins that God was sparing through gentleness.

For they too could not be without sin, since they adhered to heavenly teaching, as John bears witness when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

And behold, a voice from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

**Augustine.** Mark and Luke likewise relate this, but they vary in the wording of the voice that came from heaven, while preserving the same meaning. For what Matthew says was spoken—“This is my beloved Son”—and what the other two say—“You are my beloved Son”—serves to express the same meaning.

The heavenly voice said one of these things, but the evangelist wished to show that “This is my beloved Son” amounts to the same as what was said, so that it might indicate to those who were listening that he was the Son of God. Thus he wished to report it as “You are my Son,” as though it had been said to them, “This is my Son.” For the statement was not made to Christ, who already knew it, but to those who were present and listening, for whose sake the voice itself was produced.

As for the words “in whom I am well pleased,” one evangelist says “in you I am well pleased,” and another “in you I have been well pleased.” It is evident that, while each evangelist preserved the words of the heavenly voice, the others reported them in a more familiar form to explain the same meaning. It is understood that all of this was said, as though the statement were: “In you I have established my good pleasure,” that is, “through you I shall accomplish what pleases me.”

**Rabanus.** Thus the Son of God is baptized in a human being, the Spirit of God descends in a dove, and God the Father speaks in a voice: the mystery of the holy and indivisible Trinity is declared in the baptism.

And rightly so. Since he was going to command the ministers of his sacraments to teach all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, he first revealed personally, in his own baptism, that the whole Trinity was present.

When the Father’s voice says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” it speaks by comparison with earthly humanity. It indicates that, when the earthly human being sinned, God the Creator was, so to speak, displeased with himself, as he says: “It repents me that I made human beings on the earth” (Genesis 6:6).

Repentance, strictly speaking, does not befall God. But speaking in our manner—since we are accustomed to feel remorse when we see our actions turned against our intention—he said that he regretted having made the human being whom he saw, through sin, degenerating from the uprightness of his creation.

But in his only-begotten Son he was uniquely well pleased, because he knew that this human nature he had assumed was kept free from sin.

In this voice of the Father, as in the other mysteries of the Lord’s baptism, the fulfillment of all righteousness is also declared. The Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, is made known to human beings through the Spirit who descends upon him, so that through this human beings may learn that, having received the Holy Spirit by the grace of baptism, they can be transferred from children of the devil into children of God.

As the Apostle teaches when he speaks to the faithful: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15). And the evangelist John says: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

## CHAPTER IV. On Christ’s Fast in the Desert and the Threefold Temptation, etc.

### I.

Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil.

Some may wonder by what spirit Jesus was led into the desert, because what follows says: “The devil took him into the holy city,” and again, “he took him onto a high mountain” (Matthew 4:5, 8).

But it is truly and without any question appropriate to understand that he was led into the desert by the Holy Spirit, so that his own Spirit might lead him to the place where the evil spirit would find him for temptation.

This is also clearly indicated in the Gospel according to Luke, where it is said: “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the desert” (Luke 4:1).

Jesus was therefore not driven into the desert by the power of an evil spirit. Rather, by the will of his own good Spirit, he entered the place of combat, certain of victory, in order to overthrow his adversary.

Here he also rightly sets before us the pattern of proper conduct: after receiving the remission of sins in baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, we should equip ourselves more suitably against the new snares of the ancient enemy. Forsaking the world in our minds, we should learn to hunger only for the joys of eternal life, like the manna of the desert.

And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was afterward hungry.

**Bede.** The fast of Lent has authority both in the ancient books, from the fasting of Moses and Elijah, and in the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days. He thereby shows that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets.

Moses represents the Law, and Elijah the prophet; between them he appeared gloriously on the mountain, so that it might be made more evident what the Apostle says about him: “Having testimony from the Law and the Prophets” (Romans 3:21).

At what part of the year could the observance of Lent have been established more suitably than near and immediately adjacent to the Lord’s Passion? For in it this laborious life is signified, a life requiring self-restraint, so that we fast from friendship with the world itself.

Alternatively: the Lord fasted when he was tempted before his death, still needing food. But he ate and drank when he was glorified, after the resurrection, no longer needing food. In the former case he showed our labor in himself; in the latter, he showed his consolation in us. He defined both by forty-day periods, because the number itself—that is, forty—seems to signify the course of this age, which must be observed by those who are called by grace from the four parts of the world to him who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

There are ten commandments of the Law, and by the grace of Christ they have been spread throughout the world. The world is divided into four parts, and ten multiplied by four makes forty. For those redeemed by the Lord, “he gathered from the regions: from the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea” (Isaiah 49:12).

Thus, fasting forty days before the death of the flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Abstain from the desires of this age.” But eating and drinking forty days after the resurrection of the flesh, he seemed to cry out: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Fasting belongs to the tribulation of combat, because the one who is in the arena exercises self-restraint in all things. Food belongs to the hope of peace, which will not be perfect until our body, whose redemption we await, has put on immortality. We do not yet possess that glory, but we are already nourished by hope.

The Apostle shows that we do both at once when he says: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans 12:12). It is as though the former belonged to food and the latter to fasting.

As we travel along the Lord’s way, we both fast from the vanity of the present age and are refreshed by the promise of the future: here we do not set our hearts, while there we set our hearts above.

The Lord became hungry after completing the days of his fast, although nothing of this kind is written about Moses or Elijah when they fasted, so that the hostile enemy would not flee in fear from one who, marked by so many heavenly signs and also seen to excel in abstinence, seemed their equal.

The humble God, made man, became hungry, lest he be recognized by the enemy as the exalted God-man.

**Maurus.** Mystically, that hunger with which the Lord hungered signifies the desire he had for our salvation. He fasted, abstaining from earthly food, so that we might be refreshed by heavenly food. He was tempted so that through his victory he might enable us to conquer. He died and rose again so that we, dead in sins, might live in righteousness through him.

When, therefore, by his grace we are converted to do his will, we provide him with refreshment. Thus he asked the Samaritan woman for a drink. And when his disciples offered him earthly food, he said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to complete his work” (John 4:34). Elsewhere he says: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29).

And the tempter came and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

If the Lord had not fasted, the devil would not have had an opportunity to tempt him. He approached by permission for the purpose of temptation, although he was far away in his desire for evil. He approached, driven by the arrogance of pride, disregarding the rule of justice.

A servant rose up against his Lord, a captive against the free, the weak against the strong; and while he sought to bind the innocent, he grieved to lose the guilty.

It was therefore not unworthy of our Redeemer that he wished to be tempted, since he had come to be killed. It was just that he should overcome our temptations by his temptations, just as he had come to overcome our death by his death.

“If you are the Son of God,” he says, “command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

The ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer of the human race, his conqueror, had come into the world. He could have learned this either from the promise made through the prophets, or from the announcement given through angels, or even from John’s pointing him out with his finger.

Hence, through a possessed man, he also said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matthew 8:29).

Yet when he saw him subject to suffering, when he saw that he could endure mortal things in his humanity, everything he had suspected concerning his divinity became doubtful to him through the arrogance of his pride.

Knowing nothing except pride in himself, when he saw that Christ was humble, he doubted that he was Lord, and therefore resorted to the means of temptation.

But the soul of our Redeemer was not shaken by the necessity of temptation as we are, who are merely human beings. Temptation is carried out in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. When we are tempted, we often fall into pleasure, or even into consent, because, propagated through the sin of the flesh, we carry within ourselves the source of the struggles we endure.

But God, who came to assume flesh without sin, endured no contradiction within himself. He could therefore be tempted through suggestion, but the pleasure of sin did not bite his mind. For this reason, the whole of that diabolical temptation was external, not internal.

He graciously submitted to all these things outwardly, while inwardly his mind remained unshaken, clinging to his divinity. Even when he is said to have been troubled in spirit and to have groaned, he himself, by divine arrangement, determined the extent to which he would be troubled in his humanity.

When the Lord was hungry, the devil suggested that he make loaves not from earth or hay but from stones, because, hard in mind, he displayed hardness in his speech.

“Say,” he says, “that these stones become loaves of bread.” He did not say, “Make them,” but “Say,” because he knew what is written: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). And elsewhere: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 33:9). To speak for God is to make.

Yet the Son of God is not astonishing even if he creates loaves from stones, since he does this every day through seeds cast into the earth: “Watering the mountains from his heights, so that he may bring forth bread from the earth and make wine gladden the human heart” (Psalm 104:13, 15).

Mystically, he makes loaves from stones when, through the Gospel, he brings diverse nations—compared to stones because of the hardness of their minds—into his own body. For, according to the Apostle, “because there is one bread, we who are many are one body in Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

And he answered and said: “It is written: ‘Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’”

This testimony is taken from Deuteronomy, where Moses recalled God’s benefits to the people, saying to them: “The Lord gave you food, manna, which neither you nor your fathers knew” (Deuteronomy 8:3), so that he might show you that “human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

Therefore, if someone does not feed upon the word of God, that person does not live. For just as the human body does not live without earthly food, so the soul cannot live without the word of God.

The word is said to proceed from the mouth of God when the supreme Creator wishes to reveal his counsel and will to our weakness through the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. This does not mean that the incorporeal God possesses bodily features in his nature; rather, “his invisible attributes are understood and seen through the things that have been made,” as are his eternal power and divinity (Romans 1:20).

It should also be noted that, when our Redeemer was tempted, he answered the devil through statements from Scripture because his purpose was to conquer the devil through humility, not through power.

He gave us an example, so that whenever we suffer something from wicked people, we may be stirred toward instruction rather than revenge.

Our enemy, while we remain in this life, strives to attack us all the more fiercely the more he sees us rebelling against him. He neglects to strike those whom he believes he possesses by a peaceful right. But he is aroused against us with greater violence the more he is expelled from our hearts as though from the right of his own dwelling.

The Lord figuratively represented this in himself under a certain dispensation: he permitted the devil to tempt him only after baptism, so that he might indicate to us a sign of the future course of life—that his members, after setting out toward God, would endure more severe snares of temptation.

Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple.

**Jerome.** This taking up, as it is called, did not arise from any weakness in the Lord, but from the enemy’s pride, who thought that the Savior’s will was necessity. From this passage we understand what is meant by the other statement: “They went into the holy city, and appeared to many” (Matthew 27:53).

**Maurus.** Jerusalem was called the holy city because the temple of God and the Holy of Holies were there, as well as the worship of the one God according to the Law of Moses.

The pinnacle is the summit of the roof. The temple did not have a peaked roof rising above, any more than the tabernacle did; rather, it was flat, as is customary among all who build houses in Palestine and Egypt.

And he said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.”

**Hilary.** In all his temptations the devil is trying to discover whether he is the Son of God. But the Lord so regulates his answer that he leaves him uncertain.

“Throw yourself down,” he says, because the devil’s voice, which always desires to persuade everyone to fall downward, can persuade but cannot compel a fall.

**Maurus.** It should also be noted that, although Christ permitted the devil to place him on the pinnacle of the temple, he nevertheless refused to descend at his command.

This gives us an example: if someone commands us to ascend the narrow and heavenly way of truth, we should obey. But if someone wishes, through deceptive arguments, to hurl us from the height of truth and virtue into the depths of error and vice, we should not listen to him.

The apostolic teaching instructs us concerning both matters. Paul says to the Philippians: “Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from goodwill” (Philippians 1:15). A little later he says: “What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and I shall continue to rejoice. For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer” (Philippians 1:18–19).

Again, he says to the Galatians: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should proclaim to you a gospel contrary to the one we proclaimed to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8).

For it is written: “He will command his angels concerning you, so that they may lift you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.”

**Jerome.** We read this in Psalm 91, but there it is not a prophecy about Christ; it concerns a holy man. The devil therefore misinterprets the Scriptures. Certainly, if he truly knew that this had been written about the Savior, he ought also to have said what follows in the same psalm against himself: “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk; you will trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 91:13).

He speaks of angelic assistance as though to one who is weak, but, as a deceiver, he is silent about his own being trampled.

Then Jesus said to him again: “It is written: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’”

He breaks the devil’s false arrows drawn from Scripture with the true shields of Scripture. Note that he brought forward necessary testimonies only from Deuteronomy, in order to display the mysteries of the second Law.

“You shall not tempt,” he says, “the Lord your God.”

**Augustine.** He was being urged, as though he were merely human, to test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much he could accomplish with God. This is done wickedly whenever it is done; for it belongs to sound doctrine, when a person has something he can do, not to tempt the Lord his God.

For the Savior himself was able to protect his disciples, yet he said to them: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10:23), and he first provided an example of this.

Although he had the power to lay down his life and would not lay it down except when he willed, he nevertheless fled to Egypt as an infant, carried by his parents. He also went up to the feast not openly but secretly, although at other times he spoke publicly while the Jews were angry and listening with the most hostile intent. Yet they were unable to lay hands on him because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30).

Thus, by teaching and rebuking openly, while at the same time not allowing the rage of his enemies to have any power over him, he demonstrated God’s power. But by fleeing and hiding he also instructed human weakness, so that no one would dare to tempt God when there is something one can do to escape what ought to be avoided.

Again the devil took him onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.

**Gregory.** When it is said that the God-man was taken by the devil either onto a high mountain or into the holy city, the human mind recoils and human ears are afraid to hear it. Yet we know that these things are not incredible if we consider other things that happened to him.

Certainly, the devil is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are members of this head. What, then, is surprising if he permitted himself to be led by the devil onto a mountain, when he also endured being crucified by the devil’s members?

**Maurus.** Mystically, this mountain signifies the devil’s pride, by which he himself was deceived and seeks to deceive others. The Lord descended to humble and level places, so that he might overcome the devil through humility. But the devil hastened to lead him onto a mountain, so that, through the one by whom he himself had fallen, others too might fall.

“He showed him,” it says, “all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.”

Thus the whole power of the age is now brought to bear against the Lord, and possession of the whole universe is offered to its Creator, so that the devil, maintaining the order of his ancient fraud—by which he had neither enticed him with food nor moved him from his position—might now corrupt him through ambition.

The glory of the kingdoms of the world may be understood either as the favor of human praise, which particularly attends the kings and powerful people of this world, or as any ambition that flourishes in gold, silver, gems, and other precious things.

The devil therefore showed the Lord all the kingdoms of the world on the mountain—not because he could enlarge the Lord’s vision or show him anything unknown to him, for how could the structure of creation be hidden from its Creator? Rather, he displayed in words the vanity of worldly pomp, which he himself loved, as though it were beautiful and desirable, and sought to suggest to Christ that he should come to love it.

This may also be understood in another way. Since the devil knew that Christ had come to remove his kingdom, and that those who were under him would begin to be with Christ, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world—that is, the people of this age—and how some are ruled by fornication, others by avarice, others are swept away by popular acclaim, and others are captivated by the allure of beauty.

We should not suppose that, by showing him the kingdoms of the world, he displayed the kingdom of the Persians or, for example, that of the Indians. Rather, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world—that is, his own kingdom and the way in which he reigned in the world—so that, urging Christ to do what he wanted, he might begin to have Christ subject to him.

What is written in Luke—that all the kingdoms of the inhabited earth were shown to him in a moment of time (Luke 4:5)—indicates not so much the speed of the sight as the transience of that power. In a moment all those things pass away, and worldly honor often disappears before it has even arrived. For what in this age can be lasting, when the ages themselves do not last?

And he said to him: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

**Jerome.** The arrogant and proud devil says this boastfully—not because he possesses power over the whole world, so that he could give all the kingdoms, since we know that many holy men have been made kings by God.

“If you fall,” he says, “and worship me.” Therefore, the one who is going to worship the devil first falls.

But if we consider and weigh the order of the temptation, we perceive how greatly we are freed from temptation. The ancient enemy rose up against our first parent, the first human being, through three temptations. He tempted him through gluttony, avarice, and vain glory, and by tempting him he overcame him, subjecting him to himself through consent.

He tempted him through gluttony when he showed him the food of the forbidden tree and persuaded him to eat, saying: “Taste.” He tempted him through vain glory when he said: “You will be like gods.” And he certainly tempted him through avarice when he said: “Knowing good and evil.”

For avarice concerns not only money but also exalted status. It is rightly called avarice when exaltation is sought beyond measure.

But by the same means through which he struck down the first human being, he was overcome when he tempted the second human being.

He tempts through gluttony when he says: “Command that these stones become loaves of bread.” He tempts through vain glory when he says: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” He tempts through avarice for exalted status when he shows him all the kingdoms of the world and says: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

But he is defeated by the same means through which he boasted of having overcome the first human being, so that, captured by the very sound of these words, he may leave our hearts by the same entrance through which he had entered them.

[Col. 0785B] Then Jesus said to him, “Go, Satan.” (Jerome.) He does not condemn Satan and the apostle Peter with the same sentence, as many suppose. For Peter he says, “Get behind me, Satan,” that is, “Follow me, because you are opposed to my will.” Here, however, he hears, “Go, Satan,” and “behind me” is not added, so that the sense is: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for you and your angels.” (Maurus.) If, however, someone wishes to read, according to other copies, “Go behind me, Satan,” he can understand it in this way: that “behind” refers back to past times, when the devil held the guilty world in his power. It is as though the Lord, saying to the devil, “Go behind me, Satan,” indicated that the period of his rule—which he had held throughout past ages—was now coming to an end, as if he said: “Look back to when you deceived the first man [Col. 0785C] and deluded his descendants through various forms of idolatry. Let it be enough for you up to this point; now, however, you will not only be unable to overthrow me, but through me you will be expelled from the power over which you used to boast.” As he himself said when the hour of his passion was approaching: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, when I have been lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII). Thus *Satan* is interpreted in Latin as “adversary” or “transgressor.” And rightly the enemy of truth and transgressor of justice goes backward, because, since he did not preserve his own honor, he will appear worthy of eternal disgrace, having been driven back as an invader of another’s dominion [Col. 0786A].

For it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.” (Jerome.) When the devil says to the Savior, “If you fall down and worship me,” he hears in return that he himself ought rather to worship his Lord and God. Someone may perhaps ask how what is commanded here—that one should serve the Lord alone—can agree with the apostle’s statement: “But through love serve one another” (Galatians V). The origin of the Greek language, from which Scripture was translated, readily resolves this question. In Greek, service is ordinarily expressed in two ways and with different meanings: it is called *λατρεία* (*latreia*), and it is also called *δουλεία* (*douleia*). *Douleia* means common service—that is, service offered either to God, or to a human being, or to any part of the created order; from this word a servant, that is, *δοῦλος* (*doulos*), also receives his Greek name. *Latreia*, however, is the service owed exclusively to the worship of the divine nature and not to be shared with any creature. Hence those who offer to idols the vows, prayers, and sacrifices that ought to have been offered to the one God are called idolaters. We are therefore commanded to serve one another through love, which in Greek is *δουλεύειν* (*douleuein*); we are commanded to serve the One, which in Greek is *λατρεύειν* (*latreuein*).
