Hence the statement, “And him alone you shall serve,” is expressed in Greek by *λατρεύσεις* (*latreuseis*); and again, “For we are the circumcision, serving God in the Spirit” (Philippians III), is expressed in Greek by *λατρεύοντες* (*latreuontes*).

Then the devil left him, and behold, angels approached and ministered to him. (Jerome.) Temptation comes first, so that victory may follow; the angels minister in order to confirm the dignity of the victor. What else does this show than that the two natures belong to one person? He is both a human being whom the devil tempts and that same person is God, to whom angels minister. Let us therefore recognize our nature in him, since the devil would not have tempted him unless he had perceived him to be human. Let us venerate his divinity in him, since angels would in no way minister to him unless he existed as God above all things. But because in this book we have explained the beginning of the holy Gospel—namely, the genealogy and infancy of the Savior, his baptism and temptation—let us take another beginning with the start of his preaching.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0785]

## CHAPTER IV Follows: On the Beginning of Christ’s Preaching and the Calling of the Disciples

[Col. 0785D]

[I.] After the evangelist Matthew had related the Savior’s forty-day fast, the temptation by which he was tempted by the devil, and the ministry of the angels, he immediately added, saying:

“But when Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.”

[II.] The apostle and evangelist John, however, makes clear that this did not happen immediately, when he says that Jesus went into Galilee before John the Baptist had been sent to prison. For after he had recalled that Jesus made wine from water at Cana of Galilee, and went down with his mother and disciples, and that they remained there for not many days, he says that Jesus then went up to Jerusalem because of the Passover. After this, he says, Jesus came into the land of Judea, together with his disciples, and stayed there with them and baptized. He then continues: “John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there” (John III).

Matthew, however, as we demonstrated above, says: “But when he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.” Mark says likewise. John, on the other hand, says that after John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee. Luke says nothing about John’s being handed over, but says only that after Christ’s baptism and temptation he came into Galilee, just as those other two evangelists do. For he weaves his narrative together in this way: “When every temptation had been completed,” he says, “the devil withdrew from him until the appointed time. And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and a report about him went out through the whole region.”

From this it is understood that these three evangelists did not narrate something contrary to the evangelist John, but omitted Jesus’ first arrival in Galilee after he had been baptized, when he changed water into wine. At that time John had not yet been handed over. They connected their narratives, rather, with his later arrival in Galilee, which took place after John had been handed over. The evangelist John himself speaks of this return to Galilee as follows: “When Jesus therefore knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples were—he left Judea and went again into Galilee” (John IV).

We therefore understand that John had already been handed over at that time, and that the Jews had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John had made and baptized. Nor should I pass over what ecclesiastical history relates: that the most blessed apostle John preached the Gospel almost until the final period of his life without any written record of it. But when, it says, knowledge of the three Gospels had also reached him, he approved the faith and truth of what they said; nevertheless, he saw that certain things were lacking, especially those that the Lord had done at the beginning of his preaching. When his faithful and believing hearers in Christ asked him to describe the deeds of the Savior that the earlier writers had passed over, before John’s handing over, he therefore says in the Gospel: “This was the beginning of signs that Jesus did” (John II). And again, in another place, he indicates this by saying: “For John had not yet been sent into prison” (John III).

From these statements it is clear that he describes what Jesus did before John was handed over; that is, he composed the history of only one year—the year in which Jesus also suffered—after John’s imprisonment.

“And leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali.” (Jerome.) Nazareth, from which our Lord and Savior was called a Nazarene, is therefore a village in Galilee, opposite the region, twelve miles eastward from it, near Mount Tabor. Capernaum, however, is still a town in Galilee of the nations, beside the lake of Gennesaret, situated in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali.

A certain bishop mentioned above, Arculphus, relates that in modern times both of these cities are without any circuit of walls; that Nazareth is situated above the mountain, while Capernaum is confined within a narrow space between the mountain and the lake, having the mountain to the north and the lake to the south, and extending in a straight line from west to east.

Mystically, however, the fact that Jesus begins to preach after John has been handed over signifies that when the Law comes to an end, the Gospel consequently arises; when the dawn fails, the true Sun rises; when the disciple ceases, the Teacher is present. Yet that Teacher is humble: he did not despise or hinder the disciple’s teaching, but waited until the disciple had completed his course. He thus gives us an example, so that no one may disdain to hear the word of preaching from an inferior person; rather, he should strive to imitate apostolic humility, because it says: “If something is revealed to another who is seated, let the first be silent” (1 Corinthians XIV).

“And leaving,” he says, “the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea.” Nazareth is interpreted as “flower” or “its young shoot.” Capernaum is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” or “field of richness,” or “village of consolation.” Our Redeemer therefore rightly passes from Nazareth to Capernaum, because he teaches us to pass from the flower of figures—which remained imperfect under the Law—to the fruit of spiritual teaching, which is found in the Gospel.

For in the holy Church, which is a most beautiful village in the adornment of virtues, a field of richness in the abundance of charity and wealth of good works, or a field of consolation in the comfort of the Scriptures and the firm hope of future things, the Savior preaches the Gospel daily through teachers, because all the shoots of the virtues bear fruit in it. Therefore the Bridegroom praises it in the Song of Songs, saying:

“An enclosed garden is my sister, my bride;  
an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain.  
Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates  
with the fruits of apples;  
henna with nard,  
nard and saffron,  
calamus and cinnamon,  
with every tree of Lebanon;  
myrrh and aloe  
with all the finest perfumes.  
A fountain of gardens,  
a well of living waters  
that flow with force from Lebanon” (Song IV).

It is rightly called “by the sea,” because it is situated beside the sea of this world and is daily battered by the waves of persecutions. Nevertheless, it does not cease to free from the nets of the Gospel those who are submerged in the waves of pleasures. It is also situated in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali, because it stands among the nations to spread the word of God courageously, so that it may be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger. Zebulun is therefore interpreted as “dwelling of strength,” and Naphtali as “expansion.”

In order that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

“Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali,  
the way of the sea beyond the Jordan,  
Galilee of the nations:  
the people sitting in darkness  
have seen a great light;  
and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death,  
a light has arisen” (Isaiah IX).

According to the sense of the evangelist Matthew, the prophet Isaiah foretold this testimony concerning the coming of Christ and the illumination of the Gospel, although others interpret it as referring to the return from captivity that took place under Zerubbabel. For the true physician returns to the beginnings of the diseases: where the first captivity of the Hebrews by the Assyrians occurred and the divine Law fell into oblivion, there the Lord first kindled the fire of preaching (2 Kings XVII).

(The history of Kings relates that Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, defeated Samaria and sent Hoshea, its king, bound into prison; that Israel was transferred from its land into Assyria; and that the king of Assyria sent foreigners to guard the land of Israel, lest it be reduced to desolation. These foreigners, instructed by a priest from the Israelite people, learned to worship the God of Israel; nevertheless, they did not abandon the ancestral gods whom they had possessed in their own land.)

(Jerome.) The phrase “the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations” is placed to distinguish it from another Galilee, which is in the tribe of Zebulun. There are in fact two Galilees, one of which is called Galilee of the nations, near the territory of the Tyrians. It was there that Solomon gave twenty cities to Hiram, king of Tyre, within the allotment of the tribe of Naphtali.

(Maurus.) The other Galilee is called the region around Tiberias and the lake of Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zebulun.

“The people sitting in darkness have seen a great light,” and the rest. The holy Church, therefore, which is situated beside the sea of the present age, is itself “beyond the Jordan,” that is, through baptism it has been removed from its former errors and has become a spiritual Galilee, that is, a transmigration. Formerly it lived under pagan observance in the shadow of death—that is, in the indulgence of the flesh and the pleasure of sin—but when Christ came, it received the light of the Gospel.

From that time Jesus began to preach and to say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” (Jerome.) When the Savior preaches the same things that John the Baptist had said earlier, he shows that he is the Son of the same God of whom John was the prophet. The Savior rightly says to the repentant that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near, because through him we are lifted from the depths to the heights.

The kingdom of heaven truly drew near to the repentant at that time, when at our Savior’s coming he promised eternal life to all who, through repentance, renounced their former errors and fled to his faith and baptism. “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John I). It is also drawing near now, because after his resurrection he commanded his disciples to preach repentance and the forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations. And behold, he said, “I am with you always, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII).

[III.] As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and his brother Andrew, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen.

The Sea of Galilee is the same as the lake of Gennesaret, but it is called the Sea of Galilee because it extends beside Galilee. This same body of water is called by different names because of the places adjacent to it: the Sea of Galilee, the lake of Gennesaret, the lake of Gennesaret, the Sea of Tiberias, and the Lake of Saltpans.

As the Lord was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, therefore, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and his brother Andrew. Because the only-begotten Son of God, when he assumed the condition of our mortality in becoming incarnate, divinely saw spiritual fishermen in the sea of this world. Those whom he had foreseen before the foundation of the world as suited to the work of preaching, he called at the time of his incarnation and revealed to others what they were.

He saw two brothers because he approved the unity of fraternal love, showing that whoever does not preserve brotherly love separates himself from the order of spiritual teachers: Simon who is called Peter and his brother Andrew. Simon is interpreted as “obedient,” Peter as “one who recognizes,” [Col. 0790A] and Andrew as “manly.” This appropriately applies to the persons of teachers. For only those are suited to the work of teaching who are illumined by the light of wisdom, obey God’s commandments by good works, and courageously and manfully urge others to know and do what they themselves preserve through knowledge and action.

As they were casting their net into the sea, the Lord called them to discipleship. For often, when he sees people intent on earthly profits, he calls them back from desire for temporal things to longing for the kingdom of heaven. He not only draws them away from those things themselves, but through them also snatches others from the depths of iniquity in the nets of the Gospel.

And he said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings.” (Augustine.) Here a considerable question arises: how can John say that Andrew first followed the Lord not in Galilee but beside the Jordan, at the testimony of John the Baptist, together with another whose name he does not mention; that Peter then received his name from him; and that Philip was called third to follow him, while the other three evangelists say that they were called while fishing?

This should nevertheless be understood as follows: they did not see the Lord beside the Jordan in such a way that they also remained inseparably attached to him. They merely came to know him, marveled at him, and returned to their own affairs.

But they immediately left their nets and followed him. (Gregory.) Perhaps someone, thinking silently to himself, says: “At the Lord’s voice, what or how much did these two fishermen leave behind, since they possessed almost nothing?” In this matter, however, one must weigh their devotion rather than their wealth. Much did the one leave behind who retained nothing for himself; much did the one leave behind who abandoned everything, however little it was.

Certainly, we possess what we have with love, and we seek by desire what we do not have at all. Peter and Andrew therefore left much behind when each of them also abandoned the desire to possess. Much did the one leave behind who, along with his possessions, restrained his desires. Those who followed him therefore left behind as much as those who did not follow him could have desired.

And going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and his brother John, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. (Augustine.) It may be asked how he called fishermen two by two from their boats—first Peter and Andrew, then, after going on a little farther, two other sons of Zebedee—as Matthew and Mark relate, when Luke says that both their boats were filled with that great catch of fish and mentions Peter’s companions, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, called to help because they could not draw out the full nets. He also says that they marveled at the great quantity of fish that had been caught, and that Jesus said only to Peter, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching human beings,” while they nevertheless followed him after bringing their boats to land.

From this it should be understood that what Luke suggests happened first, and that they were not then called by the Lord; only Peter was told that he would catch human beings. This was not said as though he would never again catch fish, for we read that after the Lord’s resurrection they went fishing. It was therefore said that he would catch human beings thereafter; it was not said that he would no longer catch fish.

Thus there is room to understand that they returned, as was their custom, to the catching of fish, so that what Matthew and Mark relate might happen afterward, when he called them two by two and ordered them to follow him: first the two, Peter and Andrew, and then the other two sons of Zebedee. At that time they followed him not after bringing their boats to land, as though intending to return to their work, but as people following one who called and commanded them to follow.

These were the first called to follow the Lord. Fishermen and uneducated men are sent to preach, so that the faith of believers might not be thought to rest in human eloquence and learning rather than in the power of God [Col. 0791B].

But they immediately left their nets and their father and followed him. (Maurus.) This complete abandonment of possessions signifies a complete conversion and thereby confirms the completeness of their discipleship. For Truth himself says: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV); and again: “Whoever loves his father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew X).

Allegorically, these four disciples, called by the Lord from bodily fishing to spiritual fishing, signify two peoples called by God’s grace from anxiety over and love of this age to spiritual devotion and holy service. Peter and James signify the faithful Jews who recognize the Lord and overthrow vices. Andrew and John signify the nations that manfully believe in Christ and are saved by God’s grace.

For the two boats represent two Churches: the one called from circumcision and the one called from uncircumcision. The nets represent the preaching of the Gospel; the sea represents the world; the fish represent human beings devoted to carnal wisdom and submerged in the pleasures of this life; and the harbors represent the end of the present life.

These spiritual fishermen, who had previously been occupied only with an earthly trade and carnal concerns, now, after abandoning worldly conduct with its love of passing things—which Zebedee aptly signifies, for his name is interpreted as “this one who flows”—and having been inflamed by desire for heavenly life, daily catch chosen fish in the Lord’s seine. They draw those whom they retrieve from the deep whirlpool of sins and the hiding places of errors into the light of faith and spiritual knowledge, and thus strive to place them in the bosom of Mother Church.

Morally, each believer can possess these four names within himself if he conducts himself worthily: he can be called Simon through obedience, Peter through recognition of his sin, Andrew through manfully enduring labors, James through overthrowing vices, and John through meriting the Lord’s grace. He possesses these names most truly when he strives to display them through the four virtues.

Without doubt, each person is obedient when, through prudence, he recognizes his sins and foresees the danger threatening him because of them, so that through obedience to God’s commandments he may wipe away the guilt of all his offenses and escape the injury of punishments. He is manly when, through temperance, he endures temptations and does not weaken as he stands against the assault of lusts. He is rightly called an overthrower when, through fortitude, he conquers vices and strives to extinguish the fiery darts of the evil one with the shield of faith. And he may appropriately be called “the grace of God” when, through justice, he fulfills the commandments of his Creator and yet, in fulfilling them, attributes nothing to himself, saying with the apostle: “Yet it was not I who labored, but the grace of God with me.”

And Jesus went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.

[IV.] By his own example the Savior therefore instructed his teachers how attentive, diligent, and kind they ought to be when ministering the word of life to others. Jesus went throughout all Galilee to teach that a teacher should be tireless and preach the word of God to everyone without partiality. For, according to Peter’s statement, God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears the Lord and practices justice is acceptable to him.

He taught in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, to show that a teacher must not run about pointlessly, but must always preach the Gospel of God, especially where he finds a greater number of hearers. He must never mix anything erroneous or idle stories with true teaching, but must always present what benefits those who hear and pertains to the eternal kingdom.

He healed every disease and every sickness among the people—diseases, that is, of bodies, and sicknesses of souls—thus providing us with an example, so that wherever we are able, whether in bodily or spiritual matters, we may always be ready to confer a benefit upon our neighbors.

And his reputation went throughout all Syria. Syria, in general, is the entire region from the Euphrates River to the Great Sea, and from Cappadocia and Armenia to Egypt. It contains the greatest provinces: Commagene, Phoenicia, and Palestine, in which the Jewish people dwell.

And they brought to him all who were sick, those seized by various diseases and torments, and those who had demons, and lunatics, and paralytics; and he healed them. (Jerome.) [Col. 0792D] He calls “lunatics” those whose pain increased at the waxing of the moon—not because they truly acquired this madness through the moon’s changes, but because they were thought to be lunatics through the deception of demons. The demons, observing the lunar periods, wished to bring disgrace upon the creature so that the blasphemy might rebound upon the Creator.

(Maurus.) Paralytics are those who are bereft and stripped of bodily strength, for *παράλυσις* (*paralysis*) means “dissolution” in Greek.

Mystically, Galilee, which is interpreted as “exalted wheel,” and Syria, which signifies “exaltation,” represent this world. Although through pride it raises itself on high, it nevertheless tends toward decline and continually turns toward the depths. When the Son of God wished to assume the mortality of our nature in himself, and, preaching the Gospel either through himself or through his apostles, performed many miracles and healed various diseases of bodies and souls, his reputation spread throughout the whole world. While the heavens declare the glory of God and the firmament announces the works of his hands, their sound went out through all the earth and their words to the ends of the world.

Those who had demons were then healed when the nations were converted to the faith and abandoned their idols. Lunatics and paralytics were also healed when he strengthened by his grace those who had previously wavered amid various unstable and changeable errors and had grown sluggish in good works, and caused them to walk blamelessly in the way of justice. Hence it follows:

And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.

(Augustine.) Let us recognize in the Gospel the fourfold crowd that followed the Lord. One part consisted of those who adhered to his teaching through heavenly faith and love, such as the apostles and the other faithful, who were called disciples; he assisted these inwardly and outwardly.

The second consisted of the weak and sick, who followed the Lord because of his healings. The third consisted of those whom mere report and reputation compelled to come to the Lord, wishing to discover what the Lord’s work was, so that by seeing and hearing they might know whether they ought to believe.

The fourth consisted of those who, driven by envy, wished to dishonor the Lord’s work and to trap him in his speech, so that they might accuse him before the authorities and thereby hand him over to death—as they did when he permitted it, not when they themselves wished it.

The Decapolis, as its very name shows, is a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan, to the east, around Hippos, Pella, and Gadara, opposite Galilee. It is rightly said that great crowds followed him, because after knowledge of his name reached the ends of the earth, people from every nation under heaven gathered from all sides to his faith, and a very great crowd of the faithful followed the traces of his commandments.

# CHAPTER V On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount and Evangelical Perfection

[I.] When he saw the crowds, he went up onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples approached him, and opening his mouth he taught them, saying.

(Augustine.) Here it may appear that the Lord wished to avoid the great crowds and therefore went up onto the mountain, as though withdrawing from the crowds in order to speak only to his disciples. Luke also seems to support this interpretation, narrating as follows: “It happened in those days that he went out onto the mountain to pray, and he spent the night in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles.”

But it is difficult to understand why Luke, after saying that Jesus descended from the mountain, says that he preached this same sermon while standing in a level place among the crowds, whereas Matthew says that he taught the disciples while seated on the mountain.

This can be understood as follows: when he went up onto the mountain and chose twelve disciples from among the many whom he named apostles—a detail Matthew omitted—he then delivered the sermon that Matthew inserted and Luke passed over, namely, on the mountain. Afterward, when he descended into a level place, he delivered another similar sermon, which Matthew does not mention but Luke does; and both sermons were concluded in the same manner.

It is also possible that, at first, the Lord was with his disciples alone in some elevated part of the mountain, when he chose the twelve from among them. Then he descended with them, not from the mountain itself but from its summit to a level place—that is, to some plateau on the mountainside—which could accommodate many crowds. He stood there until the crowds gathered around him. Afterward, when he had sat down, his disciples approached more closely, and so, with them and the others present, he delivered one sermon, which Matthew and Luke both narrate in different modes of presentation but with the same truth of events and meanings.

Mystically, the mountain is rightly understood to signify the greater commandments of justice. The commandments given to the Jews were lesser; nevertheless, the one God, through his holy prophets and servants, gave lesser commandments to the people who still needed to be bound by fear, according to the most orderly distribution of times. Through his Son he gave greater commandments to the people whom it was already fitting to free by love.

When lesser things are given to lesser people and greater things to greater people, they are given by the One who alone knows how to provide the human race with medicine suited to its times. Nor is it surprising that greater commandments are given for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, while lesser commandments were given for the sake of an earthly kingdom, by the same one God who made heaven and earth.

Concerning this justice, which is greater, it is said through the prophet: “Your justice is like the mountains of God” (Psalm XXXV). This is also well signified by the fact that such great matters are taught on the mountain by the one Teacher alone who is suited to teach them. He teaches while seated, which pertains to the dignity of teaching.

And his disciples approached him. (Maurus.) They approached so that those who were physically nearer when hearing his words might also be nearer in spirit to the fulfillment of his commandments. Mystically, the Lord’s sitting is his incarnation, because unless the Lord had become incarnate, the human race could not have approached him.

The disciples approached not only in bodily location but also in faith [Col. 0794D] and devotion, so that they might receive peace for their people. For unless they had approached, salvation would not have come to us.

And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying. The circumlocution expressed by the words “opening his mouth” perhaps indicates, by the delay itself, that the sermon would be somewhat longer. It is therefore not without significance that he is now said to have opened his mouth, since in the Old Testament he used to open the mouths of the prophets.

The mouth more truly signifies the human being. By saying “he taught them,” Scripture shows through the authority of divine teaching the nature that deigned to assume human form in itself, through which it would teach.

Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. (Jerome.) Lest anyone suppose that the Lord was praising poverty that sometimes suffers want, he added “in spirit,” so that you would understand humility, not deprivation. Blessed are the poor in spirit, who are poor by their own will for the sake of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Savior also speaks through Isaiah concerning such poor people: “The Lord has anointed me; therefore he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isaiah LXI).

(Augustine.) Elsewhere, too, we read concerning the disclosure of temporal things: “All is vanity and presumption of spirit” (Ecclesiastes VI). “Presumption of spirit” signifies boldness and pride. In ordinary speech, proud people are also said to have a great spirit. And rightly so, since *spiritus* also means “wind.” Hence it is written: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind” (Psalm CXLVIII). Who does not know that proud people are called inflated, as though swollen with wind? Hence also the apostle’s statement: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians VIII).

Accordingly, the poor here are rightly understood as the humble and those who fear the Lord—that is, those who do not possess an inflating spirit.

There was no other appropriate starting point for blessedness, since it was to arrive at the summit of wisdom: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus I; Psalm CX). Conversely, “the beginning of every sin is recorded as pride” (Ecclesiasticus X). The proud desire and love earthly kingdoms, but “blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. (Jerome.) Not the land of Judea, nor the land of this world, nor the accursed earth that bears thorns and thistles, which every cruel and warlike person possesses more fully, but the earth desired by the Psalmist, who says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm CXIV).

Such a possessor and triumphant victor after victory is also described in the forty-fourth psalm: “And set out, proceed prosperously, and reign because of truth, meekness, and justice” (Psalm XLIV). For no one possesses this earth through meekness, but through pride.

(Augustine.) That earth signifies a certain solidity and stability of perpetual inheritance, where the soul rests through a good disposition as in its own place, just as the body rests in the earth, and is nourished there by its food, just as the body is nourished from the earth. It is itself the rest and life of the saints.

The meek are those who yield to wickedness and do not resist evil, but overcome evil with good (Romans XII). Let the unmeek quarrel and fight for earthly and temporal things; but “blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance,” from which they cannot be uprooted.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. (Jerome.) This mourning is not mourning for the dead according to the common law of nature, but mourning for the dead in sins and vices. Thus Samuel also wept for Saul, because the Lord regretted that he had made him king over Israel (1 Samuel XV). So also the apostle Paul says that he weeps and mourns over those who, after fornication and impurity, have not repented.

Mourning is grief over the loss of loved ones; but those who turn to the Lord lose the things that they embraced as dear in this world. They do not rejoice in the things in which they formerly rejoiced, and until the love of eternal things is established in them, they are wounded by a certain sadness. They will therefore be comforted by the Holy Spirit, who is called *παράκλητος* (*parakletos*), that is, “comforter,” especially for this reason: so that those who lose temporal things may enjoy eternal joy.

(Maurus.) It should be noted, moreover, that the mourning of the saints occurs in four ways: when they lament their former sins; when they mourn those falling into hell; when they mourn those living in sins; and when they become exceedingly sorrowful out of desire for the heavenly kingdom. Nature likewise contains four kinds of tears. Some tears are moist, so that they may wash away the filth of sins and restore the baptism that has been lost; some are salty and bitter, so that they may restrain the flow of the flesh and temper the sweetness of pleasures; some are hot, so that they may prevail against the coldness of unbelief. Some are pure, so that they may establish those cleansed from former errors in a pure way of life. These tears, then, are shed most often for beloved persons who have been lost, to remind us that we should restore the good works we have lost and return, through keeping God’s commandments, to the homeland of paradise abandoned by us through transgression. For mourning always stands between two joys: that of the world lying behind us and that of the approaching heavenly kingdom. Blessed, therefore, is the person for whom temporal sorrow will give birth to eternal joy.

**Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.** (Jerome.) It is not enough for us to desire righteousness unless we suffer hunger for righteousness, so that under this example we may understand that we are never sufficiently righteous, but always thirst for works of righteousness. Lovers, therefore, of the true and unshaken good will be filled with that food of which the Lord himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV), which is righteousness; and with that water of which, as he likewise says, whoever drinks “will have in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (ibid.).

**Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.** (Jerome.) Mercy, therefore, is understood not only in almsgiving, but in every matter concerning a brother’s sin: if we bear another’s burdens as though they were our own, if we teach the uninstructed, and if we correct the one who is in error. Mercy must be exercised not only in bodily gifts, but also in healing souls. To such people the merciful Judge repays this: that they themselves may be freed from misery.

**Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see the Lord.** The pure in heart are those whom that conscience of sin does not accuse; for the Pure One is seen by the pure heart, and God’s temple cannot be polluted. (Augustine.) How foolish, then, are those who seek God with these outward eyes, since he is seen with the heart. As it is written elsewhere: “Seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wisdom I). For this is a pure heart: a simple heart. And just as this light cannot be seen except by pure eyes, so God cannot be seen unless that by which he can be seen is pure. (Maurus.) The pure in heart see the Lord here in an enigma, through grace; but in the future they will see him face to face, because then they will know as they have been known (1 Corinthians XIII).

**Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.** (Jerome.) Those, therefore, are rightly called peacemakers who first make peace in their own hearts and then among brothers who are at variance. (Augustine.) For what benefit is it to you that others are reconciled through you, while there are wars of vices in your own soul? Perfection is in peace, where nothing resists anything else. Thus the peacemakers are sons of God, because nothing resists God; and certainly sons ought to possess the likeness of their father.

Those are peacemakers within themselves who bring all the movements of their soul into order and subject them to reason—that is, to mind and spirit—and who, having subdued carnal desires, become the kingdom of God. In that kingdom everything is so ordered that what is most important and excellent in a human being rules, while the other things that we share with animals do not resist; and that very excellence in the human being—mind and reason—is subjected to what is superior, namely, Truth itself, the only-begotten Son of God.

Nor can it rule over what is inferior unless it first subjects itself to what is superior. This is the peace given to human beings on earth who possess good will. This is the life of the perfected and complete wise person. From this great, most peaceful and perfectly ordered kingdom the ruler of this age has been cast out—the one who rules over the perverse and disordered. Once this peace has been established and strengthened within, whatever persecutions the one cast out externally stirs up from outside increase the glory that is according to God. They do not weaken anything in that structure; rather, when his engines fail, they make known how great is the strength built within. Therefore it follows:

**Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.** (Jerome.) He significantly added “for righteousness’ sake.” Many suffer persecution because of their sins and are not righteous. At the same time, consider that the eighth beatitude of true circumcision ends in martyrdom. (Augustine.) This number of sayings must therefore be considered carefully. The beatitude begins with humility, as in: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and in the seventh degree it contains wisdom itself—that is, contemplation of the truth—which brings the whole human being into peace and receives the likeness of God. It concludes in this way: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

The eighth returns, as it were, to the beginning, because it shows and proves the completed and perfected person. Thus the kingdom of heaven is named in the first and the eighth: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” and “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” When it is said, “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” there are therefore seven things that bring perfection; for the eighth makes clear and demonstrates what has been perfected, so that through these degrees the others may be perfected, beginning again from the head, as it were.

It seems to me, therefore, that the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks (Isaiah III), also corresponds to these degrees and sayings. But there is a difference in order: there the enumeration begins with the more excellent qualities, whereas here it begins with the lower. There it begins with the wisdom of God and ends with the fear of God. Yet “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.”

Accordingly, if we count them by degrees as though ascending, the first degree there is fear of the Lord, the second piety, the third knowledge, the fourth strength, the fifth counsel, the sixth understanding, and the seventh wisdom.

The fear of the Lord corresponds to the humble, of whom it is said here: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”—that is, those who are not puffed up or proud. Of them the Apostle says: “Do not be high-minded, but fear,” that is, do not be exalted.

Piety corresponds to the meek. For whoever seeks in a pious manner honors Holy Scripture and does not criticize what he does not yet understand; therefore he does not resist, which is what it means to be meek. Hence it is said here: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.”

Knowledge corresponds to those who mourn, for they have already learned from the Scriptures the evils by which they are held bound—evils which, because they were ignorant of them, they pursued as though they were good and useful. Of them it is said here: “Blessed are those who mourn.”

Strength corresponds to those who hunger and thirst. They labor, desiring joy in true goods and wishing to turn their love away from earthly and bodily things. Of them it is said here: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.”

Counsel corresponds to the merciful. For this is the one remedy by which we may escape from so many evils: that we forgive as we wish to be forgiven, and help others wherever we can, just as we desire to be helped where we cannot help ourselves. Of them it is said here: “Blessed are the merciful,” and so forth.

Understanding of the heart corresponds to the pure in heart, as to a cleansed eye by which one may see what no bodily eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart. Of them it is said here: “Blessed are the pure in heart,” and so forth.

Wisdom corresponds to the peacemakers, in whom all things are ordered and no movement rebels against reason; rather, everything obeys the human spirit when the spirit itself obeys God. Of them it is said here: “Blessed are the peacemakers.”

There is one reward for all these degrees—the kingdom of heaven—but it is named in various ways.

In the first place, as was fitting, the kingdom of heaven is set down. It is the perfect wisdom of the rational soul. Thus it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” as though it were said: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Sirach I).

An inheritance is given to the meek, as though it were the father’s testament for those who seek with piety: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.”

Consolation is given to those who mourn, as to those who know what they have lost and in what sorrows they are [Al., “immersed”]: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.”

Those who hunger and thirst receive fullness, as nourishment for those who labor and strive courageously toward salvation: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.”

The merciful receive mercy, as those who use true and excellent counsel, so that what they show to those beneath them may be shown to them by one more powerful: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.”

The pure in heart receive the ability to see God, as those who possess a pure eye for understanding eternal things: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

The peacemakers receive the likeness of God, as those who have been made perfectly wise and renewed according to the image of God through the regeneration of the human being: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

These things can indeed be fulfilled in this life, just as we believe they were fulfilled in the apostles. But that complete transformation into the evangelical form which is promised after this life cannot be expressed in words. Blessed, therefore, are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

This eighth saying, which returns to the beginning and declares the perfected human being, perhaps also signifies circumcision, which took place on the eighth day in the Old Testament; the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath, which is certainly the eighth day and also the first day; the celebration of the octave days which we observe in the regeneration of the new human being; and the very number of Pentecost. For when the number seven has been multiplied by seven, producing forty-nine, the eighth is added, as it were, so that fifty may be completed and we may return, as it were, to the beginning. On that day the Holy Spirit was sent; through him we are led into the kingdom of heaven, receive the inheritance, are comforted and nourished, obtain mercy, are cleansed and brought into peace, and thus endure external persecutions through the troubles inflicted upon us for the sake of truth and righteousness.

**Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you and utter every kind of evil against you falsely on my account.** (Augustine.) The preceding sayings were expressed generally. He did not say, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for the kingdom of heaven is yours,” but, “for theirs,” he says, “is the kingdom of heaven.” Nor did he say, “Blessed are the meek, for you shall possess the earth,” but, “for they shall possess the earth.” The same applies to the rest, up to the eighth saying, where he says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

From this point he begins to address those who are present, although both the things said above, spoken to those who were listening at the time, and the things that follow, which seem to be addressed especially to those present, also concern those who were absent or who would come afterward. He therefore turns directly to those to whom he was speaking in particular, foretelling the persecutions they would suffer for his name, because he wished to make known to them the dignity of their rank. He calls them the salt of the earth and the light of the world, so that from the painful things they might receive humility and from the joyful things consolation:

“Blessed,” he says, “are you when people hate you and persecute you and utter every kind of evil against you falsely.” That reviling which is uttered falsely by the mouth of the reviler is to be despised, and it produces blessedness.

Therefore the text specifically defines what blessed reviling is: “Every kind of reviling against you falsely, on my account.” (Augustine.) Wherever Christ is the cause, reviling is to be desired. Let anyone who seeks the pleasures of this age and the resources of temporal things observe that our blessedness, in the Christian name, is inward, as it is said prophetically of the ecclesial soul: “All the glory of the daughter of kings is within” (Psalm XLIV). For outwardly revilings, persecutions, and attacks upon one’s reputation are promised; yet from them there is a great reward in heaven.

This is experienced in the hearts of those who endure patiently and who can already say: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans V). For it is not profitable merely to endure these things; rather, one must endure them for Christ’s name not only with an even temper but also with rejoicing.

Many heretics, however, deceiving souls under the Christian name, suffer many such things. They are excluded from this reward because it was not said simply, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution,” but the addition was made: “for righteousness’ sake.” Where sound faith is absent, righteousness cannot exist, because “the righteous person lives by faith.” Nor should schismatics promise themselves anything from this reward, since where love is absent righteousness likewise cannot exist. Love does no harm to one’s neighbor; if they possessed it, they would not tear apart the body of Christ, which is the Church.

It may be asked what difference there is between “When they revile you” and “When they utter every kind of evil against you,” since reviling is itself the utterance of evil. But reviling is hurled in one way, with insult, in the presence of the person being reviled, as was said to our Lord: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII). It occurs in another way when the reputation of an absent person is injured, as it is likewise written concerning him: “Some said, ‘He is a prophet’; others said, ‘No, but he deceives the people’” (John VII).

To persecute means to inflict violence or to attack by ambush. This was done by the one who betrayed him and by those who crucified him. What is the reason that the text does not merely say, “And they will utter every kind of evil against you,” but adds “falsely,” and also adds “on my account”? I think “on my account” was added because of those who wish to glory in their persecutions and in the disgrace of their reputation, and therefore say that Christ concerns them because many evil things are said about them—although those things are true when they are spoken about their error, even if at times some false statements are also made, as commonly happens through human recklessness. Yet they do not suffer these things on Christ’s account. For the person who is not called a Christian according to the true faith and catholic discipline does not follow Christ.

**Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven.** (Augustine.) I do not think that “heaven” here means the higher regions of this visible world. Our reward, which ought to be unshaken and eternal, must not be placed in things that change and are temporary. Rather, I think “in heaven” means in spiritual strongholds, where eternal righteousness dwells.

In comparison with these heavens, the earth is called the unrighteous soul, to which, when it sinned, it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis III). Of these heavens the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III). Those who rejoice in spiritual goods already experience this reward. But it will be completed in every respect when this mortal nature also puts on immortality.

(Jerome.) I do not know which of us could fulfill this: that our reputation should be torn apart by reproaches while we rejoice in the Lord. The person who pursues empty glory cannot fulfill this. We ought therefore to rejoice and exult, so that a reward may be prepared for us in heaven. Elegantly, we read in a certain volume: “Do not seek glory, and you will not grieve when you are without glory.”

**For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.** (Augustine.) He has now spoken of persecution in general, both in reviling and in the tearing apart of one’s reputation. He rightly encouraged them by example, because those who speak the truth are accustomed to suffer persecution. Yet the ancient prophets did not, because of their accustomed persecution, abandon the preaching of truth. Therefore it very appropriately follows:

**[II.] You are the salt of the earth.** (Maurus.) The apostles are called salt because through them the whole human race is seasoned. By the name “earth,” human nature is signified; by salt, the wisdom of the word. When the Savior calls his apostles, who are filled with heavenly and divine wisdom, the salt of the earth, he shows that those who savor only earthly things are to be judged foolish. Pursuing an abundance of temporal goods or fearing their lack, they lose the eternal things that can neither be given nor taken away by human beings.

It should also be noted that the nature of salt makes the earth infertile. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “He turned a fruitful land into salt” (Psalm CVI). Certain cities were likewise sown with salt in the wrath of conquerors, so that no plant might spring up in them.

Allegorically, this aptly applies to apostolic teaching: when the strongholds of adversaries have been destroyed and the kingdom of sin overthrown, the salt of wisdom restrains the excess and foulness of the age from producing any further growth of vices in the earth of human flesh.

Likewise, since salt is suitable for seasoning food and drying meats, it properly demonstrates that through the preaching of the Gospel the flow of pleasures is restrained, and human nature, freed from the worms and corruption of sins, is preserved unharmed for its Creator through keeping his commandments.

For it is good to hear the word of God, and more frequently to have the secrets of the spiritual heart seasoned with the salt of wisdom—or rather, to become salt of the earth together with the apostles, sufficient to imbue the minds even of those who still savor earthly things. But if someone, once illuminated by the seasoning of truth, returns to apostasy, by what other teacher can he be corrected, when he has cast away the sweetness of the wisdom he himself tasted, terrified by adversity or enticed by allurements? Hence it follows:

**But if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be salted? It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled under people’s feet.** (Augustine.) That is: if you, through whom the peoples are to be seasoned, somehow lose the kingdoms of heaven through fear of temporal persecutions, who will be the people through whom your error is removed, when God has chosen you to remove the error of others?

Therefore salt that has lost its savor is useful for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled under people’s feet.

It is not the person who suffers persecution who is trampled under people’s feet, but the person who loses his savor through fearing persecution. For only what is inferior can be trampled; but the person who, although suffering many things on earth, is fixed in heaven in his heart, is not inferior.

Just as salt that has lost its savor, when it has ceased to be useful for seasoning food and drying meats, is no longer fit for any use—and, as another Evangelist testifies, is not even useful for the earth, since when it is scattered upon it plants are prevented from growing, nor useful for the agricultural manure heap, since, even when mixed with living clods, it naturally tends not to nourish the seeds of crops but to destroy them—so anyone who, after recognizing the truth, turns back is able neither to bear the fruit of a good work himself nor to cultivate others. He must be thrown outside, that is, separated from the unity of the Church, so that, in accordance with another parable, his enemies may mock him and say: “This man began to build, but he was not able to finish” (Luke XIV).

**You are the light of the world.** (Maurus.) The apostles, illuminated by the true light, which is Christ, are called the light of the world because through them the world was to be illuminated by the light of faith and knowledge. For just as above they were figuratively called the salt of the earth, so now we must understand them to be the light of the world not bodily but spiritually.

(Augustine.) “Earth” should not be understood as the earth upon which we tread with bodily feet, but as the human beings who dwell on earth, or even sinners, whose foulness the apostolic salt was sent by the Lord to season and extinguish. Here, too, “world” should be understood not as heaven and earth, but as the people who are in the world or who love the world; the apostles were sent to illuminate them.

(Hilary.) The nature of light is to emit brightness wherever it is carried, and when it is brought into a house, to destroy darkness as its light prevails.

The world, therefore, placed outside the knowledge of God, was darkened by the shadows of ignorance. Through the apostles the light of knowledge came to it, and the knowledge of God shines; from their small bodies, wherever they went, light was supplied.

**A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.** (Maurus.) This is the solidity of apostolic teaching, established upon notable and great righteousness. The mountain itself on which the Lord teaches also signifies it. This mountain, therefore, may signify Christ himself, concerning whom it is written: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isaiah II).

The city signifies the whole Church of Christ, founded upon faith in him. It is constructed from many nations, as though from many stones, and cemented by the pitch of love and the unity of faith. It becomes a place of safety for those who enter, though difficult for those who approach it; it guards its inhabitants and shuts out its enemies. Against every ambush of its enemies—that is, of Jews, pagans, and even heretics—it remains unconquerable.

The six cities of refuge set upon mountains prefigured this city, because it is itself set upon a mountain—that is, openly—and truly becomes a refuge for all who flee to it from the enemy, the devil.

**Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house.** By domestic examples and comparisons he teaches the apostles to have confidence in preaching, so that they may not hide themselves through fear and become like a lamp under a bushel. Rather, they should reveal themselves with complete freedom, so that what they have heard in private rooms they may preach from the housetops.

(Augustine.) To put a lamp under a bushel is to value bodily convenience above the preaching of truth, so that a person does not preach the truth because he fears suffering some hardship in bodily and temporal matters. Whoever obscures and conceals the light of good teaching beneath temporal advantages places the lamp under a bushel.

But the person places it on a lampstand who subjects his body to the service of God, so that the preaching of truth is superior and bodily service inferior. Yet through the strength of the body itself the teaching shines more brightly, being conveyed to learners through bodily functions—through voice, tongue, and the other movements of the body—in good works.

He places the lamp on a lampstand who says: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Corinthians IX).

This lamp may also be interpreted as the Savior’s humanity. He lights the lamp who filled the earth of human nature with the breath of his divinity. He certainly did not wish to hide this lamp from believers or place it under a bushel—that is, enclose it within the measure of the Law—or confine it within the boundaries of the single Jewish nation.

He calls the Church the lampstand, upon which he placed the lamp, because he fixed the faith of his incarnation upon our foreheads. Thus those who wish to enter the Church faithfully may behold the light of truth openly.

When he says, “so that it may give light to all who are in the house,” this can signify the Church, as we have shown above, and also the dwelling-place of human beings, that is, the world. The light of the holy preachers shines in the Church in such a way that those who are within see the light, and it spreads rays of light even to those who are outside, so that they too may flee from the darkness of errors and sins and hasten to gather into the light of true faith. Hence it follows:

**So let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.** (Augustine.) If he had said only, “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works,” he would seem to have set the goal in human praise—the praise sought by hypocrites and by those who strive after honors and pursue the emptiest glory.

Against them it is said: “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of God” (Galatians I). And through the Prophet: “Those who please people are confounded, because God has done nothing for them” (Psalm LII); and again: “God crushes the bones of those who please people” (Psalm LII). The Apostle likewise says: “Let us not become desirous of empty glory” (Galatians V). And again: “Let each person examine himself, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Galatians VI).

He therefore did not say only, “so that they may see your good works,” but added, “and glorify your Father who is in heaven,” so that the very fact that a human being pleases people through good works would not make human approval the goal. Rather, the person should refer it to the praise of God and therefore please people so that God may be glorified in him. This is beneficial for those who praise: they should honor not the human being but God.

The Lord demonstrated this in the very human being whom he bore, when the crowds marveled at his works in healing the paralytic, as it is written in the Gospel: “They were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings” (Matthew IX).

**[III.] Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.** After exhorting them to prepare themselves to endure all things for truth and righteousness, and not to hide the good things they were to receive but to learn them so that they might teach others—referring their good works not to their own praise but to the glory of God—he now begins to instruct them and teach them what they should teach.

It is as though they were asking: “Behold, we wish to endure everything for your name and not to hide your teaching; but what exactly is the thing you forbid us to hide, and for which you command us to tolerate everything? Are you perhaps going to say something contrary to what is written in the Law?”

“No,” he says. “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.” This saying has a twofold meaning, and it must be treated according to both meanings.

For the one who says, “I did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it,” either means adding what it lacks or doing what it contains. Let us therefore first consider the meaning I have placed first. The one who added what was lacking certainly did not abolish what he found; rather, by perfecting it, he confirmed it.

Whether, therefore, he came in human form to fulfill what had been prophesied about him, or to perfect the things that previously had been crude and incomplete because of the weakness of his hearers—removing anger, excluding retaliation, and forbidding the hidden desire in the mind—

**Truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things take place.** (Jerome.) New heavens and a new earth are promised, which the Lord God will make. If new things are to be created, it necessarily follows that these things will pass away.

(Augustine.) In what follows—“not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things take place”—the shape of the letter shows that even the things considered least in the Law are full of spiritual sacraments, and that everything is recapitulated in the Gospel. Among letters, iota is smaller than the others because it is made with a single stroke; the stroke is even a small mark at the top of the letter itself. By these words he shows that even the smallest things in the Law will be brought to fulfillment.

(Maurus.) Appropriately he used the Greek *iota*, and not the Hebrew *yod*, because *iota* signifies ten in number and enumerates the Decalogue of the Law, whose culmination and perfection is the Gospel.

**Therefore whoever abolishes one of the least of these commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.** (Hilary.) Thus he establishes that not even the least of God’s commandments may be abolished without guilt. He declares that those who abolish the least commandments will become “least”—that is, last and almost nothing. Nothing can be less than what is least; yet the least of all is the Lord’s passion and death on the cross. If someone does not confess it, as though it were shameful, he will be least; but to the one who confesses it he promises the glory of a great calling in heaven.

(Jerome.) In another way, this chapter attacks the Pharisees, who, having disregarded God’s commandments, established their own traditions. Their teaching among the people will not benefit them if they destroy even a small commandment prescribed in the Law.

(Augustine.) The least commandments are signified by one iota or one stroke, as was shown above. Therefore whoever abolishes and teaches others accordingly—that is, according to what he abolishes, not according to what he finds in the Law—will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Perhaps for this reason he will not be in the kingdom of heaven at all, since only the great can exist there.

(Maurus.) This may also be understood morally. The person who does not fulfill God’s commandment abolishes it, although he does not abolish the commandment itself but abolishes it in himself. God’s commandment is firm, and Scripture cannot be dissolved. The Law is, in a certain sense, a bond. Whoever transgresses God’s bonds abolishes the commandments in himself, not in the commandments themselves.

Such a person will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, because he is most despised in the Church of the saints. For “the kingdom of heaven” here also signifies the present Church, as elsewhere where it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net thrown into the sea” (Matthew XIII); and: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII).

**But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.** In doing the commandments of the Law, the person who teaches them earns the name of great. For it is not teachers or hearers of the Law who will be justified before God, but doers of the Law.

**For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.** (Augustine.) That is, unless you fulfill not only those least commandments of the Law that initiate a person, but also those that I add—since I did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it—you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore the one who does not abolish those least commandments and teaches accordingly is not yet to be regarded as great and fit for the kingdom of heaven, but is nevertheless not as least as the one who abolishes them. To be great and fit for that kingdom, he must do and teach, as Christ now teaches, so that his righteousness may exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees.

The righteousness of the Pharisees is that they do not kill; the righteousness of those who are to enter the kingdom of God is that they do not become angry. Not killing is therefore the least requirement, and the person who abolishes it will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But the person who fulfills it by not killing will not immediately be great and fit for the kingdom of heaven; nevertheless, he has ascended a certain degree.

He will be perfected if he does not even become angry. If he fulfills this, he will be much farther removed from murder. Therefore the person who teaches that we should not become angry does not abolish the Law’s commandment that we should not kill; rather, he fulfills it, so that both outwardly, by not killing, and inwardly, by not becoming angry, we may preserve innocence. Hence it follows:

**You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not kill”; and whoever kills will be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.** Because they understood murder only as the destruction of the human body, by which life is taken away, the Lord made clear that every wrongful movement directed toward harming a brother is to be counted as murder. Hence John also says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III).

“I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.” In some manuscripts “without cause” is added. But the Greek manuscripts, which ought to be trusted, do not have “without cause,” although the meaning is the same.

We must consider what it means to be angry with a brother. The person who is angry at his brother’s sin is not angry with his brother. Whoever is angry with the brother rather than with the sin is angry without cause.

**Whoever says to his brother, “Raca,” will be liable to the council.** *Raca* is properly an interjection of the Hebrew language, signifying nothing by its verbal meaning but expressing the movement of an indignant mind. Grammarians call such interjections particles of speech that signify an emotion of an agitated mind, as when a grieving person says “alas!” or an angry person “hem!” Such words belong specifically to their respective languages and are not easily transferred into another language. This is why both the Greek and Latin translators were compelled to retain the word itself, since no way of translating it could be found.

Alternatively, *raca* is properly a Hebrew word and is interpreted as *κοινός* (*koinos*), that is, “empty” or “vacant”; in the ordinary insult of our language we might call such a person “empty-headed.” If we are to give an account for an idle word, how much more for insults?

The text also significantly adds: “whoever says to his brother here, ‘Raca.’” For no one is a brother except one who has the same father as we do. Since this person likewise believes in God and knows Christ to be the Wisdom of God, by what right can he be branded with the epithet of folly?

(Hilary.) Therefore whoever accuses one full of the Holy Spirit of emptiness through an insult becomes liable to the council of the saints and will pay the penalty for insulting the Holy Spirit through the judgment of the holy judges.

Whoever, however, says, “You fool,” will be liable to the fire of Gehenna. (Jerome.) For whoever says “You fool” to one who likewise believes in God is impious toward religion. It is a grave peril of sacrilege to assail with an insult of foolishness one whom God has called salt, and to irritate by a curse the intelligence of those who are “salty” with foolish understanding. Such a person, therefore, will be fuel for the eternal fire.

Some, however, think that one should inquire what difference there is between being liable to judgment, being liable to the council, and being liable to the fire of Gehenna. For this last expression sounds most serious and suggests that certain degrees have been established, moving from lesser offenses to greater ones until one arrives at the fire of Gehenna. There are therefore degrees in these sins: first, someone becomes angry and retains in his heart the emotion he has conceived. But if that emotion of indignation forces out a sound—not signifying anything, but by its very eruption displaying the movement of the mind, so as to strike the person at whom we are angry—that is certainly more serious than if the rising anger were suppressed in silence. If, however, not only the sound of indignation is heard but also a word that clearly designates and marks the condemnation of the person against whom it is spoken, who would doubt that this is more serious than if only the sound of indignation had been uttered? Thus, in the first case there is one thing: anger alone; in the second, two: anger and the sound that signifies anger; in the third, three: anger, the sound that signifies anger, and in the sound itself a definite expression of condemnation. Hence there are here also three liabilities: judgment, council, and the fire of Gehenna.

[Col. 0807A]

For in the judgment there is still room for defense. In the council, although judgment ordinarily occurs there as well, the very distinction compels us to acknowledge that something different is intended here: the council appears to concern the pronouncement of the sentence, when the question is no longer discussed with the accused himself—whether he ought to be condemned—but those who judge deliberate among themselves with what punishment one who is certainly to be condemned ought to be punished. Gehenna, however, has neither a doubtful condemnation, as judgment does, nor merely the punishment of the condemned, as the council does. In the fire of Gehenna, both the condemnation and the punishment of the condemned are certain.

[Col. 0807B]

There therefore appear to be certain degrees both in sins and in liability. But in what ways these are invisibly manifested in accordance with the merits of souls, who can say? Here the Savior has also called Gehenna the torment of hell, where sinners and the impious will be condemned forever together with the devil and his angels. Only those can avoid and escape it who, redeemed by the grace of Christ, have performed works of righteousness, or who, after committing sins, have produced worthy fruits of repentance and have striven to recover themselves through good works.

[Col. 0807C]

They think, therefore, that the name Gehenna was taken from a valley consecrated to idols beside the wall of Jerusalem, once filled with the corpses of the dead; King Josiah is also said to have profaned it, as recorded in the Book of Kings.

## IV.

“If, therefore, you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then, when you come, offer your gift.”

[Col. 0807D]

Therefore, if it is not lawful to become angry with one’s brother, or to say “Raca,” or to say “You fool,” it is much less lawful to retain anything in the mind so that indignation may turn into hatred. To this also pertains what is said elsewhere: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV). We are therefore commanded, if we remember that our brother has something against us, to leave the gift we have brought to the altar before the altar, to go and be reconciled to our brother, and then to return and offer the gift.

If this is taken literally, perhaps someone may think that it ought to be done in this way if the brother is present; for the matter cannot be deferred longer, since we are commanded to leave our gift before the altar. If, then, something of this kind comes to mind concerning someone absent—and perhaps located across the sea—it is absurd to believe that the gift should be left before the altar, only to be offered to God after traveling over lands and seas. We are therefore compelled to retreat wholly into spiritual meanings, so that what has been said may be understood without absurdity.

[Col. 0808A]

Spiritually, then, we may understand the altar as faith itself in the inner temple of God, of which the visible altar is a sign. Whatever gift we offer to God—whether teaching, prophecy, prayer, a hymn, a psalm, or anything else of this kind that belongs to spiritual goods—cannot be acceptable to God unless it is supported by the sincerity of faith and firmly and immovably placed upon it, so that what we say may be whole and undefiled.

[Col. 0808B]

For many heretics, having no altar—that is, no true faith—have uttered blasphemies in place of praise, weighed down by earthly opinions and casting their vow upon the earth, as it were. But the intention of the one making the offering must also be sound. Therefore, when we are about to offer something of this kind in our heart—that is, in the inner temple of God—for “the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. III), and “that Christ may dwell through faith in our hearts in the inner person”—if it comes to mind that our brother has something against us, that is, if we have injured him in some way—for then he has something against us; we have something against him if he has injured us—there is no need to go to be reconciled. For you will not ask pardon from one who has done you an injury; you will merely forgive him, just as you desire to be forgiven by the Lord for what you yourself have committed.

[Col. 0808C]

One must therefore go, not with the feet of the body, but with the movements of the mind, so that with humble affection you may prostrate yourself before your brother, to whom you have hastened in loving thought, in the presence of the one to whom you are about to offer your gift. In this way, even if he is present, you will be able to soften him with a sincere disposition and restore him to friendship by asking pardon—provided that you have first done this before God, going to him not with the sluggish movement of the body but with the swiftest affection of love. Then, returning—that is, directing your intention back to what you had begun with difficulty—you will offer your gift.

“Be well-disposed toward your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Truly I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans.”

[Col. 0808D]

In place of what we have in the Latin manuscripts as “being consenting,” the Greek manuscripts have εὔνους (*eunous*), which means “well-disposed” and “kind.” From what precedes and follows, the meaning is clear: while we are running along the way of this present age, the Lord and Savior exhorts us to peace and harmony, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, living at peace with all people” (Rom. XII).

For in the preceding passage he had said: “If you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you.” Having finished this, he immediately adds: “Be well-disposed, or kind, toward your adversary,” and so forth. And in what follows he commands: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for your persecutors.”

[Col. 0809A]

(Augustine.) I understand the judge to be Christ: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). I understand the officer to be an angel: “And angels ministered to him” (Matt. IV). We believe that he will come with his angels to judge the living and the dead.

I understand the prison to mean the punishments of darkness, which elsewhere he calls “outer” punishments. I believe this because the joy of divine rewards is inward, in the mind itself—or wherever something more secret may be conceived. Concerning this joy it is said to the servant who has merited well: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV). In the same way, in the administration of the state, someone who is sent out from the judge’s secretariat or courtroom is thrust into prison.

[Col. 0809B]

A quadrans is a kind of coin worth two small coins. Hence, in one Gospel, that poor widow is said to have put a quadrans into the treasury (Mark XII), while in another she is said to have put in two small coins (Luke XXI)—not because the Gospels disagree, but because one quadrans is worth two small coins.

This, therefore, is what he says: “You will not come out of the prison until you have paid even the smallest sins.”

(Augustine.) Concerning the payment of the last quadrans, it may reasonably be understood either as referring to the fact that nothing is left unpunished—just as we also say “down to the dregs” when we wish to express something exact, leaving nothing behind—or as signifying by the name “last quadrans” earthly sins.

[Col. 0809C]

For the fourth and last part of the distinct members of this world is found in the earth: begin with heaven, count the air as the second, water as the third, and earth as the fourth.
