It may therefore appropriately be understood as saying: “Until you pay the last quadrans,” that is, until you expiate earthly sins. The sinner heard this: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III).

But when it says “until you pay,” I wonder whether it does not signify that punishment which is called eternal. For how is that debt paid where no opportunity is given for repentance and amendment of life? Perhaps “until you pay” is placed here in the same sense as in the passage where it is said: “Sit at my right hand until I place all your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. CIX). For when the enemies have been placed beneath his feet, he will not cease to sit at the right hand.

[Col. 0809D]

Or consider the Apostle’s words: “For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies beneath his feet” (1 Cor. XV). He will not cease to reign when they have been placed beneath his feet. Therefore, just as the meaning is understood there—where it says, “He must reign until he has placed all his enemies beneath his feet”—so here the meaning can be understood of the statement, “You will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans”: he will always fail to come out, because he is always paying the last quadrans while suffering the everlasting punishments of earthly sins.

Some, however, have thought that one ought to inquire more deeply who that adversary is toward whom we are commanded to be well-disposed quickly while we are with him on the way: whether he is a human being, the devil, God, or his commandment. Concerning the human being, it has already been said above how this should be understood.

[Col. 0810A]

But concerning the devil, how can it be possible that we should be commanded to show him goodwill? Wherever there is goodwill, there is friendship. No one should be told to form a friendship with the devil or to agree with him, since by renouncing him once and for all we have declared war upon him, and by conquering him we shall be crowned. Nor ought we now to consent to him; for if we had never consented to him, we would never have fallen into these accusations and miseries.

As for the flesh, I do not see how we could be commanded to be well-disposed toward it, or in harmony with it, or consenting to it. Sinners, rather, love their flesh, agree with it, and consent to it. Those who subject it to servitude, however, do not consent to it; they compel it to consent to them.

Perhaps, therefore, we are commanded to consent to God and to be well-disposed toward him, so that we may be reconciled to him, from whom we have withdrawn by sinning, as to an adversary.

[Col. 0810B]

For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV). And “the beginning of every sin is pride, and the beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Ecclus. X). The Apostle also says: “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Rom. V).

Therefore, whoever in this way—that is, in this life—has not been reconciled to God through the death of his Son is handed over by him to judgment. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). And so the remaining points written in this passage follow, concerning which we have already treated.

[Col. 0810C]

There is only one matter that creates difficulty for this interpretation. How can it rightly be said that someone is with Christ on the way, if Christ himself is to be understood here as the adversary of the impious, to whom we are commanded to be reconciled quickly? Perhaps the answer is that he is everywhere, while when we are on this way we are necessarily with him. “If I ascend into heaven,” he says, “you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings toward the sunrise and dwell at the farthest part of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

[Col. 0810D]

Or, if one does not approve of saying that the impious are with God—although God is nowhere absent—just as we do not say that the blind are with the light, even though light surrounds their eyes, one possibility remains: we should understand the adversary here to be God’s commandment.

For what so opposes those who wish to sin as God’s commandment—that is, his law and the divine Scripture—which has been given to us for this life, so that it may be with us on the way? We ought not to contradict it, lest it hand us over to the judge; rather, we ought to consent to it quickly. For no one knows when he will depart from this life.

But who consents to Scripture except the one who reads and hears it, reverently granting it the highest authority, so that he does not hate what he understands merely because he perceives that it opposes his sins, but rather loves his correction and rejoices that his diseases are not spared until they are healed?

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

[Col. 0811A]

(Augustine.) The lesser righteousness, therefore, is not to commit adultery through bodily intercourse; but the greater righteousness of the kingdom of God is not to commit adultery in the heart. Whoever does not commit adultery in the heart much more easily guards against committing adultery in the body.

He therefore confirmed what he had commanded when he said: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.” Certainly, one must consider that he did not say, “Everyone who desires a woman,” but “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her”—that is, who looks at her with this purpose and intention: that he may desire her.

[Col. 0811B]

This is no longer merely to be tickled by the pleasure of the flesh, but plainly to consent to lust, so that the unlawful desire is not restrained but, if the opportunity is given, produces the act.

The ancients distinguished these two states by calling one *propassion* and the other *passion*. The difference between passion and propassion is that passion is counted as a fault, whereas propassion, although it contains guilt, is not held to be a crime.

Therefore, when someone looks at a woman and his soul is tickled, he has been struck by propassion. But if he consents and turns the thought into an affection, as it is written of David, “They passed into the affection of the heart” (Ps. LXXII), he has passed from propassion to passion. Such a person lacks not the will to sin but only the opportunity.

Whoever, therefore, looks at a woman in order to desire her—that is, if he looks in such a way that he desires her and intends to act—is rightly said to have committed adultery with her in his heart.

[Col. 0811C]

(Augustine.) Just as sin is reached through three stages—suggestion, pleasure, and consent—so there are three forms of this sin: in the heart, in the deed, and in the habit, as though they were three deaths.

The first is as if in the house, when lust is consented to in the heart. The second, already brought outside as if beyond the gate, occurs when consent proceeds into action. The third occurs when, through the force of an evil habit, the soul is pressed down like a mass of earth, as though already rotting in a tomb.

Anyone who reads the Gospel recognizes that God raised these three kinds of dead. Perhaps he also considers the distinctions in the very voice of the one raising them: in one place he says, “Girl, arise” (Matt. IX); elsewhere, “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke VII); elsewhere he groaned in spirit and wept, and again groaned, and afterward cried out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth” (John XI).

[Col. 0811D]

Therefore, under the name of adulterers mentioned in this passage, every carnal and lustful desire must be understood. Since Scripture so frequently calls idolatry fornication, and the Apostle Paul calls greed by the name of idolatry, who would doubt that every evil desire can rightly be called fornication, when the soul, neglecting the higher law by which it is governed, is corrupted by the shameful will of lower natures, as though prostituted for payment?

Therefore, whoever feels carnal pleasure rebelling against his right will should cry out in mourning and implore the help of the true Comforter, the Lord Christ. The knowledge of one’s own unhappiness is no small approach to blessedness.

“But if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be thrown into Gehenna.”

[Col. 0812A]

Since above he had spoken of desire for a woman, he now rightly called the wandering thought and sense an eye. By the right side and the other parts of the body, the beginnings of the will and of the affections are indicated. We must take care not to complete in action what we have conceived in the mind, lest what is best in us quickly fall into vice.

If the right eye and right hand cause us to stumble, how much more those things in us that are on the left? If the soul falls, how much more the body, which is more inclined toward sin?

[Col. 0812B]

(Augustine.) It seems to me that in this passage the eye may appropriately be understood as a most beloved friend. For we can rightly call that a member which we love greatly; it is also a counselor, since the eye is like one who shows the way.

In divine matters, because it is the right eye, the left eye may be understood as a beloved counselor in matters belonging to earthly necessities and the needs of the body. It was superfluous to speak of such a counselor when he causes one to stumble, since not even the right eye must be spared.

In divine matters, however, a counselor causes one to stumble if, under the name of religion and doctrine, he attempts to lead someone into a pernicious heresy.

“And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna.”

[Col. 0812C]

The right hand, therefore, is understood as a beloved helper and minister in divine works. For just as contemplation is rightly understood in the eye, so action is rightly understood in the hand. The left hand may be understood as referring to works necessary for the body in this life.

We may also understand in the right eye and right hand the affections for brothers, a wife, children, relatives by marriage, and other close relations. If we see that these hinder us from contemplating the true light, we ought to cut off such portions, lest, while wishing to gain others, we ourselves perish forever.

Hence it is also said of the high priest, whose soul is dedicated to the worship of God: “Above mother, father, and children he shall not be defiled” (Lev. XXI)—that is, he will recognize no affection except that of the one to whose worship he has been dedicated.

[Col. 0812D]

“It was also said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce.’”

It is written in Deuteronomy as follows: “If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favor before his eyes because of some disgrace, he shall write a bill of divorce, place it in her hand, and send her away from his house,” and so forth (Deut. XXIV).

In the latter part of the Gospel the Savior explains this passage more fully: Moses commanded that a bill of divorce be given because of the hardness of the husbands’ hearts—not granting divorce, but removing murder. For it is much better that discord occur, though grievous, than that blood be shed through hatred.

“But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.”

[Col. 0813A]

(Augustine.) In the old law there were many reasons for dismissing wives. In the Gospel, however, the Lord excepted only the cause of fornication. All other troubles, if they should perhaps arise, he commands to be endured firmly, for the sake of marital fidelity and chastity.

He also calls the man who marries a woman released by her husband an adulterer. The Apostle Paul shows the limit of this matter: he says that the rule is to be observed as long as the woman’s husband lives. When he has died, he grants permission to marry.

Paul himself also maintained this rule, and in it he presents not his own advice, as in some other instructions, but the commandment of the Lord, who orders it, when he says: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife should not depart from her husband; but if she does depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband, and let the husband not dismiss his wife” (1 Cor. VII).

[Col. 0813B]

I believe that the same form applies: if he dismisses her, he should not marry another, but should be reconciled to his wife. For it may happen that he dismisses his wife on account of fornication, which the Lord wished to be excepted.

If, then, the woman who has departed is not permitted to marry the man from whom she departed, and the man is not permitted to marry another while the wife whom he dismissed is alive, it is much less lawful to commit illicit fornication with just anyone.

Certainly, those marriages should be judged more blessed in which the spouses, whether for the sake of producing children or even, having despised this earthly offspring, have been able by mutual agreement to preserve continence between themselves. For this does not violate the commandment by which the Lord forbids the dismissal of a spouse: the one who lives with her not carnally but spiritually does not dismiss her.

[Col. 0813C]

The statement made through the Apostle is also preserved: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Cor. VII).

Some are troubled by the fact that elsewhere the Lord himself says: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV).

To those who understand it less well, this may appear contrary to the present passage, where he forbids the dismissal of a wife except on account of fornication. Elsewhere, he seems to say that no one can be his disciple who does not hate his wife. If he had said this because of intercourse, he should also have placed father, mother, and brothers under the same condition.

[Col. 0813D]

Therefore, how true it is that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI)! How much force is needed for a person to love his enemies and hate his father, mother, children, and brothers! The one who calls people to the kingdom of heaven commands both.

The question is resolved in this way: the eternal kingdom, into which he has deigned to call his disciples, whom he also calls brothers, has no such temporal necessities. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither male nor female, neither slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Gal. III).

[Col. 0814A]

The Lord himself also says: “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor take wives, but are like the angels in heaven” (Luke XX; Matt. XXII).

Whoever therefore wishes already here to meditate upon the life of that kingdom ought to hate not the people themselves but these temporal relationships by which this passing life is sustained—the life that is completed through birth and death.

Many people even hate those by whom they are loved, such as lustful children who hate their parents because they restrain their lust. Someone who loves his neighbor, though he still hates his enemy, has therefore ascended one degree.

By the command of the one who came to fulfill the law, not abolish it, he will perfect goodwill and kindness when he extends them even to love of his enemy. For that degree, although it is something, is nevertheless so small that it can be shared even with tax collectors.

Nor should the statement found in the law, “You shall hate your enemy,” be understood as the voice of one commanding, but of one permitting the weak.

# CHAPTER VI

## On Giving Alms, on Praying to God, and on Avoiding Hypocrisy and Greed

## I.

“Take care that you do not perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them.”

[Col. 0814B]

In the preceding passages, therefore, the good and pious teacher gave commandments concerning the display of mercy. Now the Truth itself instructs his hearers concerning purity of heart—that is, of the eye by which God is seen. Works of mercy are approved by the Lord only when they are performed with a simple and pure intention.

“Take care,” he says, “that you do not perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them.” That is: beware of holding this intention—that when you live rightly or perform some good work, you establish your goodness there, so that people may see you, please them, and seek to receive praise from them, thereby depriving yourself of the fruit of the true reward.

Hence he adds:

[Col. 0814C]

“Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

For whoever pursues the empty favor of the crowd or seeks praise from people will have this very thing counted as his reward, for love of which he appears to have performed good works. But with the Lord he is without reward, because he is found to have done nothing for love of him or from desire for eternal life.

Hence, in another passage, the foolish virgins are described as having adorned their lamps but not possessing oil in them (Matt. XXV). They are shown not to contain within the conscience of their hearts the splendor of glory that they sought outwardly. For this reason they are deservedly driven away when they knock at the door of the eternal King’s wedding feast, since they are not worthy to see him whom, when he was absent, they neglected to love.

[Col. 0814D]

When the Apostle says, “If I were pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I), and elsewhere says, “Just as I also please everyone in all things” (1 Cor. X), those who do not understand him think these statements contradictory.

He said that he did not please people because he did not do what was right in order to please people, but in order to please God, toward whose love he wished to turn people’s hearts precisely by pleasing them.

Just as someone might reasonably say, “In this work by which I seek a ship, I am not seeking a ship but my homeland,” so the Apostle could appropriately say: “In this work by which I please people, I do not please people but God.” For I do not seek this as my goal, but I direct it toward the purpose that those whom I wish to be saved may imitate me.

[Col. 0815A]

Human praise should not be sought by the one who acts rightly; it should follow the one who acts rightly, so that those who can also imitate what they praise may advance. It should not be the case that the one who is praised thinks that those who praise him thereby benefit him.

He continues:

“Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be honored by people. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.”

“Do not,” he says, “wish to become known like the hypocrites, the pretenders, as though they were actors representing other persons, as in theatrical performances.”

[Col. 0815B]

For the person who plays the part of Agamemnon in a tragedy, for example, or of some other character belonging to the history or story being enacted, is not truly that person himself but pretends to be him and is called a hypocrite.

So, in the churches and throughout human life, whoever wishes to appear to be what he is not is a hypocrite. He pretends to be righteous but does not display righteousness, because he places the entire fruit in human praise, which even pretenders can receive while they deceive those to whom they appear good and by whom they are praised.

Such people therefore receive no reward from God, who examines the heart, but rather the punishment of deceit. “From people,” he says, “they have received their reward.”

It is most appropriately said of them: “Depart from me, deceitful workers. You have borne my name, but you have not done my works.” They have received their reward, therefore, who give alms for no other reason than to be glorified by people.

“But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.”

[Col. 0815C]

Some believed that the left hand means unbelievers; others, an enemy. But to me the left hand seems more consistently to signify the desire for praise itself. The right hand signifies the intention to fulfill the divine commandments.

When the desire for human praise mingles with the conscience of the person giving alms, the left hand becomes conscious of the work of the right hand. Therefore, “let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” means: let the desire for human praise not mingle with your conscience when, in giving alms, you strive to fulfill the divine commandment.

“So that your alms may be in secret.”

What does “in secret” mean except in the good conscience itself, which cannot be displayed to human eyes or disclosed by words, since many people tell many lies?

[Col. 0815D]

Therefore, if the right hand acts inwardly and in secret, everything outward, visible, and temporal belongs to the left hand.

Let your alms therefore be in the conscience itself. Many give alms with a good will even when they do not have money or anything else that can be given to the needy. Others give outwardly but do not give inwardly: through ambition or for the sake of some temporal advantage, they wish to appear merciful. In them only the left hand should be considered to be at work.

Others occupy a kind of middle position between the two groups: they give alms with an intention directed toward God, yet some desire for praise or for some fragile and temporal thing inserts itself into this good and excellent will.

But our Lord prohibits the left hand from working alone much more emphatically when he also forbids it to mingle with the works of the right hand. For the matter concerns the purification of the heart, which will not be pure unless it is simple.

[Col. 0816A]

But how will it be simple if it serves two masters and does not purify its vision with a single intention directed toward eternal things, but clouds it also with love of mortal and fragile things?

“And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by people. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.”

(Maurus.) The corners of the streets are places where one road crosses another and forms a crossroads.

It is not wrong for you to be seen praying somewhere by people; what is wrong is to do this in order to be seen by people. The same point is repeated so often needlessly because one rule must already be observed: it is not to be feared or avoided that people should know these things, but that they should be done with the intention that the reward of pleasing people be expected from them.

[Col. 0816B]

The Lord himself also preserves the same words when he adds similarly: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.” By this he shows that he forbids the pursuit of that reward in which fools rejoice—namely, being praised by people.

“But when you pray, enter your room, and after closing your door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

(Jerome.) This statement, understood in the same way, teaches the hearer to flee the empty glory of the world. But it seems to me that the command is rather that we should pray to the Lord with the thoughts of our breast enclosed and our lips compressed.

[Col. 0816C]

We read that Hannah did this in the Book of Kings: “Only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard” (1 Kings I). These rooms are also signified in the psalm, where it says: “What you say in your hearts, and be pierced in your chambers” (Ps. IV). “And after closing your door,” he says, “pray to your Father in secret.”

It is not enough to enter the rooms if the door is open to intrusive thoughts, through which things outside force their way in improperly and seek our inner parts. By “outside” we said that all temporal and visible things are meant; through the door—that is, through the bodily sense—they enter our thoughts, and crowds of empty phantasms disturb those who pray.

[Col. 0816D]

The door must therefore be closed—that is, resistance must be offered to the carnal power—so that spiritual prayer may be directed to the Father. Such prayer exists in the innermost part of the heart, where the Father is prayed to in secret.

“And your Father,” he says, “who sees in secret, will repay you.” It was fitting that the passage should end with such a conclusion. He is not now teaching us that we should pray, but how we should pray; nor, as above, that we should give alms, but with what intention we should give them.

Thus he commands the purification of the heart, which is purified only by a single and simple intention directed toward eternal life, through the sole and pure love of wisdom.

“But when you pray, do not speak at length like the pagans. For they think that they will be heard because of their many words. Do not therefore become like them.”

[Col. 0817A]

Just as it is characteristic of hypocrites to present themselves to be observed in prayer, their reward being to please people, so it is characteristic of pagans—that is, gentiles—to think that they will be heard because of their many words.

Indeed, all excessive talk comes from the gentiles, who devote themselves to exercising the tongue rather than purifying the mind. They also try to transfer this kind of frivolous effort to bending the Lord through prayer, imagining that, like a human judge, the Lord can be brought by words to adopt a decision.

“Do not therefore be like them,” says the one true teacher.

“For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.”

At this point a certain heresy and a perverse philosophical doctrine arise. They say: “If God knows what we are going to pray for, and knows what we need before we ask, then we speak uselessly to one who already knows.”

[Col. 0817B]

A brief answer must be given to them: we are not narrators but petitioners. It is one thing to tell something to someone who is ignorant, and another to ask someone who knows. In the former there is information; in the latter, obedience. There we faithfully make something known; here we implore in our misery.

We ought not to act upon the Lord through words in order to obtain what we want, but through the realities we carry in our minds and through the intention of thought, with pure love and a simple disposition. Yet it was necessary for the Lord to teach us these realities through words, so that, committing them to memory, we might recall them at the appropriate time of prayer.

Thus, then, you shall pray: “Our Father who art in heaven.” Nowhere is the people of Israel found to have been commanded to say “Our Father,” or to pray to the Father as Lord; rather, the Lord was revealed to them as to servants, that is, as to those still living according to the flesh. Yet the prophets often show that this same Lord, their God, could also have been their Father if they had not strayed from his commandments. Such is the passage: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isaiah 1).

Concerning the future Christian people, however, the prophets had foretold, and the Gospel bears witness, that it would have the Lord as Father, saying: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1). The apostle Paul likewise says: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a servant” (Galatians 4). And he recalls that we have received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8). A great gift, therefore, we have received through the grace of God: that we are permitted to say to God, “Our Father.” For what will he not now give to children who ask, when he has already granted this very thing—that they should be children?

Finally, how deeply this ought to touch the mind: whoever says “Our Father” must not be unworthy of so great a Father. God, however, never falls into sordid ways. And thanks be to his mercy, who requires this of us—that he should be our Father—a status that can be obtained at no cost, but solely through a good will.

Here the rich, too, and those noble according to the standards of this world, are admonished that, once they have become Christians, they must not be proud against the poor and lowly, since together they say to God, “Our Father.” They cannot say this truly and devoutly unless they recognize that they are brothers. Let the new people, therefore, of the New Testament, called to an eternal inheritance, use its voice and say: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” that is, among the holy and righteous.

[Col. 0817C]

For God is not confined by the extent of places. Just as the sinner was called “earth” when it was said to him, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3), so, conversely, the righteous may be called “heaven.” For it is said to the righteous: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3). Therefore, if God dwells in his temple, and the saints are his temple, it is rightly said, “who art in heaven”—that is, “who art among the saints.”

This likeness is especially appropriate: spiritually, the difference between the righteous and sinners appears to be as great as, bodily, that between heaven and earth. To signify this, when we stand for prayer we turn toward the East—not as though God were there, having abandoned the other parts of the world—for he is present everywhere, not through spatial extension but through the majesty of his power—but so that the mind may be reminded to turn toward the higher nature, that is, toward the Lord, when the body itself, which is earthly, turns toward the higher body, that is, toward the heavenly body.

[Col. 0818A]

“May your name be sanctified.”

This is not requested as though God’s name were not holy, but so that it may be regarded as holy by human beings; that is, so that God may become known to them, and so that they may not suppose that anything is holier, or fear offending anything more greatly.

**(Cyprian.)** We ask and entreat this in another sense: that God’s name may be sanctified in us, so that we who have been sanctified in baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be. And we pray for this daily. Daily sanctification is necessary for us, so that we who sin every day may cleanse our offenses through continual sanctification.

“May your kingdom come.”

We also ask that God’s kingdom be made manifest to us, just as we ask that his name be sanctified in us.

[Col. 0818C]

**(Augustine.)** For when does God not reign, or when does something begin with him that has always existed and never ceases to exist? “May it come,” therefore, should be understood as “May it be revealed to human beings.” For just as present light is absent to the blind and to those who close their eyes, so God’s kingdom, although it never departs from the earth, is nevertheless absent to those who do not know it.

No one, however, will be permitted to remain ignorant of God’s kingdom when his Only-begotten Son has come from heaven—not merely intelligibly but visibly, in the Lord’s humanity—to judge the living and the dead.

[Col. 0818D]

**(Cyprian.)** We do indeed ask that our kingdom may come: the kingdom promised to us by God and acquired through Christ’s blood and passion. We who formerly served in this world are to reign afterward, with Christ ruling, just as he himself promises and says: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

“May your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.”

[Col. 0819A]

**(Augustine.)** That is, just as your will is in the angels who are in heaven—that they should cling wholly to you and enjoy you, with no error clouding their wisdom and no misery hindering their blessedness—so may it be done in your saints who are on earth and, with regard to the body, have been made from earth, although they are to be taken from earth for heavenly dwelling and transformation.

The words “May your will be done” may also rightly be understood as “May your commandments be obeyed,” as in heaven and on earth—that is, by angels and by human beings alike.

The will of God is what Christ both did and taught: humility in one’s way of life, steadfastness in faith, modesty in speech, justice in actions, mercy in one’s works, discipline in one’s conduct, not knowing how to inflict injury, and being able to endure injury when it has been inflicted; keeping peace with one’s brothers; loving the Lord with one’s whole heart; fearing him as Father and revering him as God.

We must place nothing whatsoever before Christ, since he placed nothing before us. We must cling inseparably to his love and stand bravely and confidently by his cross. When there is a contest over his name and honor, we must show steadfastness in speech, by which we confess; confidence in questioning, by which we engage; and patience in death, by which we are crowned. This is to desire to be Christ’s co-heir; this is to do God’s commandment; this is to fulfill the will of the Father.

[Col. 0819B]

This sentence may also be understood in another way, so that “May your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” means: “May sinners as well as the righteous do your will, so that they may be converted to you.” Or it may mean: “May your will be done in heaven and on earth, so that each may receive what is his due.” This occurs at the final judgment, when the righteous receive their reward and sinners their condemnation, when the sheep are separated from the goats.

There is another interpretation that is not absurd but is extremely appropriate to our faith and hope: we may understand heaven and earth as spirit and flesh. For when the apostle says, “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7), we see that God’s will is done in the mind. We must pray that, just as in heaven, so also on earth God’s will may be done—that is, that just as we delight in the law with the heart according to the inner person, so also, when the body has been transformed, no part of us may oppose this delight through earthly pains or pleasures.

[Col. 0819C]

Nor is it contrary to the truth to understand “May your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” as meaning: “As in our Lord Jesus Christ, so also in the Church”—as in the man who fulfilled the Father’s will, so also in the woman who has been betrothed to him. Heaven and earth may appropriately be understood as man and woman, since earth becomes fruitful through heaven’s fertilizing power.

This is the fourth petition:

“Our daily bread, give us today.”

[Col. 0819D]

“Daily bread” may refer to all the things that sustain the needs of this life, concerning which he commands and says: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.” For this reason, “Give us today” has been added. Or it may refer to the sacrament of Christ’s body, which we receive daily. Or it may refer to spiritual food, concerning which the same Lord says: “Work for the food that does not perish.” And again: “I am the bread of life, who came down from heaven” (John 6).

Which of these three meanings is most strongly supported may be considered. Someone might perhaps be troubled as to why we pray to obtain the necessities of this life, such as food and clothing, when the Lord himself says: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will wear” (Matthew 6). As for the sacrament of the Lord’s body, those who do not communicate daily in the Lord’s Supper—of whom there are many in the eastern regions—should not raise an objection when this bread is called “daily.”

[Col. 0820A]

It remains, then, that we understand “daily bread” as spiritual bread: namely, the divine commandments, which ought daily to be meditated upon and practiced. For concerning these the Lord says: “Work for the food that does not perish.”

This food is called “daily” for as long as this temporal life is carried on through days that pass and succeed one another. Indeed, as long as the mind’s inclination alternates—now toward higher things, now toward lower, that is, now toward spiritual things, now toward carnal things—it is like someone who is sometimes nourished by food and sometimes suffers hunger. Daily bread is necessary for it, so that the hungry may be refreshed and the one who has fallen back may be raised up.

[Col. 0820B]

In other copies we read “supersubstantial bread,” or “special” or “principal bread.” This likewise signifies that bread of which he says: “I am the bread that came down from heaven,” which is above all substances and surpasses every creature.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

**(Cyprian.)** After the provision of food, forgiveness of sin is requested, so that the person who is fed by God may live in God, and so that provision may be made not only for the present and temporal life but also for the eternal life to which one can come if sins are forgiven.

The Lord calls sins “debts,” as he says in his Gospel: “I forgave you the whole debt because you asked me” (Matthew 18). How necessarily, how providently, and how beneficially we are reminded that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray concerning our sins! He who taught us to pray about our debts and sins promised paternal mercy and added the forgiveness that would follow. He plainly also added a law, binding us by a definite condition and pledge: we are to ask that our debts be forgiven in accordance with the way in which we ourselves forgive our debtors.

[Col. 0820C]

We know that what we ask for our sins cannot be obtained unless we have done the same toward our own sinners. Therefore, elsewhere he says: “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Mark 4; Luke 6). No other sentence do we pray in such a way that we seem to be making a bargain with the Lord. If we lie in this bargain, there is no fruit from the whole prayer.

“And do not lead us into temptation.”

**(Augustine.)** God does not himself lead a person into temptation, but he permits the one whom he has abandoned from his help to be led into it, according to a most hidden order and in accordance with merits. Often, too, for evident reasons, he judges someone worthy to be abandoned and permits that person to be led into temptation.

[Col. 0820D]

To be led into temptation is one thing; to be tempted is another. No one can be proved without temptation. We are not therefore praying here that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be brought into temptation. It is like someone who must be tested by fire: he does not pray that he may not come into contact with fire, but that he may not be burned. “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus 26).

Many, however, say in prayer: “Do not permit us to be led into temptation,” thereby explaining how the word “lead” is to be understood. This shows that the adversary can do nothing against us unless God has first permitted it, so that all our fear, devotion, and watchfulness may be turned toward the Lord. In our temptations, evil is permitted to do nothing unless power is granted to it from that source.

[Col. 0821A]

“But deliver us from evil. Amen.”

When we say, “Deliver us from evil,” nothing remains that ought subsequently to be requested, once we have asked for God’s protection against evil.

**(Maurice.)** Once this has been obtained, we stand secure and safe against everything the devil and the world do. But this happens in the present only to the extent that divine judgment has foreseen it to be useful for us. Hence the apostle says: “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10).

[Col. 0821B]

We must pray not only that we may not be led into the evil from which we are free—which we request in the sixth place—but also that we may be delivered from the evil into which we have already been led. When this has happened, nothing fearful will remain, and no temptation will have to be feared at all.

Yet we must not expect this to be possible in the present life, as long as we bear this mortality into which we were led through the serpent’s persuasion. We must nevertheless hope that it will one day occur. At the proper time, the blessedness that was begun in this life will be brought to completion; toward acquiring and attaining it, all our present effort is directed.

The distinction among these four petitions must also be considered and commended. Our temporal life is now being lived while eternal life is hoped for. Eternal things are superior in dignity, although one passes to them through temporal things first experienced.

[Col. 0821C]

The fulfillment of the first three petitions, although it begins in this life, which is lived in this present age—for the sanctification of God’s name began with the very coming of the Lord’s birth; and the coming of his kingdom, in which he will come in glory, will be manifested not after the age has ended but at the end of the age; and the perfection of his will, as in heaven and on earth, whether heaven and earth are understood as the righteous and sinners, or as spirit and flesh, or as the Lord and the Church, or as all these together, will be completed in the very perfection of our blessedness and therefore at the end of the age—nevertheless all three will remain forever.

The sanctification of God’s name will be everlasting; his kingdom will have no end; and eternal life is promised to our perfected blessedness. These three, therefore, will remain, completed and increased, in the life that is promised to us.

[Col. 0821D]

The remaining four petitions, however, appear to me to belong to this temporal life. The first of them is: “Our daily bread, give us today.” By calling it “daily,” spiritual bread is signified, whether it is understood as the sacrament or as visible nourishment. In either case, it belongs to the time designated by the word “today.”

This does not mean that spiritual food is not eternal, but that the food called “daily” in Scripture—or presented to the soul through the sound of speech or through various temporal signs—belongs to the present time. None of these things will exist then, when all will be taught by God and will drink in the ineffable light of truth itself, not by means of bodily movements that signify it, but through purity of mind.

[Col. 0822A]

Perhaps it is also called “bread,” rather than “drink,” because bread is converted into nourishment by being broken and chewed, just as the Scriptures feed the soul when they are opened and expounded. Drink, however, passes into the body already prepared as it is. Thus, in the present time, truth is bread when it is called “daily bread”; then it will be drink, when no labor of disputing and speaking—like breaking and chewing—will be necessary, but only the drinking in of sincere and clear truth.

Now our sins are forgiven, and now we forgive debts; this is the second of the remaining four petitions. Then there will be no forgiveness of sins, because there will be no sins. Temptations afflict this temporal life, but they will not exist when what is written has been fulfilled: “You will hide them in the secrecy of your presence” (Psalm 30). The evil from which we desire to be delivered, and the deliverance itself from evil, belong to this life, which we have deserved through God’s justice to be mortal and from which we shall be delivered through his mercy.

[Col. 0822B]

It also seems to me that this number seven of the petitions corresponds to the number seven from which the whole sermon proceeded.

If the fear of God is that by which the poor in spirit are blessed, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5), let us ask that God’s name may be sanctified among human beings, with chaste fear remaining forever and ever.

If piety is that by which the meek are blessed, because they shall possess the earth, let us ask that his kingdom may come—either upon us, so that we may become meek and not resist him, or from heaven to earth, in the glory of the Lord’s coming, in which we shall rejoice and be glad, when he says: “Come, you blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matthew 25). For the prophet says: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice” (Psalm 33).

[Col. 0822C]

If knowledge is that by which those who mourn are blessed, because they shall be comforted, let us pray that his will may be done as in heaven and on earth. When the body has consented in complete and perfect peace to the spirit, as earth to heaven, we shall no longer mourn.

For there is no other mourning of this present time except when these things struggle against one another and compel us to say: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind”; and to testify to our mourning with a tearful voice: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7).

[Col. 0822D]

If fortitude is that by which those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed, because they shall be satisfied, let us pray that our daily bread may be given to us today, so that, strengthened and sustained by it, we may be able to come to that fullest satisfaction.

If counsel is that by which the merciful are blessed, because they shall receive mercy, let us forgive the debts of our debtors and pray that our debts may be forgiven.

If understanding is that by which the pure in heart are blessed, because they shall see God, let us pray not to be led into temptation. Let us not have a divided heart by failing to desire the single good to which we may refer everything we do and by pursuing temporal and earthly things at the same time.

[Col. 0823A]

Temptations arising from those things that seem grievous and calamitous to human beings have no power over us if those temptations arising from the allurements of things that people consider good and joyful have no power over us.

If wisdom is that by which the peacemakers are blessed, because they shall be called children of God, let us pray that we may be delivered from evil. This deliverance itself makes us free—that is, children of God—so that we may cry out in the Spirit of adoption: “Abba, Father.”

**(Jerome.)** The “Amen” that is written at the end is the seal of the Lord’s prayer; Aquila rendered it as “faithfully,” and we too can truly say it.

**(Maurice.)** This signifies that in all these petitions the purest truth is established, and that everything properly requested is undoubtedly bestowed by the Lord upon those who do not neglect to keep the covenant of the final condition. Hence what follows:

[Col. 0823B]

“For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins.”

**(Jerome.)** He says, “If you do not forgive people,” as though those who forgive were not people—that is, not human or earthly. For this is what is written: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. But you shall die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes” (Psalm 81). This is said to those who, because of their sins, have deserved to become human beings instead of gods. Those, therefore, whose sins are forgiven are rightly also called “human beings.”

[Col. 0823C]

**(Augustine.)** The command concerning fasting follows and pertains to the same purification of the heart that is now under discussion. In this practice, too, care must be taken lest some display or desire for human praise creep in, dividing our heart and preventing it from being pure and single-minded for understanding the Lord. For he says:

“And when you fast, do not become like the gloomy hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.”

[III.] Whoever does not hate this has not yet come to love that life in which there will be no condition of birth and death joining earthly marriages. For we undoubtedly hate what we earnestly desire eventually not to exist.

Thus, in accordance with both of the Lord’s commandments, the good Christian loves in one woman God’s creature, which he desires to be reformed and renewed; but he hates the corruptible and mortal union and conjunction. This is to love in her what belongs to her as a human being, and to hate what belongs to her as a wife.

[Col. 0823D]

In the same way, he loves his enemy—not insofar as the enemy is an enemy, but insofar as he is a human being—so that he may wish for him what he wishes for himself: that, corrected and renewed, he may reach the kingdom of heaven.

The same is to be understood concerning father, mother, and the other bonds of blood: in them we are to hate what the human race has received through birth and death, but to love what can be brought with us to those kingdoms where no one says “my father,” but all say to the one God, “Our Father”; where no one says “my mother,” but all say to that Jerusalem, “Our mother”; and where no one says “my brother,” but everyone, from all alike, says, “Our brother.”

Here another question arises: since the Lord permits a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication, how is fornication to be understood in this passage? Is it to be understood as everyone understands it—that is, as the fornication committed in sexual offenses? Or is it to be understood in the way Scripture usually uses the word “fornication,” as was stated above, to mean every unlawful desire, such as idolatry or avarice, and from this every transgression of the law arising from unlawful desire?

[Col. 0824A]

For who could now rightly separate any unlawful desire from the category of fornication, if avarice is fornication? From this it is understood that, on account of unlawful desires—not only those committed in sexual offenses with another man or woman, but absolutely any desires that cause the mind, through wrongful use of the body, to stray from the law and to be corrupted disastrously and shamefully—a husband may dismiss his wife without sin, and a wife her husband, because the Lord makes an exception for the cause of fornication.

[Col. 0824B]

We are compelled to understand this fornication, as was mentioned above, in a general and universal sense. When he says “except for the cause of fornication,” he does not specify whose fornication it is, the man’s or the woman’s. For it is not permitted only to dismiss a wife who is committing fornication; whoever dismisses a wife by whom he himself is compelled to commit fornication dismisses her on account of fornication.

For example, if a wife compels someone to sacrifice to idols, the man who dismisses such a wife dismisses her on account of fornication—not only on account of her fornication but also on account of his own: hers, because she commits fornication; his, so that he may not commit fornication.

“Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely; rather, you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all—not by heaven, because it is the throne of God; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black.”

[Col. 0824C]

The Jews always had this extremely bad custom of swearing by the elements, as the prophetic word frequently reproves them. For whoever swears either reveres or loves the one by whom he swears.

**(Jerome.)** In the Law it was commanded that we should swear only by the Lord our God. For the Jews, swearing by angels, by the city of Jerusalem, by the temple, and by the elements, were venerating creatures and bodily things while disregarding the honor and service owed to God.

[Col. 0824D]

Finally, observe that here the Savior did not prohibit swearing by God, but by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and one’s own head. This had been permitted to them as to little children: just as they sacrificed victims to God so that they would not sacrifice them to idols, so they were permitted to swear by the Lord—not because they were doing what was right, but because it was better to offer this to God than to demons.

Evangelical truth, however, does not accept an oath, since every faithful statement serves in place of an oath. Just as one who does not speak cannot speak falsely, so one who does not swear cannot commit perjury.

**(Augustine.)** Nevertheless, since the person who calls upon God as witness does swear, this passage must be examined carefully, lest the apostle appear to have acted against the Lord’s command when he often swore in this manner.

[Col. 0825A]

He says: “As for the things I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Galatians 1). And again: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie” (2 Corinthians 11).

There is also this statement: “God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, how unceasingly I remember you always in my prayers” (Romans 1).

The Lord’s command is therefore understood to have been that one should not swear, lest anyone seek an oath as though it were a good thing and, through the habit of swearing frequently, slide into perjury. Consequently, whoever understands that an oath belongs not among goods but among necessities should restrain himself as much as possible, so that he uses it only when necessity requires it—when he sees that people are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe unless it is confirmed by an oath.

[Col. 0825B]

Thus the Lord teaches that nothing among God’s creatures is so insignificant that someone should suppose he may swear falsely by it, since divine providence governs all things created, from the highest to the lowest.

Beginning with God’s throne and continuing to the white or black hair, he forbids an oath so that you may not think that you do not owe your oath to the Lord when you are shown to swear by the one whose heaven is the throne, whose earth is the footstool, and whose entire creation is his work.

But we must not suppose, from the statement that heaven is God’s throne and earth the footstool of his feet, that God has placed bodily members in heaven and on earth in the way that we do when we sit. Rather, that seat signifies God’s judgment.

[Col. 0825C]

Since, in the whole body of the universe, heaven possesses the greatest beauty and earth the least, divine power is said to sit in heaven as though it were more present to the highest beauty, while it orders the least thing at the extremities and in the lowest places; it is said to tread upon the earth.

Spiritually, however, the name “heaven” signifies holy souls and “earth” sinful souls. Since the spiritual person judges all things but is judged by no one, he is appropriately called God’s seat. The sinner, however, to whom it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” is ordered in the lowest places because justice assigns to each what is deserved. And the one who was unwilling to remain in the law is placed under the law; accordingly, he is understood as the footstool of God’s feet.

“But let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no’; anything more than these is from evil.”

[Col. 0825D]

**(Maurice.)** Having not prohibited the taking of oaths, he taught how one ought to speak. “Let your speech,” he says, “be ‘Yes, yes; no, no,’” as though he were saying: What is, let it be enough to say “is”; what is not, let it be enough to say “is not.” Or the words “yes, yes; no, no” are repeated so that what you affirm with your mouth you may prove by your works, and what you deny in words you may not confirm by your deeds.

This is good and desirable: that the testimony of good works should commend the speech of the speaker. When he adds, “Anything more than these is from evil,” it must be understood in this way: if you are compelled to swear, this necessity arises from the weakness of those whom you are persuading—an infirmity that is itself evil.

[Col. 0826A]

This is why we daily pray to be delivered from evil when we say, “Deliver us from evil.” He therefore did not say, “Anything more is evil.” You do not do evil when you make good use of an oath, which, although not good in itself, is nevertheless necessary in order to persuade another of something that it is beneficial to persuade him of. Rather, it is “from evil”—from the weakness, namely, of the person by whom you are compelled to swear.

Yet no one knows, unless he has experienced it, how difficult it is both to extinguish the habit of swearing and never rashly to do what necessity sometimes compels.

“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist evil.”

[Col. 0826B]

**(Jerome.)** Whoever says “an eye for an eye” does not wish to take away one eye, but to preserve both. Our Lord, abolishing retaliation, cuts off the beginnings of sins, because in the Law there is retribution, whereas in the Gospel there is grace.

**(Augustine.)** There guilt is corrected; here the beginnings of sins are removed.

It should be noted that some people consider there to be four degrees of vengeance or retribution. The first is when someone who has been injured desires to take revenge more severely. It is not easy to find someone who, having received a blow, wishes to return only a blow, or who, having heard one insulting word, is content to return an equal one. Either, disturbed by anger, he takes disproportionate revenge, or, because he considers the one who inflicted the injury to deserve it, he thinks that the offender should be injured more severely than the person who had not previously injured him.

[Col. 0826C]

The Law restrained such a disposition to a considerable extent and established a certain degree in the command: “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.” These expressions signify a limit, so that revenge does not go beyond the injury. This is the beginning of peace.

Perfect peace, however, is to be entirely unwilling to take revenge. To reach this, two further degrees remain: not only must one refrain from returning as much as one has received, but one must return less—for example, returning one blow for two, or cutting off an ear for an eye that has been torn out.

Ascending from this, the person who returns no evil at all, but instead returns good for evil, approaches the Lord’s present command, although he is not yet fully there. For it still seems a small thing to the Lord if, in return for the evil one has received, one returns no evil, unless one is also prepared to receive more.

[Col. 0826D]

Accordingly, he did not say: “But I say to you, do not return evil for evil,” although this too is a great commandment. Rather, he said: “Do not resist evil,” so that you should not only refrain from returning what has been inflicted upon you, but also refrain from resisting the infliction of something else. This is what he explains next.

“But if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also.”

[Col. 0827A]

**(Augustine.)** He does not say, “If anyone strikes you, do not strike back,” but rather, “Prepare yourself to be struck again.” Those who understand this as a matter of mercy especially recognize it in the conduct of people who serve those whom they greatly love—children or other beloved persons—when they are sick, or who care for little children or the mentally disturbed, from whom they often suffer much. If the welfare of such persons requires it, they offer themselves to suffer even more, until the weakness of age or illness has passed.

Since the Lord, the physician of souls, was instructing those who care for their neighbors, what else should he have taught them except to endure with equanimity the weaknesses of those whose welfare they wished to promote? For every form of wickedness arises from weakness of mind. Nothing is more innocent than the person who is perfect in virtue.

By this saying of the Gospel, the ecclesiastical man is depicted as an imitator of the one who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11). When struck on the cheek, he confirms his promise, saying: “If I have spoken evil, testify to the evil; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” (John 18).

David says something similar in the psalm: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Psalm 7). And Jeremiah says in the Lamentations: “It is good for a man if he has sat from his youth; let him offer his cheek to the one who strikes him, and let him be filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3).

This is directed against those who think that one Lord belongs to the Law and another to the Gospel, since both there and here gentleness is taught.

[Col. 0827B]

According to the mystical interpretations, when our right cheek has been struck, we are not commanded to offer the left but the other—that is, the other right cheek. The righteous person has no left cheek.

If a heretic strikes us in debate and wishes to wound the right-hand doctrine, another testimony from the Scriptures should be set against him. We should offer successive right cheeks to the one who strikes for as long as necessary, until the enemy’s anger grows weary.

It may also appropriately be understood that the two cheeks signify two kinds of nobility: nobility according to God and nobility according to this world. Let them be distributed in this way: the right cheek belongs to divine nobility, and the left to human nobility.

[Col. 0827C]

It is therefore fitting that, in any disciple of Christ, whatever belongs to him as a Christian should be despised, while he should be prepared to have the honors of this world that he possesses despised even more.

Thus the apostle Paul, when people were persecuting in him the Christian name, would not have offered the other cheek to those striking the right one if he had kept silent about the dignity he possessed in this world. For by saying, “I am a Roman citizen,” he showed that he was prepared to have this dignity despised by those who had despised in him the name that was so precious and saving.

And to anyone who wishes to bring you to court and take your tunic, give him your cloak as well. Luke placed this passage in reverse order. For he says: “From him who takes away your garment, do not withhold even your tunic” (Luke 6). What is said about the garment and the tunic must be done not only with these things, but with everything that we say is temporarily ours by some legal right: the tunic is the inner garment, the cloak the outer one. For if this has been commanded concerning necessities, how much more fitting is it to despise superfluities, and everything that can pass from our legal possession into another’s power? Such things include clothing, a house, land, an animal, and, generally, all money. Whether this should also be understood of slaves is a serious question. A Christian ought not to possess a slave in the same way as a horse, silver, or gold. But if that slave is educated and governed by you, his master, more rightly, honorably, and suitably for the worship of God than he could be by the person who wants to take him away, I do not know whether anyone would dare say that he ought to be despised like a garment. A human being ought to love another human being as himself. The Lord of all—which the following passages will also show—commands him to love even his enemies.

[Col. 0828A] Spiritually, every teacher takes away someone’s tunic when he demands that the person confess his inward sins and those hidden in his soul, such as pride, envy, hatred, lust, and similar faults. He likewise gives up the cloak at the same time when he is not ashamed to confess the outward offenses he has committed through the body, such as the vice of drunkenness, fornication, robbery, quarrelling, theft, and murder; pouring out before the Lord every impurity and disgrace of his conduct, he says to Him with the Psalmist: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities; I said, ‘I will confess my iniquities to the Lord against myself,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm 31).

And whoever compels you to go one thousand paces, go with him another [Col. 0828B] two. (Augustine) What this testimony therefore commands must be understood not so much as an instruction to travel on foot as to be always ready in spirit to act—to offer compassion and the effort of assistance to the person who seeks it from you. For in the very Christian history, whose authority is decisive, you will find nothing of this sort literally performed by the saints or by the Lord himself, when, in the human being whom he graciously chose to receive, he offered us an example of life; yet in nearly every passage you will find that they were prepared to endure with equanimity whatever had been wickedly done to them.

He therefore set down three examples, because perfection is signified by this number, so that everyone may remember that, when doing this, he is fulfilling perfect righteousness by mercifully bearing with the weaknesses of those whom he wishes to become healthy. Nor is vengeance forbidden here when it serves correction; for it too belongs to mercy. Neither does this interfere with the resolve by which someone is prepared to endure more from the person whom he wishes to correct. But no one is fit to return such vengeance unless he has overcome, by the greatness of his love, the hatred with which those who desire to avenge themselves usually burn. We need not fear that parents appear to hate a small child when he is beaten by them for doing wrong, so that he may not sin again. Nor is anything here contradicted, except that the person to whom authority has been given in the proper order may administer punishment—and that he should do so with the same disposition as a father toward a small son, whom his age does not yet permit him to hate.

The Lord does not abolish correction through justice, nor does he forbid reproof where it is necessary; rather, through gentleness he teaches us to possess patience [Col. 0828D] and tranquillity in innocence. But since it is a small thing merely not to harm someone unless you also do as much good as you can, he appropriately adds:

“Give to anyone who asks you, and do not turn away from anyone who wishes to borrow from you.” (Jerome) If we understand this as referring only to almsgiving, it cannot stand in the case of most poor people. Wealthy people too, if they were always giving, could not always continue to give. After the good work of almsgiving, therefore, instructions are given to the apostles—that is, to teachers—so that those who have received freely may give freely. Money of this kind never runs out; rather, the more it is given, the more it is multiplied. And when it waters the fields entrusted to it, the stream of its spring never dries up.

(Augustine) But what must certainly be given is something that harms neither you nor anyone else, as far as a human being can know or reasonably believe. And when you justly refuse someone what he asks, you should explain the justice of the refusal to him, so that you do not send him away empty-handed. Thus you will give to everyone who asks you, although you will not always give him what he asks for; sometimes you will give something better, when you justly correct the person who asks.

When he says, “Do not turn away from anyone who wishes to borrow from you,” this should be referred to the soul—that is, do not estrange your goodwill from him. “God loves a cheerful giver.” We should therefore understand the Lord here to have included the two kinds of giving. For either we benevolently give what we give, or we entrust it to someone who will repay it. Often people who, because of the divine reward promised, are ready to give become reluctant to give what is requested as a loan, as though they were to receive nothing from God, since the person who receives the thing given will repay it.

Divine authority rightly urges us toward this kind of generosity, saying: “Whoever wishes to borrow from you, do not turn away from him.” That is: do not estrange your goodwill from the person who asks because your money becomes unavailable and God will not repay you once a human being has repaid you. When you do this at God’s command, it cannot be fruitless before the one who gives the command. For in the Gospel that servant is praised by his master who, after receiving talents, doubled them by trading, and for this reason is commanded to enter into the joy of his master (Matthew 25).

The spiritual teacher ought therefore to lend the capital of the divine word to his hearers, so that he may receive from them the return of good works. For this reason both parties ought to hope for eternal recompense from God and in no way grow weary in their good endeavor. It follows:

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.” (Jerome) Many people, judging God’s commands by their own weakness rather than by the strength of the saints, think that what has been commanded is impossible. They say that it is enough for virtue not to hate one’s enemies; to be commanded to love them, however, is more than human nature can endure.

We must therefore understand that Christ commands not impossibilities but perfection. David did this toward Saul and Absalom (1 Samuel 24; 2 Samuel 18). The martyr Stephen also prayed for his enemies who were stoning him (Acts 7). Paul, too, desires to become anathema for the sake of his persecutors (Romans 9). Jesus both taught and did these things when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

(Augustine) A question naturally arises here, and it seems difficult to those who understand little: many imprecations against enemies are found in the prophets, and these are thought to be curses, such as: “Let their table become a snare” (Psalm 86), along with the other words spoken there. There is also: “Let his children become orphans, and his wife a widow” (Psalm 108), as well as the other things spoken by the prophet in that psalm, above and below, concerning Judas.

Many other passages are found in Scripture that seem contrary both to this command of the Lord and to the apostolic command—“Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12)—since it is also written of the Lord that he cursed the cities that did not receive his word (Matthew 11), and it is recorded that the Apostle said of a certain person: “The Lord will repay him according to his works” (2 Timothy 4).

But these matters are easily resolved. The prophet, through an imprecation, foretold what would happen, not by the desire of one wishing it, but by the spirit of one foreseeing it. The same is true of the Lord and the Apostle. Their words do not express what they wished for, but what they predicted. When the Lord says, “Woe to you, Capernaum,” he means only that something bad will happen to it because of the merit of its unbelief. The Lord did not wish this out of malevolence; he saw it through divine knowledge. Nor does the Apostle say, “May he repay,” but “The Lord will repay him according to his works”—a statement of foretelling, not of imprecation.

In another passage the same Apostle, listing those liable to capital offenses, commands that we should not even eat with such a person (1 Corinthians 5). This is in no way contrary to the Lord’s command concerning love and benevolence toward enemies. We must love enemies not insofar as they are enemies, but insofar as they are human beings; we must love their nature and hate their vices. Everything we do toward them—whether granting benefits, reproving, admonishing, or even excommunicating them—we must do for this purpose: not that they should remain enemies, but that they should become brothers.

For what are we to pray for those who persecute us, except what the Apostle says: that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by which they are held captive to their own destruction (2 Timothy 2), so that, healed of this madness, they may turn away from evil and do good? We therefore rightly pray for them when we desire that what we wish to happen to ourselves may happen to them also: that those whom we suffer as enemies in the present time may afterward, through correction of life, become our companions in the kingdom.

(Augustine) Another question arises here. If the Lord commands us to pray for our enemies, why does the apostle John say: “If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and God will give life to the one who sins not unto death. There is sin unto death; I do not say that he should pray for that” (John 5)?

He clearly shows that there are some brothers for whom we are not commanded to pray, even though God commands us to pray for our persecutors. This question cannot be resolved unless we admit that there are sins among brothers more serious than the persecution of enemies. That “brothers” signifies Christians can be proved by many arguments from the divine Scriptures.

I think, therefore, that a brother’s sin unto death is committed when, after acknowledging God through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, someone attacks the brotherhood and is inflamed by the fires of envy against the very grace by which he has been reconciled to God. The sin is not unto death when someone has not withdrawn his love from his brother but, through some weakness of spirit, has failed to perform the duties owed to brotherhood.

For this reason the Lord also said on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” They had not yet become participants in the grace of the Holy Spirit or entered into the fellowship of holy brotherhood. This distinction between sins separates Judas, who betrayed him, from Peter—not because the person who asks should not be forgiven, since that would contradict the Lord’s command that a brother who asks his brother for forgiveness must always be forgiven, but because the stain of Judas’s sin was so great that he could not submit to the humility of seeking pardon, even though his evil conscience forced him to recognize and confess his sin.

For when Judas said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matthew 27), he nevertheless ran to the noose in despair more readily than he sought forgiveness in humility. Therefore it makes a great difference what kind of repentance God forgives. Many people confess much more quickly that they have sinned and are so angry with themselves that they intensely wish they had not sinned; yet they do not lay down their spirit in order to humble themselves, submit their hearts, and implore forgiveness. Because of the magnitude of their sin, we must believe that they already possess this disposition of mind with respect to condemnation.

Perhaps this is what it means to sin against the Holy Spirit: through malice and envy, to attack brotherly love after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Lord says that this sin will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. Let us therefore love our enemies without any hesitation, do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute us, so that what follows may come to pass:

“So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.”

The first part of this sentence [Col. 0831C] must be understood according to the principle expressed also by John: “He gave them the power to become children of God” (John 1). There is one who is naturally the Son of God, the one who is entirely incapable of sinning. We, however, become sons by the power we have received, insofar as we fulfill the commands given by him.

Hence apostolic teaching calls this adoption, by which we are called to an eternal inheritance so that we may be coheirs of Christ. We therefore become sons through spiritual rebirth and are adopted into the kingdom of God, not as strangers, but as those made and created by him—that is, brought into being [Note: “That is, brought into being” is certainly a gloss.]—so that there may be one benefit by which, through his omnipotence, he caused us to exist when previously we were nothing, and another by which he adopted us, so that, as sons, we might enjoy eternal life with him through our participation.

Thus he does not say, “Do these things because you are sons,” but, “Do these things so that you may be sons.” When he calls us to this through the Only-Begotten, he calls us to conformity with himself. For he, as the passage goes on to say, makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.

Whether you understand “his sun” not as the sun visible to bodily eyes but as that wisdom of which it is said, “For she is the brightness of eternal light” (Wisdom 7), and of which it is also said, “The sun of righteousness has risen for me,” and again, “For you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4); and whether you understand the rain as the watering of the teaching of truth, because Christ appeared to both good and wicked and was proclaimed in the Gospel to both good and wicked—

Or whether you prefer to understand this as the visible sun, displayed not only to human beings but also to animals’ bodily eyes, and the rain by which fruits are produced and given for the refreshment of the body: who is so ungrateful as not to perceive how much comfort this visible light and bodily rain provide in the present life? We see that this comfort is commonly given both to the just and to sinners.

He does not say merely, “Who makes the sun rise upon the good and the wicked,” but adds “his”—that is, the sun which he himself made and established, taking nothing from anyone in order to make it. So it is written in Genesis concerning all the heavenly lights. He alone can properly say that everything is his which he created from nothing. By this we are reminded how generously, at his command, we ought to provide for our enemies what we did not create but received as gifts.

“For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do this?”

(Maurus) The Jews called the tax collectors *publicani*, Roman collectors who were responsible for public administration. Here “tax collectors” refers to those who collect public taxes, who [or] pursue the profits of the public affairs of this world. “Gentiles” is *ethnici* in Greek and *gentes* in Latin. For ἔθνος (*ethnos*) means “nation” or “people” in Greek. Hence those are called Gentiles who are as they were born, namely, serving idols under sin.
