The sense of this sentence in the Gospel is therefore as follows: if even tax collectors and Gentiles, guided by nature, know how to show kindness toward those who love them, how much more must you—who, although your rank of profession is more exalted, must likewise have a more abundant concern for virtue—embrace, in the breadth of your love, even those who do not love you.

It therefore seems worth asking how, when the Lord testifies that those who love only those who love them, and do good to their benefactors, not only do not possess perfect love but are compared with sinners, the beloved disciple who reclined on the Lord’s breast, bringing his letter concerning the love of God and neighbor to completion, does not appear anywhere to have instructed us to love enemies, but says plainly: “If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us” (1 John 4).

If this troubles anyone, he should know that John was not teaching about love of enemies, but included them also under the name of brothers, commanding that they be loved with a view to brotherly love and that we pray for them—namely, so that they may not remain enemies forever, but may recover from the snares of the devil and be joined to us in a bond of kinship.

Nor should it seem harsh when we say that those who do not yet believe may nevertheless, because of the hope that they will believe, be called brothers. For the same John is also read to call them children of God: “Jesus,” he says, “was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered” (John 11). As long as they are scattered, they are not yet children; but by coming together into one they already become children.

“Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

Without this love by which we are commanded to love our enemies and persecutors, who can fulfill the things stated above? The perfection of mercy, by which the suffering soul receives the greatest assistance, cannot extend beyond love of one’s enemy. Therefore the passage concludes in this way: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect.” This must be understood in such a way that God is perfect as God, and the soul is perfect as a soul.

That there is nevertheless a certain level represented by the righteousness of the Pharisees, which belongs to the old law, is understood from this: these commands clearly direct all our intention toward inward joys, lest, by seeking our reward outwardly, we become conformed to this world and lose the promise of a blessedness all the more substantial and secure because it is inward—the blessedness by which God chose us to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8).

The word *exterminant*, which through the fault of translators has become customary in ecclesiastical writings, means something quite different from what it is commonly understood to mean. Exiles are *exterminated*, since they are sent outside the boundaries. In place of this expression, therefore, we should always understand “demolish.” The hypocrite demolishes his face in order to feign righteousness and, while his heart may be rejoicing, wears mourning on his face.

(Augustine) In this chapter we must be especially attentive to the fact that vanity can exist not only in the splendor and display of bodily things, but also in the very filth and squalor of mourning—and that it is more dangerous when it deceives under the name of service to God.

Someone who shines through excessive bodily adornment and clothing, or through the splendor of other things, is easily convicted by those very things of being a follower of the display of this world; no one is deceived by his deceptive appearance of holiness. But when someone, in his profession of Christianity, attracts people’s eyes to himself by unusual squalor and filth, although he does so willingly rather than suffering it by necessity, his other deeds may indicate whether he does this out of contempt for excessive adornment or from some ambition.

For the Lord also commanded us to beware of wolves under sheep’s clothing; but, he says, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7). When the very things that they have obtained or hope to obtain through this disguise begin to be taken away from them or denied to them by various temptations, then it must become clear whether there is a wolf in sheep’s clothing or a sheep in its own.

A Christian should not therefore charm people’s affections with superfluous adornment merely because hypocrites often assume a modest and necessary appearance in order to deceive the unwary. Those sheep, too, should not lay aside their own skins if wolves sometimes cover themselves with them.

“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

(Jerome) He speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where on feast days people are accustomed to anoint their heads. He therefore commands that, when we fast, we show ourselves joyful and festive.

Many readers, recalling the Psalmist’s words, “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Psalm 140), conversely wish the oil to be good, the oil of which it is said elsewhere: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44). They think that this command means that, when practicing virtues, we should anoint the ruling part of our heart with spiritual oil.

(Augustine) We rightly understand the “head” here as that which is preeminent in the soul and by which the rest of the human being is plainly ruled and governed. He does this who does not seek joy outwardly, so as to rejoice carnally in human praise. The flesh, which ought to be subject, can in no way be the head of the whole human nature.

“No one has ever hated his own flesh,” as the Apostle says (Ephesians 5), when he commands love of one’s wife: “The man is the head of the woman, and Christ is the head of the man.” Let him therefore rejoice inwardly in his fasting, precisely because by fasting in this way he turns away from the will of the world and becomes subject to Christ, who according to this command desires him to have an anointed head.

Thus he will also wash his face—that is, cleanse his heart—with which he will see the Lord, not with a veil intervening because of weakness contracted from filth, but firm and stable because it is clean and single. “Wash yourselves,” he says, “be clean; remove your wickednesses from your souls and from before my eyes” (Isaiah 1). Our face must therefore be washed of those impurities by which God’s sight is offended.

[IV.] “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.”

(Maurus) Through the three forms of adversity—rust, moth, and thieves—by which he forbids the gathering of riches on earth, he literally condemns every kind of avarice. Some things are not affected by worms but are tarnished or consumed by rust, such as gold, silver, and other metals. Others are destroyed by worms or decay, such as clothing and wooden vessels, which perish through rot. Still others, although immune to worms and rust, are nevertheless often taken away by thieves, such as gems, pearls, and precious stones.

There is no possession in the world which, once accumulated, can remain perpetually unharmed, even if carefully guarded. Hence a certain wise man says: “Every corruptible work will fail at the end, and the one who works it will perish with it. But every excellent work will be justified, and the one who performs it will be honored in it” (Ecclesiasticus 14).

Allegorically, rust can signify pride and vainglory, which, wherever they are found, obscure all the beauty and strength of the virtues and dissipate the treasure of spiritual gifts. Hence the prophet says: “God scatters the bones of those who please themselves,” and “All arrogance is an abomination before God” (Psalm 52).

The moth, which secretly gnaws clothing, signifies envy, which tears apart good endeavor and never ceases to destroy the compact unity of the community. Thieves are demons and heretics, concerning whom the Truth says: “All who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John 10). They are always intent on plundering those who possess spiritual treasures and stripping those laden with the ornaments of virtue.

Therefore, if the heart is on earth—that is, if someone acts with that heart in order to gain an earthly advantage—how can the heart that rolls about on earth be clean? But if it is in heaven, it will be clean, because whatever is heavenly is clean. Something becomes filthy when it is mixed with an inferior nature, although it is not filthy in its own kind; even gold is tarnished if it is mixed with pure silver. So our mind becomes filthy through desire for earthly things, although the earth itself is clean in its own kind and order.

I would not understand “heaven” in this passage as bodily heaven, because every body must be regarded as earth. The person who lays up treasure for himself in that heaven of which it is said, “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 113)—that is, in the spiritual firmament—must despise the whole world. We should not establish or place our treasure and our heart in what passes away, but in what always remains: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Luke 21).

“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Jerome) This should be understood [*sciendum*; alternative: *sentiendum*, “thought”] not only of money but of all passions [alternative: *possessionibus*, “possessions”]. The god of the gluttonous is their belly. Wherever the heart is held, there also is your treasure. The treasures of the luxurious are banquets; those of the wanton, amusements; those of the lover, lust. Each person serves the thing by which he is conquered.

“The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is single, your whole body will be bright. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.”

By means of an example drawn from outward things, he instructs us to consider inward matters. Those suffering from eye trouble commonly see many lamps; a single and pure eye looks upon things that are single and pure. He transfers all this to the meaning. Just as the body is entirely in darkness if the eye is not single, so the soul, if it has lost its principal brightness, will have all its understanding dwelling in darkness.

(Augustine) By “body” he means the deeds that are plainly visible to everyone; by “eye,” the intention of the mind itself by which a person acts, and by whose merit those same deeds are discerned as works of light or works of darkness.

“If,” he says, “you strive to do the good you can with a pure and upright intention, the works you do are certainly works of light, even if they appear to have some imperfection before human beings. For all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose as saints” (Romans 8).

But if the intention that precedes an action is perverse, every work that follows is perverse, even if it appears upright. “If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?”

(Jerome) If the understanding, which is the light of the soul, is darkened by vice, with what darkness do you suppose the soul itself will be enveloped?

(Augustine) A single intention, wishing to please God alone, is light. For everything that is revealed is light. It is clear to us that we do what we do with a good disposition. But the deeds themselves that proceed from us into human society have an uncertain outcome, and therefore he called them darkness.

When I extend money to a needy person who asks for it, I do not know what he will do with it or what he may suffer because of it. It may happen that he either does something with it or suffers some evil that I did not wish to occur when I gave it, nor did I give it with that intention. My deed is therefore illuminated, whatever its outcome may be.

But if the intention of the heart by which you do whatever you do—an intention known to you—is defiled and blinded by desire for earthly and temporal things, how much more filthy and dark is the deed itself, whose outcome is uncertain? Even if what you do turns out well for someone else, it will benefit you nothing if you did not do it with a right and good intention, because what is imputed to you is how you acted, not how it turned out for him.

What follows must be referred to this same intention:

“No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate one and love the other, or he will endure one and despise the other.”

(Maurus) These words must be considered carefully. Often a person serves someone whom he does not love. Yet he is rightly said to love the one whose will he obeys with a ready disposition. Who the two masters are, he shows next when he says:

“You cannot serve God and Mammon.”

(Jerome) In the Syriac language, *Mammon* means riches. “You cannot,” he says, “serve God and Mammon.” Let the avaricious person hear this; let the person who is reckoned under the Christian name hear that he cannot serve both riches and Christ.

Yet he did not say, “The person who has riches,” but “The person who serves riches.” The servant of riches guards riches as a servant; but the person who has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes them as a master.

(Augustine) The one who serves Mammon serves the one who, because of his perversity, has been placed over these earthly things, and whom the Lord calls the ruler of this age. “Either,” then, “he will hate this one and love the other”—that is, the Lord—or “he will endure one and despise the other.”

Whoever serves Mammon endures a harsh and destructive master. Entangled in his own desire, he is subjected to the devil. He does not love him—for who is there who loves the devil?—but he nevertheless endures him. For example, if someone in a great household is joined to another person’s female slave because of his own desire, he endures a harsh servitude, even though he does not love the man whose slave he loves.

He says that he will “despise” the other, not “hate” him. No one’s conscience can endure hating the Lord; but he despises him—that is, he does not fear him—when he does not keep his commandments. Those who put his threats behind their desires commonly act in this way, flattering themselves in their impurity because of his goodness.

Solomon says to such people: “My son, do not add sin upon sin, and say, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Ecclesiasticus 5). Whoever wishes to love the Lord and take care not to offend him should not suppose that he can serve two masters; rather, he should set his heart’s intention straight, free of all duplicity. In this way he will think of the Lord according to goodness and seek him in simplicity of heart.

“Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, or about your body, what you shall wear.”

(Jerome) In some manuscripts, “or what you shall drink” has been added. The words “Therefore I say” refer back to what came before: “Therefore I forbid anxiety about temporal things, lest you be convicted of laying up treasures for yourselves together with the rich of this world.”

We are therefore completely freed from concern for what nature supplies to everyone, to animals, and to beasts, and what is common to human beings as well. But we are commanded not to be anxious about what we shall eat, because “in the sweat of our face” we prepare our bread for ourselves. Labor must be undertaken; anxiety must be removed.

The words “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, or about your body, what you shall wear” should be understood of bodily food and clothing. As for spiritual foods and clothing, we must always be anxious about them.

“Is not the life more than food, and the body more than clothing?”

(Jerome) What he says means this: the one who has provided greater things will certainly provide lesser things.

(Augustine) He reminds us that we must remember that God has given us much more by making and composing us of soul and body than food and clothing are. Understand, therefore, that the one who gave the soul will much more easily give food. Likewise, the one who gave the body will much more easily give clothing.

At this point it is usually asked whether this food belongs to the soul, since the soul is incorporeal while this food is bodily. We should understand that “soul” here refers to this present life, whose support is this bodily food. In this sense it is also said: “Whoever loves his life will lose it” (John 12). Unless we understood this of the present life—which must be lost for the kingdom of God, as the martyrs clearly demonstrated—this command would contradict the statement: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16).

“Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.”

(Jerome) There are some who, wishing to exceed the boundaries set by the Fathers and fly into the heights, plunge into the depths. They say that the birds of heaven are angels and the other powers engaged in God’s service, which are fed by God’s providence without concern for themselves.

If this is understood as they wish, how does the statement addressed to human beings follow: “Are you not worth more than they?” It should therefore be understood simply. If birds, which exist today and will not exist tomorrow, whose souls are mortal, and which, once they cease to exist, will never exist again, are fed by God’s providence without anxiety or hardship, how much more will human beings be fed, to whom eternity is promised?

“Are you not worth more than they?”

(Augustine) This means that you are more precious, because a rational animal such as a human being is more exaltedly ordered in the nature of things than irrational creatures such as birds.

“Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious about clothing?”

That is: by whose power and dominion was it brought about that your body should reach this stature? By his providence it can also be clothed. It was not through your own care that your body came to this stature; this can be understood from the fact that, even if you strive and wish to add one cubit to this stature, you cannot.

Leave, then, the care of clothing the body also to the one whose care seems to have brought it about that you possess a body of such stature. A lesson concerning clothing also had to be given, just as one had been given concerning food. Therefore he continues:

“Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They do not labor, nor do they spin.”

But these examples should not be examined as allegories, so that we ask what the birds of heaven or the lilies of the field signify. They have been set forth to persuade us of greater things through lesser ones.

I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. (Jerome.) And indeed, what silk, what royal purple, what workmanship of weavers can be compared with flowers? What is so red as the rose? What is so white as the lily? But that the violet’s purple is surpassed by no purple dye is a judgment more of the eyes than of words.

But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith? In Scripture, “tomorrow” signifies future time, as Jacob says: “And tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Gen. XXX). And in the apparition of Samuel, the pythoness says to Saul: “Tomorrow you will be with me” (I Kings XXVIII). The meaning, then, is this: If the Creator of all things adorns with such beautiful appearance the plants that spring from the earth, which belong only to the use of the present time and soon, when they fall, will be consumed by fire, how much more will the providence of your Creator provide what is necessary for you, who were created in the image of God and belong to an eternal inheritance in heaven, and will not allow you to perish from nakedness?

Do not be anxious, saying, “What shall we eat?” or “What shall we drink?” or “With what shall we be clothed?” (Bede.) It should be noted that he does not say, “Do not seek, or be anxious, about food, drink, or clothing,” but more explicitly: “What you should eat, or what you should drink, or what you should wear.” Here he seems to me to rebuke those who, rejecting ordinary food or clothing, seek for themselves more luxurious or more austere nourishment or garments than those with whom they live.

For all these things the Gentiles seek. (Maurus.) That is, those who have no concern for the future but are intent only on present things, like brute animals, always desire earthly things. Of them the Prophet says: “They have been compared with foolish beasts and have become like them” (Ps. XLVIII).

For your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek therefore first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. (Augustine.) Here he most clearly shows that these things are not to be desired as though they were our goods, so that for their sake we ought to do good, if we do anything good; nevertheless, they are necessary. The difference between the good that ought to be desired and the necessity that ought to be supplied he declared in this saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” The kingdom, therefore, and the righteousness of God are our good; this is what must be desired, and in it the end must be established, for whose sake we do everything we do.

But because in this life we are engaged in service so that we may reach that kingdom, this life cannot be conducted without these necessities. “These things,” he says, “will be supplied to you; but seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.” When he says “first,” he signifies that the other is to be sought afterward—not in time, but in dignity: the one as our good, the other as our necessity; and our necessity exists for the sake of that good.

For example, we ought not to preach the Gospel in order that we may eat, but to eat in order that we may preach the Gospel. For if we preach in order that we may eat, we regard the Gospel as less valuable than food; then eating will be the good, while preaching the Gospel will be the necessity. Therefore, whatever is sought for the sake of something else is without doubt inferior to that for whose sake it is sought. Thus the first thing is that for which you seek the other, not the other for which you seek something else.

“Seek first his kingdom and the righteousness of God”—that is, putting other things after it, so that we seek the rest for its sake. We should not be troubled lest those things be lacking which are necessary for this life because of the kingdom of God. For he said above: “Your Father knows that you need all these things.” And therefore, when he had said, “Seek first the kingdom and the righteousness of God,” he did not say, “Then seek these things also,” although they are necessary; rather he said: “All these things will be supplied to you”—that is, they will follow—if you seek the former, without any hindrance on your part.

Hence, by saying not “they will be given” but “they will be added,” he plainly indicates that one thing is given as primary and another is supplied in addition. For our concern ought to be with eternity, while temporality belongs to our use. The one is given, and the other is indeed added abundantly.

Do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. (Jerome.) He granted that we ought to be concerned about present things, while he forbade us to think about future ones. Hence the Apostle also says: “Working with our own hands night and day, lest we burden any of you” (I Thess. II). As we have shown shortly before, “tomorrow” in Scripture signifies future time. (Maurus.) It is therefore unnecessary for us to be anxious about the future, which divine ordering provides for. Cold and heat, summer and winter, do not cease, and the earth produces its annual fruits: “When you open your hand, every living creature will be filled with blessing” (Ps. CXLIV). But let us gratefully receive the present benefit that has been bestowed and not fear future want; rather, let us place all our anxiety in devotion to the Creator, since he himself cares for us.

Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. (Jerome.) Here he did not use “trouble” in opposition to virtue, but for labor, affliction, and the anxieties of the world. The thought of the present time is therefore sufficient for us; let us leave the care of the future, which is uncertain. (Augustine.) I think it is called “trouble” for this reason: it is punitive for us. It belongs to that frailty and mortality which we merited by sinning. Do not add anything more burdensome to this punishment of temporal necessity, so that you not only suffer the lack of these things but also serve God in order to satisfy that lack.

Yet we must be especially careful lest, when we see a servant of God making provision that these necessities not be lacking either for himself or for those entrusted to his care, we judge him to be acting against God’s command and to be anxious about tomorrow. Even the Lord himself, although angels ministered to him, nevertheless, for the sake of example, so that no one afterward might be scandalized when he observed one of his servants providing these necessities, was willing to have a money box from which he could supply whatever was needed for necessary uses. Judas, who betrayed him, was the keeper and thief of this money box, as it is written (John XII). Hence the text continues.

## CHAPTER VII. On Not Rashly Judging One’s Neighbor; He Urges Entry through the Narrow Gate and Teaches that False Prophets Must Be Avoided, etc.

**[I.]** Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.

In this passage, I think nothing else is commanded us except that we interpret for the better those actions whose motive is uncertain. For what is written—“You will know them by their fruits”—was said of manifest acts that cannot be done with a good motive, such as sexual immorality, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and anything of that kind, about which we are permitted to judge.

Regarding kinds of food, since all human foods can be taken indifferently with a good motive and a simple heart, without the fault of desire, the Apostle forbids those who ate meat and drank wine to be judged by those who abstained from such foods: “Let the one who eats,” he says, “not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. XIV).

To this also belongs what he says elsewhere: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of the heart” (I Cor. V).

There are two circumstances in which we must beware of rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what motive something was done, or when it is uncertain what sort of person someone who now appears good or bad will eventually become. If, for example, someone complained of stomach trouble and did not wish to fast, and, not believing him, you attributed this to gluttony, you would judge rashly. Likewise, if you recognized manifest gluttony and drunkenness and rebuked someone as though these could never be corrected or changed, you would likewise judge rashly.

Let us therefore not rebuke what we do not know the motive for, nor rebuke manifest faults in such a way that we despair of healing; and thus we shall avoid the judgment of which it is now said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”

For if we judge others with rash judgment, will God therefore judge us rashly? Or if we have measured with an unjust measure, is there an unjust measure with the Lord by which it will be measured back to us? I think that the name “measure” signifies judgment itself. God in no way judges rashly or repays anyone with an unjust measure; but this was said because the rashness with which you punish another must itself punish you. Judgment often does no harm to the person rashly judged, but the rashness itself must harm the person who judges rashly.

The same rule applies to the saying: “Everyone who strikes with the sword will die by the sword”—that is, not by the sword of iron but by the sword of sin, because a person dies through the very sin that he has committed against another.

Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye but do not see the beam in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, “Let me remove the speck from your eye,” while behold, there is a beam in your eye?

Many people, overtaken by pride, hatred, avarice, or any other crime, judge these things trivial or nonexistent, yet rebuke most sharply those whom they see suddenly disturbed by anger, as though a speck had invaded and altered the eye of their mind from its customary state of purity. Forgetful of the Lord’s command, “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned,” they prefer to blame and condemn rather than amend and correct.

You act thus toward your brother if, for example, you rebuke in hatred what he did in anger. As great as the difference between a speck and a beam is the difference between anger and hatred. Hatred is anger grown old, as though through age it had become so great that it deserved to be called a beam.

It may happen that if you are angry with someone, you may wish him to be corrected; but if you hate someone, you cannot wish to correct him. For this reason it is said to be impossible for someone to remove the speck from his brother’s eye when he carries a beam in his own.

Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see how to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.

That is, first drive hatred from yourself, and afterward you will be able to correct the person whom you love. There is truly a very dangerous and troublesome class of hypocrites, that is, pretenders: while they receive accusations of every vice with hatred and jealousy, they nevertheless wish to appear to be advisers.

(Hilary.) It often happens that we assume authority to rebuke others without any example of our own correction, and boast of cleansing another’s blindness while we ourselves stand in the darkness of corrupted light. It is difficult for anyone to provide what he himself lacks, and it is better to teach by example than by words.

Care must therefore be taken regarding one’s own blindness, because the nature of things makes it impossible for anyone to become a suitable teacher for removing the speck from his brother’s eye before he has cast from the light of his own mind the beam of unbelief that burdens it.

(Augustine.) Therefore we must watch with pious caution. When necessity compels us to rebuke or reprimand someone, let us first consider whether the fault is one we have never had, or one from which we have already been free. If we have never had it, let us remember that we are human and could have had it. But if we have had it and no longer have it, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that mercy, not hatred, precedes the rebuke or reprimand. Whether this benefits the correction of the person for whom we do it, or instead contributes to his perversion—for the outcome is uncertain—let us nevertheless remain secure in the sincerity of our own eye.

But if, on examining ourselves, we find that we are in the same fault as the person whom we were preparing to rebuke, let us neither rebuke nor reprimand him, but only groan with him, and invite him not to obey us but to strive alongside us. Rebukes should therefore be used rarely and only under great necessity, and even then we should insist not on our own interests but that God be served.

This is the end: that we do nothing with a divided heart, removing from our own eye the beam of envy, malice, or pretence, so that we may see to remove the speck from our brother’s eye.

Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they perhaps trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart.

What is holy is that which it is impious to violate and corrupt. The attempt and intention to commit such a crime is held guilty, although that holy thing remains by nature inviolable and incorruptible.

Pearls, however, are to be understood as whatever spiritual mysteries there are. Since they lie hidden, they are as though drawn up from the depths; and they are found beneath the coverings of allegories, like pearls in opened shells.

It is therefore possible to understand one and the same thing as both “holy” and a “pearl”: holy because it ought not to be corrupted, and a pearl because it ought not to be despised. Everyone tries to corrupt what he does not want to remain whole, but he despises what he considers worthless and thinks beneath him. Hence whatever is despised is said to be trampled.

Accordingly, because dogs leap upon things to tear them apart, and do not allow what they tear to remain whole, while swine, although they do not attack with their bite as dogs do, nevertheless pollute things everywhere by trampling them, we may appropriately understand dogs as representing those who assault the truth and swine as representing those who despise it.

But when he says, “Turning, they will tear you apart,” he does not say that they will tear the pearls themselves apart. For they do tear the pearls apart even when they turn in order to hear something further; yet they tear apart the person from whom they have already trampled the pearls sent to them. It is not easy to find anything that can be pleasing to someone who has trampled pearls—that is, who has despised discoveries of God made with great labor.

As for those who teach such people, I do not see how they can avoid being torn apart through indignation and anger. Both animals are unclean, the dog and the swine. We must therefore be careful lest something be disclosed to one who cannot grasp it. Such a person more readily seeks what is closed than what is open, which he either attacks or neglects.

(Jerome.) It should also be noted that some wish dogs to be understood as heretics, or as those who, after the faith of Christ, return to the vomit of their sins; and swine as those who have not yet believed the Gospel and wallow in the mud of unbelief and vices. It is therefore not fitting to entrust the evangelical pearl quickly to such people, lest they trample it and, turning, begin to tear us apart.

(Augustine.) But since the command had been given that what is holy should not be given to dogs and that pearls should not be thrown before swine, a hearer conscious of his ignorance and weakness might hear himself forbidden to give these things, knowing that he himself had not yet received them, and object: “What holy thing do you forbid me to give to dogs, and what pearls do you forbid me to throw before swine, when I do not yet see that I possess them?” Most appropriately he added:

**[II.]** Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

Asking refers to obtaining health and firmness of spirit, so that we may be able to fulfill what is commanded. Seeking refers to finding the truth. Since the blessed life is completed through action and knowledge, action requires the ability of strength, while contemplation requires the disclosure of realities.

The first of these, therefore, must be asked for; the second must be sought, so that the former may be given and the latter found. But knowledge in this life belongs first to the way rather than to possession itself. When someone has found the true way, he will arrive at possession itself; yet that possession will be opened to the one who knocks.

To make these three things—that is, asking, seeking, and knocking—clear, let us set them out by an example. We see someone unable to walk because his feet are weak. First, then, he must be healed and strengthened for walking; to this belongs the command, “Ask.” But what good is it that he can now walk, or even run, if he has wandered along a wrong path? The second requirement is that he find the way that leads him where he wishes to arrive; to this belongs, “Seek.”

When he has taken and completed that way, what benefit will it be if he finds the very place where he wishes to live closed? It will have profited him nothing that he was able to walk, proceeded, and arrived, unless the place is opened. To this belongs the command, “Knock.”

He who promises gives great hope and does not deceive by promising. For he says:

“For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.”

Therefore perseverance is necessary, so that we may receive what we ask for, find what we seek, and have opened to us what we knock upon. For if what is asked for is given, the one who seeks finds, and the one who knocks has the door opened, it is clear that to the person who is not given anything, who does not find, and to whom nothing is opened, the reason is that he did not ask, seek, or knock properly.

Or what person is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, would give him a stone? Bread is understood as love, because of its greater desirability and necessity, so that without it all other things are nothing, just as without bread a table is poor. The hardness of heart is contrary to it, and this he compared to a stone.

Or if he asks for a fish, would he give him a serpent? The fish is faith in invisible things, either because of the water of baptism or because it is caught from invisible places. Since faith is not broken even when battered by the waves of this world, it is rightly compared to a fish. In opposition to it he set the serpent, because of the poisons of deceit, which it first sowed in the human race by giving evil advice.

(Maurus.) In the Gospel according to Luke, the comparison of an egg and a scorpion follows these two. The egg signifies hope: an egg is not yet a fully formed offspring, but by being warmed it is hoped that it will be perfected. In opposition to it he set the scorpion, whose venomous sting must be feared from behind. So the opposite of hope is to look backward, whereas hope attends to what lies ahead.

If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?

(Augustine.) How do the evil give good things? He called “evil” those who still love this world and are sinners. The things they give should be called good according to their judgment, because they regard them as good. Yet in the nature of things they are not good; they are temporal and belong to this weak life. Whoever among the evil gives them does not give from his own possession: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. XXIII), he who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them (Ps. CXLV).

How much, then, ought we to hope that the Lord will give good things to us who ask him, and that we cannot be deceived into receiving one thing instead of another when we ask him, since even we, although we are evil, know how to give what is asked of us? For we do not deceive our children, and whatever good things we give, we give not from our own but from his.

In another sense, the apostles, who by the excellence of their election had surpassed the human race in many ways, are called evil in view of the supreme Good. For nothing is stable in itself, nothing immutable, nothing good except the Godhead alone. All creatures, however, if they attain the blessedness of eternity or immutability, attain it not through their own nature but through participation in and grace from their Creator.

But what is said in Luke (chap. III)—“How much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?”—for which Matthew here has written, “He will give good things to those who ask him,” shows that the Holy Spirit is the fullness of God’s good gifts, and that those things supplied by God do not subsist apart from him. For all the benefits received through the grace of God’s gifts flow from this fountain.

But since nature has taught everyone to love one who loves him, while only the teaching of Christ has perfected people by instructing them to compel one who does not love them to love them through benefits—when he commanded us first to do to others what we would wish to be done to us—he immediately strengthened the same meaning by expanding it, saying:

Therefore, whatever you wish people to do to you, you also do to them. For this is the law and the prophets.

This command appears to concern love of neighbor and not also love of God, since elsewhere he says that there are two commands on which the whole law and the prophets depend. For if he had said, “Whatever you wish to be done to you, do this,” that one statement would have included both commands. It would quickly be said that everyone wishes to be loved both by God and by human beings, whereas the command would then be that he himself love God and human beings.

But since the saying is expressed more specifically in terms of human beings—“Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them”—it appears to mean nothing other than: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII).

Nevertheless, we must not carelessly overlook what he added: “For this is the law and the prophets.” Elsewhere he says that not merely “the law and the prophets” depend on these two commands, but adds “the whole law and the prophets,” meaning the whole of prophecy. Since he did not add that here, he preserved a place for the other command, which concerns love of God. Whatever was written in the prophets and the law for the salvation of human beings depends on these two commands.

Enter through the narrow gate, because the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it. How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it!

Through the narrow gate one enters the hall of salvation, because labor and fasting are necessary in order to overcome the allurements of the deceiving world. He does not call the gate narrow and the way constricted because Christ’s yoke is harsh and his burden heavy, but because few wish to bring their labors to completion, believing too little the one who cries out: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; take my yoke upon you,” and so forth (Matt. XI).

(Jerome.) The way of the world is broad toward the pleasures that people desire; the narrow way is opened through labor and fasting. The Apostle entered it and urges Timothy to enter it as well.

At the same time, consider how precisely he spoke about both ways. Many walk along the broad way; few find the narrow one. We do not seek the broad way, nor is discovery necessary: it offers itself voluntarily and is the way of those who wander. But not everyone finds the narrow way, and those who find it do not immediately enter upon it. Many, after finding the way of truth, are captivated by the pleasures of the world and turn back from the middle of the journey.

**[III.]** Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.

This can indeed be understood of all who promise one thing in appearance and speech but demonstrate another in their deeds. But it should be understood especially of heretics, who seem to surround themselves with the garment of piety—continence, chastity, and fasting—while inwardly possessing a poisoned mind and deceiving even the hearts of simpler brethren. They are compared with ravenous wolves because of the intention of their souls and the snares by which they drag the innocent to ruin.

(Origen.) It should also be noted that what he shortly before called the spacious and broad way he now reveals more openly through the false prophets, by whom many have gone into abominable destruction. For at first many appeared in Judea, and now in their unbelief they have filled the whole world. Those earlier false prophets persecuted the truest prophets of the Lord even to death, such as Jeremiah and Micah and many others.

But these false prophets and false Christians of the present day persecute true Christians without mercy and sometimes, when opportunity is given, even oppress them with swords; without interruption, however, they do so through their evil customs and examples.

Therefore, anticipating all this, the Lord exhorted them, saying: “Beware of false prophets.” Pay close attention; watch more carefully, so that you are not led astray, surrounded, or deceived.

“Beware,” that is, understand that they are not sheep but wolves in sheep’s clothing; they are not religious but irreligious under the appearance of religion; they are not Christians but empty of truth and persecutors of Christians.

The blessed Apostle also designated them when speaking to the Ephesians: “I know that after my departure ravenous wolves will enter among you” (Acts XX).

All unbelieving heretics are called grievous wolves, because they grievously oppress and persecute the holy Church or habitually harass it; without mercy they do not cease to seize and accumulate. Sometimes they invade the money of others, sometimes the very owners of the money. Much more eagerly they strive to seize souls and lead them miserably with themselves into destruction.

They are said to have the clothing of sheep because they bear the name of Christianity, or because they make themselves resemble ministers of righteousness, pretending to have the appearance of religion. Through the Christian name they therefore attempt to lead many astray, bringing scandal to many through sweet words.

These are the people of whom the Apostle again says: “By their sweet and flattering speech they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. XVI). But how they are to be recognized, he shows by what follows.

You will know them by their fruits. That is, do not attend to their appearance but to their deeds. Do not consider their clothing but inspect the form of their deceit. They preach the apostles, but announce things contrary to the apostles; they praise the martyrs, but prove to be persecutors of the martyrs.

The holy apostles and martyrs did not persecute but endured persecution; they did not curse but endured curses; they did not blaspheme the Lord but were killed by blasphemers.

(Augustine.) These most wicked people, however, have taken care to fulfill every irreligious act. They persecute the saints, oppress the faithful, and blaspheme the Lord, if not in words, then by their conduct.

Nevertheless, some seem to think that we should inquire more deeply which fruits the Lord wished us to attend to, by which we can recognize the tree. Many count among fruits certain things that belong to the clothing of all the sheep, and in this way are deceived by wolves, such as fasting, prayers, or almsgiving. If all these things could not also be done by hypocrites, he would not have said above: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.” That saying itself sets out the three things: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting.

But such people can be recognized by nothing more effectively than by their instability or impatience in adversity. When certain trials begin to take away from them or deny them the very things they obtained or hope to obtain through this disguise, then it must become apparent whether there is a wolf in sheep’s skin or a sheep in its own.

A Christian’s appearance should not therefore flatter the eyes of human beings through excessive adornment, because even pretenders often adopt a modest and necessary manner of dress in order to deceive the unwary. Nor should those sheep remove their own skins if wolves sometimes conceal themselves beneath them.

Can grapes be gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles?

(Origen.) By this comparison the Lord clearly declared that no prudent person goes to thorns seeking the sweetness of grapes from them, or walks among thistles and gathers the pleasantness of figs from them.

Thus no wise or prudent person will be able to find the sweetness, fragrance, or pleasantness of holiness and truth among empty heretics, irreligious people, or unbelievers. Rather, he will find among them what is worst and most malicious.

Just as thorns and thistles draw in, hold, and tear everything they can seize, so all unbelieving heretics—and, because of their evil lives, even those who seem to hold the right faith—through human power and corruptible authority, through wicked customs and depraved examples, tear apart, draw in, and plunder everything they can grasp.

Who would put out a hand toward thorns and thistles or approach them without being torn or cut, or find that same hand unbloodied? Who, then, extending a hand to heretics or bowing his head before them, will be found uncut by the Holy Spirit or unbloodied by a wound to the soul? Who can accommodate himself to the deeds of the wicked without being pierced by the thorn of sin through their pollutions?

The Jews of ancient times were such people. When they ought to have produced grapes, they produced thorns; and those who ought to have shown sweetness turned themselves into bitterness.

Alternatively, I think that thorns and thistles can signify the cares of the world and the prickings of vices. Of these it was said to the sinful human being: “Your land will produce thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). Figs and grapes, however, signify the sweetness of a new way of life, for which the Lord hungers in us, and the fervor of love that gladdens the human heart.

Of these things it flashes forth in the *Song of Songs*: “The voice of the turtledove resounded far and wide in the land. The fig tree produced its green figs, and the blossoming vines gave their fragrance” (Song II).

But grapes are not gathered from thorns or figs from thistles, because a mind still weighed down by the custom of the old person can pretend, but cannot bear the fruit of the new person.

If anyone should object and say that Moses also harvested a grape from a thorn when he received useful advice from his gentile kinsman, and that those gathered fruit from thistles to whom it was said concerning the Pharisees, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do,” let him know that just as a fruitful vine-shoot sometimes lies entwined in a hedge, and the thorn, bearing fruit not its own, preserves it for human use, so the words or deeds of evil people, whenever they benefit the good, do not accomplish this by their own agency; rather, it happens through them by the providence of the heavenly plan.

Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits.

(Origen.) Since God the teacher establishes the tree from which the fruit of which he was speaking arises—not nature, but either a good or an evil will—and since fruits are works, neither can the fruits of an evil will be good nor the fruits of a good will evil, this is what he says: “A bad tree does not produce good fruits, and a good tree does not produce bad fruits.”

It is as though he were saying: An evil will does not produce good works, nor does a good will produce evil works. For if the origins of those trees—that is, of those wills—are sought, what do we encounter except the natures that the good God created?

Accordingly, evils arose from good things—not evil works from good wills, but evil wills from good natures—so that the root of evil in a person is nothing other than the lack of good.

A good tree is therefore a good will, because through it a person is converted to the highest and immutable good and is filled with goodness in order to produce good fruit.

Thus God is the author of all good things, both good nature and good will. For unless God works in a person, that person does not act; the will is prepared by the Lord in a human being as good, so that, with God granting it, the person may do what he could not do from himself through the will of free choice.

(Jerome.) Let us ask the heretics, who say that there are two mutually contrary natures: if, according to their understanding, a good tree can never produce bad fruits, how did Moses, a good tree, sin at the waters of contradiction (Deut. XXXII)? How did David, after killing Uriah, lie with Bathsheba (II Sam. XI)? How did Peter deny the Lord during his Passion, saying, “I do not know the man” (Matt. XXVI)?

Or by what reasoning did Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, a bad tree who certainly did not believe in the God of Israel, give Moses good advice? How did Achior say something useful to Holofernes (Judith V)? And how could the Comic Poet have said—and the Apostle approved the saying as well spoken—“Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV)?

When they find nothing to answer, we shall add Judas, once a good tree, who produced bad fruits after he betrayed the Savior (Matt. XXV); and Paul, a bad tree at the time when he persecuted the Church of Christ, who afterward produced good fruits when he was transformed from a persecutor into a chosen vessel (Acts IX).

A good tree therefore does not produce bad fruits so long as it perseveres in the pursuit of goodness; and a bad tree remains in the fruits of sin so long as it is not converted to repentance. No one, while remaining in what he was, begins to be what he had not yet begun to be.

Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

**(MAURUS.)** Because every wicked person, uprooted from the land of the living by the forceful sentence of judgment, is thrown into the fire of Gehenna, since he is found not to have produced the fruit of good works here.

**(Origen.)** “Every,” he says, “tree that does not produce fruit”—and not merely fruit, but good fruit. Many trees indeed bear fruit, but bad and useless fruit; so also many people produce the fruit of irreligion, unbelief, and perversity. For this reason the Lord clearly demonstrated that every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. “Every tree,” that is, every human being: no one is spared, no one is accorded special honor; rather, every fruitless tree that bears no fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire—not so that it may burn and perish like wood, but that it may be thrown into that fire of which the Lord says: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV).

Therefore, by their fruits you will know them.

**(Augustine.)** What, then, are the fruits by which, once they have been discovered, we may recognize the bad tree? The Apostle says (Galatians V): “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, impurities, debaucheries, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, contentions, rivalries, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.” And who are those by whom we recognize the good tree? The same Apostle says next: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control,” and so forth.

**(MAURUS.)** Those who truly possess these qualities and serve Christ in them attain eternal life. But because many lurk falsely under the appearance of religion, we must therefore beware lest we be deceived by the very name of Christ—by heretics, by anyone who misunderstands, or by lovers of this present world. For this reason he continues and warns:

Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven—he will enter the kingdom of heaven.

**(Hilary.)** The kingdom of heaven is not obtained by verbal duties alone; nor will the one who says, “Lord, Lord,” be his fellow heir. What merit is there in saying to the Lord, “Lord”? Will he not be Lord unless we call him so? And what holiness of duty is there in pronouncing the name, when the way into the heavenly kingdom will be found in obedience to God’s will rather than in its utterance?

**(Jerome.)** Therefore, just as above he had said that those who possess the garment of a good life would not be received because of the doctrine of wickedness, so now, conversely, he asserts that faith must not be granted even to those who possess soundness of faith but live shamefully and destroy the integrity of their teaching by evil works. Both things are necessary for God’s servants: that work be confirmed by speech, and speech by works. This saying may seem contrary to the statement: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians XII). But it is customary in Scripture to take words as referring to deeds, as is immediately demonstrated in what follows, when those who boast of knowledge of the Lord without works are rejected and hear from the Savior: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke XIII). The Apostle speaks in the same sense (Titus I): “They profess that they know God in words, but they deny him by their deeds.”

**(Augustine.)** Properly and truly, those are said to speak whose utterance does not differ from their will and mind. In this sense the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” And this is especially relevant, lest we be deceived as we strive toward the contemplation of truth—not merely by those who bear the name of Christ but do not perform his works, but also by certain deeds and miracles. The Lord performed such things on account of unbelievers, yet he warned us not to be deceived by them, imagining that invisible wisdom is present wherever we have seen a visible miracle. He therefore adds and says:

Many will say to me on that day, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?”

**(Jerome.)** To prophesy, perform mighty works, and cast out demons is sometimes not the merit of the one who acts; rather, the invocation of Christ’s name accomplishes it. It is granted either for the condemnation of those who invoke it or for the benefit of those who see and hear, so that although people may despise those who perform signs, they may nevertheless honor the Lord, at whose invocation they perform such great miracles. Saul (1 Kings X), Balaam (Numbers XXIV), and Caiaphas (John XVIII) also prophesied without knowing what they were saying. Pharaoh (Genesis XLI) and Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel III, IV) learned future things through dreams. In the Acts of the Apostles, the sons of Sceva appeared to cast out demons (Acts XIX); and Judas the Apostle is reported to have performed many signs among the other apostles, even though he possessed the mind of a betrayer.

**(Augustine.)** How pure and simple an eye is needed, then, to discover the way of wisdom, when so many deceptions and errors of wicked and perverse people obstruct it—people whom one must all evade in order to arrive at the most certain peace and immovable stability of wisdom! We must fear greatly lest, through eagerness to dispute and contend, someone fail to see what only a few can see, unless he also obstructs himself. The text continues:

And then I will declare to them, “I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.”

**(Jerome.)** He significantly said, “I will declare,” because for a long time he had refrained from saying, “I do not know you.” The Lord does not know those who perish. Observe, however, why he added, “I never knew you.” If, as some maintain, all human beings have always existed among rational creatures, how can he say, “I never knew you,” when the Psalm says, “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain” (Psalm XCIII), and elsewhere it is written, “He knows the deceiver and the one who is deceived” (Job XII)? The reason is that God’s “knowing” is sometimes called knowing and sometimes approving: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the one whom he ignores will be ignored” (Psalm I). He therefore knows the reprobate whom he judges by knowing them; for he would not judge those whom he did not know at all. Yet in a certain manner he says, “I do not know you”—that is, “I do not approve you,” because he does not approve in them the mark of his faith and love. “The feasting of the legal festivals,” he says, “does not benefit the one whom devotion of faith does not commend; knowledge of the Scriptures does not make known to God the one whom the iniquity of his works displays as unworthy before his eyes.”

**(Jerome.)** Hence it follows: “Depart from me, you who work iniquity.” He did not say, “You who worked iniquity,” lest he seem to remove the possibility of repentance, but, “You who work”—that is, “up to the present hour.” When the time of judgment arrives, although you will no longer have the power to sin, you will still possess the inclination.

**(Augustine.)** We must therefore pay very close attention to how terrifyingly the conclusion of this entire sermon is introduced.

## IV

Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. Since he did not say merely, “The one who hears my words,” but added, “these words of mine,” he sufficiently indicated, as I believe, that these words which he spoke on the mountain instruct the life of those who wish to live according to them so completely that they are rightly compared to one who builds upon rock. He said this so that it might be evident that this sermon is complete with respect to all the commandments by which the Christian life is shaped.

For above, the Lord discussed many things concerning those who are openly good or bad, and many things concerning those who are truly or deceptively good. Through these three groups, I think, the whole human race is included. He concludes his entire sermon with a parable at once terrifying and loving, by which he likens some hearers of the word to the devil and others to Christ. The devil certainly does not cease building his house among human beings throughout the whole course of this age.

The comparison is fitting. For the one who hears Christ’s words and does them will be compared with Christ. Just as Christ constructs, teaches, and governs one catholic Church for himself from people of various kinds, intending at some time to dedicate it to eternal life, so also the useful hearer, advancing heavenward according to his own measure through various exercises of virtue, builds for himself a dwelling of perpetual habitation. In the present he labors to square and polish its stones and join them with the cement of charity; in the future he rejoices in its dedication with Christ.

And that person is truly wise who places his building upon what will remain, not upon what will quickly fall, and upon rock, not upon earth. No one makes firm what he hears or understands except by doing it. And if Christ is the rock, as many testimonies of Scripture proclaim, the one who builds upon Christ is the one who does what he hears from him.

And the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house; but it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock.

**(Augustine.)** This person therefore fears neither obscure superstitions—for what else is meant by “rain” when it is used as a sign of something evil?—nor human rumors, which I think are compared with winds, nor the stream of this life, flowing over the earth like carnal desires. The person who has founded his house upon rock fears none of these three: the one who is drawn in by prosperity is broken by adversity, but the one who not only hears the Lord’s commandments but also does them fears nothing of this kind.

The one who hears and does not act is dangerously exposed to all these things. He has no stable foundation; by hearing and not acting, he builds a ruin.

**(Jerome.)** This rain, which strives to overthrow the house, may also be understood as the devil; the rivers as all the Antichrists who think against Christ; and the winds as spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. Yet the house did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock.

Upon this rock the Lord founded his Church. From this rock the Apostle Peter received his name. Upon such a rock no traces of the serpent are found. The Prophet also speaks confidently of it: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm XXXIX); and elsewhere: “A rock is a refuge for rabbits or hedgehogs” (Psalm CIII). A timid animal withdraws into the cavern of a rock, while the rough skin, entirely armed with darts, protects itself by such a defense. Hence Moses too was told, at the time when he had fled from Egypt and was the Lord’s little hare: “Stand in the cleft of the rock, and you will see my back” (Exodus XXXIII).

And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand.

The foundation laid by the Apostle Paul, the architect, is one: our Lord Jesus Christ. Upon this stable and firm foundation, itself established by a solid mass, the Church of Christ is built. But upon sand, which is fluid and cannot be built up or brought together into a single bond, every saying of the heretics is constructed in such a way that it may collapse.

And the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house; and it fell.

**(Augustine.)** What did he wish to be understood by the rain except the many kinds of the devil’s temptations; by the rivers, open and manifest persecutions; and by the winds, evil spirits? For the conscience of anyone who does not remain fixed in hope upon the Lord is unable to stand either in temptations, or in persecutions, or before evil spirits.

And the conscience of each person is shaken by evil spirits all the more fiercely the more the carnal mind is separated from higher things in those matters that belong to the world, and the more tightly it is bound to lower things.

**(Gregory.)** Therefore the one who hears Christ’s words and does not do them—whether initiated into Christ’s mysteries or entirely estranged from Christ—is like a foolish man, because he builds himself badly. Of him it is said: “An enemy has done this” (Matthew XIII). All his works are unstable and prepared for collapse.

It is clear that whenever any temptation breaks in, both the genuinely wicked and the deceptively good immediately become worse, until at last they slip into everlasting punishment.

In a moral sense, it must also be said that everyone is tempted by his own desire, being drawn away and enticed. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, gives birth to death (James I). The force of the final river may also be understood as the crisis of the last judgment, when both houses have been completed, and everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, while the one who humbles himself will be exalted.

Then the wicked will go—not only human beings but also the angels who belonged to the devil—into eternal punishment, while the righteous will go into eternal life (Matthew XXIII; Luke XVIII; Matthew XXV).

And its fall was great.

**(Augustine.)** The great fall is surely to be understood as that concerning which the Lord will say to those who hear and do not act: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels. I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink,” and so forth (Matthew XXV). For according to the Apostle’s sentence: “It is not the hearers of the law who will be righteous before the Lord on that day, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans II).

And when Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astonished at his teaching. For he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees.

**(MAURUS.)** This completion refers to the perfection of his words and the integrity of his teaching, by which he instructed the disciples and the crowds on the mountain. When it is said that the crowds were astonished at the Savior’s teaching, this either signifies certain unbelievers who were amazed because they did not believe the Savior’s words, or it generally indicates all those who revered in him the excellence of such great wisdom, as his disciples must be believed to have done.

For he was teaching them as one possessing authority, not as the scribes. The scribes taught the people what had been written in Moses and the prophets; but Jesus, as God and Lord of Moses himself, according to the freedom of his will either added to what seemed deficient in the Law or proclaimed it in a changed form before the people. As we also read above: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, but I say to you.”

But since, in this book of exposition of the holy Gospel, which we began with the commencement of the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ and have brought through to the end of the sermon that the same Savior delivered on the mountain with his disciples, we consider that we should end there. From this point onward, we begin the third book, concerning the beginning of his miracles.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER VIII

After the sermon on the mountain, a leper is cleansed, a paralytic and Peter’s mother-in-law are healed; some wish to follow the Lord, who stills a storm while sailing and drives out demons

### I

When the sermons in which the Savior taught his disciples on the mountain had ended, Matthew continues and says:

When he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me.”

**(Augustine.)** This miracle may be understood to have taken place after both of the Lord’s sermons—not only the one that Matthew inserts, but also the one that Luke places in his account. Although Luke and Mark mention it in another place, the length of time that passed after the Lord’s descent from the mountain is not apparent.

Matthew wished to indicate only that, after that descent, many crowds were with the Lord when he cleansed the leper. Luke likewise, although he says that after completing all his words in the hearing of the people Christ entered Capernaum, did not specify after what interval of time he entered Capernaum once he had finished these sermons. It was during that interval that the leper was cleansed; Matthew inserted the event in its proper place, while Luke recalled it elsewhere.

Therefore the Lord’s descent from the mountain signifies his incarnation, by which “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians II).

**(Bede.)** After this, great crowds followed him. For after the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, he who had previously been known only in Judea, and whose name had been held in honor among one people, afterward became renowned throughout the whole earth.

**(Origen.)** In the literal sense also, the crowd that followed him did so for various reasons: some out of love, some because of his teaching, and some out of wonder and for the sake of healing.

**(Jerome.)** When the Lord descended from the mountain, crowds who had been unable to climb to higher things met him. The leper was the first to meet him, for while afflicted with leprosy he could not yet hear the Savior’s extensive sermon on the mountain. It is therefore rightly arranged that, after preaching and teaching, an occasion for a sign is presented, so that the sermon previously heard may be confirmed through power and miracles.

**(Augustine.)** In the mystical sense, it is fitting that no definite place is specified where the leper was cleansed, so that it may be shown that not one people of a particular city but the peoples of all nations were healed.

And because the Lord says, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it,” the man who was excluded by the Law, presuming that he could be cleansed by the Lord’s power, judged that the grace capable of washing away the leper’s stain came not from the Law but above the Law.

Yet just as the authority of power is declared in the Lord, so the steadfastness of faith is demonstrated in the leper. According to another Evangelist, he fell on his face. This is an act of humility and shame, so that each person may blush at the stains of his life, but shame may not suppress confession. He displayed his wound and asked for a remedy. His confession was itself full of religion and faith: “If you are willing,” he said, “you can cleanse me.”

He attributed this to the Lord’s will. In speaking of the Lord’s will, he did not doubt it as one unbelieving in his compassion; rather, conscious of his own defilement, he did not presume upon it.

And Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said: “I am willing; be cleansed.”

**(MAURUS.)** He stretched out the hand of healing because he extended the affection of his mercy toward curing him. He touched the sick man because he possessed the effect of health in his power. He said, “I am willing; be cleansed.” In “I am willing” he displayed the kindness of his compassion; in “be cleansed” he demonstrated the power of his majesty. For he himself spoke, and things came to be; he himself commanded, and all things were created.

**(Jerome.)** It should therefore not be joined and read, as many Latins think, “I am willing to cleanse,” but separately: first he should say, “I am willing,” and then command, “Be cleansed.”

**(Augustine.)** He says, “I am willing,” on account of Photinus; he commands, on account of Arius; he touches, on account of Mani. The Law indeed forbids lepers to be touched. But the one who is Lord of the Law does not submit to the Law; rather, he establishes the Law.

He did not touch him because he was unable to cleanse him without touching him, but to demonstrate that he was not subject to the Law. He did not fear contagion as human beings do; rather, because he could not be contaminated—the one who freed others—the leprosy that ordinarily contaminated the person who touched it was driven away by the Lord’s touch.

**(Origen.)** He touched him to demonstrate humility, teaching us to despise no one, shrink from no one, and consider no one contemptible on account of bodily injury or blemish—things sent by God for a reason known to him.

At the same time, he demonstrated the wonderful fact that he healed him in the manner in which he had been entreated. “If you are willing,” he said, “you can cleanse me.” “I am willing,” he replied, “be cleansed.”

And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.

**(Augustine.)** There is nothing intermediate between God’s work and his command, because the work is present in the command. Indeed, “He spoke, and they were made” (Psalm CXLVIII). You see, therefore, what cannot be doubted: God’s will is power. Those who assert one will necessarily assert one power.

Thus, as one possessing authority and the power to command, he does not shrink from offering testimony that he acts. The fact that, after descending from the mountain and giving commandments there to the disciples and the multitude, he immediately heals the leper by stretching out his hand signifies that those who doubt the fulfillment of those commandments are cleansed from such wavering by his help.

And Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one.”

**(Jerome.)** And indeed, what need was there to proclaim in words what he displayed in his body? Why is he ordered to tell no one except to teach that our benefits should not be publicized but kept quiet, so that we may abstain not only from monetary reward but also from praise?

But go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.

**(Jerome.)** He sends him to the priests for three reasons. First, out of humility, so that he might appear to show honor to the priests. For the Law had commanded that those cleansed of leprosy should offer gifts to the priests.

Second, so that when they saw the leper cleansed, they might either believe in the Savior or refuse to believe. If they believed, they would be saved; if they did not believe, they would become inexcusable. At the same time, this prevented him from appearing to break the Law, as they so often accused him of doing.

**(Bede.)** He is commanded to show himself to the priest so that the priest might understand that he had been healed not according to the order of the Law but by the grace of God, above the Law. He is also commanded to offer sacrifice, so that the Lord might demonstrate that he did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it: proceeding according to the Law, he healed above the Law those whom the remedies of the Law had not healed.

And he rightly adds, “as a testimony to them”—that is, if they believe in the Lord, if the leprosy of impiety departs.

**(Augustine.)** If anyone is troubled by the fact that the Lord appears to approve the Mosaic sacrifice, although the Church has not retained it, let him remember that the sacrifice of the Holy of Holies, which is his body, had not yet begun. He had not yet offered his own burnt offering in the Passion.

It was not fitting for the symbolic sacrifices to be removed before the thing they signified had been confirmed by the testimony of the apostles who preached it and by the faith of the peoples who believed.

**(Victorinus.)** Since this man typologically represents the human race, weakened by sins, he is rightly described not merely as a leper but, according to another Evangelist, as being entirely covered with leprosy. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God.

They are to be cleansed from the manifoldness of their former error by the Savior’s outstretched hand—that is, by the incarnate Word of God touching human nature—and so they may hear with the apostles: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XIII).

Those who for a long time were abhorrent and kept apart from the people of God’s camp may now at last be restored to the temple and offered to the priest—to the one of whom it is said, “You are a priest forever” (Psalm CIX). They hear the Apostle say: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians III).

For their cleansing they should offer what Moses commanded—that is, present their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God (Romans XII). Thus, according to the Prophet, they should give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and his wonders for the children of human beings, and proclaim his praises among the generations of the daughter of Zion (Psalm CVI).

Mark records that the leper did this. He did not keep silent about the benefit he had received, even though the one from whom he had received it commanded him to do so.
