Rather, performing the office of an Evangelist, he immediately went out and began to preach and spread the report, so that Jesus could no longer enter a city openly but remained outside in deserted places, while people came to him from every direction.

**(Gregory.)** Hence it is rightly asked why the Lord ordered some things he had done to be kept hidden, although they could not be hidden even for an hour. Did the only-begotten Son, coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, wish something in this matter that he was unable to accomplish?

We must observe that our Redeemer, through his mortal body, offered us in everything he did an example for our conduct. When he performed a miracle, he ordered it to be kept silent, yet it could not be kept silent. Thus his elect, following the examples of his teaching, should wish the great things they accomplish to remain hidden, but should allow them to be disclosed against their will when they benefit others.

In this way it is an example of great humility that they desire their works to be kept silent, and—[perhaps, “of great reverence”]—that their works cannot be kept silent. The Lord therefore did not wish something to happen and then prove unable to accomplish it; rather, he gave through his teaching an example of what his members ought to wish and of what happens to them even against their will.

After this Matthew continues and says:

When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, begging him and saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and suffering terribly.”

### II

It is asked how Matthew’s account—that the centurion himself approached the Lord—is consistent with Luke’s account, which says that he sent messengers. Luke writes: “A certain centurion’s servant was ill and near death, and he was precious to him. When he heard about Jesus, he sent the elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his servant” (Luke VII).

But to those who ask piously, it is readily apparent that Matthew, for the sake of brevity, said that the man himself approached. His desire and will were truly conveyed to the Lord, even though others acted as intermediaries. Mystically, he also commends to us what is written: “Approach him, and be enlightened.”

Because the centurion’s faith—the faith by which one truly approaches Jesus—was praised by him so greatly that he said, “I have not found such great faith in Israel,” the prudent Evangelist preferred to say that the centurion himself approached Christ rather than that he approached through those to whom he had entrusted his words.

Luke, for his part, disclosed the whole sequence as it happened so that from this we might understand how the other Evangelist, who could not lie, said that the man approached. Just as the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, although she touched the fringe of his garment, touched the Lord more truly because she believed than did the crowds who pressed around him (Matthew IX), so also the centurion approached the Lord all the more closely the more deeply he believed.

**(Origen.)** He approached as a foreigner by birth but a member of the household in heart; foreign in nation but eager in faith; a military commander and companion of angels.

At that time many people asked for different kinds of healing: one for a son, another for someone else, and no one for a servant except this man alone. This contributed to the increase of his blessedness and the crown of his glory: he humbly appealed to the Lord on behalf of a servant, saying, “My servant lies at home.”

His misery did not consist in only one thing—that he lay there—but in another also, that he was paralyzed, and in a third, that he was suffering terribly. He named all these things with sorrow: lying there, paralyzed, and grievously afflicted. He did this to display the anguish of his soul and move the Lord, both by showing the servant’s suffering and by inviting the Lord’s benevolence.

Thus should all who have male and female servants think, show mercy, grieve with them, plead for them, and care for their servants and maids, just as this blessed centurion did.

And Jesus said to him: “I will come and heal him.”

**(Jerome.)** Great is the sublimity of the Lord, who could heal by a single word; but no less is his humility, since he deigned to visit a suffering servant.

We must not accuse the Lord here of ostentation because he immediately promises to go and heal him. He saw the centurion’s faith, humility, and prudence: faith, because, although he was a Gentile, he believed that the servant could be healed by the Savior; humility, because he judged himself unworthy for Christ to enter under his roof; and prudence, because he perceived the divinity hidden beyond the bodily appearance, knowing that what would benefit him was not what even unbelievers could see, but what lay hidden within.

**(MAURUS.)** Elsewhere he refused to come to heal the ruler’s son, lest he appear to have honored wealth; here he immediately agrees to go, lest he seem to have despised the condition of a servant.

And the centurion replied: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

**(Bede.)** Because of his awareness of his Gentile life, he considered himself more burdened by the Lord’s condescension than helped by it, and he thought himself unable to receive Christ as a guest, since although he possessed faith, he had not yet been instructed in the sacraments.

But divine grace knows how to grant what our weakness does not presume to seek. Another centurion, who, like this man, prefigured the believing people from the nations, received the gift of the Holy Spirit before being baptized, on account of the merit of his great faith and righteousness. Likewise this man, though not yet catechized, merited that his faith should be praised by the Lord and that his servant should be saved.

[Col. 0858A]

Beautifully, another Evangelist says of him (Luke VII) that, although he did not dare invite Jesus under his roof, he did not have him far from his house, because “his salvation is near those who fear him” (Psalm LXXXIV).

The one who rightly uses the natural law, actively performing the good things he knows, thereby approaches the one who is truly good. But those who have joined crimes to the error of paganism may be compared with the crowds to whom the Lord says elsewhere: “Some have come from far away” (Mark VIII).

But only say the word, and my servant will be healed.

Great was the centurion’s faith, by which he confessed that the work could be accomplished through Christ’s word. This is suited to the mystery of our healing: although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him in that way no longer.

[Col. 0858B]

For I too am a man placed under authority, with soldiers under me.

**(Origen.)** How did such a great light proceed from the darkness of the Gentiles? How was such righteousness manifested among those who did not know their God? How did such pure faith shine from the mouth of fools who served idols?

**(Bede.)** He says that he is a man subject to the authority of either a tribune or a governor, yet able to command those beneath him. This implies that the one who is God and all-powerful possesses all the more an innumerable army of angelic power obedient to his commands. He can say to sickness, “Depart,” and it will depart; and to health, “Come,” and it will come. Everything is possible for him, because he is omnipotent. Hence it follows:

And I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.

**(Jerome.)** He wishes to show that the Lord too can accomplish what he wills not only by the arrival of his body but through the ministry of angels. Bodily illnesses and hostile powers, through which a person is often reduced to weakness, were to be driven away by the Lord’s word and by the ministries of angels.

**(Rabanus.)** Alternatively, the soldiers and servants who obey the centurion are natural powers, of which many who come to God bring a considerable supply with them. Concerning these, in praise of the centurion Cornelius, it is said that he was righteous and feared God with all his household, gave many alms to the people, and continually prayed to God (Acts X).

When Jesus heard this, he marveled.

He marveled because he saw that the centurion understood his majesty. But who had produced that faith or understanding in him except the one who marveled at it? And if someone else had produced it, why would he marvel, since he knew beforehand? We must therefore observe that when the Lord marvels at something, he signifies that it ought to be marvelous to us, who still need to be moved in this way. For all such movements, when they are attributed to God, are not signs of a troubled mind but of a teacher instructing.

And he said to those who followed him: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.”

**(Jerome.)** He is not speaking of the patriarchs and prophets of former times, but of the people of the present age. The centurion’s faith is preferred to theirs because they had been taught by the commands of the Law and the prophets, whereas this man believed spontaneously, with no one teaching him. Thus, in the centurion, the faith of the nations is placed before unbelieving Israel.

But I tell you that many will come from the East and the West.

**(Origen.)** “I tell you, I bear witness to you, I announce to you, I proclaim to you: many will come”—those of whom it was said, “that the children of God who are scattered might be gathered into one.” All these, therefore, will come.

From where will they come? From the East and the West—that is, from every nation under the sun, from East to West. For just as this Gospel must be preached among all nations, so people from all nations will come to the kingdom of heaven.

Or, alternatively, those from the East are the people who, immediately illuminated, pass onward; and those from the West are the people who, for the sake of faith, endure sufferings and persecutions even unto death.

And they will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.

**(MAURUS.)** They will recline not by lying down bodily but by resting spiritually; not by drinking temporarily but by feasting in blessedness. Since the God of Abraham, the creator of heaven, is also the Father of Christ, Abraham is therefore in the kingdom of heaven, and with him the nations that have believed in Christ, the Son of the Creator, will recline.

The other meaning we mentioned above is also fulfilled: in the centurion’s faith, the prerogative of the nations comes to pass, while the peoples who will believe are recalled as coming from East and West.

The sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there. (Hieron.) By the sons of the kingdom he signifies the Jews, among whom the Lord formerly reigned. Darkness is always inward, not outward. But [because] the one who is expelled by the Lord goes outside and leaves the light, it is for this reason that it is called “outer darkness.” There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there. If weeping belongs to the eyes, and gnashing of teeth demonstrates the bones, then the resurrection of bodies and of those same members that had fallen is real. (Greg.) Hence, too, the magnitude of the torments is expressed metaphorically. By inner darkness, to be sure, we mean blindness of heart; by outer darkness, the eternal night of condemnation. When someone is condemned, he is sent not into inner but into outer darkness, because there he is unwillingly cast into the night of condemnation who here willingly fell into blindness of heart. Weeping and gnashing of teeth are also said to be there: so that there the teeth may gnash which here rejoiced in gluttony, and there the eyes may weep which here were occupied with unlawful desires; thus each member may undergo the punishment to which here, through its several vices, it served as a subject. Weeping is usually produced by burning heat, gnashing of teeth by cold. (Beda.) Here a twofold Gehenna is indicated: that of excessive cold and that of intolerable heat. The statement of blessed Job agrees with this, when he says: “They pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24). Or certainly, the gnashing of teeth reveals the disposition of one who is indignant, because each person repents too late, groans too late, and too late grows angry with himself for having sinned with such stubborn wickedness.

And Jesus said to the centurion, “Go; and just as you have believed, [Col. 0860A] so let it be done for you.” (MAURUS.) By the merit of faith he shows that the man obtained healing for his servant, so that the strength of his faith might increase more and more as he perceived that he could obtain through it whatever he wished. (Hieron.) For if it truly happens to every person according to what he has believed, then this grace from the Lord will also be measured out to him according to the measure of his faith. Therefore the Lord said to him: “As you have believed, let it be done for you.” You have believed that I am able; you have believed that I am Lord of all. As you have believed, so shall it be done for you.

And the boy was healed in that hour. (Aug.) The master’s faith is proved, and the servant’s health is confirmed. The merit of a master can therefore also assist his servants—not only through the merit of faith, but also through devotion to discipline. (Beda.) Mystically, however, as I have said, the centurion, whose faith is preferred to that of Israel, clearly represents the elect from the nations. They are, as it were, surrounded by a hundred soldiers and raised to the perfection of spiritual virtues; they ask from the Lord nothing earthly, but only the joys of eternal salvation for themselves and their own. For the number one hundred, which is transferred from the left hand to the right, is customarily used as a sign of heavenly life. Hence the ark of Noah was built over a hundred years (Gen. 6); Abraham, at the age of one hundred, received the son of promise (Gen. 17); Isaac sowed and found a hundredfold in that same year (Gen. 26); the court of the tabernacle was one hundred cubits long (Exod. 27); and in the hundredth psalm mercy and judgment are sung to the Lord (Ps. 100), along with other things of this kind. Men of such merit must therefore intercede with the Lord for those who are still oppressed by the spirit of servitude in fear, so that, as they are gradually advanced to higher things, perfect love may cast out fear (1 John 4).

### [III.]

And when Jesus had entered Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. (Aug.) Matthew did not indicate when this happened—that is, after or before what event. For it is not necessary to understand that it happened immediately after the event he has just narrated, since Mark and Luke relate this event before speaking of the leper. But the difference in the order of narration presents no obstacle, when the same event is being reported, especially since each evangelist believed that he ought to narrate in the order in which God wished to suggest to his memory the very things he was reporting.

And he touched her hand, and the fever left her. [Col. 0860D] (Beda.) In Luke’s Gospel it is written that they pleaded with him on her behalf, and that, standing over her, he rebuked the fever. At one time, then, the Savior is asked, and at another he freely heals the sick, showing that against the passions of vices also he always responds to the prayers of the faithful, and sometimes grants them understanding of things they themselves scarcely recognize in themselves, or mercifully removes from those who ask piously things they do not understand; in accordance with what the Psalmist petitions: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults” (Ps. 18).

And she rose and ministered to them. (Hieron.) It is natural for those suffering from fever, when recovery begins, to grow weak and to feel the discomfort of their illness. But the health bestowed by the Lord’s command returns all at once; and not only does it return, but it is accompanied by such strength that she is immediately able to minister to those who had helped her. In accordance with the laws of theology, the members that served uncleanness and iniquity so as to bear fruit for death should serve righteousness unto eternal life (Rom. 6–7). (MAURUS.) Allegorically, Peter’s house is circumcision, because the apostleship to the circumcision was entrusted to him (Gal. 2). Peter’s mother-in-law is therefore the Synagogue, because in a certain sense she is the mother of the Church, which was entrusted for safekeeping to Peter by the true Bridegroom. To him he himself says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16); and elsewhere: “Feed my lambs”; and: “Feed my sheep” (John 21). Peter’s mother-in-law was therefore feverish because the Synagogue was suffering from the burning heat of envy, persecuting the Church. Hence the bride in the Song of Songs also says: “The sons of my mother have fought against me” (Song 1). The Lord touched her hand when he converted her carnal works to spiritual use. She rose and ministered to them because, after being raised by the touch of divine mercy from the carnal observance in which she was uselessly sluggish, she ministers daily to the Lord through spiritual service.

Morally, each soul that serves the desires of the flesh burns as though with fever; but when touched by the hand of divine mercy it recovers, and through the restraints of continence it curbs the wantonness of the flesh, lest, proceeding through the enticements of pleasure, it retain as diseased and dying members fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols. Rather, in those very members with which it formerly served uncleanness and iniquity so as to bear fruit for death, it should serve righteousness unto eternal life.

When evening had come, they brought him many who had demons, and he cast out the spirits by a word and healed all who were ill. (Hieron.) All are healed not in the morning or at midday, but toward evening, when the sun is about to set, when the grain of wheat dies in the earth in order to bear much fruit. The setting of the sun signifies the passion and death of the one who said: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” When the sun had set, more demoniacs than before and more sick people were healed, because the one who, while living temporally in the flesh, taught a few Jews, after trampling down the kingdom of death transmitted the gifts of faith and salvation to all the nations throughout the world. Of him the Psalmist sings to his ministers, as heralds of life and light: “Make a way for him who ascends over the setting” (Ps. 67). The Lord ascended over the setting, because from the place where he set in his passion, there he revealed his greater glory by rising again.

So that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah (chapter 53) might be fulfilled: “He himself took our infirmities and bore our illnesses.” (MAURUS.) Our Savior therefore took our infirmities, not in order to keep them for himself, but to take them away from us. For he is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1). According to the same prophet, the Lord therefore laid upon him the iniquity of us all, so that what we could not bear because of the weakness of our strength might be borne for us by him who suffered for us of his own will and who, owing nothing to death, paid the debt of death for us.

### [IV.]

When Jesus saw the large crowds around him, he ordered his disciples to go across the lake. (Aug.) Here it is clear that Matthew recalled another day on which he ordered them to cross the lake, not the day following the healing of Peter’s mother-in-law; for Mark and Luke affirm that on that day he went out into the desert. (MAURUS.) Jesus’ exhortation therefore is that we cross the bitter waves of the world in an unwavering vessel of faith, so that, with him as our pilot, we may reach the shore of paradise.

And a certain scribe approached and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” (Aug.) Matthew says that this happened when he ordered them to cross [Col. 0862B] the lake, whereas Luke says it happened while others were walking along the road. There is no contradiction, because they were certainly walking along the road in order to come to the lake. (Hieron.) This scribe of the Law, who knew only the letter that kills, would not have been rejected by the Lord if he had said, “Lord, I will follow you wherever you go.” But because he regarded him as one teacher among many, and because he was a man of letters—more significantly expressed in Greek as γραμματεύς (*grammateus*)—and not a spiritual hearer, he has no place in which Jesus may recline his head.

Jesus said to him: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the sky have nests in which they may rest; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” From the Lord’s words it is shown that this man, who promised his service, was rejected because, seeing the greatness of the signs, he wished to follow the Savior in order to seek profits from the miracles of his works. He desired the very thing that Simon Magus had wanted to buy from Peter (Acts 8). Such faith is therefore rightly condemned by the Lord’s sentence, and he is told: “Why do you wish to follow me for the sake of wealth and the profits of the world, when I am so poor that I do not even possess a lodging, and do not use a roof of my own?” (Aug.) Alternatively, it is understood that, moved by the Lord’s miracles, he wished to follow him for empty display, which is signified by the birds; but he pretended to offer discipleship, and that pretense is signified by the name of foxes. By the reclining of his head he signified his humility, which had no place in that pretender and proud man. (MAURUS.) Likewise, allegorically and not inappropriately, we may understand the foxes to signify heretics and the birds of the sky evil spirits. They have dens and nests—that is, dwelling places—in the heart of the Jewish people. A fox does nothing with courage, but everything with cunning; so heretics, trusting not in Christ’s virtues but in their own trickery, equipped with deceit and clever in the dialectical art, strive to lead astray whomever they can. Therefore the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head, because in the minds of such people Christ finds no dwelling place for his divinity. The head of Christ is God (1 Cor. 11).

Another of his disciples said to him, “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” He does not reject discipleship, but desires to pursue it more freely after first completing the duty of filial devotion at his father’s funeral. In every respect he is worthy to be a place in which the Son of Man may recline his head [Col. 0863A]—that is, in whose humble breast the divinity may rest in a kind of familiar dwelling.

But Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” (Hier.) Everyone who does not believe is dead. If a dead person buries a dead person, we should not concern ourselves with the dead but with the living, lest, while we are anxious about the dead, we too should be called dead. The addition in Luke—“But you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God”—is not placed here without reason. We must therefore note in this saying that sometimes lesser goods must be set aside in our actions for the sake of the usefulness of greater ones. For who does not know that burying the dead is the merit of a good work? Yet to the man who asked to be released in order to bury his father it was said: “Let the dead bury their own dead [Col. 0863B]; but you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” The service of this duty had to be postponed to the ministry of preaching, because by the former he would bury the dead in the flesh in the earth, whereas by the latter he would raise the dead in soul to life. (MAURUS.) How can the dead bury the dead unless you understand a twofold death: one of nature, the other of guilt; one by which the soul is separated from the flesh, the other by which God is separated from the soul? Or by “the dead” he means unbelievers, or those who, after faith, serve sins; and by “their own dead,” those who nevertheless departed from the body without faith and good works. For those who are free from their own sins must not consent to the sins of others, because not only those who commit sins but also those who consent to those who commit them have guilt before the just Judge (Rom. 1). To bury the dead is to shelter sinners in their sins. This is what those do who justify the wicked for gifts, praise sinners in the desires of their souls, and bless those who act wickedly (Isa. 5; Ps. 9).

And when he had climbed into the boat, his disciples followed him. (Orig.) They were not weak, but firm and steadfast in faith, gentle and devout, despising the world, not double-minded but single-hearted. (Beda.) In this voyage the Lord deigns to reveal both natures of his one and the same person: as man, he sleeps in the boat; as God, he restrains the fury of the sea by a word. Allegorically, the sea or lake that he wishes to cross with his own is understood as the dark and bitter turmoil of the world. The boat into which they climb is best understood as the tree of the Lord’s passion. Through its benefit each of the faithful, aided by it, crosses the waves of the world and obtains the dwelling place of the heavenly homeland, like the security of a stable shore. That the Savior himself descends into one boat with his disciples, he explains elsewhere by what it signifies, when, after announcing the mystery of his passion and resurrection, he immediately said to all: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Matt. 16).

### [V.]

And behold, a great disturbance arose in the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves. (Orig.) After he had shown many great and wondrous things on land, he crossed to the sea in order to demonstrate there works still more excellent, so that he might show to all that he was Lord of land and sea. Having entered the boat, he caused the sea to be troubled, stirred up the winds, and roused the waves. Why? In order to bring the disciples into fear, so that they would ask for his help, and so that he might reveal his power to those who entreated him. That storm did not arise of itself, but obeyed the power of the one who commanded it, who brings the winds out of his treasuries (Ps. 134), who appointed sand as the boundary of the sea. For he said to it: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall not go beyond; here your waves shall be broken within yourself” (Job 38). At his command and order, therefore, the storm arose in the sea for the reasons indicated above. A great storm, not a small one, came to pass, so that a great work, not a small one, might be displayed; and the more violently the waves rushed upon the boat, the more greatly [Col. 0864B] the disciples were disturbed, so that they might desire all the more ardently the Savior’s miracles for their deliverance.

But he himself was sleeping. O wondrous and astonishing event! He who never sleeps is sleeping. He was therefore sleeping in body, but awake in divinity. He slept, then, in order to rouse the apostles and make them awaken, and especially all of us, so that we might never sleep in mind, nor in understanding or prudence, but strive to keep watch at all times, rejoice in the Lord, and ask salvation from him. (Beda.) Mystically, however, Christ fell asleep while the disciples were sailing because, when the faithful were trampling upon the world, meditating in their hearts upon the rest of the future kingdom, and striving together to cast behind them the faithless boasts of the world, whether by the favorable breeze of the Holy Spirit or by the rowing of their own effort, the time of the Lord’s passion suddenly arrived. Hence Mark rightly says that this happened at night, so that the setting of the true Sun might be signified not only by the Lord’s sleep but also by the very hour of the departing light.

And they came and woke him, saying, “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” (Orig.) They had been so terrified by fear and almost driven out of their minds that they rushed upon him and did not make their request calmly or gently, but woke him tumultuously, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” O blessed, O truthful disciples of God! You have the Lord Savior with you, and yet you fear danger; life is with you, and you are anxious about death. The disciples wake the Lord so that, while he slept, they would not perish through the violence of the waves, because they had seen his death and were seeking his resurrection with their greatest desires, lest, if he remained asleep too long in the sleep of bodily death, their minds should perish forever in spiritual death.

And Jesus said to them: “Why are you fearful, you of little faith?” (Aug.) What Matthew says the Lord said—“Why are you fearful, you of little faith?”—Mark expresses in this way: “Why are you fearful? Do you still have no faith?” (Mark 4), namely, the perfect faith like a mustard seed. Thus he too says, “of little faith.” Luke, however, says: “Where is your faith?” (Luke 8). In fact, the whole statement could have been: “Why are you fearful? Where is your faith, you of little faith?” (Orig.) Hence one evangelist recalls one part and another recalls another. If you have recognized me as powerful on earth, why do you not believe that I am also powerful at sea? If you have accepted that I am God and Creator of all things, why do you not believe [Col. 0865A] that the things made by me are under my power? Why, then, do you doubt, you of little faith? The one who believes a little is reproved; the one who believes nothing is despised. Those weak in faith are corrected, while those wholly alien to faith are punished. Such were the Jews and pagans, and therefore they perished in their evils; such also were the heretics, and therefore they will be condemned on the day of judgment.

Those who feared in Christ’s presence are rightly reproved, since whoever clings to him cannot perish. A similar thing occurred when, after the sleep of death, he appeared to the disciples and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen (Mark 16). Likewise he said to them: “O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (Luke 24). It is as though, by a metaphor drawn from the boat, he said: “Was it not necessary for Christ to sleep, while the waves swept the boat in which he rested from side to side, and then, immediately stilling the swollen heaps of the waters, to make the power of his divinity manifest to all?”

Then, rising, he rebuked the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about. (Orig.) From the great wind and great storm, with the sea disturbed and swelling, there came a great calm. For it is fitting that this great one should do great and wondrous things. Therefore, having shortly before girded himself with great power, he magnificently troubled the depths of the sea. Now again, displaying in the same event the majesty of his power, he made a great calm. (Beda.) Rising, he rebuked the wind. For after the resurrection had been accomplished, he struck down the pride of the devil, destroying through death the one who held the power of death. Rising, he also caused the storming waters to cease, because by rising from the tomb he undermined the mad rage of the Jews, which, shaking its head, had cried: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27).

Here it should be noted literally that all creatures perceive the Creator. Those creatures to which rebukes and commands are addressed perceive the one who commands them—not through the error of the heretics, who think all things are animate [Note: Some manuscripts add “sentient”; others, conversely, “insentient.”]—but through the majesty of the Creator, by which things insentient among us are sentient to him.

But the men marveled, saying: “What kind of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” (Hieron.) It was not the disciples but the sailors and the others who were in the boat who marveled. But if someone should contentiously insist that those who marveled were the disciples, we shall answer that they were rightly called “men,” because they did not yet know the Savior’s power. They marveled, saying: “What kind of man is this, who appears to be a man and displays power like God; who is thought to be one of the fleshly but shows wonders above all fleshly things? He sleeps like a man, and he commands the sea and the winds like God; he sits in a little boat, and by his command bends every creature wherever he wishes?”

(MAURUS.) There are those who wish this boat, which Jesus boarded with his disciples, to signify allegorically the present Church, in which the Savior wishes to cross the sea of this world with his disciples. The winds that create a storm in the sea are interpreted as demons, stirring up persecution in the world against the faithful, so that the boat was covered by the waves. For this is what unclean spirits desire, and this is what wicked men desire: that the Church, overcome by severe pressures, should be submerged. But although Jesus may seem to sleep by withdrawing his help for a time, he is nevertheless awakened by worthy prayers, restrains the agitation of the evil spirits, and causes the threats of persecutors to grow mild. Thus a great calm comes about when peace is restored to his Church, so that, with the breeze of the Holy Spirit blowing upon her prosperous course, she may safely reach the desired harbor of eternal rest.

(RAB.) Theologically, each of us, instructed in the Catholic faith and imbued with the sign of the Lord’s cross, boards the boat with Jesus as we prepare to leave the world and attempt to cross the sea. Yet he who will neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel (Ps. 120), often seems to fall asleep for us as we sail, amid the roaring of the sea, whenever, as the assault grows more frequent amid our striving for virtue—whether from unclean spirits, wicked men, or the very force of our own thoughts—the splendor of faith is darkened, the height of hope withers, and the flame of love grows cold. In such storms we must hasten to that helmsman and diligently awaken him who does not serve the winds but commands them. He will immediately restrain the storms, pour back tranquility, and grant the harbor of salvation.

(Beda.) Let us also marvel when he shows kindness and benevolence toward us, when he deigns to save us from dangers, when he frees us from disturbances, and when he rescues us from enemies; let us marvel and, in our wonder, give thanks. The text continues:

And when he had crossed the lake, he came into the region of the Gerasenes. [VI.] Gerasa is a distinguished city of Arabia, beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead, which the tribe of Manasseh possessed, not far from the Lake of Tiberias, into which the pigs were hurled. It signifies the nations of the Gentiles, whom the Savior deigned to visit after the sleep of his passion and the glory of his resurrection, sending out preachers. Hence Gerasa—or Gergesa, as some wish it—may be interpreted as “driving out the settler” or “the approaching stranger.” This indicates that the people of the Gentiles drove from their hearts as an enemy the one by whom they had been wickedly inhabited, and that the one who had been far away became near through the blood of Christ.

[Col. 0866D] Two men possessed by demons came to meet him. (Aug.) Matthew says that two men were healed from a legion of demons, whereas Mark and Luke mention one. Understand that one of them was a person of greater distinction and renown, whom that region especially mourned and for whose salvation it exerted itself greatly. Since the two evangelists wished to indicate this, they judged that only the man whose affair had become more widely and more famously known should be mentioned. (Beda.) The general meaning of the allegory also agrees with this, because just as one man possessed by a demon, so also two men appropriately express the type of the Gentile peoples. For although Noah had begotten three sons, only one family was admitted into the possession of God. From the other two were born the peoples of the various nations, who were enslaved to idols.

Coming out of the tombs, exceedingly fierce. (MAURUS.) That is, displaying the foulness of evil works through their bodies. For what are the bodies of unbelievers except certain tombs of the dead, in which the word of God does not dwell, but a soul dead through sins is confined?

So that no one could pass along that road. Before the Savior’s coming, the Gentiles were an impassable road to prophets and holy teachers, because, in the savagery of their fury, they refused to obey any of them. Nor did they wish to obey human laws. Hence Mark also says that no one could any longer bind the demoniac, because, though he had often been bound with fetters and chains, he had broken the chains and crushed the fetters, and no one could tame him. Chains and fetters signify the severe and harsh laws of the Gentiles, by which sins are restrained even in their commonwealths. When the chains had been broken, as Luke writes, he was driven by the demon into the desert. Having transgressed the laws, he was driven by desire toward crimes that already exceeded ordinary custom.

(Aug.) It may also appropriately be said that these two men who were tormented by demons represent the figure of the two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles. For until the time of the Lord’s incarnation, the Gentiles, deceived by diabolical doctrines, worshiped idols instead of God, while the Jews had always been despisers and transgressors of the divine Law. Hence it happened that they did not dwell in a house—that is, they did not rest in their own consciences. They remained in tombs, because they delighted in dead works, that is, in sins. For what are the bodies of unbelievers except certain tombs of the dead, in which the word of God does not dwell, but a soul dead through sins is confined?

“Exceedingly fierce.” Their being exceedingly fierce signifies that they raged all the more violently against themselves and others insofar as they considered the divine and human laws, signified by the chains, to be worthless. “So that no one could pass along that road.” Tropologically, this road is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), and of whom the prophet Jeremiah says: “Stand and see, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls” (Jer. 6). On this road—that is, in the faith itself of Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior—while both peoples were still unbelieving and the devil raged within them, they resisted those who walked rightly, that is, those who believed rightly and preached the same faith of the Lord. For they themselves neither hastened to walk by turning away from evil, believing and doing what was right according to the way of God’s commandments, nor did they fail to attack most fiercely those who strove to walk along the way of faith.

And they cried out, saying: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God?” This is not a confession of the will, which is not followed by any reward for the one confessing, but an extortion forced by necessity, compelling those who are unwilling. It is as though runaway slaves, after a long time, should see their master and ask for nothing except to be spared the blows. So the demons, seeing the Lord suddenly dwelling on earth, believed that he had come to judge them. The Savior’s presence is the demons’ torment.

Some absurdly think that the demons know the Son of God while the devil does not, on the ground that the demons are less evil than the one whose satellites they are. Yet all knowledge must be referred from the disciples to the teacher, and demons as well as the devil should be understood to suspect rather than know that he is the Son of God. For no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.

“What have we to do with you,” they say, “Jesus, Son of God?” It is clear from these words that there was knowledge in them but no love. They feared their punishment from him; they did not love righteousness in him. They learned only as much as he wished them to learn, and he wished only as much as was appropriate. Yet he became known to them not as he is known to the holy angels, who enjoy his participated eternity according to the fact that he is the Word of God, but as it was necessary for him to be known in order to terrify them. From their tyrannical power he was about to free those predestined for his kingdom and for glory that is always truthful and truly everlasting.

The demons therefore came to know him not through what he is as eternal life and unchangeable light, which illuminates the godly and, when seen through the faith that is in him, cleanses hearts, but through certain temporal effects of his power and through signs of his most hidden might—signs that could be more conspicuous to the perceptions of angels, even evil spirits, than to human weakness.

From this one may gauge how great was the madness of Arius in believing Jesus to be a creature and not God. The demons believe and tremble that he is the Son of the Most High God. What impiety of the Jews dared to say that he cast out demons by the prince of demons, when the demons themselves confess that he has nothing in common with them? They did not cease afterward to say and confess the very thing they had then cried out in demoniacal fury in the shrines of idols: namely, that Jesus is Christ, the Son of the Most High God, and that they have no share of peace or power with him.

You have come before the appointed time to torment us. The devil and his ministers knew that their condemnation at the judgment of God was certain. To him it is said through the prophet Isaiah: “Woe to you who plunder! Will you not yourself be plundered? And you who despise, will you not yourself be despised? When you have completed your plundering, you will be plundered” (Isa. 33). But they could not know the dispensation of the divine plan that was to be revealed to us through Christ’s incarnation, because, according to the Apostle, none of the rulers of this age knew the wisdom of God. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). They therefore feared that the power of the Lord’s coming, which they marveled at, was directed toward their own condemnation. Hence, as Luke testifies, they begged him not to command them to go into the abyss.

Now there was a large herd of pigs feeding not far from them, and the demons begged him, saying: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs.” (Aug.) [Col. 0869A] It must therefore be understood that the words of the demons, reported differently by the evangelists at this point, present no difficulty, since they can either be reduced to one meaning or all be understood as having been spoken. Nor does the fact that Matthew has them speak in the plural, while the others use the singular, create a problem, since they too relate that, when asked what he was called, he answered that he was Legion, because there were many demons. Nor does Mark’s statement that the herd of pigs was near the mountain conflict with Luke’s statement that it was on the mountain; the herd was so large that some were on the mountain and others around it. For there were two thousand pigs, as Mark expressly stated.

And Jesus said, “Go.” (Hieron.) He permitted what the demons requested so that, through the destruction of the pigs, an opportunity for the salvation of human beings might be provided. Let the Manichaean be ashamed: if the souls of human beings and beasts are of the same substance and from the same creator, how can two thousand pigs be suffocated for the salvation of one human being? (Beda.) Yet in their destruction unclean people, deprived of voice and reason, are figuratively indicated—people who, grazing on the mountain of pride, take pleasure in muddy deeds. Demons can rule over such people through the worship of idols. For unless someone has lived in the manner of a pig, the devil will not receive power over him, except perhaps merely for the purpose of testing, not of destroying.

And they went out and entered into the pigs; and behold, the whole herd rushed down the cliff into the sea with great force, and they died in the waters. (Aug.) The fact that the pigs were hurled into the lake signifies that, once the Church had been glorified and the Gentile people freed from the domination of demons, those who refused to believe in Christ carry out their sacrilegious rites in hidden places, having been plunged into blind and profound curiosity. It should also be noted that the unclean spirits would not have entered even the pigs unless the gracious Savior himself, when they asked, had granted them this—he who could rightly have banished them into the abyss. He wished to teach us something necessary: namely, that we should know that they have far less power to harm human beings by their own authority, since they could not harm even animals of whatever kind. God, who is good, can grant them this power over us by his hidden justice; he cannot do so by an unjust act.

The swineherds fled and, coming into the city, reported everything, including what had happened to those who had been possessed by demons. [Col. 0869D] The fact that the swineherds fled and reported these things signifies that certain leaders even among the ungodly, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless do not cease proclaiming its power among the nations with astonishment and admiration.

And behold, the whole city went out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him they begged him to depart from their territory. (Jerome.) Those who ask him to leave their territory do not do so out of pride, as some think, but out of humility, conscious of their own weakness. The Gerasenes judged themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence: they could not receive the word of God, nor, while their mind was still weak, were they able to bear the weight of wisdom. The same is said to have happened to Peter himself when he saw the miracle of the fish (Luke V). The widow of Sarepta, too, in the story of blessed Elijah, having felt herself blessed by his lodging with her, nevertheless thought that his presence was burdensome to her. “What have I to do with you, man of God?” she said. “You have come to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and my son might be killed?” (III Kings XVII.) In the mystical sense, however, the fact that the Gerasenes came out to see what had happened, found the man clothed and sitting at Jesus’ feet with a sound mind (as Luke says), and, learning what had taken place, asked Jesus to depart from them, struck with great fear, signifies the ancient multitude, delighted with its own way of life, which indeed honors him but does not wish to endure the Christian law. They say that they cannot fulfill it, while nevertheless marveling at the faithful people healed from their former, ruined manner of life.

## CHAPTER IX

Jesus heals a paralytic and a woman from an issue of blood. [Col. 0870B] He calls Matthew, raises the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, and so forth.

### [I.]

And getting into a boat, he crossed over and came to his own city.

Here, then, a question arises between Mark and Matthew: how Matthew writes as though this had taken place in the Lord’s city, which some wish to be Nazareth, while Mark places it in Capernaum. The question would be more difficult to resolve if Matthew too had named Nazareth. But now, since Galilee itself could be called Christ’s city because Nazareth was in Galilee—just as the whole kingdom is called the Roman city, although it is constituted from so many cities—and since the city of which it is written, “Most glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm LXXXVI), is constituted among so many nations; and since the former people of God themselves, dwelling in so many cities, were also called one house, “the house of Israel”—who could doubt that Jesus did this in his own city, since he did it in Capernaum, a city of Galilee, to which he had returned by crossing over from the region of the Gerasenes? Thus, on coming to Galilee, he could rightly be said to have come to his own city, whatever town of Galilee he was in, especially since Capernaum itself so excelled in Galilee that it was regarded as a kind of metropolis.

And behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. (Bede.) The healing of this paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul sighing toward Christ after a long period of sluggishness in carnal pleasure. First of all, it needs attendants to lift it up and bring it to Christ—that is, good teachers who offer the hope of healing and the assistance of intercession. According to Mark’s account, there are found to have been four of them, either because the whole power and teaching of preachers is confirmed by the four Gospels, or because there are four virtues by which the confidence of the mind is raised toward recovering health. Of these it is said in praise of eternal Wisdom: “For she teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life” (Wisdom VIII). Some, changing the names, call these prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.” (Jerome.) O wondrous humility! He calls “son” one who was despised, weak, and dissolved in all the joints of his limbs—one whom the priests did not consider worthy to touch. Or certainly he calls him “son” because his sins are forgiven him.

(Augustine.) Matthew says that God said, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you,” whereas Luke does not say “son” but “man.” This serves to convey the Lord’s meaning more explicitly: sins were being forgiven to a human being who, precisely because he was human, could not say, “I have not sinned”; and at the same time it indicates that the one who forgave the human being was understood to be God. But if anyone is troubled about whether the Lord said what Matthew reports or what Luke reports, let him know that he could have said both at once: either, “Take courage, man; your sins are forgiven you, son,” or, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you, man.”

(John Chrysostom.) We should certainly observe how much the faith of each person counts before God, since another’s faith counted for so much that the whole man—that is, outwardly and inwardly—rose at once already healed, and the sins of some were forgiven through the merit of others. The paralytic hears the pardon and remains silent, offering no thanks, because he was more concerned with the care of his body than of his soul. He bewailed the temporal troubles of his weakened body in such a way that he did not bewail the eternal punishments of his even more weakened soul, judging the present life more precious to himself than the future one. Rightly, therefore, Christ regards the faith of those who bring him the man, and regards the insensibility of the one lying there in such a way that, with the support of another’s faith, the paralytic’s soul is healed before his body.

And behold, certain scribes said within themselves, “This man is blaspheming.” (Jerome.) What they considered blasphemy Mark explains in what follows, saying: “They said, ‘Who can forgive sins except God alone?’” We read in the prophet: “I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isaiah XLIII). Thus the scribes, because they thought he was a man while understanding that he was speaking God’s words, accused him of blasphemy. Yet, although they did not know it, they were speaking the truth, because no one can forgive sins except God—who forgives them even through those to whom he has given the power of forgiving. Christ is therefore proved truly to be God, because he can forgive sins as God. They bear true witness to God, but, by denying Christ’s person, they are mistaken.

The Jews therefore err: although they believe that Christ is God and can forgive sins, they do not believe that Jesus is the Christ. But the Arians err far more madly. Though, overcome by the words of the Gospel, they do not dare deny that Jesus is the Christ and can forgive sins, nevertheless they are not afraid to deny that he is God. Yet he himself, desiring to save the faithless, manifests that he is God both by his knowledge of hidden things and by the power of his works.

And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” He shows himself to be God, who can know the hidden things of the heart; and, in a certain sense, while remaining silent he says: “By the same majesty and power with which I look upon your thoughts, I can also forgive sins to human beings. From what happens to the paralytic, understand what he receives.”

Which is easier, to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Rise and walk”? There is a great difference between saying and doing. Only the one who forgave knew whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven. But “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the one who rose and by those who saw him rise. A bodily sign is therefore performed to prove a spiritual reality, although forgiving the ailments of body and soul belongs to the same power. We are also given to understand that many bodily weaknesses occur on account of sins. Perhaps for this reason the sins are forgiven first, so that, once the causes of the weakness have been removed, health may be restored.

(Rabanus.) There are indeed different kinds of causes for which we are afflicted in this life by bodily hardships. Sometimes the just are burdened with bodily weakness in order that their merits may be increased through patience, as were the blessed Fathers Job and Tobias and countless martyrs in both Testaments; sometimes for the protection of virtues already received, lest they perish when pride tempts them—as in the case of the Apostle Paul, to whom, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, “a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan,” was given “to buffet him” (II Corinthians XII); sometimes for the understanding and correction of our sins, as when Mary, the sister of Aaron, was struck with leprosy in the wilderness because of her rash and proud words (Numbers XII); so too the paralytic whom we are discussing, who could be healed of his weakness only after his sins had first been forgiven; sometimes for the glory of God who saves, whether by himself or through his servants, as in the case of the man born blind in the Gospel (John IX), who had sinned neither himself nor his parents, but suffered “so that the works of God might be revealed in him”; and as with Lazarus, whose sickness was not unto death but “for the glory of God, so that the Son of God might be glorified through it” (John XI); sometimes as the beginning of eternal condemnation, which is characteristic of the reprobate, as with Antiochus (II Maccabees IX) and Herod (Acts XII). Both, resisting God in their own time, showed everyone by the misery of their present afflictions how many torments they would suffer perpetually in Gehenna. To them the prophet’s words apply: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jeremiah XVII).

Therefore, whenever we suffer temporal adversity, we must give thanks to the Lord with humility; and, conscious of our weakness, we must rejoice in the remedies granted to us. Returning to our conscience, we must diligently examine both our deeds and our thoughts. Whatever we discover that we have done wrongly, we must cleanse by a fitting correction; and whatever we find has been lost to us through the fault of pride—even among those things we believed we had done rightly—we must also punish with humble satisfaction, for this very thing is often the cause of our scourging. But for the innocent and the just to be scourged for the increase of their rewards is a special gift of perfected men; whereas to be driven by temporal blows toward eternal torments is the punishment of the unrepentant reprobate.

“But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” (Bede.) If, according to the Psalmist, God is the one who “has removed our iniquities from us as far as the east is from the west” (Psalm CII), and the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, then this same one is both God and the Son of Man. Thus Christ, as man, can forgive sins through the power of his divinity, and the same Christ, as God, can die for sinners through the weakness of his humanity.

(John Chrysostom.) The searcher of souls anticipates the mind’s great deliberations. He displayed the power of his divinity by the testimony of his work, as he reassembled the limbs of the shattered body, tightened the sinews, filled out the bones, strengthened the vital organs, and raised to activity and walking the powers and steps that had already been buried in a living corpse. “Take up your bed,” he says: that is, carry the one that carried you; exchange the roles of the burden, so that what had been evidence of weakness may become proof of health. “Go to your house”: do not, having been healed by Christian faith, perish any longer on the roads of Jewish faithlessness.

Spiritually, to rise from one’s bed is to withdraw the soul from the carnal desires in which it had lain sick. To take up the bed is to separate the flesh itself, restrained by the reins of continence, from earthly pleasures through hope of heavenly rewards. To take up the bed and go home is to return to paradise. For this is our true home, which first received the human being: it was not lost by right but by fraud, and was finally restored by the one who owed nothing to the fraudulent enemy. Alternatively, the one who had been sick and is now well carries the bed home when the soul, having received forgiveness of sins, returns with the body itself to its inner guardianship, lest it admit anything perverse for which it may again justly be struck.

And he rose and went to his house. (Jerome.) If the paralytic soul rises and recovers its former strength, it carries its bed—the bed on which it had previously lain dissolved—and carries it into the house of its virtues.

But when the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings. (Bede.) How wondrous is the power of divine might, when, with no intervening delay of time, swift healing follows the Savior’s command! Therefore those who were present, condemning the darts of blasphemy, rightly turned their astonished hearts to the praise of such great majesty.

### [II.]

And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew, and he said to him, “Follow me.”

“He saw,” it says, “a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew,” and so forth. Jesus saw him not so much with the gaze of bodily sight as with the eyes of inward compassion—the same eyes with which he looked upon Peter when he denied him, so that he might recognize his guilt. He therefore saw a man—that is, he had compassion on one who was devoted only to human pursuits. He saw him sitting at the tax office, clinging obstinately to temporal profits; for τέλος (*telos*) in Greek means *tax* or *tribute* in Latin. “Matthew,” it says, “by name.” *Matthew* in Hebrew is said in Latin to mean “given.” This name most fittingly suits him, since he received so great a gift of heavenly grace.

(Jerome.) Nor should we pass over the fact that the other evangelists, out of modesty and respect for Matthew, did not wish to call him by his familiar name, but called him Levi (Luke V); for he had a double name. Matthew himself, however, in accordance with Solomon’s instruction, is a righteous accuser of himself at the beginning of his account (Proverbs XVIII), and in another passage: “Declare your sins, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah XLIII). He calls himself Matthew and publican, to show his readers that no one ought to despair of salvation if he turns toward better things, since he himself was suddenly changed from a publican into an apostle.

(Bede.) For *Levi* is interpreted as “added” or “taken up.” This name too bears witness concerning the one to whom it was given. It signifies that he was taken up by the Lord through election and added to the number of the apostolic order.

(Augustine.) It should be noted that Matthew seems here to have omitted the account of his own calling. For it must be believed that Matthew was called before the sermon on the mountain. On that mountain Luke records that all twelve were chosen from among many disciples, and that they were called apostles.

And rising, he followed him.

In Luke’s Gospel this is written more fully: “And leaving everything, he followed him.” Matthew therefore understood what it truly means to follow God and, leaving everything, followed him; for to follow is to imitate. Thus, so that he might follow poor Christ not merely in bodily steps but in affection, he abandoned his possessions—he who had been accustomed to seize the possessions of others. Giving us a perfect model of renouncing the world, he left not only the profits of the tax office but also disregarded the danger that might have come from the rulers of the world, since he had left the accounts of the taxes incomplete and unsettled. He was led by so great a desire to follow God that he retained absolutely no regard or thought for this life.

(Jerome.) At this point Porphyry and the emperor Julian accuse either the ignorance of the historian who tells lies or the folly of those who immediately followed the Savior, as though they had followed any man who called them without reason, although such great works and signs had preceded him—works which the apostles undoubtedly saw before they believed. Certainly the very radiance and majesty of the hidden divinity, which also shone forth in the human face, could draw those who saw it toward him at the first glance. If it is said that such power exists in the lodestone and in amber that they draw rings, bits of straw, and splinters to themselves, how much more could the Lord of all creatures draw to himself those whom he wished! The Lord himself, who outwardly called Matthew by human speech to follow him, kindled him inwardly by divine inspiration so that he immediately followed the one calling him; and he himself invisibly taught him how he ought to follow. Therefore, by the merit of his obedience, while despising human affairs and abandoning them, he became a faithful steward of the Lord’s talents.

And it happened, as he reclined at table in the house, that behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining at table with Jesus and his disciples.

(Augustine.) Matthew did not specify whose house Jesus was dining in, but the evangelist Luke writes that Levi gave him a great banquet in his own house. This fittingly accords with the figures of the mysteries. One who receives Christ into the dwelling place within is fed with the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures. Thus the Lord willingly enters and reclines in the affection of the one who believes; and this is the spiritual banquet of good works, at which the rich people are in need while the poor feast.

(Bede.) Tax collectors, as their name itself shows, are those who exact public taxes, or those who lease the collection of taxes belonging to the treasury or to public affairs. Those also who pursue the profits of this world through commerce are designated by the same name.

(Jerome.) Those who saw that the tax collector had turned from sins to better things and had found a place for repentance did not therefore despair of salvation.

(Bede.) Nor do they come to Jesus while remaining in their former vices, as the Pharisees and scribes complain; rather, they come in repentance, as the evangelist Mark testifies in this passage, saying: “For there were many who also followed him” (Mark II).

(Jerome.) The Lord went to the banquets of sinners in order to have an opportunity to teach and to offer spiritual food to those who invited him. In fact, although he is frequently described as going to a banquet, nothing else is reported except what he did and what he taught there. Thus both the Lord’s humility in going to sinners and the power of his teaching in the conversion of the repentant are demonstrated.

And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

The Pharisees were held by a twofold error when they disparaged the teacher of truth for receiving sinners. They considered themselves righteous, although in the arrogance of pride they had departed far from righteousness; and they accused as unrighteous those who, by turning back from their sins, were already drawing quite near to righteousness. Blinded by envy of their brothers’ salvation, they recalled that Matthew had been a tax collector, and that many other tax collectors and sinners were reclining with the Lord. But they did not wish to remember that Matthew himself, as Luke writes, left everything he possessed and followed him. Nor did they consider that the other tax collectors and sinners were reclining with him in the intention of clinging to him thereafter.

In the mystical sense, through Matthew’s election and calling the faith of the nations is expressed. They formerly longed for the profits of the world, but now they are refreshed with the Lord at the banquets of charity and with the diligent devotion of good works. The arrogance of the scribes and Pharisees clearly signifies the envy of the Jews, who are tormented by the salvation of the nations. To them he himself says (Matthew XXI): “Truly I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God.”

(Augustine.) While tax collectors were dining with the Lord, the Pharisees, murmuring about the fast, boast of their fasting. Here the great difference between the law and grace is first made clear: those who follow the law suffer the eternal hunger of a fasting mind; but those who have received the word in the depths of their soul, refreshed by the abundance of heavenly food and the fountain, cannot hunger or thirst.

And when Jesus heard this, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”

(Jerome.) He rebukes the scribes and Pharisees, who, thinking themselves righteous, avoided the company of sinners. He calls himself a physician, who, in a wondrous manner of healing, was wounded for our iniquities, and “by his bruising we were healed” (Isaiah LIII). He calls “healthy” and “righteous” those who, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to the righteousness of God (Romans X), who presume upon the law and do not seek the grace of God. But he calls sinners “those who are sick”: they are overcome by awareness of their weakness and, seeing that they cannot be justified through the law, submit their necks in repentance to the grace of Christ.

When he adds, “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’” he also shows these same Pharisees, swollen with false righteousness, the counsel of correction. He warns them to seek the rewards of heavenly mercy for themselves through works of mercy, and not, by disregarding the needs of the poor, to trust that they can please God through the offering of sacrifices. He placed before them a testimony from the prophet and commanded them to go and learn it—going, that is, from the rashness of foolish condemnation to more diligent meditation on Holy Scripture, which commends mercy above all. Hence he also sets before them his own example of mercy, saying:

“For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

(Maur.) That is: “For this purpose I came—not to exalt those who falsely justify themselves with empty approval, but mercifully to gather those who repent of their sins.”

Someone may perhaps wonder how the Lord could say that he had not come to call the righteous but rather sinners, since it is plain to all readers that he also called many whom he found righteous according to the ordinances of the Mosaic law to the heights of evangelical preaching. If he called sinners alone and not also the righteous, Nathanael would certainly not have become a companion of his discipleship. When Nathanael first came to him, he considered him worthy of such great praise that he said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John I). If he did not call the righteous, he would not have Peter and Andrew in the citadel of the apostolate. They showed how ardently they burned with love of righteousness when, at the testimony of the Forerunner, they immediately rejoiced to see and hear God.

How, then, did he come to call not the righteous but sinners? Only because, as Luke says more explicitly when relating this event, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” God calls all the elect to the heavenly kingdom, but he calls to repentance only those whom he finds entangled in more serious sins. Those whom he finds in works of righteousness he does not call to repentance for their former way of life, but rather invites them to progress toward a more perfect life. He calls sinners so that they may be corrected through repentance; he calls the righteous so that they may be justified more and more.

It may also rightly be understood in this way: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” because he did not call those who, wishing to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to the righteousness of God. Rather, he called those who, conscious of their weakness, are not ashamed to confess that “we all offend in many things.” If he also calls some of those who were falsely righteous after they have been corrected and calls them to pardon, his saying will be fulfilled in them too: he did not come to call the righteous but sinners—that is, not the proud but the humble, not those inflated by their own righteousness but those who submit with devoted mind to the one who justifies the ungodly. Such people, when they are converted, must sincerely confess that they are not righteous but sinners.

The text continues:

### [III.]

Then the disciples of John came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, while your disciples do not fast?”

Matthew reports that John’s disciples themselves said this to the Savior, whereas Mark and Luke relate it as though some others—people concerned about this matter—had brought the question to him. From this it should be inferred that the question was put to the Lord by several groups: by the Pharisees, by John’s disciples, and by the dinner guests or any others who were troubled by the question of why John’s disciples and the Pharisees fasted while the Savior’s disciples did not fast.

(Jerome.) Here John’s disciples are especially blameworthy, not only because they boasted of their fasting, but also because they slandered the one whom they knew had been proclaimed by their teacher and joined themselves to the Pharisees, whom they knew had been condemned by him.

(Bede.) In the spiritual sense, the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, while Christ’s disciples eat and drink. For whether someone follows the works of the law or the traditions of human beings, or even hears Christ’s proclamation only with the bodily ear, if he abstains from spiritual goods he wastes away with a fasting heart. But one who is incorporated into Christ’s members by faithful love cannot fast, because he feasts on his flesh and blood.

Alternatively, John does not drink wine or strong drink, while the Lord eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners. John’s abstinence increases his merit because he possesses no power over nature; but the Lord, who naturally had the power to forgive sins, why would he avoid those whom he could make purer through abstinence? Christ fasted too, so that you would not reject the commandment; he ate with sinners, so that you might see grace and recognize power.

And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.”

(Augustine.) What Matthew calls “mourning,” Mark and Luke call “fasting.” Matthew himself later says, “Then they will fast,” not, “Then they will mourn.” By the word “mourning,” however, he indicated that the Lord was speaking of a kind of fasting that pertains to the humility of tribulation. The other kind, which pertains to the joy of a soul lifted toward spiritual things and therefore in a certain sense alienated from bodily foods, the Lord is understood to have signified through the later comparisons of the new patch and the new wine. He shows that this kind of fasting is suitable for those occupied with animal and bodily matters and therefore still drawing along their former understanding.

(Jerome.) Christ is the bridegroom, and the Church is the bride. From this holy and spiritual union the apostles were born. They cannot mourn or fast as long as they see the bridegroom in the bridal chamber and know that the bridegroom is with the bride. But when the wedding has passed and the time of the Passion and Resurrection has arrived, then the children of the bridegroom will fast.

(Bede.) It should be noted that this mourning over the bridegroom’s absence has not been celebrated only now—that is, after the death and resurrection of that same bridegroom—but also before his incarnation, throughout the entire span of this world. The earliest times of the Church, before the Virgin’s childbirth, had holy people who longed for the coming of the incarnation; the present times, since he ascended into heaven, have holy people who long for his manifestation to judge the living and the dead. Nor has this desirable mourning of the Church ever ceased, except for the period when he was bodily present with his disciples. According to the laws of allegorical interpretation, we should understand that as long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in joy, we can neither fast nor mourn. But when he has withdrawn and flown away from us because of our sins, then fasting must be proclaimed; then mourning must be taken up again.

No one puts a patch of raw cloth on an old garment. For it takes away part of its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear is made.

When the Lord was asked why his disciples did not fast, he replied that those who were still carnal and not yet strengthened by faith in his Passion and Resurrection could not bear the stricter fasts and commands of continence. Otherwise, through excessive austerity, they might lose even the faith that they seemed to possess. He therefore compares the disciples, who were still such, to old garments (Augustine). A new patch is improperly sewn onto them—that is, some portion of doctrine pertaining to the moderation of the new life. If this is done, the doctrine itself is in a certain sense torn apart: the portion of it that concerns abstinence from food is inopportunely handed on, since that doctrine teaches a general fasting, not only from the desire for food but from every joy of temporal pleasures. The Lord says that a patch of this cloth—that is, the portion pertaining to food—ought not to be given to people still devoted to their former customs, because it seems to create a tear in that former cloth and is also unsuited to their oldness.

Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined. Rather, they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.

He likewise compares the same people to old wineskins, saying that they would be more easily burst by new wine—that is, by spiritual commandments—than able to contain it. But they had become new wineskins when, after the Lord’s Ascension, they were renewed by praying and hoping for his consolation. Then they received the Holy Spirit. Filled with him, they spoke in every language, and the Jews, unknowingly but nevertheless truly bearing witness, said: “These men are full of new wine.” The new wine had already come to the new wineskins: that is, the fervor of the Spirit had filled their spiritual hearts.

(Jerome.) This allegory can also be understood in another way. The Savior gave two examples: that of garments and that of old and new wineskins. By the old garments and old wineskins we should understand the scribes and Pharisees. The patch of the New Testament and the new wine signify the evangelical commandments, which the Jews cannot bear without producing a greater tear. The Galatians also wanted to do something of this kind, mixing the commandments of the law with the Gospel and putting new wine into old wineskins. But the Apostle says to them (Galatians III): “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?” The evangelical word must therefore be poured into the apostles rather than into the scribes and Pharisees, who, corrupted by the traditions of their ancestors, could not preserve the purity of Christ’s commandments. The purity of a virginal soul, unstained by any contagion of former vice, is one thing; the filth of those subjected to the lusts of many is another.

(Augustine.) A teacher must therefore beware of entrusting the secrets of new mysteries to a soul that has not yet been renewed but continues in the oldness of wickedness. If someone asks what mystical difference there is between the new wine and the new garment, the answer is readily apparent: we are inwardly refreshed and intoxicated by wine, whereas we are clothed outwardly by a garment. Since both, however, pertain to the signification of spiritual life, the garment clearly signifies our good works, which we perform outwardly and by which we shine before human beings; while the new wine expresses the fervor of faith, hope, and charity by which, in the sight of our Creator, we ourselves are inwardly renewed in the newness of our understanding.

Matthew continues, preserving the order of events, and says:

## [IV]

While he was saying this to them, behold, one ruler approached and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.”

(Aug.) Mark (Mark 5) and Luke (Luke 8) say that this ruler was the ruler of the synagogue, named Jairus, who fell at Jesus’ feet and pleaded for the healing of his daughter. Matthew, however, reports that the ruler announced to the Lord not that his daughter was about to die, was dying, or was at the point of death, but that she was entirely dead; whereas the other two say that she was already near death, though not yet dead. This must be considered lest the accounts appear contradictory. We must understand that, for the sake of brevity, Matthew wished to say rather that Jesus was asked to do what it is evident that he did—namely, to raise the dead.
