For he attended not to the father’s words about his daughter but, more importantly, to his intention, and he used words corresponding to that intention. The father had despaired so completely that he wished her to live again, not believing that she could still be found alive, since he had left her dying. Thus the other two reported what Jairus said, while Matthew reported what he intended. Both things, therefore, were requested of the Lord: either that he save the dying girl or raise the dead one. But since Matthew had undertaken to relate the whole matter briefly, he conveyed that the father requested what he certainly intended, and what Christ performed.

Mystically, however, in this passage the ruler of the synagogue asks that his daughter be saved, but as the Lord proceeds to his house, a woman with a hemorrhage gets there first and takes the healing; then the ruler’s daughter reaches the desired healing—or rather, is recalled from death to life. The salvation of the human race is shown here: when the Lord came in the flesh, certain people from Israel first came to faith; then the fullness of the nations entered, and thus all Israel would be saved.

Who, then, is this ruler of the synagogue who comes to the Lord to plead for his daughter, more appropriately understood than Moses himself? Hence he is rightly called Jairus, that is, “illuminating” or “illuminated.” He received the words of life to give to us, and through them illuminates others; and he himself was illuminated by the Holy Spirit, so that he might teach what is vital and spiritual. Seeing Jesus, he fell at his feet, according to another Evangelist, because, foreseeing in the Spirit that God would come in the flesh, he subjected himself with a humble heart to his power. He recognized that he would become human toward the end of the age, yet did not doubt that he existed as eternal God before all ages. If God is Christ’s head, what more suitably are his feet understood to be than the humanity he assumed, by which he touched the earth of our mortality? The ruler of the synagogue’s falling at Jesus’ feet means that the lawgiver, together with the whole succession of the fathers, recognized and confessed with the Apostle (1 Cor. 1) that the weakness of God is stronger than human beings, and that the mediator of God and humanity was far superior to him in the glory of his dignity.

(Maur.) Let us hear what that ruler, worshiping the Lord, requested: “My daughter,” he said, “has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.” The ruler’s daughter is therefore the Synagogue itself, formed solely by the institution of the Law, as though she were Moses’ only daughter. Hence it is written in Luke’s Gospel that she was his only daughter, about twelve years old, and that she was dying. Her father now complains that she has died, because after the noble upbringing of the lawgiver and the instruction of the prophets, after she had reached the level of understanding, and after she ought to have given birth to spiritual offspring for God, she was suddenly struck down and extinguished by the death of sins, overwhelmed by the sickness of various errors. But our Redeemer came and, finding her dead, quickly recalled her to life by the right hand of his power. Observe that this ruler said, “Come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live,” whereas the centurion said, “Lord, only say the word, and my servant will be healed.”

And Jesus rose and followed him, along with his disciples. “For his salvation is near those who fear him” (Ps. 84), and he does not forget the voices of those who seek him. For when Jesus’ arrival with his teachers draws near, there the departure of death and the entrance of life immediately become manifest.

## [V]

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment.

(Bede.) The woman flowing with blood, but healed by the Lord, is the Church gathered from the nations. Polluted by the inborn flow of carnal pleasures, she had already been separated from the assembly of the faithful. But when she saw that God’s word was saving Judea, she seized, with confident hope, the salvation that had already been prepared and promised for others.

It should be noted that the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter was twelve years old, while this woman had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years—that is, at the very time when the girl was born, the woman began to be ill. For at almost the same period of this present age, the Synagogue began to be born in the patriarchs, while the nation of the foreign peoples throughout the world began to be defiled by the corruption of idolatry. The flow of blood may rightly be understood in two ways: both as the pollution of idolatry and as the deeds performed through the pleasure of flesh and blood. Thus, as long as the Synagogue flourished, the Church suffered. The decline of the one is the strength of the other, because through their trespass salvation came to the nations.

(Maur.) Nor is it without mystery that the daughter is requested first, yet the woman with the hemorrhage is healed first. Although the patriarchs and prophets had previously asked for the salvation of the Hebrews, the great faith of the nations nevertheless obtained the gift of salvation first.

(Hieron.) The ruler’s daughter dies in the city of the Law and is raised by that same Lord in the house where the worship and confession of the one God existed. But this woman flowing with blood approaches the Lord neither in a house nor in the city—for according to the Law she was excluded from cities—but on the road, while God was walking, so that as he went toward one, the other might be healed. Hence the Apostles say: “It was necessary that the word of God be preached to you; but since you judged yourselves unworthy of salvation, we are turning to the nations” (Acts 13).

Nor should we pass over the fact that Mark and Luke say that this same woman spent her possessions on physicians and could be healed by none. By physicians we may understand either false theologians, or philosophers and teachers of secular laws, who, arguing with great subtlety about virtues and vices, promised mortals useful rules for living and believing; or certainly the unclean spirits themselves, who, as though advising human beings, thrust themselves forward to be worshiped in place of God. The more eagerly the Gentiles extended the powers of their natural ingenuity in listening to these spirits, the less were they able to be cleansed from the filth of their iniquity.

But when this woman learned that the Jewish people were sick and that the true physician from heaven had arrived, she herself began both to hope for and to seek a remedy for her illness. The Church from the nations approaches and touches the Lord, drawing near to him through the truth of faith. She approaches from behind, either in accordance with what he himself says, “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12), and with the command, “You shall walk after the Lord your God”; or because, not seeing God present in the flesh, she began, after the sacraments of his temporal dispensation had been accomplished, to follow his footsteps by faith.

She touches the fringe of his garment and stops the flow of blood, because blessed—and truly worthy of commendation—is the one who touches even the outermost part of the word with the hand of faith. Very rare indeed is the one who deserves either to recline upon his breast or to anoint his head with pure nard. Great also was the one who said that he was unworthy to carry his sandals; and great was the woman who deserved to anoint his feet and wipe them with her hair.

For she was saying within herself: “If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved.”

(Maur.) These words were an inward utterance of the mind, proceeding from the root of faith; and therefore she rightly obtained salvation, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made” (Rom. 10), and, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (ibid.). She said, “If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved”: if I receive faith in his incarnation, I shall be cleansed from all the iniquity of my sins. She believed, she spoke, she touched.

(Hieron.) In these three forms every healing is obtained: in faith, word, and deed. According to the Law (Lev. 15), whoever touches a menstruating woman or a woman flowing with blood is unclean. She therefore touches the Lord so that she herself may also be healed of the defect of blood.

And Jesus turned and, seeing her, said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you.”

(Maur.) He turned from the severity of just judgment toward the generosity of his mercy, so that he might make vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath, and so that what he had promised through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you, says the Lord” (Zech. 3). He saw her—because those whom he foreknew and predestined, he also called (Rom. 8)—and said: “Take courage, daughter.”

Why did he command her to take courage? Because, if she had not possessed faith, she would not have sought salvation from him. But he demanded from her the strength and perseverance of faith, so that she might reach certain and true salvation, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

(Hieron.) He says, “Take courage, daughter, because your faith has saved you.” She is called “daughter” because her faith saved her. He did not say, “Your faith will save you,” but “has saved you.” In the very act of believing, you have already been saved.

And the woman was saved from that hour.

(Maur.) From the hour of the Lord’s coming, therefore, this woman began to have healing; and each day those who turn from unbelief to faith are saved, as the Lord daily increases those who are being saved into the same [community].

And when Jesus had come into the ruler’s house and had seen the flute players and the crowd making a tumult, he said: “Go away.”

(Hieron.) To this day the girl lies dead in the ruler’s house, and those who appear to be teachers are flute players, singing a funeral song. The crowd of Jews is not a crowd of believers but a crowd of those making tumult. Because the Synagogue lost the joy of the Lord’s indwelling through the fault of its unbelief, it lies dead, as it were, among mourners and those who lament. Yet heavenly mercy does not allow it to perish entirely. Rather, toward the end of the age, it will restore its remnant, according to the election of grace, to salvation and life. Hence it appropriately follows:

For the girl is not dead, but sleeping.

(Bede.) She was dead to human beings, who could not raise her, but to God she was sleeping. By his ordering, her soul lived after being received, while her flesh rested in preparation for resurrection. Hence Christian custom has established that the dead, whom we do not doubt will rise again, should be called “sleeping,” as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who are sleeping, so that you may not grieve as the others do, who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4).

In the allegorical sense also, although “the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18), nevertheless it may appropriately be said that the soul whom the Lord foreknew would be raised and destined for eternal life was dead to us but sleeping to him.

(Maur.) But because it is characteristic of unbelief not to assent to the truth but to resist it, the Evangelist displays the blasphemous disposition of the Jews’ minds, saying:

And they laughed at him.

This mockery demonstrates the fickleness and childishness of their understanding, the wantonness of their behavior, and the unbelief of their spirit. Concerning them it is written: “They tested me and mocked me; they gnashed their teeth at me” (Ps. 34).

And when the crowd had been put outside, he entered.

Because they preferred to mock the word of the one raising the dead rather than believe it, they are rightly excluded, as unworthy to see the power of the one who raises and the mystery of resurrection. They were not worthy to see the mystery of the one rising, since they mocked the one who raises with unworthy insults.

Morally, the crowd is also cast outside so that the girl may be raised. For unless the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the inner chambers of the heart, the soul lying dead within will not rise. While it scatters itself among countless thoughts of earthly desires, it cannot gather itself at all for self-contemplation.

Nor should I pass over the fact that, after the crowd had been expelled, according to Luke’s Gospel the Savior allowed no one to enter the house with him except Peter, James, and John, and the girl’s father and mother. By this he showed that divine mysteries are not to be revealed to blasphemers but to the faithful; not to mockers but to teachers who know that the power of the divine work must be honored, not mocked. Thus what the Savior himself says elsewhere might be fulfilled: “Wisdom has been justified by her children” (Matt. 11). After his resurrection he said to them: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1).

Let us hear what the Savior did after entering, for it follows:

And he took her by the hand, and the girl rose.

(Hieron.) He healed the girl by taking her hand, because unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, are first cleansed, their Synagogue will not rise from death.

(Bede.) There is also a pattern of wisdom here: in the widow’s son, the Church would soon believe; in the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, the Jews would indeed believe, but only a smaller number among them. “She rose,” and rightly “she walked.” For anyone whom the mercy of the heavenly hand touches in order to raise from death through sins must not only rise from the filth and oldness of his crime but also immediately advance in good works, according to the Psalmist: “Walking blamelessly and practicing righteousness” (Ps. 14).

And this report spread throughout that whole region.

(Maur.) “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands; their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18).

According to the moral understanding, those three dead whom the Savior raised bodily signify three kinds of resurrection of souls. We shall now explain more fully what we briefly anticipated in the preceding book.

Some, by consenting to evil pleasure while the thought remains hidden, bring death upon themselves through sins. To signify that he makes such people alive, the Savior raised the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, who had not yet been carried outside but was dead in the house, as though concealing a vice secretly in her heart.

Others not only consent to harmful pleasure but also carry out the very evil in which they delight. They carry their dead person outside the gates, as it were. To show that he raises such people if they repent, he raised the widow’s young son, who had been carried outside the city gates. “And he gave him to his mother” (Luke 7), because he restores the soul turning back from the darkness of sin to the unity of the Church.

Some, however, corrupt themselves not only by thinking or doing what is unlawful but also by burying themselves, as it were, in the very habit of sinning. Yet the Savior’s power and grace are not diminished when it comes to raising them, provided that there are anxious thoughts watching over their salvation like sisters devoted to Christ.

To signify this, he raised Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb and, as his sister testified, had already begun to stink—for an evil reputation commonly accompanies harmful deeds.

It should be noted that the heavier the death of the soul becomes, the more intense must be the penitent’s fervor if he is to deserve resurrection. Lighter and daily faults can be healed by the remedy of lighter penance. The Lord wished secretly to show this by raising the girl, who lay dead in an inner room, with the easiest and briefest utterance: “Girl, arise.” He had even denied that she was already dead because of the ease of raising her.

But when the dead young man had been carried outside, he strengthened him with several words so that he might return to life, saying: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” As for the four-day-old corpse, so that it might escape the long barriers of the oppressive tomb, Jesus groaned in spirit, troubled himself, shed tears, groaned again, and cried out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out!” (John 11). Thus at last the one who had been regarded as hopeless was restored to life and light after the burden of darkness had been shaken off.

It should also be noted that, because public wrongdoing requires a public remedy, while lesser sins can be erased by lighter and private penance, the girl lying in the house rises before only a few witnesses, and they are strictly commanded to tell no one. The young man is raised outside the gate in the presence and sight of a great crowd (Matt. 21). Lazarus, called from the tomb, became so widely known among the people that, because of the testimony of those who had seen him, very large crowds came to meet the Lord with palm branches, and many Jews departed because of him and believed in Jesus.

As for the fourth dead person, the Lord heard of him through a disciple; but because there were no living people to pray for his resurrection, he said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8)—that is, let evil people burden evil people with harmful praises. Since there is no righteous person present to rebuke them in mercy, “let the oil of the sinner make their head fat” (Ps. 140).

And as Jesus was passing on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” When he had come into the house, the blind men approached him.

As the Lord Jesus was passing through the ruler’s house and proceeding to his own house, as we read above—“He got into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city”—two blind men cried out, saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” Yet they were not healed on the road, nor in passing, as some think. Rather, after he came into his own house, they approached him and entered.

The ruler’s house, as we showed above, is the Synagogue of the Jews, subject to Moses. Jesus’ house is the heavenly Jerusalem. The two blind men are two peoples blinded by observance of the letter, by Gentile ritual, or by philosophical sects. They were ignorant and unaware of future and invisible things until they were deemed worthy to follow the path of the Scriptures and the footsteps of the Savior.

As the Lord passed through this age and desired to return to his own house, the two blind men followed him. For when the Gospel had been preached through the Apostles, many from the Jews and many from the nations began to follow the Redeemer, asking him to illuminate them with the light of true knowledge. But after the Savior had completed the mystery of his passion and resurrection and had ascended into heaven, the blind men entered his house—that is, the confession of one faith, which is found in the catholic Church—and there they were truly enlightened by the Savior.

(Hieron.) Let us consider what the blind men themselves cried out to the Savior: “Son of David,” they said, “have mercy on us.” They asked for mercy because they needed light. He truly shows mercy to those to whom he grants the light of faith and good works.

But when the blind men say, “Son of David,” let Marcion, Manichaeus, and the other heretics who tear apart the Old Testament listen and learn that the Savior is called the Son of David. For if he was not born in the flesh, how is he called the Son of David?

And Jesus said to them: “Do you believe that I am able to do this for you?”

(Maur.) Knowing their faith, he asks them so that faith may be brought forth by confession, confession followed by power, and salvation accompany that power. For, as the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

They said to him: “Certainly, Lord.”

Then he touched their eyes, saying: “According to your faith, let it be done for you.”

By saying “certainly,” they outwardly affirm what they desired to believe inwardly in their hearts. Therefore their firm profession deserved the touch of divine mercy. “According to your faith,” he says, “let it be done for you”—that is, because faith already illuminates the mind, let it itself restore the light of your eyes to you.

And their eyes were opened.

According to the prophet’s saying: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” For he is the true light who illuminates every human being coming into this world (John 1).

And Jesus sternly warned them, saying: “See that no one knows.”

But they went out and spread his fame throughout that whole region.

(Hieron.) Because of his humility, the Lord was fleeing the glory of ostentation, and for that reason he had given this command. But they, because they remembered the grace they had received, could not keep the benefit silent. Observe, therefore, that there is some opposition here between the command [variant: “the just thing”] and their action.

As they were going out, people brought him a mute man who had a demon; and when the demon had been expelled, the mute man spoke.

(Maur.) This man signifies the Gentile people, who were mute because they did not have the confession of true faith in their mouths. He was also deaf, because he did not consent to hear the Law of God. The Greek term is **κωφός** (*kōphos*), which is more commonly used in ordinary speech to mean “deaf” rather than “mute.” But it is the custom of Scripture to use **κωφός** indifferently for either “mute” or “deaf.”

This man had a demon because he was entirely devoted to idolatry. When he was brought to the Savior through the preachers of the holy Gospel, the error of paganism was removed, and he began to proclaim more clearly the confession of God’s name.

And the crowds marveled, saying: “It has never appeared thus in Israel.” But the Pharisees said: “By the ruler of demons he casts out demons.”

(Hieron.) The crowd confesses God’s works and says that nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel. In the crowd of the nations there is confession. But because the Pharisees could not deny God’s power, they slandered his works and said: “By the ruler of demons this man casts out demons.” Through their slander they continue to demonstrate the unbelief of the Jews to this day.

Matthew alone records this concerning the two blind men and the mute man possessed by a demon. Those two blind men whom the other Evangelists also mention are not these men, although a similar event occurred. If Matthew himself had not also recalled the other event, it could have been thought that what he now narrates had also been reported by the other two. We must carefully commit this to memory: some events are similar. This is demonstrated when the same Evangelist mentions both, so that whenever we find individual accounts of similar events in different Evangelists and encounter in them an apparent contradiction that cannot be resolved, we may understand that it was not the same event but another similar event, or one that happened in a similar way.

And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity.

(Hieron.) You see that he preached the Gospel equally in villages, cities, and towns—that is, among great and small—so that he considered not the power of the noble but the salvation of believers. He went around the cities, carrying out the work that the Father had commanded him and possessing this hunger: to save unbelievers through his teaching.

He taught the Gospel of the kingdom in the synagogues and villages, and after preaching and teaching he healed every disease and every infirmity, so that those whom the word had not persuaded might be persuaded by his works. It is said properly of the Lord that he healed every disease and every infirmity. Nothing is impossible for him.

When he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and lying about like sheep without a shepherd.

(Maur.) Jesus therefore looked upon the human race with the compassionate gaze of his mercy and had pity on it, because it was greatly harassed by various errors under the guidance of the devil and had no shepherds to direct it into the way of truth. For this reason he appointed shepherds and rulers for it—that is, the Apostles and their successors. For it is always necessary that Christ’s sheep have shepherds and teachers.

The devil goes about like a roaring lion, always seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 4). Whenever the flock, the sheep, and the crowds are harassed, it is the fault and vice of the shepherds and teachers who ought to have come to their aid. Hence it follows:

Then he said to his disciples: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest.”

The plentiful harvest signifies the multitude of peoples; the few workers signify the scarcity of teachers. He commands them to ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest. These are the workers of whom the Psalmist speaks: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. Going forth, they went and wept, scattering their seeds; but coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 25).

To speak more plainly: the plentiful harvest is the whole crowd of believers; the few workers are the Apostles and their imitators, who are sent into the harvest.

# CHAPTER X

He sends forth the twelve Apostles with power to heal every disease, with every teaching, and with the statement that he did not come to send peace but a sword, and so forth.

## [I]

And having summoned his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, so that they might cast them out and heal every disease and every infirmity.

(Bede.) This summoning of the Apostles was not the result of their own choice or zeal but of divine condescension and grace, so that they might be called to the apostolate. Hence he says to them elsewhere: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15).

He made them twelve in number, certainly because of the grace of the mystery, so that the salvation of the world, which they would preach in word, might also be commended by their number. For three times four makes twelve, and the Apostles were sent in groups of three times four to baptize the nations throughout the four quarters of the world in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28).

Hence it is written concerning the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven from God that it had three gates in the east, three gates in the north, three gates in the south, and three gates in the west. Figuratively this showed that, through the preaching of the Apostles and their successors, all the nations throughout the world would enter the Church in the faith of the holy Trinity.

In the same mystery, the children of Israel once camped around the Tabernacle in such a way that on every side, forming a square, three tribes remained. For the primitive Church, which was in Judea, was destined to establish spiritual camps for God, in faith and confession of the holy Trinity, among the believing nations of the whole world surrounding it.

Moreover, by saying, “He gave them power over unclean spirits, so that they might cast them out,” and so forth, he shows that the kind and merciful Lord and teacher does not begrudge his servants and disciples his own powers. Just as he himself had healed every disease and every infirmity, so he granted power to his Apostles.

But there is a great difference between possessing, giving, and receiving. Whatever he does, he does by the Lord’s power; whereas they, if they accomplish anything, confess both their own weakness and the Lord’s power, saying: “In the name of the Lord Jesus, rise and walk” (Acts 3).

Now the names of the twelve Apostles are these.

The catalogue of the Apostles is placed in the Gospel so that those who will be false apostles may be excluded from their number, and so that it may be signified that their names, together with those of those who follow their teaching and faith, are contained written in the book of life.

The first is Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother.

Simon is listed first, surnamed Peter, to distinguish him from the other Simon, who is called the Cananaean, from the village of Cana in Galilee, where the Lord changed water into wine. The Lord wished the leader of the Apostles to be called by another name first, so that the vitality of the mystery might be commended through the very change of name.

Thus what is called Peter in Latin is Cephas in Syriac; and in both languages the name is derived from “rock,” undoubtedly that rock of which Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). Just as Christ, the true light, granted the Apostles that they should be called the light of the world, so he bestowed on Simon, who believed in Christ the rock, the name Peter.

Alluding elsewhere to the etymology of the name, he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16). Some, therefore, violently seeking a Hebrew ἐτυμολογία (*etymologia*, “etymology”) for the Latin or Greek name, say that Peter means “dissolving,” “unshoeing,” or “recognizing.” But the Hebrew language itself, which does not pronounce the letter P at all, testifies that this is not a Hebrew name. By an abuse, they write *Fethrum* for *Petrus*, just as they write *Faulus* and *Filatus* for *Paulus* and *Pilatus*, and violently attach a false interpretation to a fictitious name.

Simon is interpreted as “obedient.”

Andrew, moreover, is a Greek name, **ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρός** (*apo tou andros*), that is, “from a man”; he is called “manly.” These names rightly adorn the first of the Apostles, who, as soon as they learned from John that he was called the Lamb of God, took care to see and hear him.

The interpretation of Simon as “placing grief” or “hearing sadness” suits the time when, after seeing the risen Lord, he laid aside the grief of either his death or his own denial, but immediately heard the sadness of his own death, when the Lord said: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21).

James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother.

(Hieron.) He also called James the son of Zebedee because another James, the son of Alphaeus, follows. He joins the two pairs of Apostles and associates them. He joins Peter and Andrew, brothers not so much in flesh as in spirit; and James and John, who, leaving their bodily father, followed the true Father.

(Bede.) James and John were surnamed by the Lord “sons of thunder,” that is, **Boanerges**, or, as it is more correctly written, **Beneragam**, as the Syriac Gospel has it, **benai regesi**, because of the outstanding height of their virtue and spirit, as it is written in Mark’s Gospel.

Not without reason: one of them, thundering from the heavenly heights, uttered that theological voice which no one before him had known how to produce: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and so forth (John 1). He left this pregnant with such power that, if he had wished to thunder somewhat more, the world itself could not have contained it.

Both of them also often deserved to be led apart by the Lord onto a mountain and at times to hear a terrifying sound from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son.”

They bore ancient names most suited to their merits. James means “supplanter,” while John means “in whom is grace” or “the grace of the Lord.” The former, when called by the Lord, supplanted the concern of the flesh and rejoiced to despise the flesh itself when Herod slew him. The latter, because of the special grace of love that he had merited through virginal glory, reclined upon the breast of his Redeemer at the supper.

Philip and Bartholomew.

Philip is interpreted as “mouth of a lamp,” and rightly so. For when he was called by the Lord, he immediately preached to Nathanael the light he had recognized, saying: “We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote: Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth” (John 1). Later, feeling that he knew too little concerning the light, he humbly asked: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14).

Bartholomew is Syriac, not Hebrew, and is interpreted as “son of the one who suspends the waters,” that is, the Son of God, who suspends the minds of his preachers so that they may contemplate heavenly things. The more freely they fly toward the heights, the more fruitfully they saturate earthly hearts with the drops of their words.

Hence Moses, speaking mystically about the Church, rightly says: “It is not like the land that you are entering to possess, like the land of Egypt from which you came, where, after the seed is cast, the waters are led in the manner of gardens for irrigation; but it awaits the rains from heaven, which its God visits at every time” (Deut. 11).

For secular wisdom crawls along the ground like a serpent, whereas divine wisdom thunders from the heavenly realms.

Thomas and Matthew the publican.

(Hier.) The other Evangelists place Matthew first when joining the names, and Thomas afterward, and they do not add the designation “publican,” lest, by recalling his former way of life, they might appear to reproach the Evangelist. But this Evangelist, as we said above, places himself after Thomas and calls himself a publican, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more.

(Bede.) Thomas means “abyss” or “twin”; hence in Greek he is called **δίδυμος** (*didymos*, “twin”). Because he doubted longer than the others, he learned the truth of the Lord’s resurrection more profoundly.

Of him Paulinus, bishop of Nola, beautifully sang:

> Here Thomas lies near, uncertain, Didymus by his double name;  
> Christ permitted him, through the hesitation of a fearful mind, to doubt for the sake of our faith,  
> So that we too, strengthened under this guide, might confess with trembling  
> Jesus as Lord and God, living after death in a true body,  
> Displaying the wounds of his living flesh.

Matthew is said to mean “given,” because, through the great gift of the Lord, he was transferred from being a tax-collecting publican to the office of an Apostle and Evangelist.

James of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. James, indeed, is the one who in the Gospel is called “the brother of the Lord,” because Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was the sister of Mary the mother of the Lord. This Mary the evangelist John calls Mary of Clopas, perhaps because Alphaeus was also called Clopas, or because Mary herself, after Alphaeus died following the birth of James, married Clopas. Ecclesiastical history relates that she bore him a son, Simeon, who was the Lord’s cousin because Clopas had been Joseph’s brother, and that Simeon ruled the Church at Jerusalem after James—whether this apostle Simon was that Simeon, or some other Simeon.

That James was rightly surnamed “son of Alphaeus,” that is, “of the learned one,” is attested by the apostles themselves, who immediately after the Lord’s Passion appointed him bishop of Jerusalem. That even before the shedding of blood he himself was a true overthrower of carnal desire is attested by Hegesippus, a historian living near the times of the apostles:

“After the apostles, James, the brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, received the Church at Jerusalem. Many men were called James; this holy man was called the *second martyr* (*δευτερομάρτυρ*). He drank neither wine nor strong drink, ate no flesh, was never shorn, was never anointed with oil, and never used a bath. To him alone it was then [alone permitted] to enter the Holy of Holies, since he did not wear woolen garments but linen ones; and he alone entered the temple and prayed on bended knees for the people, so persistently that his knees were believed to have acquired the hardness of camels.”

(Jerome.) Thaddaeus, however, is the apostle whom the evangelist Luke calls Judas of James, and who elsewhere is called Lebbaeus, which is interpreted as *corculus*, that is, “a cultivator of the heart.” We should believe that he was *three-named* (*τριώνυμον*), just as Simon was called Peter and the sons of Zebedee were called Boanerges on account of the firmness and greatness of their faith. For he was the brother of James, the brother of the Lord, as he himself writes in his Epistle. Hence he too was called the Lord’s brother, as his fellow citizens testify. Astonished at his miracles, they said: “Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joseph, and Judas, and Simon?” (Mark VI).

Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. He listed these two with an additional designation in order to distinguish Simon from Simon Peter and Judas from Judas of James. Simon the Cananaean received his surname from Cana, a village of Galilee. The evangelist Luke rendered the name with its interpretation, calling him “Simon the Zealot”: for *Chana* means “zeal,” and *Cananaean* is called *ζηλωτής*, that is, “zealot” or “emulator.”

Judas Iscariot either took his name from the village in which he was born, or from the tribe of Issachar, receiving in his name a portent of his condemnation. For Issachar, which means “reward,” suggests the price of his betrayal; whereas Iscariot, which is interpreted as “memory of death,” shows that he was not suddenly persuaded, but committed the crime of betraying the Lord after pondering it for a long time.

(Ambrose.) He was chosen among the apostles not through lack of foresight but through providence. For how great is the truth which even an adversarial minister cannot weaken? How great is the Lord’s moral wisdom, who preferred that his judgment should be endangered among us rather than his affection? For he had assumed human weakness, and therefore did not refuse even these aspects of human frailty. He wished to be abandoned, he wished to be betrayed, he wished to be handed over by his own apostle, so that when you are abandoned by a companion and betrayed by a companion, you may bear with moderation the fact that your judgment has erred and your benefit has perished.

[Col. 0891A] **II.** Jesus sent these twelve, commanding and saying to them.

(Jerome.) It must be observed that evangelical and apostolic Scripture does not call only those twelve his disciples, but all who, believing in him, were instructed by his teaching for the kingdom of heaven. From their multitude he chose twelve, whom he called apostles, as Luke records.

(Maur.) The Lord Jesus therefore sent twelve disciples to preach, because by many indications in figures they had previously been marked out by this same number as especially suited to administer the divine mysteries. These are the twelve true sons of Jacob (Genesis XXXV); these are the twelve princes of the people of Israel (Numbers I); these are the twelve springs found at Elim (Exodus XV); these are the twelve encampments from Rameses to Sinai (Exodus XII); these are the twelve stones in the priest’s vestment (Exodus XXVIII); these are the twelve loaves of the Presence (Leviticus XXIV); these are the twelve scouts sent by Moses (Deuteronomy I; Joshua III); these are the twelve leaders of the people who entered the land (ibid.); these are the twelve stones of the altar (Joshua IV); these are the twelve stones lifted from the Jordan (ibid.); these are the twelve stones brought to the same place (ibid.); these are Solomon’s twelve prefects (1 Kings IV); these are the twelve oxen beneath the bronze sea (1 Kings VII); these are the twelve young lions on Solomon’s throne (1 Kings X); these are the twelve stars in the bride’s crown (Revelation XII); these are the twelve foundations (Revelation XXI); these are the twelve gates of the city of God (ibid.); these are the twelve months of the year (Revelation XXII); these are the twelve hours of the day; these are the arrows sent from the hand of the Mighty One into the hearts of the king’s enemies (Psalm XLIV). Through them our Peacemaker defeated the prince of the world and plundered his vessels. Let us hear, then, what he commanded them at that time:

“Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the towns of the Samaritans. But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

(Jerome.) This passage is not contrary to the command given later: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII). For the former command was given before the Resurrection, and it was necessary that Christ’s first coming be announced to the Jews, lest they have a just excuse, saying that they had rejected God because he had sent apostles to the Gentiles and Samaritans. Thus, after the preaching of the apostles had first been rejected by Judaea, it would then become our assistance, when that proud people had rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.

(Gregory.) So that, when she refused the call to conversion, the holy preachers might proceed in due order to the calling of the Gentiles. Thus the preaching of our Redeemer, rejected by his own people, would seek the Gentile nations as outsiders; and what happened to Judaea as a testimony would become an increase of grace for the Gentiles.

(Jerome.) In the tropological sense, however, we are commanded—those who are reckoned by the name of Christ—not to walk on the road of the Gentiles or in the error of heretics, so that, since their religion is separated, their life too may be separated.

(Maur.) Rather, let us strive that whoever among us—that is, among the faithful—has withdrawn from the dwelling of the Church through serious sin may return to it again through the lamentation of repentance.

“Go and preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven is near.”

(Gregory.) The kingdom of heaven is said to draw near through the faith in the invisible Creator bestowed upon us, not through any movement of the elements. For just as it was said to the sinful human being, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis III), so each person is what he loves. The righteous person, by contrast, is heaven, because he bears God within himself and loves heavenly things. God, who is unbounded, without location, and present everywhere in power but not in body, nevertheless walks locally in his saints, as he says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians VI). In this way earthly human beings become heavenly angels. To such people the Lord says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII; John XIV). Those may finally be called heavens who retain him by faith and love him in charity. To them the Son likewise promises that he will come with the Father and the Holy Spirit and make his dwelling with them. They are rightly called heavens, in whom God presides.

“Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, drive out demons: you received without payment; give without payment.”

Lest anyone refuse to believe men who were rustic, lacking elegance of speech, uneducated, and illiterate when they promised the kingdom of heaven, he gave them power to heal the sick, cleanse lepers, drive out demons, and perform the other works of power, so that the greatness of the signs might prove the greatness of the promises, the power displayed might give credibility to their words, and those who preached new things might perform new deeds.

Hence now also, although the number of the faithful has increased, there are many within the holy Church who possess a life of virtue but do not possess signs of power, because a miracle is displayed outwardly to no purpose if what should work inwardly is absent.

(Maur.) For, according to the saying of the apostle to the Gentiles, tongues are for a sign to unbelievers, not to believers. Nevertheless, the holy Church daily does spiritually what it then did bodily through the apostles. It heals the sick when, through its priests, it anoints the sick with consecrated oil in the Lord’s name, pouring out prayer to God for them at the same time so that they may receive health. It likewise does this among the rest of the faithful when it sees anyone weakened in the condition of a good work, striving through pious exhortation and example to restore such a person to his former state.

It also raises the dead when it calls unbelievers to faith or awakens those dead in sins to repentance and the practice of virtues. It cleanses lepers when it does not cease to lead those stained with various blemishes of error to the unity of faith and the purity of truth. It drives out demons when, through the grace of exorcism, it expels them from possessed persons and does not allow evil spirits to dominate their minds.

(Jerome.) But because spiritual gifts always become less valuable if payment is interposed, a condemnation of avarice is added: “You received without payment,” he says, “give without payment.” It is as though he said openly: “I, your teacher and Lord, bestowed this upon you without a price; give it also without a price, lest the grace of the Gospel be corrupted.”

[Col. 0892D] **III.** Do not possess gold, or silver, or money in your belts, no bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff. For the worker is worthy of his food.

He consequently gives this command to the preachers of truth, to whom he had previously said: “You received without payment; give without payment.” If they preach without receiving payment, then possession of gold, silver, and coins is superfluous. For if they had gold and silver, they would seem to preach not for the sake of human salvation but for the sake of profit.

Nor any bronze in your purses: he who had almost cut away riches also cuts away the necessities of life, so that the apostles, who instructed that everything should be governed by providence, might show that they thought nothing of the following day.

No bag for the road: by this command he condemns the philosophers commonly called *Bactroperitae*, who, although they despise the world and count everything as nothing, carry a storeroom with them.

Nor two tunics: by “two tunics,” it seems to me, he indicates a double garment—not that in the icy, snowbound regions of Scythia anyone should be content with a single tunic, but that by “tunic” we should understand clothing, so that we do not put on one garment while reserving another for ourselves through fear of the future.

Nor sandals: Plato too commands that the two extremities of the body should not be covered, and that softness of head and feet should not be cultivated. When these have acquired firmness, the rest are stronger.

Nor a staff: if we have God’s help, why should we seek the protection of a staff? And because he had sent the apostles to preach in a certain sense naked and unencumbered, and the condition of the teachers seemed harsh, he tempered the severity of the command with the following sentence: “The worker is worthy of his food.” “Take,” he says, “only as much as is necessary for your food and clothing.” Hence the Apostle also says of himself: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content.” And elsewhere: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.” Thus those whose disciples reap spiritual things should make them participants in their material goods—not through avarice, but according to necessity.

We must consider that one work of ours is owed two rewards: one on the road, the other in the homeland; one sustains us in labor, the other rewards us in the resurrection, making us rejoice in the vision of Truth itself.

(Jerome.) We have spoken of these matters historically. In the anagogical sense, however, teachers may not possess gold, silver, or money kept in belts. We often read gold as signifying understanding, silver as speech, and bronze as voice. We may not receive these things from others, but must possess them as gifts given by the Lord. Nor may we accept the teachings of heretics, philosophers, or perverse doctrine; nor be weighed down by the burden of the world; nor be double-minded; nor have our feet bound by deadly chains. Rather, as we enter the holy land, we must be naked. Nor should we have a staff that turns into a serpent—that is, we must not rely on any bodily support; for such a staff is a reed, which, if pressed even slightly, breaks and pierces the hand of the one leaning upon it.

(Augustine.) It is often asked how Matthew and Luke can have recorded that the Lord told the disciples not to carry a staff, when Mark says that he commanded them (Mark VI) to take nothing on the road except a staff. The matter is resolved by understanding that the staff is mentioned with different meanings: one is to be carried according to Mark, while the other is not to be carried according to Matthew and Luke. The same distinction applies to the word “temptation”: in one sense it is said, “God tempts no one” (James I), and in another, “The Lord your God is tempting you, to know whether you love him.” The former is seduction; the latter is testing.

Both statements, therefore, must be understood as having been spoken by the Lord to the apostles: both that they should not carry a staff and that they should carry nothing but a staff. For when, according to Matthew, he said to them, “Do not possess gold or silver,” and so forth, he immediately added: “For the worker is worthy of his food.”

Thus he sufficiently showed why he did not want them to possess and carry these things: not because they were unnecessary for sustaining this life, but because he was sending them in such a way as to show that these things were owed them by those to whom they announced the Gospel and who believed it.

It is clear that God did not command this as though evangelists were not to live from any other source than what was supplied by those to whom they preached the Gospel. Otherwise the Apostle would have acted against this command (1 Corinthians IV), since he supported himself by the labor of his own hands so as not to be a burden to anyone. Rather, the Lord granted them the authority by which they might know that these things were owed them. When something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is the fault of disobedience; but when authority is granted, anyone may choose not to use it and may, as it were, surrender his right.

Thus, in establishing the arrangement that the Apostle says he established—that those who announce the Gospel should live from the Gospel—the Apostle was saying that they should confidently possess and carry none of the necessities of this life, neither great nor small. Therefore he said “nor a staff,” showing that all things were owed by the faithful to their ministers, who sought nothing superfluous. By adding, “The worker is worthy of his food,” he made entirely clear and illuminated the source of all these statements.

He therefore signified this authority under the name of the staff when he said, “They should take nothing on the road except a staff,” so that it might be understood that, through the authority received from the Lord and signified by the name of the staff, even those things that are not carried will not be lacking.

The same must be understood concerning two tunics: none of them should think that, besides the one he was wearing, he ought to carry another, anxious that it might be needed, since he could receive one by virtue of that authority.

Accordingly, when Mark says that they should wear sandals or soles, this footwear suggests a mystical meaning: the foot should be neither covered nor bare to the earth—that is, the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rest upon earthly advantages. And when he prohibits them not from carrying or possessing two tunics but, more explicitly, from putting on two tunics, saying, “Nor should they be clothed in two tunics,” what does he admonish them except to walk not in a double-minded but in a simple manner?

The preacher, therefore, must have such great trust in God that, although he does not foresee the expenses of the present life, he nevertheless knows with complete certainty that they will not be lacking to him, lest, while his mind is occupied with temporal matters, he provide less adequately for the eternal needs of others. Luke also attests that he is not permitted to greet anyone along the road, so that the great haste with which he must travel the road of preaching may be shown.

If anyone wishes to understand these words of the Gospel more fully through allegory, let him take gold as signifying the understanding of secular wisdom, silver as the eloquence of rhetorical art, and money enclosed in a belt as hidden wisdom. Whoever therefore possesses the word of wisdom but neglects to distribute it to his neighbor is like one who keeps money tied up in a belt. Hence it is written: “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what benefit is there in either?” (Ecclesiasticus XX).

What else are bags than the burdens of the world? And what else are sandals in this passage than examples of dead works? Whoever has undertaken the office of preaching ought not to carry the burden of secular business, lest, while this weighs down his shoulders, he fail to rise to proclaim heavenly things. Nor should he look upon examples of foolish works, lest he believe that he can protect his own works, as it were, with dead skins.

Everyone who greets along the road greets because of the occasion of the journey, not out of eagerness to obtain that same salvation. Whoever therefore preaches salvation to his hearers not out of love for the eternal homeland but from desire for rewards is like one who greets along the road, because he wishes salvation for his hearers by occasion rather than by intention.

“Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart.”

(Jerome.) Paul speaks concerning the ordination of a bishop and a deacon: “They must also have a good testimony from those who are outside.” When the apostles entered a new city, they could not know who or what sort of person each one was. Therefore a host must be selected according to the judgment of the people and of the neighbors, lest the dignity of the preaching be disfigured by the infamy of its recipient.

Although they must preach to everyone, one host is chosen—not because he is bestowing a great benefit on the one who will stay with him, but because he is receiving one. For this is what is meant: “Who is worthy in it?”—so that he may know that he is receiving grace rather than giving it.

(Ambrose.) By saying, “Remain there until you depart,” he gives a general command concerning constancy, so that they may observe the obligations of hospitality. He declares that running from house to house is foreign to the preaching of the kingdom of heaven and causes one to lose the inviolable rights of hospitality. Nor is it without purpose that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles enter is to be selected, so that no occasion may arise for changing their lodging and violating the obligations of hospitality.

“Upon entering a house, greet it, saying: Peace to this house. And if the house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you.”

He has discreetly expressed the greeting of the Hebrew and Syriac languages. (Jerome.) What is called *χαῖρε*, and in Latin *ave*, is expressed in Hebrew and Syriac as *salomiach* or *salomalach*, that is, “Peace be with you.”

What he commands is this: “When you enter a house, invoke peace upon the host, and, as far as lies within you, calm the wars of discord. But if opposition arises, you will receive the reward for the peace you offered; they will possess the war they wished to have.”

(Maur.) For the peace offered from the preacher’s mouth either rests in the house if a son of peace is present there, or returns to the same preacher. Either a person will be predestined to life and will follow the heavenly word he hears, or, if no one wishes to listen, the preacher himself will not be without fruit, because the peace returns to him, since the Lord repays him for the labor of his work.

“And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you leave that house or city, shake the dust from your feet.”

(Jerome.) The dust is shaken from the feet as a testimony to their labor: they entered the city, and the apostolic preaching reached as far as those people. Or the dust is shaken off so that they may receive nothing from them—not even the necessities of food—because they rejected the Gospel.

(Augustine.) They are commanded to do this either as a testimony to the earthly labor that they had undertaken for them in vain, or to show that they sought nothing earthly from them to such an extent that they would not even allow the dust of their earth to cling to them.

In another sense, the disciples’ feet signify the very work and progress of preaching. The dust with which they are sprinkled signifies the lightness of earthly thought, from which even the highest teachers cannot be entirely free when, concerned for their hearers, they devote themselves without ceasing to salutary cares and, as it were, travel the roads of the world, scarcely gathering even a speck of earth’s dust upon their heel.

Those who receive the word turn the afflictions and cares of their teachers, which the teachers endured for their sake, into an argument for their own humility. But those who despise the teachers’ doctrine turn the teachers’ labors, dangers, and weariness of concern into testimony to their own condemnation. This is the dust that is shaken from those who despise the Gospel, and from which the feet of evangelists are commanded to be washed by good hearers—indeed, the feet are said to have been washed by the Savior himself.

“Amen I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city.”

(Maur.) For they despised only one law, namely, the law of nature. The Jews, however, despised both the law of nature and the written law; they did not believe the words of the prophets and did not receive the preaching of the apostles.

It should also be noted that the Sodomites, amid all the sins of flesh and soul in which they burned insatiably, were also inhospitable, as Ezekiel testifies (Ezekiel XVI). Yet no guests such as the prophets among the Jews, or such as the apostles, were found among them. Lot was righteous in sight and hearing (Genesis XVIII), but he is not reported to have taught anything there or to have performed any signs. Therefore, “from the one to whom much has been given, much will be demanded” (Luke XII), and “the powerful will suffer powerful torments.” Thus, just as there are different rewards among the righteous, so there are different punishments among sinners.

“Behold, I send you like sheep in the midst of wolves.”

“Behold,” he says, “I send you”—that is, I who foreknew you and chose you from the world, who taught you, who know everything that is going to happen to you, and who will restore to you a fitting reward when the future comes. I myself will make you, according to your name, sent forth from being disciples; for *apostles* means “those who are sent.”

“Behold,” he says, “I send you like sheep in the midst of wolves.” Since you are my sheep, I wish you to possess gentleness and humility, and not to lose your patience and steadfastness because of the sedition and threats of persecutors.

(Jerome.) He calls the scribes and Pharisees wolves, for they are the clerics of the Jews.

(Gregory.) It should be observed that the Lord’s statement according to Matthew agrees with the statement according to John: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John VI). The Father sent the Son, ordaining that he become incarnate for the redemption of the human race. He wished him to come into the world for suffering, yet he loved the Son whom he sent to suffer.

The Lord likewise sent the chosen apostles into the world not for the world’s joys but, just as he himself was sent, for sufferings. Thus, just as the Son is loved by the Father and yet is sent to suffer, so the disciples are loved by the Lord and yet are sent into the world to suffer.

When he says, “Behold, I,” this expresses the authority and strength of the Godhead among human beings: “I, God, send you, human beings. I who sent prophets to your fathers now send you equally to Jews and Gentiles.”

It should also be noted that, by one and the same command at one and the same time, they are instructed how to act among unbelieving Jews and Gentiles alike: “Like sheep in the midst of wolves.” These animals are opposed to one another, so that one is devoured by the other. But the good shepherd does not know how to fear wolves for his flock.

Therefore these disciples are sent not for prey but for grace, so that, while preserving the sense of innocence, they may not possess the bite of malice. For one who undertakes the place of preaching ought not to inflict evil but to endure it.

“Therefore be wise as serpents and simple as doves.”

(Jerome.) So that through prudence they may avoid snares and through simplicity may not create them, the cunning of the serpent is set forth as an example. Since the serpent conceals its head with its whole body and protects the part in which its life lies, so we too should guard our head, which is Christ, through every danger to the body.

(Maur.) Likewise, the serpent is said to possess prudence because it stops up its ears so as not to hear those who cast spells. For they seek the poisons in the heads of serpents for medicinal purposes. But the serpent, anticipating this, hides its head by coiling it within the spirals of its body, places one ear against a rock, and closes the other with its tail.

So the apostolic man, having gathered his entire life together as though within the circles of time, places it around the principal part of the soul. And, so that this part may remain unharmed, with the help of Christ, who is the rock, and through the subtle instruction of Scripture, signified by the tail, he strives with great care to fortify it.

Those who cast spells are those who persuade people toward bodily pleasures and gently and smoothly indulge sinners, so that they may soften the mind’s vigor within them.

Another kind of prudence is also attributed to the serpent: when it is burdened with scales, decay, and leprosy, it enters a cleft in the rocks or a narrow opening, so that it may strip off its old skin and lay aside whatever harms it, and thus emerge healthy.

[Col. 0898A] This is properly the Christian practice: through the narrowness of repentance, to strip off the old human being with his deeds, who contains within himself the leprosy of sin, and to put on the new human being, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth (Ephesians IV), who knows no corruption of guilt.

The simplicity of doves is more explicitly demonstrated by the example of the young. Hence the Apostle also says: “Be children in malice” (1 Corinthians XIV). We interpreted the genuine form of this simplicity morally above.

“But beware of human beings.”

Now he shows whom he previously called wolves. They are human beings—the same people who are also wolves—because they are sinners and fragile, yet ferocious.

“For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will be led before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.”

(Gregory.) This was either the sole or the greatest cause of the Jewish people’s destruction: after killing the Lord and Savior, they also persecuted the heralds and confessors of his name with impious cruelty.

Luke records the Lord as saying to the apostles, “It will happen to you for a testimony,” whereas Matthew has, “As a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.” This signifies that the persecution of Christ’s name becomes a testimony not only against the Jews and Gentiles on account of their wickedness, but also for the apostles themselves, as testimony to their innocence.

Whose testimony is being given, if not that of those who either inflict death by persecuting or fail to imitate when they see? The death of the righteous is an aid to the good, but a testimony against the wicked, so that the perverse perish without excuse through the very thing from which the elect take an example in order to live.

But when weak hearts could be troubled by so many terrors, consolation is added, as he immediately continues:

“When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak. For it will be given to you in that hour what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

It is as though he openly said to his weakened members: “Do not be terrified; do not be afraid. You approach the struggle, but I do the fighting.”

(Jerome.) “You utter the words, but I am the one who speaks. Therefore, when we are led before judges because of Christ, we must offer only our will for Christ. As for the rest, Christ himself, who dwells in us, will speak on his own behalf, and the Holy Spirit will supply grace in our answer.”

“A brother will hand over a brother to death, and a father his son; children will rise up against parents and put them to death, and you will be hated by all because of my name.”

(Gregory.) We often see this happening in persecutions, and there is no faithful affection among those whose faiths are different. Yet evils inflicted by strangers cause less pain; the torments we suffer from those whose minds we trusted wound us more deeply. For when bodily harm is added, these evils torture us more severely.

Hence, concerning Judas his betrayer, the Lord says through the Psalmist: “Indeed, if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have borne it; but you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food, we walked in the house of God with agreement” (Psalm LIV).

And again: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has magnified his deception against me” (Psalm XL).

It is as though he openly says concerning his betrayer: “I endured his transgression all the more grievously because I experienced it from one who seemed to be mine.”

All the elect, therefore, because they are members of the supreme Head, follow their Head in his sufferings, so that in their own death they may experience the hostility of those whose life they had trusted. Their reward for their work increases in proportion as the gain of their virtue advances through the loss of another’s charity.

“And you will be hated by all because of my name,” he says, because “all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ”; and lovers of the world have become enemies of God.

“But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

By the command of the Law, the tail of the sacrificial victim is ordered to be offered in sacrifice. The tail is the end of the body, and the one who brings sacrifice well is the one who carries the sacrifice of a good work through to the end of the required action.

Thus, in this saying about perseverance, the Lord teaches the virtue of steadfastness and patience: it is not beginning or doing a virtuous act, but completing it, that constitutes virtue.

The evangelist Luke also expresses the same thing in other words of the Lord, saying: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI).

(Gregory.) Indeed, patience is the root and guardian of all virtues. Through patience we possess our souls, as we learn to rule over ourselves; thus we begin to possess precisely what we are.

“But when they persecute you in this city, flee to another.”

(Jerome.) This refers to the time when the apostles were being sent to preach. To them it was specifically said: “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans” (Matthew X). They were not to fear persecution, but they were to avoid it. We saw believers do this at the beginning, when persecution arose in Jerusalem and they were scattered throughout all Judaea, so that the occasion of tribulation might become the seedbed of the Gospel.

“Amen I say to you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes.”

(Maur.) He foretells that they would not bring all the cities of Israel to faith by their preaching before the Lord’s Resurrection had taken place and authority to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world had been granted.

(Jerome.) Spiritually, however, we can say: When they persecute you in one city—that is, in one book or testimony of the Scriptures—let us flee to other cities, that is, to other volumes. And however contentious the persecutor may be, the protection of the Savior will arrive before victory is granted to the adversaries.

“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher and for the servant to be like his lord.”

It is as though he said: “What I, your teacher and Lord, suffer, you, my disciples and servants, should not disdain to suffer. If I, the teacher, though I could certainly as God have avenged my injuries, did not wish to do so, but preferred to make my persecutors gentler by suffering, then you disciples, who are mere human beings, must necessarily follow the same rule of perfection.”

“If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more will they call those of his household so?”

Behold, the Lord and teacher shows his disciples and servants the insults directed against him, so that by his example they may learn to endure patiently the injuries of the wicked. Thus what he said above would be fulfilled: “It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher and for the servant to be like his lord.”

He calls himself the master of the house before whom the households of heaven, earth, and the underworld bow the knee. The unbelief of the Jews blasphemed by saying that he cast out demons through Beelzebub, the prince of demons. It is therefore no wonder if, through the same impulse of wickedness, they slander his household, to whom he himself promised the kingdom of heaven.

(Jerome.) It should be noted that Beelzebub is the idol of Ekron, called in the Book of Kings the idol of the fly. *Bel* itself is Beel or Baal, while *zebub* means “fly.” They called the prince of demons by the name of the most filthy idol, which is called “fly,” because of the uncleanness that destroys the fragrance of oil.

“Therefore do not fear them.”

The following passages will show why he prohibited the disciples from fearing their persecutors: because the empty and fragile thing soon falls away.

Nothing, indeed, is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known. (Jerome) How is it, then, that in the present age the faults of many are unknown? Rather, this is written concerning the future time, when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, illuminate the secrets of darkness, and make the counsels of hearts manifest. The meaning is: Do not fear the savagery of persecutors or the fury of blasphemers, because the day of judgment will come, on which both your virtue and their wickedness will be demonstrated.

What I say to you in the darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the rooftops. What you have heard in secret, proclaim more openly; what you learn privately, speak publicly. What I have taught you in a small place of Judea, proclaim boldly in all the cities, throughout the whole world. (Bede) In saying, “Proclaim upon the rooftops,” he is speaking according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where people ordinarily sit on rooftops. For their roofs are not raised with gabled peaks according to our custom, but are made level and flat; hence the Law commands that anyone building a new house should place a wall around the roof, lest innocent blood be shed there if someone should slip and fall headlong. In the construction of the Temple, too, we read: “He also covered the house with cedar ceilings and built a paneling five cubits high over the whole house” (2 Kings 6). Therefore what is proclaimed upon the rooftops is what will be spoken openly for all to hear.

And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. If persecutors of the saints, once their bodies have been killed, have nothing further to do against them, then those who, in a superfluous frenzy, throw the dead limbs of martyrs to be torn apart by beasts and birds, or have them dispersed into the air, dissolved in the waves, or reduced to ashes by flames, rage in vain: for they cannot in any way resist the omnipotence of God, which will bring them to life by raising them again.

But rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. The name “Gehenna” is not found in the ancient books, but is first used by the Savior. Let us therefore inquire into the occasion of this expression. We read more than once that the idol of Baal stood near Jerusalem, at the foot of Mount Moriah, where the waters of Siloam flow. This valley and its small irrigated plain were wooded and full of delights, and a grove in it was consecrated to the idol. The people of Israel had fallen into such madness that, abandoning the vicinity of the Temple, they sacrificed victims there; pleasures overcame the severity of religion, and they burned their sons to the demon or initiated them into its rites. That place was called Gehennon, that is, “the valley of the sons of Hinnom.” The Book of Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah describe this very fully. God also threatens that he will fill that place with the corpses of the dead, so that it will no longer be called Topheth and Baal, but Polyandrum, that is, “a burial-place of the dead.” Thus future punishments and the everlasting penalties by which sinners are to be tormented are signified by the name of this place. That Gehenna is twofold—of fire and of cold—we read at length in Job.

Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion, and not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father? The Lord’s discourse holds together, and what follows depends upon what came before. A prudent reader should always beware of superstitious interpretation, so that you do not adapt the Scriptures to your own opinion, but join your understanding to the Scriptures and grasp what follows. Above he had said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” Now he speaks accordingly: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion, and not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father?” The meaning is: If small and worthless animals do not fall without God as their author, and if providence is present in everything, so that even what is destined to perish in them does not perish without God’s will, then you, who are eternal, ought not to fear that you live without God’s providence. This is the same meaning as was stated above.

It should be noted, however, that while Matthew says, “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion,” Luke mentions not an assarion but a dipondius: “Are not five sparrows sold for two assaria?” (Luke 12). A dipondius, therefore, for which five sparrows are sold—that is, exchanged—is a kind of very light weight composed of two assaria. The numerical difference is immaterial; the dipondius is the unit immediately following the assarion. These numbers are weights and belong to the system of weighing. What is called “one” in cardinal numbering is called an as or assis in weight; what is “two” there is called a dussis or dipondius here. Some, rather forcedly, interpret the two sparrows as soul and body; and the five sparrows, according to Luke, which are sold for two assaria, they refer to the senses. But how that interpretation can be fitted to the body of the Gospel saying is not a small difficulty. Someone may perhaps ask how the Apostle can say, “Is God concerned about oxen?” (1 Cor. 9), since an ox is certainly more valuable than a sparrow. But concern is one thing, and knowledge another. Finally, concerning the number of hairs, he says next:

But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. (Bede) This is understood not as an act of counting, but as a capacity for knowledge. God does not keep watch with the anxious care of one who counts; rather, because all things are known to him, all things are as though numbered. (Jerome) Yet they are rightly said to be numbered, because we count what we wish to preserve. Here he demonstrates God’s immense providence toward human beings and signifies his ineffable affection: nothing of ours is hidden from God, and even small and idle words do not escape his knowledge. (Augustine) Those who deny the resurrection of the flesh ridicule the ecclesiastical understanding of this passage, as though we said that the very earthly material which, when the soul departs, becomes a corpse must be restored in the resurrection in such a way that whatever disintegrates and is transformed into the various forms and shapes of other things—though it returns to the body from which it fell away—must also return to the same bodily parts where it had been. Otherwise, if the hair returns as hair after being removed by such frequent cutting, and the nails return as nails after being so often cut away by immoderate and indecorous trimming, an unseemly deformity presents itself to the thoughts of those who deny the resurrection of the flesh. But just as, if a statue of any meltable metal were liquefied by fire, crushed into powder, or mixed into a mass, and an artisan wished to restore it from the quantity of that material, it would make no difference to its integrity which particle of the material was returned to which limb of the statue, provided that he recovered the whole amount from which it was restored, so God, the wonderfully and ineffably skilled artisan, will restore our flesh with wondrous and ineffable speed from the whole substance of which it had consisted. Nor will it matter for its restoration whether hair returns to hair and nails to nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and restored to other bodily parts, since the artisan’s providence takes care that nothing improper occurs.

[Col. 0902D] Therefore do not fear, because you are worth more than many sparrows. (Maurice) He says “worth more” because they are rational, because they were created in the image of God, and because they are eternal. The irrational animals were created for the sake of human beings, so that human beings might have nourishment and service—not human beings for the sake of the animals.

Everyone, therefore, who acknowledges me before human beings, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. (Hilary) “Acknowledgment” here is to be understood in the sense of which the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).
