Since the Lord had earlier declared, “Behold, I am sending you like sheep among wolves,” and again, “They will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you, and you will be hated by everyone because of my name,” lest anyone terrified by persecutions should say to himself: “If I am not permitted to declare among human beings the faith that I owe to God alone, nevertheless I preserve it for him in my heart; I cannot declare it outwardly because of the fury of persecutors”—to this weak thought the Lord replies, saying: “Whoever denies me before human beings,” that is, denies that I was born, suffered, and died, “I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.” Even pagans cannot deny that God exists; yet no one except believers can confess that the Son is God just as the Father is. Thus a person is denied by the Son before the Father if the Son is not revealed to him in the power of divinity; and he is acknowledged by the Son before the Father if through the Son he has gained access to the Father. (Maurice) Or otherwise: This acknowledgment seeks not merely the sound of words, but the result of works, because there are some who, as the Apostle testifies, “profess in words that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1); their confession is therefore vain. For Truth itself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7).

A good Christian, therefore, acknowledges the Lord Jesus before human beings with the faith that works through love, faithfully fulfilling the Lord’s commandments; and the Lord acknowledges his confessor before his Father by happily rewarding him in eternal blessedness.

But whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. To deny Christ before human beings is to refuse to obey his commands and to display the mark of a wicked example in human sight. The Lord denies such a person before his Father because he judges him unworthy of his perpetual vision. (Gregory) But now, some say among human beings: “We are no longer ashamed of the Lord and his words, because we openly acknowledge him.” To them I reply that in this Christian people there are some who acknowledge Christ for the very reason that they see everyone to be Christian. A voice, therefore, is not sufficient as proof of faith when a general profession protects someone from shame. Yet each person should question himself in this matter, so as to prove himself truthful in confessing Christ: whether he is no longer ashamed of his name, and whether, with a mind full of courage, he has subjected human embarrassment.

Certainly, in a time of persecution, the faithful could be ashamed, stripped of their possessions, cast down from their dignities, and afflicted with blows. But in a time of peace, since these things are absent from our persecutors, there is another arena in which we are exposed to ourselves: we are often afraid of being despised by those close to us, and we disdain to endure verbal insults; if a quarrel should perhaps arise with a neighbor, we are ashamed to be the first to make amends. For the carnal heart, while it seeks the glory of this life, rejects humility.

[Col. 0904A] [IV.] Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. Above he had said: “What I say to you in the darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the rooftops.” (Jerome) Now he adds what follows after the preaching. The whole world was divided against itself over the faith of Christ. Each household contained both unbelievers and believers, and therefore a good war was sent, so that a bad peace might be broken. Something similar is also written in Genesis concerning rebellious human beings who had moved from the East and were hastening to build a tower by which they might penetrate the heights of heaven: God did this in order to divide their languages (Gen. 11).

For this reason David also prays in the Psalm: “Scatter, Lord, the nations that desire wars” (Ps. 67). Isaiah likewise prophetically foretells the same thing under the figure of Egypt, saying: “Behold, God ascends upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt; the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it; and I will set Egyptians against Egyptians” (Isa. 19)—some fighting against the faith, others for the faith.

For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household. This passage is written in almost the same words in the prophet Micah (Mic. 7). It should be noted, wherever a testimony from the Old Testament is cited, whether only the sense remains or whether the wording also agrees. (Bede) It should also be noted that the evangelist Luke, in this saying of the Savior, reports five people divided within one household: “There will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three” (Luke 12). We must therefore consider how he can speak of five divided when he appears to have listed the names of six persons: father and son, mother and daughter, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law. We must understand that the same woman is designated by the name “mother” and “mother-in-law,” because the woman who is the son’s mother is also his wife’s mother-in-law. Therefore she is said to be divided both against her daughter and against her daughter-in-law. If someone seeks to interpret these divisions allegorically as well, three are divided against two and two against three because the good think and act against the evil, and the evil against the good.

For no one doubts that the three belong to those who preserve faith in the supreme Trinity. That the two correspond to those who dissent from the unity of faith is likewise demonstrated in many passages of Scripture, and especially by the fact that unclean animals were retained in the ark under this number. The works of the second day alone in Genesis are not said by God to be good (Gen. 1). Here the father is the devil, whose children we once were—not because he created us, but because we imitated him, as the Lord says: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). But after we heard the voice of the one who warned us, “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44), that fire came—that is, spiritual grace—and separated us from one another, showing us another Father, to whom we would say: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” The mother is the Synagogue; the daughter is the primitive Church, which both endured the Synagogue from which it derived its origin as a persecutor of the faith, and itself contradicted that same Synagogue by the truth of faith. The mother-in-law of the Synagogue is the Church from the Gentiles, because Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, is the son of the Synagogue, as the Apostle says: “To them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ” (Rom. 9).

The mother-in-law, therefore—that is, the bridegroom’s mother—is divided both against her daughter-in-law, as we said above, and against her daughter, because the carnal Synagogue, whether from circumcision or from the foreskin, does not cease persecuting believers. But they themselves are also divided against their mother-in-law and mother, refusing to receive carnal circumcision, as the Acts of the Apostles show, in connection with those with whom they had previously been entangled by custom. No laws can be observed among those between whom there is a war of faith.

Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. (Jerome) After he had first said, “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword,” and to divide people against father, mother, and mother-in-law, lest anyone should put family affection before religion, he adds: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me.” In the Song of Songs we also read: “Order charity in me” (Song 2). This order is necessary in every affection. Love your father after God; love your mother; love your children. But if necessity arises, so that the love of parents and children must be compared with the love of God, and both cannot be preserved, hatred toward one’s own is devotion toward God. He therefore did not forbid loving either father or mother, but deliberately added: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.”

And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. In another Gospel it is written, “Whoever does not take up his cross daily” (Luke 9). We must not suppose that the ardor of faith can suffice once for all; the cross must always be carried, so that we may always be taught to love Christ. (Bede) The cross is so called from torment, and we carry the Lord’s cross in two ways: either when we afflict the flesh through abstinence, or when through compassion for our neighbor we regard his need as our own. Whoever shows grief in another’s need carries the cross in his mind. It must be understood, however, that some practice abstinence from the flesh not for God but for empty glory. And many show compassion to their neighbor not spiritually, so that they favor him not toward virtue but, as if pitying him, toward his faults. Such people therefore appear to carry the cross, but they do not follow the Lord. Hence Truth itself rightly says: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” To take up the cross and go after God is to practice either abstinence from the flesh or compassion for one’s neighbor with the purpose of eternal intention. For whoever practices these things for a temporal purpose carries the cross but refuses to go after God. (Maurice) When he says here and above, “is not worthy of me,” he signifies that the person is unworthy of divine fellowship who prefers the world’s pleasures and carnal love of kindred to spiritual love, and who, for the sake of trivial and transitory things, neglects to seek what is greatest and eternal.

Whoever finds his soul will lose it. (Bede) Here, therefore, by “soul” the present life is designated, by which each person desires to live as an animal does. This saying can rightly be understood in two ways, but both interpretations refer altogether to one end: that we should not fear suffering adversity for Christ, indeed, even undergoing death itself. Whoever, when a persecutor threatens death, denies Christ chooses rather to save his soul for a time; by denying him, he plainly prepares that soul for eternal destruction. Likewise, whoever seeks the eternal salvation of his soul does not hesitate to lose it temporally among the hands of persecutors—that is, to give it over to death. What follows appropriately agrees with both meanings:

And whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it. That is, whoever loses it here will bring it to life there; whoever for Christ’s sake hands it over to death, considering it all day long like a sheep destined for slaughter, will then, when Christ rises and helps, find it free for the sake of Christ’s name.

Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. (Hilary) He teaches in himself also the office of mediator: whoever is received by us, and whose progress is from God, has God poured through him into us. Thus whoever receives the apostles receives Christ; whoever receives Christ will receive God the Father, because in the apostles he receives nothing other than what is in Christ, nor in Christ anything other than what is in God. Through this order of graces, receiving the apostles is nothing other than receiving God, because Christ dwells in them and God in Christ. Behold the most beautiful order: when he sends them to preach, he teaches that dangers are not to be feared, subjects affection to the condition of religion, and had earlier told them to carry no gold and to shake the bronze from their belts—the harsh condition of evangelists.

How, then, will they obtain expenses and the necessities of food? He tempers the austerity of the commands with the hope of the promises: “Whoever receives you,” he says, “receives me; and whoever receives me, receives him who sent me.” He had taken away gold and forbidden bronze in the belt. He wishes each believer, in receiving the apostles, to consider that he has received Christ, and in Christ’s resurrection to believe that he has received God the Father. He wishes him to be believed to be such and so great as the Father is: “For,” he says, “there is no difference between me and him, to such an extent that whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. (Gregory) In these words it should be noted that he does not say, “He will receive a reward from a prophet,” or “a reward from a righteous person,” but “a prophet’s reward” and “a righteous person’s reward.” For “a reward from a prophet” is one thing, and “a prophet’s reward” another; likewise, “a reward from a righteous person” is one thing, and “a righteous person’s reward” another. What does “he will receive a prophet’s reward” mean except that the person who supports a prophet by his generosity, although he himself does not possess prophecy, will nevertheless have the rewards of prophecy before the almighty Lord? For perhaps he is righteous, and the less he possesses in this world, the greater confidence he has to speak for righteousness. When one who possesses something in this world supports him, although he himself perhaps does not yet dare to speak freely for righteousness, he makes himself a participant in that man’s freedom for righteousness, so that together with him he may receive the rewards of righteousness whom he aided by supporting him, so that he might be able freely to speak that same righteousness. The prophet is full of the spirit of prophecy, yet he needs bodily nourishment. If the body is not refreshed, it is certain that the voice itself will be withdrawn. Whoever, therefore, supplies food to a prophet because he is a prophet gives strength to that prophet’s prophecy for speaking. He will therefore receive a prophet’s reward together with the prophet, because, although he was not himself full of the spirit of prophecy, he nevertheless displayed before God what he heard [or: helped].

(Jerome) Or otherwise: Whoever receives a prophet as a prophet, and understands him to be speaking about future things, will receive a prophet’s reward. Therefore the Jews, understanding the prophets carnally, will not receive the prophets’ reward. Again, another interpretation: In every profession, weeds are mixed with wheat. He had said earlier: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” He had urged the disciples’ acceptance of their teachers. There could have been a hidden response from believers: “Then must we also receive false prophets and Judas the traitor and provide them with food?” The Lord, anticipating this, says that it is not persons who are to be received, but names, and that those who receive them will not lose their reward, even if the one received should have been unworthy.

And whoever gives one of these least ones a drink, even only a cup of cold water, in the name of a disciple—truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward. We read in the prophet David: “To excuse excuses in sins” (Ps. 140), because many put forward what appear to be just excuses for their sins, so that what they do from pleasure [or: willingness] may seem to have been done from necessity. But the Lord, who searches heart and kidneys and observes future thoughts in each person, had said: “Whoever receives you receives me.” Yet because many false prophets and false preachers could obstruct this command, he also remedied this scandal, saying: “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.” Again, another person might make an excuse and say: “Poverty prevents me; my meager means keep me from being hospitable.” He removed this excuse by the lightest of commands, so that we should offer a cup of cold water with our whole heart. He says “cold water,” not hot, so that no excuse might be sought in the cost of heating water or the scarcity of wood. The Apostle also gives a similar command to the Galatians, as we have already said: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” (Gal. 6), and he exhorts disciples to provide refreshment for their teachers. And because anyone might plead poverty and evade the command, before that person could put forward the excuse, he resolves the impending question by saying: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (ibid.). The meaning is: You plead poverty in vain, when your conscience tells another story. You may deceive me, who am exhorting you, but I know that whatever you sow, that much you will also reap.

[Col. 0908C] Since the Evangelist has here finished the Lord’s discourses that he held with the apostles, let us also, finishing this book together with him, take up in the following book another beginning of his discourses and deeds.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0907]

## CHAPTER XI

He answers the messengers sent by John and teaches the crowds about him; he rebukes the cities that refused to believe. His confession to the Father, and concerning his yoke, which is easy, and so forth.

[Col. 0907D] When Matthew had explained the Lord’s discourses concerning the calling and instruction of the apostles, he proceeded as though moving on to other matters, saying:

[I.] And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, that he departed from there to teach in their cities. The evangelist, therefore, recalling the passage in which the Lord said to his disciples, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest,” up to the place where he says, “Jesus sent these twelve, instructing them and saying: Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but rather go to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel,” shows that the Lord himself fulfilled in deeds, as a good teacher, what he had previously commanded in words. He therefore departed and preached in the cities of the Jews, so as to give them an opportunity for belief; and if they wickedly rejected the gift of heavenly grace offered to them, they would be without excuse, because he truly fulfilled what their God had promised, sending them his only-begotten Son as Savior and defender, who would set them free. He raised up for them a Prophet, namely, one from among their brothers, whom the Lawgiver had promised them (Deut. 18). For this reason what the same lawgiver foretold befell them: whoever would not listen to and receive that Prophet would have his soul exterminated from among his people. They themselves rightly became the authors and witnesses of their own destruction, because they neglected to attend to the time of their visitation. After this the evangelist continues and says:

Now when John had heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another? (Jerome) He does not ask as one ignorant. He himself, while the others were ignorant, pointed him out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1), and he had heard the voice of the Father thundering: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). But just as the Savior asks where Lazarus had been laid, so that those who pointed out the place of the tomb might at least in this way be prepared for faith and see the dead man rising, so John, about to be killed by Herod, sends his disciples to Christ so that, by this opportunity, seeing signs and mighty works, they might believe in him and learn for themselves through the question addressed to their teacher. (Hilary) He also sent them to the Lord so that his works might lend authority to John’s words, lest another Christ be expected than the one to whom those works had borne witness. But a broader understanding is offered in what John did; and, together with the efficacy of the deed, grace is perceived as expressed in him, so that the prophet himself, even by the manner of his condition, might prophesy, since in him the form of the Law had been raised up. For the Law announced Christ, preached remission of sins, and promised the kingdom of heaven; and John fulfilled the whole work of the Law. Therefore, now that the Law had ceased—the Law which, enclosed by the people’s sins and bound by the people’s vices, was confined in chains and prison so that Christ could not be understood—the Law sends people to behold the Gospel, so that unbelief may contemplate the faith of its words in deeds, and what was bound within it by the fraud of sins may be washed away [or: released] through the understanding of evangelical freedom.

(Jerome) The preceding interpretation also demonstrated that John’s disciples were arrogant toward the Lord and possessed some bitterness arising from jealousy and envy, when the evangelist reported: “Then the disciples of John approached, saying: Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” And elsewhere: “Teacher, the one to whom you bore witness at the Jordan—behold, his disciples are baptizing, and more people are coming to him.” As though they had said: “We are being abandoned; there are few with us, while the crowd rushes to him.” “Are you,” he says, “the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” He does not say, “Are you the one who has come,” but, “Are you the one who is to come.” The meaning of this sentence may be as follows: “Command me,” he says, “because I am about to descend to the underworld, whether I should announce you to those below as I announced you to those above, or whether it is unfitting for the Son of God to taste death and you are about to send another for these mysteries.”

And Jesus answered them: Go and report to John what you hear and see. The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor are evangelized; and blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me. (Jerome) John had asked through his disciples: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Christ displays signs, not answering what he had been asked, but responding to the scandal of the messengers. “Go,” he says, “and tell John the signs that you see: the blind seeing, the lame walking, and so forth, and, no less than these, the poor evangelized.” The poor may mean those poor in spirit, or certainly those poor in material possessions, so that in preaching there may be no distinction between noble and lowly, rich and needy. These things demonstrate the rigor of the teacher and confirm the truth of the instructor, since for him everyone who can be saved is equal. When he says, “And blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me,” he strikes the messengers [variant: intermediaries] for the present, as will be shown in what follows.

As they were departing, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. If the preceding statement had been spoken against John, as many think, in the words, “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me,” how is John now proclaimed with such great praises? But because the surrounding crowd did not know the mystery of the question and thought that John was doubting about Christ, whom he himself had pointed out, he speaks in this way so that they might understand that John had not asked for himself but for his disciples. “What did you go out,” he says, “into the wilderness to see? Surely not to see a man like a reed, carried about by every wind, so that through fickleness of mind he might doubt about the one whom he had previously proclaimed? Or perhaps is he driven against me by the goad of envy, and does his preaching pursue empty glory, so that he may seek profit from it? Why would he desire wealth, so that he might abound in banquets? He feeds on locusts and wild honey. Or is it so that he might be dressed in soft clothing? Garments of camel hair are his covering. Such food and clothing are received in the lodging of a prison, and such is the dwelling of the preaching of truth. But those who preach falsely are flatterers; they pursue profits, seek riches, abound in luxuries, and wear soft garments. They are in kings’ houses.” From this it is shown that a strict life and austere preaching ought to avoid royal courts and shun the palaces of soft-living people, which are frequented by those who wear linen, silk, and soft garments.

But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is the one of whom it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.” John is greater than the other prophets in this respect: they had proclaimed that the one who was to come would come, but he demonstrated with his finger that he had come, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” And to his prophetic eminence was added the privilege of the Baptist, that he should baptize his own Lord. Hence, mentioning an increase [αὔξησιν, “augmentation”; editorial suggestion: delete “mentioning”] of his merits, he brings forward the testimony of Malachi, in which he is also called an angel (Mal. 3). Let us not suppose that John is called an angel here by a sharing of nature, but by the dignity of his office—that is, as a messenger, because he announced the God who was to come. (Gregory) Rightly, therefore, the one who is sent to announce the heavenly Judge is called an angel, so that he may preserve in his name the dignity that he fulfills in his work. The name is lofty, but his life is not inferior to the name.

Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist. He says, “among those born of women.” He is therefore preferred to human beings who are born of women and from the intercourse of man, but not to the one who was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit. Yet in saying, “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist,” he did not place John above all the other prophets, patriarchs, and human beings; rather, he made all the others equal to John. For it does not immediately follow that, if no others are greater than him, he is greater than all the others, so that he should have equality with the other holy people.

But the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. Many wish this to be understood of the Savior: that the one who is later in time is greater in dignity. Let us, however, understand it simply to mean that every holy person who is already with God is greater than one who still remains in the battle. For it is one thing to possess the crown of victory and another still to fight in the line of battle, because [variant: some say that] they wish even the last angel ministering to the Lord in heaven to be considered better than any first human being who is still living on earth.

From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.

(Hilary.) The Lord had commanded the apostles to go to the lost sheep of Israel. They ought to have been established in the kingdom and retained within the family and lineage of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But all this preaching was benefiting publicans and sinners. For from among them there were already believers, from among them already apostles, and from among them already the kingdom of heaven. John, however, is not believed by the people; Christ’s works do not win them belief in his authority; the future cross was to be a stumbling block. Prophecy has now ceased, the law has now been fulfilled, all preaching is now excluded, and the spirit of Elijah is sent ahead in John’s voice [Col. 0911C]. Christ is preached to some and recognized by others; to some he is born, by others he is loved. His own reject him, strangers receive him; his relatives persecute him, enemies embrace him. Adoption seeks the inheritance, while the family rejects it. The sons repudiate the testament, while the servants acknowledge it. Thus the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who force their way into it seize it, because the glory of Israel—owed by the fathers, announced by the prophets, and offered by Christ—is occupied and seized by the faith of the Gentiles.

Alternatively, one must ask how the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence. For who can inflict violence upon heaven? And again one must ask: if the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence, why has it endured this same violence from the days of John the Baptist and not also before? But when the law says, “If anyone does this or that, let him die,” it is clear to all who read that it struck sinners with the punishment of its severity, but did not restore them to life through repentance.

When John the Baptist, going before the grace of the Redeemer, preaches repentance, so that the sinner who is dead through guilt may live through conversion, then certainly from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. What is the kingdom of heaven, except the dwelling-place of the righteous? For the rewards of the heavenly homeland are owed only to the righteous, so that the humble, chaste, meek, and merciful may attain the joys above. But when someone puffed up with pride, polluted by the sin of the flesh, inflamed with anger, or impious through cruelty returns to repentance after his sins and receives eternal life, the sinner enters, as it were, into another’s dwelling.

(Jerome.) Hence, if John was the first—as we said above—to announce repentance to the peoples, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near,” then consequently from those days the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. For it is a great act of violence that, although generated on earth, we seek a place in heaven; that by virtue we possess what we could not possess by nature.

For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John. This does not mean that he excludes prophets after John. We read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XI) that Agabus also prophesied, as did the four virgin daughters of Philip. Rather, the law and the prophets whom we read as written down prophesied everything they foretold about the Lord. Therefore, when it says, “All the prophets and the law prophesied until John,” the time of Christ is indicated, so that the one whom they had said would come might be shown by John to have come.

And if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. The statement, “If you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah,” is mystical and requires understanding; this is demonstrated by the Lord’s following words: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” For if the meaning were plain and the statement obvious, why would it have been necessary to prepare us for its understanding? John is therefore called Elijah, not according to foolish philosophers and certain heretics who introduce souls as returning into other bodies, but because, according to another testimony of the Gospel, he came “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” and possessed either the same grace or the same measure of the Holy Spirit. The austerity of life and firmness of mind in Elijah and John were also alike: the one was in the wilderness, and so was the other; the one was girded with a leather belt, and the other had a similar girdle. Because Elijah rebuked King Ahab and Jezebel for their impiety, he was compelled to flee; because John rebuked the unlawful marriage of Herod and Herodias, he was beheaded. Some think that John is called Elijah because, just as Elijah will precede the second coming of the Savior, according to Malachi (Malach. II), and announce the coming Judge, so John did this at the first coming; and that each is a messenger either of the Lord’s first coming or of his second.

To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who call to their companions and say: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a lament, and you did not mourn.”

(Augustine.) The generation of the Jews is compared to children sitting in the marketplace because formerly it received teachers and prophets, of whom it is said, “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Psalm VIII), and elsewhere, “The declaration of your words gives me light and grants understanding to the simple” (Psalm CXVIII), that is, to the humble in spirit. The Lord’s marketplace is either the synagogue or Jerusalem itself, in which the ordinances of the heavenly commandments were stored up. There, according to Luke—or according to this Matthew—they spoke to their companions, because they were accustomed daily, in their homeland, to reproach the peoples of their race and nation for refusing to heed the prophetic songs, first summoned by David’s psalms and later chastised by laments. Whenever victory over an enemy was either foretold or recalled as accomplished, they would not rise either to praises or to works of virtue.

For by the word “dancing” are signified not theatrical movements, the twisting and circling of the body, but the energetic devotion of the heart and the religious agility of the members. Whenever the lamentations of the prophets resounded over disasters either accomplished or to be avoided, even then the hearers did not take care to flee to the remedies of saving repentance. The Psalmist sings (Psalm LXXX): “Rejoice in God our helper, shout for joy to the God of Jacob; take up the psalm and give the timbrel,” and so forth. But what follows? “And my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me” (ibid.).

The prophet cries: “Thus says the Lord: Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning; and rend your hearts, not your garments” (Joel II). And again: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain; the senses of my heart are troubled within me. I will not be silent, for my soul has heard the sound of the trumpet, the cry of battle” (Jeremiah IV). A little later: “For my foolish people has not known me; they are senseless children, without understanding” (ibid.).

For John came, neither eating nor drinking, and they say, “He has a demon.” The Son of Man came, eating and drinking, and they say, “Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of publicans and sinners” [Col. 0913C]. As he says: Just as then, so also now, you reject both ways of salvation. For when he says, “We sang a lament, and you did not mourn,” this refers to John, whose abstinence from food and drink signified the mourning of repentance. But when he says, “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance,” this refers to God himself, who, by sharing food and drink with others, represented the joy of the kingdom. Yet they were unwilling either to humble themselves with John or to rejoice with Christ, saying that the former had a demon and calling the latter gluttonous, drunk, and a friend of publicans and sinners.

Then he adds:

“But wisdom is justified by her children,” that is, by the wisdom and teaching of God. It is as though he were saying openly: I, who am the power of God and the wisdom of God, am shown by my apostles to have done these things; to them the Father revealed what he had hidden from the wise and prudent in their own eyes.

(Augustine.) He shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness does not consist in eating or abstaining, but in the equanimity with which poverty is endured and in the temperance by which one is not corrupted through abundance; it consists in taking or refusing at the proper time those things whose desire, not their use, should be reproved. “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy” (Romans XIV). And because people commonly rejoice greatly in bodily feasts, he added, “in the Holy Spirit,” in whom true fullness is granted. In some Gospels it is written: “Wisdom is justified by her works,” for wisdom does not seek the testimony of words but of deeds.

[II.] Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they had not repented.

(Jerome.) The reproach of the cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum is disclosed by the title of this section. He reproached them because, after so many mighty works and signs had been performed, they did not repent.

Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida.

(Augustine.) Chorazin, which is interpreted as “my mystery,” and Bethsaida, which is called “house of fruits” or “house of hunters,” as are also Capernaum and Tiberias, which John names, are cities of Galilee situated on the shore of the lake of Gennesareth, formed by the flowing of the Jordan [Col. 0914B]. The evangelists also call it the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias. The Lord therefore mourns the cities that once possessed the mystery of God and ought by now to have produced the fruit of virtue; spiritual hunters were also sent to them. Yet after so many miracles and mighty works they did not repent. They became worse than the Gentiles, who merely destroyed the natural law, for, after disregarding the written law, they did not fear to trample upon the Son of God also and, in their ingratitude, to despise grace.

We therefore ask where it is written that the Lord performed signs in Chorazin and Bethsaida. Above we read: “And Jesus went about the cities and all the villages, healing every disease,” and so forth. Among the other cities and villages, therefore, it must be thought that the Lord also performed these works in Chorazin and Bethsaida.

For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes.

(Augustine.) Finally, we see the Savior’s statement fulfilled today. Chorazin and Bethsaida, that is, refused to believe while the Lord was present; but Tyre and Sidon, once friends of David and Solomon, later believed through the disciples who preached Christ. They received the faith with such devotion that, when the apostle Paul was departing from Tyre, all the citizens, with their wives and children, escorted him outside the city (Acts XXI). It was a most beautiful spectacle: such a multitude of people escorted a very few guests—yet guests exceedingly dear because of the faith of Christ—all the way to the ships to bid them farewell. But why the Gospel was not formerly preached to those who were able to believe, but rather to the Jews who were unwilling to believe, is known only by him whose every way is mercy and truth (Psalm XXIV).

For the Lord’s purpose had been not to go beyond the borders of Judaea, lest he give the Pharisees and priests a just occasion for persecution. Certainly, when the Lord says, “They would have repented in sackcloth and ashes,” sackcloth, which is woven from goats’ hair, signifies the harsh memory of sin that will clothe the left side on the day of judgment; ashes, meanwhile, signify consideration of death, by which the entire mass of the human race is to be reduced to dust.

It should be noted that Tyre is the metropolis of Phoenicia, in the tribe of Naphtali. It was once an island situated in the open sea, but is now joined to the mainland. Sidon also is a distinguished city of Phoenicia, formerly the boundary of the Canaanites, facing north, and later of the region of Judaea. It fell by lot to the tribe of Asher, but that tribe did not possess it, because it was entirely unable to drive out its enemies. Tyre is interpreted as “narrowness,” and Sidon as “hunting”; they signify the nations whom the hunter, the devil, enclosed in the narrowness of sin, but whom the Savior Jesus freed through the Gospel.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? Or will you descend to hell? In another copy we find: “And you, Capernaum, which have been exalted to heaven, you will be brought down to hell.” There is a twofold understanding: either you will descend to hell because you resisted my preaching with the greatest arrogance, or because you were exalted to heaven through my hospitality and my signs; having received such privilege, you will be punished with greater penalties because you were unwilling to believe even these things. In Capernaum, which is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” unbelieving Jerusalem is condemned. To it Ezekiel says: “Sodom, your sister, has been justified in comparison with you” (Ezekiel XVI). Hence what follows:

For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained until this day.

(Maurus.) Sodom is therefore said to have the lesser injustice and to be almost righteous in comparison with the greater injustice of Jerusalem: Sodom was not corrected by the examples of Lot, while Jerusalem continually proved ungrateful for the words and miracles of the Son of God. Indeed, it killed the prophets and the Savior himself, and persecuted his apostles [Col. 0915C].

Nevertheless I tell you: it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom than for you. Their punishment, therefore, will be lighter because their guilt is less; against those whose wrongdoing is greater, a stronger vengeance will proceed.

[III.] At that time Jesus answered and said: I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.

“Confession” does not always signify repentance, but also thanksgiving, as we read very frequently in the Psalms. Let those who slander the Savior by saying that he was not born but created hear that he calls God his Father, while calling him Lord of heaven and earth. For if he himself is also a creature, and a creature can likewise call its creator Father, it would have been foolish for him not likewise to call him Father or Lord of himself, of heaven, and of earth.

Because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants.

He gives thanks and rejoices in the Father because he has opened to the apostles the mysteries of his coming, which the scribes and Pharisees did not know, although they seemed wise to themselves and prudent in their own eyes. “Wisdom is justified by her children.” Here he beautifully opposed infants—not fools and dullards—to the wise and prudent, that he might show that he condemned arrogance, not intelligence. For this is the key of which he says elsewhere: “You have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke XI), that is, the humility of faith in Christ, by which you could have attained recognition of his divinity; you despised it and preferred to cast it away.

Yes, Father, for so it was pleasing before you.

(Jerome.) He speaks to the Father with an affectionate appeal, so that the benefit begun in the apostles may be completed.

(Gregory.) From these words of the Lord we receive examples of humility, lest we rashly presume to investigate the heavenly purposes concerning the calling of some and the rejection of others. For although he had introduced both matters, he did not immediately give the reason, but said that it had thus pleased God. By this he plainly showed that what has pleased the just One cannot be unjust. Hence also, when he paid the laborers in the vineyard, equating unequal workers in their labor by equality in their reward, and when the one who had labored longer sought more in payment, he said: “Did you not agree with me for a denarius? But I wish to give to this last one as to you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?” (Matthew XX). Thus, in all that is arranged outwardly, the justice of the hidden will is the cause or rationale.

All things have been handed over to me by my Father.

Understand mystically both the Father who hands over and the Son who receives. Otherwise, if we wish to understand it according to our weakness, when the one who receives begins to possess, the one who gives will begin not to possess. When you read “all things,” you recognize the omnipotent one, not unlike or degenerate from the Father. When you read “handed over,” you confess the Son, to whom all things properly belong by nature and by the right of one substance, not having been bestowed by grace as a gift. The “all things” handed over to him are not to be understood as heaven, earth, the elements, and the other things that he himself made and created, but rather those who, through the Son, have access to the Father—those who were formerly rebels and later began to know God.

(Hilary.) The things handed over are nothing other than those which are known to the Father alone in the Son; and the things that are the Father’s are known to the Son alone. Thus, in this secret of mutual knowledge, it is understood that nothing unknowable exists in the Son other than what is unknowable in the Father.

And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.

This should not be understood as though the Son can be known by no one except the Father alone, while the Father can be known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son reveals him. Rather, what he says—“and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him”—must be referred to both, so that we understand both the Father and the Son himself to be revealed through the Son, because he is the light of our mind. For the Father declares himself by his Word, and the Word declares not only what is declared through the Word but also himself. Let Eunomius blush, boasting that he possesses such knowledge of the Father and the Son as they possess of one another. But if he argues from the words “and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him,” and thereby consoles his madness, it is one thing to know by equality of nature what the Son knew, and another to know through the condescension of the one who reveals.

[IV.] Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

That sins are heavy burdens is also testified by the prophet Zechariah, who says that iniquity sits upon a talent of lead (Zechariah V). The Psalmist likewise laments: “My iniquities have become heavy above …” (Psalm XXXVII; the supplied quotation breaks off). Or certainly, he invites those who were oppressed by the very heavy yoke of the law to the grace of the Gospel. Hence it follows:

Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.

The yoke of Christ is the Gospel of Christ, which joins and unites Jews and Gentiles in the unity of faith. We are commanded to take this upon ourselves—that is, to hold it in honor—lest, placing it beneath us, we trample it with the muddy feet of our vices by perversely despising it. We are likewise commanded to learn from him, because he is meek and humble of heart.

This was also signified at his baptism when the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, because gentleness tempered his power. Of him the prophet says: “He will not cry out, nor show partiality, nor will his voice be heard outside. He will not break a bruised reed, nor extinguish a smoking flax; in strength he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad or troubled until he establishes judgment on the earth, and the islands will await his law” (Isaiah XLII).

We must therefore learn from our Savior to be meek in conduct and humble in mind, so that we harm no one, despise no one, provoke no one without cause, and through arrogance scorn no one; and so that the virtues we display outwardly in our actions may be truly held within our hearts. Whoever pretends to be meek or humble without pure intention conceals a wolf beneath a sheep’s skin and hides serpentine venom beneath the appearance of a dove. Such a person is not a disciple of Christ but an imitator of the devil. He labors in vain, for he is striving not toward eternal rest but toward everlasting fire. For true rest is what the Savior demonstrates in the following words:

And you will find rest for your souls.

Whoever follows in Christ’s footsteps and imitates, as far as he can, his meekness, humility, long-suffering, and patience—his soul already rejoices in hope and will rejoice in perpetual rest in the future, enjoying eternal blessedness with the holy angels. Through the prophet Jeremiah he himself testifies, saying: “Stand upon the ways, look, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way; walk in it, and you will find refreshment for your souls” (Jeremiah VI).

For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

(Jerome.) How is the Gospel lighter than the law, when murder is condemned in the law and likewise condemned in the Gospel? How is the grace of the Gospel easier, when adultery is punished in the law and desire is punished in the Gospel? The law contains many commandments that the Apostle teaches cannot be perfectly fulfilled. In the law works are required, and the one who performs them will live by them. In the Gospel the will is sought; even if it does not attain its effect, it nevertheless does not lose its reward. The Gospel commands what we are able to do: namely, that we should not desire; this lies within our own power. The law, since it does not punish the will, punishes the deed: “You shall not commit adultery.”

Suppose that during a persecution some virgin were violated. According to the Gospel, since she did not sin by her will, she is received as a virgin; according to the law, she is rejected as corrupted.

Likewise, this statement of the Lord—“For my yoke is easy and my burden is light”—seems to some to be sufficiently opposed to the statement that the same Truth uttered elsewhere: “Narrow is the way that leads to life.” The Prophet also says to the Lord: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult paths” (Psalm XVI). For the Apostle says: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecutions” (2 Timothy III). Whatever is difficult and filled with persecutions can be neither light nor easy.

Yet we shall prove by the testimony of experience itself that this statement of our Lord and Savior is most true. If we have legitimately undertaken the way of perfection according to Christ’s will, mortifying all our desires and cutting off harmful inclinations, then not only will we allow none of this world’s desire to remain in us—through which, whenever it wishes, the enemy will find the power to lay waste to us and tear us apart—but we shall also realize that we are not masters even of ourselves, fulfilling in truth the apostolic statement: “I live, yet it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians II).

For what could be burdensome, what could be difficult, to one who has received Christ’s yoke with his whole mind, who is grounded in true humility, and who, always looking toward the Lord’s sufferings, rejoices in every injury inflicted upon him, saying: “For this reason I am pleased with weaknesses, insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians XII).

The way of salvation is therefore called narrow because, as our blessed Father Benedict says, it can be begun only with a narrow beginning; but as one advances in the conduct of life and faith, the heart is enlarged, and one runs along the way of God’s commandments with an indescribable sweetness of love.

(Hilary.) For what is sweeter than Christ’s yoke, what lighter than his burden? To become approved, to abstain from crime, to desire the good, to refuse the evil, to love everyone, to hate no one, to attain eternal things, not to be captivated by present things, and not to inflict upon another what one would find burdensome to endure oneself.

CHAPTER XII  
The disciples pluck ears of grain. Jesus heals a withered hand and a demon-possessed blind and mute man; he gives the Pharisees the sign of Jonah, and so forth.

[I.] At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath, and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat.

(Jerome.) As we also read in another Gospel, because of excessive importunity [ejus, “of it/him,” deleted], they did not even have an opportunity to eat, and therefore, like ordinary human beings, they were hungry. That they broke the ears of grain in their hands and relieved their hunger is an indication of a more austere life: they were not seeking prepared dishes but food simply [simple food].

But when the Pharisees saw this, they said to him: Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbaths.

Note that the first apostles of the Savior destroy the letter of the Sabbath, against the Ebionites, who, although they accept the other apostles, reject Paul as a transgressor of the law.

Mystically, however, the apostles pass through the grainfields—namely, those of which the Lord says: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest, and the one who reaps will receive a reward.” The holy teachers, with the loving care of their concern, examine those whom they seek to instruct in the faith of truth, carefully considering how and in what order they ought to draw each one toward salvation. Thus they understand that nothing is more fitting than to hunger for the salvation of human beings. Once, while praying, the first of the reapers himself hungered for this; and when the foods he desired were soon offered to him, he heard: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts X).

There is a wonderful harmony of the mystery here. For there too the animals sent from heaven are commanded to be slaughtered and eaten, while here the disciples are said to have plucked ears of grain consecrated as the Lord passed through them and, according to the account of the other evangelists, to have rubbed them in their hands and eaten them.

For this is what the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth, and strip off the old man with his deeds” (Colossians III). For no one passes into the body of Christ, and no one nourishes the teacher with the fruits of his progress, except by renouncing former desires and becoming a new person through the new commandment of love.

To pluck ears of grain, therefore, is to tear human beings away from the earthly concern in which they had fixed, as it were, the root of their minds. To rub them with the hands is, through examples of virtue, to strip the purity of the mind even from the desire of the flesh, as though from the husks and coverings of the ears of grain. To eat the kernels is for each person, cleansed from the filth of vices, to be incorporated through the mouths of preachers into the members of the Church.

And it is fitting that the disciples are said to have done these things by going before the Lord. For the teacher’s word must precede, and then the heart of the hearer, following after, is enlightened by the grace of heavenly visitation. It is fitting that they did this on the Sabbaths, because the holy teachers, in preaching, themselves labor in hope of future rest, and likewise warn their hearers not to devote themselves to useless occupations for love of the world, but rather to labor earnestly for eternal rest.

Those also walk through the grainfields with the Lord who, striving to obey the divine commands, delight diligently to meditate upon the sacred words. They hunger in the grainfields when, in those same sacred words through which they pass by reading, they desire to find the bread of life—that is, when they strive to reach those words by which they may kindle within themselves a greater love for their Creator.

They do this on the Sabbaths when, with their minds quieted from turbulent thoughts, they rejoice to be free and to see how sweet the Lord is, and how blessed is the person who hopes in him (Psalm XXXIII); and, taking on an attitude of piety and humility, they strive to attain rest for their souls. They pluck the ears that happen to present themselves, rub them in their hands, and cleanse them until they reach the food within, when they take up the testimonies of Scripture encountered in reading by meditation and examine them through diligent searching until they draw out the marrow of love that seemed to lie hidden within them.

For just as the grains of wheat that nourish are covered by the roughness of the bristling awns, so the gifts of divine love that feed the minds of the faithful, who hunger and thirst for righteousness, are often concealed beneath what appears to be the lowliness of the letter. This refreshment of minds displeases the foolish defenders of the Sabbath, but it is approved by the Lord of the Sabbath, because those who follow only the surface of the letter know neither true refreshment of mind nor how to arrive at the inner rest of souls. Hence their rashness is rightly confounded by the mouth of Truth, when he adds:

But he said to them: Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?

(Jerome.) To refute the Pharisees’ accusation, he recalls an episode from ancient history. When David was fleeing from Saul, he came to Nob and was received by the priest Ahimelech; he asked for food, and since the priest had no ordinary bread, he gave him consecrated bread, which only the priests and Levites were permitted to eat (1 Samuel XXI). He asked only whether the young men were clean from women. When David answered that they had been so from yesterday and the day before, he did not hesitate to give them the bread, judging—according to the prophet’s saying, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hosea VI)—that it was better to rescue people from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God. For the sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of human beings.

The Lord therefore argues: If David is holy and Ahimelech the high priest is not reproved by you, and if both transgressed the commandment of the law with a defensible justification, with hunger as the cause, why do you not approve the same hunger in the apostles that you approve in others? Yet there is also a great difference here: these men rub ears of grain with their hands on the Sabbath, while the others ate Levitical bread.

(Bede.) The bread of the Presence was baked before the Sabbath and, on the Sabbath morning, was offered and placed upon the sacred table. It was arranged in two rows of six, facing one another, with two golden dishes placed upon them and filled with incense. The loaves remained until the following Sabbath, when others were brought in their place. The former loaves were given to the priests; after the incense had been burned in the sacred fire, in which all burnt offerings were customarily consumed, other incense was placed upon the twelve loaves. It was at this time that David, arriving, received the consecrated bread. The days of the New Moons also fell near the solemnity of the Sabbath, and David was summoned to a banquet from the royal court.

(Augustine.) Figuratively, the fact that David and his young men received sanctified bread shows that priestly food would pass over for the use of the peoples; or it shows that we should all imitate the priestly life, since all the children of the Church are priests. We have been anointed into a holy priesthood, offering ourselves to God as spiritual sacrifices.

Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt?

(Jerome.) You accuse my disciples, he says, because, passing through the grainfields, they have rubbed ears of grain, compelled by the necessity of hunger, while you yourselves violate the Sabbath in the temple by offering victims, slaughtering bulls, consuming burnt offerings in the fire upon a pile of wood, and, according to the testimony of another Gospel, circumcising infants on the Sabbath. Thus, while you wish to keep another law, you destroy the Sabbath. But God’s laws are never opposed to one another.

Wisely, where his disciples could be accused of transgression, he says that they followed the examples of David and Ahimelech. But he also refers the transgression of the Sabbath, without the excuse of necessity, back to those who had made the accusation.

But I tell you that something greater than the temple is here.

(Maurus.) In this sentence, the Gospel word “here” is not a pronoun but an adverb of place, and it signifies that the place containing the Lord of the temple is greater than the temple; as though he were saying: If the figurative temple could defend the priests who served it, why can the spiritual temple not defend the disciples who believe in it?

(Hilary.) He shows that through himself, in the apostolic teaching, salvation is given to the Gentiles while the people of the law remain unfaithfully idle; for he himself is greater than the Sabbath, and the faith of the Gospel operates in Christ without guilt arising from violation of the law. And to show that every efficacy of things contains the form of a future work, he added:

If you had known what this means, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice,” you would never have condemned the innocent.

(Jerome.) We explained above what “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” means. The words that follow, “You would never have condemned the innocent,” are to be understood of the apostles, and the meaning is this: You approve Ahimelech because he refreshed David, who was in danger from hunger, and his young men (1 Samuel XI); why, then, do you condemn my disciples, who have done nothing of the kind?

For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.

If, he says, King David may be excused for having been fed with priestly food, and if, according to the account of another evangelist, priests who violate the Sabbath through their service in the temple are without guilt, how much more is the Son of Man, who is the true king and true priest and therefore Lord of the Sabbath, free from guilt for plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath? Especially since the same Son of God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is not only the creator of the Sabbath but also of all times and of the entire world.

[II.] And when he had passed on from there, he came into their synagogue, and behold, there was a man who had a withered hand.

(Augustine.) Mark and Luke also do not omit this man who had a withered hand (Mark III; Luke VI). It might be thought that the plucking of the ears and the healing of this man occurred on the same day, since the Sabbath is mentioned in both accounts, unless Luke had made clear that the healing of the withered hand occurred on another Sabbath.

Accordingly, when Matthew says, “And when he had passed on from there, he came into their synagogue,” he certainly did not come except after passing on from there; but he does not indicate how many days later he came into their synagogue after passing through that grainfield. Thus room is left for Luke’s account, which says that this man’s hand was healed on another Sabbath.

The man who had the withered hand represents the human race, dried up in the fruitfulness of good works but healed by the Lord’s mercy. His right hand, which had withered in the first parent when he plucked the fruit of the forbidden tree, was restored to salvation through the grace of the Redeemer, when the Redeemer stretched out his innocent hands upon the tree of the cross. It is fitting that the hand was withered in the synagogue, because where the gift of knowledge is greater, there too the danger of inexcusable guilt is more serious.

And they asked him, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the sabbaths?”—so that they might accuse him. Because he had excused by a convincing example the violation of the sabbath which the Pharisees were alleging against the disciples, they wish to calumniate him himself. They therefore asked whether it was lawful to heal on the sabbaths, so that, if he did not heal, they might accuse him of cruelty or weakness, but, if he did heal, of being a transgressor. On the sabbaths especially the Lord teaches and performs miracles in the synagogue, not only to suggest the spiritual sabbath, but also because the people gathered there in greater numbers on that day. At that time, by an ancient institution of the fathers, it was customary for them—since the Law commanded them to abstain from labor—to devote themselves to reading and hearing the Scriptures. Accordingly, James says in the Acts of the Apostles: “For Moses from ancient generations has those who proclaim him in the synagogues, where he is read every sabbath” (Acts XV). For just as those skilled in hunting, when they have learned where wild animals, fish, and birds are most abundant, stretch their nets there above all, so the Lord continually taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews assembled, wishing all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

But he said to them: “Which of you will be a man who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the sabbaths, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the sabbaths.” (Jerome) He resolves the question put to him in such a way as to condemn the questioners’ greed. “If,” he says, “on the sabbath you hasten to rescue a sheep or any other animal that has fallen into a pit, consulting not the animal but your own greed, how much more should I free a human being, who is far more valuable than a sheep!” Anticipating the calumny which the Jews had prepared against him in their faithless minds, the Lord reproves them because they violated the commandments of the Law by a perverse interpretation, thinking that on the sabbath one must abstain even from good works, although the Law commands abstention from evil, saying: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Lev. XXIII), that is, sin; “for everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VII). In the same commandment he also sketches, in present things, the pattern of the age to come: those who have done good through the three ages of this world will have rest in the seventh, from evils alone and not from good things. For although worldly works cease, the activity of good work is not idle when it rests in the praise of God.

Then he said to the man: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out. The withered hand is commanded to be stretched out for healing, because the barrenness of a weakened soul is cured by no better order than by the generosity of almsgiving. Hence John the Baptist, when the crowds asked what they should do lest they be sent into the fire like withered trees, gave this sole command: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none, and let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke III). And in Ecclesiasticus it is said: “My son, do not let your hand be extended to receive and withdrawn when it is time to give” (Ecclus. IV). For in vain does one stretch out his hands to God in supplication for sins if he has not stretched them out to bring assistance to a widow who asks for aid. Hence it is beautifully added:

And it was restored to health, like the other. Before the Savior’s coming, the human race had a weak right hand and a sound left hand, because it languidly neglected the work of almsgiving and was intent only on pursuing its own advantage. But when the Lord Jesus Christ came, its right hand was healed so as to be like the left: what it had previously gathered greedily, it was now commanded to distribute generously. Thus what is written is fulfilled: “Those who use this world should be as though they did not use it” (1 Cor. VII); and: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little” (2 Cor. VIII).

(Jerome) It should also be noted that in the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes and Ebionites use, and which many call the authentic Gospel of Matthew, this man who had the withered hand is recorded as a mason, begging help in words of this kind: “I was a mason, seeking my livelihood with my hands; I beseech you, Jesus, to restore my health, so that I may not shamefully beg for food.” Finally, until the Savior’s coming, the hand in the synagogue of the Jews—whose care had been entrusted with the spiritual building—was withered, and God’s works were not being done through it. After he came upon the earth, the right hand was restored in the believing apostles and returned to its former work.

(Augustine) It may also be asked how Matthew could have said that they themselves questioned the Lord, “Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath?” wishing to find an occasion for accusing him, whereas he himself proposed to them the comparison concerning the sheep, saying: “Which of you will be a man who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the sabbaths, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the sabbaths.” For Mark and Luke report that the Lord questioned them in these words: “Is it lawful on the sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save a life or to destroy it?” (Mark III; Luke VI). It must therefore be understood that they first asked the Lord whether it was lawful to heal on the sabbath. Then, knowing their thoughts and that they were seeking an opportunity for accusation, he placed in the midst the man whom he was about to heal, and asked what Mark and Luke record him as having asked. When they remained silent, he then proposed the comparison concerning the sheep and concluded that it is lawful to do good on the sabbath.

Finally, after looking around at them with anger, as Mark says, and being grieved over the hardness of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” Matthew then follows, weaving his account together in this way.

But the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him.

(Maurice) He says “going out,” therefore, not “approaching” or “drawing near,” because their perverse mind was always turned away from the Lord, and they did not belong to the company of those to whom Scripture says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened,” and so forth (Ps. XXXIII). Going out, plainly, with their master the devil, of whom it is written: “Satan went out from the presence of the Lord” (Job I, II), they took counsel how they might destroy life, not how they themselves might find life. That the wicked plot ambushes against the Lord is due to envy. For what had he done to provoke the Pharisees to seek his death? Nothing except that a man had stretched out his hand. Which of the Pharisees had not stretched out his hand on the sabbath, carrying food, offering a cup, and doing the other things necessary for nourishment? If, then, stretching out one’s hand and lifting food or drink is not a crime on the sabbath, why do they condemn this action which they themselves are compelled to perform—especially since this mason carried nothing of the kind, but stretched out his hand at the Lord’s command for healing? Indeed, the one who said, “and they came to be” (Ps. XXXII), could not be convicted of laboring on the sabbath.

But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there. Knowing their ambushes and that they wished to destroy their Savior, he withdrew from there in order to remove from the Pharisees an occasion for impiety. (Bede) He withdrew like a man fleeing the ambushes of pursuers, because the hour of his passion had not yet come, nor was the place of his passion outside Jerusalem. He withdrew, fleeing those who pursued him out of hatred, but went to the place where he found more people following him out of love. For it follows:

And many followed him, and he healed them all. Behold: the Pharisees, namely the teachers of the people, unanimously seek to destroy the Lord; but the unlearned crowd and the populace gathered from every direction follow him with unanimous affection. Those men, seeing his mighty works and hearing the words of his teaching, were able to learn nothing more than to persecute him. These, guided only by the report of his miracles, come in a very great multitude to hear him and beg the help of salvation. Therefore they immediately deserve to obtain the fulfillment of their will and desire, with many being healed by the Lord, as is read below, where he gave his followers an example that, if they suffered persecution in one city, they should flee to another. Finally, Paul, instructed both by the Lord’s example and by his command, fled from Damascus, where he was being pursued by the plots of wicked men; but after departing from there, he found elsewhere countless peoples who followed him in devotion (2 Cor. XI).

And he commanded them not to make him known.

(Maurice) He gave this command not out of fear of death, lest he should perhaps be betrayed and killed, for his soul was in his own power, but out of mercy toward the Jews, lest they themselves should be slaughtered by envy while persecuting the innocent. Of such people it is said elsewhere: “Anger kills the foolish, and envy puts the little ones to death” (Job V). In a tropological sense, he also instructs us that, whenever we have done something great, we should not seek praise from outside ourselves.

[Col. 0925A] In order that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, when he said: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased” (Isa. XLII). For what the prophet foretold would happen concerning him had necessarily to be fulfilled in him, so that his innocence and gentleness might prove the prophetic oracle true. Jesus, therefore, is the Lord’s servant because he assumed the form of a servant and was found in appearance as a human being (Phil. III); yet he is chosen, because he himself, as Scripture says, “is chosen from among thousands” (Song V)—the true David, namely, the man found to be according to the Lord’s heart, who did all his will (Ps. LXXXVIII). He was chosen for a work which no one else performed: to redeem the human race and reconcile the world to God. For when he is chosen, he is human; when he chooses, he is God. [Col. 0925B] In two natures Christ is one person. In him God’s soul was well pleased, because he alone is the lamb without the stain of sin, concerning whom the Father’s voice also says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

I will place my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim judgment to the nations.

(Jerome) This is said through the prophet in the person of the Father. For the Spirit is placed not upon the Word of God and the Only-Begotten, who proceeded from the Father’s bosom, but upon him concerning whom it was said, “Behold my servant” (Isa. XLII). Again, he says: “The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isa. LXI). The Lord Jesus therefore proclaimed God’s judgment to the nations, because through his Gospel and the preachers of the New Testament he revealed the judgment that would come, which they had in no way believed, and taught them now to practice just judgments and avoid unjust judgments. It follows:

He will not contend, nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.

(Maurice) Christ did not contend, nor cry out, nor was his voice heard in the streets, because when he was cursed he did not curse in return, and when he suffered he did not threaten. He handed himself over to the one who judged unjustly, gave his body to those who struck him and his cheeks to those who plucked them; “like a sheep led to slaughter, he did not open his mouth” (Isa. L). Allegorically, no one heard Christ’s voice in the streets because broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many who enter by it do not hear the Savior’s voice, since they are not on the narrow way but on the spacious one.

He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish smoking flax.

(Augustine) He calls the Jews a bruised reed, because they were one people yet differed among themselves. By “smoking flax” he means the people gathered from the nations, who, after the ardor of the natural law had been extinguished, were enveloped in the errors of the most bitter smoke, harmful to the eyes, and of dark obscurity. He not only did not extinguish them and reduce them to ashes, but, on the contrary, from a small and almost dying spark he raised up the greatest conflagrations, so that the whole world burned with the fire of the Lord [Col. 0926A] Savior, whom he came to cast upon the earth (Luke XII). Or otherwise: whoever does not extend a hand to a sinner and does not carry his brother’s burden breaks the bruised reed; and whoever despises a small spark in little ones extinguishes the smoking flax. Christ did neither of these things, for he had come to save what had perished and to carry the wandering sheep back to the flock upon his sacred shoulders (Luke XIX). Hence it also follows:

Until he sends forth judgment unto victory.

He who did not crush the bruised reed and did not extinguish the smoking flax also brought judgment to victory. His judgments are true and justified in themselves (Ps. XVIII). The light of his preaching will shine in the world, and no one’s plotting will crush or overcome it, until he establishes judgment on the earth and what is written is fulfilled: “Let your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. VI). Otherwise: our Redeemer preserved his patience and gentleness until death, until the judgment being accomplished in him came to victory. For after he had powerfully overcome by rising again the death of his flesh, which he mercifully accepted for us, he returned as victor to the kingdom after expelling the prince of this world. There, seated at the Father’s right hand, he will reign until he places all his enemies beneath his feet (Ps. CIX).

And in his name the nations will hope.

Therefore the nations will rightly hope in his name, because he is the seed concerning which it was promised to Abraham that in his seed all the nations of the earth would be blessed. Concerning him the aforementioned Isaiah also says: “The root of Jesse, who will rise to rule the nations; in him they will hope” (Isa. XI), and they will entreat him.

All the nations will hope in his name, because, as Peter says, “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which they can be saved” (Acts IV). But in the name of Jesus, according to Paul’s word, “every knee will bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue will confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II).

[III.] Then a demon-possessed man was brought to him, blind and mute, and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw.
