Three signs, therefore, were performed together in one man: the blind man sees, the mute speaks, and the demon-possessed man is freed. This happened then in a bodily sense, but it is also fulfilled daily in the conduct of believers: once the demon has first been expelled, they behold the light of faith; then mouths that were previously silent are opened for the praises of God.

And all the crowds were astonished, and they said: “Is this perhaps the son of David?” But when the Pharisees heard this, they said: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” The crowds, who appeared less instructed, were always astonished at the Lord’s deeds and proclaimed him the son of David because of the mercy and benefits he bestowed upon those in need. But the Pharisees and scribes, by contrast, strove either to deny these things or to twist by sinister interpretation what they could not deny, as though these works had been performed not by divine power but by an unclean spirit—namely Beelzebub, who was the god of Ekron. For Bel himself is Baal, while Zebub is called “fly.” Contrary to certain corrupt copies, the name should not be read with the letter *l* or with *d* at the end, but with *b*, as *Beelzebub*. It is therefore interpreted as “Baal of flies,” that is, “man of flies” or “one who has flies,” evidently because of the filth of sacrificial blood; from this most unclean rite or name they gave the prince of demons his title.

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste.”

(Jerome) He answered not their words but their thoughts, so that in this way they might be compelled to believe in his power, since he saw the hidden things of the heart. If every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, then the kingdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not divided. Without any contradiction, it will not be laid waste by some force, but will remain in eternal stability. If, then, the kingdom of the holy and undivided Trinity remains undivided—or rather, because it is undivided—let the Arians cease to say that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son, for those whose kingdom is one also possess one majesty.

And every city or house divided against itself will not stand. A kingdom or city divided against itself cannot endure; but just as small things grow through harmony, so great things collapse through discord. If, therefore, Satan fights against himself, and one demon is hostile to another, the consummation of the world should already have come. Nor would the hostile powers have any place in it, since their war against one another is the peace of human beings. But if you think for this reason, O scribes and Pharisees, that the demons’ departure is obedience to their prince, so that they deceive ignorant people by fraudulent pretense, what can you say about the healings of bodies which the Lord performed? It would be otherwise only if you were also to attribute bodily weaknesses and the marks of spiritual virtues to demons.

(Hilary) This too can be understood in another way. The same reasoning applies to a house and a city as to a kingdom. But here “city” indicates Jerusalem, always glorious in its dominion over the nations. Now, after the people had kindled their fury against the Lord and driven away his apostles with the company of believers, it will not stand because of the division caused by their departure from it. Thus the destruction of that city, which soon followed through this division, is announced.

And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand? By the very manner in which they spoke, they are condemned for the wickedness of their earlier statement, in which they said that he performed these deeds by Beelzebub, without understanding that they had confessed Beelzebub to be divided. If he was compelled to divide himself, so that demon disturbed demon and, divided against himself, stood against himself, it must also be judged from this that there is more power in the one who divided them than in those who were divided. Therefore he is already divided, compelled against himself, and his kingdom has been dissolved by such division; it cannot stand, but has an end.

[Col. 0928A] (Augustine) By saying this, he wished it to be understood from their own confession that, by not believing in him, they had chosen to belong to the devil’s kingdom. That kingdom, being divided against itself, cannot stand. Let them therefore choose whichever they wish: if Satan cannot cast out Satan, they could find nothing to say against the Lord; but if he can, they should take much greater care for themselves and withdraw from his kingdom, which, being divided against itself, cannot stand. But to show in what way the Lord Christ casts out demons, lest they should think him the prince of demons, let them attend to what follows:

And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. He said this, certainly, concerning his disciples, the sons of that people, who were well aware that they had learned no evil arts from the good teacher, so as to cast out demons by the prince of demons. “Therefore,” he says, “they will be your judges.” These very men—the lowly and despised things of this world, in whom not ingenious wickedness but the holy simplicity of my power is evident—will be my witnesses and your judges.

(Jerome) Alternatively, he means the Jewish exorcists, who, according to the custom of that nation, cast out demons at an invocation. He constrains them by a prudent question to confess that this is the work of the Holy Spirit. “If,” he says, “the expulsion of demons through your sons is attributed to God and not to demons, why does the same work in me not have the same cause?” Therefore they will be your judges, not by authority but by comparison: they assign the expulsion of demons to God, while you assign it to Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. In Luke we read this passage written as follows: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI). This is the finger whom the magicians also confess when they performed signs against Moses and Aaron, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. IV); by this finger the stone tablets were also written on Mount Sinai (Deut. IX). Therefore, if the Son is the hand and arm of God, and the Holy Spirit is his finger, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one substance. Do not be scandalized by the inequality of the members, since the unity of the body establishes it.

(Augustine) Alternatively, the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God because of the distribution of gifts, by which particular gifts are given to each person, whether human or angelic. For in none of our members is division more apparent than in the fingers.

(Jerome) When he says, “The kingdom of God has come upon you,” he either signifies himself, concerning whom it is written elsewhere, “The kingdom of God is within you,” and, “He stands among you whom you do not know”; or certainly that kingdom which both John and the Lord himself proclaimed: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (John I). A third meaning is the kingdom of Holy Scripture, which is taken away from the Jews and given to a nation producing its fruits (Matt. XXI).

Or how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and seize his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.

(Augustine) He calls the devil strong because he held human beings so that they could not tear themselves away from him by their own strength, but only through God’s grace. His goods are the people deceived by him; his house is the world, which lies in the power of the evil one. Until the Savior’s coming, he possessed it as a badly pacified realm, resting without opposition in the hearts of unbelievers. The Lord bound the strong man—that is, he restrained the devil from deceiving the elect. Then he plundered his house, because he united those whom he had rescued from the devil’s snares, whom he had foreseen as his own, to the members of his Church and arranged them within it according to the distinct dignities of various ranks. Or certainly he plundered his house because he distributed all the regions of the world, over which the ancient enemy once ruled, to the apostles and their successors, so that each in his own province might convert the peoples recalled from error to the way of life. Thus, through a parable that is already utterly clear, the Lord shows that he freed people from demons not by deceitful agreement in his heart and cooperation with demons, as they accused him, but by a wholly different and opposing power of divinity. Therefore those who called what they knew to be God’s the devil’s were committing a great crime.

Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. No one should think that this was said about heretics and schismatics, although it can also be understood in that way as an additional meaning. From what follows and from the tenor of the discourse, it refers to the devil and to the fact that Beelzebub’s works cannot be compared with the Savior’s works. The devil desires to hold human souls captive; the Lord desires to free them. The devil preaches idols; the Lord the knowledge of the one God. The devil draws people to vices; the Lord recalls them to virtues. How, then, can those whose works are divided have harmony with one another?

Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings. All sins and blasphemies are not indiscriminately forgiven to all people, but to those who in this life have practiced worthy repentance for their errors. Nor does the perverse assertion of Novatian have any place, when he denies that pardon should be granted to penitents who fell during their martyrdom; nor that of Origen, who asserts that after the universal judgment, once countless ages have passed, all sinners and blasphemers will obtain forgiveness of sins and be led to the heavenly kingdom. The Lord’s subsequent words also refute this error.

But blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. Whoever clearly understands that these are works of God, yet, unable to deny their power, slanders them, driven by envy, and says that Christ, the Word of God, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub—this person will not be forgiven either in the present age or in the age to come. This does not mean that we deny that such a person could be forgiven by the one who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II), if he were able to repent. Rather, trusting in the Judge and giver of pardon, who says that he will always accept both the penitent and repentance, yet nowhere says that this blasphemy is to be repented of, we believe that this blasphemer of blasphemy, as his deserts require, will attain neither remission nor even the fruits of worthy repentance. This agrees with what John the Evangelist most truthfully wrote concerning certain people blinded on account of the merit of their blasphemy: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they might not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them’” (Isa. VI).

Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit alone, therefore, because a person in the likeness of the devil and his angels does not fear to attack the majesty of the Godhead against his own conscience, has no forgiveness forever, but is guilty of an eternal offense. The evangelist Mark plainly declares this, for after setting down this saying of the Lord he added: “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Mark III). For neither those who believe and confess that the Holy Spirit does not exist, nor those who believe that he exists but is not God, nor those who believe that he is indeed God but lesser than the Father and the Son, are held by the guilt of this unforgivable blasphemy, since they act not from diabolical envy but from human ignorance. But the leaders of the Jews, and all who are like them, corrupted by the plague of envy, blaspheme the majesty and will perish without end.

And whoever says a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him. It is as though he were saying in other words: Whoever speaks insults against me, having been scandalized by my flesh and thinking me merely human—thinking that I am the son of a carpenter and have brothers named James, Joseph, and Judas, and that I am a man who eats excessively and drinks wine—such an opinion and blasphemy, although it is not free from the guilt of error, nevertheless has forgiveness because of the lowliness of the body.

But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

(Gregory) From these words of the Lord it is understood that some faults are released in this age and others in the age to come. For what is denied in one case makes clear by implication that it is granted in certain others. Nevertheless, it must be believed that this can occur only with small and very minor sins, such as habitual idle speech, immoderate laughter, and the sin involved in managing one’s household affairs—things which are scarcely done without guilt even by those who know how guilt ought to be avoided—or errors of ignorance in matters not involving serious faults. All these burden a person even after death if they have not been released while he was still living in this life. Yet this must be known: there, at least concerning the smallest matters, no one will obtain purification unless, while still living here, he has earned through good works the attainment of it there.

Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad. For the tree is known by its fruits. He constrains them with a syllogism which the Greeks call *dilemma* (δίλημμα). [Alternatively, ἀφύκτον; we may call it “inevitable,” for it encloses those questioned from both sides and presses them with either horn.] “If,” he says, “the devil is evil, he cannot perform good works; but if the works you see being performed are good, it follows that the one performing them is not the devil. For it is impossible for good to arise from evil or evil from good.”

(Maurice) Mystically, the good tree is Christ, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “He will be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season” (Ps. I). This tree therefore gave its fruit in its season—that is, in the time of his incarnation—when he preached the Gospel, performed many miracles, bestowed healing upon the sick, granted understanding of the Scriptures, and illumined with the light of faith and truth those blinded by the darkness of unbelief and sins. Finally, after accomplishing his passion and resurrection, he raised to life by his grace the human race which had fallen into death through the forbidden fruit. Conversely, the bad tree is the devil and all who belong to him: the scribes and Pharisees, heretics, schismatics, and the other unrighteous who sprout from that most evil root. Their fruit is envy, detraction, persecution, blasphemy, heresy, the precipice of death, and the abyss of sins. For just as these two trees differ in kind, so they also differ in their offspring. Hence it follows:

Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?

(Augustine) He calls them a brood of vipers because he calls them children of the devil.

(Jerome) A person is his son to the extent that he imitates him by sinning. When he says, “How can you speak good things when you are evil?” he shows that they are a bad tree and bear fruits overflowing with blasphemy, such as the devil’s offspring possess as their seeds.

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

(Augustine) Human judgment often errs, because it does not know the neighbor’s heart except by weighing it from his mouth and his actions. But the Lord judges the action itself and our words, which the mouth of the heart speaks, since he knows from what intention words are uttered.

A good person brings good things out of a good treasure, and an evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasure.

(Augustine) The treasure of the heart is the intention of thought, from which the eternal Judge assesses the outcome of the work. Thus it often happens that certain lesser good works obtain greater rewards from heavenly grace, namely because of the intention of the heart by which people had wished to accomplish greater good works, if they could. (Jerome) Others, although displaying greater works of virtue, receive lesser rewards from the Lord because of the carelessness of a lukewarm heart. In this passage, however, he either shows the Jews themselves, who blasphemed the Lord, from what treasure—that is, from the hidden place of the heart—they bring forth blasphemy; or the statement remains connected with the preceding question: just as a good person cannot bring forth evil, nor an evil person perform good works, so Christ cannot perform evil works, nor can the devil perform good ones.

But I say to you that for every idle word which human beings speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment. This too remains connected with what precedes, and the sense is: If an idle word, which does not at all edify those who hear it, is spoken not without danger to the one who speaks, and if each person will give an account on the day of judgment for his words, how much more will you give an account for your calumny, since you slander the works of the Holy Spirit and say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. An idle word is one spoken without benefit either to the speaker or to the hearer—that is, when, setting reason aside, we talk about frivolous matters and tell ancient stories. But whoever repeats obscenity, loosens mouths in laughter, or utters something shameful will be held guilty not of idle speech but of criminal speech.

For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned. The statement still depends upon what precedes, where he said: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” It is beyond doubt that a person is condemned by God on account of the evil words he has uttered. But he cannot in any way be justified by good words unless he speaks them from the depth of his heart with a right intention. Even if words are good, if they are not spoken with a right purpose, they cannot justify the speaker. Thus Caiaphas was not found righteous in prophesying when he said: “It is better that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XI).

Those words therefore justify the speaker when he holds inwardly in his heart the good that he utters with his mouth and speaks it with a sound intention. For the testing of human life consists in the weight of words, because, as Solomon says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and whoever guards his mouth guards his soul from distress; but whoever is careless in speaking will experience evil” (Prov. XVIII). Hence James also says: “The tongue is indeed a small member, yet it boasts of great things. The tongue is a fire, the universe of iniquity. The tongue is placed among our members; it stains the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth, being set on fire by Gehenna. With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing” (James III). And again: “In many things we all offend. If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (ibid.).

By “word” he means the kind of offense which human frailty can avoid: words of blasphemy, deceit, detraction, cursing, pride, boasting, excuses for sins, jealousy, dissension, heresy, lying, perjury, and also idle or excessive speech concerning things that seem necessary. Whoever guards himself without offense in such speech is a perfect man. But whoever utters words of the catholic faith and pious confession concerning the Lord, and words pertaining to the instruction and benefit of his neighbors, will be justified eternally and judged worthy of a good reward.

[IV.] Then certain scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” (Jerome.) They ask for signs as though the signs they had seen were not signs. But in another Evangelist what they ask is explained more fully: “We wish to see a sign from you from heaven” [Col. 0933A]. Either they desired fire to come down from above in the manner of Elijah (IV Kings 1), or thunder to bellow, lightning to flash, and rain to pour down in the summertime, as in the time of Samuel (I Samuel 12). As though they could not also slander those signs and say that they had occurred through hidden and various disturbances of the air. But if you slander what you see with your eyes, hold in your hands, and experience through its usefulness, what will you do with things that have come from heaven? Surely you will answer that the magicians in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven.

He answered and said to them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign.” He aptly said “adulterous,” because it had abandoned its husband and, according to Ezekiel, had joined itself to many lovers (Ezekiel 16).

“And no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet” [Col. 0933B]. He had been pressed with a twofold question. Some were slandering him, saying that he cast out demons by Beelzebul; to these he has now given his answer. Others, testing him, were asking him for a sign from heaven; to these he now begins to reply. He does not give them the sign from heaven, which they were unworthy to see, but one from the depths of hell: the sign of Jonah the prophet, shipwrecked and swallowed by the whale, yet delivered from the abyss and the jaws of death. Jonah both received and gave this sign—namely, of the incarnation, not of divinity; of suffering, not of glorification (Jonah 2–3). To his disciples, however, he gave a sign from heaven, showing them the glory of eternal blessedness, first figuratively when he was transfigured on the mountain, and afterward truly when he was lifted up into heaven. (Augustine.) He showed, indeed, that the Jews, like the Ninevites, were entangled in grave sins [Col. 0933C] and near to destruction if they did not repent. But just as punishment was announced to the Ninevites and a remedy was shown, so the Jews also ought not to despair of pardon if they wished to repent, because the death of the Savior is the reconciliation of the world. Hence it follows:

“For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.” (Maurice.) That Jonah prefigured the Savior is evident from this passage: just as Jonah was sent to preach to Nineveh, whose name is interpreted “beautiful,” so the Savior was sent for the salvation of the nations. Jonah is indeed interpreted as “dove” or “one who mourns”; and these names fittingly apply to our Redeemer, upon whom [Col. 0933D] the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, and of whom the prophet says: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53). The fish that swallowed Jonah in the sea signifies the death that Christ suffered in the world. Jonah was therefore in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, and our Savior was in death, in the tomb, for three days and three nights. Then what is read in Hosea was fulfilled: “O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite” (Hosea 13).

And just as Jonah did not remain in the belly of the fish but was cast out onto dry land, so the soul of our Savior was not abandoned in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption, but he rose in glory. For [Col. 0934A] it seems not unworthy of inquiry how the Savior was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, since he was crucified on the Parasceve, around the sixth hour, and rose from the dead very early on the first day of the week. We must therefore understand this as spoken by synecdoche—that is, if you count the part of the day of the Parasceve during which he was buried together with the preceding night as one day and one night; then the entire night and day of the Sabbath as a whole day; and the Lord’s night together with the day that was beginning to dawn, and thus beginning with it, as the whole—then, by taking a part for the whole, you certainly have three days and three nights.

(Augustine.) Nor should we fail to consider that the single death of our Redeemer benefited our double death, and his single resurrection benefited our double resurrection. The death of his flesh and his resurrection [Col. 0934B] are the death of our flesh; and his resurrection is the death and resurrection of our soul. Two deaths of ours and two resurrections of ours make four. Add one death of the Lord and one resurrection of the Lord to our four, and they make six. Thus the Lord’s single portion and our double portion make three; and three is a division of the number six. This was signified by the thirty-three hours during which the Lord was in hell. Twelve daytime hours and twenty-four nighttime hours correspond to this single portion. Likewise, the twenty-four hours correspond to our double death, and those twelve hours to the Lord’s single death.

It was not without reason that he lay one day in the tomb and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death [Col. 0934C]. He came to us, who were held in the death of spirit and flesh; he brought to us his one death—that is, the death of the flesh—and by receiving them he dissolved our two deaths. For if he had himself assumed both, he would have freed us from neither. Instead, he mercifully accepted one and justly condemned both: he conferred his single death upon our double death, and by dying he subdued our double death.

“The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.” (Maurice.) The Ninevites will therefore condemn the Jewish people, not by the authority of judgment, but by the correction of their lives. Because the Jews did not do this, they are rightly reproved by the Lord. (Jerome.) It is as though he said to them in other words [Col. 0934D]: “Jonah preached for a few days; I have preached for so long. He preached to the Assyrians, an unbelieving nation; I to the Jews, the people of God. He to foreigners; I to citizens. He spoke with a simple voice and, performing no signs, was accepted; I, performing so many signs, endure the slander of Beelzebul. Therefore, something greater than Jonah is here”—that is, here, preaching in your midst. And for this reason the men of Nineveh will also condemn the generation of the Jews: that is, they will convict it of unbelief.

“The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it.” (Rabanus.) She will certainly condemn it, not by the power of judgment, but by comparison with her better deed. If the queen of the South, who is undoubtedly counted among the elect, will rise in the judgment with the reprobate, this shows that there will be one resurrection of all mortals, both good and evil [Col. 0935A]. And this will not occur, according to Jewish fables, a thousand years before the judgment, but in the judgment itself.

“For she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here.” Here the word “here” is not a pronoun but an adverb of place; that is, he who is incomparably greater than Solomon is now present among you. Scripture relates how the queen of Sheba came to Judea through such great difficulties, leaving behind her people and kingdom, to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and, bringing him many gifts, received even more from him (III Kings 10). She will therefore condemn the Jews in the judgment, because she sought him from the farthest ends of the earth, having learned through the gift of wisdom that he was famous [Col. 0935B]. But they, having among them one who was wise not from elsewhere but who himself is the wisdom and power of God, preferred not only not to hear him but also to blaspheme him and harass him with plots.

In another sense, in the Ninevites and the queen of the South, the faith of the Church is preferred to Israel. The Church is reconciled to the Lord no less through repentance for its former folly than through diligence in learning wisdom. For the unity of the Church is gathered from two parts: namely, from those who do not know how to sin and from those who cease from sinning. Repentance wipes out sin; wisdom guards against it. Therefore they will judge them in the resurrection, because the fear of God was found among those to whom the law had not been preached. This makes those who are unbelieving though they possess the law all the more unworthy of pardon, since greater faith was found among those who were ignorant of the law.

[Col. 0935C] “But when the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry places.” Although this may simply be understood as something the Lord added to distinguish his works from Satan’s: namely, that he always hastens to cleanse what is defiled, while Satan hastens to stain what has been cleansed with worse impurities; nevertheless, it may also suitably be understood of any heretic or schismatic, or even of a wicked Catholic. At the time of baptism, the unclean spirit that had previously dwelt in such a person is driven out through the confession of the Catholic faith and the renunciation of worldly conduct. It then traverses dry places—that is, it examines the hearts of the faithful, cleansed of the softness of wandering thought, like a crafty ambusher looking for those in whom it might perhaps plant the steps of its wickedness [Col. 0935D]. But it is rightly said:

“Seeking rest, and he does not find it.” For when the devil flees chaste minds, he can find a rest pleasing to him only in the heart of the wicked. Hence the Lord says of him: “He sleeps under the shade, in the secret place of the reed, and in moist places” (Job 40). “Under the shade,” that is, in dark consciences; “in the reed,” which is bright on the outside but hollow within, in hypocrites; and “in moist places,” insinuating himself into wanton and soft minds.

“Then he says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’” This verse is to be feared, not explained, lest the fault we believed extinguished in us should, through our negligence while we are idle [Col. 0936A], overwhelm us.

“And when he comes, he finds it empty, swept clean and adorned.” That is, chastened by baptism from the stain of sins but not enriched by any diligence in good works. Hence this Evangelist rightly says that he found the house empty, swept clean, and adorned: cleansed from former vices through baptism, empty of good deeds through negligence, and adorned with counterfeit virtues through hypocrisy.

“Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there.” By the seven evil spirits he signifies all vices. Whoever after baptism is seized either by heretical perversity or by worldly desire will soon be cast down by all vices to the depths [Col. 0936B]. Hence those spirits are rightly called more wicked when they enter him, because he will possess not only those four vices that are opposed to the four spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy to possess the virtues themselves.

“And the final state of that person is worse than the first.” For it would have been better for him not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back. We read that this was fulfilled especially in Judas the betrayer (Luke 22), Simon Magus (Acts 8), and others of the same kind. Explaining where this parable generally tends, the Savior himself immediately added:

“So will it also be with this most evil generation.” That is, what I have said is accustomed to happen specially to one person does not cease to happen generally in the whole race of this people [Col. 0936C]. The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the law. It wandered through dry places, seeking rest: driven out from the Jews, it wandered through the wildernesses of the nations. When those nations afterward believed in the Lord, and the spirit found no place among them, it said: “I will return to my former house, from which I came; I will have the Jews whom I previously abandoned.” When it came, it found the house empty and swept clean. The temple of the Jews was empty, for it did not have Christ as its guest, who said: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23).

Therefore, because they did not have the protection of God and the angels, and because they were adorned with the superfluous observances of the Pharisees, the devil returned to them. Having added to himself a sevenfold number of demons, he dwelt in the former house, and the latter state of that people became worse than the former [Col. 0936D]. For now they are possessed by a much greater number of demons, blaspheming Jesus Christ in their synagogues, than they had been possessed in Egypt before they knew the law. For it is one thing not to believe that someone will come, and another not to receive the one who has come.

Understand the number seven added to the devil either because of the Sabbath or because of the number of the Holy Spirit. Just as Isaiah says that seven spirits of virtues ascended upon the shoot from the root of Jesse and the flower that rises from the root, so, conversely, the number of vices has been consecrated in the devil (Isaiah 61).

[Col. 0937A] [V.] While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers stood outside, seeking to speak with him. But someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.” The Lord was occupied in the work of preaching—in teaching the peoples and fulfilling the office of proclamation. His mother and brothers stood outside and desired to speak with him. Then someone announces to the Savior that his brothers and mother are standing outside, seeking him. It seems to me that the messenger does not announce this accidentally and simply, but lays a trap to discover whether he prefers flesh and blood to spiritual work. For this reason he pretends not to know his mother, so that he may indicate who is his mother and who are his relatives—not through bodily kinship, but through the union of the spirit. Hence it follows:

“And he answered the one who told him and said: ‘Who is my mother [Col. 0937B], and who are my brothers?’” (Rabanus.) Certainly, when the Lord, being asked about his mother and brothers, declines to go out from the ministry of the word, he does not reject the duties of filial devotion, whose commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother.” Rather, he shows that he owes himself more to the mysteries of the Father than to maternal affections, commending the same lesson to us by his example as by his word, when he says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” He does not contemptuously disregard his brothers; instead, by preferring spiritual work to bodily kinship, he teaches that the bond of hearts is more religious than that of bodies.

Mystically, the mother and brothers of Jesus are the synagogue, from whose flesh he was born, and the Jewish people. While the Savior teaches within, they come but cannot enter, because they neglect to understand his words spiritually. For [Col. 0937C] the crowd enters the house before them and listens to his speech, because, while Judea delays, the Gentiles have flowed together to Christ. The closer they are in faith, the more capaciously they drank in the inner mysteries of life. As the psalm says: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Psalm 33); within is the word, within is the light.

(Augustine.) Hence elsewhere he says: “So that those who enter may see the light.” Thus, while his relatives stand outside, they are not themselves recognized as relatives—and perhaps they are not recognized for our example, showing how we too will be recognized if we stand outside. His relatives wish to see the Lord while standing outside, when the Jews, not seeking the spiritual meaning in the law, fixed themselves outside in the observance of the letter. They are like people who compel Christ to go out to teach carnal matters rather than consent to enter themselves to learn spiritual [Col. 0937D] matters.

(Jerome.) Some suspect that the brothers of the Lord were Joseph’s sons by another wife, following the fantasies of the apocryphal writings and inventing a certain little woman named Escha. But we understand the brothers of the Lord to be not Joseph’s sons but the Savior’s cousins, children of Mary, the Lord’s maternal aunt, who is said to have been the mother of James the younger, Joseph, and Judas. In another place in the Gospel we read that these were called the Lord’s brothers. That cousins are called brothers is demonstrated throughout Scripture.

“And stretching out his hand toward the disciples, he said: ‘Behold my mother and my brothers.’” These are my mother, who daily give birth to me in the hearts of believers. These are my brothers, who do the works of my Father [Col. 0938A]. Therefore, contrary to Marcion and Manichaeus, he did not deny his mother so that he might be thought to have been born as a phantom; rather, he preferred the apostles to bodily kinship, so that we too might prefer the spirit to the flesh in the comparison of loves.

“For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother.” Since the one who does the will of God is called the Lord’s sister and brother on account of both sexes being gathered into the faith, this is not astonishing. But it is very astonishing how such a person can also be called his mother. For he graciously called faithful disciples brothers, saying: “Go, announce to my brothers.” Therefore, since one who comes to faith can become the Lord’s brother, we must ask how that same person can become his mother [Col. 0938B]. But we must know that the one who becomes Jesus’ brother and sister by believing becomes his mother by preaching, as was said above. For that person gives birth, as it were, to the Lord when he pours him into the heart of the hearer. He becomes his mother if, through his voice, the love of the Lord is generated in the mind of his neighbor.

CHAPTER XIII. He teaches the crowds from a boat in parables, which he explains to the apostles at home; he teaches in the synagogue at Nazareth, where he is without honor

[I.] “On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea.” (Augustine.) “On that day,” unless perhaps “day,” according to the usage of Scripture, signifies a period of time, sufficiently indicates that this happened next, or that not much could have intervened [Col. 0938C]. This is especially so because Mark also maintains this order (Mark 4), while Luke, after recounting the matter of the Lord’s mother and brothers, moves on to something else (Luke 8), without making any transition that appears to conflict with this order.

(Rabanus.) Not only the Lord’s deeds and words, but also the journeys and places in which he worked miracles and preached, are filled with heavenly mysteries. After the discourse delivered in the house, where he was accused of the unspeakable blasphemy of having a demon, he went out and taught beside the sea, to show that, having abandoned Judea because of the guilt of unbelief, he would pass over to save the nations. For the proud and unbelieving hearts of the Gentiles are rightly compared to the swollen and bitter waves of the sea.

Who does not know that Judea had been the Lord’s house through faith? But after leaving the house in which he had endured the blasphemies of the ungodly, he began to teach beside the sea. For, after abandoning the synagogue because of its unbelief, he came through the apostles to gather the multitude of the Gentile people. Hence it is openly stated beforehand that, while he was preaching in the house, his mother and brothers stood outside and, as though not recognized by him, were not admitted. Thus he left the house and passed to the sea to teach, because, after the synagogue had fixed itself outside in the observance of the letter and preferred the figures of the law to the inner mysteries of the Lord’s faith, the Lord bestowed upon the nations throughout the world the mysteries of salvation that the synagogue had rejected [Col. 0938D].

“And great crowds gathered around him, so that he went up into a [Col. 0939A] boat and sat down; and the whole crowd stood on the shore.” The fact that a great crowd gathered around the Lord as he taught beside the sea signifies the multitude of peoples hastening to the faith of truth when the apostles preached. That he went up into a boat and sat on the sea prefigured the Church, which was to be built amid unbelieving and opposing nations. The Lord is seated in the boat placed in the midst of the sea when he illuminates by the grace of his visitation the minds of believers dwelling among unbelievers and consecrates among them a dwelling beloved by him.

The crowd situated on the land around the sea, listening to the Lord’s words [Col. 0939B], neither touched by the waves nor sitting with him in the boat after crossing the waves, most suitably represents those who had recently gathered to hear the word. Through the devotion of their hearts they have indeed been separated from the bitterness, darkness, and instability of the reprobate, but they have not yet been imbued with the heavenly mysteries that they desire.

(Maurice.) “And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying.” For “parable” in Greek means a figure or turn of speech, and is interpreted as “likeness.” It is a comparison of things different in kind. Things that differ in kind are compared in a likeness of their forms, in order to express what the one who utters the comparison wishes to signify.

(Jerome.) The crowd is not of one opinion but consists of diverse dispositions in different people. Therefore he speaks to it in many parables, so that, according to their various dispositions, they may receive different teachings. It should be noted that he did not speak everything to them in parables, [Col. 0939C] but many things. If he had said everything in parables, they would have departed without benefit. He mixes clear things with obscure ones, so that through what they understand they may be drawn toward knowledge of what they do not understand.

“Behold, the sower went out to sow.” In what follows, the Lord himself explains this parable, asserting that the seed is the word of God and that he himself is the sower. But by saying, “Behold, the sower went out to sow,” he has left us something to investigate. The sower therefore went out to sow because the Lord, proceeding from the bosom of the Father, came into the world and sowed among the human race the word of truth that he had seen with the Father, either through himself or through those whom he himself appointed.

Accordingly, Habakkuk says in his praise [Col. 0939D]: “You went out for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones”—that is, those whom you deign to consecrate with the anointing of your Spirit and make participants in your holy name. Or certainly he went out to sow when, after calling the chosen portion of the synagogue to his faith, he also poured out the gifts of his grace for the gathering of the nations. He signified this very thing by his journey, when, after preaching in the house, he went out to the sea.

Finally, while preaching in the house, he abandoned some because of the unforgivable crime of their blasphemy, and called others his mother and brothers because of their devotion to piety. This clearly expresses the distinction within the Jewish people, among whom many are rebellious toward the Lord, while some are worthy of divine adoption.

[Col. 0940A] “And as he sowed, some seeds fell beside the road, and the birds came and ate them.” (Jerome.) In Luke’s Gospel this seed is described as follows: “Another fell beside the road, and it was trampled, and the birds of heaven ate it” (Luke 8). Therefore whatever the Lord himself deigned to explain in this parable should be received in devout faith. What he left unsaid for our understanding should likewise be investigated with devout intention and briefly treated.

The seed that fell beside the road perished through a double injury: it was trampled by travelers and snatched away by birds. The road, therefore, is the mind worn down and dried out by the constant passage of evil thoughts, so that it is unable to receive and germinate the seed of the word. Consequently, whatever good seed falls near such a [Col. 0940B] road perishes, because, trampled by the wicked passage of evil thought, it is snatched away by demons. They are rightly called “birds of heaven,” either because they are heavenly and spiritual in nature or because they fly through the air.

“Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, because they did not have depth of soil. But when the sun rose, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered.” The Lord explained the mystery of this seed. From that explanation we learn that the same things are not always placed allegorically with one and the same meaning. He calls the rock the hardness of a rebellious mind, the soil the gentleness of an obedient soul, and the sun the heat of raging persecution, although [Col. 0940C] elsewhere he uses the sun in a good sense, saying that the righteous will shine in the future like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

In the construction of the spiritual house, he also teaches that one must dig down deeply, cast out the soil, and place the rock in the foundation. That is, he teaches that earthly thoughts must be purged from the deepest recesses of the heart and that the strength of unconquered faith must be inserted in their place as the foundation of good works.

In this passage, therefore, the depth of soil that ought suitably, when cultivated, to receive the seed of the word is the integrity of a mind trained in heavenly disciplines and regularly instructed to listen and obey the divine utterances. The rocky places, covered with a thin layer of soil, which can quickly make the seed they receive sprout but lack the strength to establish a root, are those hearts [Col. 0940D] that have been educated by no discipline and softened by no trials of temptation. They rejoice for a time merely in the sweetness of the word they have heard and in heavenly promises, but they fall away in the time of temptation.

For when they set the momentary sweetness of the heavenly oracle against the austerity implanted in them, it is as though a great heap of stones had covered a small amount of earth in places assigned to the holy seed. Such places cannot reach the fruit of righteousness because they contain too little wholesome desire to receive the seed of life and too much harmful hardness to allow the fruit of salvation to flourish.

“Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them.” (Maurice.) The Savior himself interprets the thorns as riches [Col. 0941A]. It should not seem strange that he compared riches with thorns, since thorns prick while riches delight. They are rightly called thorns because, through the prickings of their thoughts, they tear the mind. When they draw a person on to sin, they wound and make him bleed as though with an inflicted injury. At the same time, as the thorns grow, they choke the seed and prevent it from reaching fruit, because an increase of riches strangles the mind and does not permit it to produce the spiritual fruits of virtue. Rather, if it could possess any greenness, the excess of riches overwhelms it by surpassing it with its own rough barrenness and completely destroys its vital sap.

“But other seeds fell on good soil and produced fruit, one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold.” [Col. 0941B] (Jerome.) Valentinus adopts this parable to support his heresy, introducing three natures: spiritual, soulish, and earthly. Yet here there are four: one beside the road, another rocky, a third full of thorns, and a fourth good soil.

(Bede.) The good soil—that is, the faithful conscience of the elect—acts in opposition to the produce of all three kinds of bad soil, because it willingly receives the seed of the word entrusted to it and, once received, preserves it steadfastly through adversity and prosperity until the time of fruit. It bears fruit and produces one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold.

Thirtyfold, when it implants faith in the Holy Trinity in the hearts of the elect; sixtyfold, when it teaches the perfection of good works. Since the adornment of the world was completed in the number six, good works are rightly signified by this number [Col. 0941C]. A hundredfold, when it shows that in everything we do we must seek the rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

“He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” Whenever this brief admonition is inserted either in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it indicates that what is being said is mystical and salutary for hearing and learning. The ears of hearing are the ears of the heart: the ear of the inner sense, which obeys and does what has been commanded.

“And the disciples came and said to him: ‘Why do you speak to them in parables?’” (Jerome.) It must be asked how his disciples came to him when Jesus was sitting in the boat—unless perhaps we should understand that they had [Col. 0941D] gone aboard the boat with him earlier and, standing inside it, asked him about the interpretation of the parable.

He answered and said to them: “Because it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.” Mark says it this way: “But for those who are outside, everything is done in parables” (Mark 4).

(Rabanus.) Therefore let us also enter with Christ’s disciples into the sanctuary of God, so that we may understand the final things of the mysteries of God’s kingdom. For those who draw near to his feet will receive instruction from him, saying with the Psalmist: “Open our eyes, and we shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118). Rightly, then, those whose hearts are closed, who neither wish to enter nor [Col. 0942A] take care to know the truth, hear in parables and in riddles, having forgotten the Lord’s command: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

“For whoever has, to him it will be given, and he will abound. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” Apply yourselves, he says, with complete attention to the word that you hear, because whoever has love for the word will be given the understanding of what he loves. But whoever does not have love for hearing the word, even if he thinks that he is skilled either by natural intelligence or through literary training, will enjoy none of the sweetness of true wisdom.

Although this may be understood specifically of the apostles, to whom, possessing charity and faith, it was given to know the mystery of God’s kingdom, and of the faithless Jews, who, seeing in parables, did not see, and hearing, did not understand—namely, that they would lose the letter of the law [Col. 0942B] in which they gloried—it may nevertheless also be understood generally. For often an intelligent reader deprives himself through negligence of the wisdom that a simple but diligent reader tastes through labor.

(Gregory.) A lazy person is sometimes given intelligence so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence, because he scorns learning what he could have attained without labor. And sometimes a diligent person is weighed down by slowness of understanding, so that he may find greater rewards in return, in proportion as he labors more earnestly in the work of discovery.

“Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand.” (Maurice.) He now gives the apostles the reason why he speaks to the crowds in parables: those who, in their pride, considered themselves [Col. 0942C] seeing and hearing, and who, trusting in their own intelligence, thought that they could penetrate all the secrets of divine teaching and therefore refused to submit to heavenly instruction, would remain empty of spiritual understanding, while the simple and humble recognized the heavenly mysteries.

(Jerome.) He speaks of those who stand on the shore, separated from Jesus, and who, amid the noise and roar of the waves, do not hear any of the things that are said.

“And in them the prophecy of Isaiah will be fulfilled, which says: ‘You will hear with hearing and will not understand; and seeing you will see, and will not see’” (Isaiah 6). This was prophesied about the crowds that stand on the shore and are not worthy to hear the word of God. They possess bodily sight and hearing outwardly, but inwardly they have deprived themselves of the sight and hearing of the heart [Col. 0942D]. Of them it is further said:

“For the heart of this people has become dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them.” (Maurice.) The heart of the Jews became dull through the coarseness of wickedness and the abundance of sins, because they were hard and rebellious and always acted contentiously against God. To them the Lord himself says through the prophet: “Your sins separate between me and you” (Jeremiah 59). They heard the Lord’s words heavily because they received them without gratitude. They closed their eyes because they covered the vision of their minds with the veil of envy and ignorance [Col. 0943A].

Also observe that he says, “They closed their eyes,” because they are blind not by nature but by their will. He shows that the fault belongs to their free choice. And therefore they did not deserve salvation, because they refused to open their eyes and ears to receive the words of life. If they had turned to repentance, God would have turned to heal them; through the prophet he says to them: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord God” (Zechariah 1).

“For the heart of this people has become dull,” and so forth. (Augustine.) Another Evangelist says: “He has blinded their eyes.” But is this so that they may never see, or rather so that they may not see even then—so that, displeased with their blindness, grieving over it, and thereby humbled and stirred, they might confess their sins and devoutly seek God? For [Col. 0943B] Mark says: “Lest they should ever be converted and their sins be forgiven them.” From this it is understood that they had deserved through their sins not to understand. Yet even this was done mercifully to them, so that they might recognize their sins and, having been converted, deserve pardon.

But when John states this passage in the following way—“Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah again said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes and understand with their heart and be converted, and I heal them’” (John 12)—he seems to oppose this interpretation and altogether compels us to understand the words “lest they should ever see with their eyes” not as meaning “lest they should at some time see with their eyes,” but absolutely as “so that they should not see,” since he plainly says that they do not see with their eyes. And when he says, “Therefore they could not believe,” he sufficiently shows [Col. 0943C] that this blinding was not done so that, moved and grieved by the fact that they did not understand, they might at some time be converted through repentance. For they could not do this unless they first believed, so that by believing they might be converted, and by conversion healed, and by healing understand. Rather, they were blinded so that they would not believe [Col. 0943D]. For he says most plainly: “Therefore they could not believe.”

If this is so, who would not rise in defense of the Jews and proclaim that they were free from guilt because they did not believe? For they could not believe because he blinded their eyes. But since God must rather be understood to be free from guilt, we are compelled to confess that they deserved to be blinded because of certain other sins, and that through this blinding they could not believe. These, after all, are John’s words: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah again said: ‘He has blinded their eyes.’”

We therefore strive in vain to understand that they were blinded so that they might be converted, when they could not be converted precisely because they had been blinded. When what is to be believed is spoken, it cannot be believed unless what is spoken is understood. Therefore the statements must be understood so that the things that could be spoken may be believed; and the things that could be spoken must be believed so that the things that cannot be spoken may be understood.

Your eyes, however, are blessed, because they see; and your ears, because they hear. (Bede.) Not the eyes of the scribes and Pharisees, who saw only the Lord’s body; but those blessed eyes which are able to recognize his mysteries. Of these it is said: “And you have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. [Col. 0944A] 11). Blessed are the eyes of the little ones, to whom the Son deigns to reveal both himself and the Father.

“For truly I say to you, many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” Abraham rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; and he saw it and was glad. Isaiah also, and Micah, and many other prophets saw the glory of the Lord. For this reason they were called “seers”; but all these, looking from afar and greeting, saw through a mirror, in an enigma (1 Cor. 13). The apostles, however, having God present among them, dining with him, and learning by questioning whatever they wished, had no need to be taught through angels or various kinds of visions. Those whom Matthew calls prophets and righteous people, [Col. 0944B] Luke calls prophets and kings. They are indeed great kings, because they have learned not to succumb by consenting to the movements of their temptations, but to rule over them and prevail.

(Maur.) “You, then, hear the parable of the sower.” He now turns his words to those who have been granted knowledge of the mystery of the kingdom. At the same time he admonishes us with them and urges us to listen more attentively to what is said. Observe that the Lord himself explains this first parable, so that in the other things that follow he may give us confidence to expound them according to this rule. He acts, so to speak, like a nurse who carries a vessel full of nuts and brings it to her foster-children. When they marvel at it, and, because of its novelty, do not know what use it may have, she herself first takes a nut, breaks it open, removes the shell, and shows what a sweet fruit it contains and how pleasant a food it gives to those who taste it, if one breaks its outer shell. Thus also our Lord first explains his parable himself to his still inexperienced disciples and shows what sweetness lies beneath the veil of the written words. Then, when they hear similar things, they may receive them gladly and, with his grace accompanying them, diligently strive to discover for themselves what mystery is concealed within them. Thus the Lord explains:

“Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart: this is the one who was sown beside the road.” (Rabanus.) Mark writes of this seed as follows: “These are the ones beside the road, where the word is sown; and when they have heard it, Satan immediately comes and takes it away.” From this it is clearly taught that those are sown beside the road who do not deign to receive the word they hear with any faith, any understanding, or even with the opportunity of testing its usefulness. (Jerome.) Understand also that what was sown was in his heart, and that the different kinds of soil are the souls of believers.

“And the one sown upon rocky ground is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, but has no root in himself and is temporary; when tribulation or persecution occurs because of the word, he is immediately scandalized. And the one sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.” Behold, the expert in heavenly law has displayed the meaning of the rocky and thorny soil. No one can interpret anything better or more appropriately than he has. Therefore, as the Lord shows, those are sown upon rocky ground and among thorns who, although they approve the usefulness of the word they have heard and taste the desire for it, are prevented from reaching what they approve by the adversities of this life, which frighten them, or by its prosperity, which flatters them. Against both kinds of harm he endeavored to protect the seed he had received who said: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Cor. 6). Know, then, that all who fail to put into practice the Word they have heard are represented by these three kinds of soil. Attend to what is said: “He is immediately scandalized.” There is therefore some distinction between one who is compelled by many tribulations and punishments to deny Christ and one who is immediately scandalized and falls at the first, or at the nearest, persecution. Likewise, the Lord does not call the riches of this world simply “riches,” but “deceitful riches.” (Gregory.) They are deceitful because they cannot remain with us for long; they are deceitful because they do not dispel the poverty of our mind. The only true riches are those that make us rich in virtues. It should also be noted that, in explaining this, the Lord says that anxieties, pleasures, and riches choke the word. They choke it because, through their intrusive thoughts, they strangle the throat of the mind; and, by not allowing a good desire to enter the heart, they kill, as it were, the passage of vital breath. It should further be noted that he joins two things to riches—namely, anxieties and pleasures—because they oppress the mind through care and dissolve it through abundance; for by opposite effects they make their possessors both afflicted and licentious. But since pleasure cannot coexist with affliction, at one time they afflict them through the anxiety of their guardianship, and at another they soften them into pleasures through abundance.

“But the one sown in good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it, and bears fruit, producing in one case a hundredfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another thirtyfold.” (Jerome.) Just as there were three differences in the bad soil—beside the road, rocky places, and thorny places—so in the good soil there is a threefold difference: the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit. In both the former and the latter, the substance is not changed, but the will; and it is the hearts both of unbelievers and of believers that receive the seed. “Everyone,” he says, “who hears the word of faith and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart”; and a second and a third time he says: “This is the one who hears the word.” Likewise, in the explanation of the good soil: “This is the one who hears the word and understands it, and bears fruit, producing in one case a hundredfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another thirtyfold.” Therefore we must first hear, then understand, and after understanding produce the fruit of teachings, bearing either a hundredfold, or sixtyfold, or thirtyfold fruit.

Thirty refers to marriage; for the joining of the fingers themselves, as though embracing one another with a gentle kiss and binding them together, depicts husband and wife. Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in distress and tribulation; hence they are pressed down upon the upper finger. And the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the allurements of pleasures once experienced, the greater also is the reward. But as for the number one hundred, observe carefully, reader: it is transferred from the left hand to the right, with the same fingers but not the same hand by which married women are represented on the left hand; and, by forming a circle, it expresses the crown of virginity. Alternatively, one hundred, which in counting is transferred from the left to the right, is rightly understood as signifying perpetual blessedness, since thirty and sixty are still held in the left hand, while one hundred passes to the right. For although faith is great, revealing to us knowledge of our Creator, and great are the works by which faith is perfected so that it may not be idle, nevertheless both are necessary in this life. (Augustine.) The reward of faith and of the work exercised through love is to be hoped for in the life to come. Or alternatively: the good soil bears the hundredfold fruit of martyrs, because of the fullness of life and the conception of death; the sixtyfold fruit of virgins, because of inward repose, since they do not fight against the habit of the flesh—for repose is usually granted to those sixty years old after military service or public duties; and the thirtyfold fruit of married people, because this is the age of combatants. They have the sharper struggle, lest they be overcome by lust.

After these words of the Lord, Matthew continues and says:

[Col. 0946C] **II.** “He presented another parable to them, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field.’”

Notice what you hear. “He presented another parable to them,” he says. The Lord was sitting in the boat, while the crowd was on the shore of the sea; they were at a distance, while the disciples were near and listening. He presents to them another parable, like a wealthy householder refreshing invited guests with various foods, so that each might receive different nourishment according to the condition of his stomach. Hence, in the earlier parable, he did not say “another” in the sense of a different kind, but “another” in the sense of an additional one. If he had introduced it as a different one, we could not have expected a third. He introduced an additional one so that more might follow. But because this second parable was not immediately explained together with its interpretation, but was expounded after other parables had intervened, it is here proposed by the Savior and later explained, when he has dismissed the crowds and returned home, at the disciples’ request. Therefore, in the meantime, until we hear its allegorical interpretation from him, let us discuss it. Nevertheless, briefly, in contemplating the parable itself, let us attempt to say something for moral instruction, lest, hearing such a sacred reading, we pass by without some edification for ourselves. If we understand it properly, it teaches us in simple speech to possess a good will. It teaches vigilance, patience, discernment, perseverance, and justice. We shall speak of all these distinctly in their proper places, setting forth the very sayings of the Gospel that demonstrate them.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a man who sowed good seed in his field.” For only a good man sows good seed in his field: namely, the one who strives to bring the seed of good will in his body to the fruit of good works. And he is rightly said to be like the kingdom of heaven, since he is shown to be entirely suited to it.

“But while the men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds over the midst of the wheat.” This saying admonishes us to be watchful, so that, if we wish good seed to grow in our field, we may beware of the enemy’s seeds. Otherwise, while we are sluggishly numb with the sleep of idleness, we may lose the fruit of our labor.

“But when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared. The servants of the householder approached and said to him: ‘Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, does it have weeds?’ And he said to them: ‘An enemy has done this.’” In this saying, therefore, an example of patience is offered to us. For just as this householder, knowing the enemy’s trick, did not blaze up in anger or immediately wish to take vengeance on him, but waited patiently, so also, when we have received some injury from our enemies, we ought not immediately to rush to revenge, but rather to have recourse to the virtue of patience.

“But the servants said to him: ‘Do you want us to go and gather them?’ And he said to them: ‘No, lest perhaps, while gathering the weeds, you root up the wheat together with them.’” Here you have an example of discernment. Therefore we ought to bear the wicked with equanimity for the sake of the good. For if, provoked by the wicked, we were to repay them by taking vengeance, we might perhaps provide the good with an occasion for scandal.

“Let both grow until the harvest.” And what is given to us in this except an edification of perseverance? We must not possess the virtue of patience for a short time, but preserve it patiently until the end of life. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24). But let us hear what this persevering householder does at the end.

“And at harvest time I will say to the reapers: ‘Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles for burning. But gather the wheat into my barn.’” The one who previously endured patiently through perseverance now repays each according to his deserving through justice. [Col. 0947D] In this he also gives us an example, so that in suffering we may meditate upon justice, and in judging we may not neglect to possess patience. For the bond of the virtues is so established in a unity that all are distinct from one another through the diversity of their kinds, yet through their mutual opposition they are in no way hostile to one another. Let what we have said in some fashion, as we promised, according to moral interpretation, suffice.

(Augustine.) It may be asked why he says, “Bind them into bundles for burning,” rather than commanding that there be one bundle or one heap of weeds. Perhaps by the variety of heretics—who differ not only from the wheat but also from one another—he signified by the name “bundles” the separate gatherings proper to each heresy, in which they are individually bound together in their own communion. Thus they would begin to be bound for burning when, separated from Catholic communion, they began to possess their own churches, so to speak; the burning of these would occur at the end of the age, but not the binding of the bundles. Yet if this were so, many would not later repent and depart from error by returning to Catholic communion.

Therefore the binding of the bundles is also to take place at the end, so that each person may be punished not indiscriminately but according to the measure of the perversity of his own error.

“Lest perhaps, while gathering the weeds, you root up the wheat together with them.” Is this because the good, while they are still weak, also need the mixture of certain wicked people, either so that they may be exercised through them, or so that, by comparison with them, a great exhortation may be given to strive toward what is better? When these are removed, the height of charity, as though torn up by the roots, withers. This is what “to be rooted up” means; for the Apostle likewise says: “That you, being rooted and founded in charity, may be able to comprehend” (Eph. 3). Or is the wheat perhaps rooted up together with the weeds because many are first weeds and afterward become wheat, and, if they are removed, they do not attain a praiseworthy change? Thus, if they are uprooted, the wheat they would have become had they been spared is also rooted up with them.

Matthew continues and says:

[Col. 0948B] **III.** “He presented another parable to them, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. It is indeed the smallest of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is greater than all garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the sky come and dwell in its branches.’”

The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel and the knowledge of the Scriptures, which leads to life, and concerning which it is said to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruit.” The kingdom of heaven is therefore like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field (Matt. 21). By many, the Savior is understood to be the one who sows it in the minds of believers. By others, the man himself is understood as the one who sows in his field—that is, in himself and in his own heart. Who is this sower except our understanding and soul? When it receives the seed of preaching and nourishes the sowing with the moisture of faith, it makes it sprout in the field of its own breast.

The preaching of the Gospel is the smallest of all disciplines. At the beginning of its teaching it does not possess the appearance of truth, proclaiming the Lord God dead and the scandal of the cross. Compare such teaching with the doctrines of philosophers, their books, the brilliance of their eloquence, and the composition of their speeches, and you will see how much smaller the sowing of the Gospel is than the other seeds. But when those have grown, they display nothing biting, nothing vigorous, nothing living; everything is mild, withered, and softened into garden plants and herbs, which quickly grow and quickly fall. This preaching, however, which seemed small at the beginning, when it has been sown either in the soul of a believer or throughout the whole world, does not rise into garden plants but grows into a tree, so that the birds of the sky—which we should understand either as the souls of believers or as powers devoted to God’s service—come and dwell in its branches.

I think that the branches of the evangelical tree, which has grown from mustard seeds, are the varieties of doctrines, in each of which one of the birds mentioned above finds rest. Let us also assume the wings of a dove, so that, flying to higher things, we may be able to dwell in the branches of this tree and make nests for ourselves in its teachings; fleeing earthly things, let us hasten toward heavenly things.

Many people, reading that the mustard seed is the smallest of all seeds, and also what is said in the Gospel, “Lord, increase our faith,” and the Savior’s reply, “Truly I say to you, if you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, ‘Move from this place,’ and it would move” (Luke 17), think that the apostles are asking for little faith or that the Lord doubts the value of little faith. Yet the Apostle Paul judges the faith compared with a mustard seed to be exceedingly great. For what does he say? “If I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore what the Lord said could be accomplished by faith compared with a mustard seed, the Apostle teaches can be accomplished by complete faith.

(Rabanus.) The mustard seed may also be understood as the humility of the Lord’s incarnation. A man took it and placed it in his garden: Joseph, receiving the Savior’s body, buried it in a garden. It grew and became a tree when he rose again and ascended into heaven. He spread out branches in which the birds of the sky might rest, when he dispersed preachers throughout the world, in whose words and consolations the faithful might breathe again after the weariness of this life.

[Col. 0949C] **IV.** “He spoke another parable to them: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened.’”

(Jerome.) People’s tastes are different: some delight in bitter foods, others in sweet; some in harsher foods, others in mild ones. Therefore, as we said above, the Lord proposes different parables, so that according to the variety of wounds there may also be a variety of medicine. This woman who receives the leaven and hides it in three measures of flour until the whole is leavened seems to me to signify either the apostolic preaching or the Church, which has been gathered from different nations. She took the leaven—that is, the knowledge and understanding of the Scriptures mentioned above—and hid it in three measures of flour, so that spirit, soul, and body, brought together into one, might not differ among themselves; but, when two or three have agreed, they might obtain from the Father whatever they ask.

This passage is also explained in another way. We read in Plato, and it is widely circulated in the doctrine of philosophers, that there are three passions in the human soul: τὸ λογικόν, which we can interpret as “the rational”; τὸ ὀργηστικόν, which we call “full of anger,” or “the irascible”; and τὸ ἐπιποθικόν, which we call “the desiring,” or “the concupiscible.” That philosopher thinks that our rational faculty dwells in the brain, anger in the gall, and desire in the liver. Therefore, if we too receive the leaven of the Gospel together with the knowledge of the holy Scriptures mentioned above, the three passions of the human soul will be brought into unity, so that in the rational faculty we may possess prudence, in anger hatred against vices, and in desire a longing for virtues. All this will be accomplished through the evangelical teaching that Mother Church has provided for us.

I shall also give a third interpretation held by some, so that the curious reader may choose from several whatever pleases him. They too interpret this woman as the Church, which has mixed the faith of humanity into three measures of flour: belief in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When the whole has been leavened into unity, it leads us not to knowledge of a triple God but to knowledge of one divinity. The three measures of flour likewise draw us toward unity of substance, since there is not a different nature in each. This is indeed a pious interpretation, but the authority of dogmas can never be established by a parable or by the uncertain interpretation of enigmas. Some also offer a fourth opinion, finding in the three measures the descendants of Noah’s three sons, through whom the human race was restored; the woman mentioned above gathers them into the unity of faith through the leaven of the Gospel.

(Rabanus.)
