Besides these interpretations, the three measures of flour may also be understood as the fruits of the Lord’s seed: the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold—that is, of married people, the continent, and virgins. He beautifully says that the leaven was hidden in the flour until the whole was leavened, because charity, once stored in our mind, ought to grow until it transforms the whole mind into its perfection, so that the soul may be able to love, do, or remember nothing except love for its Creator. This begins here but is brought to perfection there, where, since God is “all in all” (1 Cor. 15), he warms everyone with the one and same fire of his love.

A *sat* is a kind of measure according to the custom of the province of Palestine, containing one and a half *modii*.

All these things Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them. “All these things,” he says, “Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables,” and so forth. This does not mean that he said nothing plainly, but that he scarcely explained any discourse in which he did not signify something by a parable, although in it he also spoke certain things plainly. Thus his whole discourse is often found to have been expressed in parables, but no discourse of his is found to have been entirely spoken plainly.

(Jerome.) It should be noted that he speaks in parables not to the disciples but to the crowds. To this day the crowds hear in parables, while the disciples question the Savior at home.

[Col. 0950D] “So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘I will open my mouth in parables, and I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.’”

This testimony is taken from Psalm 77, and it is also spoken in the person of the Lord: “I will open my mouth in parables,” he says, “and I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world” (Ps. 77). It must therefore be considered more attentively, and it must be discovered that in it Israel’s departure from Egypt is described and all the signs contained in the history of the Exodus are recounted. From this we understand that all those things that are written are to be understood parabolically, and that the literal surface does not correspond openly, but contains hidden mysteries. For the Savior promises that he will say these things, opening his mouth in parables and uttering things hidden since the foundation of the world, because no one has been found in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth worthy to open the book and release its seven seals, except the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Rev. 5)—the power and wisdom of God.

Then, after dismissing the crowds, he came into the house, and his disciples approached him, saying: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.”

(Jerome.) Jesus dismisses the crowds and returns home. The disciples approach him and ask him privately about things that the people neither deserved to hear nor were able to understand.

(Maur.) Mystically, however, our Savior, having dismissed the crowd of tumultuous Jews, enters the Church of the Gentiles. There, when the disciples ask—that is, when the faithful devoutly learn the divine mysteries—he explains the heavenly sacraments.

[Col. 0951B] “He answered and said: ‘The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world. The good seed, these are the children of the kingdom. The weeds are the children of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age. The reapers are angels.’”

He explained plainly that the field is the world, the sower the Son of Man, the good seed the children of the kingdom, the weeds the children of the evil one, the sower of the weeds the devil, the harvest the consummation of the world, and the reapers the angels. All scandals are referred to the weeds; the righteous are reckoned among the children of the kingdom. Therefore, as I said above, we ought to give our faith to those things explained by the Lord. But the things he left unspoken and entrusted to our understanding must be touched upon briefly.

By the men who sleep, understand the teachers of the churches. Do not understand the servants of the householder as anyone other than the angels who daily see the face of the Father. The devil is called “the enemy man” because he ceased to be God. Psalm 9 also says of him: “Arise, Lord; let not man prevail.” Therefore, the one placed over the Church must not sleep, lest through his negligence the enemy man sow weeds over the field—that is, the doctrines of heretics.

As for what is said, “Lest perhaps, while gathering the weeds, you root up the wheat together with them,” a place for repentance is granted, and we are warned not to cut off a brother too quickly. It may happen that one who today has been corrupted by a harmful doctrine may repent tomorrow and begin to defend the truth.

The statement that follows—“Let both grow until the harvest”—seems contrary to the command: “Remove the evil person from among you” (1 Cor. 5), and to the prohibition against having fellowship with those who are called brothers but are adulterers and fornicators. For if uprooting is forbidden, patience must be maintained until the harvest; but how are certain people to be expelled from among us?

Between wheat and weeds—what we call *lolium*—as long as the plants are still grass and the stalk has not yet come to the ear, there is a great similarity, and in distinguishing them there is either no difference or one that is extremely difficult to discern. The Lord therefore warns us not to pronounce judgment quickly where something is ambiguous, but to reserve the outcome for God the judge, so that when the day of judgment comes, he may expel from the assembly of the saints not someone merely suspected of a crime but one whose guilt is manifest.

[Col. 0952A] “Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals and those who practice iniquity, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Every impurity in the crop is called a weed. The weeds are said to be separated first because, after the preceding tribulation, the impious will be separated from the pious. This is understood to be done by good angels, because good beings can carry out the duties of vengeance with a good disposition, as can the law and the judge; but evil beings cannot carry out the duties of mercy.

(Jerome.) Since he decrees that the bundles of weeds be handed over to the fires and the wheat gathered into the barns, it is clear that all heretics and hypocrites are to be burned in the fires of Gehenna, while the saints, who are called wheat, are to be received into barns—that is, heavenly dwellings.

(Maur.) Observe that he says, “and those who practice iniquity,” not “those who practiced iniquity,” because not all who have practiced iniquity but have turned to repentance and a more corrected life are to be handed over to eternal torments. Only those who remain in their sins until the end of their life and have not practiced repentance are so condemned.

“Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” (Jerome.) In the present age the light of the saints shines before human beings; after the consummation of the world, the righteous themselves will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. “Whoever has ears, let him hear.” That is, whoever has understanding, let him understand: it is not mustard, garden plants, leaven of drunkenness, or flour of grasses that is being preached, but all these things must be understood mystically.

[Col. 0952C] **V.** “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and, rejoicing over it, goes and sells everything he has and buys that field.”

(Gregory.) The kingdom of heaven is therefore compared with earthly things so that, from what the mind knows, it may rise toward what it does not know; so that, by the example of visible things, it may be carried toward invisible things, and, as though rubbed against what it has learned through experience, may grow warm, in order that through what it knows it may learn to love what it does not know.

Behold, the kingdom of heaven is compared with a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and, rejoicing over it, goes and sells everything he has and buys that field. In this connection it should also be noted that the treasure, once found, is hidden so that it may be preserved, because the pursuit of heavenly desire is not sufficiently guarded by one who does not hide it from human praise. The treasure is the heavenly desire; the field in which the treasure is hidden is the discipline of heavenly study. He buys this field by selling everything who, renouncing the pleasures of the flesh, tramples all his earthly desires under the discipline of heavenly vigilance, so that he permits nothing that flatters the flesh and fears nothing that destroys carnal life.

(Jerome.) Alternatively, this treasure, in which “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2), is either the Word of God, which appears hidden in the flesh of Christ, or the holy Scriptures, in which knowledge of the Savior is stored. When someone finds him in them, he ought to despise all the profits of this age so that he may possess the one whom he has found. As for what follows—“When a man finds it, he hides it”—this is said not because he acts out of envy, but because he hides it in his heart out of the fear of one who preserves it and does not wish to lose it, having preferred it to his former possessions.

(Augustine.) Likewise, he spoke of a treasure hidden in a field: the two Testaments of the Law in the Church. When someone has reached them in some measure through understanding, he perceives that great things lie hidden there; he goes and sells all that he has and buys it—that is, through contempt for temporal things he acquires leisure for himself, so that he may be rich in the knowledge of God.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he has found one precious pearl, he goes away and sells everything he has and buys it.”

(Gregory.) Again, the heavenly kingdom is said to be like a merchant who seeks good pearls but finds one precious pearl, which, after finding it, he buys by selling everything. Whoever has perfectly recognized, insofar as ability permits, the sweetness of heavenly life gladly abandons everything he had loved on earth. In comparison with it, everything becomes cheap to him. He leaves what he possesses and scatters what he has gathered; his soul burns with desire for heavenly things. Nothing earthly pleases him. Whatever had pleased him in earthly appearance is seen as deformed, while only the love of the precious pearl shines in his mind.

The question therefore arises why he passed from the plural number to the singular, so that, while the man seeks good pearls, he finds one precious pearl, which he buys after selling everything he has. Either he is seeking good people with whom he may live usefully and finds, above all others, the one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, without sin (1 Tim. 2); or, while seeking commandments by which, when observed, he may conduct himself rightly among human beings, he finds love of neighbor. The Apostle says that all things are contained in this one commandment: “You shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, and if there is any other commandment” (Rom. 13). The individual pearls are thus gathered into this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Or a person seeks good understandings and finds that in which all are contained: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”—bright with the splendor of truth and solid with the firmness of eternity. This is to be understood as God through the shell of whose flesh one must penetrate. For he had already reached the pearl itself who had once lain hidden, as though beneath the covering of mortality, like a shell’s barrier, in the depth of this age and amid the rocky hardness of the Jews. Thus he had already reached that pearl who said: “Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer in that way.”

No understanding at all is worthy of the name “pearl” unless it is reached after all carnal coverings have been removed. Whether it is concealed beneath human words or beneath surrounding comparisons, it is so covered that it may be discerned by a sure reasoning as pure, sound, and nowhere inconsistent with itself. All true, firm, and perfect understandings are nevertheless contained by that one through whom all things were made, namely, the Word of God.

Whatever these three interpretations may be—or even if another should occur that is appropriately signified by the name of one precious pearl—its price is ourselves. We are not free to possess it unless we despise everything that is possessed temporally for the sake of our liberation. When we sell our possessions, we receive no greater price for them than ourselves, because, entangled in such things, we did not belong to ourselves; therefore we give ourselves again for that pearl—not because it is worth only so much, but because we cannot give more.

(Jerome.) Alternatively, this parable may be understood, in other words, to express the same thing that was said above. The good pearls sought by the merchant are the Law and the Prophets. Hear, Marcion; hear, Manichaeus: the good pearls are the Law and the Prophets, and the knowledge of the Old Testament. But one is the precious pearl: the knowledge of the Savior, the mystery of his passion, and the secret of his resurrection. When the merchant, like the apostle Paul, has found it, he despises all the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets and his former observances, in which he had lived blamelessly, as refuse and rubbish, so that he may gain Christ (Phil. 3). This does not mean that the discovery of one new pearl condemns the ancient ones, but that, in comparison with it, every other gem is less valuable.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it up, and, sitting beside the shore, they selected the good fish into containers but threw the bad ones outside.

**(Gregory.)** Thus, then, the kingdom of heaven is again said to be like a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it is full, it is drawn to the shore, and the good fish are selected into containers, while the bad are thrown outside. By this parable, therefore, the holy Church is compared to a dragnet, which has been entrusted to fishermen, and through which each person is drawn from the waves of the present age toward the eternal kingdom, lest he be submerged in the depths of everlasting death. It gathers fish of every kind because it calls to the forgiveness of sins the wise and the foolish, the free and the enslaved, the rich and the poor, the strong and the weak. Hence it is said to God through the Psalmist: “To you all flesh shall come” (Psalm 64). The dragnet is filled universally when, at the end, the totality of the human race is brought to completion. They draw it up and sit beside the shore because, just as the sea signifies the world, so the shore of the sea signifies the end of the world. At that end, the good fish are selected into containers, while the bad are thrown outside: each of the elect is received into the heavenly dwellings, whereas the rejected, deprived of the light of the eternal kingdom, are dragged into the outer darkness. For now the net of faith holds good and bad together, like fish mixed together; but the shore shows what the dragnet—that is, the holy Church—was drawing in. Fish that have been caught cannot be changed; we, however, are caught as bad fish but are changed into goodness. Let us therefore consider our capture, lest we be separated on the shore.

**(Jerome.)** Again, in another sense: “The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea,” and so forth. When Jeremiah’s prophecy had been fulfilled—“Behold, I am sending many fishermen to you” (Jeremiah 16)—after Peter and Andrew, James and John the sons of Zebedee, had heard, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4), they wove for themselves from the Old and New Testament a net of evangelical doctrines and cast it into the sea of this age. To this day it is spread amid the waves, catching from the false and bitter whirlpools whatever falls into it—that is, both good and bad people, and both the best and the worst fish.

**(Maurice.)** It draws them to the shore, that is, to the end of the world, so that then there may be a separation of the good fish from the bad. Hence it is added:

> For so it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and they will throw them into the furnace of fire; there there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

**(Gregory.)** This, then, must be feared rather than explained. The torments of sinners have been declared in plain language, so that no one may resort to an excuse based on ignorance if something concerning eternal punishment were said obscurely.

**(Jerome.)** When the consummation and end of the world arrive, as he himself explains more plainly below, then the dragnet will be drawn out onto the shore. Then the true judgment concerning the fish to be separated will be revealed, and, as though in a most tranquil harbor, the good will be placed into the vessels of the heavenly dwelling places; but the flame of Gehenna will receive the bad, to be burned and dried up. When the Savior had set forth the parable, he immediately added:

> “Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.”

The saying is directed particularly to the Apostles, and he asks them: “Have you understood all these things?” He does not want them merely to hear, like the crowd, but to understand, as future teachers; and he gives worthy testimony to those who understand the parables. Hence it is also added:

> And he said to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

**(Augustine.)** He did not say “old things and new,” which he certainly would have said had he preferred to preserve the order of times rather than the order of merit. The New Testament is later in time but earlier in dignity.

**(Jerome.)** The Apostles had indeed been instructed as the Savior’s scribes and secretaries. They inscribed his words and commandments on the tablets of their fleshly hearts; in the mysteries of the heavenly kingdoms they flourished and grew strong through the resources of the householder, bringing forth from the treasure of their teachings new things and old, so that whatever they preached in the Gospel might be confirmed by the words of the Law and the Prophets. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I have kept new things with old for you, my kinsman” (Song of Songs 7). Yet this can also be understood in another way.

**(Gregory.)** The old condition of the human race was to descend into the prison of hell and endure eternal punishments for its sins. Through the coming of the Mediator, something new was added: if people here strive to live rightly, they can enter the kingdoms of heaven; and a human being born on earth, if he dies to corruptible life, is to be placed in heaven. It is therefore old that the human race should perish on account of guilt, and new that, having been converted, it should live in the kingdom. What the Lord added at the conclusion of his speech is therefore precisely what he had said beforehand. First he brought forth the treasure that had been found and the good pearl as images of the kingdom; afterward he related the punishments of hell through the burning of the wicked; and in conclusion he added: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder bringing forth from his treasure new things and old.” It is as though he were saying plainly: The learned preacher in the holy Church is the one who knows how to bring forth new things concerning the sweetness of the kingdom and to speak of old things concerning the terror of punishment, so that punishments may frighten those whom rewards do not invite.

**(Maurice.)** Here, then, the fourth book of the exposition of the Gospel reaches its conclusion: the Lord’s utterance of the parables shows that the age has its end in God’s strict judgment. From this point onward, the events and sayings of the Lord that follow will be begun with another introduction.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0955]

## CHAPTER XIII FOLLOWS

[Col. 0955D]

### [VI.] When Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there and, coming into his own country, taught them in their synagogues, so that they were amazed and said: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works?”

**(Jerome.)** After speaking the parables to the people—which only the Apostles understood—the Lord passes into his own country, so that there he may teach more openly.

**(Rabanus.)** He calls Galilee the Lord’s country, or more specifically Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and where he preached in the synagogues of the Jews. For *synagōgē* (συναγωγή) is Greek and is rendered in Latin as *congregatio*, “assembly.” By this name they customarily designated not only the gathering of great crowds but also the house in which the Jews assembled to hear or proclaim the word of God. Hence the Lord says to Annas the high priest: “I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews assemble” (John 18). So we too call the places and choirs of the faithful “churches.”

There is, however, a difference between *synagōgē* (συναγωγή), which is interpreted as “assembly,” and *ecclesia* (ἐκκλησία), which is interpreted as “convocation.” The people of the Old Testament are designated by both terms, whereas the people of the New Testament are called only the Church. For animals and all inanimate things can be gathered together, but only beings endowed with reason can be summoned. Therefore it seemed more fitting to the apostolic writers and teachers to call the people of the new grace—endowed, as it were, with greater dignity—“summoned into the unity of faith” rather than “assembled”: that is, to call it the Church rather than the synagogue.

Every Sabbath they gathered in the synagogues, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45), they might set aside the business of the world and sit with tranquil hearts to meditate on the precepts of the Law. A sign of the devotion that was to be practiced on that day has continued in the Church to this point: in some places, on the Sabbath, it is customary to sing the song from Deuteronomy, which contains the entire condition of the ancient people—what they deserved from God when he was offended and when he was propitious. Otherwise it would be an inversion of order for the song of Moses to be sung last, after the verses of the Prophets had been sung on the earlier days of the week.

The Lord therefore taught in the synagogues of the Jews, as the Evangelist relates, so that they were amazed and said: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works?” But how great was the blindness of the Nazarenes! They could have recognized Christ in his words and deeds,

> “if their mind had not been perverse,”

yet they despised him merely because they knew his family. They refer “wisdom” to his teaching, and “mighty works” to the healings and miracles he performed. The Apostle recalls this with a careful and beautiful distinction, saying: “Jews demand signs, and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1). In this statement he referred “power” to signs on account of the Jews, and “wisdom” to teaching on account of the Greeks, that is, the Gentiles.

> Is this not the craftsman’s son? Is his mother not called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? And are not all his sisters among us? Where, then, did this man get all these things?

And they took offense at him. The error of the Jews is our salvation and the condemnation of heretics. They saw Christ the man so completely that they thought him the son of a craftsman and said: “Is this not the craftsman’s son?” Are you surprised that they err concerning his brothers, when they err concerning his father? His brothers and sisters are also said to be with him. Yet they should not, as the heretics think, be regarded as the children of Joseph or Mary; rather, in accordance with the custom of Sacred Scripture, they are to be understood as their relatives. Thus Abraham and Lot are called brothers, although Lot was the son of Abraham’s brother; and there are many examples of this kind.

**(Rabanus.)** It was not without the foresight of a sure mystery that the Lord, appearing in the flesh, wished to be considered and called a craftsman and the son of a craftsman. Rather, by this very fact he also taught that he was the Son, before the ages, of the one who in the beginning, as the creator of all things, made heaven and earth. Although human things must not be compared with divine things, the type is nevertheless complete: the Father of Christ works through fire and Spirit. Hence his Forerunner says of him as of a craftsman’s son: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3). In the great house of this world he fashions vessels of different kinds; indeed, by softening vessels of wrath in the fire of his Spirit, he changes them into vessels of mercy. But the Jews, ignorant of this mystery, despise the works of divine power because they contemplate a carnal lineage.

> But Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.”

That the Lord Christ is called a prophet in the Scriptures is also testified by Moses. Foretelling his future incarnation, he says to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me” (Deuteronomy 18). Not only he who is the head and Lord of the Prophets, but also Elijah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets were held in less esteem in their own country than in foreign cities.

**(Jerome.)** For it is almost natural that citizens should always envy their fellow citizens. They do not consider the present works of the man, but remember his fragile childhood, as though they themselves had not passed through the same stages of life to reach maturity.

> And he did not perform many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

Not because he could not perform many mighty works even for those unbelievers, but lest, by performing many, he condemn unbelieving fellow citizens. It can also be understood in another way: Jesus was despised in his house and in his country, that is, among the Jewish people, and therefore he performed few signs there, so that they would not become entirely without excuse. But among the Gentiles he performs greater signs every day through the Apostles—not so much in the healing of bodies as in the salvation of souls.

## CHAPTER XIV

**The beheading of John the Baptist is related, together with the miracle of the five loaves and the walking upon the waters, and so forth.**

[Col. 0958C]

### [I.] At that time Herod the tetrarch heard reports about Jesus and said to his servants: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works are performed in him.”

**(Rabanus.)** Luke writes about this as follows: “Herod the tetrarch heard all that was being done by him, and he was perplexed because some were saying that John had risen from the dead, while others said that Elijah had appeared,” and so forth (Luke 9). It must therefore be understood either that after this perplexity he confirmed in his mind what others were saying, when he declared, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead”; or that these words should be pronounced in such a way as to show that he was still uncertain. If he had said, “Could this be he?” or “Could this perhaps be John the Baptist?” there would be no need to say anything about the pronunciation by which his doubt and perplexity might be understood. But since those words are absent, the sentence can be pronounced in either way: either we may take him to have spoken as one convinced by the words of others, or as still perplexed, as Luke records.

**(Maurice.)** It should nevertheless be noted that in this statement Herod preached to his servants concerning the glory of the resurrection. He did not say, “This is John the Baptist, who performs mighty works,” but: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works are performed in him.” In every respect he had thought rightly about the power of the resurrection: the saints will possess greater power when they have risen from the dead than they possessed while still weighed down by the weakness of the flesh. But how great was the envy of the Jews, and what a fury of malice arose against the Lord, we are taught both here and in nearly every part of the Gospel. For Herod, a foreigner, declared without any witness that John—of whom it had been said that he performed no sign (John 10)—could rise from the dead. Yet they preferred to believe that Jesus had not risen but had been secretly removed, although their own Prophets had foretold him to them as a man approved by God through mighty works and signs (Acts 2), and although the elements had trembled at his death while angels, Apostles, men, and women proclaimed his resurrection and ascension in eager competition. This also shows that the minds of the Gentiles are more ready to believe than those of the Jews. For as the Prophet says of them: “Those to whom he was not announced will see”; but these, though seeing, do not see, because, as the Lawgiver testifies concerning them, “it is a crooked and perverse generation” (Deuteronomy 32), children in whom there is no faith.

> But Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother; for John was saying to him: “It is not lawful for you to have her.”

**(Jerome.)** Ancient history relates that Philip, the son of Herod the Greater, under whom the Lord fled into Egypt, and the brother of this Herod, under whom Christ suffered, married Herodias, the daughter of King Aretas. Later, when certain quarrels had arisen between her and her son-in-law, her mother took her daughter away and, to the sorrow of her former husband, joined her in marriage to his enemy. Which Philip this was, the Evangelist Luke explains more fully: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, while Philip his brother was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis” (Luke 3).

John the Baptist, therefore, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, rebuked Herod and Herodias with the same authority with which Elijah had rebuked Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21), because they had contracted an unlawful marriage. It was not lawful, while the brother was alive, to take his wife. John preferred to endanger himself before the king rather than, through flattery, forget the commandments of God.

> And although he wanted to kill him, he feared the people, because they held him as a prophet.

He feared an uprising of the people on account of John the Baptist, knowing that great crowds had been baptized by John in the Jordan. But he was overcome by love for his wife, whose passion had led him to neglect even the commandments of God.

> But on Herod’s birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced in their midst, and she pleased Herod.

**(Rabanus.)** Of mortal beings, only Herod and Pharaoh are recorded as having celebrated their birthdays with festive rejoicing (Genesis 40). Yet each king stained his festivity with blood under an evil omen. Herod, however, acted with the greater impiety, because he killed a holy and innocent teacher of truth and herald of life and the heavenly kingdom—and did so at the request and according to the desire of a dancing girl. Nor was he ashamed to bring the head of the murdered man before the guests. Pharaoh is not recorded as having committed any madness of this kind; nevertheless, by ordering that a eunuch who had offended him be deprived of life, the farther he was from the worship of true religion, the lighter was his offense in violating his festivity. From the example of both, however, it is proved that it is more beneficial for us, by fearing the future day of death and living chastely, to call it frequently to mind than to celebrate the day of birth through luxury. A human being is born into the world for labor, and those who have been raised upright pass from the world through death into rest.

**(Maurice.)** But those who are held by love of the world, blinded concerning the future, do not reflect on it. Consequently, they do not properly order even the present. Herod demonstrated this well in the luxury of his banquets. Concerning him it is added:

> So he promised her with an oath to give her whatever she might ask of him.

**(Jerome.)** Herod is not excused on the grounds that, unwillingly and against his desire, he committed murder because of his oath. Perhaps he swore for the purpose of preparing snares for a future opportunity. Otherwise, if he says that he acted because of his oath, suppose she had asked for the death of his father or mother: would he have done it? What he would have rejected in his own case, he ought to have rejected and disregarded in the case of the prophet.

> But she, having been prompted by her mother, said: “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”

Herodias feared that Herod might at some time come to his senses, or become reconciled to his brother Philip, and dissolve the unlawful marriage by repudiation. She therefore instructed her daughter to request John’s head immediately at the banquet itself: a worthy reward of blood for the worthy work of dancing.

> And the king was grieved; but because of the oath and those who were reclining with him, he ordered it to be given.

It is customary in the Scriptures for the historian to report the opinion of many people as it was believed by everyone at the time. Just as Joseph is called the father of Jesus even by Mary herself, so now Herod is said to have been grieved because this is what the reclining guests thought. Concealing his mind and acting as a contriver of murder, he displayed grief on his face while possessing joy in his heart. He excuses the crime by his oath, so that under the pretext of piety he might become impious. By adding “because of those who were reclining with him,” he wishes them all to be accomplices in his crime, so that bloody dishes might be served at a luxurious and impure banquet.

> And he sent and beheaded John in the prison, and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she took it to her mother.

**(Jerome.)** We read in Roman history that Flaminius, a Roman commander, agreed, at the request of a little courtesan reclining beside him—who said that she had never seen a beheaded man—to have a certain man accused of a capital crime be decapitated at the banquet. The censors expelled him from the Senate, because he had mixed banqueting with blood and, although the victim was guilty, had provided death for another person’s amusement, so that lust and murder might be mingled together. How much more criminal were Herod and Herodias, and the girl who danced, when she demanded the prophet’s head as the price of blood, so that she might have under her control the tongue that rebuked their unlawful marriage!

Let this be understood according to the literal sense. But to this day we see that in John’s head the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of the Prophets.

**(Rabanus.)** In another sense, John’s beheading signifies the diminution of his fame, by which Christ had been believed by the people, just as the elevation of the Lord and Savior on the cross signified the growth of faith. He who had previously been thought by the crowds to be a prophet was recognized by all the faithful as the Lord of the Prophets and the Son of God. John, therefore, was diminished by being beheaded, while the Lord was exalted on the cross, because, as John himself says, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The one who was considered a prophet had to be recognized as Christ, and the one who, because of the greatness of his mighty works, was thought to be Christ had to be understood as Christ’s prophet and Forerunner.

This same thing was also clearly indicated by the difference in the times when the two were born. John, who had to decrease, was born when the daylight was waning; but the Lord, who is the true light of the world, displayed to us the light-bearing gifts of his birth at the time of year when the days begin to grow longer.

> And his disciples came and took his body and buried it.

Here we may understand the disciples both of John himself and of the Savior. We must also not pass over what Josephus relates: John, after being bound, was taken to the fortress of Machaerus and beheaded there. Ecclesiastical History also relates that he was buried in Sebaste, a city of Palestine formerly called Samaria. In the time of the emperor Julian, pagans, out of envy toward the Christians who visited his tomb with pious devotion, invaded the monument, scattered his bones across the fields, and then gathered them up, burned them in a fire, and scattered them again over the countryside. At that time monks from Jerusalem were present there. Mixing with the pagans who were collecting the bones, they gathered a large part of them and carried them to their father Philip in Jerusalem. He sent them to the blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, where they were kept until the time of Theophilus, bishop of that city. Then, when the emperor Theodosius ordered all the temples of the Gentiles to be destroyed, the temple of Serapis was cleansed of its impurities, the bones were brought there, and a basilica was consecrated in honor of Saint John in place of the shrine of Serapis. It is called a martyrion. Read the eleventh book of *Ecclesiastical History*. It follows:

> And they came and announced it to Jesus.

The Apostles report to the Lord not only what they themselves had done and taught, but also what John had suffered while they were occupied in teaching. John himself, or his disciples, report this to him.

In a mystical sense, John, the Lord’s Forerunner, appears to signify the Law of the Old Testament. He was held in chains and prison, and the Law was held in obscure confinement and in the darkened heart of the Jewish people. He was beheaded, a foretelling of the fact that the Jews would lose Christ, who is the head of the Law and the Prophets, as we have shown above. His disciples, who buried his body and later came to announce to the Lord what had happened, appear to signify those who, recognizing that the Law had been extinguished in its carnal observances, passed over to the grace of the Lord and Savior. For John’s burial signifies the abolition of the Law.

To make this clearer, the discussion must be referred back to the beginning of the account. As we have often stated, John represented the form of the Law, because the Law proclaimed Christ, and John was the product of the Law, announcing Christ beforehand from the Law. Herod, however, is the ruler of the people; and the ruler of the people subject to him encompasses the name and cause of the whole population.

John therefore warned Herod not to take his brother’s wife. For there are, and there were, two peoples: the people of circumcision and the Gentiles. The Law warned Israel not to join to itself the works and unbelief of the Gentiles. The unbelief of the Gentiles is an associate, joined to them as though by the bond of marital love. These brothers, then, came from the same parent, the human race. For this reason, because of the truth of his harsh admonition, John, like the Law, was held in prison.

On the birthday—that is, amid the pleasures of bodily things—the daughter of Herodias danced. The will, born as it were from unbelief, was carried forward through the full course of seductions, and by an oath she offered herself entirely for sale to the peoples. Under sins and the pleasures of the age, the Israelites sold the gifts of eternal life. At the prompting of her mother—that is, of unbelief—she asked that John’s head be brought to her: that is, the glory of the Law, because the Law reproved Israel’s incestuous acts by the authority of the divine commandments.

Earlier, Herod was signified as wanting to kill John but being restrained by fear of the people, because John was regarded as a prophet. Now, when his death has been demanded and Herod is held back especially by the obligation of his oath, how does he become sad? Clearly, it is contrary to the earlier account: then he wanted it, whereas now he does not; and his present distress does not agree with his former will. In the earlier passage, however, the sequence of the event is given; here the nature of the subsequent cause is explained.

The will born from unbelief seized the glory of the Law. But the people, conscious of the good that was in the Law, were restrained by the conditions imposed by the will, not without some painful awareness of their own danger. They knew that they ought not to have surrendered such glory of the commandments; but, compelled by sins as though by oaths, corrupted by the fear and example of the surrounding rulers, and overcome by the enticements of pleasure, they obeyed even in sorrow.

Thus, amid the people’s other dissipated pleasures, John’s head is brought on a platter. Through the condemnation of the Law, the pleasure of the body is increased for worldly luxury, and it is brought by the girl to her mother, as though shameful Israel had delivered the Law to the will and unbelief of its own household, before the glory of the Gentiles.

When the times of the Law had ended, and it had been buried together with John, his disciples announced these things to the Lord. They had come from the Law to the Gospels and had become attentive hearers of the Word of God. With the Law ended, to whom else could they have migrated except to him who is its fulfillment? “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10); he caused the New Testament to succeed the Old Instrument.

> When Jesus heard this, he withdrew in a boat to a deserted place privately. [The supplied text reads *secessit mae*; the sense requires an emended reading, “he withdrew.”]

Not, as some think, through fear of death, but sparing his enemies, lest they should add murder to murder; or postponing his own death until the day of Passover, on which, because of the mystery, the Lamb had to be sacrificed and the doorposts sprinkled with the blood of believers. Or he withdrew in order to provide us with an example of avoiding the rashness of those who hand themselves over voluntarily: not all who offer themselves to be tortured persevere with the same steadfastness in torments. For this reason, knowing what evils the madness of the Jews and Gentiles would bring upon his followers, he also commanded elsewhere: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10).

The Evangelist also says elegantly not that he fled into a deserted place, but that he withdrew, so that he might be understood to have avoided his persecutors rather than feared them.

In another sense: After the head of the prophet had been severed by the Jews and by the king of the Jews, and prophecy had lost its tongue and voice among them, Jesus passed into the desert place of the Church, which previously had possessed no husband.

> And when the crowds heard this, they followed him on foot from the cities.

This can also be understood as follows: Jesus withdrew into a deserted place for another reason after hearing of John’s death, namely, to test the faith of believers. Accordingly, great crowds followed him on foot from the cities—not on beasts, not in various vehicles, but through the labor of their own feet, thereby showing the ardor of their minds. It should also be noted that, after the Lord came into the desert, the crowds followed him in great numbers. Before he came into the solitudes of the Gentiles, he was worshiped by only one people.

[Col. 0963C]

> And when he went out, he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick.

In the Gospel sayings, the spiritual meaning is always joined to the letter, and whatever at first sight appears cold becomes warm if you touch it. The Lord was in a deserted place. The crowds followed him, leaving their cities—that is, their former ways of life and their variety of doctrines. Jesus’ going out signifies that the crowds had the will to come but did not have the strength to reach him. Therefore the Savior goes out from his place and proceeds to meet them, as he also does in the parable of the repentant son (Luke 15). When he sees the crowd, he has compassion and heals their sicknesses, so that full faith may immediately receive its reward.

> When evening came, his disciples approached him, saying: “The place is deserted, and the hour has already passed. Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go to the villages and buy food for themselves.”

Everything is full of mysteries. He withdraws from Judea and comes into a deserted place; the crowds follow him, leaving their cities; Jesus goes out to meet them, has compassion on the crowd, and heals their sick. And he does this not in the morning, not as the day is growing, not at midday, but in the evening, when the sun of righteousness has set and the end of the world is approaching.

**(Maurice.)** The disciples, still carnal and ignorant of the miracle of the future nourishment, ask God to dismiss the crowds so that they may buy food for themselves in the villages—especially since at that time they had also been commanded, “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles” (Matthew 10), and so forth. Mystically, this signifies the Jews’ disdain for the crowds of the Gentiles, about whose reception they were always murmuring. They judged them more suitable to seek food for themselves in the gatherings of heretics, false prophets, or philosophers than to make use of the nourishment of the divine books. Isaiah once spoke in their voice when he said: “Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are counted as the moment on a balance.” And again: “All the nations are as nothing before him; they are regarded by him as nothing and vanity” (Isaiah 40).

But the Lord, who knows the future as though it were past, and to whom all things are present, determined that they should not be dismissed as empty but should rather be filled with heavenly food through the Apostles themselves. Hence it is added:

> But Jesus said to them: “They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat.”

**(Jerome.)** He prompts the Apostles to break the bread, so that when they testify that they do not possess any, the greatness of the sign may become more evident. At the same time he indicates that every day our fasting hearts are to be fed through them, namely, when we are aroused to love heavenly things by either their examples or their writings.

If anyone is troubled by the way in which, according to John’s account, the Lord, after seeing the crowds, asked Philip to test him where food might be obtained for them (John 6), and by the way in which the other Evangelists report that the disciples first said to the Lord that he should dismiss the crowds so that they could buy food for themselves from the nearby places (Mark 6; Luke 9), to which, according to Matthew, he replied, “They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat”—a statement with which Mark and Luke also agree, though they omit the words “they do not need to go away”—the explanation is that after these words the Lord looked upon the crowd and said to Philip what John records, while the others omitted it. Then, what Philip answers in John, Mark records as having been answered by the disciples, wishing it to be understood that Philip gave this answer through the mouth of the others as well.

> They answered him: “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.”

The whole Scripture of the Old Testament is signified by the five loaves and the two fish belonging to the Apostles. The five loaves signify the five books of the Mosaic Law, through which the knowledge of divine eternity, the creation of the world, the course of the passing age, and the true religion of serving God were made known to the human race. The two fish signify the Psalms and the Prophets, which fed the people instructed in the Law of God with the new sweetness of grace arising from the promise of the Lord’s incarnation. We are taught by the Lord’s authority that the whole sequence of the Old Instrument is contained in this threefold division of Sacred Scripture. For after his resurrection, appearing to the disciples, the Lord himself said: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke 24). When he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures and hand over what they had understood spiritually to the faithful hearers, he commanded that these things be distributed among the crowds, as though blessing the Apostles’ loaves and fish and multiplying them through the gift of inward sweetness.

According to the Gospel of John, the loaves that signify the Law are rightly reported to have been barley loaves, the food especially of beasts of burden and of rustic slaves. For beginning hearers, not yet perfected, are to be entrusted with harsher and, as it were, coarser commandments: “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2). Therefore the Lord, giving gifts to each according to his strength and always summoning him toward more perfect things, first feeds five thousand with five loaves, then four thousand with seven loaves, thirdly entrusts to the disciples the mystery of his flesh and blood, and finally gives the elect the great gift of eating and drinking at his table in his kingdom (Luke 22).

> He said to them: “Bring them here to me.”

Hear, Marcion; hear, Manichaean: the Lord commands that the five loaves and two small fish be brought to him, so that he may sanctify and multiply them. For he is the one to whom the Prophet says:

> “The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them food in due season. You open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing” (Psalm 144).

And when he had ordered the crowd to recline on the grass. The crowds are ordered to recline on the grass, and, according to another Evangelist, on the ground, in groups of fifty or one hundred, so that after they have trampled underfoot their flesh and all the flowers and pleasures of this world, and have laid dry grass, as it were, beneath themselves, they may then ascend through the repentance signified by the number fifty to the perfection signified by the number one hundred. (Gregory) The different reclining arrangements of those eating together signify the various congregations of the Churches, which together constitute the one Catholic Church. The Lord rightly commanded them to recline in groups of fifty or one hundred, so that the crowd of believers might receive its food, distinguished by place yet united in conduct. For the rest of the Jubilee is contained in the mystery of the number fifty; and fifty is taken twice in order to reach one hundred. Since one person first rests from evil action so that afterward the soul may rest more fully in thought, some recline in groups of fifty, others in groups of one hundred; for there are some who have rest from evil deeds, and others who already have rest of mind from perverse thoughts. They also reclined well upon green grass. For it is written: “All flesh is grass” (Sirach XIV). (RAB.) Those recline upon green grass and are nourished by the Lord’s provisions who, through the discipline of self-restraint and the trampling down of the allurements of carnal desires, devote themselves to hearing and fulfilling the words of God.

And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, and broke them. While the crowds were hungry, the Savior did not create new foods; rather, he blessed what the disciples had, having taken it from them. For when he came in the flesh, he preached nothing other than what had been foretold, but demonstrated how richly the writings of the Law and the Prophets were laden with the mysteries of grace. (Jerome) He looks up to heaven in order to teach that our eyes should be directed there. He took the five loaves and the two small fish into his hands, broke them, and handed them to his disciples. When the Lord breaks them, a seedbed of food is produced. For if they had remained whole and had not been torn into pieces and divided into a multiplied harvest, they could not have fed the crowds, the boys, the women, and so great a multitude. Thus the Law together with the Prophets is broken and torn into pieces, and its mysteries are brought into the midst, so that what, whole and remaining in its original condition, did not feed people may, when divided into parts, feed the multitude of the nations.

And he gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. (Maurice) Note, therefore, the order of the Lord’s banquet. First, the Lord himself blessed and broke the loaves and fish he had taken; then, having broken them into portions, he gave them to the disciples, so that they might distribute them to the crowds; afterward, the crowds ate the food received from the apostles and were satisfied. For the Lord himself first disclosed the sacraments of the Law and the Prophets, dividing them by his distribution among the apostles and preachers of the holy Gospel so that they might proclaim them throughout the whole world. Then they supplied abundant nourishment of spiritual food everywhere to the crowds of all nations. Therefore, as it is written, “they all ate and were satisfied,” because “there was not a needy person among them”; and the prophetic statement is fulfilled every day: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him shall praise God,” and so forth.

And they took up the fragments that remained, filling twelve baskets. (RAB.) What remains after the crowds have eaten is gathered up by the disciples, because the more sacred mysteries, which beginners cannot grasp, must not be carelessly neglected but sought out by the perfected. Through the twelve baskets the apostles are signified, and through the apostles all the choirs of teachers who follow: outwardly despised by human beings, but inwardly filled with the remnants of salutary food for nourishing the hearts of the humble. For it is well known that baskets are normally used for servile work; yet he filled the baskets with fragments of bread who chose the weak things of this world in order to confound the strong (I Corinthians I). Each of the apostles, therefore, fills his basket with the Savior’s remnants, so that he may have either something from which later to provide food for the needy or, from the remnants, something by which to teach that the loaves were truly loaves and were afterward multiplied.

Now the number of those who ate was five thousand men, besides women and children. The multitude corresponds to the number of the five loaves and the five thousand men who ate. For he had not yet reached, according to the account found elsewhere, the number seven, by which four thousand are fed. These numbers correspond closely to the number of the Gospels, since there are five senses of the outward person. The five thousand men who followed the Lord signify those who, while still living in a worldly condition, know how to use well the outward possessions they have. They are rightly fed with five loaves, because such people must still be instructed by the precepts of the Law. But those who renounce the world completely are four thousand and are fed with seven loaves—that is, they are exalted by evangelical perfection and instructed inwardly by spiritual grace.

Note, therefore, that it is said that five thousand men were fed by the Lord, besides women and children. (Jerome) The five thousand men who eat are those who have grown into a perfected man by advancing toward maturity and who followed him of whom Zechariah says: “Behold, a man; his name is Rising” (Zechariah VI). Women and children, representing fragile sex and lesser age, are not counted. Accordingly, whenever priests, Levites, armies, or a crowd of combatants are described in the Book of Numbers, servants, women, children, and the undistinguished multitude are mentioned beforehand without number.

(RAB.) It must not be passed over in silence that, when writing about this miracle of the loaves, the Evangelist John first stated that Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near; whereas Matthew and Mark report that it happened immediately after John’s death. From this it is inferred that John was beheaded when the same paschal feast was approaching, and that in the following year, when the paschal season returned, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was completed. Therefore, the fact that his feast is recorded in the Book of Sacraments on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and that in the Martyrology bearing the names of Eusebius and Jerome it is read that on the fourth day before the Kalends of September the birth-feast of John the Baptist was celebrated at Emesa, a city of the province of Phoenicia, on the day on which he was beheaded, does not designate specifically the day of his beheading. Rather, it designates the day on which his head was found in that same city of Emesa and placed in the church.

For, as the Chronicle of Marcellinus the Count testifies, during the reign of Marcian two Eastern monks came to Jerusalem to worship and see the holy places. The same forerunner of the Lord appeared to them in a revelation and ordered them to go to the former dwelling of King Herod, seek his head there, and, when they found it, bury it with due honor. The head, found and taken up there by them, was soon afterward lost through their negligence. It was brought to Emesa by others and ignobly hidden for a considerable time in an urn beneath the ground in a certain cave, until John once again revealed himself and his head to a certain religious abbot and priest named Marcellus, while he was living in that same cave. This head was brought, through the aforementioned priest, to Julioramus, [uncertain reading] the bishop of that city. From that time the beheading of the blessed forerunner began to be celebrated in that city, as we suppose, on the very day on which the head was found or raised.

You will find a fuller account of these matters in the aforementioned book of Chronicles. Matthew follows and says:

### III

And immediately he ordered the disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait, until he had dismissed the crowds. (Jerome) He orders the disciples to cross the water and compels them to get into the boat. By this wording it is shown that they withdrew from the Lord unwillingly, since out of love for their teacher they did not want to be separated from him.

(RAB.) Why he compelled the disciples to get into the boat, while he himself, after dismissing the people, went up onto the mountain to pray, John clearly explains. After completing that heavenly meal, he immediately adds: “When Jesus therefore perceived that they were about to come and seize him to make him king, he withdrew again to the mountain by himself.” Here he gives us a necessary example for living: in the good works we perform, we should avoid the reward of human approval, and the performance of spiritual virtues should not turn us toward desire for temporal and perishable pleasures.

For it happened to some that, while they were admired by lesser people and considered worthy of praise because of the merit of a more elevated life, and were thought rightly deserving of honor, they lost the beginnings of justice after receiving money or estates. When, through carelessness, they were corrupted by carnal allurements and greed, those very people by whom they had been honored came to regard them not only with disgust but even with hatred because of their evil deeds. It is far less dangerous to be wearied in the things we do rightly by the wickedness of those who oppose us than to be enticed by the favor of those who honor us. The latter often corrupts a soul made more secure; the former always makes it watchful and cautious.

Therefore, when the Lord was beginning for us the way of life that we should follow, those who admired his virtues wanted to make him king, and he fled to the mountain to pray. But when those who envied his virtues were preparing to hand him over to death, he came forward readily and offered himself to the enraged for binding and crucifixion. By this evident example he teaches us to be ready to endure the adversities of the world, cautious about avoiding its blandishments when they happen to smile upon us, and diligent in asking the Lord through frequent prayers that the prosperity of the world, if it overflows, may not deceive us by making us soft.

That the disciples went ahead of the Lord, Mark shows when he says that the Lord compelled his disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait toward Bethsaida while he dismissed the people. Bethsaida is in Galilee, the city of the apostles Andrew, Peter, and Philip, near the lake of Gennesareth, as we find in books about places.

(Augustine) Here it is rightly asked how Mark can say that, after the miracle of the loaves, the disciples came across the strait to Bethsaida, when Luke appears to say that the memorable miracle and heavenly meal took place in the region of Bethsaida. For he says: “Taking them, he withdrew privately into a deserted place which is Bethsaida.” When the crowds learned this, they followed him, and he received them, and so forth, up to the completion of that account of the sacred meal.

Unless perhaps we understand that, when Luke says “into a deserted place that belonged to Bethsaida,” he does not designate the vicinity of the city itself but the deserted places belonging to it. For Mark says plainly that they were to go ahead of him to Bethsaida, where the boundaries of the city itself are evidently indicated. Luke, however, who does not say “into a deserted place which is Bethsaida,” but “which is Bethsaida,” can, if I am not mistaken, rightly be understood to mean that he did not intend the city itself but its deserted place—that is, a place belonging to its boundaries.

The Evangelist John reports that the crowds ate bread near Tiberias, and that the disciples, having boarded the boat, came across the sea to Capernaum. Both are cities in Galilee, near the lake of Gennesareth, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias after the city of Tiberias.

And after dismissing the crowd, he went up onto the mountain by himself to pray. If Peter, James, and John, who had seen the glory of the Transfigured One, had been with him, perhaps they would have gone up the mountain with him. But the crowd could not follow him to the heights unless he had first taught it beside the sea, on the shore, and fed it in the wilderness. As for his going up alone to pray, do not refer this to the one who satisfied five thousand men with five loaves, besides women and children, but to the one who, having heard of John’s death, withdrew into solitude. This does not mean that we separate the Lord’s person, but that his works are divided between the divine and the human.

(Ambrose) Here it should also be noted that not everyone who prays ascends the mountain. There is a kind of prayer that produces sin. But the one who prays well, who seeks God by praying, progresses from earthly things to higher ones and ascends the summit of a more exalted concern. Whoever, however, begs anxiously for riches, worldly honor, or even the death of an enemy lies in the lowest places and sends base prayers to God.

The Lord prays not that he may plead for himself but that he may obtain something for me. For although the Father has placed all things in the power of the Son, the Son nevertheless, in order to fulfill the form of a human being, considers that he should plead with the Father on our behalf, because he is our advocate. “We have,” he says, “Jesus Christ the righteous as an advocate with the Father” (I John II). If he is an advocate, he must intercede for my sins. He pleads, therefore, not as one who is weak but as one who is compassionate. Do you wish to know how he can do everything he wills? He is both advocate and judge: in the one role there is the duty of compassion; in the other, the mark of power.

### IV

When evening came, he was there alone; but the boat was being tossed in the middle of the sea by the waves, for the wind was contrary. (Jerome) The apostles had rightly withdrawn from the Lord as though unwillingly and reluctantly, lest, while he was absent, they should suffer shipwreck. Indeed, while the Lord remained on the summit of the mountain, a contrary wind immediately arose, the sea was troubled, and the apostles were endangered; and the threatening shipwreck continued as long as Jesus did not come.

(Augustine) The disciples’ labor in rowing, and the wind contrary to them, signify the various labors of the holy Church. Amid the hostile waves of the world and the blasts of unclean spirits, she strives to reach the rest of her heavenly homeland, as though reaching a secure harbor. It is rightly said that the boat was in the middle of the sea while he himself was on land, because sometimes the Church has been not only afflicted but also defiled by such great pressures from the nations that, if it were possible, her Redeemer might seem to have completely abandoned her for a time.

Hence comes her cry when she is caught amid the waves and storms of sweeping temptations and seeks the help of his protection with a groaning shout: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why do you disregard us in times of trouble?” (Psalm IX). In the psalms that follow, she likewise sets forth the voice of the enemy pursuing her: “For he has said in his heart, ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, so that he will not see to the end.’” Yet he does not forget the prayer of the poor, nor does he turn his face away from those who hope in him. Rather, he helps those struggling with their enemies so that they may conquer, and he crowns the victorious forever.

Thus in this passage Mark also appropriately says: “He saw them laboring in rowing.” The Lord sees his own laboring on the sea, although he himself is on land, because even if he seems to delay for a time in bringing help to the afflicted, he nevertheless strengthens them by regard for his compassion, so that they may not fail in their troubles. Sometimes, too, by manifest assistance he frees them after they have overcome adversity, as though the waves’ billows had been trampled down and stilled. This is also suggested in what follows:

But in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea. (Jerome) Military watches and sentry duties are divided into three-hour periods. Therefore, when it says that the Lord came to them in the fourth watch of the night, it shows that they were in danger throughout the entire night and that help was given them toward the end of the night.

(RAB.) They labored, then, throughout the whole darkness of night. But as dawn approached, and the morning star promised the rising of the sun and the day, the Lord came and, walking upon the swollen surface of the sea, pressed it down. For when fragile humanity, burdened by troubles, considers the weakness of its own strength, it sees nothing around itself except the darkness of distress and the heat of hostile forces fighting against it. But when it raises its mind toward the light of heavenly protection and the gifts of eternal reward, it sees, as though suddenly rising amid the shadows of night, the morning star that announces the coming day.

For the morning star is said to illuminate for approximately three hours of the night—that is, the entire morning watch. The Lord will come, and when the dangers of temptation have been put to sleep, he will grant the fully delivered the confidence of his protection. It follows:

And when they saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It is a phantom.” (Jerome) If, according to Marcion and Manichaeus, our Lord was not born from a virgin but appeared in a phantom, why are the apostles now afraid that they might see a phantom?

(RAB.) The heretics still maintain that the Lord was a phantom and did not truly assume flesh from the virgin. Thus Theodore of Pharan, formerly a bishop, wrote that the Lord, according to the flesh, did not possess corporeal weight, but walked upon the sea without weight and without a body.

Against this, the Catholic faith proclaims that he possessed a body according to the flesh, bodily weight, and a bodily burden, and that he walked upon the waters with weight and corporeal burden, not with his feet immersed. For Dionysius, an outstanding ecclesiastical writer, speaks in this way in his works On the Divine Names: “For we do not know how he was formed from virginal blood by a law other than the natural one, nor how, with his feet not immersed, possessing corporeal weight and material burden, he walked upon a moist and unstable substance.”

We must therefore consider how Mark says that, around the fourth watch of the night, the Lord came to them walking upon the sea and wished to pass them by. But how did the Lord wish to pass them by as though they were strangers, when he had come to free them from the danger of shipwreck? He wished this so that, frightened and trembling for a moment but immediately delivered, they might be more profoundly astonished at the miracle of their rescue and render greater thanks to their rescuer.

The same kind of divine providence is sometimes displayed in the storms of suffering inflicted by unbelievers upon the faithful for the sake of steadfastness in the faith. Often heavenly compassion has seemed to abandon believers placed in tribulation, so that Jesus might be thought to have wished to pass by the disciples laboring on the sea. Hence comes the voice of the Church sweating through the contests of martyrdom: “Why have you forgotten me? Why have you rejected me? And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me, while all my bones are broken?” and so forth (Psalm XLII).

But let the enemies who terrify us say, “Where is their God?” To the apostles, exhausted and threatened with shipwreck, their own God says: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers will not overwhelm you. When you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not consume you” (Isaiah XLIII).

And they cried out from fear. (Jerome) A confused cry and an uncertain voice are signs of great fear.

(Maurice) But the Psalmist’s testimony is true: “The Lord is near to those who fear him, and he does not abandon all who hope in him” (Psalm CXLIV). Hence it is added:

Immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying: “Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.” (Jerome) He cures what was foremost in the situation and commands those who are afraid, saying: “Take courage; do not be afraid.” And when he adds, “It is I,” without saying who he is, they could either recognize him from his voice, since he was speaking through the darkness of night, or they could know that he was the one whom they had learned had spoken to Moses: “This you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is’ has sent me to you” (Exodus III).

But Peter answered him and said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” And he said: “Come.” In every passage Peter is found to possess the most ardent faith. When the disciples were asked whom people said Jesus was, he confessed him to be the Son of God. He tried to prevent him from going to his Passion; and although he was mistaken in the matter, he was not mistaken in his affection, since he did not want the one whom he had just confessed to be the Son of God to die.

He ascended the mountain with the Savior among the first, and in the Passion he alone followed him. He immediately washed away the sin of denial, which had arisen from sudden fear, with the bitterest tears. After the Passion, when he was at the lake of Gennesareth and they were fishing while the Lord stood on the shore, as the others sailed slowly he could not endure delay. Girded with his outer garment, he immediately threw himself into the waves.

With the same ardor of faith that he always possessed, he now also believed, while the others were silent, that by the will of his master he could do what he could not do by nature. “Command me,” he says, “to come to you upon the waters.” You command, and immediately the waves will become solid, and the body that is naturally heavy will become light.

And Peter, coming down from the boat, walked upon the waters to come to Jesus. Let those who think that the Lord’s body was not real because he walked upon soft and yielding waters, as though he were soft and aerial, answer how Peter walked, since they certainly will not deny that he was a real human being.

But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid. And when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: “Lord, save me.” The faith of his spirit was burning, but human frailty was dragging him into the depths. He is therefore abandoned to temptation for a short time, so that his faith may be increased and he may understand that he was preserved not by the ease of his request but by the Lord’s power.

And immediately extending his hand, he seized him. (Maurice) If the Lord had not extended his hand—the Lord who elsewhere looked upon Peter when he denied him—Peter himself would immediately have sunk into the depths and would not even have escaped hell. The Lord looked upon him and converted him to repentance; he extended his hand, granted forgiveness, and thus found complete salvation for his disciple. For, in Paul’s words, salvation depends “not on him who wills or on him who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Romans IX). We are not saved by our own merit but by his gift.

And he said to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” If the apostle Peter, whose faith and ardor of mind we have described above, who confidently asked the Savior, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters,” is told, because he was afraid for a little while, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” what must be said of us, who do not possess even the smallest portion of this little faith?

(Maurice) Mystically, the fact that Peter, commanded by the Lord to come, treads upon the waves of the sea in order to come to Jesus signifies the Church, whose pastor he is, pressing onward toward the heavenly homeland and trampling underfoot the waves of this world by the footprint of right faith and by steps of good works.

The fact that Peter, frightened by the storm, began to sink in the waves signifies the weaker members of the Church: those whom the storm of persecution or the whirlwind of temptation frightens and turns aside for a time from the course of faith or from the steadfastness of good deeds. Yet, lest they sink completely into unbelief and the abyss of sins, the outstretched right hand of divine mercy draws them out. And just as he placed Peter, rescued from the sea of the abyss, upon the firm ground of heavenly rest, so he will place those who have been rescued from the stumbling-block of their persecutors beside himself upon that firm ground. For it is impossible that any of those whom the judgment of the righteous Judge has predestined to eternal life should perish.

The Truth himself says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John VI). For the Lord knows how to rescue the devout from temptation (II Peter II). Nor is he powerless, amid the storms of this world, to keep his own unharmed from every wickedness of the evil.

But let us see what follows:

And when he had entered the boat, the wind ceased. (RAB.) The first assistance given to those who are trembling and in danger is to drive fear from their hearts. The second is to restrain the violence of storms by the power of his presence. It is not surprising that, when the Lord entered the boat, the wind ceased. For in whatever heart God is present through the grace of his love, all the battles of vices and of the hostile world or evil spirits are immediately restrained and become quiet.

Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying: “Truly you are the Son of God.” At a single sign—the restoration of calm to the sea, something that sometimes happens by chance after excessive storms—the sailors and passengers confess that he is truly the Son of God, while Arius proclaims in the Church that he is a creature.

(Maurice) Let us therefore believe and confess that he is not, according to the madness of the heretics, a creature among all created things, but the Creator existing and abiding before all things together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. In this confession let us also venerate him with fitting praises for his good works, and proclaim before the children of human beings that he is the only-begotten Son of God, recounting his virtues and the wonders he performed.

And when they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesar. The land of Gennesar, near the lake of Gennesareth, is, as some assert, the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Galilee is named from the neighboring province, whereas the Sea of Tiberias is named from the nearby city, which was formerly called Gennereth but was restored by Herod the tetrarch in honor of Tiberius Caesar and called Tiberias.

Moreover, according to some, Gennesar derives its name from the nature of the lake itself, since it is said to raise a breeze from itself through its rippling waters. In Greek it is therefore said to mean “generating a breeze for itself.” The water does not lie flat like that of a pond but is stirred by frequent blowing breezes; it is sweet to drink and suitable for drinking. In the customary usage of the Hebrew language, however, every gathering of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called a sea.

This lake, through which the Jordan flows, extends one hundred and sixty stadia in length and forty in breadth.
