Finally, if we know what Gennesar signifies in Latin, we will understand how Jesus, through the figure of the apostles and the boat, carries the Church, freed from the shipwreck of persecution, across to the shore and makes her rest in the calmest harbor. As we find in the book On Hebrew Names, Gennesar is interpreted as “the beginning of rising.” We shall then be granted complete tranquility, when through Christ the inheritance of paradise is restored to us and the joy of the first robe is returned.

And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent word throughout the whole surrounding region. (Jerome) They recognized him by report, not by his face; or perhaps, because of the greatness of the signs he performed among the people, he was known to many even by his appearance. And observe how great was the faith of the people of the land of Gennesareth: they were not content merely with the salvation of those who were present, but sent to the surrounding cities so that everyone might run to the physician.

And they brought to him all who were sick, and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and all who touched it were healed. (RAB.) Those who were sick do not touch the body of Jesus, nor his whole garment, but only its outermost fringe. And all who touch it will be healed. Understand the fringe of his garment as the least commandment: whoever transgresses it will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Or understand it as the assumption of flesh, through which we come to the Word of God and afterward enjoy his majesty.

# CHAPTER XV

A discourse to the Pharisees concerning what defiles a person. He heals the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman and others who are afflicted; he feeds four thousand men with seven loaves.

### I

Then scribes and Pharisees came to him from Jerusalem, saying: “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

How true was that confession of the Lord to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke X). The people of the land of Gennesareth, who seemed less learned, not only came themselves but brought their own with them—indeed, carried them to the Lord—so that they might deserve at least to touch the fringe of his garment and thus be saved. Therefore they immediately received the reward of the salvation they desired.

But the Pharisees and scribes, who ought to have been teachers of the people, came to the Lord not to hear the Word and not to seek healing, but only to stir up disputes through their questions. They criticized those whose hands had not been washed, although in their actions—performed by their hands or by the other members of their bodies—they could find no defiling impurity. They ought rather to have condemned themselves, since, though they had hands washed with water, they carried a conscience polluted by spite.

(Maurice) What remarkable foolishness on the part of the Pharisees and scribes, who accuse the Son of God because he does not observe the traditions and precepts of human beings. But because that statement of Scripture is true which says, “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs XXI), let us hear what follows:

But he answered them: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?” (Jerome) He refutes a false accusation with a true answer: “When you neglect the commandment of the Lord because of human tradition, why do you think that my disciples should be accused because they disregard the commands of human custom in order to keep God’s decrees?”

For God said: “Honor your father and your mother”; and “Whoever curses father or mother must die the death.” In Scripture, honor is understood not so much in greetings and the performance of services as in almsgiving and the bestowal of gifts. “Honor,” says the Apostle, “widows who are truly widows” (I Timothy V). Here honor means a gift. And elsewhere: “Let the presbyters who labor in the word and teaching of the Lord be honored with double honor” (ibid.). After this commandment we are also ordered not to muzzle the ox while it is threshing, so that the worker may be worthy of his reward.

But you say: “Whoever says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever gift from me would benefit you,’ and does not honor his father or his mother”—and so you have annulled the commandment of God because of your tradition.

The Lord had commanded, considering the weakness, age, or poverty of parents, that children should honor their parents, even by supplying them with the necessities of life. The scribes and Pharisees, wishing to overturn this most provident law of God and to cloak impiety under the name of piety, taught the worst children that, if someone wished to vow to God—who is the true Father—the things that ought to be offered to his parents, the offering to the Lord should be preferred to gifts for the parents.

Alternatively, the parents themselves, avoiding what had been consecrated to God lest they incur the charge of sacrilege, were worn down by poverty. Thus it happened that the offering of the children, under the pretext of the temple and God, accrued to the profit of the priests. This most wicked custom arose from such an occasion. Many people were bound by debts, and, unwilling to repay what had been lent to them, they attached themselves to priests so that the money collected might serve the services of the temple and the priests’ own needs.

This passage may also have the following brief meaning: “Whatever gift from me would benefit you.” You compel children, he says, to say to their parents: “Whatever gift I was about to offer to God, I am using for your food; it benefits you, father and mother.” Thus the parents, fearing to accept what they saw had been dedicated to God, would prefer to lead a life of poverty rather than eat what had been consecrated.

Hypocrites! Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX).

(Maurice) The prophet, foreseeing in the spirit the future hypocrisy of the Jews and their deceitful resistance to the preaching of the Gospel, prophesied well about them—not because what he says about them was good, since his statement concerned their wickedness, but because that prophecy suited their conduct well.

Speaking also in the person of the Lord, he said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” They honored him with their lips because they repeatedly studied his Law and sang hymns or psalms to him in the divine offices; but their heart was far from him. It is written of them that in their hearts they were always turned back toward Egypt.

They also honored him with their lips when they said to him: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you do not care about anyone, for you do not regard the person of human beings” (Matthew XXII). But their heart was far from him when they said: “Tell us, is it lawful to pay the census-tax to Caesar or not?” (Luke XX).

The Evangelist Luke made this clear when he said that the scribes and chief priests sent spies who pretended to be righteous in order to trap him in his speech and hand him over to the authority and power of the governor. Therefore it is rightly added:

“In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of human beings.”

They worshiped him in vain—that is, for nothing—with lips and tongue, while their hearts were turned away, because they would not receive the reward of true worshipers of God. The Truth himself testifies to this elsewhere, saying: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VII).

The Pharisees taught doctrines and commandments of human beings when, neglecting divine precepts and placing their own traditions above them, they judged that their own traditions should be observed more carefully, as was demonstrated above.

Having called the crowds to himself, he said to them: “Listen and understand: it is not what enters the mouth that makes a person unclean, but what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person.” *Communicat* is properly a term of Scripture and is not used in ordinary speech. The Jewish people, boasting that they are God’s portion, call “common” the foods that all people use—for example, pork, oysters, hares, and animals of that kind, which do not divide the hoof or chew the cud, nor have scales among the fish. Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “What God has made holy, you must not call common” (Acts X). What is common, therefore—what is open to other people and is, as it were, not part of God’s portion—is called unclean. [Col. 0976B]

“Nothing,” he says, “entering a person from outside can defile him; rather, the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” Let the prudent reader object and say: If what enters the mouth does not defile a person, why do we not eat food sacrificed to idols? And the Apostle writes: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (I Cor. X). It must therefore be understood that the foods themselves, as God’s creatures, are clean in themselves, but the invocation of idols and demons makes them unclean.

Then his disciples came and said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this saying, were scandalized?” By this one saying the whole superstition of Jewish observances had been overthrown, for they thought their religion consisted in accepting some foods and rejecting others. And since the word *scandalum* is frequently used in ecclesiastical Scripture, we should briefly explain what it means. We may render Greek *σκαλὸν* and *σκάνδαλον* as an obstacle, a ruin, or a striking of the foot. Thus, when we read, “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” we understand it to mean someone who gives another an occasion of falling through word or deed.

But he answered: “Every planting that my Father did not plant will be uprooted.” Even passages that seem straightforward in Scripture are full of questions. “Every planting,” he says, “that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.” Then that planting too will be uprooted of which the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollos watered.” But the question is resolved by what follows: “Yet God gave the growth” (I Cor. III). He himself also says: “You are God’s field, God’s building.” And elsewhere: “We are God’s fellow workers.” If we are fellow workers, then, while Paul plants and Apollos waters, God plants and waters together with his fellow workers. Those who introduce different natures misuse this passage, saying that the planting which the Father did not plant is to be uprooted. But let them hear Jeremiah: “I planted you as a choice vine; how have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” God indeed planted it, and no one can uproot his planting; but since this planting lies within the will of free choice, no one else can uproot it unless it itself gives its consent.

“Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. And if the blind leads the blind, both will fall into a pit.” This is what the Apostle commanded: “Avoid a heretical person after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a person is perverted and self-condemned” (Titus III). In this sense the Savior commands that the worst teachers be left to their own judgment, knowing that they can scarcely be drawn back to the truth: they are blind and drag a blind people into error. (MAUR.) The Pharisees were therefore blind because, observing the dark traditions of human beings, they did not consider the light of God’s commandments, which the Psalmist professed, saying: “Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Ps. CLXXXVIII). Thus they are rightly called not only blind but also guides of the blind, because such people do not merely fail to watch over themselves lest they fall into a snare; they also drag those who obey them with themselves into the precipice [Col. 0977B] of death.

Then Peter answered him: “Explain this parable to us.” But he said: “Are you still without understanding?” (Hieron.) What had been plainly spoken and was open to the hearing, the Apostles thought had been spoken as a parable; in a manifest matter they sought a hidden meaning. They are rebuked by the Lord for thinking that something had been spoken parabolically when he had spoken clearly. From this we learn that a hearer is defective when he wishes to understand obscure things plainly or plainly spoken things obscurely.

“Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the stomach and is discharged into the privy?” Among heretics and perverse people, all the Gospel passages are full of stumbling blocks. From this little statement some bring an accusation, claiming that the Lord, ignorant of physical reasoning, supposes that all foods go into the stomach and are digested in the privy, although food immediately poured in is distributed through the limbs and veins, the marrow and the nerves. They point out that many who suffer continual vomiting because of a stomach disorder immediately vomit after dinners and meals what they have swallowed, and yet remain corpulent, because at the first contact, thinner food and drink are distributed through the body. But in wishing to criticize another’s ignorance, such people display their own. For although the fluid and food may be extremely thin and liquid, once it has been digested and assimilated in the veins and limbs, it descends through the body’s hidden passages—which the Greeks call *πόροι*—to the lower parts and goes into the privy.

“But the things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and these defile a person. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and the rest.” “From the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts.” Therefore, according to Christ, the ruling faculty of the soul is not in the brain, as Plato held, but in the heart. This saying also refutes those who think that thoughts are injected by the devil and do not arise from the will itself. The devil may be an assistant and instigator of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author. If, always lying in ambush, he has kindled a small spark of our thoughts with his fuel, we must not suppose that he also searches out the hidden things of the heart; rather, from bodily appearance and gestures he judges what we are turning over within. For example, if he repeatedly sees us looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the arrow of love [Col. 0978A] and incites us to fornication. (MAUR.) If he sees us nursing resentment against a neighbor, he understands that we harbor envy and hatred in our heart and inflames us through anger to commit murder. If he sees us gazing ardently at the beauty of some object, he understands that we hold greed in our heart and urges us to theft. If he perceives that we are accustomed to frivolous speech, he understands that we are ready to lie and prompts us to give false testimony. In this way the ancient enemy probes the quality of the mind through the other dispositions of our conduct and hastens to deceive the human race, persuading it to do what divine laws forbid, so that he may pollute with his filth the creature made in the image of God. Therefore, after enumerating the vices mentioned above, the Savior added:

“These are the things that defile a person. Eating without washing the hands does not defile a person.” (RAB.) The Pharisees, however, taking the spiritual words of the prophets in a bodily sense, observed only the washing of the body, although the prophets commanded the cleansing of the heart and conduct, saying: “Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean,” and “Purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. I). In vain, then, do the Pharisees—in vain, all Jews—wash their hands and baptize themselves in the marketplace so long as they disdain to be washed in the Savior’s fountain. They preserve the baptisms of vessels to no purpose while neglecting to wash away the filth of their hearts and bodies, although it is certain that Moses and the prophets, whenever and for whatever reason they commanded the vessels of God’s people to be cleansed with water, purified by fire, or sanctified with oil, intended by this not the cleansing of material things but rather the correction of minds and deeds, holiness, and the salvation of souls [Col. 0978C].

[II.] Then Jesus went away from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. (Hieron.) Having left behind the scribes and Pharisees, his slanderers, he crossed into the region of Tyre and Sidon. There it is clearly prefigured that after his passion and resurrection the Lord would leave the faithless hearts of the Jews behind in his preachers and withdraw into the regions of foreign nations. Tyre and Sidon, cities that belonged to the Gentiles, indicate the strongholds of teaching and life in which the Gentiles place their trust.

And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from that region and cried out to him, saying: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” Appropriately, this woman, who in faith prayed to the Lord, is said to have come out from that region, because the Church would never come to Christ unless it had first abandoned the empty dwellings of its former way of life; nor would it know how to receive the new grace of faith unless it had first anathematized the doctrines of its ancient error. (Hieron.) For this reason she knows to call him Son of David: she had already gone out from her own region and, by a change of place and faith, had abandoned the error of the Tyrians and Sidonians.

“My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” (RAB.) In a figurative sense, this Gentile woman who comes to the Lord in faith, as we have said above, represents the Church gathered from the Gentiles. On behalf of her demoniac daughter she begs God, entreating divine mercy for her peoples, who do not yet believe, so that they too may be freed from the devil’s deceits [Col. 0979A]. Again, the demon-possessed daughter for whom she pleads represents any soul in the Church that is enslaved more to the deceits of wicked spirits than to the commands of its Creator. For her the Church, as mother, must earnestly intercede with the Lord, asking him to correct inwardly through inspiration the one whom it cannot correct outwardly through admonition, entreaty, and rebuke, and to awaken her, converted from the darkness of error, to the knowledge of the true light.

Again, in a tropological sense, if any one of us has a conscience polluted by the filth of greed, pride, vainglory, indignation, anger, envy, or other vices, he certainly has a daughter grievously tormented by a demon. For her healing, let him run as a suppliant to the Lord, since a thought born from the heart is endured in a state of madness through the devil’s art. He must continually—even unceasingly—beg the merciful Creator for her correction with lamentations and prayers, so that she may be healed.

Again, if someone has stained good deeds that he performed with the plague of perjury, theft, blasphemy, detraction, quarrelsomeness, bodily impurity, or other such evils, he has a daughter agitated by the frenzies of an unclean spirit. For he has foolishly destroyed through the devil’s deceits the deed that he had produced by good labor. Therefore, once such a person recognizes his guilt, he must immediately flee to prayers and tears and frequently seek the intercessions and assistance of the saints. It follows:

“He did not answer her a word.” (Hieron.) This was not because of Pharisaic pride or the arrogance of the scribes, but lest he himself should appear contrary to his own command, by which he had said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. X). For he did not wish to give the slanderers an opportunity, and he reserved the perfect salvation of the Gentiles for the time of his passion and resurrection. (RAB.) In a mystical sense, if the Lord delays answering the Church’s first tears of petition—that is, if he delays granting the requested healing of mind to those who have gone astray—even then we must not cease asking, seeking, and knocking, nor yield to despair of obtaining what we seek. Rather, the Savior must be approached with such persistence and summoned with such unwavering love; the assistance of his saints must be sought so earnestly during the litanies that they themselves may plead with the Lord from heaven for the Church to be heard. Thus, if a person does not turn his mind away from the intention he has adopted, he will by no means be deprived of the fruit of his petition; whether he has intervened for his own weakness or for others, he will obtain the desired result [Col. 0979D].

Then his disciples came and begged him, saying: “Send her away, because she is crying out after us.” (Hieron.) At that time the disciples still did not understand the Lord’s mysteries. Either moved by mercy, they pleaded for the Canaanite woman—whom the other Evangelist calls a Syrophoenician—or, wishing to be rid of her persistence, they did so because she cried out repeatedly, not recognizing him as a merciful but as a stern physician.

Mark also records this event concerning the Canaanite woman, preserving the same order of events and raising no question of contradiction, except that he says the Lord was in a house when she came to him and pleaded for her daughter. Matthew could easily be understood to have omitted the mention of the house while recounting the same event. But since he says that the disciples urged the Lord, “Send her away, because she is crying out after us,” this seems to signify nothing other than that the woman, walking behind the Lord, uttered supplicating cries. How, then, was she in the house? It must be understood that Mark said she entered where Jesus was after having stated that he had been in the house. Since Matthew says, “He did not answer her a word,” he makes known what both had left unspoken: that, during this silence, Jesus went out from that house. Thus the remaining events follow in sequence, and thereafter the two accounts differ in nothing.

But he answered: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” This does not mean that he was not also sent to the Gentiles, but that he was sent first to Israel, so that, when they did not receive the Gospel, his passage to the Gentiles might rightly take place. Significantly, he said, “To the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” so that from this passage too we may understand the one wandering sheep mentioned in another parable.

But she came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, help me.” (MAUR.) What does the statement “But she came” mean, when she has already been described as speaking to the Savior and pleading for her daughter? Since at first she cried out after Jesus, she now came by following him—that is, she caught up with him—and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, help me.”

He answered: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she said: “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” (Hieron.) Under the person of the Canaanite woman, the faith, patience, and humility of the Church are wonderfully proclaimed: faith, because she believed that her daughter could be healed; patience, because, though repeatedly rejected, she persevered in prayer; humility, because she compared herself not to dogs but to little dogs. The Gentiles are called dogs because of their idolatry; devoted to the consumption of blood, they are said to run mad over the corpses of the dead.

Notice that this Canaanite woman persistently first calls him Son of David, then Lord, and finally worships him as God. “I know,” she says, “that I do not deserve the children’s bread, nor can I receive whole loaves or sit at table with the father; but I am content with the little dogs’ leftovers, so that through the humility of crumbs I may come to the greatness of the whole bread.” O marvelous reversal of things! Israel was once the son, while we were dogs; according to the difference of faith, the order of names is changed. Of them it is later said: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. XXI). And: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers; beware of the mutilation” (Phil. III). Of us, converted from the barking of blasphemous contradiction to the grace of devotion, he says elsewhere: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice” (John X).

It should rightly be noted that the woman, believing from the Gentiles, speaks mystically, because the little dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs. The table is holy Scripture, which supplies us with the bread of life. Thus the Church says: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict me” (Ps. XXII). The children’s crumbs are the inner mysteries of Scripture, by which the hearts of the humble are accustomed to be refreshed. Concerning these it is promised elsewhere to the holy Church, when the Prophet speaks of the Lord: “He has placed peace within your borders and satisfies you with the fat of grain” (Ps. CXLVII).

The little dogs therefore eat not the crusts but the crumbs of the children’s bread, because those who have turned to the faith—once despised among the Gentiles—seek in the Scriptures not the surface of the letter but the spiritual meaning by which they may advance in good works. And they eat under the table of their masters when, humbly subject to the words of sacred discourse, they place all the faculties of their heart and body beneath the fulfillment of the commandments, so that, through the merit of due humility, they may raise themselves to hope for the rewards promised by the Lord in heaven.

[Col. 0981B] Then Jesus answered her: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you desire.” (MAUR.) In this Syrophoenician woman, therefore, the faith of the Gentiles is praised. It is rightly called great because, although they had not been instructed in the Law or taught by the voices of the prophets, they immediately obeyed the preaching of the Apostles upon hearing it and received faith in the holy Trinity with believing hearts. Adorning that faith with worthy works, they strove to preserve it inviolate unto death. Therefore they deserved to obtain perfect salvation for themselves and their people. Hence it is added:

“And her daughter was healed from that hour.” Because of the mother’s humble and faithful speech, the demon left the daughter. Here an example is given for catechizing and baptizing infants, since through the faith and confession of their parents, little ones who cannot yet understand or do any good or evil by themselves are freed from the devil in baptism [Col. 0981C].

[III.] When Jesus had crossed over from there, he came beside the Sea of Galilee; and going up the mountain, he sat there. It should therefore be noted that the Lord’s return to Judea and the Sea of Galilee after healing the daughter of the Canaanite woman was not without the rationale of a great mystery. After the dispensation of salvation among the Gentiles had been accomplished, he returns in his teachers to visit the Jewish nation, which on account of its faithlessness had rejected the Apostles and the first preachers of the Gospel. Thus what the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, long ago declared in prophetic speech comes to pass: when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered through the door of faith, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI).

The Lord therefore went up the mountain so that, just as a bird summons its tender young to fly, he might raise his hearers to meditate upon heavenly and celestial mysteries. He sat there to show that rest must be sought only in heavenly things.

And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the infirm, and many others. They cast them at his feet, and he healed them, so that the crowds marveled when they saw the mute speaking, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

While the Lord sits upon the mountain—that is, while he gloriously and wondrously reigns in the citadel of heaven—the crowds of the faithful continually approach him with devoted minds, bringing with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the infirm, and many others [Col. 0982A]. For through evangelical teachings they are converted to faith: those who had no word of confession in their mouths; those whom unbelief had blinded; those who limped through wicked works; and those whom the burden of sins had made weak. They cast them at Jesus’ feet because, confessing their sins, they submit them for healing to him alone, the mediator between God and human beings.

He heals them in such a way that the crowds marvel and glorify the God of Israel. For the hosts of the faithful then exult with immeasurable joy when they see those whom various illnesses of error had made foolish and needy now enriched with diverse resources of virtue and strong in faith, laboring well in divine service. Therefore they sing great praises to God, saying with the Prophet: “Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who alone does wonders. You have made your power known among the peoples; with your arm you have redeemed your people, the children of Israel and Joseph” (Ps. LXXVI).

But Jesus called his disciples to him and said: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have remained with me for three days now and have nothing to eat; and I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.” (Hilar.) In this reading we must consider, in one and the same Redeemer, the distinct operation of divinity and humanity; and the error of Eutyches, who presumptuously dares to teach that there is only one operation in Christ, must be driven far from Christian boundaries.

Who cannot see that the Lord’s compassion for the crowd, lest they should fail either from hunger or from the labor of a long journey, is an affection and compassion belonging to human weakness? He wishes to feed those whom he has healed. First he removes their illnesses, and afterward he offers food to those who are well. He also calls the disciples and tells them what he is about to do, either to give teachers an example of sharing their deliberations with their juniors and disciples, or so that from the conversation they may understand the greatness of the sign, replying that they have no bread in the wilderness.

“I have compassion on the crowd,” he says, “because they have remained with me for three days.” He has compassion on the crowd because, in the number of three days, they believed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. “And they have nothing to eat.” The crowd is always hungry and needs food unless it is filled by the Lord. “And I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.” They were hungry after great illnesses and, through their perseverance, awaited the food that was to come. Jesus does not want to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way [Col. 0982D]. Whoever hastens to reach the desired dwelling is therefore in danger without heavenly bread. Hence the angel says to Elijah: “Arise and eat, because you have a great journey before you” (III Kings XIX).

(Greg.) Again, the crowd bears with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, turns to the Lord in deed, speech, and thought. The Lord does not wish to send them fasting to their house, lest they faint on the way. For converted sinners faint along the road of the present life if they are sent away within their own conscience without the nourishment of holy teaching. Therefore, lest they grow weary on the journey of this pilgrimage, they must be fed with sacred admonition.

It should also be noted that in the earlier sign, when those nearby and close at hand were concerned, the Lord himself did not remember the five senses; the disciples remembered them, in the evening, when night was near and the sun was already declining. Here, however, the Lord himself remembers and says that he has compassion, explaining the reason for his compassion: they have remained with him for three days, and he does not want to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way [Col. 0983A].

For in the entire age of the human race, the third period is the time in which the grace of Christian faith has been given. The first was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. And since a fourth period still remains—the time when we shall come to the fullest peace of the heavenly Jerusalem, toward which everyone who rightly believes in Christ is journeying—the Lord says that he is refreshing that crowd so that they do not faint on the way.

[Col. 0983B] And the disciples said to him: “Where, then, shall we get so many loaves in the wilderness to satisfy such a great crowd?” (MAUR.) This statement still reveals the disciples’ inexperienced faith. They do not remember that five thousand people had shortly before been satisfied with five barley loaves. If they had perfectly understood the author and giver, they would not have hesitated about where the crowd’s nourishment would come from.

And Jesus said to them: “How many loaves do you have?” He asks not as one who is ignorant, but as one teaching them to answer.

They said: “Eight, and a few little fish.” (RAB.) Appropriately, eight loaves are placed here as a figure of the New Testament, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is more fully revealed to all the faithful for belief and given to them once believed. They are not said to have been barley loaves, as were the five by which five thousand men were satisfied, lest once again, as under the Law, the life-giving nourishment of the soul be concealed under bodily sacraments. For the kernel of barley is covered by an extremely tenacious husk.

Nor are the little fish, which the Apostles professed to have along with the loaves, without a mystery. If the seven loaves signify the Scripture of the New Testament, in whose reading we find, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the inner banquets of the mind, whom should we understand by the little fish—which the Lord likewise blessed and ordered to be set before the crowd—if not the holy men of that time through whom the same Scripture was composed, or whose faith, life, and sufferings that Scripture contains? Rescued from the turbulent waves of this age and consecrated by divine blessing, they offered us inner nourishment, so that we would not faint in the course of this passing world, through the example of either their life or their death.

And he commanded the crowd to recline upon the ground. Above, in the feeding of the five loaves, the crowd reclined upon green grass; now, when it is to be refreshed with seven loaves, it is commanded to recline upon the ground. For through the Scripture of the Law we are commanded to trample down and restrain the desires of the flesh. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL).

In the New Testament, however, we are commanded to abandon the earth itself and temporal possessions—or at least this is so because the mountain on which the crowd was refreshed with the Lord’s loaves signifies, as we said above, the exaltation of our Redeemer [Col. 0984A]. There the crowd is refreshed upon grass; here, upon the ground. There Christ’s height is covered, on account of carnal people and the earthly Jerusalem, with carnal hope and desire; here, with every carnal longing removed, the guests of the New Testament are held by the firm foundation of enduring hope, like the solidity of the mountain itself, with no grass interposed.

And Jesus took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks, broke them, and gave them to his disciples; and the disciples gave them to the people. (Venant.) The Lord took the loaves and gave them to his disciples, so that they might set before the crowd what they had received, because, granting the spiritual gifts of knowledge to the Apostles, he wished the nourishment of life to be distributed throughout the world to his Church through their ministry.

That he broke the loaves which he gave to the disciples signifies the opening of the mysteries by which the world was to be nourished for everlasting salvation [Col. 0984B]. When the Lord himself says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI), what else did he show than that the bread of life had to be opened by him, since we could not penetrate by ourselves to see its inner parts?

In contrast, the Prophet, lamenting the pitiable hunger of certain people, said: “The children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV). In other words: The unlearned sought nourishment from the word of God, by which they might be refreshed and strengthened for virtuous action, but, when teachers were lacking, there was no one to disclose the mysteries of Scripture to them and instruct them in the way of truth.

After receiving the loaves to be broken, the Lord gives thanks, both showing how much he rejoices in the salvation of the human race and teaching us to give thanks to God when, through heavenly grace, we refresh either the flesh with earthly bread or the soul with heavenly bread.

And they all ate and were satisfied. They eat of the Lord’s loaves and fish and are satisfied when, hearing the words of God and observing the examples, they hasten to be stirred and rise toward the progress of a corrected life through these things. To them the Psalmist’s words aptly apply: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied; they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their hearts shall live forever and ever” (Ps. XXI).

This plainly means: The humble will hear the word of God and do it; and they will refer everything they have done well not to their own praise but to that of the heavenly giver. Thus, rightly satisfied with the bread of life, they will attain the inner life of the inward person [Col. 0984D]. In contrast, the prophet reproaches slow hearers: “You have eaten, but you have not been satisfied” (Mic. VI). They eat and are not satisfied who taste the bread of God’s word by hearing it but, because they do not do what they hear, receive none of its inner sweetness—by which their heart might be strengthened—into the stomach of memory.

And they took up what remained of the fragments, filling seven baskets. What remained after the crowds had been satisfied the Apostles gathered up and used to fill seven baskets, because there are higher precepts of perfection—or rather, exhortations and counsels—which the general multitude of the faithful cannot reach so as to keep and fulfill. Their execution properly belongs to those who, filled with a greater grace of the Holy Spirit, surpass the general way of life of God’s people in the loftiness of mind and deed. To such people it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess,” and so forth (Matt. XIX).

Thus it is fittingly recorded that there were seven baskets in which the fragments of the Lord’s food were stored. Since baskets are usually woven from rushes and palm leaves, they are rightly used as a figure of the saints. The rush customarily grows upon water, while the palm adorns the victorious hand. The elect are rightly compared to vessels woven from rushes when they place the root of their heart at the very source of life, lest it dry up, perhaps, through separation from the love of eternity. They are also likened to things woven from palm leaves when they preserve in a pure heart the unfailing memory of eternal recompense [Col. 0985B].

And it is fittingly said that although the crowd could not contain the leftovers of the Lord’s meal, it nevertheless ate and was satisfied. For there are some who, although unable to abandon all their possessions or fulfill what is said concerning virgins—“Let the one who can accept it accept it”—and other such counsels, are nevertheless satisfied when they hunger and thirst for righteousness, because by hearing the commandments of God’s Law they attain eternal life.

There were four thousand men who had eaten, besides women and children. (RAB.) Appropriately, there were four thousand, so that by this number itself they might also be taught that they had been fed with evangelical nourishment. (Aug.) This feeding with four loaves and a few little fish, as we said above, pertains to the mystery and grace of the Church [Col. 0985C] and of the New Testament, which is recognized through that well-known sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit.

For this reason, it is not written here that there were two fish, as in the Old Testament, where only two were anointed—king and priest—but a few fish: that is, those who first believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, were anointed in his name, and were sent to preach the Gospel and to withstand the turbulent sea of this age, so that they might serve as ambassadors for the great fish, that is, for Christ, as the Apostle Paul says.

Nor were there five thousand men in the crowd, as there were in the former event, where those who receive the Law carnally—those devoted to the five bodily senses—are signified. Here there are four thousand on account of the four virtues of the soul by which one lives spiritually in this life: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The first is knowledge of what should be pursued and avoided; the second is the restraint of desire from things that delight temporarily; the third is firmness of mind against things that are temporarily burdensome; the fourth is the love of God and neighbor, which is diffused through all the others.

Indeed, both there five thousand and here four thousand are said to have been present, excluding women and children. This seems to me to signify that even among the people of the Old Testament there were some who were weak in fulfilling the righteousness that is according to the Law—within which righteousness the Apostle Paul says that he conducted himself without reproach. There were also others who could easily be led astray into the worship of idols. These two kinds—that is, weaknesses and errors—are represented figuratively by the names of women and children [Col. 0986A]. The sex of women is weak, and childhood is easily given to play. What is more like childish play than worshiping idols? The Apostle referred this kind of superstition to such play when he said: “Let us not become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (I Cor. X).

Those who did not persevere manfully through the labors of expectation until they reached God’s promises and who tested God were therefore like women; those who sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play were like children.

Nor does this apply only there. In the people of the New Testament as well, those who do not persist in attaining mature manhood are to be compared with women and children, whether because of weakness of strength or because of lightness of mind. To the former it is said: “If only we hold the beginning of his substance firm to the end” (Hebr. III). To the latter: “Do not become children in your understanding; be infants in malice, but mature in understanding” (I Cor. XIV).

Therefore, neither in the Old nor in the New Testament are such people admitted to the number. Whether five thousand there or four thousand here, they are said to have been present with the women and children excluded [Col. 0986B].

And dismissing the crowd, he went up into the boat and came to the region of Magadan. In Mark, however, it is written: “And immediately he went up into the boat with his disciples and came into the district of Dalmanutha” (Mark 8). There is no doubt that the same place is meant under both names. (Jerome.) [Col. 0986C] For many manuscripts, even in Mark, have only “Magadan.” Magadana is a region near Gerasa, and *Magada* is interpreted as “its fruits” or “heraldess.” (Maurice.) Mystically, it signifies that garden of which the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride” (Song 4), where the fruits of virtue are produced and where the Lord’s name is everywhere duly proclaimed. For “all day and not all night its watchmen upon the walls will not be silent in praising the name of the Lord” (Isa. 62). Therefore, after refreshing the crowds, the Lord went up into the boat and came to the region of Magadan, teaching us that, after we have ministered the nourishment of the word outwardly to the crowds, we must not neglect to return within for the guarding of the heart, so that we may be refreshed by the sweet food of virtues and, with the door of our chamber closed, adore the heavenly Father.

## CHAPTER XVI. [Col. 0986D]

On avoiding the leaven of the Pharisees; on Peter’s confession, and on his rebuke lest he become a stumbling block, etc.

### [I.]

And the Pharisees and Sadducees approached him, testing him, and asked him to show them a sign from heaven. (Rabanus.) They seek a sign from heaven so that he who had satisfied many thousands of people with a few loaves might now, after the example of Moses, send manna from heaven, scatter it everywhere, and refresh the whole people for a long time. We read that in the Gospel of John, after the feeding of the crowds with bread, they asked him for this, saying: “What sign, then, do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? [Col. 0987A] Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness; as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat’” (John 6).

But he answered them: “When evening comes, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’; and in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and gloomy.’ You know how to judge the appearance of the sky, but you cannot judge the signs of the times.” (Jerome.) Historically, the meaning is clear: from the order and harmony of the elements, fair and rainy days can be predicted. But the scribes and Pharisees, who appeared to be teachers of the Law, could not understand from the prophets’ predictions the coming of the Savior. (Augustine.) Spiritually, when the Lord said, “When evening comes, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red,’” he signifies that through the blood of Christ’s Passion, forgiveness of sins is granted at his first coming. And “in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red with gloom,’” signifies that at his second coming he will come with fire preceding him. “You know how to judge the appearance of the sky, but you cannot judge the signs of the times.” By “the signs of the times” he meant his coming or his Passion, to which the rosy evening sky is comparable, and likewise the tribulation that will precede his coming, to which the rosy morning sky with its gloom is comparable. [Col. 0987B]

An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah. (Rabanus.) Therefore no sign is given to that generation—that is, to those who test the Lord and resist his words—of the kind of sign they were seeking, namely, one from heaven, although he was giving them many heavenly things on earth. [Col. 0987C] To the generation, however, of those who seek the Lord and seek the face of the God of Jacob, he displayed a sign from heaven: when, in the sight of the apostles, he ascended into heaven; when, after the Spirit had been sent from above, he filled the primitive Church; and when, at the laying on of the apostles’ hands in Samaria, Caesarea, Ephesus, and many other cities and places, he supplied believers with the grace of the Holy Spirit from heaven. (Jerome.) What the sign of Jonah means has already been said above.

And he left them and went away. Having left the scribes and Pharisees, to whom he had said, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah,” he rightly went across the lake, and the people of the nations followed him.

And when the disciples had come across the lake, they had forgotten to [Col. 0987D] take bread. Someone might ask and say: How did they have no bread, when immediately after the seven baskets had been filled they went up into the boat and came to the region of Magadan, where, while sailing, they heard that they should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees? But Scripture testifies that they had forgotten to take it with them. (Rabanus.) The fact that, when they were about to sail across the lake, they forgot to take provisions with them indicates how little care they had for the flesh in other matters. The very necessity of refreshing the body, which is naturally present in all mortals, had been driven from their minds by their devotion to the Lord’s company. The one loaf which they had with them in the boat mystically signifies the bread of life itself, namely, the Lord and Savior. Because they were always inwardly refreshed by love for him, they cared less about earthly bread, by which the body is ordinarily nourished. [Col. 0988A]

He said to them: “Pay attention and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” In Mark it is written: “See to it; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod” (Mark 8). The leaven of the Pharisees is to put human traditions before the decrees of the divine Law; or certainly, to preach the Law in words while attacking it by one’s deeds. Their leaven is to test the Lord and to believe neither his teaching nor his works, but, by insulting him, to demand other things by which they ought to believe. The leaven of Herod is adultery, murder, recklessness in taking oaths, pretended religion, and—what is the head and source of all crimes—hatred and persecution of Christ and of his precursor, the first herald of the heavenly kingdom. The Apostle also forbids us both kinds of leaven when he says: “Let us therefore celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5). [Col. 0988B]

But they were reasoning among themselves, saying: “It is because we did not take bread.” Knowing this, Jesus said: “Why are you reasoning among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five loaves and the five thousand people, and how many baskets you took? Nor the seven loaves and the four thousand people, and how many baskets you took? Why do you not understand that I did not speak to you about bread when I said, ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees’?”

[Col. 0988C] Taking the occasion of the command which the Savior had given—“Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod”—he teaches them what the five loaves and the seven, or the little fish, and the five thousand and the four thousand people who were fed in the wilderness signify. Although the greatness of the signs is obvious, spiritual understanding nevertheless reveals something else. For if the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees and the leaven of Herod signify not bodily bread but perverse traditions and heretical doctrines, why should the foods by which God’s people were nourished not signify true and sound teaching? Marcion, Valentinus, and all the heretics possessed this kind of leaven, which must be avoided in every way. Leaven has this power: if it is mixed with flour, what appeared small grows larger and draws the whole mass toward its own flavor. So too, if heretical teaching casts even a small spark into your breast, in a short time a great flame will grow and draw the whole possession of the human being toward itself. This is what the Apostle also speaks of: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Gal. 5). [Col. 0988D]

Then they understood that he had not said that they should beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. (Maurice.) He persuaded them to accept what was useful and commanded them to avoid what was harmful. Superstitious and heretical teaching weighs down rather than helps; it sinks and does not raise up. Thus, instructed by the good teacher, the disciples understood that the leaven expressed the seduction of the [Col. 0989A] Pharisees and Sadducees—indeed, of all heretics who think contrary to the truth—and that it must be avoided. They themselves avoided it altogether and judged that it must be fled by us as well. After this Matthew continues and says:

### [II.]

Now Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi. This Philip is the brother of Herod, whom we have already mentioned above, tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis. In honor of Tiberius Caesar, he called Caesarea Philippi by that name; it is now called Paneas. It lies in the province of Phoenicia. He imitated his father Herod, who in honor of Augustus Caesar called Caesarea by that name, although it had previously been called Strato’s Tower; and from the name of his daughter he built Lubiade beyond the Jordan. This is the site of Caesarea Philippi, where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon. It has two springs, one called Jor and the other Dan; when joined together, they form the name Jordan. [Col. 0989B]

And he was asking his disciples, saying: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” He did not say, “Who do people say that I am?” but “the Son of Man,” so that he would not appear to be asking about himself boastfully. Note that wherever “son of man” is written in the Old Testament, the Hebrew has *son of Adam*. Thus what we read in the Psalm, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4), is expressed in Hebrew as “sons of Adam.” It was fitting, then, that he asked, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” For those who speak about the Son of Man are human beings. But those who understand his divinity are called not human beings but gods.

[Col. 0989C] And they said: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” I am astonished that certain interpreters seek out the error of each individual and weave an extremely long discussion about why some thought our Lord Jesus Christ was John, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets, since they could have erred about Elijah or Jeremiah just as Herod erred about John when he said: “This is John, whom I beheaded; he has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers are at work in him” (Matt. 14; Mark 6; Luke 9).

“But you—who do you say that I am?” (Maurice.) He does not ask as though he were ignorant of the opinion held about him by the disciples or by outsiders. Rather, he asks the disciples what they think about him so that he may reward their confession of the true [Col. 0989D] faith with a worthy recompense. He asks what others think about him so that, after the opinions of those who were in error have first been set forth, the disciples may be shown to have received the truth of their confession not from common opinion but from the mystery of the Lord’s own revelation. (Bede.) “But you,” he says, “who do you say that I am?” As though separating them from the generality of human beings and indicating that they had already become gods and sons of God by adoption, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81).

Simon Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Although the other apostles knew this, Peter answered on behalf of them all. He embraced everything, expressing both nature and name. [Col. 0990A] He calls him the living God in distinction from the false gods whom the pagan world, deceived by various errors, either fashioned for itself from dead human beings or, in still greater madness, created from lifeless matter to worship. Of these the Psalm sings: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands; they have mouths, but they do not speak,” and so forth (Ps. 113).

It should be noted how wondrously it was arranged that, when a statement about both natures of the same Lord and Savior was to be made by the Lord himself and by his faithful disciple, the Lord himself should profess the humility of the humanity he had assumed, while the disciple should display the excellence of his divine eternity. The Lord [Col. 0990B] speaks of himself what is lesser; the disciple declares of the Lord what is greater. The Lord speaks of himself as one who was made for us; the disciple declares of the Lord that he is the one who made us. Likewise, in the Gospel the Lord was accustomed to call himself the Son of Man much more frequently than the Son of God, so that he might remind us of the dispensation he undertook for our sake. But the more humbly we remember that he descended to the lowest depths of humanity for our exaltation, the more necessary it is for us to venerate the heights of his divinity.

Jesus answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” *Barjona* in Syriac is said in Latin to mean “son of a dove.” The apostle Peter is rightly called the son of a dove, since the dove is a very simple animal and he followed the [Col. 0990C] Lord with wise and devout simplicity, mindful of the command he and his fellow disciples had received from the same teacher of simplicity and truth: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.” Or, certainly, because the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, he is rightly called the son of a dove, since he is shown to have been filled with spiritual grace.

The Lord rewards with sufficiently fitting praise the one who loved and confessed him, when he testifies that he is the son of the Holy Spirit—the one by whom he himself is affirmed to be the Son of the living God—although no believer doubts that this is done in a very different manner. Christ the Lord is the Son of God by nature; Peter, like the other elect, is a son of the Holy Spirit by grace. Christ is the Son of God because he was born from him; Peter is a son of the Holy Spirit because he was reborn [Col. 0990D] from him. Christ is the Son of God before the ages, for he is the power and wisdom of God, which says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning” (Prov. 8). Peter became a son of the Holy Spirit from the time when, having been enlightened by him, he received the grace of divine knowledge.

And because the Holy Trinity has one will and one operation, after saying, “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona”—that is, “son of spiritual grace”—he immediately added: “Because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” The Father revealed this to the son of the dove because the grace of the Father and of the Holy Spirit is one, and likewise that of the Son, since the will and operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one. [Col. 0991A] Therefore it is appropriately said that the Father who is in heaven revealed to the son of the dove the mystery of faith, which flesh and blood could not reveal.

“Flesh and blood” are rightly understood as human beings puffed up with the wisdom of the flesh, ignorant of the simplicity of the dove and therefore rightly turned away from the wisdom of the Spirit. Above it was said of them that, because they did not understand Christ, some said that he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets. Of them the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 2).

And I say to you: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” (Jerome.) It is as though he were saying: Because you said to me, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” I say to you—not with an empty word devoid of action, [Col. 0991B] but because for me to speak is to accomplish—that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. Just as he gave light to the apostles so that they might be called the light of the world, and they received their other names from the Lord, so also he bestowed the name Peter upon Simon, who believed in Christ the rock. (Bede.) And, in accordance with the metaphor of the rock, he rightly says to him: “I will build my Church upon you,” because he clung with a firm and steadfast mind to the one of whom it is written: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

And upon this rock—that is, upon the Lord and Savior, who gave his faithful knower, lover, and confessor a share in his own name, so that he might be called Peter from the rock—the Church is built. For only through faith and love of Christ, through receiving [Col. 0991C] Christ’s sacraments, and through observing Christ’s commandments does one attain the lot of the elect and eternal life, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3).

And the gates of hell will not prevail against it. I think that the gates of hell are vices and sins, or certainly the doctrines of heretics, through which deceived human beings are led to Tartarus. Therefore no one should think that this is said of death, as though the apostles were not subject to the condition of death. The gates of hell are also the tortures and flatteries of persecutors, which, by terrifying and softening the weak, open for them an entrance into eternal death by drawing them away from the steadfastness of faith. Moreover, the evil works and foolish conversations of unbelievers are certainly gates of hell, in [Col. 0991D] insofar as they show the path of destruction to their authors or followers. For faith without works is dead in itself, and evil conversations corrupt good morals.

There are therefore many gates of hell, but none of them prevails against the Church founded upon the rock, because whoever has received the faith of Christ with the innermost love of his heart easily despises whatever danger the tempter may bring upon him from outside. But whoever among believers betrays the faith by corrupting it either in deed or by denial must be considered not to have built, with the Lord’s cooperation, the house of his profession upon the rock, but, according to the parable in another passage, to have placed it upon sand without a foundation (Matt. 7). That is, he did not follow Christ with simple and true intention, but assumed the appearance of a Christian for some earthly [Col. 0992A] and fragile reason. It follows:

And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. The one who confessed the King of heaven with greater devotion than the others was deservedly granted the keys of the heavenly kingdom above the others, so that it might be clear to all that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven without that confession and faith. By “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” he names the knowledge and power of discernment itself, by which he was to receive the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy from it.

And whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. Although this power of loosing and binding appears to have been given by the Lord to Peter alone, it must [Col. 0992B] nevertheless be understood without any doubt that it is also given to the other apostles. The Lord himself testifies to this when, after the triumph of his Passion and Resurrection, he appeared to them, breathed upon them, and said to all: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20).

Even now the same office is entrusted to all the bishops and priests of the Church: when they have learned the causes of sinners, they are to release, out of compassion from the fear of eternal death, all whom they see to be humble and truly penitent; but those whom they know to persist in the sins they have committed, they are to indicate as bound over to everlasting punishments. Thus, as we have said, authority to bind and loose is given to the whole Church of the elect, according to the measure of guilt or repentance.

But blessed [Col. 0992C] Peter, who confessed Christ in good faith and followed him with true love, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of judicial power in a special way, so that all believers throughout the world might understand that whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of the faith or from fellowship with Peter cannot be released from the bonds of sins or enter through the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

(Jerome.) Yet certain bishops and priests, not understanding this passage, assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or suppose that they can absolve the guilty, although before God it is not the judgment of priests but the life of the accused that is examined. We read in Leviticus about lepers, who are commanded to show themselves to the priests so that, if they have leprosy, they may then be declared unclean by the priest—not because the [Col. 0992D] priests make them lepers and unclean, but so that they may have knowledge of who is leprous and who is not, and may discern who is clean and who is unclean. Therefore, just as there the priest makes the leper unclean, so here the bishop or priest binds or looses—not those who are innocent or harmless, but, in accordance with his office, after hearing the various cases of sinners, knows who is to be bound and who is to be loosed.

Then he ordered his disciples not to tell anyone that he was Jesus the Christ. (Maurice.) Above, when sending his disciples out to preach, he had commanded them to announce his coming; here he ordered them not to say that he was Jesus. It seems to me that preaching Christ is one thing, and preaching Jesus Christ another. *Christ* is a common title of dignity [Col. 0993A]; *Jesus* is the Savior’s proper name. It may be that he did not wish to be preached before his Passion and Resurrection for this reason: after the sacrament of his blood had been completed, he could more appropriately say to the apostles, “Go and teach all nations,” and what follows. So that no one may think this is merely our interpretation and not the sense of the Gospel, what follows explains the reasons for the prohibition of preaching at that time.

### [III.]

From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, be killed, and rise again on the third day. The meaning is: Preach me when I have suffered these things, because it is of no benefit to preach Christ publicly and proclaim his majesty among the peoples when shortly afterward they will see him scourged and crucified. “To suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests.” Even now Jesus suffers many things from those who crucify the Son of God again for themselves. And when elders and chief priests are thought to exist in the Church, those who follow the simple letter kill the Son of God, because everything is understood in the Spirit. [Col. 0993B]

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you.” But he turned and said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not think the things of God, but the things of human beings.”

We have often said that Peter possessed an exceedingly ardent love and affection for the Lord and Savior. After his confession—“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”—and after hearing the Savior’s [Col. 0993C] reward—“Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven”—he suddenly hears from the Lord that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things there from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise again on the third day.

He does not want his confession destroyed, nor does he think it possible that the Son of God should be killed. Therefore he takes him into his own affection, or leads him aside privately so that he would not appear to rebuke his teacher in the presence of his fellow disciples, and begins to rebuke him with the affection of one who loves, saying with the desire that it might not happen: “Far be it from you, Lord.” Or, as it is better expressed in Greek: “Be gracious to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen”—that is, “It cannot happen, nor can my ears receive that the Son of God is to be killed.”

[Col. 0993D] The Lord turned to him and said: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me.” *Satan* means “adversary” or “opponent,” because, he says, you speak contrary to my will and ought to be called an adversary. Many think that it was not Peter who was rebuked, but the opposing spirit who was suggesting these words to the apostle. But to me an apostolic error arising from an affectionate devotion will never appear to be an incitement of the devil.

“Get behind me, Satan”—this is said to the devil: “Get behind me.” Peter hears: “Get behind me,” that is, “Follow my judgment, because you do not think the things of God, but the things of human beings.” It is my will, and that of the Father whose will I came to do, that I should die for the salvation of human beings. You, desiring only your own will, do not want the grain of wheat to fall into the earth so that it may bear much fruit.

[Col. 0994A] The prudent reader may ask how, after such great blessedness—“Blessed are you, Simon Barjona”; “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it”; “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound, and whatever you loose will be loosed in heaven”—there can now be: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me.” What was this sudden change, so that after such rewards he is called Satan and told to go behind?

But whoever asks this should consider that the blessing, blessedness, power, and building of the Church upon him were promised for the future, not given in the present. “I will build my Church upon you,” he says, “and the gates of hell will not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Everything is in the future. If he had given these things to him immediately, there would never have been room in him for the error of a misguided confession. [Col. 0994B]

Then Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” (Rabanus.) After showing his disciples the mystery of his Passion and Resurrection, he urges them to follow the example of his Passion. To all who suffer tribulation for his sake he promises the salvation of their souls in the future; yet he did not reveal this to everyone, but to those who were more perfect, telling them how much he himself would suffer and that he would rise from the dead. “If anyone,” he says, “wishes to follow me, let him deny himself.”

(Gregory.) We deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through our former life and strive toward that to which we are called through newness of life. Let us consider how Paul had denied himself when he said: [Col. 0994C] “It is no longer I who live” (Gal. 2). That savage persecutor had been extinguished, and a devout preacher had begun to live. If it were still he himself, he would certainly not be devout; but since he denies that he lives, let him say from where it is that he cries out holy words through the teaching of truth. He immediately adds: “But Christ lives in me.” It is as though he were saying openly: “I have indeed been extinguished by myself, because I do not live carnally; yet I am not dead in essence, because I live spiritually in Christ.”

Let Truth therefore speak; let it say: “If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself.” For unless someone departs from himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him; nor can he grasp what is beyond him if he does not know how to put to death what he is. But once someone has denied himself with regard to vices, he must seek the virtues in which he may grow. [Col. 0994D] For when it is said, “If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself,” it is immediately added:

And let him take up his cross and follow me. The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor. Let us consider how Paul carried his cross in both ways when he said: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be rejected” (1 Cor. 9). There we have heard of the cross of the flesh in the affliction of the body; now, in compassion for one’s neighbor, let us hear of the cross of the mind. He says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11). The perfect preacher carried the cross in his body in order to give an example of abstinence; and because he drew into himself the losses caused by another’s weakness, he carried the cross in his heart. [Col. 0995A]

For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it. (Hilary.) Great and wondrous is the saying: how a person’s love for his own soul causes it to perish, and hatred of it prevents its perishing. If you love it wrongly, then you have hated it; if you hate it rightly, then you have loved it.

(Gregory.) Blessed are those who hate their soul by guarding it, lest they lose it by loving it. Thus it is said to the faithful: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it.” It is as though one said to a farmer: “If you keep the grain, you lose it; if you sow it, you renew it.” Who does not know that, when [Col. 0995B] grain is cast into the seedbed, it perishes from sight and decays in the earth? Yet from that by which it rots in the dust it becomes green through renewal.

Since the holy Church has one season of persecution and another of peace, our Redeemer designated these seasons in his commandments. In the time of persecution, the soul must be surrendered; in the time of peace, earthly desires that are able to exercise greater dominion must be broken. Hence it is now said:

For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? When persecution from adversaries is absent, the heart must be guarded with much greater vigilance. For in a time of peace, because one is permitted to live, one is also eager to strive for worldly advancement. Often we overcome greed, but what still obstructs us is that we hold to the ways of righteousness with too little [Col. 0995C] vigilance toward perfection. Often we despise all passing things, yet we are still hindered by the habits of human embarrassment, so that we cannot yet express in our speech the righteousness we preserve in our mind. We neglect the face of God in defending justice to the same degree that we fear human faces in opposing justice.

But we must take great care lest, through greed for money, or through fear of death and love of bodily life, we neglect to seek the salvation of souls. For it will profit nothing to gain temporal things if eternal things are lost. Hence it is also added:

Or what exchange will a person give for his soul? (Jerome.) In exchange for Israel, Egypt and Ethiopia are given; but for the human soul there is only that recompense [Col. 0995D] which the Psalmist sings: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115).

For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels. The one who in human nature is less than the Father is nevertheless one with the Father in the unity of the same glory.

And then he will repay each one according to his works. Peter had been rebuked by the Lord’s sentence because he was scandalized by the prediction of the Lord’s death. The disciples were urged to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow their teacher with the disposition of those who are dying. This was a great terror for those who heard it and could instill fear even in the chief of the apostles and in the other apostles. [Col. 0996A] Therefore sorrowful things are followed by joyful ones, and he says: “The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels.” Are you afraid of death? Hear of the glory of the triumphant one. Do you dread the cross? Listen to the ministry of the angels. “And then,” he says, “he will repay each one according to his works.” There is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, man and woman, poor and rich, where it is not persons but works that are considered.

Amen I say to you: There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. (Rabanus.) The kingdom of God, in which the Son of God—the same one who is also the Son of Man—reigns, is here called the present Church. And because some of the disciples were destined to live in the body long enough to see the Church of God established and raised up against the glory of this [Col. 0996B] world through the power of its founder, it is now said by way of consolation: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom,” that is, displaying his power.

But since the Lord was giving so many commands concerning the death he had to undergo, why was it necessary for him suddenly to come to this promise? If we attend to it carefully, we recognize how great the dispensation of his compassion was. Something concerning the present life had to be promised even to the inexperienced disciples, so that they could be strengthened more firmly for the future life. Thus, when the Israelite people were being liberated from the land of Egypt, the land of promise was promised to them; and while they were being called to heavenly gifts, they were persuaded by earthly promises. Hence the Psalmist also rightly says: [Col. 0996C] “He gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed the labor of the peoples, so that they might keep his statutes and seek his law” (Ps. 104).

Thus here, too, Truth, speaking to inexperienced disciples, promises that they will see the kingdom of God on earth, so that through faith they may anticipate it in heaven. If, however, we wish to understand the kingdom of God in this statement as the future blessedness in heaven, then some of those standing there did indeed see it a few days later on the mountain. This was done in a devout act of providence, so that through the contemplation of joy that always remains—although tasted only briefly and for a moment—they might endure more strongly the adversities of the passing age that pressed upon them.

With very fitting language, then, he testifies that the saints taste death; for they taste bodily death, as it were, by taking a sip, while they truly possess the life of the soul.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 0996D]
