The Lord is transfigured on the mountain before the disciples, with Elijah and Moses. He heals a lunatic. He commands Peter to pay the tax for himself and for him.

[I.] And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother and led them up a high mountain by themselves. In Luke’s Gospel it is written as follows: “Now about eight days after these sayings, he took Peter and James and John and went up onto the mountain to pray,” etc. (Luke 9). Hence the question arises how he took them after six days and led them up a high mountain by themselves, as Matthew and Mark testify, whereas the evangelist Luke gives the number eight. The answer is easy: here the intervening days are counted, while there the first day, on which the Lord made these promises, and the last, on which he fulfilled his promises, are added. Therefore Luke does not say “after eight days,” but more cautiously, “about eight days.” In the mystical interpretation, there the saints are to rest from every labor after the six ages of the world; here, by the eighth day, resurrection is indicated. Hence the sixth Psalm is appropriately written “for the eighth,” beginning: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.” For throughout the six ages, in which it is permitted to work, we must persevere in prayer, lest in the eighth time, the time of retribution, we be rebuked by the angry Judge. The Lord himself wished to teach us this in this passage by the example of his prayer. Concerning this Luke says: “He went up onto the mountain to pray.” He therefore ascended the mountain to pray and then to be transfigured, in order to show that those who await the fruit of the resurrection and desire to see the King in his beauty ought to dwell in lofty thoughts and devote themselves to continual prayers.

He takes only three disciples with him, either because “many are called, but few are chosen,” or because those who have now preserved with an incorrupt mind the faith of the Holy Trinity with which they have been instructed will then deserve to rejoice in its eternal vision. And appropriately, when he said that he led them onto a high mountain, he added “by themselves”: for the righteous, although now oppressed by the vices of the wicked, are nevertheless entirely separated from them in mind and in the intention of faith, and in the future they will be led away from them completely, when he hides them “in the secret place of his face, from the disturbance of men.”

“And he was transfigured before them.” (Jerome.) When he says, “He was transfigured before them,” no one should suppose that he lost his former form and face, or that he lost the reality of his body and assumed either a spiritual or an aerial body. The Savior, when transfigured, did not lose the substance of true flesh, but displayed the glory of the future resurrection, whether his own or ours. As he then appeared to the apostles, so he will appear after the judgment to all the elect. For at the very time when judgment is being rendered, he will be seen by both the good and the wicked in the form of a servant, so that the impious may recognize the one they despised, the Jews the one they denied, the soldiers the one they crucified, and Pilate and Herod the one they judged—as their Judge.

“And his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow.” (Rabanus.) Here also, as an example of his future glorification, his face shone like the sun—not because the brightness and glory of the Lord and of his saints can be equal, since the Apostle says of these same saints: “Star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15), and so also with the resurrection of the dead; but because we know nothing brighter than the sun, the glory of the Lord and of the saints in the resurrection is compared to the sight of the sun, since nothing brighter than the sun could be found to provide an example for human beings.

The Lord’s garments are rightly understood as his saints, according to the Apostle’s testimony: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). These garments, while the Lord remained on earth, appeared despised and like those of other people; but when he ascends the mountain, they shine with a new whiteness. For now we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). Hence Mark rightly says of these same garments: “They became shining, exceedingly white like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make white” (Mark 9).

For since the fuller in this passage is to be understood as the one to whom the penitent Psalmist prays, “Wash me more thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. 50), he cannot give his faithful on earth the brightness that remains preserved for them in heaven. Or otherwise: No one can live on earth without contact with some sin. But what no fuller—that is, no teacher of souls or outstanding purifier of his own body—can do on earth, the Lord will do in heaven, cleansing the Church, his garment, from every pollution of flesh and spirit, and moreover restoring it with the eternal blessedness and light of flesh and spirit.

It follows:

“And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” Luke writes more explicitly what they looked like and what they said with him: “Now Moses and Elijah appeared in glory, and they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9). Moses and Elijah, therefore, who spoke with the Lord on the mountain and spoke of his passion and resurrection, signify the oracles of the Law and of prophecy. These have been fulfilled in the Lord, are now apparent to the learned, and will be revealed more clearly in the future to all the elect.

They are appropriately said to have been seen in glory, because then it will be more plainly seen with how great a dignity of truth not only the meaning but also the wording of all the divine utterances was spoken. Yet Moses and Elijah may rightly be understood as all who will reign with the Lord. In Moses, who died and was buried, are represented those who will be raised from death at the judgment; in Elijah, who has not yet paid the debt of death, those who will be found alive in the flesh at the Judge’s coming. Both groups will be caught up together in the clouds, meet the Lord in the air, and, once the judgment has been completed, be brought into eternal life. Accordingly, it is fitting that Moses and Elijah are said to have been seen in glory. Through the excellence of their majesty, the distinction of the glorious reward with which they will be crowned is displayed.

It is also fitting that they are said to have spoken of his departure, which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem, because the passion of the Redeemer is the one subject of praise for the faithful. The more they remember it, the more devotedly they always carry the memory of his grace in their hearts, and testify to it with devoted confession.

But because the more anyone tastes the sweetness of heavenly life, the more he despises everything that pleased him in the depths below, Peter deservedly, having seen the majesty of the Lord and his saints, suddenly forgets all earthly things and desires to cling forever to only those things that he sees, saying:

“Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Blessed Peter, as another evangelist testifies, did not know what he was saying in thinking that tents should be made for the heavenly way of life. In the glory of that heavenly life no house will be necessary, where the light of divine contemplation will bring peace to everything and no fear of any adversity will remain, as the apostle John testifies when describing the glory of that heavenly city: “And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

Yet he knew well what he was saying when he said, “Lord, it is good to be here,” because the only true good of a human being is to enter into the joy of his Lord and stand forever in contemplation of him. Hence one must rightly be thought never to have possessed any true good if, because his guilt demanded it, he happened never to see the face of his Creator.

If blessed Peter, contemplating Christ’s glorified humanity, is so filled with joy that he does not wish at all to be separated from its sight, what joy of blessedness must be thought to dwell in those who will have deserved to see the height of his divinity? And if, with only two saints—namely, Moses and Elijah—he considered it the greatest good to see on the mountain the transfigured form of Christ’s humanity, what speech could explain, what understanding could comprehend, how great the joy of the righteous will be when they come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, Jerusalem (Heb. 12), and to the company of many thousands of angels, and behold the very architect and creator of that city, God—not through a mirror and in an enigma, as now, but face to face? (1 Cor. 13.) Concerning this vision Peter himself says, speaking of the Lord to the faithful: “Though you do not now see him, you believe in him; and when you see him, you will rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy” (1 Pet. 1).

“While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them.” He who sought a material tent receives the shelter of a cloud, so that he may learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected not by the covering of houses but by the glory of the Holy Spirit. Of this the Psalmist says: “The children of men will hope in the protection of your wings” (Ps. 35). And John says in his Apocalypse: “And I saw no temple in it. The Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

“And behold, a voice from the cloud saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.’” (Jerome.) Because they had asked thoughtlessly, they do not deserve the Lord’s reply; instead, the Father answers for the Son, so that the Lord’s word might be fulfilled: “I do not testify concerning myself, but the Father who sent me himself testifies concerning me” (John 5). The voice of the Father speaking from heaven is also heard, bearing testimony for the Son and, once Peter’s error has been removed, teaching him the truth—or rather, teaching the other apostles through Peter: “This,” he says, “is my most beloved Son. A tent must be set up for him; he must be obeyed. He is the Son; Moses and Elijah are servants. They too ought, together with you, to prepare a tent for the Lord in the inner chambers of their hearts.”

(Rabanus.) This Gospel passage plainly agrees with the words of Moses himself, by which he bore witness to the Lord’s incarnation, saying: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me; you shall listen to him according to everything he says to you. But every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people” (Deut. 18). The one whom Moses foretold would come in the flesh and must be heard by every soul that wished to be saved, God the Father now shows to the disciples as the one who has come in the flesh and declares by a heavenly voice that he is his Son. And as though making the faith of his coming clearer to them, he says: “This man, this is the one whom that Moses repeatedly promised would be born into the world. According to the command of that same Moses, listen to his words, and command all true lovers of truth to listen.”

It should also be noted that, just as at the Lord’s baptism in the Jordan, so on the mountain at his glorification, the mystery of the whole Holy Trinity is declared. For the glory that we confess in faith at baptism, we shall praise when we see it in the resurrection. Nor is it without reason that the Holy Spirit appeared here in a bright cloud and there in a dove: whoever now preserves with a simple heart the faith he has received will then contemplate in the open light of vision what he had believed, and will be protected forever by the very grace by which he will be illumined.

“And when the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces.” (Jerome.) They are terrified with fear for three reasons: either because they recognized that they had erred, or because the bright cloud had covered them, or because they had heard the voice of God the Father speaking. Human frailty cannot endure the sight of a greater glory; trembling in soul and body, it falls wholly to the ground. For the more someone seeks great things, the more he collapses into lower things if he does not know his own measure.

“And Jesus came and touched them.” (Maurus.) Because they were lying there and could not rise, he mercifully approaches and touches them, so that by his touch he may drive away their fear and strengthen their weakened limbs.

“And he said to them: ‘Rise, and do not be afraid.’” Those whom Jesus had healed with his hand, he also heals by his command. First fear is expelled, so that instruction may afterward be given; for a mind that is frightened and occupied with various thoughts cannot attend to listening. Once fear has been removed, it admits more willingly what is said.

“But when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.” (Jerome.) If Moses and Elijah had remained with the Lord, the Father’s voice would have seemed uncertain as to whom it was chiefly bearing witness. They therefore see Jesus standing, the cloud having been removed, and Moses and Elijah having vanished. For after the shadow of the Law and the prophets, which had covered the apostles with its veil, had departed, both are found in the Gospel.

[II.] “And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: ‘Tell no one the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.’” The foretaste of the future kingdom and the glory of the triumphant one had been displayed on the mountain. He therefore does not wish this to be proclaimed among the people, lest it seem incredible because of the magnitude of the matter and, after such great glory, the ensuing cross cause scandal among inexperienced minds.

“And his disciples asked him, saying: ‘Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?’” Unless we know the reasons why the disciples asked about Elijah, their question seems foolish and out of place. For what connection does asking about Elijah and his coming have with what was said above? It is the tradition of the Pharisees, based on the prophet Malachi, who is the last of the Twelve, that Elijah will come before the Savior’s coming, “turning the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers,” and restoring everything to its former state (Mal. 4).

The disciples therefore suppose that the transfiguration of glory they had seen on the mountain was the promised event, and they say: “If you have already come in glory, how is it that your forerunner has not appeared?” Especially since they had seen Elijah depart. When they add, “The scribes say that Elijah must come first,” by saying “first” they show that, unless Elijah has come, the Savior’s coming has not occurred according to the Scriptures.

“But he answered them: ‘Elijah indeed will come, and he will restore all things.’” (Rabanus.) He will certainly restore those things that the aforementioned prophet described, saying: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he will turn the heart of fathers to their children and the heart of children to their fathers” (Mal. 4). He will also restore what is owed to death and what he postponed by living for a long time.

The Lord also made this clear immediately afterward, as Mark attests, when he added: “And how it is written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be condemned”—that is, just as the prophets wrote many things in many ways concerning Christ’s passion, so Elijah, when he comes, will suffer many things and be despised by the wicked.

He will therefore restore all things: first, by instructing the hearts of the people of that age to believe in Christ and resist the faithlessness of Antichrist; then by laying down his own life through the martyrdom of faith in Christ. This is related more fully in the Apocalypse in mystical language.

“But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished.” (Jerome.) He means the one who will come at the Savior’s second coming; according to the correspondence of the body, he has now come in John in the power and spirit of Elijah, and they did to him whatever they wished—that is, they despised and beheaded him.

“So also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.” The question arises: Since Herod and Herodias killed John, how can they also be said to have crucified Jesus, when we read that he was killed by the scribes and Pharisees? The brief answer is that Herod had agreed with the Pharisees’ action in John’s death, and in the Lord’s killing he joined his will to theirs by sending him, after mocking and despising him, to Pilate so that they might crucify him.

“Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them of John the Baptist.” (Maurus.) From the indication of the passion—both his own, which the Lord himself had often foretold to them, and that of his forerunner, which they now saw completed—the disciples understood that John had been designated to them under the name of Elijah. And rightly so, because just as Elijah is the forerunner of the final coming, so John is the forerunner of the first coming of the Lord. The one proclaimed that the Redeemer had arrived; the other will testify that the Judge is at hand.

[III.] “And when he had come to the crowds, a man approached him, kneeling before him and saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is a lunatic and suffers terribly.’” (Jerome.) It should be noted that places always correspond to events. On the mountain the Lord prays, is transfigured, and reveals to the disciples the secrets of his majesty; descending to the lower regions, he is met by a crowd and besieged by the tears of the miserable. Above, he opens the mystery of the kingdom to the disciples; below, he reproves the crowds for the sins of their unbelief. Above, he makes known the Father’s voice to those able to follow him; below, he drives evil spirits from those who are tormented. Even now, according to the quality of their merits, he does not cease to ascend for some and descend for others. For those who are still carnal and foolish he strengthens, teaches, and chastises, as though seeking the lowest places; but those whose conduct is in heaven he glorifies by raising them higher, instructs them more freely concerning eternal things, and often teaches them what the crowds are not even capable of hearing.

Mark records that this demoniac, whom the Lord healed after descending from the mountain, was deaf and mute (Mark 9), whereas Matthew records that he was a lunatic. (Maurus.) He does not call him a lunatic because the moon serves demons, but the evangelist follows popular usage in the term. For this reason the demon, watching the course of the moon, attacks human beings, so that through the creature, if possible, he may defame the Creator. In truth, everything God made is not harmful or wicked, but useful and very good.

The man continues his plea and explains the sick boy’s condition, saying:

“For he often falls into the fire and frequently into the water; and I brought him to your disciples, but they could not cure him.” (Jerome.) In the tropological sense, it seems to me that the lunatic is one who changes toward vices from moment to moment and does not persist in what he has begun, but increases and decreases. Now he is carried into the fire of lust, with which the hearts of adulterers are inflamed; now into the waters of greed, which cannot extinguish charity. When he says, “I brought him to your disciples, but they could not cure him,” he covertly accuses the apostles, since the inability to cure sometimes pertains not to the weakness of those who cure but to the faith of those who are to be cured, as the Lord says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”

“Jesus answered: ‘O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?’” He did not break out into words of anger because he was overcome by weariness, nor did the gentle one who “did not open his mouth, like a lamb before its shearer,” speak in fury. Rather, as a physician might say, if he saw a sick person acting contrary to his prescriptions: “How long must I come to your house? How long shall I waste the effort of my skill, when I command one thing and you do another?”

He was not angry with the man but with the vice; and through one man he reproved the Jews for their unbelief, so that he immediately added:

“Bring him here to me.” And Jesus rebuked him, and the demon came out of him. (Maurus.) Here it is shown that people are often handed over to unclean spirits on account of their own sins or those of their parents. For if the demon had invaded this lunatic without any preceding offenses, it should not have been the sufferer but the demon whom the Lord rebuked. But he rebuked the boy, and the demon came out of him, because the boy had been oppressed by the demon on account of his own sins or those of his parents.

Nor, I think, should it be left unsaid that, according to Mark, when this demoniac saw the Lord, the spirit immediately convulsed him, and he fell to the ground, rolling about and foaming. After the Lord commanded it to come out, the spirit, crying out loudly and tearing the boy, came out of him (Mark 9).

When the boy was brought to the Lord, therefore, the spirit convulses and throws him down, because often, when after our sins we try to turn to the Lord, we are struck by greater and new attacks of our ancient enemy. The crafty adversary does this either to instill hatred of virtue or to avenge the injury of his expulsion. Hence, passing from the particular case to the general one, the Church’s beginnings were afflicted with so many severe struggles of persecution because the enemy grieved that such a great loss of souls had suddenly been inflicted on his kingdom. As the unclean spirit was leaving the man, it tore him and terrified the onlookers with a furious cry; for often, when the devil is expelled from the heart, he generates sharper temptations in it than he had previously stirred up while possessing it undisturbed.

“And the boy was cured from that hour.” Whoever is cured by the true physician is rightly described as becoming healthy thereafter, because no infirmity remains where omnipotent power grants complete health.

“Then the disciples approached Jesus privately and said to him: ‘Why could we not cast it out?’ He said to them: ‘Because of your unbelief.’” This is what is said elsewhere: “Whatever you ask in my name, believing, you will receive” (Matt. 21). Therefore, whenever we do not receive, the failure is not the inability of the one who grants, but the fault of those who ask.

“For truly I say to you: If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move.” Some think that faith is called small because it is compared with a mustard seed, since the kingdom of heaven is compared with a mustard seed, whereas the Apostle says: “And if I have all faith, so as to move mountains” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore great faith is compared with a mustard seed.

The moving of the mountain does not signify the mountain that we see with the eyes of the flesh, but the one that had been moved by the Lord from the lunatic. For what does he say? “You will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move.” By this those who despise the apostles and all believers are rightly convicted of folly for claiming that they had not even a little faith, since none of them moved mountains. The transfer of a mountain from one place to another is not as useful, and the ostentatious display of signs is not as worth seeking, as the transfer, for the benefit of human beings, of this mountain which the prophet says corrupts the whole earth.

It should also be noted that mustard seed is extremely beneficial for cleansing the head. If it is very well ground and sifted, mixed with warm, rich honey-wine, and gargled while fasting against the heat of the sun and in a bath, it cleanses the head of every harmful humor, even if it is thicker, and also enables the dangers of impending weaknesses to be avoided.

So, surely, faith tested by the pestle of temptations, chastened by the sieve of discernment after every superficial light thought has been removed, and sweetened with the honey of perfect love, drains from the heart—all at once and for the future—the sewers of vices, which is the head of the inner person. It prevents them from gathering again, and thus makes our mind capable of heavenly gifts, so that we can obtain from the faithful Lord whatever we wish, not with difficulty but with the greatest ease. Hence it follows:

“And nothing will be impossible for you.” Therefore it is said elsewhere: “All things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark 9).

But the Lord shows how the devil’s arrogance is overcome when he says in what follows:

“But this kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” In teaching the apostles how the most wicked demon must be expelled, he instructs everyone in a way of life, so that we may know that the more serious attacks either of unclean spirits or of human temptations must be overcome by fasts and prayers. He also teaches that the Lord’s anger, when it has been kindled in punishment for our crimes, can be appeased by this singular remedy.

Fasting, in general, is not merely abstaining from food, but abstaining from all carnal allurements—in fact, restraining oneself from every passion of the vices. Likewise, prayer in general consists not only in the words by which we invoke divine mercy, but also in everything we do in the devoted service of faith toward our Creator, as the Apostle testifies: “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5). For how can anyone invoke God with words at every hour and every moment without ceasing? We pray without ceasing when we do only those works that commend us to the loving-kindness of our Creator. With the help of this fasting and prayer, we shall surely conquer and drive away all the snares of our ancient enemy.

[IV.] “While they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them: ‘The Son of Man is to be handed over into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.’ And they were greatly saddened.” (Jerome.) He always mingles sorrow with good prospects, so that when sorrow suddenly arrives it may not terrify the apostles, but may come upon minds already prepared. If it saddens you that he is to be killed, the fact that he is to rise on the third day ought to bring you joy. Their being greatly saddened does not arise from unbelief. Otherwise, they knew that Peter too had been rebuked because he did not understand the things of God but those of men; rather, out of love for the teacher, they could not bear to hear anything adverse or humiliating about him.

“And when they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said: ‘Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?’ He said: ‘He does.’” After Augustus Caesar, Judea became tributary, and everyone was registered by head. Hence Joseph also set out for Bethlehem with Mary, his kinswoman. Again, since Jesus had been raised in Nazareth, which is a town of Galilee, they demand tribute from him at Capernaum, a city; yet, because of the greatness of his signs, those who demanded it did not dare to approach him directly but confronted his disciple. Or they ask maliciously whether he pays the tribute or contradicts Caesar’s will, in accordance with what we read elsewhere: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. 22.)

“And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying”—those who collected the didrachma had approached Peter separately; and when he entered the house, before Peter could mention the matter, the Lord questioned him, so that the disciples would not be scandalized at the demand for tribute when they saw that he knew what had been done in his absence.

“‘What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?’ And he said: ‘From strangers.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Then the sons are free.’” Our Lord was the king’s son both according to the flesh and according to the spirit: either as descended from David’s line or as the Word of the almighty Father. Therefore, as the king’s son, he did not owe tribute; but because he had assumed the humility of the flesh, he had to fulfill all righteousness.

And we are wretched, who are registered under Christ’s name but do nothing worthy of so great a majesty. He endured the cross and paid the tribute for us, but we do not pay tribute for his honor and, as though we were the king’s sons, consider ourselves exempt from taxes.

“But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you.” What should I admire first in this passage, the foreknowledge or the greatness of the Savior, I do not know. His foreknowledge: that he knew a fish would have a stater in its mouth and that it would be the first one caught; his greatness and power: that at his word the stater was immediately created in the fish’s mouth, and that by speaking he brought about what was to happen.

In the mystical interpretation, this fish seemed to me to be the one that was caught first, which was in the depths of the sea and remained in salty and bitter waters, so that the first Adam might be liberated through the second Adam. What was found in its mouth—that is, in its confession—was to be paid for Peter and for the Lord.

And appropriately, the same amount is given and the price is divided: the price was paid for Peter as for a sinner, but our Lord had committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2). A stater is said to contain two didrachmas, so that the likeness of the flesh might be shown, since the Lord and the servant are both redeemed at the same price.

Even the simple interpretation edifies the hearer, since the Lord was so poor that he had nothing with which to pay the tribute. If someone should object that Judas carried money in the purse, we shall answer that he considered it wrong to convert the property of the poor to his own uses, and that he thereby gave us the same example.

**CHAPTER XVIII.** He teaches humility by the example of little children and that no one should cause them to stumble; he gives the example of the wandering sheep and teaches how often one should forgive a brother.

[I.] “At that time the disciples approached Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, will be greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’” (Jerome.) What I have often advised must also be observed here: the causes of each of the Lord’s words and deeds must be sought. After the stater had been found and the tribute paid, what is the meaning of the apostles’ sudden question? “At that time the disciples approached Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’”

They had heard that the same tribute had been paid for Peter and for the Lord. From Peter’s equality with him, they supposed that Peter had been placed above all the apostles, since he had been compared with the Lord in the payment of the tribute. Therefore they ask: “Who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” Jesus, seeing their thoughts and understanding the causes of their error, wishes to heal their desire for glory through a contest in humility.

“And Jesus, calling a little child, set him in their midst.” Either he simply set an ordinary little child before them, so that he might evoke the child’s age and demonstrate the likeness of innocence; or he set himself, in the form of a little child, in their midst, since he had come not to be served but to serve, in order to give them an example of humility. Others interpret the little child as the Holy Spirit, whom he placed in the disciples’ hearts so that they might exchange pride for humility.

(Bede.) The fact that, according to Mark, Jesus embraced the child (Mark 9) signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace and love. When such people fulfill what he commanded—“Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11)—they may rightly glory and say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”

“And he said: ‘Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.’” (Jerome.) The apostles are not commanded to possess the age of little children, but their innocence. What children possess through their years, adults must possess through deliberate effort, so that they may be children in malice, though not in wisdom.

(Rabanus.) They should preserve, after the manner of a child’s age, simplicity without arrogance, charity without envy, and devotion without anger.

“Therefore whoever humbles himself like this little child is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” (Jerome.) Like the child whose example I give you: he does not persist in anger, does not remember an injury, is not delighted when he sees a beautiful woman, does not say one thing while thinking another. So you too cannot enter the kingdom of heaven unless you possess such innocence and purity of mind.

Or otherwise: “Whoever humbles himself like this little child is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” Whoever imitates me and humbles himself as my example, so that he lowers himself as far as I lowered myself by taking the form of a servant, will enter the kingdom of heaven.

“And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” Whoever is such as to imitate Christ’s humility and innocence receives Christ in himself. And wisely, lest the apostles, once the pinnacle of honor had been offered to them, suppose that they were being honored on their own account, he added that they were to be received not for their own merit but for the honor of their teacher.

Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea. Although this sentence can be understood generally against all who cause anyone to stumble, in accordance with the context of the discourse it can also be understood as spoken against the apostles. By asking who was greater in the kingdom of heaven, they seemed to be contending among themselves over rank; and if they had persisted in these vices, they could have destroyed by their scandal those whom they were calling to the faith, while people saw the apostles fighting among themselves over honor [Col. 1007B]. When he said, “It would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck,” he was speaking according to the custom of the province: among the ancient Jews this was the punishment for greater crimes, namely, that the condemned person, tied to a stone, should be cast into the depths. (RAB.) He says, “It would be better for him,” because it is much more useful to end bodily life innocent under a punishment that is exceedingly cruel but nevertheless temporary than, by injuring a brother, to incur the perpetual death of the soul. It is rightly the case that one who can be caused to stumble is called “little”: for one who is great, whatever he may see and whatever he may suffer, does not depart from the faith; but one who is little in spirit and small seeks opportunities for being caused to stumble. Therefore we must take especial care of those who are little in faith, lest they be offended by our example and withdraw [Col. 1007C] from the faith and fall away from salvation. (Greg.) Likewise, by the millstone of a donkey the circuit and toil of secular life is expressed, and by the depth of the sea final condemnation is signified. Thus, whoever, having been led to the appearance of holiness, destroys others either by word or by example, it would certainly have been better if, beneath an outward appearance, earthly pursuits had bound him to death: for if he fell alone, the punishment of hell would torment him in some measure more tolerably. (Maximus.) Or otherwise: the donkey at the mill is the blind person at the stone, the gentile at the rock—one who worships him whom he neither sees nor recognizes. For God does not dwell in things made by hands (Acts VII), nor is he known in metal or stone. Therefore, when this gentile people inflict persecution upon a Christian, they are punished by being drowned with their sacrilegious millstone in the waves of the world that is to be judged [Col. 1007D]. (Greg.) It should certainly be noted that in our good work we must sometimes beware of causing our neighbor to stumble, and at other times disregard it as nothing. Insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid causing our neighbors to stumble. But if offense is taken at the truth, it is better to allow offense to arise than to abandon the truth.

“Woe to the world because of causes of stumbling. For it is necessary that causes of stumbling come; nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the cause of stumbling comes.” (Hieron.) This does not mean that causes of stumbling must come—otherwise those who cause others to stumble would be without blame—but that, since causes of stumbling must arise in this world, each person is exposed to them through his own fault. At the same time, Judas, who had prepared his heart for betrayal, is struck by the general sentence [Col. 1008A]. The Apostle also says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.” It is therefore impossible—as another evangelist says—for causes of stumbling not to arise very frequently in this world, which is so full of errors and hardships. But woe to the one who, through his own fault, makes that which cannot fail to come arise through him.

“But if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter life crippled than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into eternal fire.” (Beda.) Since above he had taught us not to cause those who believe in him to stumble, he now accordingly warns us how greatly we must beware of those who seek to cause us to stumble—that is, who strive by their word or example to drive us toward the ruin of sin [Col. 1008B]. He calls our hand a necessary friend, whose work and assistance we need daily. But if such a person wishes to harm us in the matter of the soul, he must be excluded from our companionship, lest, if we wish to share this life with one who is ruined, we should perish with him in the future as well. In the foot, just as in the hand, he teaches that dear but incorrigible persons are to be separated from us, lest through the uncleanness of those whom we cannot correct we ourselves also become polluted and perish. Hands, then, are so called because of the necessary work they perform for us; feet are such persons because of the service and movement useful for our affairs.

“And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you. It is better for you, having one eye, to enter into life than, having two eyes, to be cast into the gehenna of fire” [Col. 1008C]. In the eye that must be torn out because of causing offense, the same persons are indicated: carnally, they are our friends; spiritually, they are our adversaries. But when we need their counsel and foresight, while they seek by evil counsel to deceive us and turn us aside onto the path of error, their companionship must be entirely abandoned by us.

(Hieron.) Thus, by the Lord’s command every attachment is cut off and every family relationship severed, lest by an occasion of affection any believer be exposed to causes of stumbling. “If,” he says, “someone is so closely joined to you that he is as a hand, foot, or eye, and is useful, attentive, and keen in perception, but causes you to stumble and, because of a dissimilarity of character, drags you into gehenna, it is better for you to be deprived of his closeness and advantages than, while wishing to profit your relatives and friends, to become the cause of their ruin” [Col. 1008D]. Σκάνδαλον is a Greek word, which we may render “offense,” “ruin,” or “a striking of the foot.” Therefore, the one who causes a brother to stumble is the one who, by an improper word or deed, gives an occasion for ruin. Thus neither brother, nor wife, nor children, nor friends, nor any affection that can exclude us from the kingdom of heaven, should be placed before love of the Lord. Each believer knows what harms him, where his mind is troubled, and where he is often tested. It is better, therefore, to lead a solitary life than to lose eternal life for the sake of the necessities of the present life.

“See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” Above [Col. 1009A] we said that by the hand, foot, and eye all family ties and relationships that could cause offense were to be cut off. He therefore tempers the severity of that sentence with the command that follows, saying: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” “Thus,” he says, “I command a severity mixed with clemency: insofar as it lies with you, do not despise them, but seek their healing through your own salvation.” And when you see them persisting in sins and serving vices, it is better for you alone to be saved than to perish with many.

“For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” That every person, from the beginning of birth, should have an angel assigned to guard him is evidence of the great dignity of souls. Hence we read in the Apocalypse of John: “To the angel of Ephesus, of Thyatira [Col. 1009B], and of Philadelphia, and to the angels of the four remaining churches, write this” (Rev. I, II). The Apostle also commanded that women’s heads be veiled in the churches because of the angels. (MAURUS.) For the angels of the little ones—that is, of the humble—always see the face of the Father in heaven; that is, they continually enjoy the contemplation of God. He also uses “face” in the human manner to mean the clearest vision and knowledge.

“For the Son of Man came to save what had perished.” It is as though he were saying: The Son of God came to restore what had been crushed and cast down. Therefore, do not destroy what has been saved by him. No one can undo the work of God without great danger and loss to himself, nor is it right for a human being to despise what God has chosen. Hence he adds another example concerning the same matter.

[Col. 1009C] [II.] “What do you think? If someone has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go to seek the one that went astray?” (Hieron.) He appropriately calls to clemency the one who had previously said, “See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” He adds the parable of the ninety-nine sheep left on the mountains and of the one that had gone astray, which the good shepherd, because it was too weak to walk, carries back on his shoulders to the rest of the flock. Some think that this shepherd is the one who, although he was in the form of God and did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. II)—and for this reason descended to earthly things in order to save the one little sheep that had perished, that is, the human race. For what this evangelist says, that the sheep were left on the mountains—that is, in high places—another says, “in the wilderness.”

(Greg.) Why, then, is heaven called a wilderness, unless because “wilderness” means something abandoned? Humanity abandoned heaven when it sinned. The ninety-nine sheep remained in the wilderness when the Lord was seeking the one on earth, because the number of rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—which had been created to see God, had been diminished by the loss of humanity; and, in order that the perfect number of sheep might be restored in heaven, the lost human being was sought on earth. Notice that one is lacking from nine in order for there to be ten, and from ninety-nine in order for there to be a hundred. Numbers from which one is lacking can therefore vary in smallness and greatness until they are completed; but the one itself, remaining unchanged in itself, completes the others when it is added.

“And if it happens that he finds it, truly I tell you, he will rejoice over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray.” (Didym.) Others understand the number of the righteous in the ninety-nine sheep and that of sinners in the one little sheep, in accordance with what he had said elsewhere: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners; for those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX). But it should be noted that in Luke, in connection with this parable, it is written that there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance (Luke IX).

(Greg.) Hence we must consider why the Lord acknowledges that there is greater joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous persons who remain standing. Is it not because we ourselves know this through the daily experience of our observation: often those who know that they are not weighed down by any great burden of sins stand indeed on the path of righteousness and commit no unlawful acts, but they do not yearn anxiously for their heavenly homeland. They give themselves so much indulgence in lawful matters because they do not remember committing anything unlawful; and often they remain sluggish in carrying out outstanding good works because they feel very secure in having committed no more serious evil. By contrast, sometimes those who remember having committed unlawful acts, pierced by the pain itself, burn with love of God and exercise themselves in great virtues [Col. 1010C]. Thus there is greater joy in heaven over a converted sinner than over a righteous person who remains standing, because even a commander in battle loves more the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy fiercely than the one who never turned his back and never performed any act of courage.

Yet amid these things it must be understood that there are many righteous persons whose lives contain such great joy that no repentance of sinners can in any way be preferred to them. For many are conscious of no evils in themselves, yet they subject themselves to the discipline of such great fervor as though they were oppressed by every sin. They reject all that is lawful, gird themselves nobly for contempt of the world, rejoice in lamentation, humble themselves in everything, and, just as some lament the sins of their deeds, so they lament the sins of their thoughts [Col. 1010D]. From this, then, we may gather how great a joy it brings to God when a righteous person weeps humbly, if heaven rejoices when an unrighteous person condemns through repentance what he did wrongly. The Lord continues and says:

“Thus it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” (Hieron.) He refers this to the preceding point, where he had said, “See that you do not despise one of these little ones,” and he teaches that the parable just given was offered so that the little ones would not be despised. But in saying, “It is not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish,” he shows that whenever one of the little ones perishes, he has not perished by the will of the Father.

[Col. 1011A] [III.] “But if your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother.” If our brother sins against us and injures us for whatever reason, we have the power—indeed, the obligation—to forgive, so that we may forgive our debtors their debts. But if someone sins against God, that is not within our judgment. For divine Scripture says: “If a man sins against a man, the priest will pray for him; but if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. II). We, on the contrary, are lenient in offenses against God but exercise hatred in offenses against ourselves. A brother must be reproved privately, lest, if he once loses shame and modesty, he remain in sin. And if he listens, we gain his soul, and through another’s salvation our own salvation is also acquired. Thus he indicates by what order we can avoid causes of stumbling and escape perpetual woe: if we pay attention to ourselves so that we injure no one; if we reprove the sinner out of zeal for righteousness; and if we sincerely open the entrails of mercy and compassion to the penitent.

“But if he does not listen, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church; and if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican.” If he refuses to listen to you, let a brother be brought in; and if he does not listen to them either, let a third be brought in, either for the purpose of correction or for bringing the matter forward under witnesses. But if he refuses to listen to them as well, he must then be denounced to many, so that they may hold him in abhorrence; and the one who could not be saved by shame may be saved by disgrace [Col. 1011C].

When it is said, “Let him be to you as a gentile and a publican,” it is shown that the person who, under the name of believer, performs the works of unbelievers is more deserving of abhorrence than those who are wholly gentiles. For ἔθνος in Greek means “nation,” and ἔθνικοι means “gentiles.” Publicans, in the allegorical sense, are those who pursue the profits of the world and exact revenues through commerce, frauds, thefts, and wicked perjuries. Here, however, we must look carefully: we are not commanded to forgive the sinner indiscriminately, but to forgive the one who listens—that is, who obeys—and repents. First, the sinner is to be rebuked mercifully, so that afterward there may be someone whom we can justly forgive. Therefore, whoever sees his brother sinning and remains silent is no less a transgressor of the Lord’s command than the one who refuses to grant forgiveness to that same repentant person [Col. 1011D]. For the one who said, “If he repents, forgive him,” first said, “If he sins, rebuke him.” Thus forgiveness is to be granted to a brother after rebuke, but only to the one who, by repenting, turns away from error, lest forgiveness be either difficult or indulgence lax.

“Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” Because he had said, “If he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican,” and because a contemptuous brother might have responded secretly or thought silently, “If you despise me, I will despise you; if you condemn me, by contrast you will be condemned by my judgment,” he granted the apostles authority, so that they might know that those who are condemned by their tribunals are confirmed by divine judgment, and that whatever is bound on earth is likewise bound in heaven.

“Again I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about any matter whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.” Above he urged everyone in his discourse toward concord. Thus he also promises a reward, so that we may hasten more eagerly to concord, since he says that he will be in the midst of two or three. (Hilar.) For he himself is peace and love, and he has established his seat and dwelling in good and peaceful wills: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst [Col. 1012B] of them.” Whether to receive the humble penitent or to cast out the proud and obstinate, whatever they do on earth by humbly judging for the salvation of human beings is confirmed above by judgment in heaven. We may also understand this spiritually: where spirit, soul, and body agree, and do not wage among themselves the warfare of differing desires—with the flesh lusting against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—they will obtain from the Father whatever they ask, and there can be no doubt that the request concerns good things when the body wishes to possess what the spirit wishes to possess.

[IV.] “Then Peter came to him and said: Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times? Jesus says to him: I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.” (Hieron.) [Col. 1012C] The Lord’s discourse coheres with itself and cannot be broken, like a threefold cord. Above he had said, “See that you do not despise one of these little ones,” and had added, “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone.” He had also promised a reward, saying, “If two of you agree on earth, they will obtain whatever they ask, and I will be in their midst.” The apostle Peter, prompted by this, asks how often he ought to forgive a brother who sins against him, and in his question proposes the number seven. The Lord replies, “Not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven”—that is, four hundred and ninety times—so that he should forgive a brother who sinned as many times in a day as that brother could possibly sin.

(RAB.) If a brother who sins against you repents, you have the power—indeed, the obligation—to forgive him, so that the Father who is in heaven may also forgive you when you repent and ask forgiveness. But if, after being rebuked, he neglects to turn back and repent, observe what judgment the truth pronounces concerning this. We are commanded to give forgiveness in one way to a brother who asks for it, and in another way to an enemy who persecutes us. To the former, we give it so that, having received remission of the sin by which he harmed us innocent persons, he may share with us in fellowship of love; to the latter, we give it so that, although he wishes evil upon us and does it if he can, we may always wish and do him whatever good we can. For David could not offer his persecutors, who had been deprived of the remedy of repentance, the same measure of forgiveness that Joseph generously offered to his brothers, corrected by salutary remorse, although David mourned them mercifully.

“Therefore the kingdom of heaven has been likened to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.” (Hieron.) It is customary among the Syrians, and especially among the Palestinians, to join parables to almost every discourse, so that what cannot be retained by hearers through a simple command may be retained through comparison and examples. Therefore, by this parable, the Lord instructed Peter through the comparison of a king, lord, and servant: a servant who owed ten thousand talents asked his master for forgiveness and obtained it, so that he too might forgive his fellow servants who sinned in lesser matters. At the same time, he admonishes us to be kind and merciful toward our fellow servants. If that king and lord so easily forgave his indebted servant the enormous sum of ten thousand [Col. 1013B] talents, how much more ought each one of us to forgive offenses committed by his fellow servants? To make this clearer, let us give an example: if one of us has committed adultery, murder, sacrilege, or greater crimes, ten thousand talents are forgiven when those persons themselves forgive those who have committed lesser offenses. But if we are implacable because of an insult received, and maintain perpetual quarrels because of a bitter word, do we not rightly seem to deserve being handed over to prison, and, by the example of our own conduct, to ensure that forgiveness for our greater offenses is not granted?

(MAURUS.) If someone seeks an allegory in this parable, he can understand these two debtors as representing two peoples. Therefore, this man and king to whom the kingdom of heaven is likened, who settled accounts with his servants, is better understood as none other than our Redeemer. Of him the Prophet says: “He is a man; who knows him?” And the Psalmist says: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXII). He settles accounts with his servants when, examining each person’s merit strictly, he weighs it. For it is written of him: “He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in his truth” (Ps. XCV).

“And when he began to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents. But since he had nothing with which to repay, he ordered him to be sold, together with his wife, his children, and everything he had, and payment to be made.” This servant who owed ten thousand talents is the Jewish people, who, bound by the Decalogue of the Law, were liable for the debts of many transgressions. Their lord ordered that they, their wife, their children, and everything they had be sold and payment made, because he handed over not only the people but also the synagogue of the Jews—rulers and subjects alike, with all their possessions—into the power of foreign nations on account of the magnitude of their offenses, so that what they had refused to pay willingly they would be compelled to pay by punishment.

“So the servant fell down and begged him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” In the same way, that people under the Law, after realizing that they were surrounded and hemmed in by evils, at last repented and turned to supplication. What they had previously refused to do willingly, afterward, compelled by force, they promised to do.

[Col. 1014A] “And the lord, moved with compassion for that servant, released him and forgave him the debt.” For, as it is written of him, “He is merciful and compassionate, patient and very merciful” (Ps. III), receiving the prayers of the afflicted, he not only released the Jewish captivity but also promised to grant them forgiveness for all their offenses at the coming of Christ, if they persisted in what they had begun and did not break their pledge. Hence, in the person of the Lord urging them to remember those promises and their repentance, it is rightly said through Isaiah: “Remember these things, Jacob, for you are my servant; I formed you, you are my servant. Israel, do not forget me. I have wiped away your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you” (Isa. XLIV). But let us hear what this stubborn and ungrateful servant did afterward.

“But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He seized him and began to choke him, saying: Pay what you owe. So his fellow servant fell down and begged him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything. But he refused, and went away and put him in prison until he should repay the debt.” Once freed from captivity, the Jewish people not only failed to give thanks to their Redeemer but also, adding new sins to their former sins, did not refrain from oppressing their fellow servant—that is, the gentile people—as though he were subject to them, in contempt of their lord. Believing him to be their debtor, they demanded circumcision and the ceremonies of the Law from him, and, slandering the grace of Christ by claiming that it was not sufficient for their salvation, they rejected it. Hence comes the passage in the Acts of the Apostles: certain men from the sect of the Pharisees, obstructing the preaching of Paul and Barnabas, asserted that those who had believed from among the gentiles had to be circumcised and observe the Law of Moses; and they compelled them to do this not only by persuasion but also by tortures.

Likewise, the Apostle Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says: “For you became imitators, brothers, of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your fellow citizens as they did from the Jews, who both killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, and do not please God and are opposed to all human beings, forbidding us to speak to the gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby always filling up the measure of their sins. For the wrath of God has come upon them to the end” (1 Thess. II).

“But when his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly grieved; and they came and told their lord everything that had taken place.” Who are these fellow servants who report the wicked servant’s insolence to his lord, unless they are the apostles and preachers of the Gospel, who daily implore the Lord for the salvation of believers against the deceit of persecutors? We read that the apostles did the same in the Acts of the Apostles, when the priests, the magistrates of the temple, and the Sadducees, grieved that they were teaching the people and announcing the resurrection from the dead in Jesus, beat them with whips and ordered them not to speak any longer in the name of Jesus to anyone [Col. 1015A]. But they returned to their own people, raised their voice to God, and said:

“You, Lord God, who made heaven and earth and everything in them, who through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of our father David, your servant, said: Why did the nations rage and the peoples meditate on vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. For they gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate with the gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do what your hand and your counsel had decreed should be done. And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant your servants to speak your word with complete boldness, while you stretch out your hand for healings, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus, and so forth” (Acts IV).

“Then his lord summoned him and said to him: Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you begged me; should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” The Lord repeatedly forgave the Jewish people their debts when, placed in distress and repenting, they implored his mercy. But once freed from their distress, they afterward showed no compassion or mercy toward the poor among their neighbors; rather, as it is written, they cruelly demanded all their debtors’ payments. Moreover, they ungratefully despised and cruelly slaughtered the prophets and apostles who brought them the word of reconciliation. Hence they deserved to experience what follows.

“And his lord became angry and handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.” Thus the true Lord, because of their faithlessness, handed the wicked and blasphemous Jewish people over into the hands of the Romans. Some were destroyed by famine, some killed by the sword, and others led into captivity; they so devastated the whole land that they utterly destroyed Jerusalem, their capital, from its foundations, burned the temple, and dismantled their entire religious cult. Then what the Savior himself had foretold to them came to pass: the entire dwelling-place of the inhabitants of Jerusalem was so destroyed that “a stone would not be left upon a stone” (Matt. XXIV). And, according to the prophecy of Daniel, desolation would remain until the end.

Or otherwise: he handed them over to torturers—that is, to evil spirits—which, out of envy, would punish the most wicked, malicious, and incorrigible soul with eternal torments without end. What follows is:

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” (Hier.) This is a very fearful sentence, if God’s judgment is bent and changed according to our mind. If we do not forgive our brothers small offenses, God will not forgive us great ones. And because someone may say, “I have nothing against him; he knows it. He has God as his judge; I do not care what he chooses to do. I have forgiven him,” he confirms his sentence and overturns every pretense of feigned peace by saying: “If each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” (Greg.) From these words it is clear that if we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, then what we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance is demanded from us again.

BOOK SIX.

[Col. 1015]

CHAPTER XIX. He teaches that a wife must not be dismissed, and concerning eunuchs; that infants must not be barred from blessing; that the rich will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty; and that whoever abandons everything for Christ will receive a hundredfold.

Having completed the Lord’s discourses that the Savior himself delivered in Galilee to the apostles, after the tax had been demanded of him, concerning innocence and humility—prohibiting them from causing the little ones to stumble, together with the added parable—and having afterward fittingly taught about the correction of brothers and forgiveness, when Peter asked about the remission of sins and he answered that forgiveness should be granted not only seven times but also seventy times seven, confirming the same point by the following parable—after Matthew had explained all these matters in this way, he proceeds according to his custom, as though turning to other things that must be narrated, and says:

[I.] “And it happened that when Jesus had finished these discourses, he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan.” (RAB.) Here he begins to narrate what the Lord did, taught, and suffered in Judea. First, he went beyond the Jordan to the east; then also to the region on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho, Bethphage, and Jerusalem. For although the whole province of the Jews was generally called Judea in distinction from other nations, more particularly its southern region was called Judea, in distinction from Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and the other regions within the same province.

“And great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.” (Hilar.) He heals Galileans in the borders of Judea. He certainly could have spared the crowds of sick people the fatigue and offered help to the weak within Galilee itself, but the typological meaning of the places also had to be fulfilled by these privileges, so that the sins of the gentiles might be admitted into the forgiveness that was being prepared for Judea.

“And the Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying: Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any reason?” Here the difference between the minds of the crowds and of the Pharisees must also be noted: the crowds gather in order to be taught and to have their sick healed, as the evangelist Matthew clearly records; the Pharisees come in order [Col. 1017A] to deceive the Savior and teacher of truth by testing him. This is not surprising: devotion to piety brought the former, while the goad of envy brought the latter.

(Hieron.) They therefore ask whether it is lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any reason, so that they may hold him as if in a horned syllogism and make him fall into a trap whatever he answers. If he says that a wife may be dismissed for any reason and another taken, he will seem, as a preacher of chastity, to teach the opposite. But if he answers that she ought not to be dismissed for every reason, he will be held guilty of sacrilege and of acting against the teaching of Moses—and, through Moses, against God. Therefore the Lord moderates his answer in such a way as to pass through their snare, bringing Holy Scripture forward as witness, along with the natural law and God’s first judgment [Col. 1017B]. Then he introduces what was granted not by God’s will but out of necessity caused by sinners.

“He answered and said to them: Have you not read that the one who made them from the beginning made them male and female?” This is written at the beginning of Genesis. By saying “male and female,” he shows that second marriages are to be avoided. For he did not say “male and females,” which would have been sought on the basis of dismissing the former wife, but “male and female,” so that the partnership of one spouse with one spouse might be joined.

“And he said: For this reason a man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife.” Significantly he says “his wife,” not “wives.”

“And the two will be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh.” (Hilar.) The reward of marriage is that two become one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit becomes one spirit. By the eternal and salutary counsel of almighty God, it was arranged that a man should embrace in a woman a portion of his own body and should not consider as different from himself what he recognized had been fashioned from himself.

“Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.” (Hieron.) What God has joined together by making the flesh of man and woman one, no human being can separate, unless perhaps God alone. A human being separates them when, because of the desire for a second wife, we dismiss the first; God separates them—he who had joined them—when, by mutual consent for the sake of service to God, because the time is short, we have wives as though we did not have them.

“They say to him: Why, then, did Moses command that a certificate of divorce be given [Col. 1017D] and that she be dismissed?” They reveal the accusation they had prepared. Certainly the Lord had not delivered his own judgment, but had recalled the ancient history and commandments of God.

“He said to them: Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives because of the hardness of your hearts; but from the beginning it was not so.” What he says is this: Can God be inconsistent with himself, having commanded one thing earlier and then broken his own judgment by a new command? This must not be understood in that way. But when Moses saw that, because of the desire for second marriages—with women who were richer, younger, or more beautiful—the first wives were either being killed or forced to lead miserable lives, he preferred to permit separation rather than allow hatred and murder to continue. At the same time, consider that he said, “Because of the hardness of your hearts.” It was not God but Moses who permitted it, so that, according to the Apostle, it was a human counsel, not a command of God.

I say to you that whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. Fornication alone is what overcomes the marital bond. Indeed, when she has abandoned one flesh for another and separated herself from her husband through fornication, she ought not to be retained, lest she also make her husband subject to a curse, as Scripture says: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. XVIII). Therefore, wherever there is fornication or suspicion of fornication, the wife may freely be dismissed. And because it could happen that someone might bring a false accusation against an innocent woman and, for the sake of a second marriage, attach a charge to the first, he commands that the former wife be dismissed in such a way that he may not have a second wife while the first is alive. For what he says amounts to this: If you dismiss your wife not because of lust but because of injury, why, having experienced the unhappiness of a first marriage, do you expose yourself to the danger of a new one? And since it could also happen that, under the same law, a wife might give her husband a writ of divorce, the same precaution is prescribed, so that she may not take a second husband. (RAB.) And because a prostitute and a woman who had once committed adultery did not fear disgrace, the man is warned a second time that, if he marries such a woman, he incurs the charge of adultery. Thus there is only one carnal cause—that is, fornication—and one spiritual cause—that is, fear of God—for dismissing a wife, as many are recorded to have done for the sake of religion. But no cause is prescribed by God’s law for marrying another woman while the one who was left is alive.

His disciples said to him: “If this is the condition of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry.” (Hieron.) The burden of wives is heavy if it is not permitted to dismiss them except for the cause of fornication. For what if she is drunken, hot-tempered, of bad character, extravagant, gluttonous, wandering, quarrelsome, and abusive? Whether we wish it or not, such a woman must be kept and endured. For although we were free, we voluntarily subjected ourselves to slavery. Seeing, therefore, the heavy yoke of wives, the apostles express the movement of their minds and say: “If this is the condition of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry.”

He said to them: “Not everyone accepts this saying, but only those to whom it has been given.” No one should suppose that under this saying fate or fortune is being introduced—that these are virgins to whom virginity has been given by God, or that chance has led certain people to it. Rather, it has been given to those who asked, who desired it, and who labored in order to receive it. For “everyone who asks will receive, and the one who seeks will find, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.”

For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made so by men, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. There are three kinds of eunuchs: two carnal kinds and a third spiritual kind. Some are born so from their mother’s womb; others are made so either by captivity or by the indulgences of matrons; the third are those who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and who, although they could have been husbands, became eunuchs for Christ’s sake. A reward is promised to these; but to the former, whose chastity is imposed by necessity rather than chosen by will, nothing at all is owed. We may also explain it another way: Eunuchs from their mother’s womb are those who are of a colder nature and do not desire sexual pleasure. Some are made eunuchs by men—either philosophers make them so, or they are softened into women because of the worship of idols, or, through heretical persuasion, they feign charity in order to falsify the truth of religion. But none of them attains the kingdom of heaven except the one who has made himself a eunuch for Christ’s sake. Hence he adds:

“Let the one who can accept it accept it.” Let each person consider his own strength, whether he can fulfill the commands of virginity and chastity. Love is naturally pleasing and attracts everyone to itself; but one’s strength must be considered, so that the one who can accept it may accept it. It is as though the Lord’s voice were encouraging and urging his soldiers toward the reward of chastity: “Let the one who can accept it accept it.” Let the one who can fight fight, overcome, and triumph.

[II] Then little children were brought to him, so that he might lay his hands on them and pray. This happened when the Lord was speaking about chastity and declaring eunuchs blessed. For while the Lord was proclaiming the glory of continence and saying, “There are those who make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,” certain people, hearing this, brought to him little boys who were utterly pure in respect of chastity. They thought that the Lord praised only those who were bodily pure, and not those who were pure in will; they did not understand that the Lord blessed not the eunuchs whom the necessity of childhood makes chaste, but the virtue of continence.

But the disciples rebuked them. (Hieron.) This was not because they did not want the Savior to bless them both with hand and voice, but because, since they did not yet possess fully developed faith, they thought that he would grow weary, as human beings do, from the importunity of those presenting the children.

But Jesus said to them: “Allow the little children to come to me, and do not prevent them from coming to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” He pointedly said “such as these,” not “these,” to show that it is not age but character that reigns. He promised a reward also to those who possess similar innocence and simplicity. The Apostle frequently agrees with this same meaning: “Do not become children in your thinking, but be infants in malice, and mature in understanding” (I Cor. XIV).

[Col. 1019D] And after he had laid his hands on them, he departed from there. (MAUR.) The Lord lays his hands on little children when he grants the grace of his help to the humble and directs them according to his will, so that they may be able to obey his commands in all things. Hence the Psalmist says to him: “You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me” (Ps. LXXII), and so forth.

And behold, one who approached said to him: “Good Teacher, what good shall I do in order to have eternal life?” (RAB.) I think that this inquirer after eternal life had heard from the Lord that only those who wished to be like little children were worthy to enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, wishing to obtain a more certain account, he asks that it be explained to him, not through parables but openly, by what merits of works he could attain eternal life.

He said to him: “Why do you ask me about the good? There is one who is good, God.” (Hieron.) Because he had called him “good teacher” and had not confessed him to be God or the Son of God, he learned that, however holy a human being may be, he is not good in comparison with God. Of God it is said: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CXVII). But lest anyone think that, when God is called good, the Son of God is excluded from goodness, we read elsewhere: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X). The Prophet also speaks of a good Spirit and a good land. Thus the Savior did not refuse the testimony of goodness; rather, he excluded the error of calling him a teacher apart from God.

“But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He said to him: “Which ones?” Jesus then said: “You shall not commit murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not give false testimony. Honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.” We can prove that this young man was a tempter from the fact that, when the Lord said to him, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” he fraudulently asked again which commandments they were—as though he himself had not read them, or as though the Lord could command things contrary to God.

The young man said to him: “I have kept all these things; what do I still lack?” The young man is lying.
