For if he had fulfilled in deed what is contained in the commandments—“You shall love your neighbor as yourself”—how did it happen that afterward, when he heard, “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor,” he departed sorrowfully, because he had many possessions?

Jesus said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. And come, follow me.” It is within our power whether we wish to be perfect. Nevertheless, whoever wishes to be perfect must sell what he has—not sell only a portion, as Ananias and Sapphira did (Acts V), but sell everything. And when he has sold it, he must give everything to the poor and thus prepare treasure for himself in the kingdom of heaven. Yet this is not sufficient for perfection unless, after despising riches, he follows the Savior—that is, having abandoned evil, he does good. For a purse is more easily despised than the will. Many abandon riches without following God; but the one who follows Christ is his imitator and walks in his footsteps. “Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (I John II). (RAB.) Behold, we have heard of two lives proposed by our Lord Jesus Christ to human beings: the active and the contemplative. The active life belongs to the Law, the contemplative to the Gospel; for just as the Old Testament preceded the New, so good action precedes contemplation. The active life possesses perfection here; the contemplative, although it has a beginning here, will not find perfection in this life but in eternity. The active life can exist in this life without the contemplative; but the contemplative cannot attain perfection in this life without the active. For every believer has been formed by God in this life so that, through the outer person, which is the body, he may always strive to perform good works, and through the inner person, which is the soul, may strive to devote himself to contemplation. The active life includes: “You shall not commit murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and the other commandments of the Law. The contemplative life includes: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”

But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions. (Hieron.) This is the sorrow that leads to death. The reason for his sorrow is given: he had many possessions—that is, thorns and thistles—which choked the Lord’s seed.

But Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, it is difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.” How, then, did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were rich, enter the kingdom of heaven? And in the Gospel Matthew and Zacchaeus are commended by the testimony of the Lord after abandoning their riches. But we must consider that, at the time when they entered, they had ceased to be rich. Therefore, they will not enter so long as they remain rich. Yet because riches are difficult to despise, he did not say that it is impossible for the rich to enter the kingdoms of heaven, but difficult. Where “difficult” is stated, impossibility is not demonstrated, but rarity is indicated. (RAB.) When Jesus, seeing that the rich man had become sorrowful, said according to Luke, “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God” (Luke XVIII), it is clear that those who devote themselves here to multiplying riches disdain seeking the joys of the other life. But there is some difference between possessing money and loving money. Many possess it without loving it; others both possess and love it; others rejoice that they neither possess nor love the riches of the world. The safest condition is that of those who say with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). Hence Solomon does not say, “The one who possesses riches,” but, “The one who loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Eccl. V). And the Lord himself, according to Mark, explaining this saying to his disciples, who were astonished at it, added: “Children, how difficult it is for those who trust in money to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark X). Here likewise it should be noted that, as we have shown above, he did not say “impossible” but “difficult”—that is, that it is a matter of the greatest labor for those who possess money or trust in money, once stripped of the bonds of avarice, to enter the hall of the heavenly kingdom.

“And again I say to you: It is easier for a camel, with its enormous limbs, to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.” If it is easier for a camel, enormous in its massive limbs, to penetrate through the narrow opening of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God, then no rich person will enter the kingdom of God. How, then, have so many rich people entered the kingdom of God, whether in the Gospel or in the Old Testament, unless perhaps they learned, by the Lord’s inspiration, either to regard riches as nothing or to abandon them entirely? Did David trust in the riches of his kingdom, when he sings of himself: “For I am alone and poor” (Ps. XXIV)? And he exhorts others: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). I think he did not dare to say, “Do not accept them.” Is it credible that Abraham preferred his possessions to the Lord, for whose sake he did not hesitate to strike his only heir?

(Aug.) In a deeper sense, it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ. He wished himself to be understood by the name of “camel,” because he voluntarily humbled himself and bore the burdens of our weakness. And where is this more clearly understood than in the very passage that says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Eccl. III)? By the needle he signifies punctures, and by the punctures the pains endured in his passion. (Venant.) The eye of the needle therefore signifies the narrowness of the passion, by which, after the garment of our nature had been torn, he graciously repaired it, so to speak—that is, restored it—so that after the fall we might rejoice to be reformed more perfectly, in accordance with the Apostle’s testimony: “All you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying: “Who, then, can be saved?” To what does this response refer? The crowd of the poor who can be saved, in comparison with the rich who are lost, is incomparably larger—unless they understood that all who love riches, even if they cannot acquire them, are counted among the rich.

But Jesus looked at them and said: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” This should not be understood to mean that the greedy and proud—who are signified by the name of that rich man—will enter the kingdom of heaven with their greed and pride. Rather, it is possible for God, through the Word, as we see has happened and happens every day, to convert them from desire for temporal things to love of eternal things, and from destructive pride to saving humility. (MAUR.) I have also read in the expositions of certain writers that this rich man is interpreted as the Jewish people, who falsely gloried in observing the Law while rejecting evangelical perfection and, intent on earthly matters, shunned spiritual gifts. Of them it is written: “For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John XII). Hence, when conspiring in the Lord’s passion, they said: “If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John XI). Accordingly, the camel is rightly preferred to this people: that is, the Gentile people, deformed by the crookedness of sins and vices, who more readily undertook to enter the arduous way of God’s commandments, because they began sooner to honor the evangelical precepts and follow the footsteps of their Lord. Of these camels we read in Isaiah that the camels of Midian and Ephah enter the gates of Jerusalem with gifts and offerings (Isa. LX).

[III] Then Peter answered and said to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What, then, will there be for us?” (Hieron.) Great confidence! Peter was a fisherman; he had not been rich; he sought his food by hand and by skill. Yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” And because it is not enough merely to leave something, he adds what is perfect: “And we have followed you.” As though he were saying: “We have done what you commanded; what reward, then, will you give us?”

But Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” He did not say, “You who have left everything.” Socrates the philosopher did this, and many others despised riches. Rather, he said, “You who have followed me,” which is proper to the apostles and believers. “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty”: when the dead will rise incorrupt from corruption, you also will sit on seats of judgment, condemning the twelve tribes of Israel because they did not wish to believe in you who believed.

(RAB.) In this life, laboring for his name, the Lord taught us to hope for a reward in another life—that is, in the regeneration, when we shall have been regenerated by rising into immortal life, having been born mortally into a transient life. For there are clearly two regenerations, likewise two adoptions and two resurrections. One regeneration is that of which the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John IV). The other is this one, of which he now says: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty.” The first adoption is that of which the Apostle says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII). The second adoption will be that of which the same Apostle says: “But we ourselves also groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (ibid.). The first resurrection is that of which the Lord says: “The hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John IV). And in the Apocalypse: “Blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over such the second death has no power” (Apoc. XX). The second resurrection will be that of which the Lord says: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of God, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V).

As for what he says—“When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones,” and so forth—no one should suppose that only twelve apostles will then judge, since Matthias was chosen in place of Judas the traitor. Nor are only twelve tribes of Israel to be judged; otherwise the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth, will depart without judgment, and Paul, who is the thirteenth apostle, chosen in place of Judas the traitor, will be deprived of the lot of judgment, although he himself says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this life?” (I Cor. VI). For it must be understood that all who, following the example of the apostles, have left everything and followed Christ will come with him as judges, just as the entire human race will be judged. Because the number twelve often signifies universality in Scripture, the twelve seats of the judging apostles indicate the total number of those who judge, and the twelve tribes of Israel indicate the whole multitude of those who are to be judged.

Hence it should be noted that there will be two orders of the elect at the judgment. One consists of those judging with the Lord, mentioned here: those who left everything and followed him. The other consists of those who are to be judged by the Lord: those who did not likewise leave everything they possessed, but took care to give daily alms to Christ’s poor from what they had. Hence they will hear at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

The Lord also recalls these people earlier in this Gospel, when a certain ruler asked what good he could do in order to have eternal life: “If you wish,” he said, “to enter into life, keep the commandments. You shall not commit murder, you shall not steal, you shall not give false testimony; honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself” (above). Therefore, the one who keeps the Lord’s commandments enters into eternal life; but the one who not only keeps the commandments but also follows the Lord’s counsel concerning the despising of riches and luxuries will not only receive life himself, but will also judge the lives of others with the Lord. Thus, as we have said, there will be two orders of the good at the judgment.

But we also learn from the Lord’s account that there will be two orders of the reprobate. One consists of those who, having been initiated into the mysteries of the Christian faith, neglect to practice the works of faith. To them he testifies at the judgment: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth (Matt. XXV). The other consists of those who, through faith, either never received the mysteries of Christ or rejected them after receiving them through apostasy. Of them he says: “But whoever does not believe is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John III). Since they were unwilling to honor Christ even in word, they do not deserve to hear even his words by which they might be convicted at the judgment. They come to judgment only for this purpose: that they may be sent into eternal condemnation with the sinners who are judged.

“And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for the sake of my name, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.” (Hieron.) This passage agrees with that saying in which the Savior declares: “I have not come to bring peace but a sword. For I have come to separate a man from his father, and a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matt. X). Therefore, those who for the sake of faith in Christ and the preaching of the Gospel despise every affection, as well as the riches and pleasures of the world, will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.

Taking this saying as an occasion, certain people introduce a thousand years after the resurrection, saying that then we will receive a hundredfold of everything we have abandoned, and eternal life as well. They do not understand that, if the promise is worthy in other respects, it appears shameful with regard to wives: the one who has abandoned one wife for the Lord would receive a hundred in the future. The meaning, therefore, is this: Whoever has abandoned carnal things for the Savior will receive spiritual things, which in comparison with their worth and merit will be as though a hundred were compared with a small number. Hence the Apostle says that he had abandoned only one house and the small fields of one province, as though possessing nothing and possessing everything (II Cor. VI).

(RAB.) It should be noted that in Mark’s Gospel it is written: “There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields, for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now, in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and children and fields, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark X).

What he says—“He will receive a hundredfold now, in this time, houses, and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and fields, with persecutions”—can rightly be understood in a deeper symbolic sense. For the number one hundred, transferred from the left hand to the right, although it appears by the bending of the fingers to retain the same form that ten had possessed on the left, nevertheless greatly surpasses it in quantity. So all who for the sake of the kingdom of God despise temporal things and, in this life full of persecutions, taste by certain faith the joy of that kingdom, while awaiting the heavenly homeland—which is rightly signified by the right hand—enjoy the most sincere love of all the elect together.

But because many do not complete their pursuit of virtue with the same intention of devotion with which they begin it—either growing lukewarm in the love of virtue that they had begun, or falling back entirely into the whirlpool of crimes—a fearful sentence is immediately added:

“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” Consider Judas, transformed from an apostle into an apostate, because “many who are first will be last.” Consider the thief on the cross, made a confessor, rejoicing with Christ in paradise on the very day on which he was crucified for his own sins by the grace of faith; and it is said: “The last will be first.” We also see many every day who, remaining in the lay state, excel in the great merits of life, while others, fervent in spiritual devotion from their earliest years, grow weary at the end as idleness makes them sluggish, and complete in the flesh, through inactive foolishness, what they had begun in the spirit.

CHAPTER XX. The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard; the Sons of Zebedee; the First Reclining Places at the Supper; and the Two Blind Men beside the Way.

[I] “For the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.” (Hieron.) This parable, or likeness, of the kingdom of heaven is understood from what has preceded. It was written earlier: “Many who are first will be last, and the last first”—not because the Lord gives preference to time, but to faith.

(Greg.) The kingdom of heaven is said to be like a householder who hires workers to cultivate his vineyard. Who more suitably represents the likeness of a householder than our Creator, who governs those whom he created and possesses his elect in this world as a master possesses subjects in his house? He has a vineyard, namely the universal Church, because from righteous Abel to the last elect who will come at the end of the world, as many saints as it has produced, so many shoots, as it were, it has sent forth.

“Having agreed with the workers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.” (Aug.) The denarius bears the image of a king. Each person therefore approaches the worship of the divine name and draws near to the Church, which is signified by the vineyard, in order to receive in Christ the image of divinity that he had lost in paradise through the envy of the serpent. Hence it is called a denarius, which among the ancients was reckoned as ten coins, signifying by a reasonable correspondence that the more diligently someone strives to fulfill the Decalogue of the Law, the more fully he is restored to the image of the one who created him and receives in the future the more splendid reward signified by the denarius.

(Greg.) To instruct his people, therefore, the Lord never ceased sending workers to cultivate his vineyard. First through the patriarchs, afterward through the teachers of the Law and the prophets, and finally through the apostles, he labored as through workers in the cultivation of the vineyard while cultivating the character of his people. Indeed, whoever, in whatever degree or measure, has existed in faith and good action has been a worker in this vineyard.

“And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and he said to them: ‘You also go into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you.’ And they went. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hours and did likewise. About the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and he said to them: ‘Why are you standing here idle all day?’ They said to him: ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them: ‘You also go into my vineyard.’”

This householder, therefore, hires workers to cultivate his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. From the beginning to the end of the world he has never ceased predestining preachers to instruct the people of the faithful. The morning of the world was from Adam to Noah; the third hour from Noah to Abraham; the sixth from Abraham to Moses; the ninth from Moses to the coming of the Lord; and the eleventh from the coming of the Lord to the end of the world, during which the holy apostles were sent as preachers, and they received the full reward even though they came late.

The worker of the morning, the third, sixth, and ninth hours signifies that ancient Hebrew people which, in its elect, from the very beginning of the world, while striving to worship God with right faith, did not cease, as it were, to labor in cultivating the vineyard. At the eleventh hour the Gentiles are called, and to them it is said: “Why are you standing here idle all day?” For those who, after a long period of the world had passed, had neglected to labor for their life stood idle, as it were, all day.

Consider what they answer when questioned. They say: “Because no one has hired us.” No patriarch had come to them, no prophet. What does “No one has hired us for labor” mean except that no one preached to them the ways of life? What, then, shall we say in our defense, who cease from good work, when we have come to faith almost from our mother’s womb, heard the words of life from our very cradles, and drunk the nourishment of heavenly preaching from the breasts of holy Church together with the milk of the flesh?

We may also distinguish these same differences of hours according to the stages of life in each person. The morning is the childhood of our understanding. The third hour can be understood as adolescence, because the sun is already rising upward, as it were, while the warmth of age increases. The sixth is youth, because the sun seems fixed at the center while the fullness of strength is consolidated. The ninth signifies old age, in which the sun descends from its high axis, as age declines from the warmth of youth. The eleventh is the age called decrepit or very old. Hence the Greeks call the very old not γέροντας (*gerontas*) but πρεσβυτέρους (*presbyterous*), indicating that they are more than merely old.

Therefore, since one person is led to the good life in childhood, another in adolescence, another in youth, another in old age, and another in decrepitude, workers are called to the vineyard at different hours. For the one who lives for himself and feeds on the pleasures of his flesh is rightly reproved as idle, because he does not pursue the fruit of divine work. But whoever has neglected to live for God even until the final age has stood idle, as it were, until the eleventh hour. Hence it is rightly said to those who remain sluggish until the eleventh hour: “Why are you standing here idle all day?” As though it were openly said: “If you did not wish to live for God in youth and childhood, at least come to your senses in old age; and when you will soon have little time left to labor, come, even if late, to the ways of life.”

“But when evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: ‘Call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and ending with the first.’” (MAUR.) After the account of the day’s work had been rendered, when the appropriate time for announcing the promised reward had arrived, he says: “But when evening had come”—that is, when the day of the whole world had inclined toward the evening of its consummation, or when the end of any individual person was approaching. He explains a future time through the likeness of a past time. “The lord of the vineyard said to his steward,” and so forth.

Who can we understand this steward to be better than our Redeemer, to whom the Father gave all things into his hands? “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). He is rightly called a steward, because he arranges to repay the children of human beings with future goods for their good works. Of him the Apostle says: “Casting all our anxiety upon him, because he cares for us” (I Pet. V). He calls the workers and gives them their wages, because all human beings must be presented before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to him according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (II Cor. V).

As for what is subsequently said of the one who gives the reward—that he begins with the last and proceeds to the first—this often happens because those who came later are rewarded first: they depart from the body into the kingdom before those who seemed to have been called from childhood.

(Greg.) Did not the thief come at the eleventh hour? Although he had not come at the eleventh hour by reason of age, he nevertheless came late through punishment: he confessed the Lord on the cross and almost with the utterance of the sentence breathed out the spirit of life. The householder began to give the denarius from the last, because he called the thief to the rest of paradise before Peter. How many fathers existed before the Law, and how many under the Law? Yet those who were called at the Lord’s coming arrived at the kingdom of heaven without delay. Those who labored at the eleventh hour therefore received the same denarius as those who labored at the first, because those who came to the Lord at the end of the world received an equal reward of eternal life with those who had been called from the beginning of the world. Hence it follows:

“When those who had come about the eleventh hour arrived, they received a denarius each. When the first also came, they thought that they would receive more; but they too received a denarius each. And when they received it, they murmured against the householder, saying: ‘These last worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.’”

Those who were called from the beginning of the world and were destined to live here for a long time bore the burden of the day and the heat, because they necessarily endured the longer temptations of the flesh. For each person, to bear the burden of the day and the heat means to be wearied by the warmth of his flesh through the extended periods of a long life.

But it may be asked how those who were called to the kingdom only at the end are said to have murmured. No one who murmurs receives the kingdom of heaven, and no one who receives it can murmur. But because the ancient fathers, however justly they lived, were not led into the kingdom until the Lord descended—he who by the intervention of his death opened the barriers of paradise to human beings—their murmuring consists in this: they lived rightly in order to receive the kingdom, and yet they were delayed for a long time from receiving it. Since, after they had completed their righteousness, the places of hell received them, though tranquil, their experience was both to have labored in the vineyard and to have murmured. Thus, as though after murmuring, they received the denarius: after the long ages of hell, they arrived at the joys of the kingdom.

But we who come at the eleventh hour do not murmur after our labor, and we receive the denarius, because, coming into this world after the arrival of the Mediator, we are led into the kingdom as soon as we depart from the body—a kingdom that the ancient fathers received only after great labor.

But he answered one of them and said: “Friend, I am not doing you an injustice. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go.” (Jerome) I have read in a certain book that this friend, rebuked by the householder, is understood as the first-hour laborer, the first-created man, and those who believed in his time. “Did you not,” he says, “agree with me for a denarius?” The denarius bears the image of a king. You therefore received the wage I promised you—my image and likeness. What more do you seek? It is not so much that you yourself wish to receive more as that you do not want another to receive anything, as though the merit of your reward would be diminished by another’s fellowship. “Take what is yours and go.” The Jew is saved in the Law not by grace but by works: “For whoever does it will live by it” (Rom. II).

“But I wish to give to this last one also as to you.” (Hilary) Truly, the Jews had the evil eye—that is, the intention they had toward them; but the apostle Paul reproves them because they both killed the Lord Jesus and persecuted the prophets and us, and so forth (I Thess. II). (Maurus) The bestowal of the kingdom, therefore, is not a matter of human merit or rank, but a gift of divine goodness. Thus he rightly adds:

[Col. 1029B] “Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” For it is a foolish question for a human being to raise against God’s kindness. One ought not to ask whether he gave what he ought to give, but whether he failed to give what he ought to give. (Jerome) Something similar is heard in that parable of Luke, where the elder son envies the younger and does not want his repentant brother to be received, but accuses his father of injustice (Luke XV). (Gregory) Let no one exalt himself on account of his work, and let no one exalt himself on account of the time he has spent, since, when this saying has been completed, the Truth subsequently cries out:

“So the last will be first, and the first last.” (Hilary) Every former calling, therefore, envies the Gentiles, and they are tormented by the grace of the Gospel. Hence, concluding the parable, the Savior said:

[Col. 1029C] “The last will be first, and the first last.” The Jews will be turned from the head into the tail, and the Gentiles will be changed from the tail into the head. For Moses prophesied this in Deuteronomy: “The sojourner who is with you shall rise above you; he shall be the head, and you shall be the tail. He shall lend to you, and you shall not lend to him” (Deut. XXVIII). (Gregory) For even if we already know what good things, and how many, we have done, we still do not know with what subtlety the heavenly Judge examines them. Indeed, everyone ought to rejoice exceedingly in being in the kingdom of God, even if only last. Yet what follows is exceedingly terrifying:

“For many are called, but few are chosen.” For many come to the faith, but few are brought to the heavenly kingdom. Behold, how many of us gather for the festivals of the saints and fill the Church together; yet who knows how few are numbered in that flock of God’s chosen? Behold, the voice of all cries out to Christ, but the life of all does not cry out. Most follow the Lord with their voices but flee from him in their conduct. Hence Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus I). Hence James says: “Faith without works is useless” (James II). Hence, through the Psalmist, the Lord says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX). For when the Lord calls, the faithful are multiplied beyond number, because sometimes even those come to the faith who do not reach the number of the chosen. They have been mingled with the faithful in their confession, but because of their reprobate life they do not deserve to be numbered there in the lot of the faithful.

This fold of the holy Church receives both kids and lambs, but, as the Gospel testifies, when the Judge comes he separates the good from the evil, just as a shepherd separates the sheep from the kids (Matt. XXV). Those who here serve the pleasures of their flesh cannot there be numbered among the flock of sheep. There the Judge separates from the lot of the humble those who here exalt themselves on the horns of pride. Those who here, though placed within the heavenly faith, seek earth with their whole desire cannot receive the kingdom of heaven. We see many such people within the Church, but we must neither imitate them nor despair of them. For we see what someone is today, but we do not know what he will be tomorrow. Often someone who comes after us surpasses us through the vigor of his good work, and we scarcely catch up with the one whom today we seemed to precede.

Certainly, when Stephen was dying for the faith, Saul was guarding the garments of those who were stoning him (Acts VII). Thus he himself stoned him with everyone’s hands, because he made all the hands of the stoners ready. Yet the very man whom he made a martyr by persecuting him later surpassed him in the labors of the holy Church.

There are therefore two things that we must weigh carefully, because many are called but few are chosen. First, no one should presume on himself in the least, because even if he has already been called to the faith, he does not know whether he is worthy of the eternal kingdom. Second, no one should dare despair of a neighbor whom he perhaps sees lying in vices, because he does not know the riches of divine mercy.

## II. Jesus Foretells His Passion

And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside privately and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death.”

Our Redeemer, foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be disturbed by his passion, foretells to them long beforehand both the punishment of that passion and the glory of the resurrection, so that when they saw him dying as had been predicted, they would not doubt that he would also rise. (Jerome) He had often said this very thing to the disciples; but because what they had heard could slip from their memory amid many intervening discussions, as he was about to go to Jerusalem and take the apostles with him, he prepared them for the trial, so that when the persecution and disgrace of the cross came, they would not be scandalized.

“And they will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged, [Col. 1030D] and crucified, and on the third day he will rise.” (Maurus) Judas handed the Lord over to the Jews, and they themselves handed him over to the Gentiles—to Pilate and the authority of the Romans. Hence it is written: “They brought him bound and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor.” Pilate, however, seized Jesus and flogged him; and the soldiers, plaiting a crown of thorns, placed it on his head, wrapped him in a purple garment, and came to him saying, “Hail, King of the Jews,” and they struck him with their hands (Matt. XXVI). But all this disgrace was emptied of its power by the heavenly glory of the resurrection, because his flesh did not see corruption; rather, openly triumphing, he rose in glory, abolishing all principalities and powers.

[Col. 1031A] Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him with her sons, worshiping and asking something of him. He said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.”

(Jerome) Where did the mother of the sons of Zebedee get her expectation of the kingdom, so that when the Lord had said, “The Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death, and they will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged, and crucified,” and had announced the disgrace of his passion to the disciples who feared it, she should ask for the glory of the triumphant one? I think the reason was that afterward the Lord had said, “And on the third day he will rise.” The woman thought that immediately after the resurrection he would reign, and that what is promised at the second coming would first be fulfilled. Thus, with feminine eagerness, she desired the present, forgetful of the future.

When the Lord asks her, and when, in response to her request, he says, “What do you want?” this does not arise from ignorance but from his dispensation, so that, when her request had been brought forward and heard by the others, he himself might have an occasion to respond and teach—just as when he said, amid a great multitude, “Who touched me?” (Matt. IX), and concerning Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?” (John XI). The mother of the sons of Zebedee made her request through a woman’s error and an affection of piety, not knowing what she was asking. Nor is it surprising that she should be charged with ignorance, since Peter is said to have wanted to make three tents without knowing what he was saying (Matt. XVII).

But Jesus answered and said: “You do not know what you are asking.” [Col. 1031C] The mother makes the request, but the Lord speaks to the disciples, understanding that her plea arose from the will of her sons. (Rabanus) Those who seek from the Lord a seat of glory that they have not yet deserved do not know what they are asking. The summit of honor already delighted them, but first the way of labor had to exercise them. (John Chrysostom) They desired to reign sublimely with Christ, but first they had to suffer humbly for Christ: a good desire, but an inconsiderate request. Therefore, although they ought not to obtain what they asked, the simplicity of their request did not deserve to be put to shame. For this reason he did not condemn their will or intention, but reproved only their ignorance, saying: “You do not know what you are asking.”

“Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” [Col. 1031D] They say to him, “We can.” (Rabanus) By the name of the cup, or of baptism, he designates the passion of martyrdom by which it was fitting for both him and them to be brought to completion. Hence elsewhere he speaks of his passion: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished” (Luke XX); and, approaching that same passion, he prayed, saying, “Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me.” He said to them:

“You will indeed drink my cup” (Luke XXII). (Jerome) It is asked how James and John, the sons of Zebedee, drank the cup of martyrdom, or how they were baptized with the Lord’s baptism, since Scripture relates that only the apostle James was beheaded by Herod, while John ended his life by a natural death. But if we read the ecclesiastical histories, in which it is reported that John too, for the sake of martyrdom, was sent into a cauldron of boiling oil and emerged from it as Christ’s athlete to receive the crown, and was immediately exiled to the island of Patmos, we shall see that he did not lack the spirit of martyrdom and that John drank the cup of confession, which the three young men also drank in the furnace of fire, although the persecutor did not shed his blood.

But when he adds:

“But to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give to you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father”—

(Rabanus) this should be understood as follows: The kingdom of heaven is not a matter of the giver but of the receiver. For there is no favoritism with God; whoever presents himself as worthy of the kingdom of heaven will receive it. It has been prepared not for a person but for a way of life. If, therefore, you are such as to attain the kingdom of heaven that my Father has prepared for those who triumph, you too will receive it.

Again:

“It is not mine to give to you, but to those for whom it has been prepared.” (Augustine) It is not mine to give to the proud—for such you still were—but if you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are. It has been prepared for others; become others, and it has been prepared for you. What does “Become others” mean? First humble yourselves, you who already wish to be exalted.

And when the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers. (Jerome) The ten apostles were not indignant at the mother of the sons of Zebedee, nor did they attribute the boldness of the request to the woman, but to the sons, who had burned with immoderate desire while ignorant of their own measure, to whom the Lord had said, “You do not know what you are asking.” It is implied, either from the Lord’s response or from the apostles’ indignation, that the sons had sent their mother to make a grand request.

But Jesus called them to him and said: “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority over them. It will not be so among you. Rather, whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant. And whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave.”

The humble and gentle teacher neither rebukes the two who asked out of immoderate desire nor reproves the other ten for indignation and envy. Instead, he offers an example by which he teaches that the greater is the one who has been lesser, and that the one who is servant of all becomes lord. In vain, therefore, had the former sought excessively, or had the latter grieved over the desire for superiority, since one reaches the summit of the virtues not by power but by humility.

Finally, he sets forth an example, so that if they valued his words too little, they might blush before his deeds, and he says:

“Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve.”

Notice that we have often said that the one who serves is called the Son of Man.

“And to give his life as a ransom for many.”

When he took the form of a servant, he did so in order to pour out his blood for the world. He did not say, “to give his life as a ransom for all,” but “for many”—for those who would wish to believe.

## III. The Healing of the Two Blind Men

And as they were going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him; and behold, two blind men sitting beside the road heard that Jesus was passing by, and they cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.”

(Augustine) Mark also records this, but as having happened to one blind man. The question is resolved in the same way as the question concerning the two men who were suffering from a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes (Mark IX). For it is very well known that, of the two blind men whom he has just introduced, one was especially famous and widely known in that city. This is also sufficiently clear from the fact that Mark records both his name and his father’s name. Such a thing does not readily occur among the many whom the Lord healed above, except when he also gives by name Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, whose daughter Jesus raised. This makes the same interpretation still more evident, because that ruler of the synagogue was certainly a prominent man in that place.

Without doubt, therefore, that Bartimaeus whom Mark mentions, the son of Timaeus, was someone cast down from great prosperity and reduced to a misery that was especially well known and notorious, because he was not only blind but also sat begging. This is why Mark wished to mention him alone: his illumination brought as great a reputation to the miracle as his calamity had possessed notoriety.

(Jerome) Jericho is the city that Joshua destroyed after crossing the Jordan, killing its king (Josh. VI). In its place Ahiel of Bethel, of the tribe of Ephraim, built another city (III Kings XVI), which the Lord and Savior graciously honored by his presence. But this city too, at the time when Jerusalem was being attacked by the Romans, was captured and destroyed because of the faithlessness of its inhabitants. A third city was built, which still exists today, and the traces of both former cities are displayed to the present day.

Jericho, which is said to be interpreted as “moon,” signifies the waning of our mutability and mortality. This became especially clear from that parable of the Gospel in which a man descending from Jerusalem fell among robbers in Jericho (Luke X); after being wounded and stripped by them, he was restored to salvation through the compassionate diligence of the Samaritan. For clearly the human race, falling through a deadly corruption from the vision of supreme peace into desires for this world, is led back by the Lord Savior to the life it had lost through wandering.

There were many robbers in Jericho who were accustomed to go out and kill or wound those descending from Jerusalem. For this reason the Lord came to Jericho with his disciples, to free the wounded and draw a great crowd with him. Finally, after he wished to leave Jericho, a great crowd followed him. If he had remained in Jerusalem and had never descended to the lowly, the crowd would still be sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death.

There were also two blind men beside the road. He calls those blind who were not yet able to say, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). He says “beside the road” because they seemed to possess knowledge of the Law, but they did not know the way, which is Christ. Most understand them as the Pharisees and Sadducees. Others understand them as both peoples—the people of the Old Testament and the people of the New—because one, following the written Law, and the other, following natural law, was blind without Christ.

These men, who could not see by themselves, heard the proclamations of the Savior and confessed him to be the Son of David. As the Lord, his disciples, and a very great multitude were departing from Jericho, two blind men sat beside the road. For when the Lord ascended to heaven, and many of the faithful followed him—indeed, when all the elect from the beginning of the world entered the gate of the heavenly kingdom together with him—both peoples, long blinded by faithlessness, immediately began, after hearing of the Savior’s coming, to have hope of their own salvation and illumination. Through the pursuit of a saving desire, they strove to reach the point of investigating and seeking what the true worship was.

But the crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent. Yet they cried out all the more, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.”

They had to cry out until they overcame the noise of the crowd resisting them—that is, they had to apply themselves to praying and knocking with such perseverance that they might overcome either the habit of carnal desires, which, like a crowd, obstructs the mind striving to see the light of eternal truth, or the very crowd of carnal people that impedes spiritual pursuits, overcoming it by the strongest concentration.

When the blind men heard that Jesus was passing by, they begged him to have mercy on them. Although many tried to prevent them, they did not desist from crying out, because the peoples of the Gentiles, having learned the fame of Christ’s name, sought to become partakers of him. Many opposed them: first the Jews, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles; then the Gentiles too, who often pressed upon them with fiercer and stronger persecution, so that the world, which was to be illuminated and healed, would not invoke Christ. Yet the mad fury of those who attacked them could not deprive those who had been predestined for eternal life of the salvation appointed for them.

And Jesus stopped and called them, and said: “What do you want me to do for you?” They said to him: “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.”

(Jerome) They were blind and did not know where they were going; they could not follow the Savior. There were many pits in Jericho, many cliffs and precipices. Therefore the Lord stops so that they may be able to come, and he commands them to be called so that the crowd may not prevent them. He asks them as though he did not know what they wanted, so that the weakness manifested in the blind men’s confession might be made clear and his power might be recognized through the remedy.

(Gregory) Behold, the one who had previously been passing by now stands still. In this he suggests something to us that can usefully be understood of both his humanity and his divinity. For, while passing by, he heard the blind man crying out, but, standing still, he bestowed the miracle of illumination. What is it to hear while passing by and to restore light while standing still, except that in his humanity he had compassion, while through the power of his divinity he drove away from us the darkness of our mind?

For he who was born and suffered for us, who rose again and ascended into heaven, is Jesus who passed by, because this action is temporal. But he illuminated the blind man while standing still, because, unlike that temporal dispensation, the eternity of the Word did not pass away; remaining in itself, it renews all things. To stand belongs to God: in unchanging thought to dispose all mutable things. Therefore, he who heard the voices of those asking while passing by restored light while standing still, because although he endured temporal things for us, he nevertheless granted us light from that which does not know the passage of mutability.

And Jesus, having compassion on them, touched their eyes, and immediately they saw, and they followed him.

(Jerome) He touches their eyes and the craftsman supplies what nature had not given. Or rather, in his mercy he gives back what weakness had taken away. Immediately they saw and followed him. Those who had previously sat crippled in Jericho and had known only how to cry out afterward followed Jesus—not so much with their feet as with their virtues.

(Gregory) The one who sees and follows Jesus is the one who does the good he understands. He sees but does not follow when he understands the good but refuses to do it well. For he follows Jesus who imitates him. Hence he says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John XII).

Let us therefore consider by what path he walks, so that we may deserve to follow him. Behold, although he is Lord and creator of angels, he came into the womb of the Virgin, assuming the nature that he had created. He nevertheless chose to be born in this world; he did not choose wealthy parents but poor ones. Hence the lamb to be offered for him was lacking, and his mother found young pigeons and a pair of turtledoves for the sacrifice.

He did not wish to prosper in this world. He endured reproaches and mockeries, spitting, scourging, blows, a crown of thorns, and the cross. And because we have fallen from inner joy through delight in bodily things, he showed with what bitterness one returns there.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On Jesus’ Entry into Jerusalem and the Expulsion of the Sellers from the Temple; on the Pharisees’ Indignation at the Children Crying “Hosanna”; on the Withered Fig Tree and John the Baptist, etc.

And when they had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives—

(Jerome) Jesus goes out from Jericho, leading away from it a very great number of crowds and restoring health to the blind. He approaches Jerusalem enriched with great rewards. Having granted salvation to believers, he wishes to enter the city of peace, the place of the vision of God, and the fortress of the watchman: “When they had drawn near,” he says, “to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage,” and so forth.

In Luke it is written: “When he had drawn near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mountain called the Mount of Olives” (Luke XIX). Bethphage was a village of the priests on the Mount of Olives. Bethany was also a small village or town on the slope of the same mountain, about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, as the evangelist John makes clear. There Lazarus was raised from the dead, and the church now built there displays his tomb.

Bethphage means “house of the mouth” or “house of the cheeks.” Bethany is called “house of obedience.” The Savior, as he came to Jerusalem, exalted these places by the honor of his presence, because before his passion he filled many people, through his teaching, with the gifts of devout confession and spiritual obedience.

These beautiful towns are said to have been situated on the Mount of Olives—that is, in the Lord himself, who refreshes us with the anointing of spiritual gifts and with the light of knowledge and piety. Hence, when elsewhere he said, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden,” he immediately added, “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel” (Matt. V). For that same Mount of Olives—that is, the highest distributor of spiritual graces—which exalts its city so that it may stand out, also kindles it with the oil of gladness so that it may be able to shine. And because that same light did not wish to be placed under a bushel, the evangelist immediately added:

Then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them: “Go into the village that is opposite you.”

He took care to send two disciples into the village that was opposite them—that is, teachers who, by preaching, would penetrate the unlearned and barbarous shores of the whole world like the walls of a village set before them. It was right that two should be sent, either because of the knowledge of truth and purity of works, or because the mystery of the twofold love—of God and of neighbor—was to be preached throughout the whole world.

(Chrysostom) Some interpret these two as the apostles Peter and Philip, because they were the first to cross the boundaries of the Jews and bring the Gentiles to Christ. Philip brought Samaria—which is itself interpreted as “she-ass”—while Peter, receiving the Gentiles, took Cornelius from among the Gentiles as the foal of Samaria.

“And immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.”

(Venantius) Entering the world, the preachers found the people of the nations entangled in the bonds of faithlessness. Each person was bound by the cords of his sins—and not only the nations but also the Jews. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III).

Hence, fittingly, Matthew also finds a donkey tied together with its colt. The donkey, which had been subjected and tamed and had borne the yoke of the Law, signifies the synagogue. The wild and free colt of the donkey represents the people of the nations, on whom no human being had ever sat—that is, no rational teacher had imposed the bridle of correction by which he might restrain their tongue from evil or compel them to walk along the narrow way of life. No one, by offering sound advice, had given them the garments of salvation by which they might be warmed spiritually. A human being would have sat upon it if someone, using reason to suppress and correct its folly, had done so.

Therefore the two disciples sent to bring the animals to the Lord can rightly be understood, in accordance with the example of the preceding parable, as the two orders of preachers: one sent to the Gentiles, the other to the circumcision.

(Chrysostom) For because of certain such similarities, human beings who did not know God or the Son of God are here compared with animals. This is an unclean animal, and, more than almost any other beast of burden, irrational, foolish, weak, lowly, and especially burden-bearing. Such were human beings before Christ: unclean through idolatries and passions, irrational because they lacked the reason of the Word, and foolish in relation to God.

(Venantius) It should be noted that the three evangelists who wrote in the Greek language mention only the colt. Matthew alone, who wrote his Gospel in Hebrew and in Hebrew speech, also reports that the donkey was untied and brought to the Lord, to show that the salvation of that same Hebrew people too should not be despaired of if it repents.

“Untie them,” he says, “and bring them to me.” For “whatever you loose on earth will have been loosed also in heaven” (John XX).

“And if anyone says anything to you, say: ‘The Lord needs them,’ and immediately he will let them go.”

(Chrysostom) “If anyone,” he says, “says anything to you, say: ‘The Lord desires their service.’” Do not say, “your lord,” or “our lord,” or “the lord of the animals,” so that all may understand that I alone am Lord—not only of the animals, nor only of those who are subject to me, but of all human beings, even those who oppose me. For sinners are mine by their created condition, but by their will they belong to the devil. “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. XLIX).

“The Lord desires their service.” It is right that at some time the creature should serve its maker. For a time God left the Gentiles under the power of the devil, so that he might test them; he did not despise them forever in order to destroy them. But what is written must be fulfilled: “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord.”

(Jerome) The donkey was bound by many bonds of sins; the wild colt, too, uncontrolled by the bridle, had many masters together with its mother, according to Luke’s Gospel, being subject not to one error or doctrine. Yet the many masters who claimed unlawful authority for themselves, seeing the true Lord and his servants who had come to untie them, did not dare resist.

All this happened so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled:

“Tell the daughter of Zion.”

(Bede) Historically, the daughter of Zion is Jerusalem, the city situated on Mount Zion. Mystically, however, the daughter of Zion is the Church of the faithful, belonging to the heavenly Jerusalem, “which is the mother of us all” (Gal. IV), whose portion at that time was not insignificant among the people of Israel.

“Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting on a donkey and on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.”

“Behold,” he says, “your king comes to you, meek,” and so forth. “Behold” is the word of one pointing something out: that is, see—not with bodily sight, but with spiritual understanding behold the works of his virtues; do not look merely at the outward form of his appearance. If you look at his outward form, you will be deceived by his human nature. But if you consider his work, you will be saved by his divine power.

Do not say, “We have no king except Caesar alone” (John XIX). “Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting on a donkey.” If you understand, he comes to you; if you do not understand, he will come against you. That is, if you understand, he will come to save you and will subjugate the nations beneath your feet, so that you may say joyfully through the Prophet: “For God is the Most High, awesome, and a great king over all the earth; he has subjected peoples beneath us and nations beneath our feet. He chose us as his inheritance, the splendor of Jacob whom he loved” (Ps. XLVI).

But if you do not understand, he will come to destroy you, drive you from the temple of holiness, and bring another, more chaste bride from the Gentiles into the chamber of his holiness.

Would you know the meekness of the one who comes? Consider the appearance of his coming (Job XXX). He does not sit in a golden chariot shining with costly purple. He does not mount a fiery horse, a lover of discord and strife, whose breast is filled with the glory of boastfulness, who smells battle from afar and rejoices at the sound of the trumpet, and who, when he sees bloody combat, says in his heart, “Well done.” Rather, he sits upon a donkey, a friend of tranquility and peace.

You do not see shining swords or other terrible ornaments of weapons around him. But what do you see? Leafy branches, testimonies of piety. He comes meek, therefore, not to be feared because of his power but to be loved because of his gentleness, sitting on a donkey and a colt—that is, on mother and son.

(Jerome) It should be noted that this testimony is written in the prophet Zechariah (Zech. IX). Yet it must be understood that, according to the literal sense, the Lord could not have sat upon both animals within such a short span of time. Either he sat upon the donkey, with the colt remaining without a rider, or, if—as is more fitting—he used the colt for riding, the donkey was led free.

Therefore, since the historical account either contains an impossibility or something unbecoming, we are led to higher meanings, so that this donkey, which had been subjected, tamed, and had borne the yoke of the Law, may be understood as the synagogue. The wild and free colt of the donkey is the people of the Gentiles, upon whom Jesus sat—that is, in whose hearts he dwelt, saying, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI)—having sent to them two of his disciples, one to the circumcision and the other to the Gentiles.

The disciples went and did as he commanded them, and they brought the donkey and the colt.

That the apostles, going out, untied another’s donkey was indeed their ministry, but the power and authority belonged to Christ. They could not have taken an animal belonging to another master who did not know who they were, unless the superior Spirit of Christ had prepared its master’s heart to give it. Thus, when the apostles untied Jews and Gentiles from the enemy’s bond, this appeared at first sight to be their work, but in reality it was Christ’s power and grace. For the twelve established by Christ could not have loosed the whole world, bound under the devil’s power, unless Christ’s grace had broken the enemy’s strength.

It should be noted, however, that Mark writes that the colt was found outside, before the gate, at a crossroads (Mark XI). The gate is he himself who says, “I am the gate of the sheep; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out and find pasture” [Col. 1038D] (John X). This colt—that is, the people of the Gentiles—lacked these pastures of life when it still stood tied outside this gate at a crossroads. It was rightly at a crossroads, because it did not hold firmly to one way of life or faith but followed astray the many uncertain hills of sects.

And they placed their garments upon them, and made him sit on them.

The apostles’ garments are the divine commandments and spiritual grace. For just as the shame of nakedness is covered by clothing, so the natural evils of our flesh are covered by commandments and divine grace.

(Jerome) This colt and donkey, upon which the apostles spread their garments so that Jesus might sit more gently, were naked before the Savior’s coming. Many who claimed dominion over them left them exposed and shivering without covering. But after they received the apostles’ garments, they became more beautiful and had the Lord as their rider.

For, as was said above, the apostolic garment may be understood either as the teaching of the virtues or as the exposition of the Scriptures, or as the varieties of ecclesiastical doctrines. Unless the soul has been instructed and adorned with these, it does not deserve to have the Lord as its rider.

And a very great crowd spread their garments on the road.

Observe the difference among the various persons. The apostles place their garments upon the colt; the crowd, which is of lesser status, spreads them beneath the donkey’s feet, so that it may not strike against a stone, tread upon a thorn, or slip into a pit.

While the donkey carries the Lord, many spread their garments on the road, because the holy martyrs, stripping themselves of the clothing of their own flesh, prepare the way with their blood for the simpler servants of God, so that they may walk with an unhindered step of mind toward the walls of the heavenly city, where Jesus leads them.

(Gregory) Again, our Savior goes toward Jerusalem while seated on a little donkey when, governing the soul of each believer, he leads his own beast of burden to the inner vision of peace. He sits upon the beast also when he presides over the holy Church as a whole and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace. Many spread their garments on the road because they tame their bodies through abstinence, preparing a way for him to the mind or offering good examples to those who follow.

But others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.

They cut leaves or branches from the trees who select words and sayings of the fathers from their teaching of truth and, through humble preaching, lay these down on the way of God and before the soul of the hearer who is approaching.

The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest.” The Jewish people went before, while the Gentiles followed. And because all the elect—whether those who could be found in Judaea or those who now exist in the Church—have believed and do believe in the mediator between God and human beings, both those who go before and those who follow cried out, “Hosanna.” *Hosanna* means “save us” in Latin. Therefore, no one should suppose that it is composed of two words, namely, one Greek and one Hebrew; rather, it is entirely Hebrew and signifies that Christ’s coming is the salvation of the world. Hence it also follows: [Col. 1039D]

“Blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord,” as the Savior himself also confirms the same thing in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John 5).

[Gregory] From him the earlier generations sought salvation, and those of the present seek it; and they confess as blessed him who comes in the name of the Lord, since there is one hope and one faith among the peoples who go before and those who follow. For just as those people were healed through his anticipated passion and resurrection, so we are saved through his past passion and his resurrection, which endures forever. The one whom our predecessors from the Jewish people believed and loved as the one who was to come, we believe and love as having come, and we are inflamed with desire for him, so that we may behold him face to face. [Col. 1040A] Moreover, in the addition “Hosanna,” that is, “salvation in the highest,” it is clearly shown that Christ’s coming is not merely the salvation of human beings but of the whole world, joining earthly things to heavenly things, so that “every knee should bow to him, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2).

And when he had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” But the crowds were saying: “This is Jesus the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.” As Jesus entered the city with the crowd of Jerusalem, the city was stirred, wondering at the multitude but not knowing the truth, and saying: “Who is this?” We read that the same question was asked elsewhere by the angels: “Who is this King of glory?” (Psalm 23). While others were either doubting or asking, the lowly common people confess him, beginning with lesser things so as to arrive at greater ones, and say: “This is Jesus the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee” (Deuteronomy 18). Moses had also said that this prophet would come, like himself. [Col. 1040B]

And Jesus entered the temple of God.

(Rabanus) By entering the temple first after coming into the city, he gives us beforehand an example of the religious practice that we should follow: whenever we happen to enter a village, town, or any other place in which there is a place of prayer consecrated to God, we should first turn aside to it; and after commending ourselves to the Lord through earnest prayer, we should then withdraw to attend to the temporal business for which we came. As the time of his passion approached, the Lord wished to draw near to the place of his passion and remain close to it, so that, at the time established and determined before the ages, he might be found there by those through whom his passion was to be completed. [Col. 1040C] By this he also made clear to all who heard him that he would undergo death not unwillingly, as the impious supposed, but of his own accord: as the hour approached, he fearlessly went to the place in which he had long before foretold, both through himself and through the mouths of his prophets, that he would suffer.

It should be noted that this entrance of his into Jerusalem took place five days before Passover, during which he had determined to fulfill the mystery of his most holy passion. For John relates that six days before Passover he came to Bethany, where a supper was prepared for him and, while many were reclining at table, Mary, Lazarus’s sister, anointed him with mystical ointment; and on the following day, seated on a donkey and met by a very large crowd with palm branches, he came to Jerusalem (John 12). [Col. 1040D]

Here we must not pass over the concord not only of events but also of the times of the Old and New Testaments, of shadow and reality, of the Law and the Gospel. For it is written in the Law, when the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the entire assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: On the tenth day of this month, let each one take a lamb for his families and households.” And shortly afterward: “You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening” (Exodus 12).

Therefore, on the tenth day of the first month, [Col. 1041A] the great one who was to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be brought into the house, because on the tenth day of that same month—that is, five days before Passover—the Lord was to enter the city in which he would suffer. And just as a lamb chosen from the whole flock awaited the appointed day of its sacrifice, so the Lord, while the entire council of elders and chief men conspired against him, awaited with certainty the hour at which he would offer himself to God as an offering and sacrifice for the salvation of the world, as a fragrance of sweetness.

The lamb was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month in the evening. At that same hour, the Lord ate the lamb with his disciples; when he had fulfilled the ordinances of the legal Passover, he immediately went out with them to the place of prayer, where he was seized and bound by the Jews and began the sacraments of his blessed sacrifice. [Col. 1041B]

## II

And he was driving out all who were selling and buying in the temple; he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, and said to them: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.”

(Jerome) Accompanied by the crowd of believers, which had spread its garments so that the colt might proceed without injury to its feet, Jesus entered the temple. He drove out all who were selling and buying in the temple, overturned the tables of the money-changers, and scattered the seats of those selling doves. Then, producing testimony from the holy Scriptures, he said to them that his Father’s house ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of robbers or a house of commerce, as another evangelist also records him saying.

First, it must be understood that, in accordance with the commands of the Law, [Col. 1041C] innumerable victims were sacrificed in the Lord’s most august temple in the whole world, to which people from nearly every region of the Jews flocked together—especially on feast days: bulls, rams, and goats. Poorer people, so that they would not be without a sacrifice, offered young pigeons and turtledoves. It often happened that those who had come from far away did not have victims.

The priests therefore devised a way to prey upon the people: they sold all the animals needed for sacrifices, so that they could sell them to those who had none and then themselves receive back what they had sold. Their scheme was frequently disrupted by the poverty of those who came, for they needed money and not only had no victims but did not even have the means to buy birds or inexpensive offerings. [Col. 1041D]

They therefore also installed money-changers who would lend money under this guarantee. But since the Law commanded that no one should receive interest (Leviticus 25), and money lent at interest could not be profitable if it yielded no gain and sometimes even involved losing the principal, they devised another trick: instead of money-changers, they made them *collybistae*, a word whose precise sense the Latin language does not express.

In Greek it is said: τῶν κολλυβιστῶν ἐξέχει τὸ κέρμα, that is, “he drove out the money of the money-changers.” *Κόλλυβος* or *κόλλιβος* refers among them to what we call inexpensive little offerings—for example, fried chickpeas, raisins, and fruits of various kinds.

Therefore, since the *collybistae* who had lent money could not receive interest, they accepted various commodities as interest, so that what was not permitted in money they might demand in goods bought with money—as though Ezekiel had not guarded against precisely this when he said: “He shall not take interest and increase” (Ezekiel 18). [Col. 1042A]

When the Lord saw this kind of commerce, or robbery, in his Father’s house, stirred by the fervor of the Spirit, in accordance with what is written in Psalm 68, “Zeal for your house has consumed me,” he made himself a whip from cords and drove such a great multitude of people from the temple, saying: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.”

For he is a robber, and he turns the temple of God into a den of robbers, who pursues profit from religion, so that his worship is not so much worship of God as an opportunity for commerce. This is according to the historical sense.

But according to the mystical interpretations, Jesus enters the temple of the Father every day and drives out all alike—bishops, presbyters, deacons, laypeople, and the whole crowd—from the Church, treating sellers and buyers equally as guilty of one crime; for it is written: “You received without payment; give without payment.” [Col. 1042B]

He also overturns the tables of the money-changers. Observe that, because of the greed of the priests, the altars of God are called the tables of money-changers. He overturns the seats of those selling doves: those who sell the grace of the Holy Spirit and do everything so that they may devour the peoples subject to them. Of such people it is said: “They devour my people as they devour bread” (Psalm 13).

According to the literal understanding, the doves were not in seats but in stalls, unless perhaps the sellers of doves were sitting in seats—which is entirely absurd, since in the seats of teachers dignity is chiefly signified. That dignity is indeed reduced to nothing when it has been mixed with profits.

(Gregory) Who are those in the temple of God today who sell doves, except those who in the Church accept a price for the laying on of hands, through which laying on the Holy Spirit is given from heaven? A dove is therefore sold because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price. [Col. 1042C] But the Redeemer overturns the seats of those selling doves, because he destroys the priesthood of such merchants. Hence the sacred canons condemn the Simoniac heresy and command that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. The seat of those selling doves is therefore overturned because those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood, both in the eyes of human beings and in the eyes of God.

(Jerome) What we have said about churches, let each person understand of himself. For the apostle Paul says: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3; 2 Corinthians 6). Let there be no commerce in the house of your heart, no business dealings of buyers and sellers, no desire for houses, lest Jesus enter angry and severe. He cleanses his temple only by applying the whip, so that from a den of robbers and a house of commerce he may make it a house of prayer. [Col. 1042D]

(Gregory) They make the house of prayer a den of robbers who know how to stand in the temple for this purpose: either to pursue bodily those who do not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who do give them. The temple and house of God is also the very mind and conscience of the faithful. When it sometimes brings forth wicked thoughts to harm a neighbor, robbers sit, as it were, in a den and kill those who walk innocently, whenever they thrust swords into those who are guilty of no harm. [Col. 1043A] The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of robbers when, having abandoned innocence and the simplicity of holiness, it seeks to do something by which it can harm its neighbor.

And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.

(Augustine) He displayed the power of his strength in the temple before his slanderers, so that what they proclaimed in words he might demonstrate by deeds, as though he were a witness to their voice.

(Rabanus) He healed the blind so that they might see by looking, and so that their bodily illumination might become for them a spiritual lamp of the heart. [Col. 1043B] He healed the lame so that those who limped in faith might run to Christ, so that those who saw might receive better feet than those who were being healed.

But when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonders that he had done, and the children crying out in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they were indignant and said to him: “Do you hear what these people are saying?”

Most people think that the greatest of the signs was that Lazarus was raised, that the man blind from birth received light, that a voice was heard at the Jordan, and that, transfigured on the mountain, he displayed the glory of one who triumphs. To me, among all the signs that he performed, this seems more wonderful: that one man—despised at that time and so lowly that he was afterward crucified—when the scribes and Pharisees were raging against him and saw their profits being destroyed, was able with the blows of a single whip to drive out such a multitude, overturn tables, break seats, and do other things that an innumerable army could not have done. [Col. 1043C]

For something fiery and star-like radiated from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity shone upon his face. Since the priests did not dare to lay hands on him, they merely slandered his works; and they turned the testimony of the people and the children, who cried out, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” into an accusation, evidently because they claimed that this could be said only of the Son of God.

Let bishops, therefore, and holy people of any kind see how great a danger it is for them to allow these things to be said of themselves, since they were charged as a crime against the Lord, to whom they were truly said, because the faith of believers was not yet firmly established. [Col. 1043B]

But Jesus said to them: “Certainly. Have you never read: ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Psalm 8.)

How moderately he tempers his statement and his reply!
