So that the accusation would not be exposed from either side, [Al., “and the reply, inclining in both directions, would not be open to accusation,”] he did not say what the scribes wanted to hear: “The children are right to bear witness to me”; nor, again: “They were children; you ought to pardon their age.” Instead, he produces an example from the eighth Psalm, so that, while the Lord remained silent, the testimony of Scripture might confirm the children’s words.

## III

And leaving them, he went out beyond the city to Bethany, and stayed there.

He left the unbelievers and, going out from the city of those who contradicted him, went to Bethany, which is interpreted as “house of obedience,” already prefiguring the calling of the Gentiles; and he stayed there because he could not remain in Israel. [Col. 1044A] It should also be understood that he was so poor and flattered no one so completely that in the great city he found no host and no lodging, but lived in a small countryside village with Lazarus and his sisters. Their village, in fact, is Bethany.

In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he was hungry. Seeing a single fig tree beside the road, he went to it and found nothing on it except leaves, and he said to it: “May no fruit ever come from you again.” And the fig tree immediately withered.

When the darkness of night had been dispelled, the light of morning was shining, and midday was approaching—the time at which the Lord was to illuminate the world through his passion—as he was returning to the city, he was hungry, either showing the reality of human flesh or hungering for the salvation of believers and thirsting for Israel’s faith. [Col. 1044B]

When he saw a single tree, which we understand as the synagogue and the assembly of the Jews, standing beside the road because they did not believe in the Way, he came to it as it stood, fixed and immovable, without the feet of the Gospel. He found nothing in it except leaves: the noise of promises, Pharisaic traditions, boasting about the Law, and verbal ornament without any fruits of truth.

Hence another evangelist says: “For it was not yet the season” (Mark 11)—either because the time of Israel’s salvation had not yet come, since the people of the Gentiles had not yet entered, or because the time of faith had passed, since when he first came to that people and was rejected, he had passed over to the nations. [Col. 1044C]

And he said to it: “May no fruit ever come from you,” either “forever” or “for an age.” The Greek word *αἰών* signifies both. And the fig tree withered because, while the Lord was hungry, it did not possess the food he desired. Its leaves withered in such a way that the trunk itself remained and, although the branches were broken, the root lived; at the end of time, if they should wish to believe, shoots of faith may spring forth from it. And what is said is fulfilled: “There is hope for a tree.”

When the disciples saw this, they wondered, saying: “How did the fig tree wither immediately?”

(Augustine) It is understood that it did not wither at the time when they saw it, but immediately when it was cursed. For they did not see it withering but completely withered, and thus they understood that it had withered immediately at the Lord’s word. [Col. 1044B]

According to the literal sense, the Lord, who was to suffer among the peoples and bear the scandal of the cross, ought to mark the disciples’ minds beforehand by the anticipation of a sign. Hence the disciples marvel, saying: “How did the fig tree wither immediately?” The Savior could therefore, by the same power, have withered his enemies as well, had he not awaited their salvation through patience.

But Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen I say to you: If you have faith and do not waver, you will do not only what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Take yourself up and throw yourself into the sea,’ it will happen.”

Gentiles who have written insults against the Church commonly reproach us by saying that we have not had complete faith in God, because we have never been able to move mountains. They should be answered that not everything done in the Church has been written down, just as Scripture also testifies concerning the deeds of Christ himself, our God and Lord. Thus it could also have happened that, if necessity had demanded it, a mountain might have been removed from the land and cast into the sea. [Col. 1045A]

We read that something similar happened through the prayers of the blessed father Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a man distinguished in merits and virtues: a mountain yielded its place on the land only as much as the inhabitants of the city needed.

For when he wished to build a church in a suitable place and saw that it was narrower than the circumstances required—because on one side a rocky cliff by the sea and on the other a nearby mountain confined it—he came to the place at night and, kneeling, reminded God of his promise, asking him to move the mountain farther away in accordance with the faith of the petitioner. [Col. 1045B] In the morning, when he returned, he found that the mountain had left as much space for the builders of the church as they had needed.

Therefore, he could have obtained this; another man of equal merit could have done so as well, if circumstances had demanded it, obtaining from the Lord by the merit of faith that even a mountain be taken up and cast into the sea.

But because the name “mountain” sometimes signifies the devil, on account of the pride by which he raises himself against God and wishes to be like the Most High, the mountain is taken from the earth at the command of those who are strong in faith and is thrown into the sea when, through holy teachers preaching the word, the unclean spirit is driven from the hearts of those who are predestined to life and is permitted to exercise the madness of its tyranny in the turbulent and bitter minds of unbelievers—not because it did not previously have its seat and kingdom there, but because it rages all the more fiercely against those whom it is permitted to torment, the more deeply it senses that it has been torn away from harming the godly. [Col. 1045C]

A similar passage occurs in the Apocalypse: “And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and behold, a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea” (Revelation 8). When the angel sounded the trumpet, the mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea, because, when a teacher of truth preaches the word, the ancient enemy, inflamed by the fires of envy, approaches to corrupt the minds of the wicked more grievously, so that it may avenge upon the faithless the pain of its expulsion from the faithful.

“And everything that you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

In the Gospel of John we read that the Lord said to his disciples: “Amen, amen I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 14). [Col. 1045D] For this reason some ask how all believers who ask in the Savior’s name are to receive everything they ask for, when not only do people like us fail to receive many things that they appear to ask the Father for in Christ’s name, but the apostle Paul himself asked God three times that the angel of Satan, by whom he was afflicted, might depart from him, and he was unable to obtain this (2 Corinthians 12).

But the solution to this question has long been disclosed in the ancient explanation of the Fathers, who rightly understood that only those ask in the Savior’s name who ask for the things that pertain to eternal salvation. Therefore, the apostle did not ask in the Savior’s name to be free from the temptation that he had received for the preservation of humility; for if he had been free from it, he could not have been saved, as he himself affirms when he says: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me.”

Whenever, therefore, we ask and are not heard, it happens either because we ask for something contrary to the help of our salvation, and for that reason the merciful Father denies us the benefit that we foolishly request—as is shown to have happened to the same apostle Paul, who, when he asked, received this answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness”—or because we ask for useful things that truly concern salvation, but by living badly we ourselves turn away from us the hearing of the just Judge, falling under Solomon’s saying: “Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the Law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs 28). [Col. 1046A]

Or, while we pray for certain sinners to repent, although we ask beneficially and are worthy of being heard by virtue of our own merits, their perversity nevertheless prevents us from obtaining what we ask.

Sometimes it also happens that we seek things that are entirely salutary, with earnest prayers and devoted actions, yet do not immediately obtain what we ask; rather, the fulfillment of our request is deferred to the future. Thus, when we kneel each day and ask the Father, saying, “Your kingdom come,” we will nevertheless receive that kingdom not immediately when our prayer has ended but at the appropriate time. For by the gracious providence of our Creator it is arranged that the delay causes the desires of our devotion to grow, and that, advancing more and more through daily increase, they may at last receive more perfectly the joys they seek. [Col. 1046B]

Among these things it should be noted that, when we pray for sinners, even if we cannot obtain their salvation, we are nevertheless not deprived of the fruit of our prayer. For although they may not be worthy to be saved, we will nevertheless be rewarded for the love that we show them.

Thus, in such a petition also, the Lord’s promise will be fulfilled for us when he says: “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16). We must observe that he did not simply say, “He will give,” but said, “It will be given to you.” For even if he does not give it to those for whom we ask, he will nevertheless restore to us the reward of our kindness when we mercifully intercede for the errors of others. [Col. 1046C]

## IV

And when he had come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people approached him as he was teaching and said: “By what authority do you do these things? And who gave you this authority?”

(Jerome) They construct the same accusation as before in various ways, when they said: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons.” For when they say, “By what authority do you do these things?” they doubt the authority of God and imply that what he does belongs to the devil. By adding, “Who gave you this authority?” they most plainly deny that he is the Son of God, since they suppose that he performs signs not by his own powers but by those of another. [Col. 1046D]

Jesus answered and said to them: “I also will ask you one question; if you answer me, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things: The baptism of John—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?”

The Lord could have refuted the slander of his tempters with an open answer, but he questions them so that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their answer. [Col. 1047A]

But they were reasoning among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’”

(Maurus) These crafty reasoners and advocates of falsehood put forward this doubtful argument among themselves, as though the Lord would answer them in this way:

(Augustine) “The one whom you confess to have received his prophecy from heaven bore witness to me, and from him you heard by what authority I do these things.”

“But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ we fear the crowd, for they all hold John as a prophet.”

They saw, therefore, that whichever answer they gave, they would fall into a trap. They feared being stoned, but feared even more to confess the truth. For if they had answered that John’s baptism was from heaven—as they had cunningly considered in their wickedness—the inevitable reply would have been: “Why, then, were you not baptized by John?” If they wished to say that it had been devised through human deception and possessed nothing divine, they feared the people’s uprising. For the crowds had all, in groups, received John’s baptism and regarded him as a prophet. [Col. 1047B]

And they answered Jesus: “We do not know.” He also said to them: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

“I do not tell you,” he says, “what I know, because you do not wish to confess what you know.” Accordingly, the Lord ought, in keeping with their answer, to have said, “Neither do I know”; but Truth cannot lie, and he said: “Neither do I tell you.” By this he showed that they knew but refused to answer, and that he knew and therefore did not speak because they kept silent about what they knew. [Col. 1047C]

It was entirely just, then, that such plotters were driven away by these words and departed in confusion. And what God the Father says through the prophet in the Psalm was fulfilled: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” that is, John himself; “I will clothe his enemies with confusion” (Psalm 131).

[Venantius] It should be noted that the knowledge of truth is chiefly to be hidden from those who ask for two reasons: namely, when the person asking is either less capable of understanding what he asks, or is unworthy to have what he asks revealed to him because of hatred or contempt for the truth itself.

Concerning the first reason the Lord says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16). Concerning the second he commands his disciples: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7). [Col. 1047D]

After this fraudulent questioning by the priests, and after his most cautious reply, the Lord immediately presents a parable that both charges them with impiety and teaches that the kingdom of God is to be transferred to the Gentiles.

## V

“What do you think? A certain man had two sons. Approaching the first, he said: ‘Son, go today and work in my vineyard.’ But he answered: ‘I will not.’ Later, moved by repentance, he went. Approaching the other, he said the same. But he answered: ‘I am going, lord,’ and did not go.”

This man signifies God, who loves all the human beings whom he created by nature with paternal affection. He spoke to his sons not outwardly, face to face as a human being, but inwardly in the heart as God—not uttering a word in their ears, but suggesting understanding to their minds. [Col. 1048A]

(Jerome) These are the two sons who are also described in the parable in Luke: the envious, rigid one and the profligate one (Luke 15), and of whom the prophet Zechariah speaks: “I took for myself two staffs; I called one Beauty, and I called the other Bondage, and I pastured the flock” (Zechariah 11). Zechariah spoke of two staffs, that is, two sons.

To the first—the Gentile people—it is said through knowledge of the natural Law: “Go and work in my vineyard,” that is, “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.” He proudly answered, “I will not,” when he abandoned the good and chose evil. But later, at the Savior’s coming, he repented and worked in God’s vineyard, correcting his defiance in speech through labor. [Col. 1048B]

The second is the Jewish people, who answered Moses, “Everything that you have said, we will do” (Exodus 24), but did not go into the vineyard, because, after killing the son of the householder, they thought themselves heirs.

Others do not think that the parable concerns Gentiles and Jews but simply sinners and righteous people, especially since the Lord later explains his proposition: “Amen I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 21).

Now what follows:

“Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said to him: “The last.”

It should be known that in the older copies *the last* is not found, but rather *the first*, so that they might condemn themselves by their own judgment. If we wish to read *the last*, the interpretation is clear: we may say that the Jews understood the truth but evaded the question and refused to say what they thought, just as, knowing that John’s baptism was from heaven, they refused to say so. [Col. 1048C]

Jesus said to them: “Amen I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God.” And rightly so, because those who had denied serving God through evil works afterward received the baptism of repentance from John. But the Pharisees, who put forward their own righteousness and boasted that they fulfilled God’s Law, did not fulfill God’s commands after despising John’s baptism. Hence he says next:

“For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; but the tax collectors and prostitutes believed him. Yet you, seeing this, did not afterward repent so as to believe him.”

(Maurus) John therefore came preaching the way of righteousness because he pointed out with his finger that Christ, who is the fulfillment of the Law and the prophets, was present. Having become the Lord’s forerunner and preparing his way, he filled the valleys of the humble with devout teaching and humbled the hills of the proud through fitting correction. [Col. 1048D]

The Jews, therefore, despising and rejecting him, did not grasp the way of righteousness, which is Christ, because they were unwilling to repent of their evil works and wickedness.

But the Gentiles, thinking humbly and devoutly believing the prophecies of the prophets, turned from their sins to the Lord and rightly repented in the way of righteousness—that is, walking in the path of God’s commandments—and deserved to migrate swiftly into the kingdom of God. [Col. 1049A]

Here, too, the kingdom of God may be understood as the Gospel of God, which elsewhere is called the Gospel of the kingdom, or as the present Church. Hence the Savior also said to the apostles: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). In this kingdom the Gentiles go before the Jews because they were willing to believe more quickly. Thus what the Lord said in another parable comes to pass: “The last will be first, and the first last” (Matthew 21), because, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, “the head has been turned into the tail, and the tail into the head” (Isaiah 19).

“Hear another parable. There was a householder who planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, leased it to farmers, and went away to a foreign land.”

(Jerome) The chief priests and the elders of the people, who had asked the Lord, “By what authority do you do these things, and who gave you this authority?” and who had wished to catch Wisdom in his words, are defeated by their own skill and hear in parables what they had not deserved to hear openly. [Col. 1049B]

This householder is the same one who had two sons and who, in another parable, hired laborers for his vineyard; he is the one who planted the vineyard. Isaiah speaks about it fully in a song, concluding at the end: “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5). And in the Psalm he says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt, you drove out the nations, and you planted it” (Psalm 79).

He put a hedge around it, either the wall of the city or the assistance of angels. He dug a winepress in it, either an altar or those winepresses whose titles are prefixed to three Psalms: the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-sixth. [Col. 1049C] And he built a tower, undoubtedly the temple, concerning which Micah says: “And the cloudy tower of the daughter of Zion” (Micah 4). “And he leased it to farmers”—those whom elsewhere he called the laborers of the vineyard, who had been hired at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours.

“And he went away to a foreign land”—not by a change of place, for where can God be absent, through whom all things are completed? He is the one who says through Jeremiah: “I am God who is near and not far away, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 30). Rather, he appears to depart from the vineyard in order to leave the farmers free discretion to work.

When the time of the fruits had approached—

(Rabanus) He rightly said “the time of the fruits,” not “of the produce,” for no fruit arose from the disobedient people; no produce of this vineyard, although it was sought frequently and earnestly, was found. [Col. 1049D]

He sent his servants to the tenants to collect his fruit. But the tenants seized his servants: they beat one, killed another, and stoned another. The servants who were sent first are understood to be Moses himself, the lawgiver, and Aaron, God’s first priest. Of them it is written: “He sent Moses his servant, and Aaron, whom he chose” (Ps. 104), and so forth. For forty continuous years they sought from the cultivators some fruit of the law that God had given them, but after being beaten with the scourge of the tongue they sent them away empty-handed. For they provoked Moses in the camp and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord: “Moses was troubled because of them, because they embittered his spirit” (Ps. 105). This servant himself also openly declares in song what he thinks of the fruit of this vineyard, saying: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them. The wine of dragons is their fury, and the fury of asps is incurable” (Deut. 32).

[Col. 1050A] David himself too is the servant of the supreme master of the household. He established that the heart of the people should be lifted toward the desire for heavenly things amid the rites of carnal sacrifices, and that the praises of the Lord should continually be sung in sweet melody. But they also wounded this servant’s head with insults. As the Gospel of Mark relates, they treated lightly the songs of the psalmists, which summoned them to praise the Lord, and rejected David himself, who had shone forth as the head and fountain of psalmody in the Holy Spirit. For they said:

[Col. 1050B] “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (2 Sam. 20). Thus they changed both his kingdom, because of his ignoble lineage, and religion, through impiety. Nevertheless, he prayed for this vineyard, which, transplanted from Egypt, had protected the mountains of Palestine with its shade, lest it be utterly destroyed: “Lord, God of hosts, turn now; look down from heaven, and see and visit this vineyard, and direct it, which your right hand planted” (Ps. 79). There he also made clear who the man was who planted this vineyard: namely, the Lord, the God of hosts.

Again he sent other servants, more numerous than the first, and they treated them in the same way. In this statement he displays the patience of the master of the household, who sent more frequently in order to call the wicked tenants to repentance. But they, despising him,

[Col. 1050C] “stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath.” Nevertheless, understand these servants as the company of the prophets, who continually warned the people and foretold the evils that would come upon this vineyard and threaten it. But which of the prophets did they not persecute? And they killed those who proclaimed the coming of the Lord Savior. They said much about the barrenness of this vineyard, but it is enough to cite the lament of one prophet, Jeremiah: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly of genuine seed; how have you turned into a degenerate, foreign vine?” (Isa. 5).

[MAUR.] What we read above, that the tenants seized the servants of the master of the household, beat one, killed another, and stoned another, is evident in the actions of the Jews. For they beat one, such as Jeremiah;

[Col. 1050D] they killed another, such as Isaiah; and they stoned another, such as Naboth, and Zechariah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar (Luke 11).

[Hieron.] Let us read Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, and from it we shall learn most fully who God’s servants are and how much they endured.

Finally he sent his son to them.

(Chrys.) He sent him not as one carrying a sentence of punishment against the guilty, but, after so many crimes, in his patience he still reserved for them a place for mercy.

Saying: “They will respect my son.”

(Hieron.) His statement, “They will respect my son,” does not arise from ignorance on God’s part. For what could the master of the household, who here is understood to be God, fail to know? Rather, God is always said to hesitate so that human free will may be preserved. Let us question Arius and Eunomius: Behold, the Father is said to be ignorant, and he moderates his sentence; and, as far as depends on us, he is shown to have lied. Whatever they answer concerning the Father, let them understand the same concerning the Son, who says that he does not know the day of consummation.

But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.”

[Col. 1051A] (RAB.) The Lord most clearly proves that the Jewish leaders crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy. For they understood that this was the one to whom it had been said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” Therefore, as though consulting their own interests, they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him; and if we let him go on this way, everyone will believe in him” (Ps. 11). The Son’s inheritance, therefore, is the Church, given to him from all the nations. The Father did not leave it to him as a dying man, but he wonderfully acquired it through his own death and possessed it by rising again. After killing him, the wicked tenants attempted to seize it, when the Jews, by crucifying him, tried to extinguish the faith that comes through him and to prefer their own righteousness, which comes from the law, and sought to implant it among the nations whom they were trying to instruct.

And they seized him, cast him outside the vineyard, and killed him. The heir of the vineyard is slaughtered outside the vineyard because Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his blood. Or he was cast outside the vineyard and killed because he was first rejected by the heart of unbelievers and then delivered to the cross. As a figure of this, Moses placed the altar of burnt offering, on which the blood of sacrifices was poured, not inside the tabernacle but at the entrance.

[Col. 1051C] He was mystically teaching that the altar of the Lord’s cross also had to be placed outside the gate of Jerusalem, and that Christ, the true offering of the Father, was not to be received in the innermost heart by the house of the Jews, which he had approached in order to sanctify it, but was to be stained outside with his own blood. But what is said according to Mark in a different order—“They seized him and killed him, and cast him outside the vineyard” (Mark 12)—points to their obstinacy. Even when the Lord had been crucified and raised from the dead, and the apostles were preaching, they refused to believe; rather, like a worthless corpse, they cast him away, since, so far as depended on them, they excluded him from their own borders and handed him over to the Gentiles to receive.

When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?

[Col. 1051D] The Lord asks them this not because he is ignorant of what they will answer, but so that they may be condemned by their own response.

They say to him: “He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will lease the vineyard to other tenants who will render him the fruit at its proper seasons.” The vineyard has been leased to us, and leased on this condition: that we render fruits to the Lord at their proper seasons and know, at each season, what we ought either to say or to do. When they had said that, after the destruction of the wicked tenants, the lord of the vineyard would give the vineyard to others, the Lord immediately affirmed through a prophetic example that this very thing had been divinely arranged, adding:

Jesus said to them: “Have you never read in the Scriptures:

[Col. 1052A] ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes’?” (Ps. 117). How, he says, will this prophecy be fulfilled, which says that the stone rejected by the builders is to be placed as the cornerstone, unless it is because Christ, rejected and killed by you, is to be preached to the Gentiles who will believe, so that, like a stone joining two peoples in himself, he may build for himself from both peoples one city and one temple of the faithful? For he now calls the ministers of the synagogue, whom above he had called tenants, “builders,” because those who were commanded to cultivate the people subject to them, as a vineyard, so that it might bear the fruits of life, were also commanded to construct and adorn it as a house worthy of God dwelling within it. Hence the Apostle, writing to the faithful, says:

[Col. 1052B] “You are God’s agriculture, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3). But while they labored like wicked tenants to deny God the fruit of his vineyard, they also, like wicked masons, tried to remove from God’s house the precious, chosen stone that was to be placed either in the foundations or in the corner—that is, they tried to take the faith of Christ away from their hearers. But although they were unwilling, that same stone became the cornerstone, because he joined together in his faith as many as he willed from both peoples.

Therefore I say to you: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

(Hieron.) We have said several times that the kingdom of God is understood as the Holy Scriptures, which he took away from the Jews and handed over to us, so that we might produce their fruits. This is the vineyard that is entrusted to tenants and cultivators.

[Col. 1052C] Those who do not labor in it, although they possess only the name of the Scriptures, will lose the fruit of the vineyard.

“And whoever falls upon this stone will be broken to pieces; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.” It is one thing to stumble against Christ through evil works and another to deny him. “The sinner who nevertheless believes in him falls upon the stone and is broken, but is not completely crushed; for through patience he is preserved for salvation. But upon whomever that stone falls—that is, upon one whom the stone itself strikes, and who has utterly denied Christ—it will crush him, so that not even a potsherd remains from which a little water might be drawn. Or he says this about those who fall upon him because they now despise or insult him; therefore they do not yet perish completely, but are nevertheless shattered, so that they do not walk uprightly.

[Col. 1052D] But upon those upon whom he falls, he will come from above in judgment with the punishment of destruction. Therefore he said that he would grind them to dust, so that the ungodly may be like the dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth.”

When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they understood that he was speaking about them. Seeking to seize him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet. The chief priests and scribes, as though the Lord were lying against them, sought to kill him; but by this very search they were demonstrating that what he had said was true. For he is the heir whose unjust death, he had said, was to be avenged by the father. But those wicked tenants, who were held back from killing the Son of God for a brief time by human fear,

[Col. 1053A] until his hour should come, could never be restrained by divine love.

In the moral sense, whenever the mystery of baptism is entrusted to a believer to be exercised through works, it is as though a vineyard to cultivate were leased to him. One servant, then another, and a third are sent to receive the fruit when the law, psalmody, and prophecy are read, and their admonition is followed by good conduct. But the servant who is sent is insulted or beaten and driven away when the word is either despised or, worse still, blasphemed. He kills the heir sent to him, so far as depends on him, when he tramples upon the Son of God and insults the Spirit of grace by whom he was sanctified. Once the wicked cultivator has been destroyed, the vineyard is given to another, when the grace that the proud person despised enriches the humble.

But the fact that the chief priests, scribes, and elders,

[Col. 1053B] seeking to lay hands on Jesus, are restrained by fear of the crowd also occurs daily in the Church. Whenever someone who is a brother only in name, because of the multitude of good brothers living alongside him, is ashamed or afraid to attack the unity of ecclesiastical faith and peace, which he does not love, the same thing happens. Yet, as the Lord says concerning the utterly foolish bird, the ostrich: “When the time comes, it raises its wings on high” (Job 39). For he will rejoice in persecuting the Church, as though delivering the Lord to the cross, and in making him an object of public display.

## CHAPTER XXII

### On the king who made a wedding feast; on the tribute to Caesar; on the woman who had seven brothers; and whose son Christ is

[Col. 1053C] And Jesus answered and again spoke to them in parables, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.”

[I.] (Hieron.) The Pharisees, understanding that the parables were spoken about them, sought to seize and kill him. Knowing this intention of theirs, he nevertheless rebuked sinners. In the holy Gospel, the present Church is very often called the kingdom of heaven. The assembly of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven, because the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). Solomon also says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” Since heaven is called the seat of God, the soul of the righteous is therefore heaven. Concerning this, the psalmist says of the holy preachers: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). The kingdom of heaven, therefore, is the Church of the righteous.

[Col. 1053D] Since their hearts desire nothing on earth, but sigh for things above, the Lord already reigns in them as in heavenly places. Let it therefore be said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.” Who is the king, the father of the king’s son? Surely the one to whom the Psalmist says: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son, who made a wedding feast for his son” (Ps. 71). In this the Father made a wedding feast for the Son: he joined the holy Church to him through the mystery of the Incarnation. The womb of the virgin mother was the bridal chamber of this bridegroom. Hence the psalmist says:

[Col. 1054A] “He set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18). Like a bridegroom, he came forth from his bridal chamber because, having become incarnate in order to join the Church to himself, God came forth from the inviolate womb of the virgin.

And he sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding feast, and they were unwilling to come. Again he sent other servants, saying: “Tell those who have been invited: ‘Behold, I have prepared my meal; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.’” He therefore sent his servants to invite friends to this wedding feast. He sent once, and he sent again, because he appointed first the prophets and afterward the apostles as preachers of the Lord’s Incarnation. He sent these servants to invite them because he foretold through the prophets that the Only-Begotten would become incarnate, and announced through the apostles that he had done so.

But because those who were invited first did not wish to come to the wedding feast, the second invitation now says: “Behold, I have prepared my meal;

[Col. 1054B] my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready.” What are we to understand by the bulls and fattened animals except the fathers of the New and Old Testaments? For we call fattened animals *sagmata*—“fattened things”—deriving the word from *alere*, “to nourish,” as though it were *alitilia*.

But when it was written in the law, “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5), permission had then been granted to the righteous that they should suppress God’s adversaries and their own with all the strength they could, and strike them by right of the sword. This is undoubtedly restrained in the New Testament, when Truth itself proclaims: “Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you” (ibid.). What, then, are signified by the bulls except the fathers of the Old Testament? Since, by permission of the law, they had received authority to strike their adversaries in return for hatred,

[Col. 1054C] what else were they, so to speak, but bulls, who struck their enemies with the horn of bodily strength? What, moreover, are symbolized by the fattened animals except the fathers of the New Testament? As they receive the grace of inward richness, they rely upon eternal desires and are lifted on the wings of their contemplation to higher things.

But they neglected it and went away, one to his farm and another to his business. To go to one’s farm is to devote oneself excessively to earthly labor. To go to one’s business is to long for the profits of worldly activities. Since one person, intent upon earthly labor, and another, devoted to the activities of this world, pretends not to consider the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation or live according to it, he refuses to come to the king’s wedding feast, as though going to his farm or business.

[Col. 1054D] Often—and this is more serious—some not only reject the grace of the one who calls them but also persecute it. Hence it follows:

But the rest seized his servants, treated them with contempt, and killed them. When the king heard this, he was angry, and sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.

(Chrys.) This refers to the Romans under the commanders Vespasian and Titus, who, after killing the people of Judea, burned the treacherous city.

(Greg.) Or otherwise: he destroyed the murderers when he intervened against the persecutors; he burned their city with fire because not only their souls but also the flesh in which they had dwelt is tormented by the flame of eternal Gehenna.

[Col. 1055A] He is said to have destroyed the murderers by sending his armies because every judgment upon human beings is carried out through angels. For what are those hosts of angels except the armies of our king? Hence the same king is called the Lord Sabaoth; *Sabaoth* is interpreted as “of armies.” He therefore sends an army to destroy his adversaries, because the Lord exercises vengeance through angels.

Our fathers then heard of the power of this vengeance, but we now see it. Where are those proud persecutors of the martyrs? Where are those who raised the neck of their hearts against their creator and swelled with deadly pride over the glory of this world? Behold, the death of the martyrs now flourishes in the faith of the living, while those who gloried in their cruelty against them scarcely come to our memory,

[Col. 1055B] not even among the number of the dead. By events, therefore, we recognize what we hear in the parables. But he who sees that those invited despise him will not leave the king’s son’s wedding feast empty. He sends to others, because even if the word of God labors among some, it will eventually find a place where it may rest. Hence it follows:

Then he said to his servants: “The wedding feast indeed is ready.” That is, the whole mystery of the Son of God’s human dispensation—his birth, baptism, preaching, passion, resurrection, and ascension—has been accomplished.

But those who had been invited were not worthy. This refers to the Jews, who had been invited through the law and the prophets to believe in Christ but rejected the mystery of the Incarnation. Once these things had occurred, it is clear that after the Jews’ contempt and obstinacy he speaks of the calling of the Gentiles:

[Col. 1055C] “Go therefore to the exits of the roads.”

(Aug.) The roads are understood as the teachings of the Gentiles and the errors of the Gentiles; but from all of them they believed in the wedding feast—that is, in Christ.

“And invite to the wedding feast whomever you find.”

(Chrys.) That is, invite people of every condition to the faith. Just as there is no difference in the nature of human creation, so there should be no difference in their call to salvation.

(Greg.) In the moral sense, if in holy Scripture we understand the roads as actions, we understand the exits of the roads as the failures of actions, because those who are accompanied by no prosperity in earthly affairs often come easily to the Lord. Then it follows:

[Col. 1055D] And his servants went out onto the roads and gathered all whom they found, both good and bad, and the wedding feast was filled with those reclining at table. Behold, the very character of those feasting openly shows that the present Church is designated by the king’s wedding feast, in which the wicked gather together with the good. It is mixed in the diversity of its children, because it gives birth to all through faith, yet does not bring all, through the transformation of their lives, into the freedom of spiritual grace, because their sins demand otherwise.

As long as we live here, we must travel the way of the present age together in mixture. We are separated only when we arrive. The good are nowhere alone except in hell. This life, which is situated between

[Col. 1056A] heaven and hell, stands in the middle and therefore receives citizens of both parts together. Yet the holy Church now receives them indiscriminately and later separates them at their departure. We must consider with great fear what immediately follows:

But the king entered to see those reclining at table, and he saw there a man not wearing a wedding garment. And he said to him: “Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?” But he was silent.

(Hieron.) Those who had been invited to the wedding feast from hedges, corners, streets, and various places had fulfilled the supper of the law. But afterward, when the king came to see those reclining at his banquet—that is, when, as it were, he visited his guests resting in faith on the day of judgment—and to distinguish the merits of each, he found one who was not clothed in a wedding garment.

[Col. 1056B] This one represents all who are joined together in wickedness. The wedding garment consists of the Lord’s commandments and the works fulfilled from the law and the Gospel, which form the clothing of the new human being. If, therefore, at the time of judgment someone is found under the Christian name without a wedding garment—that is, without the garment of the heavenly human being, but wearing the old and polluted garment, the cast-off clothing of the old human being—he is immediately rebuked, and it is said to him: “Friend, how did you enter here?” He calls him “friend” because he had been invited to the wedding feast. He rebukes his shamelessness, because he polluted the purity of the wedding feast with a filthy garment. But he was silent. At that time there will be no place for shamelessness and no opportunity for denial, since all the angels and the world itself will be witnesses of sins.

[Col. 1056C] (Greg.) We may also understand the wedding garment as charity. A person enters the wedding feast but does not enter wearing a wedding garment when, standing in the holy Church, he possesses faith but does not possess charity. Charity is rightly called a wedding garment, because our Creator possessed it when he came to the wedding feast to join the Church to himself. It was solely through love of God that his Only-Begotten united the minds of the chosen to himself. Hence Christ says in John: “God so loved this world that he gave his Only-Begotten Son for us” (John 3). Therefore he who came to human beings through charity made known that this same charity is the wedding garment.

Everyone among us who, placed in the Church, believes in God has already entered the wedding feast; but he does not come wearing the wedding garment if he does not preserve the grace of charity.

[Col. 1056D] It must be understood, however, that just as a garment is woven from two pieces of wood, the upper and the lower, so charity is contained in two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. For it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” In this regard it should be noted that the measure of love is prescribed in love of neighbor when it says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22). But God’s love is confined by no measure: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.” No one is commanded how much he should love, but from how much—when it says “with all,”

[Col. 1057A] because the person truly loves who has kept nothing of himself for himself. Everyone who takes care to have a wedding garment at the wedding feast must therefore keep these two commandments of charity.

Behold, the king enters the wedding feast and examines the disposition of our hearts. When he does not find someone clothed in charity, he immediately says in anger: “Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?” It is very astonishing that he both calls him a friend and rejects him. It is as though he were saying more openly: “Friend, and not friend. Friend through faith, but not friend through works.” But he was silent. For in that strict final rebuke, where what cannot be said without groaning is at issue, every argument for excuse ceases. The one who rebukes outwardly is the just witness of the conscience accusing the soul within.

But amid these things it must be understood that anyone who possesses this garment of virtue, yet does not possess it perfectly,

[Col. 1057B] should not despair of pardon when the merciful king enters. For he too gives us hope through the Psalmist, saying: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. 138).

Then the king said to the attendants: “Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” At that time, by the severity of the sentence, the feet and hands of those who now refused to be restrained from evil works, so that they might reform their lives, are bound. Or certainly punishment then binds those whom guilt has now bound from good works. The feet that neglect to visit the sick, and the hands that give nothing to the needy, have already been bound from good work by their own will.

[Col. 1057C] What is now voluntarily bound in vice will then be unwillingly bound in punishment. It is rightly said that he is cast into the outer darkness. We call blindness of heart the inner darkness, but the eternal night of condemnation the outer darkness. Then each condemned person is sent not into inner darkness but into outer darkness. There he is unwillingly cast into the night of condemnation, because he voluntarily fell into blindness of heart. There is also said to be weeping and gnashing of teeth, so that there the teeth of those who here rejoiced in gluttony may gnash; there the eyes of those who here were occupied with unlawful desires may weep; so that each member may be subjected to the punishment corresponding to the particular vices to which it here served.

But after the one in whom the whole body of wicked people is represented has been rejected,

[Col. 1057D] a general sentence immediately follows:

“For many are called, but few are chosen.” What we have heard is exceedingly fearful. Behold, we have all now been called through faith and have come to the wedding feast of the heavenly king; we both believe and confess the mystery of his Incarnation, and we partake of the banquet of the divine word. But whether we are chosen, we do not know. Therefore each of us must humble himself all the more, the more he does not know whether he is chosen.

Some do not even begin to do good; others do not persist at all in the good things they have begun. One is seen to spend almost his entire life in wickedness, yet near the end of life is recalled from his wickedness through the laments of strict repentance. Another appears to lead a chosen life, yet near the end of life happens to turn toward the wickedness of error. One begins

[Col. 1058A] a good work well and completes it better. Another casts himself down through evil actions from his earliest years and is brought to a still worse end in those same works. Therefore each person should fear for himself all the more because he does not know what remains.

[II.] Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel to trap him in speech, and they sent their disciples to him with the Herodians, saying:

(Hieron.) Recently, under Caesar Augustus, Judea had been subjected to the Romans. When the registration was celebrated throughout the whole world, it had become a tributary province, and there was great dissension among the people. Some said, for the sake of security and peace, that since Rome fought for everyone, tribute ought to be paid. But the Pharisees, who applauded themselves for their righteousness,

[Col. 1058B] argued in opposition that the people of God, who paid tithes, offered the firstfruits, and observed the other things written in the law, ought not to be subject to human laws.

Caesar Augustus had appointed Herod, the son of Antipater, a foreigner and proselyte, king over the Jews, so that he might oversee the tribute and obey the Roman power. They therefore sent their disciples, who were less well known and less suspect, with the Herodians—that is, Herod’s soldiers—or, alternatively, with those whom the Pharisees mocked because they paid tribute to the Romans and were not devoted to divine worship. Thus they could either secretly deceive him with greater ease or, if rebuked, feel less shame before him.

(Chrys.) For when an evil plot has been exposed, confusion is all the less likely to arise the worse the person is.

“Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth,

[Col. 1058C] and that you care for no one, for you do not regard the status of persons.” They call him teacher and truthful so that, as one honored and praised, he might disclose the mystery of his heart to them simply, as though he wished to have them as disciples.

“Tell us, then, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” This flattering and deceitful question provokes the one answering to fear God more than Caesar and to say that tribute should not be paid, so that the Herodians, hearing it immediately, might seize him as a leader of sedition against the Romans.

But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” He did not answer them according to their peaceful and flattering words, but according to the cruel and harsh intention of their conscience.

[Col. 1058D] For God often speaks to the soul rather than to the body; he responds to intentions rather than to words.

(Hieron.) The first virtue of the one answering is to recognize the mind of those asking, and to call them not disciples but tempters. A hypocrite is one who is one thing and pretends to be another, who does one thing in action and presents another in speech.

“Show me the coin of the tribute.” And they offered him a denarius. Wisdom always acts wisely, so that the tempters may be refuted especially by their own words. “Show me,” he says, “a denarius”—that is, the kind of coin counted as ten coins and also bearing the image of Caesar.

And Jesus said to them: “Whose image and inscription is this?”

[Col. 1059A] Those who think that the Savior’s question expresses ignorance rather than a dispensation should learn from this passage that Jesus certainly could have known whose image was on the coin, but asked in order to give an appropriate answer to their speech.

They said to him: “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them: “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Here we should not think that Caesar means Augustus, but Tiberius, his stepson, who had succeeded in his stepfather’s place and under whom the Lord also suffered. All the Roman kings, beginning with Gaius Caesar, who seized the imperial power, were called Caesars.

When he says, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” let us understand this to mean the coin, tribute, and money. “And to God the things that are God’s” means tithes, firstfruits, offerings, and sacrifices. In the same way, he himself renders tribute for himself and Peter,

[Col. 1059B] and renders to God the things that are God’s by doing the Father’s will.

Alternatively: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

(Aug.) Just as Caesar demands from you the impression of his image, so God demands his image from you, so that just as the coin is rendered to Caesar, the soul, illuminated and marked by the light of his countenance, may be rendered to God. Hence the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4). This light is the whole human being and the true good, which is seen not by the eyes but by the mind. He said that it was marked upon us, just as a denarius is marked with the king’s image. For the human being was made according to the image and likeness of God, which he corrupted through sin. His true and eternal good, therefore, is to be marked anew through rebirth.

And when they heard this, they marveled.

[Col. 1059C] Those who ought to have believed marveled at such great wisdom, because their cunning attempt to lay a snare had found no opening.

And leaving him, they went away. They carried away their unbelief along with their amazement.

[III.] On that day the Sadducees approached him, who say that there is no resurrection. There were two sects among the Jews: one of the Pharisees and the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees preferred the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they call *deuterosis*—“second tradition”—and hence they were called “separated” from the people. The Sadducees, whose name was interpreted as “righteous,” also claimed for themselves what they were not. The former believed in the resurrection of both body and soul and confessed the existence of angels and spirits. The latter, according to the Acts of the Apostles, denied everything.

[Col. 1059D] These are the two houses of which Isaiah teaches more clearly.

And they questioned him, saying: “Teacher, Moses said: ‘If someone dies without having a son, his brother shall marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.’ Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and, having no offspring, left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second and the third, down to the seventh. Finally, after them all, the woman also died.”

Those who did not believe in the resurrection of bodies, judging that souls perished with bodies, rightly fabricate this kind of story, which exposes as delirious those who assert the resurrection of bodies. It is possible, however, that this really happened among their people.

[Col. 1060A] “Therefore, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be among the seven? For they all had her.”

(RAB.) They oppose an indecent story in order to deny the truth of the resurrection. Mystically, however, these seven brothers who died without children correspond to the reprobate, who throughout the whole life of this age—which turns in a cycle of seven days—remain barren of good works. When these men have been taken away one by one by miserable death, finally the worldly life itself, which they spent without the fruit of living works, will pass away like a barren wife.

But Jesus answered and said to them: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.”

(Hieron.) They are mistaken because they do not know the Scriptures; and because they are ignorant of the Scriptures, they consequently do not know the power of God—that is, Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

[Col. 1060B] For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. The Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom. Properly speaking, women are said to marry, while men take wives. But let us understand the statement simply, as though it were written that men do not marry and women are not given in marriage. If in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, then bodies capable of marrying and of being given in marriage will rise. For no one says of a stone or a tree, or of things that do not possess sexual members, that they do not marry or are not given in marriage, but of those who, although they are capable of marrying, nevertheless do not marry for another reason. But what follows—
But they are like the angels of God in heaven (RAB.). A spiritual mode of life is promised. For they are like the angels in heaven, who, renewed in the glory of the resurrection, enjoy the perpetual vision of God, without any fear of death, any stain of corruption, or any activity belonging to an earthly condition. Whoever desires to rise to that equality of angelic dignity must now, by pious conduct, humbly accommodate himself to the least of his brethren. By this humility he has answered the question proposed concerning the conditions of the resurrection. Concerning the resurrection itself, however, he spoke against their unbelief as follows:

“Concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by God, who says: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?” To prove the truth of the resurrection he could have used many other, clearer examples. Among them is this: “The dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will arise” (John 5). And elsewhere: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise, some to life and others to everlasting disgrace and confusion.” It is therefore asked what the Lord intended by presenting this testimony, which appears ambiguous or not sufficiently relevant to the truth of the resurrection. We said above that the Sadducees confessed neither angels, nor spirit, nor the resurrection of bodies, and also taught the destruction of souls. They accepted only the five books of Moses, rejecting the prophecies of the prophets. It would therefore have been foolish to produce testimonies whose authority they did not acknowledge. Rather, to prove the eternity of souls, he gives the example: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” and immediately adds:

[Col. 1061A] “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” Once he has proved that souls remain after death—for he could not be the God of those who did not in any way continue to exist—the resurrection of the bodies that did good or evil together with their souls follows as a necessary consequence. The apostle Paul treats this passage more fully in the final part of the First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 15).

And when the crowds heard this, they were astonished at his teaching. (MAUR.) The simple crowd, the uneducated populace proceeding along the way of humility, was compelled to believe in the Lord and to revere the miracles performed by him. But the Pharisees and scribes, despising this, not only did not believe; they even attacked the author of all goodness with vehement insults and slanders. [Col. 1061B] Hence elsewhere they said: “Has any one of the rulers believed in him? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed.” (Hieron.) Moreover, it seems necessary to ask: Since the Lord says, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine,” why do we find him himself saying here certain things about the glory of the resurrection, and elsewhere about the mysteries of his dispensation and even of his divinity, which many of those present did not receive, either resisting or despising them? He should not be thought to have given what was holy to dogs or to have thrown pearls before swine. For he did not give these things to those who were unable to receive them, but to those who were able to receive them and were present at the same time; and they ought not to have been neglected because of the uncleanness of others. When the tempters questioned him, he answered them in such a way that they had nothing to say in reply, although they wasted away in their own poisons rather than being nourished by his food. Others, however, who were able, heard many useful things because of the occasion provided by their questioning.

### IV.

When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together, and one of them, a lawyer, questioned him, testing him. They gathered together so that they might overcome by numbers the one whom they could not overcome by reason. By arming themselves with numbers, they declared themselves naked of truth. For they said among themselves: “Let one speak for all, and let us all speak through one, so that, if he wins, we may all appear victorious; but if he is defeated, he alone may appear confounded.”

“Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?” He calls him “Teacher” although he does not wish to be his disciple: he does not desire knowledge, but is testing him. The Lord, however, answered in such a way that in his first reply he immediately struck the false conscience underlying the question, saying: (Hieron.) What we read concerning Herod and Pontius Pilate—that they made common cause in the Lord’s death—we now see also in the Pharisees and Sadducees. Although they are opposed to one another, they agree in mind when testing Jesus. Those who had already been refuted above in the matter of the denarius, and had seen the faction of the opposing party undermined, ought to have been warned by that example not to prepare further snares. But malice and envy nourish shamelessness. One of the lawyers asks, not desiring to learn but testing whether the one being questioned knows what he is asked: which commandment is greatest? First, he does not ask which commandments are greatest, but which is the great commandment, so that, since everything commanded by God is great, whatever the Lord answers may give him an opportunity for slander, by asserting that some other commandment among the many is greater. Whoever, therefore, knows and asks not out of a desire to learn but in order to discover whether the one who will answer knows, approaches like the Pharisees—not as a disciple but as a tempter.

Jesus said to him: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind: this is the greatest and first commandment.” He calls it the first and greatest commandment because above all things each of us ought to establish it deep within the heart as the single foundation of piety.

“And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” The first and greatest commandment, therefore, is the knowledge and confession of the divine unity, together with the performance of good works. Good conduct is perfected in love of God and neighbor, which the Apostle commends briefly in other words: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5).

On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. (Aug.) He said “hang,” that is, everything is referred to them and finds its end in them. The whole law consists in two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. The entire Decalogue, therefore, pertains to these two commandments, that is, to love of God and neighbor. All the books of the prophets likewise pertain to them. For this reason two tablets of the law were given. God gave his servant Moses two tablets on the mountain, and on the two tablets the words of the covenant were written. These are the ten commandments of the law, the psalterium of ten strings, concerning which the Psalmist says: “God, I will sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psalter I will sing to you” (Ps. 32). Three commandments concerning God had been placed on one tablet, and seven concerning one’s neighbor on the other.

On the first tablet, therefore, the first commandment was written: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods” (Exod. 20), and so forth. For Christ the Son of God is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1062D] Then it was added: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold guiltless anyone who takes the name of his Lord in vain.” We must not take the name of Christ in vain, thinking that he was made—that is, that he was some creature—through whom all things were made; for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. In the Holy Spirit, that is, in the house of God, eternal rest is promised to us. Hence it follows: “Remember that you keep holy the sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work, neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter,” and so forth.

On the other tablet the first commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother”; the second, “You shall not commit adultery”; the third, “You shall not kill”; the fourth, “You shall not steal”; the fifth, “You shall not bear false witness”; the sixth, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; the seventh, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” Let us join these to the three commandments concerning the love of God, and let us sing on the ten-stringed psalter, if we wish to sing a new song as new human beings, to whom the Savior gave the new commandment that we should love one another as he loved us.

When the Pharisees had gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him: “David’s.” He said to them: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’?” (Ps. 109 [Col. 1063B]). If David therefore calls him Lord, how is he his son? Those who had gathered to test Jesus and were trying by a deceitful question to trap the truth provided the occasion for their own refutation, and they are questioned about whose son the Christ is. Jesus’ question benefits us even today against the Jews. For those who confess that Christ will come but assert that he is merely a human being and a holy man descended from David must be questioned by us, instructed by the Lord: If he is merely a human being and only David’s son, how does David call him his Lord? It was not through uncertain error or by his own will, but in the Holy Spirit. The testimony he used is taken from the one-hundred-ninth Psalm. The Lord is therefore called David’s Lord, not according to the fact that he was born from him, [Col. 1063C] but according to the fact that he had always been born from the Father, preceding even the father of his own flesh.

To evade the force of the question, the Jews invent many frivolous explanations, asserting that the psalm was written about Abraham’s servant, whose son was Damascus Eliezer, and that, in his person, the psalm says that after the slaughter of the five kings the Lord God said to Abraham, his lord: “Sit at my right hand, until I place all your enemies as a footstool for your feet.” We should ask them how God could have said to Abraham the words that follow: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” And we should compel them to answer how Abraham could have been begotten before the morning star and could have been a priest according to the order of Melchizedek—he who offered bread and wine to Melchizedek and received from him a tenth of the spoils (Gen. 14). [Col. 1064B]

And no one was able to answer him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day onward to question him further. The Pharisees and Sadducees, seeking an opportunity for slander and trying to find some word that would expose him to their snares, had been refuted in argument and therefore questioned him no further; instead, they handed him over openly to the Roman authorities. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but have greater difficulty becoming quiet. Let us not approach him as the scribes and Pharisees did, thinking wickedly, questioning the Lord deceitfully, and testing him. Rather, let us approach him with a simple heart, devout faith, and humility, so that we may be enlightened and our faces may not be put to shame, as it is written of him: “He is found by those who do not test him, and he appears to those who have faith in him” (Wis. 1).

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1063]

## CHAPTER XXIII

The Lord instructs the crowds and the disciples concerning the scribes and Pharisees; he rebukes the scribes and Pharisees in many ways by pronouncing “Woe.” He reproaches Jerusalem for the killing of the prophets and foretells its destruction.

The scribes, Pharisees, and Sadducees, the tempters of Christ, having been fittingly confounded and rejected by the very answer of truth, are shown to fulfill what was long ago said in the Book of Wisdom: “Perverse thoughts separate from God, but tested virtue rebukes the foolish. For wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subjected to sins; for the holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit and withdraw from thoughts without understanding” (Wis. 1). Since such people did not deserve to receive divine wisdom, their hearts being filled with the poison of envy, who are those whose minds can receive it through the grace bestowed by God is revealed elsewhere, where it is said: “The fountain of wisdom is the word of God on high, and its ways are eternal commandments. The root of wisdom—to whom has it been revealed? And who has known its subtleties? The discipline of wisdom—to whom has it been revealed and made manifest? And who has understood the abundance of its ways? One is the Most High, the almighty Creator, a mighty and exceedingly fearful king, seated upon his throne and ruling as God. He created her in the Holy Spirit, saw her, numbered her, and measured her. He poured her out over all his works and over all flesh according to his gift, and he gave her to those who love him” (Ecclus. 1).

Those who love God and obey his commandments receive from above a taste of true wisdom. Constantly delighting in its sweetness, they do not exalt themselves through it, but, thinking humbly, remain like little children in purity of innocence. Concerning them Truth itself, speaking to the Father in the Gospel, says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (Luke 10). It pleases God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the one almighty God, that those who recognize themselves as little in their own eyes should be exalted as great before the eyes of God. Separated from the company of the reprobate, who on account of the darkness of their sins will be condemned to the eternal prison of hell, they themselves will be perpetually illumined by the light of divine wisdom.

Therefore, having dismissed the deceitful questions of the scribes [Col. 1065A] and Pharisees, the Lord appropriately turned his instructional discourse to the disciples and the people, so that those capable of receiving it might receive the word of salvation from his mouth. The evangelist continues and says:

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore, whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do.” What could be gentler or kinder than the Lord? The Pharisees test him, their snares are shattered, and through the Psalmist “the arrows of children become their wounds” (Ps. 63); nevertheless, because of the priesthood and the dignity of their name, he exhorts the people to submit to them, considering not their works but their teaching. When he says, “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat,” he indicates by the seat the teaching of the law. (Joan. Chrys.) Thus we should also understand the statement in the Psalm, “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1), and the seats of those selling doves that he overturned: the reference is to teaching. For this reason the Lord turned his discourse toward his own people, so that the confusion of the scribes and Pharisees might become instruction for them. A word is fruitless if one person is so confounded that another is not instructed. God does not send punishment upon the earth for the sake of the wicked, but for the sake of the good; for he knows that scourges do not correct the wicked. He chastises the wicked in order to correct the good, because the good person, unless warned, fades away through negligence. In the same way, could Christ not have disregarded their questions? But he wished to teach the unworthy in an unworthy manner, so that he might edify the worthy in a worthy manner.

They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger. (Venant.) The crowds and disciples of the Lord are therefore unable to bear the burdens of the law in the manner in which the scribes and Pharisees imposed them on people. Hence they rightly hear that they did not touch these very burdens with even one finger: that is, they did not fulfill the law even in the smallest matters, although, contrary to the custom of their fathers and without the faith and grace of Jesus Christ, they presumed both to observe it and to transmit it for observance. For this reason they attempted to cast away and abolish the yoke of Christ, which is easy, and his burden, which is light (Matt. 11), in which there is rest for souls, although it is written, “The just shall live by faith” (Heb. 10), and the apostle Peter protested to those who taught that gentile believers should be circumcised, saying: “Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, just as they are” (Acts 15).

(Hieron.) It should therefore be noted that this saying of the Lord can be understood generally against all teachers who command great things but do small ones. In particular, the shoulders, fingers, burdens, and bonds by which the burdens are fastened should be understood spiritually. (Chrys.) Such are also the indiscreet priests of our own time, who command the people to practice every righteousness but themselves observe not even a little of it, evidently not in order to be righteous by doing, but to appear righteous by speaking. Such are also those who impose a heavy burden on those who come to penance, because they say and do not do. Thus, while people flee the punishment of present penance, they despise the punishment of future sin. If, when you place upon the shoulders of a young man a bundle that he cannot carry, he must either throw off the bundle or collapse under its weight, so likewise a person upon whom you impose a heavy burden of penance must either reject penance or, accepting it but unable to bear it, become scandalized and sin more. Moreover, even if we err by imposing too little penance, is it not better to give an account because of mercy than because of cruelty?

But they do all their works in order to be seen by people. [Col. 1066B] He now wishes to show the reason why they could not believe in the Lord: namely, that they do everything to be seen by people. It is impossible for someone who desires earthly human glory to believe Christ when he proclaims heavenly things. Therefore whoever performs his works in such a way as to be seen by people is like the scribes and Pharisees.

For they enlarge their phylacteries and make their fringes large. They love the first places at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and being called Rabbi by people. (Hieron.) Woe to those wretched people to whom the vices of the Pharisees pass. After giving the commandments of the law through Moses, the Lord added at the end: “You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be fixed before your eyes” (Exod. 28; Deut. 6). The sense is this: Let my commandments be in your hand, so that they may be fulfilled in action; let them be before your eyes, so that you may meditate on them day and night.

The Pharisees interpreted this badly. They wrote the Decalogue of Moses—the ten words of the law—on little strips of parchment, folding and binding them to their foreheads and making something like a crown for their heads, so that the words might always move before their eyes. The Babylonians still do this today, and anyone who possesses such things is judged religious by the people. Moses had also commanded them to make hyacinth-colored fringes at the four corners of their garments, so that the people of Israel might be distinguished; just as circumcision on the body gave the sign of the Jewish nation, so the clothing also had to bear some distinction.

The superstitious teachers, seeking popular approval and pursuing profits from women, made the fringes large and tied very sharp thorns into them, so that while walking and sitting they would sometimes be pricked and, as though by this reminder, be drawn back to the duties of God and the ministries of his service. Since the Lord had said, “They do all their works to be seen by people,” what he had accused generally he now divides into particulars.

(Hieron.) They called those little paintings of the Decalogue phylacteries, because whoever possessed them was thought to have them for his protection and defense. The Pharisees did not understand that these things should be carried in the heart, not on the body; otherwise chests and boxes also contain books, but do not possess knowledge of God. Do not superstitious women among some people still do these things today, placing them in Gospel booklets [Al.: little Gospels], [Col. 1067A] on the wood of the cross, and on objects of this kind—people who indeed have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge—“straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel”?
