Such was the small and short fringe prescribed by the law, which the woman suffering from an issue of blood touched on the Lord’s garment. But she was not pricked by the superstitious thorns of the Pharisees; rather, she was healed by touching his garment.

And while they excessively enlarge their phylacteries and make their fringes large, seeking glory from people, they are condemned in the remaining matters: why they seek the first places at banquets and the first seats in synagogues, why in public they pursue appetite and glory, and why they are called Rabbi by people—a word that in Latin means “teacher.”

(RAB.) It should nevertheless be noted that he does not forbid those to be greeted in the marketplace, or to sit or recline in the first places, to whom this belongs by the order of their office. Rather, he teaches that those who love such things improperly, whether they possess them or do not possess them, are to be avoided by all the faithful as wicked people. He rebukes the disposition, not the rank, with proper distinction. Yet it is also not free from blame if those who wish to be called teachers in the synagogue, on Moses’ seat, desire to engage in lawsuits in the marketplace.

We are rightly commanded to beware of those who desire empty glory for two reasons: lest we be deceived by their pretense and think the things they do good, or lest we be inflamed by rivalry and rejoice vainly in receiving praise for the good things they pretend to do. Finally, it follows:

But do not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher. And you are all brothers. (Chrys.) That is: Do not arrogate to yourselves what is owed to God, and do not call others Rabbi, lest you give divine honor to human beings. For one is the teacher of all, who teaches everyone by nature, as it is written: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). A human being does not give understanding to another human being by teaching; rather, through admonition, he exercises the spirit that comes from God.

And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called teachers, for one is your teacher, Christ. (Hieron.) No one else is to be called teacher or father except God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. He is Father because all things are from him; teacher because all things are through him; or because through the dispensation of the flesh we human beings have been reconciled to God.

It is asked why, contrary to this commandment, the apostle said that he was a teacher of the gentiles, or how, according to common usage, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, they call one another “Fathers.” The matter is resolved as follows: One thing is a father or teacher by nature, another by courtesy. If we call someone “father,” we pay honor to his age; we do not identify him as the author of our life. For we do not receive the beginning of life from them, but receive through them the passage of life. Someone is also called teacher by association with the true teacher. And, not to repeat endlessly, just as the one God by nature and the one Son do not prevent others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so the one Father and teacher do not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an extended sense.

Whoever is greatest among you will be your servant. When the disciples were competing for precedence, as Luke reports, the pious teacher did not rebuke them for the contention they had begun, but calmly described the form of humility they should follow (Luke 22). In maintaining this form, however, the greater and those who precede others—that is, the teachers of the Church—need no small measure of discernment, lest they rule their subjects like gentile kings and rejoice in being raised up by their empty praises. Instead, following the example of the eternal King, they should become as juniors and servants to those whom they have been appointed to govern.

For whoever wishes to precede his brother in ruling must first precede him in serving, as the Apostle says: “Outdoing one another in showing honor” (Rom. 12). Let him surpass him in service, so that he may be able to surpass him in holiness. (Greg.) Nevertheless, it is necessary that they be companions in humility with those who do good, while they stand firm through zeal for justice against the vices of wrongdoers. Thus they should not place themselves above the good in anything, yet whenever the guilt of the wicked requires it, they should immediately recognize the authority of their precedence.

Lest the mind of a ruler be carried away into arrogance by delight in his power, it is rightly said through a certain wise man: “They have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32). Hence Peter also says: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming a pattern for the flock” (1 Pet. 5). Yet sometimes one sins more gravely if equality is maintained among the wicked rather than discipline. Because Eli, overcome by false compassion, refused to strike his offending sons, he struck himself together with his sons with cruel condemnation before the strict Judge (1 Kings 2). Hence it is necessary that piety show the ruler to be a mother and discipline a father; and amid these concerns careful vigilance must ensure that neither strictness is harsh nor compassion lax.

But whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. (Venant.) Not everyone who exalts himself before people will immediately be humbled, nor will everyone who humbles himself in the sight of people be exalted by them. On the contrary, someone who raises himself either to the summit of dignity or toward the acquisition of any other glory may continue to be exalted to the end. Similarly, any humble and modest person may remain until the end of life in the modest condition with which he is content. Therefore, according to the judgment of Truth, everyone who carelessly elevates himself because of his merits will be humbled by the Lord, and whoever prudently humbles himself because of his good works will be exalted by him.

## II.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before people: for you yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit those entering to enter. (Hieron.) The scribes and Pharisees possess knowledge of the law and the prophets; they know that Christ is the Son of God. (Hilar.) They are not ignorant that he was born of a virgin. But while, by the pretense of their teaching, they conceal his bodily coming, which was proclaimed by the prophets, and seek prey from the people subject to them, they themselves do not enter the kingdom of heaven, nor permit those who could enter to do so.

This is what the Lord reproves in the prophet Hosea, saying: “The priests have hidden the way; they have killed Shechem” [that is, “a participant in the priesthood,” in the way of those who kill travelers from Shechem] (Hos. 6). And again: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’” Or certainly every teacher who builds up by his words but scandalizes his disciples by evil works shuts the kingdom of heaven before them.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you travel around sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves. We do not preserve what we seek with the same zeal with which we seek it. The scribes and Pharisees traversed the whole world for business and various profits, both to extract gains from disciples and to profit through the appearance of holiness. They took pains to make a proselyte from the gentiles—that is, to bring a foreigner and uncircumcised person into the people of God.

But someone who, while still a gentile, had previously been wandering in simple error and was once a son of Gehenna, when he sees the vices of his teachers and understands that by their deeds they destroy what they teach in words, returns to his vomit. Having become a gentile again, like a transgressor, he will deserve a greater punishment.

(RAB.) Allegorically, their traveling over sea and land signifies that they would slander the Gospel throughout the boundaries of the whole world. Proselytes are gentiles received into the synagogue; the scarcity of those who would become such in the future is indicated by the singular number. After Christ’s preaching, the faith in their teaching was not preserved. Whoever was won over to their people would be a son of Gehenna, an offspring of punishment, and an heir of eternal judgment, because adoption from the gentiles would make them members of Abraham’s family.

He will therefore be a son of doubled punishment because he has neither obtained the forgiveness of the sins of the gentiles nor followed the fellowship of those who persecuted Christ. He is called a son of Gehenna in the same way as a son of destruction and a son of this age. He is called a son of Gehenna because he is prepared for it, not because he is born from it; for each person is called the son of the one whose works he performs.

Woe to you, blind guides, who say: “Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound by his oath.” Foolish and blind men, which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And: “Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is bound by his oath.” Blind men, which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift? Whoever therefore swears by the altar swears by it and by everything that is upon it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by the one who dwells in it. And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits upon it.

Above, as it seemed to us, we explained what was signified by the Pharisees’ tradition when they said: “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you.” Now the Pharisees’ condition is condemned in two ways, since it draws everything toward one opportunity for avarice: they are shown to do everything for profit and not from fear of God.

Just as, through their enlarged phylacteries and fringes, they sought the glory of a reputation for holiness and pursued profits under the pretext of glory, so another device invented by their tradition reveals the impiety of its teachers. If someone had sworn by the temple during a dispute, some quarrel, or an uncertain case, and afterward had been convicted of lying, he was not held guilty of the offense. But if he had sworn by the gold and money offered in the temple to the priests, he was immediately compelled to fulfill what he had sworn.

Again, if someone had sworn by the altar, no one held him guilty of perjury; but if he had perjured himself concerning a gift or offering—that is, a sacrifice, victim, fine flour, or other things offered to God upon the altar—they demanded these things with the greatest insistence.

The Lord therefore rebukes them for both foolishness and fraud, because the temple is much greater than the gold sanctified by the temple, and the altar greater than the offerings sanctified by the altar. They did everything not from fear of God but from desire for riches. The temple or altar pertains to the glory of God and the salvation of spiritual people; the gold in the temple or the gift upon the altar also pertains to the glory of God, but the gold and gift themselves are offered upon the altar more for the pleasure of human beings and the benefit of the priests.

Thus the Jews said that the gold in which they themselves delighted and the gifts by which they themselves were nourished were holier than the temple and altar themselves, so that people would become more eager to offer gifts than to pour out prayers in the temple or practice righteousness. They did everything not from fear of God but from desire for riches, as was said shortly before.

Spiritually, what the Lord said—“Which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?”—and again—“Which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift?”—is to be understood as follows: the temple and altar signify Christ himself; the gold and gift signify the praises and sacrifices of prayers that we offer in him and through him. For he is not sanctified by these; rather, they are sanctified through him.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have abandoned the weightier matters: judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have done, without omitting the others. (Hieron.) There are many commandments in the law that set forth types of future things. There are also others that are clear and, according to the Psalmist, enlighten the eyes, where he says, “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes”; these immediately require action—for example: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,” and so forth (Ps. 18).

The Pharisees, because the Lord had commanded that, for the support of the priests and Levites, whose portion was the Lord, a tenth of all things should be offered in the temple—setting aside for the moment the mystical interpretations—had only this concern: that what had been commanded should be collected. Whether or not anyone practiced the other, weightier matters, they considered of little importance.

In this passage, therefore, he rebukes them because they carefully demand tithes even of the smallest herbs, while neglecting judgment in deciding cases, mercy toward the poor, orphans, and widows, and faith in God, which are great matters.

(Aug.) “These you ought to have done,” he says—that is, judgment, mercy, and faith—so that, truly judging our own misery and loving the charity of God, which he himself has bestowed, we may live piously and rightly, confessing his just judgment by which we became miserable. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Judgment indeed came from one offense unto condemnation,” while we give thanks for his great charity (Rom. 5). Concerning this same charity the preacher of grace says: “God commends his charity toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

“You ought not to have omitted the others,” that is, almsgiving from earthly produce. Let those who imagine that by whatever lavish alms from their produce or money they can purchase immunity while persisting in monstrous crimes and shameful wickedness not deceive themselves.

Blind guides, straining out the gnat but swallowing the camel. I think that, according to the meaning of the present passage and the greatness of the commandments, the camel signifies judgment, mercy, and faith; the gnat signifies the tithes of mint, dill, cumin, and the other worthless herbs. We swallow what is contrary to God’s commandments and neglect what is weighty, while displaying carefulness in small matters that bring profit under the pretext of religion.

(Aug.) These words may nevertheless be referred allegorically to the Jews. For they released Barabbas, who had not violated the Sabbath—which they observed carnally with great diligence—but killed the Lord, who was spiritually indicating the Sabbath through the judgment, mercy, and faith that they chiefly despised. Indeed, the seditious murderer is not inappropriately represented by the name “gnat,” since this creature both disturbs by its buzzing and delights in blood; and by the name “camel,” because of its greatness in humbling itself to undertake burdens, the Lord is fittingly understood. [Col. 1071C]

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of plunder and uncleanness! In different words, but with the same meaning as above, he accuses the Pharisees of pretense and falsehood: that they display one thing outwardly to human beings, but act differently at home. It was not that superstition resided in their cup and dish, but that they displayed holiness to people in their clothing, speech, phylacteries, fringes, the length of their prayers, [Col. 1071D] and other such things, while inwardly they were full of the filth of vices. For the use of a cup is internal; if it has become dirty inside, what benefit is there if it is washed externally?

(Hilar.) Therefore must the brightness of the inner conscience be secured, so that the things belonging to the body may be washed outwardly as well?

Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean. That is: first cleanse your heart and conscience from desire and evil longings, from deceit and fraud; then, through your works, you will truthfully display holiness outwardly. It should be noted, however, that in Luke it is written as follows: “Fools! Did not he who made what is outside also make what is inside?” (Luke XI.)

[Rab.] He who made both aspects of human nature desires that both should be cleansed. This is directed against the Manichaeans, who think that the soul alone was created by God, but the flesh by the devil. It is also directed against those who detest bodily sins—namely fornication, uncleanness, lust, theft, plunder, and other such things—as though they were the gravest offenses, while they regard as trivial the spiritual sins that the Apostle condemns no less: bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, blasphemy, pride, and greed, which is the service of idols.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of filth. So you too outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy [Col. 1072B] and iniquity. He also compared them to tombs which, shining through human workmanship and adornment, are inwardly defiled by the bones of the dead and the uncleanness of corpses. That is, they displayed the beauty of righteousness in empty words, but within themselves they possessed the stench of their conscience and mind.

Here he repeats by the example of tombs what he had demonstrated above concerning the cup and dish: that they were washed outwardly but filthy inwardly. For just as tombs are coated externally with whitewash, adorned with marble, and embellished with gold and colors, while inside they are full of the bones of the dead, so perverse teachers, because they teach one thing and do another, display purity through their clothing and humility of speech, while inwardly they are full of every kind of filth, greed, and lust. Finally, he expresses this even more clearly by adding: “So you too outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.” [Col. 1072C]

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and you say: “If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.” Thus you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets.

With a most judicious syllogism he proves that they are the sons of murderers, since they themselves build the tombs of the prophets whom their ancestors killed, doing so in the eyes of the people for the sake of a reputation for goodness and glory, and say: “If we had lived at that time, we would not have done what our fathers did.” Even if they do not say this in words, they proclaim it by their deeds, in that they ambitiously and magnificently build memorials for those who were killed, while not denying that their fathers slaughtered them. [Col. 1072D]

(Maur.) They did not do this out of love for truth and piety, but for the favor of empty praise; as hypocrites, they did everything deceitfully.

(Venant.) Therefore, to adorn the monuments of the prophets but to imitate the murderers of the prophets is a crime. Thus, by building monuments to the prophets, the Jews accused the deeds of their fathers, who had killed them. But by imitating their fathers’ crimes, while persecuting Christ and his apostles, they turned the sentence against themselves, doing the very things in themselves that they condemned in their parents. They pretended, in order to win the favor of the crowd, to abhor the treachery of their fathers, magnificently adorning the memorials of the prophets whom those fathers had killed; but by their very deeds they testified how much they agreed with their fathers’ wickedness, insulting the Lord who had been foretold by those same prophets. In this way they revealed themselves both as the sons of murderers and, to increase their own condemnation, as knowingly committing the sins they condemned.

And you—fill up the measure of your fathers. (Hieron.) Having established by what preceded that they were sons of murderers and of those who killed the prophets, he now concludes what he intended and supplies, as it were, the final part of the syllogism. “And you,” he says, “fill up the measure of your fathers,” that is, now complete what was lacking in them. They killed servants; you crucify the Lord. They killed prophets; you kill the one foretold by the prophets. Yet he does not command them to do what they would not have done unless he had commanded it; rather, he shows what they were going to do.

Serpents, brood of vipers. John the Baptist had said the same thing: just as vipers are born from vipers, so, he says, you have been born murderers from murderous fathers.

How will you escape the judgment of Gehenna? (Chrys.) Is it by building the tombs of the saints, or rather by cleansing your hearts from wickedness? Does God judge in the way a human being judges? A human being judges another by his works, but God judges in the heart. What kind of righteousness is it to honor the saints while despising holiness? The first step of piety is to love holiness; then to love the saints, because the saints did not exist before holiness, but holiness existed before the saints. It is therefore useless to honor the righteous while despising righteousness. How will you escape? Will the saints whose tombs you adorn deliver you? The saints cannot be friends of those whose enemy is God.

Therefore, behold, I send you prophets, wise men, and scribes; some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city. What we said earlier—“Fill up the measure of your fathers”—may refer to the person of the Lord, since he was to be killed by them; but it may also refer to his disciples, concerning whom he now says: “Behold, I send you prophets, wise men, and scribes, and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will scourge in your synagogues [Col. 1073D] and persecute from city to city,” so that you may fill up the measure of your fathers.

At the same time, observe, in accordance with the Apostle’s writing to the Corinthians, that the gifts of Christ’s disciples are various: some are prophets, who proclaim what is to come; others are wise, knowing when they ought to deliver a discourse; others are scribes, highly learned in the law. From their number Stephen was stoned, Paul was killed, Peter was crucified, and the disciples were scourged, as related in the Acts of the Apostles. They persecuted them from city to city, driving them out of Judea so that they might migrate to the people of the Gentiles to disseminate the Gospel of Christ (Acts V).

But if the same Son of God sent the prophets who were his apostles, let the heretics cease to give Christ a beginning from the Virgin, and let them stop preaching one God of the law and the prophets and another God of the New Testament.

So that all the righteous blood shed upon the earth may come upon you? (Venant.) “Let all righteous blood come upon you” means the vengeance of just retribution that they deserved for the blood of the righteous that had been shed.

It is therefore asked how the blood of all the prophets and righteous can be required from a single generation of Jews, since many saints, whether before the Incarnation or after the Savior’s death and resurrection, were killed by other nations, and the Lord himself, although the Jews cried out for it, was crucified by a Roman governor and Roman soldiers. But it is the custom of Scripture often to reckon two human generations: the good and the evil. These are, on the one hand, those who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of a man, but from God (John I), and, on the other, those to whom it is said: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII), and elsewhere: “Serpents, brood of vipers.” For there is one generation of all the wicked, persecutors, and murderers, from Cain to the end of the age. Although they do not all exist at the same time, the faithful call them all the body of the devil and the city of Babylon, that is, of confusion.

From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar? Why he begins with the blood of Abel, who first suffered martyrdom, is not surprising. But why does he continue to the blood of Zechariah, when many others after him, up to the birth of Christ, and immediately after his birth the infant Innocents in Bethlehem, were killed by this generation? Perhaps it is because Abel was a shepherd of sheep (Gen. IV), while Zechariah was a priest; the former was killed in the field, the latter in the temple court. Under their names he wished to indicate martyrs of both ranks: laymen and those devoted to the service of the altar.

(Hieron.) Literally, there is no ambiguity that Abel is righteous, since his brother Cain killed him. He is proved righteous not only by the Lord’s present judgment, but also by the testimony of Genesis, where it relates that his offerings were accepted by the Lord.

We ask who this Zechariah son of Barachiah is, since we read of many Zechariahs. And lest we be granted unrestricted freedom to err, it is added: “Whom you killed between the temple and the altar.” I have read different opinions in different sources, and I ought to set out the views of each.

Some say that Zechariah son of Barachiah is the one who is tenth among the Twelve Prophets, and that his father’s name agrees with this identification; but Scripture does not say that he was killed between the temple and the altar, especially since in his time scarcely even the ruins of the temple remained.

Others want Zechariah, the father of John, to be understood. They support this from certain apocryphal books, claiming that he was killed because he had proclaimed the Savior’s coming. Since this has no authority from Scripture, it is rejected as readily as it is accepted.

Others want this to be Zechariah who was killed by Joash, king of Judah, between the temple and the altar, as the history of Kings relates. But it must be observed that this Zechariah was not the son of Barachiah, but the son of Jehoiada the priest. Hence Scripture reports: “Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada his father had done for him” (2 Chron. XXIV). Since we have both Zechariah and the location of his killing in agreement, we ask why he is called the son of Barachiah rather than the son of Jehoiada.

Barachiah in our language means “blessed of the Lord,” while the righteousness of the priest Jehoiada is indicated by his Hebrew name. In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, we find “son of Jehoiada” written instead of “son of Barachiah.” Simpler brethren, pointing out red stones among the ruins of the temple and altar, or at the exits of the gates that lead toward Siloam, think that they were stained with Zechariah’s blood. But we do not condemn an error that has arisen from hatred of the Jews and pious faith.

[Col. 1075B] Amen, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. Clearly, upon that generation which is rightly condemned by the Lord for its impiety: the generation extending from the first parricide to the final son of perdition. It will not come upon the generation of the righteous, which will be blessed by the Lord (Ps. XXIII), the generation of those who seek the Lord and desire the face of the God of Jacob, which ascends the mountain of the Lord and stands in his holy place.

Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you. By “Jerusalem” he means not the stones and buildings of the city, but its inhabitants, and he mourns it with a father’s affection, just as we read elsewhere that he wept when he saw it (Luke XIX).

How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling? In saying against the impious city, “How often I wanted to gather your children, and you were unwilling,” he seems to suggest that God’s will was overcome by the human will, and that the most powerful one was unable to do what he wished because the weakest obstructed him by their unwillingness. Where, then, is that omnipotence which did everything in heaven and on earth that he wished (Ps. CXIII), if he wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children but did not do so? Or rather, was it Jerusalem that was unwilling for its children to be gathered by him?

Yet even though she was unwilling, he gathered the children he wished. For in heaven and on earth he did not will some things and accomplish them, but will other things and fail to accomplish them; rather, in heaven and on earth he did everything that he wished.

(Hier.) When he says, “How often I wanted to gather your children,” he testifies that all the prophets previously sent were sent by him. He also uses the likeness of a hen gathering her chicks under her wings.

(Aug.) This kind of creature has great affection for its young, so that, distressed by their weakness, it too becomes weak; and—a thing more difficult to find among other animals—while protecting its children with its wings, it fights against the kite. So too our mother, the Wisdom of God, having been made weak in a certain sense through the assumption of flesh—for the Apostle says, “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. I)—protects our weakness and resists the devil, lest he carry us away. In this protection, what the hen attempts through affection against the kite, Wisdom accomplishes through power against the devil.

(Hier.) Likewise, in the Song of Deuteronomy we read another comparison: as an eagle protects its nest and, spreading its wings over its young whom it desires, takes them up and carries them on its feathers (Deut. XXXII).

[Rab.] And fittingly, the one who had called Herod, plotting his death, a fox compares himself to a bird. For the deceitful fox never ceases to lay snares for birds.

Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. (Hieron.) He had already said the same thing earlier through the person of Jeremiah: “I have left my house; I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest” (Jer. XII). We see that the house of the Jews—that is, the temple that once shone in majestic splendor—has been left desolate. For it lost Christ, its inhabitant, and, eager to seize the inheritance, killed the heir. [Col. 1076B]

(Aug.) The city that, according to another evangelist, he had called his nest, he now calls the house of the Jews. It is not unjustly stripped of the Lord’s help and left to its own power, because it not only disdained being protected by the wings of that omnipotent bird whom Matthew calls a hen, but also handed over Christ—the same bird who wished to protect it—to the foxes, that is, to Herod and Pilate, to be devoured and crucified. Nor was there delay before those same foxes, that is, the kings of the earth, devoured the plunder itself. For after the Lord had been killed, the Romans came and, as though plundering an empty nest, took away their place, nation, and kingdom.

For I say to you: You will not see me from now on until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” (Aug.) The crowds did indeed say this to the Lord when he came to Jerusalem. But because Luke does not say that the Lord departed from there so as not to return until the time when this would already be said—for he continues on his journey until he reaches Jerusalem—this must certainly be understood mystically, that is, of his coming in which he will come in glory (Luke XIII).

(Venant.) This is especially so because Matthew testifies that the Lord said these words after the crowd had sung praises to him, so that what he says may be understood otherwise: unless you repent and confess that I am the one of whom the prophets sang, the Son of the almighty Father, you will not see my face. The Jews have been given a time for repentance. Let them confess him blessed who comes in the name of the Lord, and they will behold the face of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIV

On the structure of the temple and the signs of the last days, and on the coming of the Savior; on the vigilance of the good servant, and on the dissolution of the elements, etc.

[I.] And Jesus went out from the temple and was departing, and his disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple. But he answered and said to them: Do you see all these things? Amen, I say to you, not one stone here will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.

(Hieron.) According to the historical sense, the meaning is clear: in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion, under Vespasian and Titus, emperors of the Romans, the city itself was so utterly overthrown together with its magnificent temple that it was leveled with the ground. Even now the circuit of the walls that surrounds the site testifies to this, since it encloses within the walls the place of Calvary, where the Lord suffered outside the gate. [Col. 1077A]

(Maur.) Mystically, however, when the Lord departed from the temple, all the structures of the law and the arrangement of its commandments were destroyed, so that nothing could be fulfilled by the Jews; and, with the head removed, all the members fought among themselves. By divine providence it was arranged that, once the grace of evangelical faith had been revealed throughout the world, the temple itself, once so venerable, should be removed together with its ceremonies. Otherwise, someone still small and nursing in the faith, seeing those things remain that had been established by the holy prophets and instituted by the Lord, might, through admiration for the sacred ancient order, gradually fall away from the sincerity of faith that is in Christ Jesus [Col. 1077B] into carnal Judaism. Thus, providing for our weakness and desiring that his Church should multiply, God caused all those things to be overturned and entirely removed, so that, when the shadow and type had ceased, the truth itself, now proclaimed throughout the world, might hold the palm.

As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, his disciples came to him privately, saying: Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age? In Mark’s Gospel it is written as follows: “And when he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew questioned him privately: Tell us, when will these things happen?” (Mark XIII), and so forth.

Because, when some people were praising the buildings of the temple, the Lord had openly [Col. 1077C] answered that all these things would be destroyed, the disciples privately ask about the time and signs of the destruction foretold, saying: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?”

Here they ask three things. First: Tell us when the temple is to be overthrown. Second: What will be the sign of your coming? That is, your coming to reign temporally, which the disciples thought would occur, as may be understood from another passage where they ask: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts I.) Nevertheless, this question of the disciples may also be understood as referring to his coming for judgment. For they had recognized from these and other passages, and especially from Matthew’s words, “In the generation” (Matt. XIX), that he would be the judge of human beings.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Some material is missing here, having been lost during printing when soldiers laid everything waste, as stated in the Preface to the reader. Cologne Editor.] [lacuna] [Col. 1077D] [lacuna]

But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, except the Father alone. (Hieron.) In some manuscripts “nor the Son” has been added, although this is not found in the Greek manuscripts, and especially not in the copies of our Origen. But since it is read in some sources, it seems that the matter should be discussed.

Arius and Eunomius rejoice, as though the teacher’s ignorance were the glory of his disciples, and they say that one who knows and one who is ignorant cannot be equal. Against them the following must briefly be said. Since Jesus, that is, the Word of God, made all times—for “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I)—and since the day of judgment is included among all times, by what reasoning can he be ignorant of a part whose whole he knows?

This too must be said: what is greater, knowledge of the Father or knowledge of the judgment? If he knows what is greater, how can he be ignorant of what is less? We read: “All things that belong to the Father have been handed over to me” (Luke X). If all things belonging to the Father are the Son’s, for what reason did he reserve the knowledge of a single day for himself and refuse to share it with the Son?

We must also add this: if he is ignorant of the last day of the times, then he is ignorant of the preceding day and of all the days before it. For it cannot happen that one who does not know the first knows what the second is.

Therefore, since we have proved that the Son is not ignorant of the day of consummation, an explanation must be given for why he is said to be ignorant. The Apostle wrote concerning the Savior: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom” (Col. II). Thus all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are in Christ, but they are hidden. Why are they hidden? After the resurrection, when the apostles asked him about the day, he answered openly: “It is not for you to know the times and moments that the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts I). When he says, “It is not for you to know,” he shows that he himself knows, but that it is not beneficial for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain about the Judge’s coming, they may live each day as though they were to be judged on that day.

Finally, the subsequent discourse of the Gospel compels us to understand the same thing when it says that the Father alone knows; for in the Father it includes the Son as well, since every father is named in relation to a son.

(Aug.) The statement that the Son does not know is expressed in this way because he causes human beings not to know—that is, he does not disclose to them what they would know uselessly.

I have also read in a certain book that the son mentioned here should be understood not as the only-begotten Son but as the adopted son, that is, the Christian people. Of this people God says: “I will be a Father to them, and they will be my sons.” For if he had said this about the only-begotten Son, he would never have placed angels before him. For he says, “Neither the angels of heaven, nor the son,” thereby showing that he spoke not of the only-begotten Son but of the adopted people. No one among the holy angels or holy human beings has been granted knowledge of this day; the Father alone, and the Son and the Holy Spirit—that is, the one God—keeps it unknown to others in his own knowledge.

As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. (Rab.) He confirms by many examples that the day of his coming will be sudden. For the one whom he had compared to lightning swiftly passing over everything, he likewise compares to the days of Noah—or, according to another evangelist, to the days of Lot—when sudden destruction came upon mortals (Luke XVII).

For just as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage. Marriage and food are not condemned here according to the insane doctrine of Marcion, Manichaeus, and Tatian, the leader of the Encratites, since the former contains the means of succession and the latter the supports of nature. Rather, in accordance with what the Apostle says, “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Cor. VI), it is immoderate use of what is lawful that is criticized. They did not perish by water or fire because they engaged in these activities, but because, devoting themselves entirely to them, they disregarded God’s judgments.

(Hieron.) It is asked how it was written above, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be pestilences, famines, and earthquakes” (Matt. XXVII), while now those things are mentioned as future which are signs of peace. But, in accordance with the Apostle, it should be understood that after wars, dissensions, pestilences, famines, earthquakes, and the other calamities by which the human race is devastated, a brief peace will follow, promising quiet in all things, so that the faith of believers may be tested: whether, after the evils have passed, they expect the Judge to come. [Col. 1079B] For this is what we read in Paul: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. V), like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

Until the day when Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and swept them all away; so will be the coming of the Son of Man.

(Rab.) Mystically, Noah builds the ark when the Lord constructs the Church by joining together faithful men like smoothed pieces of wood. He enters it when it has been perfectly completed, as the eternal inhabitant illumines it on the day of judgment by the presence of his vision. But while the ark is being built, the wicked indulge themselves; when it is entered, they perish. For those who insult the saints while they struggle here will be punished there with eternal damnation when the saints are crowned.

[Col. 1079C] Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and one will be left. “Then,” he says, “two will be in the field.”

(Hieron.) When? At the time of the consummation and judgment. Two will then be found together in the field, having the same labor and, as it were, an equal sowing, but not receiving the fruits of their labor equally.

(Venant.) He signifies those who work in the ministry of the Church, as in God’s field, of which its farmer said: “You are God’s cultivation” (1 Cor. III). The one who does not corrupt the word of God, but speaks as from God, before God, in Christ, will be taken; but the one who proclaims Christ not chastely but from an ulterior motive will be left behind.

(Aug.) Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one will be left. He calls those who are established among the people and governed by teachers “women,” as they perform the activities of this age. He used the name “women” because it is beneficial for them to be governed by the counsels of the experienced, as I have said. He says “grinding” because of the world and cycle of temporal affairs; yet, according to another evangelist, he says that they are grinding at one mill, insofar as they offer service from those very affairs and occupations for the uses of the Church.

(Venant.) Every activity of this world is a mill. While it heaps up many cares, it turns human minds as though in a circle and casts out from itself, as it were, flour, because it continually gives birth to tiny thoughts in a restless heart. One will be taken and the other left. The part that has entered marriage solely for the love of procreation will be taken, and the one that has distributed earthly wealth to acquire heavenly things. But the one that has served marriage for the allurements of the flesh will be left; and if it has offered earthly goods to the Church or the poor, it will have done so in order that, as though it had purchased the Lord, it might abound in even more of them.

Two will be in bed; one will be taken and one will be left. Two will be in bed: namely, those who choose leisure and rest and are occupied neither with secular affairs nor with ecclesiastical affairs. Their rest is signified by the name “bed.” One will be taken and the other left—not as though this were said of two individuals, but of two kinds of disposition.

Whoever has devoted himself to continence for God’s sake, so that, living without anxiety, he may think about the things of God, will be taken by God. But whoever, whether from love of human praise or from some other enticement of vices, injures the state of monastic life in which he has been trained will be left behind. Where he is to be left, the Lamentations of Jeremiah indicate. Describing the fall of any idle and sinful soul under the figure of Judea, he says: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I).

(Aug.) I do not think that there are other classes of people of whom the Church consists than these three, each possessing two differences because of being taken or left. Although many differences of pursuits and desires can be found within each class, all may nevertheless converge toward harmony and unity. Hence the prophet Ezekiel saw three men delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV).

(Greg.) In these three, rulers, continent persons, and married people are signified. Noah governed the ark amid the waters and therefore represented rulers. Daniel lived in the royal court devoted to abstinence and therefore signified the life of the continent. Job, living in marriage and caring for his household, pleased God and thereby fittingly represents the order of good married people.

After the Lord had completed his discourse concerning the distinction between those who would be crowned and those who would be condemned, he now makes clear why he had said these things, adding:

Therefore keep watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. (Hieron.) He clearly shows why he had said above: “Concerning that day no one knows, neither the Son of Man nor the angels, except the Father alone.” It is not beneficial for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain in their expectant waiting, they may believe that the one whom they do not know will come.

When he says, “You do not know at what hour he will come,” he does not say, “Because we do not know at what hour the Lord will come.” After giving the example of the head of the household, he explains more clearly why he conceals the day of consummation, saying: “Be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (Matt. XXV).

But know this: if the head of the household had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have kept watch and would not have allowed his house to be broken into. From this preceding comparison the exhortation also follows:

Therefore you too must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come. Because the head of the household does not know, the thief breaks into the house. While the spirit sleeps, failing to guard itself, sudden death comes and breaks into the dwelling of our flesh and kills the master whom it finds sleeping. Because the spirit does not foresee the impending losses, death carries it away unsuspecting to punishment. Yet it would resist the thief if it were awake. By anticipating the coming of the Judge, who secretly seizes the soul, it would meet him through repentance, lest it perish unrepentant.

Our Lord wished the final hour to remain unknown to us precisely so that it might always be feared. Since we cannot foresee it, we may prepare for it without interruption.

[II.] Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom his lord has appointed over his household? In response to the questions, the Savior first teaches that judgment awaits everyone, and that each person will receive rewards or punishments according to the merit of his work and the capacity of his understanding. Then, addressing what had chiefly been asked, he shows that the grace of the virtues which he brought to the world, and which each person is able to pursue, must be sought.

“I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII.)

The phrase “Who, do you think, is…” indicates difficulty, not impossibility, in accomplishing virtue. Thus the Psalmist says, “Who is wise and will keep these things?” (Ps. CVI), meaning not no one, but only a rare person. Elsewhere the same word signifies not something difficult but something impossible: “God, who will be like you?”—that is, no one—“For you alone are Most High over all the earth” (Ps. LXXXII).

“Who, do you think,” he says, “is the faithful and prudent servant?” Faithful in giving out devotedly and not hiding his lord’s money; prudent in carefully discerning the capacity of each servant.

(Fulgent.) “Whom,” he says, “his lord has appointed over his household.” Who is this Lord except Christ, who said to his disciples: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John XIII)?

What is this Lord’s household? Surely it is the one that the Lord himself redeemed from the hand of the enemy and subjected to his dominion. This household is the holy Catholic Church, which spreads throughout the world in abundant fruitfulness and glories in having been redeemed by the precious blood of its Lord. For, as the Son of Man himself says, he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Matt. XX). He is also the good shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep (John XI). The flock of the good shepherd is the household of the Redeemer.

Who the steward is, who must be faithful and prudent, the Apostle Paul shows us. Speaking of himself and his companions, he says: “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. In stewards, moreover, it is required that one be found faithful” (1 Cor. IV).

But lest any of us think that only the apostles were made stewards and, neglecting the duty of spiritual service, sleep faithlessly and imprudently as a lazy servant, the blessed Apostle also shows that bishops are stewards, saying: “It is necessary for a bishop to be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus I).

Therefore we are servants of the head of the household and stewards of the Lord, so that we may distribute to our fellow servants the food that we have received from the Lord.

That he may give them food at the proper time. (Jerome) He inserts the example of the householder—that is, of himself—and of the faithful servants, namely, the apostles, as an exhortation to an attentive mind, so that, in hope of rewards, they may minister food of doctrine to their fellow servants at the proper time. (Fulgentius) What the food and the measure are, according to the other Evangelist—if we ask whether it is wheat—the blessed Apostle Paul shows when he says: “To each as God has apportioned the measure of faith” (Romans 12). The measure, then, or food, which Christ now names, Paul calls the measure of faith, so that we may recognize that spiritual food—or wheat, according to Luke—is none other than the venerable sacrament of the Christian faith (Luke 12). Priests distribute this food, or measure of wheat, in the name of the Lord whenever, illumined by the gift of spiritual grace, they expound according to the rule of the true faith. And the faithful receive this same food, or measure of wheat, through the Lord’s faithful stewards whenever they hear the word of truth daily from God’s servants. It is therefore concerning this measure of wheat that the prelates of the Church speak. From it all the faithful are fed with food, as God distributes it through them. From it they take nourishment for a good life, so that they may attain the rewards of eternal life, believing in him, hoping in him, loving him above all and in all things—him who gives himself to us as nourishment, so that we may not fail on the way, and preserves himself as our reward, so that we may rejoice in our homeland. (Gregory) By the measure of wheat, therefore, the manner of speech is signified. For lofty matters ought to be concealed from many hearers and disclosed only with difficulty to the few, lest, when something beyond a narrow heart’s capacity is offered, it be poured out beyond it. Thus Moses, coming forth from God’s secret presence, veils his shining face before the people, because he does not disclose to the crowds the mysteries of inward brightness. The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the quality of their hearers, so that it may suit each person individually and yet never depart from the art of the common edification.

Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing this. Amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. As great as the difference between good hearers and good teachers is, so great also is the difference between their rewards. When he comes and finds the former keeping watch, he will make them recline, and, passing by, will minister to them. But when he finds the latter faithfully and prudently distributing the grain of the word to the household entrusted to them, he will set them over all that he possesses—that is, over all the joys of the heavenly kingdom. Not, of course, so that they alone may possess dominion over these things, but so that they may enjoy eternal possession of them more abundantly than the other saints. “Those who are learned will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel 12). And the Apostle says: “Let presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine” (1 Timothy 5).

But if that evil servant says in his heart, “My lord is delaying his coming,” and begins to beat his fellow servants, while eating and drinking with drunkards—this follows from what came before: just as the attentive servant, always awaiting the Lord’s coming, gives food to his fellow servants at the proper time and is afterward set over all the householder’s possessions, so, conversely, the one who says with Ezekiel, “This will be for a long time” (Ezekiel 12), and does not think that the Lord will come soon, becoming more secure, devotes himself to banquets and debauchery; and he will find not a gentle householder but a most severe judge. (Rabanus) Just as, in the one faithful steward, the whole order of good rulers—how they should live and how they should be rewarded—is taught, so in this most wicked servant the condemned work and eternal condemnation of all wicked prelates are likewise recounted: when, neglecting the fear of the Lord, they not only devote themselves to luxury but also provoke their subjects by injuries. Yet, figuratively, “to beat his fellow servants” may be understood as corrupting the hearts of the weak, who are not yet strengthened in faith, hope, and charity, by displaying an example of wicked action or speech. Hence we also read in Luke: “And he began to beat the boys and the maidservants” (Luke 12). The weaker their age or sex, the easier their downfall. To eat, drink, and become drunk means to be occupied both with every crime and with the allurements of the world, which stupefy the mind and cause it to go astray. Notice carefully that among the vices of the evil servant it is recorded that he thought his lord’s return would be delayed. But among the virtues of the good servant it is not counted that he hoped for his lord’s swift arrival; rather, only that, whenever the lord might come, he gave his fellow servants the measure of wheat at the proper time—that is, that he displayed either the rule of divine speech or of his own example. Indeed, we read that certain good servants were rebuked by the Apostle because, trembling and anxious, they believed that the day of the Lord was imminent, whereas he himself had promised that it would come unexpectedly (2 Thessalonians 2). Hence, although we greatly desire, if it were possible, to know when the one desired by all the nations will come, it is proved best that we patiently endure not knowing what we are not permitted to know. We ought only to be ready, as an example of the good servant, to await and love his coming, whether it is near or far off.

The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him apart and appoint his portion with the hypocrites; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. (Jerome) This very thing teaches them that when the Lord is not expected, then he will come. He warns stewards to be watchful and attentive. Moreover, when he says, “He will cut him apart,” this does not mean that he will dismember him with a sword, but that he will separate him from the company of the saints. (Rabanus) Why? Because he despaired of the Lord’s coming; because he did not obey his commands; because he devoted himself to present things; because he lived the life of the nations; because, through despair of judgment, he afflicted the household entrusted to him with hunger, thirst, and slaughter. “He will appoint his portion with the hypocrites,” namely, with those who were in the field and those who were grinding, and who nevertheless were abandoned. We have often said that a hypocrite is one thing inwardly and displays another outwardly. Thus, both in the field and at the mill, he seemed to be doing the same thing as the ecclesiastical man, but the outcome revealed a different intention. When he says that there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth where the wicked servant receives his portion with the hypocrites, he expresses, as some wish, a twofold punishment of Gehenna, namely fire and cold: weeping of the eyes belongs to fire, gnashing of the teeth to cold. Hence it is also written in Job: “He passes from waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24). But, reserving these matters for divine knowledge, we earnestly warn that the torment of hell, whatever it may be, must be utterly avoided. It follows:

## CHAPTER 25

The parable of the ten virgins, of the sheep and goats, of their deeds, of the productive servants and the lazy one, etc.

### I

Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.

Having given an example concerning the day of judgment through the good and faithful servant and through the evil and faithless servant, he again sets forth another example concerning the same matter, saying: “Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins,” and so forth. (Jerome) Some interpret this parable—that is, the likeness of the ten foolish and wise virgins—simply with reference to virgins: some, according to the Apostle, are virgins both in body and in mind; others preserve only bodily virginity, while lacking the other works of righteousness; reserved for their purpose or under the guardianship of their parents, they have nevertheless married in their minds. But it seems to me that, from what precedes, another meaning is intended, and that the comparison pertains not to virginal bodies but to the whole human race. (Gregory) Nevertheless, we must first ask what the kingdom of heaven is, or why it is compared to ten virgins who are called both wise and foolish. For since the kingdom of heaven is understood to be a place into which no reprobate enters, why is it said to be like foolish virgins? We should know that sacred Scripture often calls the Church of the present time the kingdom of heaven, as we have also shown elsewhere. Concerning this the Lord says in another place: “The angels will come and separate all scandals from his kingdom” (Matthew 13). For in that kingdom of blessedness, where there is perfect peace, there can be no scandals to be gathered up. And again it is said: “Whoever does and teaches, he will be called great in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches accordingly, he will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). A person loosens a commandment and teaches this when he proclaims by his voice what he does not fulfill in his life. But he cannot attain the kingdom of eternal blessedness who refuses to fulfill by his deeds what he teaches. How, then, is he called least in it who is in no way permitted to enter it? What, then, is signified by this statement except the present Church, which is called the kingdom of heaven? In it, the teacher who loosens a commandment is called least, because when his life is despised, his preaching necessarily remains despised as well.

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.” (Augustine) As for the fact that he said the virgins went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride, I think it should be understood in such a way that the one called the bride consists of those very virgins. It is as though, when all Christians are running together into the Church, one were to say that the children are running together to their mother, although the one called the mother consists of the children gathered together. For now the Church is betrothed, and she is a virgin who is to be led to the wedding, that is, so long as she keeps herself from worldly corruption. At that time she will marry, when all mortality has passed away in her and she is made fruitful through an immortal union. “I betrothed you,” he says, “to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11). He says “you,” “a virgin,” passing from the plural number to the singular. Why they are said to be five we shall explain below. It seems to me, then, that the five virgins signify continence divided into five parts, from the allurements of the flesh. For it subsists in the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. The mind’s appetite must be restrained from the pleasure of the eyes, the pleasure of the ears, the pleasure of smelling, tasting, and touching.

(Gregory) The number five, doubled, completes the number ten. And because a multitude of the faithful is gathered from both sexes, the holy Church is declared to be like ten virgins. Since in it the wicked are mingled with the good and the reprobate with the elect, it is rightly said to be like both wise and foolish virgins. There are many continent people who guard themselves from outward desire and are carried inward by hope; they chastise the flesh and, with their whole desire, yearn for the heavenly homeland; they seek to receive eternal rewards for their labors and do not desire human praise. These certainly do not place their glory in the mouths of men but conceal it within their conscience. There are also many who afflict their bodies through abstinence but seek human favor for that very abstinence; they devote themselves to teaching and give much to those in need, but they are certainly foolish virgins, because they seek only the reward of passing praise. Hence it is plainly added:

But the five foolish, after taking their lamps, did not take oil with them. The wise, however, took oil in their vessels with their lamps. By oil, the brightness of glory is signified. The little vessels are our hearts, in which we carry all that we think. The wise have oil in their vessels because they keep the brightness of glory within their conscience, as Paul bears witness when he says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1). The foolish virgins do not take oil with them because they do not possess glory within their conscience, while they seek it from the mouths of those around them. (Augustine) Likewise, joy of mind is expressed by oil; hence it is also written: “Your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44). Whoever does not rejoice because he is pleasing to God inwardly does not have oil with him. But the wise took oil with them in their vessels along with their lamps (Galatians 6), that is, they placed the joy of good works in their hearts and conscience. As the Apostle mentioned above also exhorts and says: “Let a person examine himself, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another.” And again: “Rejoice,” he says, “in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4). (Gregory) Hence it should be noted that all have lamps, but not all have oil, because often the reprobate as well as the elect display good works outwardly, but only those come to the bridegroom with oil who seek inward glory from the things they have done outwardly. Hence the Psalmist also says concerning the holy Church of the elect: “All the glory of the daughter of kings is within” (Psalm 44).

While the bridegroom was delaying, they all grew drowsy and fell asleep. Because the Judge delays coming for the final judgment, the elect and the reprobate are lulled by the sleep of death; for to sleep is to die. Before sleep, however, to grow drowsy is to weaken in salvation before death, because through the burden of illness one reaches the sleep of death. (Jerome) The death of the saints is called sleep. It is consequently said, “They grew drowsy,” because afterward they are to be raised.

But in the middle of the night a cry arose: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.” (Gregory) The cry concerning the bridegroom’s arrival occurs in the middle of the night, because the day of judgment steals upon us in such a way that it cannot be foreseen when it comes. Hence it is written: “That day will come like a thief in the night.” (Jerome) Suddenly, as though in the deep of night, when all are secure and the heaviest sleep prevails, the cry of the angels and the trumpet of the powers that go before Christ will resound, announcing his coming. Let us say something that may perhaps be useful to the reader. It is a Jewish tradition that Christ will come in the middle of the night, in imitation of the time in Egypt when the Passover was celebrated, the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the dwellings, and the doorposts of our foreheads were consecrated with the blood of the lamb (Exodus 12). Hence I think that the apostolic tradition also remained, so that on the day of the Paschal vigil it is not permitted to dismiss the people before midnight, as they await Christ’s coming. After that time has passed, with confidence assumed, all celebrate the festive day. Hence the Psalmist also said: “At midnight I rose to confess you because of the judgments of your righteousness.”

Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. (Gregory) Then all the virgins rise, because both the elect and the reprobate are awakened from the sleep of their death. They trim their lamps because they count the works they have brought with them, for which they expect to receive eternal blessedness.

But the foolish said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” (Jerome) By complaining that their lamps are going out, they show that they shine in part, yet do not possess unfailing light or enduring works. Therefore, if anyone has a virginal soul and loves chastity, he ought not to be content with mediocre things, which quickly fade and dry up when the heat rises, but should pursue perfect virtues, so that he may have everlasting light. (Gregory) The lamps of the foolish virgins therefore go out because their works, which had appeared bright to men outwardly, are darkened inwardly at the Judge’s coming, and they find no reward from God. For they received from men the praises they loved. What does it mean that they then ask the wise for oil, except that, when they find themselves inwardly empty at the Judge’s coming, they seek testimony from outside and, deceived by their own confidence, say to their neighbors: “You see us being rejected as though without works; tell us what you have seen of our works”?

The wise answered, saying: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.” (Jerome) They answer not out of avarice but out of fear: each person will receive a reward according to his works, and on the day of judgment the virtues of some cannot lift up the vices of others. Just as, at the time of the Babylonian captivity, Jeremiah could not help sinners, and it was said to him, “Do not pray for this people” (Jeremiah 14), so that day will be full of terror, when each person will be concerned for himself. (Gregory) On that day—though I speak here of certain people resting in the peace of the Church—the testimony of each person will scarcely suffice for himself; how much less for himself and his neighbor? Hence it is immediately added by way of rebuke:

Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves. (Augustine) They should not be thought to have offered advice, but rather to have recalled their guilt indirectly. For flatterers sell oil: by praising either what is false or what they do not know, they lead souls into error, and, by procuring vain joys for them as for foolish people, they receive some payment from them, whether food, money, honor, or some other temporal advantage. They do not understand what has been said: “Those who call you happy lead you into error” (Isaiah 3). It is better to be rebuked by a righteous person than praised by a sinner: “The righteous,” he says, “will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Psalm 140). (Gregory) The principal part in us is our head. For by the name “head,” the mind that presides over the body is meant. The oil of the sinner therefore fattens the head when the favor of a flatterer caresses the mind. “Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.” (Augustine) That is: Let us now see what help those give you who were accustomed to sell you praises and lead you into error, so that you sought glory not before God but from men.

While they went to buy, the bridegroom came; those who were ready entered with him into the wedding, and the door was shut. That is, while they were bending toward the things that are outside and seeking the joys to which they were accustomed, because they did not know inward joys, he who judges came; and those who were ready—that is, those whose conscience gave good testimony before God—entered with him into the wedding, that is, where a pure soul is joined in fruitfulness to the pure and perfect word of God. The door was shut; that is, after those who had been transformed into angelic life had been received—“We shall all rise, but we shall not all be transformed” (1 Corinthians 15)—access to the kingdom of heaven was closed. After judgment there is no place for prayers or merits. (Gregory) Oh, if only the palate of the heart could taste what wonder lies in the words, “The bridegroom came”; what sweetness in, “They entered with him into the wedding”; what bitterness in, “The door was shut”! For he came whose arrival shakes the elements, before whose presence heaven and earth tremble. Hence the prophet also says: “Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Haggai 2). The whole human race is led to his tribunal, while angels, archangels, thrones, principalities, and dominions follow him to punish the wicked and reward the good. Then the door of the kingdom is closed to those who mourn, though now it is opened daily to penitents. For then there will indeed be repentance, but it will no longer be fruitful, because then the one who has lost the suitable time for pardon will by no means find forgiveness. Hence it follows:

At last the other virgins also came, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” But he answered and said: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” (Augustine) It is not said that they bought oil; therefore we should understand that, with no joy from the praises of others remaining, they return in distress and great affliction to imploring God. But great is his severity after judgment, whose ineffable mercy was extended before judgment. Therefore he answered and said: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” There the Lord can no longer have mercy on the one who here refused to hear what he commanded. Whoever has lost the appropriate time for repentance comes uselessly before the gate of the kingdom with prayers. Hence the Lord says through Solomon: “I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked. You despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes; I too will laugh at your destruction, and mock you when what you feared comes. When sudden calamity falls, when tribulation and anguish come upon you, and calamity and destruction rush upon you like a storm, then they will call upon me and I will not answer; they will rise early and will not find me” (Proverbs 1). Behold, they cry for the door to be opened, and, compelled by the grief of their rejection, they repeat the title of the Lord, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” They offer prayers, but they are not known, because then God abandons as unknown those whom he does not now recognize as his own by the merit of their life. “The Lord knows those who are his,” and “whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14). (Jerome) The Lord does not know workers of iniquity. Although they are virgins, and, according to the twofold understanding, boast of bodily purity and of confessing the true faith, nevertheless, because they do not possess the oil of knowledge and truth, it is sufficient punishment for them that they are not known by the bridegroom. From what follows, then—

“Keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour”—he made clear the meaning of everything he had said: concerning the two who are in the field, the two who are grinding, the householder who entrusted his possessions to his servants, and the ten virgins. These parables were set forth because we do not know the day of judgment, so that we may diligently prepare the lamp of good works for ourselves, lest, while we are unaware, the Judge come. (Augustine) For no one knows not only the day and hour of that final time when the bridegroom will come, but also the day and hour of his own falling asleep. Whoever is ready until sleep—that is, until death, which is owed to all—will also be found ready when that voice sounds in the middle of the night by which all will be awakened. Hence a general exhortation to the disciples is also plainly added: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” Since God receives repentance after sins, if each person knew at what time he would depart from the present age, he could set aside one time for pleasures and another for repentance. But the one who promised forgiveness to the penitent did not promise tomorrow to the sinner. Therefore we must always fear the final day, which we can never foresee. Behold, now we receive the very day on which we speak as a delay for conversion, and yet we refuse to weep over the evils we have committed. We not only do not mourn what we have done, but even increase the things that must be mourned. But if some illness seizes us, if signs of illness announce approaching death, we seek a delay in living so that we may mourn our sins, and we ask with great fervor for what we once regarded as worthless when it was granted to us. (Maurice) But because it is truly written concerning our Lord, “For his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 117), and he says through the prophet, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18), lest he come to judge us and find us unprepared, he sets forth another example concerning the same matter, saying:

### II

For just as a man going abroad called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them. Who, then, is the man who goes abroad except our Redeemer, who went up into heaven in the flesh he had assumed? For the proper place of flesh is earth, and it is led, as it were, to a foreign place when it is placed in heaven through our Redeemer. But this man, going abroad, entrusted his possessions to his servants because he granted spiritual gifts to his faithful ones.

And to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one. For there are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. The five talents therefore express the gift of the five senses, that is, knowledge of external things. The two signify understanding and action. By the name of one talent, understanding alone is signified.

To each according to his own ability, and he departed immediately. (Jerome) He therefore gave more to one and less to another not according to generosity or parsimony, but according to the capacities of those receiving. Thus the Apostle says that he gave milk to those who were unable to take solid food (1 Corinthians 3). Finally, both the one who made ten from five talents and the one who made four from two received the same joy—not because the rewarder considers the magnitude of the profit, but the willingness of the effort.

The one who had received five talents went away, worked with them, and gained five more. After receiving earthly senses, this servant doubled for himself the knowledge of heavenly things: from creatures understanding the Creator, from bodily things incorporeal things, from visible things invisible things, and from things brief eternal things. (Gregory) There are also some who, although they do not know how to penetrate inward and mystical matters, nevertheless, out of concern for the heavenly homeland, teach those whom they can about the very external things they have received. While they guard themselves from the wantonness of the flesh, from the pursuit of earthly things, and from the pleasure of visible things, they also teach rightly, by admonishing them, those whom they can.

Likewise, the one who had received two gained two more. (Jerome) This man, according to his ability, doubled in the Gospel whatever he had learned in the Law. Or else he understood knowledge and the works of the present life to be types of future blessedness. (Gregory) There are some who, as though enriched with two talents, receive understanding and action: they understand subtle matters concerning inward things and perform wondrous deeds in outward things. When, by understanding and acting, they preach to others, they bring back profit as though from a doubled investment, by which they may be rewarded with eternal blessedness. It is rightly said that another five or another two came as profit. For when preaching is devoted to both sexes, the talents received are, as it were, doubled.

But the one who had received one talent went away, dug in the earth, and hid his lord’s money. (Jerome) The wicked servant neglected and polluted God’s commands through earthly works and worldly pleasure. Although it is written in Luke’s Gospel that he bound it in a napkin—that is, he weakened the householder’s teaching by living softly and delicately (Luke 12). (Gregory) To hide a talent in the earth, therefore, is to entangle the talent of understanding one has received in earthly activities, not to seek spiritual profit, and never to lift the heart from earthly thoughts.
