There are some who have received the gift of understanding but nevertheless savor only the things of the flesh. Concerning them the Prophet says: “They are wise to do evil, but they have not known how to do good.”

But after a long time the lord of those servants came and settled accounts with them. (Jerome) A long period lies between the Savior’s ascension and his second coming. But if the apostles will have to give an account and rise under the fear of judgment, what ought we to do? (Gregory) The one who now mercifully gives spiritual gifts will strictly demand an account of merits in judgment; he will consider what each person has received and weigh what profit each has brought back from what was received.

Then the one who had received five talents came forward and offered five other talents, saying: “Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained five more.” His lord said to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.” The servant who returned doubled talents is praised by the Lord and led to eternal reward, when the Lord’s voice says to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.” (Maurice) By the word “well done” the Lord also indicates his joy, inviting the servant who has labored well into eternal joy. “Well done” is also an exclamation of one rejoicing; and the rejoicing Lord rightly commands the good and faithful servant to enter into his joy. For he alone is the one to whom the Prophet says: “You will fill us with joy by your countenance; pleasures are in your right hand forever” (Psalm 15). (Gregory) All the goods of the present life are little, although they seem many. But then the faithful servant is set over much, when, after every distress of corruption has been conquered, he rejoices in those eternal joys, even over the elements themselves, in that heavenly dwelling. He is perfectly admitted into his lord’s joy when, taken up into that eternal homeland and mingled with the ranks of angels, he rejoices inwardly in the gift in such a way that there is now nothing outwardly over which he must grieve because of corruption.

The one who had received two talents also came forward and said: “Lord, you entrusted two talents to me; behold, I have gained two more.” His lord said to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.” (Jerome) As I said earlier, the householder’s words flatter both servants—the one who made ten from five talents and the one who made four from two—and invite them to many and very great rewards, because, compared with future things that endure, all present things that pass away seem to be little. “Enter,” he says, “into the joy of your lord,” and receive what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2). What greater thing can be given to a faithful servant than to be with his lord and see the joy of his lord?

Then the one who had received one talent also came forward and said: “Lord, I know that you are a hard man; you reap where you did not sow and gather where you did not scatter. And, being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.” Truly, what is written—“to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Psalm 140)—also happened to this servant, so that the crime of pride was added to laziness and negligence. Although he ought simply to have confessed his inactivity and pleaded with the householder, instead he brings an accusation and says that he acted with prudent deliberation, lest, while seeking profit from the money, he should also risk the principal. (Gregory) It should be noted that the useless servant calls his lord hard, although he refuses to serve him for profit; he says he was afraid to spend the talent in gaining profit, when he ought to have feared only returning it to his lord without profit. There are many in the Church whom this servant represents: they fear to undertake the better paths of life, yet do not fear to lie inert in the idleness of their torpor. When they consider themselves sinners, they tremble to seize the paths of holiness, but do not fear to remain in their iniquities. Peter, while still situated in weakness, appropriately represents them when, after seeing the miracle of the fish, he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5). On the contrary, if you consider yourself a sinner, you ought not to drive the Lord away from you. But those who refuse to take hold of the paths of a better way of life and a more upright conduct because they see themselves as weak both confess themselves sinners and drive away the Lord; they flee from the one in whom they ought to have been sanctified, and, as though in confusion, have no counsel, while they fear life even as they are dying.

Some people vainly flatter themselves with this perverse reasoning, saying: “Let each person be sufficient to give an account of himself; why is it necessary to preach or minister to others, or why should anyone be compelled to give an account concerning them?” Yet before the Lord even those are without excuse to whom the Law was not given and who, without hearing the Gospel, fell asleep, because through creation they could have known the Creator, whose invisible things are perceived and understood from the foundation of the world through the things that have been made (Romans 1). Hence this servant is immediately answered:

But his lord answered and said to him: “Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter.” This means, as it were, not to reap where I did not sow: to hold even those guilty of impiety to whom the word of the Law or of the Gospel was not ministered. From the fact that the wicked servant dared to say, “You reap where you did not sow and gather where you did not scatter,” we understand that the Lord also accepts the good life of Gentiles and philosophers, distinguishing between those who act justly and those who act unjustly; and that, by comparison with the person who keeps the natural law, those who neglect the written law are condemned.

You ought therefore to have entrusted my money to the money-changers, so that when I returned I might at least have received what was mine with interest.

**(Jerome.)** What he had thought he had said in his own defense is turned against him as his guilt. The servant is called wicked because he brings an accusation against his master; lazy because he was unwilling to double the talent—so that in the one respect he may be condemned for pride, and in the other for negligence. “If,” he says, “you knew me to be harsh and cruel, and to pursue what belonged to others, reaping where I had not sown, why did such a thought not strike fear into you, so that you would realize that I would seek my own more diligently, and give the money, or silver, to the money-changers?” For the Greek word **ἀργύριον** (*argyrion*) signifies both “money” and “silver.” “The words of the Lord,” he says, “are pure words, silver tested by fire, proven upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI). Money and silver, therefore, signify the preaching of the Gospel and the divine word, which ought to have been given to the money-changers and bankers—that is, either to the other teachers, as the apostles did when they appointed presbyters and bishops throughout the various provinces, or to all believers who are able to double the money and return it with interest, so that whatever they learned in word they might fulfill in deed.

Therefore take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.

**(Gregory.)** It seemed very appropriate that, when the one talent was taken from the wicked servant, it should be given rather to the one who had received two talents than to the one who had received five: it ought to have been given to the one who had less, rather than to the one who had more. But, as we said above, by the five talents the five senses are signified—that is, knowledge of external things—whereas by the two talents understanding and action are expressed. Thus the one who received two talents had more than the one who received five, because the one who earned the administration of external things through the five talents was still empty of understanding of inward things. The one talent, therefore, which we said signifies understanding, ought to have been given to the one who had administered well the external things he had received. We see this daily in the holy Church: many, while administering well the external things they receive, are led by an accompanying grace also to mystical understanding, so that those who faithfully administer external matters may likewise excel in inner understanding.

**(Hilary.)** This parable may also be expounded allegorically in another way. The servant who received five talents is the people of believers from the Law, from which he advanced and doubled his own merit by the proper and praiseworthy exercise of evangelical faith. The accounting that must be rendered is the examination of judgment, in which the use and return of the heavenly word, represented by the entrusted talent, is demanded. Thus the one to whom five had been entrusted, when his master returned, offered ten from the five: he was found in the faith as he had been in the Law, having fulfilled, through the grace of evangelical justification, obedience to the ten commandments contained in the five books of Moses. He is therefore commanded to enter into his master’s joy—that is, he is received into the honor of Christ’s glory.

But the servant to whom two talents had been entrusted is the people of the nations, justified by faith and confession: confessing the Son, and the Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, and confessing him as human in spirit and flesh. For faith is in the heart, and confession with the mouth (Rom. X). These, then, are the two talents entrusted to him. But just as the former had understood the whole mystery in the five talents—that is, in the Law—and had doubled that very thing by faith in the Gospel, so this one earned an increase of the two talents through action. And although their entrusting and return were different, the offering of both before the Lord is equal, so that we may recognize the faith of the nations as equal to the knowledge of believers from the Law, since both are commanded with the same praise to enter into the joy of the Lord.

The doubling of the money received means adding the work of faith, and carrying out in deeds and actions what they had believed by profession. But the one who received one talent and hid it in the ground is the people who persist in the Law, wholly carnal and dull, understanding nothing spiritual, and whom the power of evangelical preaching does not penetrate. Because of envy toward the salvation of the nations, he hid in the earth the talent he had received, neither using it himself nor distributing it for the use of others, but supposing that the Law alone was sufficient for salvation. Therefore, when an account was demanded of him, he said: “I was afraid”—as though, out of reverence and fear for the ancient commandments, he abstained from using evangelical freedom—and he said, “Here is what is yours,” as though he had remained only with what had been commanded by the Lord.

To hide it in the earth means to conceal the glory of the new preaching beneath an interpretation concerned with bodily suffering. Although he could not deny that Christ the Lord had been sent for the salvation of the nations—for both his coming and his passion are found in the Law—he nevertheless refused to obey the Gospel. For he says: “I know that you are a harsh man; you reap where you did not sow and gather where you did not scatter.” The nature of present things does not allow a harvest to exist without seed, or things to be gathered that were not scattered; but this entire saying is spiritual. For we have said that this people comes from the Law: not ignorant of the Lord’s coming and the salvation of the nations, but unbelieving. Since it knows that the fruits of righteousness are to be reaped where the Law was not sown, and that those who were not scattered from Abraham’s stock are to be gathered from the nations, this man is therefore harsh—namely, one who will justify without the Law, gather without scattering, and reap without sowing.

For this reason, it will be all the more without excuse that he concealed the preaching and buried the talent entrusted to him, since he knew that the Lord would reap without seed and gather what he had not scattered. Rather, he ought to have given it to the money-changers—that is, to the whole human race, which is occupied with the affairs of this world—and shared with them the use of the talent entrusted to him, since the Lord would demand its return from each individual. Because of this guilt, the talent will be taken from him—not now the Gospel that he buried, but the Law—and it will be given to whoever has doubled it, as the Lord says:

“For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.” For to the one who has the use of the Gospels, the honor of the Law also is conferred. But from the one who does not have faith in Christ, even the honor that he seemed to possess from the Law will be taken away.

**(Jerome.)** In another sense: many who are naturally wise and possess sharp intelligence, if they are negligent and ruin the good of nature through idleness, lose that natural good in comparison with one who was somewhat slower but compensated through labor and diligence for what he lacked; and the reward promised to them seems to pass to others. It may also be understood in this way: to the one who has faith and good will in the Lord, even if, as a human being, he has had something less in action, it will be given by the good Judge; but the one who has not had faith loses even the other virtues that he seemed naturally to possess.

It is elegantly said, “what he seems to have will be taken away from him.” For whatever exists without faith in Christ ought not to be credited to him, because he used it badly, but to the one who also bestowed the good of nature upon the wicked servant.

**(Bede.)** Likewise, to the one who has love for the word, there will also be given the sense to understand what he loves. But the one who does not have love for hearing the divine word, even if he seems to possess distinction through natural intelligence or literary learning, will enjoy none of the sweetness of true wisdom.

**(Gregory.)** Or otherwise: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound,” because whoever does not have charity loses even what he seemed to have received. Therefore it is necessary that in everything we do we remain watchful in the pursuit of charity. True charity is to love a friend in God and to love an enemy for God’s sake. Whoever does not have it loses every good he possesses, is deprived of the talent he had received, and, according to the Lord’s judgment, is cast into the outer darkness.

And throw the useless servant into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

**(Jerome.)** The Lord is light, and the one who is cast out from him lacks the true light.

**(Gregory.)** Through punishment he will fall into the outer darkness who, through guilt, willingly fell into the inner darkness. There he is compelled to suffer the darkness of retribution who here willingly endured the darkness of pleasure. What weeping and gnashing of teeth mean, we have explained above.

It must be understood, however, that no lazy person is safe from receiving a talent. No one can truthfully say: “I received no talent at all; there is nothing for which I can be compelled to render an account.” For in the name of a talent, even this will be reckoned to the poor person: whatever small thing he has received.

One person has received understanding; he owes the ministry of preaching from his talent. Another has received earthly wealth; he owes the distribution of his talent from his possessions. Another receives neither inner understanding nor abundance of goods, but has learned an occupation by which he supports himself; that occupation will be reckoned to him as the talent he received. Another has acquired none of these things, but perhaps has gained a position of familiarity with a rich man; he has certainly received the talent of familiarity. If, therefore, he says nothing to him on behalf of the needy, he will be condemned for retaining his talent.

Let the one who has understanding take every care not to remain silent. Let the one who has abundance of possessions be watchful lest he grow numb toward generosity in mercy. Let the one who has an occupation by which he supports himself earnestly strive to share its use and benefit with his neighbor. Let the one who has access to speak with a rich man fear condemnation for retaining his talent if, whenever he can, he does not daily intercede with him for the poor.

The coming Judge will demand from each of us as much as he has given. Therefore, so that each person may be secure concerning the accounting of his talent when the Lord returns, let him consider daily, with trembling, what he has received. Behold, it is already near that the one who went abroad should return. He went away, as it were, to a foreign land because he departed from this earth in which he was born; but he will certainly return to demand an account of the talents, because if we grow sluggish in good action, he judges us strictly on account of the very gifts he bestowed.

Let us therefore consider what we have received and remain vigilant in distributing it. Let no earthly concern hinder us from spiritual work, lest, if the talent is hidden in the earth, the Lord of the talent be provoked to anger. For the lazy servant raises the talent from the earth when the Judge is already examining his faults. There are many who withdraw from earthly works only when, through the Judge’s punishment, they are already being dragged toward eternal suffering.

Let us therefore be watchful beforehand in rendering an account of our talent, so that when the Judge is already threatening to strike, the profit we have made may excuse us. After setting forth the parables concerning the end of the world, the Lord proceeds to explain the manner of the coming judgment and says:

### [III.] When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty.

**(Jerome.)** Since he was shortly to celebrate Passover, to be handed over to the cross, mocked by human beings, and given vinegar and gall to drink, he rightly announces beforehand the glory of the triumphant one, compensating the scandals that would follow with the reward of his promise. It must also be noted that the one who will be seen in majesty is the Son of Man.

**(Hilary.)** The expression “Son of Man” is directed against heretics who deny that our Lord Jesus Christ remains in the form of the servant he assumed, because the Apostle said: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” And what of the statement that, as he ascended, the angels testified to the apostles: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I)? Here too he says of himself: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty.”

The same one is Son of God and Son of Man, and Son of Man and Son of God: one according to humanity, the other according to divinity, yet not another, but one and the same true and proper Son of God in both natures. He is altogether one—not through confusion of substance, but through unity of person; not through the conversion of divinity into flesh, but through the assumption of humanity into God.

We must undoubtedly understand his majesty as his divinity, which, invisibly with the Father and the Holy Spirit, will judge sinners and the ungodly. Yet it has never been seen, nor will it ever be seen, by the ungodly and sinners.

**(Maurus.)** “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty,” he says—the same Son of God who is also Son of Man will then come in his majesty to judge, who previously came in his humility to be judged. Then he will come as a strict and severe judge, who previously came gentle and meek. Then he will come as king to demand, with interest, the money that he had previously freely bestowed upon his servants through grace.

He is the one of whom it is written: “He is indeed a man, and who will know him?” He will not cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice. “He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish a smoking wick” (Isa. XLII). And, “like a lamb before the one who shears him, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

He himself will then come: “God manifested, our God, and he will not keep silence.” Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him. He will summon heaven above and earth, to distinguish his people. The mountains will melt like wax before the face of the Lord; before the face of the Lord all the earth will tremble (Ps. XLIX).

“All the angels,” he says, “will come with him.” For then, if anything [Note: [Col. 1095D] Something is missing here, lost because of the soldiers’ violence. EDITOR OF COLOGNE.] [lacuna] [uncertain surviving fragment: “mor;”] whoever is scandalized, and I am not inflamed, he wholly observes the laws of true love, and for this reason earns heavenly rewards. For these words of the Lord chiefly show that those who observe the commandments of the twofold love attain an everlasting crown.

Then the righteous will answer him, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, thirsty and give you drink? When did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you? Or when did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?”

They say these words not because they distrust the Lord’s words, but either because they are astonished and amazed at the greatness and glory of Christ the King’s majesty, or because, in view of the magnitude of the terror of judgment and the abundance of the immeasurable reward, everything good they have done then seems small to them, as the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us.”

And the King will answer them: “Amen I say to you: Whatever you did for one of the least of these my brothers, you did for me.”

**(Jerome.)** It was easy for us to understand that, in every poor person, Christ is fed when hungry, given drink when thirsty, welcomed when a stranger, clothed when naked, visited when sick, and comforted by the conversation of another when confined in prison. But from what follows—“Whatever you did for one of the least of these my brothers, you did for me”—it does not seem to me that he spoke generally about the poor, but about those who are poor in spirit. Stretching out his hand toward them, he had said: “These are my brothers and my mother, those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XII).

Then he will say to those who are on the left: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

**(Maurus.)** Here is fulfilled what is written elsewhere: “On the right hand of God is the fiery law, but on his left are the rejected” (Deut. XXXIII). The rejected will therefore be placed on the Lord’s left, because they loved the left—that is, present things—through burning desire for as long as they lived, and had no longing for eternal things, which are signified by the right.

To these he says: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire.” “Depart from me,” he says. How are they commanded to depart from God, when they were never with him? Unless it is because they seemed to be with him for as long as the wicked were mixed with the good. Thus the Lord’s net draws both good and bad fish together to the shore, and the weeds still grow together with the wheat in the Lord’s field (Matt. XIII). But then, when the good fish have been gathered into vessels, the bad will be thrown out, and when the wheat has been gathered into the barn, the weeds will be collected into bundles to be burned.

Or he commands them to depart from him in the sense that they are expelled from the presence of his vision into the outer darkness. For it is written: “The wicked is taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” The accursed—that is, those who exercised their lives in wickedness—are sent into the eternal fire because they will be tortured without end. This fire is said to have been prepared for the devil and his angels because, just as God’s foreknowledge prepared the kingdom of heaven for the righteous from the foundation of the world, so for the devil and his angels, whom he foreknew would transgress, he ordained the eternal fire in which they would be tortured perpetually.

[Col. 1098A] “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink,” and so forth.

The sentence of our Redeemer is greatly to be feared and dreaded, by which he says: “Go into the eternal fire, because I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger and you did not welcome me.” If barrenness is cast into the fire, what will rapacity deserve, or what will the one who took another’s property receive, if the one who did not give from his own will burn forever? And if judgment will be without mercy for the one who did not show mercy (Jas. II), what judgment will there be for the one who both failed to show mercy and committed robbery? It continues:

Then they too will answer, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?”

They try to excuse themselves, as though they could deceive the Lord whom they had deceived human beings. But then they will have no excuse for their sins, because previously they refused to turn from their sins and neglected to give alms. Hence it is added:

Then he will answer them, saying: “Whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for me.”

For whoever disdains to help the least—that is, the humble and despised—will not rejoice that he has offered service to the King of the humble, that is, to the Judge of all. It should be noted that here too, as above, he said that mercy must be shown to one of the least, and affirmed that such mercy was shown to himself. For whatever is offered to God must be offered through the unity of faith and peace, and with a simple intention; the left hand should not know what the right hand is doing.

[Col. 1098C] And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life?

**(Maurus.)** Wise reader, observe that the punishments are eternal, and that perpetual life has no ruin.

**(Jerome.)** For this reason Origen promises in vain that, after many ages, the ungodly and sinners, and also the devil and his angels, will be released from hell. This opinion is wholly contrary to the words of Truth himself. I beseech you, Lord Jesus, that you may mercifully place me, who believe faithfully in you in all things and truly hold your faith, at your right hand, so that, according to your promise, I may receive eternal blessedness in heaven with your blessed ones, rather than, according to the fiction of heretics, seek deliverance from hell only at the end with the accursed.

## BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 1097]

### CHAPTER XXVI

Concerning the plot of the Jews to bring about Christ’s death; concerning the supper at Bethany; concerning the price requested by Judas the betrayer; concerning the final supper, and what happened there and in the garden.

### [I.]

**(Maurus.)** Since the exposition of the holy Gospel according to Matthew has been completed in seven books, from its beginning up to the Lord’s Passion, we now decide, if the Lord so wills, to begin the eighth with the Passion of the Lord and carry it through to his resurrection—or rather, to the end of the Gospel. We ask his mercy: he who rose from the dead after the Sabbath, on the Lord’s Day—that is, the eighth day after the seventh, which is also called the first day of the week—may likewise make us participants in his resurrection after the seven ages of this world, that is, in the eighth age when all the dead will rise.

After the sayings concerning the day of judgment have been completed, Matthew continues and says:

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings”—namely, all those that he had delivered concerning the consummation of the world or the separation at judgment.

**(Hilary.)** Or otherwise: all the sayings that he had completed from the beginning of his Gospel up to the time of his Passion, teaching or exhorting, and also proclaiming future events in the hearing of the disciples or the crowds—that is, he had completed them by doing and preaching.

Then he said to his disciples: “You know that after two days Passover will take place.”

**(Augustine.)** After the discourse in which he had shown that he would come again in the return of his glory, he now warns them that he will suffer, so that they may recognize that the mystery of the cross is joined to the glory of eternity.

As can therefore be gathered from John’s account, six days before Passover Jesus came to Bethany, and there took place the banquet at which the precious ointment is mentioned. From there he came to Jerusalem seated on a young donkey; afterward the events narrated as having taken place in Jerusalem after this arrival occurred (John XI).

**(Jerome.)** From the day, therefore, on which he came to Bethany and the event concerning the ointment took place, up to the day on which all these things were done and said, we understand—even though the evangelists do not mention it—that four days had elapsed, so that the day might arrive which Matthew and Mark designate as two days before Passover (Mark XIV).

Mystically, after two days of the most brilliant light of the Old and New Testaments, the true Passover is celebrated for the world. Passover, which in Hebrew is called *Phase*, is named not from suffering, as many suppose, but from passing over: because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over and did not strike them; or because the Lord himself, offering help to his people from above, passed over them.

**(Rabanus.)** Explaining the mystery of this word more profoundly, the evangelist John says: “Before the day of the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII). Here he clearly declares that the day of this solemnity was mystically called “passing over” in the Law because the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, on that day passed from this [Note: [Col. 1099D] Something is again missing here, lost for the reason stated above. EDITOR OF COLOGNE.] [lacuna] … they did not fear maintaining perpetual discord with God? There they trembled with fear where there was no fear. The arrows of the little ones also became their wounds.

### [II.]

Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper.

**(Augustine.)** Matthew and Mark, after saying retrospectively that Passover would take place after two days, return to that day in Bethany which was six days before Passover. They narrate what John reports concerning the supper and the ointment, from which Jesus was about to go to Jerusalem. After relating this event, they return again to the point from which they had digressed—that is, to narrate the Lord’s discourse delivered two days before Passover—and join Judas’s action to the council of the priests, which they held while deliberating about the Lord’s death.

**(Jerome.)** But it must be considered that the Lord, who was about to suffer for the whole world and redeem all nations with his blood, remained in Bethany, in the house of obedience, which had once belonged to Simon the leper. This does not mean that he remained a leper at that time, but that the one who had formerly been a leper was afterward cleansed by the Savior, while his former name remained, so that the power of the healer might be displayed. Likewise, in the catalogue of the apostles, Matthew is called a tax collector by his former fault, although he had certainly ceased to be a tax collector. Some wish to understand Simon the leper as the portion of the people that believed in the Lord and was healed by him. Simon also means “obedient.”

A woman approached him with an alabaster vessel of precious ointment and poured it over his head as he reclined.

**(Rabanus.)** This woman was Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, as John explicitly recalls. He also testifies that this happened six days before Passover, on the day before Jesus came to Jerusalem seated on a donkey, amid palms and the praise of the crowds.

She is the same woman, not another, who once, as Luke writes, while still a sinner, came and bathed the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance and anointed them with the ointment of pious confession; because she loved much, she obtained from the merciful Judge the forgiveness of many sins (Luke VII). Now, justified and made a familiar companion of the Lord, she poured holy oil not only on his feet, as the same John narrates, but also on his head, as Mark and Matthew testify.

It should be noted that Mark reports this ointment as follows: “When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, and was reclining, a woman came with an alabaster vessel of precious spikenard ointment; and when she had broken the alabaster vessel, she poured it over his head” (Mark XIV).

John, however, says: “Mary therefore took a pound of costly genuine nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” Where Mark has “spikenard,” John has “genuine nard”; we will explain their difference below.

Alabaster is a kind of white marble marked with various colors, which they customarily hollow out for ointment vessels, because it is said to preserve their contents especially well without corruption. It grows around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, being whiter than other varieties; the finest is found in India.

Nard is an aromatic shrub, with, as they say, a large and thick root, but short, black, and brittle, though oily, earthy-smelling, and fragrant; it resembles cypress, has a harsh taste, and small, dense leaves whose tips spread out like an ear of grain. For this reason perfumers celebrate both the ears and the leaves of nard as possessing a double value.

This is what Mark means by “precious spikenard ointment”: the ointment that Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard, but, to make it more precious, also from the addition of its ears and leaves, so that the grace of its fragrance and efficacy was increased.

“Genuine nard,” that is, faithful nard, is so called because some physicians often adulterate precious ointments with similar herbs. Just as perfumers who customarily sell aromatic compounds frequently mix certain shoots into their products by fraud, deceiving the eyes of buyers, so this ointment was not adulterated but genuine. With it Mary anointed the Lord’s head and feet. For **πίστις** (*pistis*) means “faith” in Greek, from which **πιστικόν** (*pistikon*) is derived.

Physiologists report concerning nard that it is principal among ointments; therefore it was rightly offered for the anointing of the head and feet. There are indeed many kinds of it, but all are herbs except the Indian variety, which is more precious.

Mystically, this devotion of Mary ministering to the Lord signifies the faith and piety of the holy Church, which speaks in the Song of Love: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I). She fulfilled these words once, literally, through Mary’s hands, and does not cease fulfilling them spiritually every day in all her members. Spread throughout the whole world, they glory and say: “Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place, because we are the good odor of Christ to God” (II Cor. II).

When the Church confesses and praises the power of his divine nature, which together with the Father deserves equal reverence, she pours precious ointment over his head. When, with equal reverence, she receives the mysteries of the humanity he assumed, she pours genuine and faithful nard over the feet of the Lord: because she commends through devoted preaching and honors with faithful service that nature of his by which he deigned to touch the earth—that is, to dwell among human beings.

But when the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying: “Why this waste? For it could have been sold for much and given to the poor” (John XII).

**(Augustine.)** Matthew, like Mark, speaks by **synecdoche**, using the plural number for the singular. John, speaking more distinctly, testifies that Judas said this, and that he said it out of greed, because he was a thief and, having the money box, carried what was put into it.

It may also be understood that the other disciples either felt or said this, or were persuaded by Judas when he said it, and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of all in their words. But Judas said it because he was a thief; the others because of concern for the poor. John, however, wished to mention it only of the one whose habit of stealing he believed should be disclosed on this occasion.

But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: “Why do you trouble this woman? She has performed a good work for me. For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.”

**(Jerome.)** Another question arises: why did Jesus say to the disciples after his resurrection, “I am with you always, to the consummation of the world” (Matt. XXVIII), while here he says, “You will not always have me”? It seems to me that in this passage he is speaking of bodily presence, since after the resurrection he would not be with them in the same way as now, in every companionship and intimacy. Remembering this, the Apostle says: “Even if we once knew Jesus Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (II Cor. V).

For in pouring this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial.

**(Rabanus.)** What you think is the destruction of the ointment is an act of burial. Nor is it surprising that she has given me the good fragrance of her faith, since I am about to pour out my blood for her.

Amen I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.

It is not so much this woman who is preached throughout the whole world as the Church, because she buried the Savior and anointed his head. Observe his knowledge of future events: though he was to suffer and die after two days, he knew that his Gospel would be celebrated throughout the whole world.

It should be noted that, just as Mary attained glory throughout the whole world wherever the holy Church is spread because of the pious devotion she showed to the Lord, so, conversely, the one who did not fear to disparage her service with a rash tongue has been branded far and wide with the mark of faithlessness and has rightly become hateful both to God and to human beings. But the Lord, rewarding the good with praise, passed over the insults of the wicked in silence.

### [III.]

Then one of the Twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” And they appointed for him thirty pieces of silver.

This sentence must be joined to the passage above where he reported the priests’ council concerning the killing of Christ. When, therefore, the chief priests took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him, then one of the Twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” and so forth.

**(Rabanus.)** When he says that Judas “went to the chief priests to betray him to them,” he shows that Judas was not invited by the chief priests, nor compelled by any necessity, but entered into the plot of his criminal mind of his own accord.

**(Jerome.)** Wretched Judas wished to compensate with the price of his master for the loss that he thought had resulted from the pouring out of the ointment. He did not request a fixed sum, so that profit might at least persuade him to betray him; rather, as though he were selling a worthless slave, he left it to the buyers to determine how much they wished to give.

“And they appointed for him thirty pieces of silver.” Joseph was not sold for twenty gold pieces, as many think according to the Septuagint interpreters, but for twenty pieces of silver according to the Hebrew truth; nor could a servant be more valuable than his Lord.

From then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over to them.

**(Maurus.)** The evangelist Luke explains this passage more clearly, saying: “And he sought an opportunity to hand him over without a crowd” (Luke XXII). This was the opportunity Judas was seeking: to hand over his master. The priests feared that a disturbance might arise among the people. Thus both the seller and the buyers were considering the same thing: how their fraudulent scheme might not be obstructed by an uprising of the people, and how Jesus might not be forcibly snatched from their hands.

Many people today shudder at Judas’s crime—that he sold his Lord, master, and God for money—as monstrous and unspeakable, yet they do not guard against committing the same thing. For when they give false testimony against anyone in exchange for gifts, since they deny the truth for money, they sell God for money. He himself said: “I am the truth.” When they stain the fellowship of brotherhood with the plague of discord, they betray God, because God is love.

Therefore those who despise the laws of love and truth certainly betray God, who is love and truth—especially when they sin not through weakness or ignorance, but, in the likeness of Judas, seek an opportunity to change truth through falsehood and virtue through crime while judges are absent.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples approached Jesus, saying [Col. 1103B]: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” He calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the fourteenth day of the first month, when, having discarded the leaven, they used to sacrifice—that is, slaughter—the lamb in the evening. Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (2 Cor. 5). Although he was crucified on the following day, that is, when the moon was fifteen days old, yet on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed, he handed over to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated; and, having been seized and bound by the Jews, he consecrated the beginning of that very sacrifice—that is, of his passion. “Where,” they say, “do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” That is: we have no dwelling, no tabernacle. Let those hear this whose concern is to build houses and whose thoughts are occupied with constructing imposing porticoes. [Col. 1103C] Let those who take pleasure in the display of costly marbles and ceilings ornamented with gold recognize Christ, Lord of all, who had no place where he might lay his head. And therefore the disciples ask him: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Luke 9).

But Jesus said: “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: ‘The Teacher says: My time is near; I am keeping the Passover with you at your house, together with my disciples.’” The New Scripture preserves the custom of the Old Testament. We frequently read, “he said,” “in such-and-such a place,” and “in such-and-such a place”—which in Hebrew is called *Philimoni* and *Helimoni*—and yet the names of persons and places are not given. (Aug.) Nothing in this passage, however, need be thought contrary to Mark and Luke, who relate the same event in a similar way. For when Matthew says: “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: ‘The Teacher says: My time is near; I am keeping the Passover with you at your house, together with my disciples,’” he indicates the person whom Mark and Luke call the householder, or master of the house, in which the upper room was shown to them, where they were to prepare the Passover. By inserting “to a certain man,” Matthew, as though speaking in his own person and wishing to be brief, intended to indicate him in abbreviated form. For if he had said that the Lord commanded: “Go into the city and say to him: ‘The Teacher says: My time is near; I am keeping the Passover at your house,’” it would have been understood as though the words were to be addressed to the city. Accordingly, it was not from the person of the Lord, whose command he was relating, but in his own person that he inserted “to a certain man,” saying that the Lord ordered them to go, so that it would not be necessary to state everything, since this seemed sufficient to convey the sense of the command. [Col. 1104A] (RAB.) Deliberately, however, whether the name of the water-carrier (as the other evangelists include it) or that of the master of the house is omitted, so that an opportunity may be indicated for all who wish to celebrate the true Passover—that is, to be instructed in the sacraments of Christ and to receive him as a guest in the lodging of their minds.

And the disciples did as Jesus directed them, and prepared the Passover. (Hieron.) In another Gospel it is written that they found a large upper room furnished and cleansed, and there prepared it for him. The large upper room is the spiritual law, which, emerging from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in an elevated place. For whoever still observes the letter that kills, whoever understands nothing else in the field than an animal, undoubtedly celebrates the Passover below, because he has not yet learned to comprehend the majesty of the Spirit in the words of God. [Col. 1104B] But whoever has followed the water-carrier—that is, the herald of grace—into the house of the Church, by transcending through the illuminating Spirit the surface of the letter prepares refreshment for Christ in the high chamber of the mind, because he recognizes that all the mysteries of the Passover, as well as the other decrees of the law, are sacraments.

**[IV.]** When evening had come, he was reclining with his twelve disciples. [MAUR.] Evening, then, came when the Light of the world—that is, the true sun—hastened toward the setting of death. And then the Lord reclined with his disciples, because he prepared eternal rest for them.

As they were eating, he said: “Amen I say to you: one of you will betray me.” (Hieron.) Judas does everything in such a way as to remove suspicion of the betrayer; but he who had foretold his passion also foretells the betrayer, giving an opportunity for repentance, so that when Judas understood that his thoughts and secret plans were known, he might repent of his deed. Yet he does not identify him specifically, lest, openly exposed, he become more shameless. He casts the crime into the number, so that the guilty man may repent.

And they became very sorrowful and began, each one, to say: “Surely it is I, Lord?” Certainly the eleven apostles knew that they were contemplating nothing of the sort against the Lord. But they believe the Teacher more than themselves; and, fearing their own frailty, they sorrowfully ask about a sin of which they had no awareness.

And he answered: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish is the one who will betray me.” O marvelous power of the Lord! First he had said: “One of you will betray me.” The betrayer persists in evil: he reproves him more openly, yet still does not identify him by name. While the others were sorrowful, withdrawing their hands and forbidding food to their mouths, Judas, with the boldness and shamelessness with which he was about to betray him, even puts his hand into the dish with his Teacher, so that his audacity might disguise a good conscience. (MAUR.) It should be noted that Matthew here used *paropsis*, whereas Mark wrote “in the dish.” A *paropsis*, as some say, is a square serving vessel, so called because it has equal sides—that is, sides of equal length. A dish, however, is an earthen vessel suitable for holding liquid. There is no contradiction here. It could have happened that on the very table an earthen square vessel contained sauce into which a disciple could dip his hand with the Teacher. The Lord, in the dispensation of his humility and patience, did not refuse to admit his betrayer to participation at the common table, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me” (Ps. 40).

“The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written of him. But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed.” (Hieron.) Though reproved neither the first time nor the second, he does not draw back his foot from betrayal; rather, the Lord’s patience nourishes his shamelessness, and he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath (Rom. 2). Punishment is foretold, so that the announced penalties may correct the man whom shame had not overcome. [Col. 1105B] (RAB.) But even today and forever woe to the man who approaches the Lord’s table with malice, who dares to participate in the most holy offerings of Christ’s mysteries while harboring plots in his mind and having his heart polluted by some crime. He too, after the example of Judas, betrays the Son of Man—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinners, namely, to his members, whose immeasurable and inviolable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood he presumptuously profanes. He sells the Lord who, neglecting fear and love of him, is shown to love and pursue earthly and transitory things—or rather, even criminal things—in his place.

“It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” [Col. 1105C] (Hieron.) He should not therefore be thought to have existed before he was born, on the grounds that no one could be well off unless he had existed. It is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist badly.

But Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: “Surely it is I, Rabbi?” He said to him: “You have said so.” Because the others, sorrowful and deeply sorrowful, had asked him, “Surely it is I, Lord?”—lest by remaining silent he seem to reveal himself—he too asks simply, although his conscience was already gnawing at him, having boldly put his hand into the dish. “Surely it is I, Rabbi?” He joins to the question the manner of a flatterer or a sign of disbelief. For the others, who were not betrayers, say: “Surely it is I, Lord?” This man, who was the betrayer, does not call him Lord but Teacher, as though he might have an excuse if, after denying the Lord, he had at least betrayed the Teacher. And he said to him: “You have said so.” The betrayer was refuted by the same answer with which he would later answer Pilate. (August.) But it is not explicitly stated here whether he was the one. For this can be understood as though he had said: “I did not say it.” It could also have been said in such a way that Judas and the Lord answered without everyone noticing what had been said.

**[V.]** While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” (RAB.) When the solemn rites of the old Passover, celebrated in memory of the ancient liberation of God’s people from Egypt, had been completed, he wished the Church to observe what passes over into the new Passover in memory of its redemption, so that, in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb, he might substitute the sacrament of his own body and blood, and show that he himself was the one to whom the Lord swore and would not repent: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). He himself breaks the bread that he gives to the disciples, to show that the breaking of his body would not occur without his own will and arrangement, but—as he says elsewhere—that he has authority to take it up again (John 16). He blessed this bread before breaking it, by the grace of a particular sacrament. For the human nature that he assumed and was destined to suffer, he filled with the grace of divine power together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He blessed and broke the bread because he deigned to subject the assumed human being to death in such a way as to show that the power of divine immortality truly dwelt within him, and therefore to teach that he would be raised from death more swiftly.

And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Drink from it, all of you.” (Greg.) When it is said that his passion was drawing near, he is reported, after taking the bread and the cup, to have given thanks. He gives thanks, therefore, who receives the scourges belonging to another’s iniquity; and he who has displayed nothing worthy of being struck blesses humbly under the blow, so that he may show by this what each person ought to do under the scourge of his own guilt, if he himself bears calmly the scourges belonging to another’s guilt; and so that he may show what a subject should do when corrected, if, placed under the scourge, he gives equal thanks to the Father.

“For this is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” (RAB.) Since bread strengthens, whereas wine produces blood in the flesh, this refers mystically to the body of Christ, and the other to his blood. But because Christ must also remain in us and we in Christ, water is mixed with the wine of the Lord’s cup. For, as John testifies, the waters are the peoples (Rev. 17). Nor is anyone permitted to offer either water alone or wine alone, just as no one may offer a grain of wheat by itself, without the admixture of water, as bread, lest such an offering signify that the head ought to be separated from the members, and falsely suggest either that Christ could suffer without the love of our redemption or that we could be saved and offered to the Father without Christ’s passion. If anyone is troubled by the question why, since the Savior gave his body and blood to the apostles after they had dined, we are taught by the custom of the universal Church to receive the same sacraments while fasting, let him hear briefly: the apostles communicated after dining then because it was necessary for that typological Passover to be completed and thus for the sacraments of the true Passover to be entered. Now, in honor of so great and terrible a sacrament, the teachers of the Church have deemed it fitting that we should first be fortified by participation in the Lord’s passion, first be inwardly consecrated with spiritual food, and afterward refresh the body with earthly provisions and ordinary food. When he says, “This is my blood of the new covenant,” he refers by contrast to the old covenant, which was consecrated with the blood of goats and calves, as the lawgiver said while sprinkling: “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you” (Exod. 24). For it is necessary that the copies of the true things be cleansed with these, but that the heavenly things themselves be cleansed with better sacrifices than these, in accordance with what the Apostle declares throughout the Epistle to the Hebrews, distinguishing between the law and the Gospel with a most beautiful exposition and a complete argument.

“But I say to you: I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I shall drink it with you new in the kingdom of my Father.” The synagogue is called the Lord’s vine or vineyard, as all Scripture everywhere attests, and Isaiah more clearly in the song he sang about it: “The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5). From this vineyard the Lord had long been drinking, although many of its branches had been turned into the bitterness of an alien vine. For although many in that people deviated from the straight path of faith, there nevertheless remained throughout the entire period of the law many whose pious thoughts and supreme virtues delighted God. But when the Lord had suffered in the flesh and risen from the dead, the time came for the legal and figurative observance to cease, and for what had been performed according to the letter, transferred into a spiritual meaning, to be held more perfectly in the new covenant with the aid of the grace of the Holy Spirit. As he was therefore going to his passion, the Lord said: “I shall no longer drink from this fruit of the vine until that day when I shall drink it with you new in the kingdom of my Father.” As though he were plainly saying: “I shall no longer delight in the carnal ceremonies of the synagogue, in which even the sacred rites of this paschal lamb held a chief place. The time of my resurrection will come. The day will come [Col. 1107C] when I, placed in the kingdom—that is, exalted in the glory of immortal life—shall be filled with new joy with you from the salvation of that same people, regenerated from the fountain of spiritual grace.” (Aug.) Again, alternatively: “I shall not drink from this generation of the vine from now on, until that day when I shall drink it with you new in the kingdom of my Father.” By saying that it will then be new, he wishes it understood that this is old. Since he had received a body from the stock of Adam, who is called the old man, and was going to hand that body over to death in his passion—and since he commends his blood through the sacrament of wine—what else should we understand by the new wine than the immortality of renewed bodies? When he says, “I shall drink it new with you,” he also promises them the resurrection of their bodies for the putting on of immortality. “With you” should not be understood as referring to the same time, but to the same renewal. For the Apostle also says that we have risen with Christ, so that hope of the future reality may already bring present joy. When he says that the new wine too comes from this fruit of the vine, he signifies that the very same bodies will rise according to heavenly renewal which now, according to their old condition, are destined to die. It should be noted that John says nothing about the Lord’s body and blood at this point, but speaks of it much more fully elsewhere (John 6). He testifies that the Lord spoke of it there. Here, however, after John had recorded that the Lord rose from the supper and washed the disciples’ feet, also giving the reason why he did this—and after he had stated, on the testimony of Scripture, that the Lord had indicated in that supper that he would be betrayed by one who ate his bread—he came to this passage, which the other three likewise indicate. “When Jesus had said these things,” he says, “he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said: ‘Amen I say to you: one of you will betray me.’” Then the disciples looked at one another, as that same John adds, uncertain about whom he was speaking; and, becoming sorrowful, as Matthew and Mark say, they began one by one to ask him: “Surely it is I?” But he answered, as Matthew continues: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish is the one who will betray me.” This is followed by what John relates, which the others omitted, just as John omitted certain things that they said. Therefore, after the Lord had handed over the cup, he said what Luke records: “But behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me on the table,” and so forth. Then the following passage from John is joined to it: “One of his disciples was reclining in the bosom of Jesus, whom Jesus loved.” Simon Peter therefore beckons to him and says: “Who is it about whom he speaks?” When he had reclined upon Jesus’ breast, he says to him: “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered: “It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped bread.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot; and after the morsel, Satan then entered into him (John 13). (RAB.) But here a question arises: How can this John, and likewise Luke, say that Satan had already entered Judas’s heart so that he might betray the Lord, when John says that Satan entered him after the morsel? (Aug.) The matter is resolved in this way: Satan entered the Lord’s betrayer after that bread in order to possess more fully the one already handed over to him—into whom he had previously entered in order to deceive him. For the presumption involved in the betrayal increased the sin of the sacrament, when bread entered the ungrateful man’s stomach and the enemy entered his mind. Perhaps through the dipping of the bread he signified the pretense of the man who came to the supper as a feigned friend and went to the Teacher as a false disciple.

**[VI.]** And after the hymn had been sung, they went out to the Mount of Olives. (RAB.) This is what we read in the Psalm: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him” (Ps. 21). That hymn may be understood as the one that the Lord, according to John, sang in thanksgiving to the Father, in which, lifting his eyes upward, he prayed for himself, for the disciples, and for those who were going to believe through their word. And beautifully he leads into the Mount of Olives the disciples who have been instructed in the sacraments of his body and blood and commended to the Father in the hymn of holy intercession, so that he might typologically indicate that through the celebration of his sacraments and through the aid of his intercession we ought to ascend to the higher gifts of virtues and the charisms of the Holy Spirit, with which we may be anointed in our hearts.

Then Jesus says to them: “You will all suffer scandal on this night.” (Hieron.) He foretells what they will suffer, so that when they have suffered it they may not despair of salvation, but may be freed by doing penance. He deliberately added, “You will be scandalized on this night,” because just as those who become drunk become drunk at night, so those who suffer scandal endure it at night and in darkness. [Col. 1109A] Let us instead say: “The night has passed, but the day is drawing near” (Rom. 13).

“For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’” This is written in other words in the prophet Zechariah, and, if I am not mistaken, it is spoken from the prophet’s person to God: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. 13). The sixty-eighth Psalm also, which is sung entirely by the Lord and accords with this meaning, says: “For the one whom you struck, they themselves pursued.” The good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and from many flocks of error there may become one flock and one shepherd.

“But after I have risen, I shall go before you into Galilee.” (MAUR.) Just as, hastening toward his passion, he had foretold the place of the future passion in Jerusalem, where the disciples became sorrowful, so he also foretold that there would be a place in Galilee where, rising from the dead, he would offer them the consolation of his appearance.

But Peter answered and said to him: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I shall never be scandalized.” (Hieron.) This is neither rashness nor a lie, but the faith of the Apostle Peter and his ardent affection for the Lord and Savior. He was so uplifted by affection and love for Christ that he did not consider either the weakness of his flesh or the truth of God’s words, as though what he had said could not come to pass.

Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you: on this night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Peter made his promise out of the ardor of faith, whereas the Savior, as God, knew what was to come. Note that Peter denies at night, and denies three times. But after the rooster crowed, and as the darkness diminished the approaching light was announced, he turned and wept bitterly, washing away the filth of denial with his tears. (RAB.) It should certainly not be thought contradictory that, while Mark says, “Before the rooster gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times,” the other evangelists simply say, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” (Aug.) For Peter’s entire denial is a threefold denial. He remained in the same denial and intention of lying until, warned of what had been foretold to him, he was healed by bitter weeping and sorrow of heart. If this entire denial—that is, the threefold denial—had begun after the first cockcrow, the three who said that the Lord had foretold that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed would appear to have spoken falsely. Conversely, if he had completed the entire threefold denial before the rooster began to crow, Mark would be found to have said unnecessarily, in the person of the Lord: “Amen I say to you: tonight, before the rooster gives its voice twice, you will deny me three times.” But because that threefold denial began before the first cockcrow, the other three evangelists considered not when Peter would complete it, but how great it would be and when it would begin—that is, that it would be threefold and would begin before the cockcrow, although in his mind the whole denial can be understood as present even before the first cockcrow. For although the entire threefold denial began in the words of the denier before the first cockcrow and was completed before the second cockcrow, nevertheless, in the disposition of his mind and in Peter’s fear, it was conceived in its entirety before the first cockcrow. Nor does it matter over how many intervals the threefold denial was uttered aloud, since his heart had already been entirely possessed by such great fear before the first cockcrow that he could deny the Lord not only once but, when questioned, a second and a third time. Thus, for those who attend more rightly and carefully, just as a woman has already committed adultery in her heart when she has looked upon a man in order to desire him, so whenever Peter gave voice to the fear that he had conceived so powerfully in his mind that it could persist until the third denial of the Lord, the whole threefold denial must be assigned to the moment when fear sufficient for the threefold denial seized him.

Peter said to him: “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you.” And all the disciples said likewise. [Col. 1110B] (MAUR.) Peter therefore understood the Lord to have said that he would deny him because of fear of death, and he used this as an excuse for himself, although the danger of death was imminent and he could in no way be torn away from his faith and confession. The other apostles, also driven by the same ardor, presumed the same of themselves. For since it is written, “Love is strong as death” (Song 8), they did not fear the loss of life because of the ardor of their minds. But true is the Psalmist’s statement: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. 126). (Aug.) Human presumption, therefore, was vain without divine protection. It should not be passed over that Matthew and Mark attach Peter’s denial in the same order and at the same place in their narratives: both apostles place it afterward, once the Lord had gone out from the house where they had eaten the Passover; Luke and John, however, place it before he had gone out from there. But we can readily understand either that the former two inserted it by recapitulation or that the latter two anticipated it—unless we are more troubled by the fact that they present not only very different words but also different statements of the Lord, by which Peter was moved to make that presumption of dying with or for the Lord. These differences make it more necessary to understand either that he expressed his presumption three times in different places in response to Christ’s words, and that the Lord three times answered him that he would deny him three times before the cockcrow, or that Peter was moved to presume, just as he was moved to deny, at somewhat distinct intervals of time, or that the Lord similarly answered him three times. For it is not unbelievable that, after the resurrection, he questioned Peter three times in succession, with no other matters or words inserted, whether he loved him, and that, when Peter answered three times, he himself also gave him one and the same command three times concerning the feeding of his sheep (John 21). It should therefore be believed that Peter displayed his presumption three times and heard from the Lord three times about his threefold denial. It follows:

Then Jesus came with them to a village called Gethsemane. In Luke it is written: “And he went out and proceeded, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives” (Luke 22). And in John: “When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden” (John 18). This is in no way contrary to Matthew, who related the matter concerning Gethsemane. The place of Gethsemane is still shown today, where the Lord prayed at the foot of the Mount of Olives. We understand this to have been the garden of which John spoke; a church is now known to have been built above it. *Gethsemane* is interpreted as “valley of the fertile” or “of abundance.” Since not only the words and works of our Savior but also the places and times in which he acts and speaks are, as has often been said, full of mystical figures, when the Lord prays on the mountain he silently admonishes us to seek only heavenly things in prayer and to plead for celestial goods. But when he prays in the valley—and in the valley of the fertile or of abundance—he likewise teaches us that humility must always be preserved in prayers, together with the inward abundance of love. Thus no one praying should dare, after the example of the proud Pharisee, to boast of his merits; rather, with humble voice and mind he should cry out: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). Nor should anyone with a heart dry of love for his neighbor bend his knee to win the favor of the Creator, like the man who, unwilling to forgive his brother the hundred denarii that he owed him, vainly begged the Lord to forgive him ten thousand talents (Matt. 18). Nor should anyone with a breast empty of love for the Creator seek in prayer any temporal things rather than the vision of the Creator, being counted among those of whom he himself says: “They have received their reward.” (Greg.) What else does it mean to place one’s thought below than a certain dryness of mind? But those who, through holy desires, are already nourished by the inner foods of heavenly delight, as it were, grow fat on richer nourishment. The Psalmist desired to be fattened by this abundance when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62). (RAB.) As far as the dispensation of the Lord’s passion itself is concerned, it was fitting that, as death approached, the Lord prayed in the valley of abundance: for through the valley of humility and the abundance of love he underwent death for us. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. 2). And: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

And he said to his disciples: “Sit here until I go over there and pray.” (Hieron.) Having gone out from the house in which he had eaten the Passover with his disciples, Jesus ordered them to sit for a little while and await his return, until the Lord alone should pray for all; for his prayer is the redemption of us all. (RAB.) He had therefore accepted the disciples’ faith and the constancy of their devoted will, but he also knew that they would be troubled and scattered, and he ordered them to sit in that place while he went forward to pray.

And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and distressed. (Hieron.) What we said above concerning the passion and concerning the passion itself is also shown in the present passage: the Lord, proving the reality of the human nature he had assumed, was truly sorrowful, but, so that passion would not dominate his mind, he began to be sorrowful through a preliminary movement of passion. He was sorrowful not because he feared suffering—for he had come for the purpose of suffering and had rebuked Peter for his fear—but on account of the most wretched Judas, the scandal of all the apostles, the rejection of the Jewish people, and the destruction of miserable Jerusalem. Hence Jonah too was sorrowful over the withering of the gourd or ivy, unwilling that his former shelter should perish (Jonah 4).

Then he said to them: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” The soul that is sorrowful is truly a soul, and it is sorrowful not because of death but unto death, until by his passion he should free the apostles. Let those who suppose that Jesus assumed an irrational soul say how he can be sorrowful and know the time of sorrow. For although even brute animals grieve, they nevertheless know neither the causes nor the time until which they ought to grieve. It should be noted, however, that in Mark it is written: “He began to be fearful and troubled,” clearly to demonstrate the reality of our nature. [Col. 1112B] (Aug.) But why is Christ afraid when Peter is not afraid? Christ fears, is troubled, and is sorrowful, and says: “Now my soul is troubled.” Peter says: “I shall lay down my life for you.” Both, therefore, are true, and both are fully rational: the one who is lower does not fear, while the one who is higher bears the emotion of one who fears. The former, as man, does not know the force of death; the latter, as God established in a body, displays the weakness of the flesh, so that the impiety of those who deny the sacrament of the incarnation might be excluded. Finally, he both said these things, and Manichaeus did not believe them, Valentinus denied them, and Marcion judged him to be a phantom. He so completely made the man whom he demonstrated by the reality of his body equal in emotion that he said: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” He therefore assumed my will; he assumed my sorrow. I confidently call it sorrow, because I proclaim the cross. It is my will that he called his own, because as man he assumed my sorrow and as man he spoke. And therefore he says: “Not as I will, but as you will.” It is my sorrow that he assumed with my emotion. Therefore he grieved for me, who had nothing for which he himself should grieve. And, the delight of eternal divinity having been set aside, he is affected by the weariness of my weakness. “My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful even unto death.” The Lord is not sorrowful because of death, because the bodily condition, with its human emotion, did not offend him by the fear of death. For he who assumed a body had to undergo everything belonging to a body, so that he might hunger, thirst, be distressed, and be sorrowful. Divinity, however, does not know alteration through these emotions. “Remain here and keep watch with me.” By commanding, “Remain here and keep watch with me,” he does not prohibit sleep, since the time for sleep had not come and danger was imminent, but rather the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of the mind. For he knew that, as the devil pressed upon them, their faith would be lulled to sleep. He commands equal watchfulness with himself from those for whom the same passion was approaching.

And going forward a little, he fell upon his face, praying and saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” After giving the apostles the command to remain and keep watch with the Lord, he fell forward a little and cast himself upon his face, to display the humility of his mind through the posture of his flesh. He says affectionately, “My Father,” and asks that, if possible, the cup of which we spoke above pass from him. He asks this not from fear of suffering, but from mercy for the former people, lest he drink the cup offered by them. Hence he deliberately did not say, “Let the cup pass from me,” but “this cup”—that is, the cup of the Jewish people, who cannot claim an excuse of ignorance if they kill me, since they possess the law and the prophets, who prophesy daily. Yet, returning to himself, what he had rejected hesitantly in the person of a man, he confirms by the authority of God and the Son.

Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will. (RAB.) “Let it not happen,” he says, “as I speak from human feeling, but let that happen for which I descended to earth by your will. If, then,” he says, “it is possible for the multitude of the nations to believe without the destruction of the Jews, I decline the passion; but if they must be blinded so that all the nations may see, let not my will, Father, but yours be done.” (Greg.) [Col. 1113B] Alternatively, as the Savior drew near to his passion, he took upon himself the voice of the weak, saying: “Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me”; and he assumed their fear in order to remove it. Then again, displaying the strength of his mind through obedience, he said: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done.” Thus, when what we do not want is impending, we should ask in our weakness that it not happen, so that through strength we may be prepared for the will of our Creator to be done even against our own will.

(Aug.) What was that voice except the sound of our weakness? Many who are still weak are distressed by the death that awaits them; but let them have an upright heart and avoid death as far as they can. Yet if they cannot, let them say what the Lord himself said—not for his own sake, but for ours. For what did he say? “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” [Col. 1113C] Here you have the human will expressed. Now see the upright heart: “But not what I will, but what you will.” “I have not come,” he says, “to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). He called “his own will” that which he took temporally from the Virgin; but “the will of him who sent him” signifies that will which, as the eternal Son, he had timelessly in common with the Father. He prays that the cup may pass from him, to show that he truly was also human. But, remembering the purpose for which he had been sent, he completes the dispensation for which he had been sent and cries out: “But not what I will, but what you will.” If death dies without me dying according to the flesh, namely, let this cup pass from me; but since this will not happen otherwise, he says: “Not what I will, but what you will.”

When, according to another Evangelist, he invoked the Father by the twofold name “Abba, Father,” [Col. 1113D] he showed that he is the God and Savior of both peoples—that is, of the Jews and of the Gentiles. For *Abba* means the same as *Father*. But *abba* is Hebrew, while *pater* is Greek and Latin.
