Therefore, to teach that both peoples would believe in him and that he was to be invoked by both, he himself was the first to invoke him in both languages. He is the good shepherd who, by giving his life for his sheep, made one fold from the two flocks (John 10). Therefore, with the voice of both flocks, he asks the Father’s help, so that we, formed by his example in both respects, whenever we sense adversities impending, may [Col. 1114A] seek heavenly protection with one devotion of faith and charity, we invoking God as Father and the Hebrews invoking him as *abba*. Hence the distinguished teacher, taking from the Lord the pattern of instruction, addresses his hearers in this way: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8). *Abba* applies, of course, to those from the people of Israel; “Father” to us who have come from the nations to faith in Christ.

And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter: “So, you were not able to keep watch with me for one hour?” (Hieron.) The one who had earlier said, “Even if all are scandalized, I will never be scandalized,” now cannot overcome sleep because of the greatness of his sorrow. (Hilar.) He rebukes Peter individually below the others because he had boasted above the others that he would never be scandalized.

“Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.” [Col. 1114B] It is impossible for the human soul not to be tempted. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Do not lead us into temptation,” which we cannot endure—not rejecting temptation altogether, but asking for the strength to endure amid temptations. Therefore here also he does not say, “Watch and pray that you may not be tempted,” but “that you may not enter into temptation”: that is, that temptation may not finally overcome you and hold you within its snares. For example, the martyr who shed his blood in confession of the Lord was tempted, but was not bound in the nets of temptation; whereas the one who denies falls into the traps of temptation.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” This was said against the presumptuous, who think that whatever they believe they can accomplish. Therefore, [Col. 1114C] to the extent that we trust in the ardor of the mind, let us fear the frailty of the flesh. Yet, according to the Apostle, the works of the flesh are put to death by the spirit.

(RABAN.) This passage also serves against the Eutychians, who say that in the Mediator between God and human beings, our Lord and Savior, there was one operation and one will. For when he says, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” he shows two wills: the human, namely that of the flesh, and the divine, namely that of the Godhead. The human will, because of the weakness of the flesh, refuses the passion; the divine will is utterly ready, since to fear in the passion belongs to human weakness, whereas to accept the dispensation of the passion belongs to divine will and power.

Alternatively, this saying is addressed to those who had promised that they would never deny him. Their spirit was willing, but their flesh was weak, because they had not yet been clothed with power from on high. [Col. 1114D]

Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.” (Hieron.) It was a second time, so that, if Nineveh cannot otherwise be saved unless the gourd withers, the Father’s will may be done—a will that is not contrary to the Son’s will, since he himself says through the Prophet: “To do your will, my God, I desired it” (Psalm 29). The Lord’s words concerning the Father’s possibility and will must therefore be considered carefully, because the possibility and will of God the Father disagree in nothing.

Moreover, Mark first related in his own words that [Col. 1115A] the Lord asked that, if it were possible, that hour—that is, the hour of the passion—might pass from him, which he immediately signified by the name “cup.” Then he presented the Lord’s own words in this way: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup from me.” If you add to these words what those two said—that is, Matthew and Luke—and what Mark himself likewise placed above in his own account, the meaning becomes clear: “Father, if it is possible—for all things are possible for you—take this cup from me.” No one should think that he diminished the Father’s power when he said, “If it is possible.” For he did not say, “If you can do it,” but “If it is possible.” What the Father wills can happen. Thus “if it is possible” was said as though he had said, “If you are willing.” Mark made clear in what sense “if it is possible” should be understood [Col. 1115B] when he said, “All things are possible for you.” And what they reported him as saying, “Not what I will, but what you will,” has the same force as if it were also said in this form: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done.” He sufficiently showed that “if it is possible” was spoken to the Father not because of impossibility but because of will, especially since Luke made this even clearer: he does not say, “If it is possible,” but “If you are willing.” To this clearer statement Mark more clearly joins what he wrote, so that it may be understood thus: “If you are willing—for all things are possible for you—take this cup from me.”

And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. (Hieron.) He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for all; the apostles’ eyes were growing weak and weighed down by the denial that was near. [Col. 1115C]

And, leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words. (MAURUS.) The Lord prayed three times to show us that we must devote ourselves to prayer at all times and always implore divine mercy, so that he may grant forgiveness for past sins, protection from present evils, and caution concerning future dangers; and so that we may remember that, in the name of the holy Trinity, we have been restored through the divine sacraments and instructed in the Christian religion. Let us know that the whole form of our prayer must be directed to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one almighty God, so that our spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Thessalonians 5).

(Aug.) [Col. 1115D] Just as the temptation of desire is threefold, so the temptation of fear is threefold. Opposed to the desire that consists in curiosity is the fear of death; for just as in the former there is eagerness to know things, so in the latter there is fear of losing such knowledge. Opposed to the desire for honors or praise is the fear of disgrace and insults; opposed to the desire for pleasure is the fear of pain. It is therefore not unreasonable to understand that, because of the threefold temptation of the passion, the Lord prayed three times that the cup might pass from him, but in such a way that the Father’s will might rather be fulfilled.

Then he came to his disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest.” (Hilar.) The reason why, when he returned to them and found them sleeping, he rebuked them on the first return, [Col. 1116A] was silent on the second, and ordered them to rest on the third, is this: first, after the resurrection, he rebuked them when they were scattered, doubtful, and trembling; second, after the Paraclete Spirit had been sent, he visited their burdened eyes so that they might behold the freedom of the Gospel—for some time they had been held back by love of the Law and occupied by a kind of sleep of faith; third, that is, upon the return of his glory, he restored them in security to rest.

“Behold, the hour is approaching, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go; behold, the one who betrays me is approaching.” (Aug.) This saying, according to Matthew, appears to contradict itself, because after the third prayer he came to his disciples and said to them, “Sleep now and rest,” and then added: “Behold, the hour is approaching, and the Son of Man will be handed over [Col. 1116B] into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go; behold, the one who betrays me is approaching.” For how can he first say, “Sleep now and rest,” and then add, “Behold, the hour is approaching,” and therefore say, “Rise, let us go”? Moved by this apparent contradiction, readers try to pronounce the words “Sleep now and rest” as though they had been said by one reproaching them rather than permitting them to sleep.

That would be correct if it were necessary. But Mark has related this in such a way that, after saying, “Sleep now and rest,” he added, “It is enough,” and then continued, “The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man is betrayed.” It is therefore understood that, after saying to them, “Sleep now and rest,” the Lord remained silent for a while, allowing what he had permitted to take place, and then continued: “Behold, the hour is approaching.” Hence, after those words, Mark placed “It is enough,” that is, “The rest you have now taken is enough.” But because the Lord’s intervening silence was not mentioned, the passage constrains the understanding to seek another mode of pronunciation for those words.

(Hieron.) After he had prayed a third time and, through the repentance that followed, had obtained the correction of the apostles’ fear, he proceeded confidently toward his persecutors concerning his passion and freely presented himself to be killed. He said to his disciples: “Rise, let us go; behold, the one who betrays me is near. Let them not find us as though we were afraid and hesitating; let us go freely toward death, so that they may see the confidence and joy of the one who is to suffer.”

[VII.] While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the Twelve, came, and with him a large crowd with swords and [Col. 1116D] clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders of the people. (Aug.) After the Evangelist John says that he entered the garden with his disciples, he does not relate what he did there until his betrayer came with the Jews to seize him.

(MAUR.) The deed of Judas corresponds to the change in his mind. For as long as he followed the Savior with the other apostles, he acted more peacefully. Because he pretended innocence, he brought healing to the sick, since he claimed to have been sent by the Savior. But when he had abandoned the counsel of peace and the Lamb’s most gentle passing, he rejected his peaceful companions and joined himself to murderous soldiers; abandoning the weapons of life, he proceeded against his master with clubs. He approached the author of [Col. 1117A] life while contemplating death. Hence it follows:

Now the one who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.” (Hieron.) Wretched Judas, and yet not deserving pity: with the same faithlessness with which he betrayed the Lord and master, he thought that the signs he had seen the Savior perform were accomplished not by divine majesty but by magical arts. And since he may have heard that he had been transfigured on the mountain, he feared that through a similar transformation he might slip from the hands of the attendants. Therefore he gave a sign, so that they might know that he was the one whom he would point out with a kiss.

And immediately he approached Jesus and said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. It was indeed shameless and criminal boldness to call the master “Rabbi” and to impose a kiss upon the one whom he was betraying; yet he still retained something of a disciple’s modesty, since he did not openly hand him over to the persecutors, but did so through the sign of a kiss.

(RAB.) The Lord accepts the betrayer’s kiss, not to teach us to pretend, but so that he would not appear to flee the betrayal, while also fulfilling what was said by David: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 119).

And Jesus said to him: “Friend, for what have you come?” Then they approached and laid hands on Jesus and seized him. (Hieron.) The word “friend” is to be understood *κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν*—ironically—or certainly in accordance with what we read above: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?”

And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, struck the servant of the chief priest, and cut off his ear. (RAB.) Peter did this, as the Evangelist John makes clear, with the same ardor of mind with which he had done the other things. For he knew how Phinehas had received the reward of justice and perpetual priesthood by punishing sacrilegious persons (Numbers 25). Luke adds that the Lord touched the servant’s ear and healed him. The Lord therefore never forgets his mercy: he does not even permit his enemies to be wounded. They inflict death upon the just man; he heals the wounds of his persecutors.

(Venant.) Allegorically, the servant is the Jewish people, subjected by the chief priests to an unlawful obedience, so that, at their urging, they asked for Barabbas to be released and Jesus—whom shortly before they had hailed with the cry “Hosanna,” proclaiming him the son of David and king—to be crucified. In the Lord’s passion this people lost the right ear, that is, the spiritual understanding of the Law, and remained content only with the left, that is, with the usefulness of the letter. This ear is cut off by Peter’s sword, not because Peter removes the power of understanding from those who hear, but because he reveals that it has been taken away by divine judgment from the negligent. Yet the same right ear, in those from that people who preferred to believe, was restored by the merciful favor of God to its former function.

Alternatively, the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signifies hearing renewed after the old condition has been removed, so that it exists in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter. Whoever receives this from Christ will also be granted to reign with Christ. Hence it is fitting that Malchus, the name by which that servant was called, is interpreted as “king” or “one who will reign.” That he was found to be a servant also pertains to that old condition which generates slavery, represented by Hagar (Galatians 4). But when healing came, freedom too was signified. [Col. 1118A]

Then Jesus said to him: “Put your sword back in its place.” (MAUR.) As though he had said: “Let vengeance cease; let forgiveness be granted.” For it was necessary that the author of grace should teach the evangelical people patience by his example and instruct them rather to endure adversity courageously than provoke them to vengeance. Thus Paul also says: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath; for it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Romans 12). Hence, conversely, it follows:

“For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword.” [Col. 1118B] That is, all who desire to avenge themselves in the present by retaliation do not deserve to be avenged by the Lord, but increase the punishment of their own condemnation. In other copies it is written: “All who strike with the sword will die by the sword.”

(Aug.) How many strike with the sword and yet do not die by the sword? Peter himself did not. But who can say that he escaped such a punishment through the forgiveness of sins? Yet nothing is more absurd than to think that the punishment of the sword could have been greater for Peter, who did not suffer it, than the punishment of the cross, which he did suffer. What, then, will he say about the robbers who were crucified with the Lord? One of them deserved forgiveness after he had been crucified, while the other did not deserve it at all. Or perhaps they had crucified all those whom they had killed and therefore deserved to suffer the same? It is absurd to think this. What else, then, is meant by “Everyone who strikes with the sword will die by the sword,” except that the soul dies by the very sin that it has committed?

“Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Hieron.) As though he were saying plainly: “I do not need the help of twelve apostles, even if all of them were defending me, since I can have twelve legions of the angelic army.” Among the ancients one legion comprised six thousand men. But because of the brevity of the present discussion, we do not undertake to explain the number. It is enough to have indicated the figure: seventy-two thousand angels, corresponding to the number of nations into which the human race is divided by language, are represented by the twelve legions. It is secretly suggested by this that the apostles should not be greatly concerned or afraid if all the nations of the Gentiles rise up against the Savior, since he himself possesses an army of angels much stronger than they.

Alternatively, this number signifies the whole human race, which, together with the Roman Empire, would fight against the wicked Jewish people. These are the angels of God who carried out God’s judgment when, after his resurrection, in the forty-second year—as ecclesiastical history testifies—he sent the armies of the nations under the Roman commanders Vespasian and Titus. The Lord wished to call those armies “angels” in this passage: they destroyed those murderers and burned their city.

To these words may be added what John records him as saying in that place: [Col. 1119A] “The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?” Then, as Luke relates, he touched the ear of the one who had been struck and healed him. The following sentence therefore, which says:

“How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?” shows a mind ready to suffer, since the prophets would have sung in vain unless the Lord had affirmed through his passion that they had spoken the truth.

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “As against a robber you have come out with swords and clubs to seize me. Daily I sat among you teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me.” It is foolish, he says, to seek with swords and clubs the one who freely hands himself over to your hands, and to investigate through a betrayer, as though he were hiding and avoiding your eyes at night, the one who [Col. 1119B] taught daily in the temple. But for this reason you gather against me in darkness: because your power is in darkness.

Now all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. What are the Scriptures of the prophets? These, plainly: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 21). And elsewhere: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53). And in another place: “Because of the sins of my people he was led to death,” and similar passages.

Then all the disciples, leaving him, fled. (RAB.) The saying of the Lord was fulfilled, for he had said that all the disciples would be scandalized because of him that very night. For although they fled, as John writes, when the crowd allowed it at the Lord’s request, they nevertheless displayed the fear and timidity of their minds, since they were readier to seek the protection of flight [Col. 1119C] than to endure suffering with the Lord in confidence.

Mystically, just as Peter, who washed away the guilt of his denial with repentant tears and completely eradicated it by his confession of love for the Lord, represents the restoration of those who fall in martyrdom, so the other disciples, who anticipated the moment of their arrest by fleeing, teach the prudence of flight to those who feel themselves less capable of enduring punishments. It is much safer for them to seek the protection of hiding places than to expose themselves to the danger of combat.

Thus also the young man of whom Mark reports that, after abandoning his linen cloth, he fled naked from the wicked, represents both the deed and the mind of those who, in order to become safer from the attacks of enemies, cast away whatever they seem to possess in this world and have learned to serve the Lord of the world [Col. 1119D] rather than, by clinging to worldly things, give their adversaries material for tempting them and drawing them away from God. This accords with the example of blessed Joseph, who left his cloak in the hands of the adulterous woman and leapt outside, preferring to serve God naked rather than, clothed in worldly desires, serve the prostitute (Genesis 39).

[VIII.] But they, having seized Jesus, led him to Caiaphas the chief priest, where the scribes and elders had assembled. Jesus was led, as John shows (John 18), first to Annas, who was the father-in-law of Caiaphas. Then Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, who, as the aforementioned Evangelist John writes, was high priest that year. Josephus gives corresponding testimony about him, saying that he had purchased the high priesthood for himself for only one year, without deserving the dignity, by paying Herod, the Roman ruler. It is therefore not surprising if an unjust high priest judges unjustly. [Col. 1120A]

Now Peter followed him from a distance, as far as the courtyard of the chief priest. Rightly did he follow from a distance, since he was already close to denying him. For he could not have denied him if he had clung closely to Christ. Yet in this he is greatly worthy of our admiration: he did not abandon the Lord even when he was afraid. His fear belongs to nature; his following, to devotion; his denial, to sudden weakness; his repentance, to faith.

(Aug.) Alternatively, the fact that Peter followed the Lord, who was going toward his passion, from a distance signified that the Church would indeed follow—that is, imitate—the Lord’s passions, but in a very different manner. The Church suffers for itself, whereas he suffered for the Church. [Col. 1120B]

And he entered inside and sat with the attendants to see the outcome. How Peter was able to enter the high priest’s courtyard, John makes clear when he says: “Simon Peter was following Jesus, and so was another disciple. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest; but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the woman who guarded the door, and brought Peter in.”

After entering in this way, Peter sat with the attendants beside the fire, warming himself, and waited to see the outcome—whether out of a disciple’s love or from human curiosity, wishing to know what judgment the high priest would make concerning the Lord, whether he would hand him over to death or release him after having him scourged. Here too there is a difference between the other apostles and Peter: they flee, while he, although from a distance, follows the Savior. [Col. 1120C]

Now the chief priest and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, so that they might hand him over to death, but they did not find any, although many false witnesses came forward. (MAUR.) For, as Mark testifies, their testimonies did not agree with one another. Here too is fulfilled what the Psalmist says: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2). “They searched out iniquity; they failed in their search, in the investigation. The arrows of children became their wounds” (Psalm 63).

The name “high priest” also aptly corresponds to the energy of his action. For Caiaphas is interpreted as “investigator,” or “shrewd,” or “one vomiting from the mouth.” He was shrewd in pursuing and carrying out the wickedness of his deceit, but shameless in uttering a lie and demanding murder. [Col. 1120D]

Finally, two false witnesses came forward and said: “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days.’” How are they false witnesses if they say what we read that the Lord said? A false witness is one who understands words in a sense different from that in which they are spoken. The Lord had spoken about the temple of his body, but they slander him even in the words themselves, adding or changing a few things so as to make the accusation seem just.

The Savior had said: “Destroy this temple” (John 2). They change it and say: “I will destroy this temple made with hands.” “You,” he says, “destroy it, not [Col. 1121A] I,” because it is unlawful for us to inflict death upon ourselves. Then they alter it to: “And after three days I will build another made with hands,” so that he appears to have spoken specifically about the Jewish temple. But the Lord, to show that the temple was a living and breathing thing, had said: “And I will raise it up in three days.” To build is one thing; to raise up is another.

And the chief priest rose and said to him: “Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you?” But Jesus remained silent. Impetuous and impatient anger, finding no place for accusation, drives the high priest from his seat, so that he might demonstrate the movement of his mind through the movement of his body. The more Jesus remained silent before the false witnesses unworthy of his answer and the impious priests, the more the high priest, overcome by fury, provoked him to respond, [Col. 1121B] so that from some opportunity in his words he might find a basis for accusation. Nevertheless, Jesus remained silent. For as God he knew that whatever he answered would be twisted into slander.

And the chief priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Why do you adjure him, most impious of priests? In order to accuse him, or in order to believe? If in order to accuse him, others condemn you for condemning one who remains silent. If in order to believe, why did you refuse to believe the one who confessed?

Jesus said to him: “You have said so.” (RAB.) His answer to Pilate and to Caiaphas is similar, so that they may be condemned by their own judgment. It should be noted that where Matthew has “You have said so,” Mark wrote “I am,” thereby showing that what Jesus says to him—“You have said so”—has as much force as if he had said, “I am.” [Col. 1121C]

“Nevertheless, I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven.” If, then, O pagan and heretical Judaea, weakness in Christ is an object of contempt to you and the cross an object of disgrace, see that through these very things the Son of Man will sit at the right hand of God the Father, and that the man born from the Virgin will come in his own majesty with the clouds of heaven. Hence the Apostle, after describing the abasement of the cross, saying, “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross,” added and said: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2). [Col. 1121D]

Then the chief priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. Why do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What is your judgment?” (Hieron.) The fury that had driven him from the priestly seat now provoked the same rage to tear his garments. He tears his garments to show that the Jews had lost their priestly glory and that their high priests occupied an empty seat. It is also a custom of the Jews, when they hear something blasphemous or apparently spoken against God, to tear their garments. We likewise read that Paul and Barnabas did this when they were being honored in Lycaonia with the worship due to gods (Acts 14). Herod, however, because he did not give glory to God but consented to the people’s immoderate [Col. 1122A] acclaim, was immediately struck by an angel.

(RAB.) In a higher mystery, it happened that during the Lord’s passion the Jewish priest tore his own garments, whereas the Lord’s tunic could not be torn even by the soldiers who crucified him. It was signified that the Jewish priesthood, because of the crimes of its priests, was to be torn apart and entirely removed from its state of integrity. But the solidity of the holy universal Church, which is customarily called the garment of its Redeemer, can never be torn apart. Rather, even if Jews, Gentiles, heretics, or wicked Catholics despise the humility of the Lord Savior, his chastity will nevertheless remain inviolate in those whom the lot of election has chosen, until the end.

[Col. 1122B] But they answered and said: “He is guilty of death.” Because they thought him a blasphemer, they handed him over to death. But while they imagined that they were fulfilling the prescriptions of the Law, they acted against the Law, for the Lord says: “You shall not kill the innocent and the just” (Exodus 23). They did not observe judgment but acted out their envy.

Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows. Thus was fulfilled what is written: “I gave my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isaiah 50).

Others struck him in the face with their palms, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ; who is the one who struck you?” The one who was then struck with the blows or slaps of the Jews is also struck now by the blasphemies of false Christians. [Col. 1122C] The one who was then spat upon by the saliva of unbelievers is now dishonored and provoked by insults from those who are mad, though faithful in name only.

They covered his face, as Mark records the Jews then doing—not so that he might not see their crimes, but so that they might conceal from themselves, as they once did from Moses, the grace of knowing him. For if they believed Moses, they would perhaps believe the Lord also (John 5). This veil remains to the present day over their heart, unrevealed; but for us who believe in Christ it has been removed. For it was not without reason that, at his death, the veil of the temple was torn in two, and that the holy mysteries of the Holy of Holies, which had lain hidden throughout the entire period of the Law and had been concealed from carnal Israel, were revealed to the worshipers of the New Testament.

As for what they say to him—[Col. 1122D] “Prophesy; who is the one who struck you?”—they say it as an insult to the one whom they wanted the people to regard as a prophet. Yet, by his own dispensation, he suffers everything for us, so that, as Peter urges, since Christ suffered in the flesh, we may arm ourselves with the same thought (1 Peter 4) and prepare ourselves to endure insults and mockery for his name.

(Aug.) Alternatively, the statement “They spat in his face” signifies those who reject the grace of his presence. Likewise, those who place their own honors before his strike him, as it were, with blows. They strike him in the face with their palms who, blinded by unbelief, assert that he did not come, as though they were driving away and repelling his presence. Heretical error concerning Christ ends in three forms: they are mistaken either about his divinity, or about his humanity, or about both. [Col. 1123A]

But Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. He sat outside to see the outcome of the matter, and did not approach Jesus, lest the attendants should become suspicious.

And a servant girl approached him, saying: “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” What does it mean that a servant girl is the first to expose him, when men could certainly have recognized him more readily, except that it might appear that this sex too had sinned in the Lord’s death, and that this sex might be redeemed through the Lord’s passion? Therefore a woman is the first to receive the mystery of the resurrection and to keep its commands, so that the ancient error of transgression might be erased.

But he denied it before everyone, saying: “I do not know what you are saying.” (MAUR.) He denied it openly before everyone because he was afraid of being recognized. He replied that he did not know the statement itself because he was not yet willing to die for the Savior.

As he was going out through the doorway. Here Mark completes what Matthew omitted for the sake of brevity: “He went outside,” he says, “before the courtyard, and the cock crowed.” Thus, after Peter had denied him once, he went outside, and immediately the cock crowed. When he returned to the courtyard, what follows took place:

Another servant girl saw him and said to those who were there: “This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.” In the second denial, then, he was challenged by two people: by the servant girl mentioned by Matthew and Mark, and by another person mentioned by Luke, who says: “After a little while another person saw him and said: ‘You also are one of them.’”

During this interval, which Luke calls “after a little while,” Peter went out after the first denial, and the cock crowed. He had already returned so that, as John says, standing again beside the fire, he might deny him once more: “Simon Peter,” he says, “was standing and warming himself.” Then they said to him: “Are you also one of his disciples?” and so forth.

Here, therefore, we find that Peter denied him a second time not before the doorway but while standing beside the fire. This could not have happened unless he had already returned after going outside. And when she saw him outside—that is, as he rose to go out—the servant girl noticed him. She said to those who were there—that is, to those who were gathered around the fire inside the courtyard: “This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.”

But the man who had gone outside, hearing this, returned and swore to them, while they insisted otherwise, that he did not know the man. Hence Matthew says:

[Col. 1123D] “And again he denied with an oath, ‘I do not know the man.’”

**(Augustine.)** In this denial of Peter we learn that one not only denies Christ who says that he is not the Christ, but also the one who, although he is a Christian, denies that he is one. The Lord did not say to Peter, “You will deny that you are my disciple,” but, “You will deny me.” He therefore denied him when he denied that he was his disciple.

**(Jerome.)** I know that some, out of pious affection for the apostle Peter, have interpreted this passage in such a way that they understand Peter not to have denied God, but a man; the meaning, they say, being: “I do not know the man, because I know God.” Let the prudent reader understand how frivolous this is. They defend the apostle in such a way as to make God guilty of falsehood. For if Peter did not deny him, then the Lord lied when he said: “Truly I tell you, this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Observe that he says, “You will deny me,” not “the man.”

“And after a little while those who were standing there came and said to Peter, ‘Truly, you also are one of them.’”

**(Augustine.)** What Matthew and Mark call “after a little while,” Luke makes clear as to the length of time by saying: “And when an interval of about one hour had passed.” John says nothing about this interval. Again, Matthew and Mark speak not in the singular but in the plural of those who were confronting Peter, whereas Luke mentions one, and John likewise one—namely, a relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off. It is easy to understand either that Matthew and Mark used the plural in place of the singular, as is customary in speech, or that one person, especially as someone who knew him and had seen him, made the assertion, while the others, following his lead, joined in accusing Peter. Thus two Evangelists, for the sake of concision, used the plural, while the other two intended to indicate only the person who played the principal part in this matter.

“For your speech makes you plainly recognizable.”

**(Venantius.)** This does not mean that the Galileans spoke one language and the inhabitants of Jerusalem another, since both were Hebrews. Rather, because each province and region has its own particular characteristics, no one can avoid the native sound of his speech. Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, when those upon whom the Holy Spirit had come were speaking in the languages of all nations, the inhabitants of Judaea are also reported, among the others who had gathered from different regions of the world, to have said in amazement: “Look, are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us, our own language in which we were born?” (Acts 2).

“Then he began to curse and to swear that he did not know the man.”

**(Augustine.)** How harmful are the conversations of wicked people, which compelled the apostle Peter, among unbelievers, to deny either that he knew the Lord or that he knew the man whom, among his fellow disciples, he had already confessed to be the Son of God.

**(Maurice.)** Notice that at first he answers, “I do not know what you are saying.” The second time, with an oath, he denies that he knows the man. The third time, then, he began to curse and to swear that he did not know the man. Perseverance in sin adds to the growth of crimes. For “whoever despises small things falls into greater ones” (Eccles. 19).

“And immediately the cock crowed.”

**(Augustine.)** We understand that the cock’s crow after Peter’s third denial was the second crowing, as Mark makes explicit. Sacred Scripture often indicates the merit or significance of events by the position of times. Thus Peter, who denied in the middle of the night, repented at the cockcrow. After the resurrection, in the light of day, he also professed three times that he loved the Lord whom he had denied three times. For what he had gone astray from in the darkness of forgetfulness he corrected when the remembrance of the light already hoped for returned to him; and, having obtained the presence of that same true light, he completely restored whatever in him had wavered.

I think that this cock should be understood as one of the teachers who, rousing us when we lie fallen and rebuking us in our sleep, says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15). Peter’s denial before the first cockcrow signifies those who, shaken by Christ’s death, did not believe that he was God before the resurrection. His two denials before the second cockcrow signify those who now go astray concerning him, whether according to his humanity or according to his divinity, in both substances, and therefore deny the truth. The first cockcrow is understood as the resurrection of the Head, that is, of the Lord himself; the second likewise as the resurrection of the Lord himself, but in the body of the universal Church.

“And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which he had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’”

**(Jerome.)** In another Gospel we read that, after Peter’s denial and the cockcrow, the Savior looked at Peter and by his gaze moved him to bitter tears (Luke 22). It could not happen that the one upon whom the Light of the world had looked would remain in the darkness of denial. It seems to me that this look was given by divine providence so that Peter would recall how many times he had already denied the Lord and what the Lord had foretold to him; and that, when the Lord mercifully looked upon him, he would repent and weep for his healing. Thus we say every day: “Lord, look upon me.” And the Lord has looked upon the one whom divine mercy has freed from some danger or affliction.

Just as it is said, “Look upon me,” and “Hear me,” and “Turn, Lord, deliver my soul” (Ps. 6), so, I think, it is said here: “The Lord turned and looked upon Peter,” and Peter remembered the word of the Lord.

“And he went outside and wept bitterly.”

**(Venantius.)** When the Lord looked upon him, Peter returned to his heart and wiped away the stain of denial with tears of repentance. For not only when repentance is being practiced, but also in order that it may be practiced, the mercy of God is necessary. To look upon someone is to have mercy on him. Hence the Psalmist says: “How long will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, Lord my God” (Ps. 12), that is, “Have mercy and help me.”

How harmful, indeed, were the words of the treacherous, among whom Peter denied that he knew the man whom among his fellow disciples he had confessed to be the Son of God. Yet, detained in the courtyard of Caiaphas, he could not perform his repentance there. He went outside so that, separated from the council of the impious, he might wash away the filth of his fearful denial with unrestrained tears.

For this reason, as is evident, he was permitted to waver, so that in the chief of the Church a remedy of repentance might be established, and no one might dare to trust in his own strength, since even blessed Peter could not escape the danger of changeability. The Lord Jesus, who was being held within the high priest’s council only in body, saw with divine vision the trembling of the disciple who was outside; and as soon as he looked upon the frightened soul, he strengthened it and moved it to tears of repentance.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
**Jesus Is Handed Over to Pilate; Judas Perishes by a Noose; and Concerning the Whole Passion of Christ the Lord**

**[I.]** “When morning came, the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus in order to put him to death.”

**(Augustine.)** Matthew and Mark joined together the account of what happened to the Lord up to the morning, but afterward returned to narrate Peter’s denial. When that was finished, they returned again to the morning in order to continue the rest of the account, until they had brought to completion what had happened to the Lord.

When morning came, the Jews held a wicked council against Jesus in order to put him to death. Thus the blessed man kept himself apart from the one of whom it is written: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1).

“And they brought him bound and handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the governor.”

**(Jerome.)** He was led not only to Pilate but also to Herod, so that both might mock the Lord. And observe the priests’ diligence: they stayed awake throughout the whole night for evil, in order to commit murder, and handed him over bound to Pilate. For they had this custom: whoever they had condemned to death they handed over bound to the judge.

**(Rabanus.)** Nevertheless, it should be noted that they did not bind him for the first time then. Rather, immediately after he had been seized at night in the garden, they bound him, as John declares, and thus brought him first to Annas.

“Then Judas, who had handed him over, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: ‘I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.’”

**(Jerome.)** The enormity of his avarice was outweighed by the burden of his impiety. When Judas saw that the Lord had been condemned to death, he returned the price to the priests, as though it were within his power to change the sentence of his persecutors. Thus, although he changed his own will, he did not change the outcome of his first intention.

If the one who handed over innocent blood sinned, how much more did those sin who had purchased innocent blood and, by offering the price, had provoked the disciple to betrayal? Those who attempt to introduce different natures and say that Judas the betrayer was of an evil nature and could not preserve the choice of apostleship should answer how an evil nature could have repented.

“But they said: ‘What is that to us? You see to it.’”

**(Maurice.)** “What concern of ours,” they say, “is the money we received? You approved of it; you deal with it as you wish.”

**(Jerome.)** Repentance did the wicked betrayer no good, since by it he could not correct his crime. If a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he is unable to give back what he took, he may be forgiven; but if the deeds continue, repentance is invoked in vain by words alone.

This is what the psalm says concerning that most wretched Judas: “And let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108), so that he was not only unable to amend the wickedness of his betrayal, but also added to his former crime the guilt of his own murder. The Apostle speaks similarly in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Lest the brother be swallowed up by excessive sorrow” (2 Cor. 2).

“And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed; and going away, he hanged himself with a noose.”

**(Maurice.)** Just as Judas’s repentance was fruitless, so also his offering was rejected. The silver he threw into the temple did him no good, since it did not absolve him from guilt but rather made him guilty; for it is written: “The offering of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, when it is offered from crime” (Prov. 21).

He also hanged himself with a noose as he went away, showing that he was hated by heaven and earth. Concerning him the poet appropriately sings:

> He hung his wretched soul high upon a noose:  
>   
> A milder anger, indeed, would be a fault for so great a crime,  
>   
> For whom no punishment equal to all evils could exist.  
>   
> This was the manner of his death; yet the lofty corpse  
>   
> Displayed to the peoples from what height he had fallen—  
>   
> Once a disciple, but now, guilty, abandoning the lofty  
>   
> Stars, he descended all the way to Tartarus below.

“But the chief priests, taking the thirty pieces of silver, said: ‘It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.’”

**(Jerome.)** Truly they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. If they do not put the money into the treasury—that is, into the place of offerings and gifts to God—because it is the price of blood, why is the blood itself shed?

[Col. 1127B] “And after taking counsel, they bought with them the potter’s field, for the burial of strangers.”

**(Hilary.)** This is a great sacrament of prophecy, and in the deeds of iniquity there is a meditation full of wonder. The work of a potter is to form vessels from clay; it lies in his hand, from that same clay, either to make a vessel for the intended use or to reshape it more beautifully.

That the field signifies the world is contained in the words of the Lord himself. Therefore the world is purchased at Christ’s price—that is, the whole world is acquired—and it is assigned for the burial of strangers and the poor. Israel has no part in this; the whole use of the purchased world belongs to strangers, namely those who are buried at the price of Christ’s blood, by which all things were purchased. For he received from the Father everything that is in heaven and on earth.

And so this is the potter’s field, because everything belongs to God, in whose hand it lies to reshape us as he wills. In this field, therefore, having died and been buried with Christ, we shall receive the eternal rest of our present pilgrimage.

“For this reason that field has been called Haceldama, that is, the Field of Blood, to this day.”

They did this with one intention: to leave an everlasting monument to their impiety through the purchase of the field. But we, who were strangers to the Law and the Prophets, have received their perverse undertaking for our salvation and rest at the price of his blood. The field is called the potter’s field because Christ is our potter, as we have shown above.

“Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: ‘And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose price had been set, whom the children of Israel had appraised, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord commanded me.’”

This testimony is not found in Jeremiah, but in Zechariah, who is nearly the last of the Twelve Prophets; a certain similarity is reported there (Zech. 11). Although the meaning is not very different, both the order and the words differ.

**(Augustine.)** If anyone is troubled because this testimony is not found in the writing of the prophet Jeremiah, and therefore thinks that something is thereby detracted from the Evangelist’s reliability, let him first know that not all copies of the Gospels have the words “through Jeremiah,” but only “through the prophet.” We could therefore say that those copies should rather be believed which do not contain the name Jeremiah.

This was spoken through a prophet, namely Zechariah. Hence the copies that contain the name Jeremiah are thought to be faulty, since they ought either to have contained the name Zechariah or, as some copies do, the name of no one, saying only “through the prophet,” who is plainly understood to be Zechariah.

But let whoever wishes use that defense. The reason why I do not approve of it is this: many copies contain the name Jeremiah, and those who have examined the Gospel more carefully in Greek manuscripts report that they found it so in the more ancient Greek copies. There was no reason for this name to have been added merely to create an error. But there was indeed a reason why it was removed from some copies: bold ignorance did this when people were disturbed by the question of why this testimony was not found in Jeremiah.

What, then, should we understand except that this was done by the more secret counsel of God’s providence, by which the minds of the Evangelists were governed? It could have happened that, while Matthew was writing his Gospel, Jeremiah came to mind instead of Zechariah, as often happens. Yet he would certainly have corrected it, at least after being warned by others who, while he was still alive, could have read it, unless he thought that the Spirit-governed memory had not brought the name of one prophet in place of another without reason, but that the Lord had ordained that it be written so.

Why the Lord ordained this should be understood is a matter for which the first and most useful explanation can readily be considered: it was thereby indicated that all the holy prophets spoke with one Spirit and agree with one another in a marvelous harmony—indeed, in a manner much more striking than if everything spoken by all the prophets had been said through the single mouth of one person.

Therefore everything the Holy Spirit spoke through them must unquestionably be accepted as belonging both to all individually and to each one collectively. Since what was spoken through Jeremiah belongs as much to Zechariah as to Jeremiah, and what was spoken through Zechariah belongs as much to Jeremiah as to Zechariah, why should Matthew have corrected it when, on rereading what he had written, he found one prophet’s name arising in place of another’s? Why should he not rather have followed the authority of the Holy Spirit—by whom he certainly felt his mind to be governed more than we do—and leave it written as it was, since the Lord had also established it by this reminder: that there is such agreement among the prophets in their words that we may rightly, indeed most appropriately, attribute to Jeremiah what we find spoken through Zechariah?

If today someone wishing to dictate another person’s words gives the name of someone else as their speaker, yet that other person is the speaker’s closest friend and most intimate associate, and then, immediately remembering that he has named one person in place of another, gathers himself and corrects himself while nevertheless saying, “I spoke correctly,” what else is he implying except that there is such agreement between the two—the one whose words he intended to speak and the one whose name came to mind in place of the other’s—that the first person’s having said the words is equivalent to the second person’s having said them?

How much more should this be understood and commended concerning the holy prophets, so that we might receive all their books as one book belonging to one author, in which no discrepancy of facts is believed to exist, just as none is found, and in which the consistency of truth is greater than it would be if one person, however learned, had spoken everything.

Therefore what unbelievers or ignorant people attempt to use as an argument for displaying disagreement among the holy Evangelists, the faithful and learned should instead adopt as an argument for displaying the unity even of the holy prophets.

There is another reason why the name Jeremiah was permitted—or rather commanded by the authority of the Holy Spirit—to remain in the testimony of Zechariah. In Jeremiah it is stated that he bought a field from the sons of his brother and gave them silver; not, indeed, under the name of the price given by Zechariah, thirty pieces of silver, yet the purchase of a field is not found in Zechariah.

The Evangelist clearly interpreted the prophecy concerning the thirty pieces of silver as having been fulfilled in the Lord, so that this was his price. But the matter of the purchased field, which Jeremiah mentions, could also be understood mystically as belonging here. For this reason the name of Zechariah, who spoke of the thirty pieces of silver, was not given, but the name of Jeremiah, who spoke of the purchased field.

Thus, when the Gospel has been read and the name Jeremiah found, but Jeremiah has then been read and the testimony concerning the thirty pieces of silver has not been found, while the purchased field has been found, the reader is prompted to compare the two accounts and thereby unravel the meaning of the prophecy—how it relates to what was fulfilled in the Lord.

For what Matthew added to this testimony when he said, “Whom the children of Israel priced, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord commanded me,” is found neither in Zechariah nor in Jeremiah. It should therefore rather be understood as having been elegantly and mystically inserted in the person of the Evangelist, because he also learned by the Lord’s revelation that such a prophecy belonged to this matter concerning the price of Christ.

For in Jeremiah the book of the purchased field is commanded to be placed in an earthen vessel; here the potter’s field is bought with the Lord’s price, and this is for the burial of strangers, as for the dwelling-place of their rest while they are pilgrims in this world, being buried with Christ through baptism.

Jeremiah also says that the purchase of the field signifies this: “Thus says the Lord: There shall be a dwelling-place for the captives who have been delivered in that land.”

Matthew continues and says:

“Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying: ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’”

This passage is explained more clearly in Luke. He says: “And the whole assembly of them arose and led him to Pilate. They began to accuse him, saying: ‘We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.’”

It should be noted that, according to Luke, two charges were brought against the Lord: that he forbade the payment of taxes to Caesar and that he said he was Christ the king. Pilate, however, considered only the matter of kingship worthy of inquiry. It may have happened that Pilate also heard the Lord’s judgment: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Therefore, regarding the charge as an obvious lie arising from envy and paying no attention to it, he judged only this one matter—which he did not know—to be worth questioning.

**(Venantius.)** The Jews are convicted of impiety because, when accusing the Savior, they cannot find even one plausible falsehood to bring against him. Therefore, as Mark says, their testimonies were not consistent.

“Jesus said to him: ‘You say so.’”

He responds to the governor with the same words with which he also responds to the chief priests, so that they may be condemned by their own judgment. He thus regulates his speech in such a way that he speaks the truth while leaving his words unavailable to slander. Yet his answer to the priest had been somewhat different. When the priest asked whether he was the Christ, he had said: “You have said so.”

**(Hilary.)** This is because the whole Law had foretold that Christ would come. He answers the priest as though speaking of the past, because the priest himself had always declared from the Law that Christ would come. But when this man, ignorant of the Law, asks whether he is the king of the Jews, he is told: “You say so,” because through faith in the confession of the one who is present comes the salvation of the nations. And the one who previously did not know speaks this concerning him, while those who previously spoke now deny him.

“And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.”

**(Jerome.)** To give us an example of patience, he is silent and says nothing now when accused, just as earlier when beaten. Observe that he answered Pilate, who was passing sentence almost unwillingly, in some measure; but he did not wish to answer the priests and the rulers, judging them unworthy of his words.

[Col. 1130C] “Then Pilate said to him: ‘Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?’ And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor marveled greatly.”

The pagan condemns Jesus, but attributes the charge to the Jewish people. “Do you not hear how many accusations they bring against you?” Jesus, however, did not wish to answer anything, lest, by dispelling the charge, he be released by the governor and the saving purpose of the cross be delayed.

“On the solemn day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished.”

**(Maurice.)** Pilate did not maintain this solemn release by any sanction of imperial law, but was bound to it by the annual custom of that nation, whose favor he was pleased to cultivate by such acts.

“At that time they had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.”

Luke reports that this prisoner had been sent to prison because of a certain insurrection that had taken place in the city and a murder. In the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, his name is interpreted as “son of their teacher.”

“When they had gathered, Pilate said to them: ‘Whom do you want me to release to you—Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?’”

From this it is already sufficiently clear that Mark wishes to indicate what Matthew indicates by saying “Christ” when he says “king of the Jews.” For only kings of the Jews were called christs.

“For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.”

Pilate offered them the choice of releasing either the robber or Jesus, having no doubt that they would choose Jesus, since he knew that he had been handed over out of envy. The cause of the cross, therefore, is plainly envy. The Evangelist John declares what this envy was when he says: “Look, the whole world has gone after him. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him” (John 12).

“And while he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man. For I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.’”

“While he was sitting,” he says, “on the tribunal,” that is, in the tribunal. The tribunal is the seat of judges, just as the throne is the seat of kings and the chair the seat of teachers.

His wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man,” and so forth. In visions and dreams, too, the wife of the Gentile understood what the Jews, awake, neither wished to believe nor were able to understand.

**(Jerome.)** Notice that dreams are often revealed by God to the Gentiles, and that, in Pilate and his wife confessing the Lord’s righteousness, there is a testimony from the Gentile people.

In the woman there is an image of the people of the Gentiles, who, having already become faithful, calls the unbelieving people with whom she lived to faith in Christ. Because she herself suffered greatly for Christ, she indicates that the man with whom she lived would share the glory that is to come.

Only at this point—not before—did the devil understand that through Christ’s death he would be stripped bare and lose the spoils of the human race, whether in this world or in Tartarus. Therefore he strove, through the woman by whom he had once seized the spoils of death, to rescue Christ from the hands of the Jews, lest through Christ’s death he should lose dominion over death.

“But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus.”

**(Maurice.)** This is what the Lord says elsewhere through the prophet: “Iniquity has gone forth from the elders and judges who appeared to rule the people” (Dan. 13). And again: “My people,” he says, “your exactors have stripped you” (Isa. 3).

Thus those who ought to have taught the people the Law and the Lord’s righteous judgments themselves led them astray, guiding them along trackless ways and not in the way, and became the cause of their ruin.

“But the governor answered them: ‘Which of the two do you want me to release to you?’ And they said: ‘Barabbas.’”

The request that the Jews secured with such effort remains with them to this day. For when the choice was given to them, they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Savior, and one who takes life instead of the giver of life. Therefore they deservedly lost salvation and life. They subjected themselves to robberies and insurrections to such an extent that they lost both their homeland and their kingdom, which they loved more than Christ, and to this day have not deserved to recover the freedom—of soul or body—that they sold.

“Pilate said to them: ‘What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?’ They all said: ‘Let him be crucified.’ The governor said: ‘Why, what evil has he done?’ But they shouted even more, saying: ‘Let him be crucified.’”

He gave them many opportunities to release the Savior. First he contrasted the robber with the righteous man; then he asked: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?”—that is, “who is your king.” When they answered, “Let him be crucified,” he did not immediately yield to their demand, in accordance with his wife’s message: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man.” He himself also answered: “Why, what evil has he done?” By saying this, Pilate acquitted Jesus.

But they shouted even more, saying: “Let him be crucified,” so that what had been spoken in the twenty-first Psalm might be fulfilled: “Many dogs have surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked has besieged me.” And the words of Jeremiah: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; they have raised their voice against me” (Jer. 12). Isaiah also agrees with this sentence: “I expected them to render judgment; they committed iniquity; and righteousness—behold, a cry” (Isa. 5).

**(Augustine.)** How great was the cruelty of the treacherous, who desired not only to kill an innocent man but to kill him by the worst kind of death—that is, by crucifying him. Those hung upon wood, crucified and fastened to it by nails through their hands and feet, were killed by a prolonged death. They appeared for a long time upon the cross, not because a longer life was chosen, but because death itself was prolonged, so that the pain would not end quickly.

Yet he himself, by dying the worst death, destroyed every death. It was the worst death only to those Jews who did not understand, for it had been chosen by the Lord. He was to have his cross as a sign, and was to place the cross, as a trophy over the defeated devil, upon the foreheads of the faithful, so that the Apostle might say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6).

“When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that rather a riot was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: ‘I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you see to it.’”

Pilate took water in accordance with the prophetic word: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 25). Thus, in the washing of his hands, the works of the Gentiles might be cleansed, and he might in some way declare himself separate from the impiety of the Jews who cried, “Crucify him,” saying: “I wished to release an innocent man; but since a riot is arising and I am being charged with rebellion against Caesar, I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.”

The judge who is compelled to pass sentence against the Lord does not condemn the one brought before him, but reproves those who bring him, declaring that the one who is to be crucified is righteous. “You,” he says, “see to it. I am the servant of the laws; your voice is shedding blood.”

But were they deceiving God the Judge by what Pilate did? In the very act he performed, Pilate was to some extent a participant, though by comparison he himself was far more innocent. He persisted as far as he could in trying to free Jesus from their hands.

The account continues:

“And the whole people answered: ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children.’”

This curse remains upon the Jews to the present day, and the Lord’s blood will not be removed from them. Hence he speaks through Isaiah: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will not hear you. Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1). The Jews left their children an excellent inheritance when they said: “His blood,” and so forth.

“Then he released Barabbas to them.”

**(Venantius.)** The seditious robber and author of murders was released to the Jewish people—that is, the devil, who long ago, because of the guilt of pride, was driven from his homeland of light and sent into the prison of darkness.

Therefore the Jews cannot have peace, because they preferred to choose the leader of seditions rather than the Lord. Since Barabbas is interpreted as “son of the father,” or “son of their teacher,” he can also represent a type of Antichrist, whom those to whom it is said, “You are of your father the devil” (John 8), will place before the true Son of God.

The Antichrist is called the son of the devil not because he is born from him, but because, like the other sinners, he imitates him.

“But Jesus, having been scourged, he handed over to them to be crucified.”

Let the learned reader ask how it can be consistent that Pilate washed his hands and said, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man,” and afterward handed Jesus over, having scourged him, to be crucified.

**(Rabanus.)** It should be understood that he was administering Roman laws, under which it was established that anyone who was to be crucified should first be beaten with scourges. Jesus, however, should be understood to have been scourged by Pilate himself and no other. For John writes plainly: “They all cried out again, saying: ‘Not this man, but Barabbas.’ Now Barabbas was a robber. Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.” He then adds: “And the soldiers, twisting together a crown of thorns, placed it on his head,” and so forth.

He should be believed to have done this, and to have handed him over to the soldiers to be mocked, so that the Jews, satisfied with his punishments and insults, would cease to thirst for his death. This happened so that, because it is written, “Many are the scourges of the sinner” (Ps. 31), we might be freed from blows through his scourging, as Scripture says: “The scourge will not approach your dwelling” (Ps. 90).

Mystically, however, Pilate—whose name is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammer”—signifies the devil, who according to the prophet is the hammer of the whole earth. Through him the Lord strikes his vessels so that they may be formed for service, when he permits his chosen ones to be tested by various temptations. Finally, the Lord crushes him, since at the last judgment he breaks him in eternal condemnation.

### [III]

Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the praetorium, gathered the whole cohort around him, stripped him, put a scarlet cloak around him, braided a crown of thorns and placed it on his head, and put a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!”

Because Jesus had been called King of the Jews, and because the scribes and priests had brought this charge against him—that he was arrogating rule over the people of Israel—the soldiers did these things in mockery. They stripped him of his former garments and clothed him in a scarlet cloak instead of the purple worn by ancient kings; instead of a diadem they placed a crown of thorns upon him; instead of a royal scepter they gave him a reed; and they worshiped him as though he were a king.

We, however, should understand all these things mystically. Just as Caiaphas said, “It is necessary that one man die for all,” without knowing what he was saying, so also, whatever these men did—although they did it with another intention—nevertheless they bestowed mysteries upon us who believe. In the scarlet cloak he sustains the bloody works of the nations. In the crown of thorns he abolishes the ancient curse. With the reed he kills poisonous animals; or he held a reed in his hand so as to write the sacrilege of the Jews.

It should be noted that Mark, in the same place in his narrative, says: “The soldiers led him inside, into the courtyard of the praetorium, and summoned the whole cohort. They clothe him in purple, place upon him a crown of thorns which they have braided, and begin to salute him, saying, ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ They strike his head with a reed, spit upon him, and, bending their knees, worship him.”

Here it is understood that what Matthew calls a scarlet cloak around him, Mark describes as clothing him in purple. For that cloak was used by the mockers in place of royal purple, and it was a kind of red purple, very similar to scarlet. It may also be that Mark mentioned the purple which the cloak possessed, although it was scarlet. (Venant.)

Mystically, therefore, in the purple with which the Lord was clothed, his very flesh, which he exposed to sufferings, is signified. Of this the prophecy had spoken beforehand: “Why, then, is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isa. 63). In the crown of thorns which he bore, the taking upon himself of our sins is shown, for which he deigned to become mortal. Accordingly, his precursor, bearing witness to him, says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world.”

The Lord himself testifies that thorns are customarily placed as a symbol of sins, when he said to the first-formed man after his fall into sin: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). This plainly means: “Your conscience will not cease to produce for you the pricks and barbs of vices.”

But whereas, according to the Gospel of Luke, the Lord is clothed by Herod in a white garment, while according to the other evangelists he is mocked by Pilate’s soldiers in scarlet or purple clothing, when the two accounts are compared, one expresses the innocence and chastity of the humanity he assumed, while the other expresses the truth of the Passion, through which he was to attain the glory of the immortal kingdom. For just as purple imitates the color of the blood poured out for us, so it also signifies the royal apparel into which he entered after the Passion and which he opened for us to enter.

But since the Apostle says, “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3), and Isaiah says to the Lord concerning all the elect, “You shall clothe yourself with them as with an ornament” (Isa. 49), the whole multitude of his elect—which is distinguished into revered martyrs and the remaining body of the faithful—may most fittingly be represented in these two garments of the Lord, shameful in the judgment of his enemies but most glorious by the Lord’s own choice.

He is clothed in a white garment when he is surrounded by the pure confession of the righteous. He is clothed in purple or scarlet when he rejoices in the triumph of victorious martyrs.

And spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head. What Pilate’s soldiers did then, heretics and pagans—who are certainly the soldiers of the devil—do to this day. Because Christ’s head is God, they strike his head who deny that he is truly God. And because Scripture is commonly written with a reed, they strike Christ’s head as with a reed who, contradicting his divinity, try to confirm their error by the authority of sacred Scripture.

They spit in his face who reject his gracious presence with blasphemous words conceived in the inward madness of a blind mind, and who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.

The soldiers indeed worshiped him in mockery, as though he had falsely declared himself to be God. But there are people today—what is a more serious madness—who worship him with firm faith as the true God, yet by their perverse deeds immediately despise his words as though they were fables and place the promises of his kingdom far below temporal attractions.

And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak, clothed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him. (Hieron.)

When Jesus is scourged, spat upon, and mocked, he does not have his own garments, but those which he had taken on account of our sins. But when he was crucified and the spectacle of mockery and derision had passed away, then he recovered his former garments and assumed his proper adornment. Immediately the elements were thrown into confusion, and created things bore witness to the Creator.

### [IV]

As they went out, they met a man of Cyrene coming toward them, named Simon. They compelled him to carry his cross.

Care must be taken lest anyone think it contradictory that John writes that the Lord himself carried his cross, whereas the other evangelists report that this Simon of Cyrene carried it. It was first carried by the Lord and then placed upon Simon, whom they happened to meet as they were going out, for him to carry. This accords sufficiently with the order of the mystery, because he himself suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps.

And because this Simon is said to have been not a Jerusalemite but a Cyrenian—for Cyrene is a city of Libya, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2)—the peoples of the nations are rightly represented through him. Once strangers and guests with regard to the covenants, they have now, through obedience, become fellow citizens and members of God’s household; and, as it is said elsewhere, “heirs indeed of God, but fellow-heirs of Christ” (Eph. 2).

Hence Simon is suitably interpreted as “obedient,” and Cyrene as “heir.” Nor should it be passed over that the same Simon is said to have come from the countryside. In Greek, countryside is called πάγος (*pagos*), from which we call “pagans” those whom we see alienated from the city of God and, as it were, lacking the civilized way of life.

But Simon, coming out from the countryside, carries the cross behind Jesus when the people of the nations, abandoning pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord’s Passion. (Hieron.)

It was not accidental but figurative and mystical that, while the Jews raged against Christ, a stranger came forward to suffer with him. The Apostle says, “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.” Thus, for the most sacred disgrace of the Savior, not a Hebrew or an Israelite, but a foreigner was subjected to it. Through this transfer, from circumcision to uncircumcision, from carnal sons to spiritual sons, the immaculate propitiation of the Lamb and the fullness of all the mysteries passed over.

And they came to the place called Golgotha, which means “the place of the Skull.” Golgotha is a Syriac name, not a Hebrew one, and it is interpreted as “the place of the Skull.” The place itself is in Aelia, on the northern side of Mount Zion. It is called the place of the Skull not because of the baldness of the first man—whom some misguided people foolishly suppose to have been buried there—but because of the beheading of the guilty and condemned.

We read in the book of Moses that Adam was buried not in Jerusalem but near Arbe and Hebron (Gen. 23). Thus, going out from Pilate’s praetorium, they came to the place called Golgotha, because outside the city and beyond the gate there were formerly places where the heads of the condemned were cut off; from this they took the name “the place of the Skull,” that is, the place of the beheaded.

The Lord was crucified there so that, where formerly there had been a place for the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised. And just as for the salvation of all he became the curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so he was crucified for the salvation of all as though he were guilty among the guilty.

(RAB.) The Apostle also describes the moral figure of the most holy cross when he says: “Rooted and founded in charity, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know also the charity of Christ which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. 3).

(Aug.) In breadth he signifies the good works of charity; in length, perseverance in holy conduct unto the end; in height, the hope of heavenly rewards; in depth, the inscrutable judgments of God.

Hence this grace came to human beings, and these dimensions are joined to the mystery of the cross: breadth is represented by the transverse wood on which the hands are extended, because of the signification of works; length by the wood extending from the transverse beam down to the earth, where the whole crucified body appears to stand, signifying persistence, that is, enduring patiently; height by the wood rising upward from the transverse beam toward the top, which projects above the head, signifying the contemplation of heavenly things, lest those good works and perseverance in them be thought to be undertaken for earthly and temporal benefits, but rather for that which the faith working through love hopes for from above and forever.

Depth is represented by that part of the wood which is hidden and fixed in the earth, from which all that projects above it rises—just as, from God’s hidden will, one person is called to share in such great grace in one way and another person in another way.

And the charity of Christ that surpasses knowledge is that charity, surely, in which there is that peace which surpasses all understanding.

### [Col. 1136D]

And they gave him wine to drink mixed with gall. When he had tasted it, he would not drink.

God says to Jerusalem: “I planted you as my true vine; how have you become a bitter vine of another kind?” (Isa. 5). The vine, turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine, produced bitter wine, which it offers to the Lord Jesus, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68).

When it says, “When he had tasted it, he would not drink,” this indicates that he tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again on the third day.

(Aug.) When Mark says, “He did not accept it,” this is understood as “he did not accept it in order to drink.” He did taste it, as Matthew testifies. Thus what Matthew says, “He would not drink,” Mark expressed by saying, “He did not accept,” while omitting the fact that he had tasted it.
