Moreover, when Mark says that the wine was myrrh-flavored, this is to be understood as what Matthew called “mixed with gall.” He used “gall” to mean bitterness, and wine flavored with myrrh is extremely bitter. Nevertheless, it is possible that both gall and myrrh made the wine extremely bitter.

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots.

John explains more fully how this happened. “When the soldiers,” he says, “had crucified him, they took his garments and made four portions, one portion for each soldier, and also the tunic. The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. They said to one another, ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be,’ so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, saying, ‘They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots’” (John 19).

The Lord’s four-part garment represented his four-part Church, spread throughout the whole world, which consists of four quarters, and distributed equally—that is, harmoniously—among all those quarters.

The tunic assigned by lot signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity. For if charity, according to the Apostle, possesses the more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and stands above all commandments, it is rightly said that the garment signifying it was woven from above throughout.

And what else is commended by the lot except the grace of God? In this way it reaches all as one, when the lot is acceptable to all, because God’s grace also reaches all in unity. When the lot is cast, it is not granted according to any person’s status or merits but according to God’s hidden judgment.

And because, as the Apostle says, “our old man was crucified with him on the cross, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve it” (Rom. 6), as long as our works are engaged in destroying the body of sin, as long as the outer person is being corrupted so that the inner person may be renewed day by day, it is the time of the cross.

These are indeed good works, but they are still laborious; their reward is rest. Yet it is said, “rejoicing in hope,” so that we may await future rest cheerfully amid our labors.

This cheerfulness is signified, as we said above, by the breadth of the cross in the transverse beam, where the hands are fastened. By the hands we understand works; by breadth, the cheerfulness of the worker, because sadness causes narrowness.

By the height, to which the head is joined, is signified the expectation of recompense from the sublimity of God’s justice, who will repay each according to his works: “to those who seek glory, honor, and incorruption through perseverance in good work, eternal life.”

Thus the length, by which the whole body is extended, signifies perseverance itself. Hence those who endure are called long-suffering. The depth, fixed in the earth, prefigures the secret of the mystery.

And sitting down, they kept watch over him.

The vigilance of the soldiers and priests benefits us, so that the power of the one who rose again might appear greater and more evident.

And they placed above his head the charge against him, written: “This is Jesus, King of the Jews.”

(MAUR.) The Jews found no other charge for Christ’s execution than that he was King of the Jews. Therefore it was not they but Pilate who made this inscription, just as John clearly relates: “Pilate also wrote a title and placed it above the cross. It was written: ‘Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.’ Many of the Jews read this title, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. It was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

“Therefore the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, ‘Do not write, “King of the Jews,” but, “He said, I am King of the Jews.”’ Pilate answered, ‘What I have written, I have written.’”

From this it is clear that the Jews, who accused Jesus and, out of envy, prevented him from being written as king, did not compose this title; rather, Pilate did so. As a Gentile ruler, he typologically prefigured in the writing and confirmation of the title the confession of the Gentile people.

(RAB.) Beautifully, the title testifying that Christ is king is placed not below but above the cross. Although on the cross he suffered in the weakness of a human being for our sake, above the cross he shone with the majesty of a king.

And because he is both king and priest, when he offered to the Father the outstanding sacrifice of his flesh on the altar of the cross, he also displayed the dignity conferred by the title of king, so that it might become known to all who wished to read—that is, to hear and believe—that through the cross he did not lose his dominion but rather confirmed and strengthened it.

Hence, after the Apostle had described the disgrace of the cross, he added: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2), and so forth.

The fact that this name was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin means what the same Apostle subsequently adds: “And every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

(Aug.) As far as the literal meaning is concerned, these three languages predominated there above the others: Hebrew because of the Jews who gloried in the law; Greek because of the wise among the nations; and Latin because of the Romans, who at that time ruled many, indeed almost all, nations.

(Venant.) Whether they wish it or not, therefore, every kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the mysteries of divine law testify that Jesus is King of the Jews—that is, the ruler of those who believe and confess God.

Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.

The robbers crucified on either side of the Lord signify those who, under faith in and confession of Christ, undertake either the struggle of martyrdom or any form of stricter discipline. But whoever undertakes these things solely for eternal and heavenly glory is represented by the merit and faith of the robber on the right.

Those, however, who renounce the world either for human praise or for some less worthy intention rightly imitate the mind and deeds of the blaspheming robber on the left. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “If I hand over my body so that I may be burned, if I give all my possessions as food for the poor, if I seem to do many other works of piety or to have received gifts of spiritual grace, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

Blessed are those who leave their possessions for the Lord or for the Gospel. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

But those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”

(MAUR.) Because they were passing by the road, they did not wish to walk on the true path of the Scriptures. They shook their heads because they had already moved their feet and were not standing upon the rock. Just as they limped in the steps of their deeds, so they were changeable in mind and wavering in speech.

Of them it is written in the Psalm: “All who saw me mocked me. They spoke with their lips and shook their head: ‘He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, since he desires him’” (Ps. 21).

In the same way, the foolish people, with an uncultivated voice, insulted him concerning what false witnesses had earlier fabricated in the house of the high priest, when they charged him with the destruction and rebuilding of the temple. They did not understand the Lord of the temple, and they tested the Son of God by ordering him to come down from the cross, although they possessed neither the Father as God nor the Son truly in faith and worship.

For, as John says, “Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father” (1 John 2). But those who confess the Son and the Father say, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”

(Greg.) If he had then come down from the cross, yielding to those who insulted him, he would not have shown us the power of patience. But he waited a little, endured insults, bore mockery, preserved patience, and postponed the display of his greatness.

He who did not wish to come down from the cross rose from the tomb. Therefore, it was greater to rise from the tomb than to come down from the cross. It was greater to destroy death by rising again than to preserve life by coming down.

But when the Jews did not see him come down from the cross in response to their insults, and when they saw him dying, they believed that they had conquered him. They rejoiced as though they had extinguished his name. But behold, from death his name increased throughout the world—the very death by which the unbelieving crowd thought it had extinguished him. The crowd that rejoiced at his killing mourns his death, because it recognizes that through suffering he has reached his glory.

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself.”

(Venant.) Even unwillingly, the scribes and chief priests confess that he saved others. Thus their own judgment condemns them. For he who saved others could certainly have saved himself, if he had wished.

“If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God.”

(RAB.) A deceitful promise. What is greater: to come down alive from the cross, or to rise dead from the tomb? He rose, and you do not believe. Therefore, even if he comes down from the cross, you will not believe.

“Let him deliver him now, if he wants him. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’”

O blind and foolish flock of priests, scribes, and elders! Is it impossible for him to come down from a small wooden stake, who came down from the height of heaven? Or can your bonds restrain him whom the heavens, or the heaven of heavens, cannot contain?

The robbers who were crucified with him also reproached him in the same way.

(Aug.) How could the robbers who were crucified with him reproach him, when, according to Luke’s testimony, one of them reproached him while the other rebuked that man and believed in God? We must understand that Matthew and Mark, briefly touching on the matter here, used the plural number for the singular, just as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read in the plural, “They shut the mouths of lions” (Heb. 11), although only Daniel is understood; and “They were sawn apart,” although tradition speaks of Isaiah alone.

What is more common, for example, than for someone to say, “Country people are insulting me,” even if only one is insulting him? What Luke clearly reveals about one would be contradictory only if they had said that both robbers reviled the Lord. Nevertheless, one person could be understood under the plural number.

But when it says “the robbers,” or “those who were crucified with him,” and does not add “both,” this could be said not only if both had done it, but also because one had done it, expressed in the customary manner of speech through the plural number.

(Venant.) According to Luke, one robber blasphemes the Lord, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us,” while the other rebukes him with a fitting reproach and entreats the Lord in faithful supplication, saying, “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23).

To this day we see these things taking place in the Church when true and false Christians alike are touched by the afflictions of the world. Those who bear the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion with a feigned mind desire to be freed by the Lord for the joys of the present life. But those who, with sincere intention, glory with the Apostle in nothing except the cross of our Lord, desire to be delivered from present troubles in such a way that they may commend their spirit into the hands of their Creator and desire to share with him in the kingdom of heaven.

Thus the one who prayed to the Lord with doubtful faith was rightly rejected completely by the Lord and judged unworthy of any response. But the prayers of the one who sought eternal salvation for himself the Lord soon deigned to receive with merciful hearing. For whoever, placed in tribulations, seeks only temporal consolations from the Lord deprives himself equally of temporal and eternal joys. But those who truly sigh for the good things of their heavenly homeland reach them without any doubt, through Christ’s mercy.

The two robbers may also signify the two peoples, that of the nations and that of the Jews. At first both peoples blasphemed the Lord, when Jews and Gentiles alike consented to the Lord’s death. Later, however, one of them, terrified by the greatness of the signs, repented and to this day rebukes the blaspheming Jews.

### [V]

Now from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth.

(Hieron.) Those who wrote against the Gospels suppose that this was an eclipse of the sun, which normally occurs at fixed and appointed times, and that Christ’s disciples, through ignorance, interpreted it as referring to the Lord’s resurrection. Yet an eclipse of the sun never occurs except at the moon’s conjunction.

No one doubts that at the time of Passover the moon was completely full. And lest it perhaps appear that the shadow of the earth, or the globe, or the moon passing over the sun produced a brief and rusty darkness, a period of three hours is specified, so that every opportunity for such explanations might be removed.

I think this happened so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “The sun went down at noon, and the light shall grow dark over the earth in the daytime” (Amos 8). Elsewhere also it says that the sun went down while it was still midday. It seems to me that the clearest light of the world—that is, the greater luminary—drew back its rays, lest it see the Lord hanging there or lest the impious blasphemers enjoy its light.

(RAB.) It should also be noted that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, when the sun was withdrawing from the center of the world. At dawn, however, when the sun had already risen, he celebrated the mysteries of his resurrection. He marked by the time of day what he displayed through the effect of his work: he died because of our sins and rose again because of our justification.

For it is written concerning Adam when he sinned that he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden at the breeze after midday (Gen. 3). “After midday” signifies that the light of faith had declined; “at the breeze” signifies that the fervor of charity had grown cool. He was heard walking because he had withdrawn from the sinful human being.

Therefore the order both of reason and of divine mercy required that, at the same hour when the Lord had then closed the gate against Adam’s transgression, he should now open the gate of paradise to the repentant robber; and that at the hour when the first Adam introduced death into this world by sinning, the second Adam should destroy death by dying.

(Aug.) It should not be passed over that some believe the Lord was crucified at the third hour, while darkness came from the sixth hour until the ninth, so that the three hours from his crucifixion until the darkness are understood to have elapsed.

This could indeed be understood most correctly, unless John said that at about the sixth hour Pilate returned to the tribunal at the place called the Lithostrotos, but in Hebrew Gabbatha. For he continues: “It was the preparation of Passover, about the sixth hour,” and says to the Jews, “Behold your king,” and so forth.

If, then, at about the sixth hour, while Pilate was sitting on the tribunal, he was handed over to the Jews to be crucified, how was he crucified at the third hour, as some have supposed because they did not understand the words?

Mark had already said, “And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments.” If he wished to mention the time when that deed occurred, it would have been sufficient to say, “It was the third hour.” Why did he add, “And they crucified him”? It was because, by recapitulating, he wished to signify something that would be found when the Scripture was read in those times when it was known throughout the churches at what hour the Lord was hung upon the wood. Thus either an error could be corrected or a lie refuted.

But because he knew that the Lord was crucified by the soldiers, not by the Jews, he wished secretly to show that those who shouted for him to be crucified had crucified him more than those who, according to their official duty, performed the service for their ruler.

It is therefore understood that it was the third hour when the Jews shouted for the Lord to be crucified. And it is shown most truthfully that they crucified him when they shouted, especially because they did not want it to appear that they had done this, and for that reason had handed him over to Pilate, as their words clearly indicate according to John.

Thus what they especially did not want to appear to have done, Mark shows them to have done at the third hour, judging most truthfully that the murderous tongue of the Jews was more responsible for the Lord’s death than the hands of the soldiers.

And around the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice: “Eli, Eli, Lamasabathani,” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

He used the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm. The words “Look upon me,” which are read in the middle of the verse, are superfluous. In Hebrew it reads, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

(RAB.) Do not be surprised at the humility of the words and the complaints of one who has been forsaken when you recognize the form of a servant and see the scandal of the cross. Just as hunger, thirst, and weariness did not belong properly to divinity but were bodily sufferings, so also, when he says, “Why have you forsaken me?” this belonged to bodily speech, because by nature the body ordinarily does not wish to be deprived of the life joined to it.

The Savior himself indeed said this, but he was properly displaying the frailty of the body while remaining the power and wisdom of God.

(Aug.) As a human being, therefore, he speaks, taking upon himself the emotions by which we, when placed in danger, think that we are abandoned by God. As a human being he is troubled; as a human being he weeps; as a human being he is crucified.

How could the Father abandon the Son in his Passion, when they are inseparable in nature, as the Son himself testifies: “He who sent me is with me; he has not abandoned me” (John 8)?

The Son could not therefore be abandoned by the Father, because the Father and the Son do not abandon those who hope in them. Human nature, however, had been abandoned because of sin and deserted by God. But because the Son became our advocate and legal defender, he laments the misery of those whose nature he assumed.

That nature which he assumed had been abandoned by the Father, not the Son, who is with the Father. He shows how greatly those who sin ought to weep, since he who never sinned wept in this way. And he shows how patient and hopeful sinners ought to be amid scourges, since he himself passed to immortality only through death.

Some of those standing there, when they heard this, said, “This man is calling Elijah.”

Not all of them, but some—whom I think were Roman soldiers—did not understand the proper character of the Hebrew expression. Because he said, “Eli, Eli,” they thought that he was calling upon Elijah.

But if you prefer to understand these people as Jews, they acted according to their customary practice: they slandered the Lord in his weakness, claiming that he was imploring Elijah’s help.

And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, placed it on a reed, and gave him to drink.

(RAB.) John explains more fully why vinegar was given to the Lord as a drink, saying: “Afterward, knowing that all things had now been accomplished, Jesus said, in order that the Scripture might be fulfilled, ‘I thirst.’ A vessel stood there full of vinegar. They placed a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop and offered it to his mouth.”

(Aug.) He saw, therefore, that all things which had to happen before he received the vinegar and gave up his spirit had been accomplished. He also wished to fulfill what is said: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68).

“I thirst,” he said, as if to say: “You have left this undone; give what you are.” The Jews themselves were the vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets, as though filled from a full vessel with the iniquity of this world. They had hearts like a sponge, deceitful, with cavernous and twisted hiding places.

The hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar is a low-growing herb that cleanses the breast. It fittingly signifies the humility of Christ, around which they wrapped the sponge and which they thought they had surrounded with their deceit.

Hence also the Psalm says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50). We are cleansed by Christ’s humility. For unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, his blood would not have been poured out for the remission of sins—that is, for our cleansing.

The reed upon which the sponge was placed signifies Scripture, which was fulfilled by this deed. Just as one speaks of a Greek, Latin, or any other tongue as signifying the sound expressed by the tongue, so a reed can signify the letter written with a reed. But sounds produced by the human voice are much more commonly called tongues. It is less customary to call Scripture a reed, and for that very reason it is more significantly represented mystically.

But the others said, “Let him be; let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.”

Because they wrongly understood the sound of the Lord’s voice, they foolishly awaited the coming of Elijah. The God whom the Savior invoked in the Hebrew language was therefore always inseparably with him.

But Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit.

(Venant.) What the Lord said in this loud voice Luke clearly indicates: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” And, he says, “Having said this, he expired” (Ps. 30).

John writes that, after Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up his spirit. Between the words “It is finished” and “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit,” that loud voice was uttered which John omitted but which the other three evangelists recorded.

By saying, “He gave up his spirit,” the evangelist shows that giving up the spirit was an act of divine power, as he himself had also said: “No one can take my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I shall take it up again” (John 10).

### [VII]

And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.

Josephus likewise reports that the angelic powers who had once been guardians of the temple then cried out together: “Let us depart from these dwelling places.”

The veil of the temple is torn so that the ark of the covenant and all the mysteries of the law which had been concealed might appear and pass over to the people of the nations.

Formerly it had been said: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.” But now: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory,” he says, “over all the earth” (Ps. 75).

And earlier in the Gospel he had said: “Do not go on the way of the nations”; but after his Passion: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations.”

And the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened.

No one doubts what the magnitude of the signs signifies according to the literal sense: heaven and all earthly things were showing that their Lord had been crucified.

But it seems to me that the earthquake and the other events bear the figure of the nations: those whose hearts had been softened after the former faults of their errors recognized the Creator, though previously they had been like tombs of the dead.

Alternatively, the earth was shaken because it could not endure to bear its hanging Lord. The rocks were split to indicate the hardness of the Jews, who refused to understand the Son of God present among them. And the tombs were opened as a sign of the future resurrection.

And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose, and, coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many. Thus, as a testimony to the Lord’s resurrection, many bodies of the saints arose, so that they might show that the Lord Jesus had risen; yet, when the tombs were opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn from the dead. For those who rose from the dead when the Lord rose are also to be believed to have ascended together with him when he ascended into heaven. Nor should any credence be given to the rash notion of those who think that, after returning to ashes, they were again shut up in the tombs that had been opened the previous day, as though they were dead, by those to whom they had shortly before appeared alive.

Let us understand this holy city in which they were seen rising either as the heavenly Jerusalem or as this earthly one, which had formerly been holy. Matthew likewise is called a tax collector, not because he still remained a tax collector even as an apostle, but because he retained his former designation. The city Jerusalem is called holy because of the temple and the Holy of Holies, and to distinguish it from the other cities in which idols were worshiped. When it is said, “They appeared to many,” it is shown that this was not a general resurrection visible to everyone, but a particular one witnessed by many, so that those who deserved to see might see.

Now when the centurion and those who were with him guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and what was happening, they were greatly afraid and said, “Truly this was the Son of God.” In another Gospel, after the earthquake, the more evident cause of the centurion’s wonder is explained: when he saw that Jesus had given up his spirit, he said, “Truly this was the Son of God.” For no one has the power to give up his spirit except the one who is the creator of souls. Here let us understand “spirit” as “soul,” either because the soul makes the body spiritual and living, or because the substance of the soul is spirit, in accordance with what is written: “You take away their spirit, and they perish” (Psalm 103). It should also be considered that the centurion, standing before the cross amid the very scandal of the Passion, truly confesses the Son of God, while Arius preaches a creature in the Church. At the same time, it must be weighed that not the centurion alone glorified God, but also the soldiers who were with him guarding Jesus. When they saw the earthquake and what was happening, they were greatly afraid and said, “Truly this is the Son of God.” What greater blindness, then, than that of the Jews, who, although so many mighty works had been performed by the Lord and so many signs had appeared at his death, refused to believe and, more insensitive than the Gentiles, disdained either to glorify or fear the Lord?

Hence, appropriately, the faith of the Church is represented by the centurion. Once the veil of the heavenly mysteries had been opened through the Lord’s death, she immediately confirms, while the synagogue is silent, that Jesus is both truly a righteous man and truly the Son of God. For the number one hundred itself, which—as mentioned above—passes from the left hand to the right through the bending of the fingers, most aptly corresponds to the mysteries and faith of the Church: in place of the Law, the Gospel has been entrusted to her, and in place of the riches of the earth, the kingdom of heaven has been promised.

There were many women there, watching from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. It was customary among the Jews—and, according to the ancient practice of that people, was not considered blameworthy—for women to provide their teachers with food and clothing from their own possessions. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, Paul recalls that he had rejected it, saying: “Do we not have the right to take along believing women as sisters, as the other apostles also do?” (1 Corinthians 9).

They ministered to the Lord from their own possessions, so that he might reap their material goods, while they reaped spiritual things from him. This was not because the Lord of creation needed food, but so that he might present a model for teachers: they ought to be content with food and clothing supplied by their disciples. But let us see what sort of companions he had.

Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Mary Magdalene was the woman from whom he had cast out seven demons; Mary the mother of James and Joseph was his maternal aunt, the sister of Mary the Lord’s mother; and the mother of the sons of Zebedee was the woman who shortly before had asked that the kingdom be granted to her sons. There were also the other women whom we read about in the remaining Gospels.

How, then, are we to understand that this same Mary Magdalene stood at a distance with the other women, as Matthew and Luke say, and was also near the cross, as John says? It may be that they were at such an interval that they could be said both to be near, because they were present within his sight, and to be at a distance in comparison with the crowd standing closer around the centurion and the soldiers. We may also understand that those who had been present together with the Lord’s mother began to leave after he had entrusted her to the disciple, in order to withdraw from the density of the crowd and observe the other events from farther away. Thus the other evangelists, who mention them after the Lord’s death, spoke of them as already standing at a distance.

Matthew continues:

### [VIII.]

Now when evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who himself was also a disciple of Jesus, came.

**(Jerome.)** He is called rich, not because the writer boasts in reporting that a noble and extremely wealthy man had become Jesus’ disciple, but to show why he was able to obtain Jesus’ body from Pilate. The poor and unknown could not approach Pilate, the governor of Roman authority, and obtain the body of a crucified man.

**(RAB.)** In another Gospel this Joseph is called a decurion, because he belonged to the curial order and administered the duties of the curia. He is also commonly called a curial because he managed civic offices. Arimathea is the city of Ramathaim, belonging to Elkanah and Samuel, in the Thamnitic region, near Diospolis.

He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered that the body be handed over. This Joseph is praised as having been a man of great dignity in the world, but of still greater merit before God. For it was fitting that the one who buried the Lord’s body should be such a man: by the righteousness of his merits he would be worthy of such a ministry, and by the nobility of his worldly power he would be able to obtain permission to perform it. For no unknown or ordinary person could approach the governor and obtain the body of a crucified man.

And after receiving the body, Joseph wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.

**(Jerome.)** From the Lord’s simple burial, the extravagance of the rich is condemned: they cannot be without riches even in their tombs. We may also understand this spiritually, namely, that the Lord’s body is to be wrapped not in gold, gems, or silk, but in pure linen. Yet this also signifies that the one who wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth is the person who receives him with a pure mind.

**(RAB.)** From this the custom of the Church arose: the altar sacrifice is celebrated not in silk or dyed cloth, but in earthly linen, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean linen cloth. We read that this was established by the blessed Pope Sylvester in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*.

And he placed it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock, and he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and departed.

He placed him in a new tomb so that no one might later pretend that another had risen after the resurrection while the other bodies remained. The new tomb may also signify the womb of the Virgin Mary, and the stone placed at the entrance, especially that great stone, may indicate that the tomb could not have been opened without the assistance of many people.

Those who in our time visited Jerusalem report that the Lord’s tomb was a round chamber cut out beneath the overlying rock, of such height that a person standing inside could scarcely touch its ceiling with an outstretched hand. It had an entrance from the east, to which that great stone had been rolled and fitted. In the northern part of the tomb was the tomb itself—that is, the place of the Lord’s body—made from the same rock. It was seven feet long and projected three palms above the rest of the floor. This place was open not from above but along its entire southern side, through which the body was carried in. The color of the same tomb and burial chamber is said to have been a mixture of red and white.

Now Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. In Luke we read that all his acquaintances stood at a distance, as did the women who had followed him (Luke 23). After these acquaintances of Jesus had returned home once his body had been laid down, only the women who loved the burial more ardently followed it and took care to observe how it was placed, so that at the proper time they might offer him the gift of their devotion. They persevered in their duty, awaiting what he had promised his own, and therefore deserved to be the first to see the resurrection.

Even to this day holy women do the same on Good Friday, that is, the day of Preparation. Humble souls, the more conscious they are of their own frailty and the more ardently they burn with love for the Savior, diligently follow his Passion in this world, where rest is being prepared. If perhaps they are able, through devout attentiveness, to imitate him, they consider in what order that same Passion was completed.

On the next day, which follows the day of Preparation. As we have said, *parasceve* means “preparation” in both Greek and Latin. By this name the Jews who lived among the Greeks called the sixth day of the week, because on that day they customarily prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath rest, in accordance with the ancient command concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much,” and so forth (Exodus 16).

Because the human being was made on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh day the Creator rested from his work—and therefore wished this day to be called the Sabbath, that is, rest—the Savior rightly fulfilled the mystery of humanity’s restoration on that same sixth day by being crucified. Thus, after receiving vinegar, he said, “It is finished”; that is, the entire work of the sixth day, which I undertook for the renewal of the world, has now been completed.

On the Sabbath, resting in the tomb, he awaited the outcome of the resurrection that was to come on the eighth day. Here an example of our devotion and blessed recompense shines forth together: in this sixth age of the world, we must suffer for the Lord and, as it were, be crucified to the world. In the seventh age—that is, when a person pays the debt of death—the bodies remain in tombs, but the souls remain in secret peace with the Lord. After good works, we too must rest, until at last, when the eighth age comes, the bodies themselves, glorified by the resurrection, receive immortality together with the souls as their eternal inheritance.

Hence, beautifully, the seventh day in Genesis is not said to have had an evening. For the rest of souls, which now exists in that age, is not to be consumed by any sorrow but is to be increased by the fuller joy of the future resurrection.

The chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: “Lord, we remember that while that deceiver was still alive he said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’”

The three-day period during which the Lord died and rose again cannot be correctly understood except by this manner of speaking, in which the whole is designated by a part. For he himself said: “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matthew 12).

It remains, therefore, that by that very customary mode of speech in Scripture, in which the whole is understood from a part, we take the final day to mean the time of the day of Preparation, when he was crucified and buried, and from its final portion take the whole day together with its night, which had already elapsed. The middle day, namely the Sabbath, is taken not from a part but in its entirety. The third day, in turn, is taken from its first part, namely the night, together with all its daylight hours. Thus there will be three days.

Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, “He has risen from the dead,” and the last error be worse than the first.

Although the chief priests and the Pharisees, together with the elders of the Jews, had committed an immense crime in killing the Lord, this was still not enough for them unless, even after his death, they exercised the poison of their conceived wickedness through evil counsels and deceit, and tore apart with their venomous tongues the reputation of one whom they knew to be innocent. They call him a deceiver, accuse his disciples of theft, and suspect others of what they themselves were.

Mystically, however, just as Caiaphas, unknowingly, had previously prophesied when he said, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, so that the whole nation may not perish,” so now those same priests and Pharisees, in speaking of deceivers and the theft of the disciples, prophesy the truth. Christ was indeed a deceiver—not, as they suppose, one who leads from truth into error, but one who draws people from falsehood to truth, from unbelief to faith, and from vices to virtues by his exhortations; and he leads those who obey him from death to life.

For just as the devil is a mediator toward death by deceiving human beings, so Christ is a mediator toward life by reconciling the world to God. The disciples of the Savior were also spiritual thieves—not because they fraudulently took anything from rightful owners, but because, by a just judgment, they received and used from the contemptuous and ungrateful those things that had been offered to them by the merciful Creator. These were the writings of the New and Old Testaments, which the former despised; the disciples transferred them to the use of the Church. They had also taken away from the Jews the Savior who had been promised and sent to them, while they slept by night—that is, while they lay sluggish in unbelief—and had handed him over to the Gentiles to be believed in.

Hence the Savior himself says to the Jews in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21). And in the Acts of the Apostles, when the Jews rebelled against and contradicted the Gospel of Christ, Paul and Barnabas said: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

According to the Jews’ statement, the last error will be worse than the first: for their unbelief in the resurrection is truly worse than their cruelty at the cross, and their contempt for repentance worse than the error of ignorance.

**[Note: [Col. 1147D] Several leaves are missing here; they were also lost because of the soldiers’ wantonness. EDITOR OF COLOGNE.]**

…Galilee is far away, so that he could not have been seen by them in both places on the same day; and Luke and John make it sufficiently clear that on the very day of his resurrection the Lord was seen in Jerusalem.

First by Mary Magdalene at the tomb, when, as she desired to embrace his feet, she was told, “Do not touch me.” Then, as she and the other Mary were running from the tomb, the disciples were informed of what they had learned from the angels concerning the completion of his resurrection. Of these women it is written: “They approached, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.”

He also appeared that same day, toward evening, to two men going to the village of Emmaus. They invited him to stay with them and recognized him in the breaking of bread. He also appeared to Peter. Although the evangelist does not specify exactly when or where this happened, he does not remain silent about the fact. He writes that when the two disciples mentioned above, having recognized the Lord at Emmaus, immediately returned to Jerusalem, they found the eleven gathered together, along with those who were with them, saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.” He then adds: “And they told what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of bread” (Luke 24). Immediately he attaches the account of his fifth appearance, beginning in this way: “While they were speaking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, ‘Peace to you; it is I, do not be afraid.’”

Now let us ask why he specifically foretold that he would go before them into Galilee and there be seen by the disciples, since he was seen neither only there nor there first.

**(Augustine.)** Let us consider for what mystery the risen Lord, according to Matthew and Mark, gave this command: “I will go before you into Galilee; there you will see me.” Although this was fulfilled, it was fulfilled only after many other events, even though, without prejudice to necessity, the command might have led one to expect either that this alone or that this first should have happened.

Without doubt, because these words are not the voice of an evangelist reporting that the event happened in this way, but of an angel speaking at the Lord’s command, and afterward of the Lord himself, they are to be understood prophetically. The evangelist reports that the angel and the Lord said this, but the saying itself is prophetic.

Galilee is interpreted either as “migration” or as “revelation.” First, according to the meaning “migration,” what else are we to understand by “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you,” except that the grace of Christ was to migrate from the people of Israel to the Gentiles? The apostles would not have been believed when preaching the Gospel to them unless the Lord himself had prepared the way in human hearts. This is what is meant by, “He will go before you into Galilee.”

That they would rejoice and marvel when, after difficulties had been broken through and overcome, the door in the Lord was opened to them through the illumination of believers is meant by, “There you will see him”: that is, there you will find his members; there you will recognize his living body in those who receive you.

According to the other interpretation, by which Galilee means “revelation,” this is not now to be understood as referring to the form of a servant, but to the form in which he is equal to the Father. He promised this to those who love him when he said through John: “I will love him and show myself to him” (John 14). This does not refer to what they were already seeing, and what, after rising with his scars, he later showed not only to be seen but also to be touched. Rather, it refers to that ineffable light by which he enlightens everyone coming into this world, according to which he shines in the darkness and the darkness did not comprehend him.

He went before us to the place from which, when he came to us, he did not depart, and to which, when he goes before us, he does not abandon us. That will be the revelation, true Galilee, when we shall be like him and see him as he is. It will also be the more blessed migration from this world into that eternity, if we embrace his commands in such a way that we deserve to be separated to his right hand. Then the left will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life. They will migrate from here to there and see him there, as the wicked do not see him.

For the wicked will be taken away, so that they may not see the glory of the Lord, and the wicked will not see the light. “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). In that eternity he is known by the manner in which he will lead servants through the form of a servant, so that, as free persons, they may contemplate the form of the Lord.

When they had departed, behold, some of the guard came into the city and reported to the chief priests all that had happened.

**(Maurice.)** A simple quality of mind and the uneducated rusticity of human beings often reveal the truth of a matter as it is, without deceit. By contrast, cunning malignity and the practiced wickedness of a corrupt mind, twisting deceit into plausible words, strive to commend falsehood in place of truth and hasten to turn and gather many over to its agreement. The following sentence shows this.

### [III.]

And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money, saying: “Tell people, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping.’”

**(Augustine.)** Such miracles took place around the tomb that the very soldiers who had come as guards could have become witnesses to them, if they had wished to report the truth. But the greed that had enslaved the disciple who was Christ’s companion also enslaved the soldiers guarding the tomb.

“We give you money,” they said, “and say that while you were sleeping his disciples came and took him away.” What were you saying, wretched cunning? Have you abandoned so completely the light of the counsel of piety and plunged so deeply into deceit that you say this: “Say that while you were sleeping his disciples came and took him away”?

You call upon sleeping witnesses. Truly you yourself have fallen asleep—not a priest, but a parricide, who have exhausted yourself by devising such things. If they were sleeping, how could they see? If they saw nothing, how could they be witnesses? They failed in the very execution of their plans, when they were unable to accomplish what they wished.

It follows:

And if this comes to the governor’s attention, we will persuade him and keep you out of trouble.

The guards confess the miracle, hurry back to the city, and report to the chief priests what they had seen and what they had witnessed. Those who ought to have turned to repentance and sought Jesus risen from the dead persist in wickedness. They turn the money that had been given for the needs of the temple into payment for a lie, just as earlier they had given thirty pieces of silver to Judas the betrayer. Therefore all who misuse the offerings of the temple and what is contributed for the needs of the Church for other purposes, to satisfy their own pleasure, are like the scribes and priests who purchased the lie and the blood of the Savior.

But they, after receiving the money, did as they had been instructed.

**(Maurice.)** O evil plague, avarice, always detestable to good minds—what do you leave unharmed, what unshaken? You first destroyed the human being; you confused the human race; you armed harmonious brothers for battle; you made peaceful people discordant; you cast the disciple who was Christ’s companion down from the apostolate; you enslaved the soldier guarding the tomb; you introduced the most wicked error; and you led astray an ancient and once most noble people. Hence it also follows:

And this saying has been spread among the Jews to this day.

To this day that error remains among the Jews. Just as the blood-guilt that they invoked upon themselves and their descendants presses upon them as a heavy burden of sins, so the purchase of the lie by which they deny the truth of the resurrection binds them in perpetual guilt. They reject Christ and await the Antichrist, so that those who sold the truth for a paltry price may seize the totality of error upon their own heads.

Now the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them.

**(Bede.)** It is not without a mystery that the Lord appeared to the disciples in Galilee after the resurrection, or that he appeared on a mountain. This signified that the body which, by being born, he had received from the common earth of the human race had, by rising again, been lifted above all earthly things and clothed with heavenly power.

He appeared on a mountain to admonish the faithful that, if they desire to see there the height of his resurrection, they must here pass from weak desires to heavenly longings. The name Galilee and the salvific mystery it contains are well known through the frequent exposition of the Fathers. Yet it is not out of place to repeat often in words what must always be retained in the mind.

Galilee means “a migration accomplished” or “revelation.” Both interpretations of the name look toward one end. For above we already read that the angel said to the women: “Go, tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him.”

And now, as the evangelist relates, we learn that the Savior’s disciples went into Galilee, and, seeing him, worshiped him. What, then, does it mean that Jesus goes before the disciples into Galilee to be seen by them, while they follow and, seeing him, worship him, except that Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep? Those who belong to Christ follow him, and in their own order migrate from death to life. There they see him and worship him, because, contemplating him in the form of his divinity, they praise him without end.

This vision corresponds to the fact that Galilee is also interpreted as “revelation.” Then, as the Apostle testifies, with unveiled face we shall behold the glory of the Lord and be transformed into the same image (2 Corinthians 3)—all who now unveil our way to him and follow his footsteps with sincere faith.

It follows:

And seeing him, they worshiped him. But some doubted.

If we ask how they doubted when they saw the Lord and worshiped him, no explanation presents itself more readily than the one Luke mentions when he narrates that he appeared to the disciples on the very day of his resurrection: “But they were troubled and frightened, and thought that they were seeing a spirit.”

Seeing the Lord, they recognized him. And because they had learned that he was God, they bowed their faces to the ground and worshiped him. Yet a doubt remained in their minds, not to be despised: they thought that they were seeing not the body in which he had suffered, raised again, but only the spirit that he had surrendered when his Passion was completed.

Therefore the pious teacher immediately strengthens in faith those who have already believed and calls those who still doubted to the grace of faith. He thereby makes known to all the greatness of the glory to which the humanity assumed for human beings and given over to death had attained by rising again.

And Jesus came and spoke to them, saying: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

He is not speaking here of his divinity, coeternal with the Father, but of the humanity he assumed. By assuming it, he was made a little lower than the angels; by rising from the dead, he was crowned with glory and honor, set over the works of the Father’s hands, and had all things placed beneath his feet. Among these things, death itself, which seemed for a time to prevail over him, was also placed beneath his feet.

Therefore what the Psalmist says to the Father about the Lord rising from the dead—“You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8)—is precisely what the risen Lord himself says to the disciples: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

Indeed, even before he rose from the dead, the heavenly angelic powers knew that they were rightly subject to the human being whom they saw had been specially assumed by his Creator. But human beings on earth, blinded, disdained to submit to one whom they knew to be clothed with the same mortality as themselves. They refused to recognize divine power in his miracles because they saw human weakness in his sufferings.

For this reason the mediator himself, in his kindness, wished to make known even to human beings on earth that all authority had been given to him in heaven and on earth, so that they too might have everlasting life in heaven with the angels. He therefore sent teachers to preach his Gospel to all the nations throughout the world.

[Col. 1152D]

Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything whatsoever I have commanded you.

The order of preaching is most correct, and modern preachers of the Church must follow it with the greatest care: first the hearer is to be taught; then he is to be imbued with the sacraments of faith; and then, in due course, he is to be instructed more freely in keeping God’s commandments. For the body cannot receive the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of faith. For neither can anyone untaught and ignorant of the Christian faith be washed in its sacraments, nor is it enough for anyone to be cleansed from sins by the washing of baptism if, after baptism, he does not strive to persist in good works.

[Col. 1153A]

Therefore he commands that the nations first be taught—that is, instructed in the knowledge of truth—and then baptized; for without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11), and unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, one cannot enter the kingdom of God (John 4). Finally he adds, “Teaching them to observe everything whatsoever I have commanded you.” And lest we think that what is commanded is slight or few, he adds, “Everything whatsoever I have commanded you,” so that all who have believed and been baptized in the Trinity may do everything that has been commanded; for, as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead (James 2).

[Col. 1153B]

He then indicates what a great reward for devout conduct, what a pledge of future blessedness, awaits the faithful even in the present, saying:

Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age.

It is worthwhile to compare with this testimony what Mark says: “And the Lord indeed, after he had spoken, was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God” (Mark 16). Since he is himself both God and man, he was taken up into heaven in his humanity, which he had received from the earth; in his divinity, by which he fills earth and heaven alike, he remains with the saints on earth. He remains, moreover, all the days, even to the consummation of the age. From this it is understood that, until the end of the age, there will never be lacking in the world those who are worthy of the divine indwelling and habitation. Nor should we doubt that, after the struggles of this age, they will remain with Christ in the kingdom—[Col. 1153C] those who, while struggling in this age, deserved to have Christ dwell as a guest in the lodging of their hearts.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that the divine majesty, which is present everywhere, is present to his elect in one way and to the reprobate in another. To the reprobate he is present through the incomprehensible power of nature, by which he knows all things, the most recent and the most ancient; he understands thoughts from afar and foresees all the ways of each person. To the elect he is present through the grace of loving protection, by which, through present gifts or chastisements, he specially trains them as children, and, by training them, advances them toward possession of the inheritance to come.

He is present to the elect, as it is written: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm 33). He is present to the reprobate, as it is promised: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth [Col. 1153D]” (ibid.). Therefore it is necessary that the wicked always dread their evil deeds, since each of their thoughts is open to the sight of the strict Judge. Let the good always rejoice in the practice of righteousness and in the things they suffer on account of righteousness; for those who love God, all things work together for good (Romans 8), and his mercy is never absent from those placed in whatever tribulation. Of this it is sung in the psalm: “For to you the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan. Crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (Psalm 9).

This presence of his mercy he not only promised to us in words, but also indicated by evident signs, when, after his resurrection, he appeared repeatedly to his disciples until the day on which he sought heaven, strengthening [Col. 1154A] their minds by admonishing and reproving them and by granting the gift of the Holy Spirit. Of these appearances we find only ten recorded in the writings of the Evangelists; but the Apostle teaches that there were more, saying: “And he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and he was seen by Cephas, and after this by the Eleven; then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once; then he was seen by James; then by all the apostles; and last of all, as by one born prematurely, he was seen by me.”

We do not know in what places or at what times the appearances he mentions took place. Nevertheless, we know that the appearance of the Lord which he affirms was shown to him last occurred after Christ’s ascension: either when Christ, speaking to him from heaven, made him, from a persecutor of the Church, a teacher; or when, having been caught up into paradise [Col. 1154B] and the third heaven, he heard secret words that it is not permitted a human being to speak (2 Corinthians 12). And, as he says elsewhere, he learned by revelation of Jesus Christ the mystery of the Gospel, which he had not received from a human being.

The history of the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles records, as we have said, ten appearances of the Lord after his resurrection. On the very day of his resurrection he is said to have appeared five times.

First, to Mary Magdalene, weeping at the tomb. Then he appeared to the same Mary and to another woman of the same name as they were returning from the tomb to announce to the disciples what they had discovered there; he met them on the way. Third, to Simon Peter. Fourth, to Cleopas and his companion, with whom he was walking to Emmaus and there was recognized in the breaking of the bread. They immediately returned to Jerusalem and found [Col. 1154C] the disciples saying: “The Lord has truly risen, and has appeared to Simon.” For it is not recorded more fully elsewhere when he appeared to Simon.

Fifth, he appeared to them in the same place, with the doors closed, while Thomas was absent. Sixth, after eight days, when Thomas was also with them. Seventh, to those fishing on the Sea of Tiberias. Eighth, on the mountain in Galilee, as we heard in today’s reading. Ninth, he appeared to the Eleven while they were reclining, on the day when he ascended into heaven. Tenth, on that same day they saw him no longer standing on earth, but lifted into the air and seeking heaven, while the angels said to them: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1).

By this frequent manifestation of his bodily presence, then, the Lord wished to show, as we have said, that in every place he is divinely [Col. 1154D] present to the desires of the good. He appeared at the tomb to those who were mourning; he will also be present to us when we are healthfully saddened by remembrance of his absence. He met those returning from the tomb so that, having learned of the joy of the resurrection, they might proclaim it; he will also be present to us when we rejoice faithfully in announcing to our neighbors the gifts we have come to know.

He appeared in the breaking of the bread to those who, thinking him a stranger, invited him to their lodging. He will also be present to us when we willingly bestow whatever good we can upon strangers and the poor; and he will be present in the breaking of the bread when we receive with a simple conscience the life-giving sacraments of his body—namely, bread.

He appeared in a secluded place to those who were speaking about his resurrection; he is also present to us when, by his gift, we are doing the same. He will [Col. 1155A] always be present to us when, for a time abstaining from external works, we gather to speak of his grace.

He appeared when they were sitting inside with the doors closed through fear of the Jews. He appeared when, with that fear diminished, they sought him with open steps on the summit of the mountain. He was once present to strengthen by his Spirit the Church when she was oppressed by unbelievers and forbidden to come into public and expand; he is present to her now, when royal terror has subsided as the summit of the world has inclined toward faith, and all the majesty of the world has been subjected to the apostolic footsteps.

He appeared to those who were fishing, and by appearing helped them through divine benefits; he will also be present to us when we attend to the necessities of temporal life with right intention and he adds the support [Col. 1155B] of his mercy to our righteous labors.

He appeared to those who were reclining; he will also be present to us when, in accordance with the Apostle’s admonitions, whether we eat or drink or do anything else, we do everything for the glory of God.

[Col. 1156A]

He appeared first in Judaea, then in Galilee, and afterward again in Judaea, on the day when he ascended into heaven. He was present to the Church when she was initially confined within the boundaries of Judaea alone; he is present now, when, after the Jews were abandoned on account of the guilt of their faithlessness, she migrated to the Gentiles; and he will be present in the future, when, before the end of the age, he returns to Judaea and, as the Apostle says: “When the multitude of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

Finally, he appeared to them as he ascended into heaven; he will also be present to us, so that we may deserve to follow him after death into heaven, if before death we take care to follow him to Bethany, from which he ascended—that is, into [Col. 1156B] the house of obedience.
